(With God's aid and generosity, there is no Lord besides Him.) The first thing to begin with is the discussion of its revelation (nuzul), its virtues (fadl), and what has been related about it. The same applies to every surah, if we find such material for it. So we say: Surat al-Baqarah is Madani, revealed over various periods. It has also been said that it is the first surah revealed in Madinah, except for the verse of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 281], for it is the last verse to have been revealed from the heavens. It was revealed on the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr) during the Farewell Pilgrimage (Hijjat al-Wada') at Mina. The verses on riba (usury) are also among the last of what was revealed of the Qur'an. This surah has great merit and a immense reward. It is called "the tent-pole of the Qur'an" (Fustat al-Qur'an), as said by Khalid ibn Ma'dan, because of its greatness and splendour, and the abundance of its rulings and admonitions. Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) took twelve years to learn it, with its jurisprudence and what it contains, and his son Abdullah took eight years, as has been mentioned earlier. Ibn al-Arabi said: I heard some of my teachers say: In it are a thousand commands, a thousand prohibitions, a thousand rulings, and a thousand reports. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) dispatched a expedition (ba'th) whose members were numerous, and he put over them the youngest of them in age, because he had memorized Surat al-Baqarah, and he said to him: "Go, for you are their commander." Al-Tirmidhi related it from Abu Hurayrah and authenticated it. Muslim related from Abu Umamah al-Bahili, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Recite Surat al-Baqarah, for taking it up is a blessing, abandoning it is a regret, and the sorcerers (al-batalah) cannot withstand it." Mu'awiyah said: "It has reached me that al-batalah are the sorcerers." It is also related from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not make your houses graves; indeed Satan flees from the house in which Surat al-Baqarah is recited." Al-Darimi related from Abdullah who said: No house in which Surat al-Baqarah is recited is left without Satan leaving it with a fart (dart). He also said: Indeed everything has a summit (sanam), and the summit of the Qur'an is Surat al-Baqarah; and indeed everything has a core (lubab), and the core of the Qur'an is the Mufassal. Abu Muhammad al-Darimi said: al-lubab means the pure essence. In Sahih Ibn Hibban from Sahl ibn Sa'd, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed everything has a summit, and the summit of the Qur'an is Surat al-Baqarah; whoever recites it in his house at night, Satan will not enter his house for three nights, and whoever recites it by day, Satan will not enter his house for three days." Abu Hatim al-Busti said: the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Satan will not enter his house for three days" means: the rebellious devils (maradat al-shayatin). Al-Darimi related in his Musnad from al-Sha'bi who said: Abdullah said: Whoever recites ten verses of Surat al-Baqarah in a night, no Satan will enter that house that night until morning: four from its beginning, the Ayat al-Kursi, two after it, and three at its end; the first of them being ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾ [al-Baqarah: 284]. And from al-Sha'bi, from him: no Satan nor anything that he dislikes will come near him or his family that day, and it is not recited over a madman except that he regains consciousness. Al-Mughirah ibn Subay' (or Sumay'), who was among the companions of Abdullah, said: He did not forget the Qur'an. Ishaq ibn Isa said: He did not forget what he had memorized. Abu Muhammad al-Darimi said: Some of them say: al-Mughirah ibn Sumay'. In the Kitab al-Isti'ab of Ibn Abd al-Barr: Labid ibn Rabi'ah [ibn Amir [the addition is from Kitab al-Isti'ab (vol. 1, p. 235), printed in India]] ibn Malik ibn Ja'far ibn Kilab ibn Rabi'ah ibn Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah was one of the poets of the Jahiliyyah; he lived to see Islam, his Islam was good, and he gave up composing poetry in Islam. In his caliphate, Umar asked him about his poetry and asked him to recite, and he recited Surat al-Baqarah. Umar said: "I only asked you about your poetry." He replied: "I would not say a line of poetry after Allah taught me al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran." Umar was pleased with his words, and his stipend was two thousand, so he increased it by five hundred. Many of the scholars of reports said that Labid did not compose poetry since he embraced Islam. Some said: he said nothing in Islam except his saying: "Praise be to Allah that my term did not come until I was clothed in Islam like a garment." Ibn Abd al-Barr said: It has been said that this verse belongs to Qarada ibn Nufathah al-Sululi, and that is more sound in my view. Others said: Rather the verse he said in Islam is: "A noble man is not reproached like his own self, and a man is set right by a good companion." What has come concerning Ayat al-Kursi and the ends of al-Baqarah will come [see vol. 3, pp. 268, 431], and further clarification of the merit of this surah will come at the beginning of Surat Al 'Imran [see vol. 4, p. 2], God willing.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful (Lord, make it easy and help).

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Alif Lam Mim (1). That is the Book; there is no doubt in it; it is guidance for the God-fearing (2).

[Statement of the views related concerning the disjointed letters at the beginnings of the surahs]

The interpreters differed concerning the letters that occur at the beginnings of surahs. Amir al-Sha'bi, Sufyan al-Thawri, and a group of the traditionists said: They are the secret of Allah in the Qur'an, and Allah has a secret in each of His books. They are therefore among the ambiguous (mutashabih) matters whose knowledge Allah the Exalted has reserved for Himself; it is not obligatory [in one copy of the original: "it is not permissible that we speak about them ... and they pass as they are"; in another: "and we recite them as they came"] to speak about them, but we believe in them and recite them as they came. This view has been related from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with them both. Abu al-Layth al-Samarqandi mentioned from Umar, Uthman, and Ibn Mas'ud that they said: the disjointed letters are of the hidden matter that is not explained. Abu Hatim said: We do not find the disjointed letters in the Qur'an except at the beginnings of surahs, and we do not know what Allah the Mighty and Majestic intended by them. I say: Among this meaning is what Abu Bakr al-Anbari mentioned: al-Hasan ibn al-Hubab related to us, Abu Bakr ibn Abi Talib related to us, Abu al-Mundhir al-Wasiti related to us, from Malik ibn Mighwal, from Sa'id ibn Masruq, from al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym [the author of Tahdhib al-Tahdhib said: in al-Taqrib it is al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym, with a dammed mu'jamah and an opened thaa; but in al-Khulasah it is with an opened mu'jamah and thaa, with a sukun ya between them], who said: Indeed Allah the Exalted sent down this Qur'an and reserved from it the knowledge of what He willed, and made you aware of what He willed. As for what He reserved for Himself, you cannot attain it, so do not ask about it. As for what He made you aware of, it is what you ask about and are rewarded for [in one copy: "are recompensed for by it"], and you do not know all of the Qur'an, nor do you act upon everything you know. Abu Bakr said: This makes clear that letters of the Qur'an have had their meanings concealed from the whole world, as a trial and a test from Allah the Mighty and Majestic. Whoever believes in them is rewarded and made happy, and whoever disbelieves or doubts them sins and is distanced. Abu Yusuf Ya'qub al-Qadi related to us, Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr related to us, Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi related to us, from Sufyan, from al-A'mash, from Umarah, from Hurayth ibn Zuhayr, from Abdullah, who said: No believer has believed in a better faith than belief in the unseen, then he recited: ﴿Those who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3].

I say: This view concerns the ambiguous and its ruling, and it is the sound view, as will be explained in Al 'Imran, God willing [see vol. 4, p. 2]. A large group of scholars said: Rather, it is obligatory that we speak about them, seek the benefits beneath them and the meanings that may be derived from them. They differed on this in many views. It is related from Ibn Abbas and also Ali: that the disjointed letters in the Qur'an are the Greatest Name of Allah, except that we do not know how it is composed from them. Qutrub, al-Farra' and others said: They are an indication of the letters of spelling (huruf al-hija'), by which Allah informed the Arabs when He challenged them with the Qur'an that it is composed of letters of the same kind from which their speech is built, so that their inability to produce its like would be a more decisive proof against them, since it did not depart from their language. Qutrub said: They used to turn away when hearing the Qur'an; when they heard "Alif Lam Mim" and "Alif Lam Mim Sad," they found this utterance strange, and when they listened to him (ﷺ), he approached them with the composed Qur'an in order to fix it in their hearing and ears and establish the proof against them. Some people said: It has been related that when the polytheists turned away from listening to the Qur'an in Makkah and said: "Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it," these letters were revealed so that they would be struck by them, and open their hearing to them, and then hear the Qur'an after them, so that the proof would become binding upon them. A group said: They are letters indicating names from which they were taken, with the rest omitted, as in the saying of Ibn Abbas and others: the Alif is from Allah, the Lam is from Jibril, and the Mim is from Muhammad (ﷺ). It has also been said: the Alif is the key of His name Allah, the Lam is the key of His name Latif, and the Mim is the key of His name Majid. Abu al-Duha related from Ibn Abbas concerning his saying "Alif Lam Mim": "I am Allah, the All-Knowing; 'Alif Lam Ra': I am Allah, the All-Seeing; 'Alif Lam Mim Sad': I am Allah, the Distinguisher." So the Alif conveys the meaning of "I (ana)," the Lam conveys the name of Allah, and the Mim conveys the meaning of "I know best (a'lam)." Al-Zajjaj chose this view and said: I hold that each letter of them conveys a meaning, and the Arabs have spoken with the disjointed letters in verse and in usage in place of the words of which those letters are part, as in his saying:

"I said to her: Stop (qif), and she said: Qaf"

He meant: she said: "I have stopped (waqaftu)." And Zuhayr said:

"With good, good things; and if evil, then fa..., and I do not want evil except that ta..."

He meant: "and if evil, then fa (fa-shar: then evil)." And he meant: "except that you (an ta) wish (tashaʾ)."

And another said:

"They called to them: Alla jimu (be silent)! Alla ta! They all said together: Alla fa!"

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 1–2 (part 2 of 3):

He meant: "Will you not ride?" They said: "Will you not then ride?" In a hadith: "Whoever helps in the killing of a Muslim even with half a word..." Shaqiq said: this means that one says in "iqtul" (kill): "iq," as the Prophet ﷺ said: "The sword is sufficient as a shaa," meaning: "healer" (shafiyan). Zayd ibn Aslam said: they are names of the surahs. Al-Kalbi said: they are oaths which Allah, exalted is He, swore by because of their nobility and merit, and they are among His names, related also from Ibn Abbas. Some scholars rejected this view, saying: it is not correct that they are an oath, because an oath is bound to particles such as inna, qad, la-qad and ma, and no such particle is found here, so it is not permissible that they be an oath. The answer is to say: the place of the oath is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is no doubt in it﴾. If a person swore and said: "By Allah, this Book, there is no doubt in it," the statement would be sound, and "la" would be the response to the oath. Thus it is established that the saying of al-Kalbi and what is related from Ibn Abbas is sound and correct. If it is asked: what is the wisdom in Allah's swearing, when the people of that time were of two kinds: one who believes, and one who denies? The believer believes without an oath, and the denier does not believe even with an oath? It is said to him: the Qur'an was revealed in the language of the Arabs, and when some of the Arabs wished to affirm their speech, they swore upon their speech; and Allah, exalted is He, wished to affirm the proof upon them, so He swore that the Qur'an is from Him. Some said: "Alif-Lam-Mim" means: I have sent down this Book to you from the Preserved Tablet. Qatadah said regarding His saying "Alif-Lam-Mim": it is a name of the Qur'an. It is related from Muhammad ibn Ali al-Tirmidhi that he said: Allah, exalted is He, deposited all that is in that surah of rulings and narratives in the letters He mentioned at the beginning of the surah, and none knows that except a prophet or a saint; then He clarified that throughout the surah so that people might understand. Other opinions besides this have been stated, and Allah knows best. Stopping on these letters is with sukun because of their being truncated, except when you speak about them or conjoin them, in which case you inflect them. It has been disputed: do they have a place in i'rab? It was said: no, because they are not declinable nouns nor imperfect verbs; rather they are like the letters of spelling, so they are indeclinable quoted forms. This is the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh.

Whoever says they are the names of the surahs, their place in his view is nominative, on the basis that they are, in his view, the predicate of an implied subject, i.e., "this is Alif-Lam-Mim," just as you say: "This is Surat al-Baqarah." Or they are nominative as subject and predicate: "that," just as you say: "Zayd is that man." Ibn Kaysan the grammarian said: "Alif-Lam-Mim" is in the accusative position, as you say: "Recite Alif-Lam-Mim," or "upon you Alif-Lam-Mim." It was also said: it is in the genitive position by the oath, based on Ibn Abbas's saying: they are oaths by which Allah swore.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is the Book﴾. It was said: the meaning is "this Book." "That" (dhalika) may be used to indicate something present, although it is originally for indicating something absent, as Allah, exalted and glorious is He, said in reporting about Himself: "That is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Mighty, the Merciful" [Surah al-Sajdah 6]. From this is the saying of Khufaf ibn Nudbah:

I say to him while the spear bends its shaft:
"Consider Khufaf, for indeed I am that one."

That is: "I am this one." So "that" is a reference to the Qur'an, placed in the position of "this," its summary being: "Alif-Lam-Mim, this is the Book, there is no doubt in it." This is the view of Abu Ubaydah, Ikrimah and others. From this is His saying: "And that is Our argument which We gave to Abraham" [Surah al-An'am 83], and "Those are the signs of Allah, We recite them to you in truth" [Surah al-Baqarah 252], meaning "these." But when they ended, they became as if distant, so "that" was said. In al-Bukhari: "Ma'mar said: 'That is the Book' means 'this Qur'an.'" "A guidance for the God-fearing" is an explanation and indication, like His saying: "That is the judgment of Allah, He judges between you" [Surah al-Mumtahanah 10], meaning "this is the judgment of Allah." I say: "hadha" has also come in the sense of "dhalika," and from this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ in the hadith of Umm Haram: "They ride the middle (thabaj) of this sea," meaning "that sea." And Allah knows best. It was also said: it is on its original usage, indicating something absent. Regarding that absent referent there are ten opinions. It was said: "That is the Book," meaning the Book which I wrote for the creation concerning happiness, wretchedness, the term and provision, "there is no doubt in it," meaning there is no changer of it. It was also said: "That is the Book," meaning the one which I wrote upon Myself in eternity: "that My mercy precedes My wrath." In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah who said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When Allah had decreed creation, He wrote in His Book, which is with Him, concerning Himself: 'My mercy overcomes My wrath.'" In another narration: "precedes."

It was also said: Allah, exalted is He, had promised His Prophet ﷺ that He would send down upon him a Book which water would not wash away, so He pointed to that promise, as in Sahih Muslim from the hadith of Iyad ibn Himar al-Mujashi'i that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah looked at the people of the earth and despised them, Arabs and non-Arabs, except some remnants of the People of the Book. He said: 'I have only sent you to test you and to test through you, and I have sent down upon you a Book which water does not wash away; you read it asleep and awake.'" The hadith to its end. It was also said: the reference is to what had been revealed of the Qur'an at Makkah. It was also said: when Allah, blessed and exalted is He, revealed to His Prophet ﷺ in Makkah: "Indeed We shall cast upon you a heavy word" [Surah al-Muzzammil 5], the Messenger of Allah ﷺ continued to look forward to the fulfilment of this promise from his Lord, mighty and majestic. When there was revealed to him in Madinah: "Alif-Lam-Mim. That is the Book; there is no doubt in it" [al-Baqarah 1–2], it contained the meaning of this Qur'an which I revealed to you in Madinah: that is the Book which I promised to reveal to you in Makkah. It was also said: "that" refers to what is in the Torah and the Gospel. "Alif-Lam-Mim" is a name of the Qur'an, and the implied meaning is: this Qur'an is that Book, explained in the Torah and the Gospel; that is, the Torah and the Gospel bear witness to its truth, and it encompasses what is in them and adds to them what is not in them. It was also said: "That is the Book" refers to both the Torah and the Gospel together, and the meaning is: Alif-Lam-Mim, those two Books, or like those two Books; that is, this Qur'an comprises what is in those two Books. So "that" is used for the two, with evidence from the Qur'an. Allah, blessed and exalted is He, said: ﴿It is a cow, neither old nor virgin, between that﴾ [al-Baqarah 68], meaning: between those two, the old and the virgin. This will come. It was also said: "that" refers to the Preserved Tablet. Al-Kisa'i said: "That" refers to the Qur'an which is in heaven and had not yet been sent down. It was also said: Allah, exalted is He, had promised the People of the Book that He would send down a Book upon Muhammad ﷺ, so the reference is to that promise. Al-Mubarrad said: the meaning is "this Qur'an is that Book which you used to seek victory by against those who disbelieved." It was also said: it refers to the letters of the alphabet, according to the one who said "Alif-Lam-Mim": the letters with which I challenged you to produce arrangement from them.

"Al-Kitab" is a verbal noun from kataba, yaktubu, meaning to gather, and from it is said "katibah" (a battalion), because of its gathering. And "takattabati al-khayl" means the horses became battalions. And "katabtu al-baghlah" means when I joined the two lips of its womb with a ring or a strap. He said:

Do not feel safe from a Fazari whom you have made stay upon your young she-camel, and bind her with thongs.

"Al-kutbah" (with a dammah on the kaf) is a stitch, its plural being kutab. "Al-kutb" is stitching. Dhu al-Rummah said:

A wide, tanned leather, whose stitches have been torn, its gaps left by the kutab (stitches) in disarray.

"Al-kitab" is the writing of the scribe in the letters of the alphabet, collected or scattered, and it is called a Book even though it is written, as the poet said:

She hopes for a return from me, and in it is a writing like what the glue has stuck.

"Al-kitab" also means the obligation, the judgment and the decree. Al-Ju'di said:

O daughter of my uncle, the Book of Allah has removed me from you; and would I forbid what Allah has done?

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿la rayb﴾ is a general negation, and therefore "al-rayb" is put in the accusative by it. And "al-rayb" has three meanings. One: doubt. 'Abdullah ibn al-Zib'ari said:

There is no doubt in the truth, O Umayma; doubt is only what the ignorant one says.

Second: accusation. Jamil said:

Buthaynah said: "O Jamil, you have made me doubt," so I said: "We both, O Buthaynah, are suspicious."

Third: need. He said [it is Ka'b ibn Malik al-Ansari, as in Lisan, root r-y-b]:

We settled from Tihamah every need, and Khaybar, then we gathered the swords.

So the Book of Allah, exalted is He, has no doubt in it and no suspicion. The meaning is that it is in itself true, that it is sent down from Allah, and an attribute of His attributes, uncreated and not originated, even though disbelievers may fall into doubt. It was also said: it is a statement whose meaning is a prohibition, i.e., "do not doubt," and the sentence is complete as if he said: that Book is true. You say: "This matter cast doubt upon me" when it introduces to you suspicion and fear. "Arab" means he became one who has doubt, so he is "murib." "Rabani amruhu" means his affair cast doubt upon me. "Rayb al-dahr" means its vicissitudes.

[The discussion on the guidance of the Qur'an, and it contains six issues]

﴿فِيهِ هُدىً لِلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾: In it is guidance for the God-conscious (muttaqun). This verse contains six issues.

**The first issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿فِيهِ﴾ (in it). The pronoun *ha'* in *fihi* is in the genitive position after *fi* (in). There are five possible readings, the best of which is *fihi hudan* (with the *ha'* vowelled with a *kasra*). Next is *fihu hudan* (with a *damma* on the *ha'* without a following *waw*), which is the reading of al-Zuhri and Sallam Abu al-Mundhir. Next is *fihi-yi hudan* (with the *ya'* affirmed), which is the reading of Ibn Kathir. It is also permissible to read *fihu-wa hudan* (with the *waw*), and it is permissible to read *fihh hudan* (with the consonants assimilated). *Hudan* is nominative, as the subject of a nominal sentence, with *fihi* as its predicate. In the language of the Arabs, *al-huda* (guidance) means right direction (rushd) and clarification (bayan). That is, in it is an unveiling for those who have knowledge, right direction, increased clarification and guidance.

**The second issue:** *Al-huda* has two kinds. The first is *huda dalalah* (guidance by indication), which the messengers and their followers are able to provide. God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿وَلِكُلِّ قَوْمٍ هادٍ﴾ (And for every people there is a guide) [al-Ra'd 13:7] and: ﴿وَإِنَّكَ لَتَهْدِي إِلى صِراطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ﴾ (And indeed, you guide to a straight path) [al-Shura 42:52]. Thus He affirmed for them the guidance whose meaning is indication, invitation and alerting. He alone, Glory be to Him, has the guidance whose meaning is support and enabling success (tawfiq). So He said to His Prophet ﷺ: ﴿إِنَّكَ لَا تَهْدِي مَنْ أَحْبَبْتَ﴾ (Indeed, you do not guide whom you like) [al-Qasas 28:56]. Thus *al-huda* in this sense means creating faith in the heart. From this is His saying: ﴿أُولئِكَ عَلى هُدىً مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ (Those are upon guidance from their Lord) [al-Baqarah 2:5], and His saying: ﴿وَيَهْدِي مَنْ يَشاءُ﴾ (And He guides whom He wills) [Fatir 35:8]. *Al-hudá* (being guided) means *al-ihtida'*, and its meaning returns to the meaning of guidance however it is used.

Abu al-Ma'ali said: Guidance may also be used to mean directing the believers to the paths of the Gardens and the roads leading to them. From this is His saying, Exalted is He, describing the fighters: ﴿فَلَنْ يُضِلَّ أَعْمالَهُمْ * سَيَهْدِيهِمْ﴾ (He will not let their deeds go astray. He will guide them) [Muhammad 47:4–5]. From this is His saying: ﴿فَاهْدُوهُمْ إِلى صِراطِ الْجَحِيمِ﴾ (So guide them to the path of Hellfire) [al-Saffat 37:23], meaning: lead them along it to it.

**The third issue:** *Al-huda* is a feminine noun. Al-Farra' said: Some of the Banu Asad treat *al-huda* as feminine, so they say: *hadhihi huda hasanah* (this is good guidance). Al-Lihyani said: It is masculine, and it is not inflected (i'rab) because it is a *maqsur* noun (ending in a non-moving *alif*). It is transitive with a preposition and without a preposition. This was discussed in al-Fatihah. You say: *hadaytuhu al-tariqa* and *ila al-tariqi*, and *al-dar* and *ila al-dar*, meaning: I made him know. The first usage is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and the second was transmitted by al-Akhfash. In the revelation: ﴿اهْدِنَا الصِّراطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ﴾ (Guide us to the straight path) and ﴿الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي هَدانا لِهذا﴾ (Praise be to God who guided us to this) [al-A'raf 7:43]. It was said that *al-huda* is one of the names of the day, because people are guided during it to their livelihoods and all their needs. From this is the saying of Ibn Muqbil:

*"Until I clearly discerned the guidance, and the deserts were rushing,*
*they humbled themselves in the mirage, unsheathed, or prayed for us."*

[This line is missing from all the manuscripts; the addition is from Lisan al-Arab, entry *h-d-y*, and al-Bahr al-Muhit on this topic.]

**The fourth issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿لِلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾ (for the God-conscious). God, Exalted is He, specified the God-conscious with His guidance, even though it is guidance for all creation, to honour them, because they believed in it and affirmed what is in it. It is narrated from Abu Rawq that he said: "*Hudan lil-muttaqin*" means: a dignity for them. That is, He attributed it to them out of reverence for them, honour for them and to make clear their merit.

The original form of *lil-muttaqin* is *lil-mutawqiyin*, with two light *ya'*s. The *kasra* was removed from the first *ya'* because of its heaviness, then the *ya'* was removed because of the meeting of two unvocalised letters. The *waw* was changed to a *ta'* according to their practice when *waw* and *ta'* come together, and the *ta'* was assimilated into the following *ta'*, so it became *lil-muttaqin*.

**The fifth issue:** *Al-taqwa* (God-consciousness). It is said that its root in the language is "little speech" (qillat al-kalam); Ibn Faris related this. I say: From this is the hadith: "The one who is God-conscious is restrained, and the God-conscious person is above the believer and the obedient." It is the one who guards himself, by his righteous deeds and sincere supplication, against the punishment of God, Exalted is He. It is derived from guarding oneself against what is disliked by placing a barrier between oneself and it, as al-Nabigha said:

*"The veil (nasif) fell and she did not intend to drop it,*
*so she caught it and shielded us with her hand."*

[Nasif: a garment a woman wraps over all her other clothes; it is called *nasif* because it stands between people and her, blocking their eyes from her.]

And another said:

*"She cast a covering over which the sun was shielded,*
*shielding herself with the most beautiful of joined things, a palm and a wrist."*

Abu Muhammad Abd al-Ghani al-Hafiz transmitted from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Zarbi Abu Ubaydah, from Asim ibn Bahdalah, from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: One day he said to his nephew: "O nephew, do you see how many people there are?" He said: "Yes." He said: "There is no good in them except a penitent or a God-conscious person." Then he said: "O nephew, do you see how many people there are?" I said: "Yes." He said: "There is no good in them except a scholar or a student."

Abu Yazid al-Bistami said: The God-conscious is the one who, when he speaks, speaks for God, and when he acts, acts for God. Abu Sulayman al-Darani said: The God-conscious are those from whose hearts God has removed love of desires. It was said: The God-conscious is the one who guards himself against shirk and is free of hypocrisy. Ibn Atiyyah said: This is corrupt, because a person may be like that and still be a sinner.

Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, asked Ubayy about God-consciousness. He said: "Have you ever walked a path with thorns?" He said: "Yes." He said: "What did you do there?" He said: "I girded up and was cautious." He said: "That is God-consciousness."

Ibn al-Mu'tazz took up this meaning and versified it:

*"Leave sins, the small of them and the great of them; that is piety (tuqa).*
*Act like one walking over a land of thorns, wary of what he sees.*
*Do not belittle a small sin, for mountains are made of pebbles."*

**The sixth issue:** God-consciousness contains all good. It is the commandment of God to the first and the last people, and it is the best thing a person can gain, as Abu al-Darda' said when it was said to him: "Your companions recite poetry, but nothing of yours has been preserved." He said:

*"A man wants his wish to be granted, but God refuses except what He wills.*
*A man says: My gain and my wealth... but God-consciousness is the best gain."*

Ibn Majah related in his Sunan from Abu Umamah, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he used to say: "A believer gains nothing after God-consciousness better for him than a righteous wife: if he commands her, she obeys him; if he looks at her, she pleases him; if he swears an oath concerning her, she fulfils it for him; and if he is absent from her, she is sincere to him regarding herself and his property."

The root of *al-taqwa* is *waqwa*, on the pattern *fa'la*, so the *waw* was changed to a *ta'* from *waqaytuhu uqihi*, meaning: I protected him. A man *taqiyy* means fearful; its root is *waqa*. Likewise *tuqat* was originally *wuqat*, as they said *tujah* and *turath*, when the original forms were *wujah* and *wurath*.

(With God's aid and generosity, there is no Lord besides Him.) The first thing to begin with is the discussion of its revelation (nuzul), its virtues (fadl), and what has been related about it. The same applies to every surah, if we find such material for it. So we say: Surat al-Baqarah is Madani, revealed over various periods. It has also been said that it is the first surah revealed in Madinah, except for the verse of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 281], for it is the last verse to have been revealed from the heavens. It was revealed on the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr) during the Farewell Pilgrimage (Hijjat al-Wada') at Mina. The verses on riba (usury) are also among the last of what was revealed of the Qur'an. This surah has great merit and a immense reward. It is called "the tent-pole of the Qur'an" (Fustat al-Qur'an), as said by Khalid ibn Ma'dan, because of its greatness and splendour, and the abundance of its rulings and admonitions. Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) took twelve years to learn it, with its jurisprudence and what it contains, and his son Abdullah took eight years, as has been mentioned earlier. Ibn al-Arabi said: I heard some of my teachers say: In it are a thousand commands, a thousand prohibitions, a thousand rulings, and a thousand reports. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) dispatched a expedition (ba'th) whose members were numerous, and he put over them the youngest of them in age, because he had memorized Surat al-Baqarah, and he said to him: "Go, for you are their commander." Al-Tirmidhi related it from Abu Hurayrah and authenticated it. Muslim related from Abu Umamah al-Bahili, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Recite Surat al-Baqarah, for taking it up is a blessing, abandoning it is a regret, and the sorcerers (al-batalah) cannot withstand it." Mu'awiyah said: "It has reached me that al-batalah are the sorcerers." It is also related from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not make your houses graves; indeed Satan flees from the house in which Surat al-Baqarah is recited." Al-Darimi related from Abdullah who said: No house in which Surat al-Baqarah is recited is left without Satan leaving it with a fart (dart). He also said: Indeed everything has a summit (sanam), and the summit of the Qur'an is Surat al-Baqarah; and indeed everything has a core (lubab), and the core of the Qur'an is the Mufassal. Abu Muhammad al-Darimi said: al-lubab means the pure essence. In Sahih Ibn Hibban from Sahl ibn Sa'd, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed everything has a summit, and the summit of the Qur'an is Surat al-Baqarah; whoever recites it in his house at night, Satan will not enter his house for three nights, and whoever recites it by day, Satan will not enter his house for three days." Abu Hatim al-Busti said: the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Satan will not enter his house for three days" means: the rebellious devils (maradat al-shayatin). Al-Darimi related in his Musnad from al-Sha'bi who said: Abdullah said: Whoever recites ten verses of Surat al-Baqarah in a night, no Satan will enter that house that night until morning: four from its beginning, the Ayat al-Kursi, two after it, and three at its end; the first of them being ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾ [al-Baqarah: 284]. And from al-Sha'bi, from him: no Satan nor anything that he dislikes will come near him or his family that day, and it is not recited over a madman except that he regains consciousness. Al-Mughirah ibn Subay' (or Sumay'), who was among the companions of Abdullah, said: He did not forget the Qur'an. Ishaq ibn Isa said: He did not forget what he had memorized. Abu Muhammad al-Darimi said: Some of them say: al-Mughirah ibn Sumay'. In the Kitab al-Isti'ab of Ibn Abd al-Barr: Labid ibn Rabi'ah [ibn Amir [the addition is from Kitab al-Isti'ab (vol. 1, p. 235), printed in India]] ibn Malik ibn Ja'far ibn Kilab ibn Rabi'ah ibn Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah was one of the poets of the Jahiliyyah; he lived to see Islam, his Islam was good, and he gave up composing poetry in Islam. In his caliphate, Umar asked him about his poetry and asked him to recite, and he recited Surat al-Baqarah. Umar said: "I only asked you about your poetry." He replied: "I would not say a line of poetry after Allah taught me al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran." Umar was pleased with his words, and his stipend was two thousand, so he increased it by five hundred. Many of the scholars of reports said that Labid did not compose poetry since he embraced Islam. Some said: he said nothing in Islam except his saying: "Praise be to Allah that my term did not come until I was clothed in Islam like a garment." Ibn Abd al-Barr said: It has been said that this verse belongs to Qarada ibn Nufathah al-Sululi, and that is more sound in my view. Others said: Rather the verse he said in Islam is: "A noble man is not reproached like his own self, and a man is set right by a good companion." What has come concerning Ayat al-Kursi and the ends of al-Baqarah will come [see vol. 3, pp. 268, 431], and further clarification of the merit of this surah will come at the beginning of Surat Al 'Imran [see vol. 4, p. 2], God willing.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful (Lord, make it easy and help).

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Alif Lam Mim (1). That is the Book; there is no doubt in it; it is guidance for the God-fearing (2).

[Statement of the views related concerning the disjointed letters at the beginnings of the surahs]

The interpreters differed concerning the letters that occur at the beginnings of surahs. Amir al-Sha'bi, Sufyan al-Thawri, and a group of the traditionists said: They are the secret of Allah in the Qur'an, and Allah has a secret in each of His books. They are therefore among the ambiguous (mutashabih) matters whose knowledge Allah the Exalted has reserved for Himself; it is not obligatory [in one copy of the original: "it is not permissible that we speak about them ... and they pass as they are"; in another: "and we recite them as they came"] to speak about them, but we believe in them and recite them as they came. This view has been related from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with them both. Abu al-Layth al-Samarqandi mentioned from Umar, Uthman, and Ibn Mas'ud that they said: the disjointed letters are of the hidden matter that is not explained. Abu Hatim said: We do not find the disjointed letters in the Qur'an except at the beginnings of surahs, and we do not know what Allah the Mighty and Majestic intended by them. I say: Among this meaning is what Abu Bakr al-Anbari mentioned: al-Hasan ibn al-Hubab related to us, Abu Bakr ibn Abi Talib related to us, Abu al-Mundhir al-Wasiti related to us, from Malik ibn Mighwal, from Sa'id ibn Masruq, from al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym [the author of Tahdhib al-Tahdhib said: in al-Taqrib it is al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym, with a dammed mu'jamah and an opened thaa; but in al-Khulasah it is with an opened mu'jamah and thaa, with a sukun ya between them], who said: Indeed Allah the Exalted sent down this Qur'an and reserved from it the knowledge of what He willed, and made you aware of what He willed. As for what He reserved for Himself, you cannot attain it, so do not ask about it. As for what He made you aware of, it is what you ask about and are rewarded for [in one copy: "are recompensed for by it"], and you do not know all of the Qur'an, nor do you act upon everything you know. Abu Bakr said: This makes clear that letters of the Qur'an have had their meanings concealed from the whole world, as a trial and a test from Allah the Mighty and Majestic. Whoever believes in them is rewarded and made happy, and whoever disbelieves or doubts them sins and is distanced. Abu Yusuf Ya'qub al-Qadi related to us, Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr related to us, Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi related to us, from Sufyan, from al-A'mash, from Umarah, from Hurayth ibn Zuhayr, from Abdullah, who said: No believer has believed in a better faith than belief in the unseen, then he recited: ﴿Those who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3].

I say: This view concerns the ambiguous and its ruling, and it is the sound view, as will be explained in Al 'Imran, God willing [see vol. 4, p. 2]. A large group of scholars said: Rather, it is obligatory that we speak about them, seek the benefits beneath them and the meanings that may be derived from them. They differed on this in many views. It is related from Ibn Abbas and also Ali: that the disjointed letters in the Qur'an are the Greatest Name of Allah, except that we do not know how it is composed from them. Qutrub, al-Farra' and others said: They are an indication of the letters of spelling (huruf al-hija'), by which Allah informed the Arabs when He challenged them with the Qur'an that it is composed of letters of the same kind from which their speech is built, so that their inability to produce its like would be a more decisive proof against them, since it did not depart from their language. Qutrub said: They used to turn away when hearing the Qur'an; when they heard "Alif Lam Mim" and "Alif Lam Mim Sad," they found this utterance strange, and when they listened to him (ﷺ), he approached them with the composed Qur'an in order to fix it in their hearing and ears and establish the proof against them. Some people said: It has been related that when the polytheists turned away from listening to the Qur'an in Makkah and said: "Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it," these letters were revealed so that they would be struck by them, and open their hearing to them, and then hear the Qur'an after them, so that the proof would become binding upon them. A group said: They are letters indicating names from which they were taken, with the rest omitted, as in the saying of Ibn Abbas and others: the Alif is from Allah, the Lam is from Jibril, and the Mim is from Muhammad (ﷺ). It has also been said: the Alif is the key of His name Allah, the Lam is the key of His name Latif, and the Mim is the key of His name Majid. Abu al-Duha related from Ibn Abbas concerning his saying "Alif Lam Mim": "I am Allah, the All-Knowing; 'Alif Lam Ra': I am Allah, the All-Seeing; 'Alif Lam Mim Sad': I am Allah, the Distinguisher." So the Alif conveys the meaning of "I (ana)," the Lam conveys the name of Allah, and the Mim conveys the meaning of "I know best (a'lam)." Al-Zajjaj chose this view and said: I hold that each letter of them conveys a meaning, and the Arabs have spoken with the disjointed letters in verse and in usage in place of the words of which those letters are part, as in his saying:

"I said to her: Stop (qif), and she said: Qaf"

He meant: she said: "I have stopped (waqaftu)." And Zuhayr said:

"With good, good things; and if evil, then fa..., and I do not want evil except that ta..."

He meant: "and if evil, then fa (fa-shar: then evil)." And he meant: "except that you (an ta) wish (tashaʾ)."

And another said:

"They called to them: Alla jimu (be silent)! Alla ta! They all said together: Alla fa!"

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 1–2 (part 2 of 3):

He meant: "Will you not ride?" They said: "Will you not then ride?" In a hadith: "Whoever helps in the killing of a Muslim even with half a word..." Shaqiq said: this means that one says in "iqtul" (kill): "iq," as the Prophet ﷺ said: "The sword is sufficient as a shaa," meaning: "healer" (shafiyan). Zayd ibn Aslam said: they are names of the surahs. Al-Kalbi said: they are oaths which Allah, exalted is He, swore by because of their nobility and merit, and they are among His names, related also from Ibn Abbas. Some scholars rejected this view, saying: it is not correct that they are an oath, because an oath is bound to particles such as inna, qad, la-qad and ma, and no such particle is found here, so it is not permissible that they be an oath. The answer is to say: the place of the oath is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is no doubt in it﴾. If a person swore and said: "By Allah, this Book, there is no doubt in it," the statement would be sound, and "la" would be the response to the oath. Thus it is established that the saying of al-Kalbi and what is related from Ibn Abbas is sound and correct. If it is asked: what is the wisdom in Allah's swearing, when the people of that time were of two kinds: one who believes, and one who denies? The believer believes without an oath, and the denier does not believe even with an oath? It is said to him: the Qur'an was revealed in the language of the Arabs, and when some of the Arabs wished to affirm their speech, they swore upon their speech; and Allah, exalted is He, wished to affirm the proof upon them, so He swore that the Qur'an is from Him. Some said: "Alif-Lam-Mim" means: I have sent down this Book to you from the Preserved Tablet. Qatadah said regarding His saying "Alif-Lam-Mim": it is a name of the Qur'an. It is related from Muhammad ibn Ali al-Tirmidhi that he said: Allah, exalted is He, deposited all that is in that surah of rulings and narratives in the letters He mentioned at the beginning of the surah, and none knows that except a prophet or a saint; then He clarified that throughout the surah so that people might understand. Other opinions besides this have been stated, and Allah knows best. Stopping on these letters is with sukun because of their being truncated, except when you speak about them or conjoin them, in which case you inflect them. It has been disputed: do they have a place in i'rab? It was said: no, because they are not declinable nouns nor imperfect verbs; rather they are like the letters of spelling, so they are indeclinable quoted forms. This is the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh.

Whoever says they are the names of the surahs, their place in his view is nominative, on the basis that they are, in his view, the predicate of an implied subject, i.e., "this is Alif-Lam-Mim," just as you say: "This is Surat al-Baqarah." Or they are nominative as subject and predicate: "that," just as you say: "Zayd is that man." Ibn Kaysan the grammarian said: "Alif-Lam-Mim" is in the accusative position, as you say: "Recite Alif-Lam-Mim," or "upon you Alif-Lam-Mim." It was also said: it is in the genitive position by the oath, based on Ibn Abbas's saying: they are oaths by which Allah swore.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is the Book﴾. It was said: the meaning is "this Book." "That" (dhalika) may be used to indicate something present, although it is originally for indicating something absent, as Allah, exalted and glorious is He, said in reporting about Himself: "That is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Mighty, the Merciful" [Surah al-Sajdah 6]. From this is the saying of Khufaf ibn Nudbah:

I say to him while the spear bends its shaft:
"Consider Khufaf, for indeed I am that one."

That is: "I am this one." So "that" is a reference to the Qur'an, placed in the position of "this," its summary being: "Alif-Lam-Mim, this is the Book, there is no doubt in it." This is the view of Abu Ubaydah, Ikrimah and others. From this is His saying: "And that is Our argument which We gave to Abraham" [Surah al-An'am 83], and "Those are the signs of Allah, We recite them to you in truth" [Surah al-Baqarah 252], meaning "these." But when they ended, they became as if distant, so "that" was said. In al-Bukhari: "Ma'mar said: 'That is the Book' means 'this Qur'an.'" "A guidance for the God-fearing" is an explanation and indication, like His saying: "That is the judgment of Allah, He judges between you" [Surah al-Mumtahanah 10], meaning "this is the judgment of Allah." I say: "hadha" has also come in the sense of "dhalika," and from this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ in the hadith of Umm Haram: "They ride the middle (thabaj) of this sea," meaning "that sea." And Allah knows best. It was also said: it is on its original usage, indicating something absent. Regarding that absent referent there are ten opinions. It was said: "That is the Book," meaning the Book which I wrote for the creation concerning happiness, wretchedness, the term and provision, "there is no doubt in it," meaning there is no changer of it. It was also said: "That is the Book," meaning the one which I wrote upon Myself in eternity: "that My mercy precedes My wrath." In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah who said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When Allah had decreed creation, He wrote in His Book, which is with Him, concerning Himself: 'My mercy overcomes My wrath.'" In another narration: "precedes."

It was also said: Allah, exalted is He, had promised His Prophet ﷺ that He would send down upon him a Book which water would not wash away, so He pointed to that promise, as in Sahih Muslim from the hadith of Iyad ibn Himar al-Mujashi'i that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah looked at the people of the earth and despised them, Arabs and non-Arabs, except some remnants of the People of the Book. He said: 'I have only sent you to test you and to test through you, and I have sent down upon you a Book which water does not wash away; you read it asleep and awake.'" The hadith to its end. It was also said: the reference is to what had been revealed of the Qur'an at Makkah. It was also said: when Allah, blessed and exalted is He, revealed to His Prophet ﷺ in Makkah: "Indeed We shall cast upon you a heavy word" [Surah al-Muzzammil 5], the Messenger of Allah ﷺ continued to look forward to the fulfilment of this promise from his Lord, mighty and majestic. When there was revealed to him in Madinah: "Alif-Lam-Mim. That is the Book; there is no doubt in it" [al-Baqarah 1–2], it contained the meaning of this Qur'an which I revealed to you in Madinah: that is the Book which I promised to reveal to you in Makkah. It was also said: "that" refers to what is in the Torah and the Gospel. "Alif-Lam-Mim" is a name of the Qur'an, and the implied meaning is: this Qur'an is that Book, explained in the Torah and the Gospel; that is, the Torah and the Gospel bear witness to its truth, and it encompasses what is in them and adds to them what is not in them. It was also said: "That is the Book" refers to both the Torah and the Gospel together, and the meaning is: Alif-Lam-Mim, those two Books, or like those two Books; that is, this Qur'an comprises what is in those two Books. So "that" is used for the two, with evidence from the Qur'an. Allah, blessed and exalted is He, said: ﴿It is a cow, neither old nor virgin, between that﴾ [al-Baqarah 68], meaning: between those two, the old and the virgin. This will come. It was also said: "that" refers to the Preserved Tablet. Al-Kisa'i said: "That" refers to the Qur'an which is in heaven and had not yet been sent down. It was also said: Allah, exalted is He, had promised the People of the Book that He would send down a Book upon Muhammad ﷺ, so the reference is to that promise. Al-Mubarrad said: the meaning is "this Qur'an is that Book which you used to seek victory by against those who disbelieved." It was also said: it refers to the letters of the alphabet, according to the one who said "Alif-Lam-Mim": the letters with which I challenged you to produce arrangement from them.

"Al-Kitab" is a verbal noun from kataba, yaktubu, meaning to gather, and from it is said "katibah" (a battalion), because of its gathering. And "takattabati al-khayl" means the horses became battalions. And "katabtu al-baghlah" means when I joined the two lips of its womb with a ring or a strap. He said:

Do not feel safe from a Fazari whom you have made stay upon your young she-camel, and bind her with thongs.

"Al-kutbah" (with a dammah on the kaf) is a stitch, its plural being kutab. "Al-kutb" is stitching. Dhu al-Rummah said:

A wide, tanned leather, whose stitches have been torn, its gaps left by the kutab (stitches) in disarray.

"Al-kitab" is the writing of the scribe in the letters of the alphabet, collected or scattered, and it is called a Book even though it is written, as the poet said:

She hopes for a return from me, and in it is a writing like what the glue has stuck.

"Al-kitab" also means the obligation, the judgment and the decree. Al-Ju'di said:

O daughter of my uncle, the Book of Allah has removed me from you; and would I forbid what Allah has done?

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿la rayb﴾ is a general negation, and therefore "al-rayb" is put in the accusative by it. And "al-rayb" has three meanings. One: doubt. 'Abdullah ibn al-Zib'ari said:

There is no doubt in the truth, O Umayma; doubt is only what the ignorant one says.

Second: accusation. Jamil said:

Buthaynah said: "O Jamil, you have made me doubt," so I said: "We both, O Buthaynah, are suspicious."

Third: need. He said [it is Ka'b ibn Malik al-Ansari, as in Lisan, root r-y-b]:

We settled from Tihamah every need, and Khaybar, then we gathered the swords.

So the Book of Allah, exalted is He, has no doubt in it and no suspicion. The meaning is that it is in itself true, that it is sent down from Allah, and an attribute of His attributes, uncreated and not originated, even though disbelievers may fall into doubt. It was also said: it is a statement whose meaning is a prohibition, i.e., "do not doubt," and the sentence is complete as if he said: that Book is true. You say: "This matter cast doubt upon me" when it introduces to you suspicion and fear. "Arab" means he became one who has doubt, so he is "murib." "Rabani amruhu" means his affair cast doubt upon me. "Rayb al-dahr" means its vicissitudes.

[The discussion on the guidance of the Qur'an, and it contains six issues]

﴿فِيهِ هُدىً لِلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾: In it is guidance for the God-conscious (muttaqun). This verse contains six issues.

**The first issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿فِيهِ﴾ (in it). The pronoun *ha'* in *fihi* is in the genitive position after *fi* (in). There are five possible readings, the best of which is *fihi hudan* (with the *ha'* vowelled with a *kasra*). Next is *fihu hudan* (with a *damma* on the *ha'* without a following *waw*), which is the reading of al-Zuhri and Sallam Abu al-Mundhir. Next is *fihi-yi hudan* (with the *ya'* affirmed), which is the reading of Ibn Kathir. It is also permissible to read *fihu-wa hudan* (with the *waw*), and it is permissible to read *fihh hudan* (with the consonants assimilated). *Hudan* is nominative, as the subject of a nominal sentence, with *fihi* as its predicate. In the language of the Arabs, *al-huda* (guidance) means right direction (rushd) and clarification (bayan). That is, in it is an unveiling for those who have knowledge, right direction, increased clarification and guidance.

**The second issue:** *Al-huda* has two kinds. The first is *huda dalalah* (guidance by indication), which the messengers and their followers are able to provide. God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿وَلِكُلِّ قَوْمٍ هادٍ﴾ (And for every people there is a guide) [al-Ra'd 13:7] and: ﴿وَإِنَّكَ لَتَهْدِي إِلى صِراطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ﴾ (And indeed, you guide to a straight path) [al-Shura 42:52]. Thus He affirmed for them the guidance whose meaning is indication, invitation and alerting. He alone, Glory be to Him, has the guidance whose meaning is support and enabling success (tawfiq). So He said to His Prophet ﷺ: ﴿إِنَّكَ لَا تَهْدِي مَنْ أَحْبَبْتَ﴾ (Indeed, you do not guide whom you like) [al-Qasas 28:56]. Thus *al-huda* in this sense means creating faith in the heart. From this is His saying: ﴿أُولئِكَ عَلى هُدىً مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ (Those are upon guidance from their Lord) [al-Baqarah 2:5], and His saying: ﴿وَيَهْدِي مَنْ يَشاءُ﴾ (And He guides whom He wills) [Fatir 35:8]. *Al-hudá* (being guided) means *al-ihtida'*, and its meaning returns to the meaning of guidance however it is used.

Abu al-Ma'ali said: Guidance may also be used to mean directing the believers to the paths of the Gardens and the roads leading to them. From this is His saying, Exalted is He, describing the fighters: ﴿فَلَنْ يُضِلَّ أَعْمالَهُمْ * سَيَهْدِيهِمْ﴾ (He will not let their deeds go astray. He will guide them) [Muhammad 47:4–5]. From this is His saying: ﴿فَاهْدُوهُمْ إِلى صِراطِ الْجَحِيمِ﴾ (So guide them to the path of Hellfire) [al-Saffat 37:23], meaning: lead them along it to it.

**The third issue:** *Al-huda* is a feminine noun. Al-Farra' said: Some of the Banu Asad treat *al-huda* as feminine, so they say: *hadhihi huda hasanah* (this is good guidance). Al-Lihyani said: It is masculine, and it is not inflected (i'rab) because it is a *maqsur* noun (ending in a non-moving *alif*). It is transitive with a preposition and without a preposition. This was discussed in al-Fatihah. You say: *hadaytuhu al-tariqa* and *ila al-tariqi*, and *al-dar* and *ila al-dar*, meaning: I made him know. The first usage is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and the second was transmitted by al-Akhfash. In the revelation: ﴿اهْدِنَا الصِّراطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ﴾ (Guide us to the straight path) and ﴿الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي هَدانا لِهذا﴾ (Praise be to God who guided us to this) [al-A'raf 7:43]. It was said that *al-huda* is one of the names of the day, because people are guided during it to their livelihoods and all their needs. From this is the saying of Ibn Muqbil:

*"Until I clearly discerned the guidance, and the deserts were rushing,*
*they humbled themselves in the mirage, unsheathed, or prayed for us."*

[This line is missing from all the manuscripts; the addition is from Lisan al-Arab, entry *h-d-y*, and al-Bahr al-Muhit on this topic.]

**The fourth issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿لِلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾ (for the God-conscious). God, Exalted is He, specified the God-conscious with His guidance, even though it is guidance for all creation, to honour them, because they believed in it and affirmed what is in it. It is narrated from Abu Rawq that he said: "*Hudan lil-muttaqin*" means: a dignity for them. That is, He attributed it to them out of reverence for them, honour for them and to make clear their merit.

The original form of *lil-muttaqin* is *lil-mutawqiyin*, with two light *ya'*s. The *kasra* was removed from the first *ya'* because of its heaviness, then the *ya'* was removed because of the meeting of two unvocalised letters. The *waw* was changed to a *ta'* according to their practice when *waw* and *ta'* come together, and the *ta'* was assimilated into the following *ta'*, so it became *lil-muttaqin*.

**The fifth issue:** *Al-taqwa* (God-consciousness). It is said that its root in the language is "little speech" (qillat al-kalam); Ibn Faris related this. I say: From this is the hadith: "The one who is God-conscious is restrained, and the God-conscious person is above the believer and the obedient." It is the one who guards himself, by his righteous deeds and sincere supplication, against the punishment of God, Exalted is He. It is derived from guarding oneself against what is disliked by placing a barrier between oneself and it, as al-Nabigha said:

*"The veil (nasif) fell and she did not intend to drop it,*
*so she caught it and shielded us with her hand."*

[Nasif: a garment a woman wraps over all her other clothes; it is called *nasif* because it stands between people and her, blocking their eyes from her.]

And another said:

*"She cast a covering over which the sun was shielded,*
*shielding herself with the most beautiful of joined things, a palm and a wrist."*

Abu Muhammad Abd al-Ghani al-Hafiz transmitted from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Zarbi Abu Ubaydah, from Asim ibn Bahdalah, from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: One day he said to his nephew: "O nephew, do you see how many people there are?" He said: "Yes." He said: "There is no good in them except a penitent or a God-conscious person." Then he said: "O nephew, do you see how many people there are?" I said: "Yes." He said: "There is no good in them except a scholar or a student."

Abu Yazid al-Bistami said: The God-conscious is the one who, when he speaks, speaks for God, and when he acts, acts for God. Abu Sulayman al-Darani said: The God-conscious are those from whose hearts God has removed love of desires. It was said: The God-conscious is the one who guards himself against shirk and is free of hypocrisy. Ibn Atiyyah said: This is corrupt, because a person may be like that and still be a sinner.

Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, asked Ubayy about God-consciousness. He said: "Have you ever walked a path with thorns?" He said: "Yes." He said: "What did you do there?" He said: "I girded up and was cautious." He said: "That is God-consciousness."

Ibn al-Mu'tazz took up this meaning and versified it:

*"Leave sins, the small of them and the great of them; that is piety (tuqa).*
*Act like one walking over a land of thorns, wary of what he sees.*
*Do not belittle a small sin, for mountains are made of pebbles."*

**The sixth issue:** God-consciousness contains all good. It is the commandment of God to the first and the last people, and it is the best thing a person can gain, as Abu al-Darda' said when it was said to him: "Your companions recite poetry, but nothing of yours has been preserved." He said:

*"A man wants his wish to be granted, but God refuses except what He wills.*
*A man says: My gain and my wealth... but God-consciousness is the best gain."*

Ibn Majah related in his Sunan from Abu Umamah, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he used to say: "A believer gains nothing after God-consciousness better for him than a righteous wife: if he commands her, she obeys him; if he looks at her, she pleases him; if he swears an oath concerning her, she fulfils it for him; and if he is absent from her, she is sincere to him regarding herself and his property."

The root of *al-taqwa* is *waqwa*, on the pattern *fa'la*, so the *waw* was changed to a *ta'* from *waqaytuhu uqihi*, meaning: I protected him. A man *taqiyy* means fearful; its root is *waqa*. Likewise *tuqat* was originally *wuqat*, as they said *tujah* and *turath*, when the original forms were *wujah* and *wurath*.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 3 (part 1 of 5):

There are twenty-six issues in it:

The first: His saying, (alladhina) is in the genitive position as an adjective (na't) of "al-muttaqin" (the God-conscious). It is permissible to read it in the nominative by way of a new sentence (qat'), meaning "they are those who...", and it is permissible to read it in the accusative by way of praise (madh).

(Yu'minuna) means "they believe" (yusaddiqun). Iman (faith) in the linguistic sense is tasdiq (affirmation/belief in the truth of something). In the revealed text: ﴿And you would not be a believer (bi-mu'minin) to us﴾ [Yusuf 12:17], meaning "one who affirms (bi-musaddiq) us." It takes the prepositions ba' and lam, as He said: ﴿And do not believe except to one who follows your religion﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:73], ... ﴿So none believed in Musa (fa-ma amana li-Musa)﴾ [Yunus 10:83]. Hajjaj ibn Hajjaj al-Ahwal, who was nicknamed "Ziq al-'Asal" (Honey-skin), narrated saying: I heard Qatadah say: O son of Adam, if you do not want to come to goodness except with eagerness, then your self inclines toward weariness, lethargy and boredom. But the believer is the one who exerts himself (al-mutahammil) [exerting himself in a matter means: to force oneself to it with hardship and fatigue], the believer is the one who strengthens himself, the believer is the one who is strict with himself, and indeed the believers are those who cry out (al-'ajjun) [al-'ajj: raising the voice in talbiyah] to God night and day. By God, the believer does not cease saying "Our Lord, our Lord" in secret and in public until He answers them in secret and in public.

The second: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿bil-ghayb﴾ (in the unseen). In the speech of the Arabs, al-ghayb is everything that is absent from you. It is from the roots with ya' (dhawat al-ya'), it is said from it: ghabat al-shams taghib (the sun set), and al-ghibah (absence/backbiting) is well known. Ughabat al-mar'ah, so she is mughibah, when her husband has been absent from her. We fell into a ghaybah and ghiyabah, meaning a low place in the earth. Al-ghiyabah is a thicket, which is a mass of trees in which one hides. And a lowland of the earth is called al-ghayb, because it is hidden from sight.

The third: The exegetes differed in the interpretation of al-ghayb here. One group said: al-ghayb in this verse is Allah, glorified is He. Ibn al-'Arabi weakened this view. Others said: al-qada' and al-qadar (divine decree and destiny). Others said: the Qur'an and what is in it of unseen matters. Others said: al-ghayb is everything the Messenger ('alayhi al-salam) informed of that the intellects cannot reach, such as the signs of the Hour, the punishment of the grave, the gathering, the resurrection, the Sirat, the Scale, Paradise and Hell. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: These views do not contradict one another; rather, al-ghayb applies to all of them. I say: This is the legal faith (al-iman al-shar'i) referred to in the hadith of Jibril ('alayhi al-salam) when he said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Tell me about faith." He said: "That you believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day, and that you believe in destiny, its good and its evil." He said: "You have spoken truly." And he mentioned the hadith. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: No believer has attained a better faith than faith in the unseen; then he recited: ﴿Those who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:3]. I say: In the revealed text: ﴿And We were not absent (ghaibin)﴾ [al-A'raf 7:7], and He said: ﴿Those who fear their Lord in the unseen﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:49]. So He, glorified is He, is absent from the sights, not seen in this abode, yet not absent by reflection and inference. They believe that they have a Lord, capable, who recompenses deeds, so they fear Him in their inner selves and their private moments in which they are hidden from people, knowing that He sees them. On this the verses agree and do not conflict, and all praise is due to Allah. It was also said: "bil-ghayb" means with their inner consciences and hearts, as opposed to the hypocrites, and this is a good view. The poet said:
We believed in the unseen, when our people
were praying to idols before Muhammad.

The fourth: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and establish the prayer﴾ is a clause conjoined to a clause. The establishing of prayer (iqamat al-salah) is performing it with its pillars, its sunan and its conditions, at its times, as will be explained. It is said: qama al-shay' means it lasted and was firm; it is not from standing on the foot, rather it is from your saying: qama al-haqq, meaning it became manifest and established. The poet said:
And war stood up with us upon its leg.
Another said:
And when it is said, "You have come," they do not leave until the horses set up the market of spear-thrusting.
It was also said: "yuqimuna" means they perpetuate it, and aqamahu means he made it lasting. Umar pointed to this meaning in his saying: Whoever preserves it and guards it preserves his religion, and whoever neglects it is more neglectful of what is other than it.

The fifth: The establishing of prayer is well known, and it is a sunnah according to the majority, and there is no repetition (i'adah) upon one who abandons it. According to al-Awza'i, 'Ata', Mujahid and Ibn Abi Layla, it is obligatory (wajibah), and upon one who abandons it there is repetition; this is also the view of the people of the apparent meaning (ahl al-Zahir), and it is narrated from Malik, and Ibn al-'Arabi chose it. He said: Because in the hadith of the Bedouin (al-a'rabi) there is "wa-aqim" (and establish), so He commanded him to establish it just as He commanded him to say takbir, face the qiblah, and perform wudu'. He said: As for you now, since you have come to know the hadith, it has become binding upon you to hold to one of Malik's two narrations which agrees with the hadith, namely that establishing it is an obligation (fard). Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: His saying ﷺ, "and its opening is the takbir," is evidence that one who does not begin with the takbir has not entered into prayer; so whatever occurs before the ihram, its ruling is that the prayer is not repeated from it, unless they agree upon something, and then it is submitted to the consensus, such as purity, the qiblah, the time and the like. Some of our scholars said: Whoever abandons it intentionally repeats the prayer, and this is not because it is obligatory, for if that were so, its forgetting and its intentional omission would be equal; rather it is for disregard of the sunan. And Allah knows best.

The sixth: The scholars differed concerning one who hears the iqamah, whether he should hasten or not. The majority held that he should not hasten, even if he fears missing a rak'ah, due to His saying, peace be upon him: "When the prayer is established, do not come to it running; come to it walking, and upon you is tranquility. Whatever you catch, pray, and whatever you miss, complete." Narrated by Abu Hurayrah, recorded by Muslim. And also from him, he said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When the prayer is called (thuwwiba), let none of you hasten to it, but let him walk, with tranquility and dignity upon him; pray what you catch and make up what has passed you." This is explicit text. And in terms of meaning, if he hastens he becomes breathless (infabara) [al-bahr (with a dammah): the succession of breath from exhaustion], which disturbs his entry into the prayer, its recitation and its humility. A group of the early generations, including Ibn 'Umar and Ibn Mas'ud, according to a difference reported from him, held that if he fears missing it he should hasten. Ishaq said: He hastens if he fears missing the rak'ah, and something similar is narrated from Malik, who said: There is no harm for one who is on a horse to urge the horse on. Some interpreted it as a distinction between the one walking and the one riding, since the rider hardly becomes breathless as the walker does. I say: Following the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in every situation is better; so he walks as the hadith came, with tranquility and dignity upon him, because he is in prayer, and it is impossible that his report ﷺ should be contrary to what he informed. Just as one who enters the prayer must adopt dignity and calm, so too the one walking, so that he attains the likeness of it and thereby attains its reward. Among what supports the soundness of this is the sunnah we have mentioned, and what al-Darimi transmitted in his Musnad, saying: Muhammad ibn Yusuf narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us from Muhammad ibn 'Ajlan, from al-Maqburi, from Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When you perform wudu' and then set out for the mosque, do not interlace your fingers, for you are in prayer." He ﷺ prohibited in this hadith, and it is sound, something less than hastening, and made him like one praying. These sunan clarify the meaning of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So hasten to the remembrance of Allah﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 62:9], and that it does not mean running on foot; rather it means working and acting. This is how Malik explained it. And that is the correct view in this matter, and Allah knows best.

**The seventh issue:** The scholars differed over the interpretation of the Prophet's (ﷺ) words, "And whatever you missed, complete" (ﷺ, peace be upon him), and of the Qur'anic phrase "and make up what has passed you" (ﷺ). Are these two expressions synonymous or not? It was said: they are synonymous, since *qada'* (ﷺ, to decide, complete, or make up) can be used to mean completion. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when the prayer has been concluded﴾ (62:10), and He said: ﴿And when you have completed your rites﴾ (2:200). It was also said: their meanings differ, and this is the correct view. This difference leads to a further disagreement about what the latecomer to prayer catches: is it the beginning of his prayer or its end? A group of the companions of Malik, including Ibn al-Qasim, held the first view, but he makes up what he missed with the Fatihah and a surah. So he is *bani* (building on what was done) in the actions and *qadi* (making up) in the recitations. Ibn Abd al-Barr said: this is the well-known position within the school. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: this is what our companions hold, and it is the view of al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, al-Tabari, and Dawud ibn Ali. Ashhab narrated, and it is what Ibn Abd al-Hakam mentioned from Malik, and Isa narrated it from Ibn al-Qasim from Malik, that whatever he catches is the last part of his prayer, and that he makes up in both actions and recitations. This is also the view of the Kufans. Qadi Abu Muhammad Abd al-Wahhab said: this is the well-known position of the school of Malik. Ibn Abd al-Barr said: as for those who regard what one catches as the first part of the prayer, I think they were giving weight to the *ihram* (the opening takbir), since it occurs only at the beginning of the prayer, while the *tashahhud* and the *taslim* (greeting of peace) occur only at its end. From this they said that what one catches is the beginning of his prayer, in addition to what is reported in the Sunnah (the practice of the Prophet) in his saying "complete." Completion is the end. The others argued from the phrase "then make up," and what is made up is what has been missed. However, the narration of those who report "complete" is more numerous. The view that what one catches is the beginning of the prayer is not consistent or uniform, except for what was said by Abd al-Aziz ibn Abi Salamah al-Majishun, al-Muzani, Ishaq, and Dawud, that he recites the Fatihah and a surah along with the imam if he catches that, and when he stands to make up, he recites only the Fatihah. Their statements and actions were consistent with their principle. May Allah be pleased with them.

**The eighth issue:** The iqamah (the call to standing for prayer) prevents beginning a voluntary prayer. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the prayer has been called to standing, there is no prayer except the obligatory one." Muslim and others reported it. As for one who has already begun a voluntary prayer, he should not break it, because of Allah's saying: ﴿and do not render your deeds void﴾ (47:33), especially if he has already prayed one rak'ah of it. It was also said that he should break it, due to the generality of the hadith on this matter. And Allah knows best.

**The ninth issue:** The scholars differed about one who enters the mosque and has not yet prayed the two rak'ahs of dawn, and then the iqamah is called. Malik said: he joins the imam and does not pray them. If he has not yet entered the mosque, then if he does not fear missing a rak'ah, he should pray them outside the mosque, but not in any part of the mosque's precincts (afniyah) where Friday prayer is held, adjacent to the mosque. If he fears missing the first rak'ah, he should enter and pray with the imam, and then pray the two rak'ahs after sunrise if he wishes. Praying them after sunrise is more beloved to me and better than leaving them. Abu Hanifa and his companions said: if he fears that he will miss the two rak'ahs and will not reach the imam before he rises from bowing in the second rak'ah, he joins the imam. If he hopes to catch one rak'ah, he prays the two rak'ahs of dawn outside the mosque and then joins the imam. Al-Awza'i said the same, except that it is permissible to pray them inside the mosque as long as he does not fear missing the last rak'ah. Al-Thawri said: if he fears missing one rak'ah, he joins them and does not pray the two; otherwise he prays them, even if he has entered the mosque. Al-Hasan ibn Hayy, also called Ibn Hayyan, said: once the one establishing the iqamah begins it, there is no voluntary prayer except the two rak'ahs of dawn. Al-Shafi'i said: whoever enters the mosque when the prayer has been called to standing joins the imam and does not pray them, neither outside the mosque nor inside it. Al-Tabari said the same, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal also said this, and it is reported from Malik. This is the correct view on the matter, because of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "When the prayer has been called to standing, there is no prayer except the obligatory one."

The two rak'ahs of dawn are either a sunnah (a confirmed practice of the Prophet), or a *fadilah* (a recommended virtue), or a *raghibah* (a highly desired act). When there is disagreement, the decisive authority is the authority of the Sunnah. Among the evidence for the well-known view of Malik and Abu Hanifa is what is reported from Ibn Umar: he came while the imam was leading the dawn prayer, and he prayed the two rak'ahs in the room of Hafsah, and then he prayed with the imam. Among the evidence for al-Thawri and al-Awza'i is what is reported from Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud: he entered the mosque when the iqamah had been called, and he prayed the two rak'ahs of dawn by a pillar (*ustuwanah*) in the mosque. [*Ustuwanah*: pillar.] Then he entered the prayer in the presence of Hudhayfah and Abu Musa, may Allah be pleased with them. They said: "Since it is permissible to be occupied with a voluntary prayer outside the mosque instead of the obligatory prayer, it is permissible for him to do so inside the mosque." Muslim reported from Abd Allah ibn Malik ibn Buhaynah [*Buhaynah*: his mother, daughter of al-Harith ibn Abd al-Muttalib. His father was Malik ibn al-Qashb ibn Fadhalah al-Azdi.] who said: the dawn prayer was called to standing, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw a man praying while the muezzin was calling the iqamah, and he said: "Are you praying four rak'ahs of dawn?" This was a rebuke from him (ﷺ) to the man for praying the two rak'ahs of dawn in the mosque while the imam was leading. It may also be used as evidence that if the two rak'ahs of dawn are performed in that situation, they are valid, because the Prophet (peace be upon him) did not interrupt his prayer even though he was able to do so. And Allah knows best.

**The tenth issue:** The root meaning of *salah* (prayer) in the language is supplication (*du'a*), derived from "sallā yusallī" when one supplicates. From this is the Prophet's (peace be upon him) saying: "If one of you is invited to a meal, let him accept. If he is fasting, let him pray" [i.e., let him supplicate]. Some scholars said the intended meaning is the well-known prayer, so he prays two rak'ahs and departs. The first view is better known, and the majority of scholars hold it. When Asma gave birth to Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, she sent him to the Prophet (ﷺ). Asma said: "Then he rubbed him and prayed for him," i.e., supplicated for him. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And pray for them﴾ (9:103), i.e., supplicate for them. Al-A'sha said:

My daughter says, when I was near to departing: "O Lord, keep my father far from ailments and pain."
May upon you be like what you prayed for, so rest, for a man's side needs a place to lie down.

Al-A'sha also said:

The wind met her in her jar, and he [the drinker] prayed over her jar and exulted.

*Irtasama al-rajul* means he magnified God and supplicated, as stated in *al-Sihah* [a dictionary].

Some people said: it is derived from *al-sala*, which is a vein in the middle of the back that splits at the hip and surrounds it. From this the *musalli* (the horse running second) in horse races is named, because it comes in the race with its head near the *salawa* of the leader. So *al-sala* of the horse, the rear part, gave rise to the name of prayer, either because it came second to faith and was likened to the *musalli* of horses, or because the one bowing has his *salawan* bent. *Al-sala* is the hindquarters of a horse, and "two salawan" is the dual. The *musalli* is the one following the leader, because his head is near the leader's *salah*. Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came first, Abu Bakr came second [*sallā*], and Umar came third [*thallatha*]."

It was also said: it is derived from *al-luzum* (adherence). From this comes "ṣalā bi-l-nār" (he was burnt by the fire) when he adhered to it. From this is the verse: ﴿burning in a scorching fire﴾ (88:4). Al-Harith ibn Ubad said:

I was not among its [the war's] fighters, may Allah know, but today I am burning with its heat.

That is, he adheres to its heat. It seems that the meaning in this case is persistent worship in the measure that Allah the Exalted commanded.

It was also said: it is derived from *sallaytu al-ud bil-nar*, when I straightened the wood and softened it with fire. *Al-sila'* is the heat of the fire, pronounced with a kasra on the *sad* and extended. If you put a fatha on the *sad* and shorten it, you say *sala al-nar*. So the one praying straightens himself through the hardship of it, softens, and becomes humble. Al-Kharazanji said:

Do not hasten your affair, but make it lasting, for your staff does not endure like one who lasts.

**Al-Salah** (prayer) means supplication. **Al-salah** also means mercy, as in the saying (in a hadith): "O Allah, send blessings (*salli*) upon Muhammad," and so on. **Al-salah** also means worship, as in the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Their prayer at the House was nothing but whistling and clapping﴾ [al-Anfal: 35], meaning their worship. **Al-salah** also means voluntary prayer, as in the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And enjoin your family to pray﴾ [Ta-Ha: 132]. **Al-salah** also means glorification (*tasbih*), as in the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Had he not been one of those who glorify [Allah]﴾ [al-Saffat: 143], meaning, one of those who pray. From this comes *subhat al-duha* (the forenoon prayer).
