It has also been said that the words ﴿We glorify You with Your praise﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30] mean "we pray." **Al-salah** also means recitation, as in the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And do not recite your prayer aloud﴾ [al-Isra: 110]. Thus it is a homonym (*lafz mushtarak*).

**Al-salah** also means a house in which one prays. This was stated by Ibn Faris.

It has also been said that *al-salah* is a proper noun (*ism 'alam*) assigned to this specific act of worship, since Allah, exalted is He, never left any era without a law (*shar'*), and no law was ever without prayer. This was related by Abu Nasr al-Qushayri. I say: according to this view, the word has no derivation (*ishtiqaq*). According to the view of the majority, and this is the eleventh issue, the jurists of legal theory (*usuliyyun*) differed over whether the word remains on its original linguistic, primary imposition, as with *al-iman* (faith), *al-zakah* (almsgiving), *al-siyam* (fasting) and *al-hajj* (pilgrimage), where the Law only introduced conditions and rulings. Or whether that addition from the Law makes the word assigned by the Law, like the initial imposition. This is the point of their disagreement. The first view is more correct, because the Sharia was established in Arabic, and the Qur'an was revealed in it, "in clear Arabic tongue" [al-Shu'ara: 195]. Yet the Arabs have authority over names. For example, *al-dabbah* (beast) was assigned to everything that crawls, then custom restricted it to livestock. Likewise, the custom of the Law has authority over names. And Allah knows best.

The twelfth issue: scholars differed over what is meant by *al-salah* here. It has been said that it means the obligatory prayers (*al-fara'id*). It has also been said that it means both obligatory and voluntary prayers together, and this is the sound view, because the word is general, and the God-fearing person performs both.

The thirteenth issue: prayer is a cause of provision (*rizq*). Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And enjoin your family to pray﴾ [Ta-Ha: 132], and the rest of the verse, as its explanation will come in *Ta-Ha* [see vol. 11, p. 263], Allah willing. Prayer is also a cure for stomach pain and other ailments. Ibn Majah related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) made *tahjir* (going early, hastening to something), so I hastened and prayed, then sat down. The Prophet (ﷺ) turned to me and said: "*Ashkamta dardih?*" I said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Stand and pray, for in prayer there is healing." In another narration: "*Ashkamta dard*," meaning, "You complain of your stomach," in Persian. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when a matter distressed him, would turn to prayer.

The fourteenth issue: prayer is not valid except with conditions (*shurut*) and pillars (*furud*). Among its conditions is purity (*tahara*), and the rulings on it will come in *Surat al-Nisa'* [see vol. 5, p. 204 onward] and *al-Ma'idah* [see vol. 6, p. 80 onward]. Also covering the private parts (*satr al-'awrah*), and the discussion of it will come in *al-A'raf* [see vol. 7, p. 182 onward], Allah willing. As for its pillars: facing the qiblah, intention (*niyyah*), the opening takbir (*takbirat al-ihram*) and standing for it, reciting *Umm al-Qur'an* (al-Fatihah) and standing for it, bowing (*ruku'*) and remaining still in it, rising from bowing and standing upright, prostrating (*sujud*) and remaining still in it, rising from prostration, sitting between the two prostrations and remaining still in it, and the second prostration and remaining still in it.

The basis for this whole list is the hadith of Abu Hurayrah about the man whom the Prophet (ﷺ) taught the prayer after he had performed it carelessly. He said to him: "When you stand for prayer, complete your ablution, then face the qiblah, then say *takbir*, then recite what you can of the Qur'an, then bow until you are still in bowing, then rise until you are standing straight, then prostrate until you are still in prostration, then rise until you are still sitting, then do that in all your prayer." Muslim related it. A similar hadith is that of Rifa'ah ibn Rafi', related by al-Daraqutni and others.

Our scholars said: The Prophet's (ﷺ) statement explains the pillars of prayer, and it is silent about the call to prayer (*iqamah*), raising the hands, the measure of recitation, the *takbir* for transitions, the glorification in bowing and prostration, the middle sitting, the *tashahhud*, the final sitting and the salam. As for the *iqamah* and the specification of al-Fatihah, the discussion of them has already passed [see pp. 117 and 164 of this volume]. As for raising the hands, it is not obligatory according to the majority of scholars and the common jurists, because of the hadith of Abu Hurayrah and the hadith of Rifa'ah ibn Rafi'. Dawud and some of his followers said it is obligatory at the opening *takbir*. Some of his companions said that raising the hands at the opening *takbir*, at bowing and at rising from bowing is obligatory, and whoever does not raise his hands, his prayer is invalid. This is the view of al-Humaydi, and a narration from al-Awza'i. They argued with the Prophet's (ﷺ) words: "Pray as you have seen me pray." Al-Bukhari related it. They said: "So we must do as we have seen him do, because he is the one who conveys Allah's intention."

As for the *takbir* other than the opening *takbir*, it is recommended (*masnun*) according to the majority, based on the hadith mentioned. Ibn al-Qasim, the companion of Malik, used to say: whoever omits three or more *takbirat* in prayer must perform the prostration of forgetfulness (*sujud al-sahw*) before the salam, and if he does not do it, his prayer is invalid. If he forgets one or two *takbirat*, he also performs the prostration of forgetfulness, and if he does not, there is nothing on him. It is also related from him that for a single *takbir* forgotten there is no forgetfulness prostration. This indicates that, in his view, the majority of the *takbir* and its totality are obligatory, while a little of it is excused.

Asbagh ibn al-Faraj and Abdullah ibn Abd al-Hakam said: There is nothing on the one who does not say *takbir* in prayer from beginning to end, provided he says the opening *takbir*. If he leaves it out forgetfully, he performs the forgetfulness prostration, and if he does not perform it, there is nothing on him. No one should intentionally leave out the *takbir*, because it is a sunnah of the prayer. If he does, he has done wrong, there is nothing on him, and his prayer stands.

I say: This is the sound view, and it is what the majority of the jurists of the cities (*fuqaha' al-amsar*) hold, from the Shafi'is, the Kufans, the people of hadith, and the Malikis other than those who followed the school of Ibn al-Qasim. Al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, titled a chapter: "Chapter: Completing the *takbir* in bowing and prostration," and related the hadith of Mutarrif ibn Abdullah, who said: "I prayed behind Ali ibn Abi Talib, I and Imran ibn Husayn. When he prostrated he said *takbir*, when he raised his head he said *takbir*, and when he stood up from the two rak'ahs he said *takbir*. When he finished the prayer, he took the hands of Imran ibn Husayn and said: 'This reminded me of the prayer of Muhammad (ﷺ),' or he said: 'He prayed with us the prayer of Muhammad (ﷺ).'" And the hadith of Ikrimah, who said: "I saw a man at the Maqam saying *takbir* at every lowering and raising, when he stood and when he sat down. I told Ibn Abbas, and he said: 'Is that not the prayer of the Prophet (ﷺ)? May you have no mother!'" [Note: *la umma laka* is an expression of reproach and abuse, meaning you are a foundling with no known mother. It has also been said that it may be used as praise in the sense of wonder, though this is distant.] Thus al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, indicated through this chapter that *takbir* was not practiced among them. Abu Ishaq al-Subay'i related from Yazid ibn Abi Maryam from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: "Ali led us in prayer on the day of the Camel, a prayer that reminded us of the prayer of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He used to say *takbir* at every lowering and raising, and standing and sitting." Abu Musa said: "Either we forgot it or we left it deliberately." I say: Do you think they repeated the prayer? How then can it be said that whoever leaves out the *takbir* has an invalid prayer? If that were so, there would be no difference between the sunnah and the obligation, and when a thing is not obligatory individually, it is not obligatory collectively. And success is from Allah.

The fifteenth issue: As for glorification (*tasbih*) in bowing and prostration, it is not obligatory according to the majority, because of the hadith mentioned. Ishaq ibn Rahawayh held it obligatory, and that whoever leaves it out must repeat the prayer, based on the Prophet's (ﷺ) words: "As for bowing, magnify the Lord in it, and as for prostration, strive in supplication, for it is fitting that you be answered."

The sixteenth issue: As for sitting and the *tashahhud*, scholars differed. Malik and his companions said: the first sitting and the *tashahhud* for it are two sunnahs. A group of scholars held the first sitting obligatory, and they said: it is singled out from among all the other obligations in that prostration substitutes for it, like the *'araya* (a palm grove whose fruit was given to the poor, who could not wait for it, so they were permitted to sell it for dates of their choosing) among the *muzabanah* (selling fresh dates on the palm for dried dates by measure, and selling raisins for grapes on the vine), and like *qirad* (a contract of partnership in trade for a share of its profit) among the leases, and like standing at 'Arafat after the ihram for one who finds the imam bowing. They argued that if it were a sunnah, the one who deliberately abandons it would not have his prayer invalidated, just as the prayer is not invalidated by abandoning the sunnahs of prayer. Those who did not make it obligatory argued: if it were one of the obligations of prayer, the one who forgets it would return to it until he performs it, just as if he left out a prostration or a rak'ah. And the same conditions apply to it as to bowing and prostration, of succession and order. Then he performs the forgetfulness prostration for his error, as one does who left out a rak'ah or a prostration and then performed it. In the hadith of Abdullah ibn Buhaynah: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood up after two rak'ahs and forgot to make the *tashahhud*, and the people behind him said *subhan Allah* so that he would sit, but he remained standing, and they stood up. When he finished his prayer, he performed the two prostrations of forgetfulness before the salam. Had the sitting been obligatory, forgetfulness would not have dropped it, because obligations of prayer are equal in being abandoned by forgetfulness or deliberately, except for the follower (*al-mu'tamm*).

They differed over the ruling on the final sitting in prayer and the purpose of it. This is the seventeenth issue, and there are five views. The first: sitting is obligatory, the *tashahhud* is obligatory, and the salam is obligatory. Among those who said this are al-Shafi'i and Ahmad ibn Hanbal in one narration. Abu Mus'ab related it in his *Mukhtasar* from Malik and the people of Medina, and Dawud also held this. Al-Shafi'i said: whoever leaves out the first *tashahhud* and the blessing upon the Prophet (ﷺ) need not repeat the prayer, but the two prostrations of forgetfulness are due on him for leaving it. If he leaves out the final *tashahhud*, whether forgetfully or deliberately, he must repeat. They argued that the Prophet's (ﷺ) explanation of the prayer is obligatory, because the basic obligation of prayer is general and needs explanation, except what is excluded by evidence, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Pray as you have seen me pray."

The second view: sitting, *tashahhud* and salam are not obligatory. They are all merely recommended sunnahs. This is the view of some Basran scholars, and Ibrahim ibn Ulayyah went to it, and he explicitly analogized the final sitting to the first. He opposed the majority and was an outlier, except that he holds the prayer must be repeated by one who omits any of these. Among their evidence is the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "If the imam raises his head from the last prostration of his prayer, then breaks his ablution, his prayer is complete." Abu Umar said this hadith is not sound, and we explained this in our book *al-Muqtabas* [In some copies: *al-Muftin*]. This wording only drops the salam, not the sitting.

The Second Opinion... (translation follows)

The third opinion: sitting for the length of the tashahhud is obligatory, but neither the tashahhud nor the salam is obligatory as a pillar (fard). This was said by Abu Hanifa and his companions and a group of the Kufans. They argued with the hadith of Ibn al-Mubarak from al-Ifriqi, Abd al-Rahman ibn Ziyad, and he is weak, in which the Prophet ﷺ said: "If one of you sits in the last part of his prayer and then breaks wind before he gives the salam, his prayer is complete." Ibn al-'Arabi said: Our shaykh, Fakhr al-Islam, used to recite to us in the lesson:
"He holds that leaving the prayer by a fart... where is the fart from the salam upon you?"
Ibn al-'Arabi said: Some of our scholars derived from this question two weak branches. As for the first, Abd al-Malik related from Abd al-Malik that whoever gives the salam after two rak'ahs in jest, and it becomes clear that he was on four, then it suffices him; and this is exactly the doctrine of the people of Iraq. As for the second, it occurs in the rejected books that if the imam breaks wind deliberately after the tashahhud and before the salam, it suffices those behind him. This is something that should not be turned to in giving legal rulings, even though gatherings are populated with it for reminder.

The fourth opinion: sitting is fard and the salam is fard, and the tashahhud is not obligatory. Among those who said this are Malik ibn Anas and his companions, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal in one narration. They argued by saying: there is no dhikr that is obligatory except the takbir of ihram and the recitation of Umm al-Qur'an.

The fifth opinion: the tashahhud and the sitting are obligatory, and the salam is not obligatory. This was said by a group including Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, and Ishaq argued with the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ taught him the tashahhud and said to him: "When you finish this, your prayer is complete and you have discharged what is upon you." Al-Daraqutni said: his saying "When you finish this, your prayer is complete" was inserted into the hadith by some narrators from Zuhayr, and linked to the speech of the Prophet ﷺ; but Shababa separated it from Zuhayr and made it the words of Ibn Mas'ud, and his saying is closer to the correct than that of those who inserted it into the hadith of the Prophet ﷺ. Shababa is trustworthy. And Ghassan ibn al-Rabi' followed him in this, making the end of the hadith the words of Ibn Mas'ud and not attributing it to the Prophet ﷺ.

Eighteenth: The scholars differed concerning the salam. It was said: it is obligatory, and it was said: it is not obligatory. The correct view is its obligation, based on the hadith of Aisha and the sound hadith of Ali, which Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi transmitted, and which Sufyan al-Thawri related from Abdullah ibn Muhammad ibn Aqil from Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya from Ali, who said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The key to the prayer is purification, its beginning is the takbir, and its ending is the salam." This hadith is the basis for the obligation of the takbir and the salam, and that nothing else can substitute for them, just as nothing else can substitute for purification, by consensus. Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi said: If a man opened his prayer with seventy of the names of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and did not say the takbir of ihram, it would not suffice him; and if he broke wind before giving the salam, it would not suffice him. This is an affirmation by Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi of the hadith of Ali, and he is an imam in the science of hadith and in knowing its sound from its weak. That is enough for you! The scholars differed regarding the obligation of the takbir at the opening, and it is the Nineteenth: Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Awza'i, Abd al-Rahman, and a group said: the takbir of ihram is not obligatory. It has been reported from Malik regarding the follower (ma'mum) something that indicates this view, but the correct position of his school is the obligation of the takbir of ihram, and that it is a fard and a pillar (rukn) of the prayer. This is the correct view and the majority hold it, and whoever opposes it is refuted by the Sunnah. The Twentieth: The scholars differed concerning the wording with which one enters the prayer. Malik, his companions, and the majority of scholars said: only the takbir suffices; nothing else suffices from it, neither tahlil, nor tasbih, nor ta'zim, nor tahmid. This is the view of the people of the Hijaz and most of the people of Iraq, and according to Malik only "Allahu akbar" suffices, nothing else. Likewise al-Shafi'i said, and added: "Allahu al-akbar" and "Allahu al-kabir" also suffice. The proof for Malik is the hadith of Aisha, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to begin the prayer with the takbir, and the recitation with "Al-hamdu lillahi rabbi l-'alamin." And the hadith of Ali: "and its beginning is the takbir." And the hadith of the Bedouin: "then say the takbir." In Sunan Ibn Majah: Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shayba and Ali ibn Muhammad al-Tanafisi narrated to us, they said: Abu Usama narrated to us, he said: Abd al-Hamid ibn Ja'far narrated to me, he said: Muhammad ibn Amr ibn Ata narrated to us, he said: I heard Abu Humayd al-Sa'idi say: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood to pray, he faced the qibla, raised his hands, and said: 'Allahu akbar.'" This is an explicit text and a sound hadith specifying the wording of the takbir. The poet said:
"I saw that Allah is greater than everything... in endeavour, and greater than it in hosts."

Then it includes the attribute of pre-eternity (qidam), and nothing of "great" or "mighty" includes it, so it is more eloquent in meaning, and God knows best.

Abu Hanifa said: if he opens with "There is no god but God" (la ilaha illa Allah), it suffices him; but if he says "O God, forgive me" (Allahumma-ghfir li), it does not suffice him. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said the same. Abu Yusuf said: it does not suffice him if he is able to say the takbir (Allahu akbar). Al-Hakam ibn Utayba used to say: if he mentions God in place of the takbir, it suffices him. Ibn al-Mundhir said: I do not know of any disagreement that whoever recites well, says tahlil and takbir, but does not recite, his prayer is invalid. Whoever holds this view must say that nothing other than the takbir can take its place, just as nothing other than the recitation (qira'a) can take its place. Abu Hanifa said: the takbir in Persian suffices him, even if he knows Arabic. Ibn al-Mundhir said: it does not suffice him, because it contradicts what the communities of Muslims are upon, and what the Prophet (ﷺ) taught his community. We know of no one who agreed with him in what he said. And God knows best.

The twenty-first issue: the community (al-umma) agreed on the obligation of intention (niyya) at the opening takbir (takbir al-ihram), except for something narrated from some of our companions, whose discussion will come under the verse on purification. Its reality is the intention of drawing near to the one who commands by doing what he commanded, in the manner required from him. Ibn al-Arabi said: the basic principle for every intention is that it be formed together with beginning the act intended, or before it on condition that it is sustained. If the intention precedes and heedlessness occurs, so that the engagement in worship happens in that state, it is not counted, just as an intention made after beginning the act is not counted. It has been granted leniency in advancing the intention in fasting, because of the great hardship in making it coincide with the beginning of the fast.

Ibn al-Arabi said: Abu al-Hasan al-Qarawi in the frontier town of Ascalon told us: I heard Imam al-Haramayn (al-Juwayni) say: a person should bring the intention to mind at the moment of entering prayer, and should clear his reflection of the Creator, the createdness of the world, and prophethood, until his reflection reaches the intention of the prayer. He said: this does not need a long time; it happens in a swift moment (awha [[awha: aswa', i.e., quickest]] lahza), because teaching sentences requires a long time, but recalling them happens in a moment. And it is part of the completeness of the intention that it be sustained throughout the whole prayer. However, since that is something difficult for him, the Law has allowed the intention to lapse during its course. I heard our shaykh Abu Bakr al-Fihri in the al-Aqsa Mosque say: Muhammad ibn Sahnun said: I saw my father Sahnun sometimes complete a prayer and then repeat it. I asked him about this, and he said: my intention lapsed during it, so for that reason I repeated it.

I say: this is a collection of rulings on prayer. The rest of its rulings will be explained in their places in this book, God willing: the bowing (ruku'), congregational prayer, the qibla, hastening to the prayer times, and some of the prayer of fear in this surah. The shortening of prayer and the prayer of fear will come in "al-Nisa'" [[See vol. 5, p. 351 onward.]]; the times of prayer in "Hud" [[See vol. 9, p. 109 onward.]], "Subhan" [[See vol. 10, p. 303 onward.]] and "al-Rum" [[See vol. 14, p. 14 onward.]]; the night prayer in "al-Muzzammil" [[See vol. 19, p. 51 onward.]]; the prostration of recitation in "al-A'raf" [[See vol. 7, p. 357 onward.]]; and the prostration of gratitude in "Sad" [[See vol. 15, p. 183.]]. Each in its place, God willing.

The twenty-second issue: His saying, ﴿And from what We have provided them they spend﴾. "Razaqnahum" means: We gave them. According to Ahl al-Sunna (the People of the Sunna), provision (rizq) is whatever benefit from is valid, whether lawful or unlawful. This differs from the Mu'tazila, who say that what is unlawful is not provision, because its ownership is not valid, and that God does not provide the unlawful but only the lawful, and that provision can only mean ownership. They said: if a child grew up among thieves and ate nothing except what the thieves fed him until he reached maturity and became strong and became a thief himself, and then continued to steal and eat what he stole until he died, God would not have provided him anything, since He did not make it his property, and he would die without having eaten anything from God's provision. This is false. The proof against it is that if provision meant conferring ownership, then a child would not be provided for, nor would the animals that graze in the desert, nor the young of animals, since the milk of their mothers belongs to their owner and not to the young. Since the community agreed that children, young animals and beasts are provided for, and that God provides for them while they are not owners, it is known that provision is sustenance (ghidha'). Also, since the community agrees that slaves, both male and female, are provided for, and that God provides for them while they are not owners, it is known that provision is what we have said, not what they have said. What shows that there is no provider other than Him is His saying, the Truth: ﴿Is there any creator other than God who provides for you from the heaven and the earth?﴾ [[See vol. 14, p. 321 onward.]] [Fatir: 3], and His saying: ﴿Indeed God is the Provider, the Possessor of strength, the Firm﴾ [[See vol. 17, p. 55.]] [al-Dhariyat: 58], and His saying: ﴿And there is no creature on the earth but that its provision is upon God﴾ [[See vol. 9, p. 6 onward.]] [Hud: 6]. This is decisive: God is the Provider in truth, and the son of Adam is a provider metaphorically, because he has a derived ownership, as we explained in al-Fatiha [[See p. 140 onward of this part.]]; he is provided for in truth, like the beasts that have no ownership. However, when a thing is permitted for someone to consume, it is lawful in judgment, and what is not permitted for him to consume is unlawful in judgment, yet all of it is provision. Some of the eminent scholars derived from His saying: ﴿Eat from the provision of your Lord and give thanks to Him: a good land and a forgiving Lord﴾ [[See vol. 14, p. 284.]] [Saba': 15] that He said: the mention of forgiveness indicates that provision may contain what is unlawful.

The twenty-third issue: His saying, ﴿And from what We have provided them﴾. Rizq is the verbal noun of razaqa, yarzuqu, razqan and rizqan. So razq (with a fatha) is the verbal noun, and riz (with a kasra) is the name; its plural is arzaq. Rizq means gift. Al-Raziqiyya are white linen garments. The soldiers "irtazaqa" means they took their provisions. Razqa means a single time. This is what the lexicographers said. Ibn al-Sikkit said: in the dialect of the Azd Shanu'a, rizq means thanks, and this is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And you make your provision that you deny?﴾ [[See vol. 17, p. 228 onward.]] [al-Waqi'a: 82], meaning: your thanks is denial. And one says: "razaqani" meaning "he thanked me."

The twenty-fourth issue: His saying, ﴿they spend﴾. Yunfiqun means: they bring out. Infaq is bringing money out of the hand. From it comes "nafaqa al-bay'", meaning the sale went out from the seller's hand to the buyer. "Nafaqat al-dabba" means its soul went out. From it comes "al-nafiqa'" for the hole of the jerboa, from which it exits when it is taken from another direction. From it comes "al-munafiq" (the hypocrite), because he goes out of faith, or faith goes out of his heart. "Nayfaq al-sarawil" is well known; it is the place where the leg comes out of them. "Nafaqa al-zad" means the provisions ran out, and its owner spent them. "Anfaqa al-qawm" means their provisions ran out; from it is His saying: ﴿Then you would have held back, for fear of spending﴾ [[See vol. 10, p. 335.]] [al-Isra': 100].

The twenty-fifth issue: The scholars differed about what is meant by "nafaqa" (spending) here. It was said: it is the obligatory zakat, narrated from Ibn Abbas, because it is coupled with the prayer. It was said: it is a man's spending on his family, narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, because that is the best spending. Muslim narrated from Abu Hurayra, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: (A dinar you spend in the way of God, a dinar you spend on freeing a slave, a dinar you give in charity to a poor person, and a dinar you spend on your family: the greatest of them in reward is the one you spent on your family.) And it is narrated from Thawban, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: (The best dinar a man spends is a dinar he spends on his dependents, and a dinar a man spends on his mount in the way of God, Mighty and Majestic, and a dinar he spends on his companions in the way of God.) Abu Qilaba [[Abu Qilaba: one of the narrators in this chain.]] said: he began with the dependents. Then Abu Qilaba said: and what man is greater in reward than a man who spends on young children, keeping them chaste, or whom God benefits by it and makes them independent?

It was said: what is meant is voluntary charity (sadaqat al-tatawwu'), narrated from al-Dahhak, looking at the fact that zakat only comes in its specific word, which is "zakat". When it comes in a word other than zakat, it may mean obligatory or voluntary, but when it comes in the word "infaq" (spending), it can only be voluntary. Al-Dahhak said: spending used to be an offering by which they drew near to God, Mighty and Majestic, according to their means, until the obligatory charities were revealed and abrogated (al-nasikhat) [[Like His saying: (Take from their wealth a charity) [al-Tawba: 103], the verse... See vol. 8, p. 244. Ibn al-Arabi said it abrogates the verse (And those who hoard gold and silver) [al-Tawba: 34]; see p. 381 of the first part of his tafsir, printed in Egypt in 1331 AH. Likewise al-Jassas narrated its abrogation by it from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz.]] in "Bara'a" (al-Tawba). It was said: it means the obligatory rights arising in wealth other than zakat, because God coupled it with the prayer, so it is obligatory, and because He departed from the word of zakat, it is obligatory apart from it. It was said: it is general, and this is the correct view, because it came in the manner of praise for spending from what they were provided with, and that is only from what is lawful. That is, they give what the Law obliged them to give, such as zakat and other things that occur in some circumstances, along with what they were urged to give voluntarily. It was said: faith in the unseen is the share of the heart; establishing the prayer is the share of the body; and "from what We have provided them they spend" is the share of wealth. This is clear. Some earlier scholars, in interpreting His saying, ﴿And from what We have provided them they spend﴾, said: that is, from what We have taught them they teach. This was related by Abu Nasr Abd al-Rahim ibn Abd al-Karim al-Qushayri.

It was said: the intended referent is the believers among the People of the Book, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam, and it was about them that it was revealed. The first verse was revealed concerning the believers among the Arabs. It was also said: both verses are about the believers in general. On this view, the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of *alladhina* ("those who") is in the genitive, as a conjunction (ʿatf), but it may also be in the nominative as a resumption (istinaf), meaning "and they are those who." As for one who takes the two verses to refer to two categories, *alladhina* is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾, and it may also be in the genitive as a conjunction.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and in what was sent down to you﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿and in what was sent down before you﴾, meaning the earlier scriptures. This is in contrast to what the Jews and Christians did, as God reports about them in His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Believe in what God has sent down," they say, "We believe in what was sent down to us"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91], and so on. [[See vol. 2 p. 2 (29). Akhnukh is Idris, peace be upon him.]]

It is also said: when this verse was revealed, "those who believe in the unseen," the Jews and Christians said, "We too believe in the unseen." When He said, ﴿and establish prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3], they said, "We too establish prayer." When He said, "and from what We have provided them they spend," they said, "We too spend and give charity." But when He said, "and those who believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you," they recoiled from this.

In the hadith of Abu Dharr, he said: I said, "O Messenger of God, how many books did God send down?" He said: "One hundred and four books. God sent down fifty pages to Shith, thirty pages to Akhnukh, ten pages to Ibrahim, and He sent down to Musa, before the Torah, ten pages. He sent down the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the Furqan." The hadith was recorded by al-Husayn al-Ajurri and Abu Hatim al-Busti.

Here is an issue: if someone says, "How is it possible to believe in all of them when their rulings conflict?" It is answered that there are two responses. The first is that belief means believing that all of them came from God, and this is the view of those who deny that the earlier law-codes (shara'i') remain binding. The second is that belief applies to those parts of them that were not abrogated (naskh, the replacement of a ruling by a later one), and this is the view of those who hold that the earlier law-codes are obligatory, as will be explained, God willing.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and in the Hereafter they are certain﴾, meaning: and in the resurrection and gathering they have knowledge. Yaqin (certainty) is knowledge without doubt. From it one says: *yaqintu al-amr* (with kasra) *yaqnan*, and *aqintu*, *istayqintu*, and *tayaqqantu* all have the same meaning, and "I am certain of it" (*wa-ana ʿala yaqinin minhu*). The *ya'* became a *waw* in your saying *muqin* (certain) because of the damma before it. When you make it diminutive, you return it to its root, so you say *muyayqin*, since diminutive forms return things to their origins, and the plural does the same. Sometimes they use *yaqin* to express *zann* (supposition), and from this is the saying of our scholars about the *yamin al-laghw* (idle oath): it is that a person swears by God about a matter he is certain of, then it becomes clear to him that it is otherwise, and there is no penalty for him. The poet says:

*Tahassaba Hawwas wa-ayqana annani ... biha mufdin min wahidin la ughamiruh*

He says: the lion sniffed my she-camel, thinking that I would ransom her from him, and I would spare myself and leave her to him, and I would not plunge into destruction by fighting him. [The poet is Abu Sidra al-Asadi, also said to be al-Hujaymi.]

As for *zann* in the sense of *yaqin*, it occurs in the revelation, and it is common in poetry, and this will come.

And *al-akhirah* (the Hereafter) is derived from *ta'akhkhur* (being later), because it is later than us and we are later than it, just as *al-dunya* (this world) is derived from *dunuw* (nearness), as will come.

Al-Nahhas said: The people of Najd say "ألاك" (alaka), and some of them say "ألا لك" (ala laka), and the kaf is for address (al-khitab). Al-Kisa'i said: Whoever says "أولئك" (ula'ika), its singular is "ذلك" (dhalika), and whoever says "أُلاك" (ulaka), its singular is "ذاك" (dhaka), and "أُلالِك" (ulalika) is like "أولئك" (ula'ika). Ibn al-Sikkit recited:

Alaa laka qawmi lam yakunu ushabah [[al-ushabah among people: mixtures. And ushabah in earning: what is mixed with the unlawful that has no good in it, and illicit gain.]] ... wa hal ya'izu al-dhalila illa ulalika

Sometimes they use "أولئك" (ula'ika) for non-rational beings. The poet said:

Dhamma al-manazila ba'da manzilati al-liwa ... wa al-'aysha ba'da ula'ika al-ayyam

And Allah the Exalted said: "Inna al-sam'a wa al-basara wa al-fu'ada kullu ula'ika kana 'anhu mas'ula" [[See vol. 10, p. 259.]] [al-Isra': 36]. Our scholars said: In His saying, "min rabbihim" (from their Lord), there is a refutation of the Qadariyya in their claim that they create their own faith and guidance. Exalted is Allah above their saying. Had it been as they claimed, He would have said "min anfusihim" (from themselves). The discussion of this has already passed [[See the thirty-first issue, p. 149.]] and regarding guidance [[See the second issue, p. 160 of this volume.]], so there is no point in repeating it.

(Wa ula'ika hum al-muflihun) ... "Rabbihim" may be a second subject, with "al-muflihun" as its predicate, and the second subject with its predicate is the predicate of the first. It is also permissible for "rabbihim" to be an extra element which the Basrans call "fasila" (separator) and the Kufans call "'imad" (support), and "al-muflihun" is the predicate of "ula'ika".

The root falh originally in the language means splitting and cutting. The poet said:

Inna al-hadida bi al-hadidi yuflahu

That is, it is split. From it comes the tilling of the lands (filahat al-aradin), which is only splitting them for ploughing, said Abu 'Ubayd. For this reason the one who ploughs (al-akkar) [[the one who ploughs the land.]] is called fallah. It is said of one whose lower lip is split: aflah, and he has a clear split (bayyin al-falha). So it is as if the muflih has cut through difficulties until he attained his goal. It is also used for winning and remaining, and this is also its original meaning in the language. From it is the man's saying to his wife: "Istafilhi bi-amrik" (strive for your matter), meaning: succeed in your matter. The poet said:

Law kana hayyun mudrik al-falah ... adrakahu mula'ibu al-rimah

Al-Adbat ibn Quray' al-Sa'di said in the ignorant pre-Islamic age:

Likulli hammin min al-humumi si'ah ... wa al-musiyyu wa al-subhu la falah ma'ah

He means: there is no survival along with the alternation of night and day. Another said:

Nahilla biladan kulluha hulla qablana ... wa narju al-falah ba'da 'Adin wa Himyar

That is, survival. 'Ubayd said:

Aflih bima shi'ta fa-qad yudraku bi al-di'... fi wa qad yukhad da'u al-aribu

That is, remain with whatever you wish of wisdom and foolishness, for the foolish may be provided for while the intelligent is deprived. So the meaning of "wa ula'ika hum al-muflihun" is: they are the ones who succeed with Paradise and remain therein. Ibn Abi Ishaq said: "al-muflihun" are those who attained what they sought and escaped the evil they fled from, and the meaning is one. The word falah has been used for the pre-dawn meal (al-sahur), and from it is the hadith: "Hatta kada yafutuna al-falah ma'a Rasul Allah (ﷺ)." I said: "And what is al-falah?" He said: "Al-sahur." Abu Dawud narrated it. So the meaning of the hadith is that by the suhur the fast endures, hence he called it falah. And al-fallah (with the lam doubled) is the muleteer, in the saying of the speaker:

Laha rittlun takilu al-zayta fihi ... wa fallahun yasuqu laha himaran

Then falah in common usage is: attaining the sought goal and deliverance from what is feared.

Issue: If someone asks, how did Hamza recite "'alayhum", "ilayhum" and "ladayhum", but not "min rabbuhum", "fihum" or "jannatayhum"? The answer: in 'alayhim, ilayhim and ladayhim the yaa is converted from an alif, and the original is 'alaahum, ladaahum and ilaahum, so the haa retained its damma; this does not apply to fihim, min rabbihim, or jannatayhim. Al-Kisa'i agreed with him on "'alayhimu al-dhillah" and "ilayhimu ithnayn", as is known from the recitation transmitted from them both.

Exposition of the state of the disbelievers, their end, and the meaning of kufr

When Allah mentioned the believers and their conditions, He mentioned the disbelievers and their end. Kufr (disbelief) is the opposite of iman (faith), and it is the meaning intended in the verse. It may also mean ingratitude for blessing and kindness, and from this is the Prophet's saying (ﷺ) concerning women in the hadith of the eclipse: "I saw the Fire, and I had never seen a sight more horrible than today, and I saw that the majority of its people were women." It was said: "Why, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Because of their kufr." It was said: "Do they disbelieve in Allah?" He said: "They disbelieve in the spouse (al-'Ashir) and they disbelieve in kindness. If you were to be kind to one of them all her life, and then she saw something from you, she would say, 'I have never seen any good from you.'" Related by al-Bukhari and others.

The original meaning of kufr in the speech of the Arabs is concealment and covering. From this is the poet's saying:

"In a night whose clouds had concealed the stars"

That is, it concealed them. From this the night is called kafir, because it covers everything with its darkness. The poet said: [[It is Tha'labah ibn Su'ayr al-Mazini, describing the male ostrich and the female ostrich and their returning to their eggs at sunset. Al-thiql (with a vowel on the first letter) here means the protected ostrich eggs. Al-rathid: arranged, piled one upon another or side by side. Alqat yaminaha fi kafir: that is, she began to set. Lisan al-Arab, entry (k-f-r).]]

"Then they remembered a heavy, arranged clutch, after Dhaka had cast her right hand into the kafir."

Dhaka (with a damma on the dhal and a long vowel): a name for the sun. From this is the saying of another:

"So he came before the break of dawn, while the son of Dhaka was hidden in the kafr."

That is, in the night. Also, al-kafir means the sea and the great river. Al-kafir also means the farmer, plural kuffar. Allah the Exalted said: "like a rain whose growth delighted the farmers" (al-Hadid: 20). That is, the farmers, because they cover the seed. A "makfur" ash is ash the wind has blown dust over. The kafir of the land is that which is far from people, where no one settles or passes by, and whoever dwells in those places is of the people of kufur. It is also said that al-kufur means the villages.

His saying, the Exalted: "It is the same for them" (sawa'un 'alayhim) means that warning and not warning are equal in their eyes, that is, it is the same for them whether this is done. The interrogative is used for the sake of equalization, and similar to it is His saying, the Exalted: "It is the same for us whether you admonish or are not among the admonishers" (al-Shu'ara': 136). The poet said: [[It is A'sha Qays, known as al-A'sha al-Akbar.]]

"And a night of which people say, from its darknesses, the sound-eyed and the blind are alike"

His saying, the Exalted: "Did you warn them?" (a-andhartahum). Al-indhar is informing and notifying, and it is hardly used except in a warning that leaves time for taking precaution. If its time does not allow for precaution, it is an intimation (ish'ar) and not a warning (indhar). The poet said:

"You warned 'Amr while he was at ease, before the morning; so 'Amr disobeyed."

Banu so-and-so "tanadhara" this matter when some of them warned others of it. The scholars differed in the interpretation of this verse. It was said: it is general in wording but specific in meaning, referring to the one against whom the word of punishment has become due, and it had preceded in Allah's knowledge that he would die upon his disbelief. Allah the Exalted willed to inform that among people are those whose condition is this, without specifying anyone. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Kalbi said: it was revealed concerning the chiefs of the Jews, among them Huyayy ibn Akhtab, Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, and their like. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: it was revealed concerning those of the leaders of the factions who were killed on the day of Badr. The first view is more sound, for whoever specifies someone is only giving an example of one whose death upon disbelief has been unveiled to him, and that is included within the scope of the verse.

His saying, the Exalted: "they will not believe" (la yu'minun) — its position is in the nominative as the predicate of "inna," meaning: indeed those who disbelieved will not believe. It was also said: the predicate of "inna" is "sawa'un," and what follows it takes the place of the relative clause (silah), said by Ibn Kaysan. Muhammad ibn Yazid said: "sawa'un" is nominative as the subject, "a-andhartahum am lam tundhirhum" is the predicate, and the whole clause is the predicate of "inna." Al-Nahhas said: that is, they were stupefied, so warning did not avail them anything.

The readers differed in reciting "a-andhartahum." The people of Madina, Abu 'Amr, al-A'mash and 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ishaq read: "a-andhartahum," with the first hamza realized and the second eased (between hamza and alif). This was chosen by al-Khalil and Sibawayh, and it is the dialect of Quraysh and Sa'd ibn Bakr, and upon it is the poet's saying [[It is Dhu al-Rummah, as in Sibawayh's book and al-Zamakhshari's al-Mufassal.]]:

"O gazelle of al-Wa'sa', between Julajil and al-Naqa, are you (anta) or the mother of Salim?"

The spelling of "anta" is one alif. Another said:

"I stretched up and looked at him, and recognized him, so I said to him: are you (anta) the Zayd of the hares?"

It was transmitted from Ibn Muhaysin that he read: "andhartahum am lam tundhirhum" with a single hamza and no alif after it, dropping one of the two hamzas because they met, or because "am" indicates the interrogative, as the poet said:

"Are you leaving from the tribe, or setting out early? And what harm would it do you if you waited?"

He meant: a-tarawwahu (are you leaving), and he was satisfied with "am" in place of the alif. It was transmitted from Ibn Abi Ishaq that he read "a-andhartahum," realizing both hamzas and inserting an alif between them so that they would not be joined. Abu Hatim said: it is also permissible to insert an alif between them and ease the second, and Abu 'Amr and Nafi' often do this. Hamzah, 'Asim and al-Kisa'i read with both hamzas realized: "a-andhartahum," and this is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd, though that is far-fetched according to al-Khalil. Sibawayh said: it resembles in heaviness "dananu." Al-Akhfash said: it is also permissible to ease the first of the two hamzas, but that is poor, because they only ease after finding it heavy and after the single hamza has been achieved. Abu Hatim said: it is also permissible to ease both hamzas together. These are seven aspects of the recitations, and an eighth aspect is permissible outside the Qur'an, because it contradicts the common reading (al-sawad, i.e., the great majority of people). Al-Akhfash Sa'id said: one replaces the hamza with a ha', saying "ha-andhartahum," as one says "hayyaka" and "iyyaka." Al-Akhfash also said regarding His saying, the Exalted: "Ha antum" (Al 'Imran: 66) that it is in fact "a-antum."

There are ten issues.

**The first issue: His saying, ﴿Allah has sealed﴾.** In this verse, Allah, glorified is He, explains what prevents them from faith by His saying: "Allah has sealed." *Al-khatm* (sealing) is a verbal noun: "I sealed the thing (*khatamtu al-shay'*), a sealing (*khatman*)," so it is *makhtum* or *mukhattam*, the intensive form being used for emphasis. Its meaning is covering a thing and making it secure so that nothing can enter it. From this come the expressions "he sealed the book" and "he sealed the door" and similar, so that nothing inside can be reached and nothing other than what is inside can be placed there.

The scholars of meanings (*ahl al-ma'ani*) said: Allah described the hearts of the disbelievers with ten attributes: sealing (*khatm*), stamping (*taba'*), constriction (*diq*), sickness (*maradh*), rust (*rayn*), death (*mawt*), hardness (*qasawah*), turning away (*infisar*), zealotry (*hamiyyah*), and denial (*inkar*).

Regarding denial, He said: "Their hearts deny, and they are arrogant" [al-Nahl: 22]. [See vol. 10, p. 95.]

Regarding zealotry, He said: "When those who disbelieve placed zealotry in their hearts" [al-Fath: 26]. [See vol. 16, p. 288.]

Regarding turning away, He said: "Then they turned away; Allah turned their hearts away, because they are a people who do not understand" [al-Tawbah: 127]. [See vol. 8, p. 300.]

Regarding hardness, He said: "Woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah" [al-Zumar: 22]. [See vol. 15, p. 248.] And He said: "Then your hearts hardened after that" [al-Baqarah: 74]. [See vol. 1, p. 462.]

Regarding death, He said: "Is one who was dead and We gave him life…?" [al-An'am: 122]. [See vol. 7, p. 78.] And He said: "Only those who listen will respond; as for the dead, Allah will raise them" [al-An'am: 36]. [See vol. 6, p. 418.]

Regarding rust, He said: "No! Rather, what they have earned has rusted over their hearts" [al-Mutaffifin: 14]. [See vol. 19, p. 257.]

Regarding sickness, He said: "In their hearts is a sickness" [Muhammad: 29].

Regarding constriction, He said: "And whoever Allah intends to misguide, He makes his breast constricted and narrow" [al-An'am: 125]. [See vol. 7, p. 81.]

Regarding stamping, He said: "So He stamped upon their hearts, so they do not understand" [al-Munafiqun: 3]. [See vol. 18, p. 124.] And He said: "Rather, Allah stamped upon them because of their disbelief" [al-Nisa': 155]. [See vol. 6, p. 7.]

Regarding sealing, He said: "Allah has sealed upon their hearts" [al-Baqarah: 7].

All of these will be explained in their proper places, if Allah wills.

**The second issue:** Sealing may be sensory, as we have explained, or figurative, as in this verse. Sealing upon the hearts means their failure to comprehend, from Allah, glorified is He, the meaning of His address and to reflect upon His signs. Sealing upon the hearing means their failure to understand the Qur'an when it is recited to them or when they are called to His oneness. Sealing upon the sight means its failure to be guided to contemplate His creation and the wonders of His handiwork. This is the meaning reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Qatadah, and others.

**The third issue:** In this verse is the clearest proof and the most evident path that Allah, glorified is He, is the Creator of guidance and misguidance, of disbelief and faith. So take heed, O listeners, and marvel, O thinkers, at the minds of the *Qadariyyah* (the sect who deny divine predestination) who claim that they create their own faith and guidance. For sealing is stamping, so how can they attain faith even if they strive? He has stamped upon their hearts and upon their hearing, and has placed a veil upon their sight. "Then how will they be guided? Or who will guide them after Allah, if He misguides them, makes them deaf, and blinds their sight?" "And whomever Allah misguides, there is no guide for him!" [al-Zumar: 23]

Allah's doing this is just with regard to the one whom He misguides and forsakes, since He does not withhold from him any right that was due to him, so that the attribute of justice would not be removed. He only withholds what was His to bestow as a favor upon them, not what was owed to them.

If they say: The meaning of sealing, stamping, and veiling is naming, judging, and informing that they will not believe, not the act itself, we say: This is invalid, because the reality of sealing and stamping is only the doing of that which makes the heart stamped and sealed. Its reality cannot be naming and judging. Do you not see that when it is said, "So-and-so stamped the book and sealed it," the reality is that he did what made the book stamped and sealed, not naming and judging? This is something on which there is no disagreement among the scholars of language.

Moreover, the community (*ummah*) agrees that Allah has described Himself as sealing and stamping upon the hearts of the disbelievers as a recompense for their disbelief, as He said: "Rather, Allah stamped upon them because of their disbelief" [al-Nisa': 155].

The community also agrees that stamping and sealing upon their hearts is impossible from the Prophet, peace be upon him, the angels, or the believers. If sealing and stamping were merely naming and judging, the prophets and the believers would not be prevented from doing so, for they all name the disbelievers as stamped upon in their hearts, sealed, and in misguidance who do not believe, and they judge them as such. Thus it is established that sealing and stamping is a meaning other than naming and judging. It is rather a meaning that Allah creates in the heart which prevents faith in Him. Its evidence is His saying: "Thus We insert it into the hearts of the criminals; they do not believe in it" [al-Hijr: 12]. And He said: "We have placed coverings upon their hearts so that they do not understand it" [al-An'am: 25], meaning, lest they understand it, and similar to that.

**The fourth issue:** His saying "upon their hearts" indicates the excellence of the heart over all the limbs. The heart belongs to humans and to others. The essence and most noble part of everything is its heart, so the heart is the seat of thought. Originally it is a verbal noun: "I turned the thing over (*qalabtu al-shay'*), turning (*qalban*), when I returned it to its beginning," and "I turned the vessel (*qalabtu al-ina'*)": I returned it to its face. Then this word was transferred and this noble organ, which is the most noble of living beings, was named by it, because thoughts rush to it swiftly and recur upon it, as has been said:

*The heart was only named for its turning,*
*So beware for the heart of a turning and transformation.*

Then, when the Arabs transferred this verbal noun to this noble organ, they committed to emphasizing its *qaf* (pronouncing it heavily) to distinguish it from its origin.

Ibn Majah reported from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "The parable of the heart is that of a feather that the winds turn over in an open desert." For this reason the Prophet ﷺ used to say: "O Turner of hearts, make our hearts firm upon Your obedience." If the Prophet ﷺ said this despite his great station and lofty rank, we are more deserving of it in emulation of him. Allah, the Exalted, said: "And know that Allah comes between a man and his heart" [al-Anfal: 24]. [See vol. 7, p. 390.]

**The fifth issue:** The limbs, although they follow the heart, may nevertheless affect the heart, even though it is their leader and king, because of the connection between the outward and the inward. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, when a man speaks the truth, a white spot is inscribed in his heart; and when a man tells a lie, his heart turns black." Al-Tirmidhi reported it and graded it sound, from Abu Hurayrah: "When a man commits a sin, his heart turns black; if he repents, his heart is polished." He (al-Tirmidhi) said: This is the rust (*rayn*) which Allah mentioned in the Qur'an in His saying: "No! Rather, what they have earned has rusted over their hearts" [al-Mutaffifin: 14]. [See vol. 19, p. 257.]

Mujahid said: The heart is like the palm of a hand; for every sin, a finger is folded down from it, and then it is stamped.

I say: In the saying of Mujahid, and in the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh; when it is sound, the whole body is sound, and when it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Truly, it is the heart," is evidence that sealing is real. And Allah knows best.

It has also been said that the heart resembles a pine cone (*sanubarah*), and this supports the saying of Mujahid. And Allah knows best.

Muslim reported from Hudhayfah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ related to us two hadiths; I have seen one of them while I await the other. He told us that "trust (*amanah*) descended into the root of men's hearts, then the Qur'an descended, and they learned from the Qur'an and learned from the Sunnah." Then he told us about the removal of trust. He said: "A man sleeps a sleep and trust is taken from his heart, and its trace remains like a *wakt* (faint mark). Then he sleeps another sleep and trust is taken from his heart, and its trace remains like a *majl* (blister), like a coal you roll over your foot so that it blisters; you see it swollen, but there is nothing in it." Then he took a pebble and rolled it over his foot. "People will wake up trading with one another, and hardly anyone will fulfill trust, until it is said: 'Among such-and-such a tribe there is a trustworthy man.' Until it is said of a man, 'How strong he is! How refined he is! How intelligent he is!' while there is not in his heart the weight of a mustard seed of faith. And there came upon me a time when I did not care whom among you I pledged allegiance to: if he was a Muslim, his religion would bring him back to me; if he was a Christian or a Jew, his governor would bring him back to me. But today I would only pledge allegiance to such-and-such and such-and-such."

In his saying "*al-wakt*," this is a slight mark. It is said of a date when a spot of ripening appears on it: "It has been marked (*wakkat*), so it is marked (*muwakkit*)."

His saying "*al-majl*" is when there is water between the skin and the flesh. The Prophet ﷺ explained it by his saying "like a coal you rolled," that is, you turned it over on your foot so that it blistered.

"*Mantabiran*" means raised up. This indicates that all of that is sensed in the heart, acting upon it. Likewise sealing and stamping. And Allah knows best.

In the hadith of Hudhayfah, he said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Trials are presented to the hearts like a mat, strand by strand. Whichever heart absorbs them receives a black spot, and whichever heart rejects them receives a white spot, until there are two kinds of hearts: a white one like smooth stone, which no trial will harm as long as the heavens and the earth endure, and another that is black and dim (*murbadd*), like an overturned cup, not recognizing good nor denouncing evil, except what it has absorbed of its own desire…"

*(Note on "murbadd": in another version, "mirbad," meaning its blackness is mixed with turbidity.)*

(He related the hadith, [describing the camel's gait]: *mujakhkhiyan* (leaning), meaning inclining.)

**The sixth issue:** The *qalb* (heart) is sometimes expressed by *fu'ad* (inner heart) and *sadr* (breast). Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Thus, that We may strengthen your heart thereby﴾ [al-Furqan: 32] [See vol. 13, p. 28.] and He says: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh: 1] [See vol. 20, p. 104.] meaning, in both places, your heart. It is also sometimes used to express the *'aql* (intellect). Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart﴾ [Qaf: 37] [See vol. 17, p. 23.] meaning, whoever has intellect, because the heart is the seat of the intellect according to the majority of scholars. The *fu'ad* is the seat of the heart, and the *sadr* is the seat of the *fu'ad*. And Allah knows best.

**The seventh issue:** His saying, ﴿and upon their hearing﴾. Those who prefer hearing over sight have used this verse as evidence, because hearing is mentioned before sight. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if Allah took away your hearing and your sight﴾ [al-An'am: 46] [See vol. 6, p. 427.] and He says: ﴿And He made for you hearing and sight and hearts﴾ [al-Sajdah: 9] [See vol. 10, p. 151.]

He (the one who prefers hearing) said: Hearing perceives from the six directions, and in light and in darkness, whereas sight perceives only from the direction facing it, and through an intermediary of light and radiance.

Most of the *mutakallimun* (scholastic theologians) held that sight is superior to hearing, because hearing perceives only sounds and speech, whereas sight perceives bodies, colors and all forms. They said: Since its objects are more numerous, it is superior. They also permitted perceiving by sight from the six directions.

**The eighth issue:** If someone asks: Why did He use the plural for sight (*abṣār*) and the singular for hearing (*sam'*)? It is said to him: He used the singular because it is a *maṣdar* (verbal noun) which applies to the few and the many. One says: *sami'tu al-shay' asma'uhu sam'an wa-samā'an* (I heard the thing, I hear it, hearing and listening). So *al-sam'* is the verbal noun of *sami'tu*, and *al-sam'* is also the name of the organ by which one hears, which was named by the verbal noun.

It is also said: When He attributed hearing to the group, it indicated that what was intended was the hearing of the group, as the poet said:

*bihā jīfu al-ḥasrā fa-ammā 'iẓāmuhā*
*fa-bīḍun wa-ammā jilduhā fa-ṣalību*

Upon it are the carcasses of exhausted camels; as for their bones, they are white, and as for their hides, they are dried and stiff.

[Note: This is from the commentary of al-Shantamari on the poetic evidences. The poet, Alqama ibn Abada, described a distant, arduous road, difficult for whoever travels it. *Jīf al-ḥasrā* refers to the dead, emaciated camels lying there. The line "as for their bones, they are white" means the beasts of prey and birds ate the flesh upon them, leaving the bones bare and their whiteness visible. "As for their hides..." means they are dried and not tanned, lying in the desert; *ṣalīb* here means the fat, i.e., the moisture within them has flowed out because of the heat of the sun upon them.]

He intended "their hides" but used the singular, because it is known that a group does not have one hide. Another poet said in a similar construction:

*lā tunkiri al-qatla wa-qad subīnā*
*fī ḥalqikum 'aẓmun wa-qad shajīnā*

Do not deny the killing, though we have been captured, and there is a bone in your throats, and we have been choked.

He intended "in your throats" (*ḥulūqikum*). A similar example is the saying of another:

*ka-annahu wajhu turkiyyayni qad ghaḍiba*
*mustahdafun li-ṭi'ānin ghayra tadhībi*

As if it were the face of two Turks who are angry, a target for spears, not defeated.

He intended "two faces" (*wajhayn*), but said "the face of two Turks," because it is known that two people do not have one face. There are very many examples of this.

It was also read as *wa-'alā asmā'ihim* (and upon their ears). It may be that the meaning is "and upon the places of their hearing," because hearing itself is not sealed; rather, the place of hearing is sealed. So the *muḍāf* (the governed noun) was omitted and the *muḍāf ilayhi* (the governing noun) was put in its place.

Hearing may also mean *istimā'* (listening). One says: *sam'uka ḥadīthī*, i.e., your listening to my speech pleases me. From this is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah describing a bull that listened to the sound of a hunter and dogs:

*wa-qad tawajjasa rikzan muqfirun nadusun*
*bi-nabʾati al-ṣawti mā fī sam'ihi kadhibu*

The lone, skilled bull sensed a faint sound with the alertness of the hunter's cry; there is no falsehood in his listening, i.e., his listening is truthful. *Al-nadus* means the skilled one; *al-nabʾah* means a faint sound, and likewise *al-rikz*.

*Al-simʿ* (with a kasra on the sin and sukun on the mim) means a person's good reputation. One says: *dhahaba simʿuhu fī al-nās*, i.e., his reputation went among people. *Al-simʿ* also means the cub of a wolf from a hyena.

The pause here is at ﴿and upon their hearing﴾.

﴿Ghishāwah﴾ (covering) is in the nominative as a beginning (*mubtada'*), and what precedes it is the predicate (*khabar*). The pronouns in ﴿their hearts﴾ and what is conjoined to it refer to those who, in Allah's knowledge, will not believe among the disbelievers of Quraysh. It is said they are the hypocrites, it is said the Jews, and it is said all of them, and this is the most correct, because it is general. So the sealing is upon the hearts and the hearings, and the covering is upon the sights.

*Al-ghashā'* means covering. From it comes *ghāshiyat al-sarj* (saddle cover). One says: *ghashshaytu al-shay' ughashshīhi*. Al-Nabigha said:

*halla saalti banī dhubyāna mā ḥasbī*
*idhā al-dukhānu taghashshā al-ashmaṭa al-barama*

Why did you not ask the Banu Dhubyan what my lineage is, when the smoke covers the grey-haired man and the *barm* (one who does not join the people in gambling and does not eat of their meat)?

[Note: *al-Ashmaṭ* is the one whose grey hair has mixed in; *al-barm* is the one who does not enter into gambling with the people and eats of their meat.]

Another said:

*ṣaḥibtuka idh 'aynī 'alayhā ghishāwatun*
*falammā injalat qaṭṭaʿtu nafsī ulūmuhā*

I accompanied you when my eye had a covering over it, but when it cleared, I cut myself off, blaming it.

[Note: This is by al-Harith ibn Khalid al-Makhzumi, as in Lisan al-'Arab, root *gh-sh-a*.]

Ibn Kaysan said: If you make the plural of *ghishāwah*, you say *ghishā'* with the *hā'* removed. Al-Farra' related: *ghashāwā*, like *adāwā*.

It was also read as *ghishāwatun* in the accusative (*naṣb*), meaning "and He made," so it is of the type of His saying:

*'alaftuhā tibnan wa-māan bāridan*

I fed her straw and cold water.

And the saying of another [Note: this is by Abdullah ibn al-Zib'ari, as in al-Kamil by al-Mubarrad, p. 189, Europe edition]:

*yā layta zawjaka qad ghadā*
*mutaqalladan sayfan wa-rumḥan*

Would that your husband had gone out wearing a sword and a spear.

The meaning is "and I gave her water" and "carrying a spear," because a spear is not worn around the neck. Al-Farisi said: You scarcely find this usage in a state of ease and choice, so the reading with *raf'* (nominative) is better, and the *wāw* is conjunctive of one sentence upon another sentence. He said: I have not heard from *ghishāwah* a conjugated verb with the *wāw*.

Some exegetes said: The covering is upon the hearings and the sights, and the pause is upon ﴿their hearts﴾. Others said: The sealing is upon all, and the covering is the sealing itself, so the pause according to this is upon ﴿ghishāwah﴾.

Al-Hasan read *ghushāwah* with a *ḍamma* on the ghayn, Abu Haywah read it with a *fatḥa*, and it is related from Abu 'Amr: *ghishwah*, returning it to the original form of the verbal noun. Ibn Kaysan said: *ghashwah* and *ghishwah* are also permissible, but the best is *ghishāwah*. Thus the Arabs use it for everything that encloses a thing, such as *'imāmah* (turban), *kinānah* (quiver), *qilādah* (necklace), *'iṣābah* (headband), and other such words.

**The tenth issue:** His saying, ﴿And for them﴾, i.e., for the disbelievers who deny, ﴿a great punishment﴾ is its qualifier (*na't*). *Al-'adhāb* (punishment) is like striking with a whip, burning with fire, cutting with iron, and other things that cause a person pain. In the revelation: ﴿and let a group of the believers witness their punishment﴾ [al-Nur: 2] [See vol. 12, p. 166.] It is derived from restraint and prevention. One says in the language: *a'dhibhu 'an kadhā*, i.e., restrain him and prevent him. From this is named *'udhūbat al-mā'* (sweetness of water), because it has been made sweet (*u'dhibat*), and it is made sweet by being held in a container so that it becomes clear and what mixed with it departs from it. From this is the saying of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: *a'dhibū nisā'akum 'an al-khurūj*, i.e., restrain your women from going out. And from him, may Allah be pleased with him, when he was sending off a military detachment, he said: *a'dhibū 'an dhikr al-nisā' [anfusakum] fa-inna dhālika yaksiruku 'ani al-ghazw*, i.e., keep yourselves away from mentioning women, for that will break you from the raid. Every person whom you prevent from something, you have made him *mu'dhab* (restrained). And in the proverb: *la-ulajjimannaka lijāman mu'dhaban*, i.e., I will bridle you with a bridle that prevents you from being ridden by people. It is said: *a'dhaba*, i.e., he refrained; and *a'dhaba ghayrahu*, i.e., he made another refrain. So it is both intransitive and transitive. Punishment is named *'adhāb* because its possessor is confined and prevented from everything that suits the body of good, and its opposites are poured upon him.

**Question 1:** Ibn Jurayj narrated from Mujahid that he said: Four verses of Surat al-Baqarah were revealed about the believers, two about the description of the disbelievers, and thirteen about the hypocrites. Asbat narrated from al-Suddi, concerning His saying "And among the people," that he said: They are the hypocrites. The scholars of the Sufis (*al-Sufiyyah*) said: "*al-nas*" (the people) is a generic noun (*ism jins*), and a generic noun is not used to address the friends of Allah (*awliya'*).

**Question 2:** The grammarians differed concerning the word *al-nas*. It was said: it is a collective noun (*ism min asma' al-jumu'*), the plural of *insan* and *insanah*, irregular in form, and its diminutive is *nuways*. So *al-nas* derives from *al-naws*, which means movement; one says *nasa yanusu*, meaning he moved. From this is the hadith of Umm Zar': "He made me move (*anasa*) with the ornaments of my ears." It was also said that its origin is from *nasiya* (to forget). The root of *nasin* was *nasiya*, which was transposed to become *nisiya*. The *ya'* moved and the letter before it was opened, so it became an *alif*. Then the definite article *al-* entered, and it was said *al-nas*. Ibn 'Abbas said: Adam forgot (*nasiya*) the covenant of Allah, so he was named *insan*. The Prophet (ﷺ) said, peace be upon him: "Adam forgot, so his offspring forgot." In the revelation: "And We had already made a covenant with Adam before, but he forgot (*fa-nasiya*)" (Ta-Ha 20:115), which will come later. According to this view, the *hamzah* is extra (*za'idah*). The poet said:

*Do not forget those covenants, for you were only named "insan" because you are forgetful (nasi).*

Another poet said:

*If you have forgotten former covenants made by you, then forgive; the first to forget was the first of mankind.*

It was also said: he was named *insan* because of his intimacy (*uns*) with Hawwa'. It was said: because of his intimacy with his Lord. According to this, the *hamzah* is original. The poet said:

*Man was named only for his intimacy, and the heart is named only because it turns about.*

**Question 3:** When Allah, Mighty and Exalted, mentioned the believers first, beginning with them for their nobility and excellence, He mentioned the disbelievers in contrast to them, since disbelief and faith are two extremes. Then He mentioned the hypocrites after them and joined them to the disbelievers before them, to deny faith from them, by His true saying: "And they are not believers." In this is a refutation of the Karramiyyah (followers of Muhammad ibn Karram), who said that faith is merely a statement with the tongue even if the heart does not believe. They argued with His saying: "So Allah rewarded them (*fa-athabahum Allah*) for what they said" (al-Ma'idah 5:85). He did not say: "for what they said and concealed." They also cited the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying, peace be upon him: "I have been commanded to fight people until they say, 'There is no god but Allah.' When they say it, they protect their blood and property from me." This is a deficiency, rigidity, and abandonment of reflection on what the Qur'an and the Sunnah have stated about action together with statement and belief. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Faith is knowledge in the heart, statement with the tongue, and action with the limbs." Ibn Majah recorded it in his Sunan. So what Muhammad ibn Karram al-Sijistani and his companions held is hypocrisy and the very essence of schism. We seek refuge with Allah from abandonment and bad belief.

**Question 4:** Our scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, said: The believer is of two kinds. A believer whom Allah loves and befriends, and a believer whom Allah does not love or befriend, but rather hates and opposes. Whoever Allah knows will die in faith, Allah loves him, befriends him, and is pleased with him. Whoever Allah knows will die in disbelief, Allah hates him, is angry with him, and opposes him, not because of his faith, but because of his disbelief and error with which he will die. The disbeliever is also of two kinds: a disbeliever who will certainly be punished, and a disbeliever who will not be punished. The one who will be punished is the one who dies in disbelief; Allah is angry with him and opposes him. The one who will not be punished is the one who dies in faith; Allah is not angry with this one nor does He hate him, but rather He loves him and befriends him, not because of his disbelief, but because of his faith with which he will die.

**Question 5:** It is not permissible to state absolutely that the believer deserves reward and the disbeliever deserves punishment. Rather, it is obligatory to restrict this to the outcome (*muwafah*). For this reason we say: Allah was pleased with 'Umar at the time when he was worshipping idols, and increased his reward and his entry into Paradise, not because of his worship of the idol, but because of his faith with which he died. Allah, Exalted, was angry with Iblis during his worship, because of his disbelief with which he died. The Qadariyyah (who deny predestination) differed in this and said: Allah was not angry with Iblis at the time of his worship, nor was He pleased with 'Umar at the time of his worship of the idol. This is false, because it is established that Allah, Glorified is He, knows what Iblis, may Allah curse him, would die upon, and what 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, would die upon, from eternity. Thus it is established that He was angry with Iblis and loved 'Umar. The consensus of the Muslim community also indicates this: Allah, Glorified and Exalted, does not love whom He knows to be among the people of the Fire, but rather He is angry with him; and He loves whom He knows to be among the people of Paradise. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Actions are only by their endings." For this reason the scholars of the Sufis said: Faith is not what the servant adorns himself with in statement and deed; rather, faith is the flow of happiness in the eternal preordained course. As for its appearance on the bodies, it may be empty, and it may be real.

I say: This is like what is established in Sahih Muslim and elsewhere from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who is the truthful and the one whose truthfulness is confirmed, told us: "Indeed, each of you is gathered in his mother's womb for forty days as a drop, then he is a clot for a similar period, then he is a lump of flesh for a similar period. Then Allah sends the angel, who breathes the soul into him, and he is commanded with four words: to write his provision, his term, his deeds, and whether he is wretched or happy. By Him other than whom there is no god, indeed one of you may work the deeds of the people of Paradise until there is only a cubit between him and it, and then the Decree overtakes him, and he works the deeds of the people of the Fire and enters it. Indeed one of you may work the deeds of the people of the Fire until there is only a cubit between him and it, and then the Decree overtakes him, and he works the deeds of the people of Paradise and enters it."

**Question 6:** If it is said, and this is the sixth question: The Imam, the memorizer (*al-hafiz*) Abu Muhammad 'Abd al-Ghani ibn Sa'id al-Misri has recorded from the hadith of Muhammad ibn Sa'id al-Shami, who was crucified for heresy (*zandaqah*), and he is Muhammad ibn Abi Qays, from Sulayman ibn Musa, who is al-Ashdaq, from Mujahid ibn Jabr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Abu Razin al-'Uqayli informed us that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "Indeed, you and I, O Abu Razin, will drink from milk whose taste has not changed." He said: I said: How does Allah give life to the dead? He said: "Have you not passed by a land that was barren, then you passed by it fertile, then you passed by it barren, then you passed by it fertile?" I said: Yes. He said: "Thus will be the resurrection." He said: I said: How can I know that I am a believer? He said: "No one of this nation" (Ibn Abi Qays said: or he said "of my community") "does a good deed and knows that it is good, and that Allah will reward him with good for it, or does an evil deed and knows that it is evil, and that Allah will punish him for it, or will forgive it, except a believer."

I say: Although the chain of this hadith is not strong, its meaning is sound, and it does not contradict the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, for that is conditional upon the ending (*al-khatimah*), as the Prophet (ﷺ), peace be upon him, said: "Actions are only by their endings." This only indicates that he is a believer at present, and Allah knows best.

**Question 7:** The scholars of language said: The hypocrite (*munafiq*) was only named *munafiq* because he displays other than what he conceals, by comparison to the jerboa (*al-yarbu'*), which has a burrow called *al-naqifa'* and another called *al-qasi'a'*. This is because it digs into the ground until, when it nearly reaches the surface, it leaves the soil thin. When it feels alarm, it pushes that soil away with its head and emerges. The outside of its burrow is soil, while its inside is hollow. Likewise the hypocrite: his outside is faith, and his inside is disbelief. This meaning has already been mentioned.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 9:

Our scholars said: The meaning of "yukhadi'una Allah" (they deceive Allah) is: they deceive Him in their own estimation and according to their assumption. It was also said: He spoke this way because of their action, which is the action of one who deceives. It was also said: there is an elision in the speech, its implied meaning being: "they deceive the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)," as related from al-Hasan and others. Their deception of His Messenger was made a deception of Him, because he called them to it by his message; likewise, when they deceive the believers, they have deceived Allah.

Their deception is what they displayed of faith contrary to what they concealed of disbelief, so that they might preserve their blood and their property, and they think that they have escaped and deceived; this was said by a group of the interpreters.

The lexicographers said: the root of mukhada' (deception) in the speech of the Arabs is corruption; Tha'lab related it from Ibn al-A'rabi. And he recited:

"White of hue, delicious is its taste, / good of saliva, when the saliva is corrupted (khada')." [[Said by Suwayd ibn Abi Kahil, describing a woman's mouth.]]

I say: According to this, "yukhadi'una Allah" means they corrupt their faith and their deeds between themselves and Allah, the Exalted, through showing off (riya'). Likewise it came explained from the Prophet (ﷺ), as will come. In the revelation: "They show off to the people" [[See vol. 5 p. 422]]. [An-Nisa': 142]. It was also said: its root is concealment, and from it comes makhda' al-bayt, the inner room in which a thing is kept safe; this was related by Ibn Faris and others. And the Arabs say: "The lizard (dabb) hid itself in its burrow" (inkhada'a al-dabb fi juhrihi).

His statement, exalted is He: "wa ma yakhda'una illa anfusahum" (and they deceive none but themselves) is a negation and an affirmation, meaning: the consequence of deception only falls upon them. From their sayings: "Whoever deceives one who cannot be deceived, deceives only himself." This is correct, because deception only occurs with one who does not know the inner states; but as for one who knows the inner states, whoever engages with Him in deception deceives only himself. This indicates that the hypocrites did not know Allah, for had they known Him they would have known that He cannot be deceived. And it has preceded from his statement, upon him be peace, that he said: "Do not deceive Allah, for whoever deceives Allah, Allah deceives him, and he deceives himself, if only he perceived." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, how does one deceive Allah?" He said: "By acting upon what Allah has commanded you, while seeking by it other than Him." The explanation of deception from Allah, exalted is He, how it is, will come at His statement, exalted is He: "Allah mocks them" [Al-Baqarah: 15].

Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited "yukhadi'una" in both places, so that the two words would be alike. 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Ibn 'Amir recited "yakhda'una" the second time. The verbal noun is khid' (with a kasra on the kha') and khad'ah, related by Abu Zayd. Muwarriq al-'Ijli recited "yukhadda'una Allah" (with a damma on the ya', a fatha on the kha', and a shadda on the dal), indicating intensification. Abu Talut 'Abd al-Salam ibn Shaddad and al-Jarud recited with a damma on the ya', a sukun on the kha', and a fatha on the dal, in the sense of "wa ma yukhda'una illa 'an anfusihim" (and they are deceived only regarding themselves), so the preposition was elided, as He, exalted is He, said: "And Musa chose his people" [Al-A'raf: 155], meaning from his people.

His statement, exalted is He: "wa ma yash'urun" (and they do not perceive), meaning: they do not realise that the harm of their deception returns upon them, so they think they have escaped and succeeded by their deception.
