That is only in this world; in the Hereafter it will be said to them: "Return behind you and seek light" [Al-Hadid: 13], as will come [[See vol. 17 p. 246.]]. The lexicographers said: "sha'artu bi-sh-shay'" means I perceived the thing, and from it comes the poet's name "al-Sha'ir" for his acuteness, because he perceives what others do not perceive of rare meanings. And from it is their saying: "Would that I knew (layta shi'ri)," i.e., would that I had known.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿In their hearts is a disease﴾. (*fi qulubihim maradun*) is a subject and predicate (*mubtada'* and *khabar*). "Disease" (*maradun*) is a metaphorical expression for the corruption in their beliefs. This is either doubt and hypocrisy (*nifaq*), or denial and rejection. The meaning is: their hearts are diseased, because they are empty of protection (*'ismah*), success (*tawfiq*), care (*ri'ayah*) and support (*ta'yid*). Ibn Faris the linguist said: "Disease is anything by which a person departs from the state of health, whether an ailment, or hypocrisy, or a shortcoming in a matter." The readers are unanimous in pronouncing the *ra'* of *maradun* with a fatha, except what al-Asma'i transmitted from Abu 'Amr, that he made the *ra'* sukun.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So Allah increased them in disease﴾. It has been said: this is an invocation against them, and the meaning of the statement is: Allah increased them in doubt and hypocrisy as a recompense for their disbelief, and as weakness in their ability to prevail and incapacity in their power, as the poet said:

*O sender of the winds, southern and eastern,*
*when Zayd is angry, increase her anger!*

That is, do not restrain her from prevailing in that over which she is angry. On this view, the verse contains evidence for the permissibility of invoking curses upon the hypocrites and expelling them, because they are the worst of Allah's creatures. It has also been said: this is a report from Allah, may He be exalted, about the increase of their disease, that is, Allah increased them in disease in addition to their disease, as He said in another verse: ﴿but it [the surah] increased them in uncleanness along with their uncleanness﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125] [[See vol. 8, p. 299]]. The scholars of meanings (*arbab al-ma'ani*) said: "In their hearts is a disease" means: through their inclination to the world, their love of it, their heedlessness of the Hereafter and their turning away from it. And His saying: "So Allah increased them in disease" means: He left them to themselves, and gathered upon them the worries of this world, so they had no leisure from that for concern with the religion. "And for them is a painful punishment" for what perishes in exchange for what endures. Al-Junayd said: the ailments of the hearts arise from following desire, just as the ailments of the limbs arise from sickness of the body.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾ ... "*alim*" (painful) in the speech of the Arabs means *mu'lim*, that is, causing pain, painful, like *al-sami'* in the sense of *al-musmi'* (the one who makes hear). Dhu al-Rummah, describing camels, said:

*And we urge on, from breasts of tall, long-limbed [camels]*
*whose faces are struck by a painful, scorching heat* [[Shamardalat: tall camels. Narfa'u: we urge them on in travel. Al-wahaj: intense heat that causes pain.]]

*Alama* means "to cause pain" (*awja'a*). *Al-ilam* means causing pain (*al-iljah*). *Al-alam* means pain (*al-waj'*), and one says *alima ya'lamu alaman*. *Al-ta'allum* means to feel pain (*al-tawajju'*). The plural of *alim* is *ulama'* on the pattern of *karim* and *kuramaa'*, and *alam* on the pattern of *ashraf*.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿because they used to lie﴾ (*bima kanu yakdhibun*).

*Ma* here is a verbal-source particle (*masdariyyah*), meaning: because of their denial of the Messengers and their rejection of Allah, may He be exalted, and their denial of His signs; this was said by Abu Hatim. 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with the lightened form (*al-takhfif*), and its meaning is: "because of their falsehood and their saying 'We believe,' while they are not believers." Issue: The scholars differed concerning the Prophet ﷺ refraining from killing the hypocrites, although he knew of their hypocrisy, in four opinions.

The first opinion: some scholars said: he did not kill them only because no one else knew their condition. The scholars have agreed, in its entirety (*bakrat abihim*) [[His saying: "in its entirety" is an Arab expression they use to mean abundance and completeness of number.]], that a judge does not put someone to death on the basis of his own knowledge, and they differed only regarding the rest of the rulings. Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is refuted, for he [the Prophet] killed al-Harith ibn Suwayd ibn al-Samit on account of al-Mujadhdhar ibn Ziyad, because al-Mujadhdhar had killed his father Suwayd on the day of Bu'ath [[Bu'ath: a place in the outskirts of Medina, where there were battles between the Aws and the Khazraj in the pre-Islamic period, and victory there on that day belonged to the Aws over the Khazraj.]]. Then al-Harith embraced Islam, and then he caught him off guard on the day of Uhud and killed him. Jibril informed the Prophet ﷺ of this, and he had him killed in retaliation, because his killing had been by treachery (*ghilah*), and the killing by treachery is one of the hadd-punishments of Allah. I say: this is an oversight by this Imam, for even if the aforementioned consensus is established, it is not refuted by what has been mentioned, because consensus is not formed or established except after the death of the Prophet ﷺ and the cessation of revelation. On this basis, that case is a specific case decided by revelation, so it is not cited as evidence, or else it was abrogated by the consensus. And Allah knows best.

The second opinion: the companions of al-Shafi'i said: he did not kill them only because the *zindiq*, who is the one who conceals disbelief and displays faith, is asked to repent and is not killed. Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is a mistake, for the Prophet ﷺ did not ask them to repent, nor did anyone transmit that, and no one says that asking a *zindiq* to repent is obligatory. The Prophet ﷺ turned away from them while knowing about them. As for this later companion of al-Shafi'i who said that asking the *zindiq* to repent is permissible [[Thus it is in the originals and in the copy of Ibn al-'Arabi's *Ahkam*. The correct phrasing is probably: "that asking the zindiq to repent is obligatory."]], he said a statement that was never sound for anyone.

The third opinion: he refrained from killing them as a matter of public interest, to win over hearts so that they would not flee from him. The Prophet ﷺ indicated this meaning in his saying to 'Umar: "God forbid that people should say that I kill my companions" — related by al-Bukhari and Muslim. He used to give to those whose hearts were to be won over (*al-mu'allafah qulubuhum*), while knowing their bad beliefs, as a way of winning them over. This is the view of our scholars and others. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is the approach of the companions of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, regarding the Messenger of Allah ﷺ restraining himself from the hypocrites. Muhammad ibn al-Jahm, al-Qadi Isma'il, al-Abhari and Ibn al-Majishun stated this explicitly, and they argued with His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease do not desist...﴾ [al-Ahzab: 60] up to His saying: ﴿and they will be seized and killed, a killing﴾ [al-Ahzab: 61]. Qatadah said: its meaning is: when they openly declare hypocrisy. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Hypocrisy in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is what is today called *zandaqah* among us, so the *zindiq* is killed when testimony is given against him for it, without asking him to repent, and this is one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i. Malik said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ refrained from the hypocrites only to make clear to his community that a ruler does not judge by his own knowledge, since no testimony was given against the hypocrites. Al-Qadi Isma'il said: Only Zayd ibn Arqam testified against 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, and no one else; nor did anyone testify against al-Jallas ibn Suwayd except 'Umayr ibn Sa'd, his stepson. If two men had testified against any one of them for his disbelief and hypocrisy, he would have been killed. [[The Imam al-Qurtubi will mention his story when interpreting the surah *al-Munafiqun*.]] [[He was accused of hypocrisy, and it is about him that the verse ﴿they swear by Allah that they did not say...﴾ was revealed. His story will come when interpreting this verse in the surah *Bara'ah* (al-Tawbah), if Allah wills. Ibn Hisham related it in his *Sirah*, p. 355 (Europe edition), and Ibn 'Abd al-Barr in *al-Isti'ab*, vol. 1, p. 97 (India edition).]]

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, argued for the other opinion, saying: The sunnah regarding one who has been testified against for *zandaqah*, but who denies it, and openly professes faith and disavows every religion other than Islam, is that this prevents shedding his blood. This was said by the people of opinion (*ashab al-ra'y*), Ahmad, al-Tabari and others. Al-Shafi'i and his companions said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ prevented the killing of the hypocrites only because of what they displayed of Islam while he knew of their hypocrisy, for what they displayed erases what came before it. Al-Tabari said: Allah, may He be exalted, made the rulings among His servants according to the outward, and reserved the judgment on their inner states to Himself alone, with none of His creation. So no one may rule contrary to what is apparent, for that would be a judgment based on conjecture. And had that been permitted to anyone, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would have been the most entitled to it, yet he ruled for the hypocrites by the ruling for Muslims on the basis of what they displayed, and left their inner states to Allah. And Allah proved their outward profession false in His saying: ﴿Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are liars﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 1]. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The Malikis may answer what is incumbent upon them from this verse by saying that its individuals were not specified in it; rather, it contains a rebuke for every person accused of hypocrisy, and each of them may say: "I did not mean it, and I am only a believer." And even if someone were specified, his lie would not nullify anything. I say: This answer is open to question, for the Prophet ﷺ knew them, or many of them, by name and person, by the information Allah gave him. And Hudhayfah knew this through the Prophet's informing him, to the extent that 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, would say to him: "O Hudhayfah, am I among them?" And he would say: "No."

The fourth opinion: that Allah, may He be exalted, had preserved the companions of His Prophet, peace be upon him, by making them firm, so that the hypocrites could not corrupt them or corrupt their religion. Therefore, keeping them alive did no harm. This is not the case today, for we cannot be secure from the *zanadiqah* corrupting our common people and our ignorant ones.

(إِذَا) in place of accusative (naṣb) functions as an adverb (ẓarf, adverbial complement of time), and the verb governing it is "qālū" (they said). It signals the occurrence of an awaited action. Al-Jawharī said: "idhā" is a noun denoting a future time, and it is never used except when attached to a clause. You say: "ajī'uka idhā ihmarra al-busr" (I will come to you when the unripe dates turn red), and "idhā qadima Fulān" (when so-and-so arrives). What shows that it is a noun is that it occupies the position of your saying: "ātīka yawma yaqdumu Fulān" (I will come to you on the day so-and-so arrives). So it is an adverb, and it contains the sense of conditionality (mujāzāh). The apodosis of a conditional has three forms: the verb, the fa', and idhā. The verb form is your saying: "in ta'tinī ātika" (if you come to me, I will come to you). The fa' form is: "in ta'tinī fa-anā uḥsinu ilayka" (if you come to me, I will be good to you). The idhā form is like His exalted words: ﴿وَإِنْ تُصِبْهُمْ سَيِّئَةٌ بِما قَدَّمَتْ أَيْدِيهِمْ إِذا هُمْ يَقْنَطُونَ﴾ [al-Rūm: 36] (And if an evil befalls them because of what their hands have sent forth, behold, they despair). Among the examples of conditionality with idhā in poetry is the verse of Qays ibn al-Khaṭīm:

When our swords fall short, their joining is
our steps toward our enemies, so we strike.

[He means: when our swords fall short in battle from reaching the equals, we join them with our steps, advancing against them until they reach them.]

He conjoined "fa-nuḍārib" (so we strike) with the jussive "kāna" (it was), since "kāna" is jussive. Had it not been jussive, he would have said "fa-nuḍārība" with the accusative. Sometimes "mā" is added after "idhā" for emphasis, and it too takes the jussive. From this is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

Abū Laylā stood up to him, Ibn Ẓālim,
and whenever he drew the sword, he struck.

Sībawayh said: the better usage is what Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said:

And whenever you wish, she sends forth from it
the sunset-bound, lively and terrified [wild bull].

[He described his she-camel as lively and swift after a full day's travel, so he likened her, in her swift setting out, to a lively wild bull terrified by a hunter or a predator. The nāshiṭ is the bull that leaves one land for another, so that is more frightening and startling to it.]

He means that the better usage is not to make idhā jussive, as it did not take the jussive in this verse. It is related from al-Mubarrad that in your saying in the case of sudden discovery, "kharajtu fa-idhā Zayd" (I went out and behold, Zayd), it is an adverb of place, because it implies a body. This is rejected, because the meaning is: "I went out, and behold, the presence of Zayd," so it implies a verbal noun (maṣdar), as the other adverbs of time require. From this is their saying: "al-yawma khamrun wa-ghadan amrun" (today is wine and tomorrow is a matter), meaning the existence of wine and the occurrence of a matter.

His words: (qīla) come from qawl (saying), and its root is qūla. The kasra of the waw was transferred to the qāf, and the waw turned into yā'. It is also permitted to say "qīla lahum" with the assimilation of the lām into the lām. The juxtaposition of two sākin letters is allowed, because the yā' is a letter of prolongation and softness. Al-Akhfash said: it is also permitted to say "quyila" with a ḍamma on the qāf and the yā'. Al-Kisā'ī said: it is also permitted to pronounce the qāf with a hint of ḍamma (ishmām), to show that the verb has no named agent (passive). This is the dialect of Qays, and likewise jī'a, ghīḍa, ḥīla, sīqa, sī'a and sī'at. Likewise Hishām narrated from Ibn 'Abbās [in one copy: Ibn 'Āmir], and Ruways [Ruways, like Zubayr, is Muḥammad ibn al-Mutawakkil the reciter, transmitter of Ya'qūb ibn Isḥāq] from Ya'qūb. Nāfi' gave the hint of ḍamma in sī'a and sī'at specifically. Ibn Dhakwān added ḥīla and sīqa, and the rest pronounced all of these with kasra. As for Hudhayl and Banū Dubayr of Asad and Banū Fuq'as, they say "qūla" with a silent waw.

His words: (lā tufsidū) "lā" is a prohibition. Corruption (fasād) is the opposite of righteousness (ṣalāḥ), and its essence is deviation from uprightness to its opposite. One says: fasada al-shay' yafsudu fasādan wa-fusūdan, and he is fāsid and fasīd. The meaning in the verse is: do not corrupt the earth by disbelief, by allying with its people, and by turning people away from belief in Muḥammad (ﷺ) and the Qur'an. It was also said: before the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent, the earth had corruption, and sins were committed in it; when the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent, corruption was lifted and the earth was set right. So if they commit sins, they have corrupted the earth after its reform, as He said in another verse: ﴿وَلا تُفْسِدُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ بَعْدَ إِصْلاحِها﴾ [al-A'rāf: 56] (And do not cause corruption in the earth after it has been set right). [See vol. 7, p. 226.]

His words: "fī al-arḍ" (in the earth). Arḍ is feminine, and it is a noun of genus. The singular form should have been "arḍah," but they did not say it. The plural is arḍāt, because they sometimes pluralize a feminine noun that lacks the tā' of feminization with a tā', as in their saying "'urusāt" (brides). Then they said "arḍūn" with the sound masculine plural suffix (wāw and nūn), though a feminine noun is not pluralized with wāw and nūn unless it is defective, like thubah and ẓubah. But they made the wāw and nūn a substitute for the elision of the alif and tā', and they kept the fatḥa of the rā' as it was, and sometimes it is made sākin. It may also be pluralized as Urūḍ. Abū al-Khaṭṭāb claimed that they say: arḍ and ārāḍ, as they say: ahl and āhāl. Al-arāḍī is also a plural contrary to analogy, as if they pluralized ārḍ. Everything low is arḍ. Arḍ arīḍah means a pure land with clear fertility, and it has been made arīḍ (with ḍamma), meaning purified. Abū 'Amr said: we alighted in a fertile land, meaning pleasing to the eye. It is said: lā arḍa laka (you have no land), as one says: lā umma laka (you have no mother). Arḍ also means the lower part of an animal's leg. Ḥumayd described a horse:

And the farrier did not turn over its hoof,
nor did a trace of its cords remain upon it.

[Arḍ here means a trace.] Arḍ also means a shaking and a trembling. Ḥammād ibn Salamah narrated from Qatāda, from 'Abd Allāh ibn al-Ḥārith, who said: the earth quaked in Basra, and Ibn 'Abbās said: By God, I do not know! Did the earth quake, or is there trembling in me? [i.e., a trembling in me]. Dhū al-Rummah said, describing a hunter:

When he perceives a faint sound from its hooves,
or he is a companion of arḍ, or the mūm is upon him.

[Tawajjasa: he hears. Rikz: a faint sense and sound. Sanābik: its hooves. Al-mūm: brain fever, which is the horse. It was said: al-mūm is abundant smallpox. Its meaning: the hunter stretches his self toward the sky and gapes upward constantly, lest the wild beast perceive him and flee. He is likened to one with brain fever or a cold, since brain fever causes gaping and a cold causes gaping.] (from Lisān al-'Arab).

Arḍ also means a cold. God has afflicted him with ārāḍ, meaning he caused him a cold, so he is ma'rūḍ. A fasīl musta'riḍ (a shoot with rooted growth) and a wadiyyah musta'ridah (with kasra on the rā') means one that has a root in the ground; but if it sprouts on the trunk of a palm, it is rākib. Al-Irāḍ (with kasra) is a large carpet of wool or hair. A man arīḍ means humble and fit for good. Al-Aṣma'ī said: he is ārḍuhum in doing that, meaning the most fitting of them. And shay' 'arīḍ arīḍ is an echo-formation for it, and some use it alone, saying: jady' arīḍ, meaning a fat kid.

His words: "naḥnu" (we). The origin of naḥnu is naḥun; the ḥāʾ's vowel was transferred onto the nūn and the ḥāʾ was made sākin. This was said by Hishām ibn Mu'āwiyah the grammarian. Al-Zajjāj said: naḥnu is for a group, and the sign of a group is the wāw, and ḍamma is of the same kind as wāw. When they were compelled to vowel naḥnu due to the meeting of two sākin letters, they vowelled it with what belongs to the group. He said: for this reason they gave the wāw of the plural a ḍamma in His mighty and majestic words: ﴿أُولئِكَ الَّذِينَ اشْتَرَوُا الضَّلالَةَ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16] (Those are the ones who purchased error). Muḥammad ibn Yazīd [al-Mubarrad] said: naḥnu is like qablu and ba'du, because it relates to reporting about two or more: "anā" is for one, and "naḥnu" is for the dual and plural. The speaker may report about himself with it, as in your saying: naḥnu qumnā (we stood up). God the Exalted said: ﴿نَحْنُ قَسَمْنا بَيْنَهُمْ مَعِيشَتَهُمْ﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 32] (It is We who apportion among them their livelihood). In this, the feminine speaker is treated like the masculine. A woman says: qumtu wa-dhahabtu (I stood up and went), and qumnā wa-dhahabnā (we stood up and went), and anā fa'altu dhāka (I did that), and naḥnu fa'alnā (we did). This is the speech of the Arabs, so know it.

His words, exalted be He: ﴿مُصْلِحُونَ﴾ (reformers) is an active participle from aṣlaḥa. Ṣalāḥ is the opposite of fasād. Ṣalaḥa al-shay' (with ḍamma and with fatḥa on the lām) are two dialects, said Ibn al-Sikkīt. Al-ṣulūḥ (with ḍamma on the ṣād) is the verbal noun of ṣaluḥa (with ḍamma on the lām). A poet said:

So how is my silence when you insult me,
and after insulting the two parents, there is no reconciliation?

Ṣalāḥ is also one of the names of Mecca. Al-ṣilḥ (with kasra on the ṣād) is a river. They only said this according to their assumption, since in their view their corruption is reform: that is, our backing of the disbelievers is only meant as reform between them and the believers. This was said by Ibn 'Abbās and others.

The Almighty's words: ﴿Surely it is they who are the corrupters﴾, as a refutation of them and a denial of their claim. The scholars of meanings (arbab al-ma'ani) said: whoever openly asserts a claim is lying. Do you not see that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Surely it is they who are the corrupters﴾? And this is true. "Inna" is pronounced with a kasra because it begins the sentence. Al-Nahhas said this. Ali ibn Sulayman said that it may be pronounced with a fatha, as Sibawayh permitted in: ﴿Truly you are departing﴾ (haqqan annaka muntaliq), in the sense of "alla" (unquestionably). [[The phrasing here is unclear. The probable intended meaning is: it may be read with a fatha, as Sibawayh permitted in "amma annaka muntaliq" in the sense of "haqqan annaka muntaliq" (truly you are departing). When the particles "amma" and "alla" are followed by a fatha on "inna", they carry the meaning of "haqqan"; when "inna" takes a kasra, they are introductory particles of opening. See Sibawayh's Kitab, vol. 1, p. 462, Bulaq edition.]]

"Hum" may be the subject (mubtada', the subject of the nominal clause), and "al-mufsidun" its predicate (khabar), and the subject together with its predicate forms the predicate of "inna" (khabar inna, the predicate of inna). It may also be that "hum" is an emphatic restatement (tawkid) of the hā' and mīm in "innahum". It may also be a separating pronoun (fasila). The Kufans call it an 'imad (a supporting pronoun), and "al-mufsidun" is the predicate of "inna". The underlying sense is: "alla innahumu al-mufsidun", as was discussed earlier in His words: ﴿And those are the successful﴾ [Luqman: 5].

His Exalted words: ﴿But they do not perceive﴾. Ibn Kaysan said: It is said that there is no blame on one who does not know that he is a corrupter. Blame falls only when a person knows he is a corrupter and then corrupts knowingly. He said: In this there are two answers. The first is that they used to commit corruption secretly while displaying righteousness, not realising that their affair would be exposed to the Prophet (ﷺ). The other answer is that their corruption seemed to them to be righteousness, and they did not realise that it was corruption, and they disobeyed Allah and His Messenger by refusing to clarify the truth and follow it.

"Lakin" (but) is a particle of emphasis and of contrast (istidrak, correction of a preceding idea), and it must have a negation and an affirmation: if what precedes it is a negation, what follows it is an affirmation, and if what precedes it is an affirmation, what follows it is a negation. It is not permissible, after it, to limit oneself to a single noun when an affirmation has come before it. Rather, one mentions a clause opposed to what precedes it, as in this verse, and as in your saying: "Zayd came to me, but 'Amr did not come." It is not permissible to say "Zayd came to me, but 'Amr" and then stop, because in such a position they have dispensed with "lakin" in favour of "bal". That is permissible only when a negation precedes, as in your saying: "Zayd did not come to me, but 'Amr."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 13:

Allah's words: ﴿And when it is said to them﴾: meaning the hypocrites, according to Muqatil and others. "Believe as the people have believed" means: affirm Muhammad (ﷺ) and his law, as the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun) and the verifiers (al-Muhaqqiqun) [[The muhaqqiqun here are those whose faith is joined with sincerity, free of the taints of hypocrisy, as al-Alusi and others said.]] of the people of Yathrib have affirmed. The alif in "aminu" is an alif of qat' (cutting, i.e., a hamzat al-qat' pronounced at the start), because you say yu'minu. The kaf (in "kama") is in the accusative position, because it is an adjectival qualifier of a deleted verbal noun (masdar), meaning: a faith like the faith of the people.

Allah's words: ﴿They said: "Shall we believe as the foolish have believed?"﴾: meaning the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), according to Ibn Abbas. It is also reported from him: the believers among the People of the Book. This statement by the hypocrites was only made secretly and mockingly, so Allah informed His Prophet and the believers of it, and established that foolishness, thinness of intellect and corruption of insight are found only within them and are their attribute. He informed that they themselves are the foolish, but they do not know, because of the rust that is upon their hearts. Al-Kalbi related from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, that it was revealed concerning the Jews, meaning: "And when it is said to them," i.e., the Jews, "Believe as the people have believed," namely Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions, they said, "Shall we believe as the foolish have believed," meaning the ignorant and the feeble-minded.

The root meaning of safah (foolishness) in the speech of the Arabs is lightness and thinness: it is said, "a garment is safih" when its weaving is poor and light, or when it is worn out and thin. "Tasaffahat al-rih al-shajar" means the wind bent the tree: the wind swayed it. Dhu al-Rummah said:

They walked as spears sway, when the breezes of the light winds bend their tips.

"Tasaffahtu al-shay'" means: I belittled it. Safah is the opposite of hilm (forbearance). It is said that safah is for a man to drink water excessively without being quenched.

Regarding the two hamzas of "al-sufaha'" (with the following word "ala"), there are four permitted pronunciations. The best of them is to pronounce the first as a clear hamza and change the second into a pure waw; this is the recitation of the people of Medina and what is known from the recitation of Abu 'Amr. If you wish, you may ease both: make the first between the hamza and the waw, and make the second a pure waw. If you wish, you may ease the first and pronounce the second clearly. If you wish, you may pronounce both clearly.

Allah's words: ﴿But they do not know﴾: like "but they do not perceive," which has been mentioned before. Knowledge ('ilm) is recognizing the known as it truly is. You say, "I knew (ʿalimtu) the thing, I know it ('a'lamuhu) knowledge (ʿilman): I recognized it." And "ʿalamtu al-rajul fa-ʿalimtuhu a'lamuhu" (with the vowel u in the imperfect): I overcame him in knowledge.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 2, verse 14:**

Allah's words: (When they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe.") This verse was revealed concerning the hypocrites (al-munafiqun). The original form of *laqu* is *laqiyu*. The damma was moved onto the qaf, and the ya' was dropped because two unvocalized letters came together (*iltiqa' al-sakinayn*). Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqa' al-Yamani recited: "*Laqawu alladhina amanu*." The original form is *laqayu*. The ya' took a vowel, and since a fatha came before it, it became an alif. Two unvocalized letters, the alif and the waw, then came together, so the alif was dropped, and the waw was given a damma. If it is asked why the waw is vocalized with a damma in *laqawu* during continuous recitation (*idraj*), but dropped in *laqu*, the answer is this: before the waw in *laqu* there is a damma. If the waw were vocalized with a damma, pronouncing it would be heavy on the tongue, so it was dropped because of its heaviness. In *laqawu* it is vocalized because a fatha comes before it.

Allah's words: ﴿And when they go off to their devils, they say, "Indeed, we are with you."﴾ If it is asked why *khalaw* is connected with *ila* (to), when its usual construction is with *ba'* (with), the answer is that *khalaw* here means "went off" and "departed." From this is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

*How do you see me turning my shield, striking my command's back against its belly?*
*May God slay Ziyad for me, since he made him stand in the position of "sarafa" (to turn away).*

[[The addition is taken from the book *al-Naqa'id*. Ziyad is Ziyad ibn Abih. *Majann* means the shield.]]

Some said that *ila* here means *ma'a* (with), but this is weak. Others said that *ila* means *ba'*, but al-Khalil and Sibawayh reject this. It was also said that the meaning is: "And when they go off from the believers to their devils," so *ila* keeps its original meaning. *Shayatin* is the broken plural of *shaytan*, and its derivation and meaning were discussed earlier in the section on *al-isti'adhah* (seeking refuge) [[see p. 90]]. The scholars of tafsir differed over what is meant by the devils here. Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi said they are the leaders of disbelief. al-Kalbi said they are the devils among the jinn. A group of exegetes said they are the soothsayers (*kuhhan*). The word *shaytana*, which means distance from faith and goodness, covers all of those mentioned. And Allah knows best.

Allah's words: ﴿Indeed, we are only mocking.﴾ That is, we are denying what we are being called to. It was also said: we are mockers. *Huzu'* means ridicule and play. It is said: *hazi'a bihi* and *istahza'a*. The rajaz poet said:

[[This is Sakhr al-Ghayy al-Hilali. The verse, as cited by al-Qali in his *Amali* (vol. 2, p. 284, Dar al-Kutub al-Misriyyah edition), is:

*The sister of the family of Taysalah mocks me; she said, "I see him to be broke, having no property at all."*]]

*Umm Taysalah has mocked me; she said, "I see him destitute, with no wealth at all."*

It was also said that the origin of *istihza'* (mockery) is revenge, as another poet said:

*They mocked them with two thousand armored men, their nobles in the midst of the wide plains, lying motionless.*

[[*Al-sahasih* (plural of *sahsah*) are plains with nothing in them: no plants, no trees, and no place where water settles. *Al-jathim* means one who stays in his place and does not move.]]

He (the Exalted) said: ﴿Allah mocks them﴾, meaning He takes vengeance on them and punishes them, and He mocks them and repays them for their mockery. He has named the punishment by the name of the sin. This is the view of the majority of scholars (al-jumhur). The Arabs use this often in their speech. Among examples is the verse of 'Amr ibn Kulthum:

"Let no one act ignorantly towards us,
Lest we act with more ignorance than the ignorant."

He called his retaliation "ignorance," and no person of intellect takes pride in ignorance. He said it only so that the sentence would be balanced (yazdawij), making it lighter on the tongue than if the two words differed. When the Arabs placed a word alongside another word as its reply or recompense, they would mention it with the same wording even if it differed from it in meaning. The Qur'an and the Sunnah came in this manner. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And the recompense for an evil deed is an evil deed like it﴾ [Ash-Shura: 40]. He also says: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 194]. Yet recompense is not an evil deed, and retaliation (qisas) is not transgression, because it is a right that is due. Similar to this is: ﴿And they schemed, and Allah schemed﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 54], and: ﴿Indeed, they are plotting a plot, and I am plotting a plot﴾ [At-Tariq: 15-16], and: ﴿Indeed, we are mockers... Allah mocks them﴾. Scheming, mockery and plotting do not come from Him, Glorified is He; rather, it is a recompense for their scheming and their mockery and a repayment of their plotting. Likewise: ﴿They deceive Allah, but He is the one who deceives them﴾ [An-Nisa: 142], and: ﴿They mock them, so Allah mocks them﴾ [At-Tawbah: 79].

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah does not tire until you tire, and He does not become weary until you become weary." It has been said: "Until" here means "and" (wa), i.e., "and you tire." It has also been said that the meaning is: "while you are tiring." It has further been said: the meaning is that He does not cut off the reward of your deeds until you cut off the deed.

Some people said: Allah, the Exalted, does toward them acts which, in human perception, are mockery, deception and scheming. This is in accordance with what has been narrated: "Indeed, the Fire will congeal as al-ihala (melted fat, or what is melted from the tail-fat and grease; it is also said to be solid fat) congeals, and they will walk upon it, thinking it is a means of escape, and then it will swallow them up."

Al-Kalbi narrated from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when they meet those who believe, they say: "We believe"﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 14]: they are the hypocrites among the People of the Book. He mentioned them and mentioned their mockery, and that when they went alone to their devils, meaning their leaders in disbelief, as previously mentioned, they said: "We are with you in your religion," ﴿"We are only mockers"﴾ of the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿"Allah mocks them"﴾ in the Hereafter: a door of Hell from Paradise will be opened for them, and then it will be said to them, "Come here." They will come, swimming in the Fire, while the believers, on the couches, which are the thrones in the canopies, look at them. When they reach the door, it will be closed on them, and the believers will laugh at them. This is the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Allah mocks them﴾, meaning in the Hereafter, and the believers will laugh at them when the doors are shut against them. This is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So today, those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers, reclining on couches, looking [at them]﴾ [Al-Mutaffifin: 34-35], toward the people of the Fire, ﴿Have the disbelievers been repaid for what they used to do?﴾ [Al-Mutaffifin: 36].

Some people said: deception from Allah and mockery is His drawing them on gradually (istidraj) by bestowing worldly blessings upon them. Allah, Glorified and Exalted, shows them in this world benefits contrary to what is hidden from them, and conceals from them the punishment of the Hereafter. So they think that He is pleased with them, whereas He, Exalted is He, has decreed their punishment. This, in human perception, looks like mockery, scheming and deception. This interpretation is supported by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "When you see Allah, Mighty and Majestic, giving a servant what he loves while he persists in his sins, that is only istidraj from Him." Then he recited this verse: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the doors of everything, until when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and they were then in despair. So the last remnant of the people who did wrong was cut off. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [Al-An'am: 44-45]. [[See vol. 6, p. 426. Al-Qurtubi there mentioned the hadith with a narration that differs in some wording, and in it: "Then he recited (So when they forgot) the verse," instead of "recited."]]

Some scholars said, regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We will draw them gradually from where they do not know﴾ [Al-A'raf: 182] [[See vol. 7, p. 329.]]: whenever they commit a sin, He grants them a new blessing.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He extends them﴾, meaning He prolongs their term for them, gives them respite, and lets them go on (yumli). As He said: ﴿Indeed, We grant them respite only so that they may increase in sin﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 178]. Its origin is increase. Yunus ibn Habib said: it is said "madda lahum fi al-sharr" (he extended for them in evil) and "amadda fi al-khayr" (he extended in good). Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And We increased you with wealth and sons﴾ [Al-Isra: 6], and He said: ﴿And We increased them with fruit and meat, of whatever they desire﴾ [At-Tur: 22]. It is related from al-Akhfash: "madadtu lahu" means I left him (to himself), and "amdadtuhu" means I gave him. From al-Farra' and al-Lihyani: "madadtu" is used for what increases from its own kind; one says "madda al-nahr" (the river rose), and in the revelation: ﴿And the sea, with seven seas after it, extends it﴾ [Luqman: 27]. "Amdadtu" is used for what increases from something other than itself, as when you say: "amdadtu al-jaysh bi-madad" (I supplied the army with reinforcements), and from this: ﴿Your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 125]. And "amadda al-jurh" (the wound suppurated), because the pus (midda) comes from something other than it, i.e., pus came into it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿In their transgression﴾: their disbelief and their misguidance. The root of tughyan (transgression) is exceeding the limit. From it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, when the water rose (tagha)﴾ [Al-Haqqah: 11], meaning it rose, ascended, and exceeded the measure which the keepers had determined. And His saying about Pharaoh: ﴿Indeed, he has transgressed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 24], meaning he exceeded all bounds in his claim when he said: ﴿"I am your Lord, the Most High"﴾ [An-Nazi'at: 24]. The meaning in the verse is: He extends them with long life until they increase in transgression, so He increases them in their punishment.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They wander blindly (ya'mahun)﴾: they are blind (ya'munna). Mujahid said: meaning they wander about, bewildered in disbelief. The lexicographers related: "'amiha al-rajul ya'mahu 'umuhan wa 'amahan, fa-huwa 'amih wa 'amih" (the man was bewildered, and he is bewildered and confused) when he is perplexed. And it is said: "rajul 'amih wa 'amih" means a perplexed, wandering person, and its plural is 'umh. And "dhahabat ibiluhu al-'umma" means his camels went astray and he did not know where they went. Blindness (al-'ama) is in the eye, while bewilderment (al-'amah) is in the heart. In the revelation: ﴿Indeed, it is not the eyes that are blinded, but it is the hearts within the breasts that are blinded﴾ [Al-Hajj: 46].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 16:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾. Sibawayh said: the waw in "ishtaraw" (they bought) was given a damma to distinguish it from the original waw, as in: ﴿and that if they had remained upright on the way﴾ [al-Jinn: 16]. Ibn Kaysan said: the damma on the waw is lighter than other vowels because it is of the same kind. Al-Zajjaj said: it was moved with a damma as was done in "nahnu" (we). Ibn Abi Ishaq and Yahya ibn Ya'mar [[The author of Tahdhib al-Tahdhib said: (In al-Taqrib it is with a fatha on the ya' and the mim, with a silent unpointed letter between them. In al-Mughni it is with a fatha or damma on the mim.)]] read it with a kasra on the waw, according to the original rule for joining two silent letters. Abu Zayd al-Ansari related from Qa'nab Abu al-Simmal al-'Adawi that he read it with a fatha on the waw, for the lightness of the fatha, even though the letter before it was fatha-vowelled. [[In some manuscripts: (even though what precedes it is fatha-vowelled), and in others: (even though the letter before it is fatha-vowelled).]] Al-Kisa'i permitted hamzating the waw and giving it a damma, like ad'ur. "Ishtaraw" is from purchase (shira'). The purchase here is figurative, and the meaning is that they preferred disbelief over faith, as He said: ﴿So they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fussilat: 17]. He expressed it with the word purchase because purchase is only of what the buyer loves. As for the meaning of an exchange sale, that is not intended, because the hypocrites were not believers so as to sell their faith. Ibn 'Abbas said: they took error and left guidance. Its meaning is that they substituted and chose disbelief over faith. He expressed it with the word purchase figuratively, because purchase and trade both return to substitution, and the Arabs use that for anyone who substitutes one thing for another. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

"If you claim that I was ignorant among you... then I have bought forbearance after you with ignorance."

[[Also transmitted as: (ishtaraytu). As in the Diwan of Abu Dhu'ayb: if you claim that I was ignorant in my love for you and my yearning for you, then I have bought with that ignorance and youth forbearance and reason, and I turned back from what I had been upon.

(From Sharh al-Shawahid.)]]

The root meaning of error (dalala) is bewilderment. Forgetting is called error because of the bewilderment in it. He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿I did it then while I was of the erring﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 20], meaning, of the forgetful. Perdition is also called error, as He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And they say: when we are lost in the earth﴾ [al-Sajda: 10].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So their trade did not profit﴾. Exalted is He attributed the profit to the trade, following the Arabic custom in saying: "your sale profited" (rabiha bay'uka), "your transaction was losing" (khasirat safqatuka), and their saying: "a standing night" (layl qa'im) and "a fasting day" (nahar sa'im). The meaning: you profited and lost in your sale, you stood in your night and fasted in your day; that is, they did not profit in their trade. The poet said:

"Your day is heedless and your night is asleep... thus in this world the beasts live."

Ibn Kaysan said: the plurals tijara may also be tijarat and taja'ir, and dalala may be dalalat and dala'il.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they were not guided﴾, in their buying of error. It was said: in the foreknowledge of God. Guidance is the opposite of error, and it has been discussed before. [[See p. 160 of this part.]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 17:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Their similitude is like the similitude of one who kindled a fire﴾. So "mathaluhum" (their similitude) is in the nominative by virtue of being the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate lies in the kaf (ka), which is therefore a noun (ism), as it is in the saying of al-A'sha:

"Will you desist, when one who is in excess will not desist? [He is] like a spear-thrust in which the oil and the wick sink."
[Meaning: he does not forbid those who act unjustly, [who are] like a piercing thrust, that is, one reaching through to the interior, in which the oil and the wick disappear. (From Khizanat al-Adab.)]

And the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"And we returned with a horse like a water-bird (ibn al-ma'), led at our side, the eye glancing over it at times and climbing at others."
[He says: we returned with a horse as if it were a water-bird in lightness, beauty and length of neck. "Yujnabu" means it is led and not ridden.]

He intended "like the thrust" and "like the water-bird." It is also permissible that the predicate be omitted, its estimated form being: "their similitude is established as the similitude of," so the kaf in this case is a particle (harf). "Al-mathal," "al-mithl," and "al-mathil" are one and the same, and their meaning is "the resemblance." "Al-mutamathilan" are the two that resemble each other; thus said the lexicographers.

His saying "alladhi" (the one who) may be used for the singular and the plural. Ibn al-Shajari, Hibat Allah ibn Ali, said: Among the Arabs are those who use the plural with the singular form, as the poet said:

"Indeed, those whose blood was spilled at Filj, they are the people, all of the people, O Umm Khalid."
[Filj (with a fatha on the first letter and a sukun on the second): a place between Basra and Dariyya. It is said to be a valley on the road from Basra to Makkah, in whose bottom are resting places for pilgrims. Its speaker is al-Ashhab ibn Rumayla, mourning a people who were killed in this place (from al-Lisan).]

It has been said concerning the saying of God Exalted: "And he who brought the truth and affirmed it, those are the God-fearing" [al-Zumar: 33]: that it is in this same usage. Likewise His saying: "Their similitude is like the similitude of the one who..." It is said the meaning is "like the similitude of those who kindled," and for this reason He said: "God took away their light," so He treated the beginning of the speech as singular and its end as plural. As for His saying: "And you plunged as those who plunged" [al-Tawbah: 69], "alladhi" here is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), its estimated form being: "and you plunged as the plunging which they plunged."

It is also said that He made "alladhi" and "istawqada" singular only because the one who kindled was one individual from a group who undertook the kindling for them; then when the light went out, it returned to all of them, so He said: "with their light."

"Istawqada" has the meaning of "awqada" (kindled), just as "istajaba" has the meaning of "ajaba" (answered); the sin and the ta' are extra, as said al-Akhfash, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"A caller who called out, 'O whoever answers to generosity,' but none of the answerers answered him at that time."
[He is Ka'b ibn Sa'd al-Ghanawi, mourning his brother Abu al-Maghwar (from al-Lisan).]

That is, "yujibhu" (answer him).

The grammarians differed concerning the response of "lamma" (when), and concerning the return of the pronoun in "nurihim" (their light). It has been said: the response of "lamma" is omitted, and it is "tafi'at" (it went out). On this view the pronoun in "nurihim" refers to the hypocrites, and this report concerns a state that will be in the Hereafter, as God Exalted said: "So a wall with a gate will be set up between them" [al-Hadid: 13]. It has also been said: its response is "dhahaba" (went away), and the pronoun in "nurihim" returns to "alladhi" (the one). On this view the depiction of the hypocrite by the one who kindled the fire is complete, because the kindler's remaining in darkness, unable to see, is like the hypocrite's remaining in his bewilderment and wavering.

The meaning intended by the verse is that a similitude is struck for the hypocrites. That is because what they display of faith, by which the rulings for Muslims are established for them, such as marriage, inheritance, booty, and security for their persons, children and wealth, is like one who kindled a fire on a dark night, so he was illuminated by it and saw what he should guard against and was safe from; but when it went out from him, or went away, harm reached him and he remained bewildered. Likewise the hypocrites, when they professed faith, were deceived by the word of Islam; then after death they will go to the painful punishment, as the Revelation informed: "Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest level of the Fire" [al-Nisa': 145], and their light will go away; for this reason they say: "Wait for us that we may acquire from your light" [al-Hadid: 13]. It has been said: the hypocrites' approach to the Muslims and their speech with them is like the fire, and their turning away from their affection and their reversion to disbelief among them is like its going out. And it has been said other than this.

His saying: "nara" (a fire). The fire is feminine, and it is from "nur" (light), and that also means brightness. It is from the waw, because you say in the diminutive "nuwayra," and in the plural "nur," "anwar," and "niran"; the waw changed to ya' because of the kasra before it.

"Da'a" and "adaa'a" are two dialects; it is said: the moon "da'a yadu'u du'an," and "ada'a yudi'u," which is intransitive and transitive.

Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqa' read "daat" without an alif, while the common reading has the alif. The poet said:

"Their noble ancestry and their faces lit up for them the darkness of the night, until the piercing one arranged the onyx beads."
[Al-jaza' (with a fatha or kasra on the jim): a kind of bead. It is said: it is the Yemeni bead, which has white and black in it, so the eyes were likened to it.]

"Ma" in "ma hawlahu" (what is around him) is an extra, emphasizing particle. It is also said: it is an object of "adaa'at" (illuminated). "Hawlahu" is a noun of place, and the ha' is in the place of genitive by its being attached to it. "Dhahaba" and "adhhaba" are two dialects from "dhahab" (going), which is the removal of a thing.

"Wa taraka hum" means: He left them (abqaahum).

"Fi zulumat": plural of "zulmah" (darkness). Al-A'mash read "zulmat" with the lam sukun on the original form. Whoever reads it with a damma does so to distinguish the noun from the adjective. Ashhab al-'Uqayli read "zulamat" with a fatha on the lam. The Basrans said: he substituted a fatha for the damma because it is lighter. Al-Kisa'i said: "zulamat" is a plural of a plural, the plural of "zulam."

"La yubsiruna" is an imperfect verb in the place of a circumstantial clause (hal), as if he said: "ghayra mubsirin" (not seeing). Therefore it is not permissible to stop on "zulumat" on this reading.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 18:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Deaf, dumb, blind﴾. "Deaf" means they are deaf, so it is the predicate of an implied subject (khabar li-mubtada' mudmar). In the reading of ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud and Hafsa: "ṣumman bukman ʿumyan" (deaf, dumb, blind, in the accusative). The accusative here is permitted as an accusative of censure (al-nasb ʿala al-dhamm), as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿cursed wherever they are found﴾ [al-Ahzab: 61] [[See vol. 14, p. 247.]], and as in His saying: ﴿and his wife, the carrier of firewood﴾ [al-Masad: 4] [[See vol. 20, p. 239.]], and as the poet said: [[He is ʿUrwa ibn al-Ward. He describes what the people of his wife did when they tricked him and gave him wine until he agreed to ransom her, for she had been a captive in his possession (from Sharh al-Shawahid).]]

They gave me wine to drink, then surrounded me,
enemies of God, with falsehood and lies.

Here he put "ʿudata Allah" (enemies of God) in the accusative as censure. On this view, stopping at "they do not see" (yubsirun) is correct and good. It is also permissible to make "ṣumman" accusative by "tarakahum" (He left them), as if He had said: "and He left them deaf, dumb, blind." On this view, it is not good to stop at "they do not see."

In the language of the Arabs, ṣamam (deafness) means blockage (inisad). One says: "qanah ṣammaʾ" (a solid spear) when it is not hollow, and "ṣammamtu al-qarurah" (I stopped up the bottle) when I sealed it. So the aṣamm is one whose ear-openings are blocked. The abkam is one who does not speak and does not understand; if he understands, he is the akhras (mute). It is said that the akhras and the abkam are the same. One says: "rajul abkam" and "bakim," meaning a man who is clearly mute and dumb. The poet said:

Would that my tongue were two halves of it,
one dumb, and half at the course of the stars.

ʿAma (blindness) is the loss of sight; one says "ʿamiya fa-huwa aʿma," "qawm ʿumy," and "aʿmahu Allah" (God blinded him). "Taʿama al-rajul" means he showed himself to be blind. "ʿAmiya ʿalayhi al-amr" means the matter became obscure. From this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then the news was obscured to them that day﴾ [al-Qasas: 66] [[See vol. 13, p. 304.]].

What we have mentioned is not intended to deny all perception to their senses entirely; rather the intent is to deny it in a certain respect. You say: "Fulan asamm ʿan al-khana" (So-and-so is deaf to obscenity). The poet expressed this well when he said:

Deaf to what displeases him, though he hears.

Another said:

And a crooked speech, I turned deaf to it,
though had I wished, I would have heard it.

Al-Darimi said:

Blind when my neighbour goes out,
until the walls conceal my neighbour.

Some of them said in his advice to a man who frequently entered upon kings:

Enter when you enter, blind,
and leave when you leave, mute.

Qatadah said: "ṣumm" means deaf to hearing the truth, "bukm" means mute in speaking it, and "ʿumy" means blind to seeing it. I say: this meaning is what is intended in the Prophet's (ﷺ) description of the rulers of the last age in the hadith of Jibril: "When you see the barefoot, naked, deaf, and dumb become the kings of the earth, that is among its signs." And God knows best.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So they do not return﴾, i.e., to the truth, due to God's prior knowledge concerning them. One says: "raja'a bi-nafsihi ruju'an" (he returned by himself), and "rajaʿahu ghayruhu" (another returned him); the Hudhayl tribe says "arjaʿahu ghayruhu." His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They refer the word to one another﴾ [Saba': 31], i.e., they blame one another among themselves, as the revelation clarified in surah Saba' [[See vol. 14, p. 302.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 19 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, Exalted is He: (or like a rain-cloud from the sky). Al-Tabari said: "aw" (or) here means "wa" (and), and al-Farra' said the same. He recited:
"Layla has claimed that I am a sinner... for my own self is its piety, or upon it is its sin." [The line is from a poem by Tawba al-Khafaji, composed about Layla al-Akhyaliyya.]
Another said: [It is Jarir ibn 'Atiyya, praising 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz.]
"He attained the caliphate [In his manuscript diwan: (idh) instead of (aw)], or it was for him a decree, as Musa came to his Lord at an appointed measure."
That is, "and it was." It is also said that "aw" is for choice, meaning: liken them to this or to that, not restricting it to one of the two matters. The meaning is: or like the people of a rain-cloud. Al-Sayyib (ṣayyib) is the rain. Its derivation is from ṣāba yaṣūbu, meaning it descended. 'Alqama said:
"So do not make me equal between myself and a man ignorant... may the water-skins of the clouds water you wherever they pour."
[Al-mughammar and al-ghamr: the ignorant one who has not tested affairs, as if ignorance has covered him and taken hold of him. Rawaya al-muzn: those that pour abundantly with their water.]
Its origin is ṣayyawib: the yā' and the wāw came together, and one of them was preceded by a sukūn, so the wāw was changed into a yā' and they were assimilated, as they did in mayyit, sayyid, hayyin and layyin. Some of the Kufans said: its origin is ṣawīb on the pattern of faʿīl. Al-Nahhas said: "If it were as they say, its assimilation would not be permissible, just as the assimilation of ṭawīl is not permissible." The plural of ṣayyib is ṣayāyib. The grammatical construction in Arabic is: "their likeness is like the likeness of one who kindled a fire," or "like the likeness of a rain-cloud." [In the original: (... nāran aw kaṣayyib). The correction is from Ai'rab al-Quran by al-Nahhas.]

His saying, Exalted is He: **from the sky**. Al-sama' is masculine and feminine, and its plurals are asmiyya, sumuwat and sumiyy, on the pattern fu'ul. Al-'Ajjaj said:
"The winds wrap it, and the rain (al-sumiyy)..." [Al-sumiyy: he means the rains.]
Al-sama' is everything that rises above you and shades you, and from this the roof of a house is called sama'. Al-sama' is also rain, named so because it descends from the sky. Hassan ibn Thabit said:
"Abodes of the Banu al-Hasḥas are desolate, obliterated by the dust-storms and the rain."
Another said: [He is Mu'awiya ibn Malik.]
"When the sky falls upon a people's land, we pasture upon it, even if they are angry."
Mud and herbage are also called sama', as they say: "We have not ceased to tread the sama' until we came to you," meaning the herbage and the mud. The back of a horse is also called sama' because of its height, as someone said: [The speaker is Tufayl al-Ghanawi, as in Lisan, entry (sama).]
"A red horse like brocade: its sama' is rain-watered, while its earth is barren."
Al-sama' is what is above; al-ard is what is below, as has been previously stated.

His saying, Exalted is He: **in it are darknesses**. This is a subject and predicate, and "thunder and lightning" is coordinated with it. He said "ẓulumat" in the plural, indicating the darkness of the night and the darkness of the dujn, which is the cloud; and it is pluralized because they are layered and increasing. The dialects concerning it have already passed (see p. 213 of this part), so there is no point in repeating them, and likewise everything previously mentioned, God willing.

The scholars differed concerning the thunder (al-ra'd). In al-Tirmidhi, from Ibn 'Abbas, he said: The Jews asked the Prophet ﷺ about the thunder, what is it? He said: ("It is an angel from among the angels [appointed] over the clouds, with whips of fire, driving the clouds wherever God wills"). They said: "Then what is this sound that we hear?" He said: ("Its driving of the clouds when it drives them, until it reaches where God has commanded"). They said: "You have spoken truly." The hadith in full. Most of the scholars adopt this interpretation. So al-ra'd is the name of the heard sound. This was said by 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and it is the known meaning in the Arabic language. Labid said in his pre-Islamic era:
"The thunder and the thunderbolts have bereaved me of the horseman, on the day of the harsh, valiant battle."
It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: The thunder is a wind choked between the clouds, which makes that sound. They differed concerning the lightning (al-barq). It is narrated from 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them: the lightning is an iron scourge in the hand of the angel with which he drives the clouds. I say: this is the apparent meaning of the hadith of al-Tirmidhi. Also from Ibn 'Abbas: it is a whip of light in the hand of the angel with which he drives the clouds. And also from him: the lightning is an angel that appears. The philosophers said: the thunder is the sound of the clashing of the bodies of the clouds, and the lightning is what is struck out from their clashing. This is rejected and has no sound transmission, and God knows best. It is said: the origin of ra'd is from movement, and from it comes ra'īd for the coward. And ir'ada means to tremble, and from it the hadith: ("He was brought with them, their flanks trembling") — the hadith, related by Abu Dawud. Al-barq originally comes from al-bariq and light, and from it comes al-Buraq: the beast which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ rode on the night of his Night Journey, and the prophets, peace be upon them, rode it before him. The sky "thundered" (ra'adat) from the thunder, and "flashed" (baraqat) from the lightning. A woman "ra'adat and baraqat": she beautified herself and adorned herself. A man "ra'ad and baraq": he threatened and menaced. Ibn Ahmar said:
"O most distant of our lands from you, and our seekers: then flash and thunder in your land."
And "ar'ada al-qawm wa abraqu": they were struck by thunder and lightning. Abu 'Ubayda and Abu 'Amr related: "ar'adat al-sama' wa abraqat" and "ar'ada al-rajul wa abraqa" when he threatened and menaced; al-Asma'i denied this. He was countered with the verse of al-Kumayt:
"Flash and thunder, O Yazid: your threat to me does no harm."
He said: "al-Kumayt is not a proof."

**Benefit:**
Ibn 'Abbas related: We were with 'Umar ibn al-Khattab on a journey between Madina and Syria, and with us was Ka'b al-Ahbar. He said: a wind struck us, thunder and heavy rain and hail struck us, and the people were terrified. Ka'b said to me: "Whoever says when he hears the thunder: Glory be to Him whom the thunder glorifies with His praise, and the angels out of fear of Him, he will be protected from what happens in that cloud, the hail and the thunderbolts." He said: I and Ka'b said it. When we arrived in the morning and the people gathered, I said to 'Umar: "O Commander of the Faithful, it is as if we were in other than what the people were in." He said: "And what is that?" So I related to him the report of Ka'b. He said: "Glory be to Allah! Why did you not tell us, so we could say as you said!" In another narration: a hailstone had struck 'Umar's nose and left a mark on it. [Al-barad (with vowel): the hail-grains of the cloud.] This narration will come in surah al-Ra'd, God willing [see vol. 9, p. 295]. Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn 'Ali ibn Thabit al-Khatib mentioned both narrations in *Riwayat al-Sahaba 'an al-Tabi'in*, may Allah have mercy on them all.

And from Ibn 'Umar: the Prophet ﷺ, when he heard the thunder and the thunderbolts, would say: ("O Allah, do not kill us by Your wrath, do not destroy us by Your punishment, and grant us well-being before that").

His saying, Exalted is He: **they put their fingers in their ears**. Their putting their fingers in their ears is so that they would not hear the Qur'an and believe in it and in Muhammad, peace be upon him, and that, in their view, is disbelief, and disbelief is death. For the singular of "al-asabi'" there are five dialects: iṣba' with a kasra on the hamza and a fatha on the ba'; uṣba' with a fatha on the hamza and a kasra on the ba'; it is said with both a fatha, both a damma, and both a kasra; and it is feminine. Likewise al-udhun (ear), which is lightened, made heavy, and diminutive, so it is said: udhayna. If you name a man with it and then diminutive him, you say: udhayn, and it is not made feminine because the feminine has been removed from it by transferring it to the masculine. As for their saying udhayna as a proper name, it was named with it in diminutive form. The plural is adhan. You say: adhantuhu, if you strike his ear. A man is udhun if he listens to everyone's speech, the singular and plural alike. Adhani: one with large ears. A ewe with large ears is ad'a', and a ram is adhan. Adhdhanta the sandal and other things: if you make an ear for it. Adhdhanta the child: you twisted his ear.

His saying, Exalted is He: **because of the thunderbolts**. That is, on account of the thunderbolts. Al-sawa'iq is the plural of sa'iqa. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others said: when the anger of the thunder, which is the angel, intensifies, fire flies from his mouth, and these are the thunderbolts. Al-Khalil said likewise; he said: they are the severe striking from the sound of thunder, sometimes accompanied by a piece of fire that burns whatever it reaches. Abu Zayd said: the thunderbolt is a fire that falls from the sky in severe thunder. Al-Khalil related from some people: al-sa'iqa (with sin). Abu Bakr al-Naqqash said: it is said sa'iqa, sa'qa and sa'iqa with one meaning. Al-Hasan recited: min "al-sawaqi'" (with the qaf placed first), and from this is the saying of Abu al-Najm:
"They imitate with the polished, cutting [swords] the splitting of the lightning from the thunderbolts."
Al-Nahhas said: this is the dialect of Tamim and some of Banu Rabi'a. It is said: "sa'aqathum al-sama'" when the sky cast the thunderbolt upon them. Al-sa'iqa is also the cry of punishment. God, Mighty and Majestic, said: "So the thunderbolt of the humiliating punishment seized them" [Fussilat: 17]. It is said: "su'iqa al-rajul sa'qatan wa tas'aqan", meaning he fainted. And in the saying of God, Exalted is He: "And Musa fell down in a swoon" [al-A'raf: 143], another caused him to swoon. Ibn Muqbil said:
"You see the blue gadflies beneath its chest, single and in pairs, which its neighing has struck down."
[Al-nu'ara: a large fly with a blue-green eye, which has a sting at the tip of its tail with which it stings only solid-hoofed animals. Al-labban: the chest; it is said the middle, and it is said what is between the breasts, and it applies to a human and others. Asqat-hā sawāhiluhu: its neighing killed it.]
And His saying, Exalted is He: "So all who are in the heavens and all who are on earth swooned" [al-Zumar: 68], that is, died. In this verse God has likened the states of the hypocrites to what is in the rain-cloud: darknesses, thunder, lightning and thunderbolts. The darknesses are a figure for the disbelief they hold; the thunder and lightning are a figure for what they are frightened by. It is also said: God likened the Qur'an to the rain-cloud because of the perplexity it causes them; blindness is the darknesses; what is in it of threat and warning is the thunder; what is in it of light and dazzling proofs, which sometimes nearly overwhelm them, is the lightning. The thunderbolts are a figure for what is in the Qur'an of calling to fighting in the immediate and threat in the hereafter. It is also said: the thunderbolts are the legal obligations of the Law which they dislike, such as jihad, zakat and others.

His saying: **"for fear of death."** *Hadhar* and *hidhar* have the same meaning, and both are read. Sibawayh said: it is in the accusative because it is a cause (maf'ul li-ajlihi), and its reality is that it is a verbal noun. Sibawayh recited:
"And I forgive the noble man's blemish, storing it up for him, and I turn away from the abuse of the base man, showing generosity."
[The line is by Hatim al-Ta'i. He means: if the noble one acts ignorantly toward me, I bear his ignorance out of preservation of him and storing it up for him, and if the base one reviles me, I turn away from insulting him.]
Al-Farra' said: it is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). *Al-mawt* is the opposite of life. One says *mata yamutu* and also *yamat*. The rajiz said:
"My daughter, mistress of daughters, live, and it is not assured that you will die."
So he is *mayyit* and *mayt*, and the people are *mawta*, *amwat*, *mayyitun* and *maytun*. *Al-muwat* (with damma) is death; *al-mawat* (with fatha) is that which has no spirit; *al-mawat* also is land that has no owner among the sons of Adam and from which no one benefits. *Al-mawatan* (with vowel) is the opposite of living creatures; one says: "Buy the land (al-mawatan) and do not buy the animals (al-hayawan)," meaning buy lands and houses, and do not buy slaves and beasts. *Al-muwatan* (with damma) is a death that befalls livestock; one says: "a *muwatan* has fallen upon the property." Allah caused him to die and *mawwatahu*, intensified for emphasis. And he said:
"So Urwa died a restful death, and here I am, dying every day."

And the she-camel is said to have "died" (amatat al-naqatu) when her young one dies; so she is mumit and mumitah. Abu 'Ubayd said: and likewise the woman (in that case), and its plural is mamawit. Ibn al-Sikkit said: amata fulan (he has been bereaved) when he has a son or sons die. Al-mutamawit is an attribute of the pious ascetic who makes a show (of piety, al-murai). A mawt ma'it, like your saying layl la'il (a dark night), in which something is taken from the same root to emphasize it.

Al-mustamit to a matter: one who is absorbed in it and gives himself over to it. Ru'bah said:

"The foam of the sea has for it a roar... and the night above the water is mustamit."

[[As given in the originals and in Lisan, root (w-t), i.e., (mawt). What is in his manuscript Diwan at Dar al-Kutub al-Misriyyah, no. 516, Adab:
"The foam of the sea has for it a roar,
and the fish has for it a groan,
both are immersed, overwhelmed,
and the breast of the water has for it a resting place.
And the night above the water is mustamit,
pushing away from it its hollow, the muhsut.
Al-kutayt: the roaring. Al-na'it, al-zahir, al-tahir and al-anit all mean groaning (expelling a sound or breath when labouring or in distress). Al-maghtut: the distressed. Al-mashut: one who is never satisfied."]]

Al-mustamit also means one who fights to the death, who does not care about death in battle. In the hadith: "I see the people as mustamitin," meaning those who fight to the death.

Al-mawtah (with a dammah): a kind of madness and seizure that befalls a person; when he recovers, his full reason returns to him, like one who is asleep or drunk. Mu'tah (with a dammah on the mim and a hamzah on the waw): the name of a land. It is said it is a village of the villages of al-Balqa' within the borders of Syria. It is also said it is on the outskirts of Syria, twelve miles from Adhruh. [[See Taj al-'Arus, root (m-w-t).]] Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, was killed there.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah encompasses the disbelievers﴾ is a beginning and a predicate, meaning they cannot escape Him. It is said: the ruler encircled so-and-so when he seized him by a seizure that besieges him from every side. The poet said:

"We surrounded them until, when they were certain of what they had seen, they inclined together to peace."

From this is the saying of Exalted Allah: "and his fruit was encompassed" [al-Kahf: 42]. Its origin is muhit; the vowel of the ya' was moved to the ha' and it was made sukun. So Allah, glory be to Him, encompasses all created beings, meaning they are in His grip and under His subjugation, as He said: "and the earth entirely in His grasp on the Day of Resurrection" [al-Zumar: 67]. It is also said: "encompasses the disbelievers" means He knows them. Its evidence is: "and that Allah has encompassed all things in knowledge" [al-Talaq: 12]. It is also said: He destroys them and gathers them. Its evidence is the saying of Exalted Allah: "unless you are encompassed" [Yusuf: 66], meaning unless you are all destroyed. The disbelievers were singled out for mention because they were mentioned earlier in the verse. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 20:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight﴾ ... "Yakādu" means "yuqāribu" (it approaches, comes close). It is said: "kāda yafʿalu kadhā" when he came close to doing so but did not do it. In other than the Qur'an it is permissible to say "yakādu an yafʿala", as Ru'bah said:

قَدْ كَادَ مِنْ طُولِ الْبِلَى أَنْ يَمْصَحَا [[Yamsah: goes away and is effaced.]]

It is derived from al-mashh, which is effacement. The better usage is without "an", because it indicates the approach of a present state, whereas "an" turns the speech toward the future, and this is contradictory. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿The brilliance of His lightning nearly takes away their sight﴾ [al-Nur: 43]. From the speech of the Arabs: "kāda al-naʿāmu yaṭīru" (the ostrich nearly flies) and "kāda al-ʿarūsu yakūnu amīran" (the bride nearly becomes a ruler), because they are close to that state. "Kāda" is a verb conjugated like "faʿila yafʿalu". Its predicate has also come as a noun, though this is rare, he said: "wa-mā kidtu āʾiban" [[Its speaker is Ta'abbaṭa Sharran. The full verse:

فَأُبْتُ إِلَى فَهْمٍ وَمَا كِدْتُ آئِبًا ... وَكَمْ مثلها فارقتها وهي تصفر]] (and I nearly did not return). It takes the same course as kāda, karaba, jaʿala, qāraba and ṭafiqa, in that its predicate is without "an", as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And they began to fasten upon themselves some leaves of the Garden﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 22], because all of these carry the meaning of a present state and approach, and a present state cannot be accompanied by "an". So understand this.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿snatches away their sight﴾. "Al-khaṭf" is seizing swiftly, and from it the bird is called khaṭṭāf for its swiftness. Whoever makes the Qur'an an example of intimidation, the meaning is that their fear of what will befall them nearly takes away their sights. Whoever makes it an example of the clarity in the Qur'an, the meaning is that there came to them from the clarity what dazzled them. "Yakhṭafu" and "yakhṭifu" are two dialects, both of which were recited. "Khaṭifahu" (with kasra) "yakhṭafuhu khaṭfan" is the good dialect, and the other dialect, related by al-Akhfash, is "khaṭafa yakhṭifu". Al-Jawhari said: it is rare, inferior, and hardly known. Yunus recited with it in His saying, may He be exalted, "yakādu al-barqu yakhṭifu abṣārahum". Al-Nahhas said: in "yakhṭafu" there are seven aspects. The eloquent recitation is "yakhṭafu". ʿAli ibn al-Husayn and Yahya ibn Wththab recited "yakhṭifu" with kasra on the ṭāʾ; Saʿid al-Akhfash said: it is a dialect. Al-Hasan, Qatadah, ʿAsim al-Jahdari and Abu Rajaʾ al-ʿUtaridi recited with fatḥ on the yāʾ and kasra on the khāʾ and ṭāʾ. It is also related from al-Hasan that he recited with fatḥ on the khāʾ. Al-Farra' said: some people of Madinah recited with sukūn on the khāʾ and shadda on the ṭāʾ. Al-Kisa'i, al-Akhfash and al-Farra' said: "yikhiṭifu" with kasra on the yāʾ, khāʾ and ṭāʾ is permissible. These are six aspects consistent with the script.

The seventh was related by ʿAbd al-Warith, who said: I saw in the codex of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb "yatakhaṭṭafu". Sibawayh and al-Kisa'i claimed that whoever recites "yikhiṭṭifu" with kasra on the khāʾ and ṭāʾ, the original form in his view is "yakhtatifu", then the tāʾ was assimilated into the ṭāʾ, so two sukūns met, and the khāʾ was given kasra to resolve the meeting of two sakins. Sibawayh said: whoever puts fatḥ on the khāʾ transfers the vowel of the tāʾ onto it. Al-Kisa'i said: whoever puts kasra on the yāʾ does so because the alif in "ikhtaṭafa" is kasra. As for what al-Farra' related from the people of Madinah, namely sukūn on the khāʾ with assimilation, it is not known and is not permissible, because it joins two sakins, as al-Nahhas and others said. I say: it is also related from al-Hasan and Abu Rajaʾ "yakhaṭṭafu". Ibn Mujahid said: I think it is a mistake, and he argued for this by saying that no one recited "khaṭifa al-khaṭfah" with fatḥ. "Abṣārahum" is the plural of baṣar, which is the faculty of sight. The meaning: the proofs of the Qur'an and its shining evidences nearly dazzle them. Whoever makes "al-barq" an example of intimidation, the meaning is that their fear of what will befall them nearly takes away their sights.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it﴾ ... "Kullamā" is in the accusative because it is an adverb of time. If "kullamā" has the meaning of "idhā", it is a relative construction, and the governing element is "mashaw" (they walked), which is its answer; "aḍāʾa" does not govern it, because it is within the relative clause of "mā". The object in the view of al-Mubarrad is elided, the implied sense being: "kullamā aḍāʾa lahumu al-barqu al-ṭarīq" (whenever the lightning illuminated the path for them). It was said: it is permissible that "faʿala" and "afʿala" have the same meaning, like "sakata" and "askata", so "aḍāʾa" and "ḍāʾa" are identical, and there is no need to posit an elided object. Al-Farra' said: it is said "ḍāʾa" and "aḍāʾa", and this has been mentioned before. The meaning: whenever they hear the Qur'an and the proofs appear to them, they become at ease and walk with it; but when some of the Qur'an descends in which they are blinded and go astray, or which they are obliged to follow, they "stand", that is, they remain firm in their hypocrisy, according to Ibn ʿAbbas. It was also said: the meaning is that whenever their affairs in their crops and livestock are good and blessings follow one another, they say: "the religion of Muhammad is a blessed religion"; and when a calamity strikes them and hardship befalls them, they become discontented and remain steadfast in their hypocrisy, according to Ibn Masʿud and Qatadah. Al-Nahhas said: this is a good opinion, and its soundness is supported by His saying: ﴿And among the people is he who worships Allah on an edge; if good befalls him, he is reassured by it, and if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face﴾ [al-Hajj: 11]. The Sufi scholars said: this is an example Allah set for one whose states of resolve were not sound from the beginning, who then ascended from those states through claims to the states of the eminent, as if the states of resolve would have illuminated for him had he sound them by adhering to their etiquette. When he mixed them with claims, Allah removed those lights from him, and he remained in the darkness of his claims, unable to see the way out of them. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that the intended group is the Jews: when the Prophet ﷺ was victorious at Badr they became hopeful and said: "By God, this is the Prophet whom Moses gave us good news of; his banner will not be turned back." But when he was afflicted at Uhud, they apostatized and doubted. This view is weak. The verse concerns the hypocrites, and this is more sound from Ibn ʿAbbas; the meaning encompasses all of them.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight﴾ ... "Law" is a particle of wish and carries the sense of a condition, and its answer is the "lam". The meaning: if Allah had willed, He would have made the believers aware of them, and the dignity of Islam would have departed from them through domination over them, their killing and their expulsion from among them. Hearing and sight are singled out because they were mentioned earlier in the verse, or because they are the most noble of what a human possesses. It is recited "bi-asmāʿihim" in the plural, and the discussion of this has preceded [[See the eighth issue, p. 190 of this part.]].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things Competent﴾ is general in form, and its meaning according to the theologians is in what it is permissible to describe Him, may He be exalted, as having power over. The community has agreed on naming Allah, exalted, as al-Qadir, so He, glory be to Him, is Qadir, Qadir, Muqtadir. Al-Qadir is more emphatic in description than al-Qadir (the one who is able), as al-Zajjaji said. Al-Harawi said: al-qadir and al-qadir have one meaning; it is said: "qadirtu ʿalā al-shayʾ aqdiru qadran wa-qudran wa-maqdiratan wa-maqdiratan wa-qudranan", meaning power. Iqtidar over a thing is power over it. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is Qadir, Muqtadir, Qadir over every possibility that accepts existence and non-existence. Every accountable person must know that Allah, exalted, has power, by which He acts and does whatever He wills in accordance with His knowledge and choice. He must also know that the servant has a power by which he acquires what Allah has enabled him to do according to customary course, and that he is not independent in his power. Here Allah specifically mentioned the attribute of power rather than others, because an act whose content is threat and intimidation was mentioned earlier, so mention of power is fitting for that. And Allah knows best. These are twenty verses according to the count of the Kufans: four verses describing the believers, then two verses about the disbelievers, and the rest concerning the hypocrites. The narration concerning them has been mentioned earlier from Ibn Jurayj, and Mujahid also said it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 21:

His words, glory be to Him, "O mankind, worship your Lord" (﴿يا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ اعْبُدُوا رَبَّكُمُ﴾). Alqamah and Mujahid said: every verse that begins with "O mankind" was revealed in Makkah, and every verse that begins with "O you who believe" was revealed in Madinah. I say: this is refuted by the fact that this surah and al-Nisa' are both Madinan, and in them is "O mankind." As for their statement regarding ﴿يا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾ [al-Nisa': 19], it is correct.
