Al-Bayhaqi said: his intended meaning from that, and Allah knows best, is the elevation of His command, which is the vapour of water from which the creation of the heaven occurred. It was also said: the one who istawa is the smoke. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is rejected by the description of the speech. It was also said: the meaning is istawla (took possession), as the poet said: [This is al-Akhtal, as in Sharh al-Qamus.]
"Bishr has taken possession of Iraq, without sword or spilled blood."

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This only applies to His saying, ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5]. I say: It has already been mentioned in al-Farra's statement that *'alayya* and *ilayya* have the same meaning. More detailed explanation of this topic will come, God willing, in surah al-A'raf [[See vol. 7, p. 219.]]. The principle regarding this verse and similar ones is to deny movement and transference.

The sixth issue: It appears from this verse that God created the earth before the heaven, and likewise in Ha-Mim al-Sajdah [[See vol. 15, p. 343.]]. In al-Nazi'at He said: ﴿Are you the more difficult to create, or is it the heaven? He built it﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 27], describing its creation, then He said: ﴿And the earth after that He spread out﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 30]. So it seems that, according to this, the heaven was created before the earth. And He said: ﴿Praise be to God, who created the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 1]. This is the view of Qatadah, that the heaven was created first; al-Tabari related it from him. Mujahid and others among the exegetes said: God dried up the water upon which His Throne was, and made it earth, and smoke arose from it and ascended, and He made it heaven. Thus the creation of the earth came before the creation of the heaven. Then He turned His command to the heaven and made them seven heavens, and afterwards He spread out (*daha*) the earth [[*Daha* means: he spread it out.]], and at the time of its creation it was not yet spread out.

I say: Qatadah's view can be sound, God willing, in this way: God first created the smoke of the heaven, then created the earth, then He turned toward the heaven while it was smoke and made it complete, then He spread out the earth after that.

What indicates that the smoke was created before the earth is what al-Suddi related from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Murrah al-Hamdani from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some people among the companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), concerning His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth. Then He turned to the heaven and made them seven heavens﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29]. He said:

God, blessed and exalted, His Throne was upon the water, and He had created nothing before the water. When He willed to create creation, He brought forth from the water smoke, which rose above the water, and it rose high above it, so He named it heaven. Then He dried up the water and made it one earth, then He split it and made it seven earths, in two days, on Sunday and Monday.

He placed the earth upon a fish—and the fish is the *nun* that God, blessed and exalted, mentioned in the Qur'an in His saying: ﴿Nun. By the pen﴾ [al-Qalam: 1]—and the fish is in the water, and the water [[Supplement from al-Tabari's Tafsir and History.]] is upon a *safah* [[The *safah* is a broad, smooth stone.]], and the *safah* is upon the back of an angel, and the angel is upon the rock, and the rock is in the wind—and it is the rock that Luqman mentioned: it is neither in the heaven nor in the earth. Then the fish moved and shook, so the earth quaked, and He sent the mountains upon it and it became steady. So the mountains boast over the earth, and that is His saying, exalted: ﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains lest it shake with you﴾ [al-Nahl: 15]. He created the mountains in it, and the sustenance of its people, and its trees, and what is fitting for it, in two days, on Tuesday and Wednesday. That is when He says: ﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in Him who created the earth in two days, and set up rivals to Him? That is the Lord of the worlds.﴾ And ﴿He placed in it firm mountains from above it, and blessed it, and measured in it its sustenance, in four days, equal for those who ask﴾ [Fussilat: 9–10] [[See vol. 15, p. 342.]]. He says: whoever asks, the matter is thus. ﴿Then He turned to the heaven and it was smoke﴾, and that smoke was from the breath of the water when it breathed. He made it one heaven, then split it and made it seven heavens in two days, on Thursday and Friday. It was called Friday only because in it the creation of the heavens and the earth was gathered. ﴿And He revealed in each heaven its command﴾ [Fussilat: 12]. He said: He created in each heaven its creatures, from the angels and the creation that is in it, from the seas, the mountains of hail, and what is not known. Then He adorned the lowest heaven with the stars, making them an adornment and a protection, guarding against the devils.

When He had finished creating what He loved, He established Himself upon the Throne. He said: That is when He says: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾ [al-Hadid: 4], and He says: ﴿The heavens and the earth were joined together, and We split them apart﴾ [al-Anbiya': 30]. He mentioned the story of the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, as will come in its explanation in this surah, God willing.

Waki' related from al-A'mash, from Abu Zabyan, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The first thing God created was the Pen, and He said to it: Write. It said: O Lord, what shall I write? He said: Write the decree. So it ran with what will be until the Hour rises.

He said: Then He created the *nun*, and He spread out the earth upon it, and the vapor of the water rose, and from it He split the heavens. The *nun* moved, and the earth shook, so it was made firm with the mountains, for the mountains boast over the earth until the Day of Resurrection.

In this report, the creation of the earth is before the rising of the vapor of water, which is the smoke, contrary to the first report.

The first report, from him and from others, is more preferable, because of His saying: ﴿And the earth after that He spread out﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 30] [[See vol. 19, p. 202.]]. God knows best what He did. Opinions have differed concerning it, and there is no room for independent reasoning (*ijtihad*) in it.

Abu Nu'aym related from Ka'b al-Ahbar that Iblis slipped into the fish upon whose back is the whole earth, and cast into its heart, saying: Do you know what is upon your back, O Luthiya, of nations, trees, beasts, people, and mountains? If you shook them off, you would cast them all from your back. He said: Luthiya resolved to do that, so God sent a creature which entered into his nostril, and he cried out to God because of it, and it came out. Ka'b said: By Him in whose hand my soul is, it looks at it before its eyes, and it looks at him; if he intends anything of that, it returns to where it was.

The seventh issue: The origin of the creation of all things is water, based on what Ibn Majah related in his Sunan, and Abu Hatim al-Busti in his *Sahih Musnad*, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: I said: O Messenger of God, when I see you my soul is pleased and my eye is comforted, so inform me about everything. He said: (Everything was created from water). I said: Inform me of something that, if I act upon it, I will enter Paradise. He said: (Feed the food, spread the greeting of peace, keep the ties of kinship, and pray at night while people sleep, and you will enter Paradise in peace).

Abu Hatim said: Abu Hurayrah's saying, "Inform me about everything," meant: about everything that was created from water.

The evidence for the soundness of this is the answer of the Chosen One, peace be upon him, to him when he said: (Everything was created from water), even if it is not created [[The text here is as in the source.]].

Sa'id ibn Jubayr related from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to narrate that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: (The first thing God created was the Pen, and He commanded it, and it wrote everything that will be). This is also reported from 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit as a marfu' report [[*Marfu'* means traced directly to the Prophet (ﷺ).]].

Al-Bayhaqi said: What he meant, God knows best, is that the first thing He created after the water, the wind, and the Throne was the Pen. This is made clear in the hadith of 'Imran ibn Husayn: then He created the heavens and the earth.

'Abd al-Razzaq ibn 'Umar ibn Habib al-Makki mentioned, from Humayd ibn Qays al-A'raj, from Tawus, who said: A man came to 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As and asked him: Of what were creatures created? He said: From water, light, darkness, wind, and dust. The man said: Of what were these created? He said: I do not know. He said: Then the man went to 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr and asked him, and he said the same as 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr. He said: Then the man went to 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas and asked him, and he said: Of what were creatures created? He said: From water, light, darkness, wind, and dust. The man said: Of what were these created? Then 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas recited: ﴿And He subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, all of it from Him﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 13]. The man said: No one could have brought this except a man from the household of the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Bayhaqi said: He meant that the source of all of it is from Him, that is, from His creation, His origination, and His invention. He created water first, or water and whatever else He willed of His creation, without a root and without a pattern that preceded. Then He made it a root for what He created afterward. He is the Originator and the Maker; there is no god but Him, and no creator besides Him, glorified is He, Mighty and Majestic.

The eighth issue: His saying: ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens﴾. He mentioned that the heavens are seven.

No explicit number for the earth in the revelation has come that does not admit of interpretation, except His saying: ﴿And of the earth, the like of them﴾ [al-Talaq: 12]. This has been disputed. It was said: "And of the earth the like of them" means in number, because the manner and attributes differ by observation and reports, so the number is determined. It was said: "And of the earth the like of them" means in their thickness and what is between them. It was said: They are seven, except that some of them have not been split from others; this was said by al-Dawudi.

The correct view is the first, that they are seven just as the heavens are seven.

Muslim related from Sa'id ibn Zayd, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: (Whoever takes a span of land unjustly will have it hung around his neck from seven earths). It is also reported from 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her, similarly, except that in it "min" replaces "ila". And from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah: (No one takes a span of land without its right except that God will hang it around him to seven earths [on the Day of Resurrection [[The addition is from Sahih Muslim.]]]).

al-Nasa'i related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: (Musa, peace be upon him, said: O Lord, teach me something by which I may remember You and call upon You. He said: O Musa, say: There is no god but God. Musa said: O Lord, all Your servants say this. He said: Say: There is no god but God. He said: There is no god but You; I only want something specific to me. He said: O Musa, if the seven heavens and their inhabitants other than Me, and the seven earths, were placed in one pan, and there is no god but God in the other pan, it would outweigh them: there is no god but God).

al-Tirmidhi related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: While the Prophet of God (ﷺ) was sitting with his companions, a cloud came over them. The Prophet of God (ﷺ) said: (Do you know what this is?) They said: God and His Messenger know best. He said: (This is the *anan* [cloud]; these are the water-carriers of the earth, which God drives to a people who do not thank Him nor call upon Him). He said: (Do you know what is above you?) They said: God and His Messenger know best. He said: (It is the *raqi'* [[*Raqi'* is the name of the lowest heaven.]], a protected ceiling and a restrained wave). Then he said: (Do you know how far between you and it?) They said: God and His Messenger know best. He said: (Between you and it is a distance [[Supplement from Sahih al-Tirmidhi.]] of five hundred years). Then he said: (Do you know what is above that?) They said: God and His Messenger know best. He said: ([Above that are two heavens [[Supplement from Sahih al-Tirmidhi.]], the distance between them is a distance [[Supplement from Sahih al-Tirmidhi.]] of five hundred years]), and he said so until he counted seven heavens, between every two heavens is what is between the heaven and the earth.

Then he said: (Do you know what is above that?) They said: God and His Messenger know best. He said: (Above that is the Throne, and between it and the heaven is the distance between two heavens). Then he said: (Do you know what is beneath you?) They said: God and His Messenger know best. He said: (It is the earth). Then he said: (Do you know what is beneath that?) They said:

Allah and His Messenger know best, he said:

(Indeed, beneath it is the other earth, between them a journey of five hundred years), until he counted seven earths, between every two earths a journey of five hundred years. Then he said:

(By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, if you were to lower a rope to the lowest earth, it would descend upon Allah." Then he recited: ﴿He is the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward, and He is All-Knowing of everything﴾.)

Abu Isa [al-Tirmidhi] said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ's recitation of the verse indicates that he meant: "It would descend upon the knowledge of Allah, His power and His authority [[addition from Sahih al-Tirmidhi.]] in every place, while He is upon His Throne, as He described Himself in His Book."

He said: This is a gharib (rare) hadith, and al-Hasan did not hear from Abu Hurayra.

The reports that the earths are seven are numerous, and what we have mentioned is sufficient.

Abu al-Duha, whose name is Muslim, narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said, regarding ﴿Allah is He who created seven heavens and of the earth their like﴾ [al-Talaq: 12]: "Seven earths, and in each earth is a prophet like your prophet, and Adam like Adam, Nuh like Nuh, Ibrahim like Ibrahim, and Isa like Isa."

Al-Bayhaqi said: The chain of this report from Ibn Abbas is sahih, but it is shadhdh (anomalous) in its single transmission; I know of no supporting evidence for Abu al-Duha on it [[In one copy of the original: (mutaba'an, i.e., corroborated).]]. And Allah knows best.

The ninth issue: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿He is the One who created for you all that is on the earth﴾. It is a subject and predicate (mubtada' and khabar).

"Ma" (what) is in the accusative position.

"Jami'an" (all), according to Sibawayh, is accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

"Thumma istawa" (then He rose): the people of Najd incline the vowel (imalah) to show that it is from the verbs with a ya' (dhawat al-ya'), while the people of the Hijaz use the emphatic (tafkhim) pronunciation.

"Sab'a" (seven) is in the accusative as an apposition (badal) of the ha' and nun, meaning: "so He made them seven heavens."

It may also be an object (maf'ul) with an implied verb, "yusawwi baynahunna sab'a samawat" (He arranged among them seven heavens), as Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And Musa chose from his people seventy men﴾ [al-A'raf: 155], meaning from among his people. Thus said al-Nahhas.

Al-Akhfash said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

"Wa huwa bi-kulli shay'in 'alim" (and He is All-Knowing of everything) is a subject and predicate.

The original form of "huwa" is with a vowelled ha', and the sukun (silent) pronunciation is for lightening.

The word "sama'" (heaven) may be singular and feminine, like 'anan (cloud), and its masculine usage is shadhdh (anomalous). It may be a plural of sama'a according to al-Akhfash, and of sama'a according to al-Zajjaj, and the plural of the plural is sama'at and sama'at.

"Sawwahunna" comes either because sama' is a plural, or because it is the singular of a collective noun (ism jins).

The meaning of "sawwahunna" is: He made their surfaces smooth and level. It was also said: He made them equal.

The tenth issue: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And He is All-Knowing of everything﴾, meaning: of what He created. He is the Creator of everything, so it is necessary that He be Knowing of everything. He said: ﴿Does not He who created know?﴾ [al-Mulk: 14]. He is the Knower (al-'Alim) and the Knowing (al-'Alim) of all knowable things, with an eternal, pre-existent, single knowledge subsisting in His essence. The Mu'tazila agreed with us on His being Knower, but not on His being possessed of knowledge (al-'ilmiyya). The Jahmiyya said: He is Knower by a knowledge subsisting not in any locus, exalted is Allah above the saying of the people of deviation and misguidance. The refutation of these people is in the books on creeds.

He, glorified is He, described Himself with knowledge, saying: ﴿He has sent it down with His knowledge, and the angels bear witness﴾ [al-Nisa': 166], and He said: ﴿So know that it was sent down with the knowledge of Allah﴾ [Hud: 14], and He said: ﴿Then We will surely relate to them with knowledge﴾ [al-A'raf: 7], and He said: ﴿And no female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge﴾ [Fatir: 11], and He said: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them except Him﴾ [al-An'am: 59], the verse. We will show the establishment of His knowledge and His other attributes in this surah, at His saying: ﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], if Allah wills.

Al-Kisa'i and Qalun, from Nafi', read with sukun (silencing) the ha' of "huwa" and "hiya" when preceded by a fa', waw, lam, or thumma. Abu Amr did likewise except with thumma. Abu Awn, from al-Halwani, from Qalun, added the sukun of the ha' in "an yumilla huwa" (that he dictate). The rest read with the vowel.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 30 (part 1 of 5):

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I am going to place upon the earth a vicegerent"﴾. In this there are seventeen issues.

The first issue: His saying, Exalted is He, "And when your Lord said to the angels." Idh (إذ) and idha (إذا) are both particles of time: idh is for the past and idha is for the future, though one may sometimes be placed in the position of the other. Al-Mubarrad said: when idh is used with a future verb, its meaning is past, as in His saying, ﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾ [al-Anfal: 30] and ﴿And when you said to the one on whom Allah had bestowed favor﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37]; its meaning is "when they plotted" and "when you said." And when idha is used with a past verb, its meaning is future, as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So when the Great Calamity comes﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 34], ﴿So when the deafening blast comes﴾ [Abasa: 33], and ﴿When the victory of Allah has come﴾ [al-Nasr: 1], meaning "when it comes." Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna Abu 'Ubaydah said: idh is superfluous (za'idah), and the implied sense is "And your Lord said," citing the verse of al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur:

"Then (fa-idha) that is not something whose remembrance is to be forgotten... and time follows the good with corruption."

[Note: the reading of the line is (fa-idha). The meter does not hold except with it.]

Al-Zajjaj and al-Nahhas and all the exegetes rejected this view. Al-Nahhas said: this is an error, because idh is a noun and is a temporal adverb, and it is not among the things that are added as superfluous. Al-Zajjaj said: this is a transgression by Abu 'Ubaydah. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned the creation of mankind and others, so the implied sense is "and He began your creation when He said," and so this is part of what is omitted that the speech indicates, as he said:

"Indeed, whoever fears death... it will overtake him wherever"

meaning "wherever he goes." It is possible that it is linked to an implied verb whose estimate is "and remember when He said." It has also been said: it refers back to His saying, ﴿Worship your Lord who created you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21]; the meaning then is "who created you when your Lord said to the angels." The saying of Allah, Exalted is He, and His address to the angels is an established, eternal (qadim) matter from pre-eternity, on condition of their existence and their understanding. The whole chapter is likewise regarding the commands, prohibitions and addresses of Allah, Exalted is He. This is the position of Shaykh Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, and it is what Abu al-Ma'ali approved. We have discussed it in the book al-Asna fi Sharh Asma' Allah al-Husna wa Sifat Allah al-'Ula. Al-Rabb means the owner, the master, the one who sets right, and the one who mends; its explanation has already preceded [see the eighth issue and what follows, p. 136 of this part].

The second issue: His saying, Exalted is He, "to the angels" (al-mala'ikah). Its singular is malak (ملك). Ibn Kaysan and others said: the form of malak is fa'al from al-mulk (possession/sovereignty). Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is maf'al from la'aka, meaning "he sent." Al-ala'akah, al-ma'lakah and al-ma'lukah mean "message," as Labid said:

"And a youth whose mother sent him with a message, so we gave what he asked."

Another said [this is 'Adi ibn Zayd, as in Lisan al-'Arab, root (أ ل ك). It is narrated as (innahu) instead of (inni)]:

"Convey from me to al-Nu'man a message: indeed, my imprisonment and waiting have lasted long."

It is said: "alikni," meaning "send me." So its origin according to this is ma'lak, the hamzah being the first radical of the verb, and they moved it to the place of the eye, saying ml'ak, then they eased it, saying malak. It has also been said its origin is mal'ak, from malaka yamliku, like sham'al from shamala; so the hamzah is superfluous, according to Ibn Kaysan also. It may appear in poetry in its original form, as the poet said:

"You are not human, but an angel (malak) that descended from the air of the sky, alighting."

Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: "There is no derivation (ishtiqaq) for the word *malak* (angel) among the Arabs." The *ha'* in *al-malā'ikah* is an intensifier of the feminine plural, and similar to it is *al-ṣalādimah*. *Al-ṣalādim* means hard horses, and its singular is *ṣilidim*. It was also said that the *ha'* is for emphasis (mubalaghah), as in *allamah* and *nassabah*.

The scholars of meanings (arbab al-ma'ani) said: God addressed the angels not for consultation, but to draw out what was within them of observing their movements, worship, glorification and sanctification. Then He returned them to their true worth, saying, "Mighty and Majestic is He": ﴿Prostrate yourselves to Adam﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:34].

The third point: His saying, ﴿Indeed I am placing on the earth a khalifah (vicegerent)﴾. "Ja'il" (placing) here means "creating" (khaliq). This was mentioned by al-Tabari from Abu Rawq, and its transitivity to one object supports this, as has already been discussed. It was said that "the earth" refers to Makkah. Ibn Sabit reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The earth was spread out (dahiyat) from Makkah," and for this reason it is called Umm al-Qura (Mother of Towns). He said: The graves of Nuh, Hud, Salih and Shu'ayb are between Zamzam, the Corner (al-Rukn) and the Station (al-Maqam).

*Khalifah* may mean an agent (bi-ma'na fa'il), i.e., one who succeeds whoever was before him among the angels on the earth, or whoever was before him among non-angels, as has been narrated. It is also possible that *khalifah* means a passive object (bi-ma'na maf'ul), i.e., one who is succeeded (mukhlaf), as one says *dhabihah* meaning *madhbuhah* (slaughtered). *Khalaf* (with a fatha on the lam) refers to righteous successors, and *khalf* (with a sukun) to wicked successors; this is the known usage. More detailed explanation will come in al-A'raf, God willing [see vol. 7, p. 310]. The reading *khalifah* with the fa' is the reading of the majority, except what was narrated from Zayd ibn 'Ali, who read *khaliqah* with the qaf.

The one meant by *khalifah* here, according to the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and all the commentators, is Adam (peace be upon him). He is the vicegerent of God in carrying out His judgments and commands, because he was the first messenger to the earth, as in the hadith of Abu Dharr, who said: I said, "O Messenger of God, was he a messenger?" He said, "Yes..." (the hadith). It is said: How could he be a messenger when there was no one else on the earth? It is answered: He was a messenger to his children, and they were forty children in twenty wombs, a male and a female in each womb. They multiplied until they became many, as God the Exalted said: ﴿He created you from a single soul and created from it its mate and spread from both of them many men and women﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:1] [see vol. 4, p. 2]. He sent down to them the prohibition of carrion, blood and the flesh of swine. He lived nine hundred and thirty years, as the People of the Torah mention. It was narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih that he lived a thousand years, and God knows best.

Fourth: this verse is a basis for appointing an imam and khalifah who is listened to and obeyed, so that the community is united under him and the rulings of the caliphate are carried out. There is no disagreement among the community or among the scholars regarding the obligation of this, except what was narrated from al-Asamm [al-Asamm: one of the great Mu'tazilites, whose name was Abu Bakr], who, regarding the Law, was deaf (asamm 'an al-shari'ah). Likewise, everyone who agreed with his view, followed him in his opinion and school, said: it is not obligatory in religion; rather, it is permissible, and that if the community establishes their pilgrimage and jihad, act justly among themselves, give the truth from themselves, divide the spoils, the fay' and the alms to their rightful recipients, and enforce the prescribed punishments upon those who deserve them, that suffices them, and it is not obligatory for them to appoint an imam to take charge of this.

Our proof is the saying of God the Exalted: ﴿Indeed I am placing on the earth a khalifah﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:30], and His saying: ﴿O Dawud, indeed We have made you a khalifah on the earth﴾ [Sad 38:26], and He said: ﴿God has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors (la-yastakhlifannahum) in the earth﴾ [al-Nur 24:55], meaning He will make them khulafa' (successors), along with other verses. The Companions unanimously agreed upon giving precedence to al-Siddiq (Abu Bakr) after a disagreement arose between the Muhajirun and the Ansar at the Saqifah of Banu Sa'idah about the appointment, to the point that the Ansar said: "From us a commander, and from you a commander." Abu Bakr, 'Umar and the Muhajirun repelled them from this and said to them: "The Arabs will not submit except to this clan of Quraysh," and they related the report on this matter to them. So they returned and obeyed Quraysh. Had the obligation of the imamate not been binding, neither in Quraysh nor in others, this debate and discussion over it would not have been justified, and someone would have said: "It is not obligatory, neither in Quraysh nor in others, so your dispute has no purpose and there is no benefit in a matter that is not obligatory." Then, when al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, was approaching death, he appointed 'Umar as imam, and no one said to him: "This is a matter not obligatory upon us or upon you." This indicates its obligation, and that it is a pillar of the religion upon which the Muslims are sustained. Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds.

The Rafidah (Rafidites) said: its appointment is obligatory by reason ('aql), and that the revelation (sam') came only as emphasis for a matter already established by reason. As for knowing the imam, that is known through revelation alone and not through reason. This is false, because reason does not make anything obligatory, forbid it, call it ugly, or call it good; and if that is so, it is established that it is obligatory by the Law (shar') and not by reason, and this is clear.

If it is said, and this is the fifth point: Even if we accept that the path to the obligation of the imamate is revelation, tell us: is it obligatory through revelation by explicit designation (nass) of the imam from the Messenger (ﷺ), or through the choice of the people of loosening and binding (ahl al-hall wa al-'aqd), or through the complete qualities of imams being in him, with his calling himself to it being sufficient? The answer: people have differed on this matter. The Imamiyyah (Imami Shi'a) and others maintained that the way by which the imam is known is the explicit designation (nass) from the Messenger (peace be upon him), and there is no place for choice in it. For us: reflection (nazar) is a way to knowing the imam, and the consensus of the scholars qualified for independent judgment (ijtihad) is also a way to it. Those who said there is no way to it except explicit designation built this on their principle that analogy (qiyas), opinion (ra'y) and independent judgment (ijtihad) are invalid and that nothing is known by them at all; they invalidated analogy in both its root and branch. Then they differed into three groups: one group claims an explicit designation for Abu Bakr, another claims an explicit designation for al-'Abbas, and another claims an explicit designation for 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with them all.

The proof of the absence or non-existence of an explicit designation for a specific imam is that if the Prophet (ﷺ) had made obedience to a specific imam obligatory upon the community, in such a way that it is not permissible to turn away from him to another, this would have been known, because it is impossible for the whole community to be charged with obeying God regarding an unspecified person, and they have no way to know that obligation. If knowledge of it was required, that knowledge must have come either through rational proofs or through report. Reason contains nothing that proves the imamate of a specific person, and likewise there is nothing in report that necessitates knowledge of the establishment of a specific imam, because that report is either mass-transmitted (mutawatir), producing necessary knowledge or knowledge by inference, or it is a single report (khabar al-ahad). It is not possible that its path was mass transmission producing necessary knowledge or knowledge by inference, for if it were so, every responsible person would find within himself knowledge of the obligation to obey that specific person and that this is from the religion of God for him, just as every responsible person knows that among the religion of God obligatory upon him are five prayers, fasting in Ramadan, pilgrimage to the House and the like, and no one knows this from himself by necessity. So this claim is void, and it is also void that it could be known through single reports, because knowledge of it is impossible to occur that way.

Furthermore, if it were necessary to rely on transmission of an explicit designation of the imam by any means whatsoever, it would be necessary to establish the imamate of Abu Bakr and al-'Abbas, because each of them has a people who transmit an explicit designation of his imamate. Since the establishment of all three by explicit designation is void at one time (as its explanation will follow), likewise the single one is void, since none of the groups is more entitled to an explicit designation than the other. When the establishment of explicit designation is void for lack of a path leading to it, choice and independent judgment are established.

If someone insists and claims mass transmission and necessary knowledge of the explicit designation, then immediately they should be confronted with the opposite of their claim regarding the explicit designation for Abu Bakr, and with many reports on this matter which also, taken together, stand in the place of an explicit designation. Furthermore, there is no doubt in the determination of all those other than the Imamiyyah to deny an explicit designation, and they are a vast multitude and a great throng. Necessary knowledge is not gathered in denying it by those who fall short of a tenth of the numbers of the opponents of the Imamiyyah, and if it were permissible to reject necessary knowledge in this matter, it would be permissible for a group in Baghdad, in the far East (al-Sin al-Aqsa) and elsewhere to deny it.

Sixth: regarding the rejection of the hadiths by which the Imamiyyah argued for the explicit designation of 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, and that the community disbelieved in this explicit designation, apostatized, and opposed the Messenger's command out of obstinacy. Among them is his saying (peace be upon him): "Whoever I am his mawla (master/patron), then 'Ali is his mawla. O God, befriend whoever befriends him and be an enemy to whoever is his enemy." They said: *al-mawla* in language means *awla* (more entitled), so when he said "then 'Ali is his mawla" with the fa' of consequence, it is known that by "mawla" he meant that he is more entitled and more worthy. Therefore it must be that he intended by that the imamate, and that he is one whose obedience is obligatory. And his saying (peace be upon him) to 'Ali: "You are to me in the position of Harun to Musa, except that there is no prophet after me." They said: The position of Harun is well known: he was a partner to him in prophethood, and this was not for 'Ali; he was a brother to him, and this was not for 'Ali; and he was a khalifah, so it is known that what is meant by it is the caliphate, and so on regarding other things they argued for, as will be mentioned in this book, God willing.

The answer to the first hadith: It is not mass-transmitted, and its authenticity is disputed. Abu Dawud al-Sijistani and Abu Hatim al-Razi criticized it, and they argued for its invalidity by the fact that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Muzaynah, Juhaynah, Ghifar and Aslam are clients (mawali) apart from all people; they have no mawla apart from God and His Messenger." They said: If he had said, "Whoever I am his mawla, then 'Ali is his mawla," one of the two reports would be false.

Second answer: Even if the report is sound, transmitted by a trustworthy narrator from a trustworthy one, there is nothing in it that indicates his imamate; it only indicates his excellence. This is because *mawla* means *wali* (protector/friend), so the meaning of the report would be: "Whoever I am his wali, then 'Ali is his wali." God the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed God is his mawla﴾ [al-Tahrim 66:4], meaning his wali. The purpose of the report was that people should know that 'Ali's outward is like his inward, and that is a great virtue for 'Ali.

Third answer: This report was given on a specific occasion, namely that Usamah and 'Ali disputed, and 'Ali said to Usamah: "You are my mawla." He said: "I am not your mawla; rather, I am the mawla of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)." This was mentioned to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: "Whoever I am his mawla, then 'Ali is his mawla."

Fourth answer: When 'Ali (peace be upon him) said to the Prophet (ﷺ) in the story of the slander concerning 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her: "Women other than her are many."

...the people of hypocrisy found an opening, so they criticised him and openly declared their disavowal of him. The Prophet (ﷺ) said this statement in reply to their words and to refute their claims of disavowal of him and their slander against him. For this reason, it has been related from a group of the Companions that they said:
"We did not know the hypocrites during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) except by their hatred of ʿAlī (peace be upon him)."

As for the second hadith, there is no disagreement that the Prophet (ﷺ) did not mean by the status of Hārūn in relation to Mūsā (peace be upon them both) the caliphate after him. There is also no disagreement that Hārūn died before Mūsā (peace be upon them both), as will come in the explanation of their deaths in surah al-Mā'idah [see vol. 6, p. 131]. Hārūn was not a caliph after him; rather, the successor was Yūshaʿ ibn Nūn. Had he intended by his words, "You are to me in the position of Hārūn to Mūsā," the caliphate, he would have said, "You are to me in the position of Yūshaʿ to Mūsā." Since he did not say this, it shows that he did not intend this. He only meant, "I have appointed you as my deputy over my family during my life and during my absence from my family, just as Hārūn was Mūsā's deputy over his people when he went out to converse with his Lord."

It has also been said:
This hadith was issued on a particular occasion. When the Prophet (ﷺ) set out for the Battle of Tabūk, he appointed ʿAlī (peace be upon him) as his deputy in Madīnah over his family and people. The hypocrites spread rumours about this and said, "He only left him behind out of hatred and dislike for him." ʿAlī went out and caught up with the Prophet (ﷺ) and said to him, "The hypocrites have said such and such!"
He said, "They lied. Rather, I have left you behind as Mūsā left Hārūn behind."
And he said, "Are you not pleased to be to me in the position of Hārūn to Mūsā?"

If it is established that he intended appointing a deputy according to their claim, then others shared this virtue with ʿAlī, because the Prophet (ﷺ) appointed a man from among his Companions as deputy in every campaign he undertook. Among them were Ibn Umm Maktūm, Muḥammad ibn Maslamah and others from his Companions. Moreover, the transmission of this report rests on Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqās, and it is a single report (khabar wāḥid).

It is also related, in contrast to it, concerning Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, something that is more deserving than it. It is related that when the Prophet (ﷺ) sent Muʿādh ibn Jabal to Yemen, it was said to him, "Will you not send Abū Bakr and ʿUmar?"
He said, "They are indispensable to me. Their position with respect to me is that of hearing and sight to the head."
And he said, "They are my two ministers among the people of the earth."
And it is related from him (peace be upon him) that he said, "Abū Bakr and ʿUmar are in the position of Hārūn to Mūsā."
This report was issued without a specific occasion, whereas the report about ʿAlī was issued on a specific occasion. Therefore, it is necessary that Abū Bakr is more deserving than him of the imamate. And Allah knows best.

The Seventh Issue:
There is disagreement concerning what makes a leader (imām) an imam, and this is in three ways. The first is:
Explicit designation (naṣṣ). The disagreement about it has already been mentioned. It is also upheld by the Ḥanbalīs, a group of the people of ḥadīth, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Bakr ibn Ukht ʿAbd al-Wāḥid and his followers, and a group of the Khawārij.

This is because the Prophet (ﷺ) designated Abū Bakr by indication, and Abū Bakr designated ʿUmar.

When the one who appoints a successor designates one specific person, as the Ṣiddīq did, or designates a group, as ʿUmar did, which is the second way, the choice among them in determining one of them is left to them, as the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) did [in determining ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān (may Allah be pleased with him)].[[Addition in al-ʿAllāmī's tafsir, quoting al-Qurṭubī.]]

The Third Way:
The consensus (ijmāʿ) of the people who loosen and bind (ahl al-ḥall wa al-ʿaqd), meaning the qualified leaders of the community who make binding decisions. This is because if the leader of a community in one of the cities of the Muslims dies, and there is no leader for them and he has not appointed a successor, then the people of that city, which is the seat and location of the imam, appoint an imam for themselves. They gather around him and accept him. Every Muslim behind them and in front of them in the regions is obliged to enter into obedience to that imam, provided the imam is not openly defiant or corrupt. This is because it is a comprehensive call which must be answered, and no one may hold back from it, due to the discord and disruption of unity that would result from appointing two imams. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:
"Three things in which a believer's heart will not harbour deceit (yughillu): sincerity of deed for Allah, adherence to the community, and giving sincere counsel to the rulers. For the call of the Muslims surrounds them from behind."[[It is narrated as "yughillu" with a damma on the yāʾ and kasra on the ghayn, meaning that there is no deceit, cunning or hypocrisy in the heart with them. It is also narrated with a fatḥa on the yāʾ, meaning that no resentment enters it which turns it away from the truth.]]

The Eighth Issue:
If one of the people who loosen and bind concludes the pledge, then that is valid and binding on others to follow, unlike some people who said, "It is not concluded except by a group of the people who loosen and bind." Our evidence is that ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) concluded the pledge (bayʿah) to Abū Bakr, and none of the Companions denied that. Also, it is a contract, so it must not require a specific number to conclude it, like all other contracts.

Imam Abū al-Maʿālī said:
Whoever has been granted the imamate by one contract, it becomes binding, and it is not permissible to depose him without a cause and a change in circumstances. He said:
"This is agreed upon."

The Ninth Issue:
If someone who is qualified for the imamate seizes it by force and domination, it has been said that this constitutes a fourth way. Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Tustarī was asked:
"What is obligatory upon us toward one who has prevailed over our lands and is an imam?"
He said:
"You respond to him, pay him what he demands of your rights, do not denounce his actions, do not flee from him, and if he entrusts you with a secret of religious matters, do not disclose it."

Ibn Khuwayz Mandād said:
"If someone suitable for the position leaps to it without consultation or selection, and the people pay allegiance to him, the pledge is complete for him." And Allah knows best.

The Tenth Issue:
There is disagreement about testimony (shahādah) on the conclusion of the imamate. Some of our companions said that it does not require witnesses, because testimony is only established by certain hearing, and there is no certain hearing here that establishes testimony.

Others said that it requires witnesses. Whoever holds this view argues that if testimony were not established for it, it would lead to every claimant[[In al-ʿAllāmī's tafsir: "innovator" (mubtadiʿ).]] claiming that he had been secretly granted the pledge, and this would lead to chaos and turmoil. Therefore testimony must be taken into account, and two witnesses suffice for it. This is contrary to al-Jubbāʾī, who required four witnesses, plus the one who concludes the contract and the one to whom it is concluded. His argument is that ʿUmar, when he made it a council (shūrā) among six, indicated this.[[The six are those whom ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) advised the Muslims to choose one of them for the leadership after him, when he was asked to appoint a successor. They are: ʿAlī, ʿUthmān, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf, Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwām and Ṭalḥah ibn ʿUbayd Allāh. See the story of the shūrā in Ibn al-Athīr's History (vol. 3, p. 50), printed in Europe.]]

Our evidence is that there is no disagreement between us and him that the testimony of two is valid, and anything beyond that is disputed and is not indicated by evidence, so it must not be considered.

The Eleventh Issue:
Concerning the conditions of the imam, which are eleven:

The First: that he be of the pure lineage of Quraysh, based on his (ﷺ) saying: "The imams are from Quraysh."
There has been disagreement regarding this.[[The text here appears to have a gap; the second condition follows.]]

The Second: that he be one who is qualified to serve as a judge among the judges of the Muslims, a mujtahid who does not need anyone else in seeking rulings on new matters. This is agreed upon.

The Third: that he be experienced and possess sound judgement regarding warfare, the management of armies, securing frontiers, protecting the "egg" (bayḍah), meaning the community,[[Bayḍat al-Islām: its community.]] deterring the nation, avenging the wronged and taking from the oppressor on behalf of the oppressed.

The Fourth: that he be one whom no weakness affects in carrying out the hudūd (fixed punishments), nor any fear of striking necks or cutting limbs.

The proof for all of this is the consensus of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), since there is no disagreement among them that all of this must be combined in him. Also, he is the one who appoints judges and governors, and he has the right to personally carry out judgement and ruling, and to examine the affairs of his deputies and judges. Only one who knows all of this and is competent in it can be suitable for all of that.
And Allah knows best.

The Fifth: that he be free. There is no doubt about the condition that the imam be free.
The Sixth: that he be Muslim.
The Seventh: that he be male, sound in his faculties.
The Eighth: [the same as the seventh, which is the eighth in count].

They agreed that a woman may not be an imam, though they differed on whether she may serve as a judge in matters where her testimony is accepted.

The Ninth and Tenth: that he be adult and sane. There is no disagreement on this.

The Eleventh: that he be just (ʿadl). There is no disagreement among the community that the imamate may not be conferred on a sinner. He must be among the most knowledgeable of them, based on his (peace be upon him) saying: "Your imams are your intercessors, so look at whom you seek intercession through."

In the revelation, describing Ṭālūt (Saul):
﴿Indeed, Allah has chosen him over you and increased him broadly in knowledge and physique﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:247] [see vol. 3, p. 246]. He mentioned knowledge first, then mentioned what indicates strength and soundness of the limbs.

His words "chosen" (iṣṭafāhu) mean "selected him," and this indicates the condition of lineage.

It is not a condition that he be protected from error and mistakes, nor that he know the unseen, nor that he be the most skilled horseman or the bravest of the nation, nor that he be from the Banū Hāshim alone to the exclusion of the rest of Quraysh, since consensus has been reached on the imamate of Abū Bakr and ʿUthmān, and they were not from the Banū Hāshim.

The Twelfth Issue:
It is permissible to appoint a less excellent person while a more excellent one exists, out of fear of strife and that the affairs of the community would not be set right. This is because the imam is appointed only to repel the enemy, protect the community, close gaps, recover rights, establish the hudūd, and collect funds for the treasury and distribute them to their rightful recipients.

If it is feared that appointing the most excellent would lead to chaos, corruption, and the neglect of the matters for which the imam is appointed, then that is a clear excuse for turning from the excellent to the less excellent. This is also indicated by the knowledge of ʿUmar and the rest of the community at the time of the shūrā that among the six there was one excellent and one less excellent, and he permitted the contract for each one of them when it served the public interest and their opinion converged upon him, with no one objecting to them. And Allah knows best.

The Thirteenth Issue:
If an imam is appointed and then commits sin after the contract is firmly concluded, the majority said that his imamate is terminated and he is deposed for open and known sin, because it has been established that the imam is appointed to establish the hudūd, enforce rights, guard the property of orphans and the insane, and look after their affairs, and other matters mentioned earlier. Sin in him prevents him from carrying out these duties and fulfilling them.

If we permitted him to be a sinner, it would lead to nullifying the purpose for which he was established. Do you not see that at the outset it was not permitted to conclude the contract for a sinner precisely because it would nullify the purpose for which he was appointed? The same applies here.

Others said: he is not deposed except for disbelief (kufr), or for abandoning the prayer, or for abandoning calling to it, or any part of the Sharīʿah, based on the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him) in the hadith of ʿUbādah: "And that we not dispute the affair with its people [he said[[Addition from Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim (vol. 6, p. 17), printed in Istanbul. And "bawāḥan" means openly, from "bāḥa bi al-shay'" when one makes it known.]]: except when you see manifest disbelief (kufran bawāḥan) with you, for which you have proof from Allah."

And in the hadith of Awf ibn Malik: (No, as long as they establish the prayer among you), and the hadith in full. Muslim recorded both.

And from Umm Salamah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "There will be rulers appointed over you, and you will recognise some of their deeds and disapprove of others. Whoever hates [their wrongdoing] is free of blame, and whoever denounces it is safe, but whoever approves of it and follows it [is not safe]." They said: "O Messenger of God, should we not fight them?" He said: "No, as long as they pray." (That is, one who hates [their wrongdoing] in his heart and denounces it in his heart.) Muslim also recorded this.

The Fourteenth Issue: A leader must step down if he finds in himself a deficiency that affects the imamate (leadership of the community). If he finds no such deficiency, may he dismiss himself and appoint someone else? People differ on this. Some said: he may not do so, and if he does, his imamate is not terminated. Others said: he may do so. The evidence that an imam who dismisses himself is dismissed is the statement of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him: "Relieve me, relieve me." And the statement of the Companions: "We will neither dismiss you nor ask you to resign. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) advanced you for our religion, so who could delay you? The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was pleased with you for our religion, so we will not be displeased with you!" Had he not been permitted to do this, the Companions would have rejected it from him and said: "You are not permitted to say this, and you are not permitted to do it." Since the Companions approved of this, it is known that the imam may do so. Also, the imam is a guardian of the absent [[In some manuscripts: "of others."]], so his ruling should be the ruling of a judge and of an agent (wakil) who dismisses himself. The imam is the agent of the community and its deputy. It is agreed that an agent, a judge, and anyone who acts on another's behalf in any matter may dismiss himself, and likewise the imam should be the same. And God knows best.

The Fifteenth Issue: When the imamate is established by the consensus of the people who loosen and bind (ahl al-hall wa'l-'aqd, the notables whose choice is binding), or by one person as mentioned earlier, it becomes obligatory on all people to pledge allegiance to him, to hear and obey him, and to uphold the Book of God and the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ). Whoever refuses to pledge allegiance for a valid excuse is excused, and whoever refuses without an excuse is compelled and subdued, so that the word of the Muslims does not become divided. If allegiance is given to two caliphs, the first is the caliph and the other is to be killed. It is disputed whether this killing is literal or metaphorical, so that his removal is his killing and his death. The first view is the more evident. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "If allegiance is given to two caliphs, kill the other of them." Narrated by Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, recorded by Muslim.

In the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he heard him say: "Whoever pledges allegiance to an imam, giving him the handshake of his hand and the fruit of his heart, let him obey him if he is able. If another comes to dispute with him, strike the neck of the other." Muslim also recorded it. And in the hadith of Arfajah: "Strike him with the sword, whoever he may be." This is the strongest evidence against establishing two imams. Also, that leads to discord, opposition, division, the emergence of strife, and the loss of blessings. However, if the regions are far apart and distinct, such as al-Andalus and Khurasan, it is permissible, as will be explained, God willing.

The Sixteenth Issue: If a Kharijite (rebel) rises against an imam known for his justice, it is obligatory on the people to fight him. If the imam is a sinner and the rebel displays justice, the people should not hasten to support the rebel until his matter is clarified regarding the justice he displays, or until the community agrees on deposing the first. This is because everyone who seeks such a position shows himself as righteous until he gains power, then returns to his usual conduct contrary to what he displayed.

The Seventeenth Issue: As for appointing two or three imams in one era and one land, it is not permitted by consensus, for the reasons we have mentioned. Imam Abu al-Ma'ali said: "Our companions held that the imamate may not be conferred on two people at opposite ends of the world. Then they said: If the imamate is conferred on two people by coincidence, that is treated like two guardians marrying one woman to a husband without either one knowing of the other's contract." He said: "My view is that conferring the imamate on two people in one region with narrow districts and close quarters (al-makhalif: the outskirts and areas) is not permitted, and consensus has been reached on it. As for when the distance is great and a wide separation lies between the two imams, there is room for consideration in this, and it is outside the decisive matters." Abu Ishaq (al-Isfara'ini) used to permit this in two very distant regions, so that the rights and rulings of the people would not be suspended. The Karramiyya held that appointing two imams is permitted without distinction, and this would oblige them to permit it in one land. They also held that Ali and Mu'awiya were both imams. They said: "When there are two in two lands or two regions, each of them is better at managing what is in his hands and more precise in what is near him. Also, since sending two prophets in one era was permitted and did not invalidate prophecy, the imamate is more deserving of this, and it does not invalidate the imamate." The answer is that this would be permitted were it not for the prohibition by the Law, as in His words: "kill the other of them," and because the community agrees on it. As for Mu'awiya, he did not claim the imamate for himself; he only claimed the governorship of Syria by appointment from the imams before him. Evidence for this is the consensus of the community in their time that the imam is one of them, and neither of them said: "I am the imam, and my opponent is an imam." If they say: "Reason does not rule it out, and there is nothing in revelation that forbids it." We say: The strongest revelation is consensus, and it has been established against it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said: Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?﴾ We know with certainty that the angels know only what they are taught and do not speak before Him, and this is general for all angels, since His words "They do not precede Him in speech" were given in praise of them. So how did they say: "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?" It is said: The meaning is that when they heard the word "khalifah" (successor/vicegerent), they understood that among the children of Adam there would be one who causes corruption, since the purpose of a khalifah is reform and avoiding corruption. But they generalized the judgment of disobedience to all of them. So the Lord, exalted is He, made clear that among them are those who cause corruption and those who do not, and He said, to console their hearts: "Indeed I know." He confirmed this by teaching Adam the names and revealing to them the hidden of His knowledge. It is also said: The angels had seen and known the corruption and the shedding of blood by the jinn. The earth had jinn in it before the creation of Adam, and they caused corruption and shed blood, so God sent Iblis against them with a host of angels, and he killed them and drove them to the seas and mountaintops. From then on, pride entered him. So their words "Will You place in it" came as a pure question: Will this successor follow the way of those jinn who came before, or not? This is the view of Ahmad ibn Yahya Tha'lab. Ibn Zayd and others said: God informed them that a successor would come from his descendants, a people who would cause corruption on earth and shed blood, so they said this statement, either out of astonishment that God would appoint as successor one who disobeys Him, or at the disobedience of one whom God appoints as His successor on earth and blesses with that, or out of great reverence for both matters together: the appointment and the disobedience. Qatadah said: God had informed them that if He placed on earth creatures, they would cause corruption and shed blood. So when He said, "Indeed I am placing on the earth a khalifah," they asked whether this was the one He had informed them about or someone else.

This is a good view, narrated by Abd al-Razzaq, who said: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, concerning His words "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?" He said: God had informed them that if there were creatures on earth, they would cause corruption and shed blood, so that is why they said, "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?" There is an ellipsis in the speech according to his view, and the meaning is: "I am placing on earth a successor who does such and such," so they said: "Will You place in it the one You told us about, or someone else?" The first view is also very good, because it involves drawing out knowledge and deriving it from the implications of the words, and that is only done by scholars. What lies between the two views is good, so reflect on it. It has also been said: God's question to the angels, "How did you leave My servants?" as established in Sahih Muslim and others, is only a rebuke to the one who said "Will You place in it," and a demonstration of what was already in His knowledge when He said to them: "Indeed I know what you do not know."

His words: "one who causes corruption therein" — "man" (من) is in the accusative position as the object of "taj'al" (You place), and the second object stands in its place: "therein" (فيها). "Yufsidu" (causes corruption) is singular in agreement with the form of the word "man," and it is permitted outside the Qur'an to say "yufsidun" (plural) in agreement with the meaning. In revelation: ﴿And among them is one who listens to you﴾ [al-An'am 6:25] in agreement with the form, and "wa-minhum man yastami'una" (among them are those who listen) in agreement with the meaning.

"Wa-yasfiku" (and sheds) is coordinated with it, and both readings are permitted. Usayd narrated from al-A'raj that he read "wa-yasfika al-dima'" (and shed the blood) with the accusative, making it an answer to the interrogative with the conjunction "wa," as the poet said [the speaker is al-Hutay'ah]:

"Did I not be your neighbour, and between me and you there was affection and brotherhood?"

Al-safk means pouring. One says: "safaktu al-dam asfiku-hu safkan," meaning I poured it. The same applies to tears (al-dam'). Ibn Faris and al-Jawhari reported this. Al-saffak means the one who sheds blood a lot, and the verb is also used of one who is eloquent. Al-Mahdawi said: Safk is only used of blood, though it may be used of prose speech: one says "safaka al-kalam" if he scatters it. The singular of "dima'" (blood) is "dam," which has a dropped letter. It is said its origin is "damy," and it is said "damay." No noun has only two letters without something having been dropped from it, and the dropped element is a yā', and it has been pronounced in its original form. The poet said:

"If we had been slaughtered on a stone, the two bloods would have flowed with the certain news."

His words, exalted is He: ﴿While we glorify You with Your praise﴾ meaning we exalt You above what does not befit Your attributes. In their speech, tasbih (glorification) means declaring God free from imperfection in a manner of magnification. From this is the saying of A'sha Bani Tha'labah:

"I said when his boasting came to me: Glory be to Him who [is free] from 'Alqamah the boaster."

That is, I declare him free from 'Alqamah. Talhah ibn Ubaydillah narrated: I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about the meaning of "Subhan Allah" (Glory be to God), and he said: "It is the declaring of God, Mighty and Majestic, free from every imperfection." It is derived from "sabh," which means swimming and going, as God said: ﴿Indeed for you in the day is extensive movement﴾ [al-Muzzammil 73:7]. So the one who glorifies moves in the declaring of God's freedom from imperfection and clearing Him of defect. The discussion of "nahnu" (we) has already passed, and it is not permitted to assimilate the nun into the nun, lest two unvocalised consonants come together. Issue: The interpreters differed about the glorification of the angels. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas said: their glorification is their prayer, and God's saying ﴿Had he not been of those who glorify﴾ [as-Saffat 37:143] means those who pray. It is also said: their glorification is raising the voice in remembrance. This was said by al-Mufaddal, and he cited Jarir's verse:

"May God disfigure the faces of Taghlib, whenever the pilgrims raise their hands [in supplication] and proclaim the talbiyah [at Ihram]."

Qatadah said: Their glorification (tasbih) is "Subhan Allah" (Glory be to Allah), in its customary linguistic sense, and this is the sound view, because of what Abu Dharr narrated: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked, "Which speech is most excellent?" He said: "What Allah has chosen for His angels [or for His servants[[Addition from Sahih Muslim (vol. 8, p. 86, Istanbul edition).]]] is: Subhan Allah wa-bihamdih (Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him)." Recorded by Muslim. And on the authority of Abd al-Rahman ibn Qurt, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), on the night he was taken on the Night Journey, heard glorification in the highest heavens: "Subhana al-Ali al-A'la, subhanahu wa-ta'ala" (Glory be to the Most High, the Most Exalted, glorified and exalted is He). Recorded by al-Bayhaqi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿bihamdika﴾ (with Your praise), meaning: and with Your praise we mix the glorification with praise and join it to it. Hamd (praise) is commendation, and it has been discussed previously [[See the fourth issue, p. 133 of this part.]]. It is possible that their words "with Your praise" are a parenthetical insertion between the two statements, as if they said: "And we glorify and sanctify," then they added, by way of submission: "And You are the one praised for guiding us to this." And Allah knows best.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿wa-nuqaddisu laka﴾ (and we sanctify You), meaning: we magnify You, glorify You, and purify Your remembrance from what is unfitting for You, from what the deniers attribute to You. This was said by Mujahid, Abu Salih and others. Al-Dahhak and others said: the meaning is: we purify ourselves for You, seeking Your pleasure. Some people, including Qatadah, said: "nuqaddisu laka" means "nusalli" (we pray), and taqdis means prayer. Ibn Atiyyah said: this is weak. I say: rather, its meaning is sound, for prayer includes magnification, sanctification and glorification. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say in his bowing and prostration: "Subbuhun quddusun, Rabb al-malaikati wa-al-ruh" (Most Holy, Most Pure, Lord of the angels and the Spirit). Narrated by Aisha; recorded by Muslim. The root qaddasa, in whatever form it occurs, means purification. From it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Enter the holy land﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 21], meaning the purified one [[See vol. 6, p. 125.]]. And He said: ﴿the King, the Holy﴾ [al-Hashr: 23], meaning the Pure [[See vol. 18, p. 45.]]. Similarly: ﴿in the sacred valley, Tuwa﴾ [Ta-Ha: 12] [[See vol. 11, p. 175.]]. Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) was so named because it is the place where one is made holy from sins, that is, purified. From the same root, a bucket (saṭl) is called qadas, because one performs wudu' and purifies oneself with it, and from it comes qadus (a bucket). In the hadith: "A nation is not sanctified (laa quddisat ummah) in which the weak is not given his due from its strong." He means: may Allah not purify it. Recorded by Ibn Majah in his Sunan. So al-quds is purity without any dispute. The poet said:

[[(This is Imru' al-Qais. The ha' in "adraknahu" refers to the bull, and the nun refers to the dogs. Al-nasa: a vein in the thigh. Al-shabraqah: tearing cloth and other things. Al-muqaddas (with kasra and shaddah on the dal): the monk; with fatha: the blessed one. He says: the dogs overtook the bull, seizing it by the leg and thigh, and tore its hide as the children of the Christians tear the robe of a monk who glorifies Allah, Mighty and Majestic, when he descends from his hermitage, cutting his garments seeking blessing from him.
(From the commentary on the Diwan and Lisan al-Arab).]]
"They overtook him, seizing by the leg and the thigh, as the boys tear the robe of the sanctified one."

That is, the purified one. Prayer is thus a purification for the servant from sins, and the one who prays enters it in the most perfect state, since it is the most excellent of deeds. And Allah knows best.

His saying, exalted is He: (Indi a'lamu ma la ta'lamun) (Indeed, I know what you do not know). "A'lamu" has two interpretations: it is said that it is an imperfect verb (future). It is also said that it is a noun in the sense of an active participle, as one says "Allahu akbar" meaning "Kabir" (Great), and as the poet said [[The speaker is Ma'n ibn Aws. He had a friend, and Ma'n was married to his sister. It happened that he divorced her and married another, so his friend swore never to speak to him again. Ma'n then composed verses to move his friend's heart toward him and win him back.
(From the poems of al-Hamasah).]]:

"By your life, I do not know, and indeed I am fearful: over which of us will death first run?"

So if it is a verb, then "ma" is in the position of an object of a'lamu, and it is permissible to assimilate the mim into the mim. If you make it a noun in the sense of 'alim (knower), then "ma" is in the position of the genitive by annexation. Ibn Atiyyah said: nunation (tanwin) is not valid for it by the consensus of the grammarians; the disagreement only concerns "af'al" when it is used as a proper name and is indefinite: Sibawayh and al-Khalil do not give it diptotic inflection (sarf), while al-Akhfash does. Al-Mahdawi said: it is permissible to consider there to be tanwin on "a'lamu" when you take it to mean 'alim, and to put "ma" in the accusative governed by it, as in "hawajju Bayt Allah" (pilgrims to the House of Allah). Al-Jawhari said: "niswatun hawajju Bayt Allah" with annexation when they have performed the pilgrimage; but if they have not performed it, you say "hawajjun Bayta Allah," putting the Bayt in the accusative, because you intend the tanwin on hawajj.

His saying, exalted is He: "ma la ta'lamun" (what you do not know). The scholars of interpretation differed concerning the referent of His saying: "ma la ta'lamun." Ibn Abbas said: Iblis, may Allah curse him, had become self-impressed and pride entered him when He made him keeper of the heaven and honored him, so he believed that this was due to a merit of his own, and he regarded disbelief and disobedience toward Adam, peace be upon him, as trivial. The angels said: ﴿We glorify with Your praise and sanctify You﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], while they did not know that in Iblis's soul there was something contrary to that. So Allah, exalted is He, said to them: ﴿Indeed, I know what you do not know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. Qatadah said: when the angels said ﴿Will You place in it?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], and Allah knew that among those He would make successors on the earth there would be prophets, excellent people and people of obedience, He said to them: "Indeed, I know what you do not know." I say: it is also possible that the meaning is: Indeed, I know what you do not know, of what has been, what will be, and what is yet to be; so it is general.

**Part 1 of the commentary on verse 31:**

This verse contains seven issues.

**The first issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾ ... "ʿallama" (He taught) means "ʿarrafa" (He made known). His teaching here is the inspiring of His knowledge by necessity (ḍarūratan). It is also possible that it was through an angel, namely Jibril (peace be upon him), as will come. It has been read as "wa-ʿullima" in the passive voice, though the first reading is more apparent, as will come. The scholars of the Sufis (ʿulamāʾ al-ṣūfiyya) said: He taught him by the Truth's teaching him, and he retained them by His preserving them for him, and he forgot what had been entrusted to him, because He left him to himself in that matter. So He said: "And We had certainly made a covenant with Adam before, but he forgot, and We found in him no determination" [Ṭāhā: 115] (see vol. 11, p. 251).

Ibn ʿAṭāʾ said: Had He not revealed to Adam the knowledge of those names, he would have been less able than the angels in reporting them. This is clear.

Adam (peace be upon him) is given the kunya Abu al-Bashar (father of mankind). It was also said: Abu Muhammad, a kunya taken from Muhammad, the Seal of the Prophets (may the blessings of God be upon them all), as al-Suhayli said. It was also said that his kunya in Paradise was Abu Muhammad, and on earth Abu al-Bashar.

His name originally has two hamzas, because it is of the pattern "afʿal," but they softened the second one. When you need to vocalize it, you make it a waw, so you say "awādim" in the plural, because there is no known root for it in yāʾ. So the waw became the dominant letter for it, according to al-Akhfash.

Scholars differed about its derivation. It was said: It is derived from the "adama" (surface, skin) of the earth and its "adīm" (outer layer), which is its face, so he was named after what he was created from. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas. It was also said: It is derived from "al-udma," which is brownness (al-sumra). They differed about the meaning of "udma." Al-Ḍaḥḥāk claimed it is brownness, while al-Naḍr claimed it is whiteness, and that Adam (peace be upon him) was white, derived from their saying: a female camel that is "admāʾ" when she is white. On this derivation, its plural is "udm" and "awādim," like "ḥumr" and "aḥāmir," and it is not inflected in any way. On the view that it is derived from "udma," its plural is "ādamūn," and those who hold this view are bound to make it inflected.

I say: The correct view is that it is derived from the "adīm" (surface) of the earth. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: He was named Adam only because he was created from the surface of the earth, and he was named "insān" (human) only because he "nasiya" (forgot). This was recorded by Ibn Saʿd in the Ṭabaqāt.

Al-Suddi narrated from Abu Malik, from Abu Ṣāliḥ, from Ibn ʿAbbas, and from Murra al-Hamdani, from Ibn Masʿud, concerning the story of the creation of Adam (peace be upon him). He said: God sent Jibril (peace be upon him) to the earth to bring him clay from it. The earth said: "I seek refuge in God from you, lest you diminish me or disfigure me." So he returned without taking anything and said: "O Lord, it sought refuge in You, so You granted it refuge." Then He sent Mikaʾil, and it sought refuge from him, so He granted it refuge, and he returned and said what Jibril had said. Then He sent the Angel of Death, and it sought refuge from him, and he said: "And I seek refuge in God from returning without carrying out His command." So he took from the surface of the earth and mixed it, and he did not take from one place. He took from red, white, and black soil, and that is why the children of Adam came out varied. And that is why he was named Adam, because he was taken from the adīm of the earth. Then he lifted him up, and God the Exalted said to him: "Did you not have mercy on the earth when it humbled itself before you?" He said: "I saw Your command as more binding than its plea." He said: "You are fit to seize the souls of its offspring." The dust was moistened until it became "ṭīnan lāziban," clay that sticks together. "Lāzib" is that which clings part to another. Then it was left until it became foul-smelling, and that is the meaning of His saying: ﴿from black mud, moulded﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 26]. He said: "It stank." Then He said to the angels: "Indeed, I am creating a human from clay. So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, fall down before him in prostration" [Ṣād: 71–72] (see vol. 15, p. 3).

So God created him with His own hand, so that Iblis would not be arrogant toward him. [God] says: "Will you be arrogant toward what I created with My two hands, while I am not arrogant toward it?" He created him as a human, and he was a body of clay for forty years, from the measure of a Friday. The angels passed by him, and they were terrified when they saw him, and the one most terrified of him was Iblis. He would pass by him and strike him, and the body would ring out as pottery rings, producing a clanging sound. This is when He says: ﴿from clay like pottery﴾ [al-Raḥmān: 14] (see vol. 17, p. 160). And [Iblis] would say: "For some matter you were created!" It entered through his mouth and came out through his rear. Iblis said to the angels: "Do not be frightened of this, for he is hollow and soft. I am empowered over him, and I will destroy him." It is said that whenever he passed by him with the angels, he would say: "Have you seen this one, whom you do not see as resembling any of the creatures? If he is preferred over you and you are commanded to obey him, what would you do?" They said: "We obey the command of our Lord." Then Iblis secretly said to himself: "If he is preferred over me, I will not obey him, and if I am preferred over him, I will destroy him."

When the time came for the spirit to be breathed into him, [God] said to the angels: "When I breathe into him of My spirit, fall down before him in prostration." When He breathed the spirit into him and it entered his head, he sneezed. The angels said to him: "Say: Praise be to God." He said: "Praise be to God." God said to him: "May your Lord have mercy on you." When the spirit entered his eyes, he looked at the fruits of Paradise. When it entered his belly, he desired food, so he leaped, hastening toward the fruits of Paradise, before the spirit reached his feet. This is when He says: ﴿Man was created of haste﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 37] (see vol. 11, p. 2). ﴿So all the angels prostrated themselves entirely, except Iblis; he refused to be among those who prostrated﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 30–31]. He mentioned the story.

Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu Musa al-Ashʿari, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "Indeed God, Mighty and Majestic, created Adam from a handful He took from all of the earth, so the children of Adam came in accordance with the earth's variety. Among them is the red, the white, the black, and what is between them, the easy and the hard, the wicked and the good." Abu ʿĪsā said: This is a ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ ḥadīth.

**"Adīm"** is the plural of "adam." The poet said:
"People are varied (akhyāf) and diverse in their dispositions,
yet all of them are gathered by the face of the adam."
(Akhyāf: those who differ in character and appearance.)

So Adam is derived from "adīm" and "adam," not from "udma." God knows best. It is possible that it is derived from both together. More elaboration on this topic regarding the creation of Adam will come in Surat al-Anʿām (see vol. 6, pp. 387 and vol. 7, p. 168) and elsewhere, God willing.

"Ādam" is not inflected. Abu Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās said: "Ādam is not inflected in the definite form by the consensus of the grammarians, because it is on the pattern "afʿal," and it is definite. Nothing is prevented from inflection according to the Basrans except for two reasons. If you make it indefinite and it is not an adjective, al-Khalil and Sibawayh do not inflect it, but al-Akhfash Saʿid inflects it, because it was an adjective and is on the pattern of a verb. When it is not an adjective, he inflects it." Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: The statement is Sibawayh's, and no distinction is made between an adjective and other cases, because it is the very same thing."

**The second issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the names, all of them﴾. "Al-asmāʾ" (the names) here means "al-ʿibārāt" (expressions, terms). The word "ism" (name) may be used to refer to the named thing, as when you say: "Zayd is standing," and "The lion is brave." It may also refer to the act of naming itself, as when you say: "Asad (lion) has three letters." In the first, it is said that the name is the named thing, in the sense that it refers to the named thing. In the second, it does not refer to the named thing. A "name" in language may function as the expression itself, and this is the most common usage. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾ [al-Baqara: 31], according to the most well-known interpretations. From it is also the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed God has ninety-nine names." It also functions as the essence, and it is said: "dhāt," "nafs," "ʿayn," and "ism" have the same meaning. On this basis, most of the scholars interpreted His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Aʿlā: 1], ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord﴾ [al-Raḥmān: 78], and ﴿They are nothing but names you have named﴾ [al-Najm: 23] (see vol. 20, p. 2).

**The third issue:** The interpreters differed about the meaning of the names that He taught Adam (peace be upon him). Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrima, Qatada, Mujahid, and Ibn Jubayr said: He taught him the names of all things, the great and the small. ʿĀṣim ibn Kulayb narrated from Saʿd, the client of al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, who said: I was sitting with Ibn ʿAbbas when they mentioned the name of the vessel and the name of the whip. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "And He taught Adam the names, all of them."

I say: This meaning has also been narrated as a marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet) report, as will come. It is what the wording "kullahā" (all of them) requires, since it is a term established for totality and generality. In al-Bukhari, from the ḥadīth of Anas from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "The believers will gather on the Day of Resurrection and say: If only we could seek intercession with our Lord. So they will come to Adam and say: You are the father of mankind. God created you with His hand, made His angels prostrate to you, and taught you the names of everything," and so on.
