Ibn Khuwayz Mindād said: In this verse there is evidence that language is taken by tawqīf (divine determination), and that God the Exalted taught it to Adam (peace be upon him) in its totality and in its details. Ibn ʿAbbas also said likewise: He taught him the names of everything, even the bowl and the jug.

Shaybān narrated from Qatada, who said: Adam was taught from the names the names of his creation that the angels did not know. He named each thing by its name and directed (anḥā) the benefit of each thing to its kind. Al-Naḥḥās said: This is the best of what has been narrated on this. The meaning is that He taught him the names of the kinds and made him know their benefits: this is such-and-such, and it is suitable for such-and-such.

Al-Ṭabarī said: He taught him the names of the angels and his offspring. He chose this view and preferred it, based on His saying: ﴿Then He presented them to the angels﴾. Ibn Zayd said: He taught him the names of all his offspring. Al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym said: the names of the angels specifically. Al-Qutaybī said: the names of what was created on earth. It was also said: the names of the kinds and types.

I say: The first view is more correct, for the reason we have just mentioned, and for what we will explain, God willing, the Exalted.

**Fourth:** The commentators also differed over whether He presented to the angels the names of the persons (*ashkhas*) or only the names without the persons. Ibn Mas'ud and others said that He presented the persons, based on His saying "*'aradahum*" (He presented them) and His saying "*anbi'uni bi-asma'i ha'ula'i*" (tell Me the names of these). The Arabs say: "I presented the thing (*'aradtu al-shay'*), so it appeared (*fa-a'rada*)," meaning I made it manifest and it became manifest. From this comes "I displayed the thing for sale." In a hadith it is said: "He presented them like the ants (*amthal al-dharr*)."

Ibn 'Abbas and others said that He presented the names. In the reading (*harf*, variant reading) of Ibn Mas'ud it is "*'aradahunna*" (He presented them, feminine), so the pronoun refers back to the names and not the persons, because the *ha'* and *nun* are more specific to the feminine. In the reading (*harf*) of Ubayy it is "*'aradaha*" (He presented it). Mujahid said: "the owners of the names." Whoever says that "the names" means the designations (*tasmiyat*) finds the reading of Ubayy, "*'aradaha*," consistent. As for the reading "*'aradahum*," one may say that the word "names" indicates persons, and therefore it is permissible to refer to the names with "*'aradahum*."

Regarding "*ha'ula'*" (these), the reference of the demonstrative is to the persons of the names. Although they were absent, what is connected to them through a cause was present, and that is their names.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: What appears to be the case is that God taught Adam the names and presented them to him together with those kinds and their persons. Then He presented those [persons] to the angels and asked them about their designations which Adam had learned. Then Adam said to them: "This one's name is so-and-so, and this one's name is so-and-so."

Al-Mawardi said: The more correct view is that the presentation was directed at the named things (*al-musammayn*). Then, concerning the time of presenting them, there are two opinions: one is that He presented them after He had created them; the second is that He formed them in the hearts of the angels and then presented them.

**Fifth:** It has been disputed who first spoke the Arabic tongue. It is related from Ka'b al-Ahbar that the first to set down the Arabic script, the Syriac script, and all the books, and to speak all the languages, was Adam (peace be upon him). Others than Ka'b al-Ahbar have said the same.

If it is said: It has been related from Ka'b al-Ahbar by a sound chain that he said: "The first to speak Arabic was Jibril (peace be upon him), and he is the one who cast it upon the tongue of Nuh (peace be upon him), and Nuh cast it upon the tongue of his son Sam." This was narrated by Thawr ibn Zayd from Khalid ibn Ma'dan from Ka'b.

It is also related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The first whose tongue was opened with clear Arabic was Isma'il, and he was ten years old." It has also been related that the first to speak Arabic was Ya'rub ibn Qahtan, and other things have been related.

We say: The correct view is that the first of mankind to speak all languages was Adam (peace be upon him), and the Qur'an bears witness to this. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31], and all languages are names, so they fall under this. This is also what the Sunnah has come with. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "He taught Adam all the names, even the bowl and the small bowl."

What they have mentioned may mean that the first to speak Arabic among the descendants of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was Isma'il (peace be upon him). Likewise, if what others have said is sound, it must be understood to mean that the one mentioned was the first to speak Arabic within his own tribe, based on the evidence we have cited. And God knows best.

Likewise, Jibril was the first of the angels to speak it, and he cast it upon the tongue of Nuh after God had taught it to Adam, or Jibril, as has preceded. And God knows best.

God, the Exalted, said: ﴿These﴾ is a word built on a kasra (vowel). The dialect of Tamim and some of Qays and Asad uses the shortened form (*al-qasr*) in it. Al-A'sha said:

*Ha'ula' thumma ha'ula' kullan a'ta... ta ni'alan mahdhuwwatan bi-mithal*
("These, then these, I gave each... sandals cut to a pattern.")

Some Arabs say "*hau'lau*" (with a different pronunciation) and drop the alif and the hamza.

**Sixth:** God's saying ﴿if you are truthful﴾ is a conditional clause, and its response (*jawab*) is omitted. Its estimated form is: "If you are truthful that the children of Adam will cause corruption on earth, then inform Me." This is the view of al-Mubarrad.

The meaning of "*sadiqin*" (truthful) is "knowing." For this reason, it was not fitting for the angels to exercise independent judgment (*ijtihad*), and they said: "Glory be to You!" This was related by al-Naqqash, who said: If He had required of them only truthfulness in the informing, it would have been permissible for them to exercise *ijtihad*, just as it was permissible for the one whom God caused to die for a hundred years when He said to him: "How long have you remained?" He did not stipulate for him correctness, and he said [a guess] and was not correct, and he was not rebuked. This is clear and there is no obscurity in it.

Al-Tabari and Abu 'Ubayd related that some exegetes said that the meaning of "*in kuntum*" (if you are) is "*idh kuntum*" (since you are), but the two of them said: This is an error.

"*Anbi'uni*" means "inform me." *Naba'* is information, and from it comes *nabi* (prophet) without the hamza, and its explanation will come, God willing, in God's saying: (and they kill the prophets without right...), see p. 431 of this part.

**Seventh:** Some scholars said: From this command to inform, the imposition of what cannot be borne (*taklif ma la yutaq*) follows, because He knew that they did not know. The verifying scholars of interpretation said: This is not by way of imposing an obligation, but by way of establishing a fact and questioning (*al-taqrir wa-l-tawqif*). The discussion of whether the imposition of what cannot be borne actually occurred or not will come at the end of the surah, God willing; see vol. 3, p. 428.

**The Exalted saying: ﴿They said, "Glory be to You! We have no knowledge except what You have taught us."﴾** There are three issues.

**The first issue:** His saying ﴿Glory be to You﴾ means: exalted are You above anyone other than You knowing the unseen. This is their answer to His saying, "Inform Me of their names." They answered that they know only what He has made them know, and that they did not undertake what they had no knowledge of, as the ignorant among us do. The word "mā" in "mā ʿallamtanā" (what You have taught us) means "alladhī" (that which), i.e., "except that which You have taught us." It may also be a verbal noun (maṣdariyyah), meaning "except Your teaching us."

**The second issue:** It is obligatory for one who is asked about a matter of knowledge, if he does not know it, to say: "Allah knows best" and "I do not know," following the example of the angels, the prophets, and the virtuous scholars. However, the truthful one (the Prophet ﷺ) has reported that with the death of the scholars knowledge is taken away. Then ignorant people remain who are asked for rulings and give rulings by their own opinion, and so they go astray and lead others astray.

As for the reports that came from the Prophet ﷺ, his Companions, and the Successors after them concerning the meaning of this verse: al-Bustī [[In one manuscript: "al-Nasāʾī."]] narrated in his authentic *Musnad* from Ibn ʿUmar that a man asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Which places are the worst?" He said: "I do not know until I ask Jibrīl." So he asked Jibrīl, who said: "I do not know until I ask Mīkāʾīl." Then he came and said: "The best places are the mosques, and the worst of them are the markets."

Al-Ṣiddīq (Abū Bakr) said to a grandmother: "Go back until I ask the people."

ʿAlī used to say: "Wabarda hā ʿalā al-kabid" (coolest on the liver), three times. They said: "And what is that, O Commander of the Faithful?" He said: "That a man is asked about what he does not know and says: 'Allah knows best.'"

A man asked Ibn ʿUmar about a matter, and he said: "I have no knowledge of it." When the man turned away, Ibn ʿUmar said: "How well Ibn ʿUmar spoke! He was asked about what he did not know and said, 'I have no knowledge of it!'" This was recorded by al-Dārimī in his *Musnad*.

In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, on the authority of Abū ʿAqīl Yaḥyā ibn al-Mutawakkil, companion of Buhayyah [[Buhayyah (diminutive): a freedwoman of Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, who narrated from ʿĀʾishah. Abū ʿAqīl mentioned above narrated from her.]], he said: "I was sitting with al-Qāsim ibn ʿUbayd Allah and Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd. Yaḥyā said to al-Qāsim: 'O Abū Muḥammad, it is shameful and grave for someone like you that he be asked about some matter of this religion and that he has no knowledge of it, nor a way out (of the difficulty)?' Al-Qāsim said to him: 'And why is that?' He said: 'Because you are the son of two imams of guidance: the son of Abū Bakr and ʿUmar [[Al-Qāsim here is the son of ʿUbayd Allah ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb. His mother is Umm ʿAbd Allah, daughter of al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may Allah be pleased with him. So Abū Bakr is his great-grandfather on his mother's side, ʿUmar is his great-grandfather on his father's side, and Ibn ʿUmar is his true grandfather on his father's side, may Allah be pleased with them all.

(From Sharḥ al-Nawawī ʿalā Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim.)]].' Al-Qāsim said to him: 'What is more shameful than that, in the view of one who understands from Allah, is that I should say something without knowledge, or take from someone who is not trustworthy.' He fell silent and did not answer him."

Mālik ibn Anas said: "I heard Ibn Hurmuz say: 'It is fitting for the scholar to bequeath to his companions after him 'I do not know,' so that it becomes a principle in their hands. When one of them is asked about what he does not know, he says: "I do not know."'"

al-Haytham ibn Jamīl reported: "I witnessed Mālik ibn Anas being asked about forty-eight questions, and he said 'I do not know' concerning thirty-two of them."

I say: The like of this is abundant among the Companions, the Successors, and the jurists of the Muslims. What prevents people from doing this is only leadership-seeking and lack of fairness in knowledge. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: "Among the blessings of knowledge and its etiquette is fairness in it. Whoever is not fair does not understand and does not comprehend."

Yūnus ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā reported: "I heard Ibn Wahb say: 'I heard Mālik ibn Anas say: "In our time there is nothing rarer than fairness."'" I say: This was said in Mālik's time, so how about our time today, when corruption has spread among us and the riffraff has multiplied! Knowledge is sought in it for leadership, not for understanding, but for fame in this world and for overcoming one's peers through disputation and argument, which hardens the heart and produces rancor. That is among what leads to lack of piety and abandonment of fear of Allah, the Exalted. Where is this from what was reported from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "Do not raise the dowries of women above forty ounces, even if she is the daughter of Dhū al-ʿAṣabah, meaning Yazīd ibn al-Ḥuṣayn al-Ḥārithī. Whoever exceeds this, I will put the excess into the public treasury." A tall woman from among the women, with a flat nose [[al-faṭas (with vowel): lowering and flattening of the bridge of the nose and its spreading.]], stood up and said: "That is not for you!" He said: "And why?" She said: "Because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And you have given one of them a heap of gold, do not take anything from it﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 4:20]." ʿUmar said: "A woman was right and a man erred!"

Wakīʿ reported from Abū Maʿshar, from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī, who said: "A man asked ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, about a question, and he gave an answer. The man said: 'It is not so, O Commander of the Faithful, but rather such and such.' ʿAlī said: 'You are right and I erred, and above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows.'"

Abū Muḥammad Qāsim ibn Aṣbagh mentioned: "When I traveled to the East, I stayed in al-Qayrawān and took from Bakr ibn Ḥammād the Ḥadīth of Musaddad. Then I traveled to Baghdad and met people. When I returned, I went back to him to complete the Ḥadīth of Musaddad, and I read to him one day the Ḥadīth of the Prophet ﷺ: 'That there came to him a people from Muḍar, wearing *mujtābī* [[Split and striped garments.]] al-tamar (woollen cloaks)'. He said: 'It is only *mujtābī al-thimār* (fruits).' I said: 'It is only *mujtābī al-nimār*. Thus I read it to everyone I read it to in al-Andalus and Iraq.' He said to me: 'By your entering Iraq you oppose us and boast over us!' or something like this. Then he said to me: 'Come with us to that shaykh,' (a shaykh who was in the mosque), 'for he has knowledge of such matters.' We went to him and asked him about it, and he said: 'It is only *mujtābī al-nimār*, as I said.' They were a people who used to wear split garments, their collars in front of them. *Al-nimār* is the plural of *namirah* [[Every striped wrap from the loincloths of the Bedouin, as if it were taken from the color of the leopard.]].'" Then Bakr ibn Ḥammād said, taking hold of his nose: "My nose is rubbed in the dust for the truth! My nose is rubbed in the dust for the truth!" And he left.

Yazīd ibn al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik said, and excelled:

When I speak in a gathering,
my speech ends at what I know,
and I do not reach beyond my knowledge to another,
and when it ends, I fall silent.

**The third issue:** His saying ﴿Glory be to You﴾: "Subḥāna" is in the accusative as a verbal noun according to al-Khalīl and Sībawayh, conveying the meaning "we glorify You with glorification." Al-Kisāʾī said: it is in the accusative as an annexed vocative. ﴿Al-ʿAlīm﴾ (the All-Knowing) is an intensive form (faʿīl) for emphasis and abundance in what is known in the creation of Allah, the Exalted. ﴿Al-Ḥakīm﴾ (the All-Wise) means al-Ḥākim (the Judge), and between them there is additional emphasis. It has been said that its meaning is "the one who makes firm" (al-muḥkim), and "al-Ḥakīm" in this sense is one of the attributes of action, changed from *mufʿil* to *faʿīl*, just as *musmiʿ* was changed to *samīʿ* and *mu'lim* to *alīm*; this was stated by Ibn al-Anbārī. Some people said: "al-Ḥakīm" is the one who prevents corruption, and from this the bridle is called *ḥikmah*, because it prevents the horse from running and going off without purpose. Jarīr said:

O Banū Ḥanīfah, restrain your foolish ones,
for I fear for you that I will become angry.

That is, prevent them from corruption. Zuhayr said:

The one who leads the horses, their hooves having been harmed,
the leather and the hemp-cords have been made firm.

*Al-qadd* is leather, and *al-abaq* is hemp [[*Al-qunnab* (with kasra or damma on the qāf): a kind of flax.]]. The Arabs say: "He restrained the orphan from such and such," meaning he prevented him. A *muḥkamah* sūrah is one protected from alteration and all change, from having what is not part of it attached to it, and from having added to it what is not of it. Wisdom (ḥikmah) comes from this, because it prevents its possessor from ignorance. It is said: "He made the thing firm" (aḥkama al-shayʾ) when he perfected it and prevented it from departing from what he intends. Thus it is *muḥkam* and *ḥakīm* in the intensive form.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an) on Surah 2, verse 33:**

Allah's words: ﴿He said, "O Adam, inform them of their names."﴾ In this verse there are five issues.

**The first issue:** Allah's words ﴿inform them of their names﴾. Allah commanded him to inform them of their names after presenting them to the angels, so that they would know that he (Adam) knows what they were asked about. This was a way of drawing attention to his excellence and exalted status. He was therefore superior to them: Allah placed him above them, made them prostrate to him, made them his students, and commanded them to learn from him. Thus he attained a rank of majesty and greatness by being made the one to whom prostration is performed, and by being singled out for knowledge.

**The second issue:** This verse is evidence for the excellence of knowledge (ʿilm) and of its people. In the hadith: "The angels lower their wings out of pleasure for the seeker of knowledge," meaning they humble themselves and show humility. They do this specifically for the people of knowledge among all of Allah's servants [[In one copy of the original: "for the sake of" (li-ajl)]], because Allah obligated them to do so regarding Adam, peace be upon him, and so they adopted this manner. Whenever knowledge appears in a human being, they submit to him, humble themselves, and abase themselves, out of reverence for knowledge and its people, and out of pleasure with those who seek it and occupy themselves with it. This applies to the students among them; how much more so to the scholars (aḥbār) among them and the divine scholars (rabbānīyūn)! May Allah make us among them and count us with them, for He is the Possessor of great bounty.

**The third issue:** The scholars differed on this subject: which is more excellent, the angels or the children of Adam? There are two opinions. One group held that prophets from among humans are more excellent than prophets from among the angels, and that saints (awliyāʾ) from among humans are more excellent than saints from among the angels. Others held that the Highest Assembly (al-Malaʾ al-Aʿlā, the angels) is more excellent.

Those who preferred the angels argued from Allah's words: ﴿They are honored servants. They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command﴾ [al-Anbiyaʾ 21:26–27], and ﴿They do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded﴾ [al-Tahrim 66:6], and His words: ﴿The Messiah would never disdain to be a servant of Allah, nor would the angels brought near﴾ [al-Nisaʾ 4:172], and His words: ﴿Say, "I do not tell you that I have the treasures of Allah, nor that I know the unseen, nor do I tell you that I am an angel"﴾ [al-Anʿam 6:50].

Also in al-Bukhari, Allah says: "Whoever mentions Me in a gathering, I mention him in a gathering better than theirs." And this is an explicit text.

Those who preferred the children of Adam argued from Allah's words: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, they are the best of creation﴾ [al-Bayyinah 98:7], reading the word (al-bariyyah) with a hamzah, from "barāʾa Allāh al-khalq" (Allah created the creation). They also cited the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The angels lower their wings out of pleasure for the seeker of knowledge," the full hadith, which Abu Dawud recorded. They also cited reports that Allah boasts of the people of ʿArafat to the angels, and that He only boasts of the most excellent. And Allah knows best.

Some scholars said: There is no way to decide with certainty that the prophets are more excellent than the angels, nor to decide with certainty that the angels are better than them, because the path to such a judgment is either the report of Allah, the report of His Messenger, or the consensus (ijmāʿ) of the community, and none of these exists here. This is in contrast to the Qadariyyah and to Qadi Abu Bakr (may Allah have mercy on him), who said that the angels are more excellent. He said: As for those among our companions (Ashʿarites) and the Shiʿah who said that the prophets are more excellent because Allah commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam, it is said to them: the one to whom prostration is made is not more excellent than the one who prostrates. Do you not see that the Kaʿbah is a place toward which prostration is made, and the prophets and all creation prostrate toward it, yet the prophets are better than the Kaʿbah by the consensus of the community? There is no disagreement that prostration is only due to Allah the Exalted, because prostration is worship, and worship is only for Allah. Given this, prostrating toward a direction does not indicate that the direction is better than the one who prostrates and worships. This is clear. Further clarification of this will come in the next verse.

**The fourth issue:** Allah's words: ﴿I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾ are evidence that no one knows any of the unseen except what Allah makes known to him, such as the prophets, or those whom those (prophets) inform. Therefore astrologers, fortune-tellers (kuhhān), and others are liars. The explanation of this will come in Surah al-Anʿam, God willing, at His words: ﴿With Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He﴾ [al-Anʿam 6:59] [[See vol. 7, p. 2]].

**The fifth issue:** Allah's words: ﴿And I know what you reveal﴾, i.e., of their saying: ﴿Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein?﴾ This is related by Makki and al-Mawardi. Al-Zahrawi said: What they revealed was their (the angels') concealed attitude toward prostrating to Adam.

(﴿And what you used to conceal﴾) Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Masʿud, and Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: What is meant is what Iblis concealed within himself of arrogance and disobedience. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: The word "you conceal" is in the plural, while the one who concealed (Iblis) is singular according to this view, through the Arabs' figurative and expansive usage. As one says to a people when a foolish one among them committed a crime: "You did such-and-such," meaning one of you did it. This is said with the intention of reproach. From this is Allah's words: ﴿Indeed, those who call you from behind the chambers, most of them do not reason﴾ [al-Hujurat 49:4]. Only ʿUyaynah, and some say al-Aqraʿ, called out to him from among them.

Another group said: What is revealed and what is concealed refers, in a general sense, to knowledge of all their secrets and their outward matters together.

Mahdi ibn Maymun said: We were with al-Hasan when al-Hasan ibn Dinar asked him: What was it that the angels concealed? He said: When Allah the Mighty and Majestic created Adam, the angels saw a wondrous creation, and it seems something of this affected them. He said: Then some of them turned to others and whispered this among themselves, [and said [[addition from Tafsir al-Tabari]]: and] "What concerns you about this creature? Allah has not created any creation except that we are more honored by Him than it."

As for "mā" in His words "what you reveal," it may be in the accusative governed by "aʿlamu" as a verb, or it may mean "knower" (ʿālim) with "mā" governed by it, in which case it would be like ḥawāij bayt Allāh (the needs of the House of Allah). This has already been discussed [[See p. 278]].

There are ten issues in this passage. The first concerns His saying, ﴿And when We said﴾, meaning: and remember. As for Abu 'Ubayda's claim that "idh" (when) is superfluous, it is not permissible, because "idh" is an adverb of time (zarf) and it has already been discussed [[see the first issue, p. 261.]]. He said "qulna" (We said) and not "qult" (I said), because the Almighty, the Great, speaks of Himself in the plural to express majesty and to raise His mention. "Al-Malaika" (the angels) is the plural of "malak" (angel), and this has already been discussed [[see the second issue, p. 262.]]. The discussion of Adam and his etymology has also already been given [[see the first issue, p. 279.]], so there is no point in repeating it. It is related from Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' that he vowed the feminine "ta'" of "al-malaika" with a damma, following the damma of the "jim" in "usjudu" (prostrate). A parallel to this is "al-hamdu lillah" (all praise is due to Allah).

The second issue concerns His saying, "usjudu" (prostrate). In the language of the Arabs, sujud means humbling oneself and submission. The poet said:

*Yajma'u tadillu al-bulqu fi hajarâtihi... tara al-ukama fiha sujjadan lil-hawafiri*

Al-ukam: small hills. He made them "sujjad" (prostrating) to the hooves, because the hooves overpower them and they cannot resist them. "'Ayn sajida" means a gaze that is languid, unfocused; its final stage is placing the face on the ground. Ibn Faris said: "sajada" means he lowered himself, and everything that prostrates has humbled itself. "Al-isjad" means continuing to look. Abu 'Amr said: "Asjada" means he lowered his head. He said:

*Fudula azimmatiha asjadat... sujud al-nasara li-ahbariha*

[[This is Humayd ibn Thawr describing women. He means: when they departed, they let the excess of their camels' reins, which were adorned on their wrists, hang down; "asjadat", i.e. lowered their heads, for them.
(From Lisan and Sharh al-Qamus.)]]

Abu 'Ubayda said: a Bedouin of the Banu Asad recited to me:

*Wa qulna lahu asjid li-Layla fa-asjada*

He meant the camel when it lowered its head. "Darahim al-Isjad" (Isjad coins) were coins bearing images to which people prostrated. He said:

*Wafa bihâ ka-darahim al-isjadi*

The third issue: Those who consider Adam and his descendants superior have used His saying to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam." They said: this indicates that he was superior to them. The response is that the meaning of "usjudu li-Adam" is: prostrate to Me, facing the face of Adam. This is like His saying, ﴿Establish prayer at the decline of the sun﴾ [al-Isra: 78], meaning at the decline of the sun, and His saying, ﴿And I breathed into him of My spirit, so fall down prostrate to him﴾ [Sad: 72], meaning: fall down to Me at the completion of his creation, while you face him in prostration. We have already explained that the one prostrated to is not superior to the one who prostrates, by the evidence of the qibla. If it is said: if he was not superior to them, what is the wisdom in commanding them to prostrate to him? It is said: when the angels were proud of their glorification and sanctification, He commanded them to prostrate to another, so that He might show them His independence from them and from their worship. Some said: they disparaged Adam and belittled him, and they did not know the special qualities of his creation, so they were commanded to prostrate to him in honour. It is also possible that Allah commanded them to prostrate to him as punishment for their saying, ﴿Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?﴾ when He said to them, ﴿Indeed I will make upon the earth a successive authority﴾ [al-Baqara: 30]. He knew that if He addressed them, they would say this. So He said to them: ﴿Indeed, I am creating a human from clay﴾ [Sad: 71], and I will make him a successor. When I have breathed into him of My spirit, fall down to him in prostration. The meaning is: that this be a punishment for you at that time for what you are saying to Me now. If it is said: Ibn 'Abbas used as evidence for the excellence of humanity that Allah swore by the life of His Messenger ﷺ, saying: ﴿By your life, indeed they are in their intoxication, wandering blindly﴾ [al-Hijr: 72], and gave him security from punishment by saying: ﴿That Allah may forgive you your past and future sins﴾ [al-Fath: 2], and He said to the angels: ﴿And whoever of them should say, "Indeed, I am a deity other than Him," - We would recompense him with Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya': 29]. It is said to him: He did not swear by the life of the angels, just as He did not swear by His own life, so He did not say, "By My life." He swore by the heaven and the earth, but this does not show that they are higher in rank than the Throne and the seven gardens. He swore by the fig and the olive. As for His saying, ﴿And whoever of them should say, "Indeed, I am a deity other than Him"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 29], it is like His saying to His Prophet, peace be upon him: ﴿If you were to associate partners with Allah, your deeds would surely be nullified, and you would surely be among the losers﴾ [al-Zumar: 65]. So there is no indication of superiority in it, and Allah knows best.

The fourth issue: People differed over the manner of the angels' prostration to Adam, although they agreed that it was not an act of worship. The majority said: this was a command to the angels to place their foreheads on the ground, like the customary prostration in prayer, because this is the apparent meaning of prostration in custom and in the Shari'a. On this view it was said: that prostration was an honouring of Adam and a display of his excellence, and an act of obedience to Allah, and Adam was like a qibla for us. The meaning of "li-Adam" is "towards Adam," as one says "prayed to the qibla," meaning towards the qibla. Others said: this was not the prostration customary today, which is placing the forehead on the ground, but it remains upon the original linguistic meaning, which is humbling and submission. So it means: humble yourselves before Adam and acknowledge his superiority.

(Fasajadu) means they complied with what they were commanded. It has also been disputed whether that prostration was specific to Adam, peace be upon him, so that prostration to anyone else in the whole universe is not permissible except to Allah, or whether it remained permissible after him until the time of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, by His saying: ﴿And he raised his parents upon the throne, and they fell down before him in prostration﴾ [Yusuf: 100]. Was that the last permitted form of prostration to created beings? The view of most scholars is that it was permitted until the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and that when the tree and the camel prostrated to him, his Companions said to him: "We are more deserving of prostrating to you than the tree and the stray camel." He said to them: "It is not appropriate for anyone to be prostrated to except Allah, Lord of the worlds." Ibn Majah related in his Sunan, and al-Busti in his Sahih, from Abu Waqid, who said: When Mu'adh ibn Jabal came back from Syria, he prostrated to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "What is this?" He said: "O Messenger of Allah, I came to Syria and saw them prostrating to their patriarchs and their bishops, so I wanted to do that to you." He said: "Do not do that. If I had commanded anything to prostrate to anything, I would have commanded the woman to prostrate to her husband. A woman does not fulfil the right of her Lord until she fulfils the right of her husband; even if he asked her for herself while she was on a qatab, she should not refuse him." This is the wording of al-Busti. The meaning of "qatab" is that among the Arabs, a birthing chair was rare, so they would carry their women on a qatab at the time of childbirth. [[Qatab: a small saddle, of the size of a hump.]] In some routes of Mu'adh's narration: "and he forbade prostration to humans and commanded handshaking."

I say: this prohibited prostration has been made a habit by ignorant Sufis during their sama' (listening sessions), and when they enter upon their shaykhs and seek their forgiveness. One of them, when a state overtakes him, supposedly, is seen prostrating to the feet [[In some copies of the original: "lil-aqdam" (to the feet).]] out of ignorance, whether facing the qibla or not, out of ignorance on his part. Their effort is lost and their work is ruined.

The fifth issue: His saying, "illa Iblis" (except Iblis), is in the accusative as a continuous exception (istithna' muttasil), because he was among the angels according to the majority view: Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Jurayj, Ibn al-Musayyab, Qatada and others. This is the choice of Shaykh Abu al-Hasan, al-Tabari preferred it, and it is the apparent meaning of the verse. Ibn 'Abbas said: his name was 'Azazil, and he was one of the noblest angels, and he was among the four-winged ones; then he was later driven into despair (ublis). Simak ibn Harb related from 'Ikrima from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Iblis was one of the angels, and when he disobeyed Allah, He was angry with him, cursed him, and he became a devil (shaytan). Al-Mawardi related from Qatada that he was of the best class of angels, called al-Jinna. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the jinn are a tribe of the angels created from fire, and Iblis was among them, while the rest of the angels were created from light. Ibn Zayd, al-Hasan and Qatada also said: Iblis is the father of the jinn, just as Adam is the father of humanity, and he was not an angel. Something similar was related from Ibn 'Abbas, and he said his name was al-Harith. Shahr ibn Hawshab and some of the theologians said: he was one of the jinn who were on the earth, and the angels fought them and took him captive as a child, and he worshipped with the angels and was addressed, and al-Tabari related this from Ibn Mas'ud. On this view the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), like His saying, ﴿They have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption﴾ [al-Nisa': 157], and His saying, ﴿except what you slaughter﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 3], according to one of the two opinions. The poet said:

*Laysa 'alayka 'atash wa la juw... illa al-ruqad wa al-ruqadu mamnu'*

Some of the proponents of this view argued that Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, described the angels, saying: ﴿They do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6], and His saying: ﴿except Iblis, who was of the jinn﴾ [al-Kahf: 50], and the jinn are other than the angels. Those of the first view answered that it is not impossible for Iblis to be excluded from the category of angels, because of what was already decreed in Allah's knowledge regarding his wretchedness, as an act of justice from Him, who is not questioned about what He does. Nor is there anything in his creation from fire, or in the composition of desire when he was angered by Him, that prevents him from being one of the angels. As for the one who said he was of the jinn of the earth who were taken captive, it has been related in contrast that Iblis was the one who fought the jinn on the earth together with a host of angels; this was related by al-Mahdawi and others. Al-Tha'labi related from Ibn 'Abbas that Iblis was from a tribe of the angels called the jinn, created from the scorching fire (samum), while the angels were created from light. His name in Syriac was 'Azazil, and in Arabic al-Harith. He was one of the guardians of Paradise, and he was the chief of the angels of the lowest heaven, and he had authority over it and over the earth. He was one of the most diligent angels and the most knowledgeable of them, and he governed what lay between heaven and earth. He saw in himself, because of this, nobility and greatness, and this is what led him to disbelief, so he disobeyed Allah, and He transformed him into a stoned devil. If a man's sin is due to arrogance, do not hope for him; but if his sin is disobedience, then hope for him. Adam's sin, peace be upon him, was disobedience, while Iblis's sin was arrogance. The angels are also sometimes called jinn because they are hidden, and in the revelation: ﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾ [al-Saffat: 158]. The poet said, describing Sulayman, peace be upon him:

*Wa sakhkhara min jinni al-mala'iki tis'atan... qiyaman ladayhi ya'malUna bila ajr*

Also, since he was one of the treasurers of Paradise, he was attributed to it, and his name was derived from its name, and Allah knows best. Iblis, his measure is Ifʿīl, derived from al-iblās (إِبْلَاس), which is despair of the mercy of Allah, exalted is He. He is not declined (diptote), because he is a definite proper name and there is no equivalent to him among nouns, so he was assimilated to foreign names; this was said by Abu ʿUbayda and others. It was also said: he is foreign, with no derivation, so he is not declined on account of foreignness and definiteness; this was said by al-Zajjaj and others.

The sixth point: the words of the Exalted, ﴿abā﴾ (he refused), mean he refrained from doing what he was commanded. From this is the authentic hadith from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "When the son of Adam recites the prostration verse [and prostrates [The addition is from Sahih Muslim.]], Satan withdraws weeping, saying, 'Woe is him!' – and in another narration, 'Woe is me!' – The son of Adam was commanded to prostrate and he prostrated, so for him is Paradise; and I was commanded to prostrate and I refused, so for me is the Fire." Recorded by Muslim. It is said: abā yaʾbā ibāʾan, and it is a rare verb that came in the pattern faʿala yafʿalu, in which none of the throat letters occur; but it has been said that the alif resembles the throat letters. Al-Zajjaj said: I heard Ismaʿil ibn Ishaq al-Qadi say, "My opinion is that the alif resembles the throat letters." Al-Nahhas said: I know of no statement by Abu Ishaq narrated from Ismaʿil other than this point.

The seventh point: the words of the Exalted, ﴿wa-istakbara﴾ (and he was arrogant). Al-istikbar is to deem something great, so it is as if he disliked prostrating to him and deemed it too great for Adam; thus abandoning prostration to Adam was a belittling of the command of Allah and His wisdom. Concerning this arrogance, peace be upon him said: "No one who has in his heart the weight of a mustard seed of arrogance will enter Paradise [The addition is from Sahih Muslim.]." In one narration, a man said: "Indeed a man loves that his garment be fine and his sandal be fine." He said: "Indeed Allah is beautiful and loves beauty. Arrogance is rejecting the truth and looking down on people." Recorded by Muslim. The meaning of "batar al-haqq" is belittling and nullifying it; and "ghamt al-nas" is despising them and looking down upon them. It is also narrated as "ghamṣ" with the unpointed ṣād, and the meaning is the same: one says ghamasahu yaghmisuhu ghamsan and ightamasahu, i.e., he considered him small and did not regard him as anything. Also, "ghamasa fulan al-niʿma" means he did not thank for the blessing; and "ghamastu ʿalayhi qawlan qalahu" means I found fault with him for the statement he made. The accursed one himself expressed this meaning when he said: "I am better than him; You created me from fire and created him from clay" [See vol. 7, p. 170.] [Sad: 76]. ﴿Shall I prostrate to one whom You created from clay?﴾ [al-Isra: 61]. ﴿I am not one who would prostrate to a human whom You created from dry clay, from black mud, molded﴾ [al-Hijr: 33]. Therefore Allah disbelieved him for this. So whoever belittles any of the commands of Allah the Exalted or the command of His Messenger, peace be upon him, his ruling is the same as his, and there is no disagreement about this. Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik that he said: "It has reached me that the first disobedience was envy and arrogance: Iblis envied Adam, and Adam was greedy in eating from the tree." Qatada said: Iblis envied Adam for the honour Allah had given him, and said, "I am of fire and this one is of clay." The beginning of sins was arrogance, then greed, until Adam ate from the tree, then envy, when the son of Adam envied his brother.

The eighth point: the words of the Exalted, ﴿wa-kāna min al-kāfirīn﴾ (and he was of the disbelievers). It has been said: kāna here means ṣāra (became), and from this is the words of the Exalted, ﴿fa-kāna min al-mughraqīn﴾ (so he was among the drowned). The poet said: [This is Ibn Ahmar, as in Lisan, under the root k-w-n.]
In a barren desert wilderness, the mounts seemed like sandgrouse of al-Hazn whose chicks had been their eggs.
That is, they became. Ibn Fawrak said: "kāna" here meaning "ṣāra" is an error that the principles reject. Most of the commentators said: the meaning is that it was in the knowledge of Allah the Exalted that he would disbelieve, because the true disbeliever and the true believer are the one from whom Allah has known the final state. I say: this is correct, due to the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in Sahih al-Bukhari: "Actions are only by their endings."

It has also been said that Iblis worshipped Allah the Exalted for eighty thousand years, and was given leadership and the treasury of Paradise as a gradual deception, just as the hypocrites were given the testimony that there is no god but Allah on the tips of their tongues, and just as Balaam [In the histories of Ibn al-Athir and al-Tabari, he is Balaam ibn Ba'ura, from the descendants of Lot, who lived in the time of Moses, peace be upon him, and was from the people of Canaan. See Tarikh Ibn al-Athir vol. 1, p. 140, and Tarikh al-Tabari, first part, p. 508, Europe edition.] was given the Greatest Name on the tip of his tongue, yet arrogance was firmly rooted in his soul. Ibn ʿAbbas said: he considered himself to have a virtue over the angels because of what he possessed, and therefore he said, "I am better than him." And for this reason the Exalted, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My hands? Were you arrogant, or were you of the high ones?﴾ [Sad: 75], i.e., you became arrogant and you have no pride; and I did not act arrogantly when I created him with My hands, and pride is Mine! Therefore He said: ﴿and he was of the disbelievers﴾ [Sad: 74]. The origin of his creation was from the fire of might, and therefore he swore by might, saying: ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾ [Sad: 82]. So might bequeathed him pride, until he saw superiority for himself over Adam, peace be upon him. Abu Salih said: the angels were created from the light of might, and Iblis was created from the fire of might.

The ninth point: our scholars, may Allah have mercy upon them, said: whoever Allah the Exalted manifests miracles and extraordinary events that break customary patterns through the hands of someone who is not a prophet, that does not indicate his sainthood (wilaya), in contrast to some Sufis and Rafidah who said: this indicates that he is a saint, for if he were not a saint, Allah would not have manifested through his hands what He manifested. Our proof is that knowledge that one of us is a saint of Allah the Exalted is valid only after knowing that he will die as a believer; and when it is not known that he will die as a believer, we cannot be certain that he is a saint of Allah the Exalted, because a saint of Allah the Exalted is one whom Allah knows will end only in faith. Since we agree that we cannot be certain that that man will end in faith, and the man himself cannot be certain that he will end in faith, it is known that this does not indicate his sainthood. They said: we do not deny that Allah may inform some of His saints of the goodness of their final outcome and the ending of their deeds, and other things with it; this was said by Shaykh Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari and others. Al-Tabari held that Allah the Exalted intended through the story of Iblis a rebuke to those like him among the children of Adam, namely the Jews who disbelieved in Muhammad, peace be upon him, although they knew his prophethood, and despite the ancient blessings of Allah upon them and upon their forefathers.

The tenth point: it has been disputed whether there was a disbeliever before Iblis or not. It was said: no, and Iblis was the first to disbelieve. It was said: before him there were disbelieving people, namely the jinn, who were on the earth. It is also disputed whether Iblis disbelieved out of ignorance or out of obstinacy, on two views among the People of the Sunna; and there is no disagreement that he knew Allah the Exalted before his disbelief. Whoever says he disbelieved out of ignorance says that his knowledge was taken away at his disbelief. Whoever says he disbelieved out of obstinacy says: he disbelieved while his knowledge remained with him. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: disbelief [out of obstinacy [The addition is from the tafsir of Ibn ʿAtiyya.]] with the continuing presence of knowledge is unlikely, but in my view it is possible and not impossible, given that Allah forsakes whom He wills.

**Part 1 of 4**

There are thirteen issues in this verse.

**The first issue:** the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿And We said, "O Adam, dwell﴾. There is no disagreement that Allah expelled Iblis (Satan) when he disbelieved and removed him far from the Garden. After his expulsion, He said to Adam, "Dwell" (*uskun*), meaning: remain in residence and take it as a dwelling (*maskan*), which is the place of *sukun* (dwelling/settling). One says *sakana ilayhi yaskunu sukunan* (he found rest in him/it). *Al-sakan* is fire, as the poet said:

*"It has been straightened with fire (sakan) and oils."*

*Al-sakan* is also everything that one finds rest in. *Al-sikkin* (the knife) is well known; it is so named because it stills the motion of the slaughtered animal. From the same root comes *al-miskin* (the poor man), because of the limitation of his activity and movement. The word *sukkan al-safina* (the rudder of the ship, by which it is steered) is Arabic, because it stills the ship from tossing.

**The second issue:** in the words ﴿dwell﴾ there is an indication that they would leave, because residence (*sukna*) is not ownership. For this reason, some of the knowers (*al-arifin*) said: residence is for a period and then it ends. Thus their entry into the Garden was an entry of residence, not an entry of permanent abode.

I say: if this is so, it indicates what the majority of the scholars hold: that whoever settles a man in a dwelling, the man does not own it by residence, and the owner may remove him when the period of settlement has ended.

Al-Sha'bi used to say: if a man says, "My house is yours for residence until you die," it is his for his lifetime and after his death. But if he says, "Dwell in this house of mine until you die," it returns to its owner when he dies.

Similar to residence is *al-umra* (a life-grant: the gift of the use of property for the lifetime of the grantee or the grantor), except that the disagreement regarding *al-umra* is stronger than that regarding residence. The discussion of *al-umra* will come, God willing, in (the commentary on) Surat Hud. [See vol. 9, p. 57.]

Al-Harbi said: I heard Ibn al-A'rabi say: "The Arabs have not disagreed that these things remain in the ownership of their owners, while their benefits belong to the one to whom they were granted: *al-umra*, *al-ruqba*, *al-ifqar*, *al-ikhbal*, *al-minha*, *al-ariyya*, *al-sukna*, and *al-itraq*."

This is the proof of Malik and his companions that one owns none of the gifts except their usufruct, not the substance itself. This is also the view of al-Layth ibn Sa'd, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, and Yazid ibn Qusayt.

*Al-umra* is your settling a man in a house of yours for the duration of your life or his life. Similar to it is *al-ruqba*, which is that one says, "If I die before you, it returns to me, and if you die before me, it is yours." It derives from *al-muraqaba* (mutual watching), which is that each of the two watches for the death of the other. For this reason they differed over its permissibility and prohibition. Abu Yusuf and al-Shafi'i permitted it, and in their view it is like a bequest. Malik and the Kufans prohibited it, because each of them seeks a return that he does not know whether he will obtain, and each wishes for the death of the other.

There are also two hadiths on the subject, one permitting and one prohibiting, which Ibn Majah mentioned in his Sunan. The first was narrated by Jabir ibn Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "*Al-umra* is permissible for the one to whom it is granted, and *al-ruqba* is permissible for the one to whom it is granted." In this hadith, *al-umra* and *al-ruqba* are equal in ruling.

The second was narrated by Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no *ruqba*. Whoever is granted something by *ruqba*, it is his in life and in death." He said: *Al-ruqba* is that one says to the other, "It is mine and yours, upon death."

So his saying "There is no *ruqba*" is a prohibition indicating ban, and his saying "Whoever is granted something by *ruqba*, it is his" indicates permissibility. Al-Nasa'i also recorded both.

It is reported from Ibn Abbas that he said: *al-umra* and *al-ruqba* are the same. Ibn al-Mundhir said: It is established that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "*Al-umra* is permissible for the one to whom it is granted, and *al-ruqba* is permissible for the one to whom it is granted." Ibn al-Mundhir authenticated this hadith, and it is a proof for those who say that *al-umra* and *al-ruqba* are the same.

It is reported from Ali, and al-Thawri and Ahmad held likewise, that it never returns to the first giver. Ishaq also held this view. Tawus said: whoever is granted something by *ruqba*, it is the path of inheritance.

*Al-ifqar* derives from *fiqar al-zahr* (the vertebrae of the back). One says *afqartuka naqati*: I lent you her vertebrae so that you could ride her. *Afqaraka al-sayd* means the game allowed you to reach its vertebrae so that you could shoot it. Similar to it is *al-ikhbal*: one says *akhbaltu fulanan* when I lend someone a she-camel to ride or a horse to fight on. Zuhayr said:

*"There, if they are asked for property, they lend it; and if they are asked for help, they give it; and if they prosper, they are generous."*

*Al-minha* is a gift. *Al-minha* also means the gift of milk. *Al-manihah* is a she-camel or a sheep that a man gives to another to milk, and then returns it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The borrowed item must be returned, the gift (*minha*) must be returned, the debt must be paid, and the guarantor is liable." Abu Umama narrated it; al-Tirmidhi, al-Daraqutni and others recorded it, and it is sound.

*Al-itraq* is lending a stallion for breeding. One says *istatraqa fulanun fulanan fahlahu* when someone asks another for his stallion to mate with his camels, and he lends it to him. One also says *atriqni fahlaka*, meaning: lend me your stallion to mate with my camels. *Tariqa al-fahl al-naqata yatruqu turuqan*, meaning the stallion mounted the she-camel. *Turuqat al-fahl* means its female, and one says: *naqatun taruqatu al-fahl* for the one that has reached the age at which the stallion may mate with her.

**The third issue:** the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿You and your wife﴾. The word "you" (*anta*) is an emphasis on the pronoun hidden within the verb. Similar to it is ﴿So go, you and your Lord﴾. It is not permitted to say *uskun wa-zawjuka* ("dwell, and your wife") nor *udhhab wa-rabbuka* ("go, and your Lord"), except in cases of poetic necessity, as the poet said:

*"I said when she approached, and the fair ones strutted like wild cows of the plain, stepping over sand."*

Here "the fair ones" (*zuhr*) is in apposition to the pronoun in "approached," and that pronoun was not emphasized. It is permissible outside the Qur'an, though it is weak: *qum wa-Zayd* ("stand, and Zayd").

**The fourth issue:** the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿and your wife﴾. The language of the Qur'an is *zawj* without a *ha'* (taa marbuta). This was discussed earlier. [See p. 240 of this part.]

In Sahih Muslim, however, the form *zawjah* appears: Abd Allah ibn Maslama ibn Qa'nab narrated to us, saying: Hammad ibn Salama narrated to us from Thabit al-Bunani, from Anas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) was with one of his wives, when a man passed by him. He called him, and the man came. He said: "O so-and-so, this is my wife so-and-so." The man said: "O Messenger of Allah, I did not think of anyone but you." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, Satan flows through the human being as the blood flows."

The wife of Adam, peace be upon him, is Hawwa (Eve), peace be upon her. He was the first to call her by this name when she was created from his rib, without Adam, peace be upon him, feeling it. Had he felt pain, no man would have shown affection to his wife. When he awoke, he was asked: "Who is this?" He said: "A woman." It was asked: "What is her name?" He said: "Hawwa." It was asked: "Why is she called a woman (*imra'a*)?" He said: "Because she was taken from the man (*mar'*)." It was asked: "Why is she called Hawwa?" He said: "Because she was created from a living being (*hayy*)."

It is reported that the angels asked him about this, to test his knowledge, and they said to him: "Do you love her, O Adam?" He said: "Yes." They said to Hawwa: "Do you love him, O Hawwa?" She said: "No," while in her heart there was many times the love he had for her. They said: "If a woman were truthful in her love for her husband, Hawwa would have been truthful."

Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas said: When Adam was settled in the Garden, he walked in it feeling lonely. When he slept, Hawwa was created from his rib, the lower rib on his left side, so that he might find rest in her and be at ease with her. When he awoke and saw her, he said: "Who are you?" She said: "A woman created from your rib, so that you may find rest in me." This is the meaning of the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿It is He who created you from one soul and made from it its mate, that he might find rest in her﴾ [Al-A'raf: 189]. [See vol. 7, p. 337.]

The scholars said: for this reason the woman is crooked, because she was created from something crooked, which is the rib.

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayra, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, the woman was created from a rib (in another narration: and the most crooked part of the rib is its upper part). She will never go straight for you in one manner. If you enjoy her, you enjoy her with her crookedness, and if you try to straighten her, you will break her, and breaking her is divorcing her." [The addition is from Sahih Muslim.]

The poet said:

*"She is the crooked rib, you cannot straighten her;
Indeed, the straightening of ribs is their breaking."*

*"Does she combine weakness and power over the youth?
Is it not strange, her weakness and her power?"*

Among the rulings derived from this category, the scholars used it to establish the inheritance of the ambiguous hermaphrodite (al-khunthā al-mushkil) when the signs of women and men are equal in him, such as menstruation, breasts, and the urinary organ, by the deficiency of the limbs. If his ribs are fewer than the ribs of a woman, he is given the share of a man. This is narrated from ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him), because Ḥawwāʾ (Eve) was created from one of his ribs. The explanation of this will come in the chapter on inheritance (al-mawārīth), if Allah the Exalted wills [see vol. 5, p. 65].

The fifth issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿al-Jannah﴾ (the Garden). Al-Jannah means the orchard, and the discussion of it has already passed [see p. 239 of this part]. There is no regard for what the Muʿtazilah and the Qadariyyah held, that it was not in the Garden of Eternity (jannat al-khuld) but in a garden in the land of ʿAdn. They based their innovation on the argument that, if it had been the Garden of Eternity, Iblīs would never have reached it, for Allah says: ﴿No idle talk therein nor sinfulness﴾ [al-Ṭūr: 23], and He says: ﴿They hear therein no idle talk nor lying﴾ [al-Nabaʾ: 35], and He says: ﴿They hear therein no idle talk nor sinfulness, except the saying: "Peace, peace"﴾ [al-Wāqiʿah: 25–26]. And that its people do not leave it, for His saying: ﴿And they will never be removed therefrom﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 48]. Also, the Garden of Eternity is the abode of holiness (dār al-quds), made pure from sins and disobedience as a purification of it. Iblīs idled and lied in it, and Ādam and Ḥawwāʾ were expelled from it by their disobedience. They said: how is it permissible for Ādam, with his station with Allah and his perfect intellect, to seek the tree of eternity while he was in the abode of eternity and the kingdom that does not decay? The answer: Allah the Exalted defined the Garden with the definite article (al-alif wa-l-lām), and whoever says "I ask Allah for the Garden" is understood, in the common usage of people, to mean only the seeking of the Garden of Eternity. It is not impossible in reason that Iblīs entered the Garden to deceive Ādam. Mūsā met Ādam, peace be upon them both, and Mūsā said to him: "You made your descendants wretched and expelled them from the Garden." He used the definite article to indicate that it is the well-known Garden of Eternity. Ādam did not deny that, and had it been other than it, he would have replied to Mūsā. When Ādam remained silent about what Mūsā affirmed, it is established that the abode from which Allah the Mighty and Majestic expelled them is other than the abode to which they were sent. As for what they argued from the verses, that was made by Allah in it after its people enter it on the Day of Resurrection. It is not impossible that it is the abode of eternity for whomever Allah wills to make eternal in it, and someone against whom the decree of annihilation is issued may leave it. The people of interpretation (ahl al-taʾwīl) agreed that the angels enter the Garden upon its people and leave it. Its keys were in the hand of Iblīs, then they were taken from him after the disobedience. The Prophet (ﷺ) entered it on the night of the Isrāʾ, then left it, and informed of what is in it, and that it is truly the Garden of Eternity. As for their saying that the Garden is the abode of holiness and that Allah purified it from sins, it is ignorance on their part, for Allah the Exalted commanded the Children of Israel to enter the Holy Land, which is al-Shām, and the people of the revealed laws agreed that Allah sanctified it, yet sins, unbelief, and lying were witnessed in it, and its sanctification did not prevent sins in it. The same applies to the abode of holiness. Abū al-Ḥasan Ibn Baṭṭāl said: Some of the shaykhs related that the Ahl al-Sunnah agree that the Garden of Eternity is the one from which Ādam (peace be upon him) was sent down, so there is no meaning to the saying of whoever opposes them. As for their saying, "How is it permissible for Ādam, in his perfect intellect, to seek the tree of eternity while he was in the abode of eternity," it is turned back upon them: how is it permissible for Ādam, while in his perfect intellect, to seek the tree of eternity in the abode of annihilation? This is not permissible for anyone who has the least portion of intellect, so how about Ādam, who is the most intelligent of creation, as Abū Umāmah said, as will come.

The sixth issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And eat therefrom in abundance wherever you will﴾. The reading of the majority is "raghadan" with a fatḥah on the ghayn. al-Nakhaʿī and Ibn Thabbāth read it with a sukūn on it. Raghad means a pleasant, abundant life without hardship. He said:
"While a man is seen by you, comfortable, feeling safe from misfortunes, in a life of raghad."
[The speaker is Imruʾ al-Qays, as in the tafsīrs of Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ṭabarī.]
It is said: raghuda ʿaysuhum and raghida (with ḍammah and kasrah on the ghayn), and arghada al-qawm: they became prosperous and were in abundance of life. It is in the accusative as an adjective of a deleted verbal noun. Ḥaythu, ḥaytha, ḥaythi, ḥawtha, ḥawthi, and ḥāth are all dialectal forms, mentioned by al-Naḥḥās and others.

The seventh issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not approach this tree﴾, meaning, do not approach it by eating, because permission (al-ibāḥah) regarding it had already occurred [i.e., from other than that tree]. Ibn al-ʿArabī said: I heard al-Shāshī in the assembly of al-Naḍr [ibn Shumayl] say: when it is said "lā taqrab" (with a fatḥah on the rāʾ) its meaning is "do not engage in the act," and when it is with a ḍammah on the rāʾ, its meaning is "do not come near it." In al-Ṣiḥāḥ: qaraba al-shayʾu yaqrubu qurban, meaning it drew near; qaribtuhu (with kasrah) aqrabuhu qurbānan, meaning I drew near to it; and qaraba aqrubu qarābatan (like katabtu aktubu kitābatan) when you travel toward water with a night between you and it; the noun is al-qaraba. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: I asked a Bedouin, "What is al-qaraba?" He said: "Traveling by night for the water of the next day." Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: Some of the skilled scholars said: when Allah wished to forbid eating from the tree, He forbade it with a expression that implies eating and what leads to it, which is approaching. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: This is a clear example of blocking the means (sadd al-dharāʾiʿ). Some of the masters of meanings said: His saying, "and do not approach," indicates falling into error and leaving the Garden, and that their dwelling in it would not last, because one who is eternal is not forbidden anything, nor commanded, nor prohibited. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿Indeed, I will place upon the earth a khalīfah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], which shows their departure from it.

The eighth issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿this tree﴾. The ambiguous demonstrative noun is qualified only by what has the definite article, as in your saying: "I passed by this man, this woman, and this tree." Ibn Muḥaysin read "hadhī al-shajarah" with yāʾ, and this is the original form, because the hāʾ in hādhihi is a replacement for a yāʾ, which is why the letter before it is kasrah, and there is no feminine hāʾ in the speech preceded by a kasrah other than it, because its origin is yāʾ.

The dialects are: al-shajara, al-shajara, and al-shayra, three forms. "al-shajara" is also read with a kasra on the shin (al-shijra). Al-shajara and al-shajra refer to anything that stands on a stalk from the plants of the earth. One says ardun shajirah and shajra'(land with many trees), meaning abundant in trees, and wadin shajir (a valley with many trees), but one does not say wadin ashjar. The singular of al-shajra' is shajarah. Only a few words of this pattern occur in the plural: shajarah and shajra', qasabah and qasba', tarfah and tarfa', and halfah and halfa'. Al-Asma'i used to say of the singular of al-halfa': halifah, with a kasra on the lam, to differ from its counterparts. Sibawayh said: al-shajra' is both singular and plural, and likewise al-qasba', al-tarfa' and al-halfa'. Al-mashjarah means the place of trees; one says ardun mashjarah (land with many trees), and "this land is ashjar than that," meaning it has more trees. This is from al-Jawhari.

Ninth: The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed on identifying the tree that was forbidden, so that he ate from it. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ja'dah ibn Hubayrah said: it was the vine, and for this reason wine was forbidden to us. Ibn 'Abbas also said, as did Abu Malik and Qatadah: it was the ear of grain, and its grain is like the kidneys of a cow, sweeter than honey and softer than butter; this was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih. When Allah accepted Adam's repentance, He made it food for his descendants. Ibn Juraij reported from one of the Companions: it was the fig tree, and Sa'id also related this from Qatadah [[In one copy: (Shu'bah), and both transmit from Qatadah.]]. For this reason, in dream interpretation, it signifies regret for the one who eats it, because of Adam's regret (peace be upon him) over eating it; this was mentioned by al-Suhayli. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: none of these identifications is supported by a report; rather the correct view is to believe that Allah forbade Adam a tree, and he opposed Him by going to it and disobeying Him by eating from it. Al-Qushayri Abu Nasr said: my father, the imam, may Allah have mercy on him, used to say: it is known in general that it was the tree of trial.

Tenth: They differed about how he ate from it despite the threat attached to approaching it, which is Allah's saying: ﴿so you would be among the wrongdoers﴾. Some said: they ate from a tree other than the one pointed to, so they did not understand the prohibition as applying to its entire kind; as if Iblis had deceived them into taking the matter literally. Ibn al-'Arabi said: on this view it is the first disobedience by which Allah was disobeyed. He said: this is evidence that whoever swears not to eat this bread and then eats from its kind, breaks his oath (yahnath). The detailed position is that most scholars said: he does not break it. Malik and his companions said: if the context of the oath requires specifying the indicated item, then he does not break it by eating its kind; but if the context of the oath, its cause or the intention behind it requires the kind, it is taken to mean that and he breaks it by eating anything of that kind. Adam's story is understood this way, for he was forbidden a tree that was specified for him, but what was meant was its kind; so the statement was taken according to its wording rather than its meaning. Our scholars differed on a branch of this: if he swears not to eat this wheat and then eats bread made from it, there are two opinions. The author of the Kitab said: he breaks the oath, because it is eaten in this form. Ibn al-Mawwaz said: there is nothing upon him, because he did not eat wheat but bread, and he observed the name and the description. If he had said in his oath, "I will not eat from this wheat," he would break it by eating the bread made from it. There is also disagreement regarding what is bought with its price, and regarding what it produces.

Others said: they interpreted the prohibition as recommendatory (nadb). Ibn al-'Arabi said: although this is a question of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), it falls away here because of His saying: ﴿so you would be among the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 35], since He linked the prohibition to the threat. Likewise is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿so let him not expel you from the Garden, lest you be miserable﴾ [Ta-Ha: 117]. Ibn al-Musayyib said: Adam only ate after Hawwa' had given him wine to drink, so he became drunk and was not in his right mind. Yazid ibn Qusayt said the same, and both of them would swear by Allah that he did not eat from this tree while he was in his right mind. Ibn al-'Arabi said: this is corrupt both by transmission and by reason. As for transmission, it is not established in any way, and Allah, mighty and majestic, has described the wine of Paradise, saying: ﴿neither will there be in it any intoxication﴾. As for reason, prophets after prophethood are protected (ma'sum) from what would lead to neglecting the obligations or committing grave offences.

I say: some scholars have inferred Adam's prophethood before he was made to dwell in Paradise from Allah's saying: ﴿So when he informed them of their names﴾ [al-Baqarah: 33], for Allah commanded him to inform the angels of what they did not have knowledge of from Allah, mighty and majestic. It was also said: he ate it forgetfully, and it is possible that they both forgot the threat. I say: this is the correct view, because Allah informed of it in His Book definitively and decisively, saying: ﴿And We had already taken a covenant from Adam before, but he forgot, and We did not find in him determination﴾ [Ta-Ha: 115] [[See vol. 11, pp. 251 and 253.]]. But since the prophets (peace be upon them) are obliged to a degree of watchfulness and alertness, owing to the abundance of their knowledge and the elevation of their ranks, beyond what is required of others, his preoccupation that made him neglect remembering the prohibition was a negligence for which he became disobedient, that is, one who opposed (the command). Abu Umamah said: if the intellects (ahlam) of the children of Adam, from the time Allah created creation until the Day of Resurrection, were placed in one pan of a scale and the intellect of Adam in the other pan, it would outweigh them; and Allah has said: ﴿and We did not find in him determination﴾.

I say: this saying of Abu Umamah is general over all the children of Adam. It may be that our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) is excepted from it, for he was the most forbearing and intelligent of people. It may also be that the meaning is: even if the intellects of the children of Adam were non-prophets. And Allah knows best. I say: the first view is also good, for they assumed that what was meant was the specific tree, while what was meant was the kind, like the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) when he took gold and silk and said: "These two are forbidden to the males of my community." And in another report he said: "These two destroy my community." He only meant the kind, not the specific item.

Eleventh: It is said that the first to eat from the tree was Hawwa', through Iblis's enticement of her, as will be explained. And his first speech was with her, for she was the whisperer of the pillow (wiswas al-mikhaddah), and she was the first temptation that entered upon men through women. He said: "Your Lord forbade you this tree only because it is the tree of immortality," for he knew from them that they loved eternity, so he came to them from the direction of what they loved, "Your love for a thing makes you blind and deaf." When Hawwa' spoke to Adam, he rejected it and reminded her of the covenant. Then he insisted to Hawwa' and she insisted to Adam, until she said: "I will eat before you, and if something befalls me, you will be safe." So she ate and it did not harm her, and she came to Adam and said: "Eat, for I have eaten and it has not harmed me." So he ate, and their private parts (sawat) became visible to them, and they fell under the ruling of sin, because of Allah's saying: ﴿And do not approach this tree﴾, in which He addressed them both in the prohibition. Therefore punishment did not descend upon them until the forbidden act had been committed by both of them together. This matter was obscure to Adam, and for this reason some scholars said: whoever says to his two wives or two female slaves, "If you two enter the house, then you are divorced" or "then you are free," divorce and manumission do not take effect upon the entry of only one of them. Our scholars differed on this in three opinions. Ibn al-Qasim said: neither of them is divorced or freed except by both of them entering together, following this principle and taking the requirement of the unrestricted wording. Sahnun also said this. Ibn al-Qasim said on another occasion: both are divorced and both are freed upon the entry of one of them, because partial breaking is breaking, just as if he swore not to eat these two loaves, he would break it by eating one of them, or even a morsel from them. Ashhab said: the one who entered alone is freed and divorced, because the entry of each of them is a condition for the divorce or manumission of that one. Ibn al-'Arabi said: this is far-fetched, because part of a condition is not a condition, by consensus. I say: the correct view is the first, and that when a prohibition is conditioned upon two actions, the violation is not realized except by both of them. For when you say, "Do not enter the house," and one of them enters, the violation has not occurred by them both, because Allah's saying ﴿And do not approach this tree﴾ is a prohibition for both of them, and ﴿so you would be among the wrongdoers﴾ is its consequence. So they would not be among the wrongdoers unless they both acted. When she ate, nothing afflicted her, because the forbidden act had not occurred in its entirety. This meaning was obscure to Adam, so he was tempted and forgot this ruling. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And We had already taken a covenant from Adam before, but he forgot﴾ [Ta-Ha: 115]. It was also said: he forgot His saying: ﴿Indeed, this is an enemy to you and to your wife, so let him not expel you from the Garden, lest you be miserable﴾ [Ta-Ha: 117]. And Allah knows best.

Twelfth: Scholars differed in this chapter about whether the prophets (may the blessings of Allah be upon them all) committed minor sins (saghair) for which they are held to account and rebuked, or not, after agreeing that they are protected from major sins (kaba'ir) and from every base characteristic that involves disgrace and deficiency, by consensus according to al-Qadi Abu Bakr [[He is Muhammad ibn al-Tayyib ibn Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Qasim Abu Bakr al-Baqillani.]], and according to al-Ustadh Abu Ishaq [[He is Ibrahim ibn Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Ustadh Abu Ishaq al-Isfara'ini. In the originals it reads: (according to al-Ustadh Abu Bakr), which is a distortion.]]

Al-Qurtubi's commentary on the verse, part 4 of 4:

(See the discussion on the infallibility of the prophets in the commentary on al-Mawaqif.)]] That is the requirement of the evidence of miracles. According to the Mu'tazilah, it is the requirement of the evidence of reason, according to their principles. Al-Tabari and others among the jurists, theologians and traditionists said: minor sins (saghair) do occur from them. This is in contrast to the Rafidah, who said that they are infallible from all of that. They argued with what occurred of such in the revelation and what is established of their disavowal of such in the hadith, and this is apparent and there is no obscurity in it. A majority of the jurists among the followers of Malik, Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i said: they are infallible from all minor sins, just as they are infallible from all major sins, because we have been commanded to follow them in their actions, their traces and their conduct, as an absolute command without any accompanying indication. So if we allowed minor sins upon them, it would not be possible to follow them, since not every one of their actions has a clearly distinguished purpose as to whether it is an act of devotion, permissible, forbidden or disobedient. It is not valid for a person to be commanded to comply with a command which may be a sin, especially according to those among the usulis who hold that the act takes precedence over the statement when they conflict.

Al-Ustadh Abu Ishaq al-Isfara'ini said: They differed concerning minor sins. The view of most is that these are not permissible for them, and some went to permitting them, but there is no basis for this view.

Some of the later scholars who held the first view said: What should be said is that God Most High has informed of the occurrence of sins from some of them, attributed them to them, and rebuked them for them, and they informed of them concerning themselves, disavowed them, feared them, and repented. All of this occurs in many places which, taken as a whole, do not admit of interpretation, even if individual instances may admit of it. All of this does not detract from their ranks. Rather, those matters which occurred from them occurred by way of rarity, by way of error and forgetfulness, or by an interpretation which led to them. They are, in relation to others, good deeds, and in relation to them, bad deeds, in relation to their ranks and the elevation of their stations, for a minister may be held to account for what a governor is rewarded for. So they feared that on the Day of Resurrection, while knowing that they are secure, safe and free. He said: This is the truth. Al-Junayd spoke well when he said: The good deeds of the righteous are the bad deeds of those brought near (to God). So they, may the blessings and peace of God be upon them, although the texts have testified to the occurrence of sins from them, this did not impair their ranks nor diminish their standing. Rather, He made amends for them, chose them, guided them, praised them, purified them, selected them and preferred them, may the blessings and peace of God be upon them.

The thirteenth: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿فَتَكُونا مِنَ الظَّالِمِينَ﴾ (so you would be among the wrongdoers). Its root meaning, "ẓulm," is placing a thing in other than its proper place. A "ẓalmah" land is one that has never been dug and then is dug. Al-Nabighah said:

I stopped there at dusk, questioning it,
but it was unable to answer, and in the abode there was no one,
Except the ropes (al-awari), with difficulty, which I cannot explain,
and the trench (al-nu'y) like a basin in the hard, unexcavated ground.

[[The awari (singular: ari) are ropes with which a beast is tied in its place of confinement. Al-lai: hardship and exertion. Al-nawa: a pit around the House so that water does not reach it. Al-jalad (with vowel-fatha on the lam): hard ground. See Khizanat al-Adab regarding its i'rab.]]

That soil is also called "al-ẓalim." A poet said:

So he became in the dust (ghabra') after an effort (ishahah)... over life, its "ẓalim" returned upon him.

[[Al-ishahah: caution and fear of one who tries to ward off death. The author of Lisan al-'Arab said: (meaning the grave pit, whose soil is returned upon him after the dead person is buried in it).]]

When a camel is slaughtered without any disease in it, it is said to have been wronged (ẓulima). From this is:

... ẓallamun lil-juzur
[[Second half of a line by Ibn Muqbil, whose full text is:
"They returned to the humble in a dwelling where they had been, the snorting of the flanks, wrongful toward the slaughtered camels."]]

It is also said: "He gave us a pleasant ẓalimah" when he gave them milk before it had ripened. And "he wronged his waterskin" (ẓalama waṭbahu) when he drew from it before it had fermented and its butter had come out. The milk is "maẓlum" and "ẓalim." He said:

Many a speaker said, "I wronged you with my waterskin..." — and would the ʿakad (the root of the tongue) fail to notice the ẓalim?

[[Zalamtu saqa'i: I gave them to drink from it before it had fermented. Al-'akad (with the ʿain vowelled either way, and the kaf vowelled with fatha, the plural of al-'akdah and al-'akdah): the root of the tongue.]]

A man who is "ẓalim" is one who is extremely wrongful. And "al-ẓulm" is polytheism. God Most High said: ﴿Indeed, association [with Him] is a great wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13].
[[See vol. 14, p. 62.]]

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿وَكُلا مِنْها رَغَداً﴾ (And eat from it in abundance). The nun was dropped from (kulā) because it is an imperative, and the hamzah was dropped due to frequent use, and its dropping is anomalous. Sibawayh said: Some of the Arabs say "awkul" and complete it. From it one says: "akaltu al-ṭaʿām akलan wa ma'kalan" (I ate the food). Al-akalah (with fatha): one time, until one is satisfied. Al-ukulah (with ḍammah): a morsel; you say: "akaltu ukulatan wahidah," i.e., one morsel, and it is also the bite. "Hadha al-shay'u ukulatun laka," i.e., a provision for you. Al-akl also means what is eaten. And it is said: "Fulan dhu ukul" when he has a share of worldly goods and abundant provision.
