(Raghadan) is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, i.e., an eating in abundance. Ibn Kaysan said: It may also be a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal). Mujahid said: (raghadan) means without any reckoning upon them. In the language, al-raghad is the abundant that does not concern you. It is said: "arghada al-qawm" when they fell into plenty and ease. This meaning has already been mentioned [see the sixth issue, p. 303 of this part].

(Haythu) is built on ḍammah because it differs from its sister adverbs in that it is not annexed, so it resembles qabl and ba'd when they stand alone, and so it takes ḍammah. Al-Kisa'i said: The dialect of Qays and Kinanah is ḍammah, and the dialect of Tamim is fatḥah. Al-Kisa'i said: The Banu Asad put it in the genitive in the genitive position and in the accusative in the accusative position. God Most High said: ﴿We will draw them on gradually from where they do not know﴾ [al-A'raf: 182; al-Qalam: 44]. It is both ḍammed and fatḥed.

(Wa la taqraba hadhihi al-shajarah): the hā' in (hadhihi) replaces the original yā', because the original was hadhi. Al-Nahhas said: I know of no feminine hā' in Arabic with a preceding kasrah except the hā' of (hadhihi). Some Arabs say: "hata Hind," and some say: "hati Hind." Sibawayh reported: "hadhih Hind" with the hā' sukun. Al-Kisa'i reported from the Arabs: "wa la taqraba hadhi al-shajarah." It is reported from Shibl ibn 'Abbad that Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muhaysin did not affirm the hā' in (hadhihi) throughout the Qur'an. The reading of the majority is (raghadan) with fatḥah on the ghayn. It is narrated from Ibn Wththab and al-Nakha'i that they both sukunated the ghayn. Salamah reported from al-Farra' who said: One says "hadhihi fa'alat" and "hadhi fa'alat," so there is affirmation of a yā' after the dhāl. And "hadha fa'alat," with kasrah on the dhāl without adding a yā' or hā'. And "hata fa'alat." Hisham said: it is also said "tafa'alat." And he recited:

O my two friends, had it not been for the resident of the abode, I would not have stayed at the abode of "ta," except as a passing traveller.

Ibn al-Anbari said: "ta" with the hā' dropped is like "dhi" with the hā' dropped from "hadhi," and like "dhih" with the hā' dropped from "hadhih." Al-Farra' also said: whoever says "hadhihi qamat" does not drop the hā', because a noun cannot be on a single dhāl. "Fa-takuna" is conjoined to "taqraba," and therefore the nun is dropped. Al-Jarmi [(with fatḥah on the jīm and sukūn on the rā'): Salih ibn Ishaq Abu 'Umar, client of the Jurm tribe, a well-known linguist (from Bughyat al-Wu'ah)] claimed that the fa' is the particle that puts the verb in the subjunctive, and both are permissible.

**The first issue: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then Satan caused them to slip from it﴾.** The seven readers agreed on *fa-azallahuma* without an alif, from *al-zallah*, meaning error (*al-khati'ah*). That is, he made them slip and caused them to fall into it. Hamza read *fa-azalahuma* with an alif, from *al-tanhiyah* (removing), meaning he removed them. It is said: *azaltuhu* and he departed (*fa-zal*). Ibn Kaysan said: *fa-azalahuma* is from *al-zawal* (departure), meaning he turned them from the obedience they were in to disobedience. I say: on this basis the two readings have the same meaning, but the reading of the majority is more precise in meaning. From it one says: *azlaltuhu*, and he slipped (*fa-zall*). The saying of the Exalted supports this: ﴿Satan only caused them to slip because of some of what they had earned﴾ [Al 'Imran: 155], and His saying: ﴿Satan whispered to them﴾. Whispering (*al-waswasah*) is nothing but bringing them into slipping through disobedience. Satan has no power to remove anyone from one place to another; his power is only to bring him into slipping, and that becomes a cause of his being removed from one place to another through his sin. It has also been said that the meaning of *azallahuma* comes from *zalla 'an al-makan* when he moved aside (*tanahha*), so in meaning it is like Hamza's reading from *al-zawal*. Imru' al-Qays said:

*He makes the light-bodied youth slip from his saddle-cloth,*
*and he turns with the garments of the heavy, awkward rider.*

[Note: *al-khaff* means light; *al-sahwah* is the place of the saddle-blanket on a horse's back; *yulwi bihi* means he carries him away through the intensity of his running; *al-'anif* is one who does not ride well and has no gentleness in riding horses; *al-muthaqqal* means heavy.]

And he also said:

*A bay horse whose saddle-blanket slips from the middle of its back,*
*as the smooth rock slipped the one who came down upon it.*

[Note: *al-kumayt* is a colour that is neither chestnut nor black; *al-hal* is the place of the saddle-blanket on a horse's back; *al-safwa'* (plural of *safah*) is a smooth rock; *al-mutanazzil* is one who descends onto it and slides off.]

**The second issue: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and removed them from that in which they were﴾.** If *azal* is taken as departing from a place, then His saying *fa-akhrajahuma* is an emphasis and an explanation of the departure, since they might have departed from a place they were in to another place within Paradise; but that is not the case. Their expulsion from Paradise was to the earth, because they were created from it, and so that Adam might be a khalifah (successor, vicegerent) on the earth. Iblis, may Allah curse him, did not intend to expel him from it; he intended only to cast him down from his rank and distance him, just as he himself was distanced. So he did not attain his aim nor achieve his wish, but rather his eye grew more burning (*sukhnat 'ayn*, the opposite of cooling of the eye), his soul's rage increased, and his hope was disappointed. The Exalted, may His praise be great, said: ﴿Then his Lord chose him, and turned to him, and guided him﴾ [Ta-Ha: 122]. So he, peace be upon him, became the khalifah of Allah on His earth after having been a neighbour to Him in His abode. How great is the difference between the khalifah and the neighbour! (ﷺ). This was attributed to Iblis because it occurred through his cause and his seduction. There is no disagreement among the people of interpretation (*ahl al-ta'wil*) and others that Iblis was the one who took charge of seducing Adam, but they differed on the manner. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and the majority of scholars said that he seduced them face to face (*mushafahah*). The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿And he swore to them both, "Indeed I am to you both among the sincere advisers"﴾, and *al-muqasamah* (swearing) apparently means face-to-face speech.

Some said, and 'Abd al-Razzaq reported it from Wahb ibn Munabbih: He entered Paradise in the mouth of the serpent, which had four legs like the Bactrian camel, the most beautiful creature Allah created. After presenting himself to many animals, none would admit him except the serpent. When she brought him into Paradise, Iblis came out from her belly and took from the tree which Allah had forbidden Adam and his wife, and brought it to Hawwa' (Eve). He said: "Look at this tree; how fine is its fragrance, how fine its taste, and how beautiful its colour!" He kept seducing her until Hawwa' took it and ate it. Then he seduced Adam, and Hawwa' said to him: "Eat, for I have eaten and it has not harmed me." So he ate from it, their private parts became visible to them, and they fell into the state of sin. Adam hid in the belly of the tree, and his Lord called out to him: "Where are you?" He said: "Here I am, my Lord." He said: "Will you not come out?" He said: "I am ashamed before You, my Lord." He said: "Go down to the earth from which you were created." The serpent was cursed, her legs were turned back into her belly, and enmity was placed between her and the children of Adam. For this reason we were commanded to kill her, as will be explained. It was said to Hawwa': "Just as you caused the tree to bleed, so blood will afflict you every month; you will bear and give birth in pain, approaching death many times." Al-Tabari and al-Naqqash added: "And you will become foolish, though you were forbearing."

A group said: Iblis did not enter Paradise to Adam after he had been expelled from it; rather he seduced by his devil, his authority and his whisperings which Allah gave him, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Satan flows through the son of Adam as the blood flows." And Allah knows best. It will come in *al-A'raf* [see vol. 7, p. 181] that when he ate, he remained naked and sought something to cover himself with, but the trees drew away from him and rebuked him for his disobedience. The fig tree had mercy on him, so he took from its leaves and covered himself with them, and so he was afflicted with nakedness rather than the trees. And Allah knows best. It was also said: the wisdom in Adam's expulsion from Paradise was the settling and populating of the world (*'imarat al-dunya*).

**The third issue:** It is mentioned that the serpent was Adam's servant in Paradise, but she betrayed him by allowing the enemy of Allah to enter her, and she showed enmity toward him there. When they were sent down, the enmity was strengthened, her provision was made dust, and she was told: "You are an enemy of the children of Adam, and they are your enemies; wherever one of them meets you, let him crush your head." Ibn 'Umar reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Five are killed by the one in a state of *ihram*," and he mentioned the serpent among them. It was also reported that Iblis said to her: "Let me into Paradise and you will be under my protection (*dhimmah*)." Ibn 'Abbas used to say: "Break the protection (*akhfiru*, i.e., violate its pact and guarantee) of Iblis." Sakinah bint al-Ja'd related from Sarra' bint Nabhan al-Ghanawiyyah, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Kill the serpents, small and large, black and white; for whoever kills them will have them as a ransom from the Fire, and whoever is killed by them will be a martyr." Our scholars said: It was a ransom from the Fire for him because she (the serpent) participated with Iblis and aided him in harming Adam and his offspring; therefore whoever kills a serpent is as though he killed a disbeliever. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A disbeliever and his killer will never be together in the Fire." Muslim and others recorded it.

**The fourth issue:** Ibn Juraij reported from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from Abu 'Ubayda ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) at Mina, and a serpent passed by, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Kill it." It outran us to a hole and entered it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Bring a palm-frond and fire, and set it alight over it." [Note: in all copies of the original this is "from Abu 'Ubayda"; in other tafsirs it is "from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud". It seems the original is: "from Abu 'Ubayda, from his father 'Abd Allah," etc.]

Our scholars said: This hadith specifies his prohibition, peace be upon him, against mutilation (*al-muthlah*) and against anyone punishing with the punishment of Allah, the Exalted. They said: So this enemy retained no sanctity, since it escaped him, until the destruction was delivered to it from the place where it could be reached. If it is said: It is reported from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i that he disliked burning a scorpion with fire, and said: "It is mutilation." It is answered: It is possible that this report from the Prophet (ﷺ) did not reach him, and he acted on the report that came: "Do not punish with the punishment of Allah"; so this was the course of action according to him. If it is said: Muslim reported from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) in a cave, and *al-Mursalat 'Urfan* had been revealed to him, and we were taking it from his mouth fresh; then a serpent came out at us, and he said: "Kill it." We rushed to kill it, but it outran us, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah has protected it from your evil just as He has protected you from its evil." He did not light a fire nor devise a way to kill it. It is answered: It is possible that he did not find fire and so left it, or that the hole was not of a kind in which fire could be used there, given the harm of smoke and its not reaching the animal. And Allah knows best. His saying: "Allah has protected it from your evil" means your killing of it; "just as He has protected you from its evil" means its biting.

**The fifth issue:** The command to kill serpents is part of guiding toward removing a feared harm from serpents. Whatever of them has a certain harm, there is an obligation to hasten to killing it, according to His saying: "Kill the serpents, and kill the one with two stripes (*dhu al-tufyatayn*) and the short-tailed one (*al-abtar*), for they snatch away sight and cause miscarriage." [Note: *dhu al-tufyatayn* is a serpent with two black lines like two palm-fibre ornaments.] He singled out these two by mention, though they are included in the general wording, and drew attention to them because of the great severity of their harm. As for one whose harm is not certain: whatever of them is outside the houses is killed too, because of the apparent general command, and because the species of serpents is generally harmful, so that is carried over to it; and because all of them terrify by their form and by what is in souls of aversion toward them. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah loves courage, even if it is in killing a serpent," thus encouraging their killing. And he said, in what Abu Dawud recorded from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, raised to the Prophet: "Kill the serpents, all of them; whoever fears their vengeance is not of me." And Allah knows best.

**The sixth issue:** Whatever serpents are in houses are not killed until they are warned for three days, according to his saying, peace be upon him: "Indeed in Medina there are jinn who have become Muslim; so when you see something of them, warn them for three days." Some scholars restricted this hadith to Medina alone because of the Islam of the jinn there. They said: We do not know whether any jinn outside Medina have embraced Islam or not; this was said by Ibn Nafi'. Malik said: He forbade killing the *jinan* (a kind of thin, light serpent tending toward yellow, which does not poison, and is common in people's houses) of houses in all lands. This is the correct view, because the Exalted said: ﴿And when We turned to you a company of the jinn listening to the Qur'an﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 29], and so on. In the Sahih of Muslim, from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "The caller of the jinn came to me, and I went with them and recited the Qur'an to them." And in it: they asked him for provision, and they were from the jinn of the island (*al-jazirah*)... the hadith. It will come in full in *Surat al-Jinn*, if Allah wills. When this is established, none of them should be killed until it is warned (*yuharraj*) and admonished. [Note from the margin of a copy of the original: "*al-tahrij* is that one says to it: you are in *haraj*, i.e., in constraint; if you return to us, do not blame us for narrowing upon you by tracking, chasing and killing." Likewise it is in the *Nihayah* of Ibn al-Athir and *al-Lisan*.] As will come in its explanation, if Allah the Exalted wills.

**Seventh:** The imams narrated from Abu al-Sa'ib, the client of Hisham ibn Zuhrah, that he entered upon Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him) in his house. He said: "I found him praying, so I sat waiting for him until he finished his prayer. I heard a stirring among the palm fronds (*arajin*) in a corner of the house, so I turned and there was a snake. I leapt up to kill it, but he gestured to me to sit, so I sat. When he had finished, he pointed to a room in the house and said: 'Do you see this room?' I said, 'Yes.' He said: 'There was in it a young man from among us, newly married. We went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to the Trench, and that young man used to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for permission at midday, and would return to his family. One day he asked his permission, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Take your weapon with you, for I fear for you from Qurayzah." So the man took his weapon and returned, and found his wife standing between the two doors. He lunged at her with his spear to thrust it into her, but he was seized by jealousy. She said to him: "Hold back your spear and enter the room, until you see what it was that drove me out!" So he entered, and there was a huge snake coiled on the bedding. He lunged at it with the spear and pierced it through, then came out and planted the spear in the courtyard, and the snake writhed upon it. It is not known which of the two died first, the snake or the young man!'

He said: 'We came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and told him of that, and we said: "Pray to Allah to bring him back to life for us." He said: "Ask forgiveness for your brother [[In Sahih Muslim: 'for your companion'.]]." Then he said: "Indeed, in Madinah there are jinn who have embraced Islam, so if you see anything of them, warn them for three days. If they appear to you after that, kill them, for it is only a devil."' (And in another chain, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:) "Indeed, these houses have *'awamir* [[*Al-'awamir*: the snakes that dwell in houses; its singular is *'amir* and *'amira*.]]. So if you see any of them, warn them three times. If it departs, well and good; otherwise, kill it, for it is a disbeliever." And he said to them: "Go and bury your companion."

Our scholars (may Allah have mercy on them) said: From this hadith it is not to be understood that this jinn whom the young man killed was a Muslim, and that the jinn killed him in retaliation (*qisas*), because even if it were granted that retribution (*qisas*) is prescribed between us and the jinn, it would apply only to deliberate intentional killing, and this young man did not intend or deliberately aim at killing a Muslim soul, since he had no knowledge of it. Rather, he aimed at killing something whose kind is legally permitted to be killed, so this is a killing by mistake, and there is no retaliation for it. The better view is that the disbelieving jinn, or their wicked ones, killed the young man in revenge for their companion, as an enmity and retribution. And Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah (may Allah be pleased with him) was killed by them as well; he was found dead in his bathing place, his body turned green, and they did not realize he had died until they heard someone saying, while they saw no one:

"We have killed the lord of the Khazraj, Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah,
and we shot him with two arrows, and did not miss his heart."

The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "Indeed, in Madinah there are jinn who have embraced Islam," only to explain a way by which one may guard against killing those of them who are Muslim, while being empowered to kill the disbelieving among them. It has been narrated through several routes that 'Aishah, the wife of the Prophet (ﷺ), killed a jinn, and she was shown in a dream that someone was saying to her: "You have killed a Muslim!" She said: "Had he been a Muslim, he would not have entered upon the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ)." He said: "He entered upon you only while you were wearing your garments." So in the morning she ordered twelve thousand dirhams to be given, and it was spent in the way of Allah. In another narration: "He entered upon you only while you were covered," so she gave in charity and freed slaves.

Al-Rabi' ibn Badr said: The jinn among the snakes, whose killing the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade, are those that walk and do not coil. The same was related from 'Alqamah.

**Eighth:** Concerning the manner of warning. Malik said: "I prefer that they be warned three days." 'Isa ibn Dinar said likewise, even if it appears several times in one day. It is not sufficient to warn it three times in a single day; it must be over three days. It was said: three times suffices, based on his saying (ﷺ): "Let him warn it three times," and his saying: "Warn them three times," and because *thalatha* (three) is used for feminine counts, so it is evident that what is meant is three times. Malik's view is the better, based on his saying (ﷺ): "Three days" — and this is a sound explicit text that restricts those general reports. *Thalatha* is understood to mean the nights of the three days, since the Arabs, in the matter of dating, give precedence to the night, and they give precedence to the feminine gender in it. Malik said: It suffices in the warning to say: "I adjure you by Allah and the Last Day that you do not appear to us nor harm us." Thabit al-Bunani related from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla that the snakes of houses were mentioned in his presence, and he said: "If you see any of them in your dwellings, say: 'I adjure you by the covenant which Noah (peace be upon him) took from you, and I adjure you by the covenant which Solomon (peace be upon him) took from you.' Then if you see any of them after that, kill it."

I say: This, by its apparent meaning, indicates that a single warning suffices for permission, but the hadith refutes it. And Allah knows best. Ibn Habib related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he would say: "I adjure you by the covenant which Solomon (peace be upon him) took from you, that you do not harm us and that you do not appear to us."

**Ninth:** Jubayr related from Nufayr, from Abu Tha'labah al-Khushani, whose name is Jurthum, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The jinn are of three thirds: a third have wings and fly in the air, a third are snakes and dogs, and a third move about and travel." And Abu al-Darda', whose name is 'Uwaymir, related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The jinn were created in three thirds: a third are dogs, snakes and crawling creatures of the earth; a third are a gusty wind; and a third are like the children of Adam, having reward and punishment. Allah created mankind in three thirds: a third have hearts with which they do not understand, eyes with which they do not see, and ears with which they do not hear; they are no more than cattle, rather they are more astray (cf. Qur'an 7:179). A third have bodies like the bodies of the children of Adam, but hearts like the hearts of devils. And a third are in the shade of Allah on the Day when there is no shade but His shade."

**Tenth:** Whatever among animals has harm as its basic nature is killed outright because of its harm, without any disagreement, such as the snake, the scorpion, the mouse, the gecko and the like. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Five are wicked creatures that may be killed in the sacred area and outside it..." and he mentioned the hadith. The snake revealed its wicked essence when it betrayed Adam, by bringing Iblis into the Garden between its jaws; and if it had been showing him, Ridwan would not have left it entering with him. Iblis said to it: "You are under my protection." So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded that it be killed, and said: "Kill it, even if you are in prayer," meaning the snake and the scorpion. The gecko (*wazgha* [[*Al-wazghah*: the one that is called *sam abras* (the white-spotted lizard).]]) blew upon the fire of Abraham (peace be upon him) out of all the other creatures, and so was cursed. This is of the same kind as what is related concerning the snake. And it has been related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever kills a gecko, it is as if he killed a disbeliever." In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever kills a gecko with the first blow, a hundred good deeds are written for him; with the second, less than that; and with the third, less than that." In another narration he said: "With the first blow, seventy good deeds."

The mouse revealed its wicked essence when it targeted the ropes of Noah's ship and cut them. Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Na'm related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The one in ihram may kill the snake, the scorpion, the kite, the aggressive predator, the rabid dog, and the mouse." And the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) awoke when a mouse had taken a wick to burn the house, so he commanded that it be killed. The crow revealed its wicked essence when Noah, the Prophet of Allah (peace be upon him), sent it from the ship to bring him news of the earth, and it abandoned his command and turned to a carcass. All of this concerns the meaning of the snake, which is why we mentioned it. Further elaboration on this topic, concerning the reasoning (*ta'lil*) [[See vol. 6, p. 303.]] in *al-Ma'idah* and elsewhere, will come, Allah willing.

**Verse:** Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We said: Go down, some of you being enemies to others﴾. On this there are seven issues.

**First:** His saying, the Exalted: "And We said: *ihbitu*." The alif of *ihbitu* is elided in pronunciation because it is a connecting alif (*alif wasl*). The alif of *qulna* is elided in pronunciation because of its own quiescence and the quiescence of the *ha'* after it. Muhammad ibn Musaffa related from Abu Hayawah that the *ba'* in *ihbitu* is pronounced with a *damma*, and this is a dialect supported by the fact that the verb is intransitive, and in the case of an intransitive verb the more common form is *yaf'ulu*. The address is to Adam, Eve, the snake and the devil, according to the view of Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Hasan said: "Adam, Eve and the whisperer (*al-waswasah*)." Mujahid and al-Hasan also said: "The children of Adam and the children of Iblis." *Al-hubut* is descent from above to below. Adam was sent down in Sarandib in India, at a mountain called "Buda" [[In the Lisan, the Qamus, Mu'jam al-Buldan and Muruj al-Dhahab: "Rahun."]], and with him was the fragrance of the Garden, which clung to its trees and valleys, so that everything there was filled with perfume; hence perfume is brought from the scent of Adam (peace be upon him). The clouds used to wipe his head, so he became bald, and he passed baldness on to his offspring. In al-Bukhari, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "Allah created Adam, and his height was sixty cubits," and the hadith continues; Muslim also related it, and it will come. Eve was sent down at Jeddah, and Iblis at al-Ubullah [[Al-Ubullah (with the first letter and second letter vowelled and the lam doubled and possibly with a fatha): the well-known town near Basra on its southern side.]], and the snake at Bayson [[Bayson: a town in Marw, in Syria, and a place in Yamamah.]]. It was said: at Sijistan [[Sijistan (with the first letter vowelled and the second vowelled, or the first with fatha): the name of a city among the cities of Khurasan.]].

(from Sharh al-Qamus).]] And Sijistan has the most snakes of all the lands of God; and were it not for the al-'Arbad [[al-'arbad (with a kasra on the 'ayn, sukun on the ra', and the ba' either fatha or kasra, with the dal shaddah): a snake that hisses but does not harm.]] which eats them and destroys many of them, Sijistan would have been emptied of its people because of the snakes. This was mentioned by Abu al-Hasan al-Mas'udi.

The second issue: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿some of you are enemies to others﴾ ... "some of you" is the subject (mubtada'), "enemies" is its predicate (khabar), and the clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), the implied meaning being "and this is your condition." The waw has been dropped from "some of you" because there is a returning pronoun in the sentence, as one says: "The sky rained upon you" (ra'aytuka al-sama' tumtiru 'alayka).

Al-'Aduww (the enemy) is the opposite of al-sadiq (the friend), and it derives from 'adá, meaning to wrong. One says: "A wolf 'adwan" (dhib 'adwan), i.e., it attacks people. Al-'udwan is open injustice. It has also been said that it is derived from transgression, from your saying: "This matter does not 'yaduwuka" (does not exceed you), i.e., does not pass beyond you, and "'adahu" means he passed beyond it. It is called 'aduww because it transgresses the limit in harming its companion, and from it comes al-'adw bi'l-qadam (running/passing over ground) for passing beyond a thing. The two meanings are close, for whoever wrongs has indeed transgressed.

I say: Some scholars have interpreted the saying of the Exalted, ﴿some of you are enemies to others﴾ [al-Baqarah: 36] as referring to the human being's own self, and though this is sound in meaning, it is remote. What supports it is his, peace be upon him, saying: "When the servant rises in the morning, his limbs say to his tongue: Fear God concerning us, for if you go straight we go straight, and if you go crooked we go crooked."

If it is asked: why did He say "'aduww" and not "a'da'"? There are two answers. The first: that "ba'd" and "kull" are referred to with the singular, both according to the wording and according to the meaning, and this occurs in the Qur'an. God, the Exalted, says: ﴿And all of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection, alone﴾ [Maryam: 95], according to the wording, and He says: ﴿And all came to Him, humbled﴾ [al-Naml: 87], according to the meaning. The other answer: "'aduww" is used in the singular in place of the plural, as God, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿and they are an enemy to you; wretched is the exchange for the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Kahf: 50], meaning "a'da'" (enemies), and He says: ﴿They think every cry is against them; they are the enemy﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 4]. Ibn Faris said: "'aduww" is a term that includes the singular, the dual, the plural and the feminine, and it may also be pluralized.

The third issue: God's bringing Adam out of the Garden and His sending him down from it was not a punishment for him, because He sent him down after He had accepted his repentance and turned to him. He sent him down either as a discipline or as an intensifying of the trial. The correct view regarding his descent and his dwelling on the earth is what has appeared of the eternal wisdom in that matter, which is the spreading of his offspring upon it, so that He may impose obligations upon them, test them, and make their reward and punishment in the Hereafter depend upon that, since the Garden and the Fire are not abodes of obligation. Thus that eating was the cause of his descent from the Garden. And God may do what He wills. He has said: ﴿Indeed, I am making upon the earth a vicegerent﴾. This is a great distinction and a noble, honourable virtue, and reference has already been made to it, together with the fact that he was created from the earth. We said that He sent him down after He had turned to him because of His saying a second time: ﴿We said: Go down﴾, and it will come [p. 327].

The fourth issue: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And for you on the earth is a dwelling-place﴾ — it is a beginning and a predicate, meaning a place of settlement. This was said by Abu al-'Aliyah and Ibn Zayd. al-Suddi said: "mustaqarr" means the graves. I say: the saying of God, Exalted is He, ﴿He made the earth a resting-place for you﴾ [Ghafir: 64] admits both meanings. And God knows best.

The fifth issue: His saying, ﴿and enjoyment﴾. al-Mata' is whatever is enjoyed, of food, clothing, life, conversation, companionship and other things, and from it is named mut'at al-nikah (the marriage of enjoyment), because one enjoys it. Sulayman ibn 'Abd al-Malik recited, when he stood by the grave of his son Ayyub just after his burial:
I stood by a stranger's grave in a barren waste,
a little enjoyment from a beloved who has parted.

The sixth issue: His saying, ﴿for a time﴾. The interpreters differed about al-hin (a time) in several views. One group said: until death; this is the view of those who say the dwelling-place is living in this world. It was also said: until the Hour rises; this is the view of those who say the dwelling-place is the graves. al-Rabi' said: "ila hin" means until a term, and al-hin is a long period of time, so it is a lengthening from your saying "al-an" (now). Khuwaylid said:
Abundant in ashes, great of cooking-pot is his bowl in the time of winter, like the pool of the watering-place, wide-bottomed.
Laqifa al-hawd laqfan: it sank from its bottom and widened. They sometimes add the ta' to it. Abu Wajza said:
The ones who show kindness, there is no one showing kindness in their time, and the ones who feed, where in time is the feeder?
Al-hin also means a duration, and from it is His saying: ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time from eternity?﴾ [al-Insan: 1]. Al-hin also means the hour, as God says: ﴿or say, when he sees the punishment﴾ [al-Zumar: 58]. Ibn 'Arafah said: al-hin is a portion of time, like an hour and whatever is above it. His saying: ﴿So leave them in their confusion until a time﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 54], i.e., until their terms are spent. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿it yields its produce every time﴾ [Ibrahim: 25], i.e., every year; it was also said: every six months; and it was said: morning and evening. al-Azhari said: al-hin is a name like al-waqt (time), suitable for all periods, long or short. The meaning is that one benefits from it at every time, and its benefit never ceases at all. He said: al-hin is the Day of Resurrection. Al-hin is also morning and evening. God, Exalted is He, says: ﴿So glory be to God when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾ [al-Rum: 17]. One says: "'amaltuhu muhayanatan min al-hin" (I dealt with him in a temporary arrangement from al-hin), and "ahyantu bi'l-makan" (I stayed in the place for a while) when I remained there for a time, and "hana hinu kadha" means it drew near. Buthayna said:
And my forgetting of Jamil is indeed an hour of the age that has not come near, nor has its time arrived.

The seventh issue: When the people of the language differed about al-hin, our scholars and others also differed about it. al-Farra' said: al-hin is of two kinds: a hin whose limit cannot be fixed, and the hin which God, may His praise be exalted, mentioned: ﴿It yields its produce every time by the permission of its Lord﴾ [Ibrahim: 25], which is six months. Ibn al-'Arabi said: the unknown hin has no legal ruling attached to it, while the known hin is that to which rulings attach and obligation is linked, and most of what is known is a year. Malik, in rulings and oaths, considers the most general of names and periods. al-Shafi'i takes the least. Abu Hanifah took a middle course and said: six months. There is no sense in his saying this, for estimates are not established by analogy in his view, and there is no explicit text from the Lawgiver about it; the reliance is rather on the meaning after knowing what the wording requires linguistically. So whoever vows to pray for a while, al-Shafi'i takes it to mean one rak'ah, because it is the least of supererogatory prayer, by analogy with the single rak'ah of witr. Malik and his companions said: the least of supererogatory prayer is two rak'ahs, so the time is estimated by the measure of the act. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad mentioned in his Ahkam that whoever swears not to speak to so-and-so for a while, or not to do such and such for a while, that the hin is a year. He said: they agreed in rulings that whoever swears not to do such and such for a while, or not to speak to so-and-so for a while, a period beyond a year does not enter his oath. I say: this agreement is only within the school. Malik, may God have mercy on him, said: whoever swears not to do something until a hin, or a zaman, or a dahr, all of that is a year. Ibn Wahb reported from him that he doubted whether dahr is a year. Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ya'qub and Ibn al-Hasan that dahr is six months. And from Ibn 'Abbas, the people of opinion, 'Ikrimah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Amir al-Sha'bi and 'Ubaydah, regarding God's saying: ﴿it yields its produce every time by the permission of its Lord﴾ [Ibrahim: 25], that it is six months. al-Awza'i and Abu 'Ubayd said: al-hin is six months. For al-Shafi'i there is no fixed time for al-hin, nor is there a limit to it; the hin may, in his view, be the duration of the world. He said: he will never break his oath, but the cautious course is to fulfil it before a day has passed. Abu Thawr and others said: al-hin and al-zaman are according to what the language allows; one says: "You have come from a hin," though he may not have come from half a day. Ilkiya al-Tabari al-Shafi'i said: in general al-hin has various applications, and al-Shafi'i did not consider fixing any one of these senses, because it is an ambiguous term that was not coined in the language for a specific meaning. Some scholars said regarding God's saying: ﴿until a time﴾: the benefit is a message of good tidings to Adam, peace be upon him, so that he would know that he will not remain there and that he will be moved to the Garden which he was promised he would return to; and for others than Adam, it indicates the return (to God) and nothing more. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 37:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾. In this there are eight issues.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾. Talaqqa (to receive, to take in). It has been said that its meaning is: he understood and grasped. It has also been said: he accepted and took. Peace be upon him, he used to receive (yatalaqqa) the revelation, meaning he would welcome it, take it and seize it. You say: "We went out to meet (natalaqqa) the pilgrims," meaning we went to welcome them. It has also been said that the meaning of talaqqa is talaqqana (to be taught). This is correct in meaning, but it is not permissible that talaqqa derives from talaqqana in origin, because one of the two letters is only changed into a yaa' when the two are homogeneous, such as taẓannaa from taẓannana, and taqassaa from taqassasa, and similar to it tasarraytu from tasarrartu, and amlaytu from amlaltu, and what is similar to that. For this reason one does not say taqabbaa from taqabbala, nor talaqqaa from talaqqana, so know this. Makki related that he (Adam) was inspired with them and benefited from them. Al-Hasan said: his acceptance of them is his learning of them and his acting upon them.

The second: The people of interpretation differed concerning the words. Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak and Mujahid said they are his saying: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers﴾ [al-A'raf: 23]. [See vol. 7, p. 181.] It is also reported from Mujahid: "Glory be to You, O Allah, there is no god but You; my Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me, for You are the Forgiving, the Merciful." A group said: he saw written on the leg of the Throne "Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah," so he sought intercession through it, and these are the words. Another group said: the words meant weeping, shame and supplication. It was said: regret, seeking forgiveness and sorrow. Ibn Atiyyah said: this implies that Adam, peace be upon him, said nothing except the well-known seeking of forgiveness. One of the early scholars was asked what a sinner should say, and he replied: he should say what his two parents said: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾, the verse. Moses said ﴿My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me﴾ [al-Qasas: 16] [See vol. 13, p. 261]. Yunus said ﴿There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been of the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anbiya: 87] [See vol. 11, p. 333]. It is reported from Ibn Abbas and Wahb ibn Munabbih that the words are: "Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You; there is no god but You. I have done evil and wronged myself, so forgive me, for You are the best of forgivers. Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You; there is no god but You. I have done evil and wronged myself, so turn to me, for You are the Accepter of repentance, the Merciful." Muhammad ibn Ka'b said they are his saying: "There is no god but You, glory be to You and praise be to You. I have done evil and wronged myself, so turn to me, for You are the Accepter of repentance, the Merciful. There is no god but You, glory be to You and praise be to You. I have done evil and wronged myself, so have mercy upon me, for You are the Forgiving, the Merciful. There is no god but You, glory be to You and praise be to You. I have done evil and wronged myself, so have mercy upon me, for You are the Most Merciful of the merciful." It was also said: the words are his saying when he sneezed: "Praise be to Allah."

The words (kalimat) are the plural of kalimah, and kalimah applies to the few and the many. This has already been mentioned [See p. 67 of this part].

The third: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So He turned to him﴾, meaning He accepted his repentance, or He enabled him to repent. That occurred on the day of 'Ashura', on a Friday, as will be explained, if Allah the Exalted wills. Tāba al-'abd means he returned to obedience to his Lord, and 'abd tawwab means one who frequently returns to obedience. The origin of tawbah is return. It is said: tāba, thāba, āba and anāba, all meaning he returned.

The fourth: If it is said: why did He say "upon him" and not "upon both of them", when Eve shares in the sin by consensus, and He said: ﴿And do not approach this tree﴾ [al-Baqarah: 35], and ﴿They both said: Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾ [al-A'raf: 23]? The answer: when Adam, peace be upon him, was addressed at the beginning of the story with His words "Dwell", He singled him out for mention in the receiving of the words, and therefore the story was completed by mentioning him alone. Also, because the woman is a sanctity and is veiled, Allah wished to conceal her, and for this reason He did not mention her in the disobedience in His saying: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he erred﴾ [Ta-Ha: 121]. Also, since the woman in most matters follows the man, she was not mentioned, just as Musa's servant (fata) was not mentioned along with Musa in His saying: ﴿Did I not tell you﴾ [al-Kahf: 75]. It has been said: by mentioning the repentance upon him, He indicated that He also turned to her, since their matter is the same; this was said by al-Hasan. It has also been said that it is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they saw a trade or a diversion, they dispersed towards it﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 11], meaning towards the trade, because it was the aim of the people, so He returned the pronoun to it and did not say "towards them both"; the meaning is close. The poet said: [He is 'Amr ibn Ahmar al-Bahili.]

"He hurled at me a matter of which I and my father were innocent, and from above the well (al-tawi) he hurled me..."

[What is in the commentary on the shawahid of Sibawayh is: "and because of the well (al-tawi)". Al-Tawi: a well lined with stones. Al-Shantamari said: he describes in the verse a man with whom he had a quarrel over a well, and he mentions that he accused him of a matter he disliked and accused his father with the like, though both were innocent of it, because of the quarrel that was between them.]

In the revelation: ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 62], where the pronoun is omitted for brevity and conciseness.

The fifth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed He is the Accepter of repentance, the Merciful﴾. He described Himself, glory be to Him and exalted is He, as al-Tawwab, and it is repeated in the Qur'an in definite and indefinite forms, as a noun and as a verb. It may also be applied to the servant: tawwab. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed Allah loves those who repent and loves those who purify themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 222]. Ibn al-Arabi said: our scholars have three opinions concerning describing the Lord as tawwab. The first: it is permissible regarding the Lord, glory be to Him and exalted is He, so He is called by it as in the Book and the Sunnah, and it is not to be interpreted. Others said: it is a true attribute of Allah, glory be to Him and exalted is He, and Allah's repentance upon the servant is his return from the state of disobedience to the state of obedience. Others said: Allah's repentance upon the servant is the acceptance of his repentance, which may refer to His saying, glory be to Him and exalted is He: "I have accepted your repentance," and may refer to His creatures' returning and turning in the heart of the wrongdoer and the carrying out of acts of obedience upon his outward limbs.

The sixth: It is not permissible to say concerning Allah, exalted is He, "ta'ib" as an active participle from taba yatubu, because we have no right to apply to Him of names and attributes except what He applied to Himself, or what His Prophet, peace be upon him, applied, or the community of Muslims applied, even if it is linguistically possible and permissible. This is the correct position in this matter, as we have explained in (al-Kitab al-Asna fi Sharh Asma' Allah al-Husna). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Certainly Allah turned in forgiveness to the Prophet and the Emigrants and the Helpers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 117], and He said: ﴿And it is He who accepts repentance from His servants﴾ [al-Tawbah: 104]. It is only said of Allah, mighty and majestic, that He is tawwab because of the intensity of the act and the frequency of His acceptance of His servants' repentance, owing to the multitude of those who turn to Him.

The seventh: Know that no one has the power to create repentance, because Allah, glory be to Him and exalted is He, is the sole Creator of actions, contrary to the Mu'tazilah and whoever says with their saying. Likewise, no one has the right to accept the repentance of one who has transgressed against himself, nor to pardon him. Our scholars said: the Jews and Christians have disbelieved in this great principle of the religion: ﴿They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 31], mighty and majestic, and they made it so that whoever sinned could come to the rabbi or the monk, who would give him something and remove his sins from him: ﴿a fabrication against Allah; they have certainly gone astray and were not guided﴾ [al-An'am: 140].

The eighth: Ibn Kathir recited: "Fa-talaqqa Adamu min rabbihi kalimatin" [Adam received words from his Lord, with Adam in the nominative and kalimatin in the accusative]. The rest read Adamu in the nominative and kalimatin in the accusative... Both readings return to one meaning, because when Adam receives the words, the words have received him. It has been said: since the words were the means by which Adam was rescued, through Allah's granting him success to accept them and to supplicate with them, the words became the agent. In this reading the original would be "fa-talaqqat Adama min rabbihi kalimatun", but since the distance between the feminine noun and its verb is great, dropping the feminine marker was made good. This is a principle that applies throughout the Qur'an and speech when a feminine verb comes without a marker, and from it is the saying: "a woman attended the judge today." It has also been said: since the word kalimat was not truly feminine, it was taken to the sense of kalim (words) and so was masculinised.

Al-A'mash recited "Adam min rabbihi" with idgham (assimilation). Abu Nawfal ibn Abi 'Aqrab recited "annahu" with a fatha on the hamza, meaning "because He", and the rest read it with a kasra, as a new sentence. Abu 'Amr, 'Isa and Talhah assimilated the ha' into the ha', as related by Abu Hatim from them. It has been said: it is not permissible, because between them there is a waw in pronunciation but not in writing. Al-Nahhas said: Sibawayh permitted this waw to be dropped, and he recited:

"For him is a roar as if it were the voice of a singer (hadi), when he seeks his female herd (wasiqah), or a flute (zamir)."

[The verse is by al-Shammakh. It describes a wild ass in heat: when he seeks his wasiqah, which is his female he gathers, he calls to her, and his voice, with its roar and yearning and its fine trilling and melody, is like a singer driving camels and enchanting them, or like the sound of a flute. Zajal: a sound containing yearning and trilling.

(From the commentary on the verses.)]

On this basis the assimilation is permissible: "huwa" is in the nominative as a beginning, "al-tawwab" is its predicate, and the sentence is the predicate of "inna". It is also permissible for "huwa" to be an emphasis on the ha', and it is permissible for it to be a separating pronoun, as has preceded.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: when Adam was sent down to the earth, there was nothing in it except the eagle on land and the fish in the sea. The eagle used to take refuge with the fish and spend the night with it. When the eagle saw Adam he said: "O fish, today a creature has been sent down to the earth that walks on its two legs and strikes with its two hands!" The fish said: "If you are truthful, then for me there is no escape from it in the sea, and for you there is no refuge from it on land!"

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 38:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We said: Go down﴾. He repeated the command for the sake of emphasis and reinforcement, as you say to a man: "Stand up, stand up." It was also said: He repeated the command because He attached to each of the two commands a ruling different from the ruling of the other. So He attached enmity to the first and the coming of guidance to the second. It was also said: the first descent was from the Garden to the heaven, and the second was from the heaven to the earth. On this view there is evidence that the Garden is in the seventh heaven, as indicated by the hadith of the Night Journey (isra'), as will come [see vol. 10, p. 205].

(jami'an) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal). Wahb ibn Munabbih said: When Adam, peace be upon him, descended to the earth, Iblis said to the beasts of prey: "This one is an enemy to you, so destroy him." They gathered and entrusted their affair to the dog, and said: "You are the bravest of us," and they made him their chief. When Adam, peace be upon him, saw this, he was perplexed about it, so Gabriel, peace be upon him, came to him and said to him: "Pass your hand over the head of the dog." He did so, and when the beasts of prey saw that the dog had become friendly with Adam, they dispersed. The dog sought safe conduct (istl'mana), so Adam granted him security, and he remained with him and with his children. Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim related something similar, and that when Adam, peace be upon him, was sent down to the earth, Iblis came to the beasts of prey and incited them (ashlahum) [ashlahum: incited them] against Adam to harm him, and the most hostile of them toward him was the dog, so his heart was made to die. It is related in the report that Gabriel, peace be upon him, commanded him to place his hand on its head, and he placed it, and it became calm and friendly toward him, and became among those who guard him and guard his offspring and become familiar with them. And its heart, dying, fears the sons of Adam; if it is struck with a clod it turns and flees, then comes back friendly to them. So in it is a portion of Iblis, and in it is a portion of the touch of Adam, peace be upon him. By the portion of Iblis it barks, growls, and attacks the human, and by the touch of Adam its heart died until it became humbled and submissive, and became familiar with him and with his offspring, guarding them. And its panting [lahth al-kalb: when it puts out its tongue from fatigue or thirst] is in all its states, from the death of its heart. For this reason Allah, glorified and exalted, compared the evil scholars to the dog, as will be explained in "al-A'raf" [see vol. 7, p. 323], God willing. And that staff which Allah made a sign for Musa descended upon him, and he used it to drive the beasts of prey away from himself.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If there comes to you from Me guidance﴾. There has been difference concerning the meaning of His saying "guidance" (huda). It was said: it is the Book of Allah, said by al-Suddi. It was said: it is the granting of success to guidance. A group said: the guidance is the messengers, and they are sent to Adam from the angels and to his children from mankind, as came in the hadith of Abu Dharr, which al-Ajurri transmitted. And in His saying "from Me" there is an indication that the actions of servants are the creation of Allah, may He be exalted, contrary to the Qadariyya and others, as has preceded [see the third issue, p. 186 of this volume]. Al-Jahdari read "hudaya", which is the dialect of Hudhayl, who say: "hudaya" and "as'aya" and "mahyaya". The grammarians cited Abu Dhu'ayb mourning his sons:

They preceded my "hawaya" and they hastened toward their desires, so they were cut off, and for every side there is a fatal place [[.

("Hawaya"): he means "hawaya," i.e., they died before me, and I wished to die before them.

("Wa-a'naqu li-hawahum"): he made them as if they longed for the journey to death because of their haste toward it, though they did not long for it.

("Fa-takhurrimu"): i.e., they were taken one by one.]] Al-Nahhas said: The rationale of this dialect, according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh, is that the proper form of the possessive ya' is that the letter before it be kasra; since the alif could not be moved, it was changed into ya' and assimilated. The "ma" in His saying "imma" is an addition to "in," the conditional particle, and the answer of the condition is the fa' together with the second condition in His saying "fa-man tabi'a." "Man" is in the nominative position as the subject of a nominal sentence, and "tabi'a" is in the jussive position as the condition. "Fa-la khawfun" is its answer. Sibawayh said: the second condition and its answer are both the answer of the first. Al-Kisa'i said: "fa-la khawfun 'alayhim" is the answer of both conditions together.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So there shall be no fear for them, nor shall they grieve﴾. Fear (al-khawf) is terror, and it occurs only regarding the future. "Khawwafani fulan, fa-khiftuhu" means: I was more fearful of him. Al-takhawwuf is diminution, and from it is His saying: ﴿Or He seizes them with gradual wasting﴾ [see vol. 10, p. 109] [al-Nahl: 47]. Al-Zuhri, al-Hasan, Isa ibn Umar, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Ya'qub read "fa-la khawfa" with a fatha on the fa', as absolute negation (al-tabri'a). The preferred reading among the grammarians is the raf' with tanwin on the basis of the inceptive, because the second is a definite noun, and in it only the raf' is possible, since "la" does not govern a definite noun. So they preferred the raf' in the first as well, so that the speech would be of one form. It is also permissible that "la" in your saying "fa-la khawfun" means "laysa" (not). "Al-huzn" and "al-hazan" are the opposite of joy, and it occurs only regarding the past. "Hazina al-rajulu" (with kasra) means he is "hazin" and "hazin"; "ahzanahu" means another made him sad; "hazanahu" also, like "aslakahu" and "salakahu"; and "mahzun" is built upon it. Al-Yazidi said: "hazanahu" is the dialect of Quraysh and "ahzanahu" is the dialect of Tamim, and both have been read. "Ihtazana" and "tahazzana" have the same meaning. The meaning in the verse: there is no fear for them concerning what lies before them of the Hereafter, nor do they grieve over what has escaped them of the world. It was also said: there is no evidence in it for the negation of the terrors of the Day of Resurrection and its fear for the obedient, since Allah and His Messenger described the severities of the Resurrection; rather, it lightens it for the obedient, and when they reach His mercy, it is as if they had never feared. And Allah knows best.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And those who disbelieve﴾, meaning those who associated partners with Allah (ashraku), as shown by His words: "And they denied Our signs; those are the companions of the Fire" (ﷺ is not applicable here).

"Companionship" (al-suhbah) means being associated with a thing in a certain state, at some time. If it entails constant attachment and close mixing, then it is perfect companionship, and this is precisely the companionship of the people of the Fire with it (the Fire).

With this statement the disagreement over applying the term "Companions" (al-Sahabah), may Allah be pleased with them, is resolved, since their ranks differ, as we will explain in Surat Bara'ah [[see vol. 8, p. 148]], God willing. The remaining words of the verse have had their meanings explained previously, and all praise is due to Allah.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 40:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Children of Israel﴾. This is a vocative (nida') in construction (mudaf), its sign of the accusative being the yaa', and the nun has been dropped from it for the iDafa (annexation). The singular is ibn, and the original form in it is banī; it is said also banū. Whoever says that the omitted letter is a waw argues from their saying al-bunuwwah (sonship). But this is no proof, because they have said al-futuwwah (youthfulness), and its origin is a yaa'. Al-Zajjaj said: the omitted letter, in my view, is a yaa', as if it derives from banaytu (I built). Al-Akhfash chose that the omitted letter is the waw, because its omission is more common, since it is heavy. It is said: ibn bayyin al-bunuwwah (a clearly evident sonship), and the diminutive is buniyy. Al-Farra' said: it is said yā bunayya and yā bunayyi, two dialects, like yā abatī and yā abati, and both have been read. It is derived from al-binā' (building), which is placing one thing upon another, and the son is a branch of the father, who is placed upon him.

Isra'il is Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, peace be upon them all. Abu al-Faraj al-Jawzi said: among the prophets there is none who has two names other than him, except our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), for he has many names. He mentioned this in his book "al-Athar". I say: it has been said regarding the Messiah that he is a proper name of 'Isa, peace be upon him, not derived, and Allah named him a spirit and a word; and they used to call him Abil al-Abilin. Al-Jawhari mentioned this in al-Sihah. Al-Bayhaqi mentioned in "Dala'il al-Nubuwwah" from al-Khalil ibn Ahmad: five of the prophets have two names: Muhammad and Ahmad, our Prophet (ﷺ); 'Isa and al-Masih; Isra'il and Ya'qub; Yunus and Dhu al-Nun; Ilyas and Dhu al-Kifl, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon them. I say: we have mentioned that 'Isa has four names, and as for our Prophet (ﷺ), he has many names, whose explanation is in their places.

Isra'il is a non-Arabic name, and for that reason it is not declined, and it is in the genitive position through annexation. It has seven dialectal readings: Isra'il, which is the language of the Qur'an; Isra'il with a hamzated, shortened madd, related by Shanabudh from Warsh; Isra'il with a madd after the yaa' without hamza, which is the reading of al-A'mash and 'Isa ibn 'Umar; al-Hasan and al-Zuhri read without hamza or madd; Isra'il without yaa', with a kasra-vowelled hamza; Isra'al with a fatha-vowelled hamza; and Tamim say Isra'in with a nun. The meaning of Isra'il is "servant of God". Ibn 'Abbas said: isra in Hebrew means "servant" and il means "God". It has also been said: isra means "chosen one" (safwah) of God, and il means God. It has been said: isra derives from strengthening (shadd), so that Isra'il is the one whom God strengthened and whose creation He perfected; this was mentioned by al-Mahdawi. Al-Suhayli said: he was named Isra'il because he journeyed by night (asra) when he migrated to God, exalted is He, so he was named Isra'il, meaning "one who journeyed to God"; and so part of the name is Hebrew and part agrees with Arabic. And God knows best.

His saying, exalted is He: (Remember My blessing which I bestowed upon you). Dhikr is a shared term: dhikr with the heart is the opposite of forgetfulness, and dhikr with the tongue is the opposite of silence. One says "I mentioned the thing with my tongue and heart, dhikran." And "ijʿalhu minka ʿalā dhukr" (with a dammed dhal), meaning do not forget it. Al-Kisa'i said: what is by the mind is with a dammed dhal, and what is by the tongue is with a kasra-vowelled dhal. Others said: both are dialects; one says dhikr and dhukr, and their meaning is one. Al-dhakar (with a fatha-vowelled dhal) is the opposite of the female; and al-dhikr also means nobility, and from it is His saying: "And indeed it is a reminder (dhikr) for you and for your people" [az-Zukhruf 44]. Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning in the verse is "remember the thanks for My blessing", so he omitted "thanks" by being content with mention of the blessing. It has also been said that He intended dhikr with the heart, which is what is sought, meaning: do not be heedless of My blessing which I bestowed upon you, and do not forget it; and this is good. Here "blessing" (ni'mah) is a noun of genus, so it is singular in meaning of plural, as God, exalted is He, said: "And if you count the blessing of God, you cannot enumerate it" [Ibrahim 34], meaning His blessings. Among His blessings upon them: that He rescued them from the family of Pharaoh, made prophets among them, sent down upon them the Scriptures, the manna and the quails, caused water to gush for them from the rock, and entrusted them with the Torah, in which is the description of Muhammad (ﷺ), his attributes and his mission. Blessings upon the fathers are blessings upon the sons, because they are ennobled by the nobility of their fathers.

Note: the scholars of meanings (arbab al-ma'ani) said: God, exalted is He, tied the Children of Israel to the mention of the blessing, and dropped this from the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), and called them to remember Him, saying: "Remember Me, I will remember you" [al-Baqarah 152], so that the view of the nations would be from the blessing to the Bestower, and the view of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) would be from the Bestower to the blessing.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fulfil My covenant, I will fulfil your covenant﴾. This is a command and its answer. Al-Zuhri read "uwaffi" (with a fatha on the waw and a shadda on the fa') for intensification. It has been disputed what this covenant is. Al-Hasan said its covenant is His saying: ﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾ [al-Baqarah 63], and His saying: ﴿And God had certainly taken the covenant of the Children of Israel, and We raised among them twelve leaders﴾ [al-Ma'idah 12]. It was also said it is His saying: ﴿And when God took the covenant of those given the Book: you shall make it clear to the people and not conceal it﴾ [Al 'Imran 187]. Al-Zajjaj said: "Fulfil My covenant" is what I charged you with in the Torah of following Muhammad (ﷺ); "I will fulfil your covenant" is what I guaranteed you for that, if you fulfil it, then for you is Paradise. It was said: "Fulfil My covenant" in performing the obligations according to the Sunnah and sincerity; "I will fulfil" by accepting them from you and rewarding you for them. Some said: "Fulfil My covenant" in acts of worship; "I will fulfil your covenant", meaning I will bring you to the stations of care. It was said: "Fulfil My covenant" in guarding the outward etiquettes; "I will fulfil your covenant" by adorning your inner selves. It was also said: it is general to all His commands, prohibitions and injunctions, and so the mention of Muhammad (ﷺ) in the Torah and other things enters into it. This is the view of the majority of scholars, and it is the sound one. His covenant, exalted is He, is that He admit them into Paradise. I say: what is demanded of these people in fulfilling the covenant is also demanded of us. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Fulfil the contracts﴾ [al-Ma'idah 1], ﴿Fulfil the covenant of God﴾ [al-Nahl 91], and it is much. And the phrase "fulfil the covenant of God" is a sign of God's fulfilment of His covenant to them, not a cause for it; rather that is a bounty from Him upon them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And of Me, be in awe of Me﴾. That is, fear Me. Al-rahb, al-rahab and al-rahbah all mean fear. The command to it includes the meaning of threat. The yaa' after the nun was dropped because it is the end of a verse (ra's ayah). Ibn Abi Ishaq read "fa-rhabuni" with the yaa', and likewise "fa-ttaquni", according to the original form. "Iyyaya" is in the accusative by an implied verb, and likewise the preferred construction in commands, prohibitions and questions; the estimate: "And of Me, be in awe" then "fa-rhabun". It is permissible in speech to say "wa-ana fa-rhabuni" as a beginning and predicate. And the "fa-rhabuni" being the predicate, with an elided estimate, means: "and I am your Lord, so be in awe of Me."

**Allah's words: ﴿And believe in what I have sent down﴾**, meaning: affirm it, namely the Qur'an.

**(Confirming)** is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial qualifier) referring to the pronoun in "sent down" (*anzaltu*). The sense is "what I have sent down, confirming." Its governing element is "sent down." It may also be a *ḥāl* of *mā* (what), with "believe" as its governing element, so the sense is "Believe in the Qur'an, confirming." It may also be a verbal noun (*maṣdariyya*), so the sense is "Believe in the sending down."

**(What is with you)** means: from the Torah.

**Allah's words: ﴿And do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾.** The pronoun in "in it" has been said to refer to Muhammad (ﷺ). This was said by Abu al-'Aliya. Ibn Juraij said it refers to the Qur'an, since it is implied by "what I have sent down." It has also been said to refer to the Torah, since it is implied by "what is with you."

If it is asked, "Why did he say *kāfir* (disbeliever, singular) and not *kāfirīn* (disbelievers, plural)?" the answer is that the sense is "do not be the first group to disbelieve in it." Al-Akhfash and al-Farra' claimed that it is construed according to the meaning of the verb, since the meaning is "the first one who disbelieved in it." Sibawayh reported the phrase "he is the most elegant of the youths and the most handsome," where the apparent wording would be "the most elegant youth and the most handsome." The phrase "the first disbeliever in it" is said to mean "from among the People of the Book," since they are the ones looked to in such matters, as they are the proof and are presumed to have knowledge. Although the Quraysh disbelievers had disbelieved before them, the meaning is therefore those from the People of the Book.

According to Sibawayh, *awwal* (first) is in the accusative as the predicate of *kāna* (was). It is one of the words from which no verb is derived, and its form is *afʿal*, with its 'ayn and fa' both being waw. The reason no verb is derived from it is so that it does not suffer weakness from two directions, the 'ayn and the fa'. This is the view of the Basrans (*al-Baṣriyyūn*). The Kufans (*al-Kūfiyyūn*) said it derives from *wa'ala*, meaning "to be saved." Its root is *awʾal*, then the hamza was lightened and changed to waw and assimilated, so it became *awwal*, just as the hamza of *khaṭīʾa* is lightened. Al-Jawhari said: "Its plural is *awāʾil*, and *al-ūlā* is also used, by transposition." Some people said its root is *wawwal* on the pattern *fawʿal*, so the first waw was changed to hamza. It was not pluralized as *awāwil* because they found it burdensome to have two waws together with the plural *alif* between them. It has also been said that it is *afʿal* from *āla yaʾūlu*, so its root is *awwal*, which was transposed, so it came to *aʿfal* as a transposed form of *afʿal*, then it was eased, changed and assimilated.

**Issue:** This verse provides no proof for those who reject the argument from implication (*dalīl al-khiṭāb*, the principle that a statement implies the opposite of what it leaves unstated), namely the Kufans and those who agree with them. The intended meaning of the speech is the prohibition of disbelief, both at the beginning and at the end. The first is singled out for mention because precedence in it is more serious. So the ruling on what is mentioned and what is left unmentioned is the same, and this is clear.

**Allah's words: ﴿And do not trade My verses for a small price﴾.** There are four issues in this.

*The first:* Allah's words "And do not trade" are coordinated with His words "And do not be." He forbade them from being the first to disbelieve and from taking a price for the signs of Allah, that is, from altering the description of Muhammad (ﷺ). The rabbis used to do this, so they were forbidden from it. This was said by a group of the people of interpretation, including al-Hasan and others. It has also been said that they had meals they ate in return for knowledge, like a fixed stipend, so they were forbidden from this. It has also been said that the rabbis used to teach their religion for a wage, so they were forbidden from this. In their books it is written: "O son of Adam, teach freely as you were taught freely," that is, in vain and without payment. This was said by Abu al-'Aliya.

It has also been said that the meaning is: do not trade My commands, My prohibitions and My verses for a small price, meaning this world and its duration. The "price" that is a paltry thing of no value is called "price" for what they took in exchange for that, because they made it a substitute, so the name of price applied to it even though it was not really a price. This meaning has been mentioned before. The poet said:

*If you attempted a sin or committed it,*
*you have not profited by abandoning the pilgrimage from any price.*

I say: although this verse is specific to the Children of Israel, it includes anyone who does as they did. So whoever takes a bribe to alter or nullify a right, or refrains from teaching what is obligatory upon him, or from conveying what he knows, when it has become binding upon him, unless he takes a wage for it, has entered under the implication of the verse. And Allah knows best.

Abu Dawud narrated from Abu Hurayra, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever learns knowledge of the kind by which the face of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is sought, but learns it only to obtain some worldly goods, will not find the fragrance of Paradise on the Day of Resurrection." That is, its scent.

*The second:* The scholars differed about taking a wage for teaching the Qur'an and knowledge, because of this verse and what is similar to it. Al-Zuhri and the people of opinion (*aṣḥāb al-raʾy*) prohibited it and said: it is not permitted to take a wage for teaching the Qur'an, because teaching it is one of the obligatory duties which require the intention of drawing near to Allah and sincerity, so no wage is taken for it, like prayer and fasting. Allah has said: "And do not trade My verses for a small price." Ibn 'Abbas reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The teachers of your children are the worst of you: the least merciful to the orphan and the harshest to the poor." Abu Hurayra reported: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, what do you say about teachers?" He said: "Their money is unlawful, their clothing is forbidden, and their speech is showing off."

'Ubada ibn al-Samit reported: I taught some people of the *Ṣuffa* (the people of the bench, poor companions of the Prophet) the Qur'an and writing, and one of them gave me a bow as a gift. I said: "It is not wealth, and I will shoot with it in the way of Allah." I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it, and he said: "If you would like to be encircled with a collar of fire by it, then accept it."

Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Abu Thawr and most scholars permitted taking a wage for teaching the Qur'an, because of the words of the Prophet (peace be upon him) in the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, the hadith of the incantation: "The most deserving of what you take a wage for is the Book of Allah." It was reported by al-Bukhari. This is a text that removes the disagreement, so it should be relied upon. As for what the opponent argued by analogy to prayer and fasting, it is invalid, because it contradicts the explicit text. Furthermore, there is a difference between them: prayer and fasting are acts of worship confined to the one who performs them, whereas teaching the Qur'an is an act of worship whose benefit extends to others than the teacher, so a wage is permitted for his effort in transmitting it, like teaching the writing of the Qur'an.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: Abu Hanifa disliked teaching the Qur'an for a wage, but he permitted hiring a man to write a tablet for him, or poetry, or singing for a known wage. Thus he permits hiring for what is disobedience and invalidates it for what is obedience.

*The third:* As for the answer concerning the verse: the intended people are the Children of Israel. Whether the law of those before us is law for us is a matter of disagreement, and the one who holds this view does not hold it.

*A second answer:* the verse may refer to someone for whom teaching has become obligatory, but who refuses unless he takes a wage for it. As for someone for whom it has not become obligatory, it is permitted for him to take a wage, by the evidence of the Sunna on this. Yet teaching may become obligatory for him while he has nothing to spend on himself or on his dependants; then teaching is not obligatory for him, and he may turn to his trade and craft. It is obligatory upon the ruler (*al-imām*) to help him in establishing the religion, and if he does not, then it is obligatory upon the Muslims, because when al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) was made caliph and appointed to it, he had nothing with which to support his family. So he took some clothes and went out to the market. He was asked about this, and he said: "From where shall I spend on my dependants?" They sent him back and fixed for him sufficient provision.

*The fourth:* As for the hadiths, none of them stands on its own leg, and none of them is authentic according to the experts in transmission. As for the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, it was narrated by Sa'id ibn Tarif from 'Ikrima from him, and Sa'id is abandoned (*matrūk*). As for the hadith of Abu Hurayra, it was narrated by 'Ali ibn 'Asim from Hammad ibn Salama from Abu Jurhum from him, and Abu Jurhum is unknown and not recognized. Hammad ibn Salama did not narrate from anyone called Abu Jurhum; he narrated it from Abu al-Muhazzim, who is also abandoned in hadith, and it is a hadith with no basis. As for the hadith of 'Ubada ibn al-Samit, Abu Dawud narrated it through the hadith of al-Mughira ibn Ziyad al-Mawsili from 'Ubada ibn Nusayy from al-Aswad ibn Tha'laba from him. Al-Mughira is known among the people of knowledge, [[In one copy: (known for carrying knowledge).]] but he has objectionable reports, and this is one of them, as Abu 'Umar said. Then he said: As for the hadith of the bow, it is well known among the people of knowledge, because it was narrated from 'Ubada through two routes, and it was narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b through the hadith of Musa ibn 'Ali from his father from Abu, and it is disconnected (*munqaṭi'*). There is no hadith in this chapter that must be acted upon from the standpoint of transmission. The hadith of 'Ubada and Ubayy admits of interpretation, since it is possible that he taught for the sake of Allah and then took a wage for it.

It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The best of people, and the best of those who walk on the face of the earth, are the teachers. Whenever the religion grows old, they renew it. Give them [their due], and do not hire them, lest you burden them, for when the teacher says to the child, 'Say: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate,' and the child says, 'In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate,' Allah writes..."

**Part 2 of 2**

Freedom from the Fire for the child, for the teacher, and for his parents.

The third issue: The scholars differed regarding the ruling on one who leads prayer in exchange for a wage. Ashhab related from Malik that he was asked about praying behind someone who has been hired to lead the people in prayer during Ramadan. He said: "I hope there is no harm in it, though he is more disliked in obligatory prayers." Al-Shafi'i, his companions, and Abu Thawr said: "There is no harm in that, nor in praying behind him." Al-Awza'i said: "He has no prayer." Abu Hanifa and his companions disliked it, as previously mentioned.

Ibn Abd al-Barr said: "This issue is linked to the one before it, and their origin is one."

I say: A further basis for this will come in the Book in *Bara'a* (Surat al-Tawba), God willing.

Ibn al-Qasim disliked taking a wage for teaching poetry and grammar (*nahw*, the science of Arabic syntax). Ibn Habib said: "There is no harm in being hired to teach poetry, epistles, and the battle-days of the Arabs, but poetry containing wine, obscenity, and satire is disliked."

Abu al-Hasan al-Lakhmi said: "His view entails that he should permit hiring someone for his books and permit selling his books."

As for singing (*ghina'*) and wailing (*nawh*), they are forbidden in every case.

The fourth issue: al-Darimi, Abu Muhammad, related in his *Musnad*: Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Umar ibn al-Kumayt told us, saying: Ali ibn Wahb al-Hamdani told us, saying: al-Dahhak ibn Musa informed us, saying:

Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik passed through Madina on his way to Makka and stayed there for several days. He said: "Is there anyone in Madina who met any of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ)?" They said to him: "Abu Hazim." So he sent for him. When he entered upon him, he said: "O Abu Hazim, what is this discourtesy?" Abu Hazim said: "O Commander of the Faithful, what discourtesy have you seen from me?" He said: "The notables of the people of Madina came to me, but you did not come to me!" He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, I seek refuge in God that you should say what has not happened. You did not know me before this day, nor did I see you!" He said: Then he turned to Muhammad ibn Shihab al-Zuhri and said: "The Shaykh is right, and you are wrong."

Sulayman said: "O Abu Hazim, why do we dislike death?" He said: "Because you have ruined the Hereafter and made the world prosper, so you dislike moving from the prosperous place to the ruined one." He said: "You are right, O Abu Hazim. Then how will it be to come before God the Exalted tomorrow?" He said: "As for the good-doer, he is like the absent one returning to his family; as for the wrongdoer, he is like the runaway slave returning to his master." Sulayman wept and said: "Would that I knew! What is our fate with God?" He said: "Present your deeds to the Book of God." He said: "Where can I find it?" He said: "*Indeed the righteous will be in bliss, and indeed the wicked will be in Hellfire*" [[See vol. 19 p. 247.]] [Al-Infitar: 13-14]. Sulayman said: "Then where is the mercy of God, O Abu Hazim?" Abu Hazim said: "The mercy of God is near to the good-doers." Sulayman said to him: "O Abu Hazim, which of the servants of God is most noble?" He said: "Those possessed of manliness and intellect." Sulayman said to him: "Which deeds are best?" Abu Hazim said: "Performing the obligations along with avoiding what is forbidden." Sulayman said: "Which supplication is most heard?" He said: "The supplication of the one who has been benefited for his benefactor." Then he said: "Which charity is best?" He said: "Giving to the needy beggar, and the effort of the one of little means (*juhd al-muqill*, meaning what the condition of one of little wealth can bear), with no reproach and no harm in it."
