He said: "Which speech is most just?" He said: "Speaking the truth before one whom you fear or hope for." He said: "Which of the believers is most astute?" He said: "A man who acted in obedience to God and guided the people to it." He said: "Which of the believers is most foolish?" He said: "A man who indulged in the desire of his brother while being a wrongdoer, and sold his own Hereafter for the worldly gain of another." Sulayman said to him: "You are right. What do you say about what we are in?" He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, will you excuse me?" Sulayman said to him: "No! But give me advice that you direct to me." He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, your forefathers subdued the people by the sword and took this kingship by force, without consultation with the Muslims and without their consent, until they killed a great number of them. Then they departed from it. If you knew what they said and what was said to them!" A man among his companions said to him: "What a wretched thing you have said, O Abu Hazim!" Abu Hazim said: "You lie! God took the covenant of the scholars that they should make it clear to the people and not conceal it." Sulayman said to him: "Then how can we reform?" He said: "Abandon arrogance, hold to manliness, and divide equally." Sulayman said to him: "Then how can we take hold of it?" Abu Hazim said: "Take it from its lawful source and place it with its rightful people." Sulayman said to him: "Would you, O Abu Hazim, accompany us, so that you may benefit from us and we may benefit from you?" He said: "I seek refuge in God!" Sulayman said to him: "And why is that?" He said: "I fear that I would incline toward you a little, and God would make me taste double the life and double the death." Sulayman said to him: "Raise your needs to us." He said: "Save me from the Fire and admit me to Paradise." Sulayman said to him: "That is not up to me!" Abu Hazim said to him: "Then I have no need of you other than that." He said: "Then pray for me." Abu Hazim said: "O God, if Sulayman is Your friend, then facilitate for him the good of this world and the Hereafter; and if he is Your enemy, then take hold of his forelock toward what You love and are pleased with." Sulayman said to him: "Never!" Abu Hazim said: "You have been brief and yet you have been excessive. If you are of its people, [well and good]; but if you are not of its people, then it is not fitting for me to shoot from a bow that has no string." Sulayman said to him: "Advise me." He said: "I will advise you, and I will be brief: Magnify your Lord and exalt Him above seeing you where He has forbidden you, or missing you where He has commanded you."

When he left from his presence, [Sulayman] sent him one hundred dinars and wrote [to him]: [[Addition from the Musnad of al-Darimi.]] "Spend it, and for you there is with me the like of it, many times over." He returned it to him and wrote to him: "O Commander of the Faithful, I seek refuge in God that your request of me should be in jest, or that my refusal to you should be a gift [[*Badhlan*: meaning hoping for that and your bounty.]]. And what I would not accept for you, how could I accept it for myself? When Musa ibn Imran arrived at the water of Madyan, he found on it shepherds giving drink, and he found behind them two girls holding back [their flocks]. [He asked them, and they said: 'We do not water until the shepherds have finished, and our father is a very old man.'] [[Addition from the Musnad of al-Darimi.]] So he watered for them, then turned to the shade and said: 'My Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send down to me.'" He was hungry and afraid, not feeling secure; he asked his Lord and did not ask the people. The shepherds did not perceive, but the two girls did. When they returned to their father, they informed him of the story and of his words. Their father, who was Shu'ayb (peace be upon him), said: "This is a hungry man." One of them said: "Go and call him." When she came to him, she showed him respect and covered her face and said: "My father calls you so that he may reward you the wage for what you gave us to drink." It was difficult for Musa when she mentioned "the wage for what you gave us to drink," but he had no choice but to follow her, for he was among the mountains, hungry and lonely. When he followed her, the wind blew and began to press her garments against her back, so that they described her buttocks to him, for she was large-buttocked. Musa began to turn away at one time and lower his gaze at another. When his patience was exhausted, he called to her: "O servant of God, walk behind me and show me the way with your words." When he entered upon Shu'ayb, behold, the supper was prepared. Shu'ayb said to him: "Sit down, young man, and eat." Musa (peace be upon him) said to him: "I seek refuge in God!" Shu'ayb said to him: "Why? Are you not hungry?" He said: "Yes, but I fear that this would be a recompense for what I gave them to drink. I am from a household that does not sell any of our religion for the earth filled with gold." Shu'ayb said to him: "No, young man. But it is my custom and the custom of my forefathers: we host the guest and feed the food." So Musa sat and ate. If these hundred dinars are a recompense for what I related, then carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine in a state of necessity are more lawful than this. And if it is from a right in the public treasury, then I have peers in it. So if you treat us equally, [well and good]; otherwise I have no need of it."

I say: Thus is the emulation of the Book and of the prophets. Look at this virtuous Imam and learned scholar: how he took no wage for his work, no substitute for his advice, and no gift for his counsel. Rather, he made the truth clear and spoke out, and no fear or dread reached him in that. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Let not the awe of any person prevent any of you from speaking or standing up for the truth wherever it is." In the revelation: *"They strive in the way of God and do not fear the blame of any blamer"* [[See vol. 6 p. 220.]] [Al-Ma'ida: 54].

God the Exalted said: ﴿And fear Me, and Me alone﴾. The meaning of *taqwa* (God-consciousness) has already been mentioned [[See p. 161 and following.]]. It was also read as "*fattaqunī*" with the *ya'* (in the first person), which has already been mentioned.

Sahl ibn Abd Allah said: "His saying 'And fear Me alone' refers to the place of My prior knowledge concerning you. 'And fear Me alone, so dread Me' refers to the place of scheming and gradual enticement [[The expression here is not clear. What is in al-Bahr of Abu Hayyan is: (Sahl said:) 'And fear Me, so dread Me' is the place of certainty in knowing Him, 'And fear Me alone' is the place of prior knowledge and the place of scheming and gradual enticement.]], because of God's saying: ﴿We will lead them step by step from where they do not know﴾ [[See vol. 7 p. 329 and p. 254.]] [Al-A'raf: 182], and His saying: ﴿So none feels secure from the plan of God except the losing people﴾ [[See vol. 7 p. 329 and p. 254.]] [Al-A'raf: 99]. He did not exempt any prophet or any truthful one."

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 42:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not mix the truth with falsehood﴾. *Al-labs* means mixing. One says *labastu 'alayhi al-amra albisuhu*, when I mix its clear part with its unclear part, and its truth with its falsehood. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿and We would surely have confused them over what they confuse﴾ [al-An'am: 9] [Cf. vol. 6, p. 394.]. One says *fi al-amri lubsatun*, meaning the matter is not clear. In this sense is the saying of 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) to al-Harith ibn Hawt: "O Harith, it is confusing to you. Truth is not recognised by men; recognise the truth and you will recognise its people." Al-Khansa' said:

*You see the companion who speaks the truth, and you think it is right guidance, but far from it. So look at what it is that has been confused.*

*Believe his speech and beware of his enmity, and confuse matters for him as he confused them.*

Al-'Ajjaj said:

*When they mixed the truth with false accusation, they were enriched and exchanged me for Zayd.*

Sa'id narrated from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿And do not mix the truth with falsehood﴾ [al-Baqarah: 42]: he said, "Do not mix Judaism and Christianity with Islam, when you know that the religion of Allah, which accepts no other and is not valid except by it, is Islam, and that Judaism and Christianity are innovation and not from Allah."

The apparent meaning of the saying of 'Antarah:

*And a battalion I confused with another battalion*

is that it belongs to this sense, though it may also be from *al-libas* (clothing). It has been said that this is the meaning of the verse, i.e. do not cover (the truth). From this comes *labisa al-thawb*; one says *labistu al-thawba, albasuhu*. A man's *libas* is his wife, and her *libas* is her husband. Al-Ja'di said:

*When the bedfellow bends her neck over him, she bends upon him and becomes a garment.*

Al-Akhtal said:

*I have worn this matter, its hardships, until grey hair covered my head and blazed.*

*Al-lubus* is everything worn, of garments and armour. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And We taught him the craft of making armour for you﴾ [al-Anbiya': 80] [Cf. vol. 11, p. 320.]. One says *labastu fulanan*, meaning I came to know his inner nature. One says *fi fulanin malbas*, meaning he is one who is enjoyed. Someone said:

*Indeed, after poverty there is for a man a livelihood (qinwa)[Qinwa (with the first letter vowelled with kasra or damma): earnings.] ... and after greying, a long life and enjoyment.*

*Libs al-Ka'bah* and *al-hawdaj* refers to what is upon them of covering (with a kasra on the lam).

His saying, Exalted is He, "with falsehood": *al-batil* in the speech of the Arabs is the opposite of the truth, and its meaning is that which is vanishing. Labid said:

*Surely everything other than Allah is vanity.*

*Batala al-shay'u yabtulu butlan, buhulan, butulan* (the thing became void), meaning it went to waste and was lost, and *abtalahu* ghayruhu (another made it void). One says *dhahaba dammuhu butlan*, meaning it was wasted without retribution. *Al-batil* also means Satan. *Al-batal* means a brave man, so called because he nullifies the courage of his companion. Al-Nabigha said:

*For them is a banner in the hands of a noble, brave man, which none cuts through the ranks except his spear-point.*

A woman is *batalah*. The man *batula* (with a damma) *yabtulu butulatan* and *batalatan*, meaning he became brave. [In Taj al-'Arus: "*al-batalah* with a kasra or damma are two dialect forms of *al-batalah* with a fatha, meaning courage. The kasra was transmitted by al-Layth, the damma was related by some and transmitted by the author of al-Misbah."] *Batala al-ajir* (with a fatha) *batalatan*, meaning he became idle, so he is *battal*.

The interpreters differed about what is meant by His saying "the truth with falsehood". It is related from Ibn 'Abbas and others: "Do not mix what you have of the truth in the Book with falsehood, which is alteration and substitution." Abu al-'Aliyah said: "The Jews said, 'Muhammad is sent, but to others than us.' So their acknowledgement of his mission is truth, and their denial that he was sent to them is falsehood." Ibn Zayd said: "The truth refers to the Torah, and the falsehood is what they altered in it of the mention of Muhammad (peace be upon him) and others." Mujahid said: "Do not mix Judaism and Christianity with Islam." Qatadah said the same, as has already been mentioned.

I say: the saying of Ibn 'Abbas is more correct, because it is general, so all the other sayings are included in it. And Allah is the one sought for help.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and conceal the truth﴾. It is permissible that it be conjoined to *talbisu* (تَلْبِسُوا), in which case it is in the jussive mood (*majzum*). It is also permissible that it be in the subjunctive mood (*mansub*) by the implied *an* (أَنْ), the sense being: let there not be from you the mixing of the truth and its concealment, i.e. and that you conceal it. Ibn 'Abbas said: "He means their concealment of the affair of the Prophet (ﷺ), while they recognised him." Muhammad ibn Sirin said: "A group from the descendants of Harun settled in Yathrib when what befell the Children of Israel befell them, of the dominance of the enemy over them and humiliation. That group were the bearers of the Torah at that time. So they remained in Yathrib hoping that Muhammad (ﷺ) would emerge among them, and they were believers who affirmed his prophethood. Those forefathers died while they were believers, and their sons and grandsons succeeded them. Then they encountered Muhammad (ﷺ) and disbelieved in him while they recognised him." This is the meaning of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognised, they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89] [Cf. vol. 2, p. 26.].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿while you know﴾ is a clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase (*hal*), meaning that Muhammad (peace be upon him) is the truth, so their disbelief was disbelief out of obstinacy. Allah, Exalted is He, did not testify that they had knowledge, but He only forbade them from concealing what they knew. This indicates the severity of the sin for one who commits it knowingly, and that it is more disobedient than that of the ignorant. Its explanation will come at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness on the people...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 44], the verse [p. 365.].

There are thirty-four issues (masa'il) in this verse.

**The first issue:** His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And establish the prayer﴾. It is a command whose meaning is obligation, and there is no disagreement on this. The meaning of establishing the prayer and its derivation, along with a number of its rulings, has already been discussed [[See pp. 177–164 of this part.]], and praise be to God.

**The second issue:** His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and give the zakat﴾. It is also a command that requires obligation. Ītā' (giving) means ʿaṭāʾ (bestowing). One says ātaytuhu, meaning aʿṭaytuhu (I gave him). God, exalted is He, said: ﴿If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity﴾ [al-Tawbah: 75]. Ataytuhu, without the lengthened vowel, means jiʾtuhu (I came to him). When the meaning is "coming" in the sense of "approaching," it is lengthened (ātā, with a long vowel). From this is the hadith: "I will surely come to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and inform him." It will come later.

**The third issue:** Zakat is derived from zakā al-shayʾ, when a thing grows and increases. One says zakā al-zarʿu wa'l-māl, yazkū, when it becomes abundant and increases. A man who is zakī is one of abundant goodness. The giving out of wealth is called zakat, although it is a reduction from it, in that it grows through blessing or through the reward by which the one who gives zakat is rewarded. One says zarʿun zākin, meaning a crop that is clearly thriving. Zakat al-nāqa bi-waladihā means the she-camel is rid of her offspring when she casts it out from between her hind legs. Zakā al-fard means the single number becomes a pair when the addition of another makes it an even number (shafʿ). The poet said:

"They were five or an odd number, short of four,
They were not created, and the fortunes of people are rising."

Judūd is the plural of jadd, which means fortune and luck. Taʿtalij means it rises. Iʿtalajat al-arḍ means the land's vegetation grew tall. Fa-khasā al-fard wa-zakā means the single becomes odd and the pair becomes even. It has also been said that its origin is a good praise, and from it comes zakkā al-qāḍī al-shāhid (the judge attested the witness as trustworthy). Thus the one who gives zakat acquires for himself good praise. It has also been said that zakat is derived from purification, as one says zakā fulān, meaning he was purified from the stain of blame and neglect [[In one copy: "or al-anfāl" (the spoils), and likewise in the tafsir of Ibn ʿAṭiyyah.]]. Thus the one who takes out wealth purifies it from the responsibility of the right which God placed in it for the poor. Do you not see that the Prophet (ﷺ) called what is taken out of zakat "the filth of people"? God, exalted is He, has said: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cleanse them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103]. [[See vol. 8, p. 244.]]

**The fourth issue:** Scholars differed about what is meant by zakat here. It has been said that it is the obligatory zakat, because it is paired with the prayer. It has also been said that it is ṣadaqat al-fiṭr (the charity of breaking the fast), as Mālik said in the narration of Ibn al-Qāsim. I say: According to the first view, which is the view of most scholars, zakat in the Book is general, and the Prophet (ﷺ) explained it. The imams narrated from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no charity in grain or dates until it reaches five awsuq [[The wasq (with a fatḥah) is sixty ṣāʿ, which is three hundred and twenty raṭl according to the people of the Ḥijāz.]], nor in fewer than five dhawd [[A dhawd of camels is from two to nine, and it has been said from three to ten. The word is feminine and has no singular from its own form.]] camels there is charity, nor in fewer than five awāq [[Awāq of silver.]] there is charity." Al-Bukhārī said: "five awāq of silver." Al-Bukhārī also narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "On what is watered by the sky and springs, or by a ʿathārī [[ʿAthārī, with a fatḥah on the ʿayn, a mute ʿayn, a thāʾ with three dots, lightened, and a kasrah on the rāʾ with a shaddah on the yāʾ. Ibn al-Athīr said: 'It is from the palm trees which drink from their roots from rainwater collected in a pit. It has also been said that it is the ʿidhī (crop not irrigated except by rainwater, because it is far from water). It has been said otherwise. It has also been said that it is what is watered by simply flowing, and the first is more well known.']], a tenth; and what is watered by the nadḥ [[Nadḥ (with a fatḥah on the nūn and a silent mute letter after it) is what is watered from wells.]], half a tenth." The explanation of this section will come in al-Anʿām, God willing. In Barāʾah (al-Tawbah), the zakat on gold, silver and livestock will come, and the wealth from which zakat is not taken, at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 244.]] [al-Tawbah: 103]. As for the charity of breaking the fast, there is no explicit text about it in the Book, except what Mālik interpreted here, and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿He has succeeded who purifies himself and remembers the name of his Lord and prays﴾ [al-Aʿlā: 14–15]. [[See vol. 20, p. 21.]] The exegetes discuss it in the commentary on Surat al-Aʿlā, and I saw fit to discuss it in this surah, at our discussion of the verses of fasting, because the Messenger of God (ﷺ) made the charity of breaking the fast obligatory during Ramadan, the hadith... and it will come. So he attributed it to Ramadan.

**The fifth issue:** His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and bow﴾. Rukūʿ (bowing) linguistically means bending the body, and everything that bends is rāki' (bowing). Labīd said:

"I relate the reports of the generations that passed,
I am bent down, and whenever I stand I am bowing."

Ibn Durayd said: al-rakʿah means a hollow in the ground, a Yemeni usage. It has also been said that inḥināʾ (bending) covers both rukūʿ and sujūd (prostration), and it is also used metaphorically for a decline in rank. He said:

"Do not oppose the weak, lest you
Bow one day while time has raised him."

**The sixth issue:** People differed about specifying rukūʿ by mention. Some said: because rukūʿ is one of the pillars of the prayer, it was used as an expression for the prayer. I say: This is not restricted to rukūʿ alone, for the Law made recitation [an expression [[Added to complete the sense.]]] for the prayer, and prostration an expression for the whole rakʿah. He said: "and the recitation of dawn," meaning the dawn prayer. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever catches one prostration of the prayer has caught the prayer." The people of the Ḥijāz call a rakʿah a sajdah. It has been said that he specified rukūʿ by mention only because the Children of Israel did not bow in their prayer. It has also been said that it was heavier on the people in the Jāhiliyyah, to the point that one of those who embraced Islam, I think it was ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn, said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "On condition that I do not bow except standing." Among its interpretations is "on condition that I do not bow." When Islam settled in his heart, his soul was reassured by that, and he complied with what he was commanded regarding rukūʿ.

**The seventh issue:** The Law's rukūʿ is that a man bends his back, extends his spine and neck, spreads the fingers of his hands, grips his knees, and then settles in rukūʿ, saying "Subḥāna Rabbiya al-ʿAẓīm" (Glory be to my Lord the Mighty) three times, and that is its minimum. Muslim narrated from ʿĀʾishah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) would begin the prayer with takbīr, and recite "Al-ḥamdu lillāhi rabbi al-ʿālamīn," and when he bowed he would not raise his head [al-ishkhāṣ means raising] nor lower it [al-taṣwīb means lowering], but would keep it between these. Al-Bukhārī narrated from Abū Ḥumayd al-Sāʿidī, who said: I saw the Messenger of God (ﷺ), when he said takbīr, he placed his hands level with his shoulders, and when he bowed he rested his hands on his knees, then he bent his back [haṣara ẓahrahu: he bent it toward the ground]... the hadith.

**The eighth issue:** Rukūʿ is obligatory, by the Qur'an and Sunnah, and likewise sujūd (prostration), by His saying, exalted is He, at the end of al-Ḥajj: ﴿Bow and prostrate﴾ [[See vol. 12, p. 98.]] [al-Ḥajj: 77]. The Sunnah added tuma'nīnah (calm settling) in both and separation between them. This matter has already been discussed, and we have explained the description of rukūʿ just now. As for sujūd, it has come explained in the hadith of Abū Ḥumayd al-Sāʿidī, that the Prophet (ﷺ), when he prostrated, placed his forehead and nose firmly on the ground, moved his arms away from his sides, and placed his palms level with his shoulders. Al-Tirmidhī narrated it and said: "A good, sound hadith." Muslim narrated from Anas, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Be balanced in prostration, and let none of you spread his forearms like a dog." And from al-Barāʾ, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When you prostrate, place your palms and raise your elbows." And from Maymūnah, wife of the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) prostrated, he held his arms apart [khawwā bi-yadayhi, meaning he kept them away from his body], until the whiteness of his armpits could be seen from behind him; and when he sat, he settled on his left thigh.

**The ninth issue:** Scholars differed about one who places his forehead in prostration without his nose, or his nose without his forehead. Mālik said: He prostrates on both his forehead and his nose, and this is also the view of al-Thawrī and Aḥmad, and it is the view of al-Nakhaʿī. Aḥmad said: Prostration on one of them without the other does not suffice. This is also the view of Abū Khaythamah [[This is in some copies of the original and in the tafsir of al-ʿAlāmī quoting al-Qurṭubī. In one copy: "Abū Ḥanīfah."]] and Ibn Abī Shaybah. Isḥāq said: If he prostrates on one of them without the other, his prayer is invalid. Al-Awzāʿī, Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, and it is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrimah and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Laylā, all commanded prostration on the nose. Another group said: It suffices to prostrate on the forehead without the nose. This is the view of ʿAṭāʾ, Ṭāwūs, ʿIkrimah, Ibn Sīrīn and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, and this is also the view of al-Shāfiʿī, Abū Thawr, Yaʿqūb and Muḥammad. Ibn al-Mundhir said: Someone said: If he places his forehead and does not place his nose, or places his nose and does not place his forehead, he has done wrong, but his prayer is complete. This is the view of al-Nuʿmān. Ibn al-Mundhir said: I do not know of anyone who preceded him to this view, nor who followed him in it. I say: The correct view regarding prostration is placing the forehead and the nose, on the basis of the hadith of Abū Ḥumayd, which has already been mentioned. Al-Bukhārī narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I have been commanded to prostrate on seven bones: on the forehead" [and he pointed with his hand to his nose], "and the two hands, the two knees, and the tips of the two feet, and not to gather [lā nakfit: we should not gather and bunch up] the garments and the hair." [[His saying "lā nakfit" means: we should not gather them up. He means gathering the garment with the hands during bowing and prostration.]] All of this is an explanation of the general matter of the prayer, so the view that holds it is required. And God knows best. It is narrated from Mālik that it suffices to prostrate on the forehead without the nose, like the view of ʿAṭāʾ and al-Shāfiʿī. Our chosen view is his first view, and according to Mālik it is not valid if he does not prostrate on his forehead.

**The tenth issue:** It is disliked to prostrate on the fold of the turban. If it is one or two layers, like garments that cover the knees and feet, there is no harm. The best practice is direct contact with the ground or with what one prostrates upon. If there is something that bothers him, he should remove it before entering the prayer. If he does not do so, he should wipe it once.

Muslim narrated from Muʿayqīb that the Messenger of God (ﷺ), concerning a man who levels the dust where he prostrates, said: "If you must do it, do it once." It is also narrated from Anas ibn Mālik, who said: We used to pray with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the intense heat, and when one of us could not place his forehead on the ground, he spread his garment and prostrated on it.

**The eleventh issue:** When He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Bow and prostrate﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 77], some of our scholars and others said: What is sufficient from it is what is called rukūʿ and sujūd, and likewise standing.

They did not stipulate tuma'nīnah in this, so they took the minimum of the name, and it seems they had not heard the established hadiths on invalidating the prayer.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: Neither rukūʿ, nor sujūd, nor standing after rukūʿ, nor sitting between the two prostrations suffices until one is balanced while bowing, standing, prostrating and sitting. This is the sound view in the reports, and it is the view of the majority of scholars and people of reasoning, and it is the narration of Ibn Wahb and Abū Muṣʿab from Mālik.

Al-Qāḍī Abū Bakr ibn al-ʿArabī said: The narration has been abundant from Ibn al-Qāsim and others that separation is obligatory and tuma'nīnah is dropped, and this is a great error, because the Prophet (ﷺ) did it, commanded it, and taught it. If Ibn al-Qāsim had an excuse, namely that he had not been informed of it, then what is wrong with you, when knowledge has reached you and the proof has been established against you?

Al-Nasāʾī, al-Dāraquṭnī and ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz narrated from Rifāʿah ibn Rāfiʿ, who said: I was sitting with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) when a man came, entered the mosque and prayed. When he finished the prayer he came and greeted the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the people, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said:

(Return and pray, for you have not prayed.) He returned and prayed, and we watched his prayer, not knowing what was faulty in it. When he came back and gave the salam to the Prophet ﷺ and to the people, the Prophet ﷺ said to him: (And upon you be peace. Return and pray, for you have not prayed.)

Hammam [[This Hammam is one of the narrators in the chain of this hadith.]] said: We do not know whether he ordered him to do that twice or three times. Then the man said: I have not fallen short, so I do not know what you find fault with in my prayer?

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: (Indeed, the prayer of none of you is complete until he perfects the wudu' as Allah has commanded, washing his face and his hands up to the elbows, wiping his head and his feet up to the ankles, then he says Allahu akbar and praises Allah, then he recites Umm al-Qur'an and whatever else he is permitted and is able to recite, then he says Allahu akbar and bows, placing his palms on his knees until his joints are at rest and relaxed, then he says Sami' Allahu liman hamidah, and stands upright until his spine is straight and each bone returns to its place, then he says Allahu akbar and prostrates, placing his face [Hammam said: and perhaps he said: his forehead] on the ground until his joints are at rest and relaxed, then he says Allahu akbar and sits upright on his seat, straightening his spine. He described the prayer in this way for four rak'ahs until he finished, then said: The prayer of none of you is complete until he does that.) The like of this is the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, related by Muslim, and it has already preceded.

I say: This is the explanation of the prayer that is general (mujmal) in the Book, through the teaching of the Prophet ﷺ and his conveying it to all mankind. Whoever does not stop at this explanation, neglects what the Most Merciful has enjoined upon him, and does not act upon what has reached him from His Prophet ﷺ, is among those included in the saying of Allah Most High: ﴿Then there succeeded them an evil generation who neglected the prayer and followed their desires﴾ [Maryam: 59], as will be explained there, Allah willing. [[See vol. 11, p. 121.]] Al-Bukhari related from Zayd ibn Wahb who said: Hudhayfah saw a man who did not complete his bowing or his prostration, and said: You have not prayed; and if you died, you would die upon other than the fitrah upon which Allah created Muhammad ﷺ.

The eighteenth issue: the saying of Allah Most High ﴿with those who bow﴾. The word "ma'a" (with) requires accompaniment and togetherness, and for this reason a group of the scholars of Qur'anic interpretation said: The command to pray at first did not require attending the congregation, so His saying "with" commanded them to attend the congregation. The scholars have differed regarding attending the congregation into two opinions. The view of the majority is that it is among the emphasized sunnah, and whoever persistently abandons it without an excuse deserves punishment.

Some scholars have made it an obligation as a communal duty (fard kifayah). Ibn Abd al-Barr said: This is a sound view, because there is consensus that it is not permissible for the people to collectively leave all the mosques without congregations. So when a congregation is established in the mosque, the prayer of the one praying alone in his house is permissible, due to his saying (peace be upon him): (The congregational prayer is superior to the prayer of the lone worshipper [[al-fadh: the one who prays alone.]] by twenty-seven degrees), related by Muslim from the hadith of Ibn Umar.

It is related from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: (The congregational prayer is superior to the prayer of one of you alone by twenty-five degrees).

Dawud said: Prayer in congregation is an obligation upon every individual personally, like the Friday prayer, and he argued with his saying (peace be upon him): (There is no prayer for the neighbour of the mosque except in the mosque), related by Abu Dawud, and Abu Muhammad Abd al-Haqq authenticated it. This is also the view of Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Abu Thawr and others.

Al-Shafi'i said: I do not grant a concession to one who is able to attend the congregation to leave attending it, except for an excuse; related by Ibn al-Mundhir.

Muslim related from Abu Hurayrah who said: A blind man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: O Messenger of Allah, I have no guide to lead me to the mosque. He asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to grant him a concession to pray in his house, and he granted him that. When he turned away, he called him back and said: (Do you hear the call to prayer?) He said: Yes. He said: (Then answer it.) Abu Dawud said in this hadith: (I find no concession for you). He related it from the hadith of Ibn Umm Maktum, and mentioned that he was the one who asked.

It is related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: (Whoever hears the call and nothing prevents him from answering it, [they said: And what is the excuse? He said: fear or illness,] his prayer that he prayed will not be accepted.)

Abu Muhammad Abd al-Haqq said: This is related by Maghra' al-Abdi, but the sound report is that it is stopped at Ibn Abbas: (Whoever hears the call and does not come, there is no prayer for him). Moreover, Qasim ibn Asbagh mentioned it in his book, saying: Ismail ibn Ishaq al-Qadi related to us, saying: Sulayman ibn Harb related to us, saying: Shu'bah related to us, from Habib ibn Abi Thabit, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, that the Prophet ﷺ said: (Whoever hears the call and does not answer it, there is no prayer for him, except for an excuse). And sufficient for you with this chain is its soundness. Maghra' al-Abdi, from whom Abu Ishaq related, [is the narrator].

Ibn Mas'ud said: We used to see that none would stay away from it except a hypocrite whose hypocrisy was known. The Prophet ﷺ said: (Between us and the hypocrites is attendance at the 'Isha' and Fajr prayers, which they cannot manage.) Ibn al-Mundhir said: We have also related from more than one of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ that they said: (Whoever hears the call and does not answer it without an excuse, there is no prayer for him), among them Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.

Abu Dawud related from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: (I have resolved to order my young men to gather bundles of firewood, then go to a people who pray in their houses without any excuse, and burn them upon them.)

This is what those who made the congregational prayer obligatory argued with, and it is apparent in indicating obligation. The majority interpreted it as stressing the importance of attending the prayers in congregation, on the evidence of the hadith of Ibn Umar and Abu Hurayrah, and they interpreted the statement of the Companions and what came in the hadith that (there is no prayer for him) as referring to perfection and excellence. Likewise his (peace be upon him) saying to Ibn Umm Maktum (answer it) is for recommendation.

His (peace be upon him) saying (I have resolved) does not indicate a definite obligation, because he resolved but did not do it; its purpose is a threat and warning to the hypocrites who used to stay away from the congregation and the Friday prayer.

What clarifies this meaning is what Muslim related from Abdullah who said: (Whoever wishes to meet Allah tomorrow as a Muslim, let him guard these prayers wherever they are called to, for Allah has prescribed for your Prophet ﷺ the sunan of guidance, and these are among the sunan of guidance. If you prayed in your houses as this one who stays away prays in his house, you would abandon the sunnah of your Prophet ﷺ, and if you abandoned the sunnah of your Prophet ﷺ you would go astray. There is no man who purifies himself and perfects the purification, then sets out for one of these mosques, except that Allah records for him a good deed for every step he takes, raises him by it a degree, and removes from him by it a sin. We have seen ourselves, and none would stay away from it except a known hypocrite. A man would be brought, supported between two men, until he was set in the row.)

So he (may Allah be pleased with him) made clear in his hadith that gathering is one of the sunan of guidance and abandoning it is misguidance. For this reason, Qadi Abu al-Fadl Iyad said: There has been disagreement regarding collective abandonment of the apparent sunan: whether one should fight them over it. The sound view is to fight them, because collective abandonment of it causes its death.

I say: Accordingly, when the sunnah is established and made apparent, the prayer of the one praying alone is permissible and valid.

Muslim related from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: (A man's prayer in congregation exceeds his prayer in his house and his prayer in his market by some twenty degrees, because when one of them performs wudu' and perfects it, then comes to the mosque, seeking nothing but the prayer [[al-nahz: pushing; i.e., he does not move him from his place, and it has the same meaning as his later words: "seeking nothing but the prayer."]], and takes no step except that he is raised a degree for it and a sin is removed from him by it, until he enters the mosque. When he enters the mosque, he is in prayer as long as the prayer is what detains him, and the angels send blessings upon one of you as long as he remains in his place where he prayed, saying: O Allah, have mercy on him; O Allah, forgive him; O Allah, accept his repentance, so long as he does not cause harm in it, so long as he does not break wind in it.)

It was said to Abu Hurayrah: What is "breaking wind" (yuhdith)? He said: Passing wind silently or noisily.

The thirteenth issue: The scholars have differed regarding this excellence added to the congregation: is it solely on account of the congregation wherever it is held, or is that excellence only for the congregation held in the mosque, because of the actions that are peculiar to mosques that accompany it, as came in the hadith? There are two opinions, and the first is more apparent, because the congregation is the attribute on which the ruling is based, and Allah knows best. As for increasing steps to the mosques, intending to go to them and remaining in them, that is additional reward beyond the excellence of the congregation, and Allah knows best.

The fourteenth issue: They also differed as to whether one congregation is superior to another by the number of its members and the virtue of the imam? Malik said: No. Ibn Habib said: Yes, because the Prophet ﷺ said: (A man's prayer with another man is purer than his prayer alone, and his prayer with two men is purer than his prayer with one man, and what is greater is more beloved to Allah.) Ubayy ibn Ka'b related it, and Abu Dawud recorded it, and its chain has some weakness.

The fifteenth issue: They also differed regarding one who has prayed in a congregation: may he repeat that prayer in another congregation? Malik, Abu Hanifah, al-Shafi'i and their companions said: One repeats the prayer in congregation with the imam only if he prayed alone, in his house or with his family or outside his house. As for one who prayed in a congregation, however small it was, he does not repeat it in a congregation, either more or fewer. Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishaq ibn Rahawayh and Dawud ibn Ali said: It is permissible for one who prayed in a congregation and finds another congregation for that prayer to repeat it with them if he wishes, because it is a supererogatory and sunnah prayer.

This is related from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Anas ibn Malik, Silah ibn Zufar, al-Sha'bi and al-Nakha'i, and Hammad ibn Zayd and Sulayman ibn Harb also held this view.

Malik argued with his (peace be upon him) saying: (No prayer is performed twice in one day), and some narrate it as "Do not pray," related by Sulayman ibn Yasar from Ibn Umar. Ahmad and Ishaq agreed that the meaning of this hadith is that a person prays an obligatory prayer, then stands and prays it a second time intending the obligation again. As for when he prays it with the imam considering it a sunnah or voluntary prayer, that is not a repetition of the prayer. The Prophet ﷺ said to those whom he ordered to repeat the prayer in congregation: (It is a supererogatory prayer for you) [as in the hadith of Abu Dharr and others].

The sixteenth issue: Muslim related from Abu Mas'ud, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said:

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The one who leads the people in prayer should be the one among them who best recites the Book of Allah. If they are equal in recitation, then the one among them who knows the Sunnah best. If they are equal in the Sunnah, then the one among them who emigrated earliest. If they are equal in emigration, then the one among them who embraced Islam earliest. No man should lead another man in prayer within the latter's authority, nor sit in his house on his special seat, except with his permission."

In one narration, "sinnan" (in age) is used in place of "silman" (in embracing Islam).

Abu Dawud related it and said: Shu'bah said: "I asked Isma'il, 'What is his special seat (tikrimatuhu)?'" He said: "His bedding."

At-Tirmidhi related it and said: "The hadith of Abu Mas'ud is a hasan sahih hadith, and the practice of the people of knowledge is in accordance with it. They said: 'The most deserving of people to lead in prayer is the one who recites the Book of Allah best and knows the Sunnah best.' They also said: 'The owner of the house is more deserving of leading the prayer.' Some of them said: 'If the owner of the house gives permission to another to lead, there is no harm in him praying behind that person.' Some of them disliked this and said: 'The Sunnah is that the owner of the house should lead the prayer.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir said: "It has been transmitted to us from al-Ash'ath ibn Qays that he put forward a young boy and said: 'I only put forward the one who knows the Qur'an.'" Among those who said that the one who recites best should lead the people were Ibn Sirin, al-Thawri, Ishaq and the Companions of opinion (ashab al-ra'y). Ibn al-Mundhir said: "We hold this view, because it agrees with the Sunnah." Malik said: "The one who is most knowledgeable should go forward to lead the people, provided his conduct is good, and age also has a right." Al-Awza'i said: "The most knowledgeable in jurisprudence (faqih) should lead them." Likewise al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr said: "This applies when he also recites the Qur'an." This is because the jurist is better informed about the incidents that may befall him during the prayer. They interpreted the hadith to mean that the best reciter among the Companions was also the most learned in jurisprudence, because they used to gain understanding of the Qur'an, and it was their prevalent custom to call the jurists "reciters" (qurra').

They cited as evidence the Prophet's (ﷺ) putting Abu Bakr forward during the illness in which he died, on account of his virtue and knowledge.

Ishaq said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) put him forward only to indicate that he would be his successor after him." Abu 'Umar mentioned this in at-Tamhid.

Abu Bakr al-Bazzar related with a hasan chain from Abu Hurayrah that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When you travel, let the one who recites best among you lead you in prayer, even if he is the youngest of you. When he leads you in prayer, he is your amir." He said: "We do not know this to be related from the Prophet (ﷺ) except through the narration of Abu Hurayrah with this chain."

I say: The leading of prayer by a child is permissible if he is a reciter. It is established in the Sahih of al-Bukhari from 'Amr ibn Salamah, who said: "We were at a water-place (the word *bi-mā'* is also read with the *rā'* of *mamarr* marked as a genitive adjective of *mā'*, and it may be read with a fatha, meaning the place where people pass by). The riders used to pass by us, and we would ask them, 'What is the matter with the people? Who is this man?' They would reply, 'He claims that Allah has sent him, that Allah has revealed to him such-and-such.' I used to memorise those words, and they would settle in my breast (the word *yuqarru* is read with a fatha on the qaf, from *qarar*; in another narration *yuqra'* from *al-qira'ah* or with a hamzah, and in another *yughrī*, meaning 'to stick')." The Arabs were waiting (tala'um, meaning 'to wait') with their acceptance of Islam, saying: "Leave him and his people; if he prevails over them, then he is a true prophet." When the event of the Conquest (fath) came, every people hastened to embrace Islam, and my father's people were the first of their people to do so. When he returned, he said: "I have come to you, by Allah, truly from the Prophet of Allah." He said: "Pray such-and-such a prayer at such-and-such a time; when the prayer time comes, let one of you give the adhan, and let the one with the most Qur'an among you lead you in prayer." They looked, and no one had more Qur'an than I did, because I used to learn from the riders. So they put me forward before them, and I was six or seven years old. I had a cloak which, when I prostrated, would slip away from me. A woman of the tribe said: "Will you not cover for us the backside of your reciter!" So they bought and cut a shirt for me, and I was never as happy with anything as I was with that shirt.

Among those who permitted the leading of prayer by a child who has not reached puberty were al-Hasan al-Basri and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, and Ibn al-Mundhir chose this view, provided he understands the prayer and performs it properly, because he falls under the general words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The one who leads the people should be the one who recites best," without any exception, and because of the hadith of 'Amr ibn Salamah. Al-Shafi'i, in one of his two opinions, said: he may lead in all prayers except the Friday prayer. Earlier he had said: "Whoever's leading of the obligatory prayer is valid, his leading of the festival prayers is valid too, except that I dislike the leading of anyone other than the ruler in them." Al-Awza'i said: "A boy may not lead the obligatory prayer until he reaches puberty, unless there is a group with no one among them who has any Qur'an; then the adolescent (murahiq) may lead them." Al-Zuhri said: "If they are compelled to it, he may lead them." But Malik, al-Thawri and the Companions of opinion rejected this entirely.

The seventeenth issue: Leading the prayer is permissible without any disagreement for every adult, Muslim, free man of upright character, provided he knows the limits of the prayer and does not commit a grammatical error (lahn) in Umm al-Qur'an (al-Fatihah) that alters the meaning, such as pronouncing the *kaf* of ﴿إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ﴾ with a kasra, or pronouncing the *ta'* of "an'amta" with a damma. Some scholars took into account distinguishing the *ta'* from the *dad*, and held that if he does not distinguish between them, his leading is not valid, because their meanings differ. Others permitted all of this if he is ignorant of recitation and leads someone like himself. The leading of a woman, a hermaphrodite of uncertain status (khuntha mushkil), a disbeliever, an insane person, or an unlettered person (ummi) is not permissible, and none of these may be an imam under any circumstances, according to the majority of scholars, as will be mentioned later—except the unlettered person leading someone like himself. Our scholars said: the leading of an unlettered person who cannot recite well is not valid when a reciter is present, nor for anyone else. Al-Shafi'i likewise said this. If he leads an unlettered person like himself, their prayer is valid according to us and according to al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifah said: if an unlettered person leads a group who can recite and a group of unlettered people, the prayer of all of them is invalid. Abu Yusuf disagreed with him and said: the prayer of the imam and of those who cannot recite is complete. Another group said: the prayer of all of them is valid, because each one fulfils his obligation, like the one performing tayammum who leads people who are purified with water, or the one who prays seated leading people who are standing; their prayer is valid according to those who disagree with us, because each one fulfils the obligation for himself. I say: this view may be supported by the words of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Does not the one praying look at how he prays? He is only praying for himself." Related by Muslim. And the prayer of the follower is not dependent on the prayer of the imam; Allah knows best. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah used to say: if his wife recites, he says the takbir, she recites, and when she finishes the recitation he says the takbir, bows and prostrates, while she is behind him praying. This same view is related from Qatadah.

The eighteenth issue: There is no harm in the leading of a blind person, a lame person, a paralysed person, a person with an amputated limb, a eunuch, or a slave, provided each of them knows the prayer. Ibn Wahb said: "I do not think that a person with an amputated limb or a paralysed person should lead, because he falls short of the degree of completeness, and his leading is disliked on account of the deficiency." Most of his companions disagreed with him, and this is the correct view, because it is a limb whose absence does not prevent any obligatory part of the prayer, so the regular leading is valid despite its absence, like the eye. Anas related that the Prophet (ﷺ) appointed Ibn Umm Maktum to lead the people in prayer while he was blind. (Likewise the lame, the one with an amputated limb, the paralysed and the eunuch, by analogy and reasoning; Allah knows best.) It has been related from Anas ibn Malik that he said about the blind man: "And what need do they have of him!" Ibn 'Abbas and 'Attab ibn Malik used to lead the prayer, and both of them were blind. This is the view of the majority of scholars.

The nineteenth issue: Scholars differed over the leadership of prayer (imamah) by a person born of unlawful union (walad al-zina). Malik said: "I dislike that he be appointed as a regular imam." Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz also disliked it. Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said that he may lead the prayer if he is well regarded. This is also the view of al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Zuhri, al-Nakha'i, Sufyan al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, Ahmad and Ishaq. According to the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y), the prayer behind him is valid, though praying behind someone else is more preferred by them. Al-Shafi'i said: "I dislike appointing as a regular imam one whose father is not known. Whoever prays behind him, his prayer is valid." Isa ibn Dinar said: "I do not agree with Malik's view on the imamah of a walad al-zina, for he bears nothing of the sin of his parents." Ibn Abd al-Hakam said something similar: "If he is in himself qualified for imamah." Ibn al-Mundhir said: "He may lead, because he falls under the general statement of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: 'The people should be led by the one who recites the Qur'an best.'" Abu Umar (Ibn Abd al-Barr) said: "None of the reports concerning the conditions of imamah indicate that lineage is to be considered; they only indicate knowledge of jurisprudence, recitation, and piety in religion."

The twentieth issue: As for the slave (abd), al-Bukhari reported from Ibn Umar who said: "When the first Emigrants arrived at al-Asaba (a place at Quba') before the arrival of the Prophet ﷺ, Salim, the freedman of Abu Hudhayfah, used to lead them, and he was the one who knew the most Qur'an." Also from him: "Salim, the freedman of Abu Hudhayfah, used to lead the first Emigrants and the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ in the mosque of Quba'. Among them were Abu Bakr, Umar, Zayd, and Amir ibn Rabi'ah." And: "A'ishah had her slave Dhakwan lead her in prayer, reading from the mushaf (codex)." Ibn al-Mundhir said: "Abu Sa'id, the freedman of Abu Usayd, who was a slave, led a group of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, among them Hudhayfah and Abu Mas'ud." The imamah of a slave was permitted by al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi, al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Hakam, al-Thawri, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, and the people of opinion, while Abu Mijlaz disliked it. Malik said: "He may not lead them unless the slave is a reciter, and those with him from among the free men do not recite. As for the Eid or Friday prayer, the slave may not lead them in it." According to al-Awza'i, it is valid if they pray behind him. Ibn al-Mundhir said: "The slave falls under the general statement of the Prophet ﷺ: 'The people should be led by the one who recites the Qur'an best.'"

The twenty-first issue: As for the woman, al-Bukhari reported from Abu Bakrah who said: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ heard that the people of Persia had made the daughter of Khosrow their ruler, he said: 'A people will never prosper who entrust their affairs to a woman.'" Abu Dawud mentioned from Abd al-Rahman ibn Khallad, from Umm Waraqah bint Abd Allah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to visit her in her house. He appointed a muezzin for her who would call the adhan for her, and he commanded her to lead the people of her household in prayer." Abd al-Rahman said: "I saw her muezzin, and he was an old man." Ibn al-Mundhir said: "Al-Shafi'i requires the men who pray behind a woman to repeat the prayer. Abu Thawr said there is no need for repetition, and this is the analogy of al-Muzani's view." I say: Our scholars said: "Her imamah is not valid, either for men or for women." Ibn Abi Ayman (in one manuscript: "Ibn Abi Ayman") reported the permissibility of her leading women. As for the hermaphrodite of unclear status (al-khuntha al-mushkil), al-Shafi'i said: "He may not lead men, but he may lead women." Malik said: "He may never be an imam under any circumstances," and this is the view of the majority of jurists.

The twenty-second issue: A disbelieving person who opposes the sharia, such as a Jew or a Christian, leads Muslims while they do not know of his disbelief. Al-Shafi'i and Ahmad used to say that it is not valid for them and they must repeat the prayer. This was also said by Malik and his companions, because he is not one of the people of worship (qurbah). Al-Awza'i said: "He should be punished." Abu Thawr and al-Muzani said: "There is no need to repeat the prayer for those who prayed behind him, and by his prayer he is not considered a Muslim according to al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr." Ahmad said: "He is to be compelled to accept Islam."

The twenty-third issue: As for the people of innovation (ahl al-bida') among the people of desires (ahl al-ahwa'), such as the Mu'tazilah, the Jahmiyyah and others, al-Bukhari mentioned from al-Hasan: "Pray, and his innovation is upon him." Ahmad said: "One should not pray behind any of the people of desires if he calls others to his desire." Malik said: "One prays behind rulers of injustice (a'immat al-jawr), but one does not pray behind the people of innovation, such as the Qadariyyah and others." Ibn al-Mundhir said: "Whoever his innovation has led to disbelief, the prayer behind him is not valid. Whoever is not like that, the prayer behind him is valid, and it is not permissible to put forward someone who has this description."

The twenty-fourth issue: As for the sinner in his limbs (al-fasiq bi-jawarihi), such as the adulterer, the drinker of wine, and the like, the school differed on him. Ibn Habib said: "Whoever prays behind one who drinks wine must repeat the prayer forever, unless he is the ruler to whom obedience is owed; then there is no need to repeat the prayer behind him, unless he is then intoxicated." This was said by those of the companions of Malik whom I met. It was narrated from the hadith of Jabir ibn Abd Allah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said on the minbar: "A woman should not lead a man, a bedouin should not lead an emigrant, and a wicked person should not lead a righteous one, unless that is by a ruler (dhu sultan)." Abu Muhammad Abd al-Haqq said: "This is narrated by Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, and most scholars weaken Ali ibn Zayd." Al-Daraqutni narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'If it pleases you that your prayers be purified, then put your best forward.'" In its chain is Abu al-Walid Khalid ibn Isma'il al-Makhzumi, who is weak, as al-Daraqutni said. Abu Ahmad ibn Adi said of him: "He used to fabricate hadith attributed to the trustworthy Muslims." His hadith is narrated from Ibn Jurayj, from Ata', from Abu Hurayrah. Al-Daraqutni also mentioned from Salam ibn Sulayman, from Umar, from Muhammad ibn Wasi', from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Umar who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Make your imams your best, for they are a delegation between you and Allah.'" Al-Daraqutni said: "This Umar is, in my view, Umar ibn Yazid, the judge of al-Mada'in, and Salam ibn Sulayman is also from al-Mada'in and is not strong." This was said by Abd al-Haqq.

The twenty-fifth issue: The imams narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The imam is only appointed to be followed, so do not oppose him. When he says Allahu akbar, then say Allahu akbar; when he bows, then bow; when he says 'Allah hears those who praise Him,' then say 'Our Lord, and to You be praise'; when he prostrates, then prostrate; and when he prays sitting, then pray sitting, all of you." The scholars differed concerning one who bows or lowers himself before the imam deliberately, on two views. The first: his prayer is invalid if he does that throughout the prayer or in most of it. This is the view of the Zahiriyyah, and it was narrated from Ibn Umar. Sunayd mentioned: "Ibn Ulayyah narrated to us from Ayyub, from Abu Qilabah, from Abu al-Ward al-Ansari who said: 'I prayed beside Ibn Umar, and I began to raise (my head) before the imam and to lower (my head) before him. When the imam finished the salam, Ibn Umar took my hand, twisted it, and pulled me. I said: "What is wrong with you?" He said: "Who are you?" I said: "So-and-so son of so-and-so." He said: "You are from a family of truth! What prevents you from praying?" I said: "Did you not see me beside you?" He said: "I saw you raising before the imam and lowering before him, and there is no prayer for one who opposes the imam.'" Al-Hasan ibn Hayy said concerning one who bows or prostrates before the imam and then rises from his bowing or prostration before the imam bows or prostrates: he is not counted that and it does not suffice him. Most jurists said: "Whoever does that has done wrong, but his prayer is not invalidated, because the principle in congregational prayer and following the imams in it is a good sunnah. Whoever opposes it after having fulfilled the obligation of his prayer through its purity, bowing, prostration and obligatory parts, is not required to repeat it, even if he omits some of its sunan. For if he wished to pray alone and performed that prayer before his imam, it would suffice for him, but he did wrong in leaving the congregation." They said: "Whoever enters the imam's prayer, bows with his bowing and prostrates with his prostration, and is not in a rak'ah while the imam is in another, has followed the imam, even if he raises and lowers before him, because with his bowing he bows and with his prostration he prostrates, and he rises with him; in that he is a follower of him, except that he has sinned in this act by opposing the sunnah of the follower agreed upon."

I say: What Ibn Abd al-Barr reported from the majority indicates that the prayer of the follower, according to them, is not connected to the prayer of the imam, because the physical and legal following is absent. But this is not so according to most of them, and the correct view in both the report and reasoning is the first opinion. The imam is appointed only to be followed and imitated in his actions, and from this is the saying of Allah, Most High: ﴿Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124], meaning they will follow you in what will be explained. This is the real meaning of imam linguistically and legally. Whoever opposes his imam does not follow him. Then the Prophet ﷺ explained, saying: "When he says Allahu akbar, then say Allahu akbar," the hadith. He used the fa' (then), which requires immediate sequence, and he is the one who makes clear what Allah intends. Then he threatened severely whoever raises or bows before him, saying: "Does not the one who raises his head before the imam fear that Allah will turn his head into the head of a donkey or his form into the form of a donkey?" This was recorded by Malik in the Muwatta', al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud and others. Abu Hurayrah said: "Indeed, his forelock is in the hand of a devil." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Every deed that is not in accordance with our command is rejected," meaning it is rejected. Whoever deliberately opposes his imam while knowing that he is commanded to follow him and to refrain from opposing him, has treated his prayer lightly and opposed what he was commanded. It is therefore necessary that his prayer not be valid for him. And Allah knows best.

The twenty-sixth issue: If he raises his head forgetfully...

Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The sunnah for one who forgets and does this during bowing or prostration is that he should return to bowing or prostration and wait for the imam. Doing so is an error on the part of the one who does it, because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The imam is appointed only to be followed, so do not differ from him." Ibn Abd al-Barr said: The apparent meaning of Malik's words here does not require repeating the prayer for one who does this deliberately, since he said, "and that is an error on the part of the one who does it," because the one who forgets is excused.

The twenty-seventh issue: This disagreement concerns only matters other than the opening takbir (takbir al-ihram, the takbir that begins the prayer) and the salam (the closing salutation). As for the salam, the discussion of it has already passed. As for the takbir al-ihram, the majority hold that the follower's takbir must come only after the imam's takbir. An exception is reported from one of al-Shafi'i's two opinions: that if the follower says the takbir al-ihram before his imam, it suffices for him, based on the hadith of Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to the prayer and, when he said the takbir, turned and gestured to them, meaning "stay as you are," then went out, then came back with his head dripping, and led them in prayer. When he finished, he said: "I was in a state of major impurity and forgot to wash." And from the hadith of Anas: "He said the takbir and we said the takbir with him." The explanation of this will come when Allah the Exalted says ﴿وَلَا جُنُبًا﴾ in Surah al-Nisa' [see vol. 5, p. 204], [al-Nisa': 43], if Allah wills.

The twenty-eighth issue: Muslim related from Abu Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to wipe our shoulders in prayer and say: "Straighten up and do not differ, lest your hearts differ. Let those of you who are mature and wise stand closest to me, then those who come after them, then those who come after them." Abu Mas'ud said: "And you today are more divided." It is added from the hadith of Abdullah: "Beware of the uproar (hay'at) of the markets." [Hay'ah (like hawshah): mixing, dispute, and raised voices.] His words "Straighten up" are a command to align the rows, especially the first row, which is the one nearest the imam, as will be explained in Surah al-Hijr [see vol. 10, p. 20], if Allah wills. There the discussion of the meaning of this hadith will come, by Allah's power.

The twenty-ninth issue: The scholars differed about the manner of sitting in prayer, because the reports on this differ. Malik and his companions said: The worshipper lays his buttocks on the ground, extends his right foot and folds his left foot, based on what he related in his Muwatta' from Yahya ibn Sa'id that al-Qasim ibn Muhammad showed them the sitting for the tashahhud (the testimony): he extended his right foot and folded his left foot, and he sat on his left hip and did not sit on his foot. Then he said: "Abdullah ibn Umar showed me this, and he told me that his father used to do it."

I say: This meaning has also come in Sahih Muslim from A'ishah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to begin the prayer with the takbir, and recited "Al-hamdu lillahi rabbi al-alamin." When he bowed he did not raise his head or lower it, but kept it between those two. When he raised his head from bowing, he did not prostrate until he was standing upright. When he raised his head from prostration, he did not prostrate again until he was sitting upright. He used to say the tahiyyah (greeting of testimony) after every two rak'ahs. He would lay his left foot flat and extend his right foot upright. He forbade the "uqbah al-shaytan" (the Devil's sitting) [Ibn al-Athir said: this is placing the buttocks on the heels between the two prostrations, which some people call iqa'. It is also said: it is leaving the heels unwashed during ablution], and he forbade a man to spread his forearms like a beast of prey (ifticharash al-sab'). He used to end the prayer with the salam.

I say: Because of this hadith, Allah knows best, Ibn Umar said: "The sunnah of the prayer is that you extend your right foot and fold your left." Al-Thawri, Abu Hanifah and his companions, and al-Hasan ibn Salih ibn Hayy said: One extends the right foot and sits on the left, based on the hadith of Wa'il ibn Hujr. Likewise al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq said this about the middle sitting. For the final sitting of Zuhr, 'Asr, Maghrib or 'Isha', they said the same as Malik, based on the hadith of Abu Humayd al-Sa'idi, related by al-Bukhari: "I saw the Prophet (ﷺ) when he said the takbir, raise his hands to the level of his shoulders; when he bowed he placed his hands firmly on his knees, then bent his back; when he rose he straightened until each vertebra returned to its place; when he prostrated he placed his hands without spreading out his arms or pressing them against his sides, and turned the tips of his toes toward the qiblah; when he sat in the two rak'ahs he sat on his left foot and extended the other; and when he sat in the final rak'ah he advanced his left foot, extended his right, and sat on his buttocks."

Al-Tabari said: If one does this, it is good; all of these have been established from the Prophet (ﷺ).

The thirtieth issue: Malik, from Muslim ibn Abi Maryam, from Ali ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Mu'awi, that he said: Abdullah ibn Umar saw me playing with pebbles during the prayer, and when I finished he forbade me, saying: "Do as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to do." I said: "And how did the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to do it?" He said: "When he sat in the prayer, he placed his right palm on his right thigh, closed all his fingers, and pointed with the finger next to the thumb; and he placed his left palm on his left thigh," and he said: "This is how he used to do it."

Ibn Abd al-Barr said: What Ibn Umar described, placing the right palm on the right thigh, closing all the fingers of that hand except the index finger, with which he points, and placing the left palm on the left thigh open with its fingers spread, is all sunnah in sitting in prayer, agreed upon, with no disagreement among the scholars that I know of. That is sufficient. The only difference is about moving the index finger: some scholars consider moving it, and some do not. All of this is reported in sound, connected reports from the Prophet (ﷺ), and all of it is permissible, praise be to Allah.

Sufyan ibn Uyaynah related this hadith from Muslim ibn Abi Maryam with the same meaning as Malik's, and added: Sufyan said: "Yahya ibn Sa'id had related it to us from Muslim, then I met him and heard it from him, and he added to it for me that he said: 'It is the Devil's fly-whisk. None of you will forget as long as he points with his finger,' and he said: 'like this.'"

I say: Abu Dawud related in the hadith of Ibn al-Zubayr that he (ﷺ) used to point with his finger when he supplicated, and did not move it. Some Iraqi scholars followed this and forbade moving it. Some of our scholars held that extending it signifies the continuity of tawhid (monotheism). Most scholars, including among Malik's followers and others, held that it should be moved, except that they differed about continuous movement, on two views. Those who held continuous movement interpreted it as a reminder of attentiveness in prayer, and that it is a restraint and repellent for the Devil, as Sufyan reported. Those who did not hold continuous movement regarded moving it at the utterance of the two words of the testimony (shahadah) as the motion of that limb in affirming tawhid. And Allah knows best.

The thirty-first issue: The scholars differed about the woman's sitting in prayer. Malik said: She is like the man, and she does not differ from him after the opening takbir, except in clothing and in reciting aloud. Al-Thawri said: The woman lets her outer garment (jilbab) hang down on one side, and he related this from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i. Abu Hanifah and his companions said: The woman sits in the way that is least revealing for her. This is also the view of al-Sha'bi, who said: She sits in whatever way is easiest for her. Al-Shafi'i said: She sits in the way that is most concealing for her.

Muslim related from Tawus, who said: We asked Ibn Abbas about iqa' on the two feet, and he said: "It is the sunnah." We said to him: "We see it as harsh treatment of the man." Ibn Abbas said: "Rather, it is the sunnah of your Prophet (ﷺ)." [The addition is from Sahih Muslim.] The scholars differed about what the description of iqa' is. Abu Ubayd said: Iqa' is a man sitting on his buttocks with his thighs raised, like the sitting of a dog or a beast of prey. Ibn Abd al-Barr said: This is an iqa' agreed upon, on which the scholars do not differ, and this is the explanation of the lexicographers and a group of jurists. Abu Ubayd also said: As for the people of hadith, they define iqa' as placing the buttocks on the heels between the two prostrations. Qadi Iyad said: The more likely interpretation, in my view, of the iqa' which Ibn Abbas said was from the sunnah, is the one explained by the jurists: placing the buttocks on the heels between the two prostrations. This is also reported explicitly from Ibn Abbas: "It is from the sunnah that your heel touches your buttocks," related by Ibrahim ibn Misarrah from Tawus from him, which Abu Umar mentioned. The Qadi said: It has been reported from a group of the early generations and the Companions that they used to do it, and the general body of jurists of the regions did not hold this, and they called it iqa'. Abd al-Razzaq related from Ma'mar, from Ibn Tawus, from his father, that he saw Ibn Umar, Ibn Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr doing iqa' between the two prostrations.

The thirty-second issue: Those scholars who held the salam to be obligatory and those who did not agree that the second salam is not an obligation, except what is reported from al-Hasan ibn Hayy, that he made both salams obligatory together. Abu Ja'far al-Tahawi said: We have not found from any of the people of knowledge who held that there are two salams that the second is one of its obligations except him. Ibn Abd al-Barr said: Among al-Hasan ibn Salih's proofs for making both salams obligatory is his claim that whoever breaks wudu after the first salam and before the second has invalidated his prayer, based on the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Its tahlil (release from the prayer) is the salam." Then he explained how the salam is made, that one says it to the right and to the left. The proof of those who made only the single salam obligatory rather than the second is the same saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Its tahlil is the salam." They said: The single salam is what is called a salam.

Al-Qurtubi, *al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*, commentary on Surah 2, verse 43 (part 6 of 6):

I say: This question is based on whether one takes the least part of the term or its last part. Since beginning the prayer with one *takbir* (the saying of "Allahu akbar") is agreed upon (*ijma'*, scholarly consensus), the same applies to ending it with one *taslim* (the salutation of peace). However, the established sunnahs (prophetic practices) have come down in a continuous stream (*tawaradat*; in another copy, *tawatarat*, "were transmitted by mass narration"), from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, which is the most widely transmitted of them, and from the hadith of Wa'il ibn Hujr al-Hadrami, the hadith of Ammar, the hadith of al-Bara' ibn Azib, the hadith of Ibn Umar, and the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to give two salutations.

Ibn Juraij, Sulayman ibn Bilal, and Abd al-Aziz ibn Muhammad al-Darawardi all related from Amr ibn Yahya al-Mazini, from Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Habban, from his paternal uncle Wasi' ibn Habban, who said: "I said to Ibn Umar: 'Tell me about the prayer of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): how was it?' He mentioned the *takbir* whenever he raised his head and whenever he lowered it, and he mentioned the salutation: 'As-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullah' to his right, and 'As-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullah' to his left."

Ibn Abd al-Barr said: "This is a sound chain of transmission (*isnad*) from Medina. The well-known practice in Medina is the single salutation, and it is a practice that the people of Medina inherited from generation to generation. Practice of this kind may validly be used as evidence in every land, because it cannot be hidden, since it occurs many times every day. Likewise, the practice in Kufa and elsewhere of the two salutations is widespread among them and is also inherited. Whatever falls into this category is a difference of opinion regarding what is permissible, like the call to prayer (*adhan*). Likewise, it is not reported from any scholar in the Hijaz, Iraq, Sham, or Egypt that they denied the single salutation or denied the two salutations; rather, both are known among them. The hadith of the single salutation was related by Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Aisha, and Anas, but it is defective (*ma'lulah*), and the scholars of hadith do not authenticate it."

The thirty-fourth [issue]: al-Daraqutni related from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "It is from the sunnah to recite the *tashahhud* (the testimony recited while seated in prayer) quietly." Malik chose the *tashahhud* of Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), which is: "At-tahiyyatu lillah, az-zakiyyatu lillah, at-tayyibatu as-salawatu lillah. As-salamu alayka ayyuha an-Nabiyyu wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. As-salamu alayna wa ala ibad Allahi as-salihin. Ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah wa ashhadu anna Muhammadan abduhu wa rasuluh."

Al-Shafi'i and his companions and al-Layth ibn Sa'd chose the *tashahhud* of Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to teach us the *tashahhud* just as he taught us a surah of the Qur'an. He would say: 'At-tahiyyatu al-mubarakatu as-salawatu at-tayyibatu lillah. As-salamu alayka ayyuha an-Nabiyyu wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. As-salamu alayna wa ala ibad Allahi as-salihin. Ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah wa ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasulu Allah.'"

Al-Thawri, the Kufans, and most of the people of hadith chose the *tashahhud* of Ibn Mas'ud, which Muslim also related. He said: "We used to say in the prayer behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'As-salamu ala Allah, as-salamu ala fulan' (peace upon Allah, peace upon so-and-so). Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said one day: '(Indeed Allah is As-Salam. When one of you sits in the prayer, let him say: At-tahiyyatu lillahi was-salawatu wat-tayyibat. As-salamu alayka ayyuha an-Nabiyyu wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. As-salamu alayna wa ala ibad Allahi as-salihin.) When he says it, it reaches every righteous servant [of Allah] [supplement from Muslim] in heaven and on earth. Ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah wa ashhadu anna Muhammadan abduhu wa rasuluh. Then he may choose whatever request he wishes.'"

This was also the view of Ahmad, Ishaq, and Dawud. Ahmad ibn Khalid in al-Andalus used to choose it and incline toward it. It is also related from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, both as a *marfu'* report (traced to the Prophet) and as a *mawquf* report (ending with a Companion), something similar to the *tashahhud* of Ibn Mas'ud. All of this is a difference of opinion concerning what is permissible (*mubah*), and none of it is obligatory. And all praise is due to Allah alone.

This is a summary of the rulings concerning the imam (prayer leader) and the follower (*ma'mum*), which are included in the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And bow with those who bow﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:43].

The discussion of standing in prayer will come later, at the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And stand before Allah in devotion﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:238] [see vol. 3, p. 213]. There will also come there the ruling on the sick imam and other rulings of prayer. In "Al 'Imran" will come the ruling on the prayer of a sick person who is not an imam [see vol. 4, p. 311]. In "al-Nisa'" will come, in the prayer of fear (*salat al-khawf*), the ruling on the one who performs an obligatory prayer behind one performing a voluntary prayer [see vol. 5, p. 351]. In Surah "Maryam" will come the ruling on an imam who prays at a higher place than the follower [see vol. 11, p. 85], and other matters concerning the times, the call to prayer, and the mosques. All of this is an explanation of His words, the Exalted: "And establish prayer." A portion of its rulings has already been mentioned at the beginning of the surah. And all praise is due to Allah for that.

The commentary has nine issues. The first concerns the words of God, Exalted is He: ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people?﴾ This is a rhetorical question whose meaning is rebuke. According to the people of ta'wil (interpretation), the intended subject is the scholars of the Jews. Ibn 'Abbas said: The Jews of Madinah used to say, one of them to his in-law, to his relative, and to anyone among the Muslims with whom he shared fosterage: "Hold fast to what you are upon, and do what this man commands you to do," meaning Muhammad (ﷺ), "for his command is true." So they would enjoin the people to do this, but they would not do it themselves.

It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas: The rabbis (al-ahbar) would command their followers and adherents to follow the Torah, while they themselves opposed it by denying the description of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Ibn Juraij said: The rabbis would urge obedience to God, while they themselves committed sins. Another group said: They would urge giving in charity, while they themselves were miserly. The meanings are close to one another.

Some of the people of allusive interpretation (ahl al-ishara) said: The meaning is, "Do you demand of the people the realities of the meanings, while you deviate from the outward forms of their traces?"

The second issue concerns the severity of punishment for one who has this description. Hammad ibn Salamah related from 'Ali ibn Zaid, from Anas, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "On the night I was taken on the Night Journey, I passed by people whose lips were being cut with scissors of fire. I said: 'O Jibril, who are these?' He said: 'These are the preachers from among the people of the world [[Thus in the Musnad of Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal (vol. 3, p. 120) and the Tafsir of al-Fakhr al-Razi (vol. 1, p. 496). In the original manuscripts: "from your community."]] who enjoin the people to righteousness and forget themselves, while they recite the Book. Will they not understand?'"

Abu Umamah also related: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Those who enjoin the people to righteousness and forget themselves will drag their intestines [[The meaning of al-qasab will come.]] into the Fire of Hell.
