It will be said to them: 'Who are you?' They will say: 'We are those who used to enjoin the people to good and forget ourselves.'"

I say: Although this hadith contains some weakness, because in its chain is al-Khasib ibn Jahdar, whom Imam Ahmad considered weak, and Ibn Ma'in narrates it from Abu Ghalib, from Abu Umamah Suday ibn 'Ajlan al-Bahili. Abu Ghalib, according to what Yahya ibn Ma'in reported, is Hazawwar al-Qurashi, mawla (client) of Khalid ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Usayd. It is also said he was a client of Bahilah, and it is said he was a client of 'Abd al-Rahman al-Hadrami. He used to travel to Syria for his trade. Yahya ibn Ma'in said: He is "salih al-hadith" (of acceptable narrations). Muslim related its meaning in his Sahih from Usamah ibn Zaid, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "A man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection and thrown into the Fire, and his entrails will spill out, and he will go around with them as the donkey goes around the millstone [[The addition is from Sahih Muslim.]]. The people of the Fire will gather around him and say: 'O so-and-so, what is wrong with you? Did you not used to enjoin good and forbid evil?' He will say: 'Yes, I used to enjoin good but I did not do it, and I used to forbid evil and I did it.'"

Al-qusb (with a damma on the qaf) is the intestine, and its plural is aqsab. Al-aqtab are the intestines, singular qitb. The meaning of "fatandaliq" is "it will come out quickly." We have also transmitted "fatanfaliq."

I say: The authentic hadith and the wording of the verse both indicate that the punishment of one who has knowledge of what is good and what is evil, and of the obligation to fulfil the duty of each of them, is more severe than that of one who does not have such knowledge. That is because he is like one who treats the sanctities of God, Exalted is He, with contempt and makes light of His rulings, and he is among those who do not benefit from their knowledge. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The people who will suffer the most severe punishment on the Day of Resurrection is a scholar whom God did not benefit by his knowledge." Ibn Majah related it in his Sunan.

The third issue: Know, may God grant you success, that the rebuke in the verse is for abandoning the performance of righteousness, not for enjoining righteousness. For this reason God, Exalted is He, censured in His Book a people who used to enjoin acts of righteousness but did not act upon them. He rebuked them with a rebuke that will be recited throughout the ages until the Day of Resurrection, when He said: ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people?﴾ up to the end of the verse.

Mansur al-Faqih said, excellently:
Indeed, a people who command us
to what they themselves do not do
are madmen, even if they
are not afflicted with madness.

Abu al-'Atahiyah said:
You described piety until it seemed you were its possessor,
but the scent of sins rises from your garments.

Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali said:
Do not forbid a trait while you yourself commit its like;
it is a great shame upon you when you do it.
Begin with yourself and restrain it from its error;
if it desists from it, then you are wise.
Then your admonition will be accepted, and your words will be followed,
and instruction will benefit.

Abu 'Amr ibn Mattar said: I attended the gathering of Abu 'Uthman al-Hiri, the ascetic. He came out and sat in the place where he used to sit for admonition. He remained silent until his silence lengthened. A man known as Abu al-'Abbas called out to him: "Would you like to say something during your silence?" Then he began to recite:
Anyone who is not pious yet enjoins people to piety
is a physician who treats others while the physician himself is sick.
He said: Then the voices rose in weeping and wailing.

The fourth issue: Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: "I dislike storytelling (al-qasas) because of three verses: the words of God, Exalted is He: ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 44] up to the end of the verse; His words: ﴿Why do you say what you do not do?﴾ [al-Saff: 2]; and His words: ﴿I do not intend to oppose you by doing what I forbid you from﴾ [Hud: 88]." [[See vol. 18, p. 77.]] [[See vol. 9, p. 89.]]

Salm ibn 'Amr [[Thus in the originals. The correct attribution is that the verses belong to al-Jammaz, who was the son of the sister of Salm ibn 'Amr al-Khasir. See al-Aghani (vol. 4, p. 76), Dar al-Kutub al-Misriyyah edition.]] said:
How ugly is the preacher's discouragement of worldliness,
when he discourages people from it but does not himself renounce it.
If he were sincere in his discouragement,
his house would be the mosque, morning and evening.
If he has renounced the world, then why
does he seek gifts from people and beg from them?
Provision is divided among all of you;
whoever strives for it, white or black, obtains it. [[Thus in al-Aghani. In the originals: "strives for it."]]

Al-Hasan said to Mutarrif ibn 'Abd Allah: "Admonish your companions." He said: "I fear that I will say what I do not do." He said: "May God have mercy on you! Which of us does what he says? Satan would love to have succeeded in this, so that no one would enjoin good or forbid evil."

Malik said, on the authority of Rabi'ah ibn Abi 'Abd al-Rahman: I heard Sa'id ibn Jubayr say: "If a person did not enjoin good or forbid evil until there was nothing in him [that was wrong], no one would ever enjoin good or forbid evil." Malik said: "He spoke the truth. Who is it that has nothing wrong in him?" [[In one copy: "in him" (or "upon him").]]

The fifth issue concerns the words of God, Exalted is He: ﴿righteousness﴾ (al-birr). Al-birr here means obedience and righteous deeds. Al-birr also means truthfulness. Al-birr also means the young of the fox. Al-birr also means driving sheep, and from this comes their saying: "He does not know the difference between hirr and birr," meaning he does not know the call to sheep from driving them. So the word is homonymous. A poet said:
O Lord, indeed Bakr [[Thus in al-Bahr al-Muhit of Abu Hayyan. In the originals: "bakw" with a waw. In Tafsir al-Shawkani: "in yakunu" (if they are).]] is behind You,
the people obey You and transgress against You.
By his words "yabarrukan-nas" he meant: they obey you.

It is also said that al-birr means the heart, in his words:
I would be in the place of al-birr from him, behind it,
and I would make my wealth and my commands subordinate to it. [[Thus in the originals and in Lisan al-'Arab, root b-r-r. In Sharh al-Qamus: "I would be in the place of al-birr from me, behind it."]]

Al-burr (with a damma on the ba') is grain (wheat), a well-known thing. Al-barr (with a fatha) is reverence and honour, and from it comes "a dutiful son" (walad barr and barr), meaning one who honours and respects his parents.

The sixth issue concerns the words of God, Exalted is He: ﴿and forget yourselves﴾, meaning you abandon. Al-nisyan (with a kasra on the nun) can mean abandonment, which is the meaning intended here, as in the words of God, Exalted is He: ﴿They forgot God, so He forgot them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 67], His words: ﴿And when they forgot what they had been reminded of﴾ [al-An'am: 44], and His words: ﴿And do not forget to show kindness among yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237]. It can also mean the opposite of remembering and retaining. From this is the hadith: "Adam forgot, so his descendants forgot." It will come. One says: "A man who is nasyan (with a fatha on the nun) is one who often forgets things." And "I forgot the thing, nisyanan," and do not say "nasayanan" (with a vowel on the middle letter), because nasayan is only the dual form of nasa al-'irq (the sciatic nerve).

Anfus is the plural of nafs, the paucal plural. Al-nafs means the soul (ruh). One says: "His soul departed (kharajat nafsuhu)." Abu Khirash said:
Salim escaped while his soul was in his jaw,
and nothing escaped except the sheath of a sword and a loincloth.
That is, with the sheath of a sword and a loincloth.

Among the evidence that al-nafs means the soul is the words of God, Exalted is He: ﴿God takes the souls at their death﴾ [al-Zumar: 42], meaning the spirits, according to a group of the people of ta'wil, as will come. This is clear in the words of Bilal to the Prophet (ﷺ) in the hadith of Ibn Shihab: "The one who took your soul, O Messenger of God, has taken mine." And his words (peace be upon him) in the hadith of Zayd ibn Aslam: "God took our spirits, and if He had willed He would have returned them to us at another time." Both were related by Malik, and this is the most fitting thing said about it.

Al-nafs also means blood. One says: "His soul flowed (salat nafsuhu)." The poet said [[He is al-Samaw'al.]]:
Our souls flow over the edges of swords,
and they flow only from the blades [[In Lisan al-'Arab: "hadd al-zuba."]].

Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: "Whatever has no flowing blood (nafs sa'ilah), when it dies in water, does not make the water impure."

Al-nafs also means the body. The poet said [[He is Aws ibn Hajar, inciting 'Amr ibn Hind against Bani Hanifah, who were the killers of his father al-Mundhir ibn Ma' al-Sama'. That is, they carried his blood to their tents.
(From Lisan al-'Arab.)]]:
I was informed that Bani Suhaym
brought into their tents the blood of the soul of al-Mundhir.
Al-tamur also means blood.

The seventh issue concerns the words of God, Exalted is He: ﴿while you recite the Book﴾. This is a severe rebuke for one who understands. "Tatlun" means you read. "Al-kitab" means the Torah. Likewise, whoever does what they did is like them. The root meaning of tilawah is following. For this reason it is used for recitation, because one follows some words with others in their letters until they come in their proper order. One says: "I recited him (talawtuhu) when I followed him, talwan." "I recited the Qur'an, tilawah." "I abandoned the man, talwan, when I forsook him." Al-talliyah and al-tulawah (with a damma on the ta') mean what remains. One says: "A remainder of my right remained for me (talat li min haqqi tulawah wa taliyah)," meaning it remained. "I left (atlaytu)" means "I preserved." "I pursued my right (tatallaytu haqqi)" when I pursued it until I obtained it in full. Abu Zayd said: "A man was talla" when he was at the last of his breath.

The eighth issue concerns the words of God, Exalted is He: ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ That is, will you not restrain yourselves from engaging in this destructive condition? Al-'aql means restraint. From it comes 'iqal al-ba'ir (the tether of a camel), because it restrains it from movement. From it comes al-'aql (blood money), because it restrains the guardian of the slain from killing the perpetrator. From it comes i'tiqal al-batn wa al-lisan (constipation of the belly and the tongue). From it one calls a fortress ma'qil. Al-'aql is the opposite of ignorance. Al-'aql is also a red garment that Arab women wear, with which they cover the howdahs. 'Alqamah said:
'Aqlan and ramman, which birds nearly snatch,
as if it were of the blood of the bellies, stained.

The *mudmum* (with an unpointed dal) is the red one, and this is what is meant here. The *mudmum* is also the one filled with fat, of a camel or other animal. It is said that these are two kinds of striped cloth (*burud*). Ibn Faris said: "*Al-aql* (the markings) of garments are the stripes that run lengthwise, and whatever has round markings is called *al-raqm*." Al-Zajjaj said: "The intelligent (*'aqil*) is one who acts by what Allah has made obligatory upon him, and whoever does not act is ignorant."

The ninth issue: The people of truth (*ahl al-haqq*) agree that intellect (*'aql*) is an existent thing, neither eternal nor non-existent, because if it were non-existent, it could not be peculiar to certain entities rather than others. Once its existence is established, it is impossible to say that it is eternal, since the proof has established that nothing is eternal except Allah the Exalted, as will be explained in this surah and elsewhere, Allah willing. The philosophers (*al-falasifa*) have held that intellect is eternal. Some of them held that it is a subtle substance in the body, whose ray spreads out from it like a lamp in a house, by which it distinguishes the realities of known things. Others said it is a simple substance, meaning not composite.

They then differed about its locus. One group said its locus is the brain, because the brain is the seat of sensation. Another group said its locus is the heart, because the heart is the source of life and the matter of the senses. This view, that intellect is a substance, is corrupt, since substances are alike, so if a substance were intellect, every substance would be intellect.

It was also said that intellect is that which perceives things as they are in the realities of meanings. Although this view is closer than the previous one, it is still far from the correct view, because perception is an attribute of a living being, whereas intellect is an accident, and perception is impossible for it, just as it is impossible for it to be pleasurable or desirous.

Shaykh Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, the master Abu Ishaq al-Isfarayini, and others among the verifiers (*al-muhaqqiqun*) said: intellect is knowledge, as evidenced by the fact that one does not say "I understood (*'aqaltu*)" and "I did not know," or "I knew" and "I did not understand." Al-Qadi Abu Bakr said: intellect is necessary knowledge of the obligatory being obligatory, the permissible being permissible, and the impossible being impossible. This is the view preferred by Abu al-Ma'ali in *al-Irshad*. In *al-Burhan* he chose that it is an attribute by which the apprehension of knowledge becomes possible, and he raised objections against the position of al-Qadi and argued for its invalidity.

In *al-Burhan* it is related from al-Muhasibi that he said: intellect is an innate disposition (*gharizah*). Al-Ustadh Abu Bakr related from al-Shafi'i and Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Mujahid that they both said: intellect is an instrument of discernment (*alat al-tamyiz*). It is related from Abu al-'Abbas al-Qalanisi that he said: intellect is the power of discernment (*quwwat al-tamyiz*). It is related from al-Muhasibi that he said: intellect is lights and insights (*anwar wa basa'ir*).

He then arranged these statements and interpreted them in various ways, saying: "It is preferable not to affirm this report from al-Shafi'i or from Ibn Mujahid, since an instrument is properly used for a physical, constructed instrument, and using it for accidents is metaphorical." The same applies to the saying of one who said it is a power, since by "power" one only understands capacity. Al-Qalanisi used these expressions loosely, for the sake of latitude in phrasing, and likewise al-Muhasibi.

Intellect is neither a form nor a light, but by it lights and insights are gained. Its benefit in the affirmation of God's oneness (*tawhid*) will be explained later in this surah in the verse, Allah willing. (See vol. 2, p. 191.)

**Eight issues arise from this verse.**

**The first issue:** the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Seek help through patience and prayer﴾. *Al-sabr* (patience, restraint) in the language means confining. It is said, "So-and-so was killed *sabran*," meaning he was held back until he was destroyed. And "I *sabbartu* myself upon the thing," meaning I restrained myself from it. The *maṣbūra* that is forbidden in the hadith is the animal confined to be killed, and it is the *mujaththama* (the animal shot or bound and left to die). 'Antarah said:

*So I was patient, knowing of that, a free woman*
*who stays still when the soul of the coward rises in alarm.*

**The second issue:** Allah, exalted is He, commanded patience in obedience and patience in refraining from disobedience in His Book, saying, "And be patient" (﴿Be patient﴾). It is said, "So-and-so is patient regarding sins." When he is patient regarding sins, he has been patient in obedience. This is the most accurate of what has been said. Al-Naḥḥās said: one does not say of the one who endures a calamity, "*ṣābir*" (patient) alone; one says "*ṣābir* upon such-and-such." When you say "*ṣābir*" without qualification, it has the meaning we have mentioned. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account﴾ [al-Zumar: 10]. [See vol. 15, p. 24.]

**The third issue:** the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿and prayer﴾. He singled out prayer for mention among the other acts of worship, to honour it. When a serious matter befell the Prophet (ﷺ), he would turn to prayer. Among the reports: 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas was informed of the death of his brother Qutham (and it is said, of a daughter of his) while he was on a journey. He said "*Innā lillāh*" and said: "A concealment that Allah has covered, a burden that Allah has relieved, and a reward that Allah has bestowed." Then he moved aside from the road, prayed, then went back to his mount while reciting, "Seek help through patience and prayer."

According to this interpretation, *al-ṣalāh* (prayer) is the legislated prayer (*al-shar'iyyah*). Some people said: it means supplication (*du'ā'*), in its linguistic usage, so the verse on this interpretation resembles His words: ﴿When you meet a force, stand firm and remember Allah﴾ [al-Anfal: 45], since steadfastness is patience and remembrance is supplication. A third view: Mujahid said, "Patience in this verse is fasting, and for this reason Ramadan has been called the month of patience." On this view, fasting and prayer are harmonious in the verse, since fasting restrains desires and encourages detachment from the world, while prayer forbids indecency and wrongdoing, brings humility, and the Qur'an that reminds of the Hereafter is recited in it. And Allah knows best.

**The fourth issue:** patience in the face of harm and in acts of obedience belongs to the category of striving against the self (*jihād al-nafs*), restraining it from its desires and preventing it from overreaching. It is one of the characteristics of the prophets and the righteous. Yaḥyā ibn al-Yamān said: "Patience is that you do not wish for any condition other than what Allah has granted you, and contentment with what Allah has decreed of the affairs of your worldly life and your Hereafter."

Al-Sha'bī said: 'Alī (may Allah be pleased with him) said, "Patience in relation to faith is like the head in relation to the body." Al-Ṭabarī said: 'Alī (may Allah be pleased with him) spoke the truth. That is because faith is knowledge in the heart, affirmation by the tongue, and action by the limbs. Whoever does not endure in acting with his limbs does not deserve to be called a believer without qualification. Thus patience in acting upon the legal obligations (*al-sharā'i'*) is like the head of a human being, without which the body is not complete.

**The fifth issue:** Allah, exalted is He, described the reward for deeds and set for them a limit and a measure, saying: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times the like of it﴾ [al-An'am: 160]. He made the reward for spending in the way of Allah greater than this, saying: ﴿The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a grain﴾ [al-Baqarah: 261], and so on. He made the reward of the patient without measure and praised its people, saying: ﴿Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account﴾ [al-Zumar: 10]. He also said: ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives—indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination﴾ [al-Shura: 43]. [See vol. 16, p. 44.]

It has been said that the intended meaning of "the patient" in His words ﴿Indeed, the patient will be given their reward﴾ [al-Zumar: 10] is "those who fast." This is based on His words, as recorded in the authentic Sunnah from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Fasting is for Me, and I will reward it." He did not mention a specific reward for it, just as He did not mention one for patience. And Allah knows best.

**The sixth issue:** among the excellence of patience is that Allah, exalted is He, described Himself with it, as in the hadith of Abu Musa from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "There is no one [or: nothing] more patient regarding a harm he hears from Allah, exalted is He. They attribute a son to Him, yet He grants them well-being and provides for them." Related by al-Bukhari.

Our scholars said: the description of Allah, exalted is He, as "patient" means only forbearance (*al-ḥilm*). The meaning of describing Him with forbearance is delaying punishment from those who deserve it. His description as patient did not come in the revealed text (*al-tanzīl*); it came only in the hadith of Abu Musa, and the people of the Sunnah interpreted it in the sense of forbearance. This was said by Ibn Fūrak and others. Among His names is "*al-Ṣabūr*" (the Most Patient), for emphasis in forbearance toward those who disobey Him.

**The seventh issue:** the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, it is difficult﴾. The commentators differed about what the pronoun in "*wa-innahā*" (and indeed it) refers to. It was said: it refers to prayer alone, specifically, because prayer is harder on the souls than fasting is. In this view "patience" here means fasting. Prayer involves confining the souls, whereas fasting involves only preventing desire. The one who prevents a single desire or two is not like the one who prevents all desires. The fasting person only prevents the desire for women, food and drink, then he spreads out into the other desires: speech, walking, looking at other things, and meeting people, so he consoles himself with those things for what he has been prevented from. The one who prays refrains from all of that; all his limbs are restricted by prayer from all desires. When this is the case, prayer is harder on the self and its struggle is more intense. For this reason He said, "And indeed, it is difficult."

It was also said: the pronoun refers to both, but He referred to the more prevalent, which is prayer, as in His words: ﴿Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 34], and His words: ﴿And when they see a trade or a diversion, they rush toward it﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 11]. Here the pronoun was returned to silver because it is the more prevalent and general, and to trade because it is the more excellent and important.

It was also said: since patience is included in prayer, the pronoun returns to prayer, as He said: ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 62], and He did not say "they should please them both," because the Messenger's pleasure is included in the pleasure of Allah, exalted and mighty is He. From this is the poet's saying [Ḥassān ibn Thābit]:

*Indeed, the bloom of youth and the hair of the head, as long as they are not disobeyed, are madness.*

He did not say "they are disobeyed" (*yu'āṣayā*), returning the pronoun to youth, because the hair is included within it.

It was also said: the pronoun returns to each of them separately, but it has been omitted for brevity. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 50], and He did not say "two signs." From this is the poet's saying [Ḍābi' al-Burjumī, as in *Lisān al-'Arab*, under *q-y-r*, and al-Mubarrad's *al-Kāmil*, vol. 1, p. 181, Europe edition]:

*So whoever has his dwelling in Medina, then I and Qayyār there are strangers.*

And another said [al-Aḍbaṭ ibn Qurai' al-Sa'dī, as in *Lisān al-'Arab*, under *m-s-y*]:

*For every concern among the concerns there is a remedy, but morning and evening there is no prosperity with it.*

He meant: "They are both strangers, and there is no prosperity with them."

It was also said: the pronoun refers to the worship that is implied in meaning by the mention of patience and prayer. It was said: it refers to the verbal noun, which is the seeking of help (*al-isti'āna*), required by His words "and seek help." It was said: it refers to the response of Muhammad (ﷺ), because patience and prayer are what he used to call to. It was said: it refers to the Ka'bah, because the command to pray is directed toward it.

"*Kabīrah*" means heavy and burdensome. It is the predicate of "*inna*." In other than the Qur'an it may be said: "*wa-innahu la-kabīrah*" (and indeed it is difficult). ﴿Except for the humble﴾, for it is light upon them. The scholars of meanings (*arbāb al-ma'ānī*) said: except for those who were strengthened from eternity with the special qualities of selection and guidance.

**The eighth issue:** the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿for the humble﴾. *Al-khāshi'ūn* is the plural of *khāshi'*, who is the humble, the submissive. *Al-khushū'* is a state in the soul which shows outwardly in the limbs as stillness and humility. Qatādah said: *khushū'* is in the heart, and it is fear, and lowering the gaze during prayer. Al-Zajjāj said: the *khāshi'* is one in whom the trace of humiliation and humility is seen, like the *khushū'* of a house after it has fallen into ruin. This is the original meaning. Al-Nābighah said:

*Ashes like the kohl of the eye, its remains I make clear, and a pit like the base of a pool, broken and humbled.*

A place that is *khāshi'* is one not guided to. Voices *khasha'at*, meaning they became quiet. The phlegm in his chest *khasha'at* when he spat thick saliva. He *khasha'a bi-baṣarihi* when he lowered his gaze. *Al-khush'ah* is a soft piece of ground. In the hadith: "The Kaaba was a soft ground upon the water, then the earth was spread out from it." A land *khāshi'ah* is dusty, with no dwelling in it.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: "I asked al-A'mash about *khushū'*, and he said, 'O Thawri! You want to be an imam for the people and you do not know *khushū'*!'" I asked Ibrahim al-Nakha'i about *khushū'*, and he said: "Uʿaymish! You want to be an imam for the people and you do not know *khushū'*! *Khushū'* is not eating coarse food, nor wearing coarse clothing, nor bowing the head! Rather, *khushū'* is that you see the noble and the lowly as equal in the truth, and that you humble yourself before Allah in every obligation that has been made obligatory upon you."

'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb looked at a young man who had lowered his head and said: "O you! Raise your head, for *khushū'* does not exceed what is in the heart."

'Alī ibn Abi Ṭālib said: "*Khushū'* is in the heart, and that you soften your palms for a Muslim person, and that you do not turn around in your prayer."

This meaning will come more fully explained at His words: ﴿Certainly will the believers succeed, those who are during their prayer humble﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1–2]. [See vol. 12, p. 102.]

Whoever shows people humility beyond what is in his heart has only displayed an extreme form of hypocrisy. Sahl ibn 'Abdullah said: "A person is not humble until every hair on his body is humbled, because of the words of Allah, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿From it shiver the skins of those who fear their Lord﴾ [al-Zumar: 23]." [See vol. 15, p. 248.]

I say: this is the praiseworthy *khushū'*, because when fear settles in the heart, it compels outward humility, so that its possessor cannot repel it. You see him lowering his gaze, courteous and humbled. The predecessors (*al-salaf*) used to strive to conceal what appeared of that. As for the blameworthy kind, it is affectation, feigned weeping, and bowing the head, as the ignorant do so that they may be seen with an eye of piety and reverence. That is a deception from Satan and an enticement from the human self.

Al-Ḥasan reported that a man sighed in the presence of 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb as if he were feigning grief, so 'Umar struck him with his fist, or said he punched him. When 'Umar spoke, he made himself heard; when he walked, he walked quickly; when he struck, he struck painfully. He was a truly devout and genuinely humble man.

Ibn Abi Najīḥ reported from Mujahid: "The humble ones are the truly believing."

[[Qurtubi's commentary on 2:46]]

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who think﴾. "Alladhina" (those who) is in the genitive position as an adjective (na't) for "al-khashi'in" (the humble), and it is permissible to put it in the nominative on the basis of a new sentence (qat').

The word "zann" (thinking/supposing) here, according to the majority of scholars, means "yaqin" (certainty). Among its uses is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I assumed that I would meet my account﴾ [al-Haqqah: 20], and His saying: ﴿So they assumed that they would be plunged into it﴾ [al-Kahf: 53]. Durayd ibn al-Simmah said:

"So I said to them, 'Be certain (zunnu) of two thousand armored men, their chiefs in the Persian, well-woven mail.'"

Abu Dawud said:

"How many a worry you relieved by a creditor, and hidden things you uncovered by certainties (zunun)."

It has also been said that "zann" in the verse may remain in its original sense, with an implied phrase "bi-dhunubihim" (with their sins), so that they expect to meet Him as sinners. Al-Mahdawi and al-Mawardi mentioned this. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This is far-fetched (ta'assuf)." Al-Farra' claimed that "zann" may occur in the sense of "kadhib" (lie), but the Basrans do not recognize this.

The original meaning and basic rule of "zann" is doubt with an inclination toward one of the two beliefs. It may be used in the place of certainty, as in this verse and others, but it is not used for something that has already become perceptible to the senses. The Arabs do not say of a visible, present man, "I think this is a human being." The usage is found only in matters that have not become perceptible to the senses, in the sense seen in this verse, in poetry, and in His saying, "So they assumed that they would be plunged into it." Certainty may also be used in the sense of "zann," which has been explained at the beginning of the surah. You say "su'tu bihi zannan" and "asa'tu bihi al-zann," they add the alif when they use the alif and lam.

The meaning of "mula qu rabbihim" (meeting their Lord) is meeting the recompense of their Lord. It has also been said that the form is "mufa'alah" but it comes from one party, like "'afahu Allah" (God granted him well-being).

"Wa-annahum" with a fath on the hamza is conjoined to the first (clause), and "wa-innahum" with a kasra is permissible as a new sentence.

"Ilayhi" means "to Him," i.e., to their Lord; it has also been said, "to His recompense."

"Raji'un" (returning) is an affirmation of the resurrection, the recompense, and the presentation before the Supreme King.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 47:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾ has already been discussed [[See p. 330 of this volume.]]. And (﴿and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾) means over the worlds of their time, since the people of every age are a "world" (ʿālam). It was also said: over all the worlds, because of the prophets who were raised among them, and this is a privilege specific to them and not to others.

**The exegesis of His words, Exalted is He:** ﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all﴾. This is a command whose meaning is a warning. The discussion of *taqwa* (God-consciousness, fear of God) has already passed [[See p. 161 of this volume.]]. "A Day" means His punishment and its terror, and it is the Day of Resurrection. It is in the accusative as the object of "fear" (*ittaqu*). In other than the Qur'an it could be read as *yawma la tajzi* ("a Day on which...") in the construct form. There is a disagreement among the grammarians about an ellipsis in the sentence. The Basrians said: the implied meaning is "a day on which no soul will avail another soul at all," and then the word "in it" was omitted, as in the line of poetry:

*"A day we witnessed, Sulaym and 'Amir..."* [[Sulaym and 'Amir: two tribes of Qays 'Aylan.]]

meaning "we witnessed in it." Al-Kisa'i said this is an error; the word "in it" cannot be omitted. Rather, the implied meaning is "fear a Day when no soul will avail it," and then the pronoun (the *ha'*, "it") was omitted. The omission of the *ha'* is permitted, in his view, because adverbs of time (*zuruf*) do not permit the omission of the pronoun. He said: you cannot say "this is a man I went to" (meaning "I went to him") or "I did not see a man I desire" (meaning "I desire him"). He said: if that were permitted, one could say "the one I spoke, Zayd" with the meaning "the one I spoke about, Zayd." Al-Farra' said that the omission of the *ha'* is permissible, as in *wa-fihi* ("and in it"). Al-Mahdawi reported that both opinions are permissible according to Sibawayh, al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj.

The meaning of ﴿no soul will avail another soul at all﴾ is: no soul will be held to account for the sin of another, and it will not repel anything from it. One says *jaza 'anni hadha al-amr, yajzi* ("this matter sufficed for me / served in my stead"), just as one says *qada 'anni* ("it discharged on my behalf"). And *ijtaza'tu bi-l-shay' ijtiza'an* means "I was content with the thing when I made do with it." The poet said:

*"Indeed treachery among peoples is a shame... and the free man makes do with the hoof."*

That is, he is content with it. In the Hadith of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him): "If you pour water over water, it suffices for you (*jaza 'anka*)." He means: if you pour water on urine on the ground, and the water flows over it, the place is purified, and there is no need for you to wash that spot and dry the water with a cloth or something else, as many people do. In the authentic Hadith, from Abu Burda ibn Niyar concerning the sacrifice: "You will not suffice (*lan tajzi*) for anyone after you." That is, you will not be sufficient. So the meaning of *la tajzi* is: it does not discharge, does not suffice, and does not make enough—if there is nothing owed by it. If there is something owed, then it does discharge, suffice and make enough, without its choice, from its good deeds, what is owed of rights. As in the Hadith of Abu Hurayah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has a wrong against his brother, regarding his honour or anything else, let him seek his pardon for it today, before there is no dinar or dirham. If he has good deeds, an amount will be taken from them equal to his wrong; and if he has no good deeds, some of the sins of his companion will be taken and placed upon him." Reported by al-Bukhari. Similar is his other Hadith concerning the bankrupt, which we have mentioned in *al-Tadhkira*, reported by Muslim [[See Sahih Muslim, chapter on the prohibition of injustice (vol. 2, p. 283), Bulaq edition.]].

It is read as *tujzi'* (with a *damma* on the *ta'* and a *hamza*). It is said *jaza* and *ajza* with one meaning. Some people distinguished between them, saying: *jaza* means "discharged" and "requited," and *ajza* means "sufficed" and "was enough." *Ajza'anī al-shay'* means "the thing was enough for me," that is, *kafani*. The poet said:

*"You sufficed the affair of the worlds, and it would not suffice except one perfect and son of a perfect."*

**The Third Issue** [[Note: all the copies of the original text in our hands do not mention the first and second issues concerning this verse.]]: His words, Exalted is He: ﴿nor will intercession be accepted from it﴾. *Shafa'ah* (intercession) is derived from *shaf'* ("pair, two"). One says: it was odd, so I made it even (*shaffa'tuhu shaf'an*). *Shuf'ah* (pre-emptive right of partnership) is from this, because you add the property of your partner to your property. *Shafi'* is the owner of the pre-emptive right and the one who intercedes. A she-camel is *shafi'* when she carries a foetus and a young one follows her. One says of it: *shafa'at al-naqatu shaf'an*, and a she-camel that is *shafuw* is one who combines two milkings in a single milking. *Istashfa'tuhu ila fulan* means "I asked him to intercede for me with so-and-so." *Tashaffa'tu ilayhi fi fulan fa-shaffa'anī fihi* means "I asked him to intercede regarding so-and-so and he interceded for me regarding him." Thus intercession is the joining of another to your standing and means. In reality it is a display of the intercessor's rank with the one interceded with, and the conveying of its benefit to the one for whom intercession is made.

**The Fourth Issue:** The position of the People of Truth (*Ahl al-Haqq*, the Sunni community) is that intercession is true. The Mu'tazilah [[The Mu'tazilah: a rationalist theological school which denied intercession for grave sinners.]] denied it and made the believers among the sinners who entered the Fire eternal in punishment. The reports are widely attested that whoever among the disobedient sinful monotheists from the nations of the prophets will be reached by the intercession of the intercessors: the angels, the prophets, the martyrs and the righteous. The Qadi [[The Qadi: here referring to a judge-theologian opposing the Mu'tazilah in the discussion.]] relied upon two things in his refutation of them. The first: the numerous reports that have been transmitted with consecutive chains in meaning. The second: the consensus (*ijma'*, scholarly agreement) of the earlier generations (*salaf*) in accepting these reports, and no objection was voiced by any of them in any age. So the wide transmission of these reports, their unanimous acceptance of their authenticity, and their acceptance of them is a decisive proof for the soundness of the creed of the People of Truth and the corruption of the religion of the Mu'tazilah.

If they say: texts from the Book have come that necessitate rejecting these reports, such as His words ﴿The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend nor an intercessor who is obeyed﴾ [Ghafir: 18]. They say: the people of major sins are wrongdoers. And He said: ﴿Whoever does evil will be requited for it﴾ [al-Nisa': 123], and ﴿nor will intercession be accepted from it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48].

We say: these verses are not general regarding every wrongdoer, and generality (*'umum*) has no fixed form, so these verses do not include everyone who does evil, nor every soul. Rather, what is meant by them is the disbelievers, not the believers, by the evidence of the reports transmitted on this matter. Also, Allah, Exalted is He, affirmed intercession for some people and negated it for others. He said regarding the description of the disbelievers: ﴿So the intercession of the intercessors will not benefit them﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 48]. He said: ﴿And they do not intercede except for those whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya': 28], and He said: ﴿And intercession will not benefit with Him except for one whom He has permitted﴾ [Saba': 23]. From this whole body of verses we know that intercession benefits only the believers and not the disbelievers. The exegetes have unanimously agreed that what is meant by His words, Exalted is He: "And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all, nor will intercession be accepted from it" is the disbelieving soul, not every soul.

And although we say that the punishment is general for every wrongdoer and disobedient one, we do not say that they will abide in it forever, by the evidence of the reports we have related, and by His words: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48], and His words: ﴿Indeed, none despairs of the mercy of Allah except the disbelieving people﴾ [Yusuf: 87].

If they say: He said, "And they do not intercede except for those whom He approves," and the sinful one is not approved, we say: He did not say "for those He does not approve." He said "for whom He approves," and those whom Allah approves for intercession are the monotheists, by the evidence of His words: ﴿They will not possess intercession except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾ [Maryam: 87]. It was said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "What is the covenant of Allah with His creation?" He said: "That they believe and do not associate anything with Him." The exegetes said: "except one who says: there is no god but Allah."

If they say: the one approved is the penitent who has taken a covenant with Allah by turning to Him in repentance, by the evidence that the angels sought forgiveness for them, and He said: ﴿So forgive those who have repented and followed Your way﴾ [Ghafir: 7]. And likewise the intercession of the prophets, peace be upon them, is only for the people of repentance, not the people of major sins. We say: according to you it is obligatory upon Allah, Exalted is He, to accept repentance. So when Allah accepts the repentance of the sinner, he does not need intercession nor seeking forgiveness.

The exegetes unanimously agreed that what is meant by His words "So forgive those who have repented" is: from polytheism, "and followed Your way," that is, the way of the believers. They asked Allah, Exalted is He, to forgive them what is beneath polytheism of their sins, as He said, Exalted is He: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48].

If they say: all of the community desire the intercession of the Prophet (ﷺ), so if it were only for the people of major sins, their supplication would be void. We say: every Muslim only seeks the intercession of the Messenger and turns to Allah, desiring that it reach him, because he believes he is not free from sins and is not one who has fulfilled all that Allah has obligated upon him. Rather, each one acknowledges his own shortcoming, and therefore fears punishment and hopes for deliverance. He (ﷺ) said: "No one will be saved except by the mercy of Allah, Exalted is He." It was said: "Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Not even I, unless Allah covers me with His mercy."

**The Fifth Issue:** His words, Exalted is He: ﴿nor will it be accepted﴾. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read *tuqbalu* with a *ta'*, because intercession (*shafa'ah*) is feminine. The rest read it with a *ya'* on the masculine form, because it means the intercessor (*shafi'*). Al-Akhfash said: the masculine form is good, because you have separated the verb from its subject, as was mentioned previously in His words ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾ [al-Baqarah: 37] [[See p. 326.]].

**The Sixth Issue:** His words, Exalted is He: ﴿nor will any compensation be taken from it﴾. That is, ransom (*fida'*). *Al-'adl* (with a *fatha* on the *'ayn*) means ransom, and (with a *kasra*) means an equal. One says *'idl* and *'adil* for one who resembles you in weight and measure. One says *'adl al-shay'* is what equals it in value and quantity, even if it is not of its kind. *Al-'idl* (with a *kasra*) is what equals the thing of its kind and in its substance. Al-Tabari related that some of the Arabs use a *kasra* on the *'ayn* with the meaning of ransom, but the singular of *a'dal* (equals) is only with a *kasra*, without exception.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿nor will they be helped﴾, that is, they will not be assisted. *Al-nasr* is aid, and *al-ansar* are helpers. From this is His words: ﴿Who are my helpers toward Allah?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 52], that is, who will join his support to my support. *Intasara al-rajul* means he took revenge. *Al-nasr* also means coming; one says: *nasartu ard Bani Fulan* ("I came to the land of the sons of so-and-so"). The poet said [[It is al-Ra'i, addressing a horse (from al-Lisan).]]:

*"When the sacred month has come, then bid farewell to the lands of Tamim, and go to the land of 'Amir."*

*Al-nasr* also means rain; one says *nusirat al-ard* ("the land was rained upon"). *Al-nasr* also means giving. He said:

*"Indeed, I, and lines written in writing, are one who says: O Nasr, give victory, give victory!"*

It is related that the cause of this verse was that the Children of Israel said: "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved, and the sons of His prophets, and our fathers will intercede for us." So Allah, Exalted is He, informed them about the Day of Resurrection that no intercessions will be accepted therein, and no ransom will be taken therein. He specified intercession, ransom and help for mention because they are the meanings that the children of Adam were accustomed to in this world, for the one who is in distress is not freed except by being interceded for, or helped, or ransomed.

**Issue 1:** There are thirteen issues in this verse.

**First:** His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And [remember] when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾. The word "idh" (when) is in the accusative position, in coordination with "remember My favour." This and what follows are a reminder of some of the favours He bestowed upon them. That is, "Remember My favour by saving you from your enemy and by appointing prophets among you." The address is to those present, but what is meant are the earlier fathers, as He said, ﴿Indeed, when the water rose high, We carried you in the sailing ship﴾ [al-Haqqah: 11]. That is, We carried your fathers. It has also been said that He said "We delivered you" because the deliverance of the fathers was the cause of the deliverance of these present people. The meaning of "najjaynakum" (We delivered you) is "We cast you upon a najwah (an elevated place) of the earth," which is what rises from it. This is the original meaning. Then every person who attains success was called "najiyy" (one delivered). So the najiy is one who emerges from narrowness into spaciousness. It is also read as "wa-idh najjaytukum" (and when I delivered you), in the singular.

**Second:** His saying, exalted is He, ﴿from the people of Pharaoh﴾. "Ali Fir'awn" (the people of Pharaoh) means his people, his followers, and the people of his religion. Likewise, the "people" (ali) of the Messenger ﷺ are those who follow his religion and creed in his time and in all other eras, whether or not they are related to him by blood. Whoever is not upon his religion and creed is not of his "people" or his "household," even if he is a relative and kinsman. This is contrary to the Rafidah (a Shi'i sect), who said that the people of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ are only Fatimah, al-Hasan, and al-Husayn.

Our proof is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And We drowned the people of Pharaoh﴾ [al-Baqarah: 50], and ﴿Make the people of Pharaoh enter the severest punishment﴾ [Ghafir: 46]. That is, the people of his religion, since he had no son, no daughter, no father, no paternal uncle, no brother, and no agnatic relatives. Also, there is no doubt that whoever is not a believer or monotheist is not of the people of Muhammad, even if he is a relative of his. For this reason it is said that Abu Lahab and Abu Jahl were not of his people or his household, even though they had kinship with the Prophet ﷺ. For this reason too, Allah, exalted is He, said about the son of Nuh, ﴿Indeed, he is not of your family; indeed, his conduct is unrighteous﴾ [Hud: 46].

In Sahih Muslim, from Amr ibn al-As, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ openly, not secretly, say: "Behold, the family of Abu [i.e., so-and-so]"¹ "are not my allies; my ally is only Allah and the righteous believers."

Another group said that the people of Muhammad are specifically his wives and his offspring, based on the hadith of Abu Humayd al-Sa'idi, that they said: "O Messenger of Allah, how should we send blessings upon you?" He said: "Say: O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad and upon his wives and his offspring, as You sent blessings upon the family of Ibrahim, and bless Muhammad and his wives and his offspring, as You blessed the family of Ibrahim; indeed You are Praiseworthy and Glorious." Narrated by Muslim.

A group of the scholars said: "The ahl (family) is well known, and the al (people) are the followers." The first view is more sound, for the reason we have mentioned, and because of the hadith of Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa, that when people came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with their charity, he would say, "O Allah, send blessings upon them." When my father came to him with his charity, he said, "O Allah, send blessings upon the family of Abu Awfa."

**Third:** The grammarians disagreed over whether "al" (people of) may be attached to lands/cities or not. Al-Kisa'i said: It is only said "ali fulan" (the people of so-and-so) and "ali fulanah" (the people of so-and-so, feminine), and it is not said of cities, "He is of the people of Homs," nor "of the people of Madinah." Al-Akhfash said: It is only said of a supreme leader, such as "ali Muhammad ﷺ" and "ali Fir'awn," because he is their leader in misguidance. He said: We have heard it used of cities too: they say "ahl al-Madinah" and "al al-Madinah."

**Fourth:** The grammarians also disagreed over whether "al" may be attached to a pronoun or not. Al-Nahhas, al-Zubaydi, and al-Kisa'i forbade this, so one only says, "O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad and the family of Muhammad," and does not say "wa-alihi" (and his family). The correct form is to say "ahlihi" (his family). Another group held that it is permissible, among them Ibn al-Sayyid, and this is the correct view, because the sound transmitted usage supports it. It has come in the verse of Abd al-Muttalib:

*O Allah, indeed a man defends his camp, so defend Your people (hilal-ak).*
*And give victory over the family of the Cross and its worshippers today, against your family (al-ak).*

Hilal (with a kasra) means the people who dwell and are neighbours, meaning the inhabitants of the sacred precinct.

And Nudbah said:

*I am the horseman who defends the true right of my father, and of my family (ali), as you defend the true right of your family (alika).*

Haqiqah (with two qafs) is what is binding upon a person to protect, that is, it is obligatory upon him to defend it.

**Fifth:** They also disagreed about the root of "al." Al-Nahhas said its origin is "ahl," then the ha' was replaced by an alif. If you diminutivise it, you return it to its origin and say "uhayl." Al-Mahdawi said its origin is "awl." It has also been said: it is "ahl," the ha' was changed to a hamzah, then the hamzah was changed to an alif. Its plural is "alun," and its diminutive is "uwayl," as transmitted by al-Kisa'i. Others transmitted "uhayl," which al-Nahhas has already mentioned. Abu al-Hasan ibn Kaysan said: When you pluralise "al" (in the sense of family), you say "alun"; but when you pluralise "al" which means mirage, you say "awal," like "mal" and "amwal" (wealth).

**Sixth:** His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Pharaoh﴾. It has been said that "Fir'awn" is the name of that very king. It has also been said that it is the name of every king of the Amalekites, like Kisra for the Persians, Qaysar for the Romans, and al-Najashi for the Abyssinians. And in the view of the People of the Book, the name of the Pharaoh of Moses was Qabus. Wahb said his name was al-Walid ibn Mus'ab ibn al-Rayyan, and his kunyah (byname) was Abu Murrah, and he was of the Banu Imlig ibn Lawadh ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh, peace be upon him.

Al-Suhayli said: Everyone who ruled the Copts and Egypt was called "Fir'awn." He was Persian, from the people of Istakhr. Al-Mas'udi said: No Arabic meaning is known for "Fir'awn." Al-Jawhari said: "Fir'awn" is the title of al-Walid ibn Mus'ab, king of Egypt, and every tyrant is a Fir'awn; the tyrants are the Faraina. One says "tafarra'a" (to act tyrannically), and he is "dhu far'anah," meaning cunning and cruelty. In a hadith: "Fir'awn of this community has taken us" (i.e., this community's tyrant).

"Fir'awn" is in the genitive position, but it is not declined because it is a foreign word (ajamah).

**Seventh:** His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They inflict upon you﴾. It has been said that its meaning is "they make you taste it and impose it upon you." Abu Ubaydah said: "they appoint over you," as one says "sama-hu khutat khasf" (he imposed upon him a plan of humiliation) when he assigns it to him. From this is the saying of Amr ibn Kulthum:

*When the king imposes humiliation upon people, we refuse to accept humiliation among us.*

It has also been said: "they perpetuate your torment." Al-sawm means continuance, and from it comes "sa'imat al-ghanam" (grazing sheep), because they persist in grazing. Al-Akhfash said: It is in the nominative position as a new beginning (inception)¹, and if you wish, it can be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, meaning "imposing upon you."

**Eighth:** His saying, exalted is He, ﴿the evil torment﴾ is the second object of "yasumunakum." Its meaning is "the most severe torment." It is also permissible that it means "the imposition of torment." It may also be an adjective, meaning "an evil imposition."

It is related that Pharaoh made the Children of Israel servants and dependants, and he assigned them to his tasks: one group would build, another would plough and cultivate, and another would serve. His own people were soldiers and nobles, and whoever of them was not engaged in one of these tasks was subjected to the poll-tax. This is the "evil torment."

**Ninth:** His saying, exalted is He, ﴿they slaughter your sons﴾. "Yudhabbihuna" is without a waw, as an apposition to "yasumunakum," as the poet recited, which Sibawayh cited:

*When you come to us and visit us in our homes, you will find firewood that is sturdy and a fire blazing.*

Al-Farra' and others said: "yudhabbihuna" is without a waw as an explanation of His saying ﴿they inflict upon you the evil torment﴾ [al-Baqarah: 49], just as you say, "The people came to me: Zayd and Amr," where you do not need a waw before Zayd. A parallel is His saying, ﴿And whoever does that will meet a penalty; the punishment will be doubled for him﴾ [al-Furqan: 68–69]. In Surat Ibrahim it is "wa-yudhabbihuna" with a waw, because the meaning is that they torment you by slaughtering and by other means, so His saying "wa-yudhabbihuna abna'akum" is a different kind of torment, not an explanation of what came before. And Allah knows best.

I say: It may be argued that the waw is extra (zā'idah), based on the evidence of Surat al-Baqarah. The waw may be added, as the poet said:

*When we passed the courtyard of the tribe and he set out (wa-intaha)...*

That is, "qad intaha" (he had set out). Another said:

*To the noble king and the son of the hero, and the lion of the battalion in the throng.*
