**Qurtubi's commentary on 2:49 (part 2)**

*Arrived before the king, the noble lord, son of the valiant one, lion of the battalion, who is abundant in generosity...*

**The eleventh issue:** Allah Most High attributes the act to the family of Pharaoh, though they were only carrying it out by His command and authority, because they undertook it themselves, and to make clear that the one who directly performs an act is held accountable for it. Al-Tabari said: This implies that whoever is ordered by a tyrant to kill someone, and the one ordered carries it out, is the one held accountable.

I say: The scholars have differed on this question in three opinions. One view holds that both are killed: the one who gave the order and the one who carried it out. This was said by al-Nakha'i, and also by al-Shafi'i and Malik, with some distinctions between them. Al-Shafi'i said: If the ruler orders a man to kill another man, and the one ordered knows that he has been ordered to kill him unjustly, then both bear the retaliation (*qawad*), as two killers together. If the ruler coerces him into it and he knows it is an unjust killing, the retaliation falls on the ruler, and regarding the one ordered there are two opinions: one says retaliation is due from him, the other says there is no retaliation on him, and he owes half the blood money (*diya*). This is related by Ibn al-Mundhir.

Our scholars (the Malikis) said: The one ordered is either someone obligated to obey the commander and fearful of his harm, such as a ruler or a master toward his slave, in which case retaliation is binding on both of them. Or he is someone not obligated to obey, in which case only the one who carried out the killing is killed, not the commander. An example of this is a father who orders his son, or a teacher who orders one of his students, or a craftsman who orders one of his apprentices, if the latter is an adult. If he is not an adult, the killing is charged to the commander, and half the blood money is owed by the child's paternal kin (*'aqila*).

Ibn Nafi said: A master is not killed if he orders his slave, even a non-Arabic speaker, to kill a person. Ibn Habib said: I say, in agreement with Ibn al-Qasim, that the killing is charged to both of them. As for ordering someone who has no fear of harm if he disobeys, this is not treated as coercion. Rather, the one ordered is killed and not the commander, and the commander is beaten and imprisoned.

Ahmad said, concerning a master who orders his slave to kill a man: the master is killed. This opinion is related from Ali ibn Abi Talib and Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with them both. Ali said: The slave is also placed in prison. Ahmad said: The slave is confined and beaten and disciplined. Al-Thawri said: The master is disciplined with a discretionary punishment (*ta'zir*). Al-Hakam and Hammad said: The slave is killed. Qatada said: Both of them are killed.

Al-Shafi'i said: If the slave is eloquent and understands, the slave is killed and the master is punished; but if the slave is non-Arabic speaking, retaliation is due from the master.

Sulayman ibn Musa said: The commander is not killed, but his hands are cut off, then he is punished and imprisoned; this is the second opinion, and the one who carried out the killing is killed for having committed it. This was also the view of Ata, al-Hakam, Hammad, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq concerning a man who orders another man to kill a man. Ibn al-Mundhir mentioned it.

Zufar said: Neither of them is killed. This is the third opinion, related by Abu al-Ma'ali in *al-Burhan*. He held that neither the commander nor the one who carries out the act is independently responsible for retaliation, and therefore neither of them is killed in his view. And Allah knows best.

**The twelfth issue:** The majority read *yudhabbihuna* (﴿they slaughter﴾) with the doubled *ba'* (*bi-l-tashdid*), to indicate intensity. Ibn Muhaysin read *yadhbahuna* with the single *ba'*. The first reading is preferred, since slaughter was repeated. According to what is related, Pharaoh had seen in a dream a fire come out of Jerusalem and burn the houses of Egypt. His dream was interpreted to mean that a child from the Children of Israel would be born and would grow up, and the ruin of his kingdom would come at his hands. Other accounts have been given, but the meanings are close.

**The thirteenth issue:** Allah's words, *wa-fi dhalikum* (﴿and in that﴾), point to the whole matter, since it is a report, and so it is like a single present thing. The meaning is: and in their doing that to you there is a *bala'*, that is, a test and trial. The word *bala'* can mean a blessing, as in the verse: ﴿and that He might test the believers with a good trial from Him﴾ (al-Anfal 8:17). Abu al-Haytham said: *al-bala'* can be good or bad, and its basic meaning is affliction. Allah tests His servant with good favour in order to examine his gratitude, and tests him with the hardship he dislikes in order to examine his patience. So *bala'* is used both for good and for bad. This was related by al-Harawi.

Some people said that the reference of *dhalikum* is to being saved (*al-tanjiya*), so that *bala'* here would mean good: your deliverance is a blessing from Allah upon you. But the majority said the reference is to the slaughter and similar acts, and *bala'* here means evil: the meaning is, in the slaughter there is hardship and trial.

Ibn Kaysan said: It is also said that for good one says *abla-hu Allah* and *balā-hu*, and he recited:

*May Allah reward with kindness what the two of them did with you, and what the best trial is, the one that tests.*

[The composer of this is Zuhayr.]

So he combined the two dialects. More commonly, for good one says *abliytuhu*, for evil *balawtuhu*, and for testing *ibtalaytuhu* or *balawtuhu*. This was said by al-Nahhas.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 50 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when We parted the sea for you and saved you﴾. "Idh" (when) is in the accusative position (mawdi' nasb). "Faraqna" means "faraqna" (We split), so each division became like a great mountain (tawd), that is, a great mountain. The root of al-farq (separation) is al-fasl (division), and from it comes "farq al-sha'r" (the parting of the hair). From it also comes al-Furqan (the Criterion), because it distinguishes (yafruqu) between truth and falsehood, that is, it separates. From it is His saying: ﴿By those who separate, separating﴾[[See vol. 19, p. 153.]] [al-Mursalat: 4], meaning the angels who descend with the distinction between truth and falsehood. From it is His saying: ﴿the Day of al-Furqan﴾[[See vol. 8, p. 20.]] [al-Anfal: 41], meaning the Day of Badr, in which there was a distinction between truth and falsehood. From it is His saying: ﴿And a Qur'an which We have divided (faraqnahu)﴾[[See vol. 10, p. 339.]] [al-Isra': 106], that is, We have made it detailed and firm. al-Zuhri read "farraqna" with a doubled ra', meaning We made it into separate parts. The meaning of "bikum" is "lakum" (for you), so the ba' has the sense of the lam. It was also said that the ba' keeps its own place, meaning We split the sea by your entering it, so that they came to be between the two waters, and the division came to be by them. This is more preferable, as shown by His saying "fa-infalaqa" (so it split).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the sea﴾. The sea (bahr) is well known and was so named for its vastness. It is said: "a horse is bahr" when it is wide in its running, that is, abundant in it. From this is the saying of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ concerning the horse of Abu Talha, which he praised: "And indeed we found it a bahr." Al-bahr is also salt water. It is said: "abhara al-ma'" (the water became salty). Nusayb said:
"The water of the earth has become bahr, so my sickness increased, until the sweet drink became salty."
Al-bahr is also a town; it is said: "This is our bahratuna," that is, our town. This was said by al-Umawi. Al-bahr is also al-sulal (a disease) which afflicts a person.[[Al-sulal (with the vowel of ghurab): an ulcer that occurs in the lung, or a cold and catarrh, or a long cough accompanied by a mild fever (from al-Qamus).]] They also say: "I met him ṣaḥra baḥra," that is, openly and exposed. In a report from Ka'b al-Ahbar, he said: "Allah has an angel called Sandafa'il; all the seas are in the hollow of his thumb." Abu Nu'aym related it from Thawr ibn Yazid, from Khalid ibn Ma'dan, from Ka'b.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and saved you﴾, that is, We brought you out of it. It is said: "najawtu min kadha najā'an" (with the long vowel) and "najāatan" (with the short vowel), and "al-sidq manjāh" (truthfulness is a means of salvation), and "anjaytu ghayri" and "najjaytuhu." It has been read with both: "wa-idh najjaynakum" and "fa-anjaynakum."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and We drowned the people of Pharaoh﴾. It is said: "gharika fi al-ma' gharaqan," so he is gharaq and also gharik. From it is the saying of Abu al-Najm:
"From among the slain and the drowned"
(The first half of the line: "So they became in the water and the trenches.")
Another person made him drown (aghraqahu), and "gharraqahu," so he is mughraq and gharīq. A "lijam mughraq bil-fidda" means ornamented with silver. Al-taghriq also means killing. al-A'sha said:
"Would that Qays had been destroyed by the midwives,"
(The one meant is Qays ibn Mas'ud al-Shaybani. The first half of the line: "Atwarin in a year of raid and journey.")
This is because the midwife used to drown the newborn in the water of the afterbirth in a year of famine, whether male or female, until it died; then every killing was called taghriq. From it is the saying of Dhu al-Rumma:
"When its ropes (arbad) drowned a camel of the second pregnancy in a desert where its orphan calf did not become a mother..."
Al-arbad are the ropes. Al-bakra is the young she-camel, and thaniyyuha is her second belly. She did not turn toward her young because of the exhaustion that had reached her.

The discussion of the scholars' disagreement about the manner of the deliverance of the Children of Israel:
Al-Tabari mentioned that Musa, peace be upon him, was revealed to set out by night from Egypt with the Children of Israel. Musa ordered them to borrow jewelry and goods from the Copts, and Allah made that lawful for the Children of Israel. So Musa traveled with them from the first part of the night, and Pharaoh was informed. He said: "None of them shall be followed until the roosters crow." But no rooster crowed that night in Egypt, and Allah caused many of the Copts' children to die that night, so they busied themselves with burial and went out in pursuit, entering at sunrise, as He said: ﴿So they pursued them at sunrise﴾[[See vol. 13, p. 105.]] [al-Shu'ara': 60]. Musa went to the side of the sea until he reached it. The number of the Children of Israel was over six hundred thousand, and the number of Pharaoh's army was one million and two hundred thousand. It was also said that Pharaoh pursued him with a million horses, apart from the females. It was also said that Isra'il, who is Ya'qub, peace be upon him, entered Egypt with seventy-six persons from his descendants and his descendants' descendants, and Allah multiplied their number and blessed their offspring, until they went out to the sea on the day of Pharaoh, and they were six hundred thousand fighting men, apart from the elders, the children and the women.

Abu Bakr Abdullah ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Shayba said: Shababa ibn Sawwar related to us, from Yunus ibn Abi Ishaq, from Abu Ishaq, from Amr ibn Maymun, from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, that when Musa, peace be upon him, set out with Isra'il, news reached Pharaoh. He ordered a sheep to be slaughtered and then said: "No, by Allah, its skinning will not be finished until six hundred thousand of the Copts have gathered for me." He said: So Musa set out until he reached the sea, and it was said to him: "Split!" The sea said to him: "You have become arrogant, O Musa! Have I ever split for any of the sons of Adam, so that I should split for you?" He said: With Musa was a man on his horse. That man said to him: "Where were you commanded, O Prophet of Allah?" He said: "I was commanded only in this direction." He said: So he urged his horse, and it swam and came out. He said: "Where were you commanded, O Prophet of Allah?" He said: "I was commanded only in this direction." He said: "By Allah, you have not lied, nor have you been lied to." Then he plunged a second time and swam with it until it came out. He said: "Where were you commanded, O Prophet of Allah?" He said: "I was commanded only in this direction." He said: "By Allah, you have not lied, nor have you been lied to." He said: Then Allah revealed to him: "Strike the sea with your staff" [al-A'raf: 160], and Musa struck it with his staff, "so it split, and each division was like a great mountain" [al-Shu'ara': 63]. There were twelve divisions for the twelve tribes, and for each tribe there was a path where they could see one another. This was because the mountains of water became like openings and windows through which some could see others. When the companions of Musa came out and the companions of Pharaoh stood up, the sea closed over them and drowned them. It is mentioned that the sea was the Sea of al-Qulzum, and that the man who was with Musa on the horse was his servant Yusha' ibn Nun. And that Allah the Exalted revealed to the sea: "Split for Musa when he strikes you." So the sea was agitated that night, and when morning came he struck the sea, and called it (Abu Khalid). Ibn Abi Shayba also mentioned this. The exegetes have said a great deal in narrating the stories on this matter, and what we have mentioned is sufficient, and more explanation will come, if Allah wills, in the surahs of Yunus and al-Shu'ara'[[See vol. 8, p. 377 and vol. 12, p. 105.]].

Section: Allah mentioned the deliverance and the drowning, and did not mention the day on which that happened.
Muslim related from Ibn Abbas that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to Madinah and found the Jews fasting on the day of Ashura. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to them: "What is this day that you fast?" They said: "This is a great day, on which Allah saved Musa and his people and drowned Pharaoh and his people, so Musa fasted it in gratitude, and we fast it." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "We have more right and are closer to Musa than you." So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ fasted it and commanded its fasting. Al-Bukhari also related it from Ibn Abbas, that the Prophet ﷺ said to his companions: "You have more right to Musa than they do, so fast."

Issue [on fasting the day of Ashura]
The apparent meaning of these hadiths indicates that the Prophet ﷺ fasted Ashura and commanded its fasting only in imitation of Musa, peace be upon him, as the Jews reported. This is not so, because of what A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, related: she said: "The day of Ashura was a day that Quraysh used to fast in the Jahiliyya, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to fast it in the Jahiliyya. When he came to Madinah, he fasted it and commanded its fasting. When Ramadan was made obligatory, he abandoned the fasting of the day of Ashura, so whoever wished fasted it and whoever wished left it." Related by al-Bukhari and Muslim. If it is said: it is possible that Quraysh fasted it only by the report of the Jews to them, because they used to hear from them, since they were people of knowledge among them; so the Prophet, peace be upon him, fasted it likewise in the Jahiliyya, that is, in Makkah. When he came to Madinah and found the Jews fasting it, he said: "We have more right and are closer to Musa than you," so he fasted it in following Musa, "and commanded its fasting," that is, he made it obligatory and emphasized his command, until the young ones were fasting it. We say: this is the doubt of those who say that the Prophet ﷺ was perhaps worshipping according to the law of Musa; and that is not so, as will be explained in al-An'am, at the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So follow their guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 90][[See vol. 7, p. 35.]].

Issue: There is disagreement about the day of Ashura, whether it is the ninth or the tenth of Muharram.
Al-Shafi'i held that it is the ninth, based on the hadith of al-Hakam ibn al-A'raj, who said: "I came to Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, while he was resting his cloak under Zamzam, and I said to him: 'Inform me about fasting Ashura.' He said: 'When you see the crescent of Muharram, count, and on the morning of the ninth be fasting.' I said: 'Did Muhammad ﷺ fast it like this?' He said: 'Yes.'" Muslim related it. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan al-Basri, Malik, and a group of the early generation held that it is the tenth. al-Tirmidhi mentioned the hadith of al-Hakam without describing it as sahih or hasan, then followed it with: "Qutayba informed us, 'Abd al-Warith informed us, from Yunus, from al-Hasan, from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded the fasting of Ashura on the tenth day." Abu Isa said: The hadith of Ibn Abbas is hasan sahih. al-Tirmidhi said: It is also related from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Fast the ninth and the tenth, and oppose the Jews." Al-Shafi'i, Ahmad ibn Hanbal and Ishaq follow this hadith. Others said: Ibn Abbas's words to the questioner, "count, and on the morning of the ninth be fasting," contain no evidence for abandoning the fasting of the tenth; rather, he promised to fast the ninth in addition to the tenth. They said: fasting both days is a combination of the hadiths. As for Ibn Abbas's words to al-Hakam when he said: "Did Muhammad ﷺ fast it like this?" and he answered "Yes," the meaning is: had he lived. Otherwise the Prophet ﷺ never fasted the ninth. This is clarified by what Ibn Majah related in his Sunan and Muslim in his Sahih, from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "If I live until next year, I will certainly fast the ninth day."

Virtue
- Abu Qatada related that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Fasting the day of Ashura, I hope from Allah that it will expiate the year before it." Related by Muslim and al-Tirmidhi. Al-Tirmidhi said: "We do not know of any report saying 'the fasting of the day of Ashura is an expiation for a year' except the hadith of Abu Qatada."

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 50 (part 2 of 2):**

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and you are watching﴾, is a clause in the accusative of circumstance (*jumlah fi mawdi' al-hal*, a clause functioning as a circumstantial qualifier). Its meaning is "with your eyes." It is said that the family of Pharaoh floated on the water, and they [the Children of Israel] looked at them drowning while they looked at themselves being saved. In this there is the greatest favour. It has also been said that they were brought out for them until they saw them, so this is one favour after another. It has been said that the meaning of "and you are watching" is: with your insight, through reflection (*al-i'tibar*, taking a lesson), because they were preoccupied and did not stand and look with their eyes. It has also been said that the meaning is: "and you are in the state of one who is watching, were he to look," just as you say, "this matter is before you in sight and hearing," meaning you are in a state where you can see it and hear it if you wish.

This view and the first are more fitting to the conditions of the Children of Israel, because of their continued failure to take lessons after they came out of the sea. When God rescued them and drowned their enemy, they said: "O Musa, our hearts are not at rest. Pharaoh has drowned!" until God commanded the sea and it cast him up, and they looked at him.

Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah reported from Qays ibn 'Abbad that the Children of Israel said: "Pharaoh has not died, and he would never die!" He said: When God heard their denial, He sent His Prophet, peace be upon him, and cast him onto the shore of the sea like a red bull, which the Children of Israel gazed upon. When they were reassured and sent out by land toward the cities of Pharaoh, until they carried off his treasures and became immersed in bounty, they saw a people devoted to their idols. They said: "O Musa, make for us a god just as they have gods!" Musa rebuked them and said: ﴿Shall I seek for you a god other than God, when He has favoured you over the worlds?﴾ That is, the worlds of his time.

Then He commanded them to travel to the Holy Land, which had been the dwelling of their forefathers, and to cleanse themselves from the land of Pharaoh. The Holy Land was in the hands of the tyrants (*al-jabbarin*), who had overcome them there, so they needed to repel them by fighting. They said: "Do you want to make us prey for the tyrants? It would have been better for us if you had left us in the hand of Pharaoh!" He said: ﴿O my people, enter the Holy Land which God has prescribed for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 21], up to His saying "sitting [here]," until he invoked curses upon them and named them "the defiant." So they wandered in the desert (*al-tih*) for forty years as a punishment. Then He had mercy on them and bestowed upon them the quail and the manna and the clouds (for shade), as will be explained. Then Musa went to Mount Sinai to bring them the Torah, and they took the calf for worship, as will be explained [see vol. 7, p. 273]. Then it was said to them: "You have reached Jerusalem, so enter the gate prostrating and say *hittah* (forgiveness)," as will come.

Musa, peace be upon him, was extremely shy and modest. They said: "He has a hernia (*adar*)." [Al-Adrah (with a dammah): a swelling of the testicle.] When he bathed, he placed his garment on a rock, and the rock ran off with his garment to the gatherings of the Children of Israel, while Musa followed after it, naked, saying: "O rock, my garment!" This is the meaning of God's saying: ﴿O you who believe, do not be like those who hurt Musa; then God cleared him of what they said﴾ [al-Ahzab: 69], as will be explained [see vol. 14, p. 250].

Then, when Harun died, they said to him: "You killed Harun and envied him," until the angels carried his bier while Harun was dead upon it. [This will come in al-Ma'idah; see vol. 6, p. 130.] Then they asked him to show them a sign of the acceptance of their offerings, so a fire would come down from heaven and accept their offerings. Then they asked him: "Explain to us the expiations for our sins in this world." So whoever committed a sin would find written at his door: "You did such-and-such, and its expiation is the cutting off of one of your limbs," and he would name it to him. And whoever was splashed with urine would not be purified until he cut it off and removed the skin from his body.

Then they altered the Torah, forged lies against God, wrote with their own hands, and sold it for a small price. Their affair then reached the point where they killed their prophets and messengers.

Such was their dealing with their Lord, their conduct in their religion, and their bad character. The explanation of each of these matters will come in full in its proper place, if God the Exalted wills. Al-Tabari said: The reporting of the Qur'an through the tongue of Muhammad, peace be upon him, of these unseen matters, which were not part of the knowledge of the Arabs and had only occurred to the Children of Israel, is a clear proof for the Children of Israel, standing against them, of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 51:

There are six issues in this verse.

The first concerns the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And when We made an appointment with Moses for forty nights﴾. Abu 'Amr recited "wa'adna" (We promised) without an alif. Abu 'Ubayd chose this reading, preferred it, and rejected "wa'adna" (We made an appointment, with an alif). He said: "Mutual promising (al-muwa'ada) occurs only among humans. As for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, He alone is the one who promises and threatens. On this basis we find the Qur'an, such as His saying, Mighty and Majestic: 'He promised you a promise of truth' (Ibrahim: 22), and His saying: 'Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds' (al-Fath: 29), and His saying: ﴿And when Allah promised you one of the two groups, that it would be yours﴾ (al-Anfal: 7)." Makki said: "Also, the apparent meaning of the wording is a promise from Allah, the Exalted, to Moses, and there is no promise from Moses in it. Therefore it must be understood as one-sided, in accordance with the apparent text that the action is attributed to Allah alone. This is the reading of al-Hasan, Abu Ra'ja, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, and 'Isa ibn 'Umar, and Qatada and Ibn Abi Ishaq also recited thus." Abu Hatim said: "The common reading among us is 'wa'adna' without an alif, because mutual promising occurs mostly between created beings who are equal, each of whom promises the other." Al-Jawhari said: "al-Mi'ad: the promising, the time, and the place." Makki said: "Al-muwa'ada originally comes from two parties, but the form mufa'ala (of the pattern 'fa'ala') may come from one party in the speech of the Arabs. They said: 'tarraqtu al-na'l' (I resoled the sandal), 'dawaytu al-'alil' (I treated the sick person), and ''aqabtu al-lis' (I punished the thief), and the verb is from one party. Thus the word al-muwa'ada from Allah is specifically for Moses, like the meaning of 'wa'adna,' so both readings have one meaning." The reading "wa'ada" with an alif is valid because it has the meaning of "wa'adna" in one of its senses, and because Moses necessarily had to make a promise or an acceptance that takes the place of a promise, so the mufa'ala form is correct. Al-Nahhas said: "The reading 'wa'ada' with an alif is better and finer. It is the reading of Mujahid, al-A'raj, Ibn Kathir, Nafi', al-A'mash, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i. The words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, 'Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds' are not part of this at all, because 'wa'adna Musa' belongs to the category of al-muwafat (meeting at an appointed time), and this is not part of promising and threatening at all. It comes from your saying: 'mai'aduka yawm al-jum'a' (your appointment is on Friday) and 'mai'aduka maw'i' kadha' (your appointment is at such-and-such place). The correct usage in this regard is to say 'wa'adtuhu' (I made an appointment with him)." Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: "'Wa'ada' here with an alif is good, because obedience in acceptance is equivalent to mutual promising. From Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, there is a promise; from Moses there is acceptance and following, which operates in the manner of mutual promising." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Abu 'Ubayda preferred 'wa'adna,' and this is not correct, because Moses's acceptance of Allah's promise, his commitment to it, and his waiting for it resembles mutual promising."

The second issue concerns the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Musa (Moses)﴾. Musa is a non-Arabic name, not declinable because of its foreignness (al-'ujma) and its definiteness (al-ta'rif). According to what is related, the Copts used to call water "mu" and trees "sha" [[This is as in some copies of the original; in others it reads "sa" with an unpointed sin. In the Qamus and its commentary: "... sa al-shajar" as in all copies, but Ibn al-Jawaliqi said it is with a dotted shin.]]. When Moses was found in the chest near water and trees, he was named Musa. Al-Suddi said: "When his mother feared for him, she placed him in the chest and cast him into the river, as Allah had revealed to her. She cast him into the river among trees near Pharaoh's house. The female servants of Asiya, the wife of Pharaoh, came out to bathe, and they found him, so he was named after the place." Al-Naqqash and others mentioned that the name of the one who picked him up was Sabuth. Ibn Ishaq said: "Musa is Musa son of 'Imran, son of Yash-har, son of Qahath, son of Lawi, son of Ya'qub, Israel of Allah [[Thus in the originals, and the name of Allah is an addition; it is not unlikely that the original reads 'Abd Allah, which is the meaning of Israel. See p. 331 of this part.]], son of Ishaq, son of Ibrahim, peace be upon him."

The third issue concerns the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿forty nights﴾. "Arba'in" (forty) is in the accusative as the second object, and there is an ellipsis in the sentence. Al-Akhfash said: "The estimate is: 'And when We made an appointment with Moses for the completion of forty nights,' as He said: 'And ask the town' (Yusuf: 82). All the forty are included in the appointment." According to the view of most of the exegetes, the forty are Dhu al-Qa'da and ten days of Dhu al-Hijja. This took place after he had crossed the sea and his people had asked him to bring them a Book from Allah. So he went out to Mount Sinai (al-Tur) with seventy of the best of the Children of Israel, and they climbed the mountain. He made an appointment with them for the completion of forty nights. According to what the exegetes mentioned, they counted twenty days and twenty nights, and they said: "He has broken his appointment with us." So they made the calf, and al-Samiri said to them: "This is your god and the god of Moses." They were reassured by his words. Harun forbade them and said: "O my people, you are only being tested by it, and your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my command." They said: "We will not cease to be devoted to it until Moses returns to us" (Ta-Ha: 90). Harun was not followed, and only twelve thousand obeyed him in abandoning the worship of the calf, as is related in the report. The rest of them, who were more than two million, rushed to worship it. When Moses returned and found them in that condition, he threw down the Tablets, and six parts of them were lifted up, and one part remained, which contained the lawful and the unlawful and what they needed. He burned the calf and scattered its ashes into the sea, and they drank from its water out of love for the calf, so a yellowness appeared on their lips and their bellies swelled. Then they repented, but their repentance was not accepted unless they killed themselves. This is the meaning of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So turn in repentance to your Creator and kill yourselves﴾ (al-Baqara: 54). They took up daggers and swords, some against others, from the rising of the sun until the height of the forenoon. They killed one another, and no parent would ask about his child, nor child about his parent, nor brother about his brother, nor one person about another. Everyone who met another struck him with the sword, and the other struck him with the same, until Moses cried out to Allah, shouting: "O my Lord, the Children of Israel have been destroyed!" Allah had mercy on them and bestowed His favor upon them, accepted the repentance of those who remained, and counted those who were killed among the martyrs, as will come.

The fourth issue: If it is said, "Why did He single out the nights for mention and not the days?" it is answered: Because the night precedes the day in rank, and so it comes before it, and for this reason dating is done by it. Thus the nights are the beginning of the months, and the days follow them.

The fifth issue: Al-Naqqash said: "In this verse there is an indication of the connection to fasting, because if He had mentioned the days, it would have been possible to believe that he used to break his fast at night. When He specified the nights, the strength of the speech required that he, peace be upon him, continued (wisal) for forty days with their nights." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "I heard my father say: I heard the ascetic shaykh, the imam and preacher Abu al-Fadl al-Jawhari, may Allah have mercy on him, admonishing people about seclusion with Allah and drawing near to Him in prayer and the like, and that this occupies one from every food and drink. He would say: 'Where is the state of Moses in nearness to Allah, and his continuing (wisal) for eighty days, when he said to his young man, in part of a day, "Bring us our morning meal" (al-Kahf: 62)?'" I say: Scholars of the Sufis have used this as evidence for wisal, and that its best form is forty days. The discussion of wisal will come in the verses on fasting in this surah, if Allah wills. In "al-A'raf" there will come additional rulings for this verse at His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We made an appointment with Moses for thirty nights﴾ (al-A'raf: 142). The story of the calf will come with an explanation of its manner and its lowing, and in "Ta-Ha," if Allah wills.

The sixth issue concerns the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Then you took the calf after him﴾. That is, you took it as a god after Moses. The original of "ittakhadhtum" is "i'takhadhtum," from "al-akhdh" (taking), and its pattern is "if'talatum." The second hamza was softened because two hamzas cannot be together, so it became "ittakhadhtum." The yā' fluctuated in conjugation: it came as an alif in "yattakhidhu" and as a wāw in "mu'takhidh," so it was replaced by a firm letter of the same kind as what follows it, which is the tā', and they were assimilated. Then the alif of connection (hamzat al-wasl) was brought in for pronunciation. It may be dispensed with when the meaning of the speech is affirmation (taqrir), as in His saying: ﴿Say: Have you taken a covenant with Allah?﴾ (al-Baqara: 80). Here it dispensed with the alif of connection by the alif of affirmation. The poet said: [[This is Dhu al-Rumma.]]

"Has the caravan newly received news from their companions,
or has the heart returned to its longing from its yearnings?"

Similar to this in the Qur'an are: ﴿Has he looked into the unseen?﴾ (Maryam: 78); ﴿Has He chosen daughters?﴾ (al-Saffat: 153); ﴿Have you grown arrogant, or have you been...?﴾ (Sad: 75). The view of Abu 'Ali al-Farisi is that "ittakhadhtum" is from "takhidha," which is from "akhadha."

"And you are wrongdoers" (wa antum zalimun) is a clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal). The meaning of injustice (zulm) has already been mentioned [[See p. 309.]]. And praise be to Allah.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 52:

There are four issues in it.

The first concerns His saying, ﴿Then We pardoned you﴾. *Al-'afw* (pardon) is God's pardon of His creation. It may come after punishment and before it, unlike *al-ghufran* (forgiveness), which never comes together with any punishment at all. Everyone who deserved punishment and was spared it has been pardoned. So *al-'afw* means the erasing of a sin: "We erased your sins and overlooked you." It is derived from your saying, "The wind effaced (*'afat*) the trace," meaning it removed it. And *'afa al-shay'* means "the thing increased." This is one of the words with opposite meanings (*al-adda'*). From the same root is His saying, ﴿until they multiplied﴾ [al-A'raf: 95].

The second issue concerns His saying, ﴿after that﴾, meaning after your worship of the calf. The calf was named *'ijl* because of their haste (*isti'jal*) in worshipping it, and God knows best. *Al-'ijl* is the young of a cow. *Al-'ijjul* is the same, its plural is *al-'ajajil*, and its feminine is *'ijlah*. This is related from Abu al-Jarrah.

The third issue concerns His saying, ﴿so that you may give thanks﴾, meaning that you may thank God for His pardon of you. The meaning of *la'alla* has already been mentioned (see p. 227 of this volume). As for *al-shukr* (gratitude), linguistically it means "manifestation," from the saying "a beast is *shakur* when the fat appears on it beyond what it is given as fodder." Its true meaning is praising a person for a kindness he has bestowed, as was mentioned in the Fatihah (see p. 133 of this volume). Al-Jawhari said: *Al-shukr* is praising the benefactor for the good he has bestowed upon you. One says *shakartuhu* and *shakartu lahu*, and with the preposition *lam* is more eloquent. *Al-shukran* is the opposite of *al-kufran* (ingratitude). *Tashakkartu lahu* is like *shakartu lahu*.

Al-Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud related from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "One who does not thank people does not thank God." Al-Khattabi said: This statement may be interpreted in two ways. The first is that whoever is naturally inclined to deny the favours of people and to neglect thanking them for their kindness is also inclined to deny the favours of God, the Mighty and Majestic, and to neglect thanking Him. The second is that God, glorified is He, does not accept the thanks of a servant for His kindness to him if the servant does not thank people for their kindness to him and denies their goodness, because the two matters are connected to one another.

The fourth issue concerns the statements of the scholars on the meaning of gratitude. Sahl ibn Abd Allah said: Gratitude is striving to exert obedience together with avoiding disobedience, in secret and in public. Another group said: Gratitude is the acknowledgement of one's shortcoming in thanking the Benefactor. For this reason God said, ﴿Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude﴾ [Saba': 13]. Dawud said: "How can I thank You, my Lord, when gratitude itself is a favour from You?" He said: "Now you have known Me, and you have thanked Me, since you have known that gratitude from you is a favour from Me." Dawud said: "My Lord, show me Your most hidden favour upon me." He said: "O Dawud, breathe." Dawud breathed, and God, exalted is He, said: "Who can count this favour, night and day?"

Musa, peace be upon him, said: "How can I thank You, when the smallest of Your favours that You placed in my hand cannot be repaid by all my deeds?" God revealed to him: "O Musa, now you have thanked Me."

Al-Junayd said: The reality of gratitude is the inability to thank. He also said: I was in the presence of al-Sari al-Saqati, playing, and I was seven years old, while before him was a group speaking about gratitude. He said to me: "O boy, what is gratitude?" I said: "That God not be disobeyed with His favours." He said to me: "I fear that your share from God is your tongue." Al-Junayd said: I have never stopped weeping over this word that al-Sari said to me.

Al-Shibli said: Gratitude is humility, guarding good deeds, opposing desires, exerting obedience, and being mindful of the Tyrant of the earth and the heavens.

Dhu al-Nun al-Misri, Abu al-Fayd, said: Gratitude toward one above you is obedience, toward your equal is reciprocation, and toward one below you is kindness and generosity.

"Idha" is a noun for past time, and "idha" is a noun for future time, and "atayna" means "We gave." All of this has already been mentioned [see pp. 261 and 343]. "Al-Kitab" is the Torah, by the consensus of the commentators (al-mu'awwilin). Scholars differed regarding "al-Furqan." Al-Farra' and Qutrub said: the meaning is "We gave Musa the Torah and Muhammad (ﷺ) the Furqan." Al-Nahhas said: this is an error of grammar (khata' al-i'rab), and as for the meaning: as for the grammar, what is conjoined (al-ma'tuf) to a thing is like it, and according to this view the conjoined would be the opposite of the thing it is conjoined to. As for the meaning, He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We certainly gave Musa and Harun the Furqan﴾ [al-Anbiya: 48]. Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: al-Furqan may be al-Kitab, mentioned again by another name for emphasis. It is related from al-Farra', and from it is the saying of the poet:

"And she cut the hide for her two wrists..., and she found her saying to be a lie and a falsehood" [The well-known version of the verse is "faqaddat al-adim" and it is by 'Adi ibn Zayd. al-qadd: cutting. al-adim: hide. al-rahshan: two veins in the inner part of the forearm.]

And another [poet, he is al-Hutay'a], said:

"Ah, how lovely is Hind, and a land in which is Hind... and Hind, distance and remoteness have come between her and it."

So "al-bu'd" (remoteness) is conjoined to "al-na'y" (distance), and "al-myn" (falsehood) to "al-kadhib" (lie), because the two wordings differ, for emphasis. From it is the saying of 'Antara:

"Greetings to a ruin whose traces have long aged, which has grown desolate and emptied after Umm al-Haytham."

Al-Nahhas said: this only occurs in poetry. The best that has been said about this is the view of Mujahid: "a distinction (furqan) between truth and falsehood," i.e., that which He taught him. Ibn Zayd said: al-Furqan is the splitting of the sea for him until it became separate parts (firaq), so they crossed. It was also said: al-Furqan is relief (faraj) from distress, because they were enslaved with the Copts; and from it is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿If you fear Allah, He will grant you a furqan﴾ [al-Anfal: 29], i.e., relief and a way out. It was also said: it is the proof and the clarification (al-hujjah wa al-bayan), said by Ibn Bahr. It was also said: the waw is redundant (silah), and the meaning is "We gave Musa the Book, the Furqan," and the waw may be added in descriptive phrases, as when they say "So-and-so is handsome and tall." And he recited:

"To the mighty king and the son of the lofty one... and the lion of the battalion in the crowd."

He meant "to the mighty king, the son of the lofty one, the lion of the battalion." The evidence for this interpretation is His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿Then We gave Musa the Book, completing it upon the one who did well, and a detailed explanation of all things﴾ [al-An'am: 154], i.e., it clarified the lawful and unlawful, disbelief and faith, promise and threat, and other things. It was also said: al-Furqan is the distinction between them and the people of Fir'awn: He saved these and drowned those. A parallel is His saying: "the Day of the Furqan" (yawm al-furqan). It was said: it refers to the Day of Badr, in which Allah granted victory to Muhammad (ﷺ) and his companions and destroyed Abu Jahl and his companions.

(La'allakum tahtadun) so that you may be guided (li-kay tahtadu) from misguidance, and this has been mentioned before [see p. 160 of this part].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 54:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Moses said to his people﴾. Al-qawm (the people) means the men, to the exclusion of the women. Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Let not a people ridicule another people﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11], then He said: ﴿nor let women ridicule other women﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11]. Zuhayr said:

Wa ma adri wa sawfa ukhalu adri... aqawmun Al Hisn am nisa'u
(I do not know, and I will suppose I know... are the Al Hisn a people or women?)

And Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And Lot, when he said to his people﴾ [al-A'raf: 80], meaning the men to the exclusion of the women. The word qawm may also apply to both men and women, as Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Indeed, We sent Noah to his people﴾ [Nuh: 1]. Likewise, every prophet was sent to both women and men together.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O my people﴾ is a vocative construction (munada mudaf), and the yaʾ (ي) in "ya qawmi" is omitted because it is a place of omission, and the kasra indicates it, and it is in the position of tanwin, so you omit it just as you omit tanwin from the singular. Outside the Qur'an it is permissible to affirm it as sakin, so you say ya qawmi, because it is a noun and it is in a position of jarr. If you wish, you may make it fatha; if you wish, you may add a ha' with it, so you say ya qawmiyah. If you wish, you may replace it with an alif, because it is lighter, so you say ya qawma. If you wish, you say ya qawmu, meaning ya ayyuha al-qawm (O you people). If you make them indefinite, you put them in the accusative and add tanwin, and the singular of qawm is imru' according to a non-literal form. You say qawmun, aqwamun, and aqawimu, the plural of the plural.

Here, by al-qawm is meant the worshippers of the calf, and his addressing them, peace be upon him, was by command from Allah, exalted is He.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed you have wronged yourselves﴾. He dispensed with the small plural in favour of the large one, and the large plural is nufus (souls). The large plural may be placed in the position of the small plural, and the small in the position of the large. Allah, exalted is He, says: "three periods" [al-Baqarah: 228], and He says: ﴿and therein is what the souls desire﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 71]. It is said to everyone who does an act whose harm returns upon him: "You have only harmed yourself." The root meaning of zulm (wrongdoing) is placing a thing in other than its proper place. Then He, exalted is He, said: (by your taking the calf), some scholars of meanings said: the calf of every person is his own self, so whoever abandons it and opposes its desire has been cleared of his wrongdoing. The correct view is that here it is a calf in the literal sense, which they worshipped, as the revelation has stated, and praise be to Allah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So turn in repentance to your Creator﴾. When He said to them: "So turn in repentance to your Creator," they said: "How?" He said: "Then kill yourselves." The people of inner insight said: subdue them with acts of obedience and restrain them from desires. The correct view is that "kill" is here literal. Qatl (killing) is the extinguishing of movement. And "I killed the wine" means I broke its strength with water. Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: repentance is a blessing from Allah, which Allah bestowed upon this community alone, to the exclusion of other nations, and the repentance of the Children of Israel was killing. They agreed that not every one of the calf-worshippers was commanded to kill himself with his own hand. Al-Zuhri said: when it was said to them, "So turn in repentance to your Creator and kill yourselves," they stood in two rows, and some of them killed others until it was said to them, "Stop." That was a martyrdom for the slain and a repentance for the living, as has been mentioned. Some of the exegetes said: Allah sent darkness upon them, and they did that. It is also said: those who worshipped the calf stood in a row, and those who had not worshipped it entered upon them with weapons and killed them. It is also said: the seventy who were with Moses stood up, and those who had not worshipped the calf killed those who had worshipped it. It is reported that Yusha' ibn Nun went out to them while they were sitting with their knees drawn up, and said: "Cursed is whoever unfastens his sitting-position, or extends his gaze toward his killer, or wards him off with a hand or a foot." None of them unfastened his sitting-position until those among them who were to be killed were killed, and each man began to kill the one next to him. This was related by al-Nahhas and others. The reason those who had not worshipped the calf were punished by killing themselves, according to the first view, is that they did not change the wrong when they worshipped it, but merely withdrew, whereas it was obligatory upon them to fight those who worshipped it. This is the way of Allah with His servants: when wrongdoing spreads and is not changed, all are punished. Jarir narrated, saying: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no people among whom sins are committed while they are more powerful and more able to prevent them, yet they do not change them, but that Allah will surely encompass them with punishment." Ibn Majah recorded it in his Sunan. The discussion of this meaning will come later, if Allah wills. When killing intensified among them and reached seventy thousand, Allah pardoned them, as said by Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both. Allah lifted the killing from them only because they had exerted their utmost effort in killing themselves. No blessing after Islam has been bestowed upon this community that is greater than repentance.

Qatada recited: ﴿fa-aqilu anfusakum﴾, from iqalah (pardon), meaning: receive them from their stumbling by killing.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Bari'akum﴾. Al-Bari' is the Creator, and there is a difference between them: al-Bari' is the one who originates and brings into being, while al-Khaliq is the one who determines and transfers from one state to another. Al-bariyyah means creation, and it is on the pattern fa'ila in the sense of maf'ula, except that it is not hamzated. Abu 'Amr recited "bari'kum" with a sukun on the hamza, and "yush'irkum," "yansurkum," and "ya'murkum." The grammarians differed on this. Some of them allow the sukun of the damma and the kasra in connected speech, but that is in poetry. Abu al-'Abbas al-Mubarrad said: the sukun is not permissible with the succession of vowels on the letter of i'rab, in speech or in poetry, and Abu 'Amr's recitation is a grammatical error (lahn). Al-Nahhas and others said: the early, leading grammarians permitted this, and they quoted:

Idha i'wajajna qultu sahibq qawwimi... bil-dawwi amthala al-safini al-‘awwami
(When they become crooked, I say: "Companion, straighten them," in the desert, like ships that sail.)

And Imru' al-Qays said:

Fa-al-yawma ashrab ghayra mustahqibin... ithman min Allahi wa la wa'ili
(So today I drink, not earning sin from Allah, nor as an uninvited guest.)

And another said:

Qalat Sulayma ishtir lana sawiqan
(Sulayma said: "Buy us some sawiq.")

And the other said:

Ruhti wa fi rijlayki ma fihima... wa qad bada hanikki min al-mi'zari
(You went out, and in your two feet is what is in them, and your thigh has appeared from the wrapper.)

Whoever denies the sukun on the letter of i'rab argues that this is not permissible, since it is the sign of i'rab. Abu 'Ali said: as for the vowel of construction (bina'), the grammarians have not differed about permitting its sukun with the succession of vowels. The root of bara' derives from tabarra'a al-shay' min al-shay', meaning its separation from it. So created beings have been separated from non-existence into existence, and from it comes bara'tu min al-maradh bara'an (with fatha), as the people of the Hijaz say; others say bari'tu min al-maradh bur'an (with damma). And bari'tu minka wa min al-duyun wa al-'uyub bara'atan, and from it is al-mubara'ah of a woman, and he mutually disowned his partner and his wife.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then He turned to you in forgiveness﴾. There is an omission in the speech; its estimate is: "so you did it, and then He turned to you," meaning He overlooked you, that is, toward those of you who remained.

(Indeed He is the Oft-Returning, the Most Merciful.) Its meaning has already been mentioned, and praise be to Allah.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 55–56:

There are five issues in this.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, (وَإِذْ قُلْتُمْ) "And when you said," is conjoined to "O Musa" (a single vocative). "Lan nu'mina laka" means: we will not believe you, that is, we will not accept you as truthful, "hatta nara Allaha jahrah" ("until we see God openly"). It is said: they were the seventy whom Musa chose. That was because, when he made them hear the speech of God, the Exalted, they said to him afterwards, ﴿We will not believe you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 55]. Belief in the prophets is obligatory after their miracles become manifest. So God sent down upon them fire from the sky, and it burned them. Then Musa called upon his Lord, and He brought them back to life, as the Exalted said, ﴿Then We raised you up after your death﴾ [al-Baqarah: 56]. The story of the seventy will come in al-A'raf, God willing [see vol. 7, p. 294]. Ibn Fawrak said: it is possible that their punishment was for their pursuing the request for vision by way of their saying to Musa, ﴿Show us God openly﴾ [al-Nisa': 153], and that was not within Musa's power, peace be upon him. There has been disagreement concerning the permissibility of seeing God, the Exalted. Most of the innovators (ahl al-bid'ah) deny it, both in this world and in the Hereafter. The People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) and the early generations (al-Salaf) hold that it is permissible in both and that it will occur in the Hereafter. Accordingly, they did not ask for something impossible, and Musa, peace be upon him, asked for it. The discussion of vision will come in al-An'am and al-A'raf, God willing [see vol. 7, p. 54 and p. 278].

The second: His saying, the Exalted, ﴿jahrah﴾ is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal), and its meaning is openly/manifestly; it is said: face to face ( 'iyanan), as Ibn 'Abbas said. The root of al-jahr is manifestation, and from it comes reciting aloud (al-jahr bil-qira'ah), which is only making it manifest. Al-mujaharah bil-ma'asi (openly flaunting sins) is displaying them. And "ra'aytu al-amir jiharan wa jahrah" means: I saw the ruler openly, not concealed by anything. Ibn 'Abbas read "jahrah" with a fatha on the ha', and both are dialectal forms, like zahrah and zahrah. There are two views regarding jahrah: first, that it is a qualifier of their address to Musa, that they addressed him openly and publicly, in which case there is inversion in the sentence, and the sense is: "And when you said, openly, O Musa." Second, that it is a qualifier of what they asked of him, namely that they see God openly and face to face, in which case the sentence follows its natural order without any inversion. It was emphasized with "jahr" to distinguish direct vision from vision in a dream.

The third: His saying, the Exalted, ﴿So the thunderbolt seized you﴾. The meaning of al-sa'iqah has already been mentioned at the beginning of the surah [see p. 219 of this part]. 'Umar, 'Uthman and 'Ali read "al-si'qah" (aṣ-ṣa'qah), and this is the reading of Ibn Muhaysin throughout the Qur'an.

(وَأَنْتُمْ تَنْظُرُونَ) "while you were looking" is a clause in the position of a circumstantial qualifier. It is asked: how could they die while they were looking? The answer is that the Arabs say: "the houses of the family of so-and-so face (tara'a) one another," that is, some of them face others. It is also said the meaning is "you were looking" at your own condition and at what befell you of death and the traces of the thunderbolt.

The fourth: His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Then We raised you up after your death﴾, that is, We revived you. Qatadah said: they died and their spirits departed, then they were returned so that their appointed terms might be fulfilled. Al-Nahhas said: this is an argument against those of Quraysh who did not believe in resurrection, and an argument against the People of the Book, since they were informed of this; the meaning is "so that you might give thanks" for what was done to you, namely resurrection after death. It is also said that they died a death of destruction (hamud) from which others might take warning, and then they were sent back. The original meaning of al-ba'th is sending. It is also said: rather, its origin is stirring a thing from its place; it is said: "I ba'athtu the she-camel," meaning I stirred her up, i.e., I set her in motion. Imru' al-Qays said:

"And young men of truth whom I roused at dawn ... they all rose together, some staggering and some drunken."

And 'Antarah said:

"And companions with proud noses, whom I roused at night, when sleep had inclined upon their necks."

Some have said that ﴿We raised you up after your death﴾ means: We taught you after your ignorance. I say: the first is more sound, because the basic meaning is the literal one, and it was a death of punishment. From it is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Did you not see those who went out from their homes, while they were thousands, fearing death? Then God said to them, "Die," then He revived them﴾ as will come [see vol. 3, p. 230] [al-Baqarah: 243].

The fifth: Al-Mawardi said: there is disagreement concerning whether the obligation (taklif) continues for one who is restored after his death and after witnessing the compelling states that make knowledge necessary, on two views. One: their obligation continues, so that no intelligent person is free of worship. The second: their obligation falls, the basis being inference rather than compulsion. I say: the first is more sound, for the Children of Israel saw the mountain suspended in the air above them and the fire surrounding them, and that compelled them to belief, and the obligation remained established upon them; the people of Yunus are similar. And it is impossible that they were not obligated. And God knows best.

There are eight issues in this verse.

The first issue concerns His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds﴾. That is, We made it over you like a canopy (*zullah*). *Al-ghamam* is the plural of *ghamamah*, like *sahabah* and *sahab*, as said by al-Akhfash Sa'id. Al-Farra' said: It is also permissible to say *ghama'im*, and it means clouds, because they cover (*taghumm*) the sky, that is, they conceal it, and everything that is covered is *maghmum* (covered over), and from this comes *al-maghmum 'ala 'aqlihi* (the one whose mind is clouded). And the moon is *ghumma* when the cloud covers it. *Al-ghayn* is like *al-ghaym* (cloud), and from it is his saying, peace be upon him: "Indeed, it is covered over (*layughana*) upon my heart." Sahib al-'Ayn said: *Ghiyna 'alayhi* means it was covered over. *Al-ghayn* is a dense tree. Al-Suddi said: *al-ghamam* is the white cloud.

He did this for them so that it would shield them from the heat of the sun by day, and it would clear toward its end so that they could be illuminated by the moon at night. The commentators mention that this happened in the wilderness of wandering (*al-tih*) between Egypt and Syria, when they refused to enter the city of the tyrants (*al-jabbarin*) and fight them, and they said to Musa: ﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 24]. [[See vol. 6, p. 128.]] So they were punished in that wide open plain (*al-fahs*) [[Al-fahs: every place that is inhabited (sakan). In the hadith of Ka'b: "Indeed Allah blessed Syria and singled out for sanctity the plain (fahs) from the Jordan to Rafah..." Its fahs is what has been spread out and uncovered of its regions. (From al-Qamus and al-Nihayah.)]] for forty years, wandering within a distance of five or six farsakh. It is narrated that they would walk the whole day and stop to sleep at night, and in the morning they would find themselves where they had been the day before. When they were all in the wilderness, they said to Musa: "Who will provide us with food?" So Allah sent down upon them *al-mann* and *al-salwa*. They said: "Who will protect us from the heat of the sun?" So the clouds shaded them. They said: "What will we light our lamps with at night?" So He set up for them a pillar of light in the middle of their encampment; Makki mentioned "a pillar of fire." They said: "Who will provide us with water?" So Musa was commanded to strike the rock. They said: "Who will provide us with clothing?" So they were given that their garments would not wear out, nor decay, nor become soiled, and that their children would grow as children grow. And Allah knows best.

The second issue concerns His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We sent down upon you the manna and the quails﴾. There is disagreement about what *al-mann* is and its identification, and there are several opinions. It is said that it is *al-taranjabin* [[Al-taranjabin: dew that falls from the sky, a sweet, thick, granular moisture resembling honey (from Ibn al-Baytar's Mufradat).]] (with a shadda on the ra and a sukun on the nun), mentioned by al-Nahhas, and it is also said *al-taranjabin* with a ta; and most of the commentators hold this view. It is also said to be a sweet gum, and it is said to be honey, and it is said to be a sweet drink. And it is said: it is *khubz al-riqaq* (thin bread), according to Wahb ibn Munabbih.

It is also said that *al-mann* is a verbal noun (*masdar*) that encompasses everything Allah bestows upon His servants without toil or cultivation. From this is the saying of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the hadith of Sa'id ibn Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl: "The mushroom is from the *mann* which Allah sent down upon the Children of Israel, and its water is a cure for the eye." In another narration: "from the *mann* which Allah sent down upon Musa." Narrated by Muslim. Our scholars said: This hadith indicates that the mushroom is among what Allah sent down upon the Children of Israel, that is, among what Allah created for them in the wilderness. Abu 'Ubayd said: He only compared it to the *mann* because there is no effort in it, with no sowing, no irrigation, and no treatment; so it is of its kind, that is, of the same kind as the *mann* of the Children of Israel, in that it came without exertion.

It is narrated that it used to descend upon them from the break of dawn until sunrise like snow, so a man would take what sufficed him for his day. If he saved any of it, it would spoil for him, except on Friday, when they would store up for Saturday, and it would not spoil for them, because Saturday is a day of worship; and nothing descended upon them on Saturday.

The third issue: When the Prophet, peace be upon him, stated that the water of the mushroom is a cure for the eye, some people of medical knowledge said: Either it is to cool the eye from some heat that exists in it, so it is used on its own alone; or it is for other reasons, so it is compounded with other things. Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, held to using it alone for all eye ailments. This is like Abu Wajza's use of honey for all diseases, even for kohl, as will be explained, Allah willing, in Surah al-Nahl. [[See vol. 10, p. 136.]] The lexicographers said: *al-kam'* is singular, *ka'an* is dual, and *akmu'* is plural (three or more). When they go beyond that, they say *kam'ah* with a ta, in contrast to *shajarah* and *shajar*. *Al-mann* is a collective noun (*ism jins*) with no singular from its own form, and it applies to both good and bad, as said by al-Akhfash.

The fourth issue concerns His saying: ﴿And the quails﴾. There is disagreement about *al-salwa*. It is said it is the quail itself, as said by al-Dahhak. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: *al-salwa* is a bird, by the consensus of the commentators, and al-Hudhali erred when he said:

*And he swore by Allah with all his effort, "You are*
*sweeter than al-salwa when its honey is extracted."*

He thought *al-salwa* was honey. I say: The consensus he claims is not valid. Al-Mu'arrij [[He is Mu'arrij ibn 'Amr al-Sadusi, kunya Abu Fayd. He was one of the companions of al-Khalil ibn Ahmad and died in 195 AH.]], one of the scholars of language and tafsir, said that it is honey, and he cited the verse of al-Hudhali, and mentioned that it is so in the dialect of Kinanah; it was named so because one is consoled (*yusla*) by it. From it comes *'ayn al-sulwan* [[*'Ayn al-sulwan*: a gushing spring blessed and sought for healing in Jerusalem. (From Yaqut's Mu'jam.)]], and he recited:

*"Even if I drank al-sulwan, I would not be consoled;*
*I have no independence from you, even if I am made independent."* [[The verse is by Ru'bah.]]

Al-Jawhari said: *al-salwa* is honey, and he cited the verse of al-Hudhali: "sweeter than al-salwa when its honey is extracted," and did not mention an error. *Al-sulwanah* (with a damma) is a bead (*kharazah*) which, they used to say, when rainwater is poured over it and a lover drinks it, he is consoled. He said:

*"I drank over a sulwanah water of a cloud,*
*so by the life of my glad days, O Mayy, I am not consoled."*

The name of that water is *al-sulwan*. Some said: *al-sulwan* is a medicine given to the grieving so that he is consoled, and physicians call it *al-mufarrih* (the cheerer). It is said: *salaytu* and *salawtu* are two dialects. He is in *salwah* from life, that is, in ease, according to Abu Zayd.

The fifth issue: There is disagreement about whether *al-salwa* is a plural or a singular. Al-Akhfash said: it is a plural with no singular from its own form, like *al-khayr* and *al-sharr*; and it is likely that its singular is *salwa*, like its plural, just as they said *duflah* for both singular and plural, and *sumana* and *shukaha* for both singular and plural. [[*Al-duflah* (like *dhikra*): a bitter, green, attractive shrub that grows in valleys.]] [[*Al-shukaha* (like *hubara*, and it may be pronounced with a fatha): a fine, slender plant with thin stalks, small and green, which people use as medicine.]] Al-Khalil said: its singular is *salwah*, and he recited:

*"And indeed, at the remembrance of you, a tremor seizes me,*
*as the quail shakes off the wetness of the rain."* [[In the originals it reads *salwah*, which is a distortion.]]

Al-Kisa'i said: *al-salwa* is singular, and its plural is *salawi*.

The sixth issue: *Al-salwa* is in apposition (*'atf*) to *al-mann*, and its case ending did not appear because it is a defective noun (*maqsur*). This applies to all defective nouns, because they must have an alif at the end. Al-Khalil said: the alif is an airy letter with no fixed place, so it resembles a vowel, and its vowel is therefore replaced. Al-Farra' said: if the alif were vowelled, it would become a hamzah.

The seventh issue: His saying: ﴿Eat of the good things We have provided for you﴾. The word *kulu* (eat) contains an ellipsis; its estimated form is "and We said: eat," and it was omitted because the indication is apparent. The *tayyibat* here encompasses both the lawful and the pleasant.

The eighth issue: His saying: ﴿And they did not wrong Us﴾. Before it is estimated: "so they disobeyed and did not repay the blessings with gratitude."

(﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾) by repaying the blessings with acts of disobedience.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 58 (part 1 of 2):**

There are nine issues in this verse.

The first issue concerns His saying, ﴿And when We said, "Enter this town"﴾. The alif of "qulna" (we said) is dropped because it is unvocalized and the following dal is also unvocalized. The alif with which one begins before the dal is an alif of connection (alif al-wasl), because the verb is from "yadkhulu" (to enter).

The second issue concerns His saying, ﴿this town﴾, meaning the city. It was called that because it gathers (taqarrat), that is, it is a place where people assemble. From this comes "qaraytu al-ma' fi al-hawd" (I gathered the water in the pool), meaning I collected it. The name of that water is "qira" (with a kasra on the qaf), a maqsur noun. The same applies to what is given to a guest to eat, as al-Jawhari said. "Al-miqraah" is the pool, "al-qariyy" is the channel of water, and "al-qara" is the back, from which comes the line of poetry [[This is by Hamid al-Arqat, who described a horse with a slender belly and then denied that its slenderness was due to weakness, saying: "(with fat back)". "Lahiq" means lean. (From Sharh al-Shawahid).]]:

"Lahiq batnin biqara samin" (lean of belly, with a fat back).

"Al-maqari" means large bowls, as one says:

"Izam al-maqari dayfuhum la yufazza'" (Great are the bowls; their guest is not startled).

The singular of "al-maqari" is "miqraah," and all of these words have the sense of gathering and are unhamzated. "Al-qiryah" (with a kasra on the qaf) is the dialect of Yemen. Scholars differed about which town is meant. The majority said it is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It was also said that it is Ariha, near Bayt al-Maqdis. Umar ibn Shabba said it was the capital and residence of kings. Ibn Kaysan said it was al-Sham (Greater Syria). Al-Dahhak said it was al-Ramla, al-Urdunn, Filastin and Tadmur. This is another blessing: He permitted them to enter the town and removed the wandering (al-tayh) from them.

The third issue concerns His saying, ﴿So eat﴾. It is a permission. "Raghadan" means abundant and wide. It is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "eating in abundance." It may also be in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal), as previously mentioned. The land was blessed and of great produce, and therefore He said "raghadan."

The fourth issue concerns His saying, ﴿And enter the gate prostrating﴾. "Al-bab" (gate) is pluralized as "abwab," and they have said "abwabah" for the sake of rhyme (izdiwaj). The poet said [[This is by al-Qallakh ibn Jinab. It was also said that it is by Ibn Muqbil. (From al-Lisan).]]:

"Hattak akhbiyatin wa-lajjaj abwabatin, yakhlitu bil-birri minhu al-jidda wal-linaa"

(He tears down tents and enters doors, mixing in his conduct seriousness and gentleness.)

If one were to use it in the singular, it would not be permitted. Similar to this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Welcome to the people (or to the delegation), neither disgraced nor regretful." One says "tabawwabtu bawwaban" (I took a doorkeeper), and "abwab mubawwabah," just as they say "asnaf musannafah" (sorted kinds). "Hadha shay'un min babatika" means this is suitable for you. The meaning of prostration has already been mentioned [[See p. 345.]], so there is no point in repeating it. Praise be to Allah. The gate they were commanded to enter is a gate in Bayt al-Maqdis, known today as "Bab Hittah," according to Mujahid and others. It was also said that it is the gate of the dome at which Musa and the Children of Israel used to pray. As for "sujjadan," Ibn Abbas said it means bowing in ruku'. It was also said it means humbly and submissively, without a specific form.

The fifth issue concerns His saying, ﴿And say﴾, which is conjoined to "udkhulu" (enter).

"Hittatun" (with a damma) is the reading of the majority, on the presumption of an omitted subject: "our request is hittah," or it is a quotation. Al-Akhfash said it was also read as "hittatan" (with a fatha), meaning "remove from us our sins, a removal (hittatan)." Al-Nahhas said: the report from Ibn Abbas is that it was said to them, "Say: There is no god but Allah." In another report from him, it was said to them, "Say: forgiveness." This explanation of the accusative means "say something that removes your sins," just as one says "qul khayran" (say something good). The imams among the reciters read it in the nominative, and this is preferable in the language, because of what has been transmitted from the Arabs regarding the meaning of "baddala" (to change). Ahmad ibn Yahya said: it is said "baddaltuhu," meaning I changed it, without removing its essence. And "abdaltuhu" means I removed its essence and its person, as Abu al-Najm said [[This is Abu al-Najm. (From I'rab al-Quran by al-Nahhas).]]:

"Azl al-amir lil-amir al-mubaddal" (the removal of one commander for a replacing commander).

And Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Those who do not expect to meet Us say, "Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it."﴾ [Yunus: 15]. And the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud [[In the original: "wa-lihadith Ibn Mas'ud." The correction is from al-Nahhas.]], "They said 'hittah'," is an explanation of the nominative. All of this is the statement of al-Nahhas. Al-Hasan and Ikrimah said: "hittah" means "remove our sins." They were commanded to say, "There is no god but Allah," so that their sins would be removed by it. Ibn Jubayr said its meaning is seeking forgiveness (istighfar). Aban ibn Taghlib said it means repentance. A poet said:

"Faza bil-hittati allati ja'ala Allahu biha dhanba 'abdihi maghfuran"

(He succeeded by the hittah through which Allah made His servant's sin forgiven.)

Ibn Faris said in al-Mujmal: "hittah" is a word the Children of Israel were commanded to say; if they had said it, their burdens would have been removed. Al-Jawhari also said the same in al-Sihah. I say: it is possible that they were required to worship with this exact wording, and this is the apparent meaning of the hadith. Muslim narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "It was said to the Children of Israel: Enter the gate prostrating and say 'hittah,' and We shall forgive your sins [but they changed it], so they entered the gate crawling on their buttocks and said 'habbah fi sha'rah' (a grain in a hair)." Al-Bukhari also narrated it and said: "they changed it and said 'hittah' as 'hababah fi sha'rah'." In books other than the Sahihs it is "hintah fi sha'r" (wheat in hair). It was also said that they said "hitta samaha thi" in Hebrew, and its meaning is "red wheat." Ibn Qutaybah related this, and al-Harawi related it from al-Suddi and Mujahid. Their intention was contrary to what Allah commanded them, so they disobeyed, rebelled and mocked, and Allah punished them with "rijz," which is punishment. Ibn Zayd said it was a plague that killed seventy thousand of them. It is also narrated that the gate was made low so that they would enter it bowing, but they entered it squatting on their buttocks. And Allah knows best.

The sixth issue: some scholars used this verse to show that changing the statements prescribed in the Shari'ah is of two kinds. Either worship was performed with its wording, or with its meaning. If worship was with its wording, it is not permitted to change it, because Allah censured those who changed what He had commanded them to say. If worship was with its meaning, it is permitted to change it with something that conveys that same meaning, but it is not permitted to change it with something that departs from that meaning.

Scholars have differed about this matter. It is reported from Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah and their companions that it is permitted for one who knows the contexts of discourse and who is discerning of the individual words to transmit a hadith by its meaning, but on condition that it matches the meaning completely. This is the position of the majority. However, a large group of scholars prohibited this, including Ibn Sirin, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad and Raja' ibn Haywah. Mujahid said: "Cut from the hadith if you wish, but do not add to it." Malik ibn Anas was strict regarding the Prophet's ﷺ hadith with regard to the "ta'" and the "ya'" and similar matters. Upon this stance is a group of the imams of hadith, who do not allow changing or altering the wording, to the extent that they would hear an error in speech, know it, and still not correct it. Abu Mijlaz narrated from Qays ibn Abbad who said: Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "Whoever hears a hadith and narrates it exactly as he heard it has been safe." Something similar is narrated from Abdullah ibn Amr and Zayd ibn Arqam.

The same difference applies to changing the order, adding, or omitting. Some scholars consider the meaning and do not consider the wording, while others are strict in this and do not depart from the wording. The latter is more cautious in religion, more pious and more preferable. But most scholars disagree with it. The view of permissibility is the correct one, if Allah wills, because it is known from the practice of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, that they used to narrate the same events in different wordings. This was only because they devoted their attention to meanings, and they did not insist on repeating the hadiths word for word or on writing them down. It is reported from Wathilah ibn al-Asqa' that he said: "Not everything that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ told us did we transmit to you; the meaning is enough for you." Qatadah said, from Zurarah ibn Awfa: "I met a number of the companions of the Prophet ﷺ, and they differed with me in the wording, but agreed in the meaning." Al-Nakha'i, al-Hasan and al-Sha'bi, may Allah have mercy on them, used to convey hadiths according to their meanings. Al-Hasan said: "If you hit the meaning, it suffices you." Sufyan al-Thawri, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "If I tell you that I narrate to you as I heard it, do not believe me; it is only the meaning." Waki', may Allah have mercy on him, said: "If the meaning is not broad, people have perished."

The scholars agreed on the permissibility of conveying the Shari'ah to non-Arabs in their own language and translating it for them, and that is transmission by meaning. Allah Himself did this in His Book regarding what He related of the accounts of past events. He related some of these stories in various places with different wordings while the meaning is one. He transferred them from their languages into the Arabic language, and this differs from them in order, omission, deletion, addition and subtraction. If it is permissible to replace Arabic with a non-Arabic language, then it is all the more permissible to do so within Arabic. Al-Hasan and al-Shafi'i argued with this meaning, and it is the correct position on this matter.

If it is said: the Prophet ﷺ said, "May Allah make radiant a person who hears my saying and conveys it as he heard it," and mentioned the hadith. And it is established from him ﷺ that he commanded a man to say at his bed, in a supplication that he taught him, "I believe in Your Book that You revealed and Your Prophet whom You sent," and the man said, "And Your Messenger whom You sent," and the Prophet ﷺ said, "And Your Prophet whom You sent." They said: Do you not see that he did not permit, for the one who taught him the supplication, a change of wording, and said: "He conveyed it as he heard it"? It is said to them: As for his saying "He conveyed it as he heard it," what is meant is its ruling, not its wording, because the wording is not regarded as significant. What shows that the intended meaning of the address is its ruling is his saying: "For many a bearer of knowledge is not a knower, and many a bearer of knowledge conveys it to one who is more knowing than he." Furthermore, this very hadith has been transmitted with different wordings while the meaning is one. Although it is possible that all the wordings were spoken by the Prophet ﷺ at different times, the more likely case is that it is one hadith transmitted with different wordings, and that is the strongest proof of permissibility. As for his ﷺ correction of the man from "And Your Messenger" to "And Your Prophet," this is because the wording of the Prophet ﷺ is more praiseworthy, and each of these two descriptions has its place. Do you not see that the name "Messenger" applies to all, while the name "Prophet" is deserved only by the prophets, peace be upon them? The messengers were preferred among the prophets because they combined prophethood and messengership. When he said "And Your Prophet," he used the more praiseworthy description, and then restricted it to messengership with his saying "whom You sent." Also, his moving from "And Your Messenger" to "And Your Prophet" was so that he might combine prophethood and messengership. It is considered unpleasant in speech to say, "This is the messenger of so-and-so whom he sent," or "This is the slain of Zayd whom he killed," because you suffice with saying "the messenger of so-and-so" and "the slain of so-and-so" without repeating the sender and the killer, since by it you convey only the first meaning. Rather, it is appropriate to say, "This is the messenger of Abdullah whom he sent to Amr," and "This is the slain of Zayd whom he killed yesterday, or in such-and-such battle." And Allah is the Guardian of success.

If it is permissible for the first narrator to alter the Messenger's wording, then it would be permissible for the second to alter the first's wording, and this would lead to the complete obliteration of the hadith, given how subtle and hidden the differences are. It is said in reply: the permissibility is conditional on exact correspondence and equivalence, as we have mentioned. If that is lacking, it is not permissible.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: The disagreement on this question can only be conceived with regard to the era of the Companions and the Successors, because they were equal in knowing the natural, innate linguistic taste (al-lughah al-jibilliyyah al-dhawqiyyah).
