As for those after them, we have no doubt that this is not permissible, since natures have changed, understandings have diverged, and customs have differed. This is the truth. And God knows best.

One of our scholars said: Ibn al-'Arabi, may God have mercy on him, has spoken in a non-Arabic manner. If permissibility is conditioned on correspondence, then there is no difference between the time of the Companions and the Successors and the time of others. For this reason, none of the jurists of legal theory (al-usuliyyun) or of the people of hadith (ahl al-hadith) made this distinction. Yes, if he had said: "Correspondence is further off in his time," it would have been closer to the mark. And God knows best.

The seventh issue: God's words, ﴿We will forgive you your wrongdoings﴾. The reading of Nafi' is with the yā' (يَغْفِرْ) and its damma, and of Ibn 'Amir with the tā' (تَغْفِرْ) and its damma, and this is the reading of Mujahid. The rest read it with the nūn (نَغْفِرْ) and its fatha, and this is the clearest of them, because before it is ﴿And when We said: Enter﴾, so ﴿We will forgive﴾ follows the reporting about God, the Exalted. The meaning is: "And We said: Enter the gate prostrating, [and] We will forgive." Also, after it is ﴿and We will increase﴾ with the nūn. And "khaṭāyākum" (your wrongdoings) follows the consonantal text (al-sawād, the written text of the Qur'an), and this is its proper form. The reasoning of the one who reads with the tā' is that he made the verb feminine because the word khaṭāyā is feminine, being the broken plural of khaṭī'ah. The reasoning of the reading with the yā' is that he made it masculine when a separation intervened between the feminine noun and its verb, as has preceded in God's words ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾ [al-Baqarah: 37]. The yā' and the tā' are acceptable even though before it there is a report about God in His words "And when We said," because it is known that the sins of sinners are forgiven only by God, the Exalted, so the nūn was dispensed with and the verb was referred back to the wrongdoings that are forgiven.

The eighth issue: It has been disputed regarding the original form of khaṭāyā, the plural of khaṭī'ah with a hamzah. Al-Khalil said: The original form of khaṭāyā is that one says khaṭāyi'un, then it was transposed so it became khaṭā'iyun, with a hamzah followed by a yā'. Then the yā' is changed into an alif as a necessary replacement, so one says khaṭā'. When two alifs came together with a hamzah between them, and the hamzah is of the same kind as the alif, it is as if you had combined three alifs. So you replaced the hamzah with a yā' and said khaṭāyā.

As for Sibawayh, his view is that the original form is like the first, khaṭāyi'un. Then, by this, the yā' must be given a hamzah, as you gave it a hamzah in madā'in, so you say khaṭā'i'un. Two hamzahs do not come together in one word, so you replaced the second with a yā' and said khaṭā'iy. Then you did with it what you did with the first.

Al-Farra' said: khaṭāyā is the plural of khaṭiyyah without a hamzah, just as you say hadiyyah and hadāyā. Al-Farra' also said: If you pluralized khaṭī'ah with a hamzah, you would say khaṭā'. Al-Kisa'i said: If you pluralized it with a hamzah, you would assimilate the hamzah into the hamzah, just as you say dawābb.

The ninth issue: God's words, ﴿and We will increase the good-doers﴾, meaning: in the goodness of those who did not worship the calf. It is also said: He forgives the wrongdoings of those who did not keep the manna and the quail for the next day, and He will increase the goodness of those who did not keep [any] for the next day. It is also said: He forgives the wrongdoings of whoever is disobedient, and He will increase the goodness of whoever is a good-doer, meaning: We will increase them in goodness beyond the goodness already present with them. It is the active participle of aḥsana (to do good). The muḥsin is the one who has sound belief in the oneness of God, manages his own self well, applies himself to performing his obligatory duties, and spares the Muslims his evil.

In the hadith of Gabriel, peace be upon him (he said): "What is ihsan?" He said: "That you worship God as if you see Him; and if you do not see Him, [know that] He sees you." He said: "You have spoken truly." And he mentioned the hadith. Muslim recorded it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 59:

There are four issues in this.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿But those who did wrong substituted a word﴾ ... "alladhina" (those who) is in the nominative position, meaning: the wrongdoers among them substituted a word other than the one that had been said to them. This is because they were told: "Say, ḥiṭṭah (forgiveness)," but they said ḥinṭah (wheat), as has been mentioned earlier. They added a letter to the speech, and so they met with the trials that they met with, as a lesson that adding to the religion and innovating in the Shariah is of great danger and severe harm. This concerns changing a single word that expressed repentance, and yet it brought upon them all that punishment. So what do you think of changing that which is among the attributes of the One who is worshipped! Moreover, speech is less than action, so how much more so is substitution and alteration in deed.

The second: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿fa-baddala﴾ (substituted). The meaning of baddala and abdala has already been mentioned, and it is read as "ʿasā rabbunā an yubdilanā" (perhaps our Lord will replace us) in both forms. Al-Jawhari said: "And I substituted (abdaltu) a thing for another," and "Allah substituted (baddalahu Allah) fear for security (amnan)." The substitution (tabdil) of a thing also means changing it even if no replacement comes. "Istabdala" (he took in exchange) and "tabaddalahu bihi" mean that one took it in its place. Al-Mubadalah is exchange (tabadul). Al-abdal are a people of the righteous; the world is never without them, and when one of them dies, Allah replaces him with another. Ibn Duraid said: the singular is badil, and al-badil is al-badal. The badal of a thing is its other; it is said badal and bidl, two dialects, like shabah and shibh, mithl and mathal, and nukal and nikl. Abu ʿUbayd said: "Nothing has been heard in fa'al and fi'l other than these four letters." Al-badal is an ache that occurs in the two hands and the two feet. It is said: badila (with kasra) yabdalu badalan.

The third: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So We sent down upon those who did wrong﴾. He repeated the word "dhalamu" (did wrong) and did not use a pronoun, to magnify the matter. Repetition occurs in two ways. One is its use after the completion of the sentence, as in this verse and in His saying, ﴿So woe to those who write the Book with their own hands﴾ [al-Baqarah: 79]. Then He said afterwards, "So woe to them for what their hands have written," and did not say "for what they wrote," and He repeated "woe" to intensify the gravity of their deed. From this is the saying of al-Khansa':

"Time has gnawed at me, nahsan and ḥazzan..." and "Time has afflicted me with blows (qar'an) and pinches (ghamzan)."

She meant that time had afflicted her with its great and small calamities. The second way is the repetition of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun before the sentence is complete, as in His saying, ﴿The Inevitable Reality. What is the Inevitable Reality?﴾ [al-Haqqah: 1-2] and ﴿The Striking Calamity. What is the Striking Calamity?﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 1-2]. By analogy it would have been: "The Inevitable Reality, what it is, and the Striking Calamity, what it is," but for the magnification and exaltation intended. Similar is "So the companions of the right hand, what are the companions of the right hand? And the companions of the left hand, what are the companions of the left hand?" He repeated "the companions of the right hand" to exalt what abundant reward they will receive, and repeated "the companions of the left hand" for the painful punishment they will receive. From this second kind is the saying of the poet:

"Would that the crow, when it cawed at dawn ceaselessly, had its veins cut..."

Adi ibn Zayd combined both meanings when he said: "I do not see death preceding death... death has embittered the rich and the poor," repeating the word "death" three times, and this is of the first kind. From it is also the saying of another:

"Ah, how lovely is Hind, and a land in which is Hind, and Hind, beyond whom lie distance and remoteness..."

He repeated the mention of his beloved three times to magnify her.

The fourth: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿rijzan﴾ (a punishment). The reading of the majority is "rijzan" with a kasra on the ra', and Ibn Muhaysin read it with a damma on the ra'. Rijz (with the zay) means punishment; (with the sin) rijs means filth and uncleanliness. From it is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿so it increased them in filth upon their filth﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125], meaning stench upon their stench, said al-Kisa'i. Al-Farra' said: rijz is rijs. Abu ʿUbayd said: just as it is said al-sudgh and al-zudgh, so rijs and rijz have the same meaning. Al-Farra' said: some of them mentioned that ruzz (with a damma) is the name of an idol they used to worship, and it was read thus in His saying, ﴿and the idol, avoid﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 5]. Rajaz (with a fatha on the ra' and jim) is a type of poetry, and al-Khalil denied that it is poetry. It is derived from rajaz, a disease that afflicts camels in their hindquarters; when it flares up, their thighs tremble.

﴿because they were defiantly disobeying﴾ (bi-ma kanu yafsuqun), i.e., because of their defiance. Fisq is going out (of obedience), and it has been mentioned before [see p. 245 of this part]. Ibn Wathhab and al-Nakha'i read "yafsiqun" with a kasra on the sin.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 60:

There are eight issues in this.

The first: the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿And when Moses asked for water for his people﴾. The dhal (in istasqa) is vowelled with kasra because of the meeting of two sakin letters. The sin is the sin of request, as in istaʿlama (to ask to be informed), istakhbara (to ask for news), istansara (to seek help) and the like, meaning he sought and asked for water for his people. The Arabs say saqaytuhu and asqaytuhu, two forms with the same meaning. [The line of poetry:] Labid (as in al-Lisan): "He gave drink to my people, the Banu Majd, and gave drink to Numayr and the tribes of Hilal." It is also said: saqaytuhu means to give him a drink to the lips, and asqaytuhu means I showed him the water.

The second: seeking water (istisqa') only occurs when water is absent and rain is withheld. In that case the ruling is to display servitude, poverty, neediness, humility, together with sincere repentance. The Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) sought rain, and he went out to the musalla humbly, submissively, humbled, calm and supplicating, and that is sufficient! So how about us, when we have no repentance except obstinacy and opposition to the Lord of the servants? How could we be given drink! But the Prophet (ﷺ) said in the hadith of Ibn Umar: "They did not withhold the zakat of their wealth except that they were denied rain from the sky, and were it not for the animals they would not have been rained upon." This hadith will come in full, God willing.

The third: the sunnah of istisqa' is to go out to the musalla in the manner we have described, along with the khutbah and the prayer, and this is the view of the majority of scholars. Abu Hanifa held that it is not part of its sunnah to have a prayer or to go out; it is only supplication and nothing else. He argued with the authentic hadith of Anas, related by al-Bukhari and Muslim. But there is no proof for him in it, for that was a supplication whose answer was hastened, so it sufficed on its own and did not intend to explain a sunnah. When he intended to explain, he explained by his action, as narrated by Abdullah ibn Zayd al-Mazini, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out to the musalla, sought rain, turned his cloak, then prayed two rak'ahs. Related by Muslim. More rulings of istisqa' will come in surah Hud, God willing. [Note: the author did not mention anything about istisqa' in surah Hud, but it is mentioned in surah Nuh, vol. 18, p. 302.]

The fourth: the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿So We said: Strike the rock with your staff﴾. The ʿasa (staff) is well known; it is a feminine noun with a maqsur (shortened) form, and its alif is converted from a waw. [The line of poetry, by Dhu al-Rumma, whose first half is:] "So she brought a weaving of a spider, as if it were..." on her two ʿusawayhi (the two wooden pieces crossing a bucket like a cross), a fine, thin cloth, pierced. The plural is ʿusiy and ʿisiy; it is fuʿul, and the ʿain was vowelled with kasra because of the kasra after it. Aʿsin is also similar, like zaman and azmun. In the proverb: "The staff is from the same stock," meaning some matters are from others. The saying "he cast his staff" means he settled and gave up travel, and it is a proverb. [The poetry:] "She cast her staff, and the nawa settled with her, as the traveller's eye is cooled by returning."

In the Revelation: ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Moses? He said: It is my staff, I lean upon it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 17-18]. There the discussion of its benefits will come, God willing. Al-Farra said: the first solecism heard in Iraq was "hadhihi ʿasati" (this is my staff). The staff may also be used to express unity and division; from this it is said of the Kharijites: they have split the staff of the Muslims, meaning their unity and harmony. "The staff was split" means disagreement occurred. The poet said: "When war comes and the staff is split, then sufficient for you and al-Dahhak is a sharpened sword," meaning it suffices you and suffices al-Dahhak. Their saying "do not raise your staff from your family" is meant as discipline. And Allah knows best.

The rock (al-hajar) is well known; the analogical plural in the smallest number is ahjar, in the greater number hijar and hijarah, and hijarah is rare. This is like our saying jamal and jimalah, and dhakar and dhikarah, as Ibn Faris and al-Jawhari said. I say: in the Qur'an there is ﴿then they are like rocks﴾ [al-Baqarah: 74], ﴿and indeed among rocks﴾ [al-Baqarah: 74], ﴿Say: Be rocks﴾ [al-Isra: 50], ﴿pelting them with stones﴾ [al-Fil: 4], ﴿and We rained upon them stones﴾ [al-Hijr: 74]. How then is it rare, unless they mean it is rare in analogy but common and eloquent in usage. And Allah knows best.

The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿then there gushed forth﴾: there is an omission in the speech; its estimate is "so he struck, and there gushed forth." Allah was able to make water gush forth and split the rock without striking, but He willed to link the effects to causes, as wisdom for His servants in reaching their goals, and to base upon that their reward and punishment in the hereafter. Infijar means splitting, and from it comes "the dawn broke" (infaqa al-fajr). Infajara al-ma' infijaran means it opened. The fujrah is the place where water bursts forth. Inbijas is narrower than infijar, for it is first inbijas and then becomes infijar. It is said: inbajasa, tabajjasa, tafajjara and tafattaqa have one meaning, related by al-Harawi and others.

The fifth: the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿twelve springs﴾. "Ithnata" is in the nominative position as the subject of "fanfajarat", and the sign of nominative is the alif; it is declined unlike its counterparts because the dual is always declined, for its meaning is sound. ʿAynan is accusative as an explanation (tamyiz). Mujahid, Talhah and ʿIsa read "ʿashirah" with kasra on the shin, which is the dialect of Banu Tamim; this in their dialect is rare, because their way is lightening. The dialect of the people of the Hijaz is "ʿashrah", and their way is heaviness. Jamiʿuhu al-Nahhas said this. The ʿain is among the homonymous nouns: ʿayn al-ma' (spring of water), ʿayn al-insan (eye of a person), ʿayn al-rukbah (the dip at the front of the knee, by analogy with the eye's socket; in some copies, ʿayn al-rakiyyah, the spring from which a well's water gushes), and ʿayn al-shams (the sun). The ʿayn is a cloud that approaches from the direction of the qiblah. The ʿayn is rain that lasts five or six days without ceasing. A land with little ʿayn means few people; mā bihā ʿayan (with the yaʾ vowelled) means no one is there. The ʿayn is the hole in a waterskin. The ʿayn of water is likened to the eye of an animal, because water flows out of it as tears flow from an animal's eye. It is also said: since the eye of an animal is the most noble part of it, the spring of water was likened to it, for it is the most noble thing on earth.

The sixth: when Moses (peace be upon him) asked for water for his people, he was commanded to strike with his staff a rock. It is said: a square rock of Tur stone, the size of a sheep's head, placed in a leather bag and carried; when they stopped, it was placed in the middle of their camp. It is mentioned that they did not carry the rock, but found it at every stage in its place from the first stage. This is greater in the sign and the miracle. It is also said: he was given the name "rock" so that Moses might strike whatever rock he wished, and this is more eloquent in miracle. It is also said: Allah commanded him to strike a specific rock, which He made clear to Moses (peace be upon him), and for this reason it is mentioned with the definite article. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: it is the rock upon which Moses placed his garment when he bathed, and fled with his garment until Allah cleared him of what his people accused him of. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: there is no disagreement that it was a separate, square rock, from which three springs gushed out on every side when Moses struck it, and when they no longer needed water and moved on, the springs dried up.

I say: what our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) was given of the springing of water and its gushing from his hand and between his fingers is greater in miracle, for we witness water gushing from stones at all hours of night and day. And the miracle of our Prophet (peace be upon him) was not given to any prophet before our Prophet (ﷺ): water coming out from between flesh and blood! The trustworthy imams and reliable jurists related from Abdullah who said: We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) and we found no water, so a tawr (a vessel of brass or stone from which one drinks or performs wudu) was brought, and he put his hand into it. I indeed saw the water gushing from between his fingers, and he said: "Come to the purification." Al-Amash said: Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd related to me, saying: I said to Jabir, "How many were you that day?" He said: "One thousand five hundred." This is the wording of al-Nasa'i.

The seventh: the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿Every people knew their drinking place﴾. This means that each tribe of them had a spring that they knew and drank from no other. The mashrab is the place of drinking; it is also said to mean what is drunk. The tribes among the Children of Israel are like the clans among the Arabs, and they are the descendants of the twelve sons of Jacob (peace be upon him). Each tribe had one of those springs that it did not exceed. ʿAta said: the rock had four faces, and from each face three springs gushed out, one for each tribe, which no one else shared with them. It has reached us that in each tribe there were fifty thousand fighters, apart from their horses and beasts. ʿAta said: upon every place where Moses struck there appeared something like a woman's breast on the rock, which first sweated, then flowed.

The eighth: the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿Eat and drink﴾. There is an omission in the speech; its estimate is "and We said to them: Eat the manna and the quail, and drink the water gushing from the separate rock."

﴿And do not commit abuse﴾, meaning do not cause corruption. Al-ʿaythu is the intensity of corruption; He forbade them from that. It is said: ʿathiya yaʿthā ʿuthiyyan, ʿatha yaʿthū ʿuthuwwan, and ʿaʿatha yaʿithu ʿaythan, ʿuyuthan and maʿathan; the first is the language of the Qur'an. It is also said: ʿaththa yaʿuththu in the doubled form: he corrupted, and from it comes al-ʿuththah, the moth that eats wool. ﴿Mufsidin﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal), and the meaning is repeated for emphasis through the difference of wording. In these words are the permission of blessings and their enumeration, and the prohibition of sins and warning against them.

God Almighty's words: ﴿And when you said, "O Moses, we will not endure one kind of food"﴾. This statement was made by them in the wilderness (al-tih), when they grew weary of the manna and the quails and longed for their former life in Egypt. Al-Hasan said: "They were people who stank of garlic, leeks and lentils, so they returned to their ancient (ikr) ways (ikr al-su', the evil ancestral ways), and their natures yearned for what their habits had been accustomed to. So they said: 'We will not endure one kind of food.'" [The word 'ikr (with a kasra on the first letter and sukun on the second) means origin, and it is said it also means custom and habit. 'Akr (with a fatha on the middle letter) means the sediment of anything.] They referred to the manna and the quails as "one kind of food," though they were two, because they used to eat one with the other, so they said "one food." It is also said that it was because both were their daily sustenance, repeated every day, just as you say of someone who persists in fasting, prayer and recitation, "He is on one matter," because he is constant in it. It is also said that the meaning is: "We will not endure wealth, for then all of us would be rich, and none of us could seek help from another, since each would be self-sufficient." And so it was: they were the first to take slaves and servants.

God Almighty's words: ﴿on food﴾. "Ta'am" (food) is applied to what is eaten and drunk. God Almighty said: "And whoever does not taste it, he is not of me" [Qur'an 2:249, quoted in the hadith form], and He said: ﴿There is no blame on those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have tasted﴾ [5:93], meaning what they drank of wine, as will be explained later [see vol. 6, p. 293]. Even if the quails were honey, as al-Mu'arrij related, it is also a drink. Sometimes "ta'am" is specifically applied to wheat and dates, as in the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "We used to give the zakat al-fitr (charity of breaking the fast) in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), a sa' of food or a sa' of barley..." [the hadith continues]. Custom holds that when one says, "I went to the food market," what is understood is only the place where it is sold, and not other things that are eaten or drunk. "Ta'm" (with fatha) is what the sense of taste perceives; one says, "its taste is bitter." "Ta'm" also means what is desired from something; one says, "it has no taste," and "So-and-so is not one of taste," if he is insipid. "Tu'm" (with damma) means food. Abu Khirash said:

I repel the one who is full of belly, if you only knew it,
and I prefer others of your dependents over myself with food,
and I drink plain water, and I finish
when the provision becomes for the stingy one [or the one attached to a people who is not of them; both are possible] a thing of taste.

By the first he meant food, and by the second what is desired from it. "Taama, yat'amu, fa huwa ta'im" means he ate and tasted. From this is God's words: ﴿And whoever does not taste it﴾, meaning whoever does not taste it. And He said: ﴿And when you have eaten, disperse﴾ [33:53], meaning when you have eaten. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said about Zamzam: "It is food that nourishes and a cure for sickness" [meaning it satisfies a person when he drinks its water as he is satisfied by food]. "Istat'amani fulan al-hadith" means he asked me to narrate the hadith to him. In the hadith: "If the imam asks you for food, then feed him" [meaning: if he seeks to be prompted, then prompt him]. And "So-and-so does not sleep except standing." The poet said:

Ostriches at Wajra, with yellow cheeks,
they do not taste sleep except while fasting.

[The text in the original manuscripts reads thus. Wajra (with fatha then sukun) is a place between Mecca and Basra. What is in the lexicons and gazetteers is:
Ostriches at Khatma, with yellow cheeks,
they do not taste water except while fasting.
Before it:
As for the Banu 'Amir at al-Nisar,
on the morning they met us, they were ostriches.
It is by Bishr ibn Abi Khazim. Khatma (with fatha then sukun) is a place above Medina. In the lisan, after the verse: (He means: they are fasting from it, not tasting it; and that is because ostriches do not come to water nor drink it).]

God Almighty's words: ﴿So call upon your Lord for us, that He may bring forth for us from what the earth grows﴾. The dialect of the Banu 'Amir is "fad'u" with a kasra on the 'ayn, because of the meeting of two sukun letters; they treat the weak letter as if it were sound and do not observe the elided letter. "Yukhrij" is jussive, in the sense of "ask Him and say to Him: bring forth, and He will bring forth." It is said: it is in the sense of supplication, with the lam omitted in the estimation; al-Zajjaj considered this weak. The "min" in "mimma" is extra according to al-Akhfash, and not extra according to Sibawayh, because the speech is affirmative. Al-Nahhas said: al-Akhfash was driven to this because he did not find an object for "yukhrij," so he wished to make "ma" the object. The better view is that the object is omitted and indicated by the rest of the speech; the estimated meaning is: "bring forth for us, from what the earth grows, edible." So the first "min" on this view is partitive, and the second is specifying. "Min baqlihā" is a substitute for "ma," with the particle repeated. "Al-baql" [and "qith'ihā"] is coordinated with it, and so is what follows, so understand it. "Al-baql" is well known, and it is every plant that has no stalk, while "al-shajar" is what has a stalk. "Al-qith'" is also well known, and its qaf may be vowelled with damma; this is the reading of Yahya ibn Wathhab and Talha ibn Musarrif. Both are dialects, and the kasra is more common. It is said the plural of qith' is qatha'i, like 'ilba' and 'alabi, except that qith' is from the roots with waw; you say, "aqtha'tu al-qawm," meaning I fed them that. [The words placed between the brackets were transcribed by the author from lexicons by mistake as from the root q-th-a, whereas they are actually from the root f-th-a.] "Qathha'tu al-qidr" means I calmed its boiling with water. Al-Ja'di said:

Their pot boils over us, so we keep it simmering,
and we cool it down for them when its heat has boiled.

"Fatha'tu al-rajul" means I broke him off from you with speech or otherwise, and calmed his anger. "Ada hatta afta'a" means he became exhausted and out of breath. "Afta'a al-harr" means the heat subsided and calmed. Among their proverbs about a small amount of goodness is their saying: "Indeed, al-rathi'a calms anger." Its origin is that a man was angry with a people, and being hungry along with his anger, they gave him rathi'a, and his anger subsided and he refrained from them. "Al-rathi'a" is milk milked onto something sour so that it thickens; "rathha'tu al-laban rath'an" means I milked it onto something sour so that it thickened, and the noun is rathi'a. "Raththa'a al-laban" means it thickened. Ibn Majah narrated: Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Numayr told us, Yunus ibn Bukayr told us, Hisham ibn Urwa told us, from his father, from A'isha, who said: "My mother was treating me for plumpness, wishing to bring me in to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), but that did not work for her until I ate cucumber with fresh dates, and I became plump in the best way." This chain of narration is sound.

God Almighty's words: ﴿and its fum﴾. Scholars differ about "al-fum." It is said it is garlic, because it resembles onion; this was narrated by Juwaybir from al-Dahhak. The "tha'" is exchanged for "fa'," as they say "maghafir" and "maghathir" [a sticky resin flowing from the 'arfat tree, whose smell is not pleasant], and "jadath" and "jadaf" for a grave. Ibn Mas'ud read "thumiha" with the three-dotted tha, and this was narrated from Ibn Abbas. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

Their dwellings at that time were evident,
in them were al-faradis, al-fumana and onions.

"Al-faradis," its singular is "fardis"; and "karm mufradas" means a vine trained on a trellis. Hassan said:

And you are a people of base origins,
your food is al-fum and al-hawqal.

He means garlic and onion. This is the view of al-Kisa'i and al-Nadr ibn Shumayl. It is also said: "al-fum" is wheat; this was narrated from Ibn Abbas and most of the commentators, and al-Nahhas chose it, saying: "It is better, and whoever said it is higher, and its chains are sound; and Juwaybir is not comparable in his narration." Even though al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' chose the first view on account of the Arabs' exchange of "fa'" for "tha'," and exchange is not analogized upon, and that is not frequent in Arabic speech. Ibn Abbas recited, for someone who asked him about al-fum and that it means wheat, the verse of Uhayha ibn al-Julah:

I was once the richest of people, a single person,
who came to Medina without farming fum.

Al-Zajjaj said: "How can the people seek food with no wheat in it, when wheat is the basis of nourishment?" Al-Jawhari Abu Nasr said: "al-fum is wheat," and al-Akhfash recited:

I used to think myself like the richest of anyone
who came to Medina without farming fum.

[In al-Aghani (vol. 21, p. 211, European edition): "without farming fawl" (fava beans). It is also said the verse is:
And I have looked at the suns, and between them
a barrier from the Merciful, not a little.
And by this the rhyme is lam.]

Ibn Duraid said: "al-fuma is the ear of grain," and he recited:

And their scout (rabi'uhum) said, when he came to us,
with his palm a fuma or two fumas.

["Kaffihi" (his palm): the ha' is not lengthened. Some say al-fum is chickpea, a Syrian dialect word; its seller is "fami," altered from "fumi," since they sometimes alter in the nisba, as they say "suhli" and "dahri." It is said: "fawwimu lana," meaning bake bread for us. The readers said: this is an ancient dialect. Ata and Qatada said: al-fum is every grain that is baked into bread.]

Issue: The scholars differed about eating onion, garlic and any other vegetable with an unpleasant smell. The majority of scholars held that this is permitted, on account of the established hadiths on this. A group of the people of the outward meaning (Ahl al-Zahir, the Literalist school), who hold that congregational prayer is an obligation, held that it is forbidden. They said: whatever prevents one from performing an obligation and fulfilling it is unlawful to do and to occupy oneself with. They argued that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) called them "khabitha" (foul), and God the Mighty and Majestic described His Prophet, peace be upon him, as one who makes unlawful the foul things. Among the proofs of the majority is what is established from Jabir: that the Prophet (ﷺ) was brought a tray (badr) [in the originals: "a pot" (qidr); the correction is from Sunan Abi Dawud; by badr is meant a tray, likened to the full moon for its roundness] containing green vegetables, and he smelled them, and he was informed of what was in them of vegetables, and he said: "Bring them near" to one of his companions who was with him; when he saw it, he disliked eating it, and he said: "Eat, for I converse with One you do not converse with." Related by Muslim and Abu Dawud. This is clear that it is specific to him, and that it is permissible for others. In Sahih Muslim also, from Abu Ayyub, that the Prophet (ﷺ) stayed at Abu Ayyub's house, and he prepared a meal for the Prophet (ﷺ) containing garlic; when it was returned to him, he asked about the place of the Prophet's fingers; he was told: "He did not eat." He was alarmed and went up to him and said: "Is it unlawful?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "No, but I dislike it." He said: "Then I dislike what you dislike, or what you have disliked." He said: the Prophet (ﷺ) was being approached (meaning revelation came to him). This is an explicit text that it is not unlawful. Likewise what Abu Sa'id al-Khudri related from the Prophet (ﷺ) when they ate garlic during Khaybar and its conquest: "O people, it is not for me to make unlawful what God has made lawful, but it is a plant whose smell I dislike." These hadiths indicate that the ruling is specific to him, since he is the one singled out for conversation with the angel. But we know this ruling from the hadith of Jabir with what requires equality between him and others in this ruling, where he said: "Whoever eats from this plant" (once he said "garlic," and once "whoever eats onion, garlic and leeks"), "let him not come near our mosque, for the angels are harmed by what harms the children of Adam." Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, said in a lengthy hadith: "O people, you eat two plants which I see as nothing but foul: this onion and garlic. I have seen the Messenger of God (ﷺ), when he found their smell on a man in the mosque, order him taken out to al-Baqi'; so whoever eats them, let him kill their smell by cooking." Related by Muslim.

God Almighty's words: ﴿and its lentils and its onions﴾. "Al-'adas" (lentils) is well known. "Al-'adasa" is a pimple that comes out on a person, and it may kill. "'Adas" is a call to mules; he said:

"'Adas, what authority does 'Abbad have over you?
You escaped, and this one that you carry is free."

[The verse is by Yazid ibn Mufarragh.]
"Al-'adas" also means the heavy treading and the striving; it is said: "'adasahu" (he tread him down). "'Adasa fi al-ard" means he went through the land. "'Adasat ilayhi al-maniyya" means death moved toward him. Al-Kumayt said:

I burden her with the terror of darkness, and I have always been
a brother of the night, pressed toward me and hastening.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 61 (part 2 of 2):

It means: it is brought to me at night (yusar ilayya bi-l-layl). And ʿadas is a dialect form of ḥadas, as al-Jawhari said. It is transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ), through the hadith of ʿAli, that he said: "Upon you is lentils, for it is blessed and sanctified, it softens the heart and increases tears, and seventy prophets blessed it, the last of them ʿIsa son of Maryam." Al-Tha'labi and others mention it. ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz would eat bread with oil one day, meat (in some copies of the original: with salt) another day, and lentils on another day. Al-Halimi said: lentils and oil are the food of the righteous, and even if it had no virtue except that it was the hospitality of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) in his city, it would have sufficed. It is also something that lightens the body so that it becomes light for worship, and desires are not stirred by it as they are stirred by meat. Wheat is among the grains, and according to the correct view it is the fum (garlic/wheat, as the reading goes), and barley is close to it, and it was the food of the people of Madina, just as lentils were among the food of Ibrahim's town (peace be upon him). So each of the two grains gained a virtue through one of the two prophets (peace be upon them both). It has been narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) and his household did not eat their fill of wheat bread for three consecutive days from the time he came to Madina until Allah, Mighty and Majestic, took him.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Will you exchange what is lower for what is better?﴾ Istibdal (exchange) is placing one thing in the place of another, from which comes "badal" (substitute), as has already been mentioned. According to al-Zajjaj, "adna" is derived from dunuww, meaning nearness in value, from their saying: "a thawb that is muqarib," meaning of low price. ʿAli ibn Sulayman said: it is hamzated from al-danii', clearly of baseness, in the sense of the most despicable, except that its hamza was lightened. It was also said: it is derived from al-dun, meaning the lowest, so its origin is adwan (af'al form), which was transposed to give adla', and the waw was converted into an alif because it falls at the end. In the irregular readings it is also read "adna" (the original copies have this; the books of irregular readings have: adna with hamza, which is the reading of Zuhayr al-Furqubi). The meaning of the verse: will you exchange the herbs, cucumbers, garlic, lentils and onions, which are lower, for the manna and quails, which are better?

Scholars differed about the aspects that make the manna and quails superior to what they requested, and they are five. First: since herbs have no worth compared to manna and quails, the latter are more excellent, as said by al-Zajjaj. Second: since manna and quails were food that Allah bestowed upon them and commanded them to eat, and in continuing Allah's command and thanking His blessing there is reward and treasure in the Hereafter, while what they requested is devoid of these qualities, it was lower in this respect. Third: since what Allah bestowed upon them was more pure and delicious than what they asked for, what they asked for was necessarily lower in this respect. Fourth: since what was given to them involved no burden or toil, while what they sought comes only through tilling and farming and toil, it was lower. Fifth: since what was sent down to them is undoubtedly lawful and pure, having descended from Allah, whereas grains and land are subject to sales and usurpation, and doubts enter them, they were lower in this respect.

Issue: this verse is evidence for the permissibility of eating good things and delicious foods. The Prophet (ﷺ) loved sweets and honey, and drank cool, sweet water. This matter will be discussed fully, God willing, in "al-Ma'idah" [see vol. 6 p. 263] and "al-Nahl" [see vol. 10 p. 136].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Go down to a city﴾. The meaning of descent has already been mentioned [see p. 319]. This is a command whose meaning is incapacitation, like His saying: ﴿Say: be stones or iron﴾ [al-Isra: 50], because they were in the wandering (al-tih), and this was a punishment for them. It was also said: they were given what they asked for. "Misran" with tanwin, indefinite, is the reading of the majority, and it is the script of the Mushaf. Mujahid and others said: whoever gives it tanwin intends a misr (city) among the cities, unspecified. Ikrimah related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying "Go down to a city": he said, a city from these cities. A group who also gave it tanwin said: it intends the Misr of Pharaoh specifically. Those who gave it tanwin relied on the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, which implies their being commanded to enter a town, and on the widely transmitted report that they settled in Syria after the wandering. Others relied on the Qur'an's statement that Allah made the Children of Israel inherit the dwellings and traces of Pharaoh's people, and they permitted its non-tanwin form. Al-Akhfash and al-Kisa'i said: because of its lightness and its resemblance to Hind and Da'd, and he recited:

Da'd did not wrap herself in the excess of her waist-wrapper, nor was Da'd given to drink from the ʿulab. (The line is by Jarir. The ʿulab are leather cups in which milk is milked and drunk. He means she is a townswoman, delicate in living, who does not dress like the Bedouins nor eat their food.)

Thus he combined the two dialects. Sibawayh, al-Khalil and al-Farra' do not permit this, because if you named a woman Zayd you would not give it tanwin. Other than al-Akhfash said: he intended a place, so he gave it tanwin. Al-Hasan, Aban ibn Taghlib and Talhah read "Misr" without tanwin. Likewise it is so in the Mushaf of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud. They said: it is the Misr of Pharaoh. Ashhab said: Malik said to me: in my view it is Misr, your town, the dwelling of Pharaoh. Ibn ʿAtiyyah mentioned this. Al-Misr originally means in the language a boundary, and misr al-dar means its boundaries. Ibn Faris said: it is said that the people of Hajar write in their contracts "So-and-so bought the house with its musur," meaning its boundaries. ʿAdi said:

And the one who made the sun a clear boundary, without concealment, between day and night, has distinguished them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For you is what you asked﴾. "Ma" is in the accusative governed by inna. Ibn Thabbab and al-Nakha'i read "sa'altum" with a kasra on the sin, it is said: sa'alt and salt without hamza. It is from the waw-roots, as evidenced by their saying: yatasawalun. The meaning of ﴿they were struck with humiliation and wretchedness﴾ is that these were imposed upon them and decreed upon them, derived from the striking of tents (dharb al-qibab). Al-Farazdaq said about Jarir:

The spider has struck over you with its web, and the revealed Book has decreed over you.

And the ruler "struck upon the hand," meaning he imposed and obligated it. Al-dhillah is abasement and humiliation. Al-maskanah is poverty. So no Jew is found, even if he is wealthy, free of the appearance of poverty, its submissiveness and its humiliation. It was also said: al-dhillah is the imposition of the jizyah, according to al-Hasan and Qatadah. Al-maskanah is submission, and it is derived from sukun (stillness), meaning poverty reduced their movement, as said by al-Zajjaj. Abu ʿUbaydah said: al-dhillah is humiliation, and al-maskanah is the verbal noun of al-miskin. Al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim related from Ibn ʿAbbas: "and they were struck with humiliation and wretchedness," he said: they are the people of the qaballat (the tribute-payers, i.e., the jizyah).

His saying: ﴿wa-ba'u﴾, meaning they turned back and returned, that is, this became binding upon them. From it is the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him) in his supplication and intimate prayer: "I acknowledge Your blessing upon me," meaning I confess it and bind myself to it. Its original linguistic meaning is return; one says "baa bi-kadha," meaning he returned with it, and "baa ila al-mabaʾah," which is the dwelling, meaning he returned. Al-bawa' is return with retaliation. "Hum fi hadha al-amr bawa'," meaning equal, they return in it to one meaning. The poet said:

Will not the kings cease from us and guard our sacred things? Blood will not return for blood.

That is, blood does not return for blood in retaliation. He also said:

They returned with plunder and captives, and we returned with the kings shackled.

That is, they returned and we returned. The meaning of anger has already been mentioned in al-Fatiha [see p. 149].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That﴾. "That" is a causal particle.

(Because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah) meaning they denied the Book of Allah and the miracles of His prophets, such as ʿIsa, Yahya, Zakariyya and Muhammad (peace be upon them).

(And kill the prophets) is conjoined to "they disbelieved." It is related from al-Hasan "yaqtulun," and from him also as the community reads. Nafi' read "al-nabiyyin" with hamza wherever it occurs in the Qur'an, except in two places: in Surat al-Ahzab, "if a woman gives herself to the Prophet, if he wishes" [al-Ahzab: 50], and "do not enter the houses of the Prophet except" [al-Ahzab: 53], where he read without madd and without hamza. He left the hamza in these two because of the meeting of two kasra-hamzas. The rest left the hamza in all of these. As for the one who reads with hamza, in his view it is from anba'a, when he informs, and its active participle is munbi'. The plural of nabi' is anbiya', and in the plural of nabiyy there came nubaʾ. Al-ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas al-Sulami said, praising the Prophet (ﷺ):

O seal of the prophets, you are truly sent with the truth, every guidance of the path is your guidance.

This is the meaning of the reading with hamza. Those who read without hamza differed: some derived it in the same way as the one who reads with hamza, then softened the hamza. Others said: it is derived from naba, yanbu, when it rises, so the nabi is from nubuwwah, which is elevation, so the station of the prophet is lofty. And "nabi" without hamza also means the road, so the messenger was called nabi because creation is guided by him as by a road. The poet said:

He would have become crushed pebbles in place of the nabi of the Kathib (a mountain).

Ratamtu al-shay' means I broke it; one says ratama anfahu and ratahu, with ta' and tha' both. Al-ratm also means the broken, i.e., the shattered. Al-Kathib is the name of a mountain. Thus the prophets for us are like paths upon the earth. It is narrated that a man said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Peace be upon you, O Nabi'a Allah," with hamza. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "You are not Nabi'a Allah" (with hamza), "but I am Nabi Allah" without hamza. Abu ʿAli said: the chain of this hadith is weak, and what strengthens its weakness is that he (peace be upon him) was recited to by the praiser: "O seal of the prophets...," and no objection was transmitted regarding that.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿without right﴾ is an magnification of the enormity and the sin they committed. If it is said: this is evidence that it may be right for them to be killed, whereas it is known that prophets are protected from doing anything for which they would be killed. It is said to him: it is not so; this came in the manner of a description of their killing as injustice and not as right, so this was a magnification of the enormity against them. It is known that no prophet is killed rightfully, but he is killed for the truth; so His saying "without right" expresses the enormity and clarity of the sin, and no prophet ever came with anything that would require his killing. If it is said: how could the disbelievers be allowed to kill the prophets? It is said: that is an honor for them and an increase in their stations, like one of the believers who is killed in the way of Allah, and that is not abandonment of them. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan said: no prophet was ever killed except one who was not commanded to fight, and every one who was commanded to fight was victorious.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is because they disobeyed and used to transgress﴾. "That" is a reply to the first and an emphasis on pointing to it. The "ba'" in "bima" is the ba' of cause. Al-Akhfash said: meaning because of their disobedience. Al-ʿisyan is opposition to obedience; "ista'sat al-nawah" means the date-pit became hard. Al-i'tida' is exceeding the limit in everything, and it is known in the sense of wrongdoing and sins.

**First issue:** Allah's words, ﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾, mean those who affirmed Muhammad (ﷺ). Sufyan said that what is intended is the hypocrites. It is as if He said: "Those who believe outwardly." This is why He paired them with the Jews, the Christians and the Sabians. Then He explained the ruling for whoever among all of them believes in Allah and the Last Day.

**Second issue:** Allah's words, ﴿and those who are Jews﴾. The meaning is that they became Jews (yahud). They were named after Yahudha (Judah), the eldest son of Ya'qub (Jacob), peace be upon him. The Arabs changed the dhal to a dal, because when a non-Arabic word is Arabicized, it is altered from its original pronunciation. It was also said that they were named this for their repentance from worshipping the calf. Hada means "he repented," and al-ha'id means "the penitent." The poet said:

*"Indeed, I am a man who, out of love for her, is penitent."*

That is, a penitent. In the Revelation (Tanzil) is Allah's word: ﴿Indeed, we have turned back to You﴾ (Al-A'raf: 156), meaning "we have repented." It is said: hada al-qawm yahudu hawdan wa-hiyadatan, when they repented. Ibn 'Arafa said: "hudna ilayka" means "we have settled into your command." Al-hawada means calm and reconciliation. He said: from this is Allah's word: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and those who are Jews﴾. Abu al-Sammal read "hadu" with a fatha on the dal.

**Third issue:** Allah's words, ﴿and the Christians (al-nasara)﴾. It is a plural whose singular is nasrani. It was also said: Nasran, with the yaa dropped, and this is the view of Sibawayh. The feminine is nasrana, like nadman and nadmana. It is an indefinite noun that is made definite with the alif and lam. The poet said:

*"She turned away as one turns from what is not lawful for him, from the cupbearer of the Nasara before the Fisah, who are fasting."* [[The poet is al-Namir ibn Tawlab, describing a she-camel to whom water was offered and who refused it. In the manuscripts of the original: "al-Subh" with a ba'. The correction is from Sibawayh's book. Al-Fisah: the breaking of the fast of the Christians, which is a feast for them.]]

Here he described it with the indefinite form. Al-Khalil said: the singular of al-nasara is nasri, like mahri and mahara. Sibawayh cited as evidence:

*"You see him, when the evening falls, inclining to the faith (of Abraham), and in the morning he is before him, a Christian who is bright."*

He also cited:

*"Both of them fell, and her head bowed, as the head of a Christian woman bows when she does not incline in prayer."* [[The line is by Abu al-Akhzar al-Hammani, describing two she-camels that lowered their heads from exhaustion. He likened the camel's head to the head of a Christian woman when she bows in her prayer. (From the commentary on the Qamus and Lisan.)]]

It is said: asjada, when he inclined. But nasran and nasrana are not used except with the nisba yaa, because they said: rajul nasrani (a Christian man) and imra'a nasraniyya (a Christian woman). Nassarahu means "he made him a Christian." In a hadith: "His parents make him a Jew or make him a Christian." He, peace be upon him, also said: "No one from this community hears of me, a Jew or a Christian, and then does not believe in what I was sent with, except that he will be among the companions of the Fire." Some plurals have come in forms other than their singular's usual form, and by analogy the plural is al-nasraniyyun. Then it was said: they were named after a village called Nasira, where 'Isa, peace be upon him, used to dwell, so he was attributed to it and called 'Isa al-Nasiri. When his followers were attributed to him, they were called al-Nasara. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada. Al-Jawhari said: Nasran is a village in Syria to which the Christians are attributed, and it is also called Nasira. It was also said: they were named this for the support (nusra) some of them gave to others. The poet said:

*"When I saw the Nabat as helpers, I hitched up my garment above my knees. I became for them a neighbor among the Nasara."*

It was also said: they were named this because of His word: ﴿Who are my helpers in the way of Allah?' The disciples said: 'We are the helpers of Allah'﴾ (Al 'Imran: 52).

**Fourth issue:** Allah's words, ﴿and the Sabians (al-Sabi'in)﴾. It is the plural of sabi'. It was also said: sabin. For this reason they differed about its hamza. Most readers pronounced the hamza, except Nafi'. Whoever pronounced the hamza took it from sabi'at al-nujum (the stars rose) when they appeared, and sabat thaniyyat al-ghulam (the boy's front tooth came out) when it emerged. Whoever did not pronounce the hamza took it from saba, yasbu, when he inclined. In the language, the sabi' is one who leaves and turns from one religion to another. For this reason the Arabs used to say of one who had embraced Islam: "He has sabi'a (converted)." So the Sabians had departed from the religion of the People of the Book.

**Fifth issue:** There is no disagreement that the Jews and the Christians are People of the Book. Because of their Book, it is permissible to marry their women and eat their food, as will be explained in Surat al-Ma'ida [[See vol. 6, p. 76.]], and to impose the jizya (poll tax) on them, as will come in Surat Bara'a [[See vol. 8, p. 110.]], if Allah wills. But there was disagreement about the Sabians. Al-Suddi said: they are a sect of the People of the Book. Ishaq ibn Rahawayh said the same. Ibn al-Mundhir said: Ishaq said there is no harm in eating the slaughtered animals (dhaba'ih) of the Sabians, because they are a group of the People of the Book. Abu Hanifa said: there is no harm in eating their slaughtered animals or marrying their women. Al-Khalil said: they are a people whose religion resembles the religion of the Christians, except that their qibla is toward the south wind, and they claim they are upon the religion of Nuh, peace be upon him. Mujahid, al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Najih said: they are a people whose religion is a mixture of Judaism and Magianism, and their slaughtered animals may not be eaten. Ibn 'Abbas said: nor may their women be married. Al-Hasan also said, and Qatada: they are a people who worship the angels, pray facing the qibla, recite the Zabur (Psalms), and pray the five prayers. Ziyad ibn Abi Sufyan saw them and wished to remove the jizya from them when he learned that they worshipped the angels. What has been gathered of their doctrine, according to what some of our scholars mentioned, is that they are monotheists who believe in the influence of the stars and that the stars are effective agents. For this reason Abu Sa'id al-Istakhri issued a fatwa declaring them disbelievers, when al-Qadir billah asked him about them.

**Sixth issue:** Allah's words, ﴿whoever believes﴾, mean whoever affirms. The ﴿man﴾ in His words "man amana" is in the accusative position as a substitute (badal) for ﴿those who﴾. The fa' in His words "fa-lahum" (then for them) is inserted because of the indefiniteness in "man". ﴿Then for them is their reward﴾ is an inchoative and predicate, in the position of the predicate of inna. It is also good that "man" be in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), and its meaning is the conditional. "Amana" is in the jussive position as the conditional, and the fa' is the response. "Fa-lahum ajruhum" is the predicate of "man", and the whole clause is the predicate of inna. The returning pronoun to ﴿those who﴾ is elided, and its estimate is: "whoever among them believes in Allah." Belief in Allah and the Last Day includes belief in the messengers, the books and the resurrection.

**Seventh issue:** If someone says: why is the pronoun in Allah's words, ﴿then for them is their reward﴾, plural, when "amana" is a singular word and not a plural? It would have been correct to say: "lahu ajruhu" (for him is his reward). The answer is that "man" applies to the singular, the dual and the plural. So it is permissible for the pronoun to return in the singular, the dual or the plural. Allah said: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾ (Yunus: 42), according to the meaning. He also said: "And among them is one who listens to you," according to the wording. The poet said:

*"Greet Salma on your behalf, if you pass by her, and say to her: 'Turn back toward those who stayed behind.'"*

Al-Farazdaq said:

*"Come, if you pledge to me that you will not betray me, we will be like those who, O wolf, keep company."*

He followed the meaning. If he had followed the wording, he would have said: "yasḥabu" and "takhallafu." Allah also said: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit him into gardens﴾, following the wording. Then He said: ﴿abiding therein forever﴾, following the meaning. If he had observed the wording, he would have said "khalidan fiha." When what follows "man" is in accordance with the wording, it is permissible to shift afterward to the meaning, as in this verse. But when what follows it is in accordance with the meaning, it is not permissible to shift afterward to the wording, because confusion would enter the speech. The discussion of Allah's words, ﴿no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾, has already passed [[See p. 329 of this part.]]. And praise be to Allah.

**Eighth issue:** It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that His words, ﴿Indeed, those who believe and those who are Jews﴾ (al-Hajj: 17), and the rest of the verse, are abrogated (mansukh) by His words: ﴿Whoever seeks other than Islam as religion, it will never be accepted from him﴾ (Al 'Imran: 85), and the rest of the verse. Others said: it is not abrogated. It refers to those among the believers who remained firm in their faith in the Prophet, peace be upon him.

[Tafsir]

Allah's words: ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised above you the mount, [saying], "Hold firmly to what We have given you and remember what is in it; perhaps you will become righteous."﴾ (63) ﴿Then you turned away after that. Were it not for the favor of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have been among the losers.﴾ (64)

Allah's words: ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised above you the mount﴾. This verse explains the meaning of His words: ﴿And when We shook the mountain over them as though it were a canopy﴾ (Al-A'raf: 171) [[See vol. 7, p. 313.]]. Abu 'Ubayda said: the meaning is that He shook it and uprooted it from its place. He said: everything you uproot and throw away, you have nataqtahu (torn it out). It was also said: nataqna means "We raised it." Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-nati' is the one who raises, al-nati' is the one who spreads out, and al-nati' is the one who splits open. A woman who is nati' or muntaq is one with many children. Al-Qutabi said: this is taken from natq al-siqa', which is shaking the waterskin until the butter is pulled out of it. He said: His words, "And when We shook the mountain over them as though it were a canopy," mean it was uprooted from its base.

The Tur (mount) has been disputed. It was said: al-Tur is the name of the mountain on which Allah spoke to Musa, peace be upon him, and upon which He sent down the Torah to him, and no other. Ibn Jurayj reported this from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Dahhak reported from him that al-Tur is only the mountain that produces vegetation, not the one that does not. Mujahid and Qatada said: it is any mountain. However, Mujahid said: it is the name for every mountain in Syriac, and Abu al-'Aliya also said this. The discussion of whether there are single words in the Qur'an that are not Arabicized, without further discussion, has already passed in the introduction of the book [[See p. 68 of this part.]]. And praise be to Allah. Al-Bakri claimed that it was named after Tur ibn Isma'il, peace be upon him, and Allah knows best.

**On the cause of the raising of the mount:** When Musa, peace be upon him, brought the Children of Israel the tablets from Allah, containing the Torah, he said to them: "Take them and commit yourselves to them." They said: "No! Unless Allah speaks to us with them as He spoke to you." So they were struck senseless and then revived. He said to them: "Take them." They said: "No." So Allah commanded the angels, and they tore up a mountain from the mountains of Palestine, its length a farsakh by a similar width, and their camp was like that. So it was placed over them like a canopy. They were brought a sea behind them and a fire before their faces. It was said to them: "Take them, and upon you is the covenant that you will not neglect them, or else the mountain will fall upon you." So they prostrated in repentance to Allah and took the Torah under the covenant. Al-Tabari reported from some scholars: "If they had taken it the first time, there would have been no covenant upon them. Their prostration was on one side, because they were watching the mountain out of fear. When Allah had mercy on them, they said: 'There is no prostration more excellent than a prostration which Allah accepted and by which He had mercy on His servants.' So they continued their prostration on one side." Ibn 'Atiyya said: what cannot be sound other than this is that Allah, at the time of their prostration, brought about faith in their hearts, and not that they believed under compulsion while their hearts were not at peace with it. [[Addition from the commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya.]]

Allah's words: ﴿Take﴾, meaning: "So We said: take," and it was elided.

(﴿What We have given you﴾): what We have given you.

(﴿With strength﴾): that is, with diligence and effort, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Suddi. It was also said: with intention and sincerity. Mujahid said: strength is acting upon what is in it. It was also said: with strength, meaning with much study.

(And recall what is in it) — that is, reflect upon it, preserve its commands and its warnings, and do not forget it or neglect it.

I say: this is the purpose of the Books — acting in accordance with what they require, not merely reciting them with the tongue and chanting them in measured tones, for that is (a form of) abandoning them, according to what al-Sha'bi and Ibn 'Uyaynah said. Their statement will come at the words of the Exalted: ﴿Then a party of those who were given the Book cast it behind their backs﴾ [[See vol. 2, p. 41.]] [al-Baqarah: 101].

Al-Nasa'i related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Among the worst of people is a wicked man who recites the Qur'an but does not turn back from any of it." Thus the Prophet (ﷺ) made clear that the intended goal is action, as we have explained.

Malik said: "One may recite the Qur'an while there is no good in him."

Therefore, what was binding on those before us and was taken from them as a covenant is binding on us and obligatory upon us. Allah the Exalted said: "And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord" [[See vol. 15, p. 270]] [al-Zumar: 55]. So we were commanded to follow His Book and act in accordance with its requirements, but we have abandoned that, just as the Jews and Christians abandoned it, and the physical forms of the Books and the copies of the Qur'an remain, benefiting nothing, due to the prevalence of ignorance, the pursuit of leadership, and the following of desires.

al-Tirmidhi related from Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from Abu al-Darda', who said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ), and he raised his gaze to the sky and then said: 'This is a time when knowledge will be snatched away from people, until they are unable to obtain anything from it.' Ziyad ibn Labid al-Ansari said: 'How can it be snatched from us when we have recited the Qur'an? By Allah, we will surely recite it, and we will teach it to our women and our children.' He said: 'May your mother be bereaved of you, O Ziyad! I used to count you among the jurists of Madinah. Are these not the Torah and the Gospel in the hands of the Jews and Christians? What good did they do them?'" and he mentioned the hadith, which will come.

al-Nasa'i also recorded it from the hadith of Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from 'Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i, by a sound chain, and that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Ziyad: "May your mother be bereaved of you, O Ziyad! These are the Torah and the Gospel in the hands of the Jews and Christians."

In the Muwatta', from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said to a man: "You are in a time whose jurists are many and whose reciters are few; its limits of the Qur'an are preserved while its letters are neglected; few ask and many give; they prolong the prayer and shorten the sermon; they put their deeds before their desires. And there will come upon people a time whose jurists are few and whose reciters are many; the letters of the Qur'an are preserved while its limits are neglected; many ask and few give; they prolong the sermon and shorten the prayer; they put their desires before their deeds."

These texts indicate what we have mentioned. Yahya said: I asked Ibn Nafi' about His words, "they put their desires before their deeds," and he said: "It means they follow their desires and leave off acting upon what has been made obligatory upon them."

The discussion of the meaning of His words, "that you may be God-fearing" [[See p. 227 of this part.]], has already preceded, so there is no point in repeating it.

The Exalted said: ﴿Then you turned away﴾. "Tawalla" is of the form "tafa'ala," and its root meaning is turning away and retreating from a thing physically; then it was used, by extension and metaphor, for turning away from commands, religions and beliefs. His words "after that" mean after the proof, which is the taking of the covenant and the lifting of the mountain. His words, "Had it not been for the grace of Allah upon you," — "grace" (fadl) is in the nominative as the subject according to Sibawayh, and the predicate is omitted and may not be stated, because the Arabs dispensed with stating it; but when they wish to state it, they bring "an" (that), and when they bring it they do not omit the predicate. The sense is: "Had it not been for the grace of Allah, He would have overtaken you."

"And His mercy" is conjoined to "grace," meaning His kindness and His respite.

"You would have been" is the answer to "Had it not been."

"Among the losers" is the predicate of "you were." "Loss" means deficiency, and it has already been discussed [[See p. 248.]]. It has been said: His grace is the acceptance of repentance, and "His mercy" is pardon. "Grace" (fadl) is excess beyond what is obligatory, and "ifdal" is doing what is not obligatory. Ibn Faris said in al-Mujmal: "Fadl is increase and good, and ifdal is kindness."

[Tafsir]

The Almighty's saying: ﴿And you certainly knew those among you who transgressed concerning the Sabbath﴾ "*Alimtum*" means you recognized their persons (*'arafтum a'yanahum*). It was also said: you knew their rulings (*ahkamahum*). The difference between the two is that *ma'rifah* (recognition) is directed at the essence of the named thing, while *'ilm* (knowledge) is directed at the states of the named thing. So when you say "I recognized Zayd" (*'araftu Zaydan*), the meaning is his person, and when you say "I knew Zayd" (*'alimtu Zaydan*), the meaning is knowledge of his conditions, whether good or bad. On the first usage the verb takes one object, and this is the view of Sibawayh: "*'Alimtum*" in the sense of *'arafтum*. On the second it takes two objects. Al-Akhfash related: "*Wa-laqad 'alimtu Zaydan wa-lam akun a'lamuhu*" ("I certainly knew Zayd, but I did not know him"). In the Revelation there is: ﴿You do not know them; Allah knows them﴾ [al-Anfal 8:60]. All of these carry the meaning of recognition, so understand this. ﴿Those among you who transgressed concerning the Sabbath﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:65]: "*alladhina*" is linked to the relative clause (*silah*). *I'tida'* means transgressing the limit, and this has already been discussed [see p. 432].

The second matter: al-Nasa'i related from Safwan ibn 'Assal, who said: A Jew said to his companion, "Come, let us go to this Prophet." His companion said to him, "Do not say 'Prophet'; if he hears you, he will have four eyes." (In the version of al-Nasa'i: "If he hears you, he will have four eyes," with the number also in the feminine.) So the two of them came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked him about nine clear signs. He said to them: "Do not associate anything with Allah; do not steal; do not commit adultery; do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right; do not walk with a tale-bearer to a ruler; do not practise sorcery; do not consume usury; do not falsely accuse a chaste woman; do not flee on the day of the march; and upon you, especially the Jews, is that you do not transgress concerning the Sabbath." Then they kissed his hands and feet and said: "We testify that you are a Prophet." He said: "Then what prevents you from following me?" They said: "David supplicated that there should never cease to be a prophet among his descendants, and we fear that if we follow you, the Jews will kill us." Al-Tirmidhi also narrated it and said: "A hasan sahih hadith." Its wording will come in Surah al-Isra' (*Subhan*) [see vol. 10, p. 335], if Allah the Exalted wills.

The third matter: "*fi al-sabt*" means on the day of Saturday, and it is possible that it means "in the ruling of the Sabbath." The first is the view of al-Hasan, and that they took the fish on it in the manner of making it lawful. Ashhab related from Malik, who said: Ibn Ruman claimed that a man among them would take a cord and tie to its end a noose (*wahqah*) [the *wahq* is a rope with a slipknot at one end, cast around the neck of an animal or a person until it is caught; *al-unshuwah* is a knot easily loosened, like the knot of a drawstring when pulled], and cast it into the tail of the fish, and at the other end of the cord he would fix a peg and leave it so until Sunday. Then people came to imitate what they saw, since those who did it were not tested, until the catching of fish became common and was carried on in the markets, and the wicked openly hunted it. A group then rose up, forbade it, openly voiced the prohibition, and withdrew. It is said that those who forbade said: "We will not live alongside you," so they divided the town with a wall. One day the forbidders awoke in their assemblies, and none of the transgressors had come out. They said: "The people have some matter." So they climbed the wall and looked, and behold, they were apes. They opened the door and entered upon them. The apes recognized their kin among the humans, but the humans did not recognize their kin among the apes. The apes began to come to their relatives among the humans, sniffing their clothes and weeping. He would say: "Did we not forbid you?" And she would shake her head: "Yes." Qatadah said: "The young men became apes, and the elders became swine, and none was saved except those who forbade, and the rest perished."

Al-Zajjaj said: "Some people said it is possible that these apes were of them." This was chosen by al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi. But the majority said: a transformed creature (*al-mamsukh*) does not produce offspring. The apes and swine and others were in existence before that, and those whom Allah transformed have perished and no offspring remained for them, because the wrath and the punishment had afflicted them, so they had no settled existence in the world after three days. Ibn 'Abbas said: No transformed creature ever lived beyond three days; it did not eat, did not drink, and did not produce offspring. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is established, that the transformed creature does not produce offspring, does not eat, does not drink, and does not live more than three days. I say: This is the sound of the two views.

As for what Ibn al-'Arabi and others argued in support of the first view from the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "A community of the Children of Israel was lost, and it is not known what became of it; and I do not think it was anything but the mice. Do you not see that when camel's milk is placed before them they do not drink it, but when sheep's milk is placed before them they drink it?" It was related by Abu Hurayrah and recorded by Muslim; and the hadith of the lizard (*dabb*) was also related by Muslim from Abu Sa'id and Jabir. Jabir said: The Prophet (ﷺ) was brought a lizard, and he refused to eat it and said: "I do not know, perhaps it is one of the communities that were transformed." This is interpreted according to what will come.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: In Bukhari, from 'Amr ibn Maymun, who said: "In the pre-Islamic period I saw an ape that had committed adultery, and they stoned her, and I stoned her with them." This is established in some copies of Bukhari and absent from others; the phrase "had committed adultery" is established in the text of the hadith in some copies but is absent in the copies of some. Ibn al-'Arabi said: If it is said: "Was it as if the animals retained among them knowledge of the laws, so that they inherited them from one generation to another until the time of 'Amr?" We say: Yes, it was so, because the Jews altered the stoning, so Allah willed to establish it among their transformed ones, so that it would be a stronger proof against them for what they denied and altered, and so that their books and stones and transformed ones would bear witness against them, that they might know that Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal, and counts what they change and alter, and establishes the proof against them from where they do not perceive, and gives victory to His Prophet, peace be upon him, while they are not given victory.

I say: This is his statement in *al-Ahkam*, and there is no proof in any of it. As for what he mentioned about the story of 'Amr, al-Humaydi mentioned in *Jam' al-Sahihayn* that Abu Mas'ud al-Dimashqi related that 'Amr ibn Maymun al-Awdi has in the Two Sahihs a narration through Husayn from him, who said: "In the pre-Islamic period I saw an ape around which a group of apes gathered, and they stoned her, and I stoned her with them." Thus Abu Mas'ud related it and did not mention in which place Bukhari had brought it out in his book. We searched for it and found it in some copies and not in all of them; it is mentioned in the Book of the Days of the Jahiliyyah. Nothing of this report about the apes is found at all in the narration of al-Nu'aymi from al-Firabri, and perhaps it is one of the insertions in the book of Bukhari.

What Bukhari said in *al-Tarikh al-Kabir*: Nu'aym ibn Hammad told me, Hushaym informed us from Abu Balj and Husayn, from 'Amr ibn Maymun, who said: "I saw in the pre-Islamic period an ape around which apes gathered, and they stoned her, and I stoned her with them." In it there is no "had committed adultery." If this narration is sound, then Bukhari brought it out only as an indication that 'Amr ibn Maymun had reached the pre-Islamic period, and he did not concern himself with the assumption he made about it in the pre-Islamic period.

Abu 'Umar mentioned in *al-Isti'ab*: "'Amr ibn Maymun, whose kunyah is Abu 'Abd Allah, is counted among the senior Successors (*tabi'un*) of the Kufans, and he is the one who saw the stoning in the pre-Islamic period among the apes, if that is sound, because its transmitters are unknown." Bukhari mentioned it from Nu'aym from Hushaym from Husayn from 'Amr ibn Maymun al-Awdi in abridged form: "I saw in the pre-Islamic period an ape that had committed adultery, and they stoned her—meaning the apes—and I stoned her with them." 'Abbad ibn al-'Awwam related it from Husayn, as Hushaym related it, in abridged form. As for the story in full, it revolves around 'Abd al-Malik ibn Muslim from 'Isa ibn Hittan, and neither of them is one whose narrations are used as proof. This, according to the body of scholars of knowledge, is objectionable: attributing fornication to one who is not legally accountable, and enforcing the prescribed penalties upon animals. And if it were sound, they would have been of the jinn, because the obligations of worship apply to humans and jinn and not to others."

As for his saying (ﷺ) in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah: "And I do not think it was anything but the mice," and in the case of the lizard: "I do not know, perhaps it is one of the communities that were transformed," and what is similar to it, it was only a supposition and a fear that the lizard and the mouse and others might be among those transformed, and this was a conjecture from him (ﷺ) before it was revealed to him that Allah had not granted offspring to transformed creatures. When this was revealed to him, that apprehension left him, and he knew that the lizard and the mouse were not among the transformed. At that point he informed us with his saying (ﷺ) to one who asked him about the apes and swine: "Are they of those that were transformed?" He said: "Allah does not destroy a people or punish a people and then give them offspring. The apes and swine existed before that." This is a clear, sound text, related by Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and recorded by Muslim in the Book of Destiny (*Kitab al-Qadar*). The reports are established that the lizard was eaten in his presence and at his table, and he did not object, which indicates the soundness of what we have mentioned. And with Allah is our success.

It was related from Mujahid in interpreting this verse that only their hearts were transformed, and their understandings were returned like the understandings of apes. No other exegete, as far as I know, has said this. And Allah knows best.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿So We said to them: "Be apes, despised."﴾ "*Qiradah*" is the predicate of *kana* (*khabar kana*). "*Khasi'in*" is an adjective (*na't*); if you wish, you may make it a second predicate of *kana*, or a circumstantial state (*hal*) from the pronoun in "*kuunu*." Its meaning is "driven away" (*mub'adin*). It is said: *khasa'tuhu* (I drove him away), so he was driven away (*fakhasa'a* and *khusi'a*), and *inkhasa'a*, meaning: I drove him away, so he withdrew. The Almighty's saying: ﴿The sight will return to you dazzled (*khasi'an*)﴾ [al-Mulk 67:4], meaning driven away. And His saying: ﴿Be driven away therein﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:108], meaning withdraw, withdrawal in wrath. Al-Kisa'i said: "*Khasa'a al-rajulu khusu'an*," and "*khasa'tuhu khas'an*." And *al-khasi'* may mean the abased, the humiliated. It is said: *qama'a al-rajulu qama'an wa-qama'atan*, meaning he became abased, and he is the abased, humiliated one. And *aqma'tuhu* means I belittled him and humbled him, so he is *qami*, on the pattern of *fa'il*.

**First issue:** Allah's words, ﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾, mean those who affirmed Muhammad (ﷺ). Sufyan said that what is intended is the hypocrites. It is as if He said: "Those who believe outwardly." This is why He paired them with the Jews, the Christians and the Sabians. Then He explained the ruling for whoever among all of them believes in Allah and the Last Day.

**Second issue:** Allah's words, ﴿and those who are Jews﴾. The meaning is that they became Jews (yahud). They were named after Yahudha (Judah), the eldest son of Ya'qub (Jacob), peace be upon him. The Arabs changed the dhal to a dal, because when a non-Arabic word is Arabicized, it is altered from its original pronunciation. It was also said that they were named this for their repentance from worshipping the calf. Hada means "he repented," and al-ha'id means "the penitent." The poet said:

*"Indeed, I am a man who, out of love for her, is penitent."*

That is, a penitent. In the Revelation (Tanzil) is Allah's word: ﴿Indeed, we have turned back to You﴾ (Al-A'raf: 156), meaning "we have repented." It is said: hada al-qawm yahudu hawdan wa-hiyadatan, when they repented. Ibn 'Arafa said: "hudna ilayka" means "we have settled into your command." Al-hawada means calm and reconciliation. He said: from this is Allah's word: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and those who are Jews﴾. Abu al-Sammal read "hadu" with a fatha on the dal.

**Third issue:** Allah's words, ﴿and the Christians (al-nasara)﴾. It is a plural whose singular is nasrani. It was also said: Nasran, with the yaa dropped, and this is the view of Sibawayh. The feminine is nasrana, like nadman and nadmana. It is an indefinite noun that is made definite with the alif and lam. The poet said:

*"She turned away as one turns from what is not lawful for him, from the cupbearer of the Nasara before the Fisah, who are fasting."* [[The poet is al-Namir ibn Tawlab, describing a she-camel to whom water was offered and who refused it. In the manuscripts of the original: "al-Subh" with a ba'. The correction is from Sibawayh's book. Al-Fisah: the breaking of the fast of the Christians, which is a feast for them.]]

Here he described it with the indefinite form. Al-Khalil said: the singular of al-nasara is nasri, like mahri and mahara. Sibawayh cited as evidence:

*"You see him, when the evening falls, inclining to the faith (of Abraham), and in the morning he is before him, a Christian who is bright."*

He also cited:
