*"Both of them fell, and her head bowed, as the head of a Christian woman bows when she does not incline in prayer."* [[The line is by Abu al-Akhzar al-Hammani, describing two she-camels that lowered their heads from exhaustion. He likened the camel's head to the head of a Christian woman when she bows in her prayer. (From the commentary on the Qamus and Lisan.)]]

It is said: asjada, when he inclined. But nasran and nasrana are not used except with the nisba yaa, because they said: rajul nasrani (a Christian man) and imra'a nasraniyya (a Christian woman). Nassarahu means "he made him a Christian." In a hadith: "His parents make him a Jew or make him a Christian." He, peace be upon him, also said: "No one from this community hears of me, a Jew or a Christian, and then does not believe in what I was sent with, except that he will be among the companions of the Fire." Some plurals have come in forms other than their singular's usual form, and by analogy the plural is al-nasraniyyun. Then it was said: they were named after a village called Nasira, where 'Isa, peace be upon him, used to dwell, so he was attributed to it and called 'Isa al-Nasiri. When his followers were attributed to him, they were called al-Nasara. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada. Al-Jawhari said: Nasran is a village in Syria to which the Christians are attributed, and it is also called Nasira. It was also said: they were named this for the support (nusra) some of them gave to others. The poet said:

*"When I saw the Nabat as helpers, I hitched up my garment above my knees. I became for them a neighbor among the Nasara."*

It was also said: they were named this because of His word: ﴿Who are my helpers in the way of Allah?' The disciples said: 'We are the helpers of Allah'﴾ (Al 'Imran: 52).

**Fourth issue:** Allah's words, ﴿and the Sabians (al-Sabi'in)﴾. It is the plural of sabi'. It was also said: sabin. For this reason they differed about its hamza. Most readers pronounced the hamza, except Nafi'. Whoever pronounced the hamza took it from sabi'at al-nujum (the stars rose) when they appeared, and sabat thaniyyat al-ghulam (the boy's front tooth came out) when it emerged. Whoever did not pronounce the hamza took it from saba, yasbu, when he inclined. In the language, the sabi' is one who leaves and turns from one religion to another. For this reason the Arabs used to say of one who had embraced Islam: "He has sabi'a (converted)." So the Sabians had departed from the religion of the People of the Book.

**Fifth issue:** There is no disagreement that the Jews and the Christians are People of the Book. Because of their Book, it is permissible to marry their women and eat their food, as will be explained in Surat al-Ma'ida [[See vol. 6, p. 76.]], and to impose the jizya (poll tax) on them, as will come in Surat Bara'a [[See vol. 8, p. 110.]], if Allah wills. But there was disagreement about the Sabians. Al-Suddi said: they are a sect of the People of the Book. Ishaq ibn Rahawayh said the same. Ibn al-Mundhir said: Ishaq said there is no harm in eating the slaughtered animals (dhaba'ih) of the Sabians, because they are a group of the People of the Book. Abu Hanifa said: there is no harm in eating their slaughtered animals or marrying their women. Al-Khalil said: they are a people whose religion resembles the religion of the Christians, except that their qibla is toward the south wind, and they claim they are upon the religion of Nuh, peace be upon him. Mujahid, al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Najih said: they are a people whose religion is a mixture of Judaism and Magianism, and their slaughtered animals may not be eaten. Ibn 'Abbas said: nor may their women be married. Al-Hasan also said, and Qatada: they are a people who worship the angels, pray facing the qibla, recite the Zabur (Psalms), and pray the five prayers. Ziyad ibn Abi Sufyan saw them and wished to remove the jizya from them when he learned that they worshipped the angels. What has been gathered of their doctrine, according to what some of our scholars mentioned, is that they are monotheists who believe in the influence of the stars and that the stars are effective agents. For this reason Abu Sa'id al-Istakhri issued a fatwa declaring them disbelievers, when al-Qadir billah asked him about them.

**Sixth issue:** Allah's words, ﴿whoever believes﴾, mean whoever affirms. The ﴿man﴾ in His words "man amana" is in the accusative position as a substitute (badal) for ﴿those who﴾. The fa' in His words "fa-lahum" (then for them) is inserted because of the indefiniteness in "man". ﴿Then for them is their reward﴾ is an inchoative and predicate, in the position of the predicate of inna. It is also good that "man" be in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), and its meaning is the conditional. "Amana" is in the jussive position as the conditional, and the fa' is the response. "Fa-lahum ajruhum" is the predicate of "man", and the whole clause is the predicate of inna. The returning pronoun to ﴿those who﴾ is elided, and its estimate is: "whoever among them believes in Allah." Belief in Allah and the Last Day includes belief in the messengers, the books and the resurrection.

**Seventh issue:** If someone says: why is the pronoun in Allah's words, ﴿then for them is their reward﴾, plural, when "amana" is a singular word and not a plural? It would have been correct to say: "lahu ajruhu" (for him is his reward). The answer is that "man" applies to the singular, the dual and the plural. So it is permissible for the pronoun to return in the singular, the dual or the plural. Allah said: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾ (Yunus: 42), according to the meaning. He also said: "And among them is one who listens to you," according to the wording. The poet said:

*"Greet Salma on your behalf, if you pass by her, and say to her: 'Turn back toward those who stayed behind.'"*

Al-Farazdaq said:

*"Come, if you pledge to me that you will not betray me, we will be like those who, O wolf, keep company."*

He followed the meaning. If he had followed the wording, he would have said: "yasḥabu" and "takhallafu." Allah also said: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit him into gardens﴾, following the wording. Then He said: ﴿abiding therein forever﴾, following the meaning. If he had observed the wording, he would have said "khalidan fiha." When what follows "man" is in accordance with the wording, it is permissible to shift afterward to the meaning, as in this verse. But when what follows it is in accordance with the meaning, it is not permissible to shift afterward to the wording, because confusion would enter the speech. The discussion of Allah's words, ﴿no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾, has already passed [[See p. 329 of this part.]]. And praise be to Allah.

**Eighth issue:** It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that His words, ﴿Indeed, those who believe and those who are Jews﴾ (al-Hajj: 17), and the rest of the verse, are abrogated (mansukh) by His words: ﴿Whoever seeks other than Islam as religion, it will never be accepted from him﴾ (Al 'Imran: 85), and the rest of the verse. Others said: it is not abrogated. It refers to those among the believers who remained firm in their faith in the Prophet, peace be upon him.

[Tafsir]

Allah's words: ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised above you the mount, [saying], "Hold firmly to what We have given you and remember what is in it; perhaps you will become righteous."﴾ (63) ﴿Then you turned away after that. Were it not for the favor of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have been among the losers.﴾ (64)

Allah's words: ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised above you the mount﴾. This verse explains the meaning of His words: ﴿And when We shook the mountain over them as though it were a canopy﴾ (Al-A'raf: 171) [[See vol. 7, p. 313.]]. Abu 'Ubayda said: the meaning is that He shook it and uprooted it from its place. He said: everything you uproot and throw away, you have nataqtahu (torn it out). It was also said: nataqna means "We raised it." Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-nati' is the one who raises, al-nati' is the one who spreads out, and al-nati' is the one who splits open. A woman who is nati' or muntaq is one with many children. Al-Qutabi said: this is taken from natq al-siqa', which is shaking the waterskin until the butter is pulled out of it. He said: His words, "And when We shook the mountain over them as though it were a canopy," mean it was uprooted from its base.

The Tur (mount) has been disputed. It was said: al-Tur is the name of the mountain on which Allah spoke to Musa, peace be upon him, and upon which He sent down the Torah to him, and no other. Ibn Jurayj reported this from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Dahhak reported from him that al-Tur is only the mountain that produces vegetation, not the one that does not. Mujahid and Qatada said: it is any mountain. However, Mujahid said: it is the name for every mountain in Syriac, and Abu al-'Aliya also said this. The discussion of whether there are single words in the Qur'an that are not Arabicized, without further discussion, has already passed in the introduction of the book [[See p. 68 of this part.]]. And praise be to Allah. Al-Bakri claimed that it was named after Tur ibn Isma'il, peace be upon him, and Allah knows best.

**On the cause of the raising of the mount:** When Musa, peace be upon him, brought the Children of Israel the tablets from Allah, containing the Torah, he said to them: "Take them and commit yourselves to them." They said: "No! Unless Allah speaks to us with them as He spoke to you." So they were struck senseless and then revived. He said to them: "Take them." They said: "No." So Allah commanded the angels, and they tore up a mountain from the mountains of Palestine, its length a farsakh by a similar width, and their camp was like that. So it was placed over them like a canopy. They were brought a sea behind them and a fire before their faces. It was said to them: "Take them, and upon you is the covenant that you will not neglect them, or else the mountain will fall upon you." So they prostrated in repentance to Allah and took the Torah under the covenant. Al-Tabari reported from some scholars: "If they had taken it the first time, there would have been no covenant upon them. Their prostration was on one side, because they were watching the mountain out of fear. When Allah had mercy on them, they said: 'There is no prostration more excellent than a prostration which Allah accepted and by which He had mercy on His servants.' So they continued their prostration on one side." Ibn 'Atiyya said: what cannot be sound other than this is that Allah, at the time of their prostration, brought about faith in their hearts, and not that they believed under compulsion while their hearts were not at peace with it. [[Addition from the commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya.]]

Allah's words: ﴿Take﴾, meaning: "So We said: take," and it was elided.

(﴿What We have given you﴾): what We have given you.

(﴿With strength﴾): that is, with diligence and effort, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Suddi. It was also said: with intention and sincerity. Mujahid said: strength is acting upon what is in it. It was also said: with strength, meaning with much study.

(And recall what is in it) — that is, reflect upon it, preserve its commands and its warnings, and do not forget it or neglect it.

I say: this is the purpose of the Books — acting in accordance with what they require, not merely reciting them with the tongue and chanting them in measured tones, for that is (a form of) abandoning them, according to what al-Sha'bi and Ibn 'Uyaynah said. Their statement will come at the words of the Exalted: ﴿Then a party of those who were given the Book cast it behind their backs﴾ [[See vol. 2, p. 41.]] [al-Baqarah: 101].

Al-Nasa'i related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Among the worst of people is a wicked man who recites the Qur'an but does not turn back from any of it." Thus the Prophet (ﷺ) made clear that the intended goal is action, as we have explained.

Malik said: "One may recite the Qur'an while there is no good in him."

Therefore, what was binding on those before us and was taken from them as a covenant is binding on us and obligatory upon us. Allah the Exalted said: "And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord" [[See vol. 15, p. 270]] [al-Zumar: 55]. So we were commanded to follow His Book and act in accordance with its requirements, but we have abandoned that, just as the Jews and Christians abandoned it, and the physical forms of the Books and the copies of the Qur'an remain, benefiting nothing, due to the prevalence of ignorance, the pursuit of leadership, and the following of desires.

al-Tirmidhi related from Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from Abu al-Darda', who said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ), and he raised his gaze to the sky and then said: 'This is a time when knowledge will be snatched away from people, until they are unable to obtain anything from it.' Ziyad ibn Labid al-Ansari said: 'How can it be snatched from us when we have recited the Qur'an? By Allah, we will surely recite it, and we will teach it to our women and our children.' He said: 'May your mother be bereaved of you, O Ziyad! I used to count you among the jurists of Madinah. Are these not the Torah and the Gospel in the hands of the Jews and Christians? What good did they do them?'" and he mentioned the hadith, which will come.

al-Nasa'i also recorded it from the hadith of Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from 'Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i, by a sound chain, and that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Ziyad: "May your mother be bereaved of you, O Ziyad! These are the Torah and the Gospel in the hands of the Jews and Christians."

In the Muwatta', from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said to a man: "You are in a time whose jurists are many and whose reciters are few; its limits of the Qur'an are preserved while its letters are neglected; few ask and many give; they prolong the prayer and shorten the sermon; they put their deeds before their desires. And there will come upon people a time whose jurists are few and whose reciters are many; the letters of the Qur'an are preserved while its limits are neglected; many ask and few give; they prolong the sermon and shorten the prayer; they put their desires before their deeds."

These texts indicate what we have mentioned. Yahya said: I asked Ibn Nafi' about His words, "they put their desires before their deeds," and he said: "It means they follow their desires and leave off acting upon what has been made obligatory upon them."

The discussion of the meaning of His words, "that you may be God-fearing" [[See p. 227 of this part.]], has already preceded, so there is no point in repeating it.

The Exalted said: ﴿Then you turned away﴾. "Tawalla" is of the form "tafa'ala," and its root meaning is turning away and retreating from a thing physically; then it was used, by extension and metaphor, for turning away from commands, religions and beliefs. His words "after that" mean after the proof, which is the taking of the covenant and the lifting of the mountain. His words, "Had it not been for the grace of Allah upon you," — "grace" (fadl) is in the nominative as the subject according to Sibawayh, and the predicate is omitted and may not be stated, because the Arabs dispensed with stating it; but when they wish to state it, they bring "an" (that), and when they bring it they do not omit the predicate. The sense is: "Had it not been for the grace of Allah, He would have overtaken you."

"And His mercy" is conjoined to "grace," meaning His kindness and His respite.

"You would have been" is the answer to "Had it not been."

"Among the losers" is the predicate of "you were." "Loss" means deficiency, and it has already been discussed [[See p. 248.]]. It has been said: His grace is the acceptance of repentance, and "His mercy" is pardon. "Grace" (fadl) is excess beyond what is obligatory, and "ifdal" is doing what is not obligatory. Ibn Faris said in al-Mujmal: "Fadl is increase and good, and ifdal is kindness."

[Tafsir]

The Almighty's saying: ﴿And you certainly knew those among you who transgressed concerning the Sabbath﴾ "*Alimtum*" means you recognized their persons (*'arafтum a'yanahum*). It was also said: you knew their rulings (*ahkamahum*). The difference between the two is that *ma'rifah* (recognition) is directed at the essence of the named thing, while *'ilm* (knowledge) is directed at the states of the named thing. So when you say "I recognized Zayd" (*'araftu Zaydan*), the meaning is his person, and when you say "I knew Zayd" (*'alimtu Zaydan*), the meaning is knowledge of his conditions, whether good or bad. On the first usage the verb takes one object, and this is the view of Sibawayh: "*'Alimtum*" in the sense of *'arafтum*. On the second it takes two objects. Al-Akhfash related: "*Wa-laqad 'alimtu Zaydan wa-lam akun a'lamuhu*" ("I certainly knew Zayd, but I did not know him"). In the Revelation there is: ﴿You do not know them; Allah knows them﴾ [al-Anfal 8:60]. All of these carry the meaning of recognition, so understand this. ﴿Those among you who transgressed concerning the Sabbath﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:65]: "*alladhina*" is linked to the relative clause (*silah*). *I'tida'* means transgressing the limit, and this has already been discussed [see p. 432].

The second matter: al-Nasa'i related from Safwan ibn 'Assal, who said: A Jew said to his companion, "Come, let us go to this Prophet." His companion said to him, "Do not say 'Prophet'; if he hears you, he will have four eyes." (In the version of al-Nasa'i: "If he hears you, he will have four eyes," with the number also in the feminine.) So the two of them came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked him about nine clear signs. He said to them: "Do not associate anything with Allah; do not steal; do not commit adultery; do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right; do not walk with a tale-bearer to a ruler; do not practise sorcery; do not consume usury; do not falsely accuse a chaste woman; do not flee on the day of the march; and upon you, especially the Jews, is that you do not transgress concerning the Sabbath." Then they kissed his hands and feet and said: "We testify that you are a Prophet." He said: "Then what prevents you from following me?" They said: "David supplicated that there should never cease to be a prophet among his descendants, and we fear that if we follow you, the Jews will kill us." Al-Tirmidhi also narrated it and said: "A hasan sahih hadith." Its wording will come in Surah al-Isra' (*Subhan*) [see vol. 10, p. 335], if Allah the Exalted wills.

The third matter: "*fi al-sabt*" means on the day of Saturday, and it is possible that it means "in the ruling of the Sabbath." The first is the view of al-Hasan, and that they took the fish on it in the manner of making it lawful. Ashhab related from Malik, who said: Ibn Ruman claimed that a man among them would take a cord and tie to its end a noose (*wahqah*) [the *wahq* is a rope with a slipknot at one end, cast around the neck of an animal or a person until it is caught; *al-unshuwah* is a knot easily loosened, like the knot of a drawstring when pulled], and cast it into the tail of the fish, and at the other end of the cord he would fix a peg and leave it so until Sunday. Then people came to imitate what they saw, since those who did it were not tested, until the catching of fish became common and was carried on in the markets, and the wicked openly hunted it. A group then rose up, forbade it, openly voiced the prohibition, and withdrew. It is said that those who forbade said: "We will not live alongside you," so they divided the town with a wall. One day the forbidders awoke in their assemblies, and none of the transgressors had come out. They said: "The people have some matter." So they climbed the wall and looked, and behold, they were apes. They opened the door and entered upon them. The apes recognized their kin among the humans, but the humans did not recognize their kin among the apes. The apes began to come to their relatives among the humans, sniffing their clothes and weeping. He would say: "Did we not forbid you?" And she would shake her head: "Yes." Qatadah said: "The young men became apes, and the elders became swine, and none was saved except those who forbade, and the rest perished."

Al-Zajjaj said: "Some people said it is possible that these apes were of them." This was chosen by al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi. But the majority said: a transformed creature (*al-mamsukh*) does not produce offspring. The apes and swine and others were in existence before that, and those whom Allah transformed have perished and no offspring remained for them, because the wrath and the punishment had afflicted them, so they had no settled existence in the world after three days. Ibn 'Abbas said: No transformed creature ever lived beyond three days; it did not eat, did not drink, and did not produce offspring. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is established, that the transformed creature does not produce offspring, does not eat, does not drink, and does not live more than three days. I say: This is the sound of the two views.

As for what Ibn al-'Arabi and others argued in support of the first view from the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "A community of the Children of Israel was lost, and it is not known what became of it; and I do not think it was anything but the mice. Do you not see that when camel's milk is placed before them they do not drink it, but when sheep's milk is placed before them they drink it?" It was related by Abu Hurayrah and recorded by Muslim; and the hadith of the lizard (*dabb*) was also related by Muslim from Abu Sa'id and Jabir. Jabir said: The Prophet (ﷺ) was brought a lizard, and he refused to eat it and said: "I do not know, perhaps it is one of the communities that were transformed." This is interpreted according to what will come.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: In Bukhari, from 'Amr ibn Maymun, who said: "In the pre-Islamic period I saw an ape that had committed adultery, and they stoned her, and I stoned her with them." This is established in some copies of Bukhari and absent from others; the phrase "had committed adultery" is established in the text of the hadith in some copies but is absent in the copies of some. Ibn al-'Arabi said: If it is said: "Was it as if the animals retained among them knowledge of the laws, so that they inherited them from one generation to another until the time of 'Amr?" We say: Yes, it was so, because the Jews altered the stoning, so Allah willed to establish it among their transformed ones, so that it would be a stronger proof against them for what they denied and altered, and so that their books and stones and transformed ones would bear witness against them, that they might know that Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal, and counts what they change and alter, and establishes the proof against them from where they do not perceive, and gives victory to His Prophet, peace be upon him, while they are not given victory.

I say: This is his statement in *al-Ahkam*, and there is no proof in any of it. As for what he mentioned about the story of 'Amr, al-Humaydi mentioned in *Jam' al-Sahihayn* that Abu Mas'ud al-Dimashqi related that 'Amr ibn Maymun al-Awdi has in the Two Sahihs a narration through Husayn from him, who said: "In the pre-Islamic period I saw an ape around which a group of apes gathered, and they stoned her, and I stoned her with them." Thus Abu Mas'ud related it and did not mention in which place Bukhari had brought it out in his book. We searched for it and found it in some copies and not in all of them; it is mentioned in the Book of the Days of the Jahiliyyah. Nothing of this report about the apes is found at all in the narration of al-Nu'aymi from al-Firabri, and perhaps it is one of the insertions in the book of Bukhari.

What Bukhari said in *al-Tarikh al-Kabir*: Nu'aym ibn Hammad told me, Hushaym informed us from Abu Balj and Husayn, from 'Amr ibn Maymun, who said: "I saw in the pre-Islamic period an ape around which apes gathered, and they stoned her, and I stoned her with them." In it there is no "had committed adultery." If this narration is sound, then Bukhari brought it out only as an indication that 'Amr ibn Maymun had reached the pre-Islamic period, and he did not concern himself with the assumption he made about it in the pre-Islamic period.

Abu 'Umar mentioned in *al-Isti'ab*: "'Amr ibn Maymun, whose kunyah is Abu 'Abd Allah, is counted among the senior Successors (*tabi'un*) of the Kufans, and he is the one who saw the stoning in the pre-Islamic period among the apes, if that is sound, because its transmitters are unknown." Bukhari mentioned it from Nu'aym from Hushaym from Husayn from 'Amr ibn Maymun al-Awdi in abridged form: "I saw in the pre-Islamic period an ape that had committed adultery, and they stoned her—meaning the apes—and I stoned her with them." 'Abbad ibn al-'Awwam related it from Husayn, as Hushaym related it, in abridged form. As for the story in full, it revolves around 'Abd al-Malik ibn Muslim from 'Isa ibn Hittan, and neither of them is one whose narrations are used as proof. This, according to the body of scholars of knowledge, is objectionable: attributing fornication to one who is not legally accountable, and enforcing the prescribed penalties upon animals. And if it were sound, they would have been of the jinn, because the obligations of worship apply to humans and jinn and not to others."

As for his saying (ﷺ) in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah: "And I do not think it was anything but the mice," and in the case of the lizard: "I do not know, perhaps it is one of the communities that were transformed," and what is similar to it, it was only a supposition and a fear that the lizard and the mouse and others might be among those transformed, and this was a conjecture from him (ﷺ) before it was revealed to him that Allah had not granted offspring to transformed creatures. When this was revealed to him, that apprehension left him, and he knew that the lizard and the mouse were not among the transformed. At that point he informed us with his saying (ﷺ) to one who asked him about the apes and swine: "Are they of those that were transformed?" He said: "Allah does not destroy a people or punish a people and then give them offspring. The apes and swine existed before that." This is a clear, sound text, related by Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and recorded by Muslim in the Book of Destiny (*Kitab al-Qadar*). The reports are established that the lizard was eaten in his presence and at his table, and he did not object, which indicates the soundness of what we have mentioned. And with Allah is our success.

It was related from Mujahid in interpreting this verse that only their hearts were transformed, and their understandings were returned like the understandings of apes. No other exegete, as far as I know, has said this. And Allah knows best.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿So We said to them: "Be apes, despised."﴾ "*Qiradah*" is the predicate of *kana* (*khabar kana*). "*Khasi'in*" is an adjective (*na't*); if you wish, you may make it a second predicate of *kana*, or a circumstantial state (*hal*) from the pronoun in "*kuunu*." Its meaning is "driven away" (*mub'adin*). It is said: *khasa'tuhu* (I drove him away), so he was driven away (*fakhasa'a* and *khusi'a*), and *inkhasa'a*, meaning: I drove him away, so he withdrew. The Almighty's saying: ﴿The sight will return to you dazzled (*khasi'an*)﴾ [al-Mulk 67:4], meaning driven away. And His saying: ﴿Be driven away therein﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:108], meaning withdraw, withdrawal in wrath. Al-Kisa'i said: "*Khasa'a al-rajulu khusu'an*," and "*khasa'tuhu khas'an*." And *al-khasi'* may mean the abased, the humiliated. It is said: *qama'a al-rajulu qama'an wa-qama'atan*, meaning he became abased, and he is the abased, humiliated one. And *aqma'tuhu* means I belittled him and humbled him, so he is *qami*, on the pattern of *fa'il*.

**First issue:** Allah's words, ﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾, mean those who affirmed Muhammad (ﷺ). Sufyan said that what is intended is the hypocrites. It is as if He said: "Those who believe outwardly." This is why He paired them with the Jews, the Christians and the Sabians. Then He explained the ruling for whoever among all of them believes in Allah and the Last Day.

**Second issue:** Allah's words, ﴿and those who are Jews﴾. The meaning is that they became Jews (yahud). They were named after Yahudha (Judah), the eldest son of Ya'qub (Jacob), peace be upon him. The Arabs changed the dhal to a dal, because when a non-Arabic word is Arabicized, it is altered from its original pronunciation. It was also said that they were named this for their repentance from worshipping the calf. Hada means "he repented," and al-ha'id means "the penitent." The poet said:

*"Indeed, I am a man who, out of love for her, is penitent."*

That is, a penitent. In the Revelation (Tanzil) is Allah's word: ﴿Indeed, we have turned back to You﴾ (Al-A'raf: 156), meaning "we have repented." It is said: hada al-qawm yahudu hawdan wa-hiyadatan, when they repented. Ibn 'Arafa said: "hudna ilayka" means "we have settled into your command." Al-hawada means calm and reconciliation. He said: from this is Allah's word: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and those who are Jews﴾. Abu al-Sammal read "hadu" with a fatha on the dal.

**Third issue:** Allah's words, ﴿and the Christians (al-nasara)﴾. It is a plural whose singular is nasrani. It was also said: Nasran, with the yaa dropped, and this is the view of Sibawayh. The feminine is nasrana, like nadman and nadmana. It is an indefinite noun that is made definite with the alif and lam. The poet said:

*"She turned away as one turns from what is not lawful for him, from the cupbearer of the Nasara before the Fisah, who are fasting."* [[The poet is al-Namir ibn Tawlab, describing a she-camel to whom water was offered and who refused it. In the manuscripts of the original: "al-Subh" with a ba'. The correction is from Sibawayh's book. Al-Fisah: the breaking of the fast of the Christians, which is a feast for them.]]

Here he described it with the indefinite form. Al-Khalil said: the singular of al-nasara is nasri, like mahri and mahara. Sibawayh cited as evidence:

*"You see him, when the evening falls, inclining to the faith (of Abraham), and in the morning he is before him, a Christian who is bright."*

He also cited:

*"Both of them fell, and her head bowed, as the head of a Christian woman bows when she does not incline in prayer."* [[The line is by Abu al-Akhzar al-Hammani, describing two she-camels that lowered their heads from exhaustion. He likened the camel's head to the head of a Christian woman when she bows in her prayer. (From the commentary on the Qamus and Lisan.)]]

It is said: asjada, when he inclined. But nasran and nasrana are not used except with the nisba yaa, because they said: rajul nasrani (a Christian man) and imra'a nasraniyya (a Christian woman). Nassarahu means "he made him a Christian." In a hadith: "His parents make him a Jew or make him a Christian." He, peace be upon him, also said: "No one from this community hears of me, a Jew or a Christian, and then does not believe in what I was sent with, except that he will be among the companions of the Fire." Some plurals have come in forms other than their singular's usual form, and by analogy the plural is al-nasraniyyun. Then it was said: they were named after a village called Nasira, where 'Isa, peace be upon him, used to dwell, so he was attributed to it and called 'Isa al-Nasiri. When his followers were attributed to him, they were called al-Nasara. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada. Al-Jawhari said: Nasran is a village in Syria to which the Christians are attributed, and it is also called Nasira. It was also said: they were named this for the support (nusra) some of them gave to others. The poet said:

*"When I saw the Nabat as helpers, I hitched up my garment above my knees. I became for them a neighbor among the Nasara."*

It was also said: they were named this because of His word: ﴿Who are my helpers in the way of Allah?' The disciples said: 'We are the helpers of Allah'﴾ (Al 'Imran: 52).

**Fourth issue:** Allah's words, ﴿and the Sabians (al-Sabi'in)﴾. It is the plural of sabi'. It was also said: sabin. For this reason they differed about its hamza. Most readers pronounced the hamza, except Nafi'. Whoever pronounced the hamza took it from sabi'at al-nujum (the stars rose) when they appeared, and sabat thaniyyat al-ghulam (the boy's front tooth came out) when it emerged. Whoever did not pronounce the hamza took it from saba, yasbu, when he inclined. In the language, the sabi' is one who leaves and turns from one religion to another. For this reason the Arabs used to say of one who had embraced Islam: "He has sabi'a (converted)." So the Sabians had departed from the religion of the People of the Book.

**Fifth issue:** There is no disagreement that the Jews and the Christians are People of the Book. Because of their Book, it is permissible to marry their women and eat their food, as will be explained in Surat al-Ma'ida [[See vol. 6, p. 76.]], and to impose the jizya (poll tax) on them, as will come in Surat Bara'a [[See vol. 8, p. 110.]], if Allah wills. But there was disagreement about the Sabians. Al-Suddi said: they are a sect of the People of the Book. Ishaq ibn Rahawayh said the same. Ibn al-Mundhir said: Ishaq said there is no harm in eating the slaughtered animals (dhaba'ih) of the Sabians, because they are a group of the People of the Book. Abu Hanifa said: there is no harm in eating their slaughtered animals or marrying their women. Al-Khalil said: they are a people whose religion resembles the religion of the Christians, except that their qibla is toward the south wind, and they claim they are upon the religion of Nuh, peace be upon him. Mujahid, al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Najih said: they are a people whose religion is a mixture of Judaism and Magianism, and their slaughtered animals may not be eaten. Ibn 'Abbas said: nor may their women be married. Al-Hasan also said, and Qatada: they are a people who worship the angels, pray facing the qibla, recite the Zabur (Psalms), and pray the five prayers. Ziyad ibn Abi Sufyan saw them and wished to remove the jizya from them when he learned that they worshipped the angels. What has been gathered of their doctrine, according to what some of our scholars mentioned, is that they are monotheists who believe in the influence of the stars and that the stars are effective agents. For this reason Abu Sa'id al-Istakhri issued a fatwa declaring them disbelievers, when al-Qadir billah asked him about them.

**Sixth issue:** Allah's words, ﴿whoever believes﴾, mean whoever affirms. The ﴿man﴾ in His words "man amana" is in the accusative position as a substitute (badal) for ﴿those who﴾. The fa' in His words "fa-lahum" (then for them) is inserted because of the indefiniteness in "man". ﴿Then for them is their reward﴾ is an inchoative and predicate, in the position of the predicate of inna. It is also good that "man" be in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), and its meaning is the conditional. "Amana" is in the jussive position as the conditional, and the fa' is the response. "Fa-lahum ajruhum" is the predicate of "man", and the whole clause is the predicate of inna. The returning pronoun to ﴿those who﴾ is elided, and its estimate is: "whoever among them believes in Allah." Belief in Allah and the Last Day includes belief in the messengers, the books and the resurrection.

**Seventh issue:** If someone says: why is the pronoun in Allah's words, ﴿then for them is their reward﴾, plural, when "amana" is a singular word and not a plural? It would have been correct to say: "lahu ajruhu" (for him is his reward). The answer is that "man" applies to the singular, the dual and the plural. So it is permissible for the pronoun to return in the singular, the dual or the plural. Allah said: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾ (Yunus: 42), according to the meaning. He also said: "And among them is one who listens to you," according to the wording. The poet said:

*"Greet Salma on your behalf, if you pass by her, and say to her: 'Turn back toward those who stayed behind.'"*

Al-Farazdaq said:

*"Come, if you pledge to me that you will not betray me, we will be like those who, O wolf, keep company."*

He followed the meaning. If he had followed the wording, he would have said: "yasḥabu" and "takhallafu." Allah also said: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit him into gardens﴾, following the wording. Then He said: ﴿abiding therein forever﴾, following the meaning. If he had observed the wording, he would have said "khalidan fiha." When what follows "man" is in accordance with the wording, it is permissible to shift afterward to the meaning, as in this verse. But when what follows it is in accordance with the meaning, it is not permissible to shift afterward to the wording, because confusion would enter the speech. The discussion of Allah's words, ﴿no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾, has already passed [[See p. 329 of this part.]]. And praise be to Allah.

**Eighth issue:** It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that His words, ﴿Indeed, those who believe and those who are Jews﴾ (al-Hajj: 17), and the rest of the verse, are abrogated (mansukh) by His words: ﴿Whoever seeks other than Islam as religion, it will never be accepted from him﴾ (Al 'Imran: 85), and the rest of the verse. Others said: it is not abrogated. It refers to those among the believers who remained firm in their faith in the Prophet, peace be upon him.

[Tafsir]

Allah's words: ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised above you the mount, [saying], "Hold firmly to what We have given you and remember what is in it; perhaps you will become righteous."﴾ (63) ﴿Then you turned away after that. Were it not for the favor of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have been among the losers.﴾ (64)

Allah's words: ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised above you the mount﴾. This verse explains the meaning of His words: ﴿And when We shook the mountain over them as though it were a canopy﴾ (Al-A'raf: 171) [[See vol. 7, p. 313.]]. Abu 'Ubayda said: the meaning is that He shook it and uprooted it from its place. He said: everything you uproot and throw away, you have nataqtahu (torn it out). It was also said: nataqna means "We raised it." Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-nati' is the one who raises, al-nati' is the one who spreads out, and al-nati' is the one who splits open. A woman who is nati' or muntaq is one with many children. Al-Qutabi said: this is taken from natq al-siqa', which is shaking the waterskin until the butter is pulled out of it. He said: His words, "And when We shook the mountain over them as though it were a canopy," mean it was uprooted from its base.

The Tur (mount) has been disputed. It was said: al-Tur is the name of the mountain on which Allah spoke to Musa, peace be upon him, and upon which He sent down the Torah to him, and no other. Ibn Jurayj reported this from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Dahhak reported from him that al-Tur is only the mountain that produces vegetation, not the one that does not. Mujahid and Qatada said: it is any mountain. However, Mujahid said: it is the name for every mountain in Syriac, and Abu al-'Aliya also said this. The discussion of whether there are single words in the Qur'an that are not Arabicized, without further discussion, has already passed in the introduction of the book [[See p. 68 of this part.]]. And praise be to Allah. Al-Bakri claimed that it was named after Tur ibn Isma'il, peace be upon him, and Allah knows best.

**On the cause of the raising of the mount:** When Musa, peace be upon him, brought the Children of Israel the tablets from Allah, containing the Torah, he said to them: "Take them and commit yourselves to them." They said: "No! Unless Allah speaks to us with them as He spoke to you." So they were struck senseless and then revived. He said to them: "Take them." They said: "No." So Allah commanded the angels, and they tore up a mountain from the mountains of Palestine, its length a farsakh by a similar width, and their camp was like that. So it was placed over them like a canopy. They were brought a sea behind them and a fire before their faces. It was said to them: "Take them, and upon you is the covenant that you will not neglect them, or else the mountain will fall upon you." So they prostrated in repentance to Allah and took the Torah under the covenant. Al-Tabari reported from some scholars: "If they had taken it the first time, there would have been no covenant upon them. Their prostration was on one side, because they were watching the mountain out of fear. When Allah had mercy on them, they said: 'There is no prostration more excellent than a prostration which Allah accepted and by which He had mercy on His servants.' So they continued their prostration on one side." Ibn 'Atiyya said: what cannot be sound other than this is that Allah, at the time of their prostration, brought about faith in their hearts, and not that they believed under compulsion while their hearts were not at peace with it. [[Addition from the commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya.]]

Allah's words: ﴿Take﴾, meaning: "So We said: take," and it was elided.

(﴿What We have given you﴾): what We have given you.

(﴿With strength﴾): that is, with diligence and effort, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Suddi. It was also said: with intention and sincerity. Mujahid said: strength is acting upon what is in it. It was also said: with strength, meaning with much study.

(And recall what is in it) — that is, reflect upon it, preserve its commands and its warnings, and do not forget it or neglect it.

I say: this is the purpose of the Books — acting in accordance with what they require, not merely reciting them with the tongue and chanting them in measured tones, for that is (a form of) abandoning them, according to what al-Sha'bi and Ibn 'Uyaynah said. Their statement will come at the words of the Exalted: ﴿Then a party of those who were given the Book cast it behind their backs﴾ [[See vol. 2, p. 41.]] [al-Baqarah: 101].

Al-Nasa'i related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Among the worst of people is a wicked man who recites the Qur'an but does not turn back from any of it." Thus the Prophet (ﷺ) made clear that the intended goal is action, as we have explained.

Malik said: "One may recite the Qur'an while there is no good in him."

Therefore, what was binding on those before us and was taken from them as a covenant is binding on us and obligatory upon us. Allah the Exalted said: "And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord" [[See vol. 15, p. 270]] [al-Zumar: 55]. So we were commanded to follow His Book and act in accordance with its requirements, but we have abandoned that, just as the Jews and Christians abandoned it, and the physical forms of the Books and the copies of the Qur'an remain, benefiting nothing, due to the prevalence of ignorance, the pursuit of leadership, and the following of desires.

al-Tirmidhi related from Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from Abu al-Darda', who said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ), and he raised his gaze to the sky and then said: 'This is a time when knowledge will be snatched away from people, until they are unable to obtain anything from it.' Ziyad ibn Labid al-Ansari said: 'How can it be snatched from us when we have recited the Qur'an? By Allah, we will surely recite it, and we will teach it to our women and our children.' He said: 'May your mother be bereaved of you, O Ziyad! I used to count you among the jurists of Madinah. Are these not the Torah and the Gospel in the hands of the Jews and Christians? What good did they do them?'" and he mentioned the hadith, which will come.

al-Nasa'i also recorded it from the hadith of Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from 'Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i, by a sound chain, and that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Ziyad: "May your mother be bereaved of you, O Ziyad! These are the Torah and the Gospel in the hands of the Jews and Christians."

In the Muwatta', from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said to a man: "You are in a time whose jurists are many and whose reciters are few; its limits of the Qur'an are preserved while its letters are neglected; few ask and many give; they prolong the prayer and shorten the sermon; they put their deeds before their desires. And there will come upon people a time whose jurists are few and whose reciters are many; the letters of the Qur'an are preserved while its limits are neglected; many ask and few give; they prolong the sermon and shorten the prayer; they put their desires before their deeds."

These texts indicate what we have mentioned. Yahya said: I asked Ibn Nafi' about His words, "they put their desires before their deeds," and he said: "It means they follow their desires and leave off acting upon what has been made obligatory upon them."

The discussion of the meaning of His words, "that you may be God-fearing" [[See p. 227 of this part.]], has already preceded, so there is no point in repeating it.

The Exalted said: ﴿Then you turned away﴾. "Tawalla" is of the form "tafa'ala," and its root meaning is turning away and retreating from a thing physically; then it was used, by extension and metaphor, for turning away from commands, religions and beliefs. His words "after that" mean after the proof, which is the taking of the covenant and the lifting of the mountain. His words, "Had it not been for the grace of Allah upon you," — "grace" (fadl) is in the nominative as the subject according to Sibawayh, and the predicate is omitted and may not be stated, because the Arabs dispensed with stating it; but when they wish to state it, they bring "an" (that), and when they bring it they do not omit the predicate. The sense is: "Had it not been for the grace of Allah, He would have overtaken you."

"And His mercy" is conjoined to "grace," meaning His kindness and His respite.

"You would have been" is the answer to "Had it not been."

"Among the losers" is the predicate of "you were." "Loss" means deficiency, and it has already been discussed [[See p. 248.]]. It has been said: His grace is the acceptance of repentance, and "His mercy" is pardon. "Grace" (fadl) is excess beyond what is obligatory, and "ifdal" is doing what is not obligatory. Ibn Faris said in al-Mujmal: "Fadl is increase and good, and ifdal is kindness."

[Tafsir]

The Almighty's saying: ﴿And you certainly knew those among you who transgressed concerning the Sabbath﴾ "*Alimtum*" means you recognized their persons (*'arafтum a'yanahum*). It was also said: you knew their rulings (*ahkamahum*). The difference between the two is that *ma'rifah* (recognition) is directed at the essence of the named thing, while *'ilm* (knowledge) is directed at the states of the named thing. So when you say "I recognized Zayd" (*'araftu Zaydan*), the meaning is his person, and when you say "I knew Zayd" (*'alimtu Zaydan*), the meaning is knowledge of his conditions, whether good or bad. On the first usage the verb takes one object, and this is the view of Sibawayh: "*'Alimtum*" in the sense of *'arafтum*. On the second it takes two objects. Al-Akhfash related: "*Wa-laqad 'alimtu Zaydan wa-lam akun a'lamuhu*" ("I certainly knew Zayd, but I did not know him"). In the Revelation there is: ﴿You do not know them; Allah knows them﴾ [al-Anfal 8:60]. All of these carry the meaning of recognition, so understand this. ﴿Those among you who transgressed concerning the Sabbath﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:65]: "*alladhina*" is linked to the relative clause (*silah*). *I'tida'* means transgressing the limit, and this has already been discussed [see p. 432].

The second matter: al-Nasa'i related from Safwan ibn 'Assal, who said: A Jew said to his companion, "Come, let us go to this Prophet." His companion said to him, "Do not say 'Prophet'; if he hears you, he will have four eyes." (In the version of al-Nasa'i: "If he hears you, he will have four eyes," with the number also in the feminine.) So the two of them came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked him about nine clear signs. He said to them: "Do not associate anything with Allah; do not steal; do not commit adultery; do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right; do not walk with a tale-bearer to a ruler; do not practise sorcery; do not consume usury; do not falsely accuse a chaste woman; do not flee on the day of the march; and upon you, especially the Jews, is that you do not transgress concerning the Sabbath." Then they kissed his hands and feet and said: "We testify that you are a Prophet." He said: "Then what prevents you from following me?" They said: "David supplicated that there should never cease to be a prophet among his descendants, and we fear that if we follow you, the Jews will kill us." Al-Tirmidhi also narrated it and said: "A hasan sahih hadith." Its wording will come in Surah al-Isra' (*Subhan*) [see vol. 10, p. 335], if Allah the Exalted wills.

The third matter: "*fi al-sabt*" means on the day of Saturday, and it is possible that it means "in the ruling of the Sabbath." The first is the view of al-Hasan, and that they took the fish on it in the manner of making it lawful. Ashhab related from Malik, who said: Ibn Ruman claimed that a man among them would take a cord and tie to its end a noose (*wahqah*) [the *wahq* is a rope with a slipknot at one end, cast around the neck of an animal or a person until it is caught; *al-unshuwah* is a knot easily loosened, like the knot of a drawstring when pulled], and cast it into the tail of the fish, and at the other end of the cord he would fix a peg and leave it so until Sunday. Then people came to imitate what they saw, since those who did it were not tested, until the catching of fish became common and was carried on in the markets, and the wicked openly hunted it. A group then rose up, forbade it, openly voiced the prohibition, and withdrew. It is said that those who forbade said: "We will not live alongside you," so they divided the town with a wall. One day the forbidders awoke in their assemblies, and none of the transgressors had come out. They said: "The people have some matter." So they climbed the wall and looked, and behold, they were apes. They opened the door and entered upon them. The apes recognized their kin among the humans, but the humans did not recognize their kin among the apes. The apes began to come to their relatives among the humans, sniffing their clothes and weeping. He would say: "Did we not forbid you?" And she would shake her head: "Yes." Qatadah said: "The young men became apes, and the elders became swine, and none was saved except those who forbade, and the rest perished."

Al-Zajjaj said: "Some people said it is possible that these apes were of them." This was chosen by al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi. But the majority said: a transformed creature (*al-mamsukh*) does not produce offspring. The apes and swine and others were in existence before that, and those whom Allah transformed have perished and no offspring remained for them, because the wrath and the punishment had afflicted them, so they had no settled existence in the world after three days. Ibn 'Abbas said: No transformed creature ever lived beyond three days; it did not eat, did not drink, and did not produce offspring. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is established, that the transformed creature does not produce offspring, does not eat, does not drink, and does not live more than three days. I say: This is the sound of the two views.

As for what Ibn al-'Arabi and others argued in support of the first view from the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "A community of the Children of Israel was lost, and it is not known what became of it; and I do not think it was anything but the mice. Do you not see that when camel's milk is placed before them they do not drink it, but when sheep's milk is placed before them they drink it?" It was related by Abu Hurayrah and recorded by Muslim; and the hadith of the lizard (*dabb*) was also related by Muslim from Abu Sa'id and Jabir. Jabir said: The Prophet (ﷺ) was brought a lizard, and he refused to eat it and said: "I do not know, perhaps it is one of the communities that were transformed." This is interpreted according to what will come.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: In Bukhari, from 'Amr ibn Maymun, who said: "In the pre-Islamic period I saw an ape that had committed adultery, and they stoned her, and I stoned her with them." This is established in some copies of Bukhari and absent from others; the phrase "had committed adultery" is established in the text of the hadith in some copies but is absent in the copies of some. Ibn al-'Arabi said: If it is said: "Was it as if the animals retained among them knowledge of the laws, so that they inherited them from one generation to another until the time of 'Amr?" We say: Yes, it was so, because the Jews altered the stoning, so Allah willed to establish it among their transformed ones, so that it would be a stronger proof against them for what they denied and altered, and so that their books and stones and transformed ones would bear witness against them, that they might know that Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal, and counts what they change and alter, and establishes the proof against them from where they do not perceive, and gives victory to His Prophet, peace be upon him, while they are not given victory.

I say: This is his statement in *al-Ahkam*, and there is no proof in any of it. As for what he mentioned about the story of 'Amr, al-Humaydi mentioned in *Jam' al-Sahihayn* that Abu Mas'ud al-Dimashqi related that 'Amr ibn Maymun al-Awdi has in the Two Sahihs a narration through Husayn from him, who said: "In the pre-Islamic period I saw an ape around which a group of apes gathered, and they stoned her, and I stoned her with them." Thus Abu Mas'ud related it and did not mention in which place Bukhari had brought it out in his book. We searched for it and found it in some copies and not in all of them; it is mentioned in the Book of the Days of the Jahiliyyah. Nothing of this report about the apes is found at all in the narration of al-Nu'aymi from al-Firabri, and perhaps it is one of the insertions in the book of Bukhari.

What Bukhari said in *al-Tarikh al-Kabir*: Nu'aym ibn Hammad told me, Hushaym informed us from Abu Balj and Husayn, from 'Amr ibn Maymun, who said: "I saw in the pre-Islamic period an ape around which apes gathered, and they stoned her, and I stoned her with them." In it there is no "had committed adultery." If this narration is sound, then Bukhari brought it out only as an indication that 'Amr ibn Maymun had reached the pre-Islamic period, and he did not concern himself with the assumption he made about it in the pre-Islamic period.

Abu 'Umar mentioned in *al-Isti'ab*: "'Amr ibn Maymun, whose kunyah is Abu 'Abd Allah, is counted among the senior Successors (*tabi'un*) of the Kufans, and he is the one who saw the stoning in the pre-Islamic period among the apes, if that is sound, because its transmitters are unknown." Bukhari mentioned it from Nu'aym from Hushaym from Husayn from 'Amr ibn Maymun al-Awdi in abridged form: "I saw in the pre-Islamic period an ape that had committed adultery, and they stoned her—meaning the apes—and I stoned her with them." 'Abbad ibn al-'Awwam related it from Husayn, as Hushaym related it, in abridged form. As for the story in full, it revolves around 'Abd al-Malik ibn Muslim from 'Isa ibn Hittan, and neither of them is one whose narrations are used as proof. This, according to the body of scholars of knowledge, is objectionable: attributing fornication to one who is not legally accountable, and enforcing the prescribed penalties upon animals. And if it were sound, they would have been of the jinn, because the obligations of worship apply to humans and jinn and not to others."

As for his saying (ﷺ) in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah: "And I do not think it was anything but the mice," and in the case of the lizard: "I do not know, perhaps it is one of the communities that were transformed," and what is similar to it, it was only a supposition and a fear that the lizard and the mouse and others might be among those transformed, and this was a conjecture from him (ﷺ) before it was revealed to him that Allah had not granted offspring to transformed creatures. When this was revealed to him, that apprehension left him, and he knew that the lizard and the mouse were not among the transformed. At that point he informed us with his saying (ﷺ) to one who asked him about the apes and swine: "Are they of those that were transformed?" He said: "Allah does not destroy a people or punish a people and then give them offspring. The apes and swine existed before that." This is a clear, sound text, related by Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and recorded by Muslim in the Book of Destiny (*Kitab al-Qadar*). The reports are established that the lizard was eaten in his presence and at his table, and he did not object, which indicates the soundness of what we have mentioned. And with Allah is our success.

It was related from Mujahid in interpreting this verse that only their hearts were transformed, and their understandings were returned like the understandings of apes. No other exegete, as far as I know, has said this. And Allah knows best.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿So We said to them: "Be apes, despised."﴾ "*Qiradah*" is the predicate of *kana* (*khabar kana*). "*Khasi'in*" is an adjective (*na't*); if you wish, you may make it a second predicate of *kana*, or a circumstantial state (*hal*) from the pronoun in "*kuunu*." Its meaning is "driven away" (*mub'adin*). It is said: *khasa'tuhu* (I drove him away), so he was driven away (*fakhasa'a* and *khusi'a*), and *inkhasa'a*, meaning: I drove him away, so he withdrew. The Almighty's saying: ﴿The sight will return to you dazzled (*khasi'an*)﴾ [al-Mulk 67:4], meaning driven away. And His saying: ﴿Be driven away therein﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:108], meaning withdraw, withdrawal in wrath. Al-Kisa'i said: "*Khasa'a al-rajulu khusu'an*," and "*khasa'tuhu khas'an*." And *al-khasi'* may mean the abased, the humiliated. It is said: *qama'a al-rajulu qama'an wa-qama'atan*, meaning he became abased, and he is the abased, humiliated one. And *aqma'tuhu* means I belittled him and humbled him, so he is *qami*, on the pattern of *fa'il*.

**First issue:** Allah's words, ﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾, mean those who affirmed Muhammad (ﷺ). Sufyan said that what is intended is the hypocrites. It is as if He said: "Those who believe outwardly." This is why He paired them with the Jews, the Christians and the Sabians. Then He explained the ruling for whoever among all of them believes in Allah and the Last Day.

**Second issue:** Allah's words, ﴿and those who are Jews﴾. The meaning is that they became Jews (yahud). They were named after Yahudha (Judah), the eldest son of Ya'qub (Jacob), peace be upon him. The Arabs changed the dhal to a dal, because when a non-Arabic word is Arabicized, it is altered from its original pronunciation. It was also said that they were named this for their repentance from worshipping the calf. Hada means "he repented," and al-ha'id means "the penitent." The poet said:

*"Indeed, I am a man who, out of love for her, is penitent."*

That is, a penitent. In the Revelation (Tanzil) is Allah's word: ﴿Indeed, we have turned back to You﴾ (Al-A'raf: 156), meaning "we have repented." It is said: hada al-qawm yahudu hawdan wa-hiyadatan, when they repented. Ibn 'Arafa said: "hudna ilayka" means "we have settled into your command." Al-hawada means calm and reconciliation. He said: from this is Allah's word: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and those who are Jews﴾. Abu al-Sammal read "hadu" with a fatha on the dal.

**Third issue:** Allah's words, ﴿and the Christians (al-nasara)﴾. It is a plural whose singular is nasrani. It was also said: Nasran, with the yaa dropped, and this is the view of Sibawayh. The feminine is nasrana, like nadman and nadmana. It is an indefinite noun that is made definite with the alif and lam. The poet said:

*"She turned away as one turns from what is not lawful for him, from the cupbearer of the Nasara before the Fisah, who are fasting."* [[The poet is al-Namir ibn Tawlab, describing a she-camel to whom water was offered and who refused it. In the manuscripts of the original: "al-Subh" with a ba'. The correction is from Sibawayh's book. Al-Fisah: the breaking of the fast of the Christians, which is a feast for them.]]

Here he described it with the indefinite form. Al-Khalil said: the singular of al-nasara is nasri, like mahri and mahara. Sibawayh cited as evidence:

*"You see him, when the evening falls, inclining to the faith (of Abraham), and in the morning he is before him, a Christian who is bright."*

He also cited:

*"Both of them fell, and her head bowed, as the head of a Christian woman bows when she does not incline in prayer."* [[The line is by Abu al-Akhzar al-Hammani, describing two she-camels that lowered their heads from exhaustion. He likened the camel's head to the head of a Christian woman when she bows in her prayer. (From the commentary on the Qamus and Lisan.)]]

It is said: asjada, when he inclined. But nasran and nasrana are not used except with the nisba yaa, because they said: rajul nasrani (a Christian man) and imra'a nasraniyya (a Christian woman). Nassarahu means "he made him a Christian." In a hadith: "His parents make him a Jew or make him a Christian." He, peace be upon him, also said: "No one from this community hears of me, a Jew or a Christian, and then does not believe in what I was sent with, except that he will be among the companions of the Fire." Some plurals have come in forms other than their singular's usual form, and by analogy the plural is al-nasraniyyun. Then it was said: they were named after a village called Nasira, where 'Isa, peace be upon him, used to dwell, so he was attributed to it and called 'Isa al-Nasiri. When his followers were attributed to him, they were called al-Nasara. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada. Al-Jawhari said: Nasran is a village in Syria to which the Christians are attributed, and it is also called Nasira. It was also said: they were named this for the support (nusra) some of them gave to others. The poet said:

*"When I saw the Nabat as helpers, I hitched up my garment above my knees. I became for them a neighbor among the Nasara."*

It was also said: they were named this because of His word: ﴿Who are my helpers in the way of Allah?' The disciples said: 'We are the helpers of Allah'﴾ (Al 'Imran: 52).

**Fourth issue:** Allah's words, ﴿and the Sabians (al-Sabi'in)﴾. It is the plural of sabi'. It was also said: sabin. For this reason they differed about its hamza. Most readers pronounced the hamza, except Nafi'. Whoever pronounced the hamza took it from sabi'at al-nujum (the stars rose) when they appeared, and sabat thaniyyat al-ghulam (the boy's front tooth came out) when it emerged. Whoever did not pronounce the hamza took it from saba, yasbu, when he inclined. In the language, the sabi' is one who leaves and turns from one religion to another. For this reason the Arabs used to say of one who had embraced Islam: "He has sabi'a (converted)." So the Sabians had departed from the religion of the People of the Book.

**Fifth issue:** There is no disagreement that the Jews and the Christians are People of the Book. Because of their Book, it is permissible to marry their women and eat their food, as will be explained in Surat al-Ma'ida [[See vol. 6, p. 76.]], and to impose the jizya (poll tax) on them, as will come in Surat Bara'a [[See vol. 8, p. 110.]], if Allah wills. But there was disagreement about the Sabians. Al-Suddi said: they are a sect of the People of the Book. Ishaq ibn Rahawayh said the same. Ibn al-Mundhir said: Ishaq said there is no harm in eating the slaughtered animals (dhaba'ih) of the Sabians, because they are a group of the People of the Book. Abu Hanifa said: there is no harm in eating their slaughtered animals or marrying their women. Al-Khalil said: they are a people whose religion resembles the religion of the Christians, except that their qibla is toward the south wind, and they claim they are upon the religion of Nuh, peace be upon him. Mujahid, al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Najih said: they are a people whose religion is a mixture of Judaism and Magianism, and their slaughtered animals may not be eaten. Ibn 'Abbas said: nor may their women be married. Al-Hasan also said, and Qatada: they are a people who worship the angels, pray facing the qibla, recite the Zabur (Psalms), and pray the five prayers. Ziyad ibn Abi Sufyan saw them and wished to remove the jizya from them when he learned that they worshipped the angels. What has been gathered of their doctrine, according to what some of our scholars mentioned, is that they are monotheists who believe in the influence of the stars and that the stars are effective agents. For this reason Abu Sa'id al-Istakhri issued a fatwa declaring them disbelievers, when al-Qadir billah asked him about them.

**Sixth issue:** Allah's words, ﴿whoever believes﴾, mean whoever affirms. The ﴿man﴾ in His words "man amana" is in the accusative position as a substitute (badal) for ﴿those who﴾. The fa' in His words "fa-lahum" (then for them) is inserted because of the indefiniteness in "man". ﴿Then for them is their reward﴾ is an inchoative and predicate, in the position of the predicate of inna. It is also good that "man" be in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), and its meaning is the conditional. "Amana" is in the jussive position as the conditional, and the fa' is the response. "Fa-lahum ajruhum" is the predicate of "man", and the whole clause is the predicate of inna. The returning pronoun to ﴿those who﴾ is elided, and its estimate is: "whoever among them believes in Allah." Belief in Allah and the Last Day includes belief in the messengers, the books and the resurrection.

**Seventh issue:** If someone says: why is the pronoun in Allah's words, ﴿then for them is their reward﴾, plural, when "amana" is a singular word and not a plural? It would have been correct to say: "lahu ajruhu" (for him is his reward). The answer is that "man" applies to the singular, the dual and the plural. So it is permissible for the pronoun to return in the singular, the dual or the plural. Allah said: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾ (Yunus: 42), according to the meaning. He also said: "And among them is one who listens to you," according to the wording. The poet said:

*"Greet Salma on your behalf, if you pass by her, and say to her: 'Turn back toward those who stayed behind.'"*

Al-Farazdaq said:

*"Come, if you pledge to me that you will not betray me, we will be like those who, O wolf, keep company."*

He followed the meaning. If he had followed the wording, he would have said: "yasḥabu" and "takhallafu." Allah also said: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit him into gardens﴾, following the wording. Then He said: ﴿abiding therein forever﴾, following the meaning. If he had observed the wording, he would have said "khalidan fiha." When what follows "man" is in accordance with the wording, it is permissible to shift afterward to the meaning, as in this verse. But when what follows it is in accordance with the meaning, it is not permissible to shift afterward to the wording, because confusion would enter the speech. The discussion of Allah's words, ﴿no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾, has already passed [[See p. 329 of this part.]]. And praise be to Allah.

**Eighth issue:** It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that His words, ﴿Indeed, those who believe and those who are Jews﴾ (al-Hajj: 17), and the rest of the verse, are abrogated (mansukh) by His words: ﴿Whoever seeks other than Islam as religion, it will never be accepted from him﴾ (Al 'Imran: 85), and the rest of the verse. Others said: it is not abrogated. It refers to those among the believers who remained firm in their faith in the Prophet, peace be upon him.

[Tafsir]

Allah's words: ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised above you the mount, [saying], "Hold firmly to what We have given you and remember what is in it; perhaps you will become righteous."﴾ (63) ﴿Then you turned away after that. Were it not for the favor of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have been among the losers.﴾ (64)

Allah's words: ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised above you the mount﴾. This verse explains the meaning of His words: ﴿And when We shook the mountain over them as though it were a canopy﴾ (Al-A'raf: 171) [[See vol. 7, p. 313.]]. Abu 'Ubayda said: the meaning is that He shook it and uprooted it from its place. He said: everything you uproot and throw away, you have nataqtahu (torn it out). It was also said: nataqna means "We raised it." Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-nati' is the one who raises, al-nati' is the one who spreads out, and al-nati' is the one who splits open. A woman who is nati' or muntaq is one with many children. Al-Qutabi said: this is taken from natq al-siqa', which is shaking the waterskin until the butter is pulled out of it. He said: His words, "And when We shook the mountain over them as though it were a canopy," mean it was uprooted from its base.

The Tur (mount) has been disputed. It was said: al-Tur is the name of the mountain on which Allah spoke to Musa, peace be upon him, and upon which He sent down the Torah to him, and no other. Ibn Jurayj reported this from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Dahhak reported from him that al-Tur is only the mountain that produces vegetation, not the one that does not. Mujahid and Qatada said: it is any mountain. However, Mujahid said: it is the name for every mountain in Syriac, and Abu al-'Aliya also said this. The discussion of whether there are single words in the Qur'an that are not Arabicized, without further discussion, has already passed in the introduction of the book [[See p. 68 of this part.]]. And praise be to Allah. Al-Bakri claimed that it was named after Tur ibn Isma'il, peace be upon him, and Allah knows best.

**On the cause of the raising of the mount:** When Musa, peace be upon him, brought the Children of Israel the tablets from Allah, containing the Torah, he said to them: "Take them and commit yourselves to them." They said: "No! Unless Allah speaks to us with them as He spoke to you." So they were struck senseless and then revived. He said to them: "Take them." They said: "No." So Allah commanded the angels, and they tore up a mountain from the mountains of Palestine, its length a farsakh by a similar width, and their camp was like that. So it was placed over them like a canopy. They were brought a sea behind them and a fire before their faces. It was said to them: "Take them, and upon you is the covenant that you will not neglect them, or else the mountain will fall upon you." So they prostrated in repentance to Allah and took the Torah under the covenant. Al-Tabari reported from some scholars: "If they had taken it the first time, there would have been no covenant upon them. Their prostration was on one side, because they were watching the mountain out of fear. When Allah had mercy on them, they said: 'There is no prostration more excellent than a prostration which Allah accepted and by which He had mercy on His servants.' So they continued their prostration on one side." Ibn 'Atiyya said: what cannot be sound other than this is that Allah, at the time of their prostration, brought about faith in their hearts, and not that they believed under compulsion while their hearts were not at peace with it. [[Addition from the commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya.]]

Allah's words: ﴿Take﴾, meaning: "So We said: take," and it was elided.

(﴿What We have given you﴾): what We have given you.

(﴿With strength﴾): that is, with diligence and effort, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Suddi. It was also said: with intention and sincerity. Mujahid said: strength is acting upon what is in it. It was also said: with strength, meaning with much study.

(And recall what is in it) — that is, reflect upon it, preserve its commands and its warnings, and do not forget it or neglect it.

I say: this is the purpose of the Books — acting in accordance with what they require, not merely reciting them with the tongue and chanting them in measured tones, for that is (a form of) abandoning them, according to what al-Sha'bi and Ibn 'Uyaynah said. Their statement will come at the words of the Exalted: ﴿Then a party of those who were given the Book cast it behind their backs﴾ [[See vol. 2, p. 41.]] [al-Baqarah: 101].

Al-Nasa'i related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Among the worst of people is a wicked man who recites the Qur'an but does not turn back from any of it." Thus the Prophet (ﷺ) made clear that the intended goal is action, as we have explained.

Malik said: "One may recite the Qur'an while there is no good in him."

Therefore, what was binding on those before us and was taken from them as a covenant is binding on us and obligatory upon us. Allah the Exalted said: "And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord" [[See vol. 15, p. 270]] [al-Zumar: 55]. So we were commanded to follow His Book and act in accordance with its requirements, but we have abandoned that, just as the Jews and Christians abandoned it, and the physical forms of the Books and the copies of the Qur'an remain, benefiting nothing, due to the prevalence of ignorance, the pursuit of leadership, and the following of desires.

al-Tirmidhi related from Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from Abu al-Darda', who said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ), and he raised his gaze to the sky and then said: 'This is a time when knowledge will be snatched away from people, until they are unable to obtain anything from it.' Ziyad ibn Labid al-Ansari said: 'How can it be snatched from us when we have recited the Qur'an? By Allah, we will surely recite it, and we will teach it to our women and our children.' He said: 'May your mother be bereaved of you, O Ziyad! I used to count you among the jurists of Madinah. Are these not the Torah and the Gospel in the hands of the Jews and Christians? What good did they do them?'" and he mentioned the hadith, which will come.

al-Nasa'i also recorded it from the hadith of Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from 'Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i, by a sound chain, and that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Ziyad: "May your mother be bereaved of you, O Ziyad! These are the Torah and the Gospel in the hands of the Jews and Christians."

In the Muwatta', from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said to a man: "You are in a time whose jurists are many and whose reciters are few; its limits of the Qur'an are preserved while its letters are neglected; few ask and many give; they prolong the prayer and shorten the sermon; they put their deeds before their desires. And there will come upon people a time whose jurists are few and whose reciters are many; the letters of the Qur'an are preserved while its limits are neglected; many ask and few give; they prolong the sermon and shorten the prayer; they put their desires before their deeds."

These texts indicate what we have mentioned. Yahya said: I asked Ibn Nafi' about His words, "they put their desires before their deeds," and he said: "It means they follow their desires and leave off acting upon what has been made obligatory upon them."

The discussion of the meaning of His words, "that you may be God-fearing" [[See p. 227 of this part.]], has already preceded, so there is no point in repeating it.

The Exalted said: ﴿Then you turned away﴾. "Tawalla" is of the form "tafa'ala," and its root meaning is turning away and retreating from a thing physically; then it was used, by extension and metaphor, for turning away from commands, religions and beliefs. His words "after that" mean after the proof, which is the taking of the covenant and the lifting of the mountain. His words, "Had it not been for the grace of Allah upon you," — "grace" (fadl) is in the nominative as the subject according to Sibawayh, and the predicate is omitted and may not be stated, because the Arabs dispensed with stating it; but when they wish to state it, they bring "an" (that), and when they bring it they do not omit the predicate. The sense is: "Had it not been for the grace of Allah, He would have overtaken you."

"And His mercy" is conjoined to "grace," meaning His kindness and His respite.

"You would have been" is the answer to "Had it not been."

"Among the losers" is the predicate of "you were." "Loss" means deficiency, and it has already been discussed [[See p. 248.]]. It has been said: His grace is the acceptance of repentance, and "His mercy" is pardon. "Grace" (fadl) is excess beyond what is obligatory, and "ifdal" is doing what is not obligatory. Ibn Faris said in al-Mujmal: "Fadl is increase and good, and ifdal is kindness."

[Tafsir]

The Almighty's saying: ﴿And you certainly knew those among you who transgressed concerning the Sabbath﴾ "*Alimtum*" means you recognized their persons (*'arafтum a'yanahum*). It was also said: you knew their rulings (*ahkamahum*). The difference between the two is that *ma'rifah* (recognition) is directed at the essence of the named thing, while *'ilm* (knowledge) is directed at the states of the named thing. So when you say "I recognized Zayd" (*'araftu Zaydan*), the meaning is his person, and when you say "I knew Zayd" (*'alimtu Zaydan*), the meaning is knowledge of his conditions, whether good or bad. On the first usage the verb takes one object, and this is the view of Sibawayh: "*'Alimtum*" in the sense of *'arafтum*. On the second it takes two objects. Al-Akhfash related: "*Wa-laqad 'alimtu Zaydan wa-lam akun a'lamuhu*" ("I certainly knew Zayd, but I did not know him"). In the Revelation there is: ﴿You do not know them; Allah knows them﴾ [al-Anfal 8:60]. All of these carry the meaning of recognition, so understand this. ﴿Those among you who transgressed concerning the Sabbath﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:65]: "*alladhina*" is linked to the relative clause (*silah*). *I'tida'* means transgressing the limit, and this has already been discussed [see p. 432].

The second matter: al-Nasa'i related from Safwan ibn 'Assal, who said: A Jew said to his companion, "Come, let us go to this Prophet." His companion said to him, "Do not say 'Prophet'; if he hears you, he will have four eyes." (In the version of al-Nasa'i: "If he hears you, he will have four eyes," with the number also in the feminine.) So the two of them came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked him about nine clear signs. He said to them: "Do not associate anything with Allah; do not steal; do not commit adultery; do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right; do not walk with a tale-bearer to a ruler; do not practise sorcery; do not consume usury; do not falsely accuse a chaste woman; do not flee on the day of the march; and upon you, especially the Jews, is that you do not transgress concerning the Sabbath." Then they kissed his hands and feet and said: "We testify that you are a Prophet." He said: "Then what prevents you from following me?" They said: "David supplicated that there should never cease to be a prophet among his descendants, and we fear that if we follow you, the Jews will kill us."
