Al-Tirmidhi also narrated it and said: "A hasan sahih hadith." Its wording will come in Surah al-Isra' (*Subhan*) [see vol. 10, p. 335], if Allah the Exalted wills.

The third matter: "*fi al-sabt*" means on the day of Saturday, and it is possible that it means "in the ruling of the Sabbath." The first is the view of al-Hasan, and that they took the fish on it in the manner of making it lawful. Ashhab related from Malik, who said: Ibn Ruman claimed that a man among them would take a cord and tie to its end a noose (*wahqah*) [the *wahq* is a rope with a slipknot at one end, cast around the neck of an animal or a person until it is caught; *al-unshuwah* is a knot easily loosened, like the knot of a drawstring when pulled], and cast it into the tail of the fish, and at the other end of the cord he would fix a peg and leave it so until Sunday. Then people came to imitate what they saw, since those who did it were not tested, until the catching of fish became common and was carried on in the markets, and the wicked openly hunted it. A group then rose up, forbade it, openly voiced the prohibition, and withdrew. It is said that those who forbade said: "We will not live alongside you," so they divided the town with a wall. One day the forbidders awoke in their assemblies, and none of the transgressors had come out. They said: "The people have some matter." So they climbed the wall and looked, and behold, they were apes. They opened the door and entered upon them. The apes recognized their kin among the humans, but the humans did not recognize their kin among the apes. The apes began to come to their relatives among the humans, sniffing their clothes and weeping. He would say: "Did we not forbid you?" And she would shake her head: "Yes." Qatadah said: "The young men became apes, and the elders became swine, and none was saved except those who forbade, and the rest perished."

Al-Zajjaj said: "Some people said it is possible that these apes were of them." This was chosen by al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi. But the majority said: a transformed creature (*al-mamsukh*) does not produce offspring. The apes and swine and others were in existence before that, and those whom Allah transformed have perished and no offspring remained for them, because the wrath and the punishment had afflicted them, so they had no settled existence in the world after three days. Ibn 'Abbas said: No transformed creature ever lived beyond three days; it did not eat, did not drink, and did not produce offspring. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is established, that the transformed creature does not produce offspring, does not eat, does not drink, and does not live more than three days. I say: This is the sound of the two views.

As for what Ibn al-'Arabi and others argued in support of the first view from the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "A community of the Children of Israel was lost, and it is not known what became of it; and I do not think it was anything but the mice. Do you not see that when camel's milk is placed before them they do not drink it, but when sheep's milk is placed before them they drink it?" It was related by Abu Hurayrah and recorded by Muslim; and the hadith of the lizard (*dabb*) was also related by Muslim from Abu Sa'id and Jabir. Jabir said: The Prophet (ﷺ) was brought a lizard, and he refused to eat it and said: "I do not know, perhaps it is one of the communities that were transformed." This is interpreted according to what will come.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: In Bukhari, from 'Amr ibn Maymun, who said: "In the pre-Islamic period I saw an ape that had committed adultery, and they stoned her, and I stoned her with them." This is established in some copies of Bukhari and absent from others; the phrase "had committed adultery" is established in the text of the hadith in some copies but is absent in the copies of some. Ibn al-'Arabi said: If it is said: "Was it as if the animals retained among them knowledge of the laws, so that they inherited them from one generation to another until the time of 'Amr?" We say: Yes, it was so, because the Jews altered the stoning, so Allah willed to establish it among their transformed ones, so that it would be a stronger proof against them for what they denied and altered, and so that their books and stones and transformed ones would bear witness against them, that they might know that Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal, and counts what they change and alter, and establishes the proof against them from where they do not perceive, and gives victory to His Prophet, peace be upon him, while they are not given victory.

I say: This is his statement in *al-Ahkam*, and there is no proof in any of it. As for what he mentioned about the story of 'Amr, al-Humaydi mentioned in *Jam' al-Sahihayn* that Abu Mas'ud al-Dimashqi related that 'Amr ibn Maymun al-Awdi has in the Two Sahihs a narration through Husayn from him, who said: "In the pre-Islamic period I saw an ape around which a group of apes gathered, and they stoned her, and I stoned her with them." Thus Abu Mas'ud related it and did not mention in which place Bukhari had brought it out in his book. We searched for it and found it in some copies and not in all of them; it is mentioned in the Book of the Days of the Jahiliyyah. Nothing of this report about the apes is found at all in the narration of al-Nu'aymi from al-Firabri, and perhaps it is one of the insertions in the book of Bukhari.

What Bukhari said in *al-Tarikh al-Kabir*: Nu'aym ibn Hammad told me, Hushaym informed us from Abu Balj and Husayn, from 'Amr ibn Maymun, who said: "I saw in the pre-Islamic period an ape around which apes gathered, and they stoned her, and I stoned her with them." In it there is no "had committed adultery." If this narration is sound, then Bukhari brought it out only as an indication that 'Amr ibn Maymun had reached the pre-Islamic period, and he did not concern himself with the assumption he made about it in the pre-Islamic period.

Abu 'Umar mentioned in *al-Isti'ab*: "'Amr ibn Maymun, whose kunyah is Abu 'Abd Allah, is counted among the senior Successors (*tabi'un*) of the Kufans, and he is the one who saw the stoning in the pre-Islamic period among the apes, if that is sound, because its transmitters are unknown." Bukhari mentioned it from Nu'aym from Hushaym from Husayn from 'Amr ibn Maymun al-Awdi in abridged form: "I saw in the pre-Islamic period an ape that had committed adultery, and they stoned her—meaning the apes—and I stoned her with them." 'Abbad ibn al-'Awwam related it from Husayn, as Hushaym related it, in abridged form. As for the story in full, it revolves around 'Abd al-Malik ibn Muslim from 'Isa ibn Hittan, and neither of them is one whose narrations are used as proof. This, according to the body of scholars of knowledge, is objectionable: attributing fornication to one who is not legally accountable, and enforcing the prescribed penalties upon animals. And if it were sound, they would have been of the jinn, because the obligations of worship apply to humans and jinn and not to others."

As for his saying (ﷺ) in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah: "And I do not think it was anything but the mice," and in the case of the lizard: "I do not know, perhaps it is one of the communities that were transformed," and what is similar to it, it was only a supposition and a fear that the lizard and the mouse and others might be among those transformed, and this was a conjecture from him (ﷺ) before it was revealed to him that Allah had not granted offspring to transformed creatures. When this was revealed to him, that apprehension left him, and he knew that the lizard and the mouse were not among the transformed. At that point he informed us with his saying (ﷺ) to one who asked him about the apes and swine: "Are they of those that were transformed?" He said: "Allah does not destroy a people or punish a people and then give them offspring. The apes and swine existed before that." This is a clear, sound text, related by Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and recorded by Muslim in the Book of Destiny (*Kitab al-Qadar*). The reports are established that the lizard was eaten in his presence and at his table, and he did not object, which indicates the soundness of what we have mentioned. And with Allah is our success.

It was related from Mujahid in interpreting this verse that only their hearts were transformed, and their understandings were returned like the understandings of apes. No other exegete, as far as I know, has said this. And Allah knows best.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿So We said to them: "Be apes, despised."﴾ "*Qiradah*" is the predicate of *kana* (*khabar kana*). "*Khasi'in*" is an adjective (*na't*); if you wish, you may make it a second predicate of *kana*, or a circumstantial state (*hal*) from the pronoun in "*kuunu*." Its meaning is "driven away" (*mub'adin*). It is said: *khasa'tuhu* (I drove him away), so he was driven away (*fakhasa'a* and *khusi'a*), and *inkhasa'a*, meaning: I drove him away, so he withdrew. The Almighty's saying: ﴿The sight will return to you dazzled (*khasi'an*)﴾ [al-Mulk 67:4], meaning driven away. And His saying: ﴿Be driven away therein﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:108], meaning withdraw, withdrawal in wrath. Al-Kisa'i said: "*Khasa'a al-rajulu khusu'an*," and "*khasa'tuhu khas'an*." And *al-khasi'* may mean the abased, the humiliated. It is said: *qama'a al-rajulu qama'an wa-qama'atan*, meaning he became abased, and he is the abased, humiliated one. And *aqma'tuhu* means I belittled him and humbled him, so he is *qami*, on the pattern of *fa'il*.

**The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So We made it a deterrent﴾** is in the accusative (*nasb*, the grammatical case of the object) as the second object (*al-maf'ul al-thani*) of the verb.

Scholars differ over what is meant by the thing made into a deterrent (*nakalan*). It has been said: the punishment. It has been said: the town, since the sense of the discourse requires it. It has been said: the nation that was transformed. It has been said: the fish, though this is far-fetched.

*Al-nakal* means a restraint and a punishment. *Al-nikl* and *al-ankal* mean shackles. Shackles are called *ankal* because a person is restrained by them, that is, prevented. A heavy bridle is called *nakl* and *nikl* because the animal is restrained by it.[[This word appears in some copies of the original text, but the lexicons do not support it. What is correct is only the vowelling with a kasra, and nothing else.]] One says *nakala 'an al-amr yankulu* and *nakila yankalu* when he refrains from something. *Al-tankil* means striking the enemy with a punishment that makes those behind them flinch, that is, makes them cowardly. Al-Azhari said: *al-nakal* is punishment. Ibn Duraid said: *al-minkal* is the thing by which a person is restrained. He said:

*"So hurl at their necks with a deterrent"*[[The speaker is Riyah al-Mu'ammil, and before it he says:

"O Lord, the sons of Mu'ammil have made me wretched"

and after it:

"with a boulder or a host of a massive army"

(from Sharh al-Qamus).]]

**His words: ﴿for what lay before it﴾.** Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi said: for what lay before the transformation, that is, the sins of the people that preceded it.

**﴿and what lay behind it﴾**: for those who would commit similar sins. Al-Farra' said: the transformation was made a deterrent for the sins that had passed and for what would be done after it, so that they would fear transformation for their sins. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is a good opinion, and both pronouns refer to the punishment. Al-Hakam narrated from Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas: for those who were present with them and for those who would come after them. Al-Nahhas chose this view and said: it is more fitting to the meaning, and Allah knows best. Also from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿for what lay before it and what lay behind it﴾ refers to the towns. Qatada said: ﴿for what lay before it﴾ refers to their sins, and ﴿what lay behind it﴾ refers to the hunting of the fish.

**His words: ﴿and an admonition for the God-conscious﴾.** This is conjoined (*'atf*) to *nakalan*. Its form is *maf'ala*, derived from *al-itti'az* (taking warning) and *al-inzijar* (being restrained). *Al-wa'z* means warning through fear. *Al-'iẓa* is the noun. Al-Khalil said: *al-wa'z* is reminding of goodness in matters that soften the heart. Al-Mawardi said: he specified the God-conscious, although it is an admonition for all the worlds, because they alone benefit from it, unlike the obstinate disbelievers. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the wording encompasses every God-conscious person from every nation. Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿and an admonition for the God-conscious﴾ is for the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ), that they should not violate the sanctities of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in what He has forbidden them, lest there befall them what befell the people of the Sabbath when they violated the sanctities of Allah on their Sabbath.

**The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And when Moses said to his people, "Indeed, Allah commands you to sacrifice a cow"﴾**

In this verse there are four issues.

**The first issue:** As for His words, the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you﴾, it is reported from Abu 'Amr that he recited "yamurkum" (with a sukun on the ra') by dropping the damma on the ra' because it is heavy. Abu al-'Abbas al-Mubarrad said: "This is not permissible, because the ra' is the letter of i'rab (the letter that carries the grammatical inflection). What is correctly reported from Abu 'Amr is that he used to weaken (lit. 'steal') the vowel." ﴿That you sacrifice﴾ is in a position of nasb (accusative) governed by "yamurkum," meaning "to sacrifice." "Baqarah" (a cow) is in the accusative, governed by "tadhbahu" (you sacrifice). The meaning of dhabh (slaughter) has already been discussed, so there is no need to repeat it here. [[See the tenth issue, p. 385 of this part.]]

**The second issue:** His words, the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to sacrifice a cow﴾ come first in the recitation, while His words "you killed a soul" come first in meaning before everything that began with the matter of the cow. It is also possible that the words "you killed" were revealed first, and the command to slaughter came later. It is also possible that the order of their revelation follows the order of their recitation, so that Allah commanded them to slaughter the cow and they slaughtered it, and then the matter of the killing occurred, so they were commanded to strike the body with part of the cow. In that case, "and when you killed" is first in meaning over the first view, as we have mentioned, because the conjunction "wa" (and) does not require sequence. A parallel in the revelation is the story of Noah, after the mention of the flood and its ending, in His words: ﴿until when Our command came and the oven gushed forth, We said, "Load into it two of every kind"﴾ up to His words ﴿except a few﴾. [[See vol. 9, p. 33.]] [Hud: 40]. He mentioned the destruction of those who perished among them, then joined to it His words: ﴿And He said, "Board it; in the name of Allah is its course and its anchorage"﴾ [Hud: 41]. So He mentioned the boarding later in the address, though it is known that their boarding came before the destruction. Likewise is His words, the Exalted: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who revealed to His servant the Book and did not make in it any deviance, but made it straight﴾. [[See vol. 10, p. 346.]] [Hud: 1–2]. Its implied sense is: He revealed to His servant the Book, straight, and did not make in it any deviance. Similar examples in the Qur'an are numerous.

**The third issue:** There is no disagreement among scholars that dhabh (slaughter by cutting the throat) is preferred for sheep, nahr (slaughter by cutting the base of the neck) is preferred for camels, and there is a choice regarding cows. It was said: dhabh is preferred, because it is what Allah mentioned, and because the place of nahr is near the place of dhabh. Ibn al-Mundhir said: "I do not know of anyone who forbade eating what was slaughtered by nahr of what is normally slaughtered, or what was slaughtered by dhabh of what is normally sacrificed by nahr." Malik disliked this, and a person may dislike a thing without declaring it forbidden. The rulings on slaughter, the slaughterer, and their conditions will come in full in Surat al-Ma'idah, at His words: ﴿except what you have slaughtered properly﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], Allah willing. [[See vol. 6, p. 54.]] Al-Mawardi said: "They were commanded, and Allah knows best, to slaughter a cow rather than another animal, because it is of the same kind as the calf they worshipped, so as to make easier for them what they had regarded as great of that calf, and so that their response would reveal what worship of it had been in their souls." This meaning is a reason for slaughtering a cow, but it is not a reason for the answer to the questioner. Rather, the purpose is that the slain person would be brought back to life through the slaughter of a living animal, which makes more evident His power to produce things from their opposites.

**The fourth issue:** As for His words, the Exalted, (a cow) ﴿baqarah﴾: "Baqarah" is a name for the female, and "thawr" is a name for the male, like "naqah" and "jamal," and "imra'ah" and "rajul." It was also said: "baqarah" is the singular of "baqar" (cattle), and the female and male are the same. Its root comes from your saying: baqara batnahu, meaning he split his belly open, so the cow splits the earth with ploughing and stirs it up. From this comes "al-Baqir," the title of Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn 'Ali Zayn al-'Abidin, because he split open knowledge and knew its origin, that is, he cut into it. "Al-baqirah" is a garment that is split, which the woman puts over her neck without two sleeves. In the hadith about the hoopoe concerning Ibn 'Abbas: (so it split the earth). Shamir said: "baqara" means he looked at the place of the water and saw the water beneath the earth. Al-Azhari said: "al-bakar" is a collective noun, and its plural is "baqir." Ibn 'Arafah said: it is said "baqir," "baqir," and "bayquwr." 'Ikrimah and Ibn Ya'mur recited "inna al-baqira." "Thawr" is the singular of "thiran" (bulls). "Thawr" also means a leader among men, a piece of a cut, a kind of moss, a mountain named Thawr, and a tribe of the Arabs. In the hadith: (and the time of 'isha' prayer is until the thawr of the twilight does not set), meaning its spreading out. It is said: thara yathuru thawran and thawaranan when it spreads across the horizon. In the hadith: (whoever wants knowledge, let him stir up the Qur'an). Shamir said: "tathwir al-Qur'an" means reciting it and discussing it with scholars.

**The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They said, "Do you take us for a mockery?"﴾**

This is a reply from them to Moses, peace be upon him, when he said to them: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to sacrifice a cow﴾ [al-Baqarah: 67]. The reason is that they found a slain person among them. It was said his name was 'Amil. The identity of his killer was unclear to them and a dispute arose among them, so they said: "We will fight each other while the Messenger of Allah is among us." So they came to him and asked him for clarification. This was before the revelation in the Torah of the qasamah (the procedure of oaths in homicide cases). [[The author, may Allah have mercy on him, will discuss the qasamah and its ruling at His words: (so We said, "Strike him with part of it"). See p. 457 of this part.]] They asked Moses to call upon Allah, so Moses, peace be upon him, asked his Lord, and He commanded them to slaughter a cow. When they heard that from Moses, and there was apparently no answer in it to what they had asked him about, and they had judged between themselves in his presence, they said: "Do you take us for a mockery?" Al-huzw means play and ridicule, which has been discussed before. [[See p. 207.]] Al-Jahdari recited "a-yattakhidhuna" with a ya', meaning that some of them said this to others. Moses, peace be upon him, answered them with his words: ﴿I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 67], because turning away from the answer of a seeker of guidance to mockery is ignorance, so he sought refuge from it, peace be upon him, because it is a quality that is removed from the prophets. Ignorance is the opposite of knowledge. So he sought refuge from ignorance, just as they had been ignorant in their saying "Do you take us for a mockery?" to the one who informed them about Allah, the Exalted. The apparent meaning of this statement shows the corruption of the belief of the one who said it. The faith of one who says to a prophet whose miracle has appeared, "Indeed, Allah commands you to do such-and-such," and then says, "Do you take us for a mockery?", is not valid. If anyone today said this about some statement of the Prophet (ﷺ), he would have to be declared a disbeliever. Some people held that this came from them out of coarseness of nature, harshness, and disobedience, similar to what the one who said to the Prophet (ﷺ) about the division of the spoils of Hunayn said: "This division was not intended for the sake of Allah's face," and as another said to him: "Be just, O Muhammad." In all of this there is the clearest proof of the ugliness of ignorance and that it corrupts religion.

**The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿huzuwan﴾ (a mockery)** is the second object. It is permissible to soften the hamza, by making it between the waw and the hamza. Hafs read it as an open waw, because it is an open hamza preceded by a damma, so it follows the rule of substitution, like His words: "as-sufahau wa-lakin" (the foolish, but). It is also permissible to drop the damma from the zay, as you drop it from 'adud, so you say huzu'an, as the people of Kufa recited, and likewise "wa lam yakun lahu kufuwan ahadun" (and there was none equal to Him). Al-Akhfash reported from 'Isa ibn 'Umar that every noun of three letters whose first letter is damma has two forms: the light and the heavy, such as al-'usr and al-yusr and al-huzu'. Similar to it are plurals on the pattern fu'ul, such as kutub and kutb, rusul and rusl, and 'uun and 'uun. As for His words, the Exalted: ﴿And they assigned to Him a portion of His servants﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 15], it is not like huzu' and kufu', because it is on the pattern fu'l from the root, as will be discussed in its proper place, Allah willing. [[See vol. 16, p. 69.]]

**Issue: In the verse there is evidence for the prohibition of mocking the religion of Allah, the religion of the Muslims, and whoever is obligatory to honor. Such mockery is ignorance, and its doer deserves the threat of punishment. Joking is not the same as mockery. Do you not see that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to joke, and so did the imams after him?** Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: "It has reached us that a man came before 'Ubayd Allah ibn al-Hasan, who was the judge of Kufa, and 'Ubayd Allah joked with him, saying: 'Is this robe of yours made of the wool of a ewe or of a ram?' He said to him: 'Do not be ignorant, O judge!' 'Ubayd Allah said to him: 'Where did you find joking to be ignorance?' Then he recited to him this verse, so 'Ubayd Allah turned away from him, because he saw him as ignorant, not knowing the difference between joking and mockery, and neither of them is the same as the other."

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 68:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said: "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is."﴾ This is a show of obstinacy on their part and a lack of obedience. Had they complied with the command and slaughtered any cow whatsoever, the purpose would have been achieved. But they made things hard for themselves, so Allah made things hard for them. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-'Aliyah and others. Al-Hasan al-Basri narrated something similar from the Prophet (ﷺ). The dialect of Banu 'Amir says "ud'" (for "ad'u"). This has been mentioned before [[See p. 423.]]. The verb (yubayyin) is in the jussive because it answers the imperative. (Ma hiya) is a subject and predicate. The *mahiyyah* (quiddity, essence) of a thing is its reality and its essential nature by which it is what it is.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said: "Indeed He says it is a cow neither old nor young, but of middle age between them."﴾ In this there is evidence for the permissibility of *naskh* (abrogation) before the time of performing the act, because when He commanded a cow, it required any cow whatsoever. When He then added a description, He abrogated the first ruling by another. This is like someone who says: "For thirty camels, a *bint makhad* (a one-year-old she-camel)," and then abrogates it with a *bint labun* or a *hiqqah*. Likewise here, when He specified the attribute, that became an abrogation of the earlier ruling.

*Al-Fari<u>d</u>* is the aged one. One says "faradat tafridu furudan," meaning she grew old. The word is also used for anything ancient. The rajaz poet said:

*Grey has overtaken my temples, and my head is white,*
*(like) litters, among which are old men [[In al-Sihah of al-Jawhari the word is (mahafil) with a fa', and there is another transmission reported by Ibn al-A'rabi:*
*"Mahamil bid wa qawm furad" (litters white and people aged).*
*He means they are heavy like litters. See Lisan al-Arab, root f-r-d.]] who are decrepit,*

i.e. the aged. Another said:

*By your life, you have indeed given your neighbour an aged (cow)*
*that is led to him, one that can barely stand on its legs [[The Lisan version reads "li'amri laqad" and attributes the verse to 'Alqamah ibn 'Awf, who meant an old cow.]],*

i.e. an old one. Another said:

*O Lord of a rancorous one against me who is aged,*
*who has menstrual cycles like the cycles of a menstruating woman,*

i.e. an old one.

"*La fariduun*" (neither aged) is in the nominative as an attribute of "*baqarah*" (cow). "*Wa la bikrun*" (nor young) is coordinated with it. It has been said that "*la fariduun*" is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "she is not aged," and likewise "*la dhalulun*" (not broken to work), "*la tasqi al-harth*" (not irrigating the field), and "*musallamah*" (sound). Take note of this.

It has also been said that *al-fari<u>d</u>* is the one who has borne many litters, so her belly has become wide for that; this is because the meaning of *fari<u>d</u>* in the language is "wide." This was said by one of the later scholars.

*Al-bikr* is the young one who has not yet conceived. Al-Qutabi related that it is the one who has given birth. *Al-bikr* also means the first of the offspring. Someone said:

*O firstborn of two firstborns, and O heart-liver,*
*you have become to me like the forearm to the upper arm.*

*Al-bikr* is also applied to female animals and to humans as long as the male has not mounted her; it is pronounced with a kasrah on the ba'. With a fathah on the ba' it means a young camel in its prime.

*Al-'awan* is the middle-aged one, who has borne one or two litters. She is the strongest and best of cows. This is unlike horses. A poet describing a horse said:

*A dark bay of deep colour, neither aged nor middle-aged,*
*with a mottled coat, a horse [[akhsaf: when the white patch rises from its belly to its side.]]*

Mujahid said: *al-'awan* among cows is the one that has given birth again and again. Lexicographers have transmitted this. It is also said that *al-'awan* is the tall palm tree, which is, they claim, a Yemeni usage. *Harb 'awan* means a war in which there has previously been a war that was "*bikr*" (fresh). Zuhayr said:

*When a war in its middle stage has become fierce and grievous,*
*fierce, its fangs are sharp and crooked, making people shudder at it [[In the originals it reads "tuhiz" with a zay; the correction is from the commentary on the Diwan. Meaning: it makes people push it away, i.e. makes them hate it. "Laqihat" means it intensified; "mudirrah" means sour; "darus" means harsh, bad-tempered; "'usul" means crooked.]]*

That is: she is neither young nor old, i.e. she is *'awan*. Its plural is *'un* with a damma on the 'ayn and a sukun on the waw, and it has been heard as *'uun* with a damma on the waw, like *rusul*. This has already been mentioned. Al-Farra' related from *al-'awan* the verb "'awwanat ta'wiinan" (she became middle-aged).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So do what you are commanded.﴾ This is a renewal and emphasis of the command and an admonition to abandon obstinacy, but they did not abandon it. This indicates that the requirement of a command is obligation, as the jurists say, and this is the sound view as is mentioned in the principles of jurisprudence (*usul al-fiqh*). It also indicates that a command is to be carried out immediately (*'ala al-fawr*), which is also the position of most jurists. What supports this is that He reproached them when they did not hasten to do what they were commanded, saying: ﴿So they slaughtered her, though they nearly did not do it.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 71]. It has also been said: no, rather it is to be carried out at a later time (*'ala al-taraakhi*), because He did not reprimand them for delay and for returning to the discourse. Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said this.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 69:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what its color is."﴾ "Ma" is an interrogative in the nominative (mubtada'), and "lawnuha" is the predicate (khabar). It is also permissible to put "lawnuha" in the accusative governed by "yubayyin" (makes clear), in which case "ma" is superfluous (za'idah). Al-lawn (color) is the singular of al-alwan (colors), and it is a quality (hay'ah) such as blackness, whiteness and redness. Al-lawn also means a kind (al-nau'). And a man is described as mutalawwin (of changeable character) when he does not remain fixed in one disposition or one state. [The poet] said:

"Every day you change color; other than this, you are more beautiful."

Tallawana al-busr talwinan means that when the unripe dates (busr) began to show the signs of ripening. Al-lawn also means al-daqal, which is a variety of palm tree. Al-Akhfash said: it is a collection (jama'ah), whose singular is linah.

His saying: (ṣafrā'). The majority of the exegetes hold that it means yellow in color, from the well-known yellowness. Makki reported from some of them: even the horns and hooves. Al-Hasan and Ibn Jubayr said: it was yellow in the horns and hooves only. It is also reported from al-Hasan: "ṣafrā'" means black. The poet said: [[The speaker is al-A'sha, as in Lisan al-Arab.]]

"Those are my horses from it, and those are my mounts; they are yellow, their young ones like raisins."

I say: the first view is more sound, because it is the apparent meaning, and this one is anomalous (shadhdh), used figuratively only for camels. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿As if they were yellow camels﴾ [al-Mursalat: 33], because the black camels have a blackness that is a yellowness. Had He intended blackness, He would not have emphasized it with "fuqu'" (intense brightness), and that is a description specific to yellow; blackness is not described by it. The Arabs say: "aswad halik" (intensely black), "halakuk" and "hulkuk", "dajujiyy" and "ghirbib"; "ahmar qani'" (deep red); "abyad nasi'" (pure white), "lahaq", "lihaq" and "yaqaq"; "akhdar nadir" (bright green); and "asfar faqi'" (intensely yellow). Thus the transmitters of the language have reported it from the Arabs. Al-Kisa'i said: it is said "faqa'a lawnuha yafqa'u fuqu'an" when its yellowness becomes pure. Al-Ifqa' means bad condition, and fawaqi' al-dahr are its calamities. And "faqqa'a bi-asabi'ihi" means he made a sound with his fingers; from it is the hadith of Ibn Abbas: he forbade tafqi' in prayer, which is al-farqa'ah, namely cracking the fingers until they make a sound [[Every sound of a joint or finger is a naqid.]]. "Ṣafrā'" is not declined (lam yanṣarif) whether definite or indefinite, because it has the feminine suffix alif, which is permanent, and so it differs from the ta' (ha'), since what has the ta' is declined in the indefinite, like Fatimah and A'ishah.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Intensely bright is its color﴾ means its color is pure, with no color in it other than the color of its skin.

(It delights the beholders.) Wahb said: as if the rays of the sun emerged from its skin. For this reason Ibn Abbas said: yellow delights the soul. He urged the wearing of yellow sandals; al-Naqqash related it from him. Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: whoever wears a pair of yellow leather sandals, his worry will be little, because Allah, may He be exalted, says: "Yellow, intensely bright is its color, delighting the beholders." Al-Tha'labi related it from him. Ibn al-Zubayr and Muhammad ibn Abi Kathir forbade wearing black sandals, because they cause worry. The meaning of "tasurr" is "tu'jib" (pleases/delights). Abu al-Aliyah said: its meaning concerns its appearance and its look, so it has two qualities. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 70:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the cows have become confused for us﴾. They asked a fourth question, and did not comply with the command after the clarification. He mentioned "the cow" (al-baqar) because it is used in the sense of a collective noun, and for this reason He said, "Indeed, the cows have become confused for us," so He made the verb masculine in accordance with the form of the word "cow" (al-baqar). Qutrub said: the plural of baqarah is ba'ir, ba'ur and baqar. Al-Asma'i said: al-ba'ir is the plural of ba'irah. He said: baqar is also pluralized as ba'urah, related by al-Nahhas. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "indeed the species of cow." Al-Hasan, as mentioned by al-Nahhas, and al-A'raj, as mentioned by al-Tha'labi, read "innal-baqara tashshabaha" with a ta' and a doubled shin, making it an imperfect verb and feminine. The original form is tatashabbahu, then the ta' was assimilated into the shin. Mujahid read "tashabaha" like their reading, except that it is without an alif. In the Codex of Ubayy it is "tashabbahat" with a doubled shin. Abu Hatim said: this is an error, because the ta' in this pattern is assimilated only in the imperfect. Yahya ibn Ya'mur read "inna al-ba'ira yashshabahu," making it an imperfect verb, mentioning the cow and assimilating. It is also permissible to read "innal-baqara tashabahu" with a lightened shin and a damma on the ha', related by al-Tha'labi from al-Hasan. Al-Nahhas said: "yashabahu" with a lightened shin and ya' is not permissible; it is permissible with the ta' because the original is tatashabahu, so one of the two ta's was deleted due to the coincidence of the two ta's. "Al-baqar," "al-ba'ir," "al-bayqur," and "al-biqir" are dialect forms with the same meaning, and the Arabs use it both as masculine and feminine, and the meanings of the readings of "tashabaha" return to this. It was said: they only said "indeed the cows have become confused for us" because the faces of cows resemble one another, and from this is the hadith of Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he mentioned "trials like pieces of the night, coming like the faces of cows," meaning that some of them resemble others. The faces of cows resemble one another, and for this reason the Children of Israel said: "Indeed the cows have become confused for us."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed we, if Allah wills, will surely be guided﴾. It is an exception made by them, and in their making this exception in this last question there is a sign of repentance and submission, and an indication of regret for not complying with the command. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "If they had not made the exception, they would never have been guided to it" [[In a copy of the original: "lawla" and the hadith is narrated through several chains with the wording: "law lam yastathnu" (if they had not made an exception)]]. The construction of the sentence is: "And indeed we are surely guided, if Allah wills." The mention of guidance was placed first for emphasis on it. The word "shaa'a" is in a position of jazm as a conditional, and its response according to Sibawayh is the clause "inna" and what it governs. According to Abu al-Abbas al-Mubarrad, it is omitted.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 71:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He said: Indeed, He says it is a cow, neither broken to labour﴾. The majority of reciters read *lā dhalūl* with a *ḍammah* (raised ending), as a qualifier (ṣifah) of *baqarah* (cow). Al-Akhfash said: "*Lā dhalūl* is its qualifier, and it is not permissible to put it in the accusative." Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read *lā dhalūla* with a *fatḥah* (accusative), as a negation, with the predicate (khabar) implied. It is also permissible to read: *lā hiya dhalūl*, meaning "no, she is not broken to labour; she waters the tilth; she is sound." The meaning of *lā dhalūl* is that work has not made her submissive. It is said: a cow that is *mudhallalah* (broken to labour) is clearly *dhill* (with a *kasrah* on the *dhāl*). A man who is *dhalīl* is clearly *dhull* (with a *ḍammah* on the *dhāl*). That is, she is a difficult cow, untamed, not trained, not made docile by work.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿that stirs the earth﴾. *Tuthīru* is in a place of raising (marfūʿ) as a qualifier of the cow, meaning: she is a cow neither broken to labour, stirring [the earth]. Al-Hasan said: That cow was wild, and for this reason Allah described her as one that does not stir the earth and does not water the tilth, meaning she is not used for drawing water for the crops, nor is water drawn for her. Pausing here is good (ḥasan). Others said: *tuthīru* is a new independent clause (fiʿl mustaʾnaf), and the meaning is an affirmation that tilling is hers and that she used to till but did not water. On this interpretation the pause is at *lā dhalūl*. The first view is more correct, for two reasons. The first is what al-Nahhas reported from Ali ibn Sulayman, that he said: It is not permissible for *tuthīru* to be an independent clause, because after it comes *wa-lā tasqī al-ḥarth* (and does not water the tilth), and if it were independent it would not combine the conjunction *wa* with *lā*. The second is that if she stirred the earth, the stirring would have made her submissive, while Allah has negated submission from her by His saying: *lā dhalūl* (not broken to labour).

I say: It is possible that *tuthīru al-arḍ* refers to stirring the earth outside of work, out of exuberance and vigour, as Imru' al-Qays said:

*He heaps it up, scatters its dust, and stirs it,*
*Stirring like the one who raises dust in the scorching noon, the camel-driver with the five-day thirst.*

[[Note in the source: "nabbāt al-hawājir" means the man who, when the heat became intense on him, heaped up dust to reach its moisture. *Al-ʿasir* means the owner of camels that go five days without water.]]

On this reading, *tuthīru* is an independent clause, and *wa-lā tasqī* is coordinated with it. Consider this. Stirring the earth means moving and searching it. From this comes the hadith: "Stir up the Quran, for in it is the knowledge of the first and the last," and in another narration: "Whoever desires knowledge, let him stir up the Quran." This has already been mentioned (see p. 449). In the revelation is: ﴿and they stirred up the earth﴾ [al-Rum: 9], meaning they turned it over for cultivation. *Al-ḥarth* means what is tilled and sown. This will come later.

Issue: This verse is the strongest proof for defining an animal by its attributes. When an animal is specified and restricted by its attributes, it is permissible to contract a salam (an advance-payment sale, where the price is paid now for goods delivered later). This is the view of Malik and his companions, al-Awza'i, al-Layth, and al-Shafi'i. Likewise, anything that can be specified by description. Allah described the cow in His Book with a description that stands in place of identification. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "A woman should not describe another woman to her husband in such detail that it is as if he is looking at her." Muslim narrated it. The Prophet ﷺ made the description stand in place of seeing. He also made the blood money for manslaughter (diyah) a debt owed by the one obligated to pay it, payable at a fixed term, and did not make it payable immediately. This refutes the view of the Kufans, Abu Hanifa and his companions, al-Thawri, and al-Hasan ibn Salih, who said: salam is not permissible in animals. It is also narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, Hudhayfah, and Abd al-Rahman ibn Samurah, because an animal's true attributes, such as its gait and movement, cannot be fully known, and all of these increase or decrease its price. The rules and conditions of salam will come at the end of the surah in the verse about debt, if Allah wills. (See vol. 3, p. 377 onward.)

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿unblemished﴾. That is, she is unblemished. It may also be a qualifier, meaning she is a cow free from lameness and all other defects. This was said by Qatadah and Abu al-Aliyah. One should not say "unblemished from labour," because Allah has negated labour from her. Al-Hasan said: meaning her legs are sound, with no trace of work on them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿with no mark upon her﴾. That is, there is no colour in her that differs from the majority of her colour. She is entirely yellow, with no white, no red, and no black, as He said: ﴿bright in colour﴾. The root of *shiyah* is *wishy*, with the *wāw* deleted, as it is deleted from *yashī*. The original is *yūshī*. Its parallels are *al-zinah*, *al-ʿidah*, and *al-ṣilah*. *Al-shiyah* is derived from *washy al-thawb*, when a garment is woven with two different colours. A *thawr muwashsha* (a streaked bull) has blackness on its face and legs. Ibn ʿArafah said: *al-shiyah* means colour. One is called *wāshin* (a tale-bearer) only because he alters the speech and colours it, giving it various forms and adorning it as he wishes. *Al-washy* also means abundance; "the tribes of such-and-such (*washa banū fulān*)" means they multiplied. It is said: a *fars abqa* (piebald horse), a *kabsh akhraj* (ram with spots), a *taysh abraq* (goat with mixed colour), a *ghurāb abqaʿ* (magpie-crow), and a *thawr ashyah* (bull with markings). All these mean spotted, as the lexicographers stated explicitly. These attributes of the cow came about because they were strict, so Allah was strict with them, and the religion of Allah is ease. Probing deeply into questions put to the prophets and other scholars is blameworthy. We ask Allah for well-being.

Various narrations have been transmitted about the story of this cow. Their summary is: A man from the Children of Israel had a son, and he had a young cow. He released it in a thicket and said: "O Allah, I entrust to You this young cow for this child." Then the man died. When the child grew up, his mother, who was dutiful toward her son, said to him: "Your father entrusted to Allah a young cow for you. Go and take it." He went, and when the cow saw him, she came to him until he took hold of her horns. She was wild, but he began leading her toward his mother. The Children of Israel met him and found a cow matching the description they had been commanded to find. They offered to buy her, but he overcharged them. According to what Ikrimah narrated, her price was three dinars. They brought the matter to Musa, peace be upon him, and said: "This man has overcharged us." He said to them: "Satisfy him regarding his property." So they bought her from him for her weight in gold, as Ubaydah said. Al-Suddi said: for ten times her weight. It was also said: for the amount of gold that fills her hide. Makki mentioned that this cow descended from heaven and was not of the cattle of the earth. Allah knows best.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They said: Now you have brought the truth﴾. That is, you have made the truth clear. This was said by Qatadah. Al-Akhfash reported that *qālū al-āna* cut the connecting alif (*alif al-waṣl*, the hamza used only at the start of speech), as one says *yā Allāh*. He reported another reading: *qālū lānna* with the *wāw* included. Its parallel is the reading of the people of Medina and Abu Amr: *ʿādan lūlā*. The Kufans read *qālū al-āna* with a hamza. The reading of the people of Medina is *qāl lānna*, with the hamza eased and the *wāw* deleted because two unvocalised letters came together. Al-Zajjaj said: *al-āna* is built on a *fatḥah* because it differs from all other words that have *al* in them, since the *alif* and *lām* entered without reference to a specific known thing. You say: "You are here until *al-āna*," meaning until this time. So it was built as this was built, and the *nūn* was given a *fatḥah* because two unvocalised letters came together. It refers to the interval between the past and the future.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and they nearly did not do it﴾. Sibawayh permitted *kāda an yafʿala* (he nearly did), by analogy with *ʿasā*. This was mentioned earlier at the beginning of the surah (see p. 222 of this volume). This is an announcement of their reluctance to slaughter her and their slowness to hasten to the command of Allah. Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi said: because of the high price of the cow. It was also said: out of fear of exposure, for fear that they would be shamed by the identity of the killer among them. This was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih.

The statement "And when you killed a soul and disputed about it" (﴿وَإِذْ قَتَلْتُمْ نَفْساً فَادَّارَأْتُمْ فِيها﴾) is placed before the beginning of the story. The intended sense is: "And when you killed a soul and disputed about it." Then Moses said: "Indeed, God commands you to do such-and-such." This is like His saying: "Praise be to God, who sent down the Book to His servant and did not make in it any crookedness, but made it upright" [al-Kahf: 1–2]. That is, He sent down the Book to His servant as something upright and did not make in it any crookedness. Many examples like this occur, and we have explained it at the beginning of the story.

There are two opinions about the reason for his killing. The first: he had a beautiful daughter whom his cousin (ibn 'amm) wished to marry, but her paternal uncle refused him, so the cousin killed him, carried him from his village to another village, and left him there. It was also said that he threw him between two villages. The second: he killed him in order to inherit from him, since he was poor, and he accused some of the tribes (al-asbat) of killing him. 'Ikrimah said: The Children of Israel had a mosque with twelve gates, and each gate had a group of people who entered through it. They found a slain man in one of the tribes (asbat), so these accused those, and those accused these, and then they came to Moses to settle their dispute before him. He said: ﴿Indeed, God commands you to slaughter a cow﴾ [al-Baqarah: 67], and so on.

The meaning of ﴿fa-iddaraʾtum﴾ [al-Baqarah: 72] is: you differed and disputed. This was said by Mujahid. Its original form is *tadaraʾtum*, then the *ta'* was assimilated into the *dal* (idgham, assimilation of consonants). It is not permissible to begin with the assimilated letter, because it is quiescent, so the connecting alif (hamzat al-wasl, the alif used to make pronunciation possible at the start of a word) was added. ﴿Wa-llahu mukhrijun﴾ is a subject and predicate. ﴿Ma kuntum﴾ is in the accusative position governed by *mukhrijun*, and it is permissible to drop the tanwin (nunation) by treating it as an idafa (genitive construction). ﴿Taktumun﴾ is a clause in the position of the predicate of *kana*, and the returning pronoun is omitted; the estimated form is *taktumunahu* (you were concealing it).

According to the view that he killed him in order to inherit from him, the killer of intentional homicide (qatil 'amd) did not inherit from that time on. This was said by 'Ubaydah al-Salmani. Ibn 'Abbas said: This man killed his paternal uncle so that he would inherit from him. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Our law (shar') came with the like of this. Malik, may God have mercy on him, related in his *Muwatta'* that the story of Uhayha ibn al-Jullah concerning his paternal uncle was the cause for the rule that a killer does not inherit, and then Islam confirmed this, just as it confirmed many of the incidents (nawazil) of the Jahiliyya (the pre-Islamic era).

There is no disagreement among the scholars that the killer of intentional homicide does not inherit from the blood money (diyya) or from the property, except for a sect that deviated from the majority; all of them are people of innovation (ahl bid'a). The killer of unintentional homicide (qatil al-khata') inherits from the property but does not inherit from the blood money, according to the view of Malik, al-Awza'i, Abu Thawr and al-Shafi'i, because it is not presumed that he killed him in order to inherit from him and take his property. Sufyan al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa and his companions, and al-Shafi'i in another of his opinions, said: the killer, whether intentional or unintentional, does not inherit anything of the property or of the blood money. This is the view of Shurayh, Tawus, al-Sha'bi and al-Nakha'i. Al-Sha'bi related it from 'Umar, 'Ali and Zayd, who said: the killer, whether intentional or unintentional, does not inherit anything. It is related from Mujahid that both opinions were held. A group among the Basrans said: the killer of unintentional homicide inherits from both the blood money and the property together; Abu 'Umar related this. The view of Malik is more correct, as will be explained, God willing, in the verse of inheritance [[See vol. 5, p. 55 onward.]].

**Allah's words: ﴿So We said, "Strike him with part of it."﴾**

It was said: with the tongue, because it is the instrument of speech. It was also said: with the base of the spine (*ajb al-dhanab*), since from it the human body is formed. It was said: with the thigh. It was also said: with one of its bones, and the part that was cut off was a limb of it. When he was struck with it, the dead man came back to life, named his killer, and then returned to death as he had been.

**Issue:** Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, in the narrations of Ibn Wahb and Ibn al-Qasim, used as evidence for the validity of the *qasama* (the procedure of oaths in cases of homicide) the statement of the murdered person: "My blood is with so-and-so," or "So-and-so killed me." Al-Shafi'i and the majority of scholars rejected this. They said, and this is the sound view, that the statement of the murdered person, "My blood is with so-and-so," or "So-and-so killed me," is a report that may be true or false. There is no disagreement that the blood of the accused is protected, and that its shedding is forbidden except with certainty, and there is no certainty where there is possibility. So the consideration of the murdered person's statement, "My blood is with so-and-so," is invalid. As for the murdered man of the Children of Israel, it was a miracle, and Allah informed that He would revive him. That includes an informative report about his killer, a definite report not admitting doubt. So the two cases differ.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: The miracle lay in his revival. Once he was alive, his speech became like the speech of all other people, in terms of acceptance and rejection. This is a subtle branch of knowledge that none noticed except Malik.

There is nothing in the Qur'an stating that whenever he reports, his truthfulness must be accepted. Perhaps he commanded them to take the oath with him. Al-Bukhari, al-Shafi'i and a group of scholars considered this unlikely, and they said: How can his word be accepted regarding blood when his word is not accepted regarding a dirham?

**Issue:** The scholars differed on the ruling concerning the *qasama*. It is narrated from Salim, Abu Qilabah, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz and al-Hakam ibn 'Uyayna [[In one copy: (al-Hakam ibn 'Utayba).]] that they suspended judgment on it. Al-Bukhari also inclined to this view, because he cited the hadith of the *qasama* out of its proper place.

The majority said: the ruling on the *qasama* is established from the Prophet ﷺ. Then they differed on how it is applied. One group said: the claimants begin with the oaths. If they swear, they are entitled [to the blood-money or retaliation]. If they refuse, the accused swear fifty oaths and are cleared. This is the view of the people of Madina, al-Layth, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Abu Thawr, and it is what the hadith of Huwayyisa and Muhayyisa implies, which Malik and others transmitted.

Another group held that the oaths begin with the accused, who swear and are cleared. This is narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, al-Sha'bi and al-Nakha'i, and al-Thawri and the Kufans said the same. They relied on the hadith of Shu'ba ibn 'Ubayd from Bashir ibn Yasar, in which it says: "He began with the oaths of the accused, who were the Jews." They also relied on what Abu Dawud transmitted from al-Zuhri, from Abu Salama ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from men of the Ansar, that the Prophet ﷺ said to the Jews, beginning with them: "Will fifty men of you swear?" They refused, so he said to the Ansar: "Claim [the right]." They said: "We would swear about something unseen, O Messenger of Allah!" So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ made it a blood-money (*diya*) upon the Jews, because the body was found among them. They also relied on his saying, peace be upon him: "But the oath is upon the one who denies," and they were directed to it. They said: This is the established principle in claims, which the Law pointed out the wisdom of by his saying, peace be upon him: "If people were given [claims] by their claims alone, men would claim the blood and property of others. But the oath is upon the one who denies [[This hadith is so reported in some copies of the original and in Sahih Muslim. Ibn al-Malik said: He mentioned only the oath because it is the proof in a claim at the final stage; otherwise the claimant must first establish evidence.]]."

The proponents of the first view answered them: the hadith of Sa'id ibn 'Ubayd concerning the Jews beginning is, according to the people of hadith, an error. al-Nasa'i transmitted it and said: "Sa'id was not followed in this narration as far as I know." Bashir's hadith from Sahl, that the Prophet ﷺ began with the claimants, has been transmitted with a chain by Yahya ibn Sa'id, Ibn 'Uyayna, Hammad ibn Zayd, 'Abd al-Wahhab al-Thaqafi, 'Isa ibn Hammad and Bishr ibn al-Mufaddal, these are seven. Even if Malik transmitted it as a mursal, a group of hafiz scholars have connected it, and it is more authentic than the hadith of Sa'id ibn 'Ubayd.

Abu Muhammad al-Asili said: It is not permissible to oppose the report of a group with a single report. Moreover, Sa'id ibn 'Ubayd said in his hadith: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ paid one hundred camels from the camels of charity (*sadaqa*)," and charity is not given for blood-money, nor is settlement made from it on behalf of others. And the hadith of Abu Dawud is mursal, so the sound connected hadiths are not opposed by it.

They answered the reliance on the principle: this ruling is itself a principle, due to the sanctity of blood.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: It is established that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ placed the burden of proof upon the claimant and the oath upon the accused, and judgment must be given according to the apparent meaning of this. Unless Allah in His Book, or upon the tongue of His Prophet ﷺ, specifies a ruling in some matter, which is then excepted from the general sense of this report. Among what the Book indicated is requiring the slanderer to give the slandered the punishment (*hadd*) when he does not have four witnesses to testify to the truth of what was alleged against the slandered. And Allah exempted the one who accuses his wife by removing the punishment from him if he testifies four times. Among what the Sunna specified is the Prophet's ﷺ ruling by the *qasama*.

Ibn Jurayj transmitted from 'Ata', from Abu Hurayra, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The proof is upon the one who claims, and the oath is upon the one who denies, except in the *qasama*." al-Daraqutni recorded it.

Malik has argued for this issue in his Muwatta' with what is sufficient, so reflect on it there.

**Issue:** They also differed on whether retaliation (*qawad*) is obligatory by the *qasama*. One group made retaliation obligatory by it. This is the view of Malik, al-Layth, Ahmad and Abu Thawr, relying on his saying, peace be upon him, to Huwayyisa, Muhayyisa and 'Abd al-Rahman: "Will you swear and claim the blood of your companion?" Abu Dawud transmitted from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Prophet ﷺ executed a man by the *qasama* from the Banu Nadr ibn Malik. al-Daraqutni said: The copy of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb from his father from his grandfather is sound. Likewise Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr authenticates the hadith of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb and relies upon it. al-Bukhari said: I saw 'Ali ibn al-Madini, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, al-Humaydi and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh relying upon it. This is what al-Daraqutni said in his Sunan.

Another group said: there is no retaliation by the *qasama*; it only requires blood-money (*diya*). This is narrated from 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the view of al-Nakha'i and al-Hasan. al-Thawri and the Kufans, al-Shafi'i and Ishaq also took this view. They relied on what Malik transmitted from Ibn Abi Layla ibn 'Abd Allah, from Sahl ibn Abi Hathma, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said to the Ansar: "Either pay the blood-money for your companion, or be informed of war." They said: This indicates blood-money, not retaliation. They also said: The meaning of his saying, peace be upon him, "and claim the blood of your companion," is the blood-money for your slain man, because the Jews were not their companions. Whoever is entitled to the blood-money of his companion is entitled to his blood, because blood-money may be taken for intentional killing, and so that amounts to entitlement to the blood.

**Issue:** What necessitates the *qasama* is the *lawth* (a preliminary indication), and it is indispensable. The *lawth* is a sign that predominates in the mind over the truthfulness of the claimant of killing, such as the testimony of one just witness to seeing the killing, or the murdered person being seen writhing in his blood, while the accused is near him or beside him, with traces of killing upon him.

Opinions differed concerning the *lawth* and its validity. Malik said: It is the statement of the murdered person, "My blood is with so-and-so." And a single just witness is a *lawth*. This is in the narration of Ibn al-Qasim from him.

Ashhab related from Malik that he would take an oath (qasama) together with a witness who is not trustworthy (ʿadl), and together with a woman. Ibn Wahb related that the testimony of women constitutes a lawth (a presumptive indication, from the technical term lawth, meaning a circumstantial sign that makes a claim plausible). Muhammad related from Ibn al-Qasim that the testimony of two women is a lawth, but not the testimony of a single woman.

The judge Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi said: There has been much disagreement concerning the lawth. The well-known position of the school is that it is a trustworthy (ʿadl) witness. Muhammad said: this is more beloved to me. He said: Ibn al-Qasim and Ibn ʿAbd al-Hakam adopted it.

It is reported from ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwan that if the wounded or beaten person says, "My blood is with so-and-so," and then dies, the qasama applies. This is also the view of Malik and al-Layth ibn Saʿd. Malik argued from the case of the murdered man of the Children of Israel, who said, "So-and-so killed me."

Al-Shafiʿi said: the lawth is a trustworthy witness, or the claimant brings evidence (bayyina) even if they are not trustworthy.

Al-Thawri and the Kufans made the qasama obligatory merely by the discovery of the slain person, and dispensed with considering the statement of the victim and the witness. They said: if a slain person is found in the quarter of a people, and there is a mark on him, the people of that place swear that they did not kill him, and his blood-money (ʿaql) is upon them. If there is no mark on him, the ʿaqila bear nothing, unless evidence is established against one person.

Sufyan said: "This is something on which we have a consensus (ijmaʿ)." But it is a weak opinion, opposed by the scholars, and they have no precedent for it; it contradicts the Qur'an and the Sunnah, and in it there is the imposition of wealth upon the ʿaqila without evidence established against them and without their admission.

Malik and al-Shafiʿi held that if a slain person is found in the quarter of a people, his blood is unavenged (hadar), and the nearest residents are not held liable, because the slain person may be killed and then thrown at the door of a people in order to implicate them. Therefore they are not held accountable for such a thing until the conditions they stipulated for the obligation of the qasama are met.

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz said: this is a matter in which judgment is deferred until God judges it on the Day of Resurrection.

Question: Al-Qasim ibn Masʿada said: I said to al-Nasa'i, "Malik does not hold the qasama except with a lawth, so why did he cite the hadith of the qasama in which there is no lawth?" Al-Nasa'i said: Malik treated the enmity that existed between them and the Jews as equivalent to a lawth, and treated the lawth or the statement of the deceased as equivalent to enmity. Ibn Abi Zayd said: The origin of this is the story of the Children of Israel when God revived the one who was struck with part of the cow, and he said, "So-and-so killed me," and because enmity is a lawth. Al-Shafiʿi said: we do not consider the statement of the slain person to be a lawth, as has already been mentioned. Al-Shafiʿi said: If there is clear enmity between two groups, like the enmity that existed between the Ansar and the Jews, and a slain person is found in one of the two parties, and no one else mixes with them, the qasama is obligatory in that case.

Question: They differed concerning the slain person found in a quarter whose houses were rented by their owners. The people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y) said: it is upon the people of the plot (khutta), and the residents bear nothing. If the owners sold their houses and then a slain person was found, the blood-money is upon the purchaser and the residents bear nothing. If the owners of the houses were absent and had rented out their houses, then the qasama and the blood-money are upon the absent owners, and the residents among whom the slain person was found bear nothing. Then Yaʿqub among them retracted this view and said: the qasama and the blood-money are upon the residents of the houses. He related this view from Ibn Abi Layla, and argued that the people of Khaybar were laborers residing there, and the slain person was found among them. Al-Thawri said: we say it is upon the owners of the original property, meaning the owners of the houses. Ahmad said: the view of Ibn Abi Layla is correct regarding the qasama, but not regarding the blood-money. Al-Shafiʿi said: all of that is equal, and there is no ʿaql or qawad except by an established evidence (bayyina), or by what makes the qasama obligatory, and then the heirs take the oath. Ibn al-Mundhir said: this is the more correct view.

Question: No fewer than fifty oaths are sworn in the qasama, based on his saying, peace be upon him, in the hadith of Huwayyisa and Muhayyisa: "Fifty of you shall swear concerning a man from among them." If the entitled persons number fifty, each one of them swears one oath. If they are fewer than that, or if some of them who may not pardon refuse, the oaths are returned upon them according to their number. In intentional killing, no fewer than two men swear; a single man, whether male or female, does not swear. The heirs swear, and those from the kinsmen whom the heirs enlist, fifty oaths. This is the position of Malik, al-Layth, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, Ahmad, and Dawud. Mutarrif related from Malik that no one swears together with the defendant, and they themselves swear, as if they were one or more, fifty oaths by which they clear themselves; this is also the view of al-Shafiʿi. Al-Shafiʿi said: only an heir swears the qasama, whether the killing was intentional or by error. No one swears concerning property which he claims unless he has ownership in himself, or one whom God has made owner from among the heirs, and the heirs swear in proportion to their shares of inheritance. Abu Thawr also held this view, and Ibn al-Mundhir chose it, and it is the sound view, because one against whom no claim is made has no cause that binds him to an oath. Moreover, the purpose of these oaths is clearing oneself of the claim, and whoever is not claimed against is cleared.

Malik said regarding error (khata'): one man or woman swears in it; whenever fifty oaths are completed by one person or more, the swearer inherits, and whoever refuses receives nothing. If one who was absent comes, he swears the oaths that would have been required of him had he been present, in proportion to his inheritance. This is Malik's well-known position, though it is also reported from him that he does not see a qasama in error.

The completion of the issues, branches, and rulings of the qasama is mentioned in the books of jurisprudence and disagreement, and what we have mentioned is sufficient, and God is the Granter of success.

Question: In this story of the cow there is evidence that the law of those before us is law for us. This was held by groups of theologians and some jurists, and was chosen by al-Karkhi, and Ibn Bukayr, a judge among our scholars, stated it explicitly. The judge Abu Muhammad ʿAbd al-Wahhab said: this is what the principles of Malik and his positions in his books require, and al-Shafiʿi inclined to it. God said: ﴿So follow their guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 90], as will come, God willing.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Thus God brings the dead to life﴾, meaning: just as He revived this one after his death, so God revives everyone who has died. The particle "thus" (al-kaf) is in the accusative position, as it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun.

﴿And shows you His signs﴾, meaning His indications and His power.

﴿So that you may understand﴾, meaning: so that you may reason (ta'qilun). Already mentioned: meaning you refrain from disobeying Him. "I restrained myself from such-and-such" means I prevented it from doing it, and al-maʿaqil means fortresses.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then your hearts hardened after that﴾. Al-qaswah (hardness) means solidity, severity and dryness, and it is an expression for a heart being empty of turning back in repentance (inabah) and submission (idh'an) to the signs of Allah, exalted is He. Abu al-Aliyah, Qatadah and others said: what is meant is the hearts of all the Children of Israel. Ibn Abbas said: what is meant is the hearts of the heirs of the slain man, because when he came back to life and informed them of his killer, then returned to his death, they denied his killing and said, "He lied," after they had seen this great sign. They were never more blind of heart, nor more intense in denying their Prophet, than they were at that time. But the judgement of Allah regarding his killing was carried out.

At-Tirmidhi narrated from Abdullah ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not multiply speech without remembrance of Allah, for multiplying speech without remembrance of Allah is hardness of the heart, and the people farthest from Allah are those with a hard heart." In the Musnad of al-Bazzar, from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Four things are from wretchedness: the stiffening of the eye, the hardness of the heart [[al-qasa' (with fatha and the madd): a verbal noun like al-qaswah and al-qasawah.]], long hope, and greed for this world."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so they are like stones or even harder in hardness﴾. Regarding "aw" (or), it has been said: it is here in the sense of "wa" (and), as in His saying: ﴿sinful or ungrateful﴾ [al-Insan: 24], and "excuse or warning". The poet said:

*He attained the caliphate, or it was a destiny for him*

meaning, "and it was." It has also been said: it is in the sense of "bal" (rather), as in His saying: ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand, or they increase﴾ [al-Saffat: 147], meaning, "rather they increase." [[See vol. 15, p. 130.]] The poet said:

*She appeared like the sun's horn in the brightness of the forenoon, and her image, or you in the eye are more beautiful.* [[See the line in Khizanat al-Adab, under shahid 895.]]

That is, "rather, you." It has also been said: its meaning is ambiguity toward the addressee. From this is the saying of Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali:

*I love Muhammad with an intense love, and Abbas and Hamzah, or Ali.*

*If their love is guidance, I will attain it, and I am not mistaken if it is error.*

Abu al-Aswad did not doubt that their love is clear guidance; he only intended ambiguity. It was said to Abu al-Aswad when he said that: "You doubted!" He said: "Certainly not," and then cited His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed we or you are upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [Saba': 24], and said: "Would one who reported this be in doubt?" It has also been said: the meaning is choice, i.e., liken them to stones, you will hit [the mark], or to something harder than stones, you will hit [the mark]. This is like the saying of one who says: "Sit with al-Hasan or Ibn Sirin, and learn jurisprudence or hadith or grammar." It has also been said: it retains its original meaning of doubt, and its meaning for you, O addressees, and in your view, is that if you witnessed its hardness you would doubt: is it like stones, or harder than stones? This meaning has been stated regarding His saying: ﴿to a hundred thousand or they increase﴾ [al-Saffat: 147]. A group said: Allah intended that among them is one whose heart is like a stone, and among them is one whose heart is harder than a stone. So the meaning is that they are two groups.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿or harder﴾. "Ashaddu" is in the nominative by being coordinated with the position of the kaf in His saying "ka-al-hijarah" (like stones), because the meaning is, "it is like stones or harder." It is also permissible to read "aw ashaddu" with fatha, coordinated with "al-hijarah" (stones). "Qaswatan" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). Abu Haywah read "qasawatan," and the meaning is the same.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed among stones there are those from which rivers burst forth, and indeed among them there are those that split and water comes out from them﴾. The meaning of infijar (bursting forth) has already been mentioned [[See p. 419 of this part.]]. "Yashsharaqqu" originally is "yatashaqqaqu" (it splits), the ta' being assimilated into the shin. This is an expression for springs that have not grown large enough to be rivers, or for stones that split even though no water flows out widely. Ibn Musarrif read "yanshaqqu" with a nun, and he read "lamma yatafajjaru" and "lamma yatashaqqaqu" with the shaddah on "lamma" in both places. This reading is not well supported. Malik ibn Dinar read "yanfajiru" with a nun and kasrah on the jim. Qatadah said: He excused the stones, but did not excuse the wretched sons of Adam. Abu Hatim said: it is permissible to say "lamma tatafajjaru" with a ta', but it is not permissible to say "lamma tatashaqqaqu" with a ta', because if one says "tatafajjaru" he makes it feminine in agreement with "al-anhar" (rivers), and this does not occur with "tashaqqaqa." Al-Nahhas said: what he rejected is permissible according to the meaning, because the meaning is "and indeed among them are stones that split," and as for "yashsharaqqu," it is treated as agreeing with the wording of "ma." Al-Shaqq is the singular of al-shuqqug (cracks); originally it is a verbal noun. You say: "On the hands and feet of so-and-so are shuqquq," and do not say "shiqaq." Shiqaq is a disease of beasts, a cracking that afflicts their fetlocks, and sometimes rises to their hock, according to Ya'qub. Al-Shaqq also means dawn. The "ma" in His saying "lamma yatafajjaru" is in the accusative position, because it is the subject of "inna," and the lam is for emphasis. "Minhu" follows the wording of "ma," and "minha" is permissible according to the meaning; likewise "wa-inna minha lama yashsharaqqu fa-yakhruju minhu al-ma'" (and indeed among them is that which splits, and water comes out from it). Qatadah read "wa-in" in both places, as a light form of the heavy form.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed among them is that which descends out of fear of Allah﴾. He says: among stones there is that which is more beneficial than your hearts, because water comes out of it and it falls. Mujahid said: no stone has fallen from the top of a mountain, no river has burst forth from a stone, and no water has come out of it, except out of fear of Allah; the noble Qur'an was revealed with that. Ibn Juraij said the same. Some of the theologians said regarding His saying, "And indeed among them is that which descends out of fear of Allah": it is the hail descending from the clouds. It has also been said: the word "descent" is metaphorical, because when hearts take heed from the creation of stones and humble themselves by looking at them, the humility of the one who looks at them is attributed to them, just as the Arabs said: "a she-camel that is a merchant" (tajirah), meaning one that prompts whoever sees it to buy it. Al-Tabari related from a group that the fear attributed to stones is figurative, just as will is attributed to a wall in His saying, "It wants to collapse" [al-Kahf: 77], and as Zayd al-Khayl said: [[This line is attributed in Ibn Sa'd's al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, in the biography of al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, and in Sibawayh's book, to Jarir. It should be noted that Zayd al-Khayl died in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) or at the end of the caliphate of Umar (may Allah be pleased with him). His death was before that of al-Zubayr. He described the killing of al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam when he departed on the day of the Camel and was killed on the road by treachery. He says: When news of him reached Madinah (the city of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ), its walls and mountains humbled themselves and were submissive in grief for him.]]

*When the news of al-Zubayr arrived, the walls of Madinah humbled themselves, and the humble mountains.*

Ibn Bahr mentioned that the pronoun in His saying "wa-inna minha" refers to the hearts, not to the stones, meaning: among the hearts is that which submits out of fear of Allah. I say: everything that has been said is permitted by the wording, and the first is correct, for there is nothing to prevent giving some inanimate things knowledge so that they understand, like what is reported about the trunk on which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to lean when he delivered the sermon; when he moved away from it, it moaned. And it is established from him that he said: "Indeed a stone used to greet me in the Jahiliyyah; I surely recognize it now." And as it is reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Thabir [[Thabir: a well-known mountain near Makkah.]] said to me: Descend, for I fear they will kill you on my back, and then Allah will punish me." Then Hira called out to him: "Come to me, O Messenger of Allah!" In the revelation: ﴿Indeed We offered the trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains﴾ [al-Ahzab: 72], and so on. And He said: ﴿Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled and split apart out of fear of Allah﴾ [al-Hashr: 21], meaning humbling and submission. There will come more explanation of this in Surah "Subhan" (al-Isra'), if Allah wills.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾. "Bi-ghafil" is in the accusative position according to the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and in the nominative according to the dialect of Tamim. The ba' is for emphasis. "'Amma ta'malun" means: concerning your deeds, so that He leaves neither a small thing nor a great thing except that He counts it against you: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 7-8] [[See vol. 20, p. 150.]]. "Ma" does not need a returning pronoun unless it is taken to mean "alladhi" (that which), in which case the returning pronoun is omitted because the relative clause is long, meaning: concerning that which you do. Ibn Kathir read "ya'malun" with the ya', and the address, according to this reading, is to Muhammad, peace be upon him.

The second part (of the commentary)

(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful)

[Continuation of the commentary on Surah al-Baqarah]

**Concerning this verse there are four issues.**

**The first issue:** His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Do you hope that they will believe in you?﴾ This is an interrogative with the sense of denial (inkar). It is as if He is despairing them of the belief of this group of the Jews, meaning: even if they disbelieve, they have a precedent in that. The address is to the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ. The reason is that the Ansar were eager for the Jews to embrace Islam because of the alliance and the neighbourhood that existed between them. It has also been said that the address is to the Prophet ﷺ alone, related from Ibn 'Abbas, meaning: do not grieve over their denial of you, and He informed him that they are among the people of evil who have passed away. The "an" (that) here is in the accusative position, meaning "in that they believe," governed by "an," and for this reason the nun (of the verb) is dropped from it. It is said: "Tama'a fihi tam'an wa tama'iyyatan" (he desired it), with the lightened form, so he is "tama'," on the pattern of "fa'il." And "aṭma'ahu fihi ghayruhu" (another made him desire it). It is said in exclamation: "Ṭama'a ar-rajulu" (with a damma on the mim), meaning he became greatly covetous. And aṭ-ṭama' is the provision of the soldiers; it is said: "The amir ordered them their aṭmā', that is, their provisions." And a woman who is "miṭmā'" is one who makes men desire her but does not yield.

**The second issue:** His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And there was a group of them﴾. The word "farīq" (group) is an ism jam' (collective noun) with no singular from its own form, and its plural for small numbers is "afriqah," and for large numbers "afriqā'." "Yasma'ūna" is in the accusative position as the predicate of "kāna." It is permissible that the predicate be "minhum" (from them), and "yasma'ūna" be a qualifier of "farīq," but this is far-fetched. "Kalāma Allāh" (the Speech of God) is the reading of the majority. Al-A'mash read "kalima Allāh" (the word of God) as the plural of "kalima." Sibawayh said: "Know that some people of Rabi'ah say 'minhim' with a kasra on the ha', imitating the kasra of the mim, and a silent letter was not a strong barrier in his view." "Kalāma Allāh" is the object of "yasma'ūna." What is meant is the seventy whom Musa, peace be upon him, chose; they heard the Speech of God but did not carry out His command, and they distorted the statement in reporting it to their people. This is the view of ar-Rabi' and Ibn Ishaq, and in this view there is weakness.
