Whoever says that the seventy heard what Musa heard has erred, and has removed the virtue of Musa and his particular distinction of being addressed directly. As-Suddi and others said: they could not bear hearing it, their minds were confused, and they wished that Musa would hear and repeat it to them. When they finished and went out, a group of them altered what they had heard of the Speech of God, through the tongue of their Prophet Musa, peace be upon him, as He, may He be exalted, said: "And if any of the polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection so that he may hear the Speech of God" [[See vol. 8, p. 75.]]. If it is said: Al-Kalbi related from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, that the people of Musa asked Musa to ask his Lord to let them hear His speech, so they heard a sound like the sound of the shabbur: [[Ash-shabbur (on the pattern of at-tannur): the horn.]] "Indeed I am God; there is no god but I, the Living, the Self-Subsisting. I brought you out of Egypt with a lofty hand and a mighty arm." I say: this is a false report that is not authentic. It was related by Ibn Marwan from al-Kalbi, and both of them are weak and cannot be used as evidence. Speech was rather something specific to Musa among all the children of Adam. If he had also spoken to his people until he made them hear his speech, then what would be Musa's superiority over them? And He, whose word is the truth, said: "I have chosen you above the people by My messages and by My speech" [[See vol. 7, p. 280.]]. This is clear.

**The third issue:** People differed about how Musa knew the Speech of God, since he had not previously heard His address. Some of them said: he heard speech that was not in letters and sounds, and had no division or breath, so at that point he knew that this was not the speech of human beings but the speech of the Lord of the worlds. Others said: when he heard speech not from a direction, whereas human speech is heard from one of the six directions, he knew that it was not the speech of human beings. It was also said: his whole body became ears until he heard that speech with them, and so he knew that it was the Speech of God. And it was said concerning this: the miracle indicated that what he heard was the Speech of God, because he was told: "Throw down your staff," so he threw it and it became a serpent. This was a sign of the truth of the matter, and that the One who says to him: "Indeed I am your Lord" [[See vol. 11, p. 172.]] is God, mighty and majestic. It was also said: he had concealed in himself something that none could know except the Knower of the unseen, so God, may He be exalted, informed him in His address of that inner thought, and so he knew that the One addressing him was God, majestic and mighty. What is coming in Surah al-Qasas concerning the meaning of His saying: "He was called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot, from the tree" [[See vol. 13, p. 281.]] will be explained, if God, may He be exalted, wills.

**The fourth issue:** His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then they distort it﴾. Mujahid and as-Suddi said: they are the scholars of the Jews who distort the Torah, making the forbidden lawful and the lawful forbidden, following their desires. "From after they had understood it" means they recognised it and knew it. This is a rebuke to them, meaning: these Jews had inherited from their forefathers evil deeds and obstinacy, and these are of the same course, so how can you hope for their belief!

This statement also indicates that the one who knows the truth and is obstinate against it is far from right guidance, because he knows the promise and the threat, and that has not restrained him from his obstinacy.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 76–77:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe."﴾ This refers to the hypocrites. The origin of "laqu" (they met) is "laqiyu," and this has been discussed before [[see vol. 1, p. 206, second edition]]. "And when they go apart to one another..." The verse refers to the Jews. The reason is that some of them embraced Islam and then became hypocrites, and they would inform the believers among the Arabs of what their forefathers had been punished with. The Jews then said to them: "Do you tell them of what Allah has opened (fataha) against you?" That is, what Allah has decreed of punishment against you, so that they would say, "We are more honoured by Allah than you." This is related from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi. It is also said that when 'Ali (raḍiya Allāhu 'anhu) attacked the Banu Qurayza on the day of Khaybar, he heard them reviling the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he turned toward them and said: "O Messenger of Allah, do not approach them," and he went to them. He said, "I suppose you heard my insults from them; had they seen me, they would have refrained from that." He then rose toward them, and when they saw him they fell silent. He said to them: "Have you broken the covenant, O brothers of the apes and the swine? May Allah disgrace you and send down His vengeance upon you." They said: "You were not ignorant, O Muhammad, so do not act ignorantly toward us. Who told you this? This report came out only from us!" This meaning is narrated from Mujahid.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they go apart﴾. The origin of "khala" is "khalawa." The waw was changed to an alif because it is vowelled and the letter before it is open. The meaning of "khala" was mentioned at the beginning of the surah [[see vol. 1, p. 206]]. The meaning of "fataha" is "hakama" (judged). In Arabic usage, al-fath is judgement and decision, and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, judge between us and our people with truth, and You are the best of judges﴾ [[see vol. 7, p. 251]], that is, the judges. Al-fattah means the judge in the dialect of Yemen; one says, "Between me and you is the al-fattah." It is said that this is because he supports the wronged against the wrongdoer. Al-fath also means victory, and from it is His saying: "They sought victory over those who disbelieved" [[see p. 26 of this part]], and His saying: "If you seek a victory, the victory has certainly come to you" [[see vol. 7, p. 386]]. It can also mean distinguishing between two things.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That they may argue with you﴾. It is in the accusative after the lam of purpose (lam kay), and it may also be in the accusative by an implied "an," and the sign of the accusative is the deletion of the nun. Yunus said: some of the Arabs open the lam of kay. Al-Akhfash said: because the fatha is the original. Khalaf al-Ahmar said: it is the dialect of Banu al-'Anbar. The meaning of "liyuhajjukum" is "liyu'ayyirukum" (that they may reproach you), and they say, "We are more honoured by Allah than you." It is also said that the meaning is "liyahtajjū 'alaykum bi-qawlikum" (that they may argue against you using your own words), saying, "You disbelieved in it after you had stood on its truth." It is also said that a Jewish man would meet his Muslim friend and say to him: "Hold fast to the religion of Muhammad, for he is truly a prophet." "Before your Lord" (ʿinda rabbikum) is said to refer to the Hereafter, as He said: "Then on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, you will dispute" [[see vol. 15, p. 254]]. It is also said: "ʿinda" means "at the mention of your Lord." And it is said: "ʿinda" means "fi" (in), that is, "that they may argue with you about your Lord with it," so that they would have more right to it than you, due to the clear proof against you; this is narrated from al-Hasan. The ḥujja (proof) is a correct statement in general, and from this is the word maḥajjat al-ṭarīq (the path of the road). One says ḥājajtu fulānan fa-ḥajajtuhu, meaning I overcame him by proof. From it is the ḥadith: "Adam overcame Musa in argument" (fa-ḥajja Ādam Mūsā).

His saying: ﴿Do you not then reason?﴾ It is said: this is from the words of the rabbis to their followers. It is also said: it is an address from Allah, exalted is He, to the believers, meaning: Do you not reason that the Children of Israel will not believe while they are in these states? Then He rebuked them with a rebuke that is recited, saying: ﴿Do they not know?﴾ The verse ... This is an interrogative whose meaning is reproach and censure. The majority read "ya'lamūna" with the yā', while Ibn Muḥaysin read it with the tā', addressing the believers. What they concealed is their disbelief, and what they openly declared is their denial of it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 76–77:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe."﴾ This refers to the hypocrites. The origin of "laqu" (they met) is "laqiyu," and this has been discussed before [[see vol. 1, p. 206, second edition]]. "And when they go apart to one another..." The verse refers to the Jews. The reason is that some of them embraced Islam and then became hypocrites, and they would inform the believers among the Arabs of what their forefathers had been punished with. The Jews then said to them: "Do you tell them of what Allah has opened (fataha) against you?" That is, what Allah has decreed of punishment against you, so that they would say, "We are more honoured by Allah than you." This is related from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi. It is also said that when 'Ali (raḍiya Allāhu 'anhu) attacked the Banu Qurayza on the day of Khaybar, he heard them reviling the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he turned toward them and said: "O Messenger of Allah, do not approach them," and he went to them. He said, "I suppose you heard my insults from them; had they seen me, they would have refrained from that." He then rose toward them, and when they saw him they fell silent. He said to them: "Have you broken the covenant, O brothers of the apes and the swine? May Allah disgrace you and send down His vengeance upon you." They said: "You were not ignorant, O Muhammad, so do not act ignorantly toward us. Who told you this? This report came out only from us!" This meaning is narrated from Mujahid.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they go apart﴾. The origin of "khala" is "khalawa." The waw was changed to an alif because it is vowelled and the letter before it is open. The meaning of "khala" was mentioned at the beginning of the surah [[see vol. 1, p. 206]]. The meaning of "fataha" is "hakama" (judged). From it is the ḥadith: "Adam overcame Musa in argument" (fa-ḥajja Ādam Mūsā).

Then He rebuked them with a rebuke that is recited, saying: ﴿Do they not know?﴾ The verse ... This is an interrogative whose meaning is reproach and censure. The majority read "ya'lamūna" with the yā', while Ibn Muḥaysin read it with the tā', addressing the believers. What they concealed is their disbelief, and what they openly declared is their denial of it.

**Question One:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And among them are unlettered people (ummiyyun)﴾, that is, among the Jews. It was also said: among the Jews and the hypocrites there are ummiyyun, meaning those who neither write nor read. Their singular is ummiy, which is attributed to the ummiyya (unlettered) nation, which remains in its original state since its mothers gave birth to it, having learned neither writing nor reading. From this is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "We are an unlettered nation; we do not write and we do not calculate" (al-hadith). It was said that they were called unlettered because they did not believe in Umm al-Kitab (the Mother of the Book), according to Ibn 'Abbas. Abu 'Ubayda said: they were called unlettered only because the Book was revealed to them, as if they were attributed to Umm al-Kitab. So it is as if He said: "Among them are people of the Book who do not know the Book." 'Ikrima and al-Dahhak said: they are the Christians of the Arabs. It was also said: they are a people from among the People of the Book whose scripture was lifted because of sins they committed, so they became unlettered. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: they are the Magians. I say: the first opinion is the most evident, and Allah knows best.

**Question Two:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿They know not the Book except wishful beliefs (amani)﴾. Here "illa" (except) carries the meaning of "lakin" (but), so it is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), like His saying: ﴿They have no knowledge of it except following conjecture﴾. Al-Nabigha said:

*I swore an oath without any reservation (mathnawiyya)*¹
*And I have no knowledge except a good opinion of a companion.*

Abu Ja'far, Shayba and al-A'raj read "illa amani" with a light yā' (amani), having dropped one of the two yā's for lightness. Abu Hatim said: every word of this kind whose singular is doubled may be read with shadda or without it, such as athafiyy, aghaniyy, amaniyy and the like. Al-Akhfash said: this is like what is said of miftah (key): mafatih and mafatih, and it is the yā' of the plural. Al-Nahhas said: deletion is more common in the defective (mu'tall) forms, as the poet said (Dhu al-Rumma, as in his Diwan):

*Will the greeting return, or will blindness be removed?*
*Three hearths (al-athafi) and desolate traces (al-rusum al-balaqi').*²

Al-amani is the plural of umniyya, which means recitation (tilawa). Its original form is umnuwiyya on the pattern of uf'ulah; the waw was assimilated into the yā', and the nūn took a kasra because of the yā', so it became umniyya. From this is His saying: ﴿Except when he recites (tamanna), Satan casts into his recitation (umniyyatihi)﴾, that is, when he recites, Satan casts into his recitation. Ka'b ibn Malik said:

*He recited the Book of Allah at the beginning of his night,*
*And at its end he met the death of fates.*

Another said:

*He recited the Book of Allah at the last of his night,*
*Reciting the Psalms of Dawud at a steady pace.*

Al-amani also means lies, and from this is the saying of Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him: "I have not tamanna since I embraced Islam," that is, I have not lied. And the saying of some Arabs to Ibn Da'b when he was narrating: "Is this something you have narrated, or something you have tamannaytahu?" that is, something you have fabricated. In this meaning Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid interpreted "amani" in the verse. Al-amani also means what a person wishes for and desires. Qatada said: "illa amani" means that they wish upon Allah what is not theirs. It was also said: al-amani means estimation (taqdir); it is said: "muniya lahu," meaning he was decreed for. Al-Jawhari said, and Ibn Bahr related it, and he recited the poet's verse:

*Do not feel safe, even if you have entered a sanctuary,*
*Until you meet what the decreer has decreed for you.*³

That is, the one who decrees decrees for you.

**Question Three:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And they are not but assuming (yazunnun)﴾. Here "in" (and not) has the meaning of the negating "ma" (not), as He said: ﴿The disbelievers are not but in delusion﴾. "Yazunnun" means they lie and fabricate, because they have no knowledge of the soundness of what they recite; they are only imitators of their rabbis in what they read. Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: Ahmad ibn Yahya the grammarian narrated to us that the Arabs use zann (assumption) to mean knowledge, doubt and lying. He said: when the proofs of knowledge are established and they outweigh the proofs of doubt, then the zann is certainty; when the proofs of certainty and the proofs of doubt are equal, then the zann is doubt; and when the proofs of doubt exceed the proofs of certainty, then the zann is lying. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And they are not but assuming﴾, meaning, they are not but lying.

**Question Four:** Our scholars, may Allah have mercy upon them, said: Allah the Exalted described their rabbis as those who alter and distort. He said, and His word is the truth: ﴿So woe to those who write the Book with their own hands﴾, the verse. This is because when matters among them decayed, their scholars' following was corrupted, and they turned to the world with greed and covetousness, they sought things that would turn people's faces toward them. So they introduced innovations into their law and altered it, attributed that to the Torah, and said to their foolish ones: "This is from Allah," so that they would accept it from them; thus their leadership would be secured and they would obtain the world's wreckage and its filth. Among what they introduced was saying: "We have no duty regarding the unlettered (ummiyyin), who are the Arabs," meaning: whatever we take from their wealth is lawful for us. Among what they introduced was saying: "No sin will harm us, for we are His beloved and His sons," exalted is Allah above that! Actually what was in the Torah was: "O my rabbis and O sons of My messengers," but they altered it and wrote: "O my beloved ones and O my sons." So Allah revealed their refutation: ﴿And the Jews and the Christians said: We are the sons of Allah and His beloved. Say: Why then does He punish you for your sins?﴾ Then they said: "Allah will not punish us, and if He punishes us, it will be forty days, the number of the days of the calf." So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And they said: The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days. Say: Have you taken a covenant with Allah?﴾ Ibn Miqsam said: it means monotheism (tawhid), by the evidence of His saying: ﴿Except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾, meaning "there is no god but Allah." "So Allah will not break His covenant, or do you say about Allah what you do not know?" Then He refuted them, saying: ﴿Rather, whoever earns an evil deed and his sin encompasses him, those are the companions of the Fire, they will abide therein forever. And those who believe and do righteous deeds, those are the companions of Paradise, they will abide therein forever.﴾ Thus He made clear that abiding forever in the Fire and in Paradise is only according to disbelief and faith, not according to what they claimed.

¹ *Mathnawiyya*: exception in an oath.
² *Al-athafi* (plural of uthfiyya, with the first letter vowelled with damma or kasra, the thā' sakin, and the yā' shadda): the stones on which the cooking pot is placed. *Al-rusum*: remains of buildings. *Al-balaqi'* (plural of balqa'): desolate ruins.
³ The verse is attributed in the Qamus commentary to Suwayd ibn 'Amir al-Mustaliqi.

**The first issue:** Scholars differ over the meaning of *al-Waylu* (woe, a dreadful torment or ruin).[[Abu Hayyan said in *al-Bahr al-Muhit*, after mentioning the views reported on the meaning of *al-Waylu*: "If there were a sound report from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) explaining *al-Waylu*, it would be necessary to adopt it. The Arabs spoke with the word *al-Waylu* in their verse and prose before the Qur'an came, and they did not apply it to any of these explanations. Its meaning is only what the lexicographers have explained it to be."]] `Uthman ibn `Affan reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that it is a mountain of fire. Abu Sa`id al-Khudri reported that *al-Waylu* is a valley in Hell between two mountains, into which the one who falls will plunge for forty autumns. Sufyan and `Ata' ibn Yasar reported that *al-Waylu* in this verse is a valley running in the courtyard of Hell, carrying the pus of the people of the Fire. It was also said that it is a cistern in Hell. Al-Zahrawi transmitted from others that it is a gate of the gates of Hell. Ibn `Abbas said: *al-Waylu* is the hardship of the punishment. Al-Khalil said: *al-Waylu* is the intensity of evil.[[So it appears in the manuscripts of the original, and in the *Bahr* of Abu Hayyan.]] Al-Asma`i said: *al-Waylu* expresses lamentation, and *al-Waih* expresses pity. Sibawayh said: *Waylun* is for one who has fallen into ruin, and *waihun* is a rebuke for one who is close to ruin. Ibn `Arafa said: *al-Waylu* is grief. It is said: *tawayyala al-rajulu* when a man calls out "woe." It is only said at grief and at what is disliked, and from this is His saying: "So woe to those who write the Book with their own hands." It was also said: its origin is ruin, and everyone who falls into ruin calls out "woe," and from this is His saying, Exalted is He: "Woe to us! What is this Book?" *Al-Waylu* and *al-Waylah* are both ruin, and their plural is *al-Waylat*. He said:

"Woe is his if he has become (such), and no mother of Hashim [is there]"

And he also said:

"She said: Woes upon you, for you are one who walks on foot."

"*Fa-waylun*" is in the nominative (*raf`*) as the subject of a nominal sentence (*mubtada'*), and it is permissible to begin with it although it is indefinite, because it carries the sense of supplication. Al-Akhfash said: the accusative (*nasb*) is also permissible, by supposing a verb, meaning: God imposed upon them a woe. Al-Farra' said: the original form of *al-Waylu* is *way*, meaning grief, as you say: *way li-fulan*, meaning grief for him. The Arabs joined it to the *lam*, and they treated it as part of the word and declined it. The best form when it is detached from an annexation (*idafah*) is the nominative, because it implies a settled occurrence. The accusative is also valid in the sense of supplication, as we have mentioned. Al-Khalil said: Apart from this pattern, only *waih*, *wais*, *wah*, *wayk*, *wayl* and *wayb* have been heard, and all of them are close in meaning. They are differentiated by the accusative of the verbal nouns: *waylahu*, *wa`lahu*, *waihahu*, *waisahu*. When you add the *lam*, you put it in the nominative and say: *waylun lahu* and *waihun lahu*.

**The second issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: "*lilladhina yaktubuna*" (for those who write). Writing is well known. The first to write with the pen and to inscribe with it was Idris (peace be upon him), and this is found in the hadith of Abu Dharr, which al-Ajurri and others transmitted. It has also been said that Adam (peace be upon him) was given the ability to write, and it became an inheritance among his descendants.

**The third issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: "*bi-aydihim*" (with their own hands) is an emphasis, since it is known that writing is only done by the hand. It is like His saying: "nor any bird that flies with its two wings," and His saying: "they say with their mouths." It was also said that the benefit of "*bi-aydihim*" is to clarify their guilt and to affirm their open defiance, for the one who personally performs the act is more culpable than one who merely approves of it, even if he is the one who holds the opinion. Ibn al-Sarraj said: "*bi-aydihim*" is a figurative expression meaning that they did it on their own initiative, not that it was sent down to them, even though it is not literally about the writing of their hands.

**The fourth issue:** In this verse and the one before it there is a warning against altering, changing, and adding to the Law. Everyone who alters, changes, or innovates in the religion of God what is not part of it and is not permissible in it falls under this severe threat and painful punishment. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) warned his community, knowing what would happen at the end of time, when he said: "Beware! Those before you among the People of the Book split into seventy-two sects, and this community will split into seventy-three sects, all of them in the Fire except one," and the hadith continues, and it will come later. He warned them against inventing things in the religion on their own initiative that oppose the Book of God, or His Sunnah, or the Sunnah of His Companions, so that they would lead people astray. What he warned of has occurred and spread, widespread and well known. "Surely we belong to God, and to Him we shall return."

**The fifth issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: "*liyashtaru bihi thamanan qalilan*" (to trade it for a small price). God Exalted described what they take as small, either because it is perishable and not lasting, or because it is unlawful, since what is unlawful has no blessing in it and does not grow in God's sight. Ibn Ishaq and al-Kalbi said: the description of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in their Book was "of medium height, ruddy-brown," but they made him "wheat-complexioned, straight-haired and tall." They said to their companions and followers: "Look at the description of the Prophet (ﷺ) who will be sent at the end of time; the description of this one does not resemble him." The rabbis and scholars had leadership and worldly gains, so they feared that if they made it clear, their livelihood and leadership would be lost, and for this reason they altered it. Then He said, Exalted is He: "So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they earn." It was said: "what they earn" refers to their means of livelihood. It was also said: it refers to their sins. And He repeated "woe" to intensify the gravity of their deed.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 80:

There are three issues in this verse.

The first is God's words ﴿And they say﴾, meaning the Jews, ﴿"The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days."﴾ Scholars differ concerning the occasion of its revelation. It is said that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to the Jews, "Who are the people of the Fire?" They said, "We are, and then you will succeed us." He said, "You have lied. You know well that we will not succeed you." Then this verse was revealed. This was related by Ibn Zayd.

Ikrimah related from Ibn Abbas: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) came to Madinah while the Jews were saying, "This world is only seven thousand years, and people are punished in the Fire for one day of the Otherworld for every thousand years of the days of this world, and it is only seven days." So God revealed the verse. This is also the view of Mujahid.

A group said: The Jews said that the Torah states that Jahannam is a journey of forty years, and that they would cross it at a rate of one year per day until they completed it, and Jahannam would be gone. This was related by al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas.

It is also related from Ibn Abbas: The Jews claimed that they found written in the Torah that the distance between the two edges of Jahannam is a journey of forty years, until they reach the tree of al-Zaqqum. They said, "We will only be punished until we reach the tree of al-Zaqqum, and then Jahannam will go away and perish."

Also from Ibn Abbas and Qatadah: The Jews said that God swore that He would make them enter the Fire for forty days, corresponding to the number of days they worshipped the calf. God refuted them, as has been mentioned previously.

The second issue: In this verse there is a rebuttal of Abu Hanifah and his companions, who used as evidence the Prophet's saying (peace be upon him), "Leave the prayer during the days of your menstrual periods (aqra')," to argue that the duration of menstruation (hayd) is whatever is called "days of menstruation." They held that its minimum is three days and its maximum is ten. They said: What is less than three is called "a day" or "two days," and what exceeds ten is called "eleven days," and it is not called "days" (ayyam) in that case. "Days" is only said of the range from three to ten. God the Exalted said: ﴿So fast three days during the Hajj﴾ [2:196]; ﴿Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days﴾ [11:65]; ﴿He made it prevail against them for seven nights and eight days, in succession﴾ [69:7].

It is said to them: God the Exalted has said concerning fasting: ﴿numbered days﴾ [2:184], meaning the whole month. He also said: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for numbered days﴾, meaning forty days. Furthermore, when "days" is attached to a circumstance, it is not meant to restrict the number; one says, "the days of your walking, your travel, and your residence," even if they amount to thirty, twenty, or any number. Perhaps he meant the usual period for her, and the usual period is six or seven, so the statement was framed according to that. And God knows best.

The third issue: God's words ﴿Say: Have you taken a covenant from God?﴾ The discussion of "taking" (ittakhadha) has already been given, so there is no need to repeat it. ﴿a covenant from God﴾, meaning: Have you sent forward a righteous deed, so that you believed and obeyed, thereby deserving to be brought out of the Fire? Or did you know this by the revelation that He made a covenant with you? ﴿Then God will not break His covenant﴾, ﴿or do you say about God what you do not know?﴾ This is a rebuke and reproach.

Three issues arise here.

The first concerns His saying: ﴿Bala﴾ (Nay, rather), meaning: the matter is as you have stated. Sibawayh said: "Bala" and "na'am" (yes) are not nouns; rather they are particles, like "bal" and others, and they serve as a reply to their saying: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few days﴾. The Kufans said: its origin is "bal," which is used for turning away from the first statement, and a "ya" was added to it so that pausing on it would be easier, and the "ya" was given the meaning of affirmation and assent. Thus "bal" indicates the rejection of a denial, and the "ya" indicates affirmation of what follows. They said: If someone said, "Did you not take a dinar?" and you replied, "Na'am (yes)," the meaning would be "No, I did not take it," because you confirmed the negation and what follows it. But if you say, "Bala (yes, indeed)," the meaning becomes "I did take it." Al-Farra' said: When a man says to his companion, "You owe me nothing," and the other replies, "Na'am," that is confirmation, because he owes him nothing; but if he says, "Bala," it is a rejection of his statement, and its implied meaning is, "Yes, you owe me." In the revealed text: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ They said: ﴿Bala (Yes indeed)﴾ [see vol. 7, p. 613]. Had they said "na'am," they would have disbelieved.

The second concerns His saying: ﴿sayyi'ah﴾ (evil deed). The sayyi'ah is shirk (polytheism). Ibn Juraij said: I asked 'Ata': "Whoever earns an evil deed (sayyi'ah)?" He said: "Shirk," and he recited: ﴿And whoever brings an evil deed, their faces will be thrown into the Fire﴾. Likewise said al-Hasan and Qatadah, and they said: the khati'ah is the major sin.

The third concerns the fact that when He said: ﴿Bala, whoever earns an evil deed and his sin encompasses him﴾, this shows that what is conditioned upon two requirements is not complete with only one of them. A similar example is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast﴾ [see vol. 15, p. 357]. Also His saying, peace be upon him, to Sufyan ibn 'Abd Allah al-Thaqafi, who had said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, tell me a saying in Islam about which I will not ask anyone after you." He said: "Say: I have believed in Allah, then be steadfast." Narrated by Muslim. The discussion of this meaning and what the scholars said about it has already passed at His saying to Adam and Eve: ﴿And do not approach this tree, lest you be among the wrongdoers﴾ [see vol. 1, p. 304].

Nafi' read "khati'atuhu" in the plural, while the rest read it in the singular; the meaning is abundance, like His saying: ﴿And if you count the favour of Allah, you cannot enumerate it﴾ [see vol. 9, p. 367].

Three issues arise here.

The first concerns His saying: ﴿Bala﴾ (Nay, rather), meaning: the matter is as you have stated. Sibawayh said: "Bala" and "na'am" (yes) are not nouns; rather they are particles, like "bal" and others, and they serve as a reply to their saying: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few days﴾. The Kufans said: its origin is "bal," which is used for turning away from the first statement, and a "ya" was added to it so that pausing on it would be easier, and the "ya" was given the meaning of affirmation and assent. Thus "bal" indicates the rejection of a denial, and the "ya" indicates affirmation of what follows. They said: If someone said, "Did you not take a dinar?" and you replied, "Na'am (yes)," the meaning would be "No, I did not take it," because you confirmed the negation and what follows it. But if you say, "Bala (yes, indeed)," the meaning becomes "I did take it." Al-Farra' said: When a man says to his companion, "You owe me nothing," and the other replies, "Na'am," that is confirmation, because he owes him nothing; but if he says, "Bala," it is a rejection of his statement, and its implied meaning is, "Yes, you owe me." In the revealed text: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ They said: ﴿Bala (Yes indeed)﴾ [see vol. 7, p. 613]. Had they said "na'am," they would have disbelieved.

The second concerns His saying: ﴿sayyi'ah﴾ (evil deed). The sayyi'ah is shirk (polytheism). Ibn Juraij said: I asked 'Ata': "Whoever earns an evil deed (sayyi'ah)?" He said: "Shirk," and he recited: ﴿And whoever brings an evil deed, their faces will be thrown into the Fire﴾. Likewise said al-Hasan and Qatadah, and they said: the khati'ah is the major sin.

The third concerns the fact that when He said: ﴿Bala, whoever earns an evil deed and his sin encompasses him﴾, this shows that what is conditioned upon two requirements is not complete with only one of them. A similar example is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast﴾ [see vol. 15, p. 357]. Also His saying, peace be upon him, to Sufyan ibn 'Abd Allah al-Thaqafi, who had said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, tell me a saying in Islam about which I will not ask anyone after you." He said: "Say: I have believed in Allah, then be steadfast." Narrated by Muslim. The discussion of this meaning and what the scholars said about it has already passed at His saying to Adam and Eve: ﴿And do not approach this tree, lest you be among the wrongdoers﴾ [see vol. 1, p. 304].

Nafi' read "khati'atuhu" in the plural, while the rest read it in the singular; the meaning is abundance, like His saying: ﴿And if you count the favour of Allah, you cannot enumerate it﴾ [see vol. 9, p. 367].

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 83 (part 1 of 2):**

There are ten issues concerning this verse.

**The first issue:** His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾. The discussion of the meanings of these words has already preceded [[see vol. 1, pp. 246, 330.]]. Scholars differ regarding the "covenant" (mithaq) here. Makki said: it is the covenant that was taken from them when they were brought out of the loins of Adam like atoms (al-dharr). It was also said: it is a covenant taken from them while they were sane in their lifetimes, through the tongues of their prophets. It is His saying: "Do not worship except Allah." Worship of Allah means affirming His oneness (tawhid), affirming His messengers, and acting upon what He revealed in His books.

**The second issue:** His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Do not worship﴾. Sibawayh said: "Do not worship" is connected to an oath, and the meaning is: "And when We made them successors, by Allah, you shall not worship." Al-Mubarrad, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' permitted this. Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read "Do not worship" (la ta'budu) in the prohibitive form, and for this reason the speech is connected to imperatives, so He says: "and stand up, and speak, and establish prayer, and give zakat." It was also said that it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: "We took their covenant while they were monotheists, or not opponents." This was said by Qutrub and also by al-Mubarrad. This interpretation is only tenable according to the reading of Ibn Kathir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i, "ya'budun" with the letter ya' at the beginning. Al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and a group said: the meaning is "We took their covenant that they would not worship except Allah, that they would be good to the two parents, and that they would not shed blood," then "an" (that) and the preposition (ba') were omitted, so the verb became nominative (marfu') when they were removed, as in His saying: "Do you then command me to worship other than Allah?" [[see vol. 15, p. 276.]] Al-Mubarrad said: this is an error, because everything that is elided in Arabic operates as it would if it were stated. You say: "wa-baladin qata'tu" (and a land I traversed), meaning "rubba baladin" (many a land). I say: this is not an error; rather, both are valid forms, and Sibawayh recited upon them:

*Ala ayyuha dha'l-zajiri akhḍara'l-waghā*
*wa-an ashhada'l-ladhdhati hal anta mukhlidi*

[This is a verse of Tarafa ibn al-'Abd in his Mu'allaqa.]

(Both) with the accusative and the nominative: the accusative is on the basis of implying "an," and the nominative on the basis of its omission.

**The third issue:** His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and to the parents, good treatment﴾, meaning: "And We commanded them to treat the parents well." In this verse Allah, mighty and majestic, joined the right of parents with monotheism, because the first creation is from Allah and the second upbringing (nash' al-thani, which is upbringing) is from the parents. For this reason He joined gratitude to them with gratitude to Himself, saying: "Give thanks to Me and to your parents" [[see vol. 14, p. 65.]]. Good treatment of parents means living with them in kindness (ma'ruf), humility towards them, obeying their command, praying for their forgiveness after their death, and maintaining the ties of those who were dear to them, as will be explained in detail, if Allah the Exalted wills, in "al-Isra'" [[see vol. 10, p. 238.]].

**The fourth issue:** His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and to the near kin﴾. He conjoined "the near kin" with the parents. "Al-qurba" means kinship, and it is a verbal noun like "al-ruj'a" and "al-'uqba." Meaning: "And We commanded them to do good to relatives by maintaining the ties of kinship." This will be explained in detail, if Allah the Exalted wills, in "Surat Muhammad" (al-Qital) [[see vol. 16, p. 245.]].

**The fifth issue:** His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and the orphans﴾. "Al-yatama" is also conjoined; it is the plural of "yatim," like "nadama" is the plural of "nadim." Orphanhood among the children of Adam is through the loss of the father, and among animals through the loss of the mother. Al-Mawardi related that "yatim" is said of human beings for the loss of the mother, but the first (loss of father) is the well-known usage. Its root meaning is isolation: it is said "a child is an orphan (yatim)," meaning isolated from his father; and "a pearl of unique (yatima)," meaning it has no equal. It was also said: its root is delay, so the orphan was named after it, because kindness is delayed from him. It is said: "yatama, yaytimu, yutman," like "'azuma, ya'zumu"; and "yatima, yaytamu, yutman and yatamen," like "sami'a, yasma'u." Al-Farra' mentioned both forms. "Allah has made him an orphan" (ayatamahu Allah). This indicates compassion towards the orphan, encouragement to sponsor him and to protect his property, as will be explained in "al-Nisa'" [[see vol. 5, p. 8.]].

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The one who sponsors an orphan, whether he is his own or of others, I and he will be like these two in Paradise," and Malik [[Malik: one of the narrators in the chain of this hadith.]] pointed with the index finger and the middle finger. It was narrated by Abu Hurayra and recorded by Muslim.

The Imam, the memorizer (al-Hafiz) Abu Muhammad 'Abd al-Ghani ibn Sa'id, also related, from the hadith of al-Hasan ibn Dinar Abu Sa'id al-Basri, who is al-Hasan ibn Wasil [[because he was the stepson of Dinar.]], who said: Al-Aswad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, from Hassan [[In Tahdhib al-Tahdhib: "with the first letter kasra and the unaspirated letter doubled, and at the end a nun." He is Ibn Kahim, and it is said Ibn Kahin; his father was a soothsayer (kahin) in the pre-Islamic period.]], from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "No orphan sits with a people at their dish and the Devil approaches their dish." 

It was also related from the hadith of Husayn ibn Qays, who is Abu 'Ali al-Rahabi [[al-Rahabi (with a fatha on the ra' and ha' and a single ba'): ascribed to Rahbat ibn Zar'a.]], from 'Ikrima, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever takes an orphan from among Muslims into his food and drink until Allah, mighty and majestic, enriches him, his sins will certainly be forgiven, unless he does a deed that is not forgiven. And whoever has his two precious ones taken by Allah and is patient and seeks reward, his sins will be forgiven." They said: "And what are his two precious ones?" He said: "His two eyes." And whoever has three daughters or three sisters, and spends on them and treats them well until they marry or die, his sins will certainly be forgiven, unless he does a deed that is not forgiven." A man from the Bedouins who had emigrated called out to him: "O Messenger of Allah, or two?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Or two." 

So Ibn 'Abbas, whenever he narrated this hadith, would say: "By Allah, this is among the strange and rare hadiths."

**The sixth issue:** The index finger (al-sababa) among the fingers is the one next to the thumb. In the pre-Islamic period it was called "al-sababa," because they used to insult (yasubbuna) with it. When Allah brought Islam they disliked this name, so they called it "al-mushira" (the pointing finger), because they used to point with it to Allah in affirming His oneness. It is also called "al-sabbaha" (the glorifying finger); this naming came in the hadith of Wa'il ibn Hujr and others, but the language followed what they knew in the pre-Islamic period, so it prevailed. It is related about the fingers of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that the index finger was longer than the middle finger, and the middle finger was shorter than it, and the ring finger was shorter than the middle finger.

Yazid ibn Harun narrated, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Miqsam al-Ta'ifi informed us, saying: My paternal aunt Sara bint Miqsam told me that she heard Maymuna bint Kardam say: "I went out on a pilgrimage that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) performed, and I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on his riding animal, and my father asked him about things, and I found myself amazed, while I was a young girl, at the length of his finger that is next to the thumb compared to his other fingers."

So his saying, peace be upon him: "I and he are like these two in Paradise," and his saying in the other hadith: "I and Abu Bakr and 'Umar will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection like this," and he pointed with his three fingers, he only intended the mention of ranks and elevated positions over creation. He said: "We will be gathered like this, and we will be overlooking," and likewise the sponsor of the orphan will have an elevated station.

Whoever does not know the status of the fingers of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) (may Allah bless him) interprets the meaning of the hadith as joining and drawing near to one another in the place of nearness. But this is a remote meaning, because the stations of the messengers, prophets, truthful ones, martyrs and righteous are distinct levels and different ranks.

**The seventh issue:** His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and the needy﴾ ("al-masakin") is also conjoined, meaning: "And We commanded them to do good to the needy," and they are those whom need has made quiet (askanathum) and humbled. This includes encouragement to charity, generosity, and attending to the conditions of the needy and the weak. Muslim related from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The one who strives for the widow and the needy is like the one who fights in the cause of Allah" – and I think he said – "and like the one who stands (in prayer) and never tires, and like the one who fasts and never breaks his fast." Ibn al-Mundhir said: Tawus used to regard striving for (the support of) sisters as better than jihad in the cause of Allah.

**The eighth issue:** His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And speak to people good (husnan)﴾. "Husnan" is in the accusative as a verbal noun according to the meaning, because the meaning is "let your speech be good." It was also said: the estimate is "and speak to people a speech that is good," so it is a verbal noun not according to the meaning.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "hasanan" with fatha on the ha' and the sin. Al-Akhfash said: they have the same meaning, like "al-bukhl" and "al-bakhal," and "al-rushd" and "al-rashad." Al-Akhfash related "husna" without tanwin, in the pattern fu'la. Al-Nahhas said: "This is not permitted in Arabic; nothing is said of this except with the definite article, such as al-fudla, al-kubra and al-husna. This is the view of Sibawayh." 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "husuna" with two dammas, like "al-hulm."

Ibn 'Abbas said: The meaning is: "Say to them: there is no god but Allah, and command them to it." Ibn Jurayj: "Speak to people truthfully about the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) and change his description." Sufyan al-Thawri: "Command them to what is right, and forbid them from what is wrong." Abu al-'Aliya: "Speak to them the good word, and repay them with the best that you would like to be repaid with."

All of this is encouragement to noble character. A person should be gentle in speech and have an open, cheerful face with the pious and the immoral, the Sunni and the innovator, without flattery, and without speaking to him in a way that he thinks will please his school of thought. This is because Allah, exalted is He, said to Musa and Harun: "But speak to him with gentle speech" [[see vol. 11, p. 199.]]. The speaker is not better than Musa and Harun, and the immoral person is not more wicked than Pharaoh, yet Allah the Exalted commanded them both to be gentle with him.

Talha ibn 'Umar said: I said to 'Ata': "You are a man with whom people of differing desires gather, and I am a man with a hot temper, so I say to them some harsh words." He said: "Do not do so! Allah the Exalted says: 'And speak to people good.'" So this verse includes the Jews and the Christians, so how about the Hanif [[In some copies of the original: "How about others than them."]]?

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said to 'A'isha: "Do not be obscene, for obscenity, if it were a man, would be a bad man." 

It was also said: by "people" he meant Muhammad (ﷺ), as in His saying: "Or do they envy the people for what Allah has given them of His bounty?" [[see vol. 5, p. 251.]] So it is as if He said: "Speak to the Prophet (ﷺ) good." And it was related...

al-Mahdawi, on the authority of Qatadah, reported that His saying, "And speak to people good [words]," is abrogated by the verse of the sword. Abu Nasr 'Abd al-Rahim [in some copies of the original: "'Abd al-Rahman"] relates this from Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn 'Abbas said: "This verse was revealed at the beginning, then the verse of the sword abrogated it." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This indicates that this community was addressed with this kind of wording at the beginning of Islam, whereas the report about the Children of Israel and what they were commanded is not subject to abrogation. And Allah knows best."

The ninth issue: His saying, the Exalted, "And establish prayer and give zakah." Its discussion has already passed [see vol. 1, pp. 164, 343, second edition]. The address is to the Children of Israel. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Their zakah was what they used to place (as an offering), and fire would descend upon what was accepted and would not descend upon what was not accepted. It was not like the zakah of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ)." I say: This requires a transmitted report, just as it is established concerning the spoils of war. It has been related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The zakah they were commanded with was obedience to Allah and sincerity."

The tenth issue: His saying, the Exalted, "Then you turned away." The address is to the contemporaries of Muhammad (ﷺ), and the turning away of their predecessors is attributed to them, since they all share that path in turning away from the truth, being like them, as the poet said: "Shinshinah (a disposition) I know it from Akhzam." "Except a few" refers to 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and his companions. And "qalilan" (a few) is in the accusative by way of exception. According to Sibawayh, the excepted noun is in the accusative because it is made similar to the object. Muhammad ibn Yazid said: it is truly an object; the meaning is "I excepted a few."

"And you are turning away" is a subject and predicate. Al-i'rad (turning away) and al-tawalli (turning away) have the same meaning, differing only in wording. It was said: tawalli is with the body, and i'rad is with the heart. Al-Mahdawi said: "And you are turning away" is a circumstantial clause (hal), because tawalli itself implies i'rad.

**First issue:** Concerning this verse there are two questions.

**The first question:** God's words ﴿And when We took your covenant﴾ have already been discussed (see vol. 1, p. 436). "*Lā tasfikūna dimā'akum*" (you shall not shed your blood): the intended addressees are the Children of Israel, and by implication those who came after them are included. "*Lā tasfikūna*" is grammatically like "*lā ta'budūna*" (you shall not worship) (see p. 13 of this part). Ṭalḥah ibn Muṣarrif and Shu'ayb ibn Abi Ḥamzah read "*lā tusfikūna*" with a *ḍamma* on the *fā'*, which is a dialectal form (*lughah*). Abu Nahik read "*tusaffikūna*" with a *ḍamma* on the *tā'*, a doubled *fā'*, and a *fatḥa* on the *sīn*. *Al-safk* means pouring out (see vol. 1, p. 275, second edition). "*Wa-lā tukhrijūna anfusakum*" (nor shall you expel one another from your homes) is coordinated with the preceding clause. *Al-nafs* (the self) is derived from *al-nafāsah* (preciousness), since a person's self is the most noble thing he has. *Al-dār* is the dwelling that contains structures for settled residence, as opposed to a place of temporary halt. Al-Khalīl (ibn Aḥmad) said: every place that a people settle in is their *dār*, even if it has no buildings. It has also been said that it is called *dār* because it "revolves" (*dawr*) around its inhabitants, just as a wall (*ḥā'iṭ*) is so called because it encloses (*iḥāṭah*) what it contains. "*Aqrartum*" (you acknowledged) is from *al-iqrār* (acknowledgement), that is, of this covenant that was taken from you and from your forefathers. "*Wa-antum tashhadūn*" (while you were witnesses) is from *al-shahādah* (testimony), meaning witnesses in your hearts to this. It has also been said that *shahādah* here means presence, i.e., you are present while your blood is being shed and your selves are being expelled from your homes.

**The second question:** If it is asked: does anyone shed his own blood or expel himself from his own home? It is answered: since their religion was one, their affair was one, and they were like a single person among the nations, the killing of some of them by others and the expulsion of some of them by others was treated as killing themselves and banishing themselves. It has also been said that the intended meaning is retaliation (*qiṣāṣ*): no one should kill, so that he would be killed in retaliation, and thus it is as if he had shed his own blood. Likewise, one should not commit adultery or apostatize, for these make blood permissible; and one should not cause corruption so that he is banished, and thus he would have expelled himself from his home. This interpretation is far-fetched, although its meaning is sound. The actual matter is that God Most High took a covenant from the Children of Israel in the Torah that none of them should kill another, nor banish him, nor enslave him, nor allow him to steal, along with other acts of obedience.

**I say:** All of this is binding upon us, and all of it has occurred among us through strife. *Innā lillāhi wa-innā ilayhi rāji'ūn* (Surely we belong to God and to Him we shall return). In the Revelation: ﴿or to confuse you in factions and make you taste the violence of one another﴾ (6:65), and it will come later.

Ibn Khuwayz Mandād said: It is also possible that the verse is meant in its outward sense: that a person should not kill himself, nor leave his home out of foolishness, as the Hindus kill themselves. Or that a person kills himself out of hardship and affliction that befalls him, or wanders in the desert and does not seek shelter in houses out of ignorance of his religion and foolishness in his forbearance. The verse is general in all of this.

It has been narrated that Uthman ibn Maz'un made a pledge with ten of the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and they resolved to wear woolen garments (*al-musūḥ*), to wander in the desert without seeking shelter in houses, not to eat meat, and not to approach women. When this reached the Prophet (ﷺ), he came to the house of Uthman ibn Maz'un but did not find him. He said to his wife: "What is this report that has reached me about Uthman?" She disliked to reveal her husband's secret and disliked to call the Messenger of God (ﷺ) a liar, so she said: "O Messenger of God, if what has reached you is true, then it is as it has reached you." He said: "Tell Uthman: Is it a deviation from my sunnah, or out of disregard for my way? I pray and I sleep, I fast and I break my fast, I approach women, I live in houses, and I eat meat. Whoever turns away from my sunnah is not of me." So Uthman and his companions returned from what they had been doing.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 2, verses 85–86**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then you are these [people]﴾. "Antum" (ﺃَﻧْﺘُﻢْ, "you") is in the nominative position as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'), and it has no i'rab (grammatical inflection), because it is a pronoun. The "ta'" in "antum" is given a damma, because it is fatha when addressing one masculine person and kasra when addressing one feminine person. When it is made dual or plural, only the damma remains. As for "ha'ulaa'" (ﻫَﺆُﻻَﺀِ, "these"), al-Qutabi said: the implied meaning is "O these." Al-Nahhas said: this is an error according to the view of Sibawayh, and one may not say "hadha aqbal" (this one came). Al-Zajjaj said: "ha'ulaa'" here means "alladhina" (those who). The phrase ﴿taqtulun﴾ ("you kill") falls within the relative clause, meaning: "Then you are those who kill." It was also said: "ha'ulaa'" is in the nominative as the subject, "antum" is a predicate placed before it, and ﴿taqtulun﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) describing "ha'ulaa'." It was also said: "ha'ulaa'" is in the accusative, with the verb "a'ni" (I mean) implied.

Al-Zuhri read ﴿tuqattilun﴾ with a damma on the ta' and with shadda (intensive form), and likewise ﴿fa-lima taqtulun anbiya' Allah﴾ (why then do you kill the prophets of God?).

This verse is addressed to those present, and it does not admit of being referred back to their ancestors. It was revealed concerning the Jewish tribes of Banu Qaynuqa', Quraydha and al-Nadir. The Banu Qaynuqa' were enemies of Quraydha, the Aws were allies of the Banu Qaynuqa', and the Khazraj were allies of the Banu Quraydha. The Nadir and the Aws and Khazraj were brothers, and Quraydha and the Nadir were also brothers. Then they split apart and began to fight one another; then when the war ceased they would ransom their captives. God reproached them for this, saying: ﴿And if they come to you as captives, you ransom them﴾.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿tazahiruna﴾ (you back one another). The meaning of "tazahiruna" is "tata'awwanun" (you cooperate). It is derived from "al-zahr" (the back), because one of them strengthens another so that he becomes for him like a back. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"You backed one another, the buttocks of a house gathered
upon one man; may you never cease to be a match for one."*
[[Thus it appears in some copies of the original. In others: "...the buttocks of a people..." etc. The version of this verse in the tafsir of al-Shawkani is thus:

*"You backed one another from every direction and aim..."* etc.]]

Al-ithm (sin) is the act for which its doer deserves blame. Al-'udwan (transgression) is excessiveness in wrongdoing and going beyond limits in it. The people of Madina and the people of Mecca read ﴿tazzahiruna﴾ with shadda, assimilating the ta' into the za' because they are close to each other; the original form is "tatazahiruna." The Kufans read ﴿tazahiruna﴾ without shadda, omitting the second ta' because the first indicates it; similarly ﴿wa-in tazahara 'alayhi﴾ (and if they back one another against him). [[See vol. 18, p. 189.]] Qatada read ﴿tazhiruna 'alayhim﴾ (you support against them). All of these return to the meaning of cooperation. From the same root is ﴿wa-kana al-kafiru 'ala rabbihi zahiran﴾ (and the disbeliever is ever a helper against his Lord), and his saying: ﴿wa-al-malaikatu ba'da dhalika zahir﴾ (and the angels, after that, are supporters). Know this. [[See vol. 13, p. 61; vol. 18, p. 191.]]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they come to you as captives, you ransom them, while it is forbidden to you to expel them﴾. In this there are six issues.

**The first issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they come to you as captives﴾ is a conditional clause (shart), and its answer is "tufadduhum" (you ransom them). "Asara" (captives) is in the accusative as a circumstantial (hal). Abu 'Ubayd said: Abu 'Amr used to say: whoever comes into their hands is "asara," and whoever comes as a captive who is taken is "usra." The people of the language do not know what Abu 'Amr said; rather, it is like your saying: "sukara" and "sukra" (drunk people). The reading of the majority, except Hamza, is ﴿usara﴾, but Hamza read ﴿asra﴾ on the pattern "fa'la", plural of "asir" in the sense of "ma'sur" (captive). The rule for its broken plural, when it is of this kind, is "fa'la," as you say: "qatil" and "qatla," and "jarih" and "jarha." Abu Hatim said: "asara" is not permissible. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said "asara" just as it is said "sakara," and "fu'ala" is the original, and "fa'ala" is derived from it. It is reported from Muhammad ibn Yazid that he said: it is said "asir" and "usara," like "zarif" and "zuraf'a." Ibn Faris said: the plural of "asir" is said to be "asra" and "asara," and both are read. It was also said: "asara" (with a fatha on the hamza) is not the high-register form.

**The second issue:** The "asir" (captive) is derived from "al-isar," which is the leather strap with which the saddle (mahmal) is tied. He is called "asir" because his bond is tightened. The Arabs say: "qad asara qatabahu" (he tied his saddle), meaning he tightened it. Then every captured person is called "asir," even if he was not bound. Al-A'sha said:

*"Poetry bound me in its house,
as the binding women bind the saddle-frame."*
[[The "himar" has among its meanings a piece of wood at the front of the saddle that the woman grips. It was also said: the stick on which the saddle-pads are carried. "Al-asrat": the women who tighten the saddles with leather and bind them.]]

That is, I am in its house, meaning that it has reached the extreme in him. As for "al-asr" in his saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿wa-shadadna asrahum﴾ (and We strengthened their frame), it means the creation. The "usrat" of a man is his kinsfolk, because he is strengthened by them. [[See vol. 19, p. 149.]]

**The third issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿tufadduhum﴾. Nafi', Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it thus. The rest read ﴿tafdu-hum﴾ from "al-fida'" (ransom). "Al-fida'" is seeking a ransom for a captive who is in their hands. Al-Jawhari said: "al-fida'," when its first letter is kasra, may be read with a long vowel or short; when it is fatha, it is short (maqsur). It is said: "qum fada-an laka abi" (may my father be your ransom). Among the Arabs are those who pronounce "fida'an" with tanwin (nunation) only when it is preceded by the preposition "li," so they say "fida'an laka," because it is an indefinite noun and they intend the sense of supplication. Al-Asma'i recited for al-Nabigha:

*"Enough: may all people be a ransom for you,
and whatever wealth and offspring I may gain."*

It is said: "fadahu" and "fadawahu" when he gives its ransom and so saves him. And "fadahu bi-nafsihi" (he ransomed him with his own self), and "fadayahu" when he says "ju'iltu fidaka" (may I be your ransom). "Tafadaw": that is, some of them ransomed others. "Al-fidyah," "al-fida," and "al-fida'" are all of one meaning.

"Fadaytu nafsi" means when you release it after you have paid something, in the sense of "fadaytu." From this is the saying of al-'Abbas to the Prophet (ﷺ): "I ransomed myself, and I ransomed 'Aqil." Both are verbs that take two objects, the second of which is connected by a preposition. You say: "fadaytu nafsi bi-mali" and "fadaytuhu bi-mali" (I ransomed myself with my wealth, and I ransomed him with my wealth). The poet said:

*"Stop, O ransomer of your captive, for my people
and your people—I see no unity between them."*

**The fourth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿wa-huwa muharramun 'alaykum ikhrajuhum﴾ (while it is forbidden to you to expel them). "Huwa" is the subject (mubtada'), and it is a pronoun referring to the expulsion; "muharram" is its predicate, and "ikhrajuhum" is an apposition (badal) of "huwa." If you wish, it may be a pronoun referring to the matter and the story, and the sentence after it is its predicate, meaning: "and the matter, it is forbidden to you to expel them." So "ikhrajuhum" is the second subject, "muharram" is its predicate, and the whole sentence is the predicate of "huwa." In "muharram" is the pronoun of the passive (the unnamed agent), which refers back to the expulsion. It is also permissible that "muharram" is the subject and "ikhrajuhum" is the object of the passive verb, which takes the place of the predicate of "muharram," and the sentence is the predicate of "huwa." Al-Farra' claimed that "huwa" is a pronominal support (imad), but this is, according to the Basrans, an error without meaning, because the support pronoun does not occur at the beginning of speech.

It is read "wahwa" with the h unvoweled, because the damma is heavy, as the poet said: [[He is Imru' al-Qays, as in Lisan al-'Arab and the commentary on the Diwan.]]

*"He is not increased (ghirh) by the arrow I shot..."*
[[Anmaytu al-sayd: you shoot at the game and hit it, and it goes away from you and dies after it has disappeared.]]

And likewise, if you bring it with "lam" and "thumma," which has been mentioned. [[See vol. 1, p. 261, second edition.]]

Our scholars said: God had taken four covenants from them: abandoning killing, abandoning expulsion, abandoning backing one another, and ransoming their captives. They turned away from everything they were commanded except ransoming. So God rebuked them for that, a rebuke that is recited: ﴿Do you believe in part of the Book﴾, which is the Torah, ﴿and disbelieve in part?﴾

I say: By God's life, we have indeed turned away from all of it through strife, so that some of us back others against others! Would that it were against the Muslims, but rather against the disbelievers! Until we left our brothers humiliated and abased, subject to the rule of the polytheists. There is no power and no strength except through God, the Most High, the Mighty!

Our scholars said: ransoming captives is obligatory, even if not a single dirham remains. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: the verse contains the obligation of freeing captives, and reports have come to this effect from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he freed captives and commanded that they be freed, and the practice of the Muslims went on accordingly, and consensus (ijma') was established upon it. The freeing of captives is obligatory from the public treasury (bayt al-mal). If there is none, it is an obligation upon all Muslims, and whoever among them undertakes it discharges the obligation from the rest. [[See vol. 8, p. 52.]]

**The fifth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So what is the recompense of those among you who do that except disgrace in the life of this world?﴾ It is an inceptive clause (mubtada') and predicate. "Khizy" means humiliation. Al-Jawhari said: "khazi" (with kasra) "yakhza" "khizyan" when he is humbled and degraded. Ibn al-Sikkit said: he fell into a calamity. "Akhzahu Allah" means God disgraced him. "Khazi" also means "yakhza" "khizayatan" when he is ashamed, so he is "khazyan." The people are "khaza-ya," and the woman is "khazya."

**The sixth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will be returned﴾. "Yuraddun" (they will be returned) with the ya' is the reading of the common people. Al-Hasan read "turaddun" with the ta' as an address (to you). ﴿to the severest punishment﴾. ﴿And God is not unaware of what you do﴾. The discussion of this has preceded. [[See vol. 1, p. 466.]] Likewise ﴿Those are the ones who have purchased﴾, the verse. [[See vol. 1, p. 210, second edition.]] So there is no point in repeating it. "Yawma" (the day) is in the accusative, governed by "yuraddun."

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 2, verses 85–86**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then you are these [people]﴾. The "ta'" in "antum" is given a damma, because it is fatha when addressing one masculine person and kasra when addressing one feminine person. When it is made dual or plural, only the damma remains. As for "ha'ulaa'" (ﻫَﺆُﻻَﺀِ, "these"), al-Qutabi said: the implied meaning is "O these." Al-Nahhas said: this is an error according to the view of Sibawayh, and one may not say "hadha aqbal" (this one came). Al-Zajjaj said: "ha'ulaa'" here means "alladhina" (those who). The phrase ﴿taqtulun﴾ ("you kill") falls within the relative clause, meaning: "Then you are those who kill." It was also said: "ha'ulaa'" is in the nominative as the subject, "antum" is a predicate placed before it, and ﴿taqtulun﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) describing "ha'ulaa'." It was also said: "ha'ulaa'" is in the accusative, with the verb "a'ni" (I mean) implied.

Al-Zuhri read ﴿tuqattilun﴾ with a damma on the ta' and with shadda (intensive form), and likewise ﴿fa-lima taqtulun anbiya' Allah﴾ (why then do you kill the prophets of God?).

This verse is addressed to those present, and it does not admit of being referred back to their ancestors. It was revealed concerning the Jewish tribes of Banu Qaynuqa', Quraydha and al-Nadir. The Banu Qaynuqa' were enemies of Quraydha, the Aws were allies of the Banu Qaynuqa', and the Khazraj were allies of the Banu Quraydha. The Nadir and the Aws and Khazraj were brothers, and Quraydha and the Nadir were also brothers. Then they split apart and began to fight one another; then when the war ceased they would ransom their captives. God reproached them for this, saying: ﴿And if they come to you as captives, you ransom them﴾.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿tazahiruna﴾ (you back one another). The meaning of "tazahiruna" is "tata'awwanun" (you cooperate). It is derived from "al-zahr" (the back), because one of them strengthens another so that he becomes for him like a back. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"You backed one another, the buttocks of a house gathered
upon one man; may you never cease to be a match for one."*
[[Thus it appears in some copies of the original. In others: "...the buttocks of a people..." etc. The version of this verse in the tafsir of al-Shawkani is thus:

*"You backed one another from every direction and aim..."* etc.]]

Al-ithm (sin) is the act for which its doer deserves blame. Al-'udwan (transgression) is excessiveness in wrongdoing and going beyond limits in it. The people of Madina and the people of Mecca read ﴿tazzahiruna﴾ with shadda, assimilating the ta' into the za' because they are close to each other; the original form is "tatazahiruna." The Kufans read ﴿tazahiruna﴾ without shadda, omitting the second ta' because the first indicates it; similarly ﴿wa-in tazahara 'alayhi﴾ (and if they back one another against him). [[See vol. 18, p. 189.]] Qatada read ﴿tazhiruna 'alayhim﴾ (you support against them). All of these return to the meaning of cooperation. From the same root is ﴿wa-kana al-kafiru 'ala rabbihi zahiran﴾ (and the disbeliever is ever a helper against his Lord), and his saying: ﴿wa-al-malaikatu ba'da dhalika zahir﴾ (and the angels, after that, are supporters). Know this. [[See vol. 13, p. 61; vol. 18, p. 191.]]
