Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 87:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book﴾, meaning the Torah. "Waqqaynā" means We made to follow. Al-taqfiyah (following, succession) and al-irdaf (coming after) are derived from following the qafa, which is the back of the neck. You say istaqfaytuhu when you come up behind him. From this the rhyme of poetry (qafiyat al-shi'r) is named, because it follows the rest of the speech. Al-qafiyah is the qafa (nape), and from this is the hadith: "Satan ties a knot on the qafiyat (back of the head) of one of you." Al-qafiyy and al-qafawah are what is set aside of milk and other things for someone whom you wish to honour. Qafawtu al-rajul means I accused the man of immorality. Fulan qifwati means "so-and-so is my accusation," and qifwati also means "my choice." Ibn Duraid said: it seems to be among the words with opposite meanings. The scholars said: this verse is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession﴾ [see vol. 12, p. 125]. Every messenger who came after Moses came only to confirm the Torah and to command adherence to it, up to Jesus, peace be upon him. It is said that rusul and rusl are two dialects: the first is the dialect of the Hijaz, and the second is the dialect of Tamim, whether it is in the construct state or not. Abu 'Amr would lighten it when it is followed by two letters, and make it heavy when it is followed by one letter.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, the clear proofs﴾, meaning the proofs and evidences, which are those mentioned by Allah in Al 'Imran and Al-Ma'idah [see vol. 4, p. 93; vol. 6, p. 362], as said by Ibn 'Abbas. ﴿And We strengthened him﴾ means We supported him. Mujahid and Ibn Muhaysin read "ayyadnāhu" with a long vowel, and both are dialects. ﴿With the Holy Spirit﴾: Abu Malik and Abu Salih related from Ibn 'Abbas, and Ma'mar related from Qatadah, that they both said: it is Jibril, peace be upon him. Hassan said:

"And Jibril is the Messenger of Allah among us, and the Holy Spirit, about whom there is no concealment."

Al-Nahhas said: Jibril was called a spirit and was attributed to the Holy (al-Qudus) because Allah, mighty and majestic, created for him a spirit without a parent's begetting, and likewise Jesus was called a spirit for this reason. Ghalib ibn 'Abd Allah related from Mujahid that he said: al-Qudus is Allah, mighty and majestic. Likewise al-Hasan said: al-Qudus is Allah, and His spirit is Jibril. Abu Rawq related from al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas concerning "with the Holy Spirit" that he said: it is the name by which Jesus used to revive the dead. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr also said this, and it is the Greatest Name of Allah. It is also said that the intended meaning is the Gospel, which He called a spirit just as Allah called the Qur'an a spirit in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a spirit of Our command﴾ [see vol. 16, p. 54]. The first view is more apparent, and Allah knows best. Al-qudus means purity, and it has already been discussed [see vol. 1, p. 277, second edition].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is it, whenever a messenger comes to you with what your souls do not desire, that you wax arrogant?﴾ meaning with what does not agree with them or suit them. The ha' is omitted because the noun is long, meaning: with what you do not desire. ﴿You grew arrogant﴾ means you refused to answer him, belittling the messengers and deeming the message unlikely. The root of hawa is inclination toward a thing, and its plural is ahwa', as came in the revelation, and it is not pluralized as ahwiyah, although they have said andiyah for nada. The poet said:

"On a night of Jumada, of dews, in whose darkness the dog cannot see the tent-rope."

Al-Jawhari said: this is irregular. Hawa was named hawa because it plunges its companion into the Fire, and for this reason it is generally used only for what is not true and what has no good in it, and this verse is of that kind. It may also be used for what is true, such as the saying of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, about the captives of Badr: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ inclined toward what Abu Bakr said, and did not incline toward what I said." And 'A'ishah said to the Prophet ﷺ in the sound hadith: "By Allah, I see that your Lord only hastens to fulfil your desire." Muslim transmitted both.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So a party you denied﴾: "fariqan" is in the accusative governed by "kadhdhabtum," and likewise "and a party you kill." Among those they denied were Jesus and Muhammad, peace be upon them, and among those they killed were Yahya and Zakariyya, peace be upon them, as its explanation will come in Surat Subhan [see vol. 10, p. 218], Allah willing.

"And they say, 'Our hearts are wrapped (ghulf).'" That is, the Jews. "Ghulf" is read with a sukun on the lam, the plural of aghlaf, meaning that there are coverings upon them. It is like the words: "Our hearts are in coverings (akinnah) from what you call us to" [see vol. 15, p. 339], meaning in receptacles. Mujahid said: "ghulf" means there is a veil (ghishawah) over them. 'Ikrimah said: there is a seal (taba') upon them. The lexicographers related: "ghallaftu al-sayf" means I put a sheath (ghilaf) on the sword, so the word was formed as aghlaf, meaning covered, concealed from understanding and discernment.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-A'raj and Ibn Muhaysin read "ghulf" with a damma on the lam. Ibn 'Abbas said: meaning our hearts are filled with knowledge, needing neither the knowledge of Muhammad (ﷺ) nor anyone else's. It was also said: it is the plural of ghilaf, like khimar and khumur, meaning our hearts are receptacles for knowledge, so why do they not understand from you, when we have retained a great deal of knowledge? It was also said: the meaning is, how could the knowledge of Muhammad (ﷺ) be hidden from them?

God Most High responded to them with His words: "Rather, God has cursed them for their disbelief, so little is it that they believe." Then He explained that the cause of their aversion from faith is only that they were cursed for their earlier disbelief and their audacity, and this is the recompense for a sin with something greater than it. The original meaning of la'n (curse) in the speech of the Arabs is expulsion and distancing. The wolf is called la'een, and the banished man is called la'een. Al-Shammakh said:

"I startled the sand-grouse with it, and I drove away from it the standing place of the wolf, like the accursed man."

The construction of the speech is: the standing place of the accursed wolf is like the man. So the meaning is: God has removed them far from His mercy. It was also said: from His guidance and direction. It was also said: from every good, and this is general.

"Qalilan" is an adjectival modifier of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), its estimated form being "fa-iman qalilan ma yu'minun" (so a little faith is what they believe). Ma'mar said: the meaning is that they believe only in a small part of what is in their hands and disbelieve in most of it, and "qalilan" is then in the accusative by removing the preposition. "Ma" is a supplementary particle (silah), meaning "fa-qalilan yu'minun." Al-Waqidi said: its meaning is that they believe neither a little nor a lot, just as you say, "How little does he do such-and-such," meaning he absolutely does not do it. Al-Kisa'i said: the Arabs say, "We passed through a land where little grows of the kurrath (leek) and onion," meaning nothing grows there at all.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 89:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when there came to them﴾, meaning the Jews. "A Book" meaning the Qur'an. "From Allah, confirming" is an epithet (na't) of "a Book." It is permissible, in other than the Qur'an, to put it in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), and it is so in the codex of Ubayy in the accusative, as has been reported. "What is with them" meaning the Torah and the Gospel, which inform them of what is in them. "And they had been before, seeking victory" (yastaftihun), i.e., seeking help (yastansirun). And al-istiftah (opening, in the sense of seeking) is al-istinsar (seeking victory). Istaftahtu: I sought victory. And in the hadith: The Prophet (ﷺ) used to seek opening (yastaftih) through the poor emigrants, i.e., he sought victory through their supplication and their prayer [[What is in the Nihayah of Ibn al-Athir and Lisan, root f-t-h: "i.e., he seeks victory through them."]]. And from it: ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring a victory or a command from Him﴾ [[See vol. 6, p. 217.]]. And victory (al-nasr) is the opening of something closed, so it goes back to their saying "I opened the door" (fataḥtu al-bab). Al-Nasa'i reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri [[It should be noted that the narrator of this hadith is Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas; in the Sunan of al-Nasa'i (vol. 1, p. 65, al-Matba'ah al-Maymaniyyah edition), chapter "Seeking victory through the weak," it reads: "Akhbarana Muhammad ibn Idris ... from Mus'ab ibn Sa'd from his father that he thought..." etc.]] that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: (Allah only grants victory to this nation through its weak, through their supplication, their prayer and their sincerity). Al-Nasa'i also reported from Abu al-Darda', who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say:

(Seek the weak for me, for you are only provided for and given victory through your weak). Ibn Abbas said: The Jews of Khaybar used to fight the Ghatafan, and when they met, the Jews were defeated. So the Jews resorted to this supplication and said: "We ask You by the right of the Unlettered Prophet whom You promised us to send forth for us at the end of time, that You help us against them." He said: So whenever they met, they would invoke with this supplication, and they defeated the Ghatafan. But when the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent, they disbelieved. So Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿And they had been before seeking victory over those who disbelieved﴾, i.e., through you, O Muhammad, up to His saying: ﴿So the curse of Allah is upon the disbelievers﴾.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when there came to them﴾. The response (jawab) of the first "lamma" is "fa" and what follows it in His saying "when there came to them what they recognized" according to al-Farra'. The response of the second "falamma" is "kafaru" (they disbelieved). Al-Akhfash Sa'id said: the response of "lamma" is omitted because the listener knows it, and al-Zajjaj said the same. Al-Mubarrad said: the response of "falamma" is in His saying "kafaru," and the second "falamma" was repeated because of the length of the speech. This serves to establish the sin and confirm it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 90:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Wretched is what they have sold themselves for﴾. "Bi'sa" (wretched, an expression of blame) in the speech of the Arabs fully conveys dispraise, just as "ni'ma" (excellent, an expression of praise) fully conveys praise. Each of them has four dialectal forms: bi'sa, ba'sa, ba'isa, bi'isa; ni'ma, na'ma, na'isa, ni'isa. The view of Sibawayh is that "ma" is the subject (fa'il) of "bi'sa," and that it is only followed by generic nouns (asma' al-ajnas) and indefinite nouns (al-nakirat). The same applies to "ni'ma," so you say: "ni'ma al-rajulu Zaydun" (excellent is the man Zayd) and "ni'ma rajulan Zaydun" (excellent a man is Zayd). When a noun without the definite article (alif and lam) follows it, it is always in the accusative; when it has the definite article, it is always in the nominative, and the accusative of "rajul" is as a specification (tamyiz). In "ni'ma" there is an implied pronoun (mudmar) in accordance with the condition of explanation (shart al-tafsir), and "Zayd" is in the nominative in two ways: as the predicate of an omitted subject, as if it were said: "Who is the one being praised?" You answer: "He is Zayd." The other way is that it is the subject (mubtada') and what precedes it is its predicate. Abu 'Ali permitted that "ma" follow it both as a relative pronoun (mawsulah) and as a non-relative, since it is vague (mubhamah), applying to many things and not restricted to one specific thing. According to Sibawayh the implied meaning is: "Wretched is the thing with which they have sold themselves, that they disbelieve." So "an yakfuru" (that they disbelieve) is in the nominative position as the subject, and its predicate is what precedes it, as in your saying: "bi'sa al-rajulu Zaydun" (wretched is the man Zayd). According to this view "ma" is a relative pronoun. Al-Akhfash said: "ma" is in the accusative position as a specification, as in your saying: "bi'sa rajulan Zaydun," so the implied meaning is: "wretched a thing is that they disbelieve." According to this view, "ishtaraw bihi anfusahum" (they sold themselves with it) is a descriptive clause (sifah) of "ma." Al-Farra' said: "bi'sama" as a whole is one unit, compounded like "habbadha" (how lovely). There is an objection to this view, because it leaves a verb without a subject. Al-Kisa'i said: "ma" and "ishtaraw" are like a single independent noun, and the implied meaning is: "wretched is their selling that they disbelieve." This is rejected, because "ni'ma" and "bi'sa" do not take a specific, definite noun, and "the selling" has become definite through its being attached to a pronoun. Al-Nahhas said: The clearest of these views is that of al-Akhfash and Sibawayh. Al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i said: "an yakfuru" (that they disbelieve), if you wish, may be in the genitive position, in apposition to the "ha'" in "bihi" (with it). Al-Farra' said: that is, they sold themselves by disbelieving in what Allah revealed. "Ishtara" is used with the meaning of "sold" and with the meaning of "bought," and the meaning is: wretched is the thing which they chose for themselves, in that they exchanged falsehood for truth and disbelief for faith.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿out of envy (baghyan)﴾ means out of jealousy, as said by Qatadah and al-Suddi. It is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlih), and it is literally a verbal noun (masdar). Al-Asma'i said: it is derived from the expression "qad baghā al-jurh" (the wound has festered) when it became corrupt. It was also said: its origin is seeking (al-talab), and for this reason the adulterous woman is called "baghiyy." "An yunazzila Allahu" (that Allah sends down) is in the accusative position, meaning "li-an yunazzila," that is, because of Allah's sending down of grace upon His Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub and Ibn Muhaysin recited "an yunzila" with a light pronunciation, and likewise all similar forms in the Qur'an, except "wa ma nunazziluhu" in al-Hijr [[See vol. 10, p. 14.]], and "'ala an yunazzila ayatan" in al-An'am [[See vol. 6, p. 418.]].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they earned﴾ (fa-ba'u), meaning they returned, and it is mostly said of evil. It has been mentioned before [[See vol. 1, p. 430.]]. ﴿with wrath upon wrath﴾: the meaning of Allah's wrath upon them has been mentioned before [[See vol. 1, p. 149, second edition.]], and it is His punishment. It was said: the first wrath was for their worship of the calf, and the second for their disbelief in Muhammad ﷺ; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. 'Ikrimah said: because they disbelieved in 'Isa, then they disbelieved in Muhammad, meaning the Jews. Sa'id related from Qatadah: the first was for their disbelief in the Gospel, and the second for their disbelief in the Qur'an. A group said: the intended meaning is emphasis and the severity of their condition, not that He intended two wraths caused by two disobediences. ﴿Humiliating (muhin)﴾ is derived from humiliation (al-hawan), and it is what necessitates eternal abiding in the Fire, unlike the abiding of Muslim sinners, for that is a purification and cleansing for them, like the stoning of the adulterer and the cutting of the thief's hand, as its explanation will come in surah al-Nisa' [[See vol. 5, p. 87; it also comes in al-Ma'idah and al-Nur, see vol. 6, p. 159, vol. 21, p. 159.]], from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, God willing.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 91:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Believe in what Allah has sent down,"﴾ meaning: affirm it. "[They] say, 'We believe in what was sent down to us,'" meaning: the Quran? No, meaning: "We affirm what was sent down to us," that is, the Torah. "And they reject what is beyond it," meaning: what is other than it, according to al-Farra'. Qatadah said: "what comes after it," and this is the view of Abu 'Ubaydah, and the meaning is one. Al-Jawhari said: warā' means khalf (behind), and it may also mean qudām (in front). It is one of the words with opposite meanings (al-adhdad). Allah, exalted is He, said: "And behind them was a king" (Qur'an 18:79), meaning: in front of them. Its diminutive is wuray'ah (with the ha'), which is irregular (shadhdhah). "Warā'ahu" is in the accusative as an adverb of place (zarf). Al-Akhfash said: one says "laqītuhu min warā'" (I met him from behind), and you raise it as an ending (ghāyah) when it is not followed by a genitive; you make it a noun, and it is indeclinable (ghayr mutamakkin), like your saying "min qablu" and "min ba'du." He recited:

"If I am not trusted by you, and your meeting is not
Except from behind a behind..."

[The line is by 'Ayy ibn Malik al-'Uqayli, cited from Lisan al-'Arab.]

I say: From this is the saying of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, in the hadith of intercession: "I was only a khalil (intimate friend) from behind a behind" [Noted in al-Nihayah and Lisan al-'Arab, s.v. r-w-y: "Verily I was," etc., and in both: it is narrated thus, pronounced with a fatha, i.e., from behind a veil.]. And al-warā' also means a son's son (grandson).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and it is the truth﴾: it is a subject and predicate (mubtada' and khabar). "Confirming" (musaddiqan) is a confirmatory circumstantial clause (hal mu'akkidah) according to Sibawayh. "What is with them" (limā ma'ahum): "mā" is in the genitive position through the preposition "li-", and "ma'ahum" is its relative clause. "Ma'ahum" is put in the accusative by the sense of being situated (al-istiqrar). Whoever reads it with a sukun makes it a particle (harf).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "Why then did you kill the prophets of Allah before?"﴾ This is a rebuttal from Allah, exalted is He, against them in their claim that they believed in what was sent down to them, and a denial and rebuke from Him to them. The meaning: "How, then, did you kill them when you were forbidden from that!" The address is to those present with Muhammad ﷺ, while the intended ones are their forefathers. The address was directed to their sons because they were loyal to those who killed, as He said: ﴿Had they believed in Allah, the Prophet, and what was sent down to him, they would not have taken them as allies﴾ (Qur'an 5:81). So when they were loyal to them, they are in their position. It is also said: because they were pleased with their deed, so that was attributed to them. "Taqtulun" (you kill) came in the present-future form while meaning the past, since the difficulty was removed by his saying "before" (min qablu). When there is no ambiguity, it is permissible for the past form to mean the future and the future form to mean the past. Al-Hutay'ah said:

"Al-Hutay'ah bears witness on the day he meets his Lord
That al-Walid is more deserving of the excuse."

Here "shahida" means "yashhadu" (bears witness). ﴿If you are believers﴾: that is, if you are holders of belief, then why did you consent to the killing of the prophets! It is also said: "in" means "mā," and the original of "lima" is "limā"; the alif was dropped to distinguish the interrogative from the declarative. It should not be paused upon, for if one pauses on it without the ha', it would be a grammatical error (laḥn), and if one pauses on it with the ha', it is added to the written text (zīda fī al-sawād).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And Moses certainly came to you with clear proofs﴾. The lam here is the lam of oath (lam al-qasam). "Clear proofs" (al-bayyinat) refers to His saying: ﴿And We gave Moses nine clear signs﴾ [see vol. 10, p. 335]. They are: the staff, the years of famine (al-sunun), the hand, the blood, the flood, the locusts, the lice (al-qummal), the frogs, and the splitting of the sea. It is also said that "the clear proofs" are the Torah and the indications (al-dalalat) contained in it.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Then you took the calf﴾. Here "then" (thumma) is a rebuke (tawbikh). Thumma is more emphatic than waw in reproach (al-taqri'), meaning: after you had considered the signs, or after their coming to you, you took the calf. This indicates that they did this only after a period of respite from

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 93:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised the mount above you, [saying], "Take what We have given you with determination and listen."﴾ The discussion of this has already passed [[See vol. 1, p. 436 and what follows, second edition.]]. The meaning of "listen" (isma'u) is "obey" (ati'u), and it does not mean merely the command to perceive the speech. Rather, what is meant is: act upon what you have heard and adhere to it. From this is their saying, "God hears whoever praises Him" (sami'a Allahu liman hamidah), meaning: He accepts and responds. The poet said:

I called upon God until I feared that God would not hear what I say,

meaning, would not accept. And the rajiz said:

Hearing and obedience and submission are better, and more protective for the Banu Tamim.

As for their saying, ﴿They said, "We have heard and we disobey."﴾, it is disputed whether this phrase actually came from them verbally, by speech, or whether they performed an action that took the place of speech, making it figurative, as the poet said:

The basin filled and said, "Enough, enough, I have filled my belly."

This is an argument against them in their saying, "We believe in what was sent down to us."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they were made to drink the calf into their hearts﴾, meaning, the love of the calf. The meaning is: their hearts were made to drink it. This is a metaphor and figurative expression for the calf's matter being firmly rooted in their hearts. In the hadith: "Trials are presented to the hearts like a mat, strand by strand; whichever heart absorbs them, a black spot is marked on it," the hadith in full, related by Muslim. One says: his heart was made to drink the love of such-and-such. Zuhayr said:

So I awoke from her after an inner love, and love is a disease that your heart drinks.

The expression of the love of the calf by "drinking" rather than "eating" is because the drinking of water penetrates the limbs until it reaches their interior, whereas food merely borders them without penetrating them. One of the Successors (tabi'un) went beyond this meaning, saying of his wife Athma, whom he had reproached over some matter and then divorced, though he loved her:

The love of Athma penetrated my heart, so its manifest and hidden parts travel together.

It penetrated where drink does not reach, nor sorrow, nor joy reaches.

I nearly fly when I recall the covenant with her, were a human able to fly.

As-Suddi and Ibn Juraij said: Musa, peace be upon him, burned the calf, scattered it into the water, and said to the Children of Israel: "Drink from that water." All of them drank, and whoever had loved the calf had filings of gold appear on his lips. It is also related that no one drank it without going mad; this was related by al-Qushayri. I say: as for his scattering it into the sea, this is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We will surely scatter it into the sea with scattering﴾ [[See vol. 11, p. 243.]]. As for drinking the water and the appearance of filings on the lips, His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And they were made to drink the calf into their hearts﴾ refutes it. And God knows best.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "Evil is that which your faith commands you"﴾, meaning, your faith which you claimed in your saying, "We believe in what was sent down to us." It was also said: this statement is an address to the Prophet ﷺ, who was commanded to rebuke them. That is, say to them, O Muhammad: "Evil are these things you did, and what your faith commanded you to do." The discussion of "bi'sama" has already passed [[See p. 27 of this part.]], and all praise is due to God alone.

When the Jews made false claims, Allah the Mighty and Majestic related them in His Book, such as His saying, Exalted is He: "The Fire will not touch us except for a few counted days," and His saying: "And they said, 'None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians,'" and they said, "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved" [[See vol. 6, p. 120.]]. Allah refuted them and laid the proof against them. He said: "Say to them, O Muhammad: 'If the final abode [i.e., Paradise] is yours alone, then wish for death, if you are truthful'" in your claims. This is because whoever believes he is among the people of Paradise would prefer death to life in this world, because of the bliss of Paradise he will attain and the harm of this world he will be free from. Yet they refrained from wishing for that, out of fear of Allah, because of the ugliness of their deeds and their knowledge of their own disbelief in their saying, "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved," and because of their greed for this world. For this reason, Exalted is He, speaking of them with His true word, said: "And they will never wish for it, because of what their hands have sent forward, and Allah knows the wrongdoers" as confirmation of their lying. Also, if they had wished for death, they would have died, as has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "If the Jews had wished for death, they would have died and seen their places [in some copies of the original: 'their seats'] in the Fire."

It has also been said that Allah turned them away from expressing the wish and restricted them to holding back, so that this would be a sign for His Prophet (ﷺ). These are three explanations for their not wishing. Ikrimah related from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying "so wish for death" that the meaning is: "Call down death upon the more lying of the two parties, us or you." But they did not call, because they knew they were lying.

If it is said: wishing may be by the tongue at times and by the heart at others, so how is it known that they did not wish for it in their hearts? It is said to him: the Qur'an has spoken of this in His saying "and they will never wish for it." Had they wished for it in their hearts, they would have made it known with their tongues, in refutation of the Prophet (ﷺ) and in nullification of his proof. This is clear.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿khalisatan﴾ is in the accusative as the predicate of *kana* (khabar kana, the predicate of the verb *kana*), and if you wish, it may be a *hal* (circumstantial accusative), in which case "with Allah" is in the position of the predicate. "Abadan" is an adverb of time (*zarf zaman*) that applies to both short and long periods, like *al-hin* and *al-waqt*, and here it means from the beginning of life until death. The *ma* in His saying "bima" has the meaning of *alladhi* (which), and the returning pronoun is omitted, the estimated form being "qaddamathu." It may also be verbal (masdariyya), in which case it needs no returning pronoun. "Aydihim" is in the nominative position; the damma was dropped from the ya' because of the heaviness of it together with the kasra. If it were in the accusative position, you would vocalize it, because the accusative is light. It is permissible to make it sukun in poetry. "Wa-Allahu 'alimun bi'l-zalimin" is a subject and predicate (mubtada' wa-khabar, a nominal sentence).

The Qur'anic verse: ﴿And you will surely find them the greediest of people for life﴾ means the Jews. "And of those who associated partners" (with God). It was said: the meaning is "and [those who are] more greedy," so "of those who associated partners" is elided, because they know their sins and that there is no good for them with God. The idolaters of the Arabs know only this worldly life and have no knowledge of the Hereafter. Do you not see the saying of their poet:

"Enjoy the world, for you are perishing, / from intoxicating drinks and beautiful women." [[The verse is by Imru' al-Qays. Nashawat (plural of nashwa) means intoxication.]]

The pronoun in "aḥadahum" (one of them), in this view, refers to the Jews. It was also said that the speech is complete at "ḥayah" (life), and then the report about a group of the idolaters is resumed. It was said they are the Magians (Majus), and this is clear from their supplication to one who sneezes in their languages, with something meaning "Live a thousand years." The thousand is singled out for mention because it is the end of the counting unit in calculation. Al-Hasan held that "those who associated partners" are the idolaters of the Arabs, singled out because they do not believe in the Resurrection, so they wish for a long life. The root of sanah (year) is sanhah, and it was said sanwah.

It was also said that there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech, and the meaning is: "And you will surely find them, and a group of those who associated partners, the greediest of people for life."

The Qur'anic verse: ﴿Each one of them wishes he were given a life of a thousand years﴾. The original form of "yawaddu" is "yawaddadu." It was contracted (udghimat) so that two identical letters with vowels would not be joined, and the vowel of the dal was transferred to the waw, to indicate that the action is done. Al-Kisa'i reported "wadidtu," so on this basis "yawiddu" with a kasra on the waw is permissible. The meaning of "yawaddu" is "wishes."

The Qur'anic verse: ﴿And he is not one to remove him from the punishment by being given long life﴾. The grammarians differed concerning "huwa" (he). It was said: it is a pronoun referring to the preceding "aḥad" (one), and the sense is "none of them is one to remove him," with the predicate of the subject in the prepositional phrase, and "an yu'ammara" (that he be given long life) is the agent of "bi-muzahzih." Another group said: it is a pronoun referring to the giving of long life (ta'mir), and the sense is "and the giving of long life is not one to remove him," with the predicate in the prepositional phrase, and "an yu'ammara" is then an appositive (badal) for "ta'mir" according to this view. Al-Tabari reported from a group that they said "huwa" is an 'imad (a dummy or supporting pronoun).

I say: this is far-fetched, since the proper function of the 'imad is to stand between two mutually related things, such as His saying: ﴿Indeed, this is the truth﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 398.]] and His saying: ﴿But they were the wrongdoers﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 115.]] and similar cases. It was also said: "ma" is a Ḥijazi-type operator (governing the predicate as in Ḥijazi usage), "huwa" is its subject, and the predicate is in "bi-muzahzihih." Another group said: "huwa" is the pronoun of the matter and the affair (ḍamir al-amr wa al-sha'n). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is also far-fetched, because what is transmitted from the grammarians is that it must be explained by a clause free of a preposition.

As for "bi-muzahzihih": al-zaḥzaḥah means removal and distancing. One says: "zaḥzaḥtuhu," meaning I made him distant, and "tazahzaḥa," meaning he withdrew and kept away. It is both intransitive and transitive. A poet used it transitively:

"O Seizer of the soul from a person when he is at death's door, / and Forgiver of sins, move me away from the Fire."

Dhu al-Rummah recited it:

"O Seizer of the soul from a body that has disobeyed for a time, / and Forgiver of sins, move me away from the Fire."

Another poet used it intransitively:

"My two friends, why does the darkness not withdraw, / and why does the light of dawn not become clear?"

Al-Nasa'i reported from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Whoever fasts one day in the way of Allah, Allah will remove his face from the Fire by seventy autumns."

The Qur'anic verse: ﴿And Allah is seeing of what they do﴾, that is, of what those who each wish to be given a life of a thousand years are doing. Whoever reads with the "ta'" (you), then the implied speech according to him is: "Say to them, O Muhammad: Allah is seeing of what you do." The scholars said: Allah, mighty and majestic, described Himself as "Seeing" in the sense that He is knowing of hidden matters. In the speech of the Arabs, "baṣīr" means one who knows a thing and is well-informed about it. From this is the saying: "So-and-so is baṣīr (expert) in medicine, baṣīr in jurisprudence, baṣīr in dealing with men." A poet said:

"If you ask me about women, then indeed I am / an expert in the ailments of women, a physician."

Al-Khattabi said: al-baṣīr is the knowing one, and al-baṣīr can also mean the one who sees. It was also said: Allah described Himself as "Seeing" in the sense of the Maker of things that see, that is, making them perceivers of visible things through the perceptive faculty and power He created for them. So Allah is seeing of His servants, that is, the Maker of His servants as seeing.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 97:

The occasion of its revelation: the Jews said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no prophet among the prophets except that an angel of the angels comes to him from his Lord with the message and the revelation. So who is your companion, that we may follow you?" He said: "(Jibril, Gabriel)." They said: "That is the one who descends with war and fighting; he is our enemy! If you had said Mika'il (Michael), who descends with rain and mercy, we would have followed you." So Allah revealed the verse up to His words: "for the disbelievers." Al-Tirmidhi narrated it.

As for His words, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel — indeed, it is he who has brought it down upon your heart﴾. The pronoun in "innahu" (indeed, it) may carry two meanings. The first: indeed, Allah sent down Gabriel upon your heart. The second: indeed, Gabriel descended with the Qur'an upon your heart. The heart is singled out for mention because it is the seat of intellect, knowledge, and the reception of understanding. The verse indicates the nobility of Gabriel, peace be upon him, and the blame of his opponents.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿by the permission of Allah﴾, meaning: by His will and His knowledge. "Confirming what was before it" means the Torah. "And guidance and good tidings for the believers" — its meaning has already been mentioned [[Refer to vol. 1 pp. 160, 162, and vol. 2 p. 38, second edition.]], and praise be to Allah.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 98:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Allah﴾ is a conditional clause (shart), and its response (jawab) is "then indeed Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers." This is a threat and a reproach to those who oppose Jibril, peace be upon him, and a declaration that enmity toward some of them entails Allah's enmity toward them. The servant's enmity toward Allah is his disobedience, his abandoning of obedience to Him, and his opposition to His friends. Allah's enmity toward the servant is His punishing him and manifesting the effects of enmity upon him.

If it is asked: Why did Allah single out Jibril and Mikail for mention, when the mention of the angels includes them both? It is answered: He singled them out for mention to honour them, just as He said: ﴿In them are fruit and palm trees and pomegranates﴾ [[See vol. 17, p. 185.]]. It was also said: they were singled out because the Jews mentioned them, and the verse was revealed concerning them. Therefore mentioning them is necessary, lest the Jews say: "We did not oppose Allah and all His angels," so Allah, Exalted is He, specified them by name to nullify what they were interpreting as a restriction.

Scholars of language have various dialectal forms (lughat) for Jibril and Mikail, peace be upon them. As for the forms of Jibril, there are ten:

The first: Jibril (ﺟِﺒْﺮِﻳﻞ), which is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. Hassan ibn Thabit said:

"And Jibril, the Messenger of Allah, is among us."

The second: Jabril (with a fatha on the jim), which is the reading of al-Hasan and Ibn Kathir. It is narrated from Ibn Kathir that he said: "I saw the Prophet (ﷺ) in a dream, and he was reciting Jabril and Mikail, so I have continued to recite them thus ever since."

The third: Jibra'il (with a yā' after the hamza, in the pattern of Jibra'il-like forms), as the people of Kufa recited it, and they recited poetry:

"We were present, and you will not meet against us any battalion for all time except that Jibril is at its front."

This is the dialect of Tamim and Qays. [[The verse is by Ka'b ibn Malik, as in Sharh al-Qamus.]]

The fourth: Jibra'il (on the pattern of Jibra'al), with a short final vowel (maqsur), which is the reading of Abu Bakr from 'Asim.

The fifth: similar to it, and it is the reading of Yahya ibn Ya'mur, except that he doubled the lam.

The sixth: Jibra'il (with an alif after the ra' and then a hamza), and 'Ikrima recited with it.

The seventh: similar to it, except that after the hamza there is a yā'.

The eighth: Jibrīl (with two yā's and no hamza), and al-A'mash and Yahya ibn Ya'mur also recited with it.

The ninth: Jibra'in (with a fatha on the jim, followed by a hamza with a kasra, then a yā' and a nūn).

The tenth: Jibrin (with a kasra on the jim and a sukun on the yā', with a nūn and no hamza), which is the dialect of Banu Asad. Al-Tabari said: "It was not recited with it." Al-Nahhas said, mentioning the reading of Ibn Kathir: "The pattern fa'līl is not known in the speech of the Arabs, whereas fi'lil exists, such as dihliz, qitmir, and birtil. It is not impossible that there exists in foreign speech what has no counterpart in Arabic speech, and it is not impossible that its forms are many, as they said: Ibrahim, Ibrahim, Ibrāhim, and Ibrāhām." Others said: Jibril is a non-Arabic name which the Arabs arabicised, so it has these dialectal forms, and for this reason it is not declined (lam yanṣarif, i.e. treated as ghayr munṣarif, a diptote).

I say: It has already been mentioned at the beginning of the book [[See vol. 1, p. 68, second edition.]] that the correct view regarding these words is that they are Arabic, and that Jibril brought them down in clear Arabic speech.

Al-Nahhas said: Jibril's broken plural is Jabarīl.

As for the forms of Mikail, there are six:

The first: Mikail, the reading of Nafi'. Mikāil (with a yā' after the hamza) is the reading of Hamza. Mīkāl is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and it is the reading of Abu 'Amr and Hafs from 'Asim. It is narrated from Ibn Kathir that he used all three forms. Ka'b ibn Malik said:

"On the day of Badr we met you, and we had reinforcements with us, among them, along with the victory, Mikal and Jibril."

Another poet [[It is Jarir, as in his Diwan.]] said:

"They worshipped the cross and denied Muhammad, and denied Jibra'il, and denied Mikal."

The fourth: Mīkā'īl, on the pattern of Mīka'īl, which is the reading of Ibn Muhaysin. The fifth: Mikāyīl (with two yā's), which is the reading of al-A'mash with variation from him. The sixth: Mikā'il, as is said of Isrā'il (with an open hamza). It is a non-Arabic name, and for this reason it is not declined.

Ibn 'Abbas mentioned that Jabr, Mika and Israf are all in the non-Arabic language with the meaning of "servant" and "slave." Īl is a name of Allah, Exalted is He, and from it comes the saying of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, when he heard the rhymed prose of Musaylima: "This is speech that did not come from Il." And in the revelation: ﴿They do not observe toward a believer any tie of kinship or covenant﴾ according to one of the two interpretations, and it will come [[See vol. 8, p. 79.]].

Al-Mawardi said: Jibril and Mikail are two names, one of which means "servant of Allah" (ʿAbd Allah) and the other "servant of Allah" (ʿUbayd Allah), because Il is Allah, Exalted is He, Jibr means ʿabd (servant), and Mika means ʿubayd (servant). So Jibril means ʿAbd Allah and Mikail means ʿUbayd Allah. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, and there is no opponent of it among the exegetes.

I say: Some exegetes added: Israfil means ʿAbd al-Rahman (servant of the Most Merciful). Al-Nahhas said: Whoever interprets the hadith to mean that "Jibr" is ʿabd and "Il" is Allah must say: "This is Jibrail, I saw Jibrail, I passed by Jibrail," but this is not said, so the meaning of the hadith must be that it is a name in this form. Others said: Had it been as they claimed, it would have been declined, so the non-declension indicates that it is a single, simple name, not an annexed construction (mudaf).

ʿAbd al-Ghani al-Hafiz narrated from the hadith of Aflat ibn Khalifa, who is Fulayt al-ʿAmiri and who is Abu Hassan, from Jasrah bint Dajajah, from ʿA'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, Lord of Jibril, Mikail and Israfil, I seek refuge in You from the heat of the Fire and the punishment of the grave."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 99:

Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: This is a response to Ibn Suriya [[Thus in all manuscripts of the original, in Tafsir al-Tabari, and in Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi. In Sirat Ibn Hisham (p. 379, European edition): "Abu Salluba al-Fituni".]] when he said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "O Muhammad, you have brought us nothing that we recognize, and no clear sign has been sent down to you that we might follow you by." So Allah revealed this verse, as related by al-Tabari.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Is it that whenever they make a covenant, a party of them casts it aside?﴾ The *waw* is the *waw al-'atf* (the conjunctive waw). The interrogative *alif* (*alif al-istifham*, the particle of questioning) has been placed before it, just as it is placed before the *fa'* (the conjunctive particle "then") in His saying: "*Afa-hukma al-jahiliyyah*" (see vol. 6, p. 214), "*Afa-anta tusmi'u al-summ*" (see vol. 8, p. 346), and "*Afa-tattakhidhunahu wa-dhurriyyatahu*" (see vol. 10, p. 420). It is also placed before *thumma* (then), as in His saying: "*Athumma idha ma waqa'*" (see vol. 8, p. 351). This is the view of Sibawayh. Al-Akhfash said: the *waw* is superfluous (*za'idah*). The view of al-Kisa'i is that it is *aw* (or), and its *waw* was vowelled for ease of pronunciation. Some people read it as *aw* with a silent *waw*, so that it comes in the sense of *bal* (rather), as a speaker says, "*La-adribannaka*" (I will certainly strike you), and the responder says, "*Aw yakfi Allah*" (Or does God not suffice?). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: all of this is far-fetched (*mutakallaf*), and the correct view is the view of Sibawayh.

*Kullama* (whenever) is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*zarf*). The people referred to in the verse are Malik ibn al-Sayf, also called Ibn al-Dayf. He had said: "By God, no covenant was taken from us in our Book that we should believe in Muhammad, nor any pact." So the verse was revealed. It was also said that the Jews had made a covenant that if Muhammad (ﷺ) emerged, they would certainly believe in him and stand with him against the polytheists of the Arabs; but when he was sent, they disbelieved in him. 'Ata' said: these are the covenants that existed between the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Jews, which they broke, as the Banu Qurayzah and the Banu al-Nadir did. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿Those with whom you made a covenant, then they break their covenant every time, and they do not fear God.﴾ (see vol. 8, p. 30).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿a party of them cast it aside﴾. *Al-nabdh* means to throw away and to cast down. From it come *al-nabidh* (a fermented drink) and *al-manbudh* (the discarded one). Abu al-Aswad said:

*"And someone I had sent informed me that you took my letter in your left hand, turning away,*
*You looked at its address and then cast it aside, as you cast away a sandal worn out from your sandals."*

Another said:

*"Those whom you commanded to be just have cast away your Book and made the forbidden lawful."*

This is a proverb used for one who treats a matter lightly and does not act upon it. The Arabs say: "Make this behind your back, and behind you, and under your foot," meaning leave it and turn away from it. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And you have taken it behind your backs (*wara'akum zihriyyan*)﴾ (see vol. 9, p. 91). Al-Farra' recited:

*"Tamim ibn Zayd, let not my need be behind the back, so that its answer does not tire me."*

(The verse is by al-Farazdaq, addressing Tamim ibn Zayd al-Qayni, who was in Sind; see *al-Naqa'id*, p. 381, Europe edition.)

His saying: ﴿But most of them do not believe﴾. *Bal akthanuhum* is a beginning (*mubtada'*). *La yu'minun* is a verb in the imperfect (*fi'l mustaqbal*) in the place of the predicate (*khabar*).

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And when there came to them a Messenger from Allah, confirming what was with them﴾ is an adjective (na't) of "a Messenger," and it is permissible for it to be in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). "A party" (nabadha fariq) is the answer (jawāb) of "lammā" (when). "From those who were given the Book, the Book of Allah" — it is in the accusative governed by "nabadha" (threw away). What is meant is the Torah, because their disbelief in the Prophet (peace be upon him) and their denial of him amounts to casting it away. Al-Suddi said: "They threw away the Torah and took up the book of Asif, and the sorcery of Harut and Marut." It was also said: it is possible that by it is meant the Qur'an. Al-Sha'bi said: "It is before them, they recite it, but they cast away acting upon it." Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: "They wrapped it in silk and brocade, and adorned it with gold and silver, and did not make lawful what it made lawful, nor make unlawful what it made unlawful; that is the casting away." Its explanation has already been given in full [[in the previous page.]]. "As if they did not know" is a comparison to one who does not know, since they acted as the ignorant act; and thus it follows from the wording that they disbelieved knowingly.

There are twenty-four issues concerning it. The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they followed what the devils recited during the reign of Solomon﴾. This is a report from God, exalted is He, about the group who cast away the Book, that they also followed magic, and they are the Jews. As-Suddi said: The Jews opposed Muhammad (ﷺ) with the Torah, and the Torah and the Qur'an agreed, so they discarded the Torah and adopted the book of Asif and the magic of Harut and Marut. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) mentioned Solomon among the messengers, one of their rabbis said: "Muhammad claims that the son of Dawud was a prophet! By God, he was nothing but a magician." So God, mighty and majestic, revealed: ﴿Solomon did not disbelieve, but the devils disbelieved﴾, meaning they conveyed to the children of Adam that what Solomon did, such as riding the sea and commanding the birds and the devils, was magic. Al-Kalbi said: The devils wrote down magic and the *nirnajiyyat*[[The manuscripts differ in the spelling of this word. In the Qamus it appears as "al-nirnaj." The commentator of the Qamus said: "So it is in all the copies, but what is transmitted from the text of al-Layth's statement is 'al-nirij' with the second nun dropped. It is also given thus in the Lisan. It is a kind of sorcery but is not really so; it is only imitation and deception."]] in the name of Asif, Solomon's scribe, and buried them beneath his prayer place when God took away his kingdom, without Solomon noticing. When Solomon died, they dug them up and said to the people: "It was by this that he ruled you, so learn it." As for the scholars of the Children of Israel, they said: "God forbid that this be the knowledge of Solomon!" But the base among them said: "This is the knowledge of Solomon," and they turned to learning it and abandoned the books of their prophets, until God sent Muhammad (ﷺ). Then God, mighty and majestic, revealed to His Prophet the excuse for Solomon and manifested his innocence from what was attributed to him, saying: ﴿And they followed what the devils recited﴾. 

Ata said: "Tatlu" means "recite," from recitation. Ibn Abbas said: "Tatlu" means "follow," as you say: "The people came, one following another (yatlu ba'duhum ba'dan)." At-Tabari said: "Ittaba'u" means "preferred." I say: because whoever follows something and places it before himself has preferred it over others. The meaning of "tatlu" is "tala," so it has the sense of the past tense. The poet said:

*When you pass by his grave, slaughter upon it*
*the humps of noble camels, and every swift-running horse.*
*And sprinkle the sides of his grave with their blood,*
*for indeed there may have been servants and sacrificial animals.*

That is, "for indeed there were." "Ma" is the object of "ittaba'u," meaning they followed what the devils fabricated against Solomon and recited. It was said that "ma" is a negation, but this is not valid either in the structure of the sentence or in its soundness, said Ibn al-Arabi. "Over the kingdom of Solomon" means over his law and his prophethood. Az-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "during the time of the kingdom of Solomon." It was also said: the meaning is "concerning the kingdom of Solomon," that is, concerning his stories, attributes and reports. Al-Farra said: "ʿala" and "fi" may both be used in such a context. He said "ʿala" and did not say "ba'd" because of God's saying: ﴿We did not send before you any messenger or prophet but that when he desired, Satan cast into his desire﴾, meaning into his recitation.[[See vol. 12, p. 79.]] The meaning of "shaytan" and its derivation has already been mentioned, so there is no point in repeating it.[[See vol. 1, p. 90, second edition.]] Here "the devils" is said to mean the devils of the jinn, which is what is understood from this term. It was also said that the intended meaning is the rebellious devils of mankind who persist in error, as in the saying of Jarir:

*In the days when they called me "the devil" because of my ghazal,*
*and they used to desire me when I was a devil.*

The second issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Solomon did not disbelieve﴾. This is God's exoneration of Solomon. Nothing earlier in the verse indicates that anyone attributed disbelief to him, but the Jews attributed magic to him, and since magic is disbelief, it became as if they had attributed disbelief to him. Then He said: ﴿But the devils disbelieved﴾, affirming their disbelief through teaching magic. The phrase "teaching people magic" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*), and it may also be in the nominative position as a second predicate. The Kufans, other than Asim, read ﴿wa-lakini al-shayatin﴾ with the lightened "lakin" and the nominative "al-shayatin," and likewise in al-Anfal: ﴿wa-lakinna Allaha rama﴾.[[See vol. 7, p. 384.]] Ibn Amir agreed with them. The rest read it with the intensive "lakinna" and the accusative. "Lakinna" is a word with two meanings: the negation of a past report and the affirmation of a future report. It is formed of three words: *la* (no), *ka* (you), and *inna* (indeed/certainly). *La* is a negation, *ka* is the second person address, and *inna* is affirmation and confirmation. The hamza was dropped because of heaviness. It may be pronounced heavy or light: when heavy, it governs the accusative like the heavy *inna*, and when light, it governs the nominative as the light *in* does.

The third issue: Magic. It was said: the origin of magic is the deception of the senses through tricks and illusions, namely that the magician does things and creates appearances, so that the one who is bewitched imagines them to be other than what they are, like one who sees a mirage from afar and imagines it to be water, or like a passenger on a swiftly moving ship who imagines that the trees and mountains he sees are moving along with him. It was also said that it is derived from *sahartu al-sabiyy*, meaning when you deceive a child, and likewise when you distract him; *al-tashhir* has the same sense. Labid said:

*So if you ask us what we are doing, we are but sparrows*
*from among these people who are distracted.*

Another poet, [[It is Imru' al-Qays, as in his Diwan and in the Lisan.]] said:

*We see ourselves hastening toward an unseen matter,*
*and we are distracted by food and drink.*
*Sparrows, flies, and worms,*
*and bolder than the bold wolf of the wolves.*[[Muwadi'in: hastening. Li-amr ghayb: he means death, whose time has been hidden from us, and we are distracted from it by food and drink. Dhi'ban: flies. Mujallahat al-dhi'ab: bold.]]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You are only one of the bewitched﴾ [*al-musahharin*]. It is said: "*al-musahhar*" is one who was created with a windpipe (*sahr*), and it is said: one of those distracted, that is, one who eats food and drinks drink. It was also said: its origin is concealment, since the magician performs it in secret. It was also said: its origin is turning away, as one says: "What turned you away from such-and-such (*ma saharaka 'an kadha*)," meaning what diverted you from it, so magic is something turned away from its proper direction. It was also said: its origin is attraction, since whoever attracts you has bewitched you. It was said regarding His saying: ﴿Rather, we are a bewitched people﴾, meaning we were bewitched and thus turned from our knowledge by imagination. Al-Jawhari said: magic is seizure; whatever is subtle in its grasp and fine is magic, and one says: he bewitched him (*sahara-hu*), a magic (*sihr*). The *sahir* is also the knowledgeable one, and *sahara-hu* also means "deceived him," which we have already mentioned. Ibn Mas'ud said: In the Jahiliyya we used to call magic *al-idha* (slander). *Al-idha* among the Arabs means intense false accusation and the embellishment of a lie. The poet said:

*I seek refuge in my Lord from the blowers*
*in the slander of the slanderer who slanders.*

The fourth issue: It has been disputed whether magic has a real existence or not. Al-Ghaznawi al-Hanafi mentioned in *Uyun al-Ma'ani* that according to the Mu'tazila magic is merely deception with no real basis, and according to al-Shafi'i it is whispering and sickness. He said: In our view its origin is a talisman based on the influence of the special properties of the stars, like the influence of the sun on the quicksilver in the staffs of Pharaoh, or the veneration of the devils so that they may make easy what is difficult. I say: In our view it is true, it has a real existence, and God creates through it whatever He wills, as will come. Then, among magic is that which is done by sleight of hand, like conjuring (*sha'wadha*). The *sha'wadhi* is the courier because of the lightness of his pace. Ibn Faris said in *al-Mujmal*: *sha'wadha* is not from the speech of the desert people; it is lightness in the hands and a seizing like magic. Among it is also that which is a spoken formula that is memorized, and incantations from the names of God, exalted is He. It may also come from pacts with the devils, and it may be medicines, fumigations, and other things.

The fifth issue: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) called eloquence in speech and skill in speaking "magic," when he said: "Indeed, there is magic in eloquence." Malik and others transmitted it. This is because it involves making falsehood appear right so that the listener imagines it to be true. Accordingly, his saying (peace be upon him): "Indeed, there is magic in eloquence" came as a censure of rhetoric and eloquence, since he compared them to magic. It was also said that it came as praise of rhetoric and of excellence in expression, said by a group of scholars. The first is more correct, and the proof of it is his saying (peace be upon him): "Perhaps some of you are more eloquent in his argument than others," and his saying: "The most hateful of you to me are the chatterers, the pompous-speakers (*al-mutafayhiqun*)." Chatter (*al-tharthara*) is excessive talk and its repetition; one says: "The man chattered (*tharthara*), so he is a *tharthar*, a babbler." The *mutafayhiq* is similar to it. Ibn Duraid said: "So-and-so *yatafayhaqu* in his speech" when he expands in it and goes to excess; he said: its root is *al-fahq*, which is filling, as if he filled his mouth with it. I say: In this sense which we have mentioned, Amir al-Sha'bi, the transmitter of the hadith, and Sa'sa'a ibn Suhan explained it, and they said: As for his saying (ﷺ): "Indeed, there is magic in eloquence," a man may have the right on his side while being more eloquent in arguments than the rightful party, so he bewitches the people with his speech and thus takes away the truth while it is on his side. The scholars only praise eloquence and skill in speech so long as it does not go to the extent of verbosity and prolixity, or the depicting of falsehood in the form of truth. This is clear, and praise be to God.

The sixth issue: Some magic is disbelief on the part of its practitioner, such as what they claim: changing the forms of people and turning them into the shape of beasts, traversing a month's distance in a night, and flying in the air. Whoever does this in order to make people think he is truthful, that is disbelief on his part. This was said by Abu Nasr Abd al-Rahim al-Qushayri. Abu 'Amr said: Whoever claims that the magician transforms an animal from one form to another, making a man into a donkey or the like, and that he can move bodies, destroy them, and alter them, this person would hold that the magician should be killed, because he disbelieves in the prophets, claiming the like of their signs and miracles, and with this one cannot establish the knowledge of the validity of prophethood, since something similar may be achieved by trickery. As for one who claims that magic is deception, illusions, contrivances, and imaginings, then according to his principle, the magician does not have to be killed, unless by his act he kills someone, in which case he is to be put to death for it.

**Seventh:** The People of the Sunnah hold that magic (*siḥr*) is real and has an actual existence. The majority of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school of theology) and Abu Ishaq al-Asfarayini (or al-Astarabadhi, as the text has it), one of the companions of al-Shafi'i, hold that magic has no real existence. They say it is only deception, imagination, and creating the illusion that a thing is other than what it is, a kind of trickery and sleight of hand. They cite the saying of Allah, Exalted be He: ﴿It was imagined to him, by their magic, that their ropes and staffs were moving﴾ [[See vol. 11, p. 222.]]. He did not say "they were moving in reality" but said "it was imagined to him." He also said: ﴿They bewitched the eyes of the people﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 259.]].

This argument is not conclusive, for we do not deny that imagination and other things are part of magic. But beyond that there are matters which reason allows and revelation has transmitted. Among them is what this verse mentions of magic and its teaching. Had magic had no real existence, it could not be taught, and Allah would not have informed us that they teach it to people. This shows that magic has a real existence. Also, Allah's saying about the story of Pharaoh's magicians, ﴿And they came with a great magic﴾, and the surah of *al-Falaq*, together with the agreement of the exegetes that the occasion of its revelation was the magic of Labid ibn al-A'sam. This is narrated by al-Bukhari, Muslim and others from 'Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "A Jew from the Jews of Banu Zuraiq, called Labid ibn al-A'sam, bewitched the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)," and the hadith continues. In it, when the magic was undone, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah has healed me." Healing only occurs by the removal of an ailment and the cessation of a sickness, which shows that magic has a true and real existence. Its existence and occurrence are thus definitively established by the report of Allah, Exalted be He, and His Messenger.

This is also the view of the *ahl al-ḥall wa-l-'aqd* (the qualified scholars through whom consensus, *ijma'*, is formed). Their agreement is not affected by the dregs of the Mu'tazilah or their opposition to the people of truth. Magic was widespread and well known in earlier times, and people spoke about it. No denial of its very existence appeared from the Companions or the Successors. Sufyan narrated from Abu al-A'war, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "The knowledge of magic is in a village of the villages of Egypt called *al-Farama*. Whoever denies it is an unbeliever, one who denies Allah and His Messenger, and rejects what is known through direct observation and witness."

**Eighth:** Our scholars said: It cannot be denied that acts that break customary patterns, which are beyond human capacity, may appear at the hands of a sorcerer. These include illness, separation (between spouses or friends), loss of reason, the twisting of a limb, and other things, which evidence has established are impossible to be within the power of human beings. They said: In magic it is not far-fetched that the body of the sorcerer may be made so slender that he slips through windows and small openings, stands on the top of a reed, runs on a thin thread, flies in the air, walks on water, rides a dog, and other such things. Yet magic does not, by itself, necessitate these things, nor is it their cause or a generating means. The sorcerer does not independently bring them about. Rather, Allah, Exalted be He, creates these things and brings them into being at the presence of magic, just as He creates satiety at eating and quenching at drinking. Sufyan narrated from 'Ammar al-Dhahabi that a sorcerer was with al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah. He walked on a rope and entered the rectum of a donkey and came out of its mouth. Jundub drew his sword and killed him. This is Jundub ibn Ka'b al-Azdi, also said to be al-Bajali, the one about whom the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "In my community there will be a man called Jundub who will strike a blow with the sword that will distinguish between truth and falsehood." So they regarded this Jundub as the slayer of the sorcerer. 'Ali ibn al-Madini said: Hāritha ibn Muḍarrib narrated from him.

**Ninth:** The Muslims agree that there is nothing in magic which, at its command, Allah brings about the sending down of locusts, lice and frogs, the splitting of the sea, the turning of a staff (into a serpent), the raising of the dead, the making of the dumb to speak, and similar great signs of the messengers, peace be upon them. Such things, and the like, must definitely be affirmed as not occurring through magic, nor does Allah bring them about at the will of a sorcerer. The judge Abu Bakr ibn al-Tayyib said: "We have prohibited that only by consensus, and were it not for consensus we would have permitted it."

**Tenth:** On the difference between magic and a miracle (*mu'jizah*). Our scholars said: Magic may come from a sorcerer or from others, and there may be a group who know it and are able to produce it at one time. A miracle is one which Allah does not enable anyone to produce its like or to oppose. Furthermore, the sorcerer does not claim prophethood, so what proceeds from him is distinct from a miracle, for the condition of a miracle is that it accompanies a claim to prophethood and a challenge by means of it, as was previously mentioned in the introduction of this book [[See vol. 1, p. 69 and following, second edition.]].

**Eleventh:** The jurists differed concerning the ruling on a Muslim sorcerer and a *dhimmi* (a non-Muslim under protection) sorcerer. Malik held that if a Muslim practises magic himself by a statement that amounts to disbelief, he is to be killed, is not asked to repent, and his repentance is not accepted, because this is a matter that is concealed, like the heretic (*zindiq*) and the adulterer. Also, Allah, Exalted be He, called magic disbelief in His saying: ﴿And they teach no one until they say, "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve"﴾. This is also the view of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Abu Thawr, Ishaq, al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifah. The killing of the sorcerer has been related from 'Umar, 'Uthman, Ibn 'Umar, Hafsa, Abu Musa, Qays ibn Sa'd, and from seven of the Successors. It is also related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The legal punishment for the sorcerer is striking him with the sword." Al-Tirmidhi transmitted it, but it is not strong. Isma'il ibn Muslim alone transmitted it, and he is weak according to them. Ibn 'Uyaynah narrated it from Isma'il ibn Muslim from al-Hasan as a *mursal* (a report missing its companion-link). Some of them made it from al-Hasan from Jundub. Ibn al-Mundhir said: We have also been informed from 'Aisha that she sold a female sorcerer who had bewitched her, and she put its price towards freeing slaves.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: If a man confesses that he practised magic with a statement that amounts to disbelief, he must be killed unless he repents. Likewise if evidence is established against him and the evidence describes a statement amounting to disbelief. But if the words by which he said he practised magic are not disbelief, he may not be killed. If he caused a crime against the one bewitched which entails retaliation (*qiṣāṣ*), retaliation is taken from him if he did it deliberately. If it is something for which there is no retaliation, then there is blood-money (*diyah*) for it. Ibn al-Mundhir said: When the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) differed on the question, it is obligatory to follow the one most in accordance with the Book and the Sunnah. It is possible that the magic which those among them who commanded the killing of the sorcerer had in mind was magic that amounts to disbelief, and this would accord with the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It is also possible that 'Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, ordered the sale of a sorceress whose magic was not disbelief. If someone argues from the hadith of Jundub from the Prophet (ﷺ), "The legal punishment for the sorcerer is striking him with the sword," then even if it is authentic, it allows that he commanded the killing of the sorcerer whose magic is disbelief, which would accord with the reports from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except in one of three cases..." I say: This is authentic, and the blood of Muslims is inviolable and may not be made lawful except by certainty, and there is no certainty where there is disagreement. And Allah knows best.

Some scholars said: If the practitioners of the craft say that magic is not completed except with disbelief, arrogance, or the glorification of Satan, then magic on this assumption indicates disbelief. And Allah knows best.

It is related from al-Shafi'i: The sorcerer is not killed unless he kills by his magic and says, "I intended to kill." If he says, "I did not intend it," he is not killed, and there is a blood-money for it like the blood-money for accidental killing. If he strikes someone, he is disciplined according to the degree of harm. Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is false in two respects. The first is that he has not known magic, and its reality is that it is a statement...

Second: God, glorified is He, has explicitly stated in His Book that it is disbelief, saying: "Solomon did not disbelieve," meaning by saying magic, "but the devils disbelieved," meaning by practising it and teaching it. And Harut and Marut say: "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve" (﴿We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve﴾). This is an emphatic clarification.

The companions of Malik argued that his repentance is not accepted, because magic is something hidden that its practitioner does not reveal, so his repentance cannot be known, like the zindiq (heretic who conceals unbelief). Only one who openly displays disbelief as an apostate is asked to repent. Malik said: If the magician or the zindiq comes repentant before witnesses testify against them, their repentance is accepted. The proof for this is His saying: ﴿So their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our punishment﴾ [40:85]. This indicates that their faith would have benefited them before the punishment descended, and so it is with these two.

Twelfth issue: As for the magician who is a dhimmi (a non-Muslim under protection), it has been said that he is to be killed. Malik said: He is not killed unless he kills by his magic and must pay compensation for what he caused. He is killed if something comes from him that he did not undertake to avoid.

Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: As for a dhimmi, the reports from Malik differ. Once he said: He is to be asked to repent, and his repentance is Islam. Another time he said: He is to be killed even if he embraces Islam. As for the harbi (a non-Muslim at war with the Muslims), he is not killed if he repents. Malik likewise said regarding a dhimmi who insulted the Prophet (ﷺ): He is asked to repent, and his repentance is Islam. Another time he said: He is to be killed and not asked to repent, like a Muslim. Malik also said regarding a dhimmi who was bewitched: He is punished, unless he killed by his magic or caused some harm, in which case he is held to account proportionately. Others said: He is to be killed, because he has broken the covenant. A magician's heirs do not inherit from him, because he is a disbeliever, unless his magic is not called disbelief. Malik said regarding a woman who ties up her husband by magic, whether for herself or for another: She is disciplined but not killed.

Thirteenth issue: They differed over whether a magician may be asked to undo magic from the one who has been bewitched. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib permitted it, as al-Bukhari reported, and al-Muzani inclined to this view, but al-Hasan al-Basri disliked it. Al-Sha'bi said: There is no harm in al-nushrah (a kind of incantation and treatment used for one who thinks that a jinn has touched him, because by it the ailment that has got into him is dispersed, meaning uncovered and removed).

Ibn Battal said: In the book of Wahb ibn Munabbih, it says that one should take seven green leaves of the lote tree, crush them between two stones, mix them with water, recite over it the Verse of the Throne, then sip three sips from it and bathe with it, for it will remove from him all that afflicts him, God willing. It is good for a man who has been prevented from reaching his wife.

Fourteenth issue: Most of the Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) denied the existence of devils and jinn. Their denial indicates their lack of concern and the weakness of their religious commitment. There is no rationally impossible matter in affirming them, and the texts of the Book and the Sunnah establish their existence. It is incumbent upon the intelligent person who holds fast to the rope of God to affirm what reason judges to be possible and what the Law has explicitly established. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿But the devils disbelieved﴾ and said: ﴿And among the devils are those who dive for him﴾ [21:82], besides other verses. The sura of the Jinn (72) also attests to this. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the devil flows through the son of Adam as the blood flows." Many people have denied this report, and they deemed it impossible for two spirits to be in one body. Yet reason does not rule out their moving within humans if their bodies are subtle and simple, as some people, indeed most of them, say. Even if they were dense, this would still be possible for them, just as food and drink can enter the empty spaces of the body. Likewise, worms may be in the children of Adam while they are alive.

Fifteenth issue: God's saying: ﴿And what was sent down to the two angels﴾. The "ma" here is negative, and the "waw" is conjunctive, coordinating with His saying: ﴿Solomon did not disbelieve﴾. The reason is that the Jews claimed that God sent down Gabriel and Michael with magic, and God negated that. In the sentence there is an inversion, the sense being: "Solomon did not disbelieve, and what was sent down to the two angels, but the devils disbelieved, teaching people magic at Babylon, Harut and Marut." So Harut and Marut are in apposition to "the devils" in His saying: ﴿But the devils disbelieved﴾. This is the most appropriate interpretation of the verse and the soundest of what has been said about it, and nothing else should be considered. Magic is derived from the devils' extraction, because of the subtlety of their substance and the refinement of their understanding. Among humans, it is most practised by women, especially during their menstruation. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And from the evil of the blowers in knots﴾ [113:4]. A poet said:

"I seek refuge in my Lord from the blowers..." [the poem continues]

Sixteenth issue: If someone asks: How can two be a substitute for a plural, when a substitute must match what it replaces? The answer has three aspects. First: the dual may be referred to by the name of the plural, as God said: ﴿But if he has brothers, then for his mother is a sixth﴾ [4:11]. The brothers exclude her from a third to a sixth only when there are two or more of them, as will be explained in Surat al-Nisa'. Second: since the two were the leaders in teaching, they were singled out by mention rather than their followers, as God said: ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾ [74:30]. Third: they were singled out from among them because of their rebellion, as God said: ﴿In them are fruit, palms, and pomegranates﴾ [55:68], and His saying: ﴿And Gabriel and Michael﴾ [2:98]. This is common in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech. Sometimes a specific member of a general category is named either because of his nobility, or his excellence, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the most worthy of Abraham among people are those who followed him, and this Prophet﴾ [3:68], and His saying: ﴿And Gabriel and Michael﴾. Or for his goodness, as in His saying: ﴿Fruit, palms, and pomegranates﴾. Or because of its prevalence, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The earth has been made for me a place of prayer and its dust a purifier." Or because of his rebellion and insolence, as in this verse. And God knows best.

It has also been said that "ma" is conjoined to "magic" and is in the accusative (as the object). On this view, "ma" means "that which," and magic was sent down to the two angels as a trial and test for people. God may test His servants with whatever He wills, just as He tested them with the river of Talut. Therefore the two angels say: ﴿We are only a trial﴾, meaning a test from God: "We inform you that the practice of the magician is disbelief. If you obey us, you will be saved, but if you disobey us, you will be destroyed."

It has been reported from Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Ka'b al-Ahbar, al-Suddi and al-Kalbi, something to the effect that when corruption increased among the children of Adam (peace be upon him) — and that was in the time of Idris (peace be upon him) — the angels reproached them. God, the Exalted, said: "Indeed, if you were in their place, and I had placed in you what I placed in them, you would act as they did." They said: "Glory be to You! It would not have been fitting for us." He said: "Then choose two angels from among your best." They chose Harut and Marut. He sent them down to earth and placed desire in them. Not a month passed before they were tempted by a woman whose name in Nabataean was "Bidukht," in Persian "Nahid," and in Arabic "al-Zuhra." She came to them for judgment, and they solicited her, but she refused unless they entered her religion, drank wine, and killed the soul which God had forbidden. They agreed to her, drank wine, and had intercourse with her. A man saw them, so they killed him. She asked them about the name by which they ascend to heaven, and they taught it to her. She spoke it and ascended, and she was transformed into a star.

Salim reported from his father, from Abdullah: Ka'b al-Habr told me that they did not complete their day before they did what God had forbidden them. In another report: They were given the choice between the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter, and they chose the punishment of this world. So they are punished in Babil in a pit in the earth. It is said: Babil is in Iraq. It is also said: Babil is Nahavand.

It was reported through Ata' that Ibn Umar, whenever he saw Venus and Suhayl (Canopus), cursed and reviled them, saying: "Suhayl was a tax collector in Yemen who oppressed people, and Venus was the companion of Harut and Marut." We say: All of this is weak and far from Ibn Umar and others; nothing from them is authentic. This is a claim rejected by the fundamentals regarding the angels, who are the trustees of God over His revelation and His envoys to His messengers: ﴿They do not disobey God in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded﴾ [66:6]. ﴿Rather, they are honored servants. They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command﴾ [21:26-27]. ﴿They glorify Him night and day, and they do not tire﴾ [21:20]. As for reason, it does not deny that the angels could commit sin, or that they could do something contrary to what they are commanded, or that He could create desires in them. For God's power encompasses everything imaginable, and from this comes the fear of the prophets, the excellent saints, and the scholars. However, the occurrence of this possibility can only be known through transmission, and this report is not authentic. Among the things that show it is not authentic is that God created the stars and these planets when He created the heaven. In the report: "When the heaven was created, seven revolving bodies were created in it: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, and the Moon." This is the meaning of God's saying: ﴿And each in an orbit swims﴾ [21:33]. Thus it is established that Venus and Suhayl existed before the creation of Adam.

Then, the angels' saying: ﴿It would not have been fitting for us﴾ is a flaw (ʿawrah), meaning: "He cannot test us." This is disbelief, and we seek refuge in God from it and from attributing it to the noble angels, may God's blessings be upon them all. We have declared them free of it, and they are free of everything the exegetes mentioned and related. ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Majesty, above what they describe﴾ [37:180].

Seventeenth issue: Ibn Abbas, Ibn Abza, al-Dahhak and al-Hasan read "al-malikayn" with a kasra on the lam. Ibn Abza said: They are Dawud and Sulayman. On this view too, "ma" is negative. Ibn al-Arabi weakened this view. Al-Hasan said: They were two men of Babil, two kings, so on this view "ma" is in the accusative and not negative.

**Eighteenth:** His saying, exalted is He: "in Babil" (Babil). *Babil* is not declined (ghayr munsarif, i.e. it does not take nunation) because of three features: feminine form, definiteness, and being a non-Arabic (a'jamiyy) name. It is a region of the earth. It is said to be Iraq and what borders it. Ibn Mas'ud said to the people of Kufa: "You are between al-Hirah and Babil."
