Qatadah said: "It extends from Nasibin to Ras al-'Ayn." Some people said: "It is in the West (al-Maghrib)." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This is weak." Some people said: "It is the mountain of Nahawand." Allah knows best.

There is disagreement about the reason for its name. It is said it was named Babil because of the confusion (tabalbul) of tongues there when the palace of Nimrod fell. It is also said that when Allah wished to vary the languages of the children of Adam, He sent a wind that gathered them from the horizons to Babil, Allah confused their tongues there, and then that wind scattered them throughout the lands. *Al-balbalah* means dispersal; al-Khalil stated this meaning. Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: "Among the most concise and finest things said about *al-balbalah* is what Dawud ibn Abi Hind related from 'Ilba' ibn Ahmar, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, that when Nuh (peace be upon him) descended to the foot of al-Judi, he built a town and named it Thamanin (Eighty). One day they woke up and their tongues had been confused into eighty languages, one of which was the Arabic tongue, and some of them could not understand others."

**Nineteenth:** 'Abdullah ibn Bishr al-Mazini narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Beware of this world! By the One in whose hand is my soul, it is more sorcerous than Harut and Marut." Our scholars said: "This world is only more sorcerous than them because it bewitches you with its deceptions and hides its temptation from you. It makes you covet it, compete for it, hoard it and withhold from others, until it separates you from obedience to Allah and separates you from seeing the truth and observing it. So this world is more sorcerous than them: it takes your heart away from Allah, from fulfilling His rights, and from His promise and His threat. The sorcery of this world is love for it, your delight in its desires, and your wishful thinking with its false hopes, until it captures your heart. For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Your love of something makes you blind and deaf.'"

**Twentieth:** His saying, exalted is He: "Harut and Marut." *Harut* is not declined because it is non-Arabic and definite; likewise *Marut*. Its plural is *hawarit* and *mawarit*, like *tawaghit*. It is also said *hawaratah* and *hawar*, and *mawaratah* and *mawar*. Similar to it are Jalut and Talut, so note this. It has been mentioned before whether they are two angels or other than that, and there is disagreement.

Al-Zajjaj said: "It is narrated from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: 'Yes, by the One who sent down to the two angels...', and that the two angels taught people as a warning about sorcery, not as an invitation to it." Al-Zajjaj said: "This is the view held by most linguists and thinkers. Its meaning is that they taught people by way of prohibition, saying to them: 'Do not do such and such, and do not devise such and such in order to separate a man from his wife.' What was sent down to them was the prohibition, as if they were saying to people: 'Do not do such and such.' So 'yu'allimani' (they teach) means 'yu'limani' (they inform), as in His saying: 'We have honoured (karramna) the children of Adam,' meaning 'akramna' (We honoured)."

**Twenty-first:** His saying, exalted is He: "And they do not teach anyone." The *min* here is extra (za'idah) for emphasis, and the sense is: "and they do not teach anyone." "Until they say" is in the subjunctive, governed by *hatta*, so the nun was dropped from it. The dialect of Hudhayl and Thaqif says "'ata" with an unpointed 'ayn. The pronoun in "yu'allimani" refers to Harut and Marut. There are two views on "yu'allimani": first, that it keeps its original meaning of teaching; second, that it is from informing (i'lam), not from teaching, so "yu'allimani" means "yu'limani." It has come in Arabic speech that *ta'allam* means *i'lam* (know), as related by Ibn al-A'rabi and Ibn al-Anbari. Ka'b ibn Malik said:

*"Know, O Messenger of Allah, that you will overtake me,
and that your threat is like a grip by the hand."*

al-Qutami said:

*"Know that after error there is guidance,
and that for that error there is a clearing."*

Zuhayr said:

*"Know them, by the life of Allah, as an oath,
so measure with your cubit and see where you will enter."*

[There is another piece of evidence in this line: the placing of *ha* (used for alerting) before *dha* (this), with "by the life of Allah" intervening between them. The meaning is: "Know Allah, this is what He swears by." In the Diwan it reads: "fa-aqsid bi-dhar'ika" (so aim with your cubit).]

Another said:

*"Know that there is no omen except
for one who takes omens, and that is destruction."*

"Indeed we are only a trial" (fitnah): when they informed him of their trial, the world was more sorcerous than them, because it hid its trial. "So do not disbelieve": one group said it refers to teaching sorcery, and another group said it refers to practising it. Al-Mahdawi related that it is mockery, because they were only saying it to someone whose misguidance they had already confirmed.

**Twenty-second:** His saying, exalted is He: "So they learn from them." Sibawayh said: "The implied sense is: 'so they learn.'" He said: "Similar to it is 'Be, and it is.'" It is also said that it is conjoined to the position of "wa ma yu'allimani" (and they do not teach), because His saying "wa ma yu'allimani," even though the negating *ma* enters it, implies affirmation of teaching. Al-Farra' said: "It is linked to His saying 'they teach people sorcery'... so 'fa-yata'allamun' (and so they learn)," and "fa-yata'allamun" is connected to the words "Indeed we are only a trial," so that they come and learn. Al-Suddi said: "The two would say to whoever came to them: 'Indeed we are only a trial, so do not disbelieve.' If he refused to turn back, they would say to him: 'Go to this ash and urinate on it.' When he urinated on it, a light would rise from it to the sky, which is faith, and then a black smoke would come out and enter his ears, which is disbelief. When he informed them of what he had seen, they would teach him what to use to separate a man from his wife."

A group of scholars held that the sorcerer cannot do more than what Allah has mentioned of separation, because Allah mentioned it in the context of condemning sorcery and of the extremes of teaching it; if he could do more than that, He would have mentioned it. Another group said: "That came out in terms of what is most common, and it cannot be denied that sorcery has an effect on hearts, through love and hatred, and through casting evils, so that the sorcerer separates a man from his wife and comes between a man and his heart. That happens by inflicting pains and grievous illnesses. All of this is known by observation, and denying it is obstinacy. This has been discussed before, and praise be to Allah."

**Twenty-third:** His saying, exalted is He: "And they cannot harm anyone with it except by the permission of Allah." "They" refers to the sorcerers; it is also said to refer to the Jews, and it is also said to refer to the devils. "With it" means with the sorcery. "Anyone" means anyone at all, and *min* is extra. "Except by the permission of Allah" means by His will and decree, not by His command, because He does not command indecency and does not decree it for creatures. Al-Zajjaj said: "'Except by the permission of Allah' means except by the knowledge of Allah." Al-Nahhas said: "Abu Ishaq's saying, 'except by the permission of Allah, meaning except by the knowledge of Allah,' is an error, because *adhan* is only said of knowledge in the sense of 'I have become aware' (adhina adhanan)." But since it was not permitted among them and between Him, and they kept doing it, it was as if He had permitted it, by way of metaphor.

**Twenty-fourth:** His saying: "And they learn what harms them." It means in the Hereafter, even if they gain some small benefit in this world by it. It is also said: it harms them in this world, because the harm of sorcery and separation returns to the sorcerer in this world if he is discovered, since he is disciplined and reprimanded, and the ill omen of sorcery overtakes him.

The rest of the verses are clear, since their meanings were mentioned earlier. The *lam* in "wa-laqad 'alimu" (And they had certainly known) is the emphatic lam. The *lam* in "la-man ishtarahu" (whoever purchased it) is the lam of oath, which is also for emphasis. The position of *man* is nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence, because what precedes the lam does not govern what follows it. *Man* here means "the one who." Al-Farra' said: "It is conditional." Al-Zajjaj said: "This is not a place of conditionality; *man* means 'the one who,' as you say: 'I have known, whoever came to you has no intelligence.'" The *min* in "min khalaq" (no share) is extra, and the sense is: "he has no share in the Hereafter." It is not added in an affirmative sentence; this is the view of the Basrans. The Kufans said it may be extra in an affirmative sentence, and they cited His saying: "that He may forgive you some of your sins." *Khalaq* means share (nasib); Mujahid said this. Al-Zajjaj said: "This is also its meaning according to the linguists, except that it is hardly used except for a share of good."

He was asked about His saying: "And they had certainly known that whoever purchased it, for him there is no share in the Hereafter." He informed that they had known, then He said: "And wretched is what they sold their souls for, if only they had known," informing that they do not know. The answer, which is the view of Qutrub and al-Akhfash, is that those who know are the devils, and those who sold their souls (i.e. sold them) are the humans who do not know. Al-Zajjaj said that Ali ibn Sulayman said: "In my view the better opinion is that 'wa-laqad 'alimu' refers to the two angels, because they are more entitled to know. And he said: 'alimu' as one says: 'the two Zayds stood.'" Al-Zajjaj said: "Those who knew were the scholars of the Jews, but it was said: 'if only they had known,' meaning they entered the category of one who is told: 'You are not a scholar,' because they abandoned acting on their knowledge and sought guidance from those who practised sorcery."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 103:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they had believed and feared Allah﴾, i.e., feared (ittaqaw) sorcery. "Surely a reward (lamathubah)": al-mathubah means the reward (thawab), and according to some it is the response (jawab) to "And if they had believed." Al-Akhfash Sa'id said: "Law" (if) here has no response in wording, but it has one in meaning, and the meaning is "they would be rewarded." The position of "anna" (that) in His saying "And if they had (anna-hum)" is in the nominative case, meaning: if their belief had occurred, because "law" is not followed except by a verb, either explicit or implied, since it functions like the particles of conditionality, for it must have a response, and "anna" is followed by a verb. Muhammad ibn Yazid said: The reason it cannot be a response with "law" is that the way of all particles of conditionality is to turn the past tense into the meaning of the future, and since this is not the case with "law," it is not permissible for it to be the conditional particle that takes a response.

**The first issue:** Concerning His saying, exalted is He, ﴿O you who believe, do not say, "Ra'ina"﴾. He mentions here another of the ignorant practices of the Jews, and the intention is to forbid the Muslims from the like of it. The literal meaning of "راعِنا" (*ra'ina*) in the language is "ur'ana" and "lur'ak," because the reciprocal form (*mufa'alah*) is from two parties. So it is from "ra'aka Allah," meaning "ihfazna wa-lahfazka" (protect us and we will protect you) and "irqubna wa-larqubka" (watch over us and we will watch over you). It is also permissible that it be from "arina sam'ak," meaning "farigh sam'ak li-kalamina" (empty your hearing for our speech). Addressing him with this word involves coarseness, so He commanded the believers to choose from among the words the best of them and from among the meanings the most refined of them. Ibn Abbas said: The Muslims used to say to the Prophet ﷺ, "Ra'ina," as a request and a desire, from consideration (*al-muraa'ah*), meaning "turn to us." But in the language of the Jews this was an insult, meaning "hear, may you not hear." They seized upon it and said: "We used to curse him in secret, but now we curse him openly." So they would address the Prophet ﷺ with it and laugh among themselves. Sa'd ibn Mu'adh heard it, and he knew their language, so he said to the Jews: "The curse of Allah be upon you! If I hear it from any man of you saying it to the Prophet ﷺ, I will surely strike his neck." They said: "Do you not say it yourselves?" Then the verse was revealed, and they were forbidden from it, lest the Jews follow them in the wording while intending the corrupt meaning in it.

**The second issue:** In this verse there are two proofs. The first is the avoidance of ambiguous words which contain an allusion to disparagement and belittling. From this derives the understanding of slander (*qadhf*) by allusion, and that, according to us, requires the prescribed punishment (*hadd*), contrary to Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i and their companions, who said: an allusion may imply slander or other than slander, and the *hadd* is among the things that are dropped by doubt. The explanation of this will come, God willing, in "al-Nur" [[See vol. 12, p. 175.]].

The second proof is adherence to *sadd al-dhara'i'* (blocking the means) [[The *dhara'i'* (plural of *dhari'ah*) are, linguistically, the means and cause leading to a thing.]] and protecting them. This is the position of Malik and his companions, and of Ahmad ibn Hanbal in one narration from him. The Book and the Sunnah both indicate this principle. A *dhari'ah* is an expression for a matter that is not forbidden in itself, but from whose commission one fears falling into something forbidden.

As for the Book, there is this verse. The way to adduce it is that the Jews used to say that, and it was an insult in their language. When God knew this from them, He prohibited that expression, because it was a means to insult. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not revile those whom they invoke besides Allah, lest they revile Allah in enmity without knowledge﴾ [[See vol. 7, pp. 61 and 304.]], so He forbade reviling their gods for fear of their retaliating with the like of it. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And ask them about the town which was by the sea﴾ [[See vol. 7, pp. 61 and 304.]], to the end of the verse. He forbade them hunting on the Sabbath, and the fish would come to them on the Sabbath openly (*shurra'an*), that is, visibly. So they blocked them off on the Sabbath and took them on Sunday. The blocking was a means to hunting, so God transformed them into apes and swine. God mentioned this to us in the sense of warning against it. And His saying to Adam and Eve: ﴿And do not approach this tree﴾, which has already been mentioned [[See vol. 1, p. 304.]].

As for the Sunnah, there are many established and authentic hadiths. Among them is the hadith of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that Umm Habiba and Umm Salama, may Allah be pleased with them both, mentioned to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ a church they had seen in Abyssinia, in which there were images. [So they mentioned that] to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Those people, when a righteous man among them died, they built a mosque over his grave and made in it those images. Those are the worst of creation in the sight of Allah." Related by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

Our scholars said: Their earliest ones did this so that they might feel at ease by seeing those images and remember their righteous states, and so they would strive as they had striven and worship Allah, mighty and majestic, at their graves. Times passed for them in this way. Then there succeeded them successors who did not know their purposes, and Satan whispered to them that your fathers and grandfathers used to worship this image, so they worshipped it. The Prophet ﷺ warned against the like of this, emphasized the severe denunciation and threat against whoever does it, and blocked the means leading to it. He said: "The anger of Allah has intensified against a people who took the graves of their prophets and their righteous ones as mosques." And he said: "O Allah, do not make my grave an idol that is worshipped."

Muslim related from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "The lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear, and between them are doubtful matters. Whoever avoids doubtful matters has cleared himself regarding his religion and his honor, and whoever falls into doubtful matters has fallen into the unlawful, like a shepherd who grazes around the sanctuary, about to fall into it" [[This is in Sahih Muslim, Book of Sales, with some variation in its wording.]], to the end of the hadith. So he forbade advancing into doubtful matters for fear of falling into forbidden things, and that is blocking the means.

He ﷺ also said: "A servant does not attain to being among the God-fearing until he leaves what is not harmful to him, out of caution about what is harmful." And he ﷺ said: "Among the major sins is a man cursing his parents." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, does a man curse his parents?" He said: "Yes, he curses a man's father, so he curses his father, and he curses his mother, so he curses his mother." So he made exposing oneself to the cursing of fathers equivalent to cursing them.

He ﷺ also said: "When you deal in *'ina* [[The *'ina* is a type of sale in which the seller sells to the buyer on credit and then buys back the item for less than the price.]] and take the tails of cattle and are content with agriculture and abandon jihad, Allah will impose upon you a humiliation which He will not remove from you until you return to your religion." Abu Ubayd al-Harawi said: The *'ina* is that a man sells a commodity to a man for a known price up to a specified term, then buys it back from him for less than the price at which he sold it to him. He said: If the buyer, in the presence of the one seeking the *'ina*, buys a commodity from another for a known price and takes possession of it, then sells it to the one seeking the *'ina* for a higher price than he bought it, up to a specified term, and then the buyer sells it back to the original seller for cash at less than the price, this is also an *'ina*, and it is less severe than the first, and it is permitted according to some. It was named *'ina* because the cash comes to the one seeking the *'ina*, since *al-'ayn* is the present wealth, and the buyer only buys it in order to sell it for present cash that reaches him immediately.

Ibn Wahb related from Malik that the umm walad (mother of a child) of Zayd ibn al-Arqam told Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she had sold a slave to Zayd for eight hundred up to the time of the stipend, then bought him back from him for six hundred in cash. Aisha said: "What a bad sale you made, and what a bad purchase you made! Tell Zayd that he has nullified his jihad with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, unless he repents." Such a thing is not said by opinion, because the nullification of deeds cannot be known except through revelation, so it is established that it is traced back to the Prophet ﷺ.

Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Leave usury and suspicion (*al-riba wa-l-rayba*)." Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, forbade dirhams exchanged for dirhams between which there is *huraziyyah* [[So it is in A. In B: "jarirah", and in C "jarirah", and in H "jarizah". We have not found the correct reading in them.]].

I say: These are the proofs we have for blocking the means, and upon it the Malikis built the book of *al-ajal* (deferred terms) and other issues in sales and other matters. The Shafi'is do not have a book of *al-ajal*, because according to them those are different independent contracts. They said: The original state of things is based on outward appearances, not on suspicions. The Malikis made the commodity lawful in order to reach dirhams in excess of them, and this is exactly usury, so know it.

**The third issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do not say "Ra'ina"﴾ is a prohibition which requires prohibition, as has preceded. Al-Hasan read "رَاعِنَّا" with tanwin and said: meaning *hajran min al-qawl* (abusive speech), and it is a verbal noun (*masdar*) governed by "al-qawl," meaning "do not say *ru'unah*" (foolishness). Zirr ibn Hubaysh and al-A'mash read "رَاعُونَا" (*ra'una*). It is said of a protrusion from a mountain: *ra'n*, and the mountain is *a'ran*, and an army that is *a'ran* is scattered. Similarly a man is *a'ran*, meaning scattered in his arguments and his mind not gathered, from al-Nahhas. Ibn Faris said: "Ra'una al-rajulu yar'unu ra'nan fa-huwa a'ran," meaning foolish. The woman is *ra'na'*. Basra was named *al-Ra'na'* because it resembles a protrusion of a mountain. Ibn Duraid said this, and he recited for al-Farazdaq:

Were it not for Ibn Utba, Amr, and the hope in him,
Basra, the foolish one, would not have been a homeland for me.

**The fourth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And say, "Unzurna"﴾. They were commanded to address him with reverence. The meaning is: turn toward us and look upon us, so the particle of transitivity was dropped, as the poet said:

Manifest in beauty and loveliness, they gaze
as gazelles gaze at the arak tree.

meaning "at the arak tree." Mujahid said: The meaning is "fahhimna wa-bayyin lana" (make us understand and clarify for us). It was also said: The meaning is "intazirna wa-ta'anna bina" (wait for us and be patient with us). The poet said:

Indeed, if you two look upon me for a moment
of time, it will benefit me before Umm Jundub.

The apparent meaning is seeking a look of the eye combined with contemplation of the situation, and this is the meaning of "ra'ina." So the expression was changed for the believers, and the Jews' connection to it was removed. Al-A'mash and others read "أَنْظِرْنَا" (*anzirna*) with a cut alif and a kasra on the zay, meaning "akhkhirna wa-amhilna" (delay us and give us time) until we understand from you and receive from you. The poet said:

O Abu Hind, do not hasten against us,
and give us time, and we will inform you of the certainty.

**The fifth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And listen﴾. When He forbade and commanded, He, mighty and majestic, urged listening, which contains within it obedience. He also informed that for whoever opposes His command and thereby disbelieves, there is a painful punishment.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 105:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book, nor the polytheists, would not wish﴾, i.e., would not desire (mā yawaddu, "would not wish"), and this has already been mentioned [[See p. 34 of this part.]]. "Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book" and "the polytheists" are conjoined (ma'tuf) to "ahl" (the people). It is also permissible to read "wa-lā al-mushrikūn" (nominative), conjoining it to "alladhina" (those who), as said by al-Nahhas.

"That any good should be sent down upon you" – "min" (of) here is extra (za'idah), and "khayr" (good) is the subject of the passive verb (ism mā lam yusamma fā'iluh). And "an" (that) is in the accusative position, meaning "bi-an yunazzal" (that it be sent down).

"And Allah specially chooses for His mercy whom He wills" – 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "yakhtaṣṣu bi-raḥmatihi" means "by His prophethood": He specialised Muhammad (ﷺ) with it. Some people said: the mercy is the Qur'an. It has also been said: the mercy in this verse is general, encompassing all the kinds of mercy that Allah has bestowed on His servants, past and present. It is said: "raḥima yarḥamu" means "he softened" (idha raqqa). "Al-Ruḥm," "al-marḥamah," and "al-raḥmah" have the same meaning, as said by Ibn Faris. Allah's mercy to His servants is His bestowing favours upon them and His pardoning them.

"And Allah is the Possessor of Great Bounty" – "dhū" here means "possessor" (ṣāḥib).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 106 (part 1 of 3):

There are fifteen issues in this verse. The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Whatever sign We abrogate or cause to be forgotten﴾. "Nunsiha" is conjoined to "nansakh," and the yā' is dropped for the jussive. Whoever reads "nansa'ha" drops the damma from the hamza for the jussive, and its meaning will come. "Na'ti" is the answer of the conditional, and this is a great verse concerning the rulings. Its cause was that when the Jews envied the Muslims over facing the Ka'bah in prayer, and they attacked Islam on account of that, they said: "Muhammad orders his companions to do something and then forbids them from it. This Qur'an is only from himself, and for this reason some of it contradicts other parts." So God revealed: ﴿And when We substitute a verse in place of another verse﴾ [[See vol. 10, p. 176.]] and He revealed: ﴿Whatever sign We abrogate...﴾.

The second: Knowledge of this topic is vital and its benefit is great. The scholars cannot do without knowing it, and none denies it except the ignorant fools, because of the rulings that arise from it in new cases and because of knowing what is lawful and what is unlawful. Abu al-Bakhtari narrated: 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, entered the mosque and found a man frightening the people. He said: "What is this?" They said: "A man who admonishes the people." He said: "He is not a man who admonishes the people! Rather, he is one who says, 'I am so-and-so, son of so-and-so, so recognise me.'" So he sent for him and said: "Do you know the abrogating from the abrogated?" He said: "No." He said: "Then leave our mosque and do not admonish in it." In another narration: "Do you know the abrogating and the abrogated?" He said: "No." He said: "You are ruined and you have ruined others!" The like of this is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

The third: Naskh in the speech of the Arabs has two senses. The first is transfer (naql), like copying a book from another. In this sense the whole Qur'an is abrogated, meaning from the Preserved Tablet and its sending down to the House of Honour in the lowest heaven, and this has no bearing on this verse. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We used to have copied what you used to do﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 175.]], meaning We commanded its copying and recording. The second is annulment and removal, and this is what is meant here. It is divided in the language into two kinds. One: the annulling and removal of a thing and the establishing of another in its place, as in "the sun abrogated (nasakhat) the shade" when it removes it and takes its place. This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whatever sign We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better than it or similar to it﴾. In the authentic Sahih of Muslim: "Prophethood never existed except that it was transferred (tanasakhat)," meaning it changed from one state to another, referring to the affairs of the community. Ibn Faris said: Naskh is the copying of a writing; and naskh is that you remove a matter that was previously acted upon and replace it with another new matter, as a verse is revealed with a ruling and then abrogated by another. Everything that succeeds something else has abrogated it; it is said: the sun abrogated the shade, and grey hair abrogated youth. And the heirs "tanasakhu" when heirs die one after another while the principal inheritance remains undivided; likewise is the succession of ages and generations. The second: removing a thing without another standing in its place, as in the saying: "the wind abrogated the trace." From this meaning is His saying: ﴿Then Allah abolishes what Satan throws in﴾ [[See vol. 12, p. 79.]], meaning He removes it so that it is not recited and is not preserved in the Mushaf in its place.

Abu 'Ubayd claimed that this second kind of abrogation (naskh) occurred when a surah was sent down to the Prophet (ﷺ), then lifted, so that it was neither recited nor written down. I say: among the evidence for this is what is reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b and 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with them both, that Surat al-Ahzab was as long as Surat al-Baqara, as will be explained there in detail [[see vol. 14, p. 113.]], God willing.

Something that supports this is what Abu Bakr al-Anbari reported: my father narrated to us, Nasr ibn Dawud narrated to us, Abu 'Ubayd narrated to us, 'Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, from al-Layth, from Yunus and 'Uqayl, from Ibn Shihab, who said: Abu Umama ibn Sahl ibn Hunayf told me, in the assembly of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, that a man got up at night to recite a surah of the Qur'an but could not recall any of it. Another man got up and could not recall any of it, and a third got up and could not recall any of it either. In the morning they went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). One of them said: "O Messenger of Allah, I got up last night to recite a surah of the Qur'an and I could not recall any of it." Then the other said: "And I, by Allah, O Messenger of Allah, was the same." Then the third said: "And I, by Allah, O Messenger of Allah, was the same." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "It is among what Allah abrogated last night." In one of the narrations: Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib was listening to what Abu Umama was relating, and he did not deny it.

Fourth: Some groups among those who claim to belong to Islam, the later ones, have denied the permissibility of this, but they are refuted by the consensus of the earlier scholars (salaf) that it occurred in the Shari'ah. Some groups of the Jews have also denied it, and they are refuted by what is in their Torah, according to their claim, that Allah said to Noah (peace be upon him) when he came out of the ark: "I have made every animal lawful food for you and your offspring, and I have permitted this to you as I permitted the plants of the herbage, except blood, which you must not eat." Then He forbade many animals to Moses and the Children of Israel. And (they are refuted) by the fact that Adam (peace be upon him) used to marry a brother to a sister, and Allah forbade that to Moses (peace be upon him) and to others. And (they are refuted) by the fact that Abraham the Friend (peace be upon him) was commanded to slaughter his son, and then he was told: "Do not slaughter him." And by the fact that Moses commanded the Children of Israel to kill those among them who worshipped the calf, and then commanded them to lift the sword from them. And by the fact that his prophethood was not a matter of worship before his mission, and then he was made to worship through it afterwards, and so on.

This is not a matter of bada' (a change of mind in God's knowledge). Rather, it is the transfer of servants from one form of worship to another and from one ruling to another, for some benefit, to manifest His wisdom and the perfection of His dominion. There is no disagreement among rational people that the laws of the prophets were intended for the benefit of creation, both religious and worldly. Bada' would only be necessary if He did not know the outcomes of affairs. As for the One who knows that, His commands change according to the changing of benefits, like a physician who considers the condition of the patient. He has taken this into account in His creation by His will and His determination, there is no god but Him. So His address changes, while His knowledge and His will do not change, for that is impossible with respect to God, the Exalted.

The Jews made abrogation and bada' one and the same thing, and for this reason they denied it, and so they went astray. Al-Nahhas said: The difference between abrogation and bada' is that abrogation is the transfer of worship from one thing that was permitted to something that is forbidden, or from something that was forbidden to something permitted. As for bada', it is abandoning what was resolved upon, like your saying: "Go to so-and-so today," then you say: "Do not go to him," so the change from the first statement becomes apparent to you. This happens to human beings because of their deficiency. Likewise, if you say: "Plant such-and-such this year," then you say: "Do not do it," that is bada'.

Fifth: Know that the true abrogator is Allah, the Exalted, and the legal address (al-khitab al-shar'i) is called an abrogator figuratively, since abrogation occurs through it. Similarly, figuratively, the thing ruled upon may be called an abrogator, so it is said: "The fasting of Ramadan abrogates the fasting of 'Ashura'." The abrogated (mansukh) is what is removed, and that from which it is abrogated is the one obligated to the worship that was removed, and he is the mukallaf (a person bound by the law).

Sixth: The expressions of our scholars differ in defining the abrogator (nasikh). What the skilled scholars among the People of the Sunnah hold is that it is the removal of a ruling that has been established in the Shari'ah by a later-revealed address that comes after an interval. This is how al-Qadi 'Abd al-Wahhab and al-Qadi Abu Bakr defined it, and they added: "Were it not for it, the earlier ruling would have remained established." Thus they preserved the linguistic meaning of naskh, which means lifting and removal, and guarded against the rational ruling. They mentioned "address" so that it would include all modes of indication: explicit text, apparent meaning, implication and others, and to exclude analogy (qiyas) and consensus (ijma'), since abrogation is not conceivable in them or through them. They restricted it to "after an interval," because if it were connected to the ruling, it would be an explanation of the limit of the ruling, not an abrogator, or it would be the end of the speech lifting its beginning, like your saying: "Stand up, do not stand."

Seventh: According to our scholars, the People of the Sunnah, the abrogated is the ruling itself, not its like. This is in contrast to the Mu'tazila, who say that it is the address indicating that the like of the ruling established for what will come, by the earlier text, is removed. What led them to this was their doctrine that commands are willed (murada), and that goodness is an essential attribute of the good thing, and that what God wills is good. Our scholars have refuted this in their books.

Eighth: Our scholars differed on whether abrogation enters reports (akhbar). The majority hold that abrogation is specific to commands and prohibitions, and that a report does not admit abrogation, because lying about Allah, the Exalted, is impossible. It was also said that if a report includes a legal ruling, its abrogation is permissible, as in His saying: "And from the fruits of the palm trees and the grapes you take from them an intoxicant (sakar) and good provision." The discussion of this will come there, God willing [[see vol. 10, p. 127.]].

Ninth: Specification (takhsis) of the general (al-'umum) gives the impression that it has been abrogated, but it is not. This is because the specified item was never included in the generality at all. If it were established that the generality included something and then that thing was removed from the generality, it would be abrogation, not specification. Earlier scholars use the term "abrogation" for specification loosely and figuratively.

Tenth: Know that there may come in the Shari'ah reports whose apparent meaning is absoluteness and comprehensiveness, and then a restriction of them comes in another place, so that absoluteness is lifted. An example is His saying: "And when My servants ask you about Me, I am near; I answer the call of the caller when he calls upon Me" [[p. 308 of this volume.]]. The apparent meaning of this ruling is a report about the answering of every caller in every circumstance, but there has come what restricts it in another place, such as His saying: "So He will remove what you call upon Him for, if He wills" [[vol. 6, p. 423.]]. Someone who has no insight may think that this is a matter of abrogation in reports, but it is not so. Rather, it is a matter of absoluteness and restriction. More explanation of this issue will come in its place, God willing.

Eleventh: Our scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, said: It is permissible to abrogate the heavier with the lighter, like the abrogation of the requirement for ten to stand firm against the enemy in battle by the requirement to stand firm against two [[i.e., Allah abrogated the obligation for one to stand against ten in jihad by requiring him to stand against two.]]. It is also permissible to abrogate the lighter with the heavier, like the abrogation of the day of 'Ashura' and the counted days by Ramadan, as will be explained in the verse of fasting [[p. 275 of this volume.]]. A thing may be abrogated by its like in heaviness or lightness, like the qibla (direction of prayer). A thing may be abrogated without a replacement, like the charity before private consultation (sadaqat al-najwa). The Qur'an may be abrogated by the Qur'an, and the Sunnah by the expression (of the Qur'an), and by this expression is meant the mutawatir report, which is decisive. The report of a single narrator (khabar al-wahid) may be abrogated by the report of a single narrator. The skilled imams hold that the Qur'an may be abrogated by the Sunnah, and this exists in His (peace be upon him) saying: "There is no bequest to an heir." This is the apparent position of the school of Malik. Al-Shafi'i and Abu al-Faraj al-Maliki rejected this. The first view is more sound, on the evidence that all of it is the ruling of Allah, the Exalted, and from Him, even if the names differ. Also, the flogging is dropped for the married adulterer who is stoned, and nothing removes it except the Sunnah, the act of the Prophet (ﷺ). This is clear. The skilled scholars also agree that the Sunnah may be abrogated by the Qur'an, and this exists in the qibla, for facing Syria in prayer was not in the Book of Allah, the Exalted. And in His saying: "Do not return them to the disbelievers" [[see vol. 18, p. 63.]], for their return was by the treaty of the Prophet (ﷺ) with the Quraysh.

The skilled scholars agree that the Qur'an may rationally be abrogated by a single-narrator report, but they disputed whether this has occurred in the Shari'ah. Abu al-Ma'ali and others held that it occurred in the incident of the Qubaa mosque, as will be explained [[vol. 8, p. 259.]], but others rejected this. It is not valid to abrogate a text by analogy, for one of the conditions of analogy is that it not contradict a text. All of this concerns the lifetime of the Prophet (ﷺ). As for after his death, once the Shari'ah was firmly established, the community agreed that there is no abrogation. For this reason consensus neither abrogates nor is abrogated, since it is formed after the cessation of revelation. So when we find a consensus that contradicts a text, we know that the consensus was based on an abrogating text that we do not know, and that this contradicting text is no longer acted upon, and that its ruling was abrogated while its wording remained as a Sunnah to be recited and transmitted, just as the verse about the waiting period of one year [[he means His saying: "a provision until the year..." which has had its ruling abrogated while its recitation remains. See vol. 3, p. 226.]] remains in the Qur'an and is recited. Reflect on this, for it is precious. This is a case of abrogation of the ruling without the recitation. Similar to it is the charity before private consultation. The recitation may be abrogated without the ruling, as in the verse of stoning. The recitation and the ruling may both be abrogated together, and of this is the saying of al-Siddiq (Abu Bakr), may Allah be pleased with him: "We used to recite: 'Do not turn away from your fathers, for that is disbelief.'" Similar examples are many. What the skilled scholars hold is that whoever has not received the abrogating text is bound by the first ruling, as will be explained in the discussion of the change of the qibla. The skilled scholars agree on the permissibility of abrogating a ruling before it has been carried out, and this exists in the story of the one to be sacrificed, and in the obligation of fifty prayers before performing them, five of which were reduced, as will be explained in "al-Isra'" [[vol. 10, p. 210.]] and "al-Saffat" [[vol. 15, p. 107.]], God willing.

Twelfth: There are ways to know the abrogator. Among them: that the wording contains something that indicates it, such as His (peace be upon him) saying: "I had forbidden you to visit graves, so visit them; and I had forbidden you from drinks except in containers..."

al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 2, verse 106 (part 3 of 3):

...the example of the leather vessel: "drink in every vessel, but do not drink an intoxicant" (fa-ashrabu fi kulli wi'a'in ghayra an la tashrabu muskiran), and similar ones. Among the ways of knowing abrogation (naskh) is that the narrator mentions the date, such as saying: "I heard it in the year of the Trench (al-Khandaq)," when the abrogated ruling was already known before that. Or he says: "The ruling of such-and-such has been abrogated by such-and-such." Another way is that the community (ummah) agrees that a ruling is abrogated and that its abrogating text came earlier. This topic is expounded in the books of usul al-fiqh (legal theory). We have drawn attention to what is in it for one who seeks sufficiency, and God is the One who grants success in guidance.

The thirteenth issue: The majority (al-Jumhur) read "ma nansakh" with a fatha on the nun, from nasakha, and this is the apparent and common usage, meaning: whatever ruling of a verse we abrogate while leaving its recitation, as has passed. It is possible that the meaning is: whatever ruling of a verse and its recitation we abrogate, as we have mentioned. Ibn 'Amir read "nunsikh" with a damma on the nun, from ansakhtu al-kitab, meaning "I found it abrogated." Abu Hatim said: this is an error. Al-Farisi Abu 'Ali said: it is not a valid usage, because it is not said that nasakha and ansakha have the same meaning, unless the meaning is "what we find to be abrogated," just as you say: "ahmadtu al-rajul" and "abkhaltuhu," meaning "I found him praiseworthy" and "I found him stingy." Abu 'Ali said: we do not find it abrogated except by abrogating it, so the two readings agree in meaning though they differ in wording. It was also said: "ma nansakh" means "whatever we do not make its abrogation for you"; it is said: "nasakhtu al-kitab" when I copied it, and "untasakhtuhu ghayri" when you make its copying for someone else. Makki said: it is not permissible that the hamza be causative (lil-ta'addi), because the meaning would change to "whatever verse We abrogate for you, O Muhammad," and his causing it to be abrogated (insakhuhu iyyaha) would be sending it down to him, so the meaning would become "whatever We send down to you of a verse, or cause you to forget, We bring one better than it or like it," which implies that every verse revealed is followed by a better one, so the whole Qur'an would be abrogated, and this is impossible, since only a small part of the Qur'an has been abrogated. Since it is impossible that af'ala and fa'ala have the same meaning, as it is not heard, and it is impossible that the hamza be causative because the meaning would be corrupted, no possibility remains except that it is of the type of "ahmadtuhu" and "abkhaltuhu," when I find him praiseworthy or stingy.

The fourteenth issue: His saying, exalted is He, "aw nunsiha" (or cause it to be forgotten). Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read it with a fatha on the nun, the sin and the hamza, and by this read 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', Mujahid, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, al-Nakha'i and Ibn Muhaysin, from al-ta'khir (delay), meaning: we delay the abrogation of its wording, that is, we leave it in the last part of the Mother of the Book (umm al-kitab) [in one manuscript, "in Umm al-Kitab"; in another, "then it is not abrogated"], so it is not abrogated. This is the saying of 'Ata'. Others besides 'Ata' said: the meaning of "aw nansa'ha" is: we postpone it from abrogation until a known time, from the expression "nasa'tu hadha al-amr" when you postpone it, and from this their saying: "I sold it on credit (nasa')" when you delay it. Ibn Faris said: they say: "God postponed (nasa'a) your term," and "God lengthened (ansa'a) your term." The people "intansa'a" when they delayed and went far, and "nasa'tuhum" means I delayed them. So the meaning is: we delay its sending down or its abrogation, as we have mentioned. It was also said: we remove it from you so that it is neither recited nor mentioned. The rest read "nunsiha" with a damma on the nun, from forgetting in the sense of leaving (al-tark), meaning we leave it, so we do not replace it nor abrogate it; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi, and from it is His saying, exalted is He: "They forgot God, so He forgot them" (Q. 9:67), meaning they abandoned His worship, so He abandoned them to punishment. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose this reading. Abu 'Ubayd said: I heard Abu Nu'aym al-Qari say: "I recited to the Prophet (ﷺ) in a dream with the reading of Abu 'Amr, and he did not change for me except two letters. I said: I recited to him 'arina' (Q. 2:128), and he said: 'arina; and Abu 'Ubayd said: I think the other letter was 'aw nansa'ha,' and he said: 'aw nunsiha.'" Al-Azhari related "nunsiha" as: we command its abandonment; it is said: "ansaytuhu al-shay'" meaning I commanded him to leave it, and "nasiytuhu" meaning I left it. The poet said:

"Indeed, upon me is a duty (uqbah) that I will discharge... I am not forgetting it, nor causing it to be forgotten."

That is, nor do I command its abandonment. Al-Zajjaj said: the reading with a damma on the nun does not admit the meaning of leaving, since it is not said "ansa" meaning "tarak" (left); and what 'Ali ibn Abi Talha related from Ibn 'Abbas, "aw nunsiha," he said: "we leave it, we do not replace it," is not sound; perhaps Ibn 'Abbas said "we leave it" and was not precise. What most of the people of language and reasoning hold is that the meaning of "aw nunsiha" is: "We permit you to leave it," from nasiya meaning he left, then it is made transitive. Abu 'Ali and others said: this is valid, since it means "We make you leave it." It was also said: it is from forgetting in its original sense, which is the absence of remembrance, meaning "or We cause you to forget it, O Muhammad, so you do not recall it"; it was transitivized by the hamza, so the verb takes two objects: the Prophet and the pronoun, but the object "the Prophet" is elided.

The fifteenth issue: His saying, exalted is He: "We bring one better than it or like it." The word "bi-khayr" here is a comparative adjective, and the meaning is: with what is more beneficial for you, O people, in the immediate if the abrogating verse is lighter, in the later if it is heavier, and with its like if it is equal. Malik said: [the text here is corrupt]... abrogated. It was also said: "akhyar" is not meant as a comparative, because the speech of God does not vary in excellence; it is rather like His saying: "Whoever comes with a good deed, for him is better than it" (Q. 27:89), meaning: for him from it is good, that is benefit and reward, not "khayr" in the sense of "more excellent." The first view is supported by His saying: "or like it."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 107:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do you not know﴾ is in the jussive mood because of "lam" (lam, the negative particle that jazms the verb). The interrogative particles do not change the governing work of the governing word. "Anna" is vowelled with a fatha because it is in the position of an accusative. "To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth": that is, by bringing into existence and by origination, and the sovereignty and authority, and the executing of command and will. "Mulk" is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is "Allah," and the whole clause is the predicate of "anna."

The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and what is meant is his community, because of His saying: ﴿And you have no protector or helper besides Allah.﴾ It has also been said: the meaning is, say to them, O Muhammad: "Do you not know that for Allah is the sovereignty of the heavens and the earth, and that you have no protector besides Allah?" From "walayt amr fulan" (I took charge of the affair of so-and-so), meaning I undertook it; and from this comes "waliy al-'ahd" (the heir apparent), meaning the one entrusted with what he was charged with of the affairs of the Muslims. The meaning of "min duni Allah" is "other than Allah" and "after Allah," as Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said:

O soul, you have no shield beside Allah,
and nothing that remains against the vicissitudes of time.

The reading of the majority is "wa la nasiril" with a kasra, as a conjunction (ataf) upon "waliyyin." It is permissible to read "wa la nasirun" with a damma, as a conjunction upon the position (mahal) of the noun, because the meaning is: you have no protector besides Allah and no helper.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 108:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or do you wish﴾. This "am" is the disjunctive ("am munqati'a") which carries the meaning of "bal" (rather), meaning: rather, do you wish... The meaning of the speech is rebuke (tawbikh). "An tas'alu" (that you ask) is in a place of accusative (nasb) governed by "turidun" (you wish). "Kama su'ila" (as Musa was asked): the kaf is in the place of accusative as a descriptive qualifier (na't) of a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: a question like the question. "Musa" is in the place of nominative (raf') as the substitute for the unnamed subject (naib al-fa'il). "Min qabl" (before): their asking him to show them God openly (jahrah); and they asked Muhammad to bring God and the angels as a group (qabilan). From Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid: they asked that he make al-Safa into gold for them.

al-Hasan recited "kama sil" (as it was asked), and this is according to the dialect of one who says "salt, as'alu" (I asked). It is also possible that it is on the basis of replacing the hamzah with a silent ya', contrary to analogy, so the sin before it became kasra. Al-Nahhas said: the replacement of the hamzah is remote.

And al-sawa' of everything: its middle. This was said by Abu 'Ubaydah Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna, and from it is His saying: "fi sawa' al-jahim" (in the midst of the Hellfire). 'Isa ibn 'Umar related that he said: "I kept writing until my middle (sawa'i) was cut off," and he recited the verse of Hassan lamenting the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ):

Woe to the companions of the Prophet and his kin... after his concealment in the midst of the grave (sawa' al-mulhad).

It was also said: al-sawa' is the aim (al-qasd), from al-Farra', meaning: he went astray from the aim of the path and its direction, that is, the path of obedience to Allah, mighty and majestic. Also from Ibn 'Abbas that the occasion of revelation of this verse was that Rafi' ibn Khuzaymah and Wahb ibn Zayd said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Bring us a Book from heaven that we may read it, and make rivers gush forth for us so that we may follow you."

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 2, verses 109–110:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Many of the People of the Book wish that they could turn you back from your faith to disbelief, out of envy from themselves, after the truth has become clear to them.﴾ On this verse there are two issues.

The first: *wadda* means "wished" (see page 34 of this part). *Kuffaran* (disbelievers) is the second object of *yaruddunakum* (they turn you back). Regarding *min 'indi anfusihim* (out of envy from themselves), it has been said that it is connected to *wadda*. It has also been said that it is connected to *hasadan* (envy), in which case the pause falls on *kuffaran*, and *hasadan* is an object of purpose, meaning: they wished that, because of envy. Or it is a verbal noun that indicates the action implied by what precedes it. The meaning of *min 'indi anfusihim* is "from their own initiative, without finding it in a Book, and without being commanded to do it." The word *hasad* (envy) implies this. So the phrase *min 'indi anfusihim* comes as emphasis and as a binding statement, as Allah says: ﴿They say with their mouths﴾ (see vol. 4, p. 267), ﴿they write the Book with their own hands﴾, and ﴿nor a bird that flies with its two wings﴾ (vol. 6, p. 419). This verse concerns the Jews.

The second: envy is of two kinds, blameworthy and praiseworthy. The blameworthy kind is that you wish for the removal of Allah's blessing from your Muslim brother, whether or not you also wish that it would come to you. This is the kind that Allah condemned in His Book when He said: ﴿Or do they envy people for what Allah has given them of His bounty?﴾ (vol. 5, p. 251). It is blameworthy because it implies a disparagement of the Truth (Allah, glorified is He), and that He bestowed favour upon one who does not deserve it. As for the praiseworthy kind, it is what has come in the authentic hadith, where the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no envy except in two cases: a man whom Allah has given the Qur'an, and he stands with it in the hours of the night and the hours of the day; and a man whom Allah has given wealth, and he spends it in the hours of the night and the hours of the day." This kind of envy means *ghibtah* (wholesome desire to match another's good). Al-Bukhari also titled a chapter with it: "The chapter on *al-ightibat* (wholesome desire) in knowledge and wisdom." Its reality is that you wish to have what your Muslim brother has of good and blessing, while his good does not leave him. It may also be called *munafasah* (healthy competition), and from it is Allah's saying: ﴿For this let those who compete, compete﴾ (vol. 19, p. 264).

*Min ba'di ma tabayyana lahumu al-haqq* (after the truth has become clear to them): that is, after the truth became clear to them as truth, namely Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Qur'an that he brought.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So pardon and overlook﴾. On this verse there are two issues.

The first: Allah's saying *fa'fu* (pardon). The original form is *a'fuwu*. The damma was dropped because it is heavy, then the waw was dropped because two unvocalised letters met. *Al-'afw* is leaving off blame for a sin. *Al-safh* is removing its trace from the soul. One says *safahtu 'an fulan* (I overlooked so-and-so) when one turns away from his sin, and *darabtu 'anhu safhan* (I turned away from him entirely) when one turns away from him and leaves him, and from it is Allah's saying: ﴿Shall We withdraw the Reminder from you altogether?﴾ (vol. 16, p. 62).

The second: this verse is abrogated (*mansukhah*, by *naskh*, the abrogation of one ruling by a later one) by His saying: ﴿Fight those who do not believe﴾ until His saying ﴿and they are humbled﴾ (vol. 8, p. 109), as reported from Ibn 'Abbas. It has also been said that its abrogating verse is ﴿Then kill the polytheists﴾ (vol. 8, p. 72). Abu 'Ubaydah said: every verse in which there is a leaving off of fighting is Meccan and abrogated by fighting. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: his ruling that this verse is Meccan is weak, because the opposition of the Jews occurred only in Medina. I say: this is the correct view. Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated from Usamah ibn Zayd that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rode a donkey with a Fadakiyyah saddle-cloth (*fadakiyyah*: attributed to Fadak, a village in the Hijaz two days' journey from Medina), and Usamah was behind him, visiting Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah in the clan of Banu al-Harith ibn al-Khazraj before the Battle of Badr. They passed by a gathering in which was 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul (*Salul* being the name of his mother), and that was before 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy had become Muslim. In the gathering were a mixture of Muslims, polytheists, idol-worshippers and Jews, and among the Muslims was 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah. When the dust (*'ajajah*) of the beast enveloped the gathering, Ibn Ubayy covered his nose with his garment and said: "Do not raise dust over us!" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) greeted them, then stopped and dismounted. He called them to Allah and recited the Qur'an to them. 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul said to him: "O man, there is nothing finer than what you say, if it is true! So do not harm us with it in our gatherings. Return to your abode, and whoever comes to you, relate it to him." 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah, come to us in our gatherings, for we love that." The polytheists, Muslims and Jews began to rage at one another until they nearly came to blows. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) kept calming them until they settled down. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mounted his beast and went until he entered upon Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Sa'd, did you not hear what Abu Hubab (meaning 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy) said? He said such-and-such." Sa'd said: "O Messenger of Allah, may my father and mother be your ransom! Pardon him and overlook. By Him who sent down the Book to you with truth, Allah has brought you the truth that He sent down to you. The people of this town (*al-Buhayrah*, the diminutive of *al-Bahrah*, the city of the Messenger, peace be upon him; in another narration it is *Mukayra*) had agreed to crown him and wrap him with a turban, but when Allah turned that away by the truth He gave you, he choked with it, and that is the cause of what you saw." So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) pardoned him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions used to pardon the polytheists and the People of the Book as Allah had commanded them, and endure harm patiently. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿You will surely hear much hurt from those who were given the Book before you and from those who associate others with Allah﴾ (vol. 4, p. 303), and He said: ﴿Many of the People of the Book wish...﴾. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would interpret the pardon towards them in the way Allah had commanded him, until He permitted him to deal with them. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) fought at Badr, Allah destroyed by him those of the chiefs of the disbelievers and the lords of Quraysh whom He destroyed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions returned victorious and laden with spoils, with prisoners from the chiefs of the disbelievers and the lords of Quraysh with them. 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul and those with him among the polytheists and idol-worshippers said: "This affair has been set on its course" (*ay zahara wajhuhu*, that its face has become manifest). So they pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to Islam, and they embraced Islam.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿until Allah brings His command﴾, meaning the killing of the Banu Qurayzah and the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir. ﴿Indeed Allah is Powerful over all things. And establish prayer and give zakat﴾ has already been discussed (see vol. 1, pp. 164 and following, 224, 343 and following, second edition). Praise be to Allah, the Exalted.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And whatever good you send forth for yourselves, you will find it with Allah﴾. It has come in a hadith: "When the servant dies, the people say what he left behind, and the angels say what he sent forward." Al-Bukhari and al-Nasa'i narrated from 'Abdullah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Which of you loves the wealth of his heir more than his own wealth?" They said: "O Messenger of Allah, there is none of us but that his own wealth is dearer to him than the wealth of his heir." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "None of you is there but that the wealth of his heir is dearer to him than his own wealth. Your wealth is what you have sent forward, and the wealth of your heir is what you have left behind." This is the wording of al-Nasa'i. The wording of al-Bukhari is: 'Abdullah said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Which of you loves the wealth of his heir more than his own wealth?" They said: "O Messenger of Allah, none of us is there but that his own wealth is dearer to him," and he said: "His wealth is what he sent forward, and the wealth of his heir is what he left behind."

It has also come from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he passed by Baqi' al-Gharqad (the cemetery of the people of Medina) and said: "Peace be upon you, people of the graves. The news from us is that your wives have remarried, your houses have been inhabited, and your wealth has been divided." A voice answered him: "O son of al-Khattab, the news from us is that what we sent forward we found, what we spent we have gained, and what we left behind we have lost."

The best of what has been said is the verse of the poet:

Prepare for yourself righteous deeds before your death,
and act, for there is no way back from the grave.

Another said:

Prepare for yourself a hoped-for repentance
before death and before the tongue is stilled.

Another said:

Your mother bore you weeping
while the people around you laughed with joy.
So act for a day on which, when they weep,
you will be laughing and joyful on the day of your death.

Another said:

Race towards good and hasten to it,
for what is behind you is only what you know.
Send forward good, for every person
will arrive at what he sent forward.

And better than all of this is the saying of Abu al-'Atahiyah:

Provide for yourself with your wealth during your life,
for what remains after you is either a reformer or a corrupter.
If you leave it to a corrupter, he will not leave it intact,
and the one of righteousness, even if little, will grow.
If you can, be an heir to yourself,
for the one who leaves an inheritance for his own soul is rightly guided.

﴿Indeed Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾ (see page 35 of this part).

'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul said to him: "O man, there is nothing finer than what you say, if it is true! So do not harm us with it in our gatherings. Return to your abode, and whoever comes to you, relate it to him." 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah, come to us in our gatherings, for we love that." The polytheists, Muslims and Jews began to rage at one another until they nearly came to blows. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) kept calming them until they settled down. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mounted his beast and went until he entered upon Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Sa'd, did you not hear what Abu Hubab (meaning 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy) said? He said such-and-such." Sa'd said: "O Messenger of Allah, may my father and mother be your ransom! Pardon him and overlook. By Him who sent down the Book to you with truth, Allah has brought you the truth that He sent down to you. The people of this town (*al-Buhayrah*, the diminutive of *al-Bahrah*, the city of the Messenger, peace be upon him; in another narration it is *Mukayra*) had agreed to crown him and wrap him with a turban, but when Allah turned that away by the truth He gave you, he choked with it, and that is the cause of what you saw." So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) pardoned him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions used to pardon the polytheists and the People of the Book as Allah had commanded them, and endure harm patiently. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿You will surely hear much hurt from those who were given the Book before you and from those who associate others with Allah﴾ (vol. 4, p. 303), and He said: ﴿Many of the People of the Book wish...﴾. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would interpret the pardon towards them in the way Allah had commanded him, until He permitted him to deal with them. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) fought at Badr, Allah destroyed by him those of the chiefs of the disbelievers and the lords of Quraysh whom He destroyed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions returned victorious and laden with spoils, with prisoners from the chiefs of the disbelievers and the lords of Quraysh with them. 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul and those with him among the polytheists and idol-worshippers said: "This affair has been set on its course" (*ay zahara wajhuhu*, that its face has become manifest). So they pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to Islam, and they embraced Islam.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿until Allah brings His command﴾, meaning the killing of the Banu Qurayzah and the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir. ﴿Indeed Allah is Powerful over all things. And establish prayer and give zakat﴾ has already been discussed (see vol. 1, pp. 164 and following, 224, 343 and following, second edition). Praise be to Allah, the Exalted.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And whatever good you send forth for yourselves, you will find it with Allah﴾. It has come in a hadith: "When the servant dies, the people say what he left behind, and the angels say what he sent forward." Al-Bukhari and al-Nasa'i narrated from 'Abdullah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Which of you loves the wealth of his heir more than his own wealth?" They said: "O Messenger of Allah, there is none of us but that his own wealth is dearer to him than the wealth of his heir." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "None of you is there but that the wealth of his heir is dearer to him than his own wealth. Your wealth is what you have sent forward, and the wealth of your heir is what you have left behind." This is the wording of al-Nasa'i. The wording of al-Bukhari is: 'Abdullah said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Which of you loves the wealth of his heir more than his own wealth?" They said: "O Messenger of Allah, none of us is there but that his own wealth is dearer to him," and he said: "His wealth is what he sent forward, and the wealth of his heir is what he left behind."

It has also come from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he passed by Baqi' al-Gharqad (the cemetery of the people of Medina) and said: "Peace be upon you, people of the graves. The news from us is that your wives have remarried, your houses have been inhabited, and your wealth has been divided." A voice answered him: "O son of al-Khattab, the news from us is that what we sent forward we found, what we spent we have gained, and what we left behind we have lost."

The best of what has been said is the verse of the poet:

Prepare for yourself righteous deeds before your death,
and act, for there is no way back from the grave.

Another said:

Prepare for yourself a hoped-for repentance
before death and before the tongue is stilled.

Another said:

Your mother bore you weeping
while the people around you laughed with joy.
So act for a day on which, when they weep,
you will be laughing and joyful on the day of your death.

Another said:

Race towards good and hasten to it,
for what is behind you is only what you know.
Send forward good, for every person
will arrive at what he sent forward.

And better than all of this is the saying of Abu al-'Atahiyah:

Provide for yourself with your wealth during your life,
for what remains after you is either a reformer or a corrupter.
If you leave it to a corrupter, he will not leave it intact,
and the one of righteousness, even if little, will grow.
If you can, be an heir to yourself,
for the one who leaves an inheritance for his own soul is rightly guided.

﴿Indeed Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾ (see page 35 of this part).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 111–112:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say: None will enter Paradise unless he be a Jew or a Christian.﴾ The meaning: The Jews said, "None will enter Paradise unless he is a Jew," and the Christians said, "None will enter Paradise unless he is a Christian." Al-Farra' permitted that "hudan" (Jews) could mean "yahudiyyan" (Jews), with the extra letter dropped, and that it could be the plural of "ha'id" (one who repents). Al-Akhfash Sa'id said: "illa man kana" (unless he who was): he made "kana" singular according to the wording of "man," and then said "hudan" in the plural, because the meaning of "man" is plural. It is also permissible to read "tilka amaniyyuhum" (these are their wishful thinkings), and the discussion of this has already passed [[See the second issue, p. 5 of this part.]], and praise be to God.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Bring your proof, if you are truthful.﴾ The original form of "hatu" (bring) is "hatiu". The damma was dropped because of its heaviness, then the yaʼ was dropped because of the meeting of two sukun. For the masculine singular one says "hat" (like "ram"), and for the feminine "hati" (like "rami"). "Al-burhan" (proof) is the evidence that produces certainty, and its plural is "baraheen," like "qurban" and "qarabin," and "sultan" and "salatin." Al-Tabari said: The demand for evidence here requires the establishment of reflection and refutes whoever denies it. "If you are truthful" means in your faith, or in your saying that you will enter Paradise; that is, state what you have said with proof. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Nay﴾, as a refutation of them and a denial of them, meaning: it is not as you say. It has been said that "bala" is carried by the meaning, as if it were said: "Will no one enter Paradise?" So it was answered: ﴿Nay, whoever submits his face to God﴾. The meaning of "aslama" is to surrender and humble oneself. It has been said: he sincerely devoted his deed. The face is singled out for mention because it is the most honorable part of a person that is seen, and because it is the place of the senses, and in it appear honor and humiliation. The Arabs use "the face" to refer to the whole of a thing. It is also valid that "the face" in this verse means the purpose. ﴿And he is a doer of good﴾ is a clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase. The pronoun in "wajhahu" and "lillah" returns to the wording of "man," and likewise "ajruhu." It returns in "alayhim" to the meaning, and likewise in "yahzanun." This has already been mentioned [[See vol. 1, p. 329, second edition.]].
