Its meaning: each party among them claimed that the other was not upon anything, and that it itself was more deserving of God's mercy than the other. "While they recite the Book" means the Torah and the Gospel, and the clause "they recite the Book" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). As for "those who do not know" (alladhīna lā ya'lamūn), according to the majority of scholars (al-jumhūr) it refers to the pagans of the Arabs, because they had no Book. ʿAṭāʾ said: it refers to nations that existed before the Jews and the Christians. al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said: the meaning is likewise, that the Jews said it before the Christians did. Ibn ʿAbbās said: The people of Najrān came to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the rabbis of the Jews came to them, and they disputed in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and each group said to the other, "You are not upon anything," so the verse was revealed.

**Question 1:** In this passage there are seven issues. The first concerns the words of God, Most High: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned in them?﴾ The word "مَنْ" (man) is in the nominative case as the subject (mubtada'), and "أَظْلَمُ" (aẓlamu) is its predicate (khabar). The meaning is: there is no one more unjust. The word "أَنْ" (an) is in the accusative case in apposition (badal) to "مَسَاجِدَ" (masajid). It may also be that the original is "كَرَاهِيَةَ أَنْ يُذْكَرَ" (out of aversion to its being mentioned), with the words "كَرَاهِيَةَ" (karahiyata) omitted. It may also be that the original is "مِنْ أَنْ يُذْكَرَ فِيهَا" (from its being mentioned in them), where the preposition is dropped before "أَنْ" because the clause is long. By "the mosques" here is meant Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) and its prayer niches (maḥārībuhu). It has also been said that it means the Ka'bah, and it is in the plural either because it is the qiblah of all mosques or for the sake of glorifying it. It has also been said that the intended meaning is all mosques, and the singular is "مَسْجِدٌ" (masjid, with a kasra on the jim). Some Arabs say "مَسْجَدٌ" (masjad, with a fatha on the jim). Al-Farra' said: "Every verb of the form fa'ala yaf'ulu, like dakhala yadkhulu, has its noun of place (maf'al) with a fatha, whether it is a noun or a verbal noun, and no distinction arises in it, as in dakhala yadkhulu madkhalan, and this is his madkhal. But there are some nouns for which they made the kasra on the 'ayn obligatory, among them: al-masjid, al-maṭla', al-maghrib, al-mashriq, al-masqaṭ, al-mafraq, al-majzar, al-maskan, al-mirfaq (from rafaqa yarfuqu), al-manbit, and al-mansak (from nasaka yansuku). They made the kasra a sign of the noun, although some Arabs sometimes put a fatha on it in the noun." The word "الْمَسْجَدُ" (al-masjad, with a fatha) means the forehead of a man, where the mark of prostration appears. "الْآرَابُ" (al-ārāb) [[The plural of "إرب" (irb, with a kasra and then a sukun), meaning the limbs. The seven are: the forehead, the two hands, the two knees, and the two feet.]] are the seven places of prostration. This was said by al-Jawhari.

**Question 2:** People differed about the meaning of this verse and about who it was revealed concerning. The commentators mentioned that it was revealed about Bukht Nassar (Nebuchadnezzar), because he ruined Bayt al-Maqdis. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: it was revealed about the Christians, and the meaning is: how can you claim, O Christians, that you are people of Paradise, when you have ruined Bayt al-Maqdis and prevented those who pray from praying in it? On this view the meaning of the verse is an expression of wonder at the Christians' action towards Bayt al-Maqdis, despite their glorifying it, and they only did what they did out of enmity towards the Jews. Sa'id related from Qatadah who said: "Those are the enemies of Allah, the Christians. Their hatred of the Jews led them to help Bukht Nassar the Babylonian, the Magian, in ruining Bayt al-Maqdis." It is also reported that this ruin remained until the time of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. It has been said that it was revealed about the polytheists when they prevented the worshippers and the Prophet ﷺ, and when they barred them from the Masjid al-Haram in the year of al-Hudaybiyah. It has also been said that the intended meaning is whoever prevents anyone from any mosque until the Day of Resurrection, and this is the sound view, because the wording is general and comes in the plural form, so restricting it to some mosques and some persons is weak. And Allah, Most High, knows best.

**Question 3:** The ruin of mosques may be literal, like the destruction of Bayt al-Maqdis by Bukht Nassar and the Christians, as it is mentioned that they invaded the Children of Israel together with some of their kings. It is said that his name was Nuṭus [[The manuscripts differ in the writing of this name. In A, H, and Z it is "Buṭus" with a single dotted letter. In B it is "Tuṭrus" with a two-dotted letter above. In H it is "Nuṭus" with a nun.]] ibn Asbisanus al-Rumi, according to what al-Ghaznawi mentioned. They killed and took captives, burned the Torah, threw filth into Bayt al-Maqdis, and ruined it. And it may be figurative, like the prevention of the polytheists from the Muslims when they barred the Messenger of Allah ﷺ from the Masjid al-Haram. In general, keeping mosques from prayer and suppressing the symbols of Islam in them is a form of ruin for them.

**Question 4:** Our scholars said: For this reason we have said that it is not permissible to prevent a woman who has never performed Hajj (ṣarūrah) from performing Hajj, whether or not she has a mahram. Nor is she to be prevented from praying in the mosques, so long as she is not feared to cause temptation. Likewise the Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not prevent the female servants of Allah from the mosques of Allah." For this reason we have said: it is not permissible to demolish a mosque, nor to sell it, nor to leave it unused, even if the neighbourhood has been ruined. The building of mosques is not to be prohibited, unless they intend discord and division, by building a mosque beside or near another mosque, intending by that to split the people of the first mosque, to ruin it, and to create disunity. The second mosque is then to be demolished and prevented from being built. For this reason we have said: it is not permissible for there to be two congregational mosques in one city, nor for one mosque to have two imams, nor for two congregations to pray in one mosque. Further detail on all of this will come, God willing, in Surat Bara'ah [[See vol. 8, p. 254 and p. 104.]] and in Surat al-Nur [[Vol. 12, p. 265.]], concerning the rulings on mosques and their construction, by the power of Allah, Most High. The verse also indicates the glorification of the matter of prayer, and that since it is the best of deeds and the greatest in reward, preventing it is the greatest sin.

**Question 5:** Every place where Allah can be worshipped and prostrated to is called a mosque. The Prophet ﷺ said: "The earth has been made for me a mosque and a means of purification," which the imams related. The community is unanimous that when a plot of land is designated for prayer by declaration, it leaves the category of properties belonging to its owner and becomes open to all Muslims. So if a man builds a mosque in his house, restricts it from the people, and reserves it for himself, it remains his property and does not reach the status of a mosque. But if he permits it for all people, its ruling is the ruling of all other public mosques, and it is removed from the category of private ownership.

**Question 6:** The words of God, Most High: ﴿Those, it was not for them to enter them except in fear.﴾ "أُولَئِكَ" (ulā'ika) is the subject (mubtada'), and what follows it is its predicate (khabar). "خَائِفِينَ" (khā'ifīn) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). The meaning is: when the Muslims gain control over it and it comes under their authority, the disbeliever is then unable to enter it. If they do enter, it is in fear of being expelled by the Muslims and of being disciplined for entering. This is evidence that the disbeliever has no right to enter the mosque under any circumstances, as will come in Surat Bara'ah, God willing. As for the one who applies the verse to the Christians, he related that a time passed after 'Umar built Bayt al-Maqdis in Islam when no Christian could enter it without being severely beaten, although it had been their place of worship. As for the one who applies it to the Quraysh, he said: "Likewise it was proclaimed by the command of the Prophet ﷺ: 'No polytheist shall perform Hajj after this year, and no naked person shall circumambulate the House.'" It has also been said that it is a report whose intended meaning is a command, that is: fight them and uproot them until none of them enters the Masjid al-Haram except in fear, like His words: ﴿It is not for you to harm the Messenger of Allah﴾ [[See vol. 14, p. 228.]], for it is a prohibition that came in the form of a report.

**Question 7:** The words of God, Most High: ﴿For them in this world is disgrace.﴾ It has been said that the disgrace is killing for the combatant (ḥarbī) and the poll tax (jizyah) for the protected non-Muslim (dhimmī), according to Qatadah. As-Suddi said: "Their disgrace in this world is the appearance of the Mahdi, and the conquest of 'Amuriyyah, Rumiyyah, Constantinople, and other of their cities, as we have mentioned in the book al-Tadhkirah." Whoever applies it to the Quraysh holds that the disgrace upon them is in the conquest, and the punishment in the Hereafter is for those among them who die as disbelievers.

**Part 1 of 2**

There are five issues in this verse.

**The first issue:** His saying, exalted is He, ﴿To God belong the East and the West﴾. "Al-mashriq" (the place of sunrise) is the place where the sun rises, and "al-maghrib" (the place of sunset) is the place where it sets. That is, both of them belong to Him in ownership, together with the directions and creatures between them, by bringing them into existence and originating them, as was mentioned earlier. He singled them out for mention and attributed them to Himself as an honour, like "the House of God" and "the she-camel of God." This is also because the occasion of revelation required it, as will come.

**The second issue:** His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Wherever you turn﴾. "Fa-ayna ma tuwallu" is a conditional clause, which is why the nun (of the verb) is dropped. The word "ayna" is the operative particle, "ma" is extra (zā'ida), and the response (jawāb) is "then there is the Face of God" (fa-thamma wajhu Allah). Al-Hasan read "tawallaw" with a fatha on the ta and the lam, and the original form is "tatawallaw." The word "thumma" is in the accusative position as an adverb of place. Its meaning is distance, but it is built on fatha and is not inflected, because it is indefinite (mubham). It has the same function as "hunāka" (there) for distance. If you want to indicate nearness, you say "hunā" (here).

**The third issue:** The scholars differed about the occasion in which "Wherever you turn" was revealed, and there are five opinions.

Abdullah ibn Amir ibn Rabi'ah said: it was revealed concerning those who prayed facing other than the qiblah on a dark night. At-Tirmidhi transmitted it from him, from his father, who said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) on a journey on a dark night, and we did not know where the qiblah was, so each man among us prayed in his own direction. When we woke up, we mentioned that to the Prophet (ﷺ), and then ﴿Wherever you turn, there is the Face of God﴾ was revealed." Abu Isa (at-Tirmidhi) said: "This is a hadith whose chain of transmission is not strong. We only know it from the hadith of Ash'ath as-Sammān, and Ash'ath ibn Sa'id Abu ar-Rabi' is considered weak in hadith." Most scholars have adopted this view. They said: if a person prays under cloud cover facing a direction other than the qiblah, and afterwards it becomes clear to him that he prayed facing other than the qiblah, his prayer is valid. This is the view of Sufyan, Ibn al-Mubarak, Ahmad and Ishaq.

I say: this is also the view of Abu Hanifa and Malik, except that Malik said: it is recommended for him to repeat the prayer within its time, and this is not obligatory for him, because he has fulfilled his obligation as he was commanded, and perfection can be made up within the time. Malik based this on the Sunnah concerning the one who prayed alone and then found the same prayer being performed in congregation within its time: he repeats it with them. He does not repeat within the time as a recommendation, except for the one who faced away from the qiblah, or deviated greatly to the east or west while making a good-faith effort (ijtihad). As for the one who deviated slightly to the right or left while making a good-faith effort, there is no repetition for him, either within the time or otherwise.

Al-Mughirah and ash-Shafi'i said: it does not suffice him, because facing the qiblah is one of the conditions of prayer. What Malik said is more correct, because the direction of the qiblah may be abandoned out of necessity in the heat of battle, and it is also permitted during travel by way of concession.

Ibn Umar said: it was revealed concerning the traveller who performs voluntary prayer in whatever direction his mount takes him. Muslim transmitted it from him, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to pray while he was coming from Makkah to Madinah, on his mount, facing wherever it was going," and he said: "And concerning this it was revealed, ﴿Wherever you turn, there is the Face of God﴾." There is no disagreement among the scholars on the permissibility of voluntary prayer on a mount, on the basis of this hadith and similar ones. It is not permissible for anyone to deliberately abandon the qiblah in any way, except in extreme fear, as will come.

The opinion of Malik differed concerning the sick person who prays in his litter. At one point he said: he may not pray an obligatory prayer on the back of a camel, even if his illness is severe. Sahnun said: if he does so, he must repeat it, as al-Baji reported. At another point he said: if he is one who can only pray seated by gesture (īmā'), then he should pray on the camel after it has been stopped for him, and face the qiblah.

They agreed that it is not permissible for anyone who is healthy to pray an obligatory prayer except on the ground, except in extreme fear specifically, as its explanation will come.

The jurists differed concerning the traveller on a journey in which the prayer is not shortened. Malik and his companions and ath-Thawri said: one may only perform voluntary prayer on the mount on a journey in which the prayer is shortened. They said: this is because the journeys that are reported from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), in which he used to perform voluntary prayer, were ones in which the prayer was shortened.

Ash-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and their companions, al-Hasan ibn Hayy, al-Layth ibn Sa'd and Dawud ibn Ali said: voluntary prayer on the mount is permitted outside the city on every journey, whether or not the prayer is shortened in it, because the reports do not specify one journey over another. So every journey permits this, unless some journey is singled out by something that must be accepted without question.

Abu Yusuf said: one prays in the city on a beast by gesture, on the basis of the hadith of Yahya ibn Sa'id from Anas ibn Malik, that he prayed on a donkey in the alleys of Madinah, gesturing (yūmi' īmā'an).

At-Tabari said: it is permitted for every rider and walker, whether resident or traveller, to perform voluntary prayer on his beast and mount, and on his feet, by gesture.

It is related from some companions of ash-Shafi'i that their school permits voluntary prayer on the beast both in residence and on travel.

Al-Athram said: it was asked of Ahmad ibn Hanbal about prayer on a beast in residence. He said: "As for on a journey, I have heard it, but I have not heard it for residence."

Ibn al-Qasim said: whoever performs voluntary prayer in his litter performs it seated; his standing is cross-legged (tarabbu'), and he bows placing his hands on his knees, then raises his head.

Qatadah said: it was revealed concerning the Negus (an-Najashi). When he died, the Prophet (ﷺ) called the Muslims to pray over him outside Madinah. They said: "How can we pray over a man who has died while he prayed facing other than our qiblah?" The Negus was the king of Abyssinia, whose name was Ashamah, and in Arabic it means "Atiyyah." He had prayed facing Bayt al-Maqdis until he died, and then the qiblah had been changed to the Ka'bah, so the verse was revealed. And concerning him was revealed, "And among the People of the Book are those who believe in God" [see vol. 4, p. 322]. So this was an excuse for the Negus. The Prophet's (ﷺ) prayer over him with his companions took place in the ninth year after the Hijrah.

This has been used as evidence by those who permit the funeral prayer in absentia (ṣalāt al-ghā'ib), and this is ash-Shafi'i's position. Ibn al-Arabi said: "Among the strangest issues of the funeral prayer is what ash-Shafi'i said: it is prayed over the absent person. I was in Baghdad in the majlis of Imam Fakhr al-Islam, and a man from Khurasan would come in to him and say, 'How is so-and-so?' He would say, 'He has died.' Then he would say, 'Surely we belong to God and to Him we return!' Then he would say to us, 'Stand up, so that I may lead you in prayer.' He would stand and pray over him with us. This was after six months had passed, and between him and his homeland there were six months' distance." Their basis for this is the Prophet's (ﷺ) prayer over the Negus.

Our scholars, may God have mercy on them, said: the Prophet (ﷺ) was specially permitted this for three reasons. The first is that the earth was folded up for him to the south and to the north until he saw the bier of the Negus, just as it was folded up for him to the north and south until he saw the Furthest Mosque (al-Masjid al-Aqsa). The opponent said: "What benefit is there in seeing him? The benefit lies only in his blessing reaching him." The second is that the Negus had no guardian among the believers there who would lead the prayer over him. The opponent said: "This is customarily impossible! A king upon a religion will not have no followers, and interpreting something by means of the impossible is itself impossible." The third is that the Prophet (ﷺ) only intended, by praying over the Negus, to bring mercy upon him and to win over the rest of the kings after him, when they saw the concern shown for him in life and in death. The opponent said: "The blessing of supplication from the Prophet (ﷺ) and from others reaches the deceased by general agreement."

Ibn al-Arabi said: "What I hold concerning the Prophet's (ﷺ) prayer over the Negus is that he knew the Negus and those who believed with him did not have the tradition of the funeral prayer among them, so he knew they would bury him without a prayer, and he hastened to pray over him."

I say: the first interpretation is better, because when he saw him, he was not praying over an absent person, but over one who was seen and present, whereas the absent is that which is not seen. And God, exalted is He, knows best.

**The fourth opinion:** Ibn Zayd said: the Jews had approved of the Prophet's (ﷺ) prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis, and they said, "He is only guided by us." When he was turned toward the Ka'bah, the Jews said, ﴿What has turned them away from their qiblah which they were upon?﴾ Then ﴿To God belong the East and the West﴾ was revealed. So the structure of the verse according to this opinion is: when the Jews denied the matter of the qiblah, God, exalted is He, made clear that He has the right to worship His servants in whatever way He wills. If He wills, He commands them to face Bayt al-Maqdis, and if He wills, He commands them to face the Ka'bah. It is an act against which there is no argument [in B and C: "no stone"], and He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned.

The fifth view: the verse is abrogated by His words, "And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it" [see pp. 159 and 168 of this part]. This was related from Ibn 'Abbas, as if he permitted at the beginning that a person pray however he wished, and then that was abrogated. Qatadah said: the abrogating verse is His words, Exalted is He, "So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque" (fa-walli wajhaka shatra al-Masjid al-Haram), meaning toward it (tilqa'hu). This was transmitted by Abu 'Isa al-Tirmidhi.

The sixth view: it is muhkam (not abrogated). It was related from Mujahid and al-Dahhak that the meaning is: wherever you are, east or west, there is the Face of God, which He has commanded us to face, and that is the Ka'bah. Also from Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr: when the verse "Call upon Me; I will respond to you" was revealed, they said, "To where?" Then this was revealed: "Wherever you turn, there is the Face of God." Also from Ibn 'Umar and al-Nakha'i: wherever you turn during your journeys and your comings and goings, there is the Face of God.

It was also said: it is connected to His words, "And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of God from having His name mentioned in them" (the verse). The meaning, then, is that the lands belong to God, O believers, and they are wide enough for you, so the destruction by one who destroyed the mosques of God should not prevent you from turning your faces toward the qiblah of God wherever you are in His earth.

It was also said: it was revealed when the Prophet ﷺ was prevented from the House in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, and the Muslims were grieved by that.

These are ten views. Whoever holds that it is abrogated is not open to objection on the ground that it is a report, because it is capable of the sense of a command. It may be that the meaning of "Wherever you turn, there is the Face of God" is: turn your faces toward the Face of God. This is the verse that Sa'id ibn Jubayr, may God have mercy on him, recited when al-Hajjaj ordered him to be slaughtered, [with his face] to the ground.

The fourth point: People differed in interpreting the "face" attributed to God Exalted in the Qur'an and the Sunnah. The masters (al-Huddhaq) said: that refers to existence (al-wujud), and expressing it by "face" is figurative speech, since the face is the most prominent of the limbs in what is witnessed and the most honored in rank. Ibn Furak said: the attribute of a thing is sometimes mentioned while the thing itself is intended, as an extension of meaning, as one says: "I saw the knowledge of so-and-so today," and "I looked at his knowledge," meaning: "I saw the scholar and I looked at the scholar." Likewise, when "face" is mentioned here, what is intended is the one who has the face, that is, the existence. On this basis is interpreted His words, "We feed you only for the sake of God's Face" [see vol. 19, p. 128], because what is meant is: for God, who has the Face. Likewise His words, "except the seeking of the Face of his Lord, the Most High" [see vol. 20, p. 88], that is, of Him who has the Face. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Face" is an expression for Him, Mighty and Majestic, as He said, "And there will remain the Face of your Lord, Full of Majesty and Honor" [see vol. 17, p. 165].

Some scholars said: that is an attribute established by revelation (al-sam'), beyond what the intellects necessitate of the attributes of the Eternal, Exalted is He. Ibn 'Atiyah said: Abu al-Ma'ali weakened this view, and it is indeed weak; the intended meaning is only His existence.

It was also said: the meaning of "face" here is the direction toward which we are turned, that is, the qiblah. It was also said: "face" means intention (al-qasd), as the poet said:

"I seek God's forgiveness for a sin I cannot count, the Lord of the servants; to Him are the face and the deed."

It was also said: the meaning is "There is the good pleasure of God and His reward," as He said, "We feed you only for the sake of God's Face," that is, for His pleasure and seeking His reward. From this is His ﷺ saying: "Whoever builds a mosque seeking thereby the Face of God, God will build for him the like of it in Paradise." And His saying: "On the Day of Resurrection, scrolls sealed up will be brought and placed before God, Exalted is He, and He, Mighty and Majestic, will say to His angels, 'Cast this away and accept this.' The angels will say, 'By Your might, our Lord, we have seen nothing but good,' and He knows best. He will say, 'This was not for My Face, and I accept from deeds only that which is sought thereby through My Face,'" meaning sincerely for Me. It was narrated by al-Daraqutni.

It was also said: the meaning is "There is God," and "Face" is a supplementary element (silah), as in His words, "And He is with you." This was said by al-Kalbi and al-Qutaybi, and the Mu'tazilah hold a similar view.

The fifth point: His words, Exalted is He, "Indeed, God is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing" (inna Allaha wasi'un 'alim). That is, He gives abundance to His servants in their religion, and does not burden them with what is beyond their capacity. It was also said: "Wasi'" means that His knowledge encompasses everything, as He said, "He has encompassed all things in knowledge" [see vol. 11, p. 243]. Al-Farra' said: "Al-Wasi'" is the Generous One whose bounty encompasses everything; the proof is His words, "My mercy encompasses all things" [see vol. 7, p. 296]. It was also said: "Wasi' al-maghfirah" means that no sin is too great for Him. It was also said: He is bountiful to the servants and independent of their deeds. It is said: "So-and-so is capable of what he is asked" (yasa'u ma yus'al), meaning he does not withhold; God Exalted said, "Let him who has abundance spend from his abundance" [see vol. 18, p. 170], meaning: let the rich spend from what God has given him. We have discussed this in our book "al-Asna," and praise be to God.

There are five issues in this passage.

The first concerns the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿They say: Allah has taken a son﴾. This is a report about the Christians in their saying that the Messiah is the son of Allah. It was also said to refer to the Jews in their saying that 'Uzayr is the son of Allah, and to the disbelieving Arabs in their saying that the angels are the daughters of Allah. Similar reports about ignorant disbelievers have come in Surah Maryam [See vol. 11, pp. 158 ff. and p. 281.] and Surah al-Anbiya' [See vol. 11, pp. 158 ff. and p. 281.].

The second concerns His words: ﴿Glory be to Him. Rather, to Him belongs...﴾ al-Bukhari transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: Allah the Exalted said: "The son of Adam denies Me, though it is not for him to do so, and he reviles Me, though it is not for him to do so. As for his denying Me, he claims that I cannot recreate him as he was. As for his reviling Me, he says, 'I have a son.' Glory be to Me that I should take a consort or a son."

The third concerns the word ﴿subhana﴾ (Glory be to Him), which is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar). Its meaning is clearing [Allah] of, declaring Him free from, and keeping Him beyond what is said, namely their saying that Allah has taken a son. Rather, Allah the Exalted is one in His essence and unique in His attributes. He has not begotten, so He would need a consort: ﴿How can He have a son when He has no consort and He created all things?﴾ Nor was He begotten, so that He would be preceded [by a parent]. Exalted is He far above what the wrongdoers and deniers say! ﴿Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth.﴾ The word ﴿ma﴾ (whatever) is in the nominative as a subject (mubtada', the subject of a nominal sentence), and its predicate (khabar, the complement) is the prepositional phrase that follows it. The meaning is that all of it belongs to Him as possession, by bringing it into being and originating it. The one who claims that He has taken a son is himself included among what is in the heavens and the earth. It has already been stated that the meaning of ﴿subhan Allah﴾ is the innocence of Allah from every evil [See vol. 1, p. 276, second edition.].

The fourth concerns the fact that a son can only be of the same kind as his father. How then could the Truth, glory be to Him, take a son from among His creatures, when ﴿nothing is like Him﴾? He has said: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [See vol. 11, pp. 158 ff. and p. 281.]. As He said here: ﴿Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth.﴾ Sonship requires being of the same kind and being originated, while eternity requires oneness and permanence. So He, glory be to Him, is the Eternal, the Everlasting, the One, the Unique, the Self-Sufficient, who ﴿neither begets nor is begotten, and to whom no one is comparable﴾. Furthermore, sonship contradicts slavery and servitude, as will be explained, if Allah the Exalted wills, in Surah Maryam [See vol. 11, pp. 158 ff. and p. 281.]. So how could a son be a slave? This is impossible, and whatever leads to the impossible is impossible.

The fifth concerns His words: ﴿All are devoutly obedient to Him﴾. ﴿Kull﴾ (all) is a subject (mubtada'), and ﴿qanitun﴾ (devoutly obedient) is the predicate. The implied meaning is "all of them", and then the ha' and mim (the pronoun suffix referring to them) were omitted. ﴿Qanitun﴾ means obedient and humbly submissive. So all created things are devoutly obedient to Allah, that is, they submit and obey. As for inanimate things, their ﴿qunut﴾ (devout obedience) is in the manifestation of the craftsmanship upon them and within them. Thus ﴿qunut﴾ means obedience, and it also means silence. From this is the saying of Zayd ibn Arqam: "We used to speak during the prayer, a man would speak to his companion beside him, until this was revealed: ﴿And stand before Allah in devout obedience﴾, so we were commanded to be silent and forbidden to speak." Qunut also means prayer. The poet said:

*Devoutly obedient to Allah, reciting His books,*
*and withdrawn from the people by intent.*

Al-Suddi and others said, regarding His words ﴿All are devoutly obedient to Him﴾, that it means on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Hasan said: all stand bearing witness that they are His servants. In language, ﴿qunut﴾ originally means standing, and from this is the hadith: "The best of prayer is the long qunut." This was said by al-Zajjaj. So creation is devoutly obedient, that is, standing in servitude, either by acknowledgment or, if they are otherwise, the mark of the craftsmanship upon them is clear. It was also said that its origin is obedience, and from this is His saying: ﴿The devoutly obedient men and the devoutly obedient women﴾. More explanation of this will come at His words: ﴿And stand before Allah in devout obedience﴾ [See vol. 3, p. 213.].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 117:

There are six issues in this verse.

The first: His saying, Exalted is He, "Badi' al-samawat" (the Originator of the heavens). The form fa'il (badi') is intensive (lil-mubalaghah), and it is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject. The active participle is mubdi', like basir from mubsir. One says "abda'tu al-shay'" (I originated the thing) when it is not based on a model. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is Badi' al-samawat wa al-ard, that is, their Creator (munshi'uha), their Bringer into existence (mujiduha), their Originator (mubdi'uha) and their Inventor (mukhtari'uha), without any limit or model. Everyone who creates something that has not been preceded by a precedent is called mubdi', and from this comes the word ahl al-bid'ah (people of innovation). The term bid'ah (innovation) is so called because its author originated it without any act or saying of an imam (leader). In al-Bukhari (there is the saying): "How excellent is this innovation" (wa ni'mat al-bid'ah hadhihi), meaning the night prayer of Ramadan (qiyam Ramadan).

The second: Every innovation that comes forth from a created being either has a basis in the Shari'ah or it does not. If it has a basis, it falls under the general scope of what Allah has recommended and what He singled out for His Messenger (ﷺ), and so it is within the sphere of praise. If its model does not exist, such as a kind of generosity, liberality, and doing good, then this act is among the praiseworthy acts, even if the doer was not preceded to it. This is supported by the saying of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him): "How excellent is this innovation" (ni'mat al-bid'ah hadhihi) [[He means: the night prayer of Ramadan.]], since it was among the acts of goodness and within the sphere of praise. Although the Prophet (ﷺ) had performed it, he left it and did not persist in it, nor did he gather the people for it. So 'Umar's (may Allah be pleased with him) persistence in it, his gathering of the people for it, and his urging them to it, is an innovation, but it is a praiseworthy and commendable innovation. If it contradicts what Allah and His Messenger have commanded, then it falls within the sphere of blame and rejection. This is the meaning stated by al-Khattabi and others. I say: this is the meaning of his (ﷺ) saying in his sermon: "The worst of matters are their newly invented ones, and every innovation is misguidance" (wa kullu bid'atin dalalah), meaning what does not agree with the Book, the Sunnah, or the practice of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them). This is clarified by his saying: "Whoever establishes a good practice in Islam will have its reward and the reward of whoever acts upon it after him, without that diminishing anything of their rewards. And whoever establishes an evil practice in Islam will bear its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it after him, without that diminishing anything of their burdens." This points to what is newly introduced of the evil and the good, and it is the basis of this chapter. With Allah is protection and success; there is no lord other than Him.

The third: His saying, Exalted is He, "Wa idha qada amran fa-innama yaqulu lahu kun fa-yakun" (When He decrees a matter, He only says to it: "Be," and it is). That is, when He wills its perfection and its completion, as already known in His knowledge, He says to it: "Be." Ibn 'Arafah said: The qada' (decree) of a thing is its perfection, its execution, and its completion. From this the qadi (judge) is so named, because when he rules he has finished what lies between the two disputants. Al-Azhari said: qada in the language has several meanings, all of which return to the cessation and completion of a thing. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

"And upon them two sewn coats of mail, which Dawud completed, or the skilled craftsman Tubba' made the full ones" [[Masrudatan: two sewn coats of mail. Al-sani': the one skilled in work.]]

And al-Shammakh said regarding 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him):

"You completed matters, then you left after them
bundles in their sheaths that have not opened."

Our scholars said: "qada" is a shared term (lafz mushtarak). It means creation, as Allah says: "So He completed them as seven heavens in two days" [[See vol. 15, p. 345.]], that is, He created them. It means informing, as Allah says: "And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Book" [[See vol. 10, p. 214, and vol. 2, p. 36.]], that is, We informed them. It means command, as in His saying: "And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him" [[See vol. 10, p. 214, and vol. 2, p. 36.]]. It means obligation and the execution of rulings, and from this the judge (hakim) is called qadi. It means fulfilling a right, as Allah says: "So when Musa had fulfilled the term" [[See vol. 13, p. 280.]]. It means will (iradah), as in His saying: "When He decrees a matter, He only says to it: 'Be,' and it is," that is, when He wills to create a thing. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "qada" means to measure out (qaddara), and it may also come to mean to execute (amda). Both meanings are possible in this verse according to the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah: He measured it out in eternity and executed it therein. And according to the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah: He executed it at the time of creation and bringing into existence.

The fourth: His saying, Exalted is He, "amran" (a matter). The amr is the singular of umur (affairs), and it is not the verbal noun of amara yamuru. Our scholars said: amr in the Qur'an is used in fourteen senses. The first: religion, as Allah says: "until the truth came and the command of Allah prevailed" [[See vol. 8, p. 157.]], meaning the religion of Allah, Islam. The second: speech, as in His saying: "But when Our command came" [[see vol. 9 section]], meaning Our word; and His saying: "Then they disputed their affair among themselves," meaning their saying. The third: punishment, as in His saying: "When the matter was decided" [[See vol. 9, p. 356.]], meaning when the punishment became due for the people of the Fire. The fourth: 'Isa (peace be upon him), as Allah says: "When He decrees a matter" [[See vol. 4, p. 93.]], meaning 'Isa, and it was in His knowledge that he would be born without a father. The fifth: the killing at Badr, as Allah says: "But when the command of Allah comes" [[See vol. 15, p. 334.]], meaning the killing at Badr; and His saying: "That Allah might accomplish a matter already destined" [[See vol. 8, p. 22.]], meaning the killing of the disbelievers of Makkah. The sixth: the conquest of Makkah, as Allah says: "Then wait until Allah brings His command" [[See vol. 8, p. 95.]], meaning the conquest of Makkah.

The seventh: the killing of Quraizah and the expulsion of Banu al-Nadir. Allah says: "So pardon and overlook until Allah brings His command." The eighth: the Resurrection, as Allah says: "The command of Allah has come." The ninth: the decree (qada'), as Allah says: "He arranges the affair," meaning the decree. The tenth: revelation, as Allah says: "He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth," meaning He sends down revelation from the heaven to the earth; and His saying: "The command descends among them," meaning revelation. The eleventh: the affair of creation, as Allah says: "Unquestionably, to Allah all affairs are returned," meaning the affairs of creatures. The twelfth: victory, as Allah says: "They say: 'Is there anything for us in the affair?'" meaning victory; and "Say: Indeed, the affair is entirely for Allah," meaning victory. The thirteenth: sin, as Allah says: "So it tasted the consequence of its affair," meaning the punishment for its sin. The fourteenth: the state and the deed, as Allah says: "And the affair of Pharaoh was not sound," meaning his deed and state; and He says: "Let those who oppose His command beware," meaning His act.

The fifth: His saying, Exalted is He, "kun" (Be). It has been said: the kaf is from kawnihi (His being), and the nun is from nurihi (His light), and this is what is meant by his (peace be upon him) saying: "I seek refuge in the perfect words of Allah from the evil of what He has created." And it is narrated: "by the perfect word of Allah" (bi-kalimat Allah al-tammah) in the singular. The plural is used because this word concerns all matters: when He says to every matter "Be," and to everything "Be," they are words (kalimat). What supports this is what is related from Abu Dharr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding what is related from Allah, Exalted is He: "My gift is speech, and My punishment is speech." Al-Tirmidhi recorded it in a lengthy hadith. The word in the singular also has the meaning of the plural, but since the one word is divided among matters across times, it becomes words, and they return to one word. It is said "tammah" (perfect) because, according to the people of language, the least speech consists of three letters: an initial letter, a letter in which the word is held, and a letter on which one pauses. If it is of two letters, it is among them defective (manqus), like yad, dam, and fam, and it became defective for a reason. So among human words it is defective because it has two letters, and because it is a word uttered with tools (al-adawat). But from our Lord, blessed and exalted, it is perfect, because it is without tools, exalted above resemblance to created beings.

The sixth: His saying, Exalted is He, "fa-yakun" (and it is). It was read with a raised nun (fa-yakunu) as a resumption (isti'naf). Sibawayh said: "fa-huwa yakunu" (so it is), or "fa-innahu yakunu" (indeed it is). Others said: it is conjoined to "yaqulu" (He says). According to the first, it exists after the command; and although it is non-existent, it is as the existent when it is known to Him, as will be explained. According to the second, it exists together with the command. Al-Tabari chose this and said: His command to a thing with "kun" does not precede its existence nor follow after it. So a thing is not commanded to exist unless it already exists by the command, and it does not exist unless it is commanded to exist, as will be explained. He said: Its parallel is the rising of people from their graves, which does not precede Allah's call nor follow after it, as He says: "Then when He calls you with a call from the earth, behold, you will come out" [[See vol. 14, p. 19.]]. Ibn 'Atiyyah rejected this view and said: it is an error in meaning, because it implies that the saying is together with the bringing into being and the existence. The summary of the belief in this verse is: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has never ceased to command the non-existent on condition of their existence, capable together with the delay of the things made capable, knowing together with the delay of the things known. So everything in the verse that implies the future is according to the things commanded, since created things come after they were not. And everything ascribed to Allah, Exalted is He, of power and knowledge is eternal and has never ceased. The meaning indicated by the expression "kun" is eternal and subsisting in His essence.

Abu al-Hasan al-Mawardi said: If it is asked, "In what state does He say to it 'Be' and it is? In the state of its non-existence, or in the state of its existence? If it is in the state of its non-existence, it is impossible for Him to command except one who is commanded, just as it is impossible for a command to come except from one who commands. And if it is in the state of its existence, that is a state in which it is not permissible to command it to exist and to come into being, because it is already existing and created?" It is answered that there are three replies to this question. The first: it is a report from Allah, Exalted is He, about the execution of His commands in His existing creation, just as He commanded the Children of Israel to be apes, despised; and this does not apply to the bringing into existence of the non-existent. The second: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, knows what will be before it comes to be, so the things that were not, yet are present in His knowledge before their coming to be, resemble those that exist, and so it is permissible for Him to say to them "Be," and to command them to come out from the state of non-existence into the state of existence, since all of them are present to Him and He knows them in the state of non-existence. The third: this is a general report from Allah, Exalted is He, about everything He brings into being and creates: when He wills its creation and its origination, it is, and it comes into existence without there being any saying that He says there; rather, it is a decree that He wills, and it is expressed by "saying" even though it is not a saying, like the saying of Abu al-Najm:

"The flanks said to the belly: Join!"

There is no saying there; he only meant that the back has joined the belly. And like the saying of 'Amr ibn Humamah al-Dawsi:

"She became like an eagle whose chicks have flown, when it seeks to fly it is told: Stay!"

And like the saying of another:

"Its two wings said to its legs: Cling, and be steady, lest the flesh of you two be torn."

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 118:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who do not know said﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the Jews. Mujahid said: the Christians, and al-Tabari preferred this view, because they are the ones mentioned earlier in the verse. Al-Rabi', al-Suddi and Qatadah said: the polytheists of the Arabs. And ﴿law﴾ here means "hallaa" (why not), a form of tahdid (urging/reproach), as al-Ashhab ibn Rumaylah said [[So it is in the original sources. Al-Baghdadi, author of Khizanat al-Adab, said: "Ibn al-Shajari attributed it in his Amali to al-Ashhab, but the correct view is that it is from a qasida of Jarir, with no disagreement among the transmitters that it is his, and it is a reply to a qasida previously composed by al-Farazdaq, rhyming on the same letter." The incident of hamstringing the camels is well known in the histories. Al-Nayb (with a kasra on the nun and a sukun on the ya, the plural of naab): the aged she-camel. Dwtara (ḍawṭarā): it has been said it means a large, base man who is of no use, and it has also been said it means fools. Al-Kumayy: the brave warrior. Al-Muqni': the one who has a helmet and a mail-coif on his head. See Khizanat al-Adab, the witness numbered one hundred and sixty-four, and the book al-Mughni on "law", and al-Naqa'id p. 833, printed in Europe, and the appendix to al-Qali's Amali.]]:

"You consider the hamstringing of the aged she-camels the best of your glory, sons of Dawtara, were it not for the brave warrior in his armour."

This "law" is not the one that gives the prevention of one thing due to the existence of another. The difference between them, according to the scholars of language, is that "law" meaning tahdid is followed only by a verb, either expressed or implied, whereas the "law" of imtina' (prevention) is followed by a nominal sentence, and it is customary to omit the predicate. The meaning of the speech is: why does not God speak to us about the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ so that we know that he is a prophet and believe in him, or why does He not bring us a sign that would be a proof of his prophethood. "Ayah" means a proof and a sign, and it has been discussed before [[See vol. 1, p. 66, second edition.]].

"Those who came before them": these are the Jews and the Christians according to the one who takes "those who do not know" to mean the polytheists of the Arabs, or the earlier nations according to the one who takes "those who do not know" to mean the Jews and Christians, or the Jews according to the one who takes "those who do not know" to mean the Christians.

"Their hearts are alike": it has been said this refers to their obstinacy, their making of demands, and their refusal to believe. Al-Farra' said: "Their hearts are alike" in their agreement upon disbelief.

"We have made the signs clear for a people who have certainty": this has been mentioned before [[See vol. 1, p. 180, second edition.]].

The Qur'anic verse: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good news and a warner.﴾ "Bashiran" (as a bringer of good news) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), and "nadhiran" (and a warner) is coordinated with it. Their meanings have already been discussed [[See vol. 1, pp. 184 and 238, second edition.]]. ﴿And you will not be questioned about the companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾ Muqatil said: The Prophet ﷺ said, "If God had sent down His punishment upon the Jews, they would have believed." So God revealed: ﴿And you will not be questioned about the companions of the Blazing Fire,﴾ with "tus'alu" in the nominative (marfū'). This is the reading of the majority (al-Jumhur), and it is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier, coordinated with "bashiran wa nadhiran." The meaning is: We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good news and a warner, not one who will be held accountable (for them).

Sa'id al-Akhfash said: "wa la tas'al" (with the "ta" open and the "lam" damma), and it is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier, coordinated with "bashiran wa nadhiran." The meaning: We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good news and a warner, not asking about them, because God's knowledge of their disbelief after your warning makes His asking you about them unnecessary. This is the meaning of "not asking." The meaning of "not being questioned" is that you will not be held responsible for the disbelief of those who disbelieve after the good news and the warning.

Ibn 'Abbas and Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said one day, "I wish I knew what my two parents did." Then this verse was revealed. This applies to the reading of the one who read "wa la tas'al" in the jussive (jazm) as a prohibition (nahy). This reading belongs to Nafi' alone. It has two interpretations:

The first: He was forbidden to ask about those among the living who disobeyed and disbelieved, because their state may change, so that they move from disbelief to faith and from disobedience to obedience.

The second, which is the more apparent: He was forbidden to ask about those who died in their disbelief and disobedience, as a magnification of their state and a severe judgment of their condition. This is like saying, "Do not ask about so-and-so!" meaning: he has reached beyond what you imagine.

Ibn Mas'ud read "wa lan tus'ala," and Ubayy read "wa ma tus'al." Their meanings agree with the reading of the majority, negating that he would be held responsible for them.

It was said: He only asked which of his two parents had died most recently, and then this was revealed. We have mentioned in our book "al-Tadhkira" that God gave life back to his father and mother, and they believed in him. We also mentioned his peace be upon him saying to the man, "Indeed my father and your father are in the Fire," and we clarified that matter. And praise be to God.

The Qur'an, 2:120 — "And the Jews will never be pleased with you, nor the Christians, until you follow their religion."

**First issue.** The meaning is: O Muhammad, their aim is not to believe in the signs they propose. Even if you brought them everything they ask for, they would not be pleased with you. What would please them is that you abandon what you hold, Islam, and follow them. It is said: *radiya yardha ridan wa ruduan wa ridwanan wa ruduanan wa mardatan* ("he was pleased"). It is from the *dhawat al-waw* class (roots with a medial waw). In the dual it is said *ridwan*, and al-Kisa'i reported *ridyan*. It is also reported as *ridaʾ* with a long vowel, as if it were the verbal noun of *radiya*, *yurada*, *muradah* and *ridaʾ*.

*Tattabiʿa* ("you follow") is in the subjunctive governed by *an* (that), but the *an* does not appear with *hatta* (until). This is the view of al-Khalil (ibn Ahmad), because *hatta* governs the noun in the genitive, as in His words, *hatta matliʿi al-fajr* ("until the rising of dawn"). Whatever governs a noun does not govern a verb at all, and whatever puts a noun in the genitive does not put anything in the accusative. Al-Nahhas said: *tattabiʿa* is in the subjunctive governed by *hatta*, and *hatta* is a substitute for *an*.

*Al-milla* (religion, creed) is the name for what God has prescribed for His servants in His books and through the tongues of His messengers. Thus *milla* and *shariʿa* (sacred law) are the same. As for *din* (religion, way of life), it has been distinguished from *milla* and *shariʿa*: *milla* and *shariʿa* are what God calls His servants to do, while *din* is what the servants do in obedience to His command.

**Second issue.** A group of scholars took this verse as evidence, among them Abu Hanifa, al-Shafiʿi, Dawud and Ahmad ibn Hanbal, for the view that all disbelief is one *milla*. Their evidence is His words, *milla-tahum* ("their religion"), where the word for religion is singular. They also cite His words, ﴿لَكُمْ دِينُكُمْ وَلِيَ دِينِ﴾ ("To you is your religion, and to me is my religion"), and the Prophet's words (peace be upon him): "The people of two religions do not inherit from one another," understood to mean Islam and disbelief, based on his words (peace be upon him): "A Muslim does not inherit from a disbeliever."

Malik, and Ahmad in another narration, held that disbelief comprises several *milal* (religions). Therefore a Jew does not inherit from a Christian, nor do they inherit from a Magian, relying on the apparent meaning of the Prophet's words (peace be upon him): "The people of two religions do not inherit from one another." As for His words, *milla-tahum*, the intended sense is plurality, even though the word is singular in form, as shown by its being attached to a plural pronoun. This is like saying: "I took knowledge from the scholars of the people of Madina," for example, "their knowledge," and "I heard their hadith from them," meaning their sciences and their traditions.

His words, ﴿قُلْ إِنَّ هُدَى اللَّهِ هُوَ الْهُدى﴾ ("Say: Indeed, the guidance of God is the [only] guidance"). The meaning: what you are upon, O Muhammad, of God's true guidance, which He places in the heart of whomever He wills, is the real guidance, not what these people claim.

His words, ﴿وَلَئِنِ اتَّبَعْتَ أَهْواءَهُمْ﴾ ("And if you were to follow their desires"). *Ahwaʾ* is the plural of *hawa* (desire), as in *jamal* and *ajmal*. Because the desires are varied, the plural is used; if it were taken as referring to the singular *milla*, it would say *hawahum*. This address has two readings. The first is that it is addressed to the Messenger, since the address is directed to him. The second is that it is addressed to the Messenger but intends his community (*umma*). On the first reading there is a disciplining of his community, since their rank is below his.

The occasion of the revelation: they used to ask for peace (*al-musalama*) and gifts, and they promised the Prophet ﷺ that they would become Muslims. So God informed him that they would never be pleased with him until he followed their religion, and He commanded him to fight them.

His words, ﴿مِنَ الْعِلْمِ﴾ ("from knowledge"). Ahmad ibn Hanbal was asked about someone who says: "The Qur'an is created." He said: "He is a disbeliever." It was asked: "On what basis did you declare him a disbeliever?" He said: "On the basis of verses from the Book of God: ﴿وَلَئِنِ اتَّبَعْتَ أَهْواءَهُمْ مِنْ بَعْدِ مَا جاءَكَ مِنَ الْعِلْمِ﴾ ('And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you'), and the Qur'an is from the knowledge of God. Whoever claims that it is created has disbelieved."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verses 121–123:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾. Qatadah said: They are the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, and the Book, on this interpretation, is the Qur'an. Ibn Zayd said: They are those among the Children of Israel who embraced Islam, and the Book, on this interpretation, is the Torah. The verse is general in meaning.

"Alladhina" (those) is in the nominative case by being the subject (mubtada'), "ataynahumu" (We have given them) is its relative clause (silah), and "yatluna-hu" (they recite it) is the predicate (khabar) of the subject. If you wish, the predicate may be "ulaika yu'minuna bihi" (those believe in it).

Scholars differed regarding the meaning of "yatlunahu haqqa tilawatihi" (they recite it with its due recitation). It was said: they follow it with its due following, by following its commands and prohibitions, so they make lawful what it makes lawful, forbid what it forbids, and act upon what it contains. This was said by Ikrimah. Ikrimah said: Have you not heard the saying of Allah, exalted is He: "And by the moon when it follows it" (wal-qamari idha talaha), meaning, when it follows it? This is the meaning also of the statement of Ibn Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them both. And the poet said:

"Qad ja'alat dalwi tastatlini" [[its completion:

"wa la uridu tabi'a al-qarin"]]

Nasr ibn Isa narrated from Malik, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, from the Prophet ﷺ, regarding His saying, exalted is He: "yatlunahu haqqa tilawatihi," that he said: (They follow it with its due following). In its chain of narration there are more than one of the unknown narrators, as mentioned by al-Khatib Abu Bakr Ahmad; nevertheless its meaning is sound.

Abu Musa al-Ash'ari said: Whoever follows the Qur'an, it will lead him to the gardens of Paradise. And from Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him: They are those who, when they pass by a verse of mercy, ask Allah for it, and when they pass by a verse of punishment, seek refuge from it. This meaning has also been related from the Prophet ﷺ: when he passed by a verse of mercy he asked, and when he passed by a verse of punishment he sought refuge.

Al-Hasan said: They are those who act upon its clear (muhkam) verses, believe in its ambiguous (mutashabih) verses, and leave to its knower (Allah) what is unclear to them. It was also said: they recite it with its due recitation. I say: this is far-fetched, unless the meaning is that they articulate its words properly and understand its meanings, for with understanding of the meanings, following becomes possible for whoever is granted success.

There are twenty issues in this passage.

**The first issue:** When the mention of the Ka'bah and the qiblah (direction of prayer) came up, it was connected to the mention of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and that he was the one who built the House. It was therefore the right of the Jews, who are of the offspring of Ibrahim, not to turn away from his religion. *Al-ibtila'* means testing and trial, and its meaning is a command and an act of worship. The name Ibrahim, according to what al-Mawardi mentioned, is Syriac in origin, and according to what Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned, it is Arabic, meaning "a compassionate father." Al-Suhayli said: "Often there occurs an agreement between Syriac and Arabic, or something close to it in pronunciation. Do you not see that the name Ibrahim means 'a merciful father,' because of his mercy toward children? For this reason he and his wife Sarah were made guardians of the children of believers who die young until the Day of Resurrection." I (al-Qurtubi) say: What confirms this is what al-Bukhari transmitted in the long hadith of the dream, from Samurah, in which the Prophet (ﷺ) saw Ibrahim (peace be upon him) in a garden, and around him were the children of people. We have discussed this in our book *al-Tadhkirah*, and praise be to Allah. This Ibrahim is, according to the view of some historians, the son of Tarakh, son of Nahur. In the revelation: ﴿And when Ibrahim said to his father Azar﴾ [See vol. 7, p. 22.] and likewise in Sahih al-Bukhari. There is no contradiction in this, as will be explained in *al-An'am*, if Allah the Exalted wills. He had four sons: Isma'il, Ishaq, Madyan, and Madai'in, according to what al-Suhayli mentioned. The object was placed before the subject for emphasis, since the fact that the Lord, blessed and exalted, is the one who tests is known, and the fact that the object pronoun in Arabic is attached to the subject necessitates placing the object first. So the sentence was constructed on this emphasis; understand this. The common reading is *Ibrahima* in the accusative, and *rabbuhu* in the nominative, as we have mentioned. It is narrated from Jabir ibn Zayd that he recited it the reverse way, and claimed that Ibn 'Abbas taught him to recite it so. The meaning would be: Ibrahim's Lord called upon him and asked, but this is far-fetched because of the *ba'* (with) in His words *bi-kalimat* (with words).

**The second issue:** The words of the Exalted, ﴿with words﴾. *Al-kalimat* is the plural of *kalimah* (word), and its real meaning goes back to the speech of the Creator, the Exalted. But it is used to express the duties that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was charged with. Since their imposition was by speech, they were named after it, just as Jesus was called a word, because he came into being from a word, which is "Be!" Naming a thing after its antecedent is one of the two kinds of *majaz* (figurative usage), so said Ibn al-'Arabi.

**The third issue:** The scholars differed about what is meant by *al-kalimat* (the words), in several opinions. One of them: the laws of Islam, which are thirty portions. Ten of them are in *Surat Bara'ah*: ﴿the repentant, the worshippers﴾ [See vol. 8, p. 269.] up to its end; ten in *al-Ahzab*: ﴿Indeed, the Muslim men and the Muslim women﴾ [See vol. 14, p. 185.] up to its end; and ten in *al-Mu'minun*: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded, who are humble in their prayer﴾ [See vol. 12, p. 102.] up to His words ﴿who guard their prayers﴾, and His words in *Sa'ala sa'il*: ﴿except those who pray﴾ up to His words ﴿and those who guard their prayer﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "Allah did not test anyone with these and he fulfilled all of them except Ibrahim (peace be upon him). He was tested with Islam and completed it, so Allah wrote for him freedom from blame, and said: ﴿and Ibrahim who fulfilled﴾ [See vol. 17, p. 113.]." Some said: they are the commands and prohibitions. Some said: the sacrifice of his son. Some said: the conveying of the message. The meanings are close. Mujahid said: they are His words: ﴿Indeed, I will make you a leader for the people.﴾ He said: "Will You make me a leader for the people?" He said: "Yes." He said: "And from my offspring?" He said: "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers." He said: "Will You make the House a place of return for the people?" He said: "Yes." He said: "And a sanctuary?" He said: "Yes." He said: "And show us our rites and accept our repentance?" He said: "Yes." He said: "And provide its people with fruits?" He said: "Yes." According to this view, Allah the Exalted is the One who completed them. More sound than this is what 'Abd al-Razzaq transmitted from Ma'mar, from Ibn Tawus, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿And when Ibrahim was tested by his Lord with words, and he fulfilled them﴾. He said: Allah tested him with purity: five in the head and five in the body. In the head: trimming the moustache, rinsing the mouth, sniffing water into the nose, using the miswak, and parting the hair. In the body: cutting the nails, shaving the pubic area, circumcision, plucking the armpit hair, and washing the place of defecation and urination with water. According to this view, the one who completed them is Ibrahim, and this is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. Mutarrif [in some copies: "Mutarraf"] narrated from Abu al-Jald that they are also ten, except that in place of the parting he put washing the *baraajim* (finger joints), and in place of purification after relief he put *al-istihdad* (shaving). Qatadah said: they are the rites of Hajj specifically. Al-Hasan said: they are the six features: the star, the moon, the sun, the fire, the migration, and circumcision. Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: These opinions are not contradictory, because all of this is what Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was tested with. I (al-Qurtubi) say: In the *Muwatta'* and elsewhere, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, that he heard Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab say: "Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was the first to be circumcised, the first to host a guest, the first to shave the pubic area, the first to trim the nails, the first to trim the moustache, and the first to grow white hair. When he saw the white hair he said: 'What is this?' It was said: 'Dignity.' He said: 'My Lord, increase me in dignity.'" Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah mentioned from Sa'id ibn Ibrahim, from his father, who said: "The first to deliver a sermon from pulpits was Ibrahim, the friend of Allah." Another said: "And the first to make *tharid* (bread crumbled in broth), the first to strike with the sword, the first to use the miswak, the first to clean with water, and the first to wear trousers." Mu'adh ibn Jabal narrated: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If I take a pulpit, my father Ibrahim took one, and if I take a staff, my father Ibrahim took one." I (al-Qurtubi) say: These are rulings that must be explained, understood, and discussed. The first of these is *al-khitan* (circumcision) and what has been related about it, and this is the subject of: **The fourth issue:** The scholars unanimously agreed that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was the first to be circumcised. They differed about the age at which he was circumcised. In the *Muwatta'*, from Abu Hurayrah as a statement of a companion: "He was a hundred and twenty years old, and he lived eighty years after that." Such a statement cannot be a matter of opinion. Al-Awza'i narrated it as a hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was circumcised when he was a hundred and twenty years old, then he lived eighty years after that." Abu 'Umar mentioned it. And it has been narrated as a *musnad* (traced) hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) by several routes other than that of Yahya: "He was circumcised when he reached eighty years, and he circumcised himself with the *qadum*." [Al-Nawawi said: "The narrators of Muslim agree on the light pronunciation of (*al-qadum*). The narrations of al-Bukhari differ on whether it is pronounced with a doubled letter or not. They said: The carpenter's tool is called *qadum* with a light pronunciation without emphasis. As for *al-Qadum* as a place in Syria, it may be pronounced lightly or with emphasis. Whoever reads it with emphasis means the village, while the light pronunciation may mean either the village or the tool, and most scholars read it lightly and mean the tool."] Thus in Sahih Muslim and elsewhere: "He was eighty years old," and this is the preserved version in the hadith of Ibn 'Ajlan and the hadith of al-A'raj from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ). 'Ikrimah said: "Ibrahim was circumcised when he was eighty years old." He said: "And no one performed the circumambulation of the House after that upon the religion of Ibrahim except one who was circumcised." So said 'Ikrimah, and al-Musayyab ibn Rafi' said likewise; al-Marwazi mentioned it. And *al-Qadum* is narrated both with emphasis and without. Abu al-Zinad said: *al-Qaddum* (with emphasis) is a place. **The fifth issue:** The scholars differed about circumcision. The majority of them held that it is among the emphasized *sunan* (recommended practices) and among the natural dispositions (*fitrah*) of Islam which it is not permissible to abandon for men. A group said: it is obligatory, based on His words: ﴿that follow the religion of Ibrahim, as a *hanif* (upright)﴾. Qatadah said: "This is circumcision." Some Maliki scholars inclined to this view, and it is the view of al-Shafi'i. Ibn Suraij argued for its obligation by the consensus on the prohibition of looking at the private parts, and he said: "Were circumcision not obligatory, looking at it would not be permitted for one who is circumcised." This was answered: such a thing is permitted for the benefit of the body, like the doctor's looking, and medicine is not obligatory by consensus, as will be explained in *al-Nahl*, if Allah the Exalted wills. Some of our companions argued with what al-Hajjaj ibn Arta'ah narrated from Abu al-Malih, from his father, from Shaddad ibn Aws, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Circumcision is a *sunnah* (practice) for men and an honor for women." Al-Hajjaj is not one whose narrations are used as evidence. I (al-Qurtubi) say: The strongest evidence on this subject is the hadith of Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "The natural disposition is five: circumcision..." the hadith, which will come. Abu Dawud narrated from Umm 'Atiyyah that a woman used to circumcise women in Madinah, so the Prophet (ﷺ) said to her: "Do not cut too deeply, for that is better for the woman and more loved by the husband." Abu Dawud said: "This hadith is weak; its narrator is unknown." In a narration mentioned by Razin: "And do not cut too deeply, for it brightens the face and is more pleasing to the man." **The sixth issue:** If a boy is born circumcised, then the burden of circumcision has been spared him. Al-Maymuni said: Ahmad said to me: "There is a man here who had a son born circumcised, and he was greatly distressed by this." I said to him: "If Allah has spared you the burden, why is your distress over this?" **The seventh issue:** Abu al-Faraj al-Jawzi said: I was told, from Ka'b al-Ahbar, who said: Thirteen of the prophets were created circumcised: Adam, Shith, Idris, Nuh, Sam, Lut, Yusuf, Musa, Shu'ayb, Sulayman, Yahya, 'Isa, and the Prophet (ﷺ). Muhammad ibn Habib al-Hashimi said: They are fourteen: Adam, Shith, Nuh, Hud, Salih, Lut, Shu'ayb, Yusuf, Musa, Sulayman, Zakariyya, 'Isa, Handhalah ibn Safwan (the prophet of the People of the Rass) [In *al-Lisan*: "al-Zajjaj said: It is narrated that *al-Rass* are the dwellings of a group of Thamud. He said: It is also narrated that *al-Rass* is a village in Yamamah called Falaj, and it is narrated that they denied their prophet and threw him into a well, meaning they pushed him into it until he died, and it is narrated that *al-Rass* is a well, and every well among the Arabs is a *rass*."], and Muhammad, may Allah bless him and them all. I (al-Qurtubi) say: The narrations differ regarding the Prophet (ﷺ). Abu Nu'aym al-Hafiz mentioned in *Kitab al-Hilyah* with his chain that the Prophet (ﷺ) was born circumcised. Abu 'Umar, in *al-Tamhid*, traced: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Ahmad told us, Muhammad ibn 'Isa told us, Yahya ibn Ayyub ibn Badi [in the originals: "Ziyad," and the correction is from *Tahdhib al-Tahdhib*] al-'Allaf told us, Muhammad ibn Abi al-Sarri al-'Asqalani told us, al-Walid ibn Muslim told us, from Shu'ayb, from 'Ata' al-Khurasani, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas: that 'Abd al-Muttalib circumcised the Prophet (ﷺ) on his seventh day, made a feast for him, and named him "Muhammad." Abu 'Umar said: "This is a *musnad* (traced) hadith, *gharib* (rare)." Yahya ibn Ayyub said: "I sought..."

...this hadith, and I did not find it with anyone among the people of hadith whom I met, except with Ibn Abi al-Sarri. Abu Umar (Ibn Abd al-Barr) said: It has been said that the Prophet (ﷺ) was born circumcised.

Eighth: The scholars differed over when a boy should be circumcised. It is established in the reports from a group of scholars that they said: Ibrahim circumcised Isma'il when he was thirteen years old, and he circumcised his son Ishaq on the seventh day. It is narrated from Fatimah that she used to circumcise her son on the seventh day. Malik denied this and said, "That is from the practice of the Jews." Ibn Wahb reported this from him. Al-Layth ibn Sa'd said: A boy is circumcised between the ages of seven and ten. Ibn Wahb narrated something similar from Malik. Ahmad said: "I have not heard anything about this."

In al-Bukhari, it is reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr who said: Ibn Abbas was asked, "How old were you when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed away?" He said, "I was circumcised at that time." He said: "They did not circumcise a man until he reached puberty or came close to puberty." The scholars recommended that an adult man who embraces Islam be circumcised. Ata' used to say: "His Islam is not complete until he is circumcised, even if he is eighty years old." It is narrated from al-Hasan that he granted a concession to an elderly man who embraces Islam that he need not be circumcised, and he saw no harm in his testimony, his slaughter, his Hajj, or his prayer. Ibn Abd al-Barr said: "The majority of the scholars hold this view." The hadith of Buraydah concerning the Hajj of the uncircumcised man (al-aghlaf) is not authentic. It is reported from Ibn Abbas, Jabir ibn Zayd, and Ikrimah that the meat of the uncircumcised man is not lawful to eat and his testimony is not accepted.

Ninth: As for his saying, "and the first to use the razor (istihdad)": istihdad means using iron (a razor) to shave the pubic area (al-'anah). Umm Salamah narrated that when the Prophet (ﷺ) applied depilatory paste (itlaa)[[itlaa: meaning with nura, which is a stone from which a paste is made to remove hair from the hidden parts of the body.]], he would himself treat his pubic area with his hand. Ibn Abbas narrated that a man applied depilatory paste to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and when he reached his pubic area, he said to him, "Get away from me," and then he applied the paste to his pubic area with his own hand. Anas narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) did not use depilatory paste, and when the hair on his pubic area grew thick, he would shave it. Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: "This indicates that most of his practice was shaving, and he used depilatory paste only rarely, so that the two hadiths can be reconciled."

**The tenth matter: trimming the nails.** *Taqlim al-adhfar* means cutting them, and *al-qulama* is what is cut off. Malik said: "I like that women should do the same as men regarding cutting the nails and shaving the pubic hair." This was related by al-Harith ibn Miskin and Sahnun, from Ibn al-Qasim.

al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim mentioned it in his *Nawadir al-Usul* (the twenty-ninth principle): Umar ibn Abi Umar narrated to us, saying: Ibrahim ibn al-Ala al-Zubaydi narrated to us, from Umar ibn Bilal al-Fazari, who said: I heard Abdullah ibn Bishr al-Mazini say: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Cut your nails, bury your trimmings, cleanse your finger joints, clean your gums of food, use the siwak, and do not come to me *qukhran bukhran*."[[The manuscripts are uncertain about the spelling of this word; the correction is from *Nawadir al-Usul*. The author, may Allah have mercy on him, will quote al-Tirmidhi's discussion of this hadith.]] Then he discussed it at length and excellently. Al-Tirmidhi said: As for cutting the nails, it is because they scratch, gouge and harm, and they are a gathering place for filth. Sometimes a person becomes junub (in a state of major ritual impurity requiring a full bath), and the water does not reach the skin because of the filth, so he remains junub. If, after the bath, a spot the size of a needle's point on his body is not washed, he remains junub until the bath covers his whole body. Therefore he urged them to cut their nails. *Al-adafir* is the plural of *al-udhfur*, and *al-adhfar* is the plural of *al-zufr*.

In the hadith of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he forgot something in his prayer, he said: "What is wrong with me that I do not see the *rafgh*[[al-rafgh: the filth between the fingertip and the nail.]] between the nail and the fingertip of one of you, and one of you asks me about the news of the heaven while there is janabah and *al-tafath* (uncleanliness) under his nails?"

Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Muhammad al-Tabari, known as al-Kiya, also mentioned this report in his *Ahkam al-Quran*, from Sulayman ibn Faraj Abu Wasil, who said: I came to Abu Ayyub, may Allah be pleased with him, and shook his hand. He saw that my nails were long and said: A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) asking him about the news of the heaven, and he said: "How can one of you ask about the news of the heaven while his nails are like the nails of a bird, until filth and *al-tafath* gather in them?"

As for his saying: "Bury your trimmings," the body of the believer is sacred. Whatever falls from it and separates from it still retains that sanctity, so it is right that one should bury it, just as if he died he would be buried. When part of him dies, his sanctity is likewise honoured by burying it, so that it is not scattered, does not fall into the fire, or into filthy rubbish heaps. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) also ordered that his blood be buried where he was cupped, so that dogs would not search for it. My father, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, narrated this to us, saying: Musa ibn Isma'il narrated to us, saying: al-Hunayd ibn al-Qasim ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Ma'iz narrated to us, saying: I heard Amir ibn Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr say that his father told him that he came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was being cupped. When he finished, he said: "O Abdullah, take this blood, pour it out where no one can see you." When he went away from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he went to the blood and drank it. When he returned, the Prophet said: "O Abdullah, what did you do with it?" He said: "I put it in the most hidden place I thought would be hidden from people." He said: "Perhaps you drank it?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Why did you drink the blood? [Woe to people because of you[[An addition from the book *Nawadir al-Usul*.]] and] woe to you because of people."

My father narrated to me, saying: Malik ibn Sulayman al-Harawi narrated to us, saying: Dawud ibn Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, from Hisham ibn Urwa, from his father, from Aisha, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to order that seven things from a human being be buried: hair, nail, blood, menstrual blood, tooth, foreskin, and *al-bashima*.

As for his saying: "Cleanse your finger joints": *al-barajim* are those creases at the joints, which are a gathering place for grime. Its singular is *burjuma*, which is the back of the knuckle of each joint. The back of the knuckle is called *burjuma*, and what lies between two knuckles is called *rajiba*, with plural *rawajib*, which lie on the back of the finger, namely the bone of the finger. Each finger has two *burjumas* and three *rawajib*, except the thumb, which has one *burjuma* and two *rawajib*. He ordered that they be cleaned so that they would not become grimy, so that janabah would not remain in them, and so that grime would not come between the water and the skin.

As for his saying: "Clean your gums": *al-lithah* is singular and *al-lithat* is plural; it is the flesh above the teeth and below them, and it is where the teeth grow. *Al-umur* is the small amount of flesh between two teeth, singular *amr*. He ordered that they be cleaned so that remnants of food would not remain in them, which would change the breath and make the smell offensive, and the two angels would be harmed, because it is the path of the Quran and the seat of the two angels is near the canine teeth.

A report was transmitted concerning the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Not a word does he utter but there is a watcher beside him, ready﴾[[See vol. 17, p. 11.]] that he said: "Beside his canine teeth." Muhammad ibn Ali al-Shaqiqi narrated this to us, saying: I heard my father mention it from Sufyan ibn Uyayna, and what he said was right, because *al-lafz* (pronouncing words) is the action of the two lips, expelling speech from the tongue to the outside. His saying *ladayhi* means "with him," and *al-dayy* and *al-ind* in their common usage have the same meaning, as does *ladun*, where the nun is extra. So it is as if the verse indicates that the watcher is ready near the harsh speech, which is the canine tooth.

As for his saying: "Use the siwak": it is the *siwak*, derived from *al-sinn* (tooth), that is, clean the tooth.

As for his saying: "Do not come to me *qukhran bukhran*": the version I know is *fahlan wa-qulhan* (with bad breath and yellow teeth). I heard al-Jarud mention from al-Nadr: *al-aqlah* is one whose teeth have yellowed until the inside of them has become foul-smelling.
