I do not know *al-qakhar*. *Al-bakhar* is the one whose skin gives off an offensive smell that you notice. It is said: a man is *abkhar*, and men are *bukhur*.

al-Jarud narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Mansur, from Abu Ali, from Abu Ja'far ibn Tamam ibn al-Abbas, from his father, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Use the siwak; why do you come to me with yellow teeth?"

**The eleventh matter: trimming the moustache.** This means taking from it until the edge of the lip appears, which is the *al-itar* (the border of the lip). One should not shave it off, which would make him look like a mutilated person; this was said by Malik. Ibn Abd al-Hakam reported from him: "I think the one who shaves his moustache should be disciplined." Ashhab reported from him that he said concerning shaving the moustache: "This is an innovation, and I think whoever does it should be beaten painfully." Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: Malik said: "I think whoever shaves it should be beaten painfully," as if he regards it as disfiguring oneself. Likewise, plucking the hair (is disliked), and trimming it is better than shaving it.

Similarly, it is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he had *limma* (hair reaching the shoulders), and his companions had either abundant hair or short hair. He only shaved his head, and they shaved their heads only during the rites of pilgrimage.

It is related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to trim his nails and moustache before going out to the Friday prayer.

al-Tahawi said: We did not find any explicit ruling from al-Shafi'i on this. His companions whom we have seen, al-Muzani and al-Rabi', used to trim their moustaches closely, and this indicates that they took it from al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him. He said: As for Abu Hanifa, Zufar, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, their view regarding head hair and moustache was that shaving them close is better than trimming. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad reported from al-Shafi'i that his view on shaving the moustache is the same as that of Abu Hanifa.

Abu Bakr al-Athram said: I saw Ahmad ibn Hanbal trimming his moustache very closely, and I heard him asked about the Sunnah concerning trimming the moustache, and he said: "It should be trimmed closely, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Trim the moustaches closely.'"

Abu Umar said: In this matter there are two principles. The first: "Ahfu" (trim closely), which is a word open to interpretation. The second: cutting the moustache, which is explicit, and the explicit governs the ambiguous. This is the practice of the people of Madina, and it is the best of what has been said on this matter.

al-Tirmidhi related from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to trim some of his moustache and say: "Indeed Ibrahim, the Friend of the Merciful, used to do this." He said: This is a *hasan gharib* hadith.

Muslim narrated from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The fitrah (natural disposition) consists of five: circumcision, removing pubic hair, trimming the moustache, cutting the nails, and plucking the armpit hair."

Also in it, from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Oppose the polytheists: trim the moustaches closely and let the beards grow."[[Trimming the moustache means cutting what has grown long from it. Letting the beard grow means leaving it abundant.]] The non-Arabs trim their beards and leave their moustaches long, or leave both long, and that is the opposite of beauty and cleanliness.

Razin reported from Nafi' that Ibn Umar used to trim his moustache until he could see the skin, and he would take these two, meaning what is between the moustache and the beard. In al-Bukhari: Ibn Umar used to take from the length of his beard what exceeded a fistful when he performed Hajj or Umra.

al-Tirmidhi related from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to take from his beard, both its width and its length. He said: This is a *gharib* hadith.

**The twelfth matter:** As for the armpit, the Sunnah for it is plucking, just as the Sunnah for the pubic area is shaving. If it were reversed it would be permissible, since cleanliness is achieved, but the first is better, because it is the easier and customary practice.

**The thirteenth matter: parting the hair.** This means parting it at the *mafraq* (the middle of the head).[[al-mafraq: the middle of the head.]] Regarding his description (ﷺ): if his braid parted, he would part it; it is said: "I parted the hair, I part it, parting." That is, if his head hair parted, he parted it at its middle; if it did not part, he left it as one single *wafra*.[[al-wafra: the hair gathered on the head.]]

al-Nasa'i related from Ibn Abbas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to let his hair hang down, and the polytheists used to part their hair. He loved to agree with the People of the Book in matters about which he had not been commanded anything. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) parted his hair after that. Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated it from Anas.

al-Qadi Iyad said: *Sadl* of the hair is letting it hang loose, and what is meant here according to the scholars is letting it hang over the forehead and making it like a fringe. Parting the hair is a Sunnah, because it is what the Prophet (ﷺ) returned to.

It is related that Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, whenever he left the Friday prayer, stationed guards at the door of the mosque who would shave the forelock of anyone who had not parted his hair. It has been said that parting the hair was from the Sunnah of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, but Allah knows best.

**The fourteenth matter:** As for grey hair, it is light, and plucking it is disliked. In al-Nasa'i and Abu Dawud, from the hadith of Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not pluck grey hairs. No Muslim grows a grey hair in Islam except that it will be a light for him on the Day of Resurrection, and Allah records for him a good deed and removes a sin from him."

I say: Just as plucking it is disliked, so too is dyeing it black. As for dyeing it with something other than black, it is permissible, because of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying concerning Abu Quhafa, when he was brought to him with a beard as white as *al-thughama* (a plant with white flowers and seeds, resembling white hair):[[al-thughama: a plant with white fruit and flowers, whose whiteness is compared to grey hair.]] "Change this with something and avoid black."

And whoever said it spoke well:

*Its top is blackened while its root is whitened,*
*and there is no good in the top when the root is corrupt.*

And another said:

*O you who dye grey hair with henna, hiding it:*
*ask the King to give it a cover from the Fire.*

**Fifteenth:** As for *al-tharid* (a dish of bread soaked in broth), it is the most blessed and most excellent of foods, and it is the food of the Arabs. The Prophet ﷺ affirmed its superiority over all other foods when he said: "The superiority of ʿAʾisha over the women is like the superiority of *tharid* over all other food." In *Sahih al-Busti*, it is reported from Asma' bint Abi Bakr that when she prepared *tharid*, she would cover it for a while until its steam had gone, and she would say: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'It is greater in blessing.'"

**Sixteenth:** I say: All of this is in the sense of what ʿAbd al-Razzaq reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, and what Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab and others said. The discussion of rinsing the mouth (*madmada*), sniffing water into the nose (*istinshaq*), and the siwak (tooth-stick) will come in Surat al-Nisa' [[See vol. 5, p. 212.]], the ruling on cleansing after relieving oneself (*istinja'*) in Surat al-Tawba [[See vol. 8, p. 262.]], and the ruling on hospitality in Surat Hud [[See vol. 9, p. 64.]], if Allah the Exalted wills.

Muslim reported from Anas, who said: "We were given a time limit regarding trimming the moustache, clipping the nails, plucking the armpit hair, and shaving the pubic hair, not to leave them for more than forty nights." Our scholars said: "This is a limit on the maximum period. The recommended practice is to attend to these matters from one Friday to the next." This hadith is narrated by Jaʿfar ibn Sulayman. Al-ʿUqayli said: "There is scrutiny regarding his narration." Abu ʿUmar said about him: "He is not a proof, because of his poor memory and his frequent errors." This hadith is not strong in terms of transmission, but some people have acted upon it, and most of them hold that there is no fixed limit in this matter. And success is from Allah.

**Seventeenth:** The words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, I will make you a leader (*imam*) for mankind﴾. *Al-imam* means an exemplar to be followed. From this root, a builder's plumb line is called *imam*, and so is a road, because people travel toward it, that is, it is aimed at by travellers. So the meaning is: We have made you a leader for people, whom they follow in these qualities, and whom the righteous emulate. Allah the Exalted made him a leader for those who obey Him. For this reason, the nations unanimously agree in claiming him, and Allah knows best, as one who was a *hanif* (upright monotheist).

**Eighteenth:** The words of the Exalted: ﴿And from my offspring﴾. This is a supplication made in the form of a request to Allah the Exalted, meaning: "And from my offspring, O Lord, do [make some leaders]." It was also said that this is from him in the form of an inquiry about them, meaning: "And from my offspring, O Lord, what will happen?" So Allah the Exalted informed him that among them there would be a sinner and a wrongdoer who does not deserve leadership. Ibn ʿAbbas said: Ibrahim, peace be upon him, asked that a leader be made from his offspring, so Allah informed him that among his offspring there would be those who disobey. Then He said: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾.

**Nineteenth:** The words of the Exalted: ﴿And from my offspring﴾. The root of *dhurriyya* is a form (*fi'liyya*) derived from *dharr* (scattering), because Allah the Exalted brought forth creation from the loins of Adam, peace be upon him, like tiny particles (*dharr*) when He made them bear witness against themselves. It was also said: it is derived from *dhara'a Allahu al-khalq*, meaning Allah created creation, *yadhra'uhum dharʾan* (created them). From this comes *dhurriyya*, which is the offspring of both humans and jinn. However, the Arabs dropped its hamza, and the plural is *dharari*. Zayd ibn Thabit read *dhirriyya* with a kasra on the dhal and *dharriyya* with a fatha. Ibn Jinni Abu al-Fath ʿUthman said: The root of this word may have four possible forms: first, *dhara'a*; second, *dharara*; third, *dharawa*; and fourth, *dharaya*. As for the hamza, it is from *dhara'a Allahu al-khalq*. As for *dharara*, it is from the word *dharr* and its meaning, due to what occurs in the report that "creation was like *dharr*." As for the waw and ya', they come from *dharawtu al-habba* and *dharaytuhu*, both of which are used, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So it becomes dry stubble, which the winds scatter﴾, and this is due to its fineness and lightness, and that state applies to *dharr* too. Al-Jawhari said: "The wind scattered the dust and other things, *tadhruwhu* and *tadhrawihi*, *dharwan* and *dhariyan*, meaning it blew it away. From this comes the saying: 'People winnowed the wheat' (*dharaa al-nas al-hinta*), and *adhraytu al-shay'* when I threw it, like your throwing seed for planting. And he struck him and *adhrahu* from the back of his mount, meaning he threw him off." Al-Khalil said: They were called *dhurriyya* because Allah the Exalted scattered them upon the earth just as the farmer scatters seed. It was also said: the original is *dhurruwwiyya*, but because the doubling (of the rāʾ) was frequent, one of the two rāʾs was replaced with a yāʾ, so it became *dhurruwiyya*, and then the waw was assimilated into the yāʾ, so it became *dhurriyya*. The meaning of *dhurriyya* here is specifically the children, though it may also be applied to both ancestors and descendants. From this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring﴾, meaning their forefathers [[See vol. 15, p. 34.]].

**Twentieth:** The words of the Exalted: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾. Scholars differ regarding what is meant by *ʿahd* (covenant). Abu Salih reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that it is prophethood, and al-Suddi said the same. Mujahid said: it is leadership (*imama*). Qatada said: it is faith. ʿAta' said: it is mercy. Al-Dahhak said: it is the religion of Allah the Exalted. It was also said: His covenant is His command, and *ʿahd* is used to mean a command, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, Allah enjoined upon us [[See vol. 4, p. 295.]]﴾, meaning commanded us. And He says: ﴿Did I not enjoin upon you, O children of Adam﴾, meaning, did I not previously command you? If the covenant of Allah is His commands, then His words ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ mean that it is not permissible for them to be in the position of those whose commands from Allah are accepted, nor do they uphold them, as will be explained shortly after this, if Allah the Exalted wills. Maʿmar reported from Qatada regarding the words of the Exalted ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ that he said: "The covenant of Allah does not reach the wrongdoers in the Hereafter. As for in this world, the wrongdoer has indeed attained it: he believed in it, ate, lived, and saw." Al-Zajjaj said: This is a good view, meaning: My promises do not reach the wrongdoers; that is, I do not grant them security from My punishment. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: The wrongdoer here is the polytheist. Ibn Masʿud and Talha ibn Musarrif read *la yanalu ʿahdi al-zalimuna* with the *zalimuna* in the nominative (*raf*). The rest read it in the accusative (*nasb*). Hamza, Hafs, and Ibn Muhaysin made the yāʾ in *ʿahdi* quiescent (sukun), while the rest pronounced it with a fatha.

**Twenty-first:** A group of scholars have used this verse to prove that the imam must be one of people of justice, goodness, and virtue, together with the strength to carry out that duty. He is the one whom the Prophet ﷺ commanded not to dispute the authority with its people, as was discussed earlier [[See vol. 1, p. 264, second edition.]]. As for the people of sin, oppression, and injustice, they are not fit for it, because of the words of the Exalted: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾. For this reason, Ibn al-Zubayr and al-Husayn ibn ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with them, rebelled. The best people and scholars of Iraq rose up against al-Hajjaj, and the people of Madina expelled the Umayyads and fought against them. Then there was the Battle of al-Harra, which was inflicted upon them by Muslim ibn ʿUqba [[The text in the originals reads "ʿUqba ibn Muslim," which is an error. Concerning the Day of al-Harra, Ibn al-Athir mentions in *al-Nihaya*: "It is a famous day in Islam, during the days of Yazid ibn Muʿawiya, when his army from the people of Syria, whom he had dispatched to fight the people of Madina, plundered the city. They included Companions and Successors. Muslim ibn ʿUqba al-Muri was placed in command of them in Dhu al-Hijja of the year sixty-three, and after it Yazid died. Al-Harra is an area outside Madina, containing many black stones, and the battle took place there." See also Tarikh al-Tabari, Ibn al-Athir, and al-Nujum al-Zahira, under the events of the year sixty-three.]]. The view of most scholars is that patience upon the obedience of an unjust imam is better than rebellion against him, because disputing with him and rebelling against him replaces security with fear, causes the shedding of blood, unleashes the hands of fools, launches raids against the Muslims, and spreads corruption on earth. The first view is the position of a group of the Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school), and it is the position of the Khawarij (a radical early sect). Take note of this.

**Twenty-second:** Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: Anyone who is a wrongdoer cannot be a prophet, a caliph, a judge, a mufti, or a prayer leader, and what he narrates from the Lawgiver (the Prophet ﷺ) is not accepted, and his testimony in legal matters is not accepted. However, he is not removed from office because of his wickedness until those who loose and bind (*ahl al-hall wa al-ʿaqd*) remove him. Whatever rulings he issued in the past that agree with what is correct stand and are not overturned. Malik explicitly stated this regarding the Khawarij and the rebels (*al-bughat*): their rulings are not overturned if they reached them by some form of independent reasoning (*ijtihad*) and did not break the consensus (*ijma'*) or contradict the explicit texts. We say this because of the consensus of the Companions. The Khawarij rose up in their days, but it is not reported that the imams pursued their rulings, nor did they overturn any of them, nor did they re-collect zakat or re-establish the legal punishments (*hudud*) that they had collected and enforced. This shows that if they hit upon the correct way of reasoning, their rulings were not to be challenged.

**Twenty-third:** Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: As for taking stipends (*arzaq*) from unjust imams, there are three situations. If everything in their possession was acquired in accordance with the law of Sharia, then it is permissible to take it, and the Companions and the Successors took from the hand of al-Hajjaj and others. If it is mixed, lawful and unjust, as is the case with the rulers today, then abstaining from it is the more cautious course (*al-wara'*), but it is permissible for the needy to take it. This is like a thief who has stolen property in his possession, while there is also good, lawful property, and a man has appointed him as his agent over it. The thief comes and gives charity from it to someone. It is permissible to accept that charity, even though it is possible that the thief is giving away some of what he has stolen, provided there is nothing known for certain about his plundering. Similarly, if he sells or buys, the contract is valid and binding, even though the cautious course is to keep away from it. This is because wealth is not forbidden in itself; it is forbidden only because of the means by which it was obtained. If what is in their hands is clear oppression, it is not permissible to take it from them. And if the wealth in their hands is usurped but has no known owner or claimant, then it is like property found in the hands of thieves and highway robbers. It is placed in the public treasury (*bayt al-mal*), and its owner is awaited according to the best judgment. If it is not known, the imam spends it on the interests of the Muslims.

The Almighty's words: ﴿And when We made the House a place of return for the people and a sanctuary﴾. On this there are two issues.

The first: the Almighty's words ﴿made﴾ mean "appointed," because it takes two objects, and this has already been discussed. "The House" means the Ka'bah. "A place of return" means a place to which people return. It is said: *thaba yathubu mathaban wa mathabatan wa thu'ūban wa thawabānan* (he returned). So *mathabah* is a verbal noun used as a descriptive, and it refers to the place to which one returns, that is, to which one goes back. Waraqah ibn Nawfal said about the Ka'bah [[What appears in *al-Lisan* and in the commentary on *al-Qamus*, under the root "thawb," is that the verse belongs to Abu Talib.]]:

*A place of return for all the tribes' scattered clans,*
*to which the swift she-camels hasten with their loads.*

Al-A'mash read *mathābāt* (in the plural). It may also be derived from *thawāb* (reward), meaning that people are rewarded there. Mujahid said: no one ever finishes his need from it. A poet said:

*The House was made a place of return for them;*
*never in time do they finish their need from it.*

The original form is *mathūbah*. The vowel of the *waw* was moved onto the *tha'*, and then the *waw* became an *alif*, following the pattern of *tha/yathūbu*. It is in the accusative as a second object. The *ta' marbūtah* was added for emphasis, because so many people return to it. It is said that few people leave the House without feeling they have not yet fulfilled their need of it. So it is like *nassābah* (a great genealogist) and *allāmah* (a great scholar). This was said by al-Akhfash. Others said that it is the feminine ending of the verbal noun and not for emphasis.

If it is objected that not everyone who comes to it returns to it, the answer is that the meaning is not restricted to those who come to it. Rather, the meaning is that it is never without visitors from the general public, and it never lacks people who intend it from among mankind. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: the Almighty's words ﴿and a sanctuary﴾. Abu Hanifah and a group of jurists of the major cities used this verse to argue that the prescribed punishment (*hadd*) should not be carried out within the Sacred Precinct (*haram*) against a married person (*muhsan*) or a thief who seeks refuge there. They reinforced this with the Almighty's words: "And whoever enters it is safe" [Q 3:97], as if He had said: grant safety to whoever enters the House. The correct view is that the prescribed punishments are carried out within the Sacred Precinct, and that this verse has been abrogated (*naskh*, meaning the replacement of a ruling by a later one). This is because there is agreement that one is not killed inside the House itself, but is killed outside it. The disagreement is only about whether one may be killed within the Sacred Precinct or not. The Sacred Precinct is not the House in the literal sense. They also agreed that if someone commits murder within the Sacred Precinct, he is killed for it. If he commits a prescribed offense there, the penalty is carried out on him there. If he wages war there, he is fought and killed on the spot. Abu Hanifah said: whoever takes refuge in the Sacred Precinct is not killed there, nor is he pursued, but he is constantly restricted until he dies or leaves. We kill him with the sword, while he kills himself through hunger and deprivation. What killing is more severe than this?

The Almighty's words ﴿and a sanctuary﴾ are an emphasis on the command to face the Ka'bah in prayer, that is: this virtue is not found in Jerusalem, people do not make pilgrimage to it, and whoever seeks refuge in the Sacred Precinct is safe from being raided. The explanation of this will come, Allah willing, in *al-Ma'idah* [[See vol. 6, p. 325.]].

The Almighty's words: ﴿And take the station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer﴾. On this there are three issues.

The first: the Almighty's words ﴿And take﴾. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read it with a *fathah* on the *kha'* (*wa-attakhadhū*), as a statement about those among the followers of Ibrahim who took it. It is conjoined to "We made," meaning: We made the House a place of return, and they took it as a place of prayer. It was also said that it is conjoined to an implied *idh* (when), as if He said: "And when We made the House a place of return, and when they took..." So on the first reading the speech is a single sentence, and on the second it is two sentences. The majority of reciters read *wa-attakhidhū* with a *kasrah* on the *kha'* as an imperative. They separated it from the first clause and made it a sentence conjoined to another sentence. Al-Mahdawi said: it may be conjoined to "remember My blessing," as if He said that to the Jews. Or it may be conjoined to the meaning of "when We made the House," because its meaning is "remember when We made." Or it may be conjoined to the meaning of his words "a place of return," because its meaning is "return."

The second: Ibn 'Umar narrated that 'Umar said: "I agreed with my Lord in three matters: the station of Ibrahim, the veil, and the captives of Badr." Muslim and others recorded it. al-Bukhari recorded from Anas, who said: 'Umar said: "I agreed with Allah in three matters," or "my Lord agreed with me in three matters..." the hadith. Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi recorded it in his *Musnad*, saying: Hammad ibn Salamah narrated to us, 'Ali ibn Zayd narrated to us, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: 'Umar said: "I agreed with my Lord in four matters. I said: O Messenger of Allah, what if you prayed behind the station (of Ibrahim)? Then this verse was revealed: 'And take the station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer.' And I said: O Messenger of Allah, what if you put a veil over your wives, for the good and the wicked enter upon them? So Allah revealed: 'And when you ask them for something, ask them from behind a veil' [Q 33:53]. And this verse was revealed: 'We created man from an extract of clay' [Q 23:12]. When it was revealed I said: 'Blessed is Allah, the best of creators,' and then it was revealed: 'So blessed is Allah, the best of creators' [Q 23:14]. I entered upon the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'You must desist, or Allah will replace him with wives better than you,' and then the verse was revealed: 'It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will give him wives better than you' [Q 66:5]." [[See vol. 18, p. 193.]] I say: there is no mention of the captives in this narration, so 'Umar's agreement with his Lord would be in five matters.

The third: the Almighty's words ﴿from the station﴾. *Al-maqam* in the language means the place where the two feet stand. al-Nahhas said: "*maqam*" comes from *qama yaqumu* and can be a verbal noun and a noun of place. *Muqam* comes from *aqama*. As for Zuhayr's words:

*Among them are stations of fine faces,*
*and assemblies in which speech and action are exchanged.*

its meaning is: among them are people of stations. There is disagreement about identifying the station, with several views. The most correct is that it is the stone that people know today, where they pray two rak'ahs after the tawaf of arrival. This is the view of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and others. In Muslim's *Sahih*, in the lengthy hadith of Jabir, when the Prophet (ﷺ) saw the House, he touched the corner, then did the *ramal* (quick steps) for three rounds and walked for four, then he went forward to the station of Ibrahim and recited "And take the station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer," and prayed two rak'ahs, reciting in them "Say: He is Allah, the One" and "Say: O disbelievers." This indicates that the two rak'ahs of tawaf and others of the prayers [for the people of Makkah [[An addition required by the context; we relied on it from what appears in the sixth issue on p. 116 of this volume.]] are superior, and it indicates in one respect that tawaf is superior for outsiders, as will come. In al-Bukhari: it is the stone on which Ibrahim stood when he became too weak to lift the stones that Isma'il was handing him while building the House, and his feet sank into it. Anas said: "I saw in the station the mark of his fingers, his heel, and the soles of his feet, but people's hands wiping it removed it." al-Qushayri related this. al-Suddi said: the station is the stone that the wife of Isma'il placed under the feet of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) when she washed his head. From Ibn 'Abbas also, and Mujahid, 'Ikrimah [[This name is missing from b, j, z.]], and 'Ata': the station is the whole Hajj. From 'Ata': 'Arafat, Muzdalifah and the stoning pillars. This was said by al-Sha'bi. al-Nakha'i: the whole Sacred Precinct is the station of Ibrahim. This was said by Mujahid. I say: the correct view about the station is the first, according to what is established in the *Sahih*.

Abu Nu'aym transmitted from the hadith of Muhammad ibn Suqah, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, from Jabir, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) saw a man between the corner and the station, or between the door and the station, supplicating and saying: "O Allah, forgive so-and-so." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "What is this?" He said: "A man entrusted me to supplicate for him at this station." He said: "Go back, for your companion has been forgiven." Abu Nu'aym said: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Qadi narrated this to us, saying: Muhammad ibn 'Asim ibn Yahya al-Katib narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim al-Qattan al-Kufi narrated to us, saying: al-Harith ibn 'Imran al-Ja'fari narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Suqah, and he mentioned it. Abu Nu'aym said: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated it thus from al-Harith, from Muhammad, from Jabir, but it is known from the hadith of al-Harith, from Muhammad, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas.

The meaning of "a place of prayer" (*musalla*): a place to which one calls people (*mudda'an*) to pray there. Mujahid said this. It was also said: the place of prayer where one prays nearby. Qatadah said this. It was also said: a direction (*qiblah*) at which the imam stands. al-Hasan said this.

The Almighty's words: ﴿And We charged Ibrahim and Isma'il: Purify My House for those who circle it, those who stay in it for worship, and those who bow and prostrate﴾. On this there are six issues.

The first: the Almighty's words ﴿And We charged﴾. It was said: the meaning is "We commanded." It was also said: "We revealed." ﴿That purify﴾: the *an* is in a position of accusative by implied deletion of the preposition. Sibawayh said: it means "that," explanatory, so it has no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis). The Kufans said: it means "saying." ﴿Purify﴾: it was said that the meaning is: from idols, according to Mujahid and al-Zuhri. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: from afflictions and doubts. It was also said: from disbelievers. al-Suddi said: build it and found it in purity and with the intention of purity, which is like His words: "founded upon piety" [Q 9:108]. Yaman said: fumigate it and make it fragrant. ﴿My House﴾: He attributed the House to Himself as an attribution of honor and dignity, which is the attribution of a creature to its Creator, and of a possession to its Owner. al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, the people of Madinah, Hisham and Hafs read *baytiya* with a *fathah* on the *ya'*, and the others read it with a *sukun*.

The second: the Almighty's words ﴿for those who circle﴾. Its apparent meaning is those who circumambulate it. This is the view of 'Ata'. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it means for strangers who arrive at Makkah, but this is far-fetched. ﴿Those who stay﴾: the residents, both locals and strangers, according to 'Ata'. The same applies to His words "for those who circle." *Al-'ukuf* in the language means staying with something and devoting oneself to it, as the poet said [[It is al-'Ajjaj, describing a bull. The first half of the verse is: "So they cling to it when they go on pilgrimage."]]:

*They cling like the Nabataeans playing the fanzaja* [[*Al-fanzaja* and *al-fanzaj* (with a *fathah* and a silent letter): the dance of foreigners when some of them take hold of each other's hands while dancing.]]

Mujahid said: "al-'Akifun" means those who stay (in the sanctuary), i.e. the residents. Ibn 'Abbas said: those who pray. It was also said: those who sit without circumambulating, and the meanings are close. "wal-Ruka'i al-Sujud" means those who pray near the Ka'bah. Ruku' and sujud were singled out for mention because they are the closest states of the one praying to Allah, the Exalted. The linguistic meaning of ruku' and sujud has already been discussed (see vol. 1, pp. 291 and 344, second edition), and all praise is due to Allah.

The third issue: When Allah, the Exalted, said, ﴿that you purify My House﴾, its meaning includes all of the houses of Allah, the Exalted, so their ruling is the same as His regarding purity and cleanliness. The Ka'bah was singled out for mention either because there was nothing else there at that time, or because it has the greatest sanctity; the first is more evident, and Allah knows best. In the Revelation, ﴿in houses which Allah has permitted to be raised﴾ (see vol. 12, p. 264). The ruling on mosques will come there, Allah willing.

It is related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he heard the voice of a man in the mosque and said: "What is this! Do you know where you are?"

Hudhayfah said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah revealed to me: O brother of the warners, O brother of the messengers, warn your people that they should not enter any of My houses except with sound hearts, truthful tongues, clean hands and pure private parts; and that they should not enter any of My houses while anyone among them has a wrongful claim (against another), for I curse him as long as he stands before Me until he returns that injustice to its people. Then I will be his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, and he will be among My friends and chosen ones, and he will be my neighbour along with the prophets, the truthful ones, the martyrs and the righteous."

The fourth issue: Al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah, al-Thawri and a group of the early scholars used this verse as evidence for the permissibility of performing the obligatory and voluntary prayers inside the House. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: If one prays inside it facing one of its walls, his prayer is valid; if he prays facing the door while the door is open, his prayer is invalid; and likewise whoever prays on its roof, because he has not faced any part of it.

Malik said: The obligatory prayer and the sunnah prayers are not performed in it, but voluntary prayer may be performed in it; however, if one performs the obligatory prayer in it, he must repeat it within its time. Asbagh said: he must repeat it forever. I say: this is the sound view, because of what Muslim related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Usamah ibn Zayd informed me that when the Prophet (ﷺ) entered the House, he supplicated in all its corners and did not pray in it until he came out of it; and when he came out, he prayed two rak'ahs in front of the Ka'bah and said: "This is the qiblah." This is an explicit text.

If it is objected: al-Bukhari related from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), together with Usamah ibn Zayd, Bilal and 'Uthman ibn Talhah al-Hajabi, entered the House and they closed the door behind them. When they opened it, I was the first to enter, and I met Bilal and asked him: Did the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) pray in it? He said: Yes, between the two Yemeni pillars. Muslim also related it, and in it he said: He placed two pillars to his left, one pillar to his right, and three pillars behind him, and the House at that time was on six pillars.

We say: this may mean that he prayed in the sense of supplicating, as Usamah said, and it may mean that he performed the prayer in its customary form; and when it admits of both possibilities, the argument from it falls.

If it is objected: Ibn al-Mundhir and others related from Usamah, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) saw images in the Ka'bah, so I used to bring him water in a bucket with which he would strike those images. Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi also related it, saying: Ibn Abi Dhi'b narrated to us from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mihran, who said: 'Umayr, the freedman of Ibn 'Abbas, narrated to us from Usamah ibn Zayd, who said: I entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the Ka'bah and he saw images. He said: He called for a bucket of water, and I brought it to him, and he began erasing them and saying: "May Allah destroy a people who make images of what they cannot create." It is possible that the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed while Usamah was away seeking water, so Bilal witnessed what Usamah did not witness; thus the one who affirms is more worthy than the one who denies. Usamah himself said: "The people took the saying of Bilal and abandoned my saying."

Mujahid related from 'Abd Allah ibn Safwan, who said: I asked 'Umar ibn al-Khattab: How did the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) act when he entered the Ka'bah? He said: He prayed two rak'ahs. We say: this is to be understood as referring to voluntary prayer, and we know of no disagreement among the scholars concerning the validity of voluntary prayer in the Ka'bah; as for the obligatory prayer, it is not valid there, because Allah, the Exalted, specified the direction by His saying: ﴿So turn your faces toward it﴾, as will be explained, and by the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying when he came out: "This is the qiblah," thereby specifying it as Allah, the Exalted, specified it. Had the obligatory prayer been valid inside it, he would not have said: "This is the qiblah." By this the traditions can be reconciled, which is better than discarding some of them, so there is no contradiction, and all praise is due to Allah.

The fifth issue: The scholars also differed concerning prayer on the roof of the Ka'bah. Al-Shafi'i held the view we have mentioned. Malik said: whoever prays on the roof of the Ka'bah must repeat it within its time. It has been related from some of Malik's companions that he must repeat it forever. Abu Hanifah said: whoever prays on the roof of the Ka'bah, there is nothing upon him.

The sixth issue: The scholars also differed over which is more excellent: prayer beside the House or circumambulation of it? Malik said: circumambulation is more excellent for the people of the other regions, and prayer is more excellent for the people of Makkah. This is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' and Mujahid. The majority hold that prayer is more excellent. In a report: "Were it not for humble men, bowing elders, nursing infants and grazing animals, the punishment would have been poured upon you in a torrent." Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn 'Ali ibn Thabit al-Khatib mentioned in his book (al-Sabiq wal-Lahiq) from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Were it not for humble men among you, grazing animals and nursing children, punishment would have been poured upon the sinners in a torrent." In it, "and bowing elders" is not mentioned. In the hadith of Abu Dharr: "Prayer is the best of things to be undertaken, so increase it or lessen it." Related by al-Ajurri. The reports on the excellence of prayer and prostration are numerous, and they support the view of the majority, and Allah the Exalted knows best.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 126:**

In this verse there are three issues (masa'il).

**The first issue:** His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿a secure land﴾, meaning Makkah. So he (Ibrahim) prayed for his descendants and others to have security and abundant livelihood. It is narrated that when he made this supplication, God commanded Jibril, and he uprooted al-Ta'if from al-Sham and circled it around the House seven times. For this reason it was named al-Ta'if. Then he set it down in Tihama. At that time Makkah and its surroundings were a barren wasteland with no water and no vegetation, so God blessed the areas around it, such as al-Ta'if and others, and caused all kinds of fruits to grow in it, as will be explained, God willing, in the commentary on surah Ibrahim [[see vol. 9, p. 368 onward.]].

**The second issue:** The scholars differed over whether Makkah became a sanctuary (haram) of security through Ibrahim's request, or whether it was already so before him. There are two opinions.

The first is that it had always been a sanctuary, free from tyrannical oppressors, from earthquakes and landslides, and from all the calamities that befall lands. God placed in the hearts of rebellious people a reverence and awe for it, so that its people were distinguished by security from other people of the settlements. God, glory be to Him, also placed in it a great sign of His oneness: the hunting there. A dog and its prey may gather together, and the dog does not stir the prey or make it flee. But when both leave the sanctuary, the dog attacks it and returns to chasing it and it flees. Ibrahim asked his Lord only to make it secure from famine, drought and raids, and to provide its people with fruits. He did not mean what some people thought, that it was a prohibition on shedding blood against one who deserved execution, for that would make it very unlikely that Ibrahim (ﷺ) intended this, such that it could be said he asked God to establish in His law the prohibition of killing whoever seeks refuge in the sanctuary. This is very far-fetched.

The second opinion is that Makkah was lawful (halal) before the prayer of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), like other lands, and that by his prayer it became a secure sanctuary, just as Madinah became secure through the prohibition of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) after it had been lawful. Those who held the first opinion argued with the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said on the day of the Conquest of Makkah: (Indeed this land, God Most High made it sacred on the day He created the heavens and the earth, so it is sacred by the sanctity of God until the Day of Resurrection. Fighting in it was not made lawful for anyone before me, and it was made lawful for me only for an hour of a day. So it is sacred by the sanctity of God until the Day of Resurrection. Its thorn bush is not to be cut, its game is not to be frightened, and its lost property is not to be picked up except by one who will announce it, and its herbage (khala) is not to be cut.) Al-'Abbas said: "O Messenger of God, except for the idhkhir [[al-Idhkhir (with a kasra on the hamza and kha'): a fragrant grass with which houses are roofed over wooden beams, and which is burned instead of wood and charcoal. Al-Qayn: the blacksmith.]], for it is for their smiths and their houses." He said: (Except the idhkhir.) A similar hadith is that of Abu Shurayh. Both were narrated by Muslim and others. Also in Sahih Muslim, from 'Abd Allah ibn Zayd ibn 'Asim, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: (Indeed Ibrahim made Makkah sacred and prayed for its people, and I have made Madinah sacred as Ibrahim made Makkah sacred, and I have prayed for its measure of grain (sa') and its mudd [[measures of volume]] twice what Ibrahim prayed for the people of Makkah.)

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "There is no contradiction between the two hadiths. The first is an announcement of God's prior knowledge concerning it and His decree, and that the sanctity is for the duration of Adam and the times of the inhabiting of the region by faith. The second is an announcement of Ibrahim renewing its sanctity and making it manifest after it had been effaced. The first statement from the Prophet (ﷺ) on the second day of the Conquest was an announcement of magnifying the sanctity of Makkah for the believers by attributing the prohibition to God Most High. He mentioned Ibrahim at the making of Madinah sacred as an example for himself. Without doubt, the making of Madinah sacred is also from God Most High, and from His executed decree and His prior knowledge."

Al-Tabari said: Makkah was sacred, but God had not imposed this as an act of worship on creation until Ibrahim asked Him, and He made it sacred.

**The third issue:** His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And provide its people with fruits, those of them who believe﴾. The meaning of provision (rizq) has already been discussed [[see the twenty-second issue, vol. 1, p. 177.]]. The word thamarat (fruits) is the plural of thamara (fruit), and it has already been discussed [[see the fourth issue, vol. 1, p. 229.]]. The phrase "those of them who believe" (man amana) is a substitute (badal) for "its people", a substitution of part for whole (badal al-ba'd min al-kull). Faith (iman) means affirmation (tasdiq), which has already been discussed [[see the first issue, vol. 1, p. 162, second edition.]].

His saying: ﴿He said: And whoever disbelieves﴾. The word "man" (whoever) in His saying "And whoever disbelieves" is in the accusative position, and the implied meaning is "and provide whoever disbelieves." It may also be in the nominative position as the subject of an inceptive sentence (mubtada'), in which case it is a conditional, and the predicate (khabar) is "then I will let him enjoy" (fa-umatti'uhu), which is the response (jawab).

There is a disagreement as to whether this statement is from God Most High or from Ibrahim (peace be upon him). Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn Ishaq and others said: it is from God Most High. They read "fa-umatti'uhu" with a damma on the hamza, a fatha on the mim, and a shadda on the ta', and "thumma adtarruhu" with a hamza of cutting (qat') and a damma on the ra'. The seven readers (al-qurra' al-sab'a) did likewise, except Ibn 'Amir, who read the mim with a sukun and lightened the ta'. Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj reported that in the reading of Ubayy it is "fa-numatti'uhu qalilan thumma nadtarruhu" with the letter nun. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada said: this statement is from Ibrahim (peace be upon him). They read "fa-amti'hu" with a fatha on the hamza and a sukun on the mim, and "thumma idtarrahu" with a connecting alif and a fatha on the ra'. Then Ibrahim (peace be upon him) prayed for the believers and against the disbelievers. Accordingly, the pronoun in "qala" (he said) refers to Ibrahim, and "qala" is repeated either because the speech is long, or because he moved from praying for one group to praying against others. According to the reading of the community (jama'a), the subject of "qala" is the name of God Most High. Al-Nahhas chose this, and considered the reading with a fatha on the hamza, a sukun on the mim and a connecting alif to be anomalous (shadhdha). He said: "The sequence of the speech and the explanation both indicate other than it. As for the sequence of the speech, God Most High reported about Ibrahim (peace be upon him) that he said: 'My Lord, make this a secure land,' then He came with His saying, mighty and majestic: 'And provide its people with fruits, those of them who believe in God and the Last Day,' without separating it with 'qala'. Then after that He said: 'He said: And whoever disbelieves,' so this was a response from God, and it does not say after that 'Ibrahim said.'" As for the explanation, it is authentically reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Muhammad ibn Ka'b. This is the wording of Ibn 'Abbas: Ibrahim (peace be upon him) prayed for those who believe only, among the people, specifically. So God, mighty and majestic, informed him that He provides for whoever disbelieves just as He provides for whoever believes, and that He will let him enjoy for a little while, then compel him to the torment of the Fire.

Abu Ja'far said: God, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿To each We extend, to these and to those, from the gift of your Lord﴾ [[see vol. 10, p. 236.]], and He, whose praise is exalted, said: ﴿And nations We will let enjoy, then...﴾ [[see vol. 9, p. 48.]].

Abu Ishaq said: Ibrahim (peace be upon him) only knew that among his descendants there would be disbelievers, so he singled out the believers, because God, Most High, said: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on surah 2, verse 127 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted:
﴿And when Abraham and Ishmael were raising the foundations of the House﴾

*Al-qawa'id* (the foundations): its base, according to Abu 'Ubayda and al-Farra'.

Al-Kisa'i said: they are the walls.

What is well known is that they are the base.

In a hadith: "When the House was demolished, large stones were taken out of it." Ibn al-Zubayr said: "These are the foundations which Abraham, peace be upon him, raised."

It was also said: the foundations had been effaced, so Allah made Abraham aware of them.

Ibn 'Abbas said: He (Abraham) set the House upon foundations which he had seen two thousand years before the world was created, and then the earth was spread out beneath it.

*Al-qawa'id*, its singular is *qa'ida*. *Al-qawa'id* among women (*al-qawa'id min al-nisa'*) has as its singular *qa'id*.

People differed about who first built the House and laid its foundation. It was said: the angels.

It is narrated from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, who said: My father was asked, while I was present, about the beginning of the creation of the House. He said: When Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Indeed, I am going to place upon the earth a successor﴾, the angels said: ﴿Will You place upon it one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood, while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You?﴾ He was angry with them, so they sought refuge in His Throne and circumambulated it seven times, seeking the pleasure of their Lord, until Allah was pleased with them. He said to them: "Build Me a house on the earth, in which one who has incurred My wrath among the children of Adam may seek refuge, and which will be circumambulated as you circumambulated My Throne. Then I shall be pleased with him as I was pleased with you." So they built this House.

'Abd al-Razzaq mentioned, from Ibn Jurayj, from 'Ata' and Ibn al-Musayyib and others, that Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed to Adam: "When you descend, build Me a house, then circle around it as you saw the angels circling around My Throne which is in the heaven."

'Ata' said: People claim that he built it from five mountains: from Hira', from Tur Sina', from Lubnan, from al-Judi, and from Tur Zayta. Its *rabd* (foundation) [[*al-rabd* (with the *ra'* vowelled and the *ba'* either sukun or damma): the foundation. With both vowelled as fatha: what surrounds the city.]] was from Hira'.

Al-Khalil said: *al-rabud* here means the foundation of stone encircling the House, and from this the surroundings of a city are called *rabd*.

Al-Mawardi mentioned, from 'Ata', from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When Adam was sent down from Paradise to the earth, He said to him: "O Adam, go and build Me a house, circumambulate it, and remember Me there, as you saw the angels doing around My Throne." Adam set out, striding, and the earth was folded up for him, and the desert was gathered for him, so that his foot would not fall on any part of the earth without it becoming inhabited, until he reached the site of the Sacred House. Gabriel, peace be upon him, struck the earth with his wings and revealed a foundation fixed in the lowest seventh earth, and the angels cast stone to him, and not even thirty men could lift one of its stones. He built it from the five mountains as we have mentioned.

It has been narrated in some reports that a tent from the tents of Paradise was sent down for Adam, peace be upon him, and was pitched at the place of the Ka'ba so that he would find comfort in it and circumambulate it. It remained there until Allah, mighty and majestic, took Adam, and then it was lifted up.

This is from the chain of Wahb ibn Munabbih.

In another report: a house was sent down with him, and he used to circumambulate it, and the believers among his offspring did likewise until the time of the Flood. Then Allah raised it and it became in the heaven, and it is the one called the *al-Bayt al-Ma'mur* (the Frequented House).

This was narrated from Qatada. Al-Halimi mentioned it in his book *Minhaj al-Din*, and said: It is possible that the meaning of what Qatada said, that a house was sent down with Adam, is that there was sent down with him the measure of the *al-Bayt al-Ma'mur* in length, breadth and height, and then he was told: "Build to its measure," and it was intended that it be exactly opposite it. So the place opposite it was the site of the Ka'ba, and he built it there.

As for the tent, it is possible that it was sent down and pitched at the site of the Ka'ba. When he was commanded to build it and did so, there was around the Ka'ba a tranquillity for the heart of Adam, peace be upon him, for as long as he lived, and then it was lifted. Thus these reports agree.

This is the building of Adam, peace be upon him. Then Abraham, peace be upon him, built it.

Ibn Jurayj said: Some people said: Allah sent a cloud in which there was a head. The head said: "O Abraham, your Lord commands you to take the measure of this cloud." So he began to look at it and to mark out its size. Then the head said: "You have done it." So he dug, and a foundation fixed in the earth was revealed.

It is narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him: When Allah commanded Abraham to rebuild the House, he set out from Syria with his son Ishmael and his mother Hajar, and Allah sent with him *al-sakina* (the tranquillity) [[*al-sakina* (with fatha then kasra): a swift, hot wind, i.e. a quick hot wind.]], which had a tongue with which it spoke. Abraham went along with it when it moved in the morning, and went along with it when it halted, until it brought him to Mecca. It said to Abraham: "Build the foundation on my location" [[In j: "Build on the site of the foundation." And Abu Qubays: the name of the mountain overlooking Mecca.]]. So Abraham and Ishmael raised the House until they reached the place of the Corner (*al-Rukn*). He said to his son: "My son, bring me a stone which I may place as a sign for the people." He brought him a stone, but he did not accept it and said: "Bring me another." So he went to seek one, and when he came back, Gabriel had brought the Corner Stone and placed it in its place. Abraham said: "O father, who brought you this stone?" He said: "The one who did not leave you to yourself." 

Ibn 'Abbas: Abu Qubays [[In j: "Build on the site of the foundation." And Abu Qubays: the name of the mountain overlooking Mecca.]] called out: "O Abraham, O Friend of the Merciful, you have a deposit with me, so take it." Behold, there was a white stone of the rubies of Paradise, which Adam had brought down from Paradise. When Abraham and Ishmael raised the foundations of the House, a square cloud came with a head in it, and it called out: "Raise them up according to my squaring."

This is the building of Abraham, peace be upon him.

It is narrated that when Abraham and Ishmael finished building the House, Allah gave them horses as a reward for raising the foundations of the House.

Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim narrated to us: 'Umar ibn Abi 'Umar narrated to me: Nu'aym ibn Hammad narrated to us: 'Abd al-Wahhab ibn Hammam, brother of 'Abd al-Razzaq, narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from Ibn Abi Mulayka, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said:

The horses were wild beasts like the rest of the wild beasts. When Allah permitted Abraham and Ishmael to raise the foundations, Allah, blessed is His name, said: "Indeed I am giving you both a treasure which I have stored up for you both." Then He revealed to Ishmael: "Go out to Ajyad and call, and the treasure will come to you."

So he went out to Ajyad, which was his homeland, not knowing what the call was or what the treasure was. Then He inspired him, and there remained on the face of the earth no horse in the land of the Arabs except that it came to him, and it submitted its forelocks to him, and he tamed them for himself. "So ride them and feed them, for they are blessed, and they are the inheritance of your father Ishmael." That is why the horse was called *'arabi* (Arab), because Ishmael was commanded to call and to him it came.

'Abd al-Mun'im ibn Idris narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: The first to build the House with clay and stones was Shith, peace be upon him.

As for the building of Quraysh of it, it is well known, and the story of the serpent in that connection is mentioned. It used to prevent them from demolishing it until the Quraysh gathered at the Maqam and cried out to Allah, mighty and exalted, and said: "Our Lord, we were not frightened! We wanted to honour Your House and adorn it. If You are pleased with that, well and good; otherwise, do what You will." Then they heard a *khawat* from the sky (*al-khawat*: the rustling of the wing of a large bird). Behold, there was a bird larger than an eagle, black on its back and white on its belly and legs. It thrust its talons into the nape of the serpent, then carried it off, dragging its tail, larger than such-and-such, until it took it toward Ajyad. Then Quraysh demolished it and began to build it with stones of the valley, which Quraysh carried on their necks, and they raised it twenty cubits into the sky.

While the Prophet ﷺ was carrying stones from Ajyad, wearing a *namira* (*al-namira*: every striped wrap of the Arabs' loincloths), the *namira* became too tight for him, so he tried to lift the *namira* onto his shoulder, and his private part was seen because the *namira* was small. He was called: "O Muhammad, cover your nakedness!" After that he was never seen naked.

Between the building of the Ka'ba and his receiving revelation there were five years, and between his coming forth and its building there were fifteen years.

This was mentioned by 'Abd al-Razzaq, from Ma'mar, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Uthman, from Abu al-Tufayl.

It is mentioned from Ma'mar, from al-Zuhri: When they built it and reached the place of the Corner, the Quraysh disputed about the Corner: which of the tribes should have the honour of raising it? They quarrelled among themselves, and said: "Come, let us make the first one who enters upon us from this road the judge." They agreed upon that, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ appeared to them, while he was a youth wearing a striped *namira* sash. They made him the judge. He commanded that the Corner be placed in a cloth, then he had the chief of each tribe take a side of the cloth, then he himself climbed up and they raised the Corner to him, and he placed it, ﷺ.

Ibn Ishaq said: It was related to me that the Quraysh found in the Corner a writing in Syriac, which they did not understand, until a man of the Jews read it for them. In it was: "I am God, Possessor of Bakka. I created it on the day I created the heavens and the earth, and I formed the sun and the moon, and I surrounded it with seven angels, upright, which will not cease until its two mountains cease. It is blessed for its people in water and milk."

From Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn 'Ali, who said: The door of the Ka'ba, in the time of the 'Amaliq and Jurhum and Abraham, peace be upon him, was at ground level, until Quraysh built it.

Muslim transmitted from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: I asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the *Jadr* [[*al-jadr* (with fatha on the jim and the dal silent): the stone enclosure of the Ka'ba (with kasra on the ha')]]: is it part of the House? He said: "Yes." I said: "Why then did they not include it in the House?" He said: "Your people were short of expenses." I said: "Then why is its door raised?" He said: "Your people did that so that they could admit whom they wished and prevent whom they wished. Had your people not been recent in their pre-Islamic disbelief, and had I not feared that their hearts would reject it, I would have considered including the *Jadr* in the House and making its door level with the ground."

It is also transmitted from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: My maternal aunt (meaning 'A'isha), may Allah be pleased with her, told me: The Prophet ﷺ said: "'A'isha, had your people not been recent in shirk, I would have demolished the Ka'ba and levelled it with the ground, and made for it two doors, an eastern door and a western door, and I would have added six cubits of the *Hijr* to it, for Quraysh reduced it when they built the Ka'ba."

From 'Urwa, from his father, from 'A'isha, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me: "Had the recent disbelief of your people not been so, I would have pulled down the Ka'ba and placed it upon the foundations of Abraham, for Quraysh, when they built the Ka'ba, shortened it. And I would have made for it a back door."

In al-Bukhari, Hisham ibn 'Urwa said: That is, a door.

Also in al-Bukhari: "I would have made for it two back doors," meaning two doors.

This is the building of Quraysh.

Then, when the people of Syria (Ahl al-Sham) attacked ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, and the Kaʿba was weakened by their burning of it, Ibn al-Zubayr demolished it and rebuilt it according to what ʿĀʾisha had told him. He added five cubits from the Hijr to it, until he exposed a foundation (ussan) which people looked at, and he built upon it. The Kaʿba had been eighteen cubits in length, and when he extended it he found it too short, so he added ten cubits to its length. He also made for it two doors: one through which people enter and another through which they exit. This is as it is in Sahih Muslim, though the wordings of the hadith differ.

Sufyan related from Dawud ibn Shapur, from Mujahid, who said:

When Ibn al-Zubayr wished to demolish the Kaʿba and rebuild it, he said to the people: "Demolish it." [The text reads: "he said"] They refused to demolish it, fearing that punishment would descend upon them.

Mujahid said: We went out to Mina and stayed there three days, awaiting the punishment.

He said: Ibn al-Zubayr himself climbed onto the wall of the Kaʿba. When they saw that nothing had befallen him, they became bold regarding it, and he said: They demolished it.

When he rebuilt it, he made for it two doors: a door through which they enter and a door through which they exit. He added six cubits on the side adjoining the Hijr and extended its length by nine cubits.

Muslim said in his narration: When Ibn al-Zubayr was killed, al-Hajjaj wrote to ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwan informing him of this, and informing him that Ibn al-Zubayr had set the building upon a foundation which the trustworthy (ʿudul) people of Makka had seen. ʿAbd al-Malik wrote back to him:

"We are not [concerned with] smearing Ibn al-Zubayr in any matter" [Al-Nawawi said: "He intends by this to revile him and disparage his deed; one says: lataktahu, meaning I accused him of a foul thing."]. As for what he extended in its length, keep it; as for what he added to it from the Hijr, return it to its former construction, and block up the door he opened. So he tore it down and restored it to its former construction.

In another version: ʿAbd al-Malik said: "I did not think Abu Khubayb (meaning Ibn al-Zubayr) had heard from ʿĀʾisha what he claimed to have heard from her." al-Harith ibn ʿAbd Allah said: "Indeed, I heard it from her." He said: "What did you hear her say?" He said: She said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Your people fell short in building the House, and were it not for the recency of their conversion from polytheism, I would have restored what they left out of it. If your people after me decide to build it, come and I will show you what they left out." So she showed him about seven cubits.

In another version: ʿAbd al-Malik said: "Had I heard it before I demolished it, I would have left it as Ibn al-Zubayr built it."

This is what has come down in the reports concerning the building of the Kaʿba.

It is narrated that al-Rashid mentioned to Malik ibn Anas that he intended to demolish what al-Hajjaj had built of the Kaʿba and restore it to the building of Ibn al-Zubayr, because of what had come from the Prophet (ﷺ) and that Ibn al-Zubayr had acted upon it. Malik said to him: "I beseech you by Allah, O Commander of the Faithful, not to make this House a plaything for kings, where whenever any of them wishes he demolishes the House and rebuilds it, so that its awe departs from the hearts of people."

Al-Waqidi mentioned: Maʿmar related to us from Hammam ibn Munabbih, who heard Abu Hurayra say: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade reviling Asʿad al-Himyari, who is Tubbaʿ, and he is the first who clothed the House, and he is the other Tubbaʿ.

Ibn Ishaq said: The Kaʿba used to be clothed with qabati [cloth, a fine white thin fabric woven in Egypt, attributed to the Copts (al-Qibt) irregularly], then it was clothed with burud, and the first who clothed it with dibaj was al-Hajjaj.

The scholars said: Nothing from the covering of the Kaʿba should be taken, for it is a gift made to it, and nothing should be reduced from it.

It is related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr that he disliked that anything be taken from the perfume of the Kaʿba to seek healing by it, and whenever he saw the attendant taking from it, he would strike the attendant's head with a slap (qafda) from the back of the hand, not failing to cause pain.

ʿAta said: Whenever one of us wished to seek healing by it, he would bring perfume from his own possession, wipe it upon the Stone, and then take it.

Allah's words: ﴿Our Lord, accept from us﴾. The meaning: and they both say "Our Lord," so it is elided. Likewise it is in the recitation of Ubayy and ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud: "And when Ibrahim and Isma'il were raising the foundations of the House, saying: Our Lord, accept from us." The meaning of Isma'il: Hear, O Allah, for "il" in Syriac is Allah, and this has been previously mentioned [see p. 36 of this part]. It was said: when Ibrahim called upon his Lord, he said: "Hear, O Il," and when his Lord answered him and granted him a son, he named him by what he had called upon. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Allah's words: ﴿Indeed, You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾. These are two of Allah's names, which we have addressed in the book "al-Asna fi Sharh Asma' Allah al-Husna."

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 128:**

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, and make us submissive to You﴾. That is, make us. "Muslimayn" (submissive) is the second object. They asked for steadfastness and continuance. In this passage, "Islam" (submission) means faith and deeds together, and from it is His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ [[See vol. 4, p. 43.]]. In this there is evidence for those who say that faith (iman) and Islam are one thing. They reinforced this with His words, Exalted is He, in another verse: ﴿So We brought out those who were in it of the believers. But We found not there except one house of the submissive﴾ [[See vol. 17, p. 48.]]. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Awf al-A'rabi read "muslimin" in the plural.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And from our descendants, a community submissive to You﴾. That is, "and from our descendants, make [a community submissive to You]." It is said that no prophet supplicated except for himself and his community, except Ibrahim, who, along with his supplication for himself and his community, supplicated for this community as well. The "min" (from) in His words "and from our descendants" is partitive (lil-tab'id), because Allah had already informed him that among them there would be wrongdoers. Al-Tabari related that by His words "and from our descendants" he meant specifically the Arabs. Al-Suhayli said: "Their descendants are the Arabs, because they are the sons of Nabit ibn Isma'il, or the sons of Taymin ibn Isma'il. It is also said: Qaydar ibn Nabit ibn Isma'il. The Adnanites are from Nabit, and the Qahtanites are from Qaydar ibn Nabit ibn Isma'il, or from Taymin according to one of the two opinions." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is weak, because his supplication became manifest among the Arabs and among those of other peoples who believed."

"Ummah" here means a group. It may also refer to a single person when he is a model to be followed in goodness, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was a community (ummah), devoutly obedient to Allah﴾ [[See vol. 10, p. 197.]]. The Prophet (ﷺ) said about Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl: "He will be raised as a community by himself," because he did not associate anyone with Allah in his religion. And Allah knows best. The word "ummah" may also be used in other senses. Among these is His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a community (ummah)﴾, meaning upon a religion and creed [[See vol. 16, p. 74.]]. Among them is His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, this, your community (ummah), is one community﴾ [[See vol. 11, p. 338.]]. It may also mean a period and a span of time, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And he remembered after a period (ummah)﴾ [[See vol. 9, p. 201.]], meaning after a while and a time. It is said: "This is the ummah of Zayd," meaning the mother of Zayd. "Ummah" also means stature: it is said, "So-and-so has a fine ummah," meaning fine stature. The poet said:

*And Mu'awiya, the generous ones... fair of faces, tall of statures.*

It is also said that "ummah" is a wound that reaches the mother of the brain (umm al-dimagh). It is said: "a man is ma'mum and amim" [i.e., one with such a wound].

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And show us our rites﴾. "Arina" (show us) is from the sight of the eye, so it transitively takes two objects. It is also said that it is from the sight of the heart, in which case the verb would require three objects. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is resolved by the fact that it is found transitive by the hamza (of causation) from the sight of the heart to two objects [like the non-causative form]." The poet Hutaytat ibn Ya'fur, brother of al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur, said:

*Show me a horse that died of emaciation, for indeed I... [would see] what you see, or a miserly, eternal one.*

[Note: in one version "li-'anni" is "la'alli," and "li-anna" here means "perhaps."]

Umar ibn 'Abd al-Aziz, Qatadah, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, al-Suddi, Rawh (on the authority of Ya'qub), Ruways, and al-Susi read "arna" with a sukun on the ra' throughout the Qur'an, and Abu Hatim preferred this reading. Abu 'Amr read with the kasra of the ra' slightly reduced (ikhtilas), and the rest read with a full kasra, and Abu 'Ubayd preferred this. The original form is "arina" with a hamza. Whoever reads with the sukun says: the hamza was dropped along with its vowel, and the ra' remained sukun in its state. They cite the verse of the poet:

*Show us the water-skin of 'Abdullah, which we will fill with water of Zamzam, for the people have become thirsty.*

Whoever reads with the kasra transferred the vowel of the dropped hamza to the ra'. Abu 'Amr sought lightness.

It is related on the authority of Shuja' ibn Abi Nasr, who was trustworthy and truthful, that he saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in a dream, and he discussed with him some matters of Abu 'Amr's readings, and he [the Prophet] did not object except to two letters: this one, and the other, "ma nansakh min ayatin aw nansa'ha" (whatever We abrogate of a verse or cause it to be forgotten), which should be read with a hamza.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Our rites﴾. It is said that the original meaning of "nusk" in the lexicon is washing; it is said from it: "nasaka thawbahu" (he washed his garment) when he washed it. In the Shari'ah it is a name for worship. It is said: "rajul nasik" (a man who is a nasik) when he is a worshipper. The scholars differed concerning the meaning of "manasik" here. It is said: the rites of Hajj and its landmarks, as said by Qatadah and al-Suddi. Mujahid, 'Ata', and Ibn Jurayj said: "al-manasik" means the places of slaughter, that is, the sites of sacrifice. It is also said: all acts of worship. Everything by which one worships Allah, Exalted is He, is called "mansak" and "masak." And "nasik" means worshipper. Al-Nahhas said: it is said "nasaka yansuku," so by this analogy it should be "mansuk," but there is no pattern "maf'ul" in the speech of the Arabs (in this form).

Zuhayr ibn Muhammad related: When Ibrahim, peace be upon him, finished building the Sacred House, he said: "O Lord, I have finished; so show us our rites." Allah sent Jibril to him, and he performed Hajj with him. When he returned from 'Arafat and came to the day of sacrifice (yawm al-nahr), Iblis appeared to him and said to him: "Pelt him," so he pelted him with seven pebbles. Then the next day, and then the third day. Then he climbed Thabir [[Thabir: a mountain between Makkah and Mina, on the right of one going to Makkah.]] and said: "O servants of Allah, respond!" He heard his call from between the ends of the earth from everyone who had in his heart an atom's weight of faith. He said: "Labbayka, Allahumma labbayk." He said: "There have always been, on the face of the earth, seven or more submissive ones; were it not for that, the earth and whoever is upon it would have been destroyed." The first to respond to him were the people of Yemen.

On the authority of Abu Mijlaz: When Ibrahim finished the House, Jibril, peace be upon him, came to him and showed him the circumambulation (tawaf) around the House. He said: "And I think he said: 'and al-Safa and al-Marwa.'" Then they set off towards al-'Aqabah, where Satan appeared to them. Jibril took seven pebbles and gave Ibrahim seven pebbles. He threw and said "Allahu akbar," and said to Ibrahim: "Throw and say 'Allahu akbar'." They threw and said "Allahu akbar" with every throw until Satan vanished. Then they set off to the middle jamrah, where Satan appeared to them again. Jibril took seven pebbles and gave Ibrahim seven pebbles and said: "Throw and say 'Allahu akbar'." They threw and said "Allahu akbar" with every throw until Satan vanished. Then they came to the farthest jamrah (al-jamrah al-quswa), where Satan appeared to them, and Jibril took seven pebbles and gave Ibrahim seven pebbles, and said: "Throw and say 'Allahu akbar'." They threw and said "Allahu akbar" with every throw until Satan vanished. Then he brought him to Jam' [[Jam': (with fatha and then sukun) Muzdalifah.]] and said: "Here the people gather for the prayers." Then he brought him to 'Arafat and said: "Do you recognize ('arafta)?" He said: "Yes." Hence it was named 'Arafat. It is also reported that he said to him: "'Arafta? 'Arafta? 'Arafta?" meaning Mina, Jam', and this [place]. He said: "Yes," so that place was named 'Arafat.

On the authority of Khusayf ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, that Mujahid related to him: When Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said: "And show us our rites," this meant al-Safa and al-Marwa, which are among the symbols of Allah by the explicit text of the Qur'an. Then Jibril went out with him, and when he passed the Jamrat al-'Aqabah, Iblis was there. Jibril said to him: "Say 'Allahu akbar' and pelt him," so Iblis moved to the middle jamrah, and Jibril said: "Say 'Allahu akbar' and pelt him," and likewise at the farthest jamrah. Then he set off with him to al-Mash'ar al-Haram, then brought him to 'Arafah and said to him: "Have you recognized what I showed you?" He said: "Yes." It was therefore named 'Arafat for this reason, it is said. He said: "Proclaim to the people the Hajj." He said: "How shall I say it?" He said: "Say: 'O people, respond to your Lord,'" three times. He did so, and they said: "Labbayka, Allahumma labbayk." He said: "Whoever responded on that day is a pilgrim (hajj)."

In another narration: when he called out, he turned around and supplicated in every direction, so the people responded from every east and west, and the mountains humbled themselves until his voice reached far.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: When Ibrahim, the Friend of the Most Merciful, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, finished building the Sacred House, Jibril, peace be upon him, came to him and said: "Circumambulate it seven times." He circumambulated it seven times, he and Isma'il, peace be upon them both, touching all the corners in every circuit. When they completed seven, they prayed two rak'ahs behind the Maqam. He said: Jibril then stood and showed him all the rites: al-Safa and al-Marwa, Mina, and Muzdalifah. He said: When he entered Mina and descended from al-'Aqabah, Iblis appeared to him... and he mentioned something similar to what came before.

Ibn Ishaq said: It has reached me that Adam, peace be upon him, used to touch all the corners before Ibrahim, peace be upon him. And he said: Ishaq and Sarah performed Hajj from al-Sham, and Ibrahim, peace be upon him, used to perform Hajj every year on al-Buraq, and after that the prophets and the nations performed Hajj.

Muhammad ibn Sabit related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whenever a prophet's community was destroyed, he would come to Makkah and worship there, he and whoever believed with him, until they died. Nuh, Hud, and Salih died there, and their graves are between Zamzam and the Hijr." Ibn Wahb mentioned that Shu'ayb died in Makkah, he and those believers who were with him, and their graves are in the west of Makkah between Dar al-Nadwah and the Banu Sahm. Ibn 'Abbas said: "In the Masjid al-Haram there are two graves, and there is nothing else in it besides them: the grave of Isma'il and the grave of Shu'ayb, peace be upon them both. The grave of Isma'il is in the Hijr, and the grave of Shu'ayb is opposite the Black Stone." 'Abdullah ibn Damrah al-Salouli said: "Between the Corner and the Maqam to Zamzam are the graves of ninety-nine prophets who came as pilgrims and were buried there, may the blessings of Allah be upon them all."

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And turn to us in forgiveness﴾. Scholars differed concerning the meaning of the words of Ibrahim and Isma'il, peace be upon them both: "And turn to us," while they are infallible prophets. One group said: they sought steadfastness and continuance, not that they had any sin. I say: this is good, and better than it is that when they had learned the rites and built the House, they wished to make clear to the people and inform them that this standing place and those locations are places of disavowal of sins and seeking repentance. It is also said: the meaning is "and turn [in forgiveness] to the wrongdoers among us." The discussion of the infallibility of the prophets, peace be upon them, has already passed in the story of Adam, peace be upon him [[See vol. 1, p. 30, second edition.]], and the meaning of His words, "Indeed, You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful" has already been mentioned, so there is no need to repeat it [[See vol. 1, p. 325, second edition.]].

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Our Lord, and raise among them a messenger from among them﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ). In the reading of Ubayy it is "and raise among their last ones a messenger from among them." Khalid ibn Ma'dan narrated that a group of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, tell us about yourself." He said: "Yes, I am the answer to the prayer of my father Abraham and the glad tidings of Jesus."

"Rasulan" means "mursalan" (one who is sent), and it is on the pattern fa'ul from the risalah (mission). Ibn al-Anbari said: Its origin may be from the saying of the Arabs: "a female camel that is mirsal and rasla," when she is easy in her pace and goes ahead of the (other) she-camels. It is also said of a group that is sent off: "rasl," and its plural is "arsal." It is said: "The people came arsalan," meaning some of them following others. From this, milk is called "risl," because it is sent (released) from the udder.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿and teach them the Book and the Wisdom﴾. "The Book" is the Qur'an, and "the Wisdom" is knowledge of the religion, understanding of the interpretation, and the comprehension that is a disposition and a light from Allah the Exalted. This was said by Malik, narrated from him by Ibn Wahb, and said by Ibn Zayd. Qatadah said: "The Wisdom" is the Sunnah and the explanation of the laws. It is also said: it refers specifically to judgment and decision, and the meanings are close. The teaching is attributed to the Prophet (ﷺ) insofar as he provides the matters that are to be considered and teaches the method of reflection through what Allah casts to him of revelation. ﴿And purify them﴾, that is, cleanse them from the filth (wadar) of polytheism, according to Ibn Jurayj and others. And zakah means purification, and it has been discussed earlier (see vol. 1, p. 343, 2nd edition). It is also said: the verses are the recitation of the apparent wording, the Book is the meanings of the words, and the Wisdom is the ruling, which is what Allah intends by the address, whether general or specific, explicit or implicit, absolute or restricted, universal or particular; and this is the meaning of what preceded. And Allah knows best.

﴿The Mighty﴾: its meaning is the unassailable one who cannot be reached or overcome.
