Ibn Kaysan said: its meaning is the one whom nothing can incapacitate, its evidence being: ﴿And Allah was not one to be frustrated by anything in the heavens or on earth﴾ (see vol. 14, p. 361). Al-Kisa'i said: "al-Aziz" is the Overpowering, and from it is the verse: ﴿and he overpowered me in speech﴾ (see vol. 15, p. 174). There is a proverb: "Whoever is mighty plunders," meaning whoever overpowers despoils. It is also said: "al-Aziz" is the One who has no like, its clarification being: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ (see vol. 16, p. 8). We have expanded on this meaning in explaining His name al-Aziz in the book "al-Asna fi Sharh Asma' Allah al-Husna." The meaning of "al-Hakim" has already been mentioned (see the third issue, vol. 1, p. 287, 2nd edition). And praise be to Allah.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 130:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And who would turn away from the religion of Ibrahim, except one who makes a fool of himself?﴾ "Man" is an interrogative in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), and "yarghabu" is the relative clause (silah) of "man." ... "Illa man safiha nafsahu" (except one who makes a fool of himself) is in the position of the predicate (khabar). This is a rebuke and reproach in which the meaning of negation is implied, i.e., "and no one turns away," as stated by al-Nahhas. The meaning is: one renounces it and keeps himself away from it, that is, from the religion (millah), which is the faith and the law (shari'ah). "Illa man safiha nafsahu": Qatadah said: they are the Jews and the Christians, who turned away from the religion of Ibrahim and took Judaism and Christianity as innovations that are not from Allah, may He be exalted. Al-Zajjaj said: "safiha" means "jahila" (he was ignorant), i.e., he was ignorant of the matter of his own self and did not reflect upon it. Abu Ubaydah said: the meaning is "ahlaka nafsahu" (he destroyed himself). Tha'lab and al-Mubarrad related that "safiha" with a kasrah on the fa' is transitive like "saffaha" with a fathah on the fa' and a shaddah. It is related from Abu al-Khattab and Yunus that this is a dialectal usage. Al-Akhfash said: "safiha nafsahu" means he did to himself from folly what made him a fool. He also said, from him as well, that it is a dialect meaning "saffaha," as related by al-Mahdawi, and the first view was mentioned by al-Mawardi. As for "safuha" with a dammah on the fa', it is not transitive, as stated by al-Mubarrad and Tha'lab. al-Kisa'i related from al-Akhfash that the meaning is "jahila fi nafsihi" (he was ignorant regarding himself), and the preposition "fi" (in) was deleted, so the noun became accusative. Al-Akhfash said: and similar to it is "'uqdata al-nikah" [[i.e., in His saying, may He be exalted: "and do not determine the binding of the marriage contract" (2:235); see vol. 3, p. 192.]], meaning "'ala 'uqdati al-nikah" (upon the binding of the marriage contract). This runs according to the view of Sibawayh regarding what he related from their saying: "daraba fulanun al-zahra wa al-batna," meaning "fi al-zahri wa al-batni" (he struck the back and the belly, i.e., on the back and the belly). al-Farra' said: it is a specificative accusative (tamyiz). Ibn Bahr said: its meaning is that he was ignorant of his own self and of the signs and indications within it that point to the fact that it has a Maker, "laysa kamithlihi shay'" (there is nothing like Him), so that by it the oneness of Allah and His power are known. I say: this is the meaning of the statement of al-Zajjaj, that he reflects upon his own self: from two hands with which he grasps, and two legs upon which he walks, and an eye with which he sees, and an ear with which he hears, and a tongue with which he speaks, and molars that grow for him when he no longer needs suckling and needs food, so that he may grind the food with them, and a stomach prepared for cooking food, and a liver to which the purest part ascends, and veins and channels through which it passes to the extremities, and intestines into which the residue of food settles and which exits from the lower part of the body. By this one is guided to the conclusion that He has a Creator who is capable, knowing, and wise. This is the meaning of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And within yourselves; will you not see?﴾ (51:21). al-Khattabi, may Allah have mercy on him, pointed to this. More explanation of this will come in surah al-Dhariyat, if Allah wills [[see vol. 17, p. 40.]]. This verse has been used as evidence by those who say: the law (shari'ah) of Ibrahim is a law for us, except what has been abrogated (nusikha, i.e., naskh) of it. This is like His saying: ﴿the religion of your father Ibrahim﴾ (22:78) [[see vol. 12, p. 101.]], and ﴿Follow the religion of Ibrahim﴾ (16:123) [[see vol. 10, p. 198.]]. Its explanation will come.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We had chosen him in this world﴾ means: We chose him for the message, and made him pure from defilements. The original form of "iṣṭafaynāhu" is "iṣtafaynāhu," and the tā' was changed to ṭā' to harmonize with the ṣād in emphatic articulation. The word is derived from "ṣafwah" (the choice part), and its meaning is to select the purest.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous﴾. The righteous in the Hereafter are the successful. Then it was said: how is it permissible to place "in the Hereafter" first when it is part of the relative clause? Al-Nahhas said: the answer is that the intended meaning is not "indeed he is among the righteous in the Hereafter," so that the relative clause would have been placed first. The people of Arabic grammar have three views on this. One of them is that the meaning is "and indeed he is righteous in the Hereafter," and then it was deleted. It was also said: "in the Hereafter" is connected to a deleted verbal noun (maṣdar), i.e., "his righteousness in the Hereafter." The third view is that "al-ṣāliḥīn" (the righteous) does not mean "those who became righteous," but is an independent noun, just as one says "al-rajul" (the man) and "al-ghulam" (the boy). I say: a fourth view is that the meaning is "and indeed he is among the righteous in the works of the Hereafter," so the speech contains an elision of a noun in construct (mudaf). al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: in the speech there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir); its implied meaning is: "and We had chosen him in this world and the Hereafter, and indeed he is among the righteous." Hajjaj ibn Hajjaj, who is Hajjaj al-Aswad, and who is also Hajjaj al-Ahwal, known as "Ziqq al-'Asal," related and said: I heard Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah say: "O Allah, indeed You made the righteous righteous, and You granted them the provision to act in obedience to You, so You were pleased with them. O Allah, just as You made them righteous, make us righteous, and just as You granted them the provision to act in obedience to You, so You were pleased with them, grant us the provision to act in Your obedience, and be pleased with us."

The governing element of "idh" (when) is His saying "ṣṭafaynāhu" (We chose him), meaning: We chose him when his Lord said to him, "Submit (aslim)." This statement from God, Exalted is said to have been made when He tested him with the star, the moon and the sun. Ibn Kaysan and al-Kalbi said: meaning, purify your religion for God through monotheism. It was also said: humble yourself and be submissive. Ibn 'Abbas said: He only said this to him when he came out of the *sarab* [[al-sarab (with a vowel on the root): a pit, a hollow dug beneath the ground.]], as will be mentioned in commentary on *al-An'am* [[See vol. 7, p. 24.]]. Islam here is in its most complete sense. In the speech of the Arabs, Islam (*islam*) means submission and yielding to the one who is surrendered to. Not every Islam is faith (*iman*), and every faith is Islam, because whoever believes in God has submitted and yielded to God. And not everyone who submits has believed in God, for a person may utter the words out of fear of the sword, and that is not faith. This is contrary to the Qadariyya and the Khawarij, who said: Islam is faith, so every believer is a Muslim and every Muslim is a believer, based on His saying: "Indeed, the religion with God is Islam" [[See vol. 4, p. 43.]]. This indicates that Islam is the religion, and that whoever is not a Muslim is not a believer. Our proof is His saying, Exalted: "The Bedouins say, 'We have believed.' Say, 'You have not believed; rather say, "We have submitted"'" [[See vol. 16, p. 348.]], and so on. God, Exalted, informed us that not everyone who submits is a believer, which indicates that not every Muslim is a believer. The Prophet ﷺ said to Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas when he said to him: "Give to so-and-so, for he is a believer," and the Prophet ﷺ said: "Or a Muslim," the hadith, which Muslim recorded. This indicates that faith is not the same as Islam, for faith is inward and Islam is outward, and this is clear. Faith may be used in the sense of Islam, and Islam may be used to mean faith, because each of them entails the other and proceeds from it, like Islam, which is the fruit of faith and evidence of its soundness. So understand this. And success is from God.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 2, verse 132:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Abraham enjoined it upon his sons﴾, meaning the religion (*millah*). It was also said: meaning the word that is His saying, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds." This second view is more correct, because it is the nearest thing mentioned, so the sense is: say, "We have submitted."

*Wassa* and *awsa* are two dialects, one of the Quraysh and another of other tribes, with the same meaning, like *karramana* and *akramana* (both meaning "he honored us"). Both are read in the recitations. In the *mushaf* (codex) of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) it is *wassa*, and in the *mushaf* (codex) of Uthman it is *awsa*. The latter is the reading of the people of Madina and Syria. The rest read *wassa*, which carries the sense of intensification (*al-taktheer*).

*Ibrahim* is in the nominative case, being the agent of the verb. *Ya'qub* is coordinated (*ma'tuf*) to it. It was also said that it is a separate, new sentence (*maqta' mustanaf*), and the meaning is: "Ya'qub also enjoined, and said, 'O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you the religion.'" In that case Ibrahim enjoined his sons, and then after him Ya'qub enjoined his sons.

The sons of Ibrahim: Isma'il, whose mother was Hajar the Copt. He was Ibrahim's eldest son. Ibrahim carried him to Makka while he was still a suckling infant. It was said that he was two years old, and it was said that he was fourteen years old. The first view is more sound, as will be explained, God willing, in Surah Ibrahim [[See vol. 9, p. 368.]]. Ishaq was born before his brother Isma'il by fourteen years. Isma'il died at the age of one hundred and thirty-seven. It was said: one hundred and thirty. When his father Ibrahim died, his age was eighty-nine. He is the one who was to be sacrificed according to one opinion. Ishaq's mother was Sarah, and he is the one who was to be sacrificed according to another opinion, which is the more sound, as will be explained, God willing, in Surah al-Saffat [[See vol. 15, p. 99.]]. From his descendants came the Romans, the Greeks, the Armenians, those who follow their path, and the Children of Israel.

Ishaq lived one hundred and eighty years. He died in the Holy Land and was buried beside his father Ibrahim, the Friend (*al-Khalil*), peace be upon them both.

Then, after Sarah died, Ibrahim, peace be upon him, married Qanturah, daughter of Yaqtan the Canaanite. She bore him Midian, Madai, Nahshan, Zimran, Nashiq, and Shuyukh [[These names are given as they appear in the manuscripts of the original. What appears in *Tarikh al-Rusul wa'l-Muluk* by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari, first part, p. 345, the Europe edition, is: "Yaqsan, Zimran, Madyan, Yasbaq, Suh, and Basr." And in *Tarikh* of Ibn al-Athir, vol. 1, p. 87, the Europe edition, is: "Nafshan, Maran, Madyan, Madan, Nashq, and Sarh."]]. Then he, peace be upon him, died.

The period between his death and the birth of the Prophet (ﷺ) was about two thousand six hundred years, while the Jews reduce this by about four hundred years.

The enumeration of the sons of Ya'qub will come in Surah Yusuf, God willing [[See vol. 9, p. 130.]].

Amr ibn Fa'id al-Asawari and Isma'il ibn Abdullah al-Makki read *Ya'qub* in the accusative case, as a coordination (*'atfan*) upon *banihi* ("his sons"). In that case Ya'qub is included among those who were enjoined.

Al-Qushayri said: *Ya'qub* was also read in the accusative, coordinated upon *banihi*, but this is far-fetched, because Ya'qub was not among Ibrahim's sons when he enjoined them. It is not reported that Ya'qub met his grandfather Ibrahim; he was born only after Ibrahim's death. And Ya'qub enjoined his own sons too, just as Ibrahim had done. The enumeration of the sons of Ya'qub will come, God willing, the Exalted.

Al-Kalbi said: When Ya'qub entered Egypt, he saw them worshipping idols, fires, and cows. So he gathered his sons, feared for them, and said: "What will you worship after me?" It is also said: Ya'qub was named so because he and al-Is were twins, and he came out of his mother's womb grasping the heel (*'aqib*) of his brother al-Is. There is a problem with this, because this is an Arabic derivation, whereas Ya'qub is a non-Arabic name, even though it coincided with Arabic in being used as a name, like *al-hajal* (the partridge). *Al-Hajal* (with a vowel on the first letter): a bird the size of a pigeon, like the sand grouse, red of beak and legs, also called the wild hen. Its male is called *ya'qub*, and its plural is *ya'aqib* and *ya'aqib* (the plural forms of *ya'qub*).

He, peace be upon him, lived one hundred and forty-seven years and died in Egypt. He directed that he be carried to the Holy Land and buried beside his father Ishaq. Yusuf carried him and buried him beside him.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O my sons﴾. Its meaning is "that O my sons," and it is the same in the recitation of Ubayy, Ibn Mas'ud, and al-Dahhak. Al-Farra' said: *An* has been dropped (*ulghiyat*), because enjoining is like speech, and every statement that goes back to speech may take *an* and may omit it. He said: The statement of the grammarians that the intention was *an*, which was then dropped, is not valid.

Al-Nahhas said: "*Ya banī*" is a vocative with a possessive suffix (*nida' mudaf*). This is the suffix of the first person singular (*ya' al-nafs*), and here it may only be vowelled with a fatha, because if it were given a sukun, two consecutive unvowelled letters would meet. Similar to this is *bi-musrikhiyya* [[See vol. 9, p. 357.]].

*Inna Allah*: *inna* is given a kasra because *awsa* and *qala* (enjoin and say) are one verb. It was also said that it is based on an implied *qawl* (saying).

*Istafa* means "he chose." The reciter (*rajiz*) said:

O son of kings who inherited dominions,
the caliphate of Allah which He gave you.
He chose it for you, and it chose you for itself.

﴿For you the religion﴾, that is, Islam. The definite article in *al-din* is for a known reference (*al-'ahd*), because they had already known it.

﴿So do not die except while you are Muslims﴾ is a concise, eloquent expression (*ijaz baligh*). The meaning is: adhere to Islam, persist in it, and do not depart from it until you die. So He used a concise wording that contains the intended meaning, and it also contains an admonition and a reminder of death. The reason is that a person is certain that he will die but does not know when. So when he is commanded to do something that death will not reach him except while he is upon it, the address has been directed at him from the time of the command, continuously and binding.

*La* is a prohibition. *Tamutunna* is in a position of jussive (*jazm*) by the prohibition, emphasized with the heavy *nun*, and the *waw* was dropped because two unvowelled letters met.

*Illa wa-antum muslimun* is a subject and predicate (*ibtida' wa-khabar*) in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*). That is, "while you are those who think well of your Lord (*muhsinun bi-rabbikum al-zann*)." It was also said: "sincere (*mukhlisun*)," it was also said: "entrusting (*mufawwidun*)," and it was also said: "believers (*mu'minun*)."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on Surah 2, verse 133:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or were you witnesses﴾. "*Shuhadā'*" (witnesses) is the predicate (*khabar*) of *kāna* (the verb "to be"), and it is not declined (*lam yuṣrif*) because it contains the feminine *alif* (*alif al-ta'nīth*). The feminine marker was added for the feminine plural, just as the *hā'* is added (for the same purpose). The address is to the Jews and the Christians who attribute to Abraham what he did not enjoin upon his sons, and who claim that they follow Judaism and Christianity. So God refuted their claim, rejected it, and said to them, by way of rebuke: "Were you present when Jacob was dying, and did you know what he enjoined, so that you may claim it on knowledge?" That is, you were not present, but rather you are fabricating! The *alif* of "*am*" here means "rather" (*bal*), that is, "rather, did your forefathers witness Jacob?" The governing element of the first "*idh*" (when) is the meaning of witnessing, and the second "*idh*" is an apposition (*badal*) of the first. "*Shuhadā'*" is the plural of *shāhid*, meaning present. The phrase "Jacob was visited by death" means its preliminary stages and causes, for if death had actually arrived, he could not have spoken at all.

He referred to the object of worship with "*mā*" (what) and did not say "*man*" (who), because he wanted to test them. Had he said "*man*," his intention would have been to see who among them was guided, but he intended to test them, so he said "*mā*." Also, the commonly known objects of worship apart from God are inanimate things such as idols, fire, the sun, and stones, so he asked about what they worship from among these. The phrase "*min ba'dī*" (after me) means after my death.

It is related that when Jacob was given the choice, as prophets are given the choice, he chose death and said: "Give me respite until I enjoin my sons and my family." So he gathered them and said this to them, and they were guided and said: "We shall worship your God..." (the verse). Thus they showed him their steadfastness upon the religion and their knowledge of God, may He be exalted.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said: We shall worship your God and the God of your fathers, Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac﴾. "*Ibrāhīma wa-Ismā'īla wa-Is'hāqa*" (Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac) are in the genitive position as an apposition (*badal*), and they are not declined because they are non-Arabic (*a'jamiyya*) names. Al-Kisa'i said: "If you wish, you may decline "*Is'hāq*" and make it derived from *al-sahq* (grinding/wearing away), and decline "*Ya'qūb*" and make it derived from *al-ṭayr* (flying)." God called each of the paternal uncle and the grandfather a father, and He began with mention of the grandfather, then Ishmael, the paternal uncle, because he was older than Isaac.

"*Ilāhan*" (a God) is an apposition of "*ilāhaka*" (your God), an apposition of an indefinite noun to a definite noun (*badal al-nakira min al-ma'rifa*), and He repeated it for the benefit of the attribute of oneness (*al-wahdāniyya*). It has also been said that "*ilāhan*" is a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*). Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is a good opinion, because the purpose is to establish the state of oneness."

Al-Hasan, Yahya ibn Ya'mar, al-Jahdari and Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi recited "*wa-ilāha abīka*" (and the God of your father). In this there are two possibilities. The first is that he used the singular and meant Abraham alone, and it was disliked to make Ishmael a father because he was an uncle. Al-Nahhas said: "This is not necessary, because the Arabs call an uncle a father." The second, according to the view of Sibawayh, is that "*abīka*" is a sound masculine plural, since Sibawayh related *ab*, *abūn* and *abīn*, as the poet said:

*Fa-qulnā aslimū inna akhūkum*
(So we said: "Submit, for indeed your brother...")

The witness in it is "*akhūkum*," which is a plural with the *wāw* and *nūn* (ending), and the *nūn* was dropped because of the annexation (*iḍāfa*), so that it may be correctly predicated of the plural pronoun. The complete verse is:

*Fa-qad salimat min al-iḥan al-ṣudūr*
(Then the breasts were freed from enmities.)

It describes women who were taken captive, when a delegation came to them from their people to ransom them, and the women wept before them and ransomed them with their fathers out of joy at the delegation's arrival to them.

(From *Sharḥ al-Shawāhid*.)

Another poet said:

*Fa-lammā tabayyannā aṣwātanā*
*Bakayna wa-faddaynanā bil-abīnā*
(When they recognized our voices, they wept and ransomed us with our fathers.)

[See *Khizānat al-Adab*, the twenty-eighth witness after the three hundredth.]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and to Him we are submitting﴾. "*Wa-naḥnu lahu muslimūn*" is a nominal sentence, a subject (*mubtada'*) and predicate (*khabar*). It is possible that it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), and the governing element would be "*na'budu*" (we worship).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 134:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is a community that has passed away﴾. "That" (تِلْكَ) is the subject (mubtada'), and "a community" (أُمَّةٌ) is the predicate (khabar), and "that has passed away" (قَدْ خَلَتْ) is a qualifying clause (na't) for "a community." If you wish, it may be the predicate of the subject, and "a community" would then be an appositive (badal) for "that." ﴿For it is what it earned﴾: "what" (مَا) is in the nominative position, as the subject (mubtada') or as a qualifier according to the view of the Kufans. ﴿And for you is what you have earned﴾: the same applies, meaning good and evil. In this is evidence that deeds and earnings are attributed to the servant, even though God Most High has empowered him to do so: if it is good, then it is by His bounty, and if it is evil, then it is by His justice. This is the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah, and the verses in the Qur'an with this meaning are many. Thus the servant is an acquirer (muktasib) of his actions, in the sense that a power accompanying the act has been created in him, by which he perceives the difference between a voluntary movement and, for example, the movement of trembling. That capacity is the basis of moral responsibility (taklif). The Jabriyyah (Determinists) said that the servant has no acquisition, and that he is like a plant that is turned by the winds. The Qadariyyah and the Mu'tazilah said contrary to these two views, and that the servant creates his own actions.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you will not be questioned about what they used to do﴾, meaning that no one is held to account for the sin of another, like His saying, exalted is He: "And no bearer bears the burden of another" (Q. 6:164; 35:18), meaning that no burdened one carries the load of another. This will come later [[see vol. 7, p. 157.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 135:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they say: Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided.﴾ Each group invited to what it itself followed, so Allah, Exalted is He, refuted them by saying: "Rather [we follow] the religion (millah)," that is, say, O Muhammad: "Rather we follow the religion (millah)." For this reason, al-Millah is in the accusative case (nusiba). It was also said: the meaning is "Rather we are guided by the religion of Ibrahim (Abraham)," and when the preposition was omitted, it became accusative (mansub).

Al-A'raj and Ibn Abi Abla read "Bal millatu" in the nominative (marfu') case. The implied sense is "Rather, the guidance is the religion (millah)," or "Our religion is the religion of Ibrahim."

"Hanifan" means inclining away from the disliked religions toward the truth, the religion of Ibrahim. It is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (hal), as stated by al-Zajjaj, meaning: "Rather we follow the religion of Ibrahim in this state."

Ali ibn Sulayman said: it is in the accusative as an object of "a'ni" (I mean), and the circumstantial state here is incorrect; one may not say "The servant of Hind came to me hastening (musri'a)."

Ibrahim was called hanif because he inclined (hanifa) toward the religion of Allah, which is Islam. Al-hanaf means inclination, and from it comes "a crooked leg (rijl hanfa')" and "a man who is ahnaf," who is one whose feet each lean toward the other with their toes. The mother of al-Ahnaf said:

By Allah, were it not for a crookedness in his leg,
there would not be among your youths one like him.

And the poet said:

When the shadow turns in the evening, you see it
hanif, and at the height of forenoon it turns Christian (yatanassar).

That is, the chameleon faces the qiblah in the evening and the east in the morning, and the east is the qiblah of the Christians.

Some said: al-hanaf means uprightness (istiqamah), so the religion of Ibrahim was called hanif for its uprightness. The one with bowed legs was called ahnaf out of optimism (tafa'ul) for straightness, just as the one stung is called salim (safe) and the deadly desert is called mafazah (a safe passage), according to the view of most of them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 136:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "We believe in God"﴾. Al-Bukhari transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The People of the Book would read the Torah in Hebrew and explain it in Arabic to the people of Islam. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: (Do not believe the People of the Book, nor disbelieve them, but say: 'We believe in Allah and in what has been revealed...') the verse." Muhammad ibn Sirin said: "If you are asked, 'Are you a believer?', say: 'We believe in Allah and in what has been revealed to us and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac...' the verse." Most of the early scholars (al-salaf) disliked that a man should say, "I am a believer in truth," and its explanation will come in Surat al-Anfal [see vol. 7, p. 763], God willing, exalted is He. Some of the earlier scholars were asked about a man to whom it was said: "Do you believe in so-and-so the Prophet?", and he named him by a name he did not know. If he said "Yes," perhaps he was not a prophet, and he would have testified to prophethood for someone who was not a prophet; and if he said "No," perhaps he was a prophet, and he would have denied one of the prophets. So what should he do? He said: he should say, "If he is a prophet, then I believe in him." The address in this verse is to this community, teaching them faith. Ibn Abbas said: "A group of Jews came to the Prophet ﷺ and asked him about which prophets he believed in, so the verse was revealed. When the mention of Jesus came, they said: 'We do not believe in Jesus, nor in anyone who believed in him.'"

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and what was revealed to us, and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes﴾. The plural of Ibrahim is Baraahim, and Isma'il is Sama'il, as said by al-Khalil and Sibawayh, and as said by the Kufans, who also related Baraahimah and Sama'ilah, and related Barahim and Sama'il. Muhammad ibn Yazid said: "This is an error, because the hamza is not a place for its addition. Rather, I say: Abarih and Asami', and it is permissible to say Abarih and Asami'." Ahmad ibn Yahya permitted Birah, as one says in diminutive Buraihah. The plural of Ishaq is Asahiq, and the Kufans related Asahiqah and Asahiq. Likewise Ya'qub: Ya'aqib, and Ya'aqibah and Ya'aqib. Al-Nahhas said: "As for Israil, we know of no one who permits dropping the hamza from its beginning; rather it is said Asaril, and the Kufans related Asarilah and Asaril." The rule in all of this is that it is pluralized as a sound masculine plural, so one says Ibrahimun, Ishaqun and Ya'qubun, and the sound plural has no inflection (amal) in it. The Asbat are the children of Jacob, peace be upon him; they are twelve sons, and from each of them arose a nation of people, and the singular is sibt. The sibt among the Children of Israel is in the position of the tribe among the descendants of Ishmael. They were called the Asbat from al-sabt, which means continuity, so they are a group in succession. It was also said: its origin is from al-sabat (with a vowel), which is a tree, meaning that in their multitude they are like trees, the singular being sabatah. Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: "What clarifies this for you is what Muhammad ibn Ja'far al-Anbari narrated to us, saying: Abu Nujayd [in vol. J and in Ibn Kathir's tafsir at this place; in all other manuscripts it is 'Abu Mujayd' with a mim] al-Daqqaq narrated to us, saying: al-Aswad ibn Amir narrated to us, saying: Isra'il narrated to us from Simak from Ikrimah from Ibn Abbas, who said: 'All the prophets were from the Children of Israel except ten: Noah, Shu'ayb, Hud, Salih, Lot, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Ishmael, and Muhammad ﷺ.' No one had two names except Jesus and Jacob." And al-sibt: the group and the tribe that trace back to one origin. And "sha'r sabt" and "sabit" means hair that is not curly. ﴿We make no distinction between any of them﴾. Al-Farra' said: that is, we do not believe in some of them and disbelieve in others, as the Jews and Christians did.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 137:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So if they believe in the like of what you have believed, then they are [rightly] guided﴾. The address is to Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community. The meaning: if they believe with a belief like your belief, and affirm with an affirmation like your affirmation, then they are rightly guided. Thus the likeness occurs between the two beliefs. It was also said [[This sentence is part of the first opinion and not a separate opinion, as the context might suggest.]] that the particle "bi" (bi, "with") is superfluous and emphatic. Ibn 'Abbas, as related by al-Tabari, used to read: "So if they believe in that which you have believed in, then they are rightly guided." This is the meaning of the reading, even though it contradicts the Mushaf. In this case "mithl" (like) is superfluous, as it is in His saying: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 8]], meaning: there is nothing like Him. A poet said [[He is Humayd al-Arqat, who described a people who were uprooted, and he likened them to the chaff whose grain has been eaten. "Al-'asf" is straw.

(From Sharh al-Shawahid.)]]:

"So they were made like chaff eaten [up]"

Baqiyyah related to us: Shu'bah related to us from Abu Hamzah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Do not say, ﴿So if they believe in the like of what you have believed﴾, for Allah has no like. Rather say: 'in that which you have believed.'" 'Ali ibn Nasr al-Jahdami followed him in this from Shu'bah; al-Bayhaqi mentioned it. The meaning is: that is, if they believe in your Prophet and in the prophets in general, and do not make distinctions between them as you do not, then they are rightly guided; but if they refuse anything except distinction, then they are those who have swerved from the religion [[In vol. C: "from the tabyin." In vols. B and Z: "from the tadayyun."]] into dissension, ﴿so Allah will suffice you against them﴾. It is related from a group of the people of reasoning that they said: it is possible that the kaf in His saying "There is nothing like unto Him" is superfluous. He said: What is related from Ibn 'Abbas, of his prohibiting the common reading, is a matter he adopted for the sake of emphasis in negating comparison from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is from Ibn 'Abbas by way of interpretation, meaning: this is how it should be understood. It has also been said that "bi" means "ala" (upon), and the meaning is: if they believe upon the like of your belief. It was also said: "mithl" retains its own sense, meaning: with the like of what was revealed, its proof being His saying: ﴿Say: I believe in whatever Allah has sent down of Scripture﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 13.]], and His saying: ﴿And say: We believe in what has been sent down to us and sent down to you﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 351.]].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But if they turn away﴾, that is, from belief, ﴿then they are only in dissension﴾. Zayd ibn Aslam said: "al-shiqaq" is contention. It was also said: "al-shiqaq" is opposition, hostility and enmity. Its origin is from "al-shiqq," which is the side, as though each of the two parties is on a side other than the side of its companion. A poet said:

"How long will they kill the scholars by force... and commit wickedness with dissension and hypocrisy?" [[In A: "... yaqtulu ... wayafjuru ..." with the yā'.]]

Another said:

"Otherwise know that we and you are transgressors, as long as we remain in dissension."

It was also said: "al-shiqaq" is derived from doing what is difficult and hard, as though each of the two parties eagerly does what is hard for its companion.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So Allah will suffice you against them﴾, that is, Allah will suffice His Messenger against his enemy. This was a promise from Allah, may He be exalted, to His Prophet (peace be upon him) that He would suffice him against whoever opposed him and contended with him among those who turned away, by means of those among the believers whom He would guide; so He fulfilled the promise to him. That occurred in the killing of Banu Qaynuqa', the killing of Banu Qurayzah, and the expulsion of Banu al-Nadir. The kaf, the ha' and the mim are in the position of the two objects in the accusative. Outside the Qur'an it is permissible to say: "fa-sayakfika [iyyahum]" [[Addition from I'rab al-Qur'an of al-Nahhas.]]. This letter, "fa-sayakfikahumu Allah," is the one upon which the blood of 'Uthman fell when he was killed, by the Prophet's (ﷺ) informing him of that. And "al-Sami'" hears the speech of every speaker, and "al-'Alim" knows what He executes among His servants and what He carries out upon them.

It is related that Abu Dulamah entered upon al-Mansur wearing a long cap and a durra'ah [[The durra'ah and the mudarra': a robe with a slit in its front.]], on whose back between the shoulders was written: "So Allah will suffice you against them, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing," and a sword hung at his waist. Al-Mansur had ordered the troops to wear this attire. Al-Mansur said to him: "How are you, O Abu Dulamah?" He said: "In evil, O Commander of the Faithful." He said: "And how is that?" He said: "What is your opinion of a man whose face is in the middle of him, and whose sword is in his backside, and who has cast the Book of Allah behind his back!" Al-Mansur laughed at him, and ordered that this attire be changed at once.

There are two issues in this passage. The first concerns His saying, ﴿The colouring of Allah﴾. Al-Akhfash and others said: it means the religion of Allah, and it is a *badal* (apposition) to "the religion" (millah) in the preceding words. Al-Kisa'i said: it is in the accusative by implication of "follow," or by *al-ighra'* (exhortation), meaning "adhere to." If it were read in the nominative, it would be permissible, meaning: "It is the colouring of Allah."

Shayban related from Qatadah that he said: "The Jews colour their sons as Jews, and the Christians colour their sons as Christians, and the colouring of Allah is Islam." Al-Zajjaj said: "What indicates this is that *ṣibgha* is a *badal* of *millah*."

Mujahid said: it means the *fitrah* (natural disposition) of Allah upon which He created mankind. Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: "Mujahid's statement returns to Islam, because the *fitrah* is the beginning of creation, and the beginning on which they were created is Islam."

It is related from Mujahid, al-Hasan, Abu al-Aliyah and Qatadah that *al-ṣibgha* is the religion.

The origin of this is that the Christians used to dip their children in water, which they call *al-ma'mudiyyah* (baptism), and they would say: "This is purification for them." Ibn Abbas said: the Christians, when a child was born to them and seven days had passed, would immerse him in water which they call the water of baptism, and so they would colour him with it, to purify him in place of circumcision, because circumcision is purification. When they did this they would say: "Now he has truly become a Christian." So Allah rejected this from them by saying: "The colouring of Allah," meaning: the colouring of Allah is the best colouring, and it is Islam. Thus religion is called *ṣibgha* by *isti'arah* (metaphor) and *majaz* (figurative usage), from the standpoint that its effects and its mark appear upon the one who adheres to it, just as the trace of dye appears on cloth.

One of the poets of the kings of Hamdan said:

Every people has a colouring for themselves,
but the colouring of Hamdan is the best of colourings.

We colour our sons upon that,
so how excellent is our colouring among colourings!

It has also been said that *al-ṣibgha* is the ritual washing for one who wishes to enter Islam, in place of the baptism of the Christians; al-Mawardi mentioned this. I say: according to this interpretation, the washing of the unbeliever is obligatory as an act of worship. This is the second issue: because the meaning of ﴿the colouring of Allah﴾ is "the washing of Allah," that is, wash yourselves upon your Islam with the washing which Allah has made obligatory upon you. It is in this sense that the established Sunnah came concerning Qays ibn Asim and Thumamah ibn Uthal when they embraced Islam.

Abu Hatim al-Busti related in his *Sahih al-Musnad* from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him: that Thumamah al-Hanafi [[Thumamah al-Hanafi is Thumamah ibn Uthal mentioned earlier.]] was taken captive, and the Prophet ﷺ passed by him one day, and he embraced Islam. So the Prophet ﷺ sent him to the orchard [[al-ha'it: a garden of palm trees that has a wall around it.]] of Abu Talhah, and commanded him to wash, so he washed, prayed two rak'ahs, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Your companion's Islam is good."

He also related from Qays ibn Asim that he embraced Islam, and the Prophet ﷺ commanded him to wash with water and lote-leaves. This was mentioned by al-Nasa'i, and Abu Muhammad Abd al-Haqq authenticated it.

It has been said that *qurbah* (act of drawing near) to Allah the Exalted is called *ṣibgha*; this was related by Ibn Faris in *al-Mujmal*. Al-Jawhari said: "The colouring of Allah" is His religion.

It has also been said that *al-ṣibgha* is circumcision: Ibrahim was circumcised, so the term *ṣibgha* was applied to circumcision because of the Christians' dipping of the boys in water; this was said by al-Farra'.

﴿And to Him we are worshippers.﴾

"Mubtada' and khabar" (subject and predicate).

Al-Hasan said: The argument was that they said, "We are closer to God than you, because we are the sons of God and His beloved." It was also said: "Because of the antiquity of our fathers and our scriptures, and because we did not worship idols."

So the meaning of the verse is: Say to them, O Muhammad, that is, say to these Jews and Christians who claim that they are the sons of God and His beloved, and who assert that they are closer to God than you because of the antiquity of their fathers and their scriptures: "Do you argue with us" (*ataḥājjūnanā*), that is, do you contend with us over the proof of your claim, when the Lord is one and each person is recompensed for his own deeds, so what effect does the antiquity of a religion have? The phrase "concerning God" means concerning His religion, nearness to Him, and standing before Him.

[[The editor's note in the source reads: "As in the manuscripts, though the correct reading is probably 'and standing with Him'."]]

The recitation of the majority is *ataḥājjūnanā*. It is permissible for two identical letters of the same kind to come together with both vowelled, because the second is treated as separate. Ibn Muhsin recited *ataḥājjūnnā* with assimilation (*idghām*), because the two identical letters meet. Al-Nahhas said: This is permissible, but it contradicts the written text (*al-sawād*). It is also permissible to read *ataḥājjūna* with the second nūn deleted, as Nafi' recited *fa-bima tubashshirūn* [[See vol. 10, p. 35.]].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And we are sincere to Him﴾, means: we are sincere in worship. There is in this a sense of rebuke, that is: you have not been sincere yourselves, so how do you claim what we are closer to than you? Sincerity (*al-ikhlāṣ*) in its reality is the purifying of an act from observing created beings.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God, may He be exalted, says: I am the best partner. Whoever associates a partner with Me in an act, it belongs to My partner. O people, make your deeds sincere for God, may He be exalted, for God, may He be exalted, accepts only what is sincerely done for Him. Do not say, 'This is for God and for the kinship tie,' for it is for the kinship tie and nothing of it is for God. Do not say, 'This is for God and for your faces,' for it is for your faces and nothing of it is for God, may He be exalted." Al-Dahhak ibn Qays al-Fihri narrated it, saying: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said... and he mentioned it. Al-Daraqutni recorded it.

Ruwaym said: Sincerity in action is that its doer does not seek in return any compensation in either of the two abodes, nor any share of the two angels.

Al-Junayd said: Sincerity is a secret between the servant and God, which no angel knows so as to record it, nor any devil so as to corrupt it, nor any desire so as to incline it.

Abu al-Qasim al-Qushayri and others related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "I asked Jibril about sincerity, what it is. He said: I asked the Lord of Might about sincerity, what it is. He said: It is one of My secrets, which I deposit in the heart of whomever I love of My servants."

The Qur'anic phrase ﴿Or do you say﴾ means "they say" (this is the view that *am* is *munqati'ah*, disjunctive [[This is the view that "am" is munqati'a.]]). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and 'Asim in Hafs's transmission read "تَقُولُونَ" (*taqulun*) with the *ta'*, and this is a good reading, because the discourse is coherent. It is as if the meaning is: "Do you dispute with us about God, or do you say that the prophets were upon your religion?" Here *am* is *muttasilah* (connecting). On the reading with the *ya'* (*yaqulun*), it is disjunctive, so it forms two separate statements, and *am* carries the meaning of *bal* (rather). "Hudan" is the predicate (*khabar*) of *kana*, and the predicate of *inna* is in the sentence. Outside the Qur'an it is permissible to put "هوداً" in the nominative as the predicate of *inna*, with *kana* being cancelled (*mulghah*); al-Nahhas mentioned this.

The Qur'anic phrase ﴿Say: Are you more knowing, or is God?﴾ is a rebuke and reproach for their claim that they were Jews or Christians. God refuted them by saying that He knows about them better than you do, meaning they were neither Jews nor Christians.

The Qur'anic phrase ﴿And who is more unjust﴾ is in the form of a question, but the meaning is: no one is more unjust, "than one who conceals a testimony," meaning their knowledge that the prophets were upon Islam. It was also said that what they concealed was the description of Muhammad (ﷺ); Qatadah said this, but the first view fits the context of the verse better. The phrase ﴿And God is not unaware of what you do﴾ is a threat and an announcement that He has not left their affair neglected (*sudan*) and that He will recompense them for their deeds. The *ghafil* (unaware) is one who does not pay attention to affairs out of negligence. It is derived from *al-ardh al-ghufl*, which is land with no knowledge of it and no trace of cultivation. A *naqah ghufl* is a she-camel with no brand. A *rajul ghufl* is a man who has not tested affairs. Al-Kisa'i said: "ardh ghufl" is land that has not been rained upon. "Ghafaltu 'an al-shay' ghaflatan wa ghufulan" (I was unaware of the thing), and "aghfaltu al-shay'" means I left it without remembering it.

The verse is repeated because it contains a meaning of warning and admonition. That is, if those prophets, despite their leadership and virtue, are recompensed according to what they earned, then you are more deserving of that (i.e., of being held to account), so emphasis was required, and for this reason it was repeated.

There are eleven issues (masa'il) in this verse.

**First:** His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The foolish among the people will say...﴾ God the Exalted informed that they would say about the turning of the believers from Syria to the Ka'bah, "What has turned them away from their qiblah?" "Sa-yaqulu" means "qala" (said), but the future form is used in place of the past, indicating the continuation of this and that they would persist in that saying. He specified "among the people" because foolishness occurs in inanimate objects and animals as well. By "the foolish" is meant all who said, "What has turned them away?" *Al-sufaha'* is the plural of *safih*, which means one of light mind, from their saying "a safih garment" when it is thin in weave. This has been mentioned before [[See vol. 1, p. 205, second edition.]]. Women are called *saqa'ih*. Al-Mu'arrij said: the *safih* is the one who lies and fabricates, deliberately opposing what he knows. Qutrub said: the *zalum* (wrongdoer) and the *jahul* (ignorant). The *sufaha'* here refers to the Jews who were in Medina; this is the view of Mujahid. Al-Suddi said: the hypocrites. Al-Zajjaj said: the disbelievers of Quraysh, when they denied the change of the qiblah, said, "Muhammad has longed for his birthplace, and soon he will return to your religion." The Jews said, "His matter has become confused for him and he is bewildered." The hypocrites said, "What has turned them away from their qiblah?" and they mocked the Muslims. "Wallahum" means "he diverted them and turned them away."

**Second:** The imams have related, and the wording is that of Malik, from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "While the people were at Quba' [[Quba' (with a damma): a village two miles from Medina, on the left for one heading to Mecca, with many remains of buildings, and there is the Mosque of Piety. (From Yaqut's Mu'jam.)]] in the morning prayer, a messenger came to them and said: 'The Messenger of God (ﷺ) has had a Qur'an revealed to him tonight, and he has been commanded to face the Ka'bah, so face it.' Their faces had been toward Syria, so they turned toward the Ka'bah." Al-Bukhari related from al-Bara' that the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis for sixteen or seventeen months, and he liked that his qiblah be toward the House. He first prayed the 'Asr prayer [[The version of al-Bukhari in his Sahih: "And he prayed—or prayed—the 'Asr prayer..."]] and some people prayed with him. A man who had prayed with the Prophet (ﷺ) went out and passed by people of the mosque who were bowing, and he said: "I testify before God that I prayed with the Prophet (ﷺ) facing Mecca," so they turned around as they were, toward the House. Some men who had died while facing the former qiblah before it was changed toward the House had been killed, and we did not know what to say about them, so God the Mighty and Majestic revealed: "God would not let your faith be lost" [Qur'an 2:143]. So in this narration it is the 'Asr prayer, and in Malik's narration it is the morning prayer. It is also said that this was revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) in the Mosque of Banu Salimah while he was in the noon prayer, after two units of it, and he turned during the prayer; so that mosque was named the Mosque of the Two Qiblahs. Abu al-Faraj mentioned that 'Abbad ibn Nahik was with the Prophet (ﷺ) in this prayer. Abu 'Umar mentioned in al-Tamhid, from Nuwaylah [[In the Isti'ab and al-Qamus it is "Nawlah" with a nun, and the author of al-Qamus said: "or it is like Juhaynah." I have mentioned it in the diminutive in al-Isabah under the letters ta' and nun; with nun it is the narration of Ishaq ibn Idris from Ja'far ibn Mahmud, and with ta' it is the narration of Ibrahim ibn Hamzah. The author of al-Isabah said: "the latter is more reliable."]] daughter of Aslam, who was among those who pledged allegiance, who said: "We were at the noon prayer when 'Abbad ibn Bishr ibn Qayzi came and said: 'The Messenger of God (ﷺ) has faced the qiblah'—or said: 'the Sacred House'—so the men moved to the place of the women, and the women moved to the place of the men."

It is also said that the verse was revealed outside of prayer, and this is the more common view. The first prayer toward the Ka'bah was the 'Asr, and God knows best. It is related that the first to pray toward the Ka'bah when the qiblah was turned away from Bayt al-Maqdis was Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla, because he was passing by the mosque and heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) addressing the people about the change of the qiblah from the pulpit, reciting this verse: "We have seen you turning your face about in the sky" [Qur'an 2:144], until he finished the verse. So I said to my companion: "Come, let us pray two units before the Messenger of God (ﷺ) descends, and we will be the first to pray." So we hid behind a camel [[Nu'am is a term for camels.]] and prayed the two units. Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) descended and led the people in the noon prayer that day. Abu 'Umar said: Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla has no narration other than this hadith and the hadith "I used to pray" concerning the virtue of al-Fatihah, which al-Bukhari related; and it has been mentioned before [[See vol. 1, p. 108, second edition.]].

**Third:** There is disagreement about the time of the change of the qiblah after his arrival in Medina. It is said it was changed after sixteen or seventeen months, as in al-Bukhari. Al-Daraqutni also related it from al-Bara', who said: "We prayed with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) after his arrival in Medina for sixteen months toward Bayt al-Maqdis; then God knew the inclination of His Prophet, and the verse was revealed: 'We have seen you turning your face about in the sky'..." So in this narration it is sixteen months without doubt. Malik related from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, that the change occurred two months before the Battle of Badr. Ibrahim ibn Ishaq said: that was in Rajab of the second year [after the Hijrah]. Abu Hatim al-Busti said: the Muslims prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis for seventeen months and three days exactly; that is because his arrival in Medina was on Monday, twelve nights into Rabi' al-Awwal, and God the Mighty and Majestic commanded him to face the Ka'bah on Tuesday, the middle of Sha'ban.

**Fourth:** The scholars also differed on the manner of his facing Bayt al-Maqdis, in three views. Al-Hasan said: that was from him by opinion and independent reasoning (ijtihad), and this was said by 'Ikrimah and Abu al-Aliyah. The second: he was given the choice between it and the Ka'bah, and he chose Jerusalem out of hope for the faith of the Jews and winning them over; this was said by al-Tabari. Al-Zajjaj said: it was a test for the polytheists, because they were accustomed to the Ka'bah. The third, which is the view of the majority, Ibn 'Abbas and others: it was obligatory for him to face it by the command of God the Exalted and His revelation without doubt; then God abrogated (naskh) that, and commanded him to face the Ka'bah in his prayer. They cited the saying of the Exalted: "We did not make the qiblah which you used to face except that We might know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels" [Qur'an 2:143].

**Fifth:** They also differed, when prayer was first prescribed for him in Mecca, whether it was toward Bayt al-Maqdis or toward Mecca, on two views. One group said: toward Bayt al-Maqdis, and in Medina for seventeen months, then God turned him toward the Ka'bah; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Others said: the prayer was first prescribed toward the Ka'bah, and he continued praying toward it throughout his stay in Mecca, in the same manner as the prayer of Abraham and Ishmael. When he came to Medina he prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis for sixteen or seventeen months, according to the disagreement, then God turned him to the Ka'bah. Abu 'Umar said: this is the more correct of the two views in my opinion. Another said: that is because when the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Medina he wanted to win over the Jews, so he faced their qiblah so that this would be more attractive to them; but when their obstinacy became clear and he despaired of them, he loved to be turned toward the Ka'bah, so he would look toward the sky. His love for the Ka'bah was because it is the qiblah of Abraham; this is from Ibn 'Abbas. It is also said: because it was more appealing to the Arabs for Islam. It is also said: to oppose the Jews; this is from Mujahid. It is related from Abu al-Aliyah al-Riyahi that he said: "The mosque of Salih (peace be upon him) had its qiblah toward the Ka'bah." He said: "Moses (peace be upon him) used to pray toward the rock, facing the Ka'bah, and it is the qiblah of all the prophets, God's blessings be upon them all." [[The wording here is unclear. In the Tafsir of al-Tabari (vol. 2, p. 21, Bulaq edition): "...al-Rabi' said: a Jew disputed with Abu al-Aliyah and said: Moses (peace be upon him) used to pray toward the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis. Abu al-Aliyah said: he prayed at the rock toward the Sacred House. He said: 'Then between me and you is a righteous mosque, for beneath it is part of the mountain.' Abu al-Aliyah said: I have prayed in it, and its qiblah was toward the Sacred House. Al-Rabi' said: Abu al-Aliyah informed me that he passed by the mosque of Dhu al-Qarnayn, and its qiblah was toward the Ka'bah."]]

**Sixth:** In this verse there is clear evidence that in the rulings of God the Exalted and His Book there is abrogating (naskh) and abrogated (mansukh) material. The community agreed on this except for one who deviated, as has been mentioned before [[At His saying: "What We abrogate of a verse or cause to be forgotten" [Qur'an 2:106], p. 61 of this part.]]. The scholars agreed that the qiblah was the first thing abrogated in the Qur'an, and that it was abrogated twice, according to one of the two views mentioned earlier in the issue.

**Seventh:** It also indicates the permissibility of abrogating the Sunnah by the Qur'an. This is because the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis, and there was no Qur'an about that; so the ruling came only from the Sunnah, and then that was abrogated by the Qur'an. On this view, "you used to face it" (kunta 'alayha) means "you face it" (anta 'alayha).

**Eighth:** It also contains evidence for the permissibility of acting with certainty on a report of a single transmitter (khabar al-wahid). This is because facing Bayt al-Maqdis was, according to them, certainly prescribed by the Law. Then when the messenger came to the people of Quba' and informed them that the qiblah had been changed to the Sacred Mosque, they accepted his word and turned toward the Ka'bah. Thus they abandoned what was mutawatir (widely transmitted, certain) in favor of a single report, which is only probable. The scholars differed over whether this is possible by reason and whether it has occurred. Abu Hatim said: "The preferred view is that it is possible by reason, if the Law had made it a form of worship, and it has occurred in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), as evidenced by the story of Quba', and by the fact that he (peace be upon him) would send single governors to the frontiers, and they would convey both the abrogating and the abrogated material." But that is prohibited after his death (ﷺ), by the consensus of the Companions that the Qur'an and what is known through mass transmission cannot be annulled by a single report; so no one among the earlier or later generations holds that it is permissible. Whoever prohibited it argued that it leads to an impossibility, namely the removal of what is certain by what is probable.

As for the story of the people of Quba'—

And the case of the Prophet's (ﷺ) governors is to be interpreted in terms of the indicators that yield certain knowledge, whether transmitted and verified or merely probable and presumed. The discussion of this, in question and answer form, is completed in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh).

The ninth issue: This verse is evidence that whoever has not received the news of the abrogating ruling (al-nasikh) is still bound (mut'abbad) by the first ruling. This differs from the view of those who say that the first ruling is lifted by the existence of the abrogating ruling itself, not by knowledge of it. The first view is more sound, because the people of Quba' continued to pray toward Bayt al-Maqdis until the one who came to them informed them of the abrogating ruling, and then they turned toward the Ka'bah. So the abrogating ruling, once it comes into existence, certainly lifts the earlier ruling, but on condition that one knows of it, because the abrogating ruling is an address (khitab), and it is not an address with respect to one who has not received it. The benefit of this disagreement appears in acts of worship performed after the abrogation and before the news reached the person, namely whether they must be repeated or not. On the same basis is built the question of the agent (wakil) who acts after his principal has dismissed him or died, before he knows of it, which is held to be one of two opinions. The same applies to the muqarid [[Qiradh (with a kasra on the qaf) in the Maliki school is what is called mudaraba in the Hanafi school. It is when the muqarid (with a kasra on the ra', who is the owner of the capital) gives the muqarid (with a fatha on the ra', who is the worker) money to trade with, on condition that he has a known share of the profit.]], and to the judge (hakim) when the one who appointed him dies or dismisses him. The sound view is that what each of these does is valid, and his ruling is not rejected. Al-Qadi Iyad said: The school (madhhab) has not differed regarding the rulings applying to one who has been freed without knowing of his manumission, that they are the rulings of a free person in his dealings with people. As for his dealings with Allah the Exalted, they are valid. They have also not differed concerning a freed woman that she does not have to repeat what she prayed after her manumission and before she knew of it, if she prayed without a covering. They have only differed concerning one who encounters a binding condition (mujib) while in the act of worship, and his worship is still in progress, by analogy with the case of Quba'. So whoever prayed in one state and then his state changed before he completed his prayer, he completes it and does not break it, and what has passed is sufficient for him. Likewise is one who prayed naked and then found a garment during the prayer, or one who began his prayer healthy and then fell ill, or sick and then recovered, or seated and then became able to stand, or a slave-woman who was freed while in prayer: she takes her covering and builds upon her prayer. I say: Likewise is one who entered the prayer by tayammum (dry ablution) and then water became available to him. He does not break his prayer, as Malik and al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on them both, and others say. It is also said that he must break it, and this is the view of Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, and it will come later.

The tenth issue: This verse is also evidence for the acceptance of solitary reports (khabar al-wahid). This is agreed upon among the early generations (al-salaf), and it is known by continuous practice (tawatur) from the custom of the Prophet (ﷺ) in sending his messengers as individuals to the regions, so that they would teach the people their religion, and then convey to them the Sunnah of their Prophet (ﷺ) concerning commands and prohibitions.

The eleventh issue: This verse is also evidence that the Qur'an was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) piece by piece, at one time after another, according to the need for it, until Allah perfected His religion, as He said: ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾ [[See vol. 6, p. 16.]].

His saying the Exalted: ﴿Say: To Allah belong the east and the west﴾. He established it as an argument, meaning: to Him belongs the dominion of the easts and the wests and what is between them. So He may command turning toward whichever direction He wills, and this has already been discussed.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿He guides whom He wills﴾ is a reference to Allah the Exalted guiding this community to the qiblah of Ibrahim, and Allah the Exalted knows best. As for al-sirat, it is the path. And al-mustaqim is that in which there is no crookedness, and this has already been discussed [[Vol. 1, p. 147.]].

This is the first of two parts. The first issue concerns the verse ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾. The meaning is: just as the Ka'bah is the center of the earth, so We have made you a middle nation, that is, We have placed you below the prophets and above the (other) nations. Al-wasat means al-'adl (the just, the upright), and the root of this is that the best of things is their middle. al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning the words of Allah, "And thus We have made you a middle nation," that he said: "(Just)." He said: This is a hasan sahih hadith. In the revelation (it is said): ﴿The most moderate of them said﴾ [[Vol. 18, p. 244.]], meaning the most just of them and the best of them. Zuhayr said:

*They are a middle (wasat), whom the people accept as judges*
*when one of the nights of great calamity descends.*

Another said:

*You are the most middle of a tribe, who know*
*the small matters and the great ones.*

Another said:

*Do not go to extremes in affairs,*
*do not ask excessively if you are asked.*
*And be among the people, all of them, in the middle (wasat).*

The middle (wasat) of a valley is its best place, where there is the most pasture and water. Since the middle is far from excess and deficiency, it is praiseworthy. That is, this community did not exaggerate (ghuluww) about its prophets as the Christians did, nor did it fall short (taqsir) about its prophets as the Jews did. There is a hadith: "The best of matters is their middle." And it is reported from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "Upon you is the middle path (al-namat al-awsat); to it the one who has gone too far returns, and to it the one who has fallen behind rises." [[In al-Lisan and al-Nihayah: "...The best of this community is the middle path, the one who lags behind joins them, and the one who exaggerates returns to them." Al-namat means a group of people whose affair is one. It is also said it means a way (tariqah).]] One says: Fulan is among the middle of his people (awsat qawmihi), and he is their wasitah (intermediary/mediator), and wasat qawmihi, meaning among their best and those of noble descent. The verb is wasata, wasatah, wasitah. It is not from the wasat meaning "between two things." As for al-wasṭ (with a sukun on the sin), it is an adverb of place: you say, "I prayed wasṭa al-qawm (in the midst of the people)," and "I sat wasṭa al-dar (in the middle of the house)" with a fatha on the sin, because it is a noun. al-Jawhari said: Every place where "bayn" (between) can fit is wasṭ, and where "bayn" cannot fit, it is wasat with a fatha; and it is sometimes pronounced with a sukun, but that is not the correct form.

The second issue: Allah's words ﴿so that you may be﴾ are in the accusative by the lam of purpose (lam kay), meaning "in order that you may be." ﴿witnesses﴾ (shuhada') is the predicate of kana (to be). ﴿over the people﴾ ('ala al-nas) means on the Day of Gathering, for the prophets over their nations, as is established in Sahih al-Bukhari from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Nuh (peace be upon him) will be called on the Day of Resurrection, and he will say, 'At your service, O Lord, and at your pleasure.' He will be asked, 'Did you convey (the message)?' He will say, 'Yes.' Then his nation will be asked, 'Did he convey to you?' They will say, 'No warner came to us.' He will be asked, 'Who will bear witness for you?' He will say, 'Muhammad and his nation.' They will bear witness that he conveyed, and the Messenger will be a witness over you." That is the meaning of His words, mighty and majestic: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation, so that you may be witnesses over the people, and the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾ [[The hadith was also related at length by Ibn al-Mubarak in meaning, and in it: "Those nations will say, 'How can he bear witness against us, when he did not reach us?' The Lord, glorified is He, will say to them, 'How can you bear witness about those you did not reach?' They will say, 'Our Lord, You sent to us a Messenger and sent down to us Your covenant and Your Book, and You related to us that they had conveyed, so we bear witness to what You covenanted to us.' The Lord will say, 'They have spoken truly.' That is His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ — and al-wasat means al-'adl (the just) — ﴿so that you may be witnesses over the people, and the Messenger may be a witness over you.'"]]. Ibn An'um said: It has reached me that on that day the community of Muhammad (peace be upon him) will bear witness, except those who harbor enmity (hinnah, with a kasrah on the ha', meaning enmity, a rare dialect form of ihnah) against their brother. Another group said: The meaning of the verse is that some of you will bear witness over others after death, as is established in Sahih Muslim from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that when a funeral bier passed by him and good was said of the deceased, he said: "It is due, it is due, it is due." Then another bier passed by him and bad was said of the deceased, and he said: "It is due, it is due, it is due." 'Umar said: May my father and mother be ransomed for you, a bier passed by you and good was said of it, and you said, "It is due, it is due, it is due," and a bier passed by and bad was said of it, and you said, "It is due, it is due, it is due." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whomever you praise with good, Paradise is due to him; and whomever you praise with evil, the Fire is due to him. You are the witnesses of Allah on earth. You are the witnesses of Allah on earth. You are the witnesses of Allah on earth." Al-Bukhari related it in meaning. In some of its chains outside the two Sahihs, he recited: ﴿so that you may be witnesses over the people, and the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾.

Abban and Layth related from Shahr ibn Hawshab, from 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "My community has been given three things that were not given except to the prophets. Whenever Allah sent a prophet, He said to him, 'Call upon Me, and I will answer you,' and He said to this community, 'Call upon Me, and I will answer you.' And whenever Allah sent a prophet, He said to him, 'He has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion,' and He said to this community, 'And He has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion.' And whenever Allah sent a prophet, He made him a witness over his people, and He made this community witnesses over the people." al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim Abu 'Abd Allah related it in Nawadir al-Usul.

The third issue: Our scholars said: Our Lord, blessed and exalted is He, has informed us in His Book of what He has bestowed upon us, by preferring us with the title of justice (al-'adalah) and entrusting us with the weighty responsibility of witnessing over all His creation. So He placed us first in rank, even though we are last in time, as he (peace be upon him) said: "We are the last (in time) and the first (in rank)." This is evidence that only the just may bear witness, and that the word of one person is not binding on another unless that person is just. The explanation of justice and its rulings will come, if Allah wills, at the end of the surah [[See Vol. 3, p. 383.]].

The fourth issue: In this is evidence for the soundness of al-ijma' (scholarly consensus) and the obligation to act upon it (al-ijma', consensus of the scholars, is the agreement of the jurists of the community on a ruling). Since they are just, they bear witness over the people. Every generation is a witness over those after it, so the word of the Companions is a proof and a witness over the Successors, and the word of the Successors is over those after them. And since the community has been made witnesses, it is obligatory to accept their word. There is no sense in the view of one who says that it means the entire community, because then no consensus would be established until the Hour arrives. The explanation of this is in the books of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh).

The words of Allah: ﴿and the Messenger will be a witness over you﴾. It is said: its meaning is over your deeds on the Day of Resurrection. It is also said: "over you" means "for you," that is, he will bear witness for you to faith. And it is said: that is, he will bear witness against you concerning his conveying (the message) to you.

The words of Allah: ﴿And We did not make the qiblah which you used to face﴾. It is said: the qiblah here refers to the first qiblah, because of His words, "which you used to face." It is also said: the second, so the kaf (in "kuntu 'alayha") is redundant, meaning "you are now facing it," as has already been said, and as He said, "You are the best community brought forth for mankind," meaning "you are," according to some of them; and it will come [[See Vol. 4, p. 170.]].

The words of Allah: ﴿except that We might know who follows the Messenger﴾. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The meaning of "li-na'lama" (that We might know) is "li-naraa" (that We might see). The Arabs use knowledge in place of sight and sight in place of knowledge, as in His words: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt﴾ [[See Vol. 20, p. 44.]], meaning, "Have you not known?" It is also said: the meaning is "that you might know that We know," for the hypocrites were in doubt about Allah's knowledge of things before they occurred. It is also said: the meaning is "to distinguish the people of certainty from the people of doubt," related by Ibn Furak, and al-Tabari mentioned it from Ibn 'Abbas. It is also said: the meaning is "that the Prophet and his followers might know," and He informed of that about Himself, as one says, "The commander did such-and-such," when in fact his followers did it; this was mentioned by al-Mahdawi, and it is good. It is also said: its meaning is "that Muhammad might know," and He attributed his knowledge to Himself as a mark of honor and distinction, just as He referred to Himself in His words in the hadith: "O son of Adam, I was sick and you did not visit Me" [[He attributed sickness to Himself, and the intended meaning is the servant, as an honor to the servant and bringing him near. In a hadith: "He said, 'O Lord, how shall I visit You, when You are the Lord of the worlds?' He said, 'Did you not know that My servant so-and-so was sick and you did not visit him? Did you not know that if you had visited him, you would have found Me with him?'..." See Sahih Muslim, "The Virtue of Visiting the Sick."]]. The first (interpretation) is more apparent: that its meaning is the knowledge of witnessing (ilm al-mu'ayanah) which necessitates reward, and He, glorified is He, is the Knower of the unseen and the seen; He knows what will be before it is, and the circumstances differ with respect to the known things, but His knowledge does not differ; rather it relates to all things with one single relation. Likewise every occurrence in the Book of this meaning, such as His words: ﴿And that Allah may know those who believe and take martyrs from among you﴾ [[See Vol. 4, p. 218.]], and ﴿And We will surely test you until We know those who strive among you and the patient﴾ [[See Vol. 16, p. 253.]], and what is similar to them. The verse is a reply to the Quraysh in their saying, "What has turned them away from their qiblah which they used to face?" The Quraysh were attached to the Ka'bah, so Allah, mighty and majestic, wished to test them with something other than what they were accustomed to, so that it would become manifest who follows the Messenger from among those who do not follow him. al-Zuhri recited "ila li-yu'lama," and on this reading "man" is in the nominative position, since it is the substitute for the passive subject (ism ma lam yusamma fa'iluh). On the reading of the majority, it is in the accusative position as the object. "Who follows the Messenger" means in what he was commanded regarding facing the Ka'bah. "Who turns back on his heels" means who apostatizes from his religion, for when the qiblah was changed, some of the Muslims apostatized and some became hypocrites. Therefore He said: ﴿and indeed it was a great thing﴾, meaning its change, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Qatadah. In Arabic grammar the estimated sense is: "and indeed the change was (a great thing)."

The words of Allah: ﴿and indeed it was a great thing﴾. al-Farra' held that "in" (inna) and the lam here mean "ma" (not) and "illa" (except). The Basrans say: it is the heavy "inna" that has been lightened. al-Akhfash said: meaning, "and indeed the qiblah, or the change, or the turning, was a great thing." ﴿except for those whom Allah guided﴾, meaning He created the guidance, which is faith, in their hearts, as He said: ﴿Those, He has written faith upon their hearts﴾ [[See Vol. 17, p. 308.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 143 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah would never make your faith (iman) go to waste﴾. The scholars agreed that it was revealed concerning one who died while praying toward Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), as established in al-Bukhari from the hadith of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, as mentioned earlier [[See p. 148 of this part.]]. At-Tirmidhi related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) was turned toward the Ka'bah, they said: "O Messenger of Allah, what of our brothers who died while praying toward Bayt al-Maqdis?" So Allah, may He be exalted, revealed: "And Allah would never make your faith go to waste," to the end of the verse. He said: This is a hadith that is hasan sahih. Thus He called the prayer "faith" because it comprises intention, speech and action. Malik said: "I indeed take this verse as a refutation of the Murji'ah who say that prayer is not part of faith." Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: "And Allah would never make your faith go to waste" means by your facing the qiblah and your affirmation of your Prophet, and this is the view of the majority of Muslims and of the usuliyyun (scholars of legal theory). Ibn Wahb, Ibn al-Qasim, Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam and Ashhab related from Malik regarding "And Allah would never make your faith go to waste" that he said: "Your prayer."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Kind (ra'uf) and Merciful to the people﴾. Ra'fah is stronger than rahmah. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: ra'fah is greater than rahmah, though the meaning is close. We have already discussed its lexical usage, its poetry and its meanings in the book "al-Asna fi Sharh Asma' Allah al-Husna" (The Most Sublime in Explaining the Names of Allah), so refer to it there. The Kufans and Abu 'Amr read "la-ra'ufun" on the pattern fa'ul, and this is the dialect of Banu Asad, and from it is the saying of al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah:

"And the worst of seekers, do not be one who fights his paternal uncle, the Kind (al-ra'uf), the Merciful (al-rahim)."

Al-Kisa'i related that the dialect of Banu Asad is "la-ra'fun," on the pattern fa'l. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' read "la-Ru'uf" with a doubled letter and without hamzah, and he likewise facilitated every hamzah in the Book of Allah, whether it was sakinah (quiescent) or mutaharrikah (vowelled).

The scholars said: this verse comes after the revelation of His words, "The foolish among the people will say..." The meaning of "the turning of your face" is the turning of your face toward the sky, as al-Tabari said. Al-Zajjaj said: it is the turning of your eyes in looking toward the sky, and the meanings are close. He singled out the sky for mention because it is the place of what is ascribed to it and what comes down from it, such as rain, mercy and revelation. The meaning of "you are pleased with" is that you love it. Al-Suddi said: when he prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis, he would raise his head toward the sky, looking for what he would be commanded, and he loved to pray toward the direction of the Ka'bah. So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the sky﴾. Abu Ishaq narrated from al-Bara', who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis for sixteen or seventeen months, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) loved to be turned toward the Ka'bah, so Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the sky﴾. This meaning and its discussion have already been mentioned, and praise is due to Allah.

His words, the Exalted: ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾. In it there are five issues.

The first: His words, ﴿So turn﴾, are an imperative. "Your face toward" means the side of "the Sacred Mosque," meaning the Ka'bah, and there is no disagreement on this. It was said: facing the whole House, from Ibn Abbas. Ibn Umar said: facing the spout (al-mizab) of the Ka'bah, as Ibn Atiyyah said. The mizab is the qiblah of the people of Madinah and of Syria, and there is the qiblah of the people of al-Andalus. I say: Ibn Jurayj narrated from Ata', from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: (The House is the qiblah for the people of the Mosque, the Mosque is the qiblah for the people of the Haram, and the Haram is the qiblah for the people of the earth in its east and its west, from among my nation).

The second: His words, ﴿toward the Sacred Mosque﴾. The word shatr (side) has several usages: it means the side and the direction, as in this verse, and it is a locative adverb (zarf makan), as you say: tilqa'hu (in front of it) and jihatahu (in its direction). The adverb is in the accusative because it is a supplementary element (fadlah) in the position of the direct object (al-maf'ul bihi) [[Supplement from I'rab al-Quran by al-Nahhas.]], and also because the action falls upon it. Dawud ibn Abi Hind said: in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is: "So turn your face tilqa'a the Sacred Mosque." The poet said [[He is Abu Zinba' al-Judhami (from Lisan al-Arab).]]:

I say to Umm Zinba', "Stand the chests of the camels toward the Banu Tamim."

Another said:

And there has overtaken you from the side of your frontier a terror whose darkness covers you in pieces.

Another said:

Is there anyone to convey to Amr a message, though the message does not avail toward the side of Amr?

The shatr of a thing is its half, and from this is the hadith: (Purity is half of faith).
