It may also be one of the words with opposite meanings: it is said shatara ila kadha when he turned toward such a thing, and shatara 'an kadha when he was removed from it and turned away from it. As for the shatir among men, it is because he has taken a course other than straightness, and he is the one who wearied his people with his wickedness; he has been shatara and shatura (with a damma) shatarah in both senses. Some were asked about the shatir, and he said: he is one who has set out to distance himself from what Allah has forbidden.

The third: There is no disagreement among the scholars that the Ka'bah is the qiblah in every horizon. They agreed that whoever sees it and beholds it, it is obligatory for him to face it, and that if he leaves facing it while he is beholding it and knows its direction, then he has no prayer, and he must repeat everything he prayed. Abu Umar mentioned this. They agreed that everyone who is absent from it must face its side, its direction and its front. If it is hidden from him, he must seek guidance to it by everything possible of the stars, the winds, the mountains and other things by which its direction may be known. Whoever sits in the Sacred Mosque, let his face be toward the Ka'bah and let him look at it in faith and seeking reward, for it is narrated that looking at the Ka'bah is an act of worship, as said by Ata' and Mujahid.

The fourth: They differed over whether the obligation for one who is absent is facing the exact building (ayn) or the direction (jihah). Some of them said the former. Ibn al-Arabi said: this is weak, because it is an obligation to what one cannot reach. Others said the direction, and this is the correct view, for three reasons. The first: it is what is possible, to which the obligation is tied. The second: it is what is commanded in the Quran, by His words: ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque, and wherever you are﴾, meaning from the earth, from east or west, ﴿turn your faces toward it﴾. The third: the scholars argued from the long rows, which are certainly many times the width of the House.

The fifth: In this verse there is clear proof for what Malik and those who agreed with him held, that the one praying should look ahead of himself and not at the place of his prostration. Al-Thawri, Abu Hanifah, al-Shafi'i and al-Hasan ibn Hayy said: it is recommended that his gaze be at the place of his prostration. Shurayk al-Qadi said: he looks, while standing, at the place of prostration; in bowing, at the place of his feet; in prostration, at the place of his nose; and in sitting, at his lap. Ibn al-Arabi said: he only looks ahead, for if he bows his head, some of the obligatory standing is lost in the head, which is the most noble of the limbs; and if he keeps his head upright and forces his gaze downward, that is a great hardship and difficulty. ﴿And He has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion﴾. Yet that is better for one who is able to do it.

His words, the Exalted: ﴿And indeed, those who were given the Scripture﴾, meaning the Jews and the Christians, ﴿know that it is the truth from their Lord﴾, meaning the changing of the qiblah from Bayt al-Maqdis. If it is asked: how do they know this, when it is not part of their religion nor in their scripture? It is answered that there are two answers. One: when they knew from their scripture that Muhammad (ﷺ) is a prophet, they knew that he says nothing but the truth and commands nothing but it. The second: they knew from their religion the permissibility of naskh (abrogation), even though some of them denied it, so they became knowers of the permissibility of changing the qiblah.

His words, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what they do﴾. Its meaning has already been mentioned [[See vol. 1, p. 466.]]. Ibn Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "ta'malun" with the ta, addressing the People of the Book or the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ). On both readings it is an announcement that Allah the Exalted does not neglect the deeds of His servants nor is He heedless of them, and it carries a warning. The rest read it with the ya, from below. [[In manuscript B: "that Allah the Exalted knows the deeds ..."]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 145:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you were to bring to those who were given the Book every sign, they would not follow your qiblah﴾, because they disbelieved although the truth had become clear to them, and signs do not benefit them; "signs" means the indications (al-'alamat). The plural of qiblah in the broken plural (taksir) is qibal, and in the sound feminine plural (taslim) it is qiblat. It is permissible to replace the kasrah with a fathah, so you say qiblat (with fathah on the ba'). It is also permissible to drop the kasrah and make the ba' sukun, so you say qiblat. "Law'in" (if indeed) is answered with the answer of "law" (if), though they are opposites in that "law" in its answer requires the past and the occurrence, while "la'in" requires the future. Al-Farra' and al-Akhfash said: it is answered with the answer of "law" because the meaning is "and if you had come (wa-law atayta)". Likewise "law" is answered with the answer of "la'in"; you say: "law ahsanta uhsinu ilayka" (if you had done good, I would do good to you). A similar example is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if We were to send a wind and they saw it turn yellow, they would surely remain disbelievers﴾ [[See vol. 14, p. 45.]], meaning "and if We had sent a wind." Sibawayh disagreed with them and said: the meaning of "la'in" differs from the meaning of "law," so neither of them enters upon the other. So the meaning is: "And if you were to bring to those who were given the Book every sign, they would not follow your qiblah." Sibawayh said: the meaning of "And if We were to send a wind and they saw it turn yellow, they would surely remain" is "they would surely remain (layazallunna)."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And you are not one who will follow their qiblah﴾. This is a statement in the form of a report, but it implies a command, meaning: do not incline toward anything of that. Then Allah, may He be exalted, informed that the Jews do not follow the qiblah of the Christians, nor the Christians the qiblah of the Jews, related from al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. This is an announcement of their disagreement, their opposition to one another, and their misguidance. Some said: the meaning is that whoever of them embraced Islam and followed you does not follow the qiblah of those who did not embrace Islam, nor do those who did not embrace Islam follow the qiblah of those who embraced Islam. The first is more apparent, and Allah knows best.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, then indeed you would be among the wrongdoers﴾. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and what is meant is his community, those who may follow their own desire and thereby become wrongdoers by following it. It is not permissible that the Prophet (ﷺ) would do anything by which he would become a wrongdoer, so it is understood as directed at his community, owing to the infallibility (ismah) of the Prophet (ﷺ), and we are certain that this does not occur from him. The Prophet (ﷺ) was addressed to magnify the matter, and because he is the one to whom it was revealed. "Al-ahwa'" is the plural of hawa (desire), which has been discussed earlier [[See vol. 9, p. 94 of this part.]]. Likewise "min al-'ilm" was discussed earlier as well [[See p. 95 of this part.]], so there is no point in repeating it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book know it as they know their own sons﴾. "Alladhina" (those who) is in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate (khabar) is "ya'rifunahu" (they know it). It is also permissible for it to be in the genitive position as a qualifier (sifah) of "al-zalimin" (the wrongdoers), and "ya'rifun" (they know) is then in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: they know his prophethood and the truthfulness of his message. The pronoun refers back to Muhammad (ﷺ), as said by Mujahid, Qatadah and others. It was also said that "ya'rifun" refers to the change of the qibla from Bayt al-Maqdis to the Ka'bah, that it is the truth, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jurayj, al-Rabi' and Qatadah also.

He specified the sons for knowing, mentioning them rather than the selves, although the self is closer, because a person passes through a period of his life in which he does not know himself, but there is no time in which he does not know his son. It is related that Umar said to Abdullah ibn Salam: "Do you know Muhammad (ﷺ) as you know your son?" He said: "Yes, and more. Allah sent His trustworthy one in His heaven to His trustworthy one on His earth with his description, so I knew him. As for my son, I do not know what his mother did."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, a group of them conceal the truth﴾. This means Muhammad (ﷺ), as said by Mujahid, Qatadah and Khusayf. It was also said that it means facing the Ka'bah, as we mentioned just above.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿while they know﴾. This is clear evidence of the validity of disbelief out of obstinacy (mu'anadah). Similar to it is: "And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them" [See vol. 13, p. 163.], and His saying: "So when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 147:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿The truth is from your Lord﴾, meaning the direction of the Ka'bah (qiblah), not what the Jews informed you of regarding their qiblah. It is narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he recited "al-haqq" in the accusative, governed by "ya'lamun", meaning: they know the truth. Its accusative may also be justified by the assumed verb "ilzam al-haqq" (hold fast to the truth). The nominative is valid as a subject (ibtida'), or by the implied subject (mubtada'), the estimate being "huwa al-haqq" (it is the truth), or by an implied verb, meaning "jaka al-haqq" (the truth has come to you). Al-Nahhas said: As for the one in al-Anbiya' (﴿al-haqq fa-hum mu'ridun﴾), we do not know anyone who recited it except in the accusative. The difference between them is that the one in Surat al-Baqarah is the beginning of a verse, whereas the one in al-Anbiya' is not so.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿So do not be of those who doubt﴾, meaning of those who are skeptical. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), but the intended meaning is his community (ummah). It is said: "Fulan tamara fi kadha" when certainty confronts him at one time and doubt at another, so he repels one with the other. From this comes al-mira' (disputation), because each of the two doubts the other's statement. And al-imtira' regarding a thing is doubting it, and likewise al-tamari. Al-Tabari cited as evidence that al-mumtarun means the doubters the verse of al-A'sha:

"He pours out upon the flanks of the mumtarin, from those who spur on, when the mirage quivers."

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: He erred in this, because Abu 'Ubaydah and others said: the mumtarun in the verse are those who stroke the horses with their feet to make them run, as though they were milking the running out of them; and there is no meaning of doubt in the verse, as al-Tabari said. I say: the meaning of doubt is present in it, because the owner may be testing the horse to know whether it is still of the running it was known for, lest it have suffered some harm; or this may be at the time of its first purchase, so he makes it run to learn the measure of its running. Al-Jawhari said: "Maraytu al-faras" means when you extract what it has of running by a whip or otherwise; the noun is al-miryah (with kasrah), and it may be pronounced with dammah. "Maraytu al-naqah maryan" means when I stroked its udder so that it would yield milk; "amrat hiya" means when its milk flowed, and the noun is al-miryah (with kasrah), while the dammah is an error. Al-miryah is doubt, and it may be pronounced with dammah, and both have been read.

**The first issue: ﴿For each there is a direction﴾**

The word *al-wijhah* (direction) is of the form *fi'lah*, derived from *al-muwajahah* (facing). *Al-wijhah*, *al-jihah* and *al-wajh* have one meaning. What is meant here is the *qiblah* (direction of prayer). That is, they do not follow your *qiblah*, and you do not follow their *qiblah*. And ﴿for each there is a direction﴾ is either in truth or in whim.

**The second issue: ﴿and he is its facer﴾**

The pronoun *huwa* refers to the word *kull* (each) in its form, not its meaning. If it referred to its meaning, it would have said *hum muwalloha wujuhahum* (they are its facers, their faces toward it). The *ha'* and the *alif* are the first object, and the second object is omitted. That is, *huwa muwalliha wajhahu wa-nafsahu* (he faces it with his face and himself).

The meaning is: for every owner of a religious community (*millah*) there is a *qiblah*, and the owner of the *qiblah* faces it with his face. This is in the form of *kull*. This is the view of al-Rabi', 'Ata' and Ibn 'Abbas.

Ali ibn Sulayman said: *"wallaha"* means *mutawalliha* (the one who faces it).

Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Amir read *"muwallaha"* in the passive voice (*ma lam yusamma fa'iluhu*). In this reading the pronoun refers to a singular noun. That is: for every one of the people there is a *qiblah*, and the one who is faced toward it (*muwalla*) is the one turned toward it. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

It is possible that, according to the reading of the majority, *"huwa"* is a pronoun referring to the name of Allah, may He be glorified and exalted, even though He has not been mentioned, because it is known that Allah, may He be glorified and exalted, is the one who does this. The meaning is: for every owner of a religious community there is a *qiblah*, and Allah turns him toward it.

Al-Tabari narrated that some people read *"wa-li-kulli wijhatun"* with *kull* in the construct form with *wijhah*. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: al-Tabari rejected this reading, but it is valid (*muttajihah*). That is: *fa-stabiqu al-khayrat* (so race toward good deeds), for each direction He has turned you toward (*wallakumuha*). Do not object in what He commanded you between this and that. That is, you are only obligated to obey in all of them.

The phrase *"li-kulli wijhatun"* was placed before the command in His words *"istabiqu al-khayrat"* for the sake of giving attention to the direction, just as the object is placed first. Abu 'Amr al-Dani mentioned this reading from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

The *waw* in *"wijhah"* was kept (not dropped) to distinguish between *'iddah* and *zinah*, because *jihah* is a noun of place (*zarf*) while these are verbal nouns (*masadir*). Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) said: some people held that it is a verbal noun which deviated from analogy (*qiyas*) and so kept its *waw*. Others held that it is a noun, not a verbal noun. Someone other than Abu 'Ali said: when you want the verbal noun you say *wijhah*, and *jihah* may be used for the place (*zarf*).

**The third issue: ﴿race toward the good deeds﴾**

That is, *ila al-khayrat* (toward the good deeds), so the preposition was omitted. That is: hasten to what Allah, may He be glorified and exalted, has commanded you regarding facing the Sacred House (*al-Bayt al-Haram*). Although it includes encouragement to hasten and rush toward all acts of obedience in general, what is meant here is the facing mentioned, due to the context of the verses. The meaning intended is hastening to pray at the beginning of its time. Allah the Exalted knows best.

al-Nasa'i narrated from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The likeness of one who goes early to prayer is like the one who sacrifices a camel, then the one after him is like the one who sacrifices a cow, then the one after him is like the one who sacrifices a ram, then the one after him is like the one who sacrifices a hen, then the one after him is like the one who sacrifices an egg."

al-Daraqutni narrated from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed one of you prays the prayer at its time, but has left from the first part of the time what is better for him than his family and his wealth."

Malik narrated it from Yahya ibn Sa'id as his statement.

al-Daraqutni also narrated from Ibn 'Umar, who said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The best of deeds is prayer at the beginning of its time."

In the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud it is *"awwala waqtiha"* without *"fi"*.

It was also narrated from Ibrahim ibn 'Abd al-Malik, from Abu Mahdhurah, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The beginning of the time is the pleasure of Allah, the middle of the time is the mercy of Allah, and the end of the time is the pardon of Allah."

Ibn al-'Arabi added: Abu Bakr said: "The pleasure of Allah is more beloved to us than His pardon, for His pleasure is toward the good-doers and His pardon is toward those who fall short." This is the view chosen by al-Shafi'i.

Abu Hanifah said: the end of the time is better, because it is the time of obligation (*wujub*).

As for Malik, he gave a detailed position. For the dawn (*subh*) and the sunset (*maghrib*) prayers, the beginning of the time is better. As for the dawn prayer, it is based on the hadith of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ would pray the dawn prayer, and the women would leave wrapped in their cloaks, not recognized because of the darkness (*ghalas*)." In one narration: *"mutalaffifat"*.

As for the sunset prayer, it is based on the hadith of Salamah ibn al-Akwa' that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to pray the sunset prayer when the sun set and disappeared behind the veil. Muslim narrated both.

As for the night prayer ('Isha'), delaying it is better for one who is able. Ibn 'Umar narrated: "We stayed one night waiting for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for the late night prayer. He came out to us when a third of the night had passed or after it, and we do not know whether something had occupied him with his family or otherwise. He said when he came out: 'Indeed you are waiting for a prayer that no people of any religion other than you wait for. Were it not that it would be burdensome upon my community, I would have led them in prayer at this hour.'"

In al-Bukhari, from Anas, who said: "The Prophet ﷺ delayed the night prayer until midnight, then prayed..." and he mentioned the hadith.

Abu Barzah said: "The Prophet ﷺ used to prefer delaying it."

As for the noon prayer (*zuhr*), it comes to people when they are heedless, so it is preferred to delay it a little until they prepare themselves and gather. Abu al-Faraj said: Malik said: "The beginning of the time is better in every prayer except the noon prayer in intense heat." Ibn Abi Uways said: "Malik disliked praying the noon prayer at the moment of the sun's decline (*zawal*), but rather after that, and he would say: 'That is the prayer of the Kharijites.'"

In the Sahih of al-Bukhari and the Sahih of al-Tirmidhi, from Abu Dharr al-Ghifari, who said: "We were with the Prophet ﷺ on a journey, and the caller to prayer (*mu'adhdhin*) wanted to call for the noon prayer. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Cool (it down).' Then he wanted to call, and he was told: 'Cool (it down).' until we saw the shadows of the dunes (*tulul*). Then the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Indeed the intensity of the heat is from the blast (*fayh*) of Jahannam, so when the heat intensifies, cool the prayer.'"

In the Sahih of Muslim, from Anas, that the Prophet ﷺ used to pray the noon prayer when the sun had declined. The way to reconcile the two hadiths is what Anas narrated: when the heat is intense, he would cool the prayer, and when it is cool, he would hasten it.

Abu 'Isa al-Tirmidhi said: "A group of the people of knowledge (*ahl al-'ilm*) chose to delay the noon prayer in intense heat. This is the view of Ibn al-Mubarak, Ahmad and Ishaq. al-Shafi'i said: 'Cooling the noon prayer is only when the mosque is one to which its people travel (*yantabu*) from a distance. As for the one who prays alone, and the one who prays in the mosque of his own people, what I love for him is that he not delay the prayer in intense heat.'" Abu 'Isa said: "The meaning of those who held that the noon prayer is to be delayed in intense heat is more correct and closer to following the Sunnah. As for what al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, held, that the concession is for one who travels from a distance and for the hardship upon people, the hadith of Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, indicates the opposite of what al-Shafi'i said. Abu Dharr said: 'We were with the Prophet ﷺ on a journey, and Bilal called the adhan for the noon prayer. The Prophet ﷺ said: "O Bilal, cool it down, then cool it down."' So if the matter were as al-Shafi'i held, there would be no meaning to cooling at that time, since they were gathered on the journey and did not need to travel from a distance."

As for the afternoon prayer ('Asr), hastening it is better. There is no disagreement in our school (*madhhab*) that delaying the prayer in hope of congregation (*jama'ah*) is better than hastening it, for the virtue of congregation is known, while the virtue of the beginning of the time is unknown, and attaining what is known is better. This was said by Ibn al-'Arabi.

**The fourth issue: ﴿wherever you are, Allah will bring you all together﴾**

*"Ayna ma takunu"* (wherever you are) is a conditional clause (*shart*), and its answer is ﴿Allah will bring you all together﴾, meaning on the Day of Resurrection. Then He described Himself with power over everything, to match the attribute with what was mentioned of the restoration after death and decay.

**The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verses 149–150:**

Allah's words: ﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾. It was said: this is an emphasis on the command to face the Ka'bah and a concern for it, because the matter of the change of direction (qiblah) was very difficult in their souls. So He emphasized the command so that people would see the importance attached to it, and it would become light for them and their souls would settle toward it. It was also said: by the first [phrase] He meant "turn your face toward the Ka'bah," that is, look at it when you pray facing it. Then He said: "And wherever you are, O Muslims, in all the mosques in Medina and elsewhere, turn your faces toward it." Then He said: "And from wherever you set out," meaning the obligation of facing [the Ka'bah] during journeys. So this is a command to face the Ka'bah in all places, from all regions of the earth. I say: this view is better than the first, because it assigns each verse a separate benefit. Al-Daraqutni narrated from Anas ibn Malik, who said: "The Prophet ﷺ, when he was on a journey and wished to pray on his mount, would face the qiblah, say the takbir, and then pray wherever his mount turned him." Abu Dawud also narrated it, and this was the view of al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Abu Thawr. Malik held that facing the qiblah is not obligatory in this case, based on the hadith of Ibn Umar, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to pray on his mount while traveling from Mecca to Medina." He said: and concerning this was revealed ﴿Wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾, and this has already been mentioned. I say: there is no contradiction between the two hadiths, because this falls under the category of the absolute (al-mutlaq) and the restricted (al-muqayyad). So the view of al-Shafi'i is preferable, and the hadith of Anas on this matter is authentic. It is related that Ja'far ibn Muhammad was asked: what is the meaning of the repetition of narratives in the Qur'an? He said: Allah knew that not everyone would memorize the Qur'an, so if the narrative were not repeated, it could be with some people and not with others; therefore it was repeated so that it would be with whoever had memorized part of it.

Allah's words: ﴿So that people will have no argument against you, except those of them who do wrong﴾. Mujahid said: they are the polytheists of the Arabs, and their argument was their saying: "You have reverted to our qiblah." This was answered by His saying: ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west﴾. It was also said: the meaning of "so that people will have no argument against you" is: so that they do not say to you, "You were commanded to face the Ka'bah, and you do not see it." When He said, "And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it," this objection was removed. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "illa" (except) here means "wa" (and), that is, "and those who did wrong," so it is an exception in the sense of "wa." From this is the saying of the poet (it is al-Farazdaq, and he meant Marwan ibn al-Hakam; from Sharh al-Shawahid):

*"There is no dwelling in Medina other than one: the dwelling of the caliph, except the dwelling of Marwan."*

It is as if he said: "except the dwelling of the caliph and the dwelling of Marwan." Likewise it was said regarding His words: ﴿except those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them is a reward never cut off﴾ [see vol. 20, p. 116], meaning: those who believe. Al-Zajjaj rejected this view and said: this is an error according to the skilled grammarians, and it nullifies the meanings; "illa" and what follows it would then be dispensable. Their view is that this is an exception that is not from the first part, meaning: "but those among them who did wrong, for they will argue." Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: that is, Allah informed you of the matter of argument concerning the qiblah in His words: ﴿For each there is a direction toward which he turns﴾ [2:148]; and ﴿so that people will have no argument against you, except one who does wrong by arguing about what has already become clear to him.﴾ Just as you say: "You have no argument against me, except injustice," or "except that you wrong me," meaning: you have no argument at all, but you are wronging me. So He called their wrongdoing an argument, because the one who presents it calls it an argument, even though it is void. Qutrub said: it is possible that the meaning is: "so that people will have no argument against you, except against those who did wrong," so "those who" is a substitute (badal) for the kaf and mim in "against you." A group said: "illa alladhina" is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil); this meaning was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and others, and al-Tabari chose it and said: Allah negated that anyone could have an argument against the Prophet ﷺ and his companions regarding their facing the Ka'bah. The meaning is: there is no argument against you except the invalid argument, when they said: "He turned them away, Muhammad is confused in his religion, and he only turned to our qiblah because we were more guided than he." And other such statements, which came only from an idol-worshipper, a Jew, or a hypocrite. The word "hujjah" (argument) here means "muhajjah" (disputation), which is contention and debate. Allah called it an argument and ruled it corrupt, since it came from wrongdoers. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it was also said that the exception is disconnected (istithna' munqati'), and this is on the basis that the intended "people" are the Jews; then He excepted the disbelieving Arabs, as if He said: "But those who did wrong will dispute with you." His words "from among them" refute this interpretation. The meaning is: "but those who did wrong," meaning the disbelievers of Quraysh in their saying: "Muhammad has returned to our qiblah and will return to all of our religion." Included in this is everyone other than the Jews who spoke about this incident. Ibn 'Abbas, Zayd ibn 'Ali and Ibn Zayd read "ala alladhina zalamu" with a fatha on the hamzah and a lightened lam, in the sense of opening speech (istiftah al-kalam), so that "alladhina zalamu" is an inceptive phrase (mubtada'); or in the sense of warning or inciting (al-igra'), so that "alladhina" is in the accusative governed by a supposed verb.

Allah's words: ﴿So do not fear them, but fear Me﴾, meaning the people. Khashyah (awe) originally is tranquility in the heart that prompts caution. Khawf (fear) is the alarm of the heart, by which the limbs tremble, and because of the trembling of the limbs it is called khawf. The meaning of the verse is to belittle everyone other than Allah the Exalted, and to command disregarding them and attending to the command of Allah the Exalted.

Allah's words: ﴿and that I may complete My favour upon you﴾. It is in coordination with "so that there will not be" (li-alla yakuna), that is, "and so that I may complete," as said by al-Akhfash. It was also said: it is a new sentence (maqtu') in the nominative position as an inceptive, with an implied predicate; the estimate is: "And that I may complete My favour upon you, I have made known to you My qiblah," as said by al-Zajjaj. Completing the favour is guidance to the qiblah. It was said: it is entry into Paradise. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "The favour of Allah upon a servant is never completed until He admits him into Paradise." And ﴿so that you may be guided﴾ has been mentioned before [see vol. 1, p. 160, second edition].

**The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verses 149–150:**

Allah's words: ﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾. It was said: this is an emphasis on the command to face the Ka'bah and a concern for it, because the matter of the change of direction (qiblah) was very difficult in their souls. So He emphasized the command so that people would see the importance attached to it, and it would become light for them and their souls would settle toward it. It was also said: by the first [phrase] He meant "turn your face toward the Ka'bah," that is, look at it when you pray facing it. Then He said: "And wherever you are, O Muslims, in all the mosques in Medina and elsewhere, turn your faces toward it." Then He said: "And from wherever you set out," meaning the obligation of facing [the Ka'bah] during journeys. So this is a command to face the Ka'bah in all places, from all regions of the earth. I say: this view is better than the first, because it assigns each verse a separate benefit. Al-Daraqutni narrated from Anas ibn Malik, who said: "The Prophet ﷺ, when he was on a journey and wished to pray on his mount, would face the qiblah, say the takbir, and then pray wherever his mount turned him." Abu Dawud also narrated it, and this was the view of al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Abu Thawr. Malik held that facing the qiblah is not obligatory in this case, based on the hadith of Ibn Umar, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to pray on his mount while traveling from Mecca to Medina." He said: and concerning this was revealed ﴿Wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾, and this has already been mentioned. I say: there is no contradiction between the two hadiths, because this falls under the category of the absolute (al-mutlaq) and the restricted (al-muqayyad). So the view of al-Shafi'i is preferable, and the hadith of Anas on this matter is authentic. It is related that Ja'far ibn Muhammad was asked: what is the meaning of the repetition of narratives in the Qur'an? He said: Allah knew that not everyone would memorize the Qur'an, so if the narrative were not repeated, it could be with some people and not with others; therefore it was repeated so that it would be with whoever had memorized part of it.

Allah's words: ﴿So that people will have no argument against you, except those of them who do wrong﴾. It was also said: the meaning of "so that people will have no argument against you" is: so that they do not say to you, "You were commanded to face the Ka'bah, and you do not see it." When He said, "And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it," this objection was removed. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "illa" (except) here means "wa" (and), that is, "and those who did wrong," so it is an exception in the sense of "wa." From this is the saying of the poet (it is al-Farazdaq, and he meant Marwan ibn al-Hakam; from Sharh al-Shawahid):

*"There is no dwelling in Medina other than one: the dwelling of the caliph, except the dwelling of Marwan."*

It is as if he said: "except the dwelling of the caliph and the dwelling of Marwan." The Exalted's saying: ﴿As We have sent﴾. The kaf (ك) is in the accusative position, as a description (na't) of an omitted verbal noun (masdar). The meaning: "and that I may complete My favour upon you by completing it in the manner of how We sent [a messenger]." This is said by al-Farra'. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is the best of the opinions," that is, "and that I may complete My favour upon you in explaining the sunnah of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, in the manner of how We sent [a messenger]."

It has also been said: the meaning is "and that you may be guided with a guidance like how We sent [a messenger]." And it has been said: it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), and the meaning is: "and that I may complete My favour upon you in this state." The comparison holds in that the favour in the qibla is like the favour in the messengership, and that the remembrance commanded is in its greatness like the greatness of the favour.

It has also been said that the meaning of the speech is by inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), that is, "remember Me as We have sent," narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and preferred by al-Zajjaj, that is, "as We sent among you a messenger whom you know for truthfulness, so remember Me with monotheism and affirmation of him." According to this opinion, stopping at "tahtadun" (you are guided) is permissible.

I say: This is the view chosen by al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim in his book, that is, "as I have done with you this bounty of favours which I have enumerated for you, so remember Me with gratitude and I will remember you with increase, because in your remembrance of that there is thanks to Me, and I have promised you increase in return for thanks, which is His saying: ﴿If you give thanks, I will surely increase you﴾ [see vol. 9, p. 343]." The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verses 152–153:

Allah's words: ﴿So remember Me, and I will remember you﴾. This is a command (amr) and its response (jawab), and it carries the meaning of a conditional, which is why the verb is jussive (majzum). The root meaning of dhikr is the heart's awareness of the thing remembered and its being alert to it. Remembrance by the tongue is called dhikr because it indicates the remembrance of the heart. However, since the term dhikr was used very frequently for spoken utterance, that meaning became the one that comes first to the mind. The meaning of the verse is: remember Me through obedience, and I will remember you with reward and forgiveness. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. He also said: remembrance is obedience to Allah. Whoever does not obey Him has not remembered Him, even if he multiplies glorification (tasbih), declaration of God's oneness (tahlil), and recitation of the Qur'an. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever obeys Allah has remembered Allah, even if his prayer, his fasting, and his charitable deeds for good are few; and whoever disobeys Allah has forgotten Allah, even if his prayer, his fasting, and his charitable deeds for good are many." This was mentioned by Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Khuwayz Mindad in his book Ahkam al-Quran. Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi said: "I know the hour in which Allah remembers us." It was asked of him: "How do you know it?" He said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: 'So remember Me, and I will remember you.'" Al-Suddi said: "There is no servant who remembers Allah except that Allah remembers him, Mighty and Majestic. No believer remembers Him except that Allah remembers him with His mercy, and no disbeliever remembers Him except that Allah remembers him with punishment." Abu 'Uthman was asked: "We remember Allah but we do not find sweetness in our hearts?" He said: "Praise Allah that He has adorned one of your limbs with His obedience." Dhu al-Nun al-Misri (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "Whoever remembers Allah the Exalted with true remembrance forgets everything in comparison with His remembrance, Allah preserves everything for him, and He becomes a substitute for everything." Mu'adh ibn Jabal (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "No action of the son of Adam saves him from the punishment of Allah more than the remembrance of Allah." The hadiths on the virtue of remembrance and its reward are numerous, and the imams have transmitted them. Ibn Majah related from 'Abd Allah ibn Busr that a Bedouin said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "The laws of Islam have become numerous for me, so inform me of something I can hold on to." He said: "Let your tongue always be moist with the remembrance of Allah, Mighty and Majestic." It was also transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: 'I am with My servant when he remembers Me and his lips move with Me.'" More explanation on this topic will come at Allah's words: "O you who believe, remember Allah with much remembrance" [see vol. 14 p. 197]. The intended meaning is the remembrance of the heart, which must be continued in all circumstances.

Allah's words: ﴿And give thanks to Me and do not deny Me﴾. Al-Farra' said: it is said "shakartuka" and "shakartu laka," and "nasahtuka" and "nasahtu laka," and the eloquent form is the first [the dictionaries of language state that the eloquent form is the second]. Thanks (shukr) is recognition of a favor and speaking of it. Its root meaning in the language is manifestation, and this has been discussed before [see the third issue and what follows, vol. 1 p. 397, second edition]. The servant's thanks to Allah, Exalted is He, is his praise of Him by mentioning His favor to him, and the Truth's (the Exalted's) thanks to the servant is His praise of him for his obedience to Him. However, the servant's thanks is speech with the tongue and acknowledgment in the heart of the Lord's bounty together with acts of obedience.

Allah's words: ﴿and do not deny Me﴾. This is a prohibition (nahy), and for this reason the nun of the plural (nun al-jama'a) has been dropped from it, and this is the nun of the first person singular. The yā' has been dropped because it falls at the end of a verse (ra's ayah), and its affirmation is better outside the Qur'an. The meaning is: do not deny My blessing and My favors. Thus kufr here means concealing the blessing, not denying (takdhib). The meaning of kufr linguistically has been discussed before [see vol. 1 p. 183]. The meaning of seeking help (isti'anah) through patience and prayer has been discussed before [see vol. 1 p. 371, second edition], so there is no point in repeating it.

This is like His saying, in another verse: ﴿And do not think of those who have been killed in the way of Allah as dead; rather, they are alive with their Lord, being provided for﴾ [[See vol. 4, p. 268.]]. And since God revives them after death in order to provide for them, as will be explained, it is possible that He revives the disbelievers in order to punish them, and this would be evidence for the punishment of the grave. The martyrs are alive, as God said, but this does not mean that they will be brought back to life, for if it were so, there would be no difference between the martyrs and others, since everyone will be brought back to life. **Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 155:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We will surely test you﴾. This *waw* is vowelled with a fatha according to Sibawayh (the grammarian), because two unvowelled letters came together. Others said: when it was joined to the heavy *nun*, the verb was built (on that form), so it became like *kham'sata 'ashara* (fifteen, a compound form). *Al-bala'* (trial) may be good or bad, and its origin is *al-mihna* (testing). It has already been discussed [[See the thirteenth issue in volume 1, page 387, second edition.]]. The meaning is: We will test you in order to know the one who strives and the one who is patient, a knowledge of witnessing, so that the reward falls upon him, as has already been explained. It was also said: they were tested with this so that it would be a sign for those after them, that they would know that they only endured this when the truth had become clear to them. It was also said: He informed them of this so that they would be certain it would befall them, and would prepare themselves for it, so that they would be further from despair, and in this is the hastening of Allah's reward for resolve and the preparing of the self.

His saying, the Exalted: "*bi-shay'in*" (with something). It is a singular word but its meaning is plural. Al-Dahhak recited "*bi-ash'ya'*" (with things) in the plural, while the majority recited it in the singular, meaning: with something of this and something of this, and he suffices with the first for brevity. "*Min al-khawf*" (from fear) means fear of the enemy and terror in battle, as said by Ibn Abbas. Al-Shafi'i said: it is the fear of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. "*Wa'l-ju'*" (and hunger) means famine through drought and dearth, according to the view of Ibn Abbas. Al-Shafi'i said: it is hunger in the month of Ramadan. "*Wa naqsin min al-amwal*" (and loss of wealth) is due to being occupied with fighting the unbelievers. It was also said: the destroying calamities. Al-Shafi'i said: through the obligatory zakat. "*Wa'l-anfus*" (and lives). Ibn Abbas said: by killing and death in jihad. Al-Shafi'i said: he means by sicknesses. "*Wa'l-thamarat*" (and fruits). Al-Shafi'i said: what is meant is the death of children, and a man's child is the fruit of his heart, as is found in the report, as will come. Ibn Abbas said: what is meant is the scarcity of crops and the cutting off of blessings.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And give good tidings to the patient﴾, that is, of the reward for patience. *Al-sabr* (patience) originally means restraint, and its reward is not measured, and this has already been discussed [[See volume 1, page 371.]]. However, that (reward) is only attained through patience at the first shock, as al-Bukhari narrated from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Patience is only at the first shock." Muslim also recorded it in a more complete form. That is, the patience that is difficult for the self, and for which the reward is great, is only at the onset of calamity and its heat, for it indicates the strength of the heart and its firmness in the station of patience. As for when the heat of the calamity cools, everyone becomes patient at that time. For this reason it has been said: every intelligent person must, at the time of calamity, adopt what even the foolish must adopt after three (days).

Sahl ibn Abd Allah al-Tustari said: when He, the Exalted, said "*And give good tidings to the patient*," patience became a way of life [[This is how it appears in all the copies in our hands.]]. Patience is of two kinds: patience against disobedience to Allah, and this is the striver (*mujahid*); and patience upon obedience to Allah, and this is the worshipper (*'abid*). When one is patient against disobedience to Allah and patient upon obedience to Allah, Allah bequeaths to him contentment with His decree, and the sign of contentment is the stillness of the heart with what comes upon the self of things disliked and things loved.

Al-Khawwas said: patience is steadfastness upon the rulings of the Book and the Sunnah. Ruwaym said: patience is leaving off complaint. Dhu al-Nun al-Misri said: patience is seeking help from Allah, the Exalted. Al-Ustadh Abu Ali said: its limit is that you do not object to the decree. As for displaying one's affliction not in the manner of complaint, it does not contradict patience. Allah, the Exalted, said in the story of Ayyub: ﴿Indeed, We found him patient; an excellent servant﴾ [[See volume 15, page 215.]], ﴿with what He reported about him, that he said: "Harm has touched me"﴾.

**Sixth issue**

There are six issues in this passage.

**First issue:** God's words, ﴿*muṣībah*﴾ (calamity). *Muṣībah* means anything that harms the believer and befalls him. One says *aṣābahu iṣābatan wa muṣābatan wa muṣābāan* (it befell him). *Muṣībah* is the singular of *maṣāʾib* (calamities). *Maṣūbah* (with a ḍammah on the ṣād) is like *muṣībah*. The Arabs agreed on hamzating the plural *maṣāʾib*, though its root is *wāw*. It is as if they made the original letter resemble the added one. It is also pluralized as *maṣāwib*, which is the original form. *Al-muṣāb* is the same as *al-iṣābah*. The poet said:

*Oh Sulaym, your calamity, a man* ... *who sent greetings as a salutation, is a wrong.*

*Ṣāba al-sahmu al-qirṭās yuṣību ṣaybā* is a dialectal variant of *aṣābahu*. *Al-muṣībah* is a misfortune that a person suffers, even if it is small, and it is used for evil. ʿIkrimah narrated that the lamp of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out one night, and he said, "Indeed we belong to God and to Him we return." It was said, "Is it a calamity, O Messenger of God?" He said, "Yes, everything that harms the believer is a calamity." I say: the meaning of this is established in the Ṣaḥīḥ. Muslim transmitted from Abū Saʿīd and Abū Hurayrah, may God be pleased with them both, that they both heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "No fatigue, weariness, sickness, or grief afflicts the believer, not even the worry that troubles him,[[Al-Nawawī said in his commentary on Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim: "Al-Qāḍī said: it is with a ḍammah on the yāʾ and a fatḥah on the hāʾ, in the passive form (yuhamm, from the unnamed agent). Others vocalized it with a fatḥah on the yāʾ and a ḍammah on the hāʾ, meaning 'he grieves him.' Both are correct."]] except that God expiates some of his sins because of it."

**Second issue:** Ibn Mājah transmitted in his Sunan: Abū Bakr ibn Abī Shaybah narrated to us, Wakīʿ ibn al-Jarrāḥ narrated to us, from Hishām ibn Ziyād, from his mother, from Fāṭimah bint al-Ḥusayn, from her father, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is afflicted with a calamity and mentions his calamity, then utters *istirjāʿ* (the saying 'We belong to God and to Him we return'), even if its time has long passed, God will record for him a reward like the reward he had on the day he was afflicted."

**Third issue:** Among the greatest calamities is the calamity in one's religion. Abū ʿUmar mentioned, from al-Firyābī, who said: Fiṭr ibn Khalīfah narrated to us, ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ narrated to us, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "If any of you is afflicted with a calamity, let him remember his calamity through me, for it is among the greatest of calamities." Al-Samarqandī Abū Muḥammad transmitted it in his Musnad: Abū Nuʿaym informed us, saying: Fiṭr informed us, and he mentioned the same thing exactly. He also transmitted something similar from Makḥūl as a *mursal* (a report in which the Companion is omitted). Abū ʿUmar said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) spoke truthfully, because the calamity of his death is greater than every calamity a Muslim suffers after him until the Day of Resurrection. Revelation ceased and prophethood died. The first appearance of evil was the apostasy of the Arabs and other things, and that was the first cutting off of good and the first decrease of it. Abū Saʿīd said: "We did not shake the dust from our hands after the grave of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) until we denied our hearts." Abū al-ʿAtāhiyah composed beautifully the meaning of this ḥadīth when he said:

*Be patient with every calamity and endure it, and know that a man is not immortal.*

*Do you not see that calamities are many, and that death lies in wait for the servants?*

*Of those you see, who has not been struck by a calamity? This is a path in which you are not unique.*

*So when you remember Muḥammad and his calamity, then remember your calamity through the Prophet Muḥammad.*

**Fourth issue:** God's words, ﴿They say, "Indeed we belong to God and to Him we return."﴾ God made these words a refuge for the afflicted and a protection for those being tested, because of the blessed meanings they contain. His saying "Indeed we belong to God" is a declaration of monotheism and an affirmation of servitude and ownership. His saying "and to Him we return" is an acknowledgment of our own perishing, and of our resurrection from our graves, and a certainty that the return of all matters is to Him, as it belongs to Him. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, may God have mercy on him, said: "These words were not given to any prophet before our Prophet. Had Jacob known them, he would not have said, 'Oh my grief over Joseph.'"

**Fifth issue:** Abū Sinān said: "I buried my son Sinān while Abū Ṭalḥah al-Khawlānī was at the edge of the grave. When I wanted to leave, he took hold of my hands, comforted me, and said: 'Shall I not give you good news, O Abū Sinān? al-Ḍaḥḥāk narrated to me from Abū Mūsā that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When a servant's child dies, God says to His angels, 'Have you taken the child of My servant?' They say, 'Yes.' He says, 'Have you taken the fruit of his heart?' They say, 'Yes.' He says, 'What did My servant say?' They say, 'He praised You and said *istirjāʿ*.' God the Exalted says, 'Build for My servant a house in Paradise, and name it the House of Praise.'"'" Muslim also transmitted from Umm Salamah, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "No Muslim is afflicted with a calamity and says what God, the Mighty and Majestic, commanded: 'Indeed we belong to God and to Him we return. O God, reward me in my calamity and replace it for me with something better,' except that God replaces it for him with something better." This is an indication of His words: ﴿And give good tidings to the patient﴾, either with a replacement, as God replaced for Umm Salamah the Messenger of God (ﷺ), since he married her after her husband Abū Salamah died, or with a great reward, as in the ḥadīth of Abū Mūsā. It may also be both.

**Sixth issue:** God's words, ﴿Upon them are blessings from their Lord and mercy﴾. These are favors from God, the Mighty and Majestic, upon those who are patient and say *istirjāʿ*. God's blessing (*ṣalāt*) upon His servant is His pardon, His mercy, His blessing, and His honoring of him in this world and the Hereafter. Al-Zajjāj said: "The blessing from God, the Mighty and Majestic, is forgiveness and good praise." From this comes the prayer over the dead, which is only praise of him and supplication for him. He repeated "mercy" when the wording differed, for emphasis and to fully convey the meaning, as in His words, ﴿from the clear proofs and the guidance﴾, and His words, ﴿Do they think that We do not hear their secret and their private talk?﴾ The poet said:

*May a Generous Lord bless Yaḥyā and his followers, and an obeyed intercessor.*

It was also said that by mercy He meant the removal of distress and the fulfilling of need. In al-Bukhārī, ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, said: "What an excellent pair, and what an excellent addition: ﴿Those who, when a calamity strikes them, say, 'Indeed we belong to God and to Him we return.' Those are upon them blessings from their Lord and mercy, and those are the guided.﴾" By "the pair" he meant the blessing and the mercy, and by "the addition" he meant the guidance. It was said that this refers to deserving the reward and abundant recompense, and it was also said that it refers to making calamities easier and lightening grief.
