There are nine issues concerning this verse.

The first issue: al-Bukhari related from Asim ibn Sulayman, who said: "I asked Anas ibn Malik about al-Safa and al-Marwah, and he said: 'We used to regard them as part of the affairs of the Jahiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance). When Islam came, we refrained from them, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah. So whoever makes the pilgrimage to the House or performs 'umrah, there is no blame upon him for going back and forth between them﴾.'"

al-Tirmidhi related from Urwah, who said: "I said to Aisha, 'I do not see any blame on anyone who does not circumambulate between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and I do not mind not going back and forth between them.' She said: 'Evil is what you have said, nephew! The Messenger of Allah ﷺ circumambulated, and the Muslims circumambulated. It was only those who used to assume the ihlal (the raising of the voice with the talbiyah at the start of the pilgrimage) for Manat, the idol at al-Mushallal, who did not go back and forth between al-Safa and al-Marwah. So Allah, Exalted is He, revealed: ﴿So whoever makes the pilgrimage to the House or performs 'umrah, there is no blame upon him for going back and forth between them﴾. Had it been as you say, it would have been: ﴿there is no blame upon him that he not go back and forth between them﴾.'" [[Manat: a place name denoting an idol on the side of the sea facing Qudayd, at al-Mushallal (a mountain that descends to Qudayd on the seaward side), seven miles from Madinah. The Azd and Ghassan used to assume ihlal for it and make pilgrimage to it, and the first to erect it was Amr ibn Luhayy al-Khuza'i.
(See the Mu'jam of Yaqut under the entry Manat.)]]

Abu Bakr ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn Hisham said: "I mentioned that to Abu Bakr ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn Hisham, and he was impressed by it and said: 'This is indeed knowledge. I have heard men of learning say: the Arabs who did not go back and forth between al-Safa and al-Marwah used to say that our circuit between these two stones is part of the affairs of the Jahiliyyah. Others among the Ansar said: We were only commanded to circumambulate [the House [[Addition from al-Tirmidhi.]]] and were not commanded to do so between al-Safa and al-Marwah. So Allah, Exalted is He, revealed: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah﴾.'" Abu Bakr ibn Abd al-Rahman said: "I think it was revealed concerning both of these groups." He said: "This is a hadith that is hasan sahih (good and authentic)." It was related by al-Bukhari in similar meaning, and in it, after his saying "Allah, Exalted is He, revealed: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah﴾", is: "Aisha said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had established the circumambulation between them, so no one has the right to abandon the circumambulation between them." Then she informed Abu Bakr ibn Abd al-Rahman, and he said: "This is indeed knowledge that I had not heard. I have heard men of learning mention that the people, except those whom Aisha mentioned, who used to assume ihlal for Manat, all used to circumambulate between al-Safa and al-Marwah. When Allah, Exalted is He, mentioned the circumambulation of the House but did not mention al-Safa and al-Marwah in the Qur'an, they said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we used to circumambulate between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and Allah has revealed the circumambulation of the House but did not mention al-Safa. Is there any blame upon us if we circumambulate between al-Safa and al-Marwah?' So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah﴾, to the end of the verse." Abu Bakr said: "I think this verse was revealed concerning both groups: concerning those who used to avoid circumambulating between al-Safa and al-Marwah in the Jahiliyyah, and those who circumambulated but then avoided doing so in Islam, because Allah, Exalted is He, had commanded the circumambulation of the House and did not mention al-Safa until He mentioned it after mentioning the circumambulation of the House."

al-Tirmidhi related from Asim ibn Sulayman al-Ahwal, who said: "I asked Anas ibn Malik [[So it is in the original manuscripts, in Sahih al-Bukhari and in Tafsir al-Tabari. What is in Sahih al-Tirmidhi is "Anas ibn Sirin ...", and he was a client of Anas ibn Malik and among those who related from him.]] about al-Safa and al-Marwah, and he said: 'They were among the symbols of the Jahiliyyah. When Islam came, we refrained from them, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah. So whoever makes the pilgrimage to the House or performs 'umrah, there is no blame upon him for going back and forth between them﴾.'" He said: "They are voluntary (tatawwu'), and ﴿whoever volunteers good, then indeed Allah is Appreciative, Knowing﴾." He said: "This is a hadith that is hasan sahih." He (al-Tirmidhi) also related it.

It is also related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "In the Jahiliyyah there were devils who would play music all night between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and between them were gods. When Islam appeared, the Muslims said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we do not circumambulate between al-Safa and al-Marwah, for they are polytheism (shirk).' So the verse was revealed."

al-Sha'bi said: "In the Jahiliyyah, on al-Safa there was an idol called 'Isaf, and on al-Marwah an idol called Na'ilah. They used to touch them when they circumambulated, so the Muslims refrained from circumambulating between them on account of that, and the verse was revealed."

The second issue: The root meaning of al-Safa in the language is the smooth rock, and here it is a well-known mountain in Makkah. Likewise al-Marwah is also a mountain. For this reason the verse mentions them with the definite article. al-Safa is mentioned first because Adam, the chosen one (ﷺ), stood upon it and it was named after him, while Eve stood upon al-Marwah and it was named after the feminine form of the word, so it was made feminine for that reason. And Allah knows best.

al-Sha'bi said: "On al-Safa there was an idol called 'Isaf, and on al-Marwah an idol called Na'ilah." The masculine and feminine forms were then made consistent, and the masculine was placed first. This is good, because the hadiths mentioned indicate this meaning. The aversion of those who disliked circumambulating between them was only on account of this, until Allah lifted the blame in that matter. The People of the Book claimed that the two (the man and woman) had committed fornication in the Ka'bah, so Allah transformed them into two stones and placed them on al-Safa and al-Marwah as a lesson for others. When the time passed, they were worshipped besides Allah. And Allah, Exalted is He, knows best.

al-Safa (with a short final vowel, maqsur) is the plural of safah, which means smooth stones. It is also said: al-Safa is a singular noun whose plural is sufiyy (with a damma on the sad) and asfa', on the pattern of arha'. The rajiz (a poet of rajaz verse) said:

"As if its two sides, from the stream of [water] drawn up, are the places where birds alight upon the sufiyy."

[[This is al-Akhyal, as in Lisan al-Arab.]]

[[In Lisan al-Arab: "Ibn Sida said: Abu Ali recited it thus, and Ibn Duraid recited it in al-Jamharah: 'As if its two sides (matnayh).' He said: This is correct, because of what comes after it: 'from the length of my climbing upon the high (al-'alawi).' Al-Naf: the scattering of water from the rope when drawing water. Naf al-matar: what the rain cleans and sprinkles. The author of Lisan said: Tha'lab explained it and said: he likened the water which has fallen upon the back of the one drawing water to the droppings of a bird upon a smooth stone."]]

It is also said: among the conditions of al-Safa are whiteness and hardness, and its derivation is from safa yasfu, meaning it became pure of dust and mud.

al-Marwah (the singular of al-marw) is small stones that have some softness. It has also been said that they are hard stones. The correct view is that al-marw is stones, both hard and soft, the soft kind being that which breaks into pieces and whose edges are thin. In this regard it is said: "al-marw" is the more common, and it is said of the hard kind as well. The poet said:

"And he turned the land, with a dry gait, and when he met the marw it crumbled."

Abu Dhu'ayb said:

"Until I am, for the calamities, like a marwah at the rock of al-Mushaqqar, struck every day."

[[Al-Mushaqqar: a great fortress of the tribe of Abd al-Qays in Bahrain, adjacent to another fortress called al-Safa before the city of Hajar. It is also narrated as "Safa al-Mashriq." Abu Ubaydah said: al-Mashriq is the market of Ta'if. Al-Asma'i said: al-Mashriq is the place of prayer.
(From the commentary on the Diwan and Yaqut's Mu'jam.)]]

It has also been said that they are black stones, and it has been said that they are white, shining stones in which there is fire.

The third issue: Allah's words ﴿from the symbols of Allah﴾ mean from His landmarks and places of His worship. It is the plural of shi'irah. The sha'a'ir are the acts of worship which Allah has made conspicuous (ashara), that is, made them markers for people: from the standing place (at 'Arafat), the sa'y (going between al-Safa and al-Marwah), and the sacrifice. Al-shi'ar means the sign. It is said: ash'ara al-hadiy means he marked the offering by piercing its hump with an iron, from your saying: ash'artu, meaning I informed. al-Kumayt said:

"We slay them generation after generation; you see them as symbols of sacrifice by which they draw near."

The fourth issue: Allah's words ﴿whoever makes the pilgrimage to the House﴾ mean whoever intends it. The root meaning of hajj is intention. The poet said:

[[He is al-Mukhabbal al-Sa'di, as will come.]]

"I witness from the tribe of Awf many gatherings, many of them making pilgrimage to the sibb of al-Zibriqan, the saffron-dyed one."

al-Sibb is a homonymous word. Abu Ubaydah said: al-sibb (with a kasra) is one who insults much. Your sibb is also the one who insults you. The poet said:

[[He is Abd al-Rahman ibn Hassan, satirizing Miskin al-Darimi.
(From Lisan.)]]

"Do not insult me, for you are not my sibb; my sibb is the noble one among men."

Al-sibb also means a head covering, and likewise a turban. al-Mukhabbal al-Sa'di said:

"They make pilgrimage to the sibb of al-Zibriqan, the saffron-dyed one."

Al-sibb also means a rope in the dialect of Hudhayl. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

"It hangs down upon it between a rope and a stitched patch, on a bare desert like a drop, its crow stumbling."

Al-subub are ropes. Al-sibb is a piece of thin linen, and al-sabibah is the same, and the plural is al-subub and al-sababi'. Al-Jawhari said so. Hajja al-tabib al-shajjah means the physician probed the wound with a probe. The poet said:

[[He is Udhar ibn Durrah al-Ta'i, as in Lisan. The complete line is:
"Fast al-tabib qadhaha ka-l-mugharid."]]

"He probes a deep wound, at its bottom a crumbling."

[[Al-ma'mumah: the wound that reaches the cranium, the membrane that encloses the brain. In Lisan: "Ibn Duraid explained this poetry, saying: this poet described a physician treating a wound of great depth, so he recoils from its horror, and the filth falls from its anus like the mughārīd." Al-mugharid: plural of mughrud, a well-known gum.]]

Al-lajaf means subsidence. Talajjafat al-bi'r means the bottom of the well subsided. Then this term became specifically applied to intending the Sacred House for specific acts.

The fifth issue: Allah's words ﴿or performs 'umrah﴾ mean visits. al-'Umrah means the visit. The poet said:

[[He is al-'Ajjaj, praising Umar ibn Ubayd Allah al-Qurashi.
(From Lisan.)]]

"Indeed Ibn Ma'mar rose high when he performed 'umrah, a far-off raid beyond the far, with powerful legs."

[[Dabr: plural of its limbs, to leap.]]

The sixth issue: Allah's words ﴿there is no blame upon him﴾ mean there is no sin. Its root is from junuh, which is inclination, and from it come the jawanih, the ribs of the body, because of their curvature. Aisha's interpretation of this verse has already been mentioned. Ibn al-Arabi said: "The truth of the matter is that the saying of the speaker, 'there is no blame upon you that you do it,' is permission for the act. And his saying, 'there is no blame upon you that you not do it,' is permission for abandoning the act. When Urwah heard the words of Allah, Exalted is He, ﴿there is no blame upon him that he go back and forth between them﴾, he said: 'This is evidence that abandoning the circumambulation is permissible.' Then he saw that the Shari'ah was unanimous that there is no concession in abandoning the circumambulation, so he sought to reconcile these two conflicting matters. Aisha said to him: 'His saying ﴿there is no blame upon him that he go back and forth between them﴾ is not evidence for abandoning the circumambulation. It would only be evidence for abandoning it if it were ﴿there is no blame upon him that he not go back and forth between them﴾. This wording was not used to permit abandoning the circumambulation, nor is there evidence for it in it. It came only to convey the permissibility of circumambulating for those who used to be averse to it in the Jahiliyyah, or for those who used to circumambulate in the Jahiliyyah intending the idols that were there. So Allah, Glorified is He, informed them that circumambulating is not forbidden when the one circumambulating does not intend a false purpose.'" If it is said: Ata related from Ibn Abbas that he recited ﴿there is no blame upon him that he not go back and forth between them﴾, and this is the recitation (qira'ah) of Ibn Mas'ud, and it is narrated that it was in the Mushaf of Ubayy in this way, and it is narrated from Anas something similar. The answer is that this differs from what is in the Mushaf, and what is established in the Mushaf is not abandoned for a recitation whose soundness is unknown. Ata used to narrate much from Ibn Abbas without direct hearing (mursal). As for the narration from Anas, it has been said that it is not a reliable transmission, or that the "la" is an extra particle for emphasis, as the poet said:

"I do not blame the fair ones for not mocking, when they saw the grey-haired, ugly old man."

[[Al-qafandar: the one ugly in appearance.]]

The Seventh Issue: al-Tirmidhi narrated from Jabir that when the Prophet (ﷺ) arrived in Makkah, he circled the House seven times, then recited: "And take the Station of Abraham as a place of prayer" [Qur'an 2:125], and prayed behind the Station. Then he came to the Black Stone and touched it, and said: (We begin with what God began with). So he began with al-Safa, and recited [[In Sahih al-Tirmidhi: "wa qara'a" (and he recited).]] "Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of God" [Qur'an 2:158]. He said: This is a hadith that is hasan sahih (good and sound), and the practice among the scholars is that one begins with al-Safa before al-Marwah. If one begins with al-Marwah before al-Safa, it does not suffice, and one should begin again with al-Safa.

The Eighth Issue: The scholars differed over whether the sa'i (ritual running) between al-Safa and al-Marwah is obligatory. Al-Shafi'i and Ibn Hanbal said it is a rukn (pillar of the rite), which is also the well-known position in the school of Malik, based on his (peace be upon him) saying: (Perform the sa'i, for God has prescribed for you the sa'i). Al-Daraqutni narrated it. The word "kataba" here means "awjaba" (made obligatory), as in God's saying: "Fasting has been prescribed for you" [Qur'an 2:183], and the Prophet's (peace be upon him) saying: (Five prayers which God has prescribed for the servants). Ibn Majah narrated from a slave-mother of Shaybah, who said: I saw the Messenger of God (ﷺ) performing the sa'i between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and he was saying: (The valley of al-Abtah is not crossed except running [[Shadda: i.e., running.]]). Whoever abandons it, or abandons a round of it, forgetfully or deliberately, must return from his land, or from the place where he remembered, to Makkah, and then circle and perform the sa'i, because the sa'i is only valid when connected to the tawaf.

According to Malik, this applies equally whether it is in Hajj or in 'Umrah, even though it is not an obligation (fard) in 'Umrah. If he has had intercourse with women, then according to Malik he owes an 'Umrah and a hadi (sacrificial animal), together with completing his rites. Al-Shafi'i said: he owes a hadi, and there is no meaning to 'Umrah if he returns, circles and performs the sa'i. Abu Hanifa and his companions, al-Thawri and al-Sha'bi said: it is not obligatory; if any pilgrim abandons it until he returns to his country, he compensates for it with a blood sacrifice, because it is a sunnah (recommended practice) of the Hajj. This is also the view of Malik in al-'Utbiyyah [[Al-'Utbiyyah: a book on the school of Imam Malik, named after its author, the Andalusian jurist Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz al-'Utbi al-Qurtubi, who died in 254 AH.]]. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Zubayr, Anas ibn Malik and Ibn Sirin that it is voluntary (tatawwu'), based on God's saying: "And whoever volunteers good" [Qur'an 2:158]. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "yatatawwa'" in the present tense, jussive, and similarly "Whoever volunteers good, it is better for him" [Qur'an 2:184]; the rest read "tatawwa'" in the past tense. It means what a believer does on his own initiative. Whoever performs any of the supererogatory acts (nawafil), God will reward him, and God's appreciation of a servant is his reward for obedience.

The correct view is that of al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, for the reasons we have mentioned, and the Prophet's (peace be upon him) saying: (Take your rites from me). Thus it became an explanation of the general (mujmal) Hajj, so it must be obligatory, like his explanation of the number of rak'ahs, and whatever is like that, when there is no agreement that it is a sunnah or voluntary.

Tulayb said: Ibn 'Abbas saw people circling between al-Safa and al-Marwah and said: This is what your mother Umm Isma'il left you.

I say: This is established in Sahih al-Bukhari, as will be explained in the commentary on Surah Ibrahim [[See vol. 9, p. 368.]].

The Ninth Issue: No one may circle the House or perform the sa'i between al-Safa and al-Marwah while riding, except for a valid excuse. If one circles while riding with an excuse, he owes a blood sacrifice. If one circles without an excuse, he must repeat it if he is near the House, and if he is far from it, he must send a sacrificial animal. We say this because the Prophet (ﷺ) circled on foot himself and said: (Take your rites from me). We permitted it with an excuse because the Prophet (ﷺ) circled on his camel and touched the corner with his staff (mihjan) [[Al-mihjan: a staff with a curved head used by a rider to reach what has fallen from him.]], and he said to 'A'ishah, when she said to him: I am unwell, and he said: (Circle behind the people while you are riding). Our companions distinguished between circling on a camel and circling on a person's back. If one circles on a person's back, it does not suffice, because then he is not the one circling; rather, the one circling is the one carrying. If one circles on a camel, the rider is the one circling. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: This is a distinction of preference; as for validity, it is valid. Do you not see that if he fainted and was carried around while being carried, or was made to stand at 'Arafat while being carried, it would be valid for him?

The commentary contains seven issues (masa'il).

**First issue:** God, exalted is He, informs us that whoever conceals the clear proofs and the guidance that He has sent down is cursed. Scholars differ over who is meant. It has been said: the rabbis of the Jews and the monks of the Christians who concealed the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ), and the Jews concealed the matter of stoning. It has also been said: the meaning is everyone who conceals the truth. The verse is therefore general, covering everyone who conceals knowledge of the religion of God that people need to have disseminated. This is explained in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever is asked about knowledge that he possesses and conceals it, God will bridle him on the Day of Resurrection with a bridle of fire." Abu Hurayrah and Amr ibn al-As related it, and Ibn Majah recorded it. It is opposed by the saying of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud: "You will not speak to a people with a saying that their minds cannot reach without it becoming a trial for some of them." The Prophet (ﷺ) also said: "Speak to people in what they can understand. Do you want God and His Messenger to be called liars?" This is to be understood as applying to certain sciences, such as the science of kalam (theological discourse), or to matters that not all common people can grasp equally. The duty of the scholar is to speak in a way that is understood by those he addresses, and to place each person in his own station. And God knows best.

**Second issue:** This verse is the one that Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him, had in mind when he said: "Were it not for two verses in the Book of God, I would not have related a single hadith to you." (In al-Bukhari and Ibn Majah the wording is "Were it not for two verses.") By this verse the scholars have proven that it is obligatory to convey true knowledge and to explain knowledge in general, without taking payment for it, since one does not deserve payment for what it is obligatory for one to do, just as one does not deserve payment for Islam. This matter has already been discussed (see the second issue in volume 1, page 335, second edition). The true meaning of the verse is this: if the scholar intends to conceal knowledge, he sins; if he does not intend it, he is not obliged to convey it when it is known that he is with others (who will convey it). But whoever is asked is obliged to convey it, by this verse and by the hadith. It is not permissible to teach the Qur'an and knowledge to a disbeliever until he becomes Muslim. Likewise it is not permissible to teach an innovator (mubtadi', one who holds a heretical view) the methods of disputation and argument so that he may dispute with the people of truth. Nor should one teach a litigant an argument with which he may defeat his opponent unjustly, nor should a ruler be taught an interpretation (ta'wil) through which he may reach the harms of his subjects, nor should concessions (rukhas) be spread among fools so that they make that a path to committing what is forbidden and abandoning what is obligatory, and the like. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Do not withhold wisdom from its people, lest you wrong them, and do not place it with those who are not its people, lest you wrong it." It is also related from him (ﷺ) that he said: "Do not hang pearls around the necks of swine," meaning teaching jurisprudence (fiqh) to one who is not qualified for it. Sahnun said: "The hadith of Abu Hurayrah and Amr ibn al-As only concerns testimony." Ibn al-Arabi said: "The correct view is the opposite of this, because the hadith says, 'Whoever is asked about knowledge,' and it does not say 'about testimony.' Remaining with the apparent meaning is required until something arrives that removes it." And God knows best.

**Third issue:** God's saying, "from the clear proofs and the guidance," includes both what is explicitly stated and what is derived by inference, since the name guidance applies to all of it. This also contains proof that the report of a single person must be acted upon, because it is not obligatory on him to explain unless the acceptance of his word has become obligatory. And He says: "Except those who repent, make amends and clarify," so He judged that clarification takes place through their report. It might be objected: "It is possible that each of them was forbidden to conceal and commanded to clarify, so that the reporters would be numerous and the report would become mass-transmitted (mutawatir)." We reply: This is a mistake, because they were not forbidden to conceal except that they were among those who could conspire together to conceal. Whoever among them could conspire to conceal, their report does not produce certain knowledge. And God knows best.

**Fourth issue:** When He said, "from the clear proofs and the guidance," this indicates that what is other than that may be permissible to conceal, especially if there is fear along with it, since fear makes concealment more emphatic. Abu Hurayrah left this when he feared, and he said: "I memorized two vessels (of knowledge) from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). As for one of them, I disseminated it. As for the other, if I disseminated it, my throat would be cut." Al-Bukhari recorded it. Abu Abdullah (i.e., al-Bukhari, may God be pleased with him) said: "The bulʿum is the passage of food." Our scholars said: What Abu Hurayrah did not disseminate, and feared for himself a trial or death because of it, relates only to matters concerning times of civil strife and the naming of individual apostates and hypocrites, and the like of this, which does not relate to the clear proofs and the guidance. And God knows best.

**Fifth issue:** God's saying, "after We have made it clear," the pronoun in "made it clear" refers to what was sent down of the clear proofs and the guidance. "The Book" is a noun of genus, so the meaning is all the books that were sent down.

**Sixth issue:** God's saying, "Those, God curses them," means: He disowns them, removes them far from His reward, and says to them: "My curse is upon you," as He said to the accursed one: "And indeed My curse is upon you." The original meaning of cursing (la'n) in the language is distancing and expelling. This has already been discussed (see page 25 of this part).

**Seventh issue:** God's saying, "and the cursers curse them." Qatadah and al-Rabi' said: the cursers are the angels and the believers. Ibn Atiyyah said: "This is clear and follows the implication of the speech." Mujahid and Ikrimah said: they are the insects and the animals, which are afflicted with drought because of the sins of the wicked scholars who conceal, so they curse them. Al-Zajjaj said: "The correct view is the view of the one who said the cursers are the angels and the believers. As for whether this applies to the beasts of the earth, its reality cannot be known except through an explicit text or a binding report, and we have found neither of these."

I say: A report has come concerning this, related by al-Bara' ibn Azib, may God be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ), regarding His saying, "God curses them and the cursers curse them," said: "The beasts of the earth." Ibn Majah recorded it from Muhammad ibn al-Sabbah, from Ammar ibn Muhammad, from Layth, from Abu al-Minhal, from Zadhan, from al-Bara'. Its chain is good (hasan).

If it is said: How is that which does not reason given the plural form used for those who reason? It is said: Because the act of those who reason is attributed to them, as He said: "I saw them prostrating to me" (and He did not say "prostrating females"), and He said: "Why did you testify against us?" and He said: "And you see them looking at you." There are many similar examples, and more will come, God willing.

Al-Bara' ibn Azib and Ibn Abbas said: "The cursers" means every creature except the two weighty ones, jinn and humans. This is because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When the disbeliever is struck in his grave and he cries out, every creature hears him except the two weighty ones, and every hearer curses him."

Ibn Mas'ud and al-Suddi said: "It is the man who curses his companion, and the curse rises to the heaven, then descends, and does not find its target worthy of it, so it returns to the one who uttered it and does not find him worthy, so it goes and falls upon the Jews who concealed what God sent down. This is His saying: 'and the cursers curse them.' Whoever of them dies, the curse is lifted from him, and it remains upon those of the Jews who are left."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 160:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Except those who repent﴾. Exalted is He excepted those who repent, who are righteous in their deeds and their words, and who turn back (in devotion) to their repentance. According to our scholars (ʿulamāʾunā), saying "I have repented" is not sufficient for repentance (tawbah) until there appears from him, in the second state, the opposite of the first. If he was an apostate, he returns to Islam, manifesting its laws (sharaʾiʿ). If he was among the people of sins, righteous deeds appear from him, and he keeps away from the people of corruption and from the circumstances in which he used to be. If he was among the people of idols, he keeps away from them and associates with the people of Islam. And so on: what appears is the reverse of what he was upon. The explanation of repentance (tawbah) and its rulings will come, God willing, in (surah) al-Nisaʾ [[See vol. 5, p. 91.]]. Some scholars said regarding His saying, "and made it clear" (wa-bayyanū), meaning: by breaking the wine and pouring it out. It was also said: "made it clear" means what is in the Torah concerning the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the obligation to follow him. The general meaning is preferable, according to what we have explained, that is, they made clear the opposite of what they had been upon, and God, exalted is He, knows best. ﴿Those, I turn back to them, and I am the Accepting of repentance, the Most Merciful﴾ has already passed [[Refer to the fifth issue and what follows, vol. 1, p. 325, second edition.]]. And praise be to God.

**Third-person commentary of al-Qurtubi on 2:161–162**

There are three issues in this passage.

**The first issue:** God's words, ﴿and they are disbelievers﴾. The *waw* is the *waw* of circumstance (*waw al-hal*), indicating a state.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: Many of my teachers told me that it is not permissible to curse a specific disbeliever, because his state at the time of his *muwafat* (dying upon a particular state, i.e., his final condition at death) is not known. In this verse, God made the permission to curse conditional upon dying in disbelief. As for what is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he cursed specific groups of disbelievers by name, that was because he knew their final end.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: In my view, the sound position is that it is permissible to curse a specific disbeliever, based on his outward state and because it is permissible to kill him and fight him. It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "O God, 'Amr ibn al-'As satirized me, though he knew that I am not a poet. So curse him and satirize him, as many times as he satirized me." Then he cursed him, even though faith, religion and Islam were his eventual end. The Prophet (ﷺ) showed moderation by his words, "as many times as he satirized me," and did not exceed that, so that justice and fairness would be known. He attributed the satire to God in the matter of retribution, not in initiating the description with it, just as scheming, mockery and deception are attributed to Him. Glory be to Him, high above what the wrongdoers say, a great exaltation.

I say: As for cursing disbelievers collectively, without specifying individuals, there is no disagreement about it, based on what Malik narrated from Dawud ibn al-Husayn, that he heard al-A'raj say: "I did not find people except that they were cursing the disbelievers during Ramadan." Our scholars said: It makes no difference whether they have a protected covenant (*dhimma*) or not. This is not obligatory, but it is permissible for the one who does it, because of their rejection of the truth and their enmity toward the religion and its people. Likewise, anyone who openly commits sins, such as drinkers of wine and consumers of usury, and women who imitate men and men who imitate women, and others whose cursing is mentioned in the hadiths.

**The second issue:** Cursing the disbeliever is not intended as a deterrent from disbelief. Rather, it is a retribution for disbelief and a display of the ugliness of his disbelief, whether the disbeliever is dead or insane. Some of the early scholars (*al-salaf*) said: There is no benefit in cursing someone among them who has gone insane or died, neither as retribution nor as deterrence, since he is not affected by it. According to this view, the meaning of the verse is that people will curse him on the Day of Resurrection so that he will be affected by it, suffer harm, and his heart will be pained, and that will be a retribution for his disbelief, as God said: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection, some of you will disavow others and some of you will curse others﴾. This position is supported by the fact that the verse indicates a report from God about their being cursed, not a command.

Ibn al-'Arabi mentioned that cursing a specific sinner is impermissible by consensus (*ittifaq*), based on what is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that a man who drank wine was brought to him several times. One of those present said: "May God curse him, how often he is brought!" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do not be a helper of Satan against your brother." He thus gave him the sanctity of brotherhood, and this requires compassion. This is a sound hadith. I say: al-Bukhari and Muslim recorded it. Some scholars have mentioned a difference of opinion regarding cursing a specific sinner. They said: The Prophet (ﷺ) only said, "Do not be a helper of Satan against your brother," concerning Nu'aym,¹ after the prescribed punishment (*hadd*) had been carried out on him. Whoever has had God's prescribed punishment carried out upon him should not be cursed. Whoever has not had the prescribed punishment carried out upon him, cursing him is permissible, whether he is named or not, because the Prophet (ﷺ) only cursed the one upon whom the curse was obligatory, as long as he remained in that state which warrants the curse. When he repents of it, desists, and the prescribed punishment purifies him, no curse is directed at him. This is clarified by the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "If the slave-girl of one of you commits fornication, let him flog her with the prescribed punishment and not reproach her (*yuthrib*)."² 

This hadith, together with its soundness, indicates that reproach and cursing occur only before the prescribed punishment is taken and before repentance. And God knows best.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: As for cursing the sinner in general, it is permissible by consensus (*ijma'*), based on what is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "God curses the thief who steals an egg, so his hand is cut off."

**The third issue:** God's words, ﴿Those—upon them is the curse of God, and of the angels, and of mankind, all together﴾. That is, their removal from His mercy. The root meaning of *la'n* (cursing) is expulsion and banishment, which has already been discussed.³ So the curse from people is expulsion, and the curse from God is punishment.

Al-Hasan al-Basri read *"wal-mala'ikatu wal-nasu ajma'un"* with the nominative (*raf'*). Its interpretation: ﴿Those—their recompense is that God curses them, and the angels curse them, and mankind curses them all together﴾, just as you say: "I disliked the standing of Zayd, 'Amr and Khalid," because the meaning is: "I disliked that Zayd stood." This reading of al-Hasan contradicts the codices (*al-masahif*).

If it is said: All of mankind does not curse them, because their own people do not curse them, there are three answers to this. The first: the curse of most people is attributed to "the curse of mankind," giving the ruling of the majority precedence over the minority. The second: al-Suddi said: Everyone curses the wrongdoer, and when the disbeliever curses the wrongdoer, he has cursed himself. The third: Abu al-'Aliyah said: What is meant is the Day of Resurrection, when their own people will curse them along with all of mankind, as God said: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection, some of you will disavow others and some of you will curse others﴾.

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Abiding therein﴾, meaning in the curse, that is, in its recompense. It was also said: their abiding in the curse means that it is everlasting upon them. ﴿Nor will they be reprieved﴾, meaning they will not be delayed from punishment for any moment.

﴿Abiding﴾ (*khalidin*) is in the accusative as a state (*hal*) from the *ha'* and *mim* in ﴿upon them﴾, and the element governing it is the adverbial phrase in "upon them," because the curse contains the sense of being fixed (*istiqrar*).

¹ Nu'aym: he is Ibn 'Amr ibn Rifa'ah. He witnessed al-'Aqabah, Badr and the battles after them. He was very playful, and the Prophet (ﷺ) would laugh at his jokes. (From *Usd al-Ghabah*.)

² Ibn al-Athir said in *al-Nihayah*: "That is, he should not rebuke her or reproach her with fornication after the flogging. It was also said: he meant that in her punishment he should not be content with reproach, but should flog her with the prescribed punishment."

This is clarified by the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "If the slave-girl of one of you commits fornication, let him flog her with the prescribed punishment and not reproach her (*yuthrib*)."² 

This hadith, together with its soundness, indicates that reproach and cursing occur only before the prescribed punishment is taken and before repentance. And God knows best.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: As for cursing the sinner in general, it is permissible by consensus (*ijma'*), based on what is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "God curses the thief who steals an egg, so his hand is cut off."

**The third issue:** God's words, ﴿Those—upon them is the curse of God, and of the angels, and of mankind, all together﴾. That is, their removal from His mercy. The root meaning of *la'n* (cursing) is expulsion and banishment, which has already been discussed.³ So the curse from people is expulsion, and the curse from God is punishment.

Al-Hasan al-Basri read *"wal-mala'ikatu wal-nasu ajma'un"* with the nominative (*raf'*). Its interpretation: ﴿Those—their recompense is that God curses them, and the angels curse them, and mankind curses them all together﴾, just as you say: "I disliked the standing of Zayd, 'Amr and Khalid," because the meaning is: "I disliked that Zayd stood." This reading of al-Hasan contradicts the codices (*al-masahif*).

If it is said: All of mankind does not curse them, because their own people do not curse them, there are three answers to this. The first: the curse of most people is attributed to "the curse of mankind," giving the ruling of the majority precedence over the minority. The second: al-Suddi said: Everyone curses the wrongdoer, and when the disbeliever curses the wrongdoer, he has cursed himself. The third: Abu al-'Aliyah said: What is meant is the Day of Resurrection, when their own people will curse them along with all of mankind, as God said: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection, some of you will disavow others and some of you will curse others﴾.

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Abiding therein﴾, meaning in the curse, that is, in its recompense. It was also said: their abiding in the curse means that it is everlasting upon them. ﴿Nor will they be reprieved﴾, meaning they will not be delayed from punishment for any moment.

﴿Abiding﴾ (*khalidin*) is in the accusative as a state (*hal*) from the *ha'* and *mim* in ﴿upon them﴾, and the element governing it is the adverbial phrase in "upon them," because the curse contains the sense of being fixed (*istiqrar*).
