Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 163:

There are two issues here.

The first: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And your God is one God﴾. When the Exalted warned against concealing the truth, He made clear that the first thing that must be made manifest, and whose concealment is not permitted, is the matter of tawhid (affirming God's oneness). He connected this with the mention of proof and taught the method of reflection (nazar), which is contemplation of the wonders of creation, so that it may be known that there must be a Creator who is not similar to anything. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: The disbelievers of Quraysh said: "O Muhammad, describe your Lord for us." So Allah sent down Surah "al-Ikhlas" and this verse. The idolaters had three hundred and sixty idols, so Allah made clear that He is One.

The second: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿There is no god but He﴾. It is a negation and an affirmation. Its first part is disbelief and its last part is faith, and its meaning is: there is no worshipped one except Allah. It is related from al-Shibli, may Allah have mercy on him, that he used to say "Allah" and would not say "There is no god". When asked about this, he said: "I fear that I would begin with the word of denial and not reach the word of affirmation." I say: This is one of their subtle sciences which have no reality, for Allah, mighty is His name, mentioned this meaning in His Book by negation and affirmation and repeated it, and promised a great reward to the one who says it, on the tongue of His Prophet ﷺ. It was recorded by al-Muwatta', al-Bukhari, Muslim and others. And the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever's last words are 'There is no god but Allah' will enter Paradise." Recorded by Muslim. What is intended is the heart, not the tongue. So if one says "There is no god" and dies while his belief and inner conviction are the oneness of God and what is due to Him of attributes, he would be among the people of Paradise by the consensus of the People of the Sunnah. We have already explained the meaning of His name "the One", and "There is no god but He" and "the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate" in "al-Kitab al-Asna fi Sharh Asma' Allah al-Husna". And praise be to Allah.

In it are fourteen issues.

**The first issue:** 'Ata' said: When "And your God is One God" was revealed, the disbelievers of Quraysh said: "How can one God be sufficient for the people?" Then "Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth" was revealed. Sufyan narrated this from his father, from Abu al-Duha, who said: When "And your God is One God" was revealed, they said: "Is there any proof of that?" So Allah the Exalted revealed "Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth." It was as if they had asked for a sign, and so He made clear to them the proof of Tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness), and that this world and this wondrous structure must have a builder and a maker. He used the plural "heavens" because they are different kinds, each heaven being of a kind different from the others. He used the singular "earth" because it is all dust, and Allah knows best.

The sign in the heavens is their elevation without pillars beneath them and without ties above them, and this points to power and to the breaking of normal custom. If a prophet had come and challenged people with a mountain standing in the air without support, it would have been a miracle. Then, what is in them of the sun, the moon, the wandering stars and the shining planets, rising and setting, luminous and effaced, is a second sign. The sign in the earth is its seas, its rivers, its minerals, its trees, its plains and its rugged places.

**The second issue:** As for the words of Allah the Exalted: "and the alternation of the night and the day." It has been said: their alternation is by the coming of one and the going of the other, from a direction that is not known. It has also been said: their alternation is in their attributes, of light and darkness, of length and shortness.

"Layl" (night) is the plural of "laylah," like "tamrah" and "tamr," and "nakhlah" and "nakhl." It is also pluralized as "layali" and "layal" with the same meaning, and this is among what departs from the standard pattern of plurals, like "shabah" and "mushabih," "hajah" and "hawa'ij," and "dhakar" and "madhakir." It is as if "layali" by analogy is the plural of "laylah" (in the form "laylaah"). They have used this in poetry, and someone said:

*In every day and every night (laylaah)*

Another said:

*Every day, whatever it is, and every one of its nights,*
*until everyone who sees him says:*
*Woe to him, what a camel, how wretched he is!*

Ibn Faris said in al-Mujmal: It is said that some birds are called "layl," but I do not know it. [[Al-Jawhari said in al-Sihah: "Some people have mentioned that the night is the offspring of the kurwan (a bird), and that the day is the offspring of the hubara (bustard), and this has come in some poems."]]

"Nahar" (day) is pluralized as "nuhur" and "anhirah." Tha'lab, Ahmad ibn Yahya, said: "nahr" is the plural of "nuhr," and "nuhr" is the plural of "nahar." It has also been said that "nahar" is a singular noun not pluralized, because it has the meaning of a verbal noun, like your saying "al-diya'" (light), which applies to the few and the many. The first view is the more common. The poet said:

*Had it not been for the two dishes of thareed, we would have perished from the lean camels;*
*the thareed of the night and the thareed in the day (nuhr).*

Ibn Faris said: "Nahar" is well known, and its plural is "nuhr" and "anhar." It is said that "nahar" is pluralized as "nuhr." "Nahar" is the light between the rising of dawn and the setting of the sun. A man who is "nahir" is one who keeps the day. It is said that "nahar" is the chick of the hubara. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: The beginning of the day is the rising of the sun, and what comes before that is not counted as day. Tha'lab said: Its beginning according to the Arabs is the rising of the sun, citing the words of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

*The sun rises each last night (of the night),*
*red, its color turning rosy.*

He also recited the words of 'Adi ibn Zayd:

*And the one who made the sun a barrier (misr), with no concealment in it,*
*which separated between the day and the night.*

Al-Kisa'i recited:

*When the sun of the day rises, indeed it*
*is the sign of my greeting to you, so greet me.*

Al-Zajjaj said in the Book of Anwa': The beginning of the day is the first light of the sun. Ibn al-Anbari divided time into three parts: one part he made pure night, which is from the setting of the sun to the rising of dawn; one part he made pure day, which is from the rising of the sun to its setting; and one part he made shared between day and night, which is from the rising of dawn to the rising of the sun, because of the remnants of the darkness of night and the beginnings of the light of day.

I say: The correct view is that the day is from the rising of dawn to the setting of the sun, as Ibn Faris narrated in al-Mujmal. This is shown by what is established in Sahih Muslim from 'Adi ibn Hatim, who said: When "until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread at dawn" was revealed, 'Adi said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, I put two cords under my pillow, a white cord and a black cord, and I know by them the night from the day." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Your pillow is indeed wide; it is only the blackness of the night and the whiteness of the day." This hadith decides that the day is from the rising of dawn to the setting of the sun, and this is what jurisprudence of oaths requires, and by it the rulings are tied. So whoever swears not to speak to a certain person by day, and then speaks to him before sunrise, has broken his oath; but on the first view he has not broken it. The saying of the Prophet ﷺ is the decisive judgment in this matter. As for the apparent meaning of the language and its derivation from the Sunnah, it is from the time of brightening when the time of day has widened, as the poet said [[He is Qays ibn al-Khatim, describing a spear-thrust.]]:

*I held it in my hand and widened its opening,*
*so that a standing man could see what lay behind it through it.*

There has come from Hudhayfah what points to this view, which al-Nasa'i recorded. It will come in the verses on fasting, if Allah the Exalted wills. [[See p. 273 of this part.]]

**The third issue:** The words of Allah the Exalted: "and the ships that run in the sea." "Fulk" means ships. Its singular and plural are with one form, and it may be masculine or feminine. The vowels of the singular are not the same as those of the plural; rather it is as if the plural is built with a different pattern, which is shown by the dual form in their saying "fulkan," where the middle is kept. The singular "fulk" is masculine, as Allah said: "in the laden ship (al-fulk al-mashhun)" [[See vol. 15, p. 34.]], so He brought it masculine; and He said: "and the ships (al-fulk) that run in the sea," so He made it feminine. It may be singular or plural. He said: "until when you are in the ships (al-fulk), and they run with them by a good wind" [[See vol. 8, p. 324.]], so He used the plural. It seems that when it is singular, one takes it to refer to the vessel (al-markab) and makes it masculine, and to the boat (al-safinah) and makes it feminine.

It has also been said: its singular is "falak," like "asad" and "usd," and "khashab" and "khushb." Its origin is from rotation, and from this comes "falak al-sama'," the sphere on which the stars revolve. "Fallakat al-jariyah" means her breast became round, and from this comes "falkat al-mighzal," the whorl of the spindle. The boat was named "fulk" because it turns easily on the water with the greatest ease of turning.

The meaning of the verse concerning ships is that Allah subjects them so that they run on the surface of the water and remain upon it despite their weight. The first to make them was Nuh (Noah), peace be upon him, as Allah the Exalted informed us, and Jibril said to him: "Make it on the breast (juju') of a bird," and Nuh, peace be upon him, made it by inheritance among the worlds with what Jibril showed him. So the ship is an inverted bird, and the water beneath it is like the air above it. This was said by Ibn al-'Arabi.

**The fourth issue:** This verse and what is like it is evidence for the permissibility of sailing the sea in general, whether for trade or for worship, such as the pilgrimage (hajj) and jihad. From the Sunnah is the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: A man came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we sail the sea and carry with us only a little water." The hadith [continues]. And the hadith of Anas ibn Malik concerning the story of Umm Haram, both of which the imams recorded: Malik and others. A group narrated the hadith of Anas from him, from Ishaq ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Talhah, from Anas. But Bishr ibn 'Umar narrated it from Malik, from Ishaq, from Anas, from Umm Haram, making it part of Umm Haram's narrations rather than Anas's narrations. In this way Bundar Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated it to him. In it is clear evidence for sailing the sea in jihad for men and women. If it is permissible to sail for jihad, then sailing for the obligatory hajj is more fitting and more binding.

It is reported from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they forbade sailing. The Qur'an and the Sunnah refute this view, and if sailing were disliked or impermissible, the Prophet ﷺ would have forbidden those who said to him: "We sail the sea." This verse and what is like it is a clear text on the matter, and to it one returns for refuge. What was reported from the two 'Umars on this has been interpreted as meaning caution and avoiding the exposure of lives in seeking worldly gain and multiplying it; but as for performing the obligations, that is not the case. From what indicates the permissibility of sailing in terms of meaning is that Allah the Exalted set the sea across the middle of the earth and placed people on its two banks (al-'adwatayn), and divided benefits between the two sides, so that they cannot be reached except by cutting through the sea; so Allah made the way easy for them by the ship. This was said by Ibn al-'Arabi.

Abu 'Umar said: Malik disliked for a woman to ride the sea for the pilgrimage, and for jihad he disliked it even more. The Qur'an and the Sunnah refute his view. However, some of our companions from the people of Basra said: Malik only disliked it because the ships in the Hijaz were small, and women could not conceal themselves when relieving themselves in them because of their narrowness and the crowding of people in them, and the land route from Madinah to Makkah was possible; therefore Malik disliked it. As for large ships, like the ships of the people of Basra, there is no harm in them. He said: The principle is that the hajj is obligatory upon everyone who is able to reach it by a way, from free adult men and women, when the safer part of the route is secure, and it does not single out sea from land.

I say: the Book, the Sunnah, and the meaning all indicate the permissibility of sailing for both purposes together: worship and trade. The Book is the proof, and in it there is a model. However, people differ in their condition when sailing. Some find it easy and it does not trouble them, while others find it hard and it weakens them, like the one who is severely seasick (al-ma'id, the one who sails and whose soul is so overcome that he is turned about and nearly faints) and who cannot perform the obligatory prayer or other obligations while aboard. For the first, sailing is permitted. For the second, it is forbidden and he is prevented from it. There is no disagreement among the scholars on this.

The fifth matter: When the sea becomes turbulent (irtaja al-bahr, meaning it rages; it is said that it means its water becomes abundant and covers everything), it is not permitted for anyone to sail on it in any way at the time of its turbulence, nor in a period in which safety is unlikely. Sailing is permitted, in their view, only in a period in which safety is the more likely outcome. Those who sail in calm conditions and are saved are countless, while those who perish in it are limited in number.

The sixth matter: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿with what benefits people﴾, means with that which benefits them from trade and all the other needs by which their conditions are made good. Through sailing, profits are gained, and those to whom goods are carried also benefit. Some of those who attacked the religion said: "Allah, Exalted is He, says in your Book: 'We have neglected nothing in the Book' (cf. Qur'an 6:38). So where is the mention of the condiments that improve food, such as salt, pepper, and other things?" It was answered regarding His saying: "with what benefits people."

The seventh matter: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and what Allah sends down from the sky of water﴾ means by it the rains, by which the world is revived, plants and provisions are brought forth. He made some of it stored for use at times other than when it falls, as He, Exalted is He, said: "Then We made it settle in the earth" (Qur'an 23:18).

The eighth matter: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and He spread in it every kind of moving creature﴾: "baththa" means He scattered and spread out, and from it comes "like scattered moths" (Qur'an 101:4). "Dabbah" comprises all animals. Some people excluded birds, but this is rejected, since Allah, Exalted is He, said: "There is no creature on earth but its provision is upon Allah" (Qur'an 11:6). Birds do crawl (yadibbu) on their feet in some of their conditions. Al-A'sha said:

"Crawling like the sandgrouse of the sandy valley at every watering place."

And Alqama ibn Abada said:

"Its thunderbolts for their birds are a crawling."

The ninth matter: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and the turning of the winds﴾. Its turning (tasrif) is sending them as barren (aqim) and fertilizing, as gentle breezes (sirr) and as help, as destruction, as hot and cold, and as gentle and violent. It is said that its turning is sending them south and north, east and west, and the nakba' (the wind that comes between the directions of two winds). It is said that its turning is that the large ships and the small ones come to the extent that they carry them, and that what would strike them is turned away from them. The size or smallness of the sails does not matter, for if the wind came as one mass, it would strike the sails and sink the ships.

"Riyah" is the plural of "rih," which is so named because it generally brings "rawh" (relief, comfort). Abu Dawud related from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "The wind is from the mercy of Allah; it brings mercy and it brings punishment. So when you see it, do not curse it, but ask Allah for its good and seek refuge in Allah from its evil." [Note: This is as it appears in the Sunan of Abu Dawud. In the original manuscripts it reads: "The wind is from the spirit of Allah." Salamah said: "The spirit of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, comes..." etc. Salamah is one of those from whom Abu Dawud related this hadith.]

Ibn Majah also related it in his Sunan: Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us: Yahya ibn Sa'id narrated to us from al-Awza'i, from al-Zuhri, from Thabit al-Zuraqi, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not curse the wind, for it is from the mercy of Allah; it brings mercy and punishment. But ask Allah for its good and seek refuge in Allah from its evil."

It is also narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Do not curse the wind, for it is from the breath of the Most Merciful."

The meaning is that Allah, Exalted is He, placed in it relief, breathing space, and refreshment, and the attribution is by way of action. The meaning is that Allah, Exalted is He, made it so.

In Sahih Muslim, from Ibn Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "I was helped (on the day of the Confederates) by the east wind (al-Sabā), and the people of 'Ad were destroyed by the west wind (al-Dabur)." The meaning of al-Sabā and al-Dabur will come later.

This is the meaning of what came in the report that Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, relieved His Prophet (ﷺ) by the wind on the day of the Confederates, when He said: "So We sent upon them a wind and hosts you did not see" (Qur'an 33:9). It is said: "Allah gave relief (naffasa) to so-and-so from a distress of this world," meaning He relieved him of it.

In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him): "Whoever relieves a believer of a distress of this world, Allah will relieve him of a distress of the Day of Resurrection." That is, relieves him.

The poet said:

"As if the east wind, when it breathes,
upon a sorrowful heart, dispels its sorrows."

Ibn al-A'rabi said: "Al-Nasim is the first blowing of the wind."

The origin of "rih" is "rawh," and for this reason the plural of paucity is said to be "arwah." It is not said "ayrah," because it is from the root with waw. "Riyah" is said as the plural of abundance and to seek harmony with the yā'.

In the Mushaf of Hafsa (may Allah be pleased with her), it reads: "wa-tasrifi al-arwah."

The tenth matter: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and the turning of the winds﴾. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "al-rih" in the singular. Likewise in al-A'raf, al-Kahf, Ibrahim, al-Naml, al-Rum, Fatir, al-Shura, and al-Jathiyah, there is no difference between them in this. Ibn Kathir agreed with them in al-A'raf, al-Naml, al-Rum, Fatir, and al-Shura. Hamza read "al-rih" in the singular in "winds fertilizing" (Qur'an 15:22). Ibn Kathir read it in the singular in "It is He who sends the wind" (Qur'an 25:48) in al-Furqan. The rest read it in the plural in all of these, except for the one in Ibrahim and al-Shura, which only Nafi' read in the plural. The Seven (ahl al-sab'ah, the seven canonical readers) did not differ except in these places.

What we mentioned in al-Rum is the second: "It is Allah who sends the winds" (Qur'an 30:48). There is no disagreement among them regarding "winds bearing good tidings" (Qur'an 30:46).

Abu Ja'far Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa' used to read "al-riyah" in the plural whenever it had the definite article (alif and lam) throughout the Qur'an, except for "the wind blows him away" and "the barren wind." If there was no alif and lam, he read it in the singular.

Whoever reads it in the singular does so because it is a noun of genus that indicates both the few and the many. Whoever reads it in the plural does so because of the differing directions from which the winds blow. Whoever reads it in the plural with mercy and in the singular with punishment does so by taking into account what predominates in the Qur'an, such as "winds bearing good tidings" and "the barren wind." Thus in the Qur'an it appears in the plural with mercy and in the singular with punishment, except in Yunus in His saying: "and they sailed with them in a good wind" (Qur'an 10:22).

It is related that when the wind blew, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would say: "O Allah, make it winds (riyah) and do not make it a wind (rih)."

This is because the wind of punishment is strong, its parts fitted together as if it were one body, while the wind of mercy is gentle and broken up, so for that reason it is plural.

It was made singular together with the ship (al-fulk) in Yunus, because the wind that makes ships run is one continuous wind, and then it was described as good, so the shared term between it and the wind of punishment ceased.

The eleventh matter: The scholars said: The wind stirs the air, and it may strengthen or weaken. When the movement of the air appears from the direction of the qiblah, going toward the qiblah's line, that wind is called "al-Sabā" (the east wind). When the movement of the air appears from behind the qiblah and goes toward the front of the qiblah, that wind is called "al-Dabur" (the west wind). When the movement of the air appears from the right of the qiblah going toward its left, it is called "rih al-janub" (the south wind). When the movement of the air appears from the left of the qiblah going toward its right, it is called "rih al-shamal" (the north wind).

Each of these winds has a nature, so its benefit is according to its nature. Al-Sabā is hot and dry, al-Dabur is cold and moist, al-Janub is hot and moist, and al-Shamal is cold and dry.

The difference in their natures is like the difference in the natures of the seasons of the year. Allah, Exalted is He, set four seasons for time, whose return is to the change of the states of the air. He made spring, which is the first of the seasons, hot and moist, and arranged in it growth and increase, so waters descend in it, the earth brings forth its blossoms and shows its plants, people begin to plant trees and much crops, animals breed in it, and milk becomes abundant.

When spring passes, it is followed by summer, which resembles spring in one of its two natures, which is heat, and differs from it in the other, which is moisture, because the air in summer is hot and dry. In it fruits ripen, and the grains sown in spring dry.

When summer passes, it is followed by autumn, which resembles summer in one of its two natures, which is dryness, and differs from it in the other, which is heat, because the air in autumn is cold and dry. In it the ripening of fruits is completed, they become dry and parched, and reach the state of storage. Fruits are picked, grapes are harvested, and the trees are cleared of their gathering.

When autumn passes, it is followed by winter, which accords with autumn in one of its two natures, which is cold, and differs from it in the other, which is dryness, because the air in winter is cold and moist. Rains and snow increase, and the earth is smoothed like a resting body, so it does not stir unless Allah, Blessed and Exalted, sends to it the heat of spring. When it combines with moisture, then at that time there is growth and increase by the permission of Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He.

Many other winds may blow besides what we have mentioned, but the roots are these four. So every wind that blows between two winds, its ruling is the ruling of the wind that in its blowing is nearer to its place, and it is called "al-Nakba'."

The twelfth matter: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and the clouds subjected between heaven and earth﴾. The cloud (sahab) is so named because it is drawn (insihab) through the air. "I dragged my train (sahbtu dhaili sahban)." "So-and-so dragged himself (tasahhaba) upon so-and-so," meaning he dared. "Al-sahb" means intense eating and drinking. "Al-musakhkhar" means the subdued, and its subjection (taskhir) is sending it from one place to another. It is said that its subjection is its remaining between heaven and earth without pillars or ties, and the first is more apparent. It may be with water and with punishment.

Muslim related from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "While a man was in a barren land of the earth, he heard a voice in a cloud saying: 'Water the garden of so-and-so.' That cloud moved away and poured its water on a black stony land (harrah), and a watercourse (sharjah) from those watercourses had absorbed all that water. He followed the water and found a man standing in his garden turning the water with his spade. He said to him: 'O servant of Allah, what is your name?' He said: 'So-and-so,' by the name he had heard in the cloud. He said to him: 'O servant of Allah, why do you ask me my name?' He said: 'I heard a voice in the cloud whose water this is saying: Water the garden of so-and-so, by your name. So what do you do with it?' He said: 'As you have said this, I look at what comes out of it, and I give a third of it in charity, and my family and I eat a third, and I return a third of it to it.'"

And in another narration: "And I will make a third of it for the poor, the beggars, and the wayfarer."

In the revelation: "And it is Allah who sends the winds, so they stir up clouds, and We drive them to a dead land" [see vol. 14, p. 326]; and He said: "Until, when they carry heavy clouds, We drive them to a dead land" [see vol. 7, p. 229]. And it is abundant in the revelation.

Ibn Majah related from Aisha that when the Prophet ﷺ saw a cloud approaching from one of the horizons, he would leave whatever he was doing, even if he was in prayer, until it came over him, and he would say: "O Allah, we seek refuge in You from the evil of what it was sent with." If it rained, he would say: "O Allah, let it be beneficial rain" twice or thrice. If Allah removed it and it did not rain, he would praise Allah for that.

Muslim related it in meaning from Aisha, the wife of the Prophet ﷺ, who said: When there was a day of wind and cloud, the effect of that would be seen on the face of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; he would come and go. When it rained, he would be pleased and that would leave him.

Aisha said: I asked him, and he said: "I feared that it might be a punishment sent upon my community." And when he saw rain, he would say: "A mercy."

In another narration he said: "Perhaps, O Aisha, it is as the people of 'Ad said: 'When they saw it as a cloud coming toward their valleys, they said: This is a cloud bringing us rain'" [see vol. 16, p. 205].

These hadiths and verses indicate the correctness of the first view, and that their being subjected (to movement) is not their being fixed in place. Allah knows best.

For fixity indicates non-movement. If by fixity is meant that they are in the air, neither in the heaven nor on the earth, this is correct, due to His saying "between" (bayn), and they are, along with that, subjected and carried, and that is greater in power, like the bird in the air. Allah the Exalted said: "Have they not seen the birds subjected in the air of the sky? None holds them up except Allah" [see vol. 10, p. 152]. And He said: "Have they not looked at the birds above them, spreading their wings and folding them? None holds them except the Most Merciful" [see vol. 18, p. 217].

The thirteenth: Ka'b al-Ahbar said: "The cloud is the sieve of the rain; were it not for the cloud, when the water descends from the sky, it would ruin what it falls upon of the earth." Ibn Abbas related it from him.

Al-Khatib Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn Ali mentioned it from Mu'adh ibn Abd Allah ibn Khubayb al-Juhani, who said: I saw Ibn Abbas pass by on a mule while I was among Banu Salama, and Tubay' ibn the wife of Ka'b passed by him. He greeted Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Abbas asked him: "Have you heard Ka'b al-Ahbar say anything about the cloud?" He said: "Yes." He said: "The cloud is the sieve of the rain; were it not for the cloud, when the water descends from the sky, it would ruin what it falls upon of the earth." He said: "I heard Ka'b say about the earth: it produces one plant this year and a different one the next year?" He said: "Yes, I heard him say: the seed descends from the sky." Ibn Abbas said: "I too have heard that from Ka'b."

The fourteenth: His saying, Exalted is He: "Surely there are signs (la-ayat)", that is, indications pointing to His oneness and power. For this reason He mentioned these matters right after His saying: "And your God is One God," so that by them He would demonstrate the truth of the report about His oneness, which precedes them, and the mention of His mercy and compassion toward His creation.

It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Woe to him who recites this verse and passes over it without reflection," that is, he did not contemplate it or take heed of it.

If it is said: "What prevents you from saying that they brought themselves into being?"

It is said to him: "This is impossible, for if they brought themselves into being, they would have to be either bringing themselves into being while existing, or while non-existent. If they brought themselves into being while non-existent, that would be impossible, because bringing into being is possible only from a living, knowing, powerful, willing being, and what does not exist cannot be described with that. If they existed, then their existence makes their bringing themselves into being unnecessary."

Also, if what they say were valid, then a building could bring itself into being, and likewise carpentry and weaving, and that is impossible; and whatever leads to the impossible is impossible.

Then Allah the Exalted did not limit His signs of His oneness to mere reports, but joined that with reflection and consideration in several verses of the Qur'an. He said to His Prophet ﷺ: "Say: Look at what is in the heavens and the earth" [see vol. 8, p. 386], and the address is to the disbelievers, as His saying Exalted: "But signs and warnings avail not a people who do not believe." And He said: "Have they not looked into the dominion of the heavens and the earth" [vol. 7, p. 330], meaning by "dominion" the signs.

And He said: "And in yourselves; will you not see?" [vol. 17, p. 40].

He says: Have they not looked at these things with a look of reflection and contemplation, so that they might infer from their being loci of events and changes that they are created things, and that a created thing cannot do without a maker who makes it, and that this Maker is wise, knowing, powerful, willing, hearing, seeing, speaking? For if He were not characterized by these attributes, a human being would be more perfect than Him, and that is impossible.

And Allah the Exalted said: "And We created man from an extract of clay" [vol. 12, p. 109], meaning Adam, peace be upon him. "Then We made him" — that is, We made his offspring and progeny — "a drop in a secure lodging," up to His saying: "you will be raised."

When a human being reflects, through this admonition and the intellect given to him, upon himself, he sees himself as governed and turned through various states.

He was a drop, then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, then bone and flesh. Thus he knows that he did not transfer himself from the state of deficiency to the state of perfection, because he cannot bring about for himself, in the better state which is the completeness of his intellect and the attainment of his maturity, any organ, nor can he add any limb to his body. This indicates to him that in his state of deficiency and the time of his weakness he was even less able to do that.

He may see himself as a youth, then a middle-aged man, then an old man, yet he did not transfer himself from the state of youth and strength to the state of old age and decrepitude, nor did he choose it for himself, nor is it within his power to leave the state of gray hair and return to the strength of youth. Thus he knows that he is not the one who performed those acts on himself, and that there is a Maker who made him and a transferrer who moved him from state to state; otherwise his states would not change without a transferrer or a governor.

Some of the sages said: Everything in the great world has a counterpart in the small world, which is the human body. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: "We have certainly created man in the best of stature," and said: "And in yourselves; will you not see?"

So the human senses are nobler than the shining stars, and the hearing and sight among them are like the sun and moon in perceiving what is perceived through them. His limbs, at decay, become dust of the same kind as the earth; in him is of the kind of water the sweat and all the moisture of the body; and of the kind of air in him is the spirit and breath; and of the kind of fire in him is the yellow bile.

His veins are like rivers in the earth, and his liver is like the springs from which the rivers are fed, since the veins draw from the liver. His bladder is like the sea, because what is in the vessels of the body flows down to it as rivers flow to the sea. His bones are like the mountains which are the pegs of the earth. His limbs are like trees: just as every tree has leaves and fruit, so every organ has an action or effect. Hair on the body is like plants and grass on the earth.

Then man, with his tongue, imitates every animal's voice, and with his limbs imitates the doing of every animal. Thus he is the small world together with the great world, a created thing made by one Maker, there is no god but Him.

His saying, Exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 165:

When Allah, glorified and exalted is He, informed in the previous verse of His oneness, His power and the greatness of His dominion, He then informed that alongside these overpowering signs for people of intellect there are those who take rivals (andad) besides Him. Its singular is nidd, and it has already been discussed (see the sixth issue in vol. 1, p. 230, second edition). The intended meaning is the idols and images that they worshipped, giving them the worship due to Allah despite their helplessness. This is the view of Mujahid.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They love them as they love Allah﴾, meaning: they love their idols in falsehood as the believers love Allah in truth. This is the statement of al-Mubarrad. Al-Zajjaj said its meaning is that, despite the helplessness of the idols, they love them as the believers love Allah despite His power. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi said: the intended meaning of the rivals (andad) is the leaders who are followed, whom they obey in acts of disobedience to Allah. On this view the pronoun in "yuhibbunahum" (they love them) follows the original form, whereas on the first view the pronoun for the idols is used in the form for rational beings, contrary to the original usage. Ibn Kaysan and al-Zajjaj also said: the meaning of "they love them as they love Allah" is that they set the idols and Allah equal in love. Abu Ishaq said: this is the correct view, and the evidence for its correctness is: ﴿But those who believe are stronger in love for Allah﴾.

Abu Raja' read "yahibbunahum" with a fatha on the ya', and likewise wherever it occurs in the Qur'an. This is a dialect form; one says: habibtu al-rajul, fa-huwa mahbub (I made the man beloved, so he is beloved). Al-Farra' said: Abu Turab recited to me:

I love, for her love, the black men, until
I have been made beloved by her love, black dogs.

The "man" in His saying, "man yattakhidh" (those who take), is in the nominative position as the subject of the sentence. "Yattakhidh" is in the singular form in accordance with the wording; outside the Qur'an it is permissible to say "yattakhidhun" in accordance with the meaning, and "yuhibbunahum" in accordance with the meaning, while "yuhibbuhum" is in accordance with the wording. It occupies the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "yattakhidh", meaning "loving them". If you wish, it may be a qualifier of the rivals (andad), meaning "beloved". The kaf in "ka-hubbi" is a qualifier of a deleted verbal noun (masdar), meaning: they love them with a love like the love of Allah. "But those who believe are stronger in love for Allah" means: stronger than the love of the people of the idols for their idols, and the followers for their leaders. It has been said: He said "those who believe are stronger in love for Allah" because Allah loved them first, and then they loved Him. Whoever is witnessed by his beloved as being loved, his love is more complete. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He loves them and they love Him﴾. The explanation of the love of the believers for Allah and His love for them will come in surah Al 'Imran, if Allah the Exalted wills.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If only those who have done wrong could see, when they see the punishment, that all power belongs to Allah, and that Allah is severe in punishment﴾. The reading of the people of Madina and the people of Syria is with the ta' (tarawn/"if you could see"), while the people of Makka, the people of Kufa and Abu 'Amr read with the ya' (yaraw/"if they could see"), and this is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd. There is a difficulty and an ellipsis in the verse. Abu 'Ubayd said: the meaning is, "If those who did wrong in this world could see the punishment of the Hereafter, they would know, when they see it, that all power belongs to Allah." On this view "yara" is from sight by the eye. Al-Nahhas said in his book Ma'ani al-Qur'an: this is the view that the exegetes follow. He said in his book I'rab al-Qur'an: it is related from Muhammad ibn Yazid that he said: this interpretation which Abu 'Ubayd brought is remote, and his expression in it is not good, because he supposes: "If those who did wrong could see the punishment," as though he makes it doubtful, whereas Allah has made it certain. Rather the estimate, which is the view of al-Akhfash, is: "If those who did wrong could see that power belongs to Allah." "Yara" here means "yalam" (to know), that is: if they knew the reality of the power of Allah, mighty and majestic, and the severity of His punishment. So "yara" takes effect upon "that power belongs to Allah", which fills the place of the two objects. "Those who" (alladhina) is the subject of "yara", and the answer to "law" (if) is omitted, meaning: they would have clarified the harm of taking gods, as He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿If only you could see when they are made to stand before their Lord﴾ and ﴿If only you could see when they are made to stand over the Fire﴾. No answer to "law" is stated. Al-Zuhri and Qatada said: the omission is more intense as a threat, and similar to it is the saying of a speaker: "If only you saw so-and-so while the whips were taking hold of him!" As for whoever reads with the ta', the estimate is: "If you could see, O Muhammad, those who did wrong in the state of seeing the punishment, and their terror of it, and their magnifying of it, they would acknowledge that power belongs to Allah." So the answer is omitted in this way of meaning, and it is the governing element of "anna" (that). Another estimate: "If you could see, O Muhammad, those who did wrong in the state of their seeing the punishment and their terror of it, you would know that all power belongs to Allah." The Prophet (ﷺ) already knew this, but he was addressed while the intended audience is his community, for among them are those who need the strengthening of their knowledge through witnessing such a thing. It is also possible that the meaning is: "Say, O Muhammad, to the wrongdoer, this." It has been said: "anna" is in the accusative position as an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), meaning: because all power belongs to Allah. Sibawayh recited:

And I forgive the faults of the noble, saving them up,
and I turn away from the abuse of the base, out of nobility.

Meaning: for the sake of saving them up. The meaning is: "If you could see, O Muhammad, those who did wrong in the state of their seeing the punishment, because power belongs to Allah, you would know the extent of their torment and you would magnify what has befallen them." The word "idh" (when), which refers to the past, is used in affirming these future events, to bring the matter near and to confirm its occurrence. Ibn 'Amir alone read "yurawna" with a damma on the ya', while the rest read it with a fatha. Al-Hasan, Ya'qub, Shayba, Sallam and Abu Ja'far read "inna al-quwwata" and "inna Allaha" with a kasra on the hamza in both, as a new sentence or by implying a verb of saying, meaning: "If you could see those who did wrong, when they see the punishment, saying: indeed power belongs to Allah." By the explicit text of this verse, power is established for Allah, in contrast to the claim of the Mu'tazila, who deny the meanings of the eternal attributes. Exalted is Allah above what they say.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 166:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed﴾. He means the leaders and chiefs disowned those who followed them in disbelief. This is related from Qatadah, ʿAta' and al-Rabi'. Qatadah also said, and al-Suddi: they are the misleading devils, who disowned humankind. And it is said: it is general, covering every leader who is followed. ﴿And they see the punishment﴾: he means the followers and the followed. It was said: by their certainty of it at the moment of witnessing it in this world. And it was said: at the time of the presentation and questioning in the Hereafter. I say: both are attained. They witness at death what they are coming to of humiliation, and in the Hereafter they taste the painful punishment and retribution.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And their ties are cut off from them﴾, that is, the connections by which they used to be linked in this world, such as kinship and other things; this is related from Mujahid and others. The singular is sabab (means of connection) and wusla (link). The original meaning of sabab is a rope tied to a thing so that it pulls it; then everything that draws something was called a sabab. Al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: the asbab are their deeds. And sabab also means a direction or side, and from it is the saying of Zuhayr:

"And whoever shrinks from the causes of death, they will reach him, even if he tries to climb the causes of the sky with a ladder."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 167:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who followed said: "If only we had a return (karrah), so that we might disassociate ourselves from them just as they have disassociated themselves from us."﴾ "Anna" is in the position of the nominative (raf'), meaning: if it were established that we have a return (raj'ah), "fa-natabarra'a minhum" (so that we might disassociate ourselves from them) is the answer to the wish (jawab al-tamanni). The karrah is the return (raj'ah) and the coming back (al-'awdah) to a state that once existed; that is, the followers said: "If we were returned to the world until we act righteously and disassociate ourselves from them," "kama tabarra'u minna" (just as they disassociated themselves from us). The kaf here is in the position of the accusative (nasb) as an attribute (na't) of an omitted verbal noun (masdar mahdhuf); that is, "tabarra'an kama" (a disassociation like theirs). It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), its implied sense being "mutabarri'in" (disassociating themselves). Al-tabarru' (disassociation) is separation (al-infisal).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Thus Allah will show them their deeds as regrets upon them.﴾ The kaf is in the position of the nominative (raf'), meaning: the matter is thus; that is, just as Allah showed them the punishment, thus Allah will show them their deeds. As for "yuriyhimu Allah" (Allah will show them), it has been said that it is from the sight of the eye (ru'yat al-basar), in which case it is transitive to two objects: the first is the ha' and mim in "yuriyhim" (them), and the second is "a'malahum" (their deeds), and "hasarat" (as regrets) is a circumstantial state (hal). It is also possible that it is from the sight of the heart (ru'yat al-qalb), in which case "hasarat" is the third object. As for "a'malahum" (their deeds), al-Rabi' said: that is, the corrupt deeds which they committed, for which the Fire became obligatory for them. Ibn Mas'ud and al-Suddi said: they are the righteous deeds which they abandoned, so the Garden escaped them, and traditions have been narrated in support of this view. Al-Suddi said: the Garden will be raised up for them, and they will look at it and at their houses in it, had they obeyed Allah, then it will be divided among the believers, and that is the time they will regret. These deeds are attributed to them in terms of their being commanded to perform them, while the attribution of the corrupt deeds to them is in terms of their having done them. "Al-hasrah" is the singular of "al-hasarat," like tamrah and tamarat, jafnah and jafanat, and shahwah and shahawat. This is when it is a noun; if you make it an adjective, you add a sukun, as when you say: dakhmah and dakhmat, and 'abalah and 'abalat. Al-hasrah is the highest degree of regret over a thing that has been lost. Al-tahassur is al-talahhuf (anguish), and it is said: "hasirtu 'alayhi" (with kasrah) ahsaru hasaran wa hasratan. It is derived from the word hasir, meaning something that has been exhausted and whose strength has departed, like a camel when it becomes weary. It has also been said that it is derived from hasara, meaning to uncover, and from it comes al-hasir in war: one who has no armor with him. Al-infisar means al-inkishaf (exposure).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they will never emerge from the Fire.﴾ This is evidence for the eternal abiding of the disbelievers in it and that they will not come out of it. This is the view of the body of the People of the Sunnah, based on this verse and on His saying, may He be exalted: "And they will not enter the Garden until the camel passes through the eye of the needle." And it will come [[see vol. 7, p. 206.]].

In this regard there are four issues.

The first concerns His saying, ﴿O mankind﴾. It is said that it was revealed concerning Thaqif, Khuza'ah and Banu Mudlij regarding what they had forbidden themselves of livestock, but the wording is general. Here "good" (al-tayyib) means "lawful" (al-halal). In that case it is an emphasis on the difference in wording, and this is the view of Malik regarding "good." Al-Shafi'i said: "good" means "pleasing to the taste" (al-mustaladh), so it is a classification of types, and for this reason eating a filthy animal is prohibited. The explanation of this will come in "al-An'am" [[See vol. 7, p. 115, 00 3.]] and "al-A'raf" [[See vol. 7, p. 115, 00 3.]], God willing.

The second issue concerns His saying, ﴿lawful and good﴾. "Halalan" (lawful) is a circumstantial accusative (hal), and it is said it is an object (maf'ul). Lawful (halal) is so called because the knot of danger (al-khatar) is loosened (inhalal) from it. Sahl ibn Abd Allah said: "Salvation lies in three things: eating what is lawful, performing the obligatory duties, and following the Prophet (ﷺ)." Abu Abd Allah al-Saji, whose name is Sa'id ibn Yazid, said: "There are five qualities through which knowledge is complete: knowing God, may He be exalted and glorified; knowing the truth and making the action sincerely for God; acting according to the sunnah (the prophetic practice); and eating what is lawful. If any one of them is missing, the action is not raised up." Sahl said: "Eating what is lawful is not valid without knowledge, and wealth is not lawful until it is purified of six things: usury (riba), the forbidden (haram), suht (illicit gain, a comprehensive term), embezzlement (ghulul), the disliked (makruh), and doubtful matters (shubhah)."

The third issue concerns His saying, ﴿And do not follow the footsteps of Satan﴾, a prohibition. "Khutuwat" is the plural of khatwah, and khutwah has the same meaning. Al-Farra' said: "Khutuwat is the plural of khatwah, with a fatha." And khutwah with a damma is the distance between the two feet. Al-Jawhari said: "The plural of paucity (jam' al-qillah) is khatawat, khutuwat and khatawat, and the plural of abundance is khuta." Khatwah with a fatha is a single step, and its plural is khatawat (with a movement on the middle letter) and khita', like rakwah and rika'. Imru' al-Qays said:

"For her are leaps like the leaps of gazelles... a heart that halts and a valley that rains."

[[It means: at one time she steps and stops from the enemy, and at another time she runs a running like rain. From the explanation of the Diwan.]]

Abu al-Sammal al-Adawi and Ubayd ibn Umayr read "khatawat" with a fatha on the kha' and the ta'. It is also transmitted from Ali ibn Abi Talib, Qatadah, al-A'raj, Amr ibn Maymun and al-A'mash that they read "khuta'at" with a damma on the kha' and the ta' and a hamzah in place of the waw. Al-Akhfash said: "They took this reading to mean that it is the plural of khati'ah, from error (khata'), not from stepping (khatw)." The meaning according to the reading of the majority is: do not follow the traces and the works of Satan. Whatever the Law has not sanctioned is attributed to Satan. Ibn Abbas said: "The footsteps of Satan" are his works. Mujahid said: "His sins." Al-Suddi said: "His obedience." Abu Mijlaz said: "They are vows in acts of disobedience."

I say: The correct view is that the wording is general for everything other than the sunan (the prophetic traditions) and the lawful religious prescriptions (shara'i'), namely innovations (bida') and acts of disobedience. The discussion of "Satan" has already been presented in full [[See the tenth issue, vol. 1, p. 90, second edition.]].

The fourth issue concerns His saying, ﴿Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾. God, may He be exalted, informed that Satan is an enemy, and His report is true and sincere. Therefore it is obligatory for the sensible person to take precaution against this enemy, whose enmity has been manifest since the time of Adam, and who has expended himself and his lifetime in corrupting the conditions of the children of Adam. God, may He be exalted, has commanded caution against him, saying, may He who speaks be exalted: ﴿And do not follow the footsteps of Satan; indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾; ﴿He only commands you to evil and immorality and to say about God that which you do not know﴾; He said: ﴿Satan threatens you with poverty and orders you to immorality﴾ [[See vol. 3, p. 328.]]; He said: ﴿And Satan wants to lead them far astray﴾; He said: ﴿Satan only wants to cause between you animosity and hatred through intoxicants and gambling and to avert you from the remembrance of God and from prayer. So will you not desist?﴾ [[See vol. 6, p. 292.]]; He said: ﴿Indeed, he is an enemy, a misleader, clear﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 261.]]; He said: ﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy. He only invites his party that they may be among the companions of the Blaze﴾ [[See vol. 14, p. 323.]]. This is the utmost in warning, and its like in the Qur'an is abundant.

Abd Allah ibn Umar said: "Iblis is bound in the lowest earth. When he stirs, every evil in the earth between two or more people comes from his stirring." Al-Tirmidhi transmitted from the hadith of Abu Malik al-Ash'ari, in which: (And I command you to remember God, for the likeness of that is like a man whom the enemy pursued swiftly, until he came to a strong fortress and secured himself from them. Likewise, the servant does not secure himself from Satan except through the remembrance of God.) And he said concerning it: "A hasan sahih gharib hadith" (a good, sound, rare hadith).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 169:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, He only commands you to evil and immorality﴾. Evil (al-su') is called "evil" because it distresses its possessor through the evil of its consequences. It is the verbal noun of sa'ahu, yasu'uhu, su'an and musa'atan, meaning he grieved him. And su'tuhu, so he became distressed (fa-si'a), means: when you grieved him, so he grieved. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿The faces of those who disbelieved became distressed﴾ [see vol. 18, p. 220]. And the poet said:

If this age has distressed me,
then it has often gladdened me.

The matter, for me, regarding both is one;
for this there is thankfulness, and for that there is patience.

And al-fahsha' (immorality) originally means ugliness of appearance, as he said:

And a neck like the neck of a gazelle (al-rim: the white antelope of pure whiteness), not ugly.

Then the word was used for what is reprehensible among meanings. The Shari'ah is what makes things good and makes them reprehensible, so everything the Shari'ah has forbidden is among the immorality. Muqatil said: Indeed, everything in the Qur'an that mentions al-fahsha' refers to fornication, except His saying: ﴿The Satan promises you poverty and commands you to immorality﴾, for it refers to withholding zakat. I say: On this basis it has been said: evil is what carries no prescribed punishment (hadd), and immorality is what carries a prescribed punishment. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas and others, and Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that you say about Allah what you do not know﴾. Al-Tabari said: He means what they prohibited of the bahirah [Abu Ishaq al-Nahwi said: "The most correct of what we have related from the lexicographers about the bahirah is that it was a she-camel which, when she had borne five offspring and the last of them was a male, they would slit her ear, leave her back free from riding, load and slaughter, and she would not be driven away from water she came to, nor prevented from pasture; and if the one who was cut off from her met her, he would not ride her."] and the sa'ibah [In the Jahiliyyah, when a man returned from a long journey, or recovered from an illness, or was relieved of a hardship with his mount or in war, he would say: "My she-camel is sa'ibah," meaning she is set free, so her back is not used for riding, she is not driven away from water, nor prevented from grazing, nor ridden (from Lisan al-Arab)], and the like of them, which they had made into law. "And that you say" is in the genitive position (mawdi' khafd) by coordination (atf) upon His saying: "with evil and immorality."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 170:

There are seven issues in this verse. The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And when it is said to them﴾, meaning the disbelievers of the Arabs. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed concerning the Jews. al-Tabari said: the pronoun in "lahum" (to them) refers to "mankind" (al-nas) in His saying, exalted is He, "O mankind, eat..."

It is also said that it refers to "min" (some of) in His saying, exalted is He, "And among mankind is he who takes, besides Allah, rivals..." up to the end of the verse. His saying, exalted is He, "Follow what Allah has sent down," means: accept it and act upon it. "They say: Nay, we will follow what we found our fathers upon." Alfayna (we found) means: we found. The poet said:

"So I found him, not one who seeks to make amends, nor one who remembers Allah except a little."

The second issue: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Even though their fathers did not understand anything, nor were they guided?﴾ The alif is an interrogative particle, and the waw is vocalized with a fatha because it is a conjunctive waw (waw al-'atf), linking one clause of speech to another, since the utmost corruption in their adherence is that they would say: "We follow our fathers even though they did not understand," so they are held to this commitment, since this is the condition of their fathers. Issue: Our scholars said: the strength of the wording of this verse gives the invalidation of taqlid (blind imitation). A parallel is His saying: "And when it is said to them: Come to what Allah has sent down and to the Messenger, they say: Sufficient for us is what we found our fathers upon," and so on. This verse and the one before it are connected to what precedes them, because Allah, glorified is He, informed of the ignorance of the Arabs in what they decided by their foolish opinions regarding the bahira, the sa'iba and the wasila [[The exegetes said: the wasila was specific to the sheep; when a sheep gave birth to a female, it was theirs, and when it gave birth to a male, they dedicated it to their gods; and when it gave birth to a male and a female, they said: it has joined its brother, so they did not slaughter the male for their gods. There are other meanings as well.

(See Lisan al-Arab, entry "wsl"). The meaning of "bahira" and "sa'iba" was mentioned earlier, p. 210.]], so they argued that it was a matter upon which they found their fathers, and so they followed them in it, and abandoned what Allah sent down to His Messenger and commanded in His religion. Thus the pronoun in "lahum" refers to them in both verses.

The third issue: Some people have relied upon this verse to condemn taqlid, because Allah condemned the disbelievers for following their fathers in falsehood and imitating them in disbelief and disobedience. This is correct regarding falsehood. As for taqlid in truth, it is one of the foundations of the religion and a safeguard among the safeguards of the Muslims, to which the ignorant person who falls short of grasping reasoning resorts. The scholars differed concerning its permissibility in matters of the fundamentals (usul) as will come, and as for its permissibility in matters of the subsidiaries (furu') it is correct.

The fourth issue: Taqlid according to the scholars is in reality accepting a statement without evidence. On this basis, whoever accepts the saying of the Prophet ﷺ without considering his miracle is a muqallid (one who follows by taqlid); but whoever considers it is not a muqallid.

It is also said: it is the belief in the validity of a fatwa from one whose statement's validity is not known. Linguistically it is derived from the necklace of a camel, for the Arabs say: "qalladtu al-ba'ir" (I put a collar on the camel) when you place a rope on its neck by which it is led. So it is as if the muqallid places his whole affair in the hands of the one who leads him wherever he wishes. Likewise their poet said:

"And entrust your affair to Allah, may you be blessed, [a man] steadfast of heart, resolute in the matter of war."

The fifth issue: Taqlid is not a path to knowledge nor a means leading to it, neither in the fundamentals nor in the subsidiaries. This is the view of the majority of the intelligent and the scholars, in contrast to what is reported from the ignorant Hashwiyya and Tha'labiyya, that it is a path to knowing the truth, that this is what is obligatory, that reflection and inquiry are forbidden, and the argument against them is in the books of usul. 

The sixth issue: The obligation upon the layman who does not engage in deriving rulings from their sources, for lack of qualification in what he does not know of his religious matters and needs, is to intend the most knowledgeable person of his time and city and ask him about his case, and act in accordance with his fatwa, based on His saying: "So ask the people of remembrance if you do not know" [[See vol. 10 p. 108 and vol. 11 p. 272.]]. It is also incumbent upon him to strive to identify the most knowledgeable of the people of his time through inquiry about him, until consensus of the majority of people falls upon him. Also upon the scholar is the obligation to follow (yuqallid) a scholar like himself in a case where the evidence and reasoning are obscure to him, and he wishes to renew his thought and inquiry therein until he reaches the sought-after answer, but time runs short for that, and he fears that the worship will be missed or the ruling will be lost; whether that other mujtahid was a Companion or otherwise. This is the view of al-Qadi Abu Bakr and a group of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun).

The seventh issue: Ibn 'Atiyya said: the Ummah has unanimously agreed on the invalidation of taqlid in creed ('aqa'id). Others besides him have mentioned disagreement on it, such as al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi, Abu 'Umar, and 'Uthman ibn 'Isa ibn Darbas al-Shafi'i. Ibn Darbas said in his book "al-Intisar": Some people said that taqlid is permissible in the matter of tawhid, and this is an error, because of His saying: "Indeed we found our fathers upon a community" [[See vol. 16 p. 74.]]. So He condemned them for their taqlid of their fathers and their abandonment of following the Messengers, like the conduct of the people of desires in their taqlid of their great men and their abandonment of following Muhammad ﷺ in his religion. And because it is an obligation upon every responsible person to learn the matter of tawhid and to be certain of it, and that is only attained from the Book and the Sunnah, as we explained in the verse of tawhid [[p. 190 of this part.]]. And Allah guides whom He wills.

Ibn Darbas said: The people of deviation have greatly insisted that those who hold fast to the Book and the Sunnah are muqallids. This is an error on their part; rather, it is more fitting for them and more appropriate for their doctrines, since they accepted the statement of their masters and great men in matters where they opposed the Book of Allah, the Sunnah of His Messenger, and the consensus of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. So they became among those whom Allah condemned by His saying: "Our Lord, indeed we obeyed our masters and our great men" to His saying: "a great [sin]" [[See vol. 14 p. 249.]], and His saying: "Indeed we found our fathers upon a community, and indeed we are following in their footsteps" [[See vol. 16 p. 74 and onward.]]. Then He said to His Prophet: "He said: Even if I bring you what is better guidance than what you found your fathers upon?" They said: "Indeed we disbelieve in what you have been sent with" [[See vol. 9 p. 191.]], then He said to His Prophet, upon him be peace: "So We took vengeance upon them" [[See vol. 16 p. 74 and onward.]], up to the verse. Thus Allah, exalted is He, made clear that guidance lies in what His messengers, peace be upon them, brought. The saying of the people of transmitted narration regarding their creed, "We found our imams and our fathers and the people upon the taking of the Book and the Sunnah and the consensus of the righteous predecessors of the Ummah," is not on a par with the saying of those (the deviants): "We found our fathers and obeyed our masters and great men," because these ones attributed their position to the revelation and to following the Messenger, whereas those attributed their falsehood to the people of baseless doctrines, and thereby increased in misguidance. Do you not see that Allah, glorified is He, praised Yusuf, peace be upon him, in the Qur'an when He said: "Indeed I have forsaken the creed of a people who do not believe in Allah, and they in the Hereafter are disbelievers. And I follow the creed of my fathers, Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub; it was not for us to associate anything with Allah. That is from the bounty of Allah upon us and upon mankind" [[See vol. 9 p. 191.]]. Since his fathers, upon them and him be peace, were prophets following the revelation, which is the pure religion that Allah approved, his following of his fathers was among the attributes of praise. And there did not come in what they brought any mention of accidents (a'rad) and their attachment to substances (jawahir) and their transformation within them, so this shows that there is no guidance in them and no rectitude in their originators. Ibn al-Hassar said: The utterance of these terms appeared only in the time of al-Ma'mun after the year 200, when the books of the ancients were translated and their disagreement became apparent concerning the eternity of the world and its origination, and their disagreement about the substance (jawhar) and its establishment, and the accident (arad) and its essence. So the innovators and whoever had deviation in his heart rushed to memorize those technical terms, intending by them to bewilder the people of the Sunnah and to introduce doubts upon the weak among the people of the religion. The matter remained so until innovation appeared and the innovators had a party, and the affair became confused for the ruler, until the Amir declared the createdness of the Qur'an and compelled the people to it, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal was beaten over that.

Then men from the people of the Sunnah stood up for the task, such as Shaykh Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, 'Abd Allah [[In the originals: "Abi 'Abd Allah," and the correction is from al-Qamus and its commentary; he is 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'id ibn Kullab al-Tamimi al-Basri, the head of the Kullabi sect among the people of the Sunnah.]] ibn Kullab, Ibn Mujahid, al-Muhasibi and their peers, so they plunged with the innovators into their technical terms, then fought them and killed them with their own weapons. Those among the Muslims of this community who passed on were holding fast to the Book and the Sunnah, turning away from the doubts of the heretics, and did not examine substance and accident; upon this was the early generation. I say: whoever now examines the terminology of the theologians to the point of defending the religion with it, his station is close to that of the prophets. As for those extreme theologians who disparage the path of those who adhere to transmitted narration among the believers, and urge the study of books of kalam, and claim that the truth is only known through them with those technical terms, they become blameworthy for overturning the path of the earlier imams who preceded them; and Allah knows best. As for disputation and argument with evidence and proof, that is clear in the Qur'an, and its explanation will come, if Allah the Exalted wills [[See vol. 12 p. 94, vol. 13 p. 350.]].

Allah, exalted is He, compared the preacher of the disbelievers and their caller, who is Muhammad (ﷺ), to the shepherd who shouts to the sheep and camels, so that they hear nothing but his calling and his shouting, and do not understand what he is saying. This is how Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, al-Suddi, al-Zajjaj, al-Farra' and Sibawayh explained it, and this is the utmost in concision. Sibawayh said: "They were not likened to the one who shouts; rather, they were likened to the one who is shouted at." The meaning is: "Your likeness, O Muhammad, and the likeness of those who disbelieve, is like the likeness of the one who shouts and the one shouted at among the beasts that do not understand," so the second element was omitted, the meaning making it clear.

Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is that the likeness of those who disbelieve in their calling upon the gods that are unable to hear is like the one who cries out in the depth of the night and the echo answers him; he cries out to what does not hear, and what answers him has no reality and no benefit.

Qutrub said: the meaning is that the likeness of those who disbelieve in their calling upon what does not understand, meaning the idols, is like the shepherd who shouts at his sheep while not knowing where they are.

al-Tabari said: what is meant is the likeness of the disbelievers in their calling upon their gods is like one who shouts at something far away, so it does not hear because of the distance; the shouter gets nothing from that except the calling which tires and exhausts him.

In these three interpretations, the disbelievers are likened to the one who shouts and cries out, and the idols to the one who is shouted at.

Al-na'iq (النَّعِيق) means driving sheep and calling out to them. It is said: "The shepherd shouted at his sheep (naʿaqa al-rāʿī bi-ghanamihi yanʿiqu naʿīqan, wa-niʿāqan, wa-naʿāqan), meaning he called out to them and drove them." al-Akhtal said:

"Shout at your ewes, O Jarir, for indeed
Your own soul deceived you into error in the wilderness."

al-Qutabi said: Jarir was not a shepherd of ewes; rather he meant that the Banu Kulayb were reproached for tending ewes, and Jarir was among them, so he is in their ignorance. The Arabs use the shepherd of sheep as a proverb for ignorance, saying: "More ignorant than a shepherd of ewes." al-Qutabi said: whoever takes this as the meaning of the verse has a valid view, though to our knowledge none of the scholars has adopted it.

Al-nida' (النِّدَاءُ) is for the distant, and al-du'a' (الدُّعَاءُ) is for the near; for this reason the call to prayer is called nida', because it is addressed to those far away. The consonant nun in al-nida' may be vowelled with a damma, though the original is with a kasra.

Then Allah, exalted is He, likened the disbelievers to being deaf, dumb and blind. This has been discussed at the beginning of the surah.

This is an emphasis on the first command, and here the believers are singled out for mention as a mark of honour. By "eating" is meant benefiting in every way. It has also been said that it means ordinary eating.

In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O people, Allah is Pure (Tayyib) and accepts only what is pure. Allah commanded the believers with what He commanded the messengers, so He said: 'O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds; indeed I am Knowing of what you do' [23:51]. And He said: 'O you who believe, eat of the good things We have provided you' [2:172]." Then he mentioned [[This sentence is part of the narrator's speech, and the pronoun refers to the Prophet (ﷺ). "The man" (al-rajul) in the nominative is the subject, quoted from the Messenger's words (peace be upon him). It is also permissible to put it in the accusative as the object of "mentioned".]] the man who travels far, dishevelled and dusty, who stretches his hands towards the sky, saying, "O Lord, O Lord," while his food is unlawful, his drink is unlawful, his clothing is unlawful, [and he is nourished by what is unlawful [[The addition is from Sahih Muslim.]]], so how could his supplication be answered?

"And give thanks to Allah, if it is Him that you worship" [2:172]. The meaning of thanks (shukr) has already been discussed [[See the third issue and what follows, vol. 1, p. 397, second edition.]], so there is no point in repeating it.

**Question 1:** There are thirty-four issues in this verse.¹

Concerning His words, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, He has forbidden for you carrion﴾: *innama* is a particle established for restriction (*hasr*). It contains both negation and affirmation. It affirms what the address covers and negates whatever lies beyond it. Here it restricts the prohibition, especially since it follows the permission in His words, exalted is He, ﴿O you who have believed, eat of the good things We have provided for you﴾. That verse grants permission absolutely. Then He follows it with the mention of what is forbidden, using the restrictive *innama*. This requires that the two categories be comprehensive, so nothing forbidden falls outside this verse. The verse is Medinan. It is reinforced by another verse, which is reported to have been revealed at Arafat: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to an eater who eats it﴾, to its end. Thus the explanation is complete at the beginning and at the end. Ibn al-Arabi said this. The discussion of that will come under *al-An'am*, God willing.²

**Question 2:** *Al-maytatu* is in the accusative because of *harrama* (forbade). *Ma* is *kaffah* (a particle that removes the governing force of *inna*). It is also permissible to make *ma* mean *alladhi* (that which), written separately, and then *al-maytatu wa'l-dammu wa-lahmu'l-khinzir* (carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine) would be in the nominative as the predicate of *inna*. This is the reading of Ibn Abi Ablah. In *harrama* there is a pronoun referring back to *alladhi*. A parallel is His words, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, what they have made is only the plot of a magician﴾.³ Abu Ja'far read *hurrima* with a damma on the *ha'* and a kasra on the *ra'*, and with the following nouns in the nominative. This is either the passive form (*ma lam yusamma fa'iluhu*) or the predicate of *inna*. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' also read *al-mayyitata* with the shaddah.

Al-Tabari said: Some linguists said that *maytun* and *mayyitun* (with and without the shaddah) are two dialects. Abu Hatim and others said: They are both used of what has died. Of what has not yet died, *maytun* with the lightened form is not used. The proof is His words, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed you will die, and indeed they will die﴾.⁴ A poet said:

*He who has died and found rest is not a dead one (mayyit);*
*the dead one is the dead one of the living (mayyit al-ahya').*

No one read the lightened form for what has not died, except what al-Bazzi reported from Ibn Kathir: ﴿And he is not dead (bi-mayyit)﴾.⁵ The well-known reading from him is the heavy form. As for the poet's words:

*When a dead man (mayyit) of Tamim dies,*
*if it pleases you to live, bring provisions.*

There is no stronger satire than that he meant the one who is truly dead. Some people held that he meant one who is near death, but the first view is more well known.

**Question 3:** *Al-maytatu* is what has departed from life without slaughter (*dhakah*) among animals that are slaughtered. Whatever is not eaten, its slaughter is like its death, such as predatory beasts and others. This will be explained here and in *al-An'am*, God willing.⁶

**Question 4:** This verse is general, and specification (*takhsis*) has entered it through His words, peace be upon him: "Two carcasses are made lawful for us: fish and locusts; and two bloods: liver and spleen." Al-Daraqutni reported it. Likewise the hadith of Jabir about the *anbar* (a large sea creature whose hide is used for shields; the shield is also called *anbar*, and the fish is so named because of what is found in its belly)⁷ specifies the generality of the Qur'an, because its chain is sound. Al-Bukhari and Muslim recorded it, along with His words, exalted is He, ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea﴾, which will be explained there, God willing.⁸ Most scholars hold that it is permissible to eat all sea creatures, whether alive or dead. This is the position of Malik. Malik hesitated to answer about the sea hog and said: You people call it "hog"! Ibn al-Qasim said: I avoid it and do not consider it forbidden.

**Question 5:** People have differed about whether the Book of God may be specified by the Sunnah. Despite their disagreement on this, they agreed that it may not be specified by a weak hadith. Ibn al-Arabi said this. This verse may also be taken as specified by what is in Sahih Muslim from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa, who said: We fought seven campaigns with the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, and we used to eat locusts with him. Its apparent meaning is that it is eaten however it dies, whether by treatment or by natural death. Ibn Nafi', Ibn Abd al-Hakam, and most scholars said this. It is the position of al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah, and others. Malik and the majority of his companions forbade eating it if it dies a natural death, because it is game of the land. Do you not see that a person in the state of ihram may be liable for killing it, so it resembles the gazelle? Ashhab said: If it dies from the cutting of a leg or a wing, it is not eaten, because it is a condition in which it may still live and walk. More explanation of the ruling on locusts will come under *al-A'raf* when its mention arises, God willing.⁹

**Question 6:** Scholars differed about whether it is permissible to benefit from carrion or from any impurities. Malik's position on this also varied. At one time he said: Benefit from them is permitted, because the Prophet, peace be upon him, passed by a sheep of Maymunah and said: "Why did you not take its hide?" (the hadith). At another time he said: Carrion as a whole is forbidden, so it is not permissible to benefit from any part of it, nor from any impurity in any way of benefit. Thus it is not permissible to water crops or animals with impure water, nor to feed animals impurities, nor to let dogs and predators eat carrion. If they eat it, they are not prevented. The apparent meaning of this view is His words, exalted is He, ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion and blood﴾, without specifying any aspect over another. It is not permissible to say that this address is *mujmal* (ambiguous), because the *mujmal* is what the meaning cannot be understood from its outward sense. The Arabs understood the meaning of His words, exalted is He, ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾. Also, the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Do not benefit from carrion in any way." In the hadith of Abdullah ibn Ukaym: "Do not benefit from carrion by means of hide or sinew." This was the last thing his letter contained before his death, by a month. The explanation of these reports and the discussion of them will come under *al-Nahl*, God willing.¹⁰

**Question 7:** As for a she-camel that is slaughtered, or a cow or sheep that is slaughtered, and there is a dead fetus in its belly, it is permissible to eat it without its own slaughter, unless it comes out alive and is slaughtered, and then it has the ruling of its own self. This is because when a fetus comes out of the animal dead after slaughter, it takes the place of one of its limbs. What clarifies this is that if one sells a sheep and excepts what is in its belly, it is not valid, just as if he excepted one of its limbs. What is in its belly follows it like all its other limbs. Likewise, if he frees it without directing a separate act of manumission to what is in its belly, but if it were separate from it, it would not follow it in sale or manumission.

Jabir, may God be pleased with him, reported that the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, was asked about a cow or sheep that is slaughtered, or a she-camel that is slaughtered, and there is a dead fetus in its belly. He said: "If you wish, eat it, for its slaughter is the slaughter of its mother." Abu Dawud recorded it with this meaning, from the hadith…¹¹

The Eighth Issue: The reports from Malik differ on whether the hide of a carcass becomes pure through tanning (dibagh). It is reported from him that it does not become pure, and this is the apparent position of his school.
