It is also reported from him that it does become pure, based on the Prophet's saying (peace be upon him): "Whatever hide is tanned has become pure." The reasoning of those who say it does not become pure is that the hide is a part of the carcass, and if it had been taken from the animal while alive, it would have been impure. Therefore tanning should not purify it, by analogy with the flesh. The reports about purity are interpreted to mean that tanning removes the dirt from the hide so that it may be used for dry things and for sitting upon. It is also permissible to use it for water by making it a water-skin, because water remains in its original state of purity so long as no attribute of it has changed, as will be discussed in its ruling in Surat al-Furqan [see vol. 13, p. 39 onward]. In the language, purity (tahara) is directed toward the removal of dirt, just as it is directed toward legal purity. And God knows best.

The Ninth Issue: As for the hair and wool of a carcass, they are pure, based on what is reported from Umm Salamah, may God be pleased with her, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "There is no harm in the hide of a carcass if it is tanned, nor in its wool and hair if they are washed." Also, these were pure if taken from the animal while alive, so they must be likewise after death. Yet the flesh, being impure during life, remains so after death. Therefore the wool must be the opposite of that in the state of death, just as it was the opposite in the state of life, by way of inference from the reverse. This does not apply to the milk and the egg of a dead hen, because milk is pure according to us even after death, and so is the egg. But they became contained in an impure vessel, so they became impure through contact with the vessel, not because they were made impure by death. The further explanation of this issue, and the disagreement of the scholars concerning it and the preceding one, will come in Surat al-Nahl, God willing [see vol. 10, p. 195].

The Tenth Issue: As for a mouse that falls into food, there are two situations. If the mouse is taken out alive, the food is pure. If it dies in the food, there are two further situations: if the food is liquid, all of it becomes impure; and if the food is solid, what is adjacent to the mouse becomes impure, so that it is thrown away along with what surrounds it, and what remains is used and remains pure. This is based on the report that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about a mouse that falls into ghee and dies, and he said (peace be upon him): "If it is solid, throw it away and what is around it; and if it is liquid, pour it out." The scholars differed concerning whether it becomes pure when washed. It was said: it does not become pure by washing, because it is a liquid that is impure, so it resembles blood, wine, urine, and all other impurities. Ibn al-Qasim said: it becomes pure by washing, because it is a body that became impure through contact with an impurity, so it resembles a garment. This does not apply to blood, because it is impure in itself; nor to wine and urine, because washing would destroy them and it cannot be carried out on them.

The Eleventh Issue: If we rule that it becomes pure by washing, it returns to its original state regarding purity and all other ways of benefiting from it. However, one may not sell it until one makes its condition known, because that is a defect in the eyes of people, and their souls reject it. Some of them believe it to be forbidden and impure, so it is not permissible to sell it until the defect is made known, like all other defective items. As for before washing, it is in no way permissible to sell it, because impure things are not permitted to be sold according to him, and because it is an impure liquid, so it resembles wine. Also, the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the price of wine, and he said: "May God curse the Jews. Fat was forbidden to them, so they melted it down (jamalu), sold it, and ate its price." And when God forbids something, He forbids its price. This liquid is forbidden because of its impurity, so its price must be forbidden by apparent ruling.

The Twelfth Issue: It has been disputed when an animal, a bird or something else, falls into a cooking pot and dies. Ibn Wahb reported from Malik that he said: what is in the pot is not to be eaten, because it has become impure through being mixed with the carcass. Ibn al-Qasim reported from him that he said: the meat is to be washed and the broth is to be poured out. Ibn Abbas was asked about this issue and said: the meat is to be washed and eaten. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad mentioned that there is no one among his companions who disagrees with him concerning the broth [in some of the sources and the Azhari copy: "there is no one who disagrees with him among the Companions"].

The Thirteenth Issue: As for the rennet (infaha) of a carcass and the milk of a carcass, al-Shafi'i said: this is impure, because of the general wording of His saying ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾. Abu Hanifa said that they are pure, and he did not regard the place of origin as having any effect in making impure what is adjacent to it which came into being from it. He said: for this reason the flesh is eaten with the veins in it, despite the certainty that blood is adjacent to its inner parts, without purification or washing, by consensus (ijma'). Malik said something similar to Abu Hanifa's view: that these do not become impure through death, but they become impure through contact with an impure vessel, and this is something that washing cannot accomplish.

Likewise the hen, from which an egg comes forth after its death, because the egg is soft, having the status of a liquid before it comes out, and it only solidifies and hardens through exposure to air. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: if it is said that your view leads to a contradiction of the consensus, since the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims after him used to eat cheese, which was brought to them from the land of the non-Arabs, and it is known that the slaughter of the non-Arabs, who were Magians, is carrion, and they did not take into account whether it had been set with the rennet of a carcass or of a slaughtered animal. It is said to him: the amount of rennet that falls into cheese-milk is small, and a small amount of impurity is excused when it is mixed with a large amount of liquid. This is a reply according to one of the two reports. According to the other report, that was only at the beginning of Islam, and no one can transmit that the Companions ate cheese brought from the land of the non-Arabs. Rather, cheese was not part of the food of the Arabs. When the Muslims spread into the land of the non-Arabs through the conquests, slaughtered animals became theirs. So from where do we know that the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Companions ate cheese, let alone cheese brought from the land of the non-Arabs and made with the rennet of their slaughtered animals?

Abu Umar said: there is no harm in eating the food of idol-worshippers, Magians, and all unbelievers who have no scripture, as long as it is not from their slaughtered animals and does not require ritual slaughter (dhakah), except cheese, because of the rennet of a carcass in it. In the Sunan of Ibn Majah, under "Cheese and Ghee," it is narrated to us by Isma'il ibn Musa al-Suddi, who said: Sayf ibn Harun narrated to us from Sulayman al-Taymi, from Abu Uthman al-Nahdi, from Salman al-Farisi, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about ghee, cheese, and furs. He said: "The lawful is what God has made lawful in His Book, and the unlawful is what God has made unlawful in His Book, and what He has been silent about is among what He has pardoned."

The Fourteenth Issue: God's saying ﴿and blood﴾. The scholars agree that blood is forbidden, impure, not to be eaten, and not to be benefited from. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: as for blood, it is forbidden unless it becomes widespread as a trouble, and what becomes widespread as a trouble is excused. What becomes widespread as a trouble is the blood in meat and its veins, and a small amount of blood on the body or on a garment in which one prays. We only say this because God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion and blood﴾, and He said in another place: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to an eater who would eat it, except that it be carrion or blood poured forth﴾ [see vol. 7, p. 151].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 173 (part 3 of 6):

﴿So He forbade the poured-forth blood.﴾ 'Ā'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, related: "In the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ we would cook the cooking-pot, and a yellowness of blood would be on its surface, and we would eat from it and not object to it, because guarding against this is a burden (iṣr) and a hardship, and burden and hardship in the religion have been removed." This is a principle in the Sharia: whenever the community finds performing an act of worship difficult and burdensome, the obligation to perform it in that respect is lifted. Do you not see that the one compelled eats carrion, and that the sick person breaks the fast and performs tayammum (dry ablution) in similar cases?

I say: Allah, glorified and exalted is He, mentioned blood here without qualification (mutlaq), and He restricted it in al-An'am by His saying: ﴿poured forth﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 123.]]. The scholars, by consensus (ijma'), applied the unqualified (mutlaq) here to the qualified (muqayyad) there. Thus "blood" here means the poured-forth blood, because what mixes with the flesh is not forbidden by consensus, and likewise the liver and the spleen are agreed upon as permitted. As for the blood of fish that leaves it, there is a difference of opinion. It is related from al-Qabisi that it is pure (tahir), and it follows from its purity that it is not forbidden. This is the view chosen by Ibn al-'Arabi, who said: "If the blood of fish were impure, its slaughter (dhakah) would have been prescribed." I say: This is also the position of Abu Hanifah regarding fish blood. I heard some Hanafis say: "The proof that it is pure is that when it dries it turns white, unlike other bloods, which turn black." This point is their argument against the Shafi'is.

**The fifteenth issue:** His saying: ﴿and the flesh of swine﴾. Allah specified the mention of the flesh of swine in order to show the prohibition of the animal itself, whether it was slaughtered or not, and to include the fat, the cartilage (ghada-rif, every soft bone, wherever it is) and other parts.

**The sixteenth issue:** The community has agreed on the prohibition of swine fat. Malik and his companions used this to rule that whoever swears not to eat fat and then eats meat does not break his oath by eating meat. But if he swears not to eat meat and then eats fat, he breaks his oath, because meat together with fat is called "meat," so fat falls within the meaning of "meat," but meat does not fall within the meaning of "fat." Allah forbade the flesh of swine, so mention of its flesh stands in place of its fat, because the fat falls under the name "flesh." Allah also forbade the fats to the Children of Israel by His saying: "We forbade them their fats" (6:146). By this, the prohibition of flesh did not fall upon them, and it did not enter the name of fat. For this reason Malik distinguished between one who swears regarding fat and one who swears regarding meat, unless the one swearing had an intention regarding meat and not fat, in which case he does not break his oath. And Allah knows best.

According to al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr and the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y), he does not break his oath if he swears not to eat meat and then eats fat. Ahmad said: "If he swears not to eat meat and then eats fat, there is no harm, unless he intended to avoid greasy foods (al-dasam)."

**The seventeenth issue:** There is no disagreement that the whole body of the swine is forbidden except its hair, for it is permitted to use it in stitching (al-kharazah). It is related that a man asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about stitching with swine hair, and he said: "There is no harm in that." Ibn Khuwayz Mandad mentioned it. He said: "Stitching was practised in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and was widespread after him, and we do not know that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ denounced it, nor did any of the imams after him. What the Messenger ﷺ permitted is, in effect, the initiation of the Sharia by him."

**The eighteenth issue:** There is no disagreement about the prohibition of the land swine, as we have mentioned, but there is disagreement about the sea swine. Malik refused to give a ruling on it and said: "You people say 'swine'!" This has already been discussed and will be explained in al-Ma'idah [[See vol. 6, p. 320]], if Allah wills.

**The nineteenth issue:** Most lexicographers held that the word khinzir (swine) is quadriliteral. Ibn Sidah related from some of them that it is derived from kharaz al-'ayn (squint of the eye), because the swine looks that way, and on this view the word is triliteral. In al-Sihah: "Takhazara al-rajul" means the man narrowed his eyelid in order to sharpen his gaze. Al-kharaz is narrowness and smallness of the eye. A man is akhzar, clearly squinting. It is also said that it is when a person seems to look with the back of his eye. The plural of khinzir is khanazir. Al-khanazir is also a known ailment, which is hard sores that appear on the neck.

**The twentieth issue:** His saying: ﴿and that over which other than the name of Allah has been invoked﴾, meaning: over which the name of other than Allah, exalted is He, has been mentioned. This refers to the slaughter of the Magian (majus), the idolater (wathani) and the mu'attil (one who denies the Creator). The idolater slaughters for an idol, the Magian for fire, and the mu'attil believes in nothing, so he slaughters for himself. There is no disagreement among the scholars that what the Magian slaughters for his fire or the idolater for his idol is not eaten, and their slaughter is not eaten according to Malik, al-Shafi'i and others, even if they did not slaughter for their fire or idol. Ibn al-Musayyab and Abu Thawr permitted it if the slaughter was done for a Muslim at his command. More on this will come, if Allah wills, in surah al-Ma'idah [[See vol. 6, p. 76.]].

Al-ihlal (intoning) is raising the voice. It is said: "ahalla bi-kadhā" means he raised his voice with such-and-such. Ibn Ahmar, describing a desert, said:

It raises its voice with the lone one's riders, as the pilgrim on the way to 'umrah raises his voice.

And al-Nabighah said:

Or a pearl of Sadaf whose diver is delighted; when he sees it, he cries out and prostrates.

And among these is the raising of the voice by the newborn (ihlal, "the crying out"), and its istihlal, which is its crying out at birth. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: what is meant is what was slaughtered for the idols (anṣab) and the images (awthan), not what had the name of al-Masih mentioned over it, as its explanation will come in Surat al-Ma'idah [[See vol. 6, p. 76.]] "if Allah the Exalted wills." It was the custom of the Arabs to call out the name of the one for whom the sacrifice was made, and this became so common in their usage that it was used to refer to the intention, which is the cause of the prohibition. Do you not see that 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, took the intention into account concerning the camels that Ghalib, the father of al-Farazdaq, had slaughtered, and said: "They are among what was dedicated to other than Allah," so the people left them?

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: I found in the reports of al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan that he was asked about a pampered woman who made a wedding feast for her idol and slaughtered a camel. al-Hasan said: "Its eating is not lawful, for it was slaughtered only for an idol."

I say: Among this meaning is what we have related from Yahya ibn Yahya al-Tamimi, the shaykh of Muslim, who said: Jarir informed us from Qabus, who said: My father sent a woman to 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, and commanded her to convey his greetings to her, and to ask her which prayer was most beloved to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, the one he maintained regularly. She said: He used to pray four rak'ahs before the noon prayer, lengthening the standing in them and performing the bowing and prostration well. As for the two rak'ahs before the dawn prayer, he never abandoned them, whether in health, sickness, or travel. A woman among the people said at that point: "O Mother of the Believers, we have foreign (ajam) foster-families (azhar) among whom there is always a festival, and they send us gifts from it. Shall we eat anything from it?" She said: "As for what was slaughtered for that day, do not eat it, but eat from their trees."

The twenty-first matter concerns His Exalted saying: ﴿So whoever is compelled﴾ It is recited with a damma on the nun for the sake of harmony (ittiba'), and with a kasra, which is the original form, because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters (iltiqa' al-sakinayn). In it there is an ellipsis (idmar), meaning: so whoever is compelled to any of these prohibited things, i.e., is made to need them. The verb is of the form ifta'ala from al-darurah (necessity). Ibn Muhaysin recited "fa-man ittarra" with the dad assimilated into the ta' (idgham). Abu al-Sammal recited "fa-man idtirra" with a kasra on the ta'. Its original form is idtarra; when it was assimilated, the vowel of the ra' was transferred to the ta'.

The twenty-second matter: compulsion (idtirar) is either due to coercion by an oppressor, or due to hunger in a famine (makhmasah). The majority of jurists and scholars hold, regarding the meaning of the verse, that it refers to one whom poverty and deprivation (al-gharath), which is hunger, have brought to that, and this is the correct view. It was also said: its meaning is that he is forced and overcome into eating these prohibited things. Mujahid said: that is, he is forced to it, like a man whom the enemy seizes and forces to eat pork or other things that disobey Allah the Exalted, except that coercion permits that until the coercion ends. As for famine, it is either constant or not. If it is constant, there is no disagreement about the permissibility of eating one's fill of carrion, except that it is not lawful for him to eat it while he finds the property of a Muslim about which he is certain he will not be punished, such as hanging dates and the sheep stolen at night from a mountain (hariasat al-jabal), and similar things for which there is no amputation (qat') and no harm. This is a matter on which there is no disagreement, based on the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "While we were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on a journey, we saw camels whose udders were tied [[Musarrah: tied at the udders; it was the custom of the Arabs that when they sent their milk-camels to pasture they tied their udders.]] among the acacia trees, so we rushed toward them. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ called out to us, and we returned to him. He said: 'These camels belong to a household of the Muslims; they are their sustenance and their blessing [[Thus in the Sunan of Ibn Majah, meaning their blessing and their good. In the originals it reads "qaymuhum" (their value).]] after Allah. Would it please you if you returned to your water-skins and found what was in them had been taken away? Do you consider that just?' They said: 'No.' He said: 'Then these are likewise.' We said: 'What do you think if we are in need of food and drink?' He said: 'Eat but do not carry away, and drink but do not carry away.'" Ibn Majah, may Allah have mercy on him, narrated it and said: "This is the principle in my view." Ibn al-Mundhir also mentioned it and said: We said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is lawful for one of us from the property of his brother when he is compelled to it?" He said: "He may eat and not carry away, and drink and not carry away." Ibn al-Mundhir said: Every matter disputed after this is referred back to Allah's prohibition of property. Abu 'Umar said: The summary of the matter is that when a Muslim is obligated to restore the breath of life (raqam) of a Muslim's soul (muhjah), and the obligation falls upon him that there be no one else able to do so, then he is judged to be obliged to sustain that human soul. The one who is denied that which he needs has the right to fight the one who withholds it, even if that leads to his own death. This is the view of the scholars when there is only one person and no other; then the obligation becomes an individual duty (fard 'ayn). If there are many, or a group or a number of people, it becomes a collective obligation (fard kifayah) upon them. Water, in that regard and other things that restore and sustain a Muslim's life, are the same. However, they differed about whether the value of that thing is obligatory upon the one whose soul was restored by it and whose breath was sustained by it: some scholars made it obligatory, and others rejected it, and in our school both opinions exist. There is no disagreement among the scholars, past and present, that it is obligatory to restore the soul of a Muslim when there is fear of death and destruction, with a small thing that causes no harm to its owner and that suffices for subsistence (al-bulghah).

The twenty-third matter: Ibn Majah narrated: Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah informed us, Shababah informed us (ḥ) [[When a hadith has two or more chains, they write at the transition from one chain to another "ḥ," taken from "al-taḥawwul" ... etc. See the books of hadith terminology.]] and Muhammad ibn Bashshar and Muhammad ibn al-Walid told us, both saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far told us, Shu'bah told us from Abu Bishr Ja'far ibn Iyas, who said: I heard 'Abbad ibn Shurahbil, a man of the Banu Ghubar, say: "A year of famine struck us, so I came to Madinah and went to one of its orchards (ha'it), which is a garden of palms or other trees that has a wall. I took an ear of grain, rubbed it, ate it, and put some in my garment. The owner of the orchard came, struck me, and took my garment. I came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and informed him. He said to the man: 'Did you not feed him when he was hungry or starving, nor teach him when he was ignorant?' The Prophet ﷺ commanded him, and he returned his garment to him, and commanded that he be given a wasq of food or half a wasq." I say: This is a sound hadith, on whose narrators al-Bukhari and Muslim agree, except Ibn Abi Shaybah, for whom it is only in Muslim. 'Abbad ibn Shurahbil al-Ghubari al-Yashkuri, al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated nothing from him, and he has nothing from the Prophet ﷺ other than this story. Abu 'Umar, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned it, and it negates amputation and discipline in case of famine.

Abu Dawud narrated from al-Hasan, from Samurah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "If one of you comes upon livestock, and its owner is present, let him ask his permission; if he permits him, let him milk and drink; and if the owner is not present, let him call out three times. If someone answers, let him ask permission; if he is permitted, let him milk and drink, and not carry away."

And al-Tirmidhi mentioned, from Yahya ibn Sulaym, from 'Ubayd Allah, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Whoever enters an orchard, let him eat, and let him not take a fold of his garment (khubnah)."

He said: "This is a gharib hadith; we do not know it except from the hadith of Yahya ibn Sulaym."

It was also mentioned from the hadith of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Prophet ﷺ was asked about hanging dates, and he said: "Whoever takes from it out of need, not making a khubnah, there is no fault upon him." He said concerning it: "This is a hasan hadith."

In the hadith of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "When one of you passes by an orchard, let him eat, and let him not take a thiban."

Abu 'Ubayd said, and Abu 'Umar said: It is the container in which a thing is carried. If you carry it in front of you, it is a thiban; one says: "I have made a thiban." If you carry it on your back, it is a hal (a load), from which one says: "I have made my garment a hal" when you put something in it and then carry it on your back. If you put it in your lap (hidn), it is a khubnah, and from it is the marfu' hadith of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb: "and let him not take a khubnah." From it one says: "I took a khubnah, akhbinu khabnan."

Abu 'Ubayd said: This hadith is to be understood as meaning that a concession was given to the hungry person in necessity who has nothing with which to buy, that he should carry only what is in his stomach, the amount of his sustenance.

I say: Because the established principle is the prohibition of another's property except with his free consent. If there is a custom of doing this, as was the case at the beginning of Islam or as is now the case in some lands, then that is permissible. This is to be understood as applying to times of famine and necessity, as has been mentioned, and Allah knows best.

If the second case [[He means by "the second" one of the two forms of famine mentioned in the twenty-second matter, namely the non-constant one.]], which is rare at any time, arises, the scholars differ concerning it on two views:

One of them is that he eats until he is satisfied and fully sated, and takes provision if he fears need in what lies ahead of him of desert and barren land; and when he finds himself independent of it, he discards it. This is what Malik said in his Muwatta', and al-Shafi'i and many scholars said the same. The proof for that is that necessity lifts the prohibition, so it returns to being permitted. The measure of necessity is only from the state of lacking food to the state of having it. The hadith of al-'Anbar is explicit on this, for when the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ returned from their journey and their provisions had run out, they went to the seashore, and there rose on its shore something like a huge sand dune. When they reached it, it was an animal called al-'Anbar. Abu 'Ubaydah, their commander, said: "It is carrion." Then he said: "No, we are the messengers of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and in the way of Allah, and you have been compelled, so eat." He said: "We stayed by it for a month, and we were three hundred, until we became fat," and the hadith continues. They ate and were satisfied, may Allah be pleased with them, from what they believed to be carrion, and they took provision from it to Madinah. They mentioned that to the Prophet ﷺ, and he informed them that it was lawful, and said: "Do you have any of its meat with you, so that you may feed us?" They sent to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ some of it, and he ate it.

Another group said: He eats only the amount that stops the breath from failing (sadd al-ramaq). Ibn al-Majishun and Ibn Habib said the same. The companions of al-Shafi'i distinguished between the state of the resident and the traveler, and they said: "The resident eats only what stops his breath from failing, while the traveler eats his fill and takes provision. When he finds himself independent of it, he discards it; and if he finds a needy person, he gives it to him, and does not take a return for it, for carrion may not be sold."

The twenty-fourth matter: If one is compelled to drink wine (khamr): if it is by coercion, he drinks it without disagreement; if it is by hunger or thirst, he does not drink it. Malik said likewise in al-'Utbiyyah, saying: "Wine does not increase him except in thirst." This is also the view of al-Shafi'i, for Allah the Exalted prohibited wine absolutely, and prohibited carrion on condition of the absence of necessity. Al-Abhari said: If wine repels hunger or thirst from him, he may drink it, because Allah the Exalted said concerning pork: "for indeed it is rijs (filth)," then permitted it in necessity. And He the Exalted said concerning wine that it is "rijs," so it enters into the permission granted for pork in necessity by the clear meaning, which is stronger than analogy. It must quench thirst even for an hour, and repel hunger even for a period.

**The twenty-fifth issue:** Ashhab reported from Ibn al-Qasim that he said: The one compelled by necessity (al-mudtarr) may drink blood but not wine, and he may eat carrion (al-maytah) but not approach the strayed camels. Ibn Wahb also said this. He may drink urine but not wine, because the prescribed punishment (al-hadd) applies to wine, so it is more severe.

The companions of al-Shafi'i stated this explicitly.

**The twenty-sixth issue:** If someone chokes on a morsel, may he wash it down with wine or not? It has been said: No, for fear that he would claim this [falsely].

Ibn Habib permitted it, because it is a state of necessity.

Ibn al-Arabi said: "As for the one who chokes on a morsel, he is permitted this in what lies between him and Allah the Exalted. As for what lies between us, if we witness it, the true nature of the choking cannot be hidden from us by the circumstantial evidence, so he is believed if it becomes evident. If it does not become evident, we apply the prescribed punishment to him outwardly, and he is safe from punishment before Allah the Exalted inwardly.

Then, if the one compelled by necessity finds carrion, swine, and human flesh, he eats the carrion, because it is lawful in one state. Swine and human flesh are never lawful in any state.

The lighter prohibition should be undertaken before the heavier prohibition, just as if he were compelled to have intercourse with his sister or with a stranger, he should have intercourse with the stranger, because she is lawful to him in some state.

This is the governing principle of these rulings.

He may not eat human flesh even if the person has died. This is what our scholars said, and Ahmad and Dawud also said it.

Ahmad relied on the words of the Prophet (peace be upon him): 'Breaking the bone of a dead person is like breaking it while he is alive.'

Al-Shafi'i said: He may eat human flesh.

It is not permitted for him to kill a dhimmi (a non-Muslim under Muslim protection), because his blood is protected, nor a Muslim nor a captive, because he is the property of another. If he is a combatant (harbi) or a married adulterer, it is permitted to kill him and to eat from him."

Dawud criticized al-Muzani by saying: "You have permitted eating the flesh of the prophets!"

Ibn Shurayh overcame him by saying: "You have exposed yourself to killing the prophets, since you forbade them from eating the disbeliever."

Ibn al-Arabi said: "In my view, the sound position is that a person should not eat a human being unless it is certain that this will save him and keep him alive. And Allah knows best."

**The twenty-seventh issue:** Malik was asked about one compelled to eat carrion while finding the property of another: dates, crops, or sheep. He said: If he is safe from harm to his body, such that he is not considered a thief and his word is believed, he may eat from whichever of these he finds enough to repel his hunger, and he should not carry any of it away. That is more beloved to me than eating carrion. This meaning has already been discussed in full.

If he fears that they will not believe him and will consider him a thief, then eating carrion is more permissible in my view, and he has latitude to eat carrion in this situation.

**The twenty-eighth issue:** Abu Dawud reported: He said, Musa ibn Isma'il narrated to us, he said, Hammad narrated to us, from Simak ibn Harb, from Jabir ibn Samura, that a man came to settle at al-Harra [[al-Harra (with a fatha on the ha and a shadda on the ra): land on the outskirts of Madina with black stones.]], and his family and children were with him. A man said: "My she-camel has strayed. If you find her, hold on to her." He found her but could not find her owner. She fell ill, and his wife said: "Slaughter her." He refused, and she died.

She said: "Skin her so that we can dry her meat and fat and eat it." He said: "Until I ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." He came to him and asked him, and he said: "Do you have enough wealth to suffice you?" He said: "No." He said: "Then eat it."

Then her owner came and told him the story, and he said: "Why did you not slaughter her?" He said: "I was too shy before you."

Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: In this hadith there are two proofs.

The first: the one compelled by necessity eats carrion even if he does not fear death, because he asked him about wealth and did not ask him about his fear for his own life.

The second: he may eat, be satisfied, store, and take provisions, because he permitted him to store and did not stipulate that he must not be satisfied.

Abu Dawud said: Harun ibn Abd Allah narrated to us, he said, al-Fadl ibn Dukayn narrated to us, he said, Uqba ibn Wahb ibn Uqba al-Amiri informed us, he said: I heard my father narrate from al-Fujay' al-Amiri that he came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "What makes carrion lawful for us?"

He said: "What is your food?" We said: "We drink in the evening and in the morning."

Abu Nu'aym [[Abu Nu'aym: the kunya of al-Fadl ibn Dukayn.]] said: Uqba explained it to me: a bowl in the morning and a bowl in the evening.

He said: "By my father, that is hunger."

He said: So he made carrion lawful for them in this state.

Abu Dawud said: Al-ghabuq is from the end of the day, and al-subuh is from the beginning of the day.

Al-Khattabi said: Al-ghabuq is the evening meal, and al-subuh is the morning meal. The bowl of milk in the morning and the bowl in the evening keep the spirit alive and sustain the soul, even though they do not nourish the body or fully satisfy. Despite this, he permitted them to consume carrion. Its implication is that consuming carrion is permitted until the soul has taken its need of food.

Malik held this view, and it is one of the two positions of al-Shafi'i.

Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: If it is permitted for them to drink in the morning and in the evening, then it is permitted for them to be satisfied and take provisions.

Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i, in the other position, said: It is not permitted for him to take from carrion except the amount that keeps his soul alive. This was also the view of al-Muzani.

They said: If he were in this condition from the start, it would not be permitted for him to eat any of it, so likewise when he reaches it after having taken it.

Something similar is reported from al-Hasan.

Qatada said: He should not fill himself with it at all.

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: He should not exceed three mouthfuls.

The sound position is contrary to this, as has already been discussed.

**The twenty-ninth issue:** As for treatment with it, it is either necessary to use it while intact or burned. If it has been changed by burning, Ibn Habib said: It is permitted to use it for treatment and for prayer.

Ibn al-Majishun made it more lenient, on the basis that burning is a purification, since it changes its attributes.

In al-Utbiyya, from the narration of Malik, concerning al-mirtak [[al-mirtak (like maq'ad): a type of medicine.]] which is made from the bones of carrion: if he applies it to his wound, he should not pray with it until he washes it.

If the carrion is still intact, Sahnun said: It should not be used for treatment in any case, nor should swine, because from the carrion there is a lawful substitute, unlike in cases of starvation. If a substitute is found during starvation, the carrion should not be eaten.

Likewise, wine is not to be used for treatment, as Malik said, and this is the apparent position of al-Shafi'i. It is also the preference of Ibn Abi Hurayra among his companions.

Abu Hanifa said: It is permitted to drink it for treatment, but not for thirst. This is the preference of al-Qadi al-Tabari among the companions of al-Shafi'i, and it is the view of al-Thawri.

Some of the Baghdadi Shafi'is said: It is permitted to drink it for thirst, but not for treatment, because the harm of thirst is immediate, unlike treatment.

It has been said: It is permitted to drink it for both reasons together.

Some companions of al-Shafi'i prohibited treatment with every forbidden thing except camel urine specifically, on account of the hadith of the 'Uraynis.

Some of them prohibited treatment with every forbidden thing, on account of the words of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Allah has not made the cure of my community in what has been forbidden to them." And because of his words (peace be upon him) to Tariq ibn Suwayd, when he asked him about wine. He forbade him, or disliked that he make it, so he said: "I make it only for medicine." He said: "It is not medicine, but it is a disease."

Narrated by Muslim in the Sahih.

This may be restricted to the state of necessity, for it is permitted to use poison for treatment but not to drink it. And Allah knows best.

**The thirtieth issue:** The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿without being a rebel nor transgressing﴾. "Ghayr" is in the accusative case as a circumstantial qualifier (hal), and it has been said that it is an exception (istithna').

When you see that "ghayr" could be replaced by "fi" (in), it is a circumstantial qualifier; when its position could be replaced by "illa" (except), it is an exception. Measure other cases by this.

"Bagh" originally was "baghin." The dammah on the ya' was made heavy, then it was sukun-ed, and the tanwin is sukun, so the ya' was deleted and the kasrah indicates it.

The meaning, according to Qatada, al-Hasan, al-Rabi', Ibn Zayd, and Ikrima, is ﴿without being a rebel﴾ in eating more than his need, ﴿nor transgressing﴾ by finding an alternative to these prohibited things and eating them anyway.

Al-Suddi said: ﴿without being a rebel﴾ in eating them out of desire and pleasure, ﴿nor transgressing﴾ by continuing to eat until satiety.

Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, and others said: The meaning is ﴿without being a rebel﴾ against the Muslims, ﴿nor transgressing﴾ against them. Thus included among the rebel and the transgressor are highway robbers, one who rebels against the ruler, one who travels to sever kinship ties, one who raids the Muslims, and whatever resembles them.

This is correct, for the root of "baghy" in the language is seeking corruption. It is said: "The woman committed baghā' (prostitution) if she committed fornication," and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution﴾ [al-Nur: 33]. [[See vol. 12, p. 254.]]

Sometimes "baghy" is used for seeking something other than corruption.

The Arabs say: "The man went out in search (bigha') of his camels," meaning in seeking them. From this is the saying of the poet:

Let not the seeking of good (bagha') keep you from the pursuit of the ... ,
Indeed, the inauspicious are like the days, and the auspicious are like the inauspicious.

The thirty-first issue: His words, exalted is He, ﴿and not transgressing﴾. The original form of "ʿādin" is "ʿāʾid," so it is of the transposed type (maqlūb, metathesis), like "shākī al-silāḥ" (for shāʾik, "sharp-edged"), "hār" (for hāʾir, "collapsing"), and "lāth" (for lāʾith). The original forms are shāʾik, hāʾir, and lāʾith, from "luthtu al-ʿimāmah" (I wrapped the turban). So God permitted, in the state of necessity, eating all the forbidden things, because one is unable to obtain all the permitted things, as we have explained. Thus the absence of a permitted option becomes a condition for permitting the forbidden.

The thirty-second issue: The scholars differed when the necessity is accompanied by an act of disobedience, such as highway robbery and terrorizing travelers. Mālik and one of al-Shāfiʿī's two opinions prohibited it for him because of his disobedience, since God, glorified is He, permitted this as a means of help, and a disobedient person may not be helped. So if he wants to eat, let him repent and then eat. Abū Ḥanīfah and al-Shāfiʿī, in his other opinion, permitted it for him, and they treated his permission as equal whether he was obedient or disobedient.

Ibn al-ʿArabī said: "It is strange that someone would permit this for him while he persists in disobedience. I do not think anyone says it, and if someone says it, he is certainly mistaken."

I say: The correct view is the opposite of this, for a person destroying himself during a journey of disobedience is a greater sin than what he is already doing. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 29]. This is general, and perhaps he will repent in a later state, and repentance will erase what had happened.

Masrūq said: "Whoever is compelled to eat carrion, blood, and pork, and does not eat until he dies, enters the Fire, unless God pardons him."

Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ṭabarī, known as Ilkiyā, said: "Eating carrion in cases of necessity is not a concession (rukhṣah, a relaxation of the ruling) but a mandatory obligation (ʿazīmah, the original ruling). If he refrains from eating carrion, he is sinful. Eating carrion is not one of the concessions of travel, nor connected to travel. Rather, it is one of the results of necessity, whether one is traveling or resident. It is like breaking the fast for a sick resident who is disobedient, and like tayammum (dry ablution) for a disobedient traveler when water is unavailable." He said: "This is the correct view according to us."

I say: The reports from Mālik on this differ. The well-known position of his school, as reported by al-Bājī in al-Muntaqā, is that it is permissible for him to eat during a journey of disobedience, but it is not permissible for him to shorten the prayer or break the fast.

Ibn Khuwayz Mandād said: "As for eating when necessity arises, the obedient and the disobedient are equal in it, because carrion may be eaten during travel and at home. Leaving home for acts of disobedience does not remove from him the ruling of the resident; rather, it is at worst a state of being a resident. The case is not the same with breaking the fast and shortening the prayer, because these two are concessions connected to travel. So whenever the journey is a journey of disobedience, it is not permitted to shorten the prayer during it, because this concession is specific to travel. For this reason we say that he performs tayammum when water is unavailable during a journey of disobedience, since tayammum is the same at home and during travel. How is it permissible to prohibit him from eating carrion and from tayammum because of a disobedience he committed, when refraining from eating would cause the destruction of his life, which is the greatest of sins, and refraining from tayammum would cause the loss of prayer? Is it permissible to say to him: 'You have committed a sin, so commit another'? Is it permissible to say to a drinker of wine: 'Commit adultery,' and to an adulterer: 'Disbelieve,' or to say to them both: 'Neglect the prayer'?" He mentioned all of this in his book Aḥkām al-Qurʾān, and he did not mention any disagreement from Mālik or from any of his companions.

Al-Bājī said: "Ziyād ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Andalusī reported that the disobedient traveler shortens the prayer and breaks the fast in Ramadan. So he treated all of these alike, and this is the view of Abū Ḥanīfah. There is no disagreement that it is not permissible for him to kill himself by abstaining from food, and that he is commanded to eat as an obligation. Whoever is on a journey of disobedience is not relieved of the obligatory duties and requirements of fasting and prayer; rather, he must perform them. Likewise, what we have mentioned applies. The argument for the first view is that these allowances were permitted during journeys because people need them, so he may not use them as aids for disobedience, and he has a way not to kill himself."

Ibn Ḥabīb said: "That is by repenting, and then eating carrion after his repentance." Ibn Ḥabīb relied in this on God's words, exalted is He: ﴿But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing﴾, so he made the condition for permitting carrion in necessity that the person not be a transgressor. A traveler who is engaged in armed robbery or highway banditry, or in severing kinship ties, or who pursues sin, is a transgressor and an aggressor, so the conditions of permission are not met in him. And God knows best."

I say: This is an argument from the implication of the text (mafhūm al-khiṭāb, implicit meaning), which is disputed among the jurists of legal theory (uṣūliyyūn). The explicit wording of the verse is that the one compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, bears no sin. Other cases are left unmentioned, and the default is the generality of the address. So whoever claims that this generality has been removed for some reason must provide the evidence.

The thirty-fourth issue: His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning He forgives sins. So, all the more, He does not hold to account for what He has permitted, and it is part of His mercy that He granted the concession.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 174:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has revealed of the Book﴾ means the scholars of the Jews, who concealed what Allah had revealed in the Torah concerning the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the authenticity of his prophethood. The meaning of "revealed" (anzala) here is "made manifest" (azhara), as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And who says, "I will reveal (sa-unzilu) the like of what Allah has revealed"﴾ [al-An'am: 93], i.e., "I will make manifest." It has also been said: it is on its original sense of descent, i.e., what Allah sent down with His angels to His messengers. "And exchange it" means, with the concealed matter, "for a small price" (thamanan qalilan), meaning the taking of bribes (al-rishaa). He called it "small" because its duration is cut off and its outcome is evil. It has also been said: because what they took as bribes was little. I say: although this verse concerns the People of the Book, it also encompasses those among the Muslims who knowingly conceal the truth for the sake of some worldly gain they obtain, and this meaning has already been mentioned previously.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿into their bellies﴾. He mentioned the bellies to indicate and emphasize the literal reality of eating, since the word may be used figuratively, as in "so-and-so ate my land" and similar expressions. In the mention of the bellies there is also an indication of their greed, and that they sold their Hereafter for their share of food that has no worth. The meaning of ﴿only the Fire﴾ is that it is unlawful, and Allah will punish them with the Fire for it. What they consumed of bribes was called "fire" because it leads them to the Fire; this is what most of the exegetes said. It has also been said: that is, He will punish them for their concealment by eating the fire in Hell in actuality. Thus He reports the outcome by the present state, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the properties of orphans unjustly, they only consume fire into their bellies﴾ [al-Nisa': 10], i.e., its end will lead to that. From this is the saying of the poets:

Give birth for death, and build for ruin.

[It is disputed whether this is a hadith or not. See Kashf al-Khafa, vol. 2, p. 140.]

He said:

So for death is what the mother bears.

Another said:

And our dwellings, for the ruin of time, we build them.

This usage is abundant in the Qur'an and in poetry.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah will not speak to them﴾ is an expression for anger toward them and the removal of His good pleasure from them. It is said: "So-and-so does not speak to so-and-so" when he is angry with him. Al-Tabari said: the meaning of "He will not speak to them" is, with what they would love. In the revelation: ﴿Remain in it with disgrace, and do not speak to Me﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 108]. It has also been said: the meaning is that He will not send the angels to them with greetings. ﴿Nor will He purify them﴾, i.e., He will not correct their evil deeds so as to cleanse them. Al-Zajjaj said: He will not praise them with goodness, nor name them "the pure." ﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾: "painful" (alim) is in the sense of "causing pain" (mu'lim), and this has been mentioned previously.

In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Three whom Allah will not speak to on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them, nor look at them, and for them is a painful punishment: an old adulterer, a lying king, and a proud pauper." He singled these out for painful punishment and severe retribution because their sins are pure defiance and contempt, which drive them to those disobediences, since no need compelled them to it, nor did necessity urge them to it as it does those who are not like them. The meaning of "He will not look at them" is that He will not show mercy to them nor incline toward them. It will come in Al 'Imran, Allah willing, Exalted is He.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance, and punishment in exchange for forgiveness﴾. Its discussion has already preceded [see vol. 1, p. 210, second edition]. Since punishment follows error, and forgiveness follows the guidance which they discarded, both fall under the figurative use of purchase (tajawwuz al-shira', the metaphorical sense of "buying").

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So what has made them endure the Fire?﴾ The position of the majority of scholars (al-jumhur), including al-Hasan and Mujahid, is that "مَا" here means exclamation (al-ta'ajjub), and it is directed at the created beings. It is as if He said: marvel at their endurance of the Fire and their remaining in it. In the revelation: ﴿Man is killed; how disbelieving he is!﴾ [Abasa: 17], and ﴿How well they will hear and see!﴾ [Maryam: 38]. Abu 'Ali began with this meaning. Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ibn Jubayr and al-Rabi' said: By God, they have no endurance for it; rather, "مَا أَجْرَأَهُمْ عَلَى النَّارِ" (how bold they are toward the Fire!). This is a well-known Yemeni usage. Al-Farra' said: Al-Kisa'i informed me, saying: The judge of Yemen informed me that two litigants came before him, and the oath became obligatory upon one of them, so he swore. His companion said to him: "مَا أَصْبَرَكَ عَلَى اللَّهِ؟" meaning: how bold you are against God! The meaning is: how brave they are toward the Fire, in that they do deeds that lead to it. Al-Zajjaj related that the meaning is: "مَا أَبْقَاهُمْ عَلَى النَّارِ", from their saying: "مَا أَصْبَرَ فُلَانًا عَلَى الْحَبْسِ" (how long so-and-so has been kept in prison!), i.e., how long he has been kept in it. It was also said: the meaning is how little their impatience is at the Fire, so the lack of impatience is called endurance. Al-Kisa'i and Qutrub said: that is, how constant they are at the deeds of the people of the Fire. It was also said: "مَا" is interrogative, meaning rebuke, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi, 'Ata' and Abu 'Ubaydah Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna, and its meaning is: "أَيُّ شَيْءٍ صَبَّرَهُمْ عَلَى عَمَلِ أَهْلِ النَّارِ؟!" (what made them endure the deeds of the people of the Fire?!). It was also said: this is in the manner of belittling them and making light of their affair.

"His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That﴾. "That" is in the nominative position (marfu') and refers to the ruling, as if He said: That ruling is the Fire. Al-Zajjaj said: its estimated sense is "the matter is that," or "that matter," or "that punishment is for them." Al-Akhfash said: the predicate (khabar) of "that" is implied, its meaning being "that is known to them." It has also been said that its position is accusative (nasb), meaning: We did that to them. ﴿Because Allah sent down the Book﴾ — meaning the Qur'an in this context — ﴿with the truth﴾, i.e., with sincerity (al-sidq). It has also been said: with proof (al-hujjah). ﴿And indeed those who differ concerning the Book﴾ — meaning the Torah. The Christians claimed that it contains the description of Jesus, while the Jews denied his description. It has also been said: they opposed their forefathers and predecessors in adhering to it. It has also been said: they opposed what is in the Torah concerning the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and differed about it. It has also been said: the intended meaning is the Qur'an, and those who differ are the disbelievers of Quraysh: some of them say it is sorcery, some say it is the fables of the ancients, and some say it is fabricated, and so on. The discussion of the meaning of shiqaq has already been presented earlier, and praise be to Allah. [[See p. 143 of this part.]]"

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 177 (part 1 of 2):**

There are eight issues concerning it.

**The first issue:** His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿It is not righteousness﴾. Scholars differ over who is addressed by this discourse. Qatadah said: "It has been reported to us that a man asked the Prophet ﷺ about righteousness, and so Allah revealed this verse." He said: "Before the obligatory duties, the man who bore witness that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger, and then died in that state, was assured of Paradise. So Allah revealed this verse." Al-Rabi' and Qatadah also said: the address is to the Jews and the Christians, because they disagreed about the direction of prayer (tawajjuh) and the orientation (tawalli). The Jews faced west towards Bayt al-Maqdis, and the Christians faced east towards the rising of the sun. They argued about the changing of the qiblah, and each group preferred its own orientation. So it was said to them: "It is not righteousness that you are upon, but righteousness is in whoever believes in Allah."

**The second issue:** Hamzah and Hafs read *al-birra* with a fatha (accusative). This is because *laysa* (not) is among the sisters of *kana* (was), and two definite nouns follow it, so you may make whichever of them you wish the subject (*ism*) or the predicate (*khabar*). Since *al-birru* came after *laysa*, he put it in the accusative, and made *an tuwallu* (that you turn) the subject. The verbal noun is more suitable to be the subject, because it is not indefinite, whereas *al-birr* may be indefinite, and the verb is stronger in definiteness. The rest read *al-birru* with a damma (nominative), as the subject of *laysa*, with *an tuwallu* as its predicate. The sense is: "It is not righteousness that you turn your faces..." On the first reading the sense is: "It is not your turning your faces that is righteousness," like His saying: ﴿Their argument was only that they said...﴾ (Surah al-Jathiyah 25), ﴿Then the end of those who did evil was that they denied...﴾ (Surah al-Rum 10), ﴿So the end of both of them was that they were in the Fire...﴾ (Surah al-Hashr 17), and similar examples. What strengthens the nominative reading is that the second noun is accompanied by the preposition *bi-* (with) by consensus, in His saying: ﴿It is not righteousness that you enter the houses from their backs﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah 189), and in that position only the nominative is permitted. So it is better to make the first (reading) conform to the second than to oppose it. Likewise, in the codex of Ubayy it is written with *bi-*: *laysa al-birru bi-an tuwallu*, and likewise in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud. Most of the readers follow this, and both readings are good.

**The third issue:** His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿But righteousness is in whoever believes in Allah﴾. *Al-birr* here is a comprehensive term for good. The implied meaning is: "But the righteousness is the righteousness of whoever believes," so the noun modified (*al-mudaf*) has been omitted, as in His saying: ﴿And ask the town﴾ (Surah Yusuf 82), and ﴿And the calf was made to sink into their hearts﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah 93). This was said by al-Farra', Qutrub and al-Zajjaj. A poet said:

*"For it is only advance and retreat"*

meaning: possessing advance and possessing retreat. Al-Nabighah said:

*"How can you maintain the friendship of one whose friendship has become like that of Abu Marhab?"*

Al-Khalalah (friendship; it may be read with fatha, kasra or damma) means companionship. Abu Marhab is a kunyah for the shade, and it is said that it is also a kunyah for 'Aqrab. He means: the friendship and union of this woman does not endure, just as the friendship of Abu Marhab does not endure, so one should not feel at ease with her or rely upon her. [From the Lisan and the explanation of the verses.] That is: like the friendship of Abu Marhab, so the phrase has been omitted. It was also said: the meaning is "But the one of righteousness (*dhal-birr*) is..." as in His saying: ﴿They are of degrees with Allah﴾ (Surah Al 'Imran 163), meaning: they are people of degrees. This is because when the Prophet ﷺ migrated to Madinah, the obligatory duties were prescribed, the qiblah was turned to the Ka'bah, and the limits (hudud) were fixed, Allah revealed this verse and said: "It is not righteousness in its entirety that you pray and do nothing else. But righteousness, that is, the one who has righteousness, is whoever believes in Allah..." to the end of the verse. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, 'Ata', Sufyan and also al-Zajjaj. It is also permissible that *al-birr* be used in the sense of *al-barr* and *al-barr* (the pious or righteous one), and the active participle is sometimes used in the sense of the verbal noun, as one says: *rajul 'adl* (a just man), *sawm* and *fitr* (fasting and breaking the fast). In the revelation: ﴿If your water should become sunken (*ghawran*)﴾ (Surah al-Mulk 30), meaning sunken (*ghair*). This is the view chosen by Abu 'Ubaydah. Al-Mubarrad said: "If I were one of those who recite the Qur'an, I would have read *wa-lakinna al-birra* with a fatha on the *ba'*."

**The fourth issue:** His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And those who fulfil their covenant when they make a covenant, and the patient...﴾. It was said: *al-muwfuna* (those who fulfil) is in apposition (*'atf*) to *man* (whoever), because *man* is in the position of a plural and in the place of the nominative, as if He had said: "But righteousness is the believers and those who fulfil..." This was said by al-Farra' and al-Akhfash. *Al-sabirina* (the patient) is in the accusative for praise (*madh*), or by an implied verb. The Arabs use the accusative both for praise and for blame, as if they intend by this to single out the one praised or blamed, and do not make it follow the beginning of the sentence, but place it in the accusative. As for praise, there is His saying: ﴿And those who establish prayer﴾ (Surah al-Nisa' 162). Al-Kisa'i recited:

*"Every people obeyed the command of their guide, except Numayr, who obeyed the command of their misguider."*

*"The travellers, though they have not made anyone travel, and those who say: 'For whom is the abode that we may leave it?'"*

Abu 'Ubaydah recited:

*"Let not my people be far away, those who are the poison of the enemies and the calamity of the slaughtered camels,*
*Those who alight in every battlefield, and those who are good at tying the knots of the loincloths."*

Another said:

*"We are the sons of Dabbah, the companions of the camel."*

So it is in the accusative for praise. As for blame, there is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Cursed, wherever they are found﴾ (Surah al-Ahzab 61), and the verse. 'Urwah ibn al-Ward said:

*"They gave me wine, then surrounded me, the enemies of Allah, with falsehood and lies."*

This is a broad and well-known usage in qualifying descriptions (nu'ut). There is no objection to it from the standpoint of grammar, and it is found in the speech of the Arabs as we have shown. Some of those who pursued obscure points in their speech said: "This is an error by the scribes when they wrote the codex of the Imam." He said: "The evidence for this is what is reported from 'Uthman, that he looked at the codex and said: 'I see a grammatical error in it, and the Arabs will correct it with their tongues.'" [This statement is among the most wicked things that forgers attributed to 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, and scholars have denied the authenticity of its attribution to him. Moreover, 'Uthman did not alone undertake the compilation of the codex; the Companions shared with him in its compilation and writing, and they did not circulate it among the Muslims until they had collated it with the leaves on which the Qur'an had been collected in the time of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. Therefore, the Muslims did not circulate it except that, by the consensus of the Companions, it was in complete agreement with the final recitation (al-'ardah al-akhirah) by which the Prophet ﷺ presented the Qur'an to Jibril, peace be upon him. Would anyone suppose that 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, the third of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, would see in the codex a grammatical error contrary to what Allah revealed, and leave it, saying: "The Arabs will correct it with their tongues"? How could he say that in the presence of the Companions, without them standing against him and rejecting his statement, when they were the helpers of the religion and its defenders? Among those who denied the attribution of this statement to 'Uthman were the author (al-Musannif), al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi, in the commentary on Surah al-Nisa' at His saying: "And those who establish prayer" (verse 162); see vol. 6, p. 13.] in it, and the Arabs will correct it with their tongues." He said the same in Surah al-Nisa': ﴿And those who establish prayer﴾ (Surah al-Nisa' 162), and in Surah al-Ma'idah: *wa-l-sabi'un* (and the Sabians) (Surah al-Ma'idah 69). The answer is what we have mentioned.

It was also said: *al-muwfuna* is in the nominative as a beginning (mubtada'), and its predicate is omitted; the implied meaning is: "and they are the ones who fulfil." Al-Kisa'i said: *al-sabirina* is in apposition (*'atf*) to *dhawi al-qurba* (the kinsmen), as if He had said: "and gave to the patient." Al-Nahhas said: "This view is an error and a clear mistake, because if you put *al-sabirina* in the accusative and make it coordinate with *dhawi al-qurba*, it enters into the relative clause (*silah*) of *man*; and if you make *al-muwfuna* in the nominative as coordinate with *man*, you have made it coordinate with *man* before the relative clause is complete, and you have separated the relative clause from the relative pronoun with a coordinated word." Al-Kisa'i said: "In the reading of 'Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) it is: *wa-l-muwfina wa-l-sabirina*." Al-Nahhas said: "Both may be coordinated with *dhawi al-qurba*, or be in the accusative for praise." Al-Farra' said: "In the reading of 'Abdullah in Surah al-Nisa' it is: *wa-l-muqimina l-salata wa-l-mu'tuna l-zakah*" [So it is in the book *I'rab al-Qur'an* by al-Nahhas; what the context of the discussion in *al-Bahr al-Muhit* by Abu Hayyan, in Surah al-Nisa', indicates is otherwise. In the originals: "*wa-l-muqimina ... wa-l-mu'tina*."] (Surah al-Nisa' 162). Ya'qub and al-A'mash read *al-muwfuna wa-l-sabirun* with the nominative in both words. And [the text breaks off here].

Al-Jahdari read "bi-ʿuhudihim" (in their covenants).

It has been said that "wal-mūfūna" (وَالْمُوفُونَ) is in the nominative as a conjunction with the pronoun in "āmana" (آمَنَ, "believed"). Abu ʿAli rejected this and said: "The meaning does not support it, for it is not intended that the righteousness of the one who believes in God is the righteousness of him and of those who fulfil [their covenants], as if they all believed together. It is like saying: 'The brave man is the one who advances, he and ʿAmr.' Rather, what comes after 'man āmana' is an enumeration of the deeds and attributes of those who believe."

**The fifth matter.** Our scholars said: This is a great verse among the foundational rulings, for it contains sixteen principles: belief in God and in His names and attributes (we have discussed these in *al-Kitab al-Asna*), the Resurrection, the Gathering, the Balance, the Bridge (al-Sirat), the Basin (al-Hawd), intercession, Paradise and Hell (we have discussed these in the book *al-Tadhkira*), the angels, the revealed Books and that they are the truth from God (as has preceded), the prophets, spending wealth on what is obligatory and recommended, maintaining kinship ties and not severing them, caring for the orphan and not neglecting him, the needy likewise, the wayfarer (*ibn al-sabil*), said to mean the one cut off from his means, and said to mean the guest, the beggar, and the freeing of slaves. The explanation of this will come in the verse on charities (see vol. 8, p. 167). Also: maintaining the prayer, giving the zakat, fulfilling covenants, and patience in hardship. Each of these principles requires a book of its own, and many of them have already been pointed out; the explanation of the rest will come in their proper places, God willing.

It has been disputed whether an orphan may be given from voluntary charity merely because he is an orphan, as a gift, even if he is wealthy, or whether he may not be given unless he is poor. Scholars hold two opinions on this. This applies if the giving of wealth is other than the obligatory zakat, as we will explain shortly (*ānifan*: that is, just now).

**The sixth matter.** God's words: ﴿And gives wealth, despite loving it﴾. Whoever said that there is a right in wealth beyond zakat used this as evidence, and that with it righteousness is complete. It has also been said that what is meant is the obligatory zakat. The first view is more correct, because of what al-Daraqutni narrated from Fatima bint Qays, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, there is a right in wealth beyond zakat," and then he recited this verse: "Righteousness is not that you turn your faces..." to the end of the verse. Ibn Majah included it in his Sunan, and al-Tirmidhi in his Jami', and said: "This hadith does not have a strong chain, and Abu Hamzah Maymun al-Aʿwar is weak. Bayan and Ismaʿil ibn Salim narrated this hadith from al-Shaʿbi as his own statement, and this is more correct." I say: Although this hadith has criticism, the meaning of the verse itself confirms its soundness, through God's words: ﴿and establishes the prayer and gives zakat﴾. He mentioned zakat alongside the prayer, which is evidence that what is meant by ﴿and gives wealth despite loving it﴾ is not the obligatory zakat, for otherwise it would be a repetition. And God knows best.

The scholars agreed that if the Muslims face a need after the zakat has been paid, it is obligatory to spend wealth on it. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is obligatory upon the people to ransom their captives, even if that consumes all their wealth. This is also a consensus, and it strengthens what we have chosen. And success is from God.

**The seventh matter.** God's words: ﴿despite loving it﴾. Scholars differed about what the pronoun in "ḥubbihi" (حُبِّهِ, "his love") refers to. It has been said it refers to the giver of the wealth, and the object, which is the wealth, is omitted. The phrase "dhawi al-qurba" (ذَوِي الْقُرْبى, "relatives") may be read in the accusative with "al-ḥalab" (the verbal noun of love), so the sense is "despite the giver's love for the relatives." It has also been said that it refers to the wealth, so the verbal noun is annexed to its object. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: The phrase "ʿala ḥubbihi" comes as an eloquent interjection within the statement. I say: Its parallel is God's words: ﴿and they give food, despite loving it, to the needy﴾ (see vol. 19, p. 126). It combines both meanings: the interjection and the annexation of the verbal noun to its object, that is, "despite love of the food." Among the interjections is God's words: ﴿Whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female, while being a believer, those will enter Paradise﴾ (see vol. 5, p. 399). Scholars call this *tatmim* (completion, adding a phrase that perfects the meaning), a kind of eloquence, and it is also called *ihtiras* (safeguarding) or *ihtiyat* (precaution). Thus the verse is completed by "despite loving it" and "while he is a believer." From it is the saying of Zuhayr:

*Whoever meets, one day, in his faults, an old man,*
*Will meet from him generosity and munificence as a character.*

Imru al-Qays said:

*Upon a sturdy steed that gives you, before you ask,*
*Varied paces of running, neither stiff nor slack.*

So his words "in his faults" and "before you ask" are a fine *tatmim*. From it is the saying of ʿAntarah:

*Let him praise me for what he knows of me, for I am*
*Easy to deal with when I am not wronged.*

So his words "when I am not wronged" are a fine *tatmim*. Tarafah said:

*So may the rain-cloud of spring water your abodes, not ruining them,*
*And a steady, flowing downpour.*

And al-Rabiʿ ibn Dabiʿ al-Fazari said:

*I have perished, yet my deeds and my speech do not perish,*
*And every man perishes except his tales.*

So his words "not ruining them" and "except his tales" are *tatmim* and *ihtiras*. Abu Haffan said:

*Death has consumed our souls, not unjustly,*
*And generosity has consumed our wealth, not blamefully.*

So his words "not unjustly" and "not blamefully" are *tatmim* and *ihtiyat*, and this is abundant in poetry.

It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the giving (*al-iʾtaʾ*), because the verb indicates its verbal noun, as in God's words: ﴿And let not those who withhold what God has given them of His bounty think that it is better for them﴾ (see vol. 4, p. 290), meaning: the withholding is better for them. So when people face need or poverty, giving wealth becomes beloved to them. It has also been said that it refers to the name of God in His words: "whoever believes in God." The intended meaning is that a person gives charity in these ways while he is healthy and miserly, fearing poverty and hoping to remain.

**The eighth matter.** God's words: ﴿And those who fulfil their covenant when they make it﴾, that is, both in what is between them and God and in what is between them and people. ﴿And the patient in misfortune and in adversity﴾. *Al-basaʾ* (الْبَأْسَاءُ) is hardship and poverty. *Al-ḍarraʾ* (الضَّرَّاءُ) is illness and affliction; this was said by Ibn Masʿud. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "God the Exalted says: Whichever of My servants I afflict with a trial in his bed, and he does not complain to his visitors, I will replace his flesh with flesh better than his flesh and his blood with blood better than his blood. If I take him, it is to My mercy; and if I restore him to health, I restore him, and he has no sin." It was said: "O Messenger of God, what is flesh better than his flesh?" He said: "Flesh that has not sinned." It was said: "And what is blood better than his blood?" He said: "Blood that has not sinned."

*Al-basaʾ* and *al-ḍarraʾ* are two nouns formed on the pattern *faʿlaʾ*, and they have no verb of their own, because they are nouns and not adjectives. "Wa-ḥina al-basi" (وَحِينَ الْبَأْسِ, "and at the time of violence") means the time of conflict (in manuscript B: "the time of drought").

God's words: ﴿Those are the ones who are truthful, and those are the God-fearing﴾. He described them with truthfulness and piety in their affairs and in fulfilling them, and that they were earnest in religion. This is the utmost praise. *Al-sidq* (الصدق, truthfulness) is the opposite of lying. It is said: "They faced each other in battle" (*ṣadaqūhumu al-qitāl*). A *ṣiddīq* (صِدِّيق) is one who constantly adheres to truthfulness. In a hadith: "Hold to truthfulness, for truthfulness leads to righteousness, and righteousness leads to Paradise. A man continues to speak truth and seek truthfulness until he is recorded with God as a *ṣiddīq*."

There are seventeen issues in it.

**The first issue:** Al-Bukhari, al-Nasa'i and al-Daraqutni narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Among the Children of Israel there was retaliation (al-qisas) but there was no blood money (al-diyah). So God said to this Ummah: ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain: the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female. But whoever is pardoned by his brother in any way...﴾" "Pardon" means accepting the blood money in cases of intentional killing. ﴿...then pursue it with fairness and pay him with good conduct.﴾ "He pursues it fairly and pays with good conduct." ﴿That is a lightening from your Lord and a mercy.﴾ "This is a relief from what was prescribed for those before you." ﴿Whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment.﴾ "He who kills after accepting the blood money."

This is the wording of al-Bukhari: Al-Humaydi narrated to us, Sufyan narrated to us, 'Amr narrated to us [he said [[The addition is from Sahih al-Bukhari.]]], I heard Mujahid [he said [[The addition is from Sahih al-Bukhari.]]], I heard Ibn 'Abbas [saying [[The addition is from Sahih al-Bukhari.]]].

Al-Sha'bi said regarding God's words, ﴿the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female﴾, that it was revealed concerning two tribes of the Arab tribes who fought each other. They said, "We will kill for our slave So-and-so son of So-and-so, and for our female slave So-and-so daughter of So-and-so." Qatadah narrated something similar.

**The second issue:** God's words, ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you﴾. "Kutiba" (it was prescribed) means it was made obligatory and established. From this is the statement of 'Umar ibn Abi Rabi'ah:

*Killing and fighting have been prescribed for us,*
*and for the young women, the trailing of skirts.*

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 178 (part 2 of 5):**

It has been said that "kutiba" (it is prescribed) here is a report about what was written on the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) and what had already been decreed. *Al-qisas* (retaliation) is derived from *qass al-athar*, which means following the trail, and from it comes *al-qass* (the storyteller), because he follows traces and reports. *Qass al-sha'r* (trimming hair) means following its line. So it is as if the killer took a path of killing and then followed its traces, walking in its way. From this comes the verse ﴿So they went back, retracing their steps﴾ [al-Kahf 18:64]. It has also been said that *al-qass* means cutting. One says, "I cut between them" (*qassatu ma baynahuma*). From this comes the taking of *qisas*, because the one who takes retaliation wounds the offender with a wound like his, or kills him in return. One says, "The ruler exacted retaliation (*aqassa*) from so-and-so on behalf of so-and-so," and "He ordered him and he complied, so he took retaliation from him," meaning he exacted retaliation from him.

**The third issue:** The form of *qisas* is that when the victim's guardian (*al-waliy*) wishes to kill, the killer is obligated to submit to God's command and to yield to the lawful retaliation against him. The guardian is obligated to stop at the killer of his relative and not to transgress against others, as the Arabs used to transgress by killing someone other than the killer. This is the meaning of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Among the most rebellious people against God on the Day of Resurrection are three: a man who kills someone other than his killer, a man who kills within the sacred precinct (*al-haram*), and a man who seeks vengeance for the blood feuds of the Jahiliyya (*dhuhul al-jahiliyya*)."[[*Dhahl* (with a fatha on the dhal and a sukun on the ha): it is said to mean enmity and rancor, and it is said to mean the fire and the seeking of compensation for an offence committed against him, such as killing or wounding, and the like.]]

Al-Sha'bi, Qatada and others said: The people of the Jahiliyya were given to rebellion and obedience to Satan. If a tribe had power and protection, and one of its slaves was killed by a slave of another tribe, they said, "We will not kill for him except a free man." If a woman of theirs was killed, they said, "We will not kill for her except a man." If a lowly person of theirs was killed, they said, "We will not kill for him except a noble." They would say, "Killing is more protective against killing" (*al-qatlu awqa li-l-qatl*), with the waw and the qaf. It is also narrated as *abqa* (with the ba and the qaf), and as *anfa* (with the nun and the fa). So God forbade them from rebellion and said: "Retaliation is prescribed for you in the matter of the slain: the free for the free, and the slave for the slave..." up to the end of the verse. And He said: ﴿And in retaliation there is life for you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:179]. There is a great difference between the two statements in eloquence and forcefulness.

**The fourth issue:** There is no disagreement that *qisas* for killing is carried out only by those in authority (*ulu al-amr*). They are obligated to undertake the execution of *qisas* and the enforcement of the prescribed punishments (*hudud*) and other matters. This is because God, glory be to Him, addressed all the believers with *qisas*, but it is not possible for all the believers to gather together to carry out *qisas*. So they placed the ruler (*al-sultan*) in their stead for carrying out *qisas* and the other prescribed punishments. *Qisas* is not obligatory in the sense that it must always be enforced. What is obligatory is that *qisas* and the other prescribed punishments not be exceeded into aggression. As for when agreement is reached without *qisas*, through blood money (*diyya*) or pardon, that is permitted, as its explanation will come. If it is said: The words of God, "Retaliation is prescribed for you" (*kutiba 'alaykum*), mean that it is decreed and imposed, so how can *qisas* not be obligatory? It is answered: Its meaning is "if you wish," which informs us that *qisas* is the final resort when there is dispute. *Al-qatla* is the plural of *qatil*, a word of feminine form with the feminine of collectives (*ta'nith al-jama'a*). It is one of the things that befall people against their will, so it came in this pattern, like *jarha* (wounded), *zamna* (disabled), *hamqa* (fools), *sarha* (fallen), *gharqa* (drowned), and similar words.

**The fifth issue:** God's words: "The free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female..." up to the end of the verse. Its interpretation has been disputed. One group said: The verse came to clarify the ruling for each category when a person kills someone of his own category. It explains the ruling for a free man who kills a free man, a slave who kills a slave, and a woman who kills a woman, and it does not address the case of one category killing the other. So the verse is definitive (*muhkama*), and it contains a general statement (*ijmal*) which is clarified by God's words: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:45]. The Prophet (ﷺ) also clarified it by his Sunnah when a Jew was killed for a woman. This is what Mujahid said, and Abu 'Ubayd mentioned it from Ibn 'Abbas. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the verse was abrogated (*mansukha*) by the verse of al-Ma'idah.[[See vol. 6, p. 191.]] This is the view of the people of Iraq.

**The sixth issue:** The Kufans and al-Thawri said: A free man is killed for a slave, and a Muslim for a *dhimmi* (a non-Muslim living under Muslim protection). They argued with God's words: "O you who believe, retaliation is prescribed for you in the matter of the slain," which is general.
