They also argued with God's words: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:45]. They said: The *dhimmi* and the Muslim are equal in the sanctity that suffices for retaliation, which is the sanctity of blood established permanently, because the *dhimmi*'s blood is protected permanently, and so is the Muslim's, and both have become people of the abode of Islam. What confirms this is that a Muslim's hand is cut for stealing the property of a *dhimmi*. This shows that the property of the *dhimmi* is equal to the property of the Muslim, and so it indicates equality in blood, since property is sacred only through the sanctity of its owner. Abu Hanifa and his companions, al-Thawri, and Ibn Abi Layla agreed that a free man is killed for a slave just as a slave is killed for a free man. This is also the view of Dawud. It is narrated from 'Ali and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them both, and this was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Qatada, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, and al-Hakam ibn 'Uyayna. But the majority of scholars do not kill a free man for a slave, because of the division and categorization in the verse.

Abu Thawr said: Since they all agreed that there is no *qisas* between slaves and free persons for injuries less than killing, then killing is more deserving of this rule. Whoever among them distinguished between these matters has contradicted himself. Also, there is consensus (*ijma'*) that whoever kills a slave by mistake is liable only for the slave's value, so just as he is not treated like a free man in unintentional killing, he is not treated like one in intentional killing. Also, the slave is a commodity among commodities, bought and sold, and a free man may dispose of him as he wishes, so there is no equality between him and a free man, and no comparability.

I say: This consensus is sound. As for his earlier statement, "Since they all agreed..." up to "...then he has contradicted himself," Ibn Abi Layla and Dawud held that there is *qisas* between free persons and slaves in killing and in all limbs. Dawud argued with the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "The blood of the Muslims is equal" (*al-muslimuna tatakafa'u dimauhum*), and so he did not distinguish between a free man and a slave. Its explanation will come in *al-Nisa'*, God willing.[[See vol. 5, p. 314.]]

**The seventh issue:** The majority also hold that a Muslim is not killed for a disbeliever, based on the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "A Muslim is not killed for a disbeliever." Al-Bukhari reported it from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib. What they narrated from the hadith of Rabi'a, that the Prophet (ﷺ) killed a Muslim for a disbeliever on the day of Khaybar, is not sound, because it is *munqati'* (with a broken chain). And from the hadith of Ibn al-Baylamani, who is weak, from Ibn 'Umar from the Prophet (ﷺ), as a *marfu'* (traced to the Prophet) report, al-Daraqutni said: "No one transmitted it with a chain except Ibrahim ibn Abi Yahya, who is abandoned in hadith (*matruk al-hadith*). The correct version from Rabi'a from Ibn al-Baylamani is *mursal* (with a missing companion) from the Prophet (ﷺ). Ibn al-Baylamani is weak in hadith and cannot be used as proof when he connects a hadith, so how much less when he transmits it without a link." I say: Nothing authentic on this subject is established except the hadith of al-Bukhari, and it specifies the generality of God's words: "Retaliation is prescribed for you in the matter of the slain" up to the end of the verse, and the generality of His words: ﴿the life for the life﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:45].

**The eighth issue:** It is narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan al-Basri that the verse was revealed to clarify the ruling for those mentioned, so that this would indicate the distinction between them and cases where a free man kills a slave, or a slave kills a free man, or a male kills a female, or a female kills a male. Both said: If a man kills a woman, then if her guardians wish, they may kill his companion (the killer) and render to his guardians half the blood money; and if they wish to spare him, they may take from him the blood money of the woman. If a woman kills a man, then if his guardians wish to kill her, they may kill her and take half the blood money; otherwise they take the blood money of their companion and spare her. Al-Sha'bi narrated this from 'Ali, but it is not sound, because al-Sha'bi did not meet 'Ali. Al-Hakam narrated from 'Ali and 'Abd Allah (ibn Mas'ud), who both said: If a man kills a woman intentionally, then he is liable to *qawad* (retaliatory killing) for her. This contradicts the narration of al-Sha'bi from 'Ali.

The scholars agreed that if a one-eyed man or a man with a paralyzed limb kills a man who is sound in all his limbs, the guardian has no right to kill the one-eyed man and take from him half the blood money on the grounds that he killed one who had two eyes while he himself has only one, or killed one with two hands while he is paralyzed. This shows that a soul is equivalent to a soul, and that a child is equivalent to an adult in this respect. It is said to the one who holds this view: If a man is not equivalent to a woman, and she does not fall under the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying, "The blood of the Muslims is equal," then why did you kill the man for her, when she is not his equal, and then take half the blood money? The scholars have agreed that blood money and *qisas* are not combined, and that when blood money is accepted, the killing becomes unlawful for retaliation and *qisas* is cancelled. So your view is neither based on a principle nor on analogy. Abu 'Umar (Ibn 'Abd al-Barr), may Allah be pleased with him, said this.

If a free man kills a slave, then if the slave's master wishes, he may kill the killer and give the heirs of the free man the blood money of a free man minus the value of the slave. If he wishes, he may spare him and take the value of the slave. This is reported from 'Ali and al-Hasan, but this has also been denied of them.

**The ninth issue:** The scholars agreed on killing a man for a woman and a woman for a man. The majority do not hold that any return of the difference is required. A group holds that the difference in blood money is to be pursued (*al-ittiba' bi-fadl al-diyat*). Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, al-Thawri and Abu Thawr said: Likewise, *qisas* between them applies to injuries less than killing. Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman and Abu Hanifa said: There is no *qisas* between them for injuries less than killing; it applies only to killing for killing. Both are refuted by the extension of what is less than killing to killing, through the method of the stronger and the more fitting, as previously explained.

**The tenth issue:** Ibn al-'Arabi said: Ignorance has reached such a point among some people that they said: A free man is killed for his own slave. They narrated a hadith in this regard from al-Hasan, from Samura, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever kills his slave, we will kill him." It is a weak hadith. Our proof is God's words: ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have given his heir authority, but let him not commit excess in killing﴾ [al-Isra' 17:33].

[[See vol. 10, p. 254.]] " [Al-Isra: 33] Here "al-wali" means the master (al-sayyid), so how can he be given authority over his own self?" Everyone agrees that if a master kills his slave by mistake, no blood money (qimah) is taken from him for the public treasury (bayt al-mal). 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb reported from his father, from his grandfather, that a man killed his slave deliberately, and the Prophet (ﷺ) flogged him, banished him for a year, erased his share from the Muslims' booty, and did not impose retaliation (qisas) on him for it. If it is said: when a man kills his wife, why do you not say that marriage (nikah) creates a doubt (shubha) that averts retaliation from the husband, since marriage is a kind of servitude (riqq)? Al-Layth ibn Sa'd said this. We reply: the marriage contract creates rights for her over him just as it creates rights for him over her, as proven by the fact that he may not marry her sister or more than four others besides her, and she may demand from him sexual fulfilment just as he may demand it from her. But he has over her the superiority of guardianship (qiwamah), which God has given him "because they spend from their wealth", that is, because of the dowry and maintenance that became obligatory upon him. Had it created a doubt, it would have created one on both sides. I say: this hadith, which Ibn al-'Arabi declared weak, is sound. It was transmitted by al-Nasa'i and Abu Dawud, and the completion of its text is: "Whoever slits his slave's nose, we slit his nose; whoever castrates him, we castrate him." Al-Bukhari said, quoting 'Ali ibn al-Madini: "The hearing of al-Hasan from Samurah is sound, and he acted upon this hadith." Al-Bukhari also said: "And I hold to it." Had the hadith not been sound, these two imams would not have adopted it, and that is sufficient for you! A free man is killed for killing his own slave. Al-Nakha'i and al-Thawri, in one of his two opinions, said so. It has been said that al-Hasan did not hear from Samurah except the hadith of the 'aqiqah, and God knows best. [They differed concerning retaliation between slaves in matters short of killing. This is the view of 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, Salim ibn 'Abd Allah, al-Zuhri, Qiran [Qiran (with a damma on the qaf and a shadda on the ra') ibn Tammam al-Asadi, who died in the year 181 AH], Malik, al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr. Al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, al-Thawri and Abu Hanifah said: there is no retaliation between them except in killing. Ibn al-Mundhir said: the first view is more sound.] The eleventh issue: al-Daraqutni and Abu 'Isa al-Tirmidhi transmitted from Suraqah ibn Malik, who said: "I was present with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) when he imposed retaliation on a father for his son, but did not impose retaliation on a son for his father." Abu 'Isa said: "This is a hadith we do not know from the narration of Suraqah except through this route, and its chain is not sound. Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash transmitted it from al-Muthanna."

Its chain runs through Ibn al-Sabbah, and al-Muthanna is weak in hadith. This hadith was also related by Abu Khalid al-Ahmar, from al-Hajjaj, from Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, from Umar, from the Prophet ﷺ. It has also been related from Amr ibn Shu'ayb as a mursal (a report lacking a companion in its chain). This hadith contains idtirab (confusion or inconsistency in its transmission). The practice of the scholars according to this is that a father who kills his son is not executed for it, and if he slanders him he is not subjected to the hadd (prescribed punishment).

Ibn al-Mundhir said: The scholars differed concerning a man who deliberately kills his son. One group said: there is no qisas (retaliation) against him, but he owes the diyah (blood money). This is the view of al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq and the Ashab al-Ra'y (the Hanafis), and it is narrated from 'Ata' and Mujahid. Malik, Ibn Nafi' and Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam said: he is to be executed for it. Ibn al-Mundhir said: We hold this view, because of the apparent meaning of the Book and the Sunnah. As for the apparent meaning of the Book, it is the words of the Most High: ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you in the case of the slain: the free for the free, the slave for the slave﴾. And what is established from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is: "The believers' blood is equal" (tatakafa'u dima'uhum). We know of no authentic report that requires excepting the father from the general statement of the verse, and we have transmitted reports on this matter that are not authentic. Ilkiya al-Tabari related from 'Uthman al-Batti that a parent is to be executed for his child, on account of the general statements concerning qisas. Something similar is related from Malik. Perhaps they (al-Batti and Malik) did not accept solitary reports (akhbar al-ahad) against the general statements of the Qur'an.

I say: There is no disagreement in the school of Malik that if a man deliberately kills his son, such as by throwing him down and slaughtering him, or by pinning him (sabr: to hold a person or animal and shoot or stone it until it dies) [[Sabr of a human or other being upon killing: that he is confined and shot at until he dies. In A and J: "or strikes him."]] in a manner for which he has no excuse and there is no doubt about claiming accident, he is to be executed for it, by unanimous opinion. But if he struck him with a weapon out of discipline or anger and killed him, there are two opinions within the school: he is executed for it, or he is not executed for it and the diyah is made heavier; and this is the view of a group of scholars. And a grandfather (al-jaddi) is to be executed for this kind of act.

Ibn al-'Arabi: "I heard our shaykh Fakhr al-Islam al-Shashi say in a discussion: The father is not executed for his son, because the father was the cause of his existence, so how could he be the cause of his non-existence? This is refuted by the case where he commits fornication with his daughter, for he is stoned, though he was the cause of her existence and she would be the cause of his non-existence. [Then what jurisprudence is there in this, and why should he not be the cause of his non-existence when he has disobeyed Allah the Most High in that? [[Addition from Ibn al-'Arabi.]]] They have transmitted from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he said: 'A parent is not to be retaliated against for his child,' but this is a false hadith. Their argument is that Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, ruled for a heavier diyah against the killer of his son, and none of the Companions objected to him. So the jurists, may Allah be pleased with them, took the matter in its general form [[That is, unrestricted and absolute.]], [and they said [[Addition from Ibn al-'Arabi.]]: the parent is not executed for his child]. But Malik took it in its specified and detailed form and said: if he strikes him with a sword, and this is a state that admits of both the intent to kill and its absence, and the compassion of fatherhood is an apparent doubt testifying to the absence of intent to kill, which drops retaliation; but if he pins him down, that uncovers his intent, and so he is joined to the original ruling (of execution)."

Ibn al-Mundhir said: Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq used to say: if the son kills the father, he is executed for him.

Twelfth issue: Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal used this verse as evidence for his view that a group is not executed for one person. He said: Because Allah, glorified is He, stipulated equality, and there is no equality between a group and one person. And the Most High said: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life, and the eye for the eye﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 45]. The answer is that what is meant by qisas in the verse is the killing of whoever kills, regardless of who he is, in response to the Arabs who used to want to kill in retaliation for one who had been killed someone who had not killed, and would kill a hundred in exchange for one, out of pride and reliance on status and power. So Allah, glorified is He, commanded justice and equality, and that is that the killer is killed. Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, executed seven men for one man in San'a' and said: "If the people of San'a' were to collude against him, I would kill them all for him." 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, also killed the Harurites [[al-Harusiyyah: a group of Kharijites named after Harura' (a place near Kufa), because their first gathering and their arbitration took place there.]] for 'Abd Allah ibn Khabbab, for he had delayed fighting them until they committed an act (of hostility); when they slaughtered 'Abd Allah ibn Khabbab as a sheep is slaughtered, and 'Ali was informed of this, he said: "Allahu akbar! Call out to them: bring out to us the killer of 'Abd Allah ibn Khabbab." They said: "We all killed him," three times. Then 'Ali said to his companions: "Take the people," and it was not long before 'Ali and his companions had killed them. Al-Daraqutni recorded the two hadiths in his Sunan. And in al-Tirmidhi, from Abu Sa'id and Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he said: "If the people of the heavens and the people of the earth were to share in the blood of one believer, Allah would hurl them all into the Fire." He said of it: "It is a gharib hadith." Also, if the group knew that when they killed one person they would not be executed, the enemies would cooperate in killing their enemies by sharing in the killing and attain their desire for revenge; and observing this principle is more important than observing the wording. And Allah knows best.

[Ibn al-Mundhir said: al-Zuhri, Habib ibn Abi Thabit and Ibn Sirin said: two are not executed for one. This is related from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, Ibn al-Zubayr and 'Abd al-Malik. Ibn al-Mundhir said: This is the more sound view, and there is no proof for those who permit the execution of a group for one. And it is established from Ibn al-Zubayr what we have mentioned [[What is between the brackets is missing from B, J, Z.]].]

Nineteenth issue: The imams recorded from Abu Shurayh al-Ka'bi, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed, you, the assembly of Khuza'ah, have killed this victim from Hudhayl, and I am responsible for his diyah. Whoever is killed after this statement of mine, his family has a choice between two: they may take the diyah or they may execute (the killer)." This is the wording of Abu Dawud. And al-Tirmidhi said: a hasan sahih hadith. And it is related from Abu Shurayh al-Khuza'i [[Abu Shurayh al-Khuza'i: he is Abu Shurayh al-Ka'bi, and his name is disputed; the well-known view is that it is Khuwaylid ibn 'Amr ibn Sakhr. He embraced Islam on the day of the Conquest.]] from the Prophet ﷺ who said: "Whoever has a victim killed, he has the right to kill or to pardon or to take the diyah." Some scholars held this view, and it is the view of Ahmad and Ishaq.

Fourteenth issue: The scholars differed concerning accepting diyah from the killer in deliberate homicide. One group said: the guardian of the victim has the choice: if he wishes he may take qisas, and if he wishes he may take the diyah, even if the killer does not consent. This is narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, 'Ata' and al-Hasan, and Ashhab related it from Malik; and this is the view of al-Layth, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq and Abu Thawr. Their evidence is the hadith of Abu Shurayh and what has the same meaning, and it is explicit on the point of disagreement. Also, from the standpoint of reasoning: the diyah became binding on him without his consent, because it is an obligation upon him to preserve his own life, and Allah the Most High said: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 29]. As for His words: ﴿whoever is pardoned something by his brother﴾, meaning he leaves his blood-claim for him, according to one interpretation, and is content with the diyah from him; ﴿then pursuit in kindness﴾, meaning the guardian of the blood must pursue the diyah in a reasonable manner, and the killer must pay it to him with good grace, that is, without procrastination or delay beyond the due time; ﴿That is a lightening from your Lord and a mercy﴾, meaning that those before us were not prescribed anything except life for life, so Allah bestowed on this community the diyah if the guardian of the blood agrees to it, as will be explained. Others said: the guardian of the victim has only qisas, and he may not take the diyah unless the killer consents. This was transmitted by Ibn al-Qasim from Malik, and it is the well-known view from him; and al-Thawri and the Kufans held it. They argued with the hadith of Anas concerning the case of al-Rubay' [[al-Rubay' (with a damma on the ra', fath on the ba', shadda on the ta' with kasra after it, and an unpointed ayn): she was the paternal aunt of Anas ibn Malik.]] when the front tooth of a woman was broken, which the imams recorded. They said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ruled for qisas and said, "Qisas is the Book of Allah, qisas is the Book of Allah," and did not give the injured party a choice between qisas and diyah, it was thereby established that what is obligatory in deliberate killing by the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger is qisas. But the first view is more sound, because of the hadith of Abu Shurayh mentioned above. Al-Rabi' related from al-Shafi'i, who said: Abu Hanifah ibn Simak ibn al-Fadl al-Shihabi informed me, and Ibn Abi Dhi'b related to me from al-Maqburi, from Abu Shurayh al-Ka'bi, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said in the year of the Conquest: "Whoever has a victim killed, he has the better of two options: if he wishes he may take the diyah, and if he wishes he has the right of retaliation." Abu Hanifah said: I said to Ibn Abi Dhi'b: "Do you act on this, O Abu al-Harith?" He struck my chest and shouted at me vehemently and abused me, and said: "I relate to you from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and you say: Do you act on it? Yes, I act on it, and that is an obligation upon me and upon whoever hears it. Indeed, Allah, mighty and majestic, chose Muhammad ﷺ from among people and guided them through him and at his hands, and chose for them what He chose for him and through his tongue, so it is incumbent upon creation to follow him, willingly or unwillingly; there is no escape for a Muslim from that." He said: He did not stop with me until I wished he would be silent.

Fifteenth issue: The Most High said: ﴿So whoever is pardoned something by his brother, then pursuit in kindness and payment to him with good grace﴾. The scholars differed concerning the interpretation of "man" (whoever) and "ufiya" (is pardoned) according to five interpretations. The first: "man" refers to the killer, "ufiya" implies that the one pardoning is the guardian of the blood, the "brother" is the victim, and "shay'" (something) is the blood that is pardoned and reverts to taking the diyah. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Mujahid and a group of scholars. In this view, pardon retains its original meaning, which is leaving (remitting). The meaning is: if the guardian of the victim pardons the killer for the blood of the victim and waives qisas, then he takes the diyah, pursuing it in a reasonable manner, and the killer pays it to him with good grace.

The second, which is the view of Malik: "man" refers to the guardian, "ufiya" means made easy (not in its literal sense of pardon), the "brother" refers to the killer, and "shay'" is the diyah. That is, if the guardian inclines toward pardoning qisas in exchange for the diyah, the killer is given the choice between paying it or surrendering himself; thus sometimes it is made easy and sometimes it is not. Other than Malik say: if the guardians are content with the diyah, the killer has no choice, but it is binding upon him. This view is related from Malik, and many of his companions preferred it. Abu Hanifah said: the meaning of "ufiya" is "budhila" (was given), and pardon in the language means giving, and for this reason Allah the Most High said: ﴿Take the pardon﴾ [al-A'raf: 199], meaning what is easy. Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali said:

"Take the pardon from me, that my affection may endure"

[And he said, [[What is between the two brackets is in manuscript ḥ and is missing from all other manuscripts.]] ﷺ: "The beginning of the time is Allah's good pleasure, and its end is Allah's pardon"] meaning that Allah bears witness over His servants. It is as if He said: whoever is offered some of the blood money (diyya) should accept it and pursue it fairly. Others said: the killer should pay it to him with good conduct. So Allah, exalted is He, urged the taking of the wealth when the killer makes it easy to do so, and informed that this is a lightening from Him and a mercy, as He said after mentioning retaliation (qisas) in Surat al-Ma'idah: ﴿But whoever forgoes it, it is an expiation for him﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 45]. So He urged the mercy of pardon and charity. Likewise, in this verse He urged acceptance of the blood money when the offender offers it by paying the diyya, then He commanded the guardian (walī) to follow up, and commanded the offender to pay with good conduct.

Some people said: these expressions all concern the specific individuals about whom the verse was revealed, and they waived the blood money between themselves by mutual retaliation (muqāṣṣa). The meaning of the verse is: whoever has an excess of some of those blood payments over the other party, then let him... and "ʿufiya" would mean "fuḍila" (was given an excess).

[Sufyān ibn Ḥusayn ibn Shawdhab narrated from al-Shaʿbī, who said: There was fighting between two tribes of the Arabs, and people were killed from both sides. One of the two tribes said: "We will not be satisfied until a man is killed for a woman and a woman for a man." So they brought the matter to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he, peace be upon him, said: "Killing is equal." So they agreed on blood money, and one of the two tribes had an excess over the other. This is His saying: "It is prescribed" up to His saying: "and whoever is pardoned anything by his brother" — meaning, whoever has an excess over his brother, let him pay it with fairness. Thus al-Shaʿbī informed about the occasion of the revelation of the verse, and Sufyān mentioned that "al-ʿafw" here means "al-faḍl" (the excess), which is a meaning the wording can bear.]

A fifth interpretation [[It should be noted that the author, may Allah have mercy on him, did not mention the third and fourth interpretations.]] — this is the view of ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, and al-Ḥasan, concerning the excess between the blood money of a man and a woman, and of a free person and a slave. That is, whoever has that excess should follow up fairly, and "ʿufiya" in this place also means "fuḍila" (was given an excess).

The sixteenth matter: This verse is an exhortation from Allah, exalted is He, to good conduct in demanding by the claimant and good conduct in payment by the one who pays. Is that obligatory or recommended? The reading in the nominative (al-rafʿ), ﴿fa-ittibāʿun﴾, indicates obligation, because the meaning is: "then upon him is following up fairly." Al-Naḥḥās said: "Whoever is pardoned" is a conditional clause, and the response is "ittibāʿun" [fa-ittibāʿun], which is in the nominative by being a subject (mubtada'), and the implied meaning is: upon him is following up fairly. In other than the Qur'an it may be read "ittibāʿan" and "adāʾan," making them both verbal nouns (maṣdar) in the accusative. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: Ibrahim ibn Abi ʿAbla read "fa-ittibāʿan" in the accusative. The nominative indicates what is obligatory, as in His saying: ﴿Then retention in kindness﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 229]. As for what is recommended, it comes in the accusative, as in His saying: ﴿So strike the necks﴾ [Muhammad: 4].

The seventeenth matter: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is a lightening from your Lord and a mercy﴾, because the People of the Torah had retaliation (qiṣāṣ/qawad) and had nothing other than that, while the People of the Gospel had pardon and had neither retaliation nor blood money. So Allah made that a lightening for this nation: whoever wills may kill, whoever wills may take the blood money, and whoever wills may pardon.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But whoever transgresses after that, for him there is a painful punishment﴾ — the conditional clause and its response. That is, he kills after taking the blood money and the blood of the killer's guardian's [victim] has been waived. "For him there is a painful punishment." Al-Ḥasan said: In the Jahiliyya, when a man killed a victim, he fled to his people, and his people came and made peace by blood money. Then the victim's guardian would say: "I accept the blood money," until the killer felt safe and came out, and then he would kill him and then throw the blood money to them.

The scholars differed concerning the one who kills after taking the blood money. A group of scholars, including Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī, said: he is like one who kills initially; if the guardian wills he may kill him, and if he wills he may pardon him, and his punishment is in the Hereafter. Qatādah, ʿIkrimah, al-Suddī and others said: his punishment is that he is killed absolutely, and the ruler does not allow the guardian to pardon. Abū Dāwūd narrated from Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "May I not pardon [aʿfā] the one who kills after taking the blood money." [Aʿfā: from ʿafā the thing, when it increased and grew; this is a supplication against him, meaning: may his wealth not increase and may he not become rich.] Al-Ḥasan said: his punishment is that he returns the blood money only, and his sin remains for the punishment of the Hereafter. ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: his matter is for the imam, who does with him what he sees fit.

In Sunan al-Dāraquṭnī, from Abū Shurayḥ al-Khuzāʿī, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Whoever is afflicted by blood or by injury [khabl — and khabl is lameness] has a choice among three things. If he wants a fourth, then restrain him by the hands: [he may choose] between retaliation, or pardon, or taking the compensation [ʿaql]. If he accepts any of those, and then transgresses after that, then for him is the Fire, abiding therein forever."

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 2, verse 179:

There are four issues in this verse.

The first concerns His saying, ﴿And in retribution (al-qisas) there is life for you﴾. This is from eloquent and concise speech, as has already been explained. Its meaning is: none of you should kill another. This was related by Sufyan from al-Suddi, from Abu Malik. The meaning is that when retribution is carried out and the ruling in it is enforced, whoever intends to kill another is deterred, fearing that retribution will be exacted from him, and so both of them live. The Arabs, when one man killed another, would become enraged, their tribes would fight one another, and this would lead to the killing of large numbers. When God legislated retribution, everyone was content with it and abandoned fighting, and so they had life in it.

The second issue: the jurists of legal opinion (a'immat al-fatwa) agree that it is not permissible for anyone to exact his right from another without the ruler (al-sultan). People may not exact retribution from one another. It belongs only to the ruler or to whomever the ruler appoints for this purpose. For this reason God placed the ruler to restrain people's hands from one another.

The third issue: the scholars unanimously agree that the ruler must exact retribution from himself if he wrongs any of his subjects, since he is one of them. His only distinction is that he watches over their interests, like a guardian (wasi) or an agent (wakil), and this does not prevent retribution. There is no difference between them and the common people in the rulings of God, the Mighty and Majestic, due to His saying, ﴿Retribution is prescribed for you in cases of killing﴾. It is also established from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said to a man who complained to him that an official had cut off his hand: "If you are truthful, I will certainly have you retaliate against him." Al-Nasa'i related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: While the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was distributing something, a man rushed at him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) struck him with a palm-stalk (u'rjun) that he had with him. The man cried out, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Come and retaliate." He said: "Rather, I forgive you, O Messenger of Allah."

Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi related from Abu Firas, who said: Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, delivered a sermon and said: "Whoever has been wronged by his commander, let him raise it to me, and I will have him retaliate against him." Then Amr ibn al-As stood up and said: "O Commander of the Faithful, if a man among us disciplines a man from among his subjects, will you exact retaliation from him?" He said: "How could I not exact it from him, when I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) exact retaliation from himself!"

The wording of Abu Dawud al-Sijistani, from him, is: Umar ibn al-Khattab addressed us and said: "I did not send my agents to beat your skins or to take your wealth. Whoever has been treated thus, let him raise it to me, and I will exact retaliation from him." He mentioned the hadith in meaning.

The fourth issue concerns His saying, ﴿so that you may have taqwa﴾. Its meaning has already been explained (see vol. 1, p. 226 and following, second edition). Here it means: that you may refrain from killing, and so be safe from retribution. Then this becomes a motive toward various kinds of taqwa in other matters, since God rewards obedience with further obedience.

Abu al-Jawza' Aws ibn Abd Allah al-Rabi'i recited, ﴿And in retribution (al-qasas) there is life for you﴾. Al-Nahhas said: the recitation of Abu al-Jawza' is shadhdh (an irregular, non-canonical reading). Others said: it may be a verbal noun (masdar) like al-qisas. It was also said: by al-qasas he meant the Qur'an, that is, in the Book of God, in which the narratives (al-qasas) were legislated, there is life for you, that is, salvation (najah).

**Issue 1:** It contains twenty-one issues. The first concerns the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Prescribed for you﴾. This is the verse of bequest (wasiyyah). There is no mention of bequest in the Qur'an except in this verse, [and in "al-Nisa'": "after a bequest" [[See vol. 5, p. 73.]] [An-Nisa': 12], and in "al-Ma'idah": "when the bequest" [[See vol. 6, p. 348.]] [Al-Ma'idah: 106]. The one in al-Baqarah is the most complete and perfect of them. [It was revealed before the laws of inheritance and shares were revealed, as will be explained.] In the sentence there is an implied conjunction "wa" (and), meaning "and it is prescribed for you," but when the sentence was long, the "wa" was dropped. A similar case, according to some opinions, is the words: ﴿None will enter it except the most wretched, who denied and turned away﴾ [[See vol. 20, p. 86.]] [Al-Layl: 15-16], meaning "and the one who," so it was omitted. It has also been said: when it was mentioned that the victim's guardian has the right to retaliate, this [person] who is about to be retaliated against, and whose act is the cause of death, is as if death has come to him; so this is the time for bequest. Thus the verse is connected to what precedes it and linked to it, which is why the conjunction was dropped. The word "kutiba" means "was obligated and established," as previously mentioned [[See p. 244 of this part.]]. The "presence of death" means its causes. Whenever the cause is present, the Arabs use it to refer to the effect. Their poet said:

*O rider who urges on his mount,*
*ask the Banu Asad what this clamor is.*

[[The word "sawt" (clamor) is masculine, but here it is made feminine because the poet meant by it the noise and uproar, in the sense of a cry. (From al-Lisan).]]

*Say to them: hasten with your excuse and seek a word that will clear you, for I am Death.*

And 'Antarah said:

*Death is at the command of my hand whenever I clasp its fingertips with an Indian sword.*

And Jarir said in his satire against al-Farazdaq:

*I am the Death you have heard of,*
*so there is no escape for one who flees from me.*

**Issue 2:** If it is asked: why did He say "kutiba" (was prescribed) and not "kataibtu" (I prescribed), when "wasiyyah" (bequest) is feminine? It is said in reply: that is because He meant by "wasiyyah" the act of bequeathing. It has also been said: because a separating element intervened, and the separating element served as a substitute for the feminine ending "ta'," as the Arabs say: "The judge came today, a woman." Sibawayh has also related: "Stood a woman." But the good usage of this is only with a long intervening separation.

**Issue 3:** The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿If he leaves behind good﴾. "In" (if) is a conditional particle. Concerning its answer (jawab), Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash has two opinions. Al-Akhfash said: the implied meaning is "then the bequest," and then the "fa'" (then) was dropped, as the poet said:

*Whoever does good deeds, Allah will reward them,*
*and evil with evil is equal in the sight of Allah.*

The second answer is that the past tense may have its response both before and after it. The sense would then be: "the bequest is for the parents and the relatives, if he leaves wealth." If you take the *fa'* as present, then *al-wasiyyah* (the bequest) is in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence. If you do not take the *fa'* as present, you may still make *al-wasiyyah* the subject of a nominal sentence, or make it the deputy subject of the passive verb, meaning "the bequest has been prescribed for you." According to the majority of grammarians, *al-wasiyyah* cannot govern *idha* (when), because *idha* is in the position of a relative clause for the verbal noun *al-wasiyyah*, which has already come before it, so it cannot govern a word that precedes it. The governing word for *idha* may be *kutiba* (it has been prescribed), and the meaning is: the command of God has been directed at you, and the requirement of His Book takes effect when death approaches. The verb is expressed as *kutiba* to convey that the obligation is directed at them, and in order to include the further sense that it is written in eternity. The governing word for *idha* may also be an implied verb of bequeathing (*al-iya'*) indicated by *al-wasiyyah*, meaning: "the bequeathing has been prescribed for you, then."

The fourth point concerns God's words ﴿khayran﴾ (wealth). Here *al-khayr* means wealth, without any disagreement. The scholars differed over its amount. It was said that it means a large amount of wealth, which is reported from ʿAli, ʿAʾishah and Ibn ʿAbbas, and they said seven hundred dinars is a small amount. Qatadah reported from al-Hasan that *khayr* means a thousand dinars or more. Al-Shaʿbi said it is between five hundred dinars and a thousand.

*Al-wasiyyah* is an expression for anything that a person is commanded to do and entrusted with during life and after death. Custom has restricted it to what is entrusted to be carried out after death. Its plural is *wasaya*, like *qadaya*, the plural of *qadiyyah*. The *wasi* (executor) may be the one who bequeathes or the one to whom the bequest is made, and its root is from *wasa*, in its lightened form. *Tawassa al-nabt* means the plants became interconnected, when they grew together. *Ard wasiyah* means land with interconnected vegetation. *Awsaytu lahu bi-shay'* means I bequeathed something to him, and *awsaytu ilayhi* means I made him my executor, by making him your *wasiy*. The noun is *al-wisayah* and *al-wisayah* (with kasra and fatha). *Awsaytuhu* and *wassaytuhu* also mean the same thing in the verbal noun *tawsiyah*, and the noun is *al-wusat*. *Tawassa al-qawm* means some of them bequeathed to others. In a hadith: "Advise one another to treat women well, for they are *ʿawan* (captives) with you." *ʿAwan* is the plural of *ʿaniyah*, meaning the captive; the meaning is that they are with you in the position of prisoners. *Wassaytu al-shay' bi-kadha* means I joined the thing to that.

The fifth point concerns the scholars' disagreement over whether the bequest is obligatory for one who leaves wealth, after they had agreed that it is obligatory for one who has deposits held for others or debts owed. Most scholars hold that the bequest is not obligatory for one who has none of these, and this is the view of Malik, al-Shafiʿi and al-Thawri, whether the testator was wealthy or poor. A group said: the bequest is obligatory according to the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. This is the view of al-Zuhri and Abu Mijlaz, whether the wealth was little or much. Abu Thawr said: the bequest is not obligatory except for a man who owes a debt or holds money belonging to people. It is obligatory for him to write his bequest and to declare what he owes. As for one who has no debt and holds no deposit, the bequest is not obligatory for him unless he wishes it. Ibn al-Mundhir said: this is good, because God has required the return of trusts to their owners, and one who has no right owed and no trust in his keeping is not obliged to make a bequest.

The earlier scholars argued with what the imams narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "No Muslim man has anything he wants to bequeath about which he should spend two nights without his bequest written and kept with him." In another narration, "three nights." In one of these narrations, ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar said: "Not a single night has passed over me since I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say that without my bequest being with me."

Those who did not make it obligatory argued: if it were obligatory, He would not have made it dependent on the testator's wish, and it would be binding in every case. Furthermore, even if its apparent meaning is obligation, the view that it is obligatory for one who has such (debts or deposits) rejects that, and that applies to one who owes rights to people and fears losing them for them, as Abu Thawr said. Likewise if he has rights held by people and fears their loss to the heirs; then the bequest is obligatory for him, and there is no disagreement about this. If it is said: God has said, ﴿It is prescribed for you﴾, and *kutiba* means *furida* (was made obligatory), which indicates the obligation of the bequest. It is said to them: the answer to this has already been given earlier in the verse, and the meaning is: "if you wish to make a bequest"; and God knows best.

Al-Nakhaʿi said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) died without making a bequest, and Abu Bakr made a bequest. If one makes a bequest, it is good, and if one does not make a bequest, there is nothing upon him.

The sixth point: God did not specify in His Book the amount of wealth to be bequeathed, but He only said, ﴿if he leaves wealth﴾, and *al-khayr* means wealth, as in His words: ﴿and whatever wealth you spend﴾ [al-Baqarah: 272], and ﴿and indeed he is intense in his love of wealth﴾ [al-ʿAdiyat: 8]. The scholars differed over this amount. It is reported from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may God be pleased with him) that he bequeathed one-fifth. ʿAli (may God be pleased with him) said: from the spoils of the Muslims, one-fifth. Maʿmar reported from Qatadah: ʿUmar bequeathed one-quarter. al-Bukhari mentioned it from Ibn ʿAbbas. It is reported from ʿAli (may God be pleased with him) that he said: "To bequeath one-fifth is dearer to me than to bequeath one-quarter, and to bequeath one-quarter is better for me than to bequeath one-third." A group chose, for one whose wealth is little and who has heirs, to abstain from making a bequest. This is reported from ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿAʾishah, may God be pleased with them all. Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from the hadith of Ibn Abi Mulaykah from ʿAʾishah that a man said to her: "I wish to make a bequest." She said: "How much is your wealth?" He said: "Three thousand." She said: "How many dependents do you have?" He said: "Four." She said: "God the Exalted says: ﴿if he leaves wealth﴾, and this is a small amount, so leave it for your dependents, for that is better for you."

The seventh point: most scholars hold that it is not permissible for anyone to bequeath more than one-third, except Abu Hanifah and his companions. They said: if the testator leaves no heirs, it is permissible for him to bequeath all his wealth. They said: restricting the bequest to one-third was only so that his heirs might be left wealthy, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "That you leave your heirs wealthy is better than leaving them dependent, begging from people," the hadith, which the imams narrated. One who has no heir is not among those intended by the hadith. This view is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Abu ʿUbaydah and Masruq said the same, and Ishaq and Malik in one of his two opinions held it, and it is reported from ʿAli. The cause of the disagreement, together with what we have mentioned, is the disagreement over whether the public treasury (*bayt al-mal*) is an heir or a keeper of what is placed in it, two opinions.

The eighth point: the scholars agreed that whoever dies leaving heirs may not bequeath all his wealth. It is reported from ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs (may God be pleased with him) that when death approached him, he said to his son ʿAbdullah: "I wish to make a bequest." He said to him: "Make your bequest, and your wealth is part of my wealth." So he called a scribe and dictated. ʿAbdullah said: "I said to him: I do not see you but that you have encroached upon my wealth and yours. Had you called my brothers and sought their pardon."

The ninth point: the scholars agreed that a person may change his bequest and retract whatever part of it he wishes, except that they differed concerning the *mudabbar* (a slave freed upon his master's death). Malik (may God have mercy on him) said: "The matter agreed upon among us is that if the testator makes a bequest in his health or sickness that includes manumission of one of his slaves or something else, he may change whatever he wishes of it and do with it what he chooses until he dies. If he wishes to abandon that bequest and cancel it, he may do so, except that if he has made a slave *mudabbar*, then there is no way for him to change what he has made *mudabbar*. This is because the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'No Muslim man has anything he wants to bequeath about which he should spend two nights without his bequest written and kept with him.'"

Abu al-Faraj al-Maliki said: analogically, the *mudabbar* is like one freed upon a fixed term, because it is a term that inevitably comes. They agreed that one cannot retract an oath of manumission, and manumission upon a term is likewise; so is the *mudabbar*. This is the view of Abu Hanifah. Al-Shafiʿi, Ahmad and Ishaq said: it is a bequest, because they agreed that it is within the one-third like the other bequests. The permission they gave for intercourse with a female *mudabbar* contradicts their analogy of the *mudabbar* to manumission upon a term. It is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) sold a *mudabbar*, and that ʿAʾishah made a slave-girl of hers *mudabbar* and then sold her. This is also the view of a group of the Successors (*tabiʿun*). A group said: a man may change whatever he wishes of his bequest except manumission. This is what al-Shaʿbi, Ibn Sirin, Ibn Shubrumah and al-Nakhaʿi said, and it is the view of Sufyan al-Thawri.

The tenth point: they differed concerning a man who says to his slave: "You are free after my death," intending a bequest. According to Malik, he may retract that. If he says: "So-and-so is *mudabbar* after my death," he may not retract it. If he intended *tadbir* (making a slave *mudabbar*) by his first statement, he also may not retract it, according to most of Malik's companions. As for al-Shafiʿi, Ahmad, Ishaq and Abu Thawr, all of this is a bequest according to them, because it is within the one-third, and whatever is within the one-third is a bequest. However, al-Shafiʿi said: retraction concerning the *mudabbar* does not happen except by taking him out of his ownership through sale or gift. His saying, "I have retracted," is not a retraction, and even if he does not take the *mudabbar* out of his ownership until he dies, he is freed upon his death. In his older view he said: one may retract concerning the *mudabbar* as one may retract a bequest. Al-Muzani chose this, by analogy with their agreement that one may retract concerning one who bequeathed his manumission. Abu Thawr said: if he says, "I have retracted concerning my *mudabbar*," the *tadbir* is void, and if he dies he is not freed.

Ibn al-Qasim and Ashhab differed concerning one who says: "My slave is free after my death," without intending a bequest or *tadbir*. Ibn al-Qasim said: it is a bequest. Ashhab said: it is *mudabbar*, even if he did not intend a bequest.

The eleventh point: the scholars differed over whether this verse is abrogated (*mansukh*) or clear and not abrogated (*muhkam*). It was said: it is *muhkam*; its apparent meaning is general, but its intended meaning is specific to the two parents who do not inherit, such as the two disbelieving parents and the two slave parents, and to relatives other than heirs. This was said by al-Dahhak, Tawus and al-Hasan, and al-Tabari chose it. It is reported from al-Zuhri that the bequest is obligatory whether the wealth is little or much. Ibn al-Mundhir said: all the people of knowledge whom we have from them agreed that a bequest to the two parents who do not inherit, and to the relatives who do not inherit, is permissible. Ibn ʿAbbas said:

Al-Hasan and Qatadah also said: the verse is general, and the ruling was established by it for a period of time, and every heir who would inherit under the verses of inheritance (ayat al-fara'id) was abrogated (naskh) from it. It has also been said that the verse of inheritance did not abrogate it on its own, but together with another text, namely his saying ﷺ: "Allah has given every person with a right his right, so there is no bequest to an heir." Abu Umamah narrated it, and al-Tirmidhi recorded it and said: "This is a hasan sahih hadith." So the abrogation of the verse was by the established Sunnah and not by inheritance, according to the sounder of the scholars' opinions. Were it not for this hadith, it would have been possible to reconcile the two verses by having people take the property from the deceased by bequest, and by inheritance if he did not bequeath, or what remained after the bequest. But this hadith and the consensus (ijma') prevent that. Al-Shafi'i and Abu al-Faraj, although they both prohibited abrogating the Book by the Sunnah, the sounder view is that it is permissible, on the proof that all of it is the command of Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, and from Him, even if the names differ. This meaning has already been mentioned [[See item 65 of this part.]]. Although this report reached us as a single-transmission report (ahad), the consensus of the Muslims has joined it, that a bequest to an heir is not permitted. It is thus clear that the obligation of bequest to the closest relatives who are heirs has been abrogated by the Sunnah, and that the consensus rests upon it. And Allah knows best.

Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said: the bequest to parents was abrogated by the obligatory shares in Surah al-Nisa', and it remained for the closest relatives who do not inherit. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, most of the Malikis, and a group of scholars. In al-Bukhari, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, he said: "Property belonged to the child, and the bequest was for the parents. Then part of that was abrogated: the male was given the share equal to two females, the parents were each given a sixth, the wife was given an eighth or a quarter, and the husband a half or a quarter."

Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd said: the whole verse is abrogated, and the bequest remained as a recommendation (nadb). Something similar is the view of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him. al-Nahhas reported it from al-Sha'bi and al-Nakha'i.

Al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym [[Khuthaym: its first letter is pronounced with a damma and the mutaqqal letter with a fatha, as in al-Taqrib. In al-Khulasah, it is with a fatha on the mu'jamah and the thaa' with a silent yaa' between them.]] said: there is no bequest. 'Urwah ibn Thabit said: I said to al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym, "Bequeath your Qur'an-copy to me." He looked at his child and recited: ﴿And those of blood ties are closer to one another in the Book of Allah﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 58.]] [al-Anfal: 75]. Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, did something similar.

Twelfth issue: The words of the Exalted: ﴿and the closest relatives﴾. Al-aqrabun is the plural of aqrab. Some people said: a bequest to the closest relatives takes priority over strangers, because of the explicit text of Allah regarding them. Al-Dahhak even said: if someone bequeaths to someone other than his relatives, he has ended his deeds with disobedience. It is reported from Ibn 'Umar [[In manuscripts B and J: "from 'Umar." The known fact is that our master 'Umar died in debt.]] that he bequeathed to the mothers of his children, to each one four thousand. It is reported that 'A'ishah bequeathed household furniture to a freedwoman of hers. Similar is reported from Salim ibn 'Abd Allah. al-Hasan said: if someone bequeaths to someone other than the closest relatives, the bequest is returned to the closest relatives. If it was for a stranger, it is shared with them, and it is not permitted for anyone else while they are left out. When Abu al-'Aliyah died, people said: "How strange! A woman from the tribe of Riyah freed him, and he bequeathed his property to the Banu Hashim!" al-Sha'bi said: "He had no right to that, and there is no honor in it." Tawus said: if he bequeaths to someone other than his relatives, the bequest is returned to his relatives and his act is annulled. Jabir ibn Zayd said the same, and similar is reported from al-Hasan too, and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh said so. Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah and his companions, al-Awza'i and Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: whoever bequeaths to someone other than his relatives while leaving his needy relatives has done a bad thing. Yet his act remains permissible and binding for each person he bequeathed to, whether rich or poor, near or distant, Muslim or disbeliever. This is the meaning of what is reported from Ibn 'Umar and 'A'ishah, and it is the view of Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas.

I say: the first view is better. As for Abu al-'Aliyah, may Allah be pleased with him, perhaps he considered that the Banu Hashim had a greater claim than his freedwoman, because of his companionship with Ibn 'Abbas, his teaching him, and his elevation to the rank of scholars in this world and the next. This fatherhood, though it is spiritual, is the true one, and his freedwoman's merit is only that she placed him among the free in this world, so her reward for freeing him suffices her. And Allah knows best.

Thirteenth issue: The majority of scholars held that a sick person is restricted in his property (yuhjar 'alayhi), while the people of the apparent meaning (Ahl al-Zahir) deviated, saying: he is not restricted, and he is like the healthy. The hadith and the reasoning refute them. Sa'd said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ visited me during the Farewell Pilgrimage from an illness from which I came close to death. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, my illness has reached what you see, and I have wealth, and only one daughter inherits from me. Shall I give away two-thirds of my wealth in charity?' He said: 'No.' I said: 'Shall I give away half of it?' He said: 'No. A third, and a third is a lot. It is better that you leave your heirs wealthy than that you leave them poor, begging from people'" [and the rest of the hadith]. The people of the apparent meaning also prohibited bequeathing more than a third, even if the heirs permit it. The majority permitted it if the heirs permit it, and this is the sounder view, because a sick person is only prevented from bequeathing more than a third for the right of the heir. So if the heirs waive their right, it is permissible and valid, and it is like a gift from them. al-Daraqutni narrated on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "A bequest to an heir is not permitted unless the heirs wish." And it is reported from 'Amr ibn Kharijah who said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There is no bequest to an heir unless the heirs permit it."

Fourteenth issue: They differed regarding the retraction, after the testator's death, of those who permitted a bequest to an heir during the testator's lifetime. One group said: it is binding on them, and they have no right to retract it. This is the view of 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, Tawus, al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Zuhri, Rabi'ah and al-Awza'i. Another group said: they have the right to retract if they wish. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Shurayh, al-Hakam, Tawus, al-Thawri, al-Hasan ibn Salih, Abu Hanifah, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Abu Thawr, and Ibn al-Mundhir chose it. Malik made a distinction, saying: if they gave permission while he was healthy, they may retract; but if they gave permission to him during his illness, when he was restricted from his property, then it is binding on them. This is also the view of Ishaq.

The proponents of the first view argued that the prohibition came only for the sake of the heirs, so when they permit it, it is valid. They also agreed that if someone bequeaths more than a third to a stranger, it is valid by their permission, so it is the same here. The proponents of the second view argued that they permitted something they did not own at that time, since property is owned only after the testator's death. The heir who gave permission may die before him and not be an heir, and someone else may inherit him, so one who had no right gave permission, and nothing is binding on him. Malik argued: if a man is healthy, he has the most right to all his property and may dispose of it as he wishes. So if the heirs give him permission while he is healthy, they have waived something that was not due to them. But if they give him permission during his illness, they have waived a right that was due to them. So they have no right to retract it once he has executed it, because it has already taken effect.

Fifteenth issue: If the sick person does not execute that, the heir may retract it, because it has not become final by execution. This was stated by al-Abhari. Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ishaq ibn Rahawayh that Malik's view on this issue is more consistent with the Sunnah than others. Ibn al-Mundhir said: the views of Malik, al-Thawri, the Kufans, al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr agree that if they permit it after his death, it binds them.

Sixteenth issue: They differed regarding a man who bequeaths property to one of his heirs and says in his bequest: "If the heirs permit it, it is for him; if they do not permit it, it goes to the cause of Allah." The heirs did not permit it. Malik said: if the heirs do not permit it, it reverts to them. According to the view of al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah and Ma'mar, the companion of 'Abd al-Razzaq, it goes to the cause of Allah.

Seventeenth issue: There is no disagreement regarding the bequest of a sane adult who is not restricted. They differed regarding others. Malik said: "The matter agreed upon among us is that the weak-minded, the foolish, and the afflicted who recovers at times, their bequests are permitted if they have enough sense to know what they bequeath. Likewise a young child who understands what he bequeaths and does not say anything objectionable, his bequest is permitted and binding." Abu Hanifah and his companions said: the bequest of a child is not permitted. al-Muzani said: this is the analogy of al-Shafi'i's view, but I did not find anything from al-Shafi'i on this that he stated explicitly. His companions differed on two views: one like Malik's, and the other like Abu Hanifah's. Their argument is that his divorce is not valid, nor is his manumission, nor is retaliation taken from him for a crime, nor is he punished for slander, so he is not like the adult restricted from his property, and so his bequest is likewise not valid.

Abu 'Umar said: these scholars agreed that the bequest of an adult restricted from his property is permitted. It is known that a child who understands what he bequeaths is in the same position as one restricted in his property, and the reason for restriction is the squandering and wasting of property, which is a cause that ends with death. He resembles the restricted person more than the insane person who does not understand. So his bequest must be permitted, along with the report that came from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. Malik said: it is the matter agreed upon among them in Medina. And success is from Allah.

Muhammad ibn Shurayh said: whoever bequeaths, whether young or old, and hits the truth, then Allah has decreed it upon his tongue, and there is no repelling of the truth.

Eighteenth issue

Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 180 (part 4 of 4):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿bil-ma'ruf﴾ (in a fair manner) means with justice, with no deficiency in it and no excess. This was left to the discretion of the deceased and the judgment of the testator. Then God, glory be to Him, determined that amount through the tongue of His Prophet, peace be upon him, who said: "The third, and the third is much." The positions of the scholars on this have already been mentioned earlier. And the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God has granted you a charity from a third of your wealth at the time of your death, as an addition to your good deeds, so that He may make it a purification (zakah) for you." (Recorded by al-Daraqutni from Abu Umamah, from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, from the Prophet (ﷺ).)

Al-Hasan said: a bequest is not valid except within a third. This is also the view of al-Bukhari, who cited as evidence the verse: ﴿And judge between them by what God has revealed﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 49]. [[See vol. 6, p. 212.]] The Prophet's (ﷺ) ruling that a third is much is the ruling by what God has revealed. Whoever exceeds what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) set as a limit and bequeaths more than a third has done what the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade, and by such an act he is disobedient if he knows the ruling of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

Al-Shafi'i said: His saying "the third is much" means that it is not little.

The nineteenth matter: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿haqqan﴾ (as an obligation) means established, an established matter of prudence and caution, not an established matter of obligation and duty. This is shown by His saying: ﴿upon the God-fearing﴾, and this indicates that it is recommended, for if it were obligatory it would be upon all Muslims. Since God restricted it to those who are mindful (yattaqi), that is, who fear falling short, this shows that it is not binding except where its loss is anticipated should one die. In that case it becomes obligatory to hasten to write it and to make a bequest concerning it, because if one remains silent about it, that would be neglect of it and a shortcoming on his part. This meaning has already been mentioned. "Haqqan" is in the accusative as an emphatic verbal noun (masdar mu'akkid). Outside the Qur'an it may be read "haqqun," meaning "that is a truth."

The twentieth matter: The scholars said: the hastening to write a bequest is not derived from this verse; rather it is from the hadith of Ibn Umar. Its benefit lies in exaggerating in securing the matter further and in its being written and attested to, and this is the bequest on which practice is agreed. If he calls upon upright witnesses and they bear witness to it verbally, it is acted upon even if it is not written down. If he writes it in his own hand without calling witnesses, there is no disagreement in the view of Malik that it is not acted upon except for what it contains of acknowledgment of a right in favour of one who is not suspected in it, in which case its execution is binding.

The twenty-first matter: al-Daraqutni narrated from Anas ibn Malik, who said: "They used to write at the head of their bequests: 'This is what so-and-so son of so-and-so bequeaths: that he bears witness that there is no god but God alone, without partner, and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger, and that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt in it, and that God will raise those who are in the graves. And he enjoins upon those he leaves behind of his family the fear of God, as is His due, and that they set right their affairs among themselves, and obey God and His Messenger if they are believers, and he enjoins upon them what Abraham enjoined upon his sons and Jacob: "O my sons, God has chosen for you the religion, so do not die except as Muslims."'"

**Fourth issue (*masa'il*)**: It contains four issues.

**The first issue:** The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿Whoever alters it﴾, form a conditional clause (*shart*). Its response (*jawab*) is "then its sin falls only upon those who alter it." The *ma* is a *kafffa* (a particle that prevents the governing particle from operating) for *inna*, so it stops *inna* from governing its noun. "Ithmuhu" (its sin) is in the nominative as the subject (*mubtada'*), and "upon those who alter it" occupies the position of the predicate (*khabar*). The pronoun in "baddalahu" (alters it) refers to the bequest (*al-iy~sa'*), because *al-wasiyyah* (the bequest) has the sense of *al-i~sa'* (the instruction). The pronoun in "sami'ahu" (heard it) is similar. It is like His saying, ﴿Whoever has received an admonition from his Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 275], meaning "an exhortation" (*wa'z*). And His saying, ﴿When the division is attended﴾ [an-Nisa': 8], meaning "the property," as shown by His saying "from it" (*minhu*). A similar usage is the poet's line:

"What is this *al-sawt*?"

meaning "the cry" (*al-sayhah*). Imru' al-Qays said:

"A slender, soft, tender woman, like the shoot of a fresh *al-ban* tree that has sprouted."

*Al-barhar­hah* means one with delicate skin, or one with smooth, shining skin. *Al-ru'dah* and *al-ra'udah* mean a beautiful young woman, quick in youth and of good nourishment. *Al-rakhsah* means gentle in disposition. *Al-kharu'ubah* means a tender, supple young shoot. *Al-banah* refers to the *al-ban* tree.

*Al-munfatir* means swollen with leaves, and this is at its most luxuriant. He referred to the shoot and left out the word *kharu'ubah*. The pronoun in "sami'ahu" may mean that he heard it from the executor (*al-wasi*) himself, or that he heard it from someone through whom the matter is established for him. Both are acceptable, as they are two just witnesses. The pronoun in "ithmuhu" refers back to the alteration, meaning that the sin of the alteration falls on the one who alters it, not on the deceased. The testator is free from blame by the bequest, and the obligation is placed on the heir or guardian. It has also been said: if this testator is changed, that is, the bequest is abandoned or not carried out in the manner prescribed by the Shari'ah, then the sin is upon him.

**The second issue:** This verse is evidence that if the deceased bequeaths a debt, he is released from his obligation to it, and the guardian becomes responsible for it. He receives the reward for paying it and bears the burden for delaying it. Al-Qadi Abu Bakr Ibn al-'Arabi said: "This is valid only if the deceased did not neglect to pay it. But if he was able to pay it and left it undone, and then made a bequest concerning it, the guardian's neglect does not remove it from his obligation."

**The third issue:** There is no disagreement that if someone bequeaths something impermissible, such as wine, pork, or any sin, then it is permissible to alter it, and it is not permissible to carry it out, just as it is not permissible to carry out anything exceeding one-third. This was stated by Abu 'Umar.

**The fourth issue:** The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾, are two attributes of Allah the Exalted, by which nothing of the deviation (*janf*) of the testators or the alteration of the transgressors remains hidden.

There are six issues (masa'il) in this verse.

The first: God's words, "fa-man khafa" ("whoever fears"). "Man" is a conditional particle, and "khafa" means "feared" (khashiya). It is also said to mean "knew" ('alima). The original form is "khawifa," and the waw was changed to alif because it is vowelled and the letter before it is vowelled too. The people of Kufa pronounce "khafa" with imala (inclination toward the vowel i), to indicate the kasra of the form "fa'iltu."

"Min mu-sin" with tashdid (doubled letter) is the reading of Abu Bakr from 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i, while the rest read it without tashdid. The lighter reading is clearer, because most grammarians say "muwassin" for intensive emphasis (tikthir). It is also permissible that it be like "karrama" and "akrama."

"Janafan" comes from "janifa yajnafu" meaning "he acted unjustly" (idha jara). Its noun forms are "janif" and "jani f," according to al-Nahhas. It is also said that janaf means inclination (al-mail). Al-A'sha said:

Tajanafa 'an hijri (al-yamama) naqati... wa ma qasadat min ahliha lasawa'ika

In al-Sihah: "janaf" is inclination. Janifa (with kasra) yajnafu janafan when he inclined, and from this is God's words: ﴿Whoever fears from a testator inclination or wrongdoing﴾. A poet said:

Hum al-mawla wa in janafu 'alayna... wa inna min liqa'ihim lazuru

Abu 'Ubayda said: "al-mawla" here stands in the place of "al-mawali," i.e., cousins (banu al-'amm), like God's words: ﴿Then He brings you out as a child﴾. Labid said:

Inni imru'un mana'at uru'atu 'Amirin... daymi wa qad janafat 'alayya khusumi

Abu 'Ubayda said: likewise "al-jani'" (with hamza) means the one who inclines. It is also said: "ajnafa al-rajul," i.e., he committed janaf, as one says "alama" (he did something blameworthy) and "akhassa" (he did something base). "Tajanafa li-ithmin" means he inclined. A "ajnaf" man is one whose back is bent. "Junafa" (on the pattern fu'ala, with damma on the fa' and fatha on the 'ayn) is the name of a place, according to Ibn al-Sikkit. It is narrated from 'Ali that he read "hayfan" with ha' and ya', meaning injustice.

Mujahid said: "fa-man khafa" means whoever feared that the testator would act unjustly and cut off the inheritance of a group, and intentionally harm them, or would do so without intention; that is janaf without sin. If he does it intentionally, it is janaf with sin. So the meaning is: whoever is admonished in this matter and turned back from it, and thereby corrects what is between him and his heirs and between the heirs themselves, then there is no sin upon him. ﴿Indeed God is Forgiving﴾ toward the testator when the admonition takes effect in him and he returns from what he intended of harm.

Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Rabi' and others said: the meaning of the verse is: whoever knows and is aware, after the death of the testator, that the testator acted unjustly and intentionally harmed some of his heirs, and then corrects the discord and dispute that arose among the heirs, ﴿then there is no sin upon him﴾, i.e., the sin of the one who alters, mentioned earlier, does not reach him. Although there must be some alteration in his action, it is an alteration for the sake of good. The alteration that carries sin is only the alteration of one's desire.

The second: The address in "fa-man khafa" is to all Muslims. It is said to them: if you fear from a testator inclination in the bequest, deviation from truth, and falling into sin, and he did not give it according to what is fair, such as bequeathing property to the husband of his daughter or to the son of his daughter, so that the property goes to his daughter, or to the son of his son, while the aim is that the property goes to his son; or if he bequeaths to a distant person and leaves the near one, then hasten to strive for reconciliation among them. When reconciliation takes place, the sin falls from the one who reconciles. Reconciliation is a communal obligation (fard 'ala al-kifaya): if one of them undertakes it, it drops from the rest, and if none of them does, all are sinful.

The third: In this verse there is evidence for judgment based on conjecture (zann), because if one presumes an intention of corruption, it becomes obligatory to strive for correction. When corruption is established, it is not reconciliation but a ruling of repulsion, nullifying the corruption and cutting it off.

God's words: ﴿fa-aslaha baynahum﴾ are conjoined to "khafa." The pronoun refers to the heirs, and no mention of them preceded because the meaning is known. The answer to the condition is "fa-la ithma 'alayhi" (then there is no sin upon him).

The fourth: There is no disagreement that charity during life and health is better than charity at the time of death, based on his words ﷺ when he was asked: "Which charity is best?" He said: "That you give charity while you are healthy and miserly..." — the hadith, which the people of the Sahih collections have recorded. Al-Daraqutni narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "For a man to give charity of a dirham during his life is better for him than to give charity of a hundred at his death." Al-Nasa'i narrated from Abu al-Darda', from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The likeness of one who spends or gives charity at his death is like one who gives a gift after he is full."

The fifth: Whoever does not harm in his bequest, it will be an expiation for what he left of his zakat. Al-Daraqutni narrated from Mu'awiya ibn Qurra, from his father, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is visited by death and makes a bequest, and his bequest is according to the Book of God, it will be an expiation for what he left of his zakat."

If he harms in the bequest, which is the sixth issue: Al-Daraqutni also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: "Harm in bequest is among the grave sins." Abu Dawud narrated from Abu Hurayra, may God be pleased with him, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed a man or a woman may work by the obedience of God for sixty years, then death attends them, and they harm each other in the bequest, so the Fire becomes obligatory for them." Al-Nasa'i titled a chapter: "Prayer over one who acts unjustly in his bequest." He narrated to us: 'Ali ibn Hujr, who narrated to us: Hushaym, from Mansur, who is Ibn Zadhan, from al-Hasan, from 'Imran ibn Husayn, may God be pleased with him, that a man manumitted six of his slaves at his death, and he had no property other than them. This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and he became angry at that and said: "I was determined not to pray over him." Then he summoned his slaves, divided them into three parts, then cast lots among them, freed two and kept four in bondage. Muslim also narrated it with the same meaning, except that at its end he said: "and he spoke a harsh word to him," in place of his saying: "I was determined not to pray over him."

**Issue 1: Six matters.**

**The first matter:** His statement, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, fasting has been prescribed for you﴾. When He mentioned what had been prescribed for those responsible (*mukallafin*) regarding retaliation (*qisas*) and bequest (*wasiyyah*), He also mentioned that fasting had been prescribed for them, obligated them to it, and made it incumbent upon them. There is no disagreement about this. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Islam is built upon five: the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establishing the prayer, paying the zakat, fasting Ramadan, and the Hajj." Narrated by Ibn Umar.

Linguistically, its meaning (*sawm*) is abstention (*al-imsak*) and ceasing to move from one state to another. Silence is called *sawm* because it is abstention from speech. Allah, exalted is He, related of Mary: ﴿Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast﴾ [Maryam: 26], meaning silence from speech. *Sawm* also means the stillness of the wind, which is its ceasing to blow. *Sammat al-dabbah ʿala aryiha* (the animal stood still on its tether) means it stood and remained still and did not eat fodder. [*Al-aryy*: a rope with which an animal is tied in its stall, also called *al-akhiyyah*.] *Sawm al-nahar* means the day became balanced (at midday). *Masamm al-shams* is the place where the sun stands at the middle of the day. From this is the saying of al-Nabighah:

*Horses that are still (siyam), and horses that are not still, under the dust, and horses chewing their bits.*

That is, steady horses holding back from running and movement. As Imru' al-Qays said: [The full line is: *"With ropes upon hard rocks"*]

*As if the Pleiades were hung in their station.*

That is, they are fixed in their places and do not move. And his saying:

*And the pulleys, the worst of them is the one that is still (al-saʾimah).*

meaning the one that does not turn. Imru' al-Qays also said:

*Leave it [the text reads "leave this" in the originals, corrected from the Diwan and Lisan] and drive away your worry with a swift she-camel, when the day stands still and heats up.*

That is, the sun was slow to move and proceed, so by its slowness it became like something stationary. Another said:

*Until, when the day stood still and balanced, and saliva dripped down to the sun, and it descended.*

Another said:

*Ostriches at Wajrah with yellowish cheeks, who taste no sleep except standing (siyaman).*

That is, standing. There is much poetry on this meaning. In the Sharia, *sawm* is abstention from the things that break the fast, together with the intention, from the break of dawn until sunset. Its completeness and perfection come through avoiding prohibited acts and not falling into forbidden things, because of his saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever does not give up false speech and acting upon it, Allah has no need that he give up his food and drink."

**The second matter:** The virtue of fasting is great and its reward is abundant. Many reports, sound and fair (*sihah* and *hisan*), have come concerning this, which the imams mentioned in their *masanid*, and some of them will come later. For now, it is enough for you regarding the virtue of fasting that Allah singled it out by attributing it to Himself, as is established in the hadith from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said, relating from his Lord: "Allah, blessed and exalted, says: every deed of the son of Adam is for him except fasting; it is for Me, and I will reward it." The hadith continues.

Fasting was singled out as being for Him, even though all acts of worship are for Him, for two reasons which set fasting apart from all other acts of worship:

First, fasting prevents the soul from its pleasures and desires in a way that other acts of worship do not.

Second, fasting is a secret between the servant and his Lord, which none sees except Him. Therefore it became specific to Him. All other acts of worship are visible, and a person may perform them out of showing off (*tasannuʿ*) and ostentation (*riyaʾ*). Therefore fasting became the most specific to Him among acts of worship. It has also been said other than this.

**The third matter:** His statement, exalted is He: ﴿as it was prescribed﴾. The *kaf* (the particle "as") is in a position of accusative as a qualifier (*naʿt*), the implied meaning being "a prescription like [it]" or "a fast like [it]." Or it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from *al-siyam*, meaning: fasting has been prescribed for you in a manner resembling how it was prescribed for those before you.

Some grammarians said: the *kaf* is in the position of nominative as a qualifier for *al-siyam*, since its definiteness is not pure (*mahd*), because of the generality (*ijmal*) that is in it, which the Sharia has explained. Therefore it is permissible to qualify it with "as" (*kama*), since only indefinite nouns are qualified by it. So it is in the status of "fasting has been prescribed for you" (*kutiba ʿalaykum siyam*). This view has been regarded as weak.

The *ma* (in *kama*) is in the position of genitive, and its relative clause is "was prescribed upon those before you." The pronoun in *kutiba* refers back to *ma*.
