The exegetes differed about the aspect in which the comparison lies.

**The fourth matter:** Al-Sha'bi, Qatadah and others said: the comparison refers to the time of fasting and the quantity of fasting. Allah, exalted is He, prescribed the fasting of Ramadan upon the people of Musa and Isa, but they altered it. Their rabbis added ten days to it. Then one of their rabbis fell ill and vowed that if Allah cured him, he would add ten days to their fasting, and he did so. So the fasting of the Christians became fifty days. It became difficult for them in the heat, so they moved it to spring. Al-Nahhas chose this view and said: "It is the most fitting with what is in the verse." There is a hadith that supports its soundness, which he transmitted from Dagfal ibn Handhalah from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "The Christians had a month of fasting. A man among them fell ill, so they said: 'If Allah cures him, we will add ten days.' Then another [king] came, and he ate meat and his mouth became sore, so they said: 'If Allah cures him, we will add seven days.' Then there was another king, and they said: 'We will complete these seven days and make our fasting in spring.' So it became fifty days."

Mujahid said: Allah, mighty and majestic, prescribed the fasting of the month of Ramadan upon every nation.

It was also said: they took the matter with caution (*bi-l-wathiqah*), [*al-wathiqah* in matters means making it firm and taking it with certainty], so they fasted a day before the thirtieth and a day after it, generation after generation, until their fasting reached fifty days. It became difficult for them in the heat, so they moved it to the solar season (*al-fasl al-shamsi*). Al-Naqqash said: "There is a hadith on this from Dagfal ibn Handhalah, al-Hasan al-Basri and al-Suddi."

I say: for this reason, and Allah knows best, fasting on the day of doubt (*yawm al-shakk*) and the six days of Shawwal immediately after the day of Fitr (joined to it) is now disliked. Al-Sha'bi said: "Even if I fasted the whole year, I would break my fast on the day of doubt. The Christians were obligated to fast the month of Ramadan just as we were, but they moved it to the solar season, because it used to coincide with the summer heat. So they counted thirty days. Then after them came a generation which took the matter with caution for themselves, fasting a day before the thirtieth and a day after it. Then the next generation continued to follow the practice of those before them until they reached fifty days." That is his saying, exalted is He: ﴿as it was prescribed for those before you﴾.

It was also said: the comparison refers to the basic obligation upon those who preceded, not to the time and the manner.

It was also said: the comparison falls upon the description of the fast which was upon them, of abstaining from eating, drinking and intercourse, such that when the time of breaking the fast came, whoever slept would not do these things. This was similarly the case for the Christians at first, and it was the case at the beginning of Islam. Then Allah abrogated (*naskh*) it with His statement: ﴿It has been made lawful for you to go to your wives on the night of fasting﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187], as its explanation will come. This was said by al-Suddi, Abu al-Aliyah and al-Rabi'.

Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Ata' said: the comparison falls upon the fasting itself, not upon the description nor the number, even if the two fasts differ by addition and subtraction.

The meaning is: ﴿fasting has been prescribed for you﴾, that is, at the beginning of Islam, three days of every month and the day of Ashura; ﴿as it was prescribed for those before you﴾, meaning the Jews according to the view of Ibn Abbas, three days and the day of Ashura. Then this was abrogated for this nation by the month of Ramadan. Mu'adh ibn Jabal said: it was abrogated by ﴿a number of set days﴾, then the days were abrogated by Ramadan.

**The fifth matter:** His statement, exalted is He: ﴿so that you may become righteous﴾. *La'alla* (so that) here expresses hope with regard to them, as was mentioned before. And *tattaqun* (you may become righteous). It was said: its meaning here is "you may weaken," for whenever eating decreases, desire weakens, and whenever desire weakens, sins decrease. This is a fine figurative meaning. It was also said: so that you may guard against sins. It was also said: it is general, because fasting, as he, peace be upon him, said: "Fasting is a shield and a castration (*wija'*)." [*Wija'* is when the testicles of a stallion are crushed severely, removing sexual desire and making it like being castrated. He meant that fasting cuts off intercourse as castration does.] And it is a means to righteousness (*taqwa*), because it kills desires.

**The sixth matter:** His statement, exalted is He: ﴿a number of set days﴾. *Ayyaman* is the second object of *kutiba*, said al-Farra'. It was also said: it is in the accusative as a time expression (*zarf*) for *kutiba*, meaning: fasting has been prescribed for you during days. The "set days" are the month of Ramadan. This indicates something contrary to what was narrated from Mu'adh, and Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 183–184 (part 2 of 6):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So whoever among you is ill or on a journey, then [an equal number of] other days.﴾ On this there are sixteen issues.

The first issue: His saying ﴿ill﴾. The sick person has two states. The first: he cannot fast in any way, so for him breaking the fast is obligatory. The second: he is able to fast but with harm and hardship; for such a person breaking the fast is recommended (mustahabb), and only the ignorant would fast. Ibn Sirin said: Whenever a person is in a state that makes him deserving of the name "sick," breaking the fast is valid, by analogy with the traveller, whose cause is travel, even if it does not compel him to break the fast out of necessity. Tarif ibn Tammam al-Utaridi said: I entered upon Muhammad ibn Sirin during Ramadan while he was eating, and when he finished he said: "This finger of mine has been hurting." The majority of scholars said: If he has an illness that pains and harms him, or he fears its prolongation or its worsening, breaking the fast is valid for him. Ibn Atiyyah said: This is the position of the most skilled scholars of the school of Malik, and they argue on its basis. As for the wording of Malik, it is: the illness that burdens a person and reaches him (i.e., becomes severe). Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: The transmission from Malik differed regarding the illness that permits breaking the fast. He said once: it is fear of destruction from fasting. He said at another time: severity of the illness, its increase, and grievous hardship. This is the sound position of his school, and it is what the apparent meaning requires, since he did not single out one illness over another; so it is permitted in every illness, except what evidence has excluded, such as headache, fever, and a slight illness that involves no difficulty in fasting. Al-Hasan said: If a person due to illness cannot pray standing, he breaks the fast; al-Nakha'i also said this. A group said: One breaks the fast due to illness only if the necessity of the illness itself compels him to break it, and whenever he can bear the necessity with it, he does not break the fast. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him. I say: The statement of Ibn Sirin is the most just thing in this chapter, God willing. Al-Bukhari said: I fell ill in Nishapur with a slight illness, and that was in the month of Ramadan; a group of his companions visited me, and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh said to me: "Have you broken the fast, Abu Abd Allah?" I said: "Yes." He said: "You feared you would be too weak to accept the concession." I said: Abdan narrated to us from Ibn al-Mubarak from Ibn Jurayj who said: I said to Ata: "From which illness may one break the fast?" He said: "From any illness, as Allah the Exalted said: 'So whoever among you is ill.'" Al-Bukhari said: This hadith was not in Ishaq's possession. Abu Hanifa said: If a man fears for himself while fasting that if he does not break the fast his eye will increase in pain or his fever will intensify, he breaks the fast.

The second issue: His saying ﴿or on a journey﴾. The scholars differed regarding the journey that permits breaking the fast and shortening the prayer, after they agreed on the journey of obedience such as the Hajj and jihad. Connected to these two is the journey for maintaining family ties and seeking essential livelihood. As for journeys for trade and permissible purposes, there is disagreement between prohibiting and permitting, and the view of permissibility is stronger. As for the journey of a sinner, there is disagreement between permitting and prohibiting, and the view of prohibition is stronger; this was said by Ibn Atiyyah. The distance for breaking the fast according to Malik is the distance at which the prayer is shortened. The scholars differed on the measure of this. Malik said: a day and a night; then he reverted and said: forty-eight miles. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: this is the apparent position of his school. He said at another time: forty-two miles; and at another time: thirty-six miles; and at another time: the distance of a day and a night. It is also transmitted from him: two days, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i. He once distinguished between land and sea: at sea, the distance of a day and a night, and on land forty-eight miles; and in his school thirty miles; and in other than his school three miles. Ibn Amr, Ibn Abbas and al-Thawri said: breaking the fast applies to a journey of three days; this was related by Ibn Atiyyah. I say: What is in al-Bukhari is that Ibn Umar and Ibn Abbas would break the fast and shorten the prayer over four barids, which are sixteen farsakhs.

The third issue: The scholars agreed that the traveller in Ramadan may not make the intention to break the fast before dawn, because the traveller is not a traveller by intention, unlike the resident; rather he becomes a traveller through action and setting out, whereas the resident does not need action, for if he intends to reside he is a resident immediately, since residence does not require action; so they differ. There is also no disagreement among them regarding one who intends to travel that he may not break the fast before he sets out. If he breaks it, Ibn Habib said: if he has prepared for his journey and has begun the means of departure, there is nothing upon him. This is related from Asbagh and Ibn al-Majishun. If something prevents him from travelling, he owes expiation (kaffarah), and it suffices him that he would be safe if he travelled. Ibn al-Qasim related from Isa that he owes only the making up of one day, because he is interpreting in his breaking of the fast. Ashhab said: he owes no expiation whether he travelled or not. Sahnun said: he owes expiation whether he travelled or not, and he is in the position of a woman who says: "Tomorrow my menstruation will come to me," and so breaks the fast for that reason; then he reverted to the view of Abd al-Malik and Asbagh, and said: "It is not like a woman, for a man initiates travel whenever he wishes, while a woman does not initiate menstruation." I say: The view of Ibn al-Qasim and Ashhab regarding the negation of expiation is good, because he is doing what he is permitted to do, and the obligation is free, so nothing is established in it except by certainty, and there is no certainty amid disagreement; moreover, it is the implication of the words of Allah the Exalted: "or on a journey." Abu Umar said: This is the soundest of their opinions on this issue, because he is not violating the sanctity of the fast with deliberate intent to that end; he is merely interpreting. And if eating with the intention of travel obliged expiation, then what would have removed it from him when he set out? So reflect on this and you will find it so, God willing. Al-Daraqutni related: Abu Bakr al-Nisaburi narrated to us, Isma'il ibn Ishaq ibn Sahl narrated to us in Egypt, Ibn Abi Maryam narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, Zayd ibn Aslam informed me, who said: Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir informed me, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, that he said: I came to Anas ibn Malik in Ramadan while he was about to travel, his mount had been saddled, he had put on travelling clothes, and the sun was about to set; he called for food, ate from it, then mounted. I said to him: "Is it the sunnah?" He said: "Yes." It is also related from Anas that he said: Abu Musa said to me: "Did I not inform you: when I go out, I go out fasting, and when I come in, I come in fasting; so when you go out, go out breaking the fast, and when you come in, come in breaking the fast." Al-Hasan al-Basri said: He may break the fast in his house, if he wishes, on the day he intends to...

and he would break his fast when he goes out... [continuing]. Ahmad said: he breaks his fast once he has come out of the houses. Ishaq said: No, rather when he puts his foot in the riding-saddle (ril). Ibn al-Mundhir said: Ahmad's view is sound, because they say of one who woke up healthy and then fell ill, that he breaks his fast for the rest of his day; likewise if he woke up in the settled area (al-hadar) and then set out on a journey (al-safar), he too may break his fast. A group said: he does not break his fast that day even if he sets out on his journey. This was the view of al-Zuhri, Makhul, Yahya al-Ansari, Malik, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr and the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y). They differed as to whether, if he did break it, he must make up the day and also expiate; all of them said he makes it up (qada') and does not expiate (kaffara). Malik said: because travel is an accidental excuse, so it is like illness that befalls him. It is narrated from some of Malik's companions that he makes it up and expiates; this is the view of Ibn Kinana and al-Makhzumi, al-Baji related it from al-Shafi'i, and Ibn al-Arabi chose it and held it, saying: because travel is an excuse that arose after the obligation of worship became binding, and it differs from illness and menstruation, because illness permits him to break the fast and menstruation forbids her to fast, whereas travel does not permit him that; therefore expiation is obligatory upon him for violating its sanctity. Abu Umar said: this is no valid argument, for Allah the Exalted has permitted him to break the fast in the Book and the Sunnah. As for their saying "he does not break it," that is merely a recommendation (istihbab) on account of what he has undertaken; if he takes the concession of Allah, he owes making up the day, but expiation has no basis; whoever makes it obligatory has made obligatory what neither Allah nor His Messenger (ﷺ) made obligatory. It is narrated from Ibn Umar on this question: he may break his fast if he wishes on that day when he sets out as a traveller; this is the view of al-Sha'bi, Ahmad and Ishaq.

I say: al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, titled a chapter on this question "Chapter: whoever breaks his fast during travel so that people may see him," and related the hadith from Ibn Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out from Madinah toward Makkah and fasted until he reached 'Usfan [[Usfan (with a dammah on the ʿayn and a sukun on the sin, both unpointed-letter forms): a village eight-and-forty miles from Makkah.]], then he asked for water, raised it to his hands so that he might show it to the people, and broke his fast until he reached Makkah, and that was in Ramadan. Muslim also related it from Ibn Abbas, and in his version: then he asked for a vessel containing a drink, drank it in daylight so that the people might see him, then broke his fast until he entered Makkah. This is a clear text on the matter, so whatever contradicts it falls away; and success is from Allah. In it is also a proof against those who say that fasting is not valid during travel. This was narrated from Umar, Ibn Abbas, Abu Hurayrah and Ibn Umar. Ibn Umar said: whoever fasts during travel must make it up at home. And from Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf: the one who fasts during travel is like the one who breaks his fast at home. A group of the Zahiris held this, and they argued with the words of the Exalted, "then a number of other days" (Q 2:184), as its explanation will come, and with what Ka'b ibn Asim narrated, saying: I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "It is not righteousness to fast during travel." In it is also a proof against those who say that whoever formed the intention to fast during travel may break it even without an excuse; this was the view of Mutarrif, one of al-Shafi'i's two opinions, and a body of the people of hadith hold it. Malik used to require making up and expiation for him, because he had been free to fast or not, and when he chose fasting and formed the intention, it became binding on him and he was no longer permitted to break it; so if he broke it deliberately without an excuse, he owes making up and expiation. It is also narrated from him that there is no expiation, and this is the view of most of his companions, except 'Abd al-Malik, who said: if he breaks it by intercourse, he must expiate, because he is not strengthened thereby for his journey and has no excuse, since the traveller is only permitted to break the fast in order to be strengthened thereby for his journey. The rest of the jurists of Iraq and the Hijaz said: there is no expiation upon him, among them al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and all the jurists of Kufa; said Abu Umar.

The fourth matter: the scholars differed about which is better, breaking the fast or fasting while travelling. Malik and al-Shafi'i, in one of what is narrated from them, said: fasting is better for one who is able to do it. Most of Malik's school holds the option (takhyir), and so does al-Shafi'i's school. Al-Shafi'i and those who followed him said: he has the choice, and made no distinction; so did Ibn Ulayyah, on the hadith of Anas who said: We travelled with the Prophet (ﷺ) in Ramadan, and the one fasting did not reproach the one breaking the fast, nor the one breaking the fast reproach the one fasting; related by Malik, al-Bukhari and Muslim. It is narrated from Uthman ibn Abi al-As al-Thaqafi and Anas ibn Malik, the two companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that they said: fasting during travel is better for one who is able to do it; this is the view of Abu Hanifa and his companions. It is narrated from Ibn Amr and Ibn Abbas: the concession is better; this was held by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Sha'bi, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Awza'i, Ahmad and Ishaq. All of these say breaking the fast is better, because of the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185].

The fifth issue: God's words, "so a number of other days" (fa-'iddatun min ayyamin ukhar). The sentence contains an ellipsis, meaning: whoever among you is sick or on a journey and breaks the fast, then let him make up (fa-liyaqdi) the number of days. The majority of scholars hold that if the people of a town have fasted twenty-nine days, and there is a sick man in the town who did not recover, he makes up twenty-nine days. Some scholars, including al-Hasan ibn Salih ibn Hayy, said that he makes up a full month for a month, without regard to the number of days. Ilkiya al-Tabari said: This is far-fetched, because of God's words, "so a number of other days," and He did not say "so a month of other days." Also, His words "a number" require matching the number of days in which he broke the fast. There is no doubt that if he broke the fast for part of Ramadan, he must make up the days he missed after it by their exact number. Likewise, the ruling for breaking the fast for all of it must be the same in regard to its number.

The sixth issue: God's words, ﴿fa-'iddah﴾ ("so a number"). The word "'iddah" is in the nominative as the predicate of an implied subject, with the sense "so the ruling is" or "so what is obligatory is a number." It is also permissible to read it as "fa-'alayhi 'iddah" ("so upon him is a number"). Al-Kisa'i said: It is also permissible to read "fa-'iddatan" in the accusative, meaning "so let him fast a number of days." It was also said: The meaning is "so upon him is the fasting of a number," so the noun "fasting" (sawm) is omitted and "'iddah" is put in its place. The word "'iddah" is of the pattern fi'lah from the root "to count" ('add), and it has the sense of the thing counted, like "tahn" (grinding) meaning "the thing ground." One says: "I hear a clamor but I see no flour" (a proverb for a man who talks a lot but does nothing, or for one who promises and does not act). From the same root comes the "'iddah" of a woman (her waiting period). As for "min ayyamin ukhar" ("from other days"), the word "ukhar" is not declined according to Sibawayh, because it is a form diverted from the definite article (al-), since the usual pattern of fu'al in this category is to take the article, as in "al-kubar" and "al-fudal." Al-Kisa'i said: It is diverted from "akhar," as you say "hamra'" and "humar," and therefore it is not declined. It was also said: It is not declined because it is of the pattern of plurals, and it is an adjective of "days." The feminine "ukhra" was not used so that it would not appear to be an adjective of "'iddah." It was also said: "Ukhar" is the plural of "ukhra," as if it were "ayyam ukhra" ("other days") and then it was made plural, so it became "ayyam ukhar." It was also said: The adjective of "days" is feminine, and therefore it is described as "ukhar."

The seventh issue: People differ on whether these days must be consecutive, in two views mentioned by al-Daraqutni in his Sunan. It is narrated from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: "So a number of other days, consecutive" (muta-tabi'at) was revealed, and then it was dropped. Al-Daraqutni said: This is a sound chain. (Al-Zarqani in his commentary on the Muwatta' said: The meaning of "dropped" is "abrogated." He said: The word "consecutive" is not between the two covers, meaning it is not a word in the written Qur'an. Al-Daraqutni said: The expression "dropped" is reported only by 'Urwa.)

It is narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has a fast owed from Ramadan, let him continue it (fal-yasrudhu) [meaning: let him make it consecutive] and not break it." In its chain is 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ibrahim, who is weak in narration. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning making up Ramadan: "Fast it however you wish." Ibn 'Umar said: "Fast it as you broke it." It is reported from Abu 'Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayrah, Mu'adh ibn Jabal, and 'Amr ibn al-'As.

From Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, who said: It reached me that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about breaking up the fasting of Ramadan, and he said: "That is up to you. Do you not see that if one of you owed a debt and paid a dirham and two dirhams, would he not have paid it? God is more worthy to pardon and forgive." Its chain is good, but it is mursal (a report in which the Companion's name is omitted from the chain), and it is not established as connected.

In the Muwatta' of Malik, from Nafi', that 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar used to say: "Whoever broke a fast of Ramadan due to illness or while traveling should fast it consecutively." (The wording in the Muwatta' is: "He fasts the making-up of Ramadan consecutively, whoever broke it due to illness or during a journey.") Al-Baji said in al-Muntaqa: "It is possible that he means to report the obligation, and it is possible that he means to report what is recommended. Most jurists hold it is recommended. If he separates them, it suffices for him, and this is the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i. The evidence for the validity of this is God's words, ﴿so a number of other days﴾, and He did not specify separated from consecutive. If he fasts them separately, he has fasted a number of other days, so it must suffice for him." Ibn al-'Arabi said: Consecutiveness was required in the month of Ramadan only because it is fixed in time, and since there is no fixed time for making up, separation is permitted.

The eighth issue: When God said, ﴿so a number of other days﴾, this indicates the obligation of making up without a fixed time, because the wording runs over all times and is not restricted to some of them rather than others. In the two Sahihs (of al-Bukhari and Muslim), from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, she said: "I would have to make up a fast of Ramadan, and I could not make it up except in Sha'ban, because of being busy with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)" (or "because of the place of the Messenger of Allah"). (Al-Nawawi said: The word "al-shughl" (busyness) is in the nominative as the subject of an implied verb, meaning "being busy prevents me.") In another narration: "And that was because of the position of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." This is a clear text and an added explanation of the verse. This refutes Dawud's statement that it is obligatory for him to make it up on the second day of Shawwal, and that whoever did not make it up and then died is a sinner in his view. He built on this that if someone was obligated to free a slave and found a slave being sold for a price, he is not allowed to go beyond it and buy another, because the obligation on him is to free the first slave he finds, and another will not suffice. If he already had a slave, he is not allowed to buy another. If the slave he has dies, the emancipation is not invalidated, just as a vow to free a specific slave is invalidated if she dies. That would undermine his statement.

Some of the jurists of principles said: If he dies after the second day of Shawwal has passed, he is not disobedient, on condition that he had the intention (to make it up). The correct view is that he is neither sinful nor negligent, and this is the view of the majority, except that it is recommended for him to hasten the making-up so that death does not overtake him while the obligation remains upon him.

The ninth issue: If someone had to make up days of Ramadan, and the number of days passed after the end of Ramadan while he could have fasted them, but he delayed that, and then an obstacle prevented him from making them up until the next Ramadan, then there is no feeding (kaffarah of feeding the poor) for him, because he was not negligent when he did what was permissible for him in delaying. This is the view of the Baghdadi Malikis, and they regard it as the view of Ibn al-Qasim in al-Mudawwana.

The tenth issue: If he delayed making up his fast beyond Sha'ban, which is the final limit of the time in which Ramadan may be made up, is he then obliged to pay an expiation (kaffarah) for that or not? Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, and Ishaq said: Yes. Abu Hanifah, al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, and Dawud said: No.

I say: Al-Bukhari adopted this view, based on his statement, and it is mentioned from Abu Hurayrah in a mursal report, and from Ibn 'Abbas, that he should feed (the poor). God did not mention feeding; He only said, ﴿so a number of other days﴾.

I say: It has come down from Abu Hurayrah in a connected (musnad) report concerning one who was negligent in making up Ramadan until another Ramadan came upon him. He said: "He fasts this one with the people, and he fasts the one he neglected, and he feeds a poor person for each day." Al-Daraqutni transmitted it and said: "This is a sound chain." It is also reported from him as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet (ﷺ)) concerning a man who broke the fast of Ramadan due to illness, then recovered but did not fast until another Ramadan came upon him. He said: "He fasts the one that came upon him, then he fasts the month in which he broke the fast, and he feeds a poor person for each day." In its chain are Ibn Nafi' and Ibn Wajih, both weak.

The eleventh issue: If the illness continued for him and he did not recover until another Ramadan came, al-Daraqutni reported from Ibn 'Umar that he feeds, in place of each day, one poor person with a mudd of wheat (a measure of about three-quarters of a kilogram), and then there is no making-up required of him. It is also reported from Abu Hurayrah that he said: "If he did not recover between the two Ramadans, he fasts for this one and feeds for the second, and there is no making-up upon him. If he recovered and did not fast until another Ramadan came upon him, he fasts for this one and feeds for the past one, and then if he breaks it he makes it up." Its chain is sound. Our scholars said: The statements of the Companions that go against analogy (qiyas) may be used as evidence.

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that a man came to him and said: "I was ill for two Ramadans?" Ibn 'Abbas said to him: "Did your illness continue, or did you recover between them?" He said: "No, I recovered." He said: "Fast two Ramadans and feed sixty poor people." This is a substitute for the statement that if his illness continued, there is no making-up upon him. This resembles their position on the pregnant woman and the nursing woman, that they feed and there is no making-up upon them, as will come (see p. 288 of this part).

The twelfth issue: Those who made feeding obligatory differed on the amount that must be fed. Abu Hurayrah, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, Malik, and al-Shafi'i said: One feeds a mudd for each day. Al-Thawri said: One feeds half a sa' (another measure) for each day.

The thirteenth issue: They differed about the one who broke the fast or had intercourse while making up a fast of Ramadan, what is obligatory for him. Malik said: Whoever breaks a day of making-up of Ramadan forgetfully, there is nothing upon him except making it up. It is recommended for him to continue the fast as a way of stepping out of disagreement, and then make it up. If he broke it intentionally, he is sinful, and there is nothing upon him except making up that day, and he should not continue it, because there is no point in refraining here from what restrains the fasting person, since he is not fasting according to the majority of scholars, due to his intentionally breaking it. As for expiation (kaffarah), there is no disagreement among Malik and his companions that it is not obligatory in this case, and this is the view of the majority of scholars. Malik said: Whoever breaks a day of making-up of Ramadan by having intercourse with his wife or otherwise, there is no expiation upon him; he is only obliged to make up that day. Qatadah said: Whoever has intercourse during the making-up of Ramadan must make up the day and pay expiation.

Ibn al-Qasim transmitted from Malik that whoever breaks the fast during the making-up of Ramadan must fast two days. Ibn al-Qasim used to give this ruling, then he retracted it and said: If he intentionally breaks the fast during the making-up of making-up, he must fast two days in its place, like someone who invalidates his pilgrimage by intercourse with his wife, and then performs it the following year and again invalidates it by intercourse with his wife, so he must perform two pilgrimages. Abu 'Umar said: Ibn Wahb and 'Abd al-Malik disagreed with him concerning the pilgrimage, and it is not obligatory to analogize from a principle on which there is disagreement.

The correct view in my opinion, and God knows best, is that in both cases there is nothing upon him except making up one day, because it is one day that he broke twice.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verses 183–184 (part 5 of 6):**

I say: This is what is implied by His saying, ﴿a number of other days﴾. So whenever a person makes up a full day in place of the day he broke his fast on during the making-up of Ramadan, he has fulfilled what is obligatory upon him, and nothing beyond that is required of him, and Allah knows best.

**The Fourteenth Issue:** The majority hold that whoever broke his fast in Ramadan due to an illness and died from that illness, or who traveled and died during his journey, owes nothing. Tawus and Qatadah said, regarding a sick person who dies before he recovers: food is to be given on his behalf.

**The Fifteenth Issue:** They differed concerning one who dies with an obligation of fasting from Ramadan that he did not make up. Malik, al-Shafi'i and al-Thawri said: no one fasts on behalf of anyone else. Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, al-Layth, Abu 'Ubayd and Ahl al-Zahir (the literalists) said: it is fasted on his behalf, except that they restricted this to a vow. A similar view is reported from al-Shafi'i. Ahmad and Ishaq said, regarding making up Ramadan: food is to be given on his behalf.

Those who argue for fasting cite what Muslim narrated from 'A'isha, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever dies with fasting owed upon him, his guardian shall fast on his behalf." However, this is general regarding fasting, and it is specified by what Muslim also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: A woman came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, my mother has died and she owed a fast of a vow," and in another narration, "a fast of a month." "Shall I fast on her behalf?" He said: "Think about it: if your mother had a debt and you paid it, would that have discharged it for her?" She said: "Yes." He said: "Then fast on behalf of your mother."

Malik and those who agreed with him argued with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164], and His saying: ﴿And that man will have nothing except what he strives for﴾ [al-Najm: 39], and His saying: ﴿And every soul earns only against itself﴾ [al-An'am: 164]. They also cited what al-Nasa'i narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "No one prays on behalf of anyone else, and no one fasts on behalf of anyone else, but food is given on his behalf for every day a mudd of wheat."

I say: This hadith is general, so it is possible that his saying, "No one fasts on behalf of anyone else," refers to the fast of Ramadan. As for the fast of a vow, it is permissible, by the evidence of the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas and others. Sahih Muslim also contains, from the hadith of Buraydah, something similar to the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas. In some of its chains: "a fast of two months." "Shall I fast on her behalf?" He said: "Fast on her behalf." She said: "She never performed Hajj. Shall I perform Hajj on her behalf?" He said: "Perform Hajj on her behalf." Her saying "two months" makes it unlikely that this refers to Ramadan, and Allah knows best.

The strongest thing cited for Malik's view is that it is the practice of the people of Medina (amal Ahl al-Madina). It is supported by clear analogy (al-qiyas al-jali), namely that it is a physical act of worship in which wealth has no role, so it is not performed on behalf of someone who was obligated to it, like prayer. This is not undermined by Hajj, because wealth has a role in it.

**The Sixteenth Issue:** Whoever holds that fasting is not valid during travel, and that making it up is obligatory forever, uses this verse as evidence. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿So whoever among you is ill or on a journey, then a number of other days﴾, meaning: then upon him is a number (of days). There is no omission or implication in the speech. [And by His saying, peace be upon him: "It is not righteousness to fast while traveling." He said: Whatever is not righteousness is sinful, so this indicates that fasting Ramadan is not permitted while traveling.] The majority say that there is an omitted element in it, "so he broke his fast," as has been mentioned earlier. This is the correct view, based on the hadith of Anas, who said: "We traveled with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in Ramadan, and the one fasting did not criticize the one not fasting, nor the one not fasting criticize the one fasting." Malik narrated it from Humayd al-Tawil, from Anas. Muslim also narrated it from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "We went on a military campaign with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sixteen days into Ramadan. Some of us fasted and some of us broke their fast, and the one fasting did not criticize the one not fasting, nor the one not fasting criticize the one fasting."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 183–184 (part 6 of 6):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And for those who are able to fast [yuṭīqūnahu], there is a redemption: feeding a needy person. But whoever volunteers good, it is better for him. And that you fast is better for you, if you only knew.﴾ On this there are five issues.

The first: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿yuṭīqūnahu﴾ (those who are able to, or "who are able to [do] it"). The majority read it with a kasra on the ṭāʾ and a sukūn on the yāʾ. Its original form is yuṭawwiqūnahu; the kasra was transferred to the ṭāʾ, and the wāw became a yāʾ because the letter before it was kasra. Ḥumayd read it according to the original form without the change (iʿtilāl), and analogically the change is what is expected. The well-known reading of Ibn ʿAbbas is "yuṭawwiqūnahu," with a fatḥa on the ṭāʾ, lightened, and a shaddah on the wāw, meaning "they are burdened with it" (yukallafūnahu). Mujahid transmitted "yaṭīqūnahu" with a yāʾ after the ṭāʾ, on the pattern of "yakīlūnahu," but this is false and impossible, because the verb is derived from ṭawq (a collar), so the wāw is obligatory and necessary in it, and there is no place for a yāʾ in this form. Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: Ahmad ibn Yahya the grammarian recited to us from Abu Dhuʾayb:

"It was said: 'Bear beyond your collar (ṭawq), for it is full (muṭabbaʿah)
Whoever comes to it, it will not harm it.'"

Here the wāw appears in ṭawq, and by this it is established that the one who puts a yāʾ in its place departs from what is correct. Ibn al-Anbari transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas "yaṭṭayyaqūnahu," with a fatḥa on the yāʾ and a shaddah on the ṭāʾ, with both the yāʾ and the ṭāʾ fatḥa, meaning "yuṭīqūnahu." It is said: ṭāqa, aṭāqa and uṭīqu have the same meaning. Also from Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿĀʾishah, Ṭawus and ʿAmr ibn Dinar: "yaṭṭawwaqūnahu," with a fatḥa on the yāʾ and a shaddah on the ṭāʾ fatḥa; this is correct in the language, because the original is yatawwaqūnahu, the tāʾ was made sukūn and merged into the ṭāʾ, becoming a shaddah ṭāʾ. It is not part of the Qur'an, contrary to those who count it as Qur'an; it is only a reading by way of explanation (tafsir).

The people of Medina and Syria read "fidyatu ṭaʿāmin" as an idafah (construct), and "masākīn" in the plural. Ibn ʿAbbas read "ṭaʿāmu miskīnin" in the singular, as reported by al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i from ʿAṭāʾ from him. This is a good reading, because it clarifies the ruling regarding each day. Abu ʿUbayd preferred it, and it is the reading of Abu ʿAmr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i. Abu ʿUbayd said: It makes clear that for each day there is one feeding, so the singular stands for the plural, but the plural does not stand for the singular. As for the plural "masākīn," one does not know how many of them there are in a day from outside the verse. The reading of the plural in "masākīn" may be explained: since those who are able to do it are plural, and each one of them is obliged to feed one needy person, the word is pluralised, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not bring four witnesses, flog them eighty lashes﴾ [al-Nur: 4], meaning: flog each one of them eighty lashes, so the eighty are not spread across all of them together, but each one receives eighty. Abu ʿAli said this is its meaning. Al-Nahhas preferred the plural reading and said: What Abu ʿUbayd preferred is rejected, because this is known by implication: it is known that the meaning of "and for those who are able to do it, there is a redemption: feeding a needy person" is that for each day there is one needy person. So choosing this reading is to answer plural with plural. Al-Nahhas said: Abu ʿUbayd preferred that it be read "fidyatu ṭaʿāmin" and said: because the food is the redemption, and it is not permissible for ṭaʿām to be an adjective, since it is a substance, but it is permissible as an apposition (badal). And it is clearer than reading "fidyatu ṭaʿāmin" as an idafah, because "fidyah" is general and falls upon food and other things, so it is like your saying: "this is a garment of silk (khazz)."

The second: The scholars differed concerning the intended meaning of the verse. It was said: it is abrogated (mansukhah). Al-Bukhari reported: "Ibn Numayr said: al-A'mash narrated to us, ʿAmr ibn Murrah narrated to us, Ibn Abi Layla narrated to us: the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) said: Ramadan came down and it was hard upon them, so whoever fed a needy person each day was excused from fasting, of those who were able to, and they were given leave in this; then 'and that you fast is better for you' abrogated it." On this basis, the majority's reading "yuṭīqūnahu" means "they are capable of it," because the obligation of fasting was thus: whoever wished fasted, and whoever wished fed a needy person. Ibn ʿAbbas said: this verse was revealed as a concession specifically for the elderly and the decrepit when they break the fast while they are able to fast; then it was abrogated by His saying ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], so the concession was removed except for those among them who are incapable. Al-Farra' said: the pronoun in "yuṭīqūnahu" may refer to the fast, meaning: "and for those who are able to fast, that they feed when they break the fast," then it was abrogated by His saying "and that you fast." It may also refer to the redemption, meaning: "and for those who are able to [bear] the redemption, a redemption."

As for the reading "yuṭawwiqūnahu," in the sense of "they are burdened with it along with the hardship that befalls them," such as the sick person and the pregnant woman: they are able to do it, but with a hardship that reaches them in themselves. If they fast, it suffices for them; and if they pay the redemption, that is theirs. Ibn ʿAbbas, if the chain from him is sound, explained "yuṭīqūnahu" as "yuṭawwiqūnahu" and "yatakallafūnahu," and so some transmitters introduced it into the Qur'an. Abu Dawud reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding "and for those who are able to do it": he said: it was confirmed for the pregnant and the nursing woman. And it is also reported from him: "and for those who are able to do it, there is a redemption: feeding a needy person," he said: it was a concession for the aged old man and the aged old woman, who are able to fast, that they break the fast and feed a needy person for each day; and the pregnant and nursing woman, if they fear for their children, break the fast and feed. Al-Daraqutni also transmitted from him: he said: a concession was granted to the aged old man to break the fast and feed a needy person for each day, with no qadaʾ upon him; this is a sound chain. And it is reported from him that he said: "and for those who are able to do it, there is a redemption: feeding" is not abrogated; it refers to the aged old man and the aged old woman who cannot fast, so they feed a needy person in place of each day; and this is sound. It is also reported from him that he said to a umm walad of his who was pregnant or nursing: "You are of those who are unable to fast; upon you is the compensation (jaza'), and upon you is no qadaʾ"; this is a sound chain. In another narration: he had a umm walad who was nursing, without doubt, and she was overwhelmed, so he commanded her to break the fast and not make up; this is sound. I say: it has thus been established by sound chains from Ibn ʿAbbas that the verse is not abrogated, and that it is muhkam (established) regarding those who have been mentioned. The first view is also sound, except that it is possible that the abrogation there means specification (takhsis), for the early scholars often use "naskh" in its broad sense; and God knows best.

Al-Hasan al-Basri, ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abi Rabah, al-Dahhak, al-Nakha'i, al-Zuhri, Rabi'ah, al-Awza'i and the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y) said: the pregnant and the nursing woman break the fast and there is no feeding upon them, in the position of the sick person who breaks the fast and makes up. This was also the view of Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Thawr. Abu ʿUbayd related this from Abu Thawr, and Ibn al-Mundhir preferred it. It is the view of Malik regarding the pregnant woman if she breaks the fast; as for the nursing woman, if she breaks the fast, then upon her is qadaʾ and feeding. Al-Shafi'i and Ahmad said: they break the fast, feed, and make up. They all agreed that the old men and old women who are unable to fast, or who are able to fast only with severe hardship, may break the fast. They differed about what is upon them. Rabi'ah and Malik said: nothing is upon them, except that Malik said: if they feed a needy person for each day, that would be dearer to me. Anas, Ibn ʿAbbas, Qays ibn al-Sa'ib and Abu Hurayrah said: upon them is the redemption. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, the people of opinion, Ahmad and Ishaq, following the saying of the companions, may God be pleased with all of them, and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So whoever of you is sick or on a journey, then a number of other days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184], then He said: ﴿And for those who are able to do it, there is a redemption: feeding a needy person﴾; and these are neither sick nor travellers, so the redemption became obligatory upon them. The evidence for Malik's view is that this person breaks the fast for an existing excuse in him, namely old age and decrepitude, so feeding is not obligatory upon him, like the traveller and the sick person. This was also reported from al-Thawri and Makhul, and Ibn al-Mundhir preferred it.

The third: Those who made the redemption obligatory upon those mentioned differed about its quantity. Malik said: a mudd by the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ) for each day he broke the fast; al-Shafi'i also said this. Abu Hanifah said: the expiation (kaffarah) for each day is a ṣāʿ of dates or half a ṣāʿ of wheat. It was reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: half a ṣāʿ of grain (ḥintah); al-Daraqutni mentioned it. It was reported from Abu Hurayrah that he said: whoever reaches old age and is not able to fast, upon him for each day is a mudd of wheat. And it was reported from Anas ibn Malik that he grew weak with regard to fasting in a year, so he prepared a large dish of food, then called thirty needy persons and fed them to satisfaction.

The fourth: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But whoever volunteers good, it is better for him.﴾ Ibn Shihab said: whoever wishes to feed in addition to fasting. Mujahid said: whoever adds to feeding beyond the mudd. Ibn ʿAbbas said regarding "whoever volunteers good": another needy person, and it is better for him. Al-Daraqutni mentioned this and said: its chain is sound and established. The second "khayr" is a comparative adjective (ṣifat tafḍīl), and so is the third; and the first "khayran" is likewise. ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "yaṭṭawwaʿa khayran" with a shaddah and a sukūn on the ʿayn, in the sense of "yatatawwaʿa." The rest read "tatawwaʿa," with a tāʾ and a lightened ṭāʾ and a fatḥa on the ʿayn, as a past tense verb.

The fifth: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And that you fast is better for you﴾, meaning: and fasting is better for you. Ubayy also read thus, meaning: better than breaking the fast together with the redemption; and this was before the abrogation. It was said: "and that you fast" refers to travel and to illness that is not burdensome; and God knows best. In general, it implies urging fasting, meaning: know this, and fast.

**Issue 1: Six matters.**

**The first matter:** His statement, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, fasting has been prescribed for you﴾. When He mentioned what had been prescribed for those responsible (*mukallafin*) regarding retaliation (*qisas*) and bequest (*wasiyyah*), He also mentioned that fasting had been prescribed for them, obligated them to it, and made it incumbent upon them. There is no disagreement about this. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Islam is built upon five: the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establishing the prayer, paying the zakat, fasting Ramadan, and the Hajj." Narrated by Ibn Umar.

Linguistically, its meaning (*sawm*) is abstention (*al-imsak*) and ceasing to move from one state to another. Silence is called *sawm* because it is abstention from speech. Allah, exalted is He, related of Mary: ﴿Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast﴾ [Maryam: 26], meaning silence from speech. *Sawm* also means the stillness of the wind, which is its ceasing to blow. *Sammat al-dabbah ʿala aryiha* (the animal stood still on its tether) means it stood and remained still and did not eat fodder. [*Al-aryy*: a rope with which an animal is tied in its stall, also called *al-akhiyyah*.] *Sawm al-nahar* means the day became balanced (at midday). *Masamm al-shams* is the place where the sun stands at the middle of the day. From this is the saying of al-Nabighah:

*Horses that are still (siyam), and horses that are not still, under the dust, and horses chewing their bits.*

That is, steady horses holding back from running and movement. As Imru' al-Qays said: [The full line is: *"With ropes upon hard rocks"*]

*As if the Pleiades were hung in their station.*

That is, they are fixed in their places and do not move. And his saying:

*And the pulleys, the worst of them is the one that is still (al-saʾimah).*

meaning the one that does not turn. Imru' al-Qays also said:

*Leave it [the text reads "leave this" in the originals, corrected from the Diwan and Lisan] and drive away your worry with a swift she-camel, when the day stands still and heats up.*

That is, the sun was slow to move and proceed, so by its slowness it became like something stationary. Another said:

*Until, when the day stood still and balanced, and saliva dripped down to the sun, and it descended.*

Another said:

*Ostriches at Wajrah with yellowish cheeks, who taste no sleep except standing (siyaman).*

That is, standing. There is much poetry on this meaning. In the Sharia, *sawm* is abstention from the things that break the fast, together with the intention, from the break of dawn until sunset. Its completeness and perfection come through avoiding prohibited acts and not falling into forbidden things, because of his saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever does not give up false speech and acting upon it, Allah has no need that he give up his food and drink."

**The second matter:** The virtue of fasting is great and its reward is abundant. Many reports, sound and fair (*sihah* and *hisan*), have come concerning this, which the imams mentioned in their *masanid*, and some of them will come later. For now, it is enough for you regarding the virtue of fasting that Allah singled it out by attributing it to Himself, as is established in the hadith from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said, relating from his Lord: "Allah, blessed and exalted, says: every deed of the son of Adam is for him except fasting; it is for Me, and I will reward it." The hadith continues.

Fasting was singled out as being for Him, even though all acts of worship are for Him, for two reasons which set fasting apart from all other acts of worship:

First, fasting prevents the soul from its pleasures and desires in a way that other acts of worship do not.

Second, fasting is a secret between the servant and his Lord, which none sees except Him. Therefore it became specific to Him. All other acts of worship are visible, and a person may perform them out of showing off (*tasannuʿ*) and ostentation (*riyaʾ*). Therefore fasting became the most specific to Him among acts of worship. It has also been said other than this.

**The third matter:** His statement, exalted is He: ﴿as it was prescribed﴾. The *kaf* (the particle "as") is in a position of accusative as a qualifier (*naʿt*), the implied meaning being "a prescription like [it]" or "a fast like [it]." Or it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from *al-siyam*, meaning: fasting has been prescribed for you in a manner resembling how it was prescribed for those before you.

Some grammarians said: the *kaf* is in the position of nominative as a qualifier for *al-siyam*, since its definiteness is not pure (*mahd*), because of the generality (*ijmal*) that is in it, which the Sharia has explained. Therefore it is permissible to qualify it with "as" (*kama*), since only indefinite nouns are qualified by it. So it is in the status of "fasting has been prescribed for you" (*kutiba ʿalaykum siyam*). This view has been regarded as weak.

The *ma* (in *kama*) is in the position of genitive, and its relative clause is "was prescribed upon those before you." The pronoun in *kutiba* refers back to *ma*.

The exegetes differed about the aspect in which the comparison lies.

**The fourth matter:** Al-Sha'bi, Qatadah and others said: the comparison refers to the time of fasting and the quantity of fasting. Allah, exalted is He, prescribed the fasting of Ramadan upon the people of Musa and Isa, but they altered it. Their rabbis added ten days to it. Then one of their rabbis fell ill and vowed that if Allah cured him, he would add ten days to their fasting, and he did so. So the fasting of the Christians became fifty days. It became difficult for them in the heat, so they moved it to spring. Al-Nahhas chose this view and said: "It is the most fitting with what is in the verse." There is a hadith that supports its soundness, which he transmitted from Dagfal ibn Handhalah from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "The Christians had a month of fasting. A man among them fell ill, so they said: 'If Allah cures him, we will add ten days.' Then another [king] came, and he ate meat and his mouth became sore, so they said: 'If Allah cures him, we will add seven days.' Then there was another king, and they said: 'We will complete these seven days and make our fasting in spring.' So it became fifty days."

Mujahid said: Allah, mighty and majestic, prescribed the fasting of the month of Ramadan upon every nation.

It was also said: they took the matter with caution (*bi-l-wathiqah*), [*al-wathiqah* in matters means making it firm and taking it with certainty], so they fasted a day before the thirtieth and a day after it, generation after generation, until their fasting reached fifty days. It became difficult for them in the heat, so they moved it to the solar season (*al-fasl al-shamsi*). Al-Naqqash said: "There is a hadith on this from Dagfal ibn Handhalah, al-Hasan al-Basri and al-Suddi."

I say: for this reason, and Allah knows best, fasting on the day of doubt (*yawm al-shakk*) and the six days of Shawwal immediately after the day of Fitr (joined to it) is now disliked. Al-Sha'bi said: "Even if I fasted the whole year, I would break my fast on the day of doubt. The Christians were obligated to fast the month of Ramadan just as we were, but they moved it to the solar season, because it used to coincide with the summer heat. So they counted thirty days. Then after them came a generation which took the matter with caution for themselves, fasting a day before the thirtieth and a day after it. Then the next generation continued to follow the practice of those before them until they reached fifty days." That is his saying, exalted is He: ﴿as it was prescribed for those before you﴾.

It was also said: the comparison refers to the basic obligation upon those who preceded, not to the time and the manner.

It was also said: the comparison falls upon the description of the fast which was upon them, of abstaining from eating, drinking and intercourse, such that when the time of breaking the fast came, whoever slept would not do these things. This was similarly the case for the Christians at first, and it was the case at the beginning of Islam. Then Allah abrogated (*naskh*) it with His statement: ﴿It has been made lawful for you to go to your wives on the night of fasting﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187], as its explanation will come. This was said by al-Suddi, Abu al-Aliyah and al-Rabi'.

Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Ata' said: the comparison falls upon the fasting itself, not upon the description nor the number, even if the two fasts differ by addition and subtraction.

The meaning is: ﴿fasting has been prescribed for you﴾, that is, at the beginning of Islam, three days of every month and the day of Ashura; ﴿as it was prescribed for those before you﴾, meaning the Jews according to the view of Ibn Abbas, three days and the day of Ashura. Then this was abrogated for this nation by the month of Ramadan. Mu'adh ibn Jabal said: it was abrogated by ﴿a number of set days﴾, then the days were abrogated by Ramadan.

**The fifth matter:** His statement, exalted is He: ﴿so that you may become righteous﴾. *La'alla* (so that) here expresses hope with regard to them, as was mentioned before. And *tattaqun* (you may become righteous). It was said: its meaning here is "you may weaken," for whenever eating decreases, desire weakens, and whenever desire weakens, sins decrease. This is a fine figurative meaning. It was also said: so that you may guard against sins. It was also said: it is general, because fasting, as he, peace be upon him, said: "Fasting is a shield and a castration (*wija'*)." [*Wija'* is when the testicles of a stallion are crushed severely, removing sexual desire and making it like being castrated. He meant that fasting cuts off intercourse as castration does.] And it is a means to righteousness (*taqwa*), because it kills desires.

**The sixth matter:** His statement, exalted is He: ﴿a number of set days﴾. *Ayyaman* is the second object of *kutiba*, said al-Farra'. It was also said: it is in the accusative as a time expression (*zarf*) for *kutiba*, meaning: fasting has been prescribed for you during days. The "set days" are the month of Ramadan. This indicates something contrary to what was narrated from Mu'adh, and Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 183–184 (part 2 of 6):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So whoever among you is ill or on a journey, then [an equal number of] other days.﴾ On this there are sixteen issues.

The first issue: His saying ﴿ill﴾. The sick person has two states. The first: he cannot fast in any way, so for him breaking the fast is obligatory. The second: he is able to fast but with harm and hardship; for such a person breaking the fast is recommended (mustahabb), and only the ignorant would fast. Ibn Sirin said: Whenever a person is in a state that makes him deserving of the name "sick," breaking the fast is valid, by analogy with the traveller, whose cause is travel, even if it does not compel him to break the fast out of necessity. Tarif ibn Tammam al-Utaridi said: I entered upon Muhammad ibn Sirin during Ramadan while he was eating, and when he finished he said: "This finger of mine has been hurting." The majority of scholars said: If he has an illness that pains and harms him, or he fears its prolongation or its worsening, breaking the fast is valid for him. Ibn Atiyyah said: This is the position of the most skilled scholars of the school of Malik, and they argue on its basis. As for the wording of Malik, it is: the illness that burdens a person and reaches him (i.e., becomes severe). Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: The transmission from Malik differed regarding the illness that permits breaking the fast. He said once: it is fear of destruction from fasting. He said at another time: severity of the illness, its increase, and grievous hardship. This is the sound position of his school, and it is what the apparent meaning requires, since he did not single out one illness over another; so it is permitted in every illness, except what evidence has excluded, such as headache, fever, and a slight illness that involves no difficulty in fasting. Al-Hasan said: If a person due to illness cannot pray standing, he breaks the fast; al-Nakha'i also said this. A group said: One breaks the fast due to illness only if the necessity of the illness itself compels him to break it, and whenever he can bear the necessity with it, he does not break the fast. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him. I say: The statement of Ibn Sirin is the most just thing in this chapter, God willing. Al-Bukhari said: I fell ill in Nishapur with a slight illness, and that was in the month of Ramadan; a group of his companions visited me, and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh said to me: "Have you broken the fast, Abu Abd Allah?" I said: "Yes." He said: "You feared you would be too weak to accept the concession." I said: Abdan narrated to us from Ibn al-Mubarak from Ibn Jurayj who said: I said to Ata: "From which illness may one break the fast?" He said: "From any illness, as Allah the Exalted said: 'So whoever among you is ill.'" Al-Bukhari said: This hadith was not in Ishaq's possession. Abu Hanifa said: If a man fears for himself while fasting that if he does not break the fast his eye will increase in pain or his fever will intensify, he breaks the fast.

The second issue: His saying ﴿or on a journey﴾. The scholars differed regarding the journey that permits breaking the fast and shortening the prayer, after they agreed on the journey of obedience such as the Hajj and jihad. Connected to these two is the journey for maintaining family ties and seeking essential livelihood. As for journeys for trade and permissible purposes, there is disagreement between prohibiting and permitting, and the view of permissibility is stronger. As for the journey of a sinner, there is disagreement between permitting and prohibiting, and the view of prohibition is stronger; this was said by Ibn Atiyyah. The distance for breaking the fast according to Malik is the distance at which the prayer is shortened. The scholars differed on the measure of this. Malik said: a day and a night; then he reverted and said: forty-eight miles. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: this is the apparent position of his school. He said at another time: forty-two miles; and at another time: thirty-six miles; and at another time: the distance of a day and a night. It is also transmitted from him: two days, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i. He once distinguished between land and sea: at sea, the distance of a day and a night, and on land forty-eight miles; and in his school thirty miles; and in other than his school three miles. Ibn Amr, Ibn Abbas and al-Thawri said: breaking the fast applies to a journey of three days; this was related by Ibn Atiyyah. I say: What is in al-Bukhari is that Ibn Umar and Ibn Abbas would break the fast and shorten the prayer over four barids, which are sixteen farsakhs.

The third issue: The scholars agreed that the traveller in Ramadan may not make the intention to break the fast before dawn, because the traveller is not a traveller by intention, unlike the resident; rather he becomes a traveller through action and setting out, whereas the resident does not need action, for if he intends to reside he is a resident immediately, since residence does not require action; so they differ. There is also no disagreement among them regarding one who intends to travel that he may not break the fast before he sets out. If he breaks it, Ibn Habib said: if he has prepared for his journey and has begun the means of departure, there is nothing upon him. This is related from Asbagh and Ibn al-Majishun. If something prevents him from travelling, he owes expiation (kaffarah), and it suffices him that he would be safe if he travelled. Ibn al-Qasim related from Isa that he owes only the making up of one day, because he is interpreting in his breaking of the fast. Ashhab said: he owes no expiation whether he travelled or not. Sahnun said: he owes expiation whether he travelled or not, and he is in the position of a woman who says: "Tomorrow my menstruation will come to me," and so breaks the fast for that reason; then he reverted to the view of Abd al-Malik and Asbagh, and said: "It is not like a woman, for a man initiates travel whenever he wishes, while a woman does not initiate menstruation." I say: The view of Ibn al-Qasim and Ashhab regarding the negation of expiation is good, because he is doing what he is permitted to do, and the obligation is free, so nothing is established in it except by certainty, and there is no certainty amid disagreement; moreover, it is the implication of the words of Allah the Exalted: "or on a journey." Abu Umar said: This is the soundest of their opinions on this issue, because he is not violating the sanctity of the fast with deliberate intent to that end; he is merely interpreting. And if eating with the intention of travel obliged expiation, then what would have removed it from him when he set out? So reflect on this and you will find it so, God willing. Al-Daraqutni related: Abu Bakr al-Nisaburi narrated to us, Isma'il ibn Ishaq ibn Sahl narrated to us in Egypt, Ibn Abi Maryam narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, Zayd ibn Aslam informed me, who said: Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir informed me, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, that he said: I came to Anas ibn Malik in Ramadan while he was about to travel, his mount had been saddled, he had put on travelling clothes, and the sun was about to set; he called for food, ate from it, then mounted. I said to him: "Is it the sunnah?" He said: "Yes." It is also related from Anas that he said: Abu Musa said to me: "Did I not inform you: when I go out, I go out fasting, and when I come in, I come in fasting; so when you go out, go out breaking the fast, and when you come in, come in breaking the fast." Al-Hasan al-Basri said: He may break the fast in his house, if he wishes, on the day he intends to...

and he would break his fast when he goes out... [continuing]. Ahmad said: he breaks his fast once he has come out of the houses. Ishaq said: No, rather when he puts his foot in the riding-saddle (ril). Ibn al-Mundhir said: Ahmad's view is sound, because they say of one who woke up healthy and then fell ill, that he breaks his fast for the rest of his day; likewise if he woke up in the settled area (al-hadar) and then set out on a journey (al-safar), he too may break his fast. A group said: he does not break his fast that day even if he sets out on his journey. This was the view of al-Zuhri, Makhul, Yahya al-Ansari, Malik, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr and the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y). They differed as to whether, if he did break it, he must make up the day and also expiate; all of them said he makes it up (qada') and does not expiate (kaffara). Malik said: because travel is an accidental excuse, so it is like illness that befalls him. It is narrated from some of Malik's companions that he makes it up and expiates; this is the view of Ibn Kinana and al-Makhzumi, al-Baji related it from al-Shafi'i, and Ibn al-Arabi chose it and held it, saying: because travel is an excuse that arose after the obligation of worship became binding, and it differs from illness and menstruation, because illness permits him to break the fast and menstruation forbids her to fast, whereas travel does not permit him that; therefore expiation is obligatory upon him for violating its sanctity. Abu Umar said: this is no valid argument, for Allah the Exalted has permitted him to break the fast in the Book and the Sunnah. As for their saying "he does not break it," that is merely a recommendation (istihbab) on account of what he has undertaken; if he takes the concession of Allah, he owes making up the day, but expiation has no basis; whoever makes it obligatory has made obligatory what neither Allah nor His Messenger (ﷺ) made obligatory. It is narrated from Ibn Umar on this question: he may break his fast if he wishes on that day when he sets out as a traveller; this is the view of al-Sha'bi, Ahmad and Ishaq.

I say: al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, titled a chapter on this question "Chapter: whoever breaks his fast during travel so that people may see him," and related the hadith from Ibn Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out from Madinah toward Makkah and fasted until he reached 'Usfan [[Usfan (with a dammah on the ʿayn and a sukun on the sin, both unpointed-letter forms): a village eight-and-forty miles from Makkah.]], then he asked for water, raised it to his hands so that he might show it to the people, and broke his fast until he reached Makkah, and that was in Ramadan. Muslim also related it from Ibn Abbas, and in his version: then he asked for a vessel containing a drink, drank it in daylight so that the people might see him, then broke his fast until he entered Makkah. This is a clear text on the matter, so whatever contradicts it falls away; and success is from Allah. In it is also a proof against those who say that fasting is not valid during travel. This was narrated from Umar, Ibn Abbas, Abu Hurayrah and Ibn Umar. Ibn Umar said: whoever fasts during travel must make it up at home. And from Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf: the one who fasts during travel is like the one who breaks his fast at home. A group of the Zahiris held this, and they argued with the words of the Exalted, "then a number of other days" (Q 2:184), as its explanation will come, and with what Ka'b ibn Asim narrated, saying: I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "It is not righteousness to fast during travel." In it is also a proof against those who say that whoever formed the intention to fast during travel may break it even without an excuse; this was the view of Mutarrif, one of al-Shafi'i's two opinions, and a body of the people of hadith hold it. Malik used to require making up and expiation for him, because he had been free to fast or not, and when he chose fasting and formed the intention, it became binding on him and he was no longer permitted to break it; so if he broke it deliberately without an excuse, he owes making up and expiation. It is also narrated from him that there is no expiation, and this is the view of most of his companions, except 'Abd al-Malik, who said: if he breaks it by intercourse, he must expiate, because he is not strengthened thereby for his journey and has no excuse, since the traveller is only permitted to break the fast in order to be strengthened thereby for his journey. The rest of the jurists of Iraq and the Hijaz said: there is no expiation upon him, among them al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and all the jurists of Kufa; said Abu Umar.

The fourth matter: the scholars differed about which is better, breaking the fast or fasting while travelling. Malik and al-Shafi'i, in one of what is narrated from them, said: fasting is better for one who is able to do it. Most of Malik's school holds the option (takhyir), and so does al-Shafi'i's school. Al-Shafi'i and those who followed him said: he has the choice, and made no distinction; so did Ibn Ulayyah, on the hadith of Anas who said: We travelled with the Prophet (ﷺ) in Ramadan, and the one fasting did not reproach the one breaking the fast, nor the one breaking the fast reproach the one fasting; related by Malik, al-Bukhari and Muslim. It is narrated from Uthman ibn Abi al-As al-Thaqafi and Anas ibn Malik, the two companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that they said: fasting during travel is better for one who is able to do it; this is the view of Abu Hanifa and his companions. It is narrated from Ibn Amr and Ibn Abbas: the concession is better; this was held by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Sha'bi, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Awza'i, Ahmad and Ishaq. All of these say breaking the fast is better, because of the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185].

The fifth issue: God's words, "so a number of other days" (fa-'iddatun min ayyamin ukhar). The sentence contains an ellipsis, meaning: whoever among you is sick or on a journey and breaks the fast, then let him make up (fa-liyaqdi) the number of days. The majority of scholars hold that if the people of a town have fasted twenty-nine days, and there is a sick man in the town who did not recover, he makes up twenty-nine days. Some scholars, including al-Hasan ibn Salih ibn Hayy, said that he makes up a full month for a month, without regard to the number of days. Ilkiya al-Tabari said: This is far-fetched, because of God's words, "so a number of other days," and He did not say "so a month of other days." Also, His words "a number" require matching the number of days in which he broke the fast. There is no doubt that if he broke the fast for part of Ramadan, he must make up the days he missed after it by their exact number. Likewise, the ruling for breaking the fast for all of it must be the same in regard to its number.

The sixth issue: God's words, ﴿fa-'iddah﴾ ("so a number"). The word "'iddah" is in the nominative as the predicate of an implied subject, with the sense "so the ruling is" or "so what is obligatory is a number." It is also permissible to read it as "fa-'alayhi 'iddah" ("so upon him is a number"). Al-Kisa'i said: It is also permissible to read "fa-'iddatan" in the accusative, meaning "so let him fast a number of days." It was also said: The meaning is "so upon him is the fasting of a number," so the noun "fasting" (sawm) is omitted and "'iddah" is put in its place. The word "'iddah" is of the pattern fi'lah from the root "to count" ('add), and it has the sense of the thing counted, like "tahn" (grinding) meaning "the thing ground." One says: "I hear a clamor but I see no flour" (a proverb for a man who talks a lot but does nothing, or for one who promises and does not act). From the same root comes the "'iddah" of a woman (her waiting period). As for "min ayyamin ukhar" ("from other days"), the word "ukhar" is not declined according to Sibawayh, because it is a form diverted from the definite article (al-), since the usual pattern of fu'al in this category is to take the article, as in "al-kubar" and "al-fudal." Al-Kisa'i said: It is diverted from "akhar," as you say "hamra'" and "humar," and therefore it is not declined. It was also said: It is not declined because it is of the pattern of plurals, and it is an adjective of "days." The feminine "ukhra" was not used so that it would not appear to be an adjective of "'iddah." It was also said: "Ukhar" is the plural of "ukhra," as if it were "ayyam ukhra" ("other days") and then it was made plural, so it became "ayyam ukhar." It was also said: The adjective of "days" is feminine, and therefore it is described as "ukhar."

The seventh issue: People differ on whether these days must be consecutive, in two views mentioned by al-Daraqutni in his Sunan. It is narrated from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: "So a number of other days, consecutive" (muta-tabi'at) was revealed, and then it was dropped. Al-Daraqutni said: This is a sound chain. (Al-Zarqani in his commentary on the Muwatta' said: The meaning of "dropped" is "abrogated." He said: The word "consecutive" is not between the two covers, meaning it is not a word in the written Qur'an. Al-Daraqutni said: The expression "dropped" is reported only by 'Urwa.)

It is narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has a fast owed from Ramadan, let him continue it (fal-yasrudhu) [meaning: let him make it consecutive] and not break it." In its chain is 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ibrahim, who is weak in narration. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning making up Ramadan: "Fast it however you wish." Ibn 'Umar said: "Fast it as you broke it." It is reported from Abu 'Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayrah, Mu'adh ibn Jabal, and 'Amr ibn al-'As.

From Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, who said: It reached me that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about breaking up the fasting of Ramadan, and he said: "That is up to you. Do you not see that if one of you owed a debt and paid a dirham and two dirhams, would he not have paid it? God is more worthy to pardon and forgive." Its chain is good, but it is mursal (a report in which the Companion's name is omitted from the chain), and it is not established as connected.

In the Muwatta' of Malik, from Nafi', that 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar used to say: "Whoever broke a fast of Ramadan due to illness or while traveling should fast it consecutively." (The wording in the Muwatta' is: "He fasts the making-up of Ramadan consecutively, whoever broke it due to illness or during a journey.") Al-Baji said in al-Muntaqa: "It is possible that he means to report the obligation, and it is possible that he means to report what is recommended. Most jurists hold it is recommended. If he separates them, it suffices for him, and this is the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i. The evidence for the validity of this is God's words, ﴿so a number of other days﴾, and He did not specify separated from consecutive. If he fasts them separately, he has fasted a number of other days, so it must suffice for him." Ibn al-'Arabi said: Consecutiveness was required in the month of Ramadan only because it is fixed in time, and since there is no fixed time for making up, separation is permitted.

The eighth issue: When God said, ﴿so a number of other days﴾, this indicates the obligation of making up without a fixed time, because the wording runs over all times and is not restricted to some of them rather than others. In the two Sahihs (of al-Bukhari and Muslim), from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, she said: "I would have to make up a fast of Ramadan, and I could not make it up except in Sha'ban, because of being busy with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)" (or "because of the place of the Messenger of Allah"). (Al-Nawawi said: The word "al-shughl" (busyness) is in the nominative as the subject of an implied verb, meaning "being busy prevents me.") In another narration: "And that was because of the position of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." This is a clear text and an added explanation of the verse. This refutes Dawud's statement that it is obligatory for him to make it up on the second day of Shawwal, and that whoever did not make it up and then died is a sinner in his view. He built on this that if someone was obligated to free a slave and found a slave being sold for a price, he is not allowed to go beyond it and buy another, because the obligation on him is to free the first slave he finds, and another will not suffice. If he already had a slave, he is not allowed to buy another. If the slave he has dies, the emancipation is not invalidated, just as a vow to free a specific slave is invalidated if she dies. That would undermine his statement.

Some of the jurists of principles said: If he dies after the second day of Shawwal has passed, he is not disobedient, on condition that he had the intention (to make it up). The correct view is that he is neither sinful nor negligent, and this is the view of the majority, except that it is recommended for him to hasten the making-up so that death does not overtake him while the obligation remains upon him.

The ninth issue: If someone had to make up days of Ramadan, and the number of days passed after the end of Ramadan while he could have fasted them, but he delayed that, and then an obstacle prevented him from making them up until the next Ramadan, then there is no feeding (kaffarah of feeding the poor) for him, because he was not negligent when he did what was permissible for him in delaying.
