This is the view of the Baghdadi Malikis, and they regard it as the view of Ibn al-Qasim in al-Mudawwana.

The tenth issue: If he delayed making up his fast beyond Sha'ban, which is the final limit of the time in which Ramadan may be made up, is he then obliged to pay an expiation (kaffarah) for that or not? Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, and Ishaq said: Yes. Abu Hanifah, al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, and Dawud said: No.

I say: Al-Bukhari adopted this view, based on his statement, and it is mentioned from Abu Hurayrah in a mursal report, and from Ibn 'Abbas, that he should feed (the poor). God did not mention feeding; He only said, ﴿so a number of other days﴾.

I say: It has come down from Abu Hurayrah in a connected (musnad) report concerning one who was negligent in making up Ramadan until another Ramadan came upon him. He said: "He fasts this one with the people, and he fasts the one he neglected, and he feeds a poor person for each day." Al-Daraqutni transmitted it and said: "This is a sound chain." It is also reported from him as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet (ﷺ)) concerning a man who broke the fast of Ramadan due to illness, then recovered but did not fast until another Ramadan came upon him. He said: "He fasts the one that came upon him, then he fasts the month in which he broke the fast, and he feeds a poor person for each day." In its chain are Ibn Nafi' and Ibn Wajih, both weak.

The eleventh issue: If the illness continued for him and he did not recover until another Ramadan came, al-Daraqutni reported from Ibn 'Umar that he feeds, in place of each day, one poor person with a mudd of wheat (a measure of about three-quarters of a kilogram), and then there is no making-up required of him. It is also reported from Abu Hurayrah that he said: "If he did not recover between the two Ramadans, he fasts for this one and feeds for the second, and there is no making-up upon him. If he recovered and did not fast until another Ramadan came upon him, he fasts for this one and feeds for the past one, and then if he breaks it he makes it up." Its chain is sound. Our scholars said: The statements of the Companions that go against analogy (qiyas) may be used as evidence.

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that a man came to him and said: "I was ill for two Ramadans?" Ibn 'Abbas said to him: "Did your illness continue, or did you recover between them?" He said: "No, I recovered." He said: "Fast two Ramadans and feed sixty poor people." This is a substitute for the statement that if his illness continued, there is no making-up upon him. This resembles their position on the pregnant woman and the nursing woman, that they feed and there is no making-up upon them, as will come (see p. 288 of this part).

The twelfth issue: Those who made feeding obligatory differed on the amount that must be fed. Abu Hurayrah, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, Malik, and al-Shafi'i said: One feeds a mudd for each day. Al-Thawri said: One feeds half a sa' (another measure) for each day.

The thirteenth issue: They differed about the one who broke the fast or had intercourse while making up a fast of Ramadan, what is obligatory for him. Malik said: Whoever breaks a day of making-up of Ramadan forgetfully, there is nothing upon him except making it up. It is recommended for him to continue the fast as a way of stepping out of disagreement, and then make it up. If he broke it intentionally, he is sinful, and there is nothing upon him except making up that day, and he should not continue it, because there is no point in refraining here from what restrains the fasting person, since he is not fasting according to the majority of scholars, due to his intentionally breaking it. As for expiation (kaffarah), there is no disagreement among Malik and his companions that it is not obligatory in this case, and this is the view of the majority of scholars. Malik said: Whoever breaks a day of making-up of Ramadan by having intercourse with his wife or otherwise, there is no expiation upon him; he is only obliged to make up that day. Qatadah said: Whoever has intercourse during the making-up of Ramadan must make up the day and pay expiation.

Ibn al-Qasim transmitted from Malik that whoever breaks the fast during the making-up of Ramadan must fast two days. Ibn al-Qasim used to give this ruling, then he retracted it and said: If he intentionally breaks the fast during the making-up of making-up, he must fast two days in its place, like someone who invalidates his pilgrimage by intercourse with his wife, and then performs it the following year and again invalidates it by intercourse with his wife, so he must perform two pilgrimages. Abu 'Umar said: Ibn Wahb and 'Abd al-Malik disagreed with him concerning the pilgrimage, and it is not obligatory to analogize from a principle on which there is disagreement.

The correct view in my opinion, and God knows best, is that in both cases there is nothing upon him except making up one day, because it is one day that he broke twice.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verses 183–184 (part 5 of 6):**

I say: This is what is implied by His saying, ﴿a number of other days﴾. So whenever a person makes up a full day in place of the day he broke his fast on during the making-up of Ramadan, he has fulfilled what is obligatory upon him, and nothing beyond that is required of him, and Allah knows best.

**The Fourteenth Issue:** The majority hold that whoever broke his fast in Ramadan due to an illness and died from that illness, or who traveled and died during his journey, owes nothing. Tawus and Qatadah said, regarding a sick person who dies before he recovers: food is to be given on his behalf.

**The Fifteenth Issue:** They differed concerning one who dies with an obligation of fasting from Ramadan that he did not make up. Malik, al-Shafi'i and al-Thawri said: no one fasts on behalf of anyone else. Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, al-Layth, Abu 'Ubayd and Ahl al-Zahir (the literalists) said: it is fasted on his behalf, except that they restricted this to a vow. A similar view is reported from al-Shafi'i. Ahmad and Ishaq said, regarding making up Ramadan: food is to be given on his behalf.

Those who argue for fasting cite what Muslim narrated from 'A'isha, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever dies with fasting owed upon him, his guardian shall fast on his behalf." However, this is general regarding fasting, and it is specified by what Muslim also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: A woman came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, my mother has died and she owed a fast of a vow," and in another narration, "a fast of a month." "Shall I fast on her behalf?" He said: "Think about it: if your mother had a debt and you paid it, would that have discharged it for her?" She said: "Yes." He said: "Then fast on behalf of your mother."

Malik and those who agreed with him argued with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164], and His saying: ﴿And that man will have nothing except what he strives for﴾ [al-Najm: 39], and His saying: ﴿And every soul earns only against itself﴾ [al-An'am: 164]. They also cited what al-Nasa'i narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "No one prays on behalf of anyone else, and no one fasts on behalf of anyone else, but food is given on his behalf for every day a mudd of wheat."

I say: This hadith is general, so it is possible that his saying, "No one fasts on behalf of anyone else," refers to the fast of Ramadan. As for the fast of a vow, it is permissible, by the evidence of the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas and others. Sahih Muslim also contains, from the hadith of Buraydah, something similar to the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas. In some of its chains: "a fast of two months." "Shall I fast on her behalf?" He said: "Fast on her behalf." She said: "She never performed Hajj. Shall I perform Hajj on her behalf?" He said: "Perform Hajj on her behalf." Her saying "two months" makes it unlikely that this refers to Ramadan, and Allah knows best.

The strongest thing cited for Malik's view is that it is the practice of the people of Medina (amal Ahl al-Madina). It is supported by clear analogy (al-qiyas al-jali), namely that it is a physical act of worship in which wealth has no role, so it is not performed on behalf of someone who was obligated to it, like prayer. This is not undermined by Hajj, because wealth has a role in it.

**The Sixteenth Issue:** Whoever holds that fasting is not valid during travel, and that making it up is obligatory forever, uses this verse as evidence. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿So whoever among you is ill or on a journey, then a number of other days﴾, meaning: then upon him is a number (of days). There is no omission or implication in the speech. [And by His saying, peace be upon him: "It is not righteousness to fast while traveling." He said: Whatever is not righteousness is sinful, so this indicates that fasting Ramadan is not permitted while traveling.] The majority say that there is an omitted element in it, "so he broke his fast," as has been mentioned earlier. This is the correct view, based on the hadith of Anas, who said: "We traveled with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in Ramadan, and the one fasting did not criticize the one not fasting, nor the one not fasting criticize the one fasting." Malik narrated it from Humayd al-Tawil, from Anas. Muslim also narrated it from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "We went on a military campaign with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sixteen days into Ramadan. Some of us fasted and some of us broke their fast, and the one fasting did not criticize the one not fasting, nor the one not fasting criticize the one fasting."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 183–184 (part 6 of 6):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And for those who are able to fast [yuṭīqūnahu], there is a redemption: feeding a needy person. But whoever volunteers good, it is better for him. And that you fast is better for you, if you only knew.﴾ On this there are five issues.

The first: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿yuṭīqūnahu﴾ (those who are able to, or "who are able to [do] it"). The majority read it with a kasra on the ṭāʾ and a sukūn on the yāʾ. Its original form is yuṭawwiqūnahu; the kasra was transferred to the ṭāʾ, and the wāw became a yāʾ because the letter before it was kasra. Ḥumayd read it according to the original form without the change (iʿtilāl), and analogically the change is what is expected. The well-known reading of Ibn ʿAbbas is "yuṭawwiqūnahu," with a fatḥa on the ṭāʾ, lightened, and a shaddah on the wāw, meaning "they are burdened with it" (yukallafūnahu). Mujahid transmitted "yaṭīqūnahu" with a yāʾ after the ṭāʾ, on the pattern of "yakīlūnahu," but this is false and impossible, because the verb is derived from ṭawq (a collar), so the wāw is obligatory and necessary in it, and there is no place for a yāʾ in this form. Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: Ahmad ibn Yahya the grammarian recited to us from Abu Dhuʾayb:

"It was said: 'Bear beyond your collar (ṭawq), for it is full (muṭabbaʿah)
Whoever comes to it, it will not harm it.'"

Here the wāw appears in ṭawq, and by this it is established that the one who puts a yāʾ in its place departs from what is correct. Ibn al-Anbari transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas "yaṭṭayyaqūnahu," with a fatḥa on the yāʾ and a shaddah on the ṭāʾ, with both the yāʾ and the ṭāʾ fatḥa, meaning "yuṭīqūnahu." It is said: ṭāqa, aṭāqa and uṭīqu have the same meaning. Also from Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿĀʾishah, Ṭawus and ʿAmr ibn Dinar: "yaṭṭawwaqūnahu," with a fatḥa on the yāʾ and a shaddah on the ṭāʾ fatḥa; this is correct in the language, because the original is yatawwaqūnahu, the tāʾ was made sukūn and merged into the ṭāʾ, becoming a shaddah ṭāʾ. It is not part of the Qur'an, contrary to those who count it as Qur'an; it is only a reading by way of explanation (tafsir).

The people of Medina and Syria read "fidyatu ṭaʿāmin" as an idafah (construct), and "masākīn" in the plural. Ibn ʿAbbas read "ṭaʿāmu miskīnin" in the singular, as reported by al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i from ʿAṭāʾ from him. This is a good reading, because it clarifies the ruling regarding each day. Abu ʿUbayd preferred it, and it is the reading of Abu ʿAmr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i. Abu ʿUbayd said: It makes clear that for each day there is one feeding, so the singular stands for the plural, but the plural does not stand for the singular. As for the plural "masākīn," one does not know how many of them there are in a day from outside the verse. The reading of the plural in "masākīn" may be explained: since those who are able to do it are plural, and each one of them is obliged to feed one needy person, the word is pluralised, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not bring four witnesses, flog them eighty lashes﴾ [al-Nur: 4], meaning: flog each one of them eighty lashes, so the eighty are not spread across all of them together, but each one receives eighty. Abu ʿAli said this is its meaning. Al-Nahhas preferred the plural reading and said: What Abu ʿUbayd preferred is rejected, because this is known by implication: it is known that the meaning of "and for those who are able to do it, there is a redemption: feeding a needy person" is that for each day there is one needy person. So choosing this reading is to answer plural with plural. Al-Nahhas said: Abu ʿUbayd preferred that it be read "fidyatu ṭaʿāmin" and said: because the food is the redemption, and it is not permissible for ṭaʿām to be an adjective, since it is a substance, but it is permissible as an apposition (badal). And it is clearer than reading "fidyatu ṭaʿāmin" as an idafah, because "fidyah" is general and falls upon food and other things, so it is like your saying: "this is a garment of silk (khazz)."

The second: The scholars differed concerning the intended meaning of the verse. It was said: it is abrogated (mansukhah). Al-Bukhari reported: "Ibn Numayr said: al-A'mash narrated to us, ʿAmr ibn Murrah narrated to us, Ibn Abi Layla narrated to us: the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) said: Ramadan came down and it was hard upon them, so whoever fed a needy person each day was excused from fasting, of those who were able to, and they were given leave in this; then 'and that you fast is better for you' abrogated it." On this basis, the majority's reading "yuṭīqūnahu" means "they are capable of it," because the obligation of fasting was thus: whoever wished fasted, and whoever wished fed a needy person. Ibn ʿAbbas said: this verse was revealed as a concession specifically for the elderly and the decrepit when they break the fast while they are able to fast; then it was abrogated by His saying ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], so the concession was removed except for those among them who are incapable. Al-Farra' said: the pronoun in "yuṭīqūnahu" may refer to the fast, meaning: "and for those who are able to fast, that they feed when they break the fast," then it was abrogated by His saying "and that you fast." It may also refer to the redemption, meaning: "and for those who are able to [bear] the redemption, a redemption."

As for the reading "yuṭawwiqūnahu," in the sense of "they are burdened with it along with the hardship that befalls them," such as the sick person and the pregnant woman: they are able to do it, but with a hardship that reaches them in themselves. If they fast, it suffices for them; and if they pay the redemption, that is theirs. Ibn ʿAbbas, if the chain from him is sound, explained "yuṭīqūnahu" as "yuṭawwiqūnahu" and "yatakallafūnahu," and so some transmitters introduced it into the Qur'an. Abu Dawud reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding "and for those who are able to do it": he said: it was confirmed for the pregnant and the nursing woman. And it is also reported from him: "and for those who are able to do it, there is a redemption: feeding a needy person," he said: it was a concession for the aged old man and the aged old woman, who are able to fast, that they break the fast and feed a needy person for each day; and the pregnant and nursing woman, if they fear for their children, break the fast and feed. Al-Daraqutni also transmitted from him: he said: a concession was granted to the aged old man to break the fast and feed a needy person for each day, with no qadaʾ upon him; this is a sound chain. And it is reported from him that he said: "and for those who are able to do it, there is a redemption: feeding" is not abrogated; it refers to the aged old man and the aged old woman who cannot fast, so they feed a needy person in place of each day; and this is sound. It is also reported from him that he said to a umm walad of his who was pregnant or nursing: "You are of those who are unable to fast; upon you is the compensation (jaza'), and upon you is no qadaʾ"; this is a sound chain. In another narration: he had a umm walad who was nursing, without doubt, and she was overwhelmed, so he commanded her to break the fast and not make up; this is sound. I say: it has thus been established by sound chains from Ibn ʿAbbas that the verse is not abrogated, and that it is muhkam (established) regarding those who have been mentioned. The first view is also sound, except that it is possible that the abrogation there means specification (takhsis), for the early scholars often use "naskh" in its broad sense; and God knows best.

Al-Hasan al-Basri, ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abi Rabah, al-Dahhak, al-Nakha'i, al-Zuhri, Rabi'ah, al-Awza'i and the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y) said: the pregnant and the nursing woman break the fast and there is no feeding upon them, in the position of the sick person who breaks the fast and makes up. This was also the view of Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Thawr. Abu ʿUbayd related this from Abu Thawr, and Ibn al-Mundhir preferred it. It is the view of Malik regarding the pregnant woman if she breaks the fast; as for the nursing woman, if she breaks the fast, then upon her is qadaʾ and feeding. Al-Shafi'i and Ahmad said: they break the fast, feed, and make up. They all agreed that the old men and old women who are unable to fast, or who are able to fast only with severe hardship, may break the fast. They differed about what is upon them. Rabi'ah and Malik said: nothing is upon them, except that Malik said: if they feed a needy person for each day, that would be dearer to me. Anas, Ibn ʿAbbas, Qays ibn al-Sa'ib and Abu Hurayrah said: upon them is the redemption. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, the people of opinion, Ahmad and Ishaq, following the saying of the companions, may God be pleased with all of them, and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So whoever of you is sick or on a journey, then a number of other days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184], then He said: ﴿And for those who are able to do it, there is a redemption: feeding a needy person﴾; and these are neither sick nor travellers, so the redemption became obligatory upon them. The evidence for Malik's view is that this person breaks the fast for an existing excuse in him, namely old age and decrepitude, so feeding is not obligatory upon him, like the traveller and the sick person. This was also reported from al-Thawri and Makhul, and Ibn al-Mundhir preferred it.

The third: Those who made the redemption obligatory upon those mentioned differed about its quantity. Malik said: a mudd by the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ) for each day he broke the fast; al-Shafi'i also said this. Abu Hanifah said: the expiation (kaffarah) for each day is a ṣāʿ of dates or half a ṣāʿ of wheat. It was reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: half a ṣāʿ of grain (ḥintah); al-Daraqutni mentioned it. It was reported from Abu Hurayrah that he said: whoever reaches old age and is not able to fast, upon him for each day is a mudd of wheat. And it was reported from Anas ibn Malik that he grew weak with regard to fasting in a year, so he prepared a large dish of food, then called thirty needy persons and fed them to satisfaction.

The fourth: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But whoever volunteers good, it is better for him.﴾ Ibn Shihab said: whoever wishes to feed in addition to fasting. Mujahid said: whoever adds to feeding beyond the mudd. Ibn ʿAbbas said regarding "whoever volunteers good": another needy person, and it is better for him. Al-Daraqutni mentioned this and said: its chain is sound and established. The second "khayr" is a comparative adjective (ṣifat tafḍīl), and so is the third; and the first "khayran" is likewise. ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "yaṭṭawwaʿa khayran" with a shaddah and a sukūn on the ʿayn, in the sense of "yatatawwaʿa." The rest read "tatawwaʿa," with a tāʾ and a lightened ṭāʾ and a fatḥa on the ʿayn, as a past tense verb.

The fifth: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And that you fast is better for you﴾, meaning: and fasting is better for you. Ubayy also read thus, meaning: better than breaking the fast together with the redemption; and this was before the abrogation. It was said: "and that you fast" refers to travel and to illness that is not burdensome; and God knows best. In general, it implies urging fasting, meaning: know this, and fast.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 185 (part 1 of 5):

There are twenty-one issues (masa'il) in it.

The First: His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿The month of Ramadan﴾. The historians (ahl al-tarikh) said: The first to fast Ramadan was Nuh (Noah), peace be upon him, when he came out of the ark. Mujahid's statement has already been mentioned: "Allah prescribed Ramadan for every nation" [[See p. 274 of this volume.]]. It is known that there were nations before Nuh, and Allah knows best. The word "shahr" (month) is derived from "ishhar" (making known), because it is well known and its knowledge is not difficult for anyone who seeks it. From the same root one says: "shahartu al-sayf" (I drew the sword) when I unsheathed it. "Ramadan" is taken from "ramida al-sa'im yurmadu" (the fasting person was scorched), when his insides became hot from intense thirst. "Al-ramda'" (with a long vowel) is intense heat, and from it is the hadith: "The prayer of the penitents (salat al-awwabin) is when the young camels are scorched" [[This is the prayer that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ instituted at the time of duha (forenoon).]]. Muslim transmitted it. "Ramida al-fisal" means the heat of the sand burns their hooves so that they kneel down because of its intensity. So Ramadan, as they mentioned, coincided with intense heat, and therefore it is derived from al-ramda'. Al-Jawhari said: The plural of "shahr Ramadan" is "ramadanat" and "armida'". It is said that when they transferred the names of the months from the ancient language, they named them after the seasons in which they fell, and this month fell during the days when the heat was intense (ramida al-harr), so it was named after that. It was also said: Ramadan was named so because it scorches sins (yarmidu al-dhunub), i.e., burns them away with righteous deeds, from al-irmad, which is burning. From the same root: "ramidat qadamuhu min al-ramda'" (his foot was scorched by the sand), i.e., it burned. "Armadatni al-ramda'" (the sand scorched me), i.e., it burned me, and from this it is said: "armadani al-amr" (the matter distressed me). It was also said: It is because hearts take in it from the heat of admonition and reflection on the matter of the Hereafter, just as the sand and stones take in the heat of the sun. "Al-ramda'" also means heated stones. It was also said: It derives from "ramadtu al-nasl, armiduhu wa armuduhu ramdan", meaning when you pound the blade between two stones to make it thin. From this comes "nasl ramid" and "marmud" (a thinned blade), according to Ibn al-Sikkit. The month was named after this because they used to polish their weapons in Ramadan in order to fight with them in Shawwal before the entry of the sacred months (al-ashhur al-hurum). Al-Mawardi reported that its name in the pre-Islamic period was "Nataq," and he recited, quoting al-Mufaddal:

"In Nataq they were routed at the mass of battle,
and the knights of Khath'am turned their backs in flight."

"Shahr" with a nominative ending (raf') is the reading of the majority, as the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is ﴿which the Quran was sent down in﴾. Or it is nominative by implying a subject (idmar mubtada'), the meaning being: "The fasting that is obligatory upon you is the month of Ramadan," or "among what has been prescribed for you is the month of Ramadan." It is also permissible for "shahr" to be the subject, with ﴿in which the Quran was sent down﴾ as a qualifying clause (sifah), and the predicate being ﴿so whoever of you witnesses the month﴾. The word "the month" is repeated for glorification, as in His words: ﴿The Inevitable Reality, what is the Inevitable Reality?﴾ [al-Haqqah: 1-2]. It is permissible that the meaning of a conditional (jaza') enters it, because the month of Ramadan, although it is a definite noun (ma'rifah), is not a definite noun specifically, since it is common to all the times that recur. This was stated by Abu 'Ali. It is reported from Mujahid and Shahr ibn Hawshab that "shahr" is in the accusative (nasb), and Harun al-A'war transmitted it from Abu 'Amr. Its meaning: "Keep to the month of Ramadan," or "Fast." And ﴿in which the Quran was sent down﴾ is a qualifier of it. It is not permissible for it to be governed by "tasumu" (fast), lest the relative clause (silah) and the relative pronoun (mawsul) be separated by the predicate of "anna," which is ﴿it is better for you﴾. Al-Rummani said: It is permissible to put it in the accusative as an apposition (badal) from His words ﴿for a number of days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184].

The Second: It has been disputed whether it is said "Ramadan" without being attached to "shahr" (month). Mujahid disliked this and said: It is said as Allah said. In a report: "Do not say 'Ramadan,' but attribute it (ansibuhu) as Allah attributed it in the Quran, when He said 'the month of Ramadan.'" He used to say: "It has reached me that it is one of the names of Allah." He disliked that its word be used in the plural for this meaning. He used as evidence what is narrated: "Ramadan is one of the names of Allah, the Exalted." This is not authentic, for it comes from the hadith of Abu Ma'shar Najih, and he is weak. The correct view is the permissibility of using "Ramadan" without attachment, as it is established in the Sahihs and elsewhere. Muslim transmitted from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When Ramadan comes, the gates of mercy are opened, the gates of the Fire are closed, and the devils are shackled." In the Sahih of al-Busti, from him, he said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When Ramadan comes, the gates of mercy are opened for it, the gates of Jahannam are closed, and the devils are chained." It is narrated from Ibn Shihab, from Anas ibn Abi Anas, that his father told him that he heard Abu Hurayrah say ... and he mentioned it. Al-Busti said: This Anas ibn Abi Anas is the father of Malik ibn Anas. The name of Abu Anas is Malik ibn Abi 'Amir, one of the trustworthy people of Madinah, and he is Malik ibn Abi 'Amir ibn 'Amr ibn al-Harith ibn 'Uthman [[In Ibn Khallikan: "Ghaymam (with a dotted ghayn and a letter ya with two dots beneath it), and it is said 'Uthman (with an undotted 'ayn and a three-dotted tha'), ibn Jutheyl (with a jim, a three-dotted tha', and a silent ya with two dots beneath it). Ibn Sa'd said: it is Khutheyl with a dotted kha'." This lineage appears corrupted in the manuscripts.]] ibn Jutheyl ibn 'Amr, from Dhi Asbah, one of the crowned kings (aqyal) of Yemen. Al-Nasa'i narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Ramadan has come to you, a blessed month. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has made its fasting obligatory upon you. The gates of heaven are opened in it, the gates of the Hellfire are closed in it, and the rebellious devils are chained in it. In it there is a night better than a thousand months. Whoever is deprived of its good has indeed been deprived." Abu Hatim al-Busti also transmitted it and said: His words "the rebellious devils" specify his words "the devils are shackled and chained." Al-Nasa'i also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to a woman of the Ansar: "When Ramadan comes, perform 'umrah, for an 'umrah in it equals a Hajj." Al-Nasa'i also narrated from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah, the Exalted, has made the fasting of Ramadan [upon you] obligatory, and I have established its night prayer (qiyam) as a sunnah for you. Whoever fasts it and stands in prayer during it, out of faith and seeking reward, will come out of his sins like the day his mother bore him." The reports on this are numerous, all of them without the word "shahr." Sometimes the Arabs omitted the word "month" from Ramadan.

The poet said:

"A girl in her loose-fitting garment,
whiter than the sister of the Banu Ibad,
a girl in the past Ramadan,
breaking off speech with winks."

The virtue of Ramadan is great and its reward is abundant. This is indicated by the meaning of its derivation from its burning sins, and by what we have written of the hadiths.

The Third: Allah prescribed the fasting of the month of Ramadan, i.e., the duration of its crescent, and by this the month was named, as came in the hadith: "If the month is hidden from you" (fa-in ghumma 'alaykum al-shahr), i.e., the crescent, and it will come later. The poet said:

"Two brothers from Najd, upon a firm promise,
and the month is like a fingernail paring,
until it becomes complete in its circle,
in four days beyond ten."

It is obligatory upon us, when the crescent is hidden by clouds, to complete the count of Sha'ban as thirty days and the count of Ramadan as thirty days, so that we enter into worship with certainty and exit from it with certainty. He said in His Book: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Reminder, that you may make clear to people what has been sent down to them﴾ [al-Nahl: 44] [[See vol. 10, p. 108.]]. The authoritative imams narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Fast when you see it, and break your fast when you see it; but if it is hidden from you, then complete the count (fa-akmiluu al-'adad)." In another narration: "If the month is hidden from you, then count thirty." Mutarrif ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Shikhkhir, who was one of the senior Successors (kibar al-tabi'in), and Ibn Qutaybah, one of the linguists, went to the view that when there are clouds one relies on calculation, by estimating the lunar mansions and considering their calculation for the fasting of Ramadan; they said even if it were clear, one would act upon it, based on his saying, peace be upon him: "If it is hidden from you, then estimate for it" (fa-in ughmiya 'alaykum fa-qduru lahu), i.e., derive evidence for it from its mansions, and estimate the completion of the month by its calculation. The majority said: The meaning of "fa-qduru lahu" is "then complete the measure," which is explained by the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, "then complete the count." Al-Dawudi mentioned that it was said regarding the meaning of his words "fa-qduru lahu": i.e., estimate the mansions. We do not know anyone who said this except some of the companions of al-Shafi'i, who held that one relies in this on the statement of the astrologers (al-munajjimin). The consensus (ijma') is a proof against them. Ibn Nafi' narrated from Malik concerning the imam who does not fast upon sighting the crescent, nor break his fast upon its sighting, but fasts and breaks his fast according to calculation: that he is not to be followed or obeyed. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Some of our companions have slipped, reporting from al-Shafi'i that he said: "One relies upon calculation," and this is a stumble for which there is no recovery (la la'a laha) [[In manuscripts a, b, j, z, and w, "la la'a" with tanwin is a phrase invoked for one who stumbles; its meaning is raising up and pardon from the stumble. When a curse is intended, one says "la la'a." In H: "la yuqalu biha." In Ibn al-'Arabi's Ahkam al-Quran: "la yuqalaha."]].

The Fourth: Malik and al-Shafi'i disagreed over whether the crescent of Ramadan is established by the testimony of one witness or two. Malik said: The testimony of one is not accepted regarding it, because it is testimony concerning a crescent, so less than two is not accepted in it. Its basis is the testimony concerning the crescent of Shawwal and Dhu al-Hijjah. Al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifah said: One is accepted, because of what Abu Dawud narrated from Ibn 'Umar who said: "The people were looking for the crescent, so I informed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that I had seen it, and he fasted and commanded the people to fast." Al-Daraqutni also transmitted it and said: "Marwan ibn Muhammad alone transmitted it from Ibn Wahb, and he is trustworthy." Al-Daraqutni narrated that "a man testified before 'Ali ibn Abi Talib that he had seen the crescent of Ramadan, so he fasted, I think he said: and he commanded the people to fast, and he said: 'To fast one day of Sha'ban is dearer to me than to break my fast on one day of Ramadan.'" Al-Shafi'i said: If the general public do not see the crescent of the month of Ramadan but a just man (rajul 'adl) sees it, I think it right to accept him, based on the report and as a precaution. Al-Shafi'i later said: For Ramadan, only two witnesses are permissible. Al-Shafi'i said: Some of our companions said: "I do not accept on it except two witnesses, and this is the analogy for every matter that is unseen (mughayyab)."

The Fifth: They differed regarding the one who sees the crescent of Ramadan alone, or the crescent of Shawwal. Al-Rabi' narrated from al-Shafi'i: "Whoever sees the crescent of Ramadan alone should fast it, and whoever sees the crescent of Shawwal alone should break his fast, and he should keep that quiet." Ibn Wahb narrated from Malik concerning the one who sees the crescent of Ramadan alone that he fasts, because it is not right for him to break his fast while he knows that this day is from the month of Ramadan. As for one who sees the crescent of Shawwal alone, he does not break his fast, because people would suspect that someone who is not trustworthy among them breaks his fast, and then those people would say when it appears to them: "We saw the crescent." Ibn al-Mundhir said: Al-Layth ibn Sa'd and Ahmad ibn Hanbal also said this. 'Ata' and Ishaq said: He neither fasts nor breaks his fast. Ibn al-Mundhir said: He fasts and breaks his fast.

**The sixth issue:** Scholars differ on the case where someone reports having seen the new moon in another place. If that place is near, the ruling is one. If it is far, each people follow their own sighting. This view is narrated from ʿIkrimah, al-Qasim and Salim, and is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas. Ishaq (ibn Rahawayh) held it, and al-Bukhari alluded to it when he titled a chapter: "For the people of every land, their own sighting." Others said: when it is established among the people that the people of a certain land have seen the moon, then those who broke their fast must make up the days. This was the view of al-Layth ibn Saʿd and al-Shafiʿi. Ibn al-Mundhir said: "I know of no one who holds it except al-Muzani and al-Kufi."

I say: Ilkiya al-Tabari mentioned in his book *Ahkam al-Quran*: "The companions of Abu Hanifa agreed that if the people of one land fast thirty days on the basis of sighting, and the people of another land fast twenty-nine days, then those who fasted twenty-nine days must make up one day." The companions of al-Shafiʿi do not hold this, since the horizons (*matali*, the places where the moon is first visible) in different lands may differ.

The evidence of the companions of Abu Hanifa is the words of God Most High: ﴿and that you complete the prescribed period﴾. By the sighting of one land it is established that the period is thirty days, so it became obligatory on these people to complete it. Their opponents argue from the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Fast when you see it, and break your fast when you see it," and this requires taking into account the custom of each people in their own land.

Abu ʿUmar (Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr) related a consensus that the sighting is not taken into account for places far away, such as al-Andalus relative to Khurasan. He said: "Every land has its own sighting, except for a great city and the lands of the Muslims whose regions are close together."

Muslim narrated from Kurayb that Umm al-Fadl bint al-Harith sent him to Muʿawiya in Syria. He said: "I arrived in Syria, did her errand, and Ramadan began while I was in Syria. I saw the crescent on Friday night. Then I came to Medina at the end of the month, and ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) asked me, and he mentioned the crescent and said: 'When did you see the crescent?' I said: 'We saw it on Friday night.' He said: 'Did you see it yourself?' I said: 'Yes, and the people saw it too, and they fasted, and Muʿawiya fasted.' He said: 'But we saw it on Saturday night, so we will keep fasting until we complete thirty days or see it.' I said: 'Are you not satisfied with the sighting of Muʿawiya and his fasting?' He said: 'No. This is how the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded us.'"

Our scholars said: Ibn ʿAbbas's words "This is how the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded us" are an explicit statement that this is traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ) and to his command. It is therefore evidence that when the lands are far apart, as Syria is from the Hijaz, it is obligatory on the people of each land to act on their own sighting and not on the sighting of others, even if it is established before the supreme ruler (*al-imam al-aʿzam*), so long as he has not compelled the people to act on it. If he does compel them, then opposing him is not permitted.

Ilkiya al-Tabari said: The words "This is how the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded us" may be understood as an interpretation of the Prophet's saying: "Fast when you see it, and break your fast when you see it."

Ibn al-ʿArabi said: "There is disagreement about the interpretation of Ibn ʿAbbas's statement. It was said: he rejected it because it was a report from a single person (*khabar wahid*). It was also said: he rejected it because the regions differ in their horizons, and this is the correct view, because Kurayb did not witness the sighting himself; he only reported a ruling that had been established by testimony. There is no disagreement that a ruling already established may be transmitted by a single reporter. A parallel case: if it were established that the crescent was seen on Friday night in Aghmat, a town of the Berbers in the land of Morocco near Marrakesh, and was seen in Ishbiliya (Seville), a great city in al-Andalus, on Saturday night, then each land has its own sighting, because Suhayl (Canopus, a star) is visible from Aghmat but not visible from Ishbiliya, and this shows that the horizons differ."

I say: As for the school of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, on this question Ibn Wahb and Ibn al-Qasim related from him in *al-Majmuʿa* that if the people of Basra saw the crescent of Ramadan, and this reached the people of Kufa, Medina and Yemen, then they are obliged to fast or, if the time of performance has passed, to make it up.

Al-Qadi Abu Ishaq related from Ibn al-Majishun that if the sighting was established in Basra by a widely known and publicized matter that needs no testimony or certification of the witnesses, then it obliges the people of other lands to make it up. But if it was established only before their judge on the testimony of two witnesses, then it does not oblige the people of other lands, except those who are subject to that judge's ruling within his jurisdiction, or unless it was established before the commander of the believers (the caliph), in which case making it up is obligatory on the whole body of Muslims. He said: "This is the view of Malik."

**The seventh issue:** Most readers recited *shahru* (شَهْرُ) in the nominative case, as the predicate of an implied subject, meaning: that (which is prescribed) is the month, or: the obligatory fasting for you is the month of Ramadan, or: the fasting, or: the days. It was also said that it is in the nominative as the object of the passive verb *kutiba* (it was prescribed), meaning: the month of Ramadan was prescribed for you. *Ramadan* (رَمَضَانَ) is not declined, because the *nun* in it is an added letter. It may be nominative as a subject (mubtada'), with its predicate being: ﴿the month in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾. It was also said that its predicate is: ﴿whoever of you witnesses﴾, and ﴿in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾ is a qualifying clause. It was also said that it is nominative as an apposition (badal) of *al-siyam* (the fasting).

Whoever says that *al-siyam* in the phrase ﴿fasting is prescribed for you﴾ refers to the three days and ʿAshura, must read *shahru* here as a subject. Whoever says that *al-siyam* there refers to Ramadan must read *shahru* here either as a subject, or as an apposition of *al-siyam*, meaning: the month of Ramadan was prescribed for you.

Mujahid and Shahr ibn Hawshab read *shahra* (شَهْرَ) in the accusative. Al-Kisai said: the meaning is: fasting was prescribed for you, and that you fast the month of Ramadan. Al-Farra' said: that is, fasting was prescribed for you, namely that you fast the month of Ramadan.

Al-Nahhas said: "It is not permissible for *shahra Ramadan* to be in the accusative governed by *tasumu* (you fast), because it would then fall within the relative clause (*silah*) and there would be a separation between the relative clause and the relative pronoun. The same applies if you put it in the accusative governed by *al-siyam* (the fasting). But it is permissible to put it in the accusative as an exhortation (*ighra'*), meaning: keep to the month of Ramadan, and fast the month of Ramadan. This is also weak, because the month has not been mentioned before, so one would not be exhorted to it."

I say: The phrase ﴿fasting is prescribed for you﴾ points to the month, so the exhortation is permissible. This is the view chosen by Abu ʿUbayd. Al-Akhfash said: it is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*zarf*).

It is reported from al-Hasan and Abu ʿAmr that they assimilated the *ra'* into the following *ra'* (idgham). This is not permissible, because two consonants would then come together without a vowel between them. It is permissible to transfer the vowel of the *ra'* onto the *ha'* (of *Ramadan*?), so that the *ha'* takes a *damma* and then the letters are assimilated. This is the view of the Kufan grammarians.

**The eighth issue:** God Most High's words ﴿the month in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾ are explicit that the Qur'an was sent down in the month of Ramadan. This clarifies His words, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Ha Mim. By the clear Book. Indeed, We sent it down during a blessed night﴾ [al-Dukhan 44:1–3], meaning the Night of Decree (*Laylat al-Qadr*), and His words: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ [al-Qadr 97:1]. In this there is evidence that the Night of Decree occurs only in Ramadan and not in any other month.

There is no disagreement that the Qur'an was sent down from the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh al-mahfuz*) on the Night of Decree, as we have explained, all at once, and was placed in the House of Honour (*bayt al-ʿizza*) in the lowest heaven. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) would bring it down piece by piece, with commands, prohibitions and occasions of revelation, over twenty years.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: the Qur'an was sent down from the Preserved Tablet all at once to the scribes (*al-kataba*, the angels who record) in the lowest heaven. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) brought it down in installments, meaning verse by verse or two verses at a time, at different times over twenty-one years.

Muqatil, regarding God's words ﴿the month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾, said: it was sent down from the Preserved Tablet every year on the Night of Decree to the lowest heaven. Then it was brought down to the *safara* (the angels who transcribe) from the Preserved Tablet over twenty months, and Jibril brought it down over twenty years.

I say: The statement of Muqatil contradicts the reported consensus that "the Qur'an was sent down all at once." And Allah knows best.

Wathila ibn al-Asqaʿ related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The scrolls of Ibrahim were sent down on the first night of Ramadan, the Torah on the sixth night of it, the Gospel on the thirteenth night, and the Qur'an on the twenty-fourth night."

I say: In this hadith there is evidence for what al-Hasan says, that the Night of Decree is the night of the twenty-fourth. Its explanation will come, God willing.

**The ninth issue:** God Most High's words ﴿the Qur'an﴾. *Al-Qur'an* is a name for the speech of God Most High. It has the meaning of the thing recited, as a drink is called a drink (*shara'b*) and a thing written is called a book (*kitab*). On this basis it was said that it is the verbal noun of *qara'a* (he recited), *yaqra'u*, *qira'atan* and *qur'anan* with the same meaning. A poet said:

*They sacrificed a grey-haired one, whose forehead marks the prostrations,*
*Who cuts the night with glorification and recitation (qur'anan).*

That is, recitation. In the authentic *Sahih Muslim*, from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, there are chained shayatin in the sea whom Sulayman (peace be upon him) bound, and they are about to come out and recite to the people *qur'anan*, that is, recitation. In the revelation: ﴿And the recitation of dawn; indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed﴾ [al-Isra' 17:78], that is, the recitation of dawn.

The thing recited is called *Qur'an* according to the Arabs' custom of naming the thing acted upon by the verbal noun, as they name the known thing *ʿilm*, the beaten thing *darb* and the drunk thing *shurb*, as we have mentioned. Then the usage became well known and was joined by religious custom (*al-ʿurf al-shar'i*), so that *al-Qur'an* became the name of the speech of God. So when it is said "the Qur'an is uncreated," what is meant is the thing recited, not the act of reciting.

The codex in which the speech of God is written is sometimes also called "Qur'an" by extension. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do not travel with the Qur'an to the land of the enemy," meaning the codex. It is derived from *qara'tu al-shay'* (I gathered the thing), meaning I collected it.

It was also said that *al-Qur'an* is a proper name for the Book of God, not derived, like the Torah and the Gospel. This is reported from al-Shafiʿi. But the correct view is that all of them are derived, as will come.

**The tenth issue:** God Most High's words ﴿a guidance for mankind﴾. *Huda* (هُدىً) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*) of *al-Qur'an*, meaning: guiding them. ﴿And clear proofs﴾ is conjoined to it. *Al-huda* means guidance and explanation, as has been mentioned, that is, an explanation for them and a guidance. The intended meaning is the Qur'an in its entirety, including the decisive (*muhkam*) and the ambiguous (*mutashabih*), and the abrogating (*nasikh*, the ruling that cancels an earlier ruling) and the abrogated (*mansukh*). Then the clear proofs within it are singled out and mentioned specifically, meaning the lawful and the unlawful, the admonitions and the rulings. ﴿Clear proofs﴾ is the plural of *bayyina*, from *bana al-shay'* (the thing became manifest) when it became clear. ﴿And the criterion﴾ is what distinguishes truth from falsehood, that is, it separates them, and this has been mentioned before.

**The eleventh issue:** God Most High's words ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾. The reading of the common people has the *lam* (لَامُ) jussive (with sukun). Al-Hasan and al-A'raj read it with a *kasra* on the *lam*, and this is the *lam* of command, whose basic form is the *kasra* when it stands alone. When it is joined to something, there are two possibilities: the jussive (sukun) and the *kasra*. It is joined only to three letters: with the *fa'* as in His words ﴿fa-l-yasumhu﴾ ("let him fast it"), and with the *waw* ... and with the *lam*... as in His words ﴿li-ya'budu﴾ ("so let them worship"), [the passage ends here]

﴾ [Quraysh: 3]. The waw (و) is like His words, ﴿and let them fulfil﴾ [al-Hajj: 29], and thumma (ثم) is like His words, ﴿then let them complete﴾ [al-Hajj: 29]. "Shahida" (شَهِدَ) means "attended" (حَضَرَ), and it contains an implied element. That is, "whoever among you attends the place of residence (al-misr) during the month, being sane, mature, healthy and resident, let him fast." It is said to be general (ʿamm) and is specified by His words, ﴿but whoever among you is ill or on a journey [must fast the same number of other days]﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184]. "The month" is not an object (maf'ul) but a time adverb (zarf zaman).

The scholars differed in interpreting this. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, Ibn ʿAbbas, Suwayd ibn Ghaflah and ʿAʾishah, four of the Companions, together with Abu Mijlaz Lahiq ibn Humayd and ʿUbaydah al-Salmani, said: "Whoever attends," that is, whoever is present at the entry of the month and was resident at its beginning in his town and with his family, let him complete his fast, whether he travels afterwards or stays. And one only breaks the fast while travelling if Ramadan began while he was on a journey. Their meaning is: whoever is overtaken by Ramadan while travelling may break his fast, and he owes a number of other days; but whoever is overtaken by it while resident, let him fast.

The majority of the Ummah said: whoever attends the beginning and the end of the month, let him fast for as long as he is resident; if he travels, he may break his fast. This is the sound view, and the authentic reports indicate it. Al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, in reply to the first view, titled a chapter: "Chapter: If one fasts some days of Ramadan and then travels." He related to us: ʿAbdullah ibn Yusuf said, Malik informed us, from Ibn Shihab, from ʿUbaydullah ibn ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUtbah, from Ibn ʿAbbas, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out to Makkah during Ramadan and fasted until he reached al-Kadid [[al-Kadid (with a fatha on the kaf and a kasra on the dal): a place about seven stages or so from Madinah, and about two stages from Makkah.]] and then broke his fast, and the people broke their fast too. Abu ʿAbdullah (al-Bukhari) said: "al-Kadid is the area between ʿUsfan and Qudayd [[ʿUsfan: a village with farms and palm trees two stages from Makkah; Qudayd (with a damma on the qaf): the name of a place near Makkah.]]."

I say: It is possible to interpret the view of ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, and those who agreed with him, as referring to recommended travel, such as visiting virtuous brothers and righteous people, or permissible travel in seeking wealth beyond sufficiency. As for obligatory travel in seeking essential sustenance, or conquering a land when that is established, or repelling an enemy, then the person has a choice in it, and it is not obligatory for him to abstain; rather, breaking the fast in it is better, to gain strength. This is so even if he attended the month in his own town and fasted part of it there, based on the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas and others. There will be no disagreement in this, Allah willing, and Allah knows best.

Abu Hanifah and his companions said: whoever attends the month with the conditions of legal responsibility (taklif), not being insane or unconscious, let him fast it. And whoever is overtaken by Ramadan while insane and remains so for the whole month, there is no qada' (making up) for him, because he did not attend the month in a state that requires fasting. And whoever becomes insane at the beginning and end of the month, he makes up the days of his insanity. The accusative of "the month" under this interpretation is the explicit object (maf'ul sarih) of "shahida."

Twelfth issue: It has been established that the obligation of fasting is incumbent upon Islam, puberty and knowledge of the month. So if a disbeliever embraces Islam, or a child reaches puberty, before dawn, fasting becomes obligatory for them on that day's morning. If it is after dawn, abstaining is recommended for them, and they do not have to make up the past part of the month, nor the day on which they reached puberty or embraced Islam.

The scholars differed concerning a disbeliever who embraces Islam on the last day of Ramadan: is it obligatory on him to make up the whole of Ramadan or not? And is it obligatory on him to make up the day on which he embraced Islam? Imam Malik and the majority said: he does not have to make up what has passed, because he only attended the month from the time of his Islam. Malik said: "It is more beloved to me that he makes up the day on which he embraced Islam." ʿAta' and al-Hasan said: he fasts what remains and makes up what has passed. ʿAbd al-Malik ibn al-Majishun said: he refrains from eating during that day and makes it up. Ahmad and Ishaq said the same. Ibn al-Mundhir said: he does not have to make up what has passed of the month, nor that day. Al-Baji said: whoever among our companions says that disbelievers are addressed by the laws of Islam (and this is the implication of the view of Malik and most of his companions) obligates him to abstain for the rest of his day. Ibn Nafi' related it in the Mudawwanah from Malik, and Shaykh Abu al-Qasim said it. And whoever among our companions says they are not addressed says: he is not obliged to abstain for the rest of his day. This is the implication of the view of Ashhab and ʿAbd al-Malik ibn al-Majishun, and Ibn al-Qasim said it.

I say: And this is the sound view, because of His saying, "O you who have believed," so He addressed the believers and not others. This is clear. Therefore it is not obligatory on him to abstain for the rest of the day, nor to make up what has passed. The discussion of the meaning of His words, "and whoever is ill or on a journey [must fast the same number of other days]," has preceded (see the first issue and what follows it, p. 276 of this part). And praise be to Allah.

Thirteenth issue: His words, ﴿Allah intends for you ease﴾. The reading of a group is "al-yusr" (الْيُسْرَ) with a damma on the sin; both are dialects, and likewise "al-ʿusr" (الْعُسْرَ). Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: "al-yusr" is breaking the fast while travelling, and "al-ʿusr" is fasting while travelling. The correct view is the general meaning of the wording in all matters of religion, as He said, ﴿and He has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion﴾ [al-Hajj: 78] [[See vol. 12, p. 100.]]. It is related from the Prophet ﷺ: "The religion of Allah is ease," and he ﷺ said: "Make things easy and do not make them difficult." "Al-yusr" comes from ease (al-suhulah), and from it comes "al-yasar" (affluence/wealth). The left hand (al-yad al-yusra) was named so as an optimistic omen, or because affairs become easy for him through its help to the right hand; there are two views. And His words, "and He does not intend for you hardship," have the same meaning as His words, "Allah intends for you ease," and so it is repeated for emphasis.

Fourteenth issue: The verse indicates that Allah, glory be to Him, wills by an eternal, pre-eternal will that is additional to His essence. This is the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah (the people of the Prophetic tradition), just as He is knowing by knowledge, powerful by power, living by life, hearing by hearing, seeing by sight, and speaking by speech. All of these are existential, eternal attributes additional to the essence. The philosophers and the Shiʿah went to the denial of these, may Allah be exalted above the words of the deviators and the falsehood of the falsifiers. What cuts off the roots of the people of negation (ahl al-taʿtil) is to say: if it were not affirmed that He is one with will, it would be affirmed that He is not one with will; and if that were correct, then everything that does not have will would be deficient in comparison with whoever has will. For whoever possesses volitional attributes can specify a thing or can refrain from specifying it. Sound reason decides that this is a perfection for Him and not a deficiency. Indeed, if one were to suppose by imagination that this attribute were removed from Him, His earlier state would be more perfect than His later state. So there remains only that what does not possess an attribute is more deficient than what possesses it, and the impossibility in this is not hidden: how can it be conceived that the created is more perfect than the Creator, and the Creator more deficient than it? Immediate understanding requires its rejection and refutation.

He, may His majesty be great and His names be sanctified, described Himself as willing, saying, ﴿Doer of what He wills﴾ [Hud: 107] [[See vol. 19, p. 295.]], and He, glory be to Him, said, ﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], and He said, ﴿Allah wants to lighten [the burden] for you﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 28] [[See vol. 5, p. 148.]]. When He wills a thing, He only says to it, "Be," and it is. Moreover, this world is in the utmost wisdom, perfection, order and firm structure, and yet its existence is possible and its non-existence is possible. So the One who specified it with existence must be willing it, powerful over it, and knowing of it. If He were not knowing and powerful, nothing could proceed from Him. And whoever is not knowing, even if powerful, what proceeds from him would not be in an order of wisdom and perfection. And whoever is not willing, the specification of some possibilities with certain states and times over others is not more fitting than the reverse, since their relation to Him is one and the same. They said: once it is established that He is powerful and willing, it must be that He is living, since life is a condition of these attributes; and it follows from His being living that He is hearing, seeing and speaking. If these attributes were not established for Him, then necessarily He would be characterised by their opposites, such as blindness, deafness and muteness, as is known in the observable world. The Creator, glory be to Him and exalted, is sanctified above being characterised by anything that would necessitate deficiency in His essence.

Fifteenth issue: His words, ﴿and that you complete the period﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: completing the number of days of performance (ʿiddat al-adaʾ) for one who broke his fast on a journey or during illness. The second: the number of the lunar month, whether it is twenty-nine or thirty days. Jabir ibn ʿAbdullah said: the Prophet ﷺ said, "The month may be twenty-nine days." In this there is a refutation of the interpretation of those who interpreted his words ﷺ, "The two months of festival, Ramadan and Dhu al-Hijjah, do not decrease," as meaning that they do not fall short of thirty days; it was related by Abu Dawud. The majority of scholars interpreted it as meaning that they do not decrease in reward and expiation of sins, whether they are of twenty-nine or thirty days.

Sixteenth issue: There is no consideration of the sighting of the crescent of Shawwal on the thirtieth day of Ramadan during the day; rather, it belongs to the night that follows. This is the sound view. The narrators differed from ʿUmar on this question. Al-Daraqutni related from Shaqiq, who said: ʿUmar's letter came to us while we were in Khanaqin, and in his letter he said: "The crescents vary in size, so when you see the crescent during the day, do not break your fast until two witnesses testify that they saw it yesterday."

Al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 2, verse 185 (part 4 of 5):

Abu 'Umar (Ibn 'Abd al-Barr) also reported it through the hadith of 'Abd al-Razzaq, from Ma'mar, from al-A'mash, from Abu Wa'il [Abu Wa'il: the kunya of Shaqiq mentioned earlier], who said: "'Umar wrote to us ..." and then he mentioned it.

Abu 'Umar said: It is also narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib the same as what 'Abd al-Razzaq mentioned, and it is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Umar and Anas ibn Malik. Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, al-Layth and al-Awza'i also held this view, and so did Ahmad and Ishaq.

Sufyan al-Thawri and Abu Yusuf said: If the crescent is seen after midday (zawal), it belongs to the night that comes next; if it is seen before midday, it belongs to the night that has passed. The same has been narrated from 'Umar: 'Abd al-Razzaq reported it from al-Thawri, from Mughira, from Shibak, from Ibrahim, who said: 'Umar wrote to 'Utba ibn Farqad: "If you see the crescent during the day before the sun has passed its zenith, on the completion of thirty days, then break your fast; and if you see it after the sun has passed its zenith, do not break your fast until you have reached the evening."' The same has been narrated from 'Ali. Nothing in this matter is authentic in terms of its chain of transmission from 'Ali.

It is also narrated from Sulayman ibn Rabi'a the same as the view of al-Thawri, and this was the view of 'Abd al-Malik ibn Habib, and it was by this that fatwas were given in Cordoba.

Opinions differ from 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Aziz on this question. Abu 'Umar said: The hadith from 'Umar in accordance with the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa is connected (muttasil), whereas the report from him in accordance with the view of al-Thawri is disconnected (munqati'), and turning to the connected report is more appropriate.

Those who adopted the view of al-Thawri argued: "The hadith of al-A'mash is general (mujmal), not specifying whether before or after midday, whereas the hadith of Ibrahim is explicit (mufassar), so it is more fitting to act upon it."

I say: A report has been transmitted with a raised (marfu') chain, with the same meaning as what was narrated from 'Umar, connected and halted (mawquf), related by 'A'isha, the wife of the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) woke up fasting on the morning of the thirtieth day, and he saw the crescent of Shawwal during the day, and did not break his fast until evening." Al-Daraqutni transmitted it from the hadith of al-Waqidi, and said: al-Waqidi said: Mu'adh ibn Muhammad al-Ansari narrated to us, saying: I asked al-Zuhri about the crescent of Shawwal when it is seen early, and he said: I heard Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab say: "If the crescent of Shawwal is seen after dawn has risen, until the afternoon or until the sun sets, then it belongs to the night that is coming." Abu 'Abd Allah said: This is agreed upon (muj'ma' 'alayhi).

The seventeenth issue: al-Daraqutni narrated from Rib'i ibn Hirash, from a man of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "People disagreed about the last day of Ramadan, so two Bedouins came and testified before the Prophet (ﷺ) that they had sighted (ahalla) the crescent the previous evening. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered the people to break their fast and to go out early to their place of prayer." Al-Daraqutni said: This chain is good and established (hasan thabit).

Abu 'Umar said: There is no disagreement from Malik and his companions that the 'Id prayer is not performed on a day other than the day of 'Id, nor on the day of 'Id after midday. It is also reported from Abu Hanifa. The view of al-Shafi'i on this question varied: at one time he said the same as Malik, and al-Muzani adopted it and said: "If it is not permissible to pray on the day of 'Id after midday, then the second day is further from its time, and it is even more fitting that it not be prayed on it." Another narration from al-Shafi'i is that it is prayed on the second day in the forenoon (duha). Al-Buwayti said: It is not prayed unless a hadith establishes it.

Abu 'Umar said: If the 'Id prayer were performed after its time had passed, it would resemble the obligatory prayers, yet they agree that in the remaining sunan it is not made up; so this is similar to them.

Al-Thawri, al-Awza'i and Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: They go out the next day. Abu Yusuf said so in al-Imla'. Al-Hasan ibn Salih ibn Hayy said: They do not go out for 'Id al-Fitr, but they go out for 'Id al-Adha. Abu Yusuf said: As for 'Id al-Adha, he leads them in the prayer on the third day. Abu 'Umar said: This is because 'Id al-Adha consists of days of 'Id and its prayer is an 'Id prayer, whereas 'Id al-Fitr is a day of 'Id only as a single day; so if the prayer is not performed on it, it is not made up on another day, because it is not an obligation that would be made up.

Al-Layth ibn Sa'd said: They go out for both al-Fitr and al-Adha the next day.

I say: The view of going out, if Allah wills, is more sound, due to the established Sunna regarding this, and there is nothing to prevent the Lawgiver from exempting from the sunan whatever He wishes, commanding that it be made up after its time has passed. Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has not prayed the two rak'as of Fajr, let him pray them after the sun has risen." Abu Muhammad authenticated it. Al-Tirmidhi said: Action is in accordance with this among some scholars, and Sufyan al-Thawri, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq and Ibn al-Mubarak say so. And it has been narrated from 'Umar that he did it.

I say: Our scholars have said: Whoever runs out of time, prays Subh and leaves the two rak'as of Fajr, then he may pray them after sunrise if he wishes. It was also said: He should not pray them at that time. Then, if we say he should pray them, is what he does a qada' (making up), or do the two rak'as earn him the reward of the two rak'as of Fajr? Shaykh Abu Bakr said: This is what follows from the basic principle of the school, and the use of the term qada' is figurative. I say: It is not far-fetched that the ruling for the 'Id al-Fitr prayer on the second day is based on this principle, especially since it occurs only once a year, along with what has been established from the Sunna. Al-Nasa'i narrated: Amr ibn 'Ali told me, saying: Yahya narrated to us, saying: Shu'ba narrated to us, saying: Abu Bishr narrated to me, from Abu 'Umayr ibn Anas, from some paternal uncles of his: that a group saw the crescent, so they came to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he ordered them to break their fast after the day had risen, and to go out to the 'Id the next day. In another narration: "and to go out to their place of prayer the next day."

The eighteenth issue: Abu Bakr [ibn 'Ayyash], reading from 'Asim, and Abu 'Amr in some of what is narrated from him, and al-Hasan, Qatada and al-A'raj read "wa-litukammilu al-'idda" with tashdid (doubled letter). The rest read it with takhfif (no doubling). Al-Kisa'i preferred the takhfif, as in His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 3]. Al-Nahhas said: They are two dialects with one meaning, as He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿So give respite to the disbelievers; give them a little respite﴾ [al-Tariq: 17]. "Wa-litukmilu" with a sukun on the lam is not permissible. The difference between this and what preceded is that the estimated sense is: "and He wants you to complete (la-an tukmilu)," and the omission of "an" together with the kasra is not permitted; this is the view of the Basrans. A similar statement is the verse of Kathir Abu Sakhr:

"I want to forget her remembrance (li-ansa dhikraha)"

meaning: "li-an ansa" (in order that I forget). This lam is the one that governs the object, like the one in your saying: "I hit for Zayd" (darabtu li-Zayd), meaning: "He wants the completion of the period." It was also said: it is linked to a verb implied afterward, its estimated form being: "And in order that you complete the period, He granted you this concession." This is the view of the Kufans, and al-Nahhas related it from al-Farra'. Al-Nahhas said: This is a good view, and similar to it is: ﴿And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth, that he might be among the certain [in faith]﴾ [al-An'am: 75], meaning: "and that he might be among the certain, We did that." It was also said: the waw is superfluous (muqhama). It was also said: it is possible that this lam is the lam of command, and the waw is conjoining one speech to another. Abu Ishaq Ibrahim ibn al-Sarri said: It is to be understood according to the meaning, and the estimate is: "God did that so that He would make it easy for you, and so that you would complete the period." He said: Similar to it is what Sibawayh recited:

"They have perished, and the signs of them have been changed by decay, except the still embers of their fire, which is dust (haba')
And the one struck with a tent-peg, as for the middle of his temple (qadhalihi), then it appeared and concealed its traveller (sarah)
al-Ma'za' (a hard land of pebbles)."

...the word *shāda, yashīdu, shaydan* means he plastered it with gypsum (*jiṣṣa*), because its meaning is that the ruins were destroyed except for remnants of it (*rawākid*) remaining, so it is as if he said: "and in it is a plastered thing, or there is a plastered thing."

**The nineteenth issue:** God's words, ﴿and that you may magnify God﴾, are coordinated (*'aṭf*) with what precedes them. Their meaning is an exhortation to magnify God (*takbīr*, saying "Allahu akbar") at the end of Ramadan, according to the view of the majority of the people of interpretation (*ahl al-ta'wīl*).

People differ over the limits of this takbīr. Al-Shafi'i said: It is narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Urwa and Abu Salama that they used to magnify God and praise Him on the night of Eid al-Fitr. He said: The night of Eid al-Adha is likened to it.

Ibn Abbas said: It is incumbent upon the Muslims, when they see the new moon of Shawwal, that they magnify God. It is also narrated from him: A person magnifies God from the sighting of the crescent until the end of the sermon (*khuṭba*), and he remains silent at the time the imam comes out, and he magnifies God along with the imam's magnification.

Some people said: One magnifies God from the sighting of the crescent until the imam comes out for the prayer.

Sufyan said: It is the magnification on the day of Fitr.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: They magnify God when they go out to the musalla (prayer ground), and when the prayer is finished the Eid is over.

This is the position of Malik. Malik said: It is from the moment one leaves his house until the imam comes out.

Ibn al-Qasim and Ali ibn Ziyad narrated that if one goes out before the sun rises, he does not magnify God on his way or while sitting until the sun rises; but if he goes out after sunrise, he magnifies God on his way to the musalla, and when he sits, until the imam comes out.

According to Malik, Fitr and Adha are the same in this matter, and al-Shafi'i also said so.

Abu Hanifa said: One magnifies God on Adha and does not magnify God on Fitr. The proof for him is God's words, ﴿and that you may magnify God﴾, and because this is a day of Eid which does not recur within the year, so magnifying God is recommended when going out to it, as on Adha.

Al-Daraqutni narrated from Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami that he said: They were more strenuous in magnifying God on Fitr than on Adha.

It is narrated from Ibn Umar that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to magnify God on the day of Fitr from the moment he went out of his house until he reached the musalla.

It is also narrated from Ibn Umar that when he went out on the day of Adha and the day of Fitr, he would proclaim the takbīr aloud until he reached the musalla, then he would continue magnifying God until the imam arrived.

Most of the scholars, from among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) and others, hold that one magnifies God on the Eid of Fitr, as Ibn al-Mundhir reported. He said: Al-Awza'i narrated this from Ilyas.

Al-Shafi'i used to say, when he saw the new moon of Shawwal: I like people to magnify God together and individually, and they should not cease magnifying God and openly proclaiming the takbīr until they go in the morning to the musalla and at the time the imam goes out to the prayer. Likewise, I like this on the night of Adha for one who is not performing Hajj.

The ruling on the Eid prayers and the takbīr in them will come in the commentary on "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High" [al-A'la] and "Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar" [al-Kawthar], God willing. [Editorial note: See vol. 20, pp. 22 and 218.]

**The twentieth issue:** The wording of the takbīr according to Malik and a group of scholars is: "Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar," three times. It is narrated from Jabir ibn Abd Allah. Some scholars magnify God, declare the tahlīl (saying "La ilaha illa Allah") and glorify God (tasbīḥ) in the midst of the takbīr. Others say: "Allahu akbar kabīran, wal-hamdu lillahi kathīran, wa subhan Allahi bukratan wa aṣīlan" (God is greatest, great; and praise belongs to God abundantly; and glory be to God morning and evening).

Ibn al-Mubarak used to say when he went out on the day of Fitr: "Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, la ilaha illa Allah, wa Allahu akbar, wa lillahi al-hamd, Allahu akbar 'ala ma hadana" (God is greatest, God is greatest, there is no god but God, and God is greatest, and praise belongs to God; God is greatest for what He has guided us to).

Ibn al-Mundhir said: Malik did not set a limit to it. Ahmad said: It is broad.

Ibn al-Arabi said: "Our scholars chose the unrestricted takbīr, and it is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, and towards it I incline."

**The twenty-first issue:** God's words, ﴿for what He has guided you to﴾. It has been said: This is because of what the Christians erred in, by altering their fasting [in some copies: "their book"]. It has also been said: It is in place of what the Jahiliyya (pre-Islamic period) used to do, namely boasting of ancestors, displaying lineage, and enumerating virtues. It has also been said: It is so that you may glorify Him for what He has guided you to of the sacred laws, so it is general.

The meaning of ﴿so that you may be thankful﴾ has already been mentioned [vol. 1, pp. 227, 397, second edition].

This passage contains four issues. The first concerns the verse ﴿When My servants ask you about Me, then I am near﴾.

The meaning is: if they ask you about the One who is worshipped, tell them that He is near. He rewards obedience, answers the one who calls upon Him, and knows what the servant does, such as fasting, prayer and other acts. Scholars differed about the occasion of revelation. Muqatil said that ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, had intercourse with his wife after he had prayed the ʿisha' prayer. He regretted this and wept, came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), informed him of it, and returned with remorse. This happened before the dispensation (rukhsa) was revealed, and so this verse was revealed: ﴿When My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near﴾. It was also said that at the beginning it was obligatory for them to abstain from eating after sleeping, and some of them ate and then regretted it. So this verse was revealed concerning the acceptance of repentance and the abrogation (naskh) of that ruling, as will be explained later [[See p. 314 of this part.]]. Al-Kalbi related from Abu Salih, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The Jews said, "How can our Lord hear our supplication when you claim that between us and the heaven is a distance of five hundred years, and the thickness of each heaven is the same?" So this verse was revealed. Al-Hasan said: Its occasion was that some people said to the Prophet (ﷺ), "Is our Lord near so that we may confide in Him, or far so that we must call out to Him?" So it was revealed. ʿAta' and Qatada said: When the verse ﴿And your Lord says: Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ [Ghafir: 60] was revealed, some people said, "At what hour should we call upon Him?" So this verse was revealed [[See vol. 15, p. 326.]].

The second issue concerns His words ﴿then indeed I am near﴾. That is, near in answering. It was also said: near in knowledge. It was also said: He is near to His friends through bounty and favour.

The third issue concerns His words ﴿I answer the call of the caller when he calls Me﴾. That is, I accept the worship of whoever worships Me. So "supplication" (duʿaʾ) here means worship, and "answering" means acceptance. The evidence for this is what Abu Dawud related from al-Nuʿman ibn Bashir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Supplication is worship," and then recited: "Your Lord says: Call upon Me, I will respond to you." Thus supplication was called worship. From the same usage is His saying: ﴿Indeed those who disdain My worship will enter Hell, humbled﴾ [Ghafir: 60], meaning My supplication [[See vol. 15, p. 326.]]. So Allah commanded supplication, emphasised it, named it worship, and promised to respond to them.

Layth related from Shahr ibn Hawshab, from ʿUbada ibn al-Samit, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "My community has been given three things that were not given except to the prophets. Whenever Allah sent a prophet, He said to him, 'Call upon Me, I will respond to you,' and to this community He said, 'Call upon Me, I will respond to you.' Whenever Allah sent a prophet, He said to him, 'He has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion,' and to this community He said, 'He has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion.' And whenever Allah sent a prophet, He made him a witness over his people, and He made this community witnesses over mankind."

Khalid al-Rabaʿi used to say: "I am amazed at this community regarding ﴿Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ [Ghafir: 60]. He commanded them to supplicate and promised them an answer, with no condition between them." Someone said to him, "Like what?" He said: "Like His saying: ﴿And give good tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Baqara: 25]. Here there is a condition. And His saying: ﴿And give good tidings to those who believe that they have a sure standing with their Lord﴾ [Yunus: 2], where there is no condition of action. And like His saying: ﴿So call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [Ghafir: 14], where there is a condition. But His saying ﴿Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ has no condition."

Nations used to turn to their prophets in their needs, asking the prophets to intercede for them.

If it is asked: why does the supplicant sometimes supplicate and yet is not answered? The answer is that one should know that His word of truth in the two verses, "I answer" and "I will respond," does not necessarily entail an answer absolutely, for every caller in every detail, nor for every request in every detail. Our Lord, blessed and exalted, said in another verse: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly. Indeed He does not like transgressors﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 55]. Every person who persists in a major sin, whether knowingly or ignorantly, is a transgressor, and He has informed us that He does not love transgressors, so how would He answer him? The kinds of transgression are many, and their explanation will come here and in al-Aʿraf, if Allah wills.

Some scholars said: "I answer if I wish," as He said: ﴿He removes that for which you call upon Him, if He wills﴾ [al-Anʿam: 41]. This falls under the category of the absolute (mutlaq) and the restricted (muqayyad). The Prophet (ﷺ) supplicated for three things, was given two, and was refused one, as will be explained in al-Anʿam, if Allah wills.
