It was also said: The purpose of this statement is to inform all believers that this is the attribute of their Lord, glorified is He, that in general He answers the supplications of those who supplicate; that He is near to the servant, hears his supplication, knows his distress, and so answers him with what He wills and however He wills. And who is more astray than one who calls upon other than Allah, one who will not answer him? [al-Ahqaf: 5], and so on.

A master may answer his servant, and a father his son, and yet not give him what he asked. So the answer was certainly present whenever the supplication occurred, because "I answer" and "I will respond" is a report that cannot be abrogated, for otherwise the one reporting would be a liar. This interpretation is supported by what Ibn ʿUmar related from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever has the door of supplication opened for him, the doors of answer will be opened for him."

Allah revealed to Dawud: "Tell the wrongdoers among My servants not to call upon Me, for I have made it binding upon Myself to answer whoever calls upon Me, and if I answer the wrongdoers, I curse them."

Some people said: Allah answers every supplication, but the answer may come in one of three forms: either it is realised in this world, or it is expiated from him, or it is stored up for him in the Hereafter. This is based on what Abu Saʿid al-Khudri related, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No Muslim supplicates with a supplication that contains no sin and no severing of kinship except that Allah gives him one of three things: either He hastens his supplication for him, or He stores it up for him, or He averts from him an evil of similar kind." They said, "Then we shall increase our supplications?" He said: "Allah is more abundant [in giving]." Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr transmitted it, and Abu Muhammad ʿAbd al-Haqq graded it sound. It is in the Muwatta' with a broken chain (munqatiʿ al-sanad). Abu ʿUmar said: This hadith is cited in the sound exegesis (tafsir) concerning Allah's words ﴿Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ [Ghafir: 60]. All of this is from answering.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: Every servant who supplicates is answered. If what he asks for is provision for him in this world, he is given it; and if it is not provision for him in this world, it is stored up for him.

I say: Although the hadith of Abu Saʿid al-Khudri gives permission for the answer in one of three forms, it indicates the soundness of what preceded concerning avoiding transgression, which prevents answer, since it says: "so long as he does not supplicate for a sin or the severing of kinship." Muslim added: "so long as he does not hasten." He related from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "The servant will continue to be answered so long as he does not supplicate for a sin or the severing of kinship, so long as he does not hasten." It was asked, "O Messenger of Allah, what is hastening?" He said: "He says, 'I have supplicated, and I have supplicated, but I see that He does not answer me,' and then he becomes weary (yastahsir) and abandons supplication" [[yastahsir: he ceases supplicating and becomes bored with it.]].

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and Abu Dawud related from Abu Hurayra that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "One of you will be answered so long as he does not hasten, saying, 'I supplicated, but I was not answered.'" Our scholars, may Allah have mercy upon them, said: His words "one of you will be answered" may mean a report of the necessity (wujub) of the answer occurring, or a report of its permissibility (jawaz). If it means a report of the necessity and occurrence, then the answer means one of the three things mentioned earlier. So if he says, "I have supplicated but I was not answered," then the occurrence of any of these three things is negated, and the supplication is empty of all of them. But if it means the permissibility of the answer, then the answer in that case is the doing of exactly what he asked for, and the supplicant's saying "I supplicated but was not answered" is prohibited, because that belongs to despair, weakness of certainty, and discontent.

I say: What also prevents the answer of supplication is eating what is unlawful (haram) and what is similar to it. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A man travels a long journey, dishevelled and dusty, raising his hands to the sky, saying, 'O Lord, O Lord,' while his food is unlawful, his drink is unlawful, his clothing is unlawful, and he has been nourished with the unlawful. How could he be answered?" This is an interrogative used to express that it is far-fetched that the supplication of one with such a description would be accepted.

The answer to supplication necessarily has conditions in the supplicant, in the supplication, and in the thing supplicated for. Among the conditions of the supplicant is that he knows that no one is able to fulfil his need except Allah, that intermediaries are in His grip and subjected by His subjugation, that he supplicates with a sincere intention and presence of heart, for Allah does not answer a supplication from a heedless, distracted heart; that he avoids eating the unlawful; and that he does not tire of supplicating. Among the conditions of what is supplicated for is that it be among matters permissible in request and in deed according to the Sacred Law, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "so long as he does not supplicate for a sin or the severing of kinship." Sin includes every wrong for which one incurs guilt, and severing of kinship includes all the rights of Muslims and their injustices.

Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Tustari said: The conditions of supplication are seven: first, humility (tadarruʿ); fear; hope; persistence; humbleness (khushuʿ); generality; and eating what is lawful (halal).

Ibn ʿAta' said: Supplication has pillars, wings, causes and times. If it accords with its pillars, it is strong; if it accords with its wings, it flies into the sky; if it accords with its times, it succeeds; and if it accords with its causes, it is effective. Its pillars are presence of heart, tenderness, lowliness and humbleness; its wings are sincerity; its times are the pre-dawn hours; and its causes are sending blessings upon Muhammad (ﷺ).

It was said: Its conditions are four. The first is guarding the heart when alone; guarding the tongue in the presence of people; guarding the eye from looking at what is unlawful; and guarding the belly from the unlawful.

It has also been said: among the conditions of supplication is that it be free from grammatical error (laḥn), as one of them recited:

He calls upon his Lord with a grammatical error (laḥn),
and so when he calls upon Him, He does not answer.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 186 (part 2 of 2):

It was said to Ibrahim ibn Adham: "Why is it that we supplicate but are not answered?" He said: "Because you know Allah but do not obey Him; you know the Messenger but do not follow his Sunnah; you know the Qur'an but do not act upon it; you eat the blessings of Allah but do not render their thanks; you know Paradise but do not seek it; you know the Fire but do not flee from it; you know Satan but do not fight him, rather you agree with him; you know death but do not prepare for it; you bury the dead but do not take warning; and you leave your own faults and occupy yourselves with the faults of people."

Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said to Nawf al-Bakali: "O Nawf, Allah revealed to Dawud: 'Command the Children of Israel that they should not enter any of My houses except with pure hearts, humble glances and clean hands, for I will not answer any of them so long as there is any injustice (mazlimah) in any of My creatures.' O Nawf, do not be a poet, nor an 'arif (chief), nor a shurtah (police officer), nor a jabi (tax collector), nor an 'ashshar (tithe collector) [[al-'arif: one who is in charge of the affairs of a group of people, knows their affairs and conveys them to the ruler. Al-shurti (like turki and kujhani): the assistants of the ruler. Al-'ashshar: one who undertakes the collection of the tenth of wealth.]], for Dawud stood up at a certain hour of the night and said: 'This is an hour in which no servant supplicates except that he is answered, except for an 'arif, a shurtah, a jabi, an 'ashshar, a possessor of 'arṭaba, which is the tanbur (lute), or a possessor of kawba, which is the drum.'"

Our scholars said: The supplicant should not say: "O Allah, give me if You wish; O Allah, forgive me if You wish; O Allah, have mercy on me if You wish." Rather, he should make his request and supplication free of the word "if it be Your will," and he should ask as one who knows that He does nothing except by His will. Moreover, in the saying "if You wish" there is a kind of self-sufficiency regarding His forgiveness, His giving and His mercy, like the saying of one who says: "If you wish to give me such-and-such, then do it." This is only used with one who is free of need of it, whereas one who is compelled to it resolves in his request and asks as a poor, compelled person asks for what he requests.

The imams narrated, and the wording is that of al-Bukhari, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When any one of you supplicates, let him resolve in his request, and let him not say: 'O Allah, if You wish, give me,' for there is no one who can compel Him." And in the Muwatta': "O Allah, forgive me if You wish; O Allah, have mercy on me if You wish."

Our scholars said: His saying (ﷺ) "let him resolve in his request" is evidence that the believer should strive in supplication, be hopeful of being answered, and not despair of the mercy of Allah, for he is calling upon One who is Generous.

Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: Let nothing prevent anyone from supplicating because of what he knows of himself, for Allah has answered the supplication of the worst of creation, Iblis, when he said: "My Lord, give me respite until the day they are resurrected," and He said: "Indeed, you are among those given respite."

For supplication there are times and states in which answering is most likely, such as the pre-dawn hour, the time of breaking the fast, the period between the adhan and the iqamah, the period between dhuhr and 'asr on Wednesday, times of distress, the state of travel and illness, at the descent of rain, and when lined up in the way of Allah. All of this has been reported in narrations, and its explanation will come in its places.

Shahr ibn Hawshab narrated that Umm al-Darda' said to him: "O Shahr, do you not feel the goosebumps?" I said: "Yes." She said: "Then supplicate to Allah, for supplication is answered at that time."

Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) supplicated in the Mosque of Victory (Masjid al-Fath) three times, on Monday and Tuesday, and it was answered for him on Wednesday between the two prayers. I recognized the joy in his face. Jabir said: "Whenever a serious and grave matter befell me, I would choose that hour, supplicate in it, and I would recognize the answer."

The fourth matter: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So let them respond to Me﴾. Abu Raja' al-Khurasani said: "So let them supplicate to Me." Ibn 'Atiyya said: The meaning is: so let them seek that I answer them. This is the pattern of "istaf'ala" meaning to seek something, except in rare cases, such as "istaghna Allah" (Allah is self-sufficient). Mujahid and others said: The meaning is: so let them respond to Me in what I have called them to of faith, that is, obedience and action. It is said that "ajaba" and "istajaba" have the same meaning, and from this is the saying of the poet:

"Then no answerer answered him at that time."

That is, no one answered him. The sin (in istajaba) is extra, and the lam is the lam of command. Likewise "and let them believe" (wal-yu'minu). The lam of command jussed the verb because it makes the verb refer only to the future, so it resembled "in" (if), which is the conditional particle. It was also said: because it occurs only before verbs.

Al-rushd is the opposite of al-ghayy (error). One says: rashada yarshudu rushdan, and rashida (with kasra) yarshadu rashadan, a dialectal variant of it. Arshadahu Allah (Allah guided him). Al-maradid: the intended paths of the roads. Al-tariq al-arshad: like al-aqsad (the most direct). You say: he is of legitimate birth (li-rushdah), which is the opposite of your saying: of fornication (li-zaniyah). [[With a kasra on the ra', and it may be opened; its meaning: if he is from a valid marriage.]] Umm Rashid: a kunya for the mouse. Banu Rashdan: a clan of the Arabs, according to al-Jawhari. Al-Harawi said: al-rushd, al-rashad and al-rashad are guidance and uprightness, and from it is His saying: "that perhaps they may be rightly guided" (la'allahum yarshudun).

There are thirty-six issues (masa'il) in this verse. The first: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Permitted for you﴾. The word "permitted" (uhilla) implies that it was prohibited before that and then abrogated (naskh, the cancellation of an earlier ruling by a later one). Abu Dawud narrated from Ibn Abi Layla, who said: "Our companions told us: When a man broke his fast [[In the text of Musnad Abi Dawud: "When he fasted and slept..."]] and slept before eating, he would not eat until morning. Umar came and wanted his wife, and she said, 'I have already slept.' He thought she was making an excuse, so he approached her. A man from the Ansar wanted food, and they said, 'Wait until we heat something for you.' He fell asleep. When they woke in the morning, this verse was revealed, and in it: ﴿It is permitted for you on the night of the fast to approach your wives﴾."

Al-Bukhari narrated from al-Bara', who said: "The companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) followed this practice: if a man was fasting and the time of iftar arrived, but he slept before breaking his fast, he would not eat that night or the next day until evening. Qays ibn Sirma al-Ansari was fasting. [In another narration: he worked in the palm groves by day and was fasting.] When the time of iftar came, he went to his wife and said to her, 'Do you have any food?' She said, 'No, but I will go and find some for you.' He had been working all day, and sleep overcame him. When his wife came back and saw him, she said, 'What a disappointment for you!' When midday came, he fainted. This was mentioned to the Prophet (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed: ﴿It is permitted for you on the night of the fast to approach your wives﴾. They rejoiced greatly, and the verse was revealed: ﴿Eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread at dawn﴾."

Also in al-Bukhari, from al-Bara': "When the fasting of Ramadan was prescribed, they would not approach women for the whole month, and some men would betray themselves. So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Allah knew that you were betraying yourselves, so He turned to you and pardoned you﴾."

It is said: "khana" and "ikhtana" have the same meaning, from treachery (khiyana), meaning: you betray yourselves by intercourse during the nights of fasting. Whoever disobeys Allah has betrayed himself, since he brings punishment upon himself. Al-Qutabi said: The root of treachery is that a man is entrusted with something and does not fulfill that trust regarding it.

Al-Tabari mentioned that Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, returned from the Prophet (ﷺ) after spending a night talking with him. He found his wife asleep and wanted her, but she said, "You have slept." He said, "I have not slept," and he had intercourse with her. Ka'b ibn Malik did the same. Umar went to the Prophet (ﷺ) in the morning and said, "I seek forgiveness from Allah and from you. My soul adorned this for me, and I had intercourse with my wife. Do you find any concession for me?" He said: "You were not deserving of that, O Umar." When he reached his house, he sent for him and informed him of his excuse in a verse of the Qur'an.

Al-Nahhas and Makki also mentioned that Umar slept and then had intercourse with his wife, and that he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him of that, and so this was revealed: ﴿Allah knew that you were betraying yourselves, so He turned to you and pardoned you. So now, have intercourse with them...﴾, to the end of the verse.

The second issue: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿On the night of the fast, the rafath (approaching)﴾. "Layla" (night) is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf), and it is a noun of genus, which is why it is singular. Rafath is a euphemism for intercourse, because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is generous and uses euphemism. This was said by Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi. Al-Zajjaj said: Rafath is a comprehensive word for everything a man desires from his wife. Al-Azhari also said this. Ibn Arafa said: Rafath here means intercourse. Rafath is explicitly mentioning intercourse and speaking about it openly. The poet said:

"And they show, from the pleasant talk of their eyes, flirtation,
and by them they keep away from the rafath of men."

It is also said that rafath originally means obscene speech. It is said: "rafatha" and "arfatha" when one speaks coarsely. From this is the poet's saying:

"How many a flock of pilgrims restrained
from idle talk and the rafath of speech."

The verb rafatha takes "ila" in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The rafath to your wives﴾. You do not say "rafathtu ila al-nisa'" (I committed rafath with women), but it has been used in the sense of ifda' (going unto), which means close contact, as in His saying: "And some of you have gone unto others" [An-Nisa' 21]. [See vol. 5, p. 102.] From this meaning is His saying: ﴿And when they go alone to their devils﴾ [Al-Baqara 14], as mentioned before [See vol. 1, p. 206.]. And His saying: ﴿On the day it will be heated in the fire﴾ [At-Tawba 35], meaning it will be kindled, because you say, "The iron was heated in the fire." This will come later [See vol. 8, p. 129.]. From this is His saying: ﴿Let those who oppose His command beware﴾ [An-Nur 63], which is understood as meaning "deviate from His command" or "turn away from His command," because you say, "I opposed Zayd." Similarly, His saying: ﴿And He was merciful to the believers﴾ [Al-Ahzab 43], which is understood in the sense of ra'uf (compassionate) as in: ﴿Compassionate and merciful to the believers﴾ [At-Tawba 128]. Do you not see that you say "ra'uftu bihi" (I was compassionate to him), and you do not say "rahimtu bihi"? But since it agrees with it in meaning, it takes its place in governing the object. Among this type is the saying of Abu Kabir al-Hudhali:

"She carried him in a night of terror [mazuda: frightened],
unwillingly, and the knot of her belt was not untied."

Here "hamalat" (she carried) takes "bi" (with), and it should take its object directly, as in the revelation: ﴿His mother carried him with hardship and gave birth to him with hardship﴾ [Al-Ahqaf 15 [See vol. 16, p. 193.]], but he said "hamalat bihi" because it has the meaning of "habilat bihi" (she became pregnant with him).

The third issue: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They are a garment for you﴾. It is a subject and predicate. The nun in "hunna" is doubled because it stands in the position of the mim and waw in the masculine. "And you are a garment for them." The original meaning of libas (garment) is clothing. Then the intermingling of each spouse with the other was called libas, because of the joining of the bodies, their mixing, and their closeness, likening it to a garment. Al-Nabigha al-Ja'di said:

"When the bedfellow turns her neck,
they cling together and she becomes a garment over him."

He also said:

"I have worn people and worn them out,
and after people, I wore out people."

Some said: What covers a thing and conceals it is called libas. It is permissible that each of them is a covering for the other against what is not lawful, as was reported in a hadith. It was also said: each of them is a covering for the other regarding what happens between them of intercourse from the eyes of people. Abu Ubayd and others said: A wife is called your garment, your bedding, and your waist-wrap. A man said to Umar ibn al-Khattab:

"Shall I not convey to Abu Hafs a message,
ransomed for you by my trustworthy brother, my waist-wrap?"

Abu Ubayd said: that is, my women. It was also said: my self. Al-Rabi' said: They are bedding for you, and you are a covering for them. Mujahid said: That is, a place of rest for you, meaning that each of you rests with the other.

The fourth issue: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah knew that you were betraying yourselves﴾. Some of you seek the advice of others about violating the prohibition of intercourse and eating after sleep during the nights of fasting, as in His saying: ﴿You kill yourselves﴾ [Al-Baqara 85], meaning some of you kill others. It may also mean each one of them individually betrays himself, and He called him a traitor to himself because the harm returns to him, as mentioned before. His saying: ﴿So He turned to you﴾ may have two meanings: first, accepting the repentance for their betrayal of themselves; second, lightening for them by permission and allowance, as in His saying: ﴿He knew that you would not be able to count it, so He turned to you﴾ [Al-Muzzammil 20], meaning He lightened it for you. His saying after the accidental killing: ﴿Whoever does not find [the means], then fasting two consecutive months is a repentance from Allah﴾ [An-Nisa' 92 [See vol. 5, p. 327.]], meaning a lightening, because the one who kills by mistake has not done anything requiring repentance from him. And He said: ﴿Allah has turned in mercy to the Prophet and the Emigrants and the Helpers who followed him in the hour of hardship﴾ [At-Tawba 117 [See vol. 8, p. 277.]], even though the Prophet (ﷺ) had done nothing requiring repentance. His saying: ﴿And He pardoned you﴾ may mean pardon from sin, and may mean expansion and facilitation, like the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "The beginning of the time is Allah's pleasure, and its end is Allah's pardon," meaning its facilitation and expansion. So the meaning of "Allah knew" is: He knew the occurrence of this from you by witnessing, "so He turned to you" after it occurred, meaning He lightened it for you, "and pardoned" meaning He made it easy. "Takhtanun" comes from khiyana (betrayal), as mentioned before.

Ibn al-Arabi said: "The scholars of asceticism said: Likewise, let there be care and nobility of station. Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, betrayed himself, so Allah the Exalted made it a legislation and lightened it for the Ummah because of him. May Allah be pleased with him and make him content."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So now, have intercourse with them﴾ is a euphemism for intercourse, meaning: what was forbidden to you has now been made lawful for you. Intercourse is called mubashara (close contact) because the two skins touch in it. Ibn al-Arabi said: "This indicates that the cause of the verse was Umar's intercourse, not Qays's hunger, because if the cause had been Qays's hunger, it would have said: 'So now, eat.' It begins with it because it is the important matter for which the verse was revealed."

**The fifth issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And seek what Allah has prescribed for you﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hakam ibn 'Uyayna, 'Ikrimah, al-Hasan, al-Suddi, al-Rabi' and al-Dahhak said: its meaning is "and seek the child," and this is supported by the fact that it comes directly after His saying, "So now, have intercourse with them." Ibn 'Abbas also said: "What Allah has prescribed for us" is the Qur'an. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, seek the Qur'an through what is permitted to you in it and what you have been commanded in it. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Mu'adh ibn Jabal that the meaning is "and seek the Night of Power." It has also been said: the meaning is "seek the concession and the ease," as Qatadah said. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is a good view. And it has been said: "seek what Allah has prescribed for you" refers to female slaves and wives. Al-Hasan al-Basri and al-Hasan ibn Qurrah read "wa-ittabi'u" (and follow) from ittiba' (following). Ibn 'Abbas permitted this reading, but preferred "ibtaghu" (seek), from ibtigha' (seeking).

**The sixth issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And eat and drink﴾. This is the answer to the case of Qays, and the earlier verse is the answer to the case of 'Umar. It began with the case of 'Umar because it is the more important, so it is placed first.

**The seventh issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread of dawn﴾. "Until" marks the limit of the distinction. It is not valid for the distinction to occur for someone and for eating to become forbidden to him unless a period of time has already passed since the break of dawn. Scholars differed over the threshold at which, once it becomes clear, abstention becomes obligatory. The majority said: it is the dawn that stretches across the horizon, to the right and to the left, and the reports came to this effect and the regions acted upon it. Muslim reported from Samurah ibn Jundub, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Let not the call of Bilal, nor the spreading whiteness of the horizon that rises like this, deceive you about your suhur, until it spreads like this" (ﷺ). Hammad [[Hammad here is Hammad ibn Zayd, one of the narrators in this chain.]] illustrated it with his two hands and said: that is, stretching across the horizon. In the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud: "The dawn is not the one that says [[Ibn al-Athir said in al-Nihayah: "The Arabs use 'said' (qala) as an expression for all actions, and apply it to things other than speech and tongue. They say: 'He said with his hand,' meaning he took. 'He said with his foot,' meaning he walked. 'He said with his garment,' meaning he lifted it. All of this is figurative and extended usage." So the meaning of "says" here is "appears."]] like this," and he joined his fingers and then turned them downward toward the ground, "but the dawn is the one that says like this," and he placed the index finger upon the index finger and extended his hands. Al-Daraqutni reported from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Abbas that it had reached him that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There are two dawns. As for the one that is like the tail of the sirhan [[al-Sirhan (with a kasra and sukun): the wolf, and it is said the lion; its plural is siraH and sarahin.]], it does not make anything lawful or unlawful. As for the one that stretches across and crosses the horizon, in it the prayer becomes lawful and eating becomes unlawful." This is a mursal [[A mursal hadith is one in which the Successor (tabi'i) reports directly from the Prophet ﷺ, omitting the Companion from the chain.]]. Another group said: that is after the break of dawn and its becoming clear in the roads and houses. This was reported from 'Umar [[In some copies: 'Uthman.]], Hudhayfah, Ibn 'Abbas, Talq ibn 'Ali, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, and al-A'mash Sulayman and others, that abstention becomes obligatory when the dawn becomes clear on the roads and on the tops of the mountains. Masruq said: They did not count the dawn as your dawn; they only counted the dawn that fills the houses. Al-Nasa'i reported from 'Asim, from Zirr, who said: We said to Hudhayfah: At what hour did you eat suhur with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ? He said: It was daytime, except that the sun had not yet risen. Al-Daraqutni reported from Talq ibn 'Ali that the Prophet of Allah said: "Eat and drink, and let not the ascending glow deceive you. Eat and drink until the reddish light appears to you." Al-Daraqutni said: Qays ibn Talq [[The completion from Sunan al-Daraqutni is required by the context.]] is not strong. Abu Dawud said: this is among what the people of al-Yamamah alone transmitted. Al-Tabari said: What led them to this view is that fasting is only during the day, and for them the day begins at sunrise and ends at sunset. The disagreement among the linguists on this matter has already passed. The clarification by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ of this, with his saying, "It is only the blackness of the night and the whiteness of the day," is decisive in this matter, along with His saying: ﴿for a specified number of days﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 184]. Al-Daraqutni reported from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Whoever does not set his intention to fast before the break of dawn, there is no fast for him." This was transmitted alone by 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbad from al-Mufaddal ibn Fadalah with this chain, and all of them are trustworthy. It is also reported from Hafsah that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever does not resolve to fast before dawn, there is no fast for him." 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr raised it, and he is among the trustworthy raisers of hadith. It is also reported from Hafsah as a marfu' statement, being her own words. In these two hadiths there is evidence for what the majority said about the dawn, and it prevents fasting without intention before dawn, contrary to the view of Abu Hanifah.

**The eighth issue:** This is because fasting is among the acts of worship, so it is not valid except with intention, and the Lawgiver has fixed the time for it before dawn. How, then, can it be said that eating and drinking after dawn is permitted?

Al-Bukhari and Muslim reported from Sahl ibn Sa'd, who said: The verse "And eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread" was revealed, and "of dawn" was not yet revealed. Some men, when they wished to fast, would tie a white thread and a black thread to their feet, and would continue eating and drinking until they could distinguish them. Then Allah revealed afterwards "of dawn," and they understood that what was meant was the whiteness of the day.

'Adi ibn Hatim reported that he said: I said: O Messenger of Allah, what is the white thread from the black thread? Are they two threads? He said: "You have a broad nape [[A broad nape is used as an indication of a person's lack of perceptiveness.]] if you can see the two threads." Then he said: "No, rather it is the blackness of the night and the whiteness of the day." Al-Bukhari recorded it.

The dawn is called a "thread" because the whiteness that appears is seen extending like a thread. The poet said:

The white thread is the morning light breaking open,
and the black thread is the darkness of the night, concealed.

In their speech, "thread" is an expression for colour. The word "fajr" (dawn) is a verbal noun from "fajjartu al-ma' ufajjiruhu fajran," meaning when water flowed and gushed forth. Its root is splitting. For this reason, the first emergence of the light of the sun from its rising, which is the first whiteness of the day that is visible, spreading across the horizon, is called "fajr," because its light gushes forth. The Arabs call it the white thread, as we have explained. Abu Dawud al-Iyadi said:

When a dimness [[al-Sudfah (with a damma or fatha on the sin, and sukun on the dal): in the dialect of Najd, it means the darkness of night, and in the dialect of others, it means light. It is one of the words with opposite meanings.]] lit up for us
and a thread of the morning appeared, shining.

Another said:

It was about to appear, and it appeared, touching it,
while the pitch-dark shadows of the night were covering it.

It is also called "al-sadi'" (the splitting), and from this comes their saying: "The dawn split." Bishr ibn Abi Khazim or 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib said:

You see the sirhan [wolf] spreading its forelegs,
as if the whiteness of its chest were a split in the dawn.

Al-Shammakh likened it to the parting of the head, and said:

When the night was there, the morning in it
split, like the parting of the oiled head.

They also say about a clear matter: "This is like the break of dawn," and "like the breaking open of the dawn," and "like the first glimmers of the morning." A poet said:

So I came before the breaking of the dawn,
while the son of Dhakka' was hidden in the darkness [[The speaker of this verse is Humayd al-Arqat, as in al-Sihah. Dhakka' (with a damma) is a name for the sun, and the morning is called "son of Dhakka'" because it comes from its light. Al-Kafr (with a fatha) means the darkness and blackness of the night.]].

**Ninth issue:** Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, made the night the time for eating, drinking and intercourse, and the day the time for fasting. He thus explained the rulings for the two periods and distinguished between them. So nothing that He permitted at night is lawful during the day, except for the traveler or the sick person, as was explained earlier. ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾.

Whoever breaks the fast in Ramadan without being one of those mentioned falls into one of two cases: either he did so deliberately or he did so forgetfully. If it is the first, Malik said: whoever deliberately breaks the fast in Ramadan by eating, drinking or intercourse, is liable for the make-up fast (qada') and the expiation (kaffarah). This is based on what Malik narrated in his Muwatta', and Muslim in his Sahih, from Abu Hurayrah, that a man broke his fast in Ramadan, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered him to make expiation by freeing a slave, or fasting two consecutive months, or feeding sixty poor people. The hadith continues. This was also the view of al-Sha'bi.

Al-Shafi'i and others said: this expiation applies only to the one who broke the fast by intercourse, based on the hadith of Abu Hurayrah also, who said: A man came to the Messenger of Allah and said, "I am ruined, O Messenger of Allah!" He said, "What has ruined you?" He said, "I had intercourse with my wife in Ramadan." The hadith continues. In it there is mention of the expiation in sequence, narrated by Muslim. They applied this case to the first case, saying: they are one and the same. But this is not accepted; rather they are two different cases, because their contexts differ. The expiation was attached to one who broke the fast without any qualifying circumstance, so it applies generally. This was the view of Malik and his companions, al-Awza'i, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, al-Tabari and Ibn al-Mundhir. It was also narrated from 'Ata' in one report, and from al-Hasan and al-Zuhri. Al-Shafi'i is bound to hold this view, for he says: the omission of enquiry (tark al-istifsal) in the presence of differing circumstances indicates the generality of the ruling. Al-Shafi'i made punishment obligatory in addition to the make-up fast, for violating the sanctity of the month.

**Tenth issue:** The scholars also differed regarding what is obligatory upon a woman whose husband has intercourse with her during Ramadan. Malik, Abu Yusuf and the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y) said: she is liable for the same as the husband. Al-Shafi'i said: she is liable for only one expiation, whether she consented or was forced, because the Prophet (ﷺ) answered the questioner with one expiation and did not distinguish. It was narrated from Abu Hanifa: if she consented, then each of them is liable for an expiation; if he forced her, then he is liable for one expiation only and nothing more. This is also the view of Sahnun ibn Sa'id, the Maliki. Malik said: he is liable for two expiations, and this is the established position of his school according to the majority of his companions.

**Eleventh issue:** The scholars also differed regarding one who has intercourse or eats while forgetful of his fast. Al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and his companions, and Ishaq said: there is nothing upon him in either case, neither make-up fast nor expiation. Malik, al-Layth and al-Awza'i said: he must make up the fast but owes no expiation. The same was narrated from 'Ata'. It was also narrated from 'Ata' that he owes the expiation if he had intercourse, and he said, "Such a thing is not forgotten." Some of the people of the Zahiri school said: whether he had intercourse forgetfully or deliberately, he owes both the make-up fast and the expiation. This is the view of Ibn al-Majishun, 'Abd al-Malik, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal also adopted it, because the hadith that makes the expiation obligatory does not distinguish between the forgetful and the deliberate. Ibn al-Mundhir said: there is nothing upon him.

**Twelfth issue:** Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr and the people of opinion said: if one eats forgetfully, thinks that this has broken his fast, and then has intercourse deliberately, he owes the make-up fast but no expiation. Ibn al-Mundhir said: we also say this. It has been said within the school: he owes both the make-up fast and the expiation if he intended to violate the sanctity of his fast out of boldness and carelessness. Abu 'Umar (Ibn 'Abd al-Barr) said: according to the principle of Malik, he should not owe expiation, because whoever eats forgetfully is, in his view, one who has broken the fast and must make up that day; so what sanctity has he violated while he is already one who has broken the fast? According to others than Malik: not everyone who eats forgetfully has broken his fast.

I say: this is the correct view, and the majority have said so: whoever eats or drinks forgetfully, there is no make-up fast upon him and his fast is complete, based on the hadith of Abu Hurayrah who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If the fasting person eats forgetfully or drinks forgetfully, it is only a provision that Allah has brought to him, and there is no make-up fast upon him." In another version: "Let him complete his fast, for Allah has fed him and given him drink." Narrated by al-Daraqutni, who said: its isnad is sound and all its narrators are trustworthy. Abu Bakr al-Athram said: I heard Abu 'Abd Allah (Ahmad) being asked about one who ate forgetfully during Ramadan. He said: there is nothing upon him, based on the hadith of Abu Hurayrah. Then Abu 'Abd Allah Malik said: "They claim that Malik says he must make up the fast!" And he laughed. Ibn al-Mundhir said: there is nothing upon him, because of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying to one who ate or drank forgetfully: "Let him complete his fast." And when he said "Let him complete his fast," and he completed it, then it is a complete and perfect fast.

I say: if one who broke his fast forgetfully owes no make-up fast and his fast is complete, then if he has intercourse deliberately he owes the make-up fast and the expiation, Allah knows best, just as one who did not break his fast forgetfully. Our scholars (the Malikis) have argued for the obligation of the make-up fast by saying: what is required of him is to fast a complete day in which no breach occurs, based on the words of Allah, ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾. He has not completed it, so it remains upon him. Perhaps the hadith concerns voluntary fasting, given its lighter nature. It has come in the Sahihayn of al-Bukhari and Muslim: "Whoever forgets while fasting and eats or drinks, let him complete his fast," and it does not mention a make-up fast nor refer to it. What it does address is the removal of blame and the command to continue and complete his fast. If this was obligatory, it indicates what we have mentioned regarding the make-up fast. As for voluntary fasting, there is no make-up fast for one who ate forgetfully, based on the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "There is no make-up fast upon him."

I say: this is what our scholars have argued, and it is sound, were it not for what is established from the Lawgiver (ﷺ), which we have mentioned. There is an explicit and sound text, which is what Abu Hurayrah narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever breaks his fast in the month of Ramadan forgetfully, there is no make-up fast upon him and no expiation." Narrated by al-Daraqutni, who said: Ibn Marzuq, who is trustworthy, uniquely narrated it from al-Ansari. Thus the possibility vanishes and the difficulty is removed, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of Majesty and Perfection.

**Thirteenth issue:** When Allah, glorified is He, explained the prohibitions of fasting, which are eating, drinking and intercourse, and did not mention physical contact (mubashara), which is the touching of skin to skin, such as kissing, touching and other things, this indicates the validity of the fast of one who kisses or makes physical contact. This is because the implication of the speech (fahwa al-kalam) only indicates the prohibition of what the night permitted, which is those three things, and there is no indication in it regarding anything else. Rather, this depends on evidence. For this reason disagreement has spread about it, and the scholars of the early generations differed about it. Among these is physical contact. Our scholars said: it is disliked for one who does not trust himself and does not control himself, lest it become a cause of what invalidates the fast. Malik narrated from Nafi' that 'Abd

Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) used to forbid kissing and intimate touching for one who is fasting, and this, Allah knows best, was out of fear of what might result from them. So if one kisses and is safe, there is no blame on him; likewise if he engages in intimate touching. Al-Bukhari related from Aisha, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) would kiss and engage in intimate touching while he was fasting." Among those who disliked kissing for the fasting person were Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Urwa ibn al-Zubayr. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud that he would make up a day in its place, but the hadith is a proof against them. Abu Umar (Ibn Abd al-Barr) said: "I do not know of anyone who permitted it for one who knows that it will lead to what invalidates his fast. If he kisses and then ejaculates, he must make up the day but owes no expiation (kaffarah). This is the view of Abu Hanifa and his companions, al-Thawri, al-Hasan and al-Shafi'i, and Ibn al-Mundhir chose it, saying: 'There is no proof for those who make expiation obligatory.'" Abu Umar said: "If he kissed and emitted madhy (pre-seminal fluid), there is nothing upon him according to them." Ahmad said: "Whoever kisses and emits madhy or semen must make up the day but owes no expiation, except for one who has intercourse by penetration, whether deliberately or forgetfully." Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik concerning one who kisses or touches and becomes erect without any fluid coming out: he must make up the day. Ibn Wahb related from him: he owes no making up until he emits madhy. The Qadi Abu Muhammad said: "Our companions agree that there is no expiation upon him. If it was semen, is expiation obligatory along with making up? There are two cases: either he kissed once and ejaculated, or he kissed, became aroused, repeated it and ejaculated. If he kissed once, or engaged in intimate touching or caressing once, Ashhab and Sahnun said: there is no expiation upon him unless he repeats it. Ibn al-Qasim said: he owes expiation in all of this, except for looking, where there is no expiation unless he repeats it. Among those who held that expiation is obligatory if he kisses, touches, plays with his wife, or has intercourse without penetration and ejaculates: al-Hasan al-Basri, Ata, Ibn al-Mubarak, Abu Thawr and Ishaq, and this is Malik's view in the Mudawwana. The argument of Ashhab is that kissing, touching and intimate contact do not break the fast in themselves; they only lead to what breaks it. So if he does it once, without intending ejaculation and the breaking of the fast, there is no expiation upon him, like looking at her. If he repeats it, he has intended to break his fast, so he owes expiation, just as if looking were repeated. Al-Lakhmi said: they all agree that in the case of ejaculation from looking there is no expiation unless he continues. The principle is that expiation is obligatory only upon one who intends to break the fast and violate its sanctity. So when this is the case, one must consider the habit of the person affected: if it is his habit to ejaculate from kissing or intimate contact once, or his habit varies, sometimes ejaculating and sometimes not, I consider expiation obligatory upon him, because one who does this intends to violate his fast or exposes himself to it. But if his habit is safety, and it happens to him contrary to his habit, there is no expiation upon him. Malik's view on the obligation of expiation may be understood as applying only to one whose nature is like this, and he relied on what was apparent from him. Ashhab took the matter according to the general case of people, that they are safe from this, and their view on looking is evidence for that." I say: what he reported as agreement regarding looking, and made into a principle, is not so. Al-Baji in al-Muntaqa related that if he looks once intending pleasure [and ejaculates] (an addition from the book al-Muntaqa required by the context), Shaykh Abu al-Hasan said: he owes both making up and expiation. Al-Baji said: "This is the correct view in my opinion, because if he intends enjoyment by it, it is like kissing and other kinds of enjoyment. And Allah knows best." Jabir ibn Zayd, al-Thawri, al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr and the people of opinion said concerning one who repeatedly looks at a woman until he ejaculates: there is no making up and no expiation, as related by Ibn al-Mundhir. Al-Baji said: Ibn Nafi related in the Madaniyya from Malik that if he looks at a woman who is undressed and becomes aroused and ejaculates, he owes making up but not expiation.

The Fourteenth Issue: The majority of scholars hold that the fast of one upon whom dawn breaks while he is in a state of janabah (major ritual impurity) is valid. Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi said: "This is permissible by consensus. There had been some dispute among the Companions about it, but the matter settled on the view that whoever wakes up in a state of janabah, his fast is valid." I say: as for the mention of a dispute having occurred, it is sound and well known. It was the statement of Abu Hurayra: "Whoever wakes up in janabah has no fast," related by Malik in the Muwatta and others. In the Sunan of al-Nasa'i, it is reported that when he was told of it, he said: "By Allah, I did not say it; Muhammad (ﷺ) said it, by Allah." His retraction has been disputed, and the most well-known of his two positions among scholars is that he has no fast, as related by Ibn al-Mundhir, and it is reported from al-Hasan ibn Salih. There is also a third view from Abu Hurayra: he said, "If he knows of his janabah and then sleeps until morning, he is a breaker of the fast; but if he did not know until morning, he is fasting." This was related from Ata, Tawus and Urwa ibn al-Zubayr. It is also related from al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i that this suffices for a voluntary fast but must be made up for an obligatory one. I say: these are four views of scholars concerning one who wakes up in janabah, and the sound among them is the view of the majority, based on the hadith of Aisha and Umm Salama (may Allah be pleased with them) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would wake up in janabah from intercourse, not from wet dreams, and then fast. Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) also said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would be overtaken by dawn in Ramadan while he was in janabah from intercourse, not from wet dreams, so he would bathe and fast." Both are related by al-Bukhari and Muslim. This is what is understood from the necessary implication of the verse, "So now, have intercourse with them..." and so on, for when He extended the permissibility of intercourse until dawn breaks, it is necessarily known that dawn would break upon one in janabah, and bathing is only possible after dawn. Al-Shafi'i said: if the male organ was inside the woman and he withdrew it at the time of dawn, there is no making up upon him. Al-Muzani said: he must make it up, because it is part of the completion of intercourse. The first view is more correct for the reasons we have mentioned, and it is the view of our scholars.

The Fifteenth Issue: They differ concerning a woman who becomes pure before dawn but delays her ritual bath until morning. The majority hold that fasting is obligatory for her and valid, whether she deliberately or inadvertently delays it, like the one in janabah; this is the view of Malik and Ibn al-Qasim. Abd al-Malik said: if a menstruating woman becomes pure before dawn but delays her bath until dawn breaks, her day is a day of breaking the fast, because for part of it she is not pure, and she is not like the one in janabah, because a wet dream does not nullify the fast while menstruation does. This is how Abu al-Faraj mentioned it in his book from Abd al-Malik. Al-Awza'i said: she must make it up, because she was negligent in bathing. Ibn al-Jallab related from Abd al-Malik that if she became pure before dawn at a time when it was possible for her to bathe, but she was negligent and did not bathe until morning, it does not harm her, like the one in janabah; but if the time was too short for her to bathe, her fast is not valid and her day is a day of breaking the fast. Malik also said this: she is like one upon whom dawn breaks while menstruating. Muhammad ibn Maslama said concerning this: she fasts and makes it up, like the view of al-Awza'i. It is related from him that he anomalously required expiation together with making up for one who became pure before dawn but was negligent, delayed and tarried until morning.

The Sixteenth Issue: If a woman becomes pure at night in Ramadan and does not know whether that was before dawn or after it, she fasts and makes up that day as a precaution, and there is no expiation upon her.

The Seventeenth Issue: It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The one who cups and the one who is cupped have broken their fast." This is from the hadiths of Thawban, Shaddad ibn Aws and Rafi ibn Khadij, and Ahmad and Ishaq held this view. Ahmad authenticated the hadith of Shaddad ibn Aws, and Ali ibn al-Madini authenticated the hadith of Rafi ibn Khadij. Malik, al-Shafi'i and al-Thawri said: there is no making up upon him, except that it is disliked for him because of the risk. In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Anas, he was asked: "Did you used to dislike cupping for the fasting person?" He said: "No, except because of weakness." Abu Umar said: the hadiths of Shaddad, Rafi and Thawban are, in our view, abrogated by the hadith of Ibn Abbas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was cupped while fasting and in the state of ihram. This is because in the hadith of Shaddad ibn Aws and others, he (ﷺ) passed by a man who was being cupped in the eighteenth night of Ramadan in the year of the conquest of Makka, and said: "The cupper and the one cupped have broken their fast." He (ﷺ) himself was cupped in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage while in ihram and fasting. So if his pilgrimage was in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage, it is necessarily abrogating, because he (ﷺ) did not live to see another Ramadan, for he died in Rabi al-Awwal, (ﷺ).

The Eighteenth Issue: The words of the Most High: ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾. The imperative "complete" requires obligation without dispute. "Until" (ila) marks an endpoint; if what follows it is of the same kind as what precedes it, it is included in its ruling, as when you say: "I bought the field up to its boundary," or "I bought from you this tree up to that tree," the thing sold being trees, for the tree is included in what is sold. This is unlike your saying: "I bought the field up to the house," for the house is not included in what was bounded, since it is not of its kind. So He stipulated the completion of the fast until the night arrives, just as He permitted eating until the day becomes distinct.

The Nineteenth Issue: Part of the completion of the fast is maintaining the intention without cancelling it. If one cancels it during part of the day and intends to break the fast, though he does not eat or drink, the Mudawwana considers him a breaker of the fast who owes making up. In the book of Ibn Habib, he remains in his fast, and only actual breaking by deed, not by intention, removes him from the fast. It is also said: he owes both making up and expiation. Sahnun said...

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 187 (part 5 of 7):

It is only the one who intends the fast at night that breaks it. As for the one who intends it during the day, it does no harm to him, and he makes it up out of juristic preference (istihsan). I say: this is good. The twentieth point: ﴿until the night﴾. When the night has clearly appeared, breaking the fast becomes sunna (the Prophetic practice), whether or not one has eaten. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Imam Abu Ishaq al-Shirazi was asked about a man who swore, three times over, by divorce, that he would not break his fast on anything hot or cold. He replied that once the sun has set he has broken his fast and nothing is incumbent upon him. He based this on the Prophet's saying (ﷺ): "When the night comes from here and the day withdraws from here, the fasting person has broken his fast." Imam Abu Nasr ibn al-Sabbagh, author of al-Shamil, was asked about the same case and said: he must break his fast on something hot or cold. What Imam Abu Ishaq answered is better, because it is what the Book and the Sunna require.

The twenty-first point: if a person thinks the sun has set because of cloud or something else, and breaks his fast, and then the sun appears, he must make up the day according to the opinion of most scholars. In al-Bukhari, it is related from Asma' bint Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with them both, that she said: "We broke our fast on a cloudy day during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then the sun rose." It was said to Hisham [[He is Ibn Urwa, one of the narrators in the chain of this hadith.]]: "Were they ordered to make it up?" He said: "Was there any choice but to make it up?" Umar said in the Muwatta' concerning this: "The matter is light, and we exerted ourselves [in the time [[Addition from the Muwatta'.]]]," meaning the making-up. It is also related from Umar that he said: "There is no making-up for him." Al-Hasan al-Basri said: "There is no making-up for him, like the forgetful person." This is also the view of Ishaq and the Zahiris. But the words of Allah, "until the night," refute this view, and Allah knows best.

The twenty-second point: if a person breaks his fast while doubting whether the sun has set, he must expiate along with making up the day, as Malik said, unless it is most likely in his judgment that the sun has set. Whoever doubts whether dawn has come must refrain from eating. If he eats while in doubt, he must make up the day like the forgetful person, and Malik's opinion on this is unchanged. Some scholars in Medina and elsewhere hold that he bears nothing until dawn has clearly appeared to him, and Ibn al-Mundhir held this view. Ilkiya al-Tabari said: "Some people have thought that when eating is permitted until the beginning of dawn, if he eats believing dawn has not yet risen, he has eaten by the permission of the Law during a time when eating is allowed, so there is no making-up for him. Mujahid and Jabir ibn Zayd said the same." There is no disagreement that making up is required if the new moon of the first night of Ramadan was obscured and he ate, and then it became clear that it was Ramadan. What we are discussing is similar to this. Likewise, a captive in the land of war who eats thinking it is still Sha'ban, and then it turns out otherwise.

The twenty-third point: the words of Allah, ﴿until the night﴾, contain an implication forbidding continuous fasting (wisal, fasting without breaking the fast between days), since the night is the limit of the fast. Aisha said this too. This is a matter on which there is disagreement. Among those who practised continuous fasting were Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, Ibrahim al-Taymi, Abu al-Jawza', and Abu al-Hasan al-Dinawari, among others. Ibn al-Zubayr would fast continuously for seven days, and when he broke his fast he drank ghee and aloe until his intestines were split open. He said: "His intestines would dry out." Abu al-Jawza' would fast continuously for seven days and seven nights, and if he gripped a strong man's forearm he would crush it. The apparent meaning of the Qur'an and the Sunna requires prohibition. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When the sun has set from here and the night has come from here, the fasting person has broken his fast." Muslim transmitted it from the hadith of Abd Allah ibn Abi Awfa. He forbade continuous fasting, and when they refused to stop, he fasted continuously with them for a day, then another day, then they saw the new moon, and he said: "If the new moon had been delayed, I would have increased it for you," as a punishment for them when they refused to stop. Muslim transmitted this from Abu Hurayra. In the hadith of Anas: "If the month were extended for us, we would fast continuously in a way that would make those who go to extremes give up their excess." Muslim also transmitted this. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Beware of continuous fasting, beware of continuous fasting," as an emphatic prohibition for them. Al-Bukhari transmitted it. Most scholars hold that continuous fasting is disliked, for the reasons we have mentioned and because it weakens one's strength and wears down the body. Some have forbidden it, because it contradicts the apparent sense (of the text) and imitates the People of the Book. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The difference between our fast and the fast of the People of the Book is the pre-dawn meal (suhur)." Muslim and Abu Dawud transmitted it. In al-Bukhari, it is related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that he heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Do not fast continuously. Whoever wants to fast continuously, let him fast until the pre-dawn." They said: "But you fast continuously, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "I am not like you. I spend the night being fed by one who feeds me and given drink by one who gives me drink." They said: This is a permission to delay breaking the fast until the pre-dawn, which is the limit of continuous fasting for whoever wishes it, and it prohibits continuing from one day into the next. This is the view of Ahmad, Ishaq, and Ibn Wahb, a companion of Malik. Those who permit continuous fasting argue that the prohibition was only because they were recent converts to Islam, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) feared they would overburden themselves with continuous fasting and the highest levels of devotion, and then they would tire or grow weak in what was more beneficial to them, namely jihad and strength against the enemy, and they needed that at that time. He himself kept continuous fasting and the highest levels of acts of worship as a personal practice. When they asked him about their continuous fasting, he showed them a distinction between himself and them, and informed them that his state in this was not like theirs, and he said: "I am not like you. My Lord feeds me and gives me drink." When faith was perfected in their hearts, firmly established and deeply rooted, the Muslims increased in number and prevailed over their enemy, the friends of Allah practised continuous fasting and bound themselves to the highest levels (of devotion). And Allah knows best.

I say: abandoning continuous fasting, while Islam is manifest and the enemies are subdued, is more excellent, and that is the highest rank, the loftiest station and degree. The evidence for this is what we have mentioned. Also, the night is not a time of legally prescribed fasting, so that if a person begins a fast during it with the intention of reward, he would not be rewarded for it. The Prophet (ﷺ) did not report of himself that he fasted continuously. Rather, the Companions assumed this and said: "You fast continuously," and he informed them that he is fed and given drink. The apparent meaning of this reality is that he (ﷺ) is brought the food and drink of Paradise. It was also said that this is to be understood as referring to the meanings and subtleties that come upon his heart. When a word admits both the literal and the figurative sense, the original is the literal sense, until a proof that removes it appears. Then, when they refused to stop continuous fasting, he fasted continuously with them while he was in his customary state, as he reported of himself, and they were in their customary state, so that they would weaken, their endurance would diminish, and they would stop fasting continuously. This is the real meaning of punishment, so that they would give up their excess and the strictness they wanted to impose upon themselves. Also, even if we suppose that what is meant by his saying "I am fed and given drink" is figurative, he would be considered as having broken his fast in legal ruling, just as one who backbites during his fast or gives false testimony has broken his fast in legal ruling, and there is no difference between them. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever does not give up false speech and acting upon it, Allah has no need that he give up his food and drink." In this sense, the Prophet (ﷺ) did not fast continuously, nor did he command it, so abandoning it is more excellent. And success is from Allah.

The twenty-fourth point: when the fasting person breaks his fast, it is recommended that he break it with fresh dates, or dates, or a few sips of water, based on what Abu Dawud related from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to break his fast with fresh dates before praying. If there were no fresh dates, then with dates. If there were no dates, he would take a few sips of water." Al-Daraqutni also transmitted it and said concerning it: "Its chain is sound." Al-Daraqutni related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) broke his fast he would say: 'O Allah, for You we fasted, and with Your provision we break our fast. So accept from us, You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.'" And from Ibn Umar, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say when he broke his fast: 'The thirst has gone, the veins are moistened, and the reward is established, if Allah wills.'" Abu Dawud also transmitted this. Al-Daraqutni said: "Al-Husayn ibn Waqid alone related it, and its chain is good." Ibn Majah related from Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) broke his fast at the house of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, and he said: 'The fasting ones have broken their fast with you, the righteous have eaten your food, and the angels have sent blessings upon you.'" It is also related from Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever gives a fasting person something to break his fast with will have a reward like theirs, without any reduction in their rewards." It is also related from Abd Allah ibn Amr ibn al-As, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "For the fasting person, at the time of breaking his fast, there is a supplication that is not rejected." Ibn Abi Mulayka said: "I heard Abd Allah ibn Amr say, when he broke his fast: 'O Allah, I ask You by Your mercy which encompasses everything, that You forgive me.'" In Sahih Muslim, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The fasting person has two joys: he rejoices when he breaks his fast, and he rejoices when he meets his Lord because of his fast."

The twenty-fifth point: it is recommended for him to fast six days in Shawwal, based on what Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, and Ibn Majah related from Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever fasts Ramadan and then follows it with six from Shawwal, it is as if he had fasted the whole time." This is a sound hadith from the hadith of Sa'd ibn Sa'id al-Ansari al-Madani, who is one whom al-Bukhari did not take any narrations from. It has come with a good chain, explained, from the hadith of Abu Asma' al-Rahbi, from Thawban, the freed slave of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace

وسلم يقول: "جعل الله الحسنة بعشر أمثالها، فشهر رمضان بعشرة أشهر، وستة أيام بعد الفطر تمام السنة". رواه النسائي. واختُلف في صيام هذه الأيام، فكرهها مالك في موطئه خوفًا أن يُلحق أهل الجهالة برمضان ما ليس منه، وقد وقع ما خافه، حتى إنه كان في بعض بلاد خراسان يقومون لسحورها على عادتهم في رمضان. وروى مطرف عن مالك أنه كان يصومها في خاصة نفسه. واستحب صيامها الشافعي، وكرهه أبو يوسف.

السادسة والعشرون: قوله تعالى: ﴿ولا تباشروهن وأنتم عاكفون في المساجد﴾. بيّن جل تعالى أن الجماع يفسد الاعتكاف. وأجمع أهل العلم على أن من جامع امرأته وهو معتكف عامدًا لذلك في فرجها أنه مفسد لاعتكافه، واختلفوا فيما عليه إذا فعل ذلك، فقال الحسن البصري والزهري: عليه ما على الموقع أهله في رمضان. فأما المباشرة من غير جماع فإن قصد بها التلذذ فهي مكروهة، وإن لم يقصد لم يُكره، لأن عائشة كانت ترجّل رأس رسول الله ﷺ وهو معتكف، وكانت لا محالة تمسّ بدن رسول الله ﷺ بيدها، فدل بذلك على أن المباشرة بغير شهوة غير محظورة، هذا قول عطاء والشافعي وابن المنذر. قال أبو عمر: وأجمعوا على أن المعتكف لا يباشر ولا يقبّل. واختلفوا فيما عليه إن فعل، فقال مالك والشافعي: إن فعل شيئًا من ذلك فسد اعتكافه، قاله المزني. وقال في موضع آخر من مسائل الاعتكاف: لا يفسد الاعتكاف من الوطء إلا ما يوجب الحد، واختاره المزني قياسًا على أصله في الحج والصوم.

السابعة والعشرون: قوله تعالى: ﴿وأنتم عاكفون﴾ جملة في موضع الحال. والاعتكاف في اللغة: الملازمة، يقال عكف على الشيء إذا لازمه مقبلًا عليه. قال الراجز:
عكف النبيط يلعبون الفنزجا [[تقدم صدر هذا البيت وقائله ومعناه في هامش ص ١١٤ من هذا الجزء.]]
وقال شاعر:
وَظَلَّ بَنَاتُ اللَّيْلِ حَوْلِي عُكَّفًا ... عُكُوفَ الْبَوَاكِي بَيْنَهُنَّ صَرِيعُ
ولما كان المعتكف ملازمًا للعمل بطاعة الله مدة اعتكافه لزمه هذا الاسم. وهو في عرف الشرع: ملازمة طاعة مخصوصة في وقت مخصوص على شرط مخصوص في موضع مخصوص. وأجمع العلماء على أنه ليس بواجب، وهو قربة من القرب ونافلة من النوافل عمل بها رسول الله ﷺ وأصحابه وأزواجه، ويلزمه إن ألزمه نفسه، ويُكره الدخول فيه لمن يُخاف عليه العجز عن الوفاء بحقوقه.

الثامنة والعشرون: أجمع العلماء على أن الاعتكاف لا يكون إلا في المسجد، لقول الله تعالى: "في المساجد". واختلفوا في المراد بالمساجد، فذهب قوم إلى أن الآية خرجت على نوع من المساجد، وهو ما بناه نبي كالمساجد الحرام ومسجد النبي ﷺ ومسجد إيلياء [[إيلياء (بكسر أوله واللام): اسم مدينة بيت المقدس.]]، روي هذا عن حذيفة بن اليمان وسعد بن المسيّب، فلا يجوز الاعتكاف عندهم في غيرها. وقال آخرون: لا اعتكاف إلا في مسجد تُجمع فيه الجمعة، لأن الإشارة في الآية عندهم إلى ذلك الجنس من المساجد، روي هذا عن علي بن أبي طالب وابن مسعود، وهو قول عروة والحكم وحماد والزهري وأبي جعفر محمد بن علي، وهو أحد قولي مالك. وقال آخرون: الاعتكاف في كل مسجد جائز، يُروى هذا القول عن سعيد بن جبير وأبي قلابة وغيرهم، وهو قول الشافعي وأبي حنيفة وأصحابهما. وحجتهم حمل الآية على عمومها في كل مسجد له إمام ومؤذن، وهو أحد قولي مالك، وبه يقول ابن علية وداود بن علي والطبري وابن المنذر. وروى الدارقطني عن الضحاك عن حذيفة قال: سمعت رسول الله ﷺ يقول: "كل مسجد له مؤذن وإمام فالاعتكاف فيه يصلح". قال الدارقطني: والضحاك لم يسمع من حذيفة.

التاسعة والعشرون: وأقل الاعتكاف عند مالك وأبي حنيفة يوم وليلة، فإن قال: لله عليّ اعتكاف ليلة لزمه اعتكاف ليلة ويوم. وكذلك إن نذر اعتكاف يوم لزمه يوم وليلة. وقال سحنون: من نذر اعتكاف ليلة فلا شيء عليه، وقال أبو حنيفة وأصحابه: إن نذر يومًا فعليه يوم بغير ليلة، وإن نذر ليلة فلا شيء عليه. كما قال سحنون. قال الشافعي: عليه ما نذر، إن نذر ليلة فليلة، وإن نذر يومًا فيومًا. قال الشافعي: أقله لحظة ولا حد لأكثره. وقال بعض أصحاب أبي حنيفة: يصح الاعتكاف ساعة. وعلى هذا القول فليس من شرطه صوم، وروي عن أحمد بن حنبل في أحد قوليه، وهو قول داود بن علي وابن علية، واختاره ابن المنذر وابن العربي. واحتجوا بأن اعتكاف رسول الله ﷺ كان في رمضان، ومحال أن يكون صوم رمضان لرمضان ولغيره. ولو نوى المعتكف في رمضان بصومه التطوع والفرض فسد صومه عند مالك وأصحابه. ومعلوم أن ليل المعتكف يلزمه فيه من اجتناب مباشرة النساء ما يلزمه في نهاره، وأن ليله داخل في اعتكافه، وأن الليل ليس بموضع صوم، فكذلك نهاره ليس بمفتقر إلى الصوم، وإن صام فحسن. وقال مالك وأبو حنيفة وأحمد في القول الآخر: لا يصح إلا بصوم. وروي عن ابن عمر وابن عباس وعائشة رضي الله عنهم. وفي الموطأ عن القاسم بن محمد ونافع مولى عبد الله بن عمر: لا اعتكاف إلا بصيام، لقول الله تعالى في كتابه: "وكلوا واشربوا" إلى قوله: "في المساجد" وقالا: فإنما ذكر الله الاعتكاف مع الصيام. قال يحيى قال مالك: وعلى ذلك الأمر عندنا. واحتجوا بما رواه عبد الله بن بديل عن عمر بن دينار عن ابن عمر أن عمر جعل عليه [أن يعتكف [[الزيادة عن سنن أبي داود.]]] في الجاهلية ليلة أو يومًا [عند الكعبة [[الزيادة عن سنن أبي داود.]]] فسأل النبي ﷺ فقال: "اعتكف وصم". أخرجه أبو داود. وقال الدارقطني: تفرد به ابن بديل عن عمرو وهو ضعيف. وعن عائشة أن النبي ﷺ قال: "لا اعتكاف إلا بصيام". قال الدارقطني: تفرد به سويد بن عبد العزيز عن سفيان بن حسين عن الزهري عن عروة عن عائشة. وقالوا: ليس من شرط الصوم عندنا أن يكون للاعتكاف، بل يصح أن يكون الصوم له ولرمضان ولنذر ولغيره، فإذا نذره الناذر فإنما ينصرف نذره إلى مقتضاه في أصل الشرع، وهذا كمن نذر صلاة فإنما تلزمه، ولم يكن عليه أن يتطهر لها خاصة بل يجزئه أن يؤديها بطهارة لغيرها.

الموفية ثلاثين: وليس للمعتكف أن يخرج من معتكفه إلا لما لا بد له منه، لما روى الأئمة عن عائشة قالت: كان رسول الله ﷺ إذا اعتكف يدني إلى رأسه فأرجله، وكان لا يدخل البيت إلا لحاجة الإنسان، تريد الغائط والبول. ولا خلاف في هذا بين الأمة ولا بين الأئمة، فإذا خرج المعتكف لضرورة وما لا بد له منه ورجع في فوره بعد زوال الضرورة بنى على ما مضى من اعتكافه ولا شيء عليه. ومن الضرورة المرض البيّن والحيض. واختلفوا في خروجه لما سوى ذلك، فمذهب مالك ما ذكرنا، وكذلك مذهب الشافعي وأبي حنيفة. وقال سعيد بن جبير والحسن والنخعي: يعود المريض ويشهد الجنائز، وروي عن علي وليس بثابت عنه. وفرّق إسحاق بين الاعتكاف الواجب والتطوع، فقال في الاعتكاف الواجب: لا يعود المريض ولا يشهد الجنائز، وقال في التطوع: يُشترط حين يبتدئ حضور الجنائز وعيادة المرضى والجمعة. وقال الشافعي: يصح اشتراط الخروج من معتكفه لعيادة مريض وشهود الجنائز وغير ذلك من حوائجه. واختلف فيه عن أحمد، فمنع منه مرة، وقال مرة: أرجو ألا يكون به بأس. وقال الأوزاعي كما قال مالك: لا يكون في الاعتكاف شرط. قال ابن المنذر: لا يخرج المعتكف من اعتكافه إلا لما لا بد له منه، وهو الذي كان النبي ﷺ يخرج له.

الحادية والثلاثون: واختلفوا في خروجه للجمعة، فقالت طائفة: يخرج للجمعة ويرجع إذا سلّم، لأنه خرج إلى فرض ولا ينتقض اعتكافه. وrواه ابن الجهم عن مالك، وبه قال أبو حنيفة، واختاره ابن العربي وابن المنذر. ومشهور مذهب مالك أن من أراد أن يعتكف عشرة أيام أو نذر ذلك لم يعتكف إلا في المسجد الجامع، وإذا اعتكف في غيره لزمه الخروج إلى الجمعة وبطل اعتكافه. وقال عبد الملك: يخرج إلى الجمعة فيشهدها ويرجع مكانه ويصح اعتكافه. قلت: وهو صحيح لقوله تعالى: "وأنتم عاكفون في المساجد" فعمّ. وأجمع العلماء على أن الاعتكاف ليس بواجب وأنه سنة، وأجمع الجمهور من الأئمة على أن الجمعة فرض على الأعيان، ومتى اجتمع واجبان أحدهما آكد من الآخر قُدِّم الآكد، فكيف إذا اجتمع مندوب وواجب، ولم يقل أحد بترك الخروج إليها، فكان الخروج إليها في معنى حاجة الإنسان.

**Thirty-second issue:** When a person in i'tikaf (seclusion in the mosque for worship) commits a major sin, his i'tikaf is invalidated, because a major sin is the opposite of worship, just as ritual impurity (hadath) is the opposite of purity (ṭahara) and prayer. Allah the Exalted has forbidden him the highest ranks of i'tikaf in worship. This was stated by Ibn Khuwayz Mandad, on the authority of Malik.

**Thirty-third issue:** Muslim narrated from Aisha, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) intended to observe i'tikaf, he would pray the dawn prayer and then enter his place of i'tikaf..." and the rest of the hadith. The scholars differed over the time at which the one observing i'tikaf enters into it. Al-Awza'i followed the apparent meaning of this hadith. It is also reported from al-Thawri and al-Layth ibn Sa'd in one of his two opinions, and Ibn al-Mundhir and a group of the Successors (tabi'un) held the same view.

Abu Thawr said: "Only the one who vowed ten days does this. If he extends it beyond that, he enters before sunset."

Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and their companions said: "If one makes it obligatory upon himself to observe i'tikaf for a month, he enters the mosque before sunset on the evening of that day." Malik said: "Likewise everyone who intends to observe i'tikaf for one day or more." Abu Hanifa and Ibn al-Majishun, Abd al-Malik, also held this view, because the first night of the days of i'tikaf is included in them, and because it is a period for i'tikaf, so it is not divided, just like the day.

Al-Shafi'i said: "If one says, 'For Allah I owe a day,' he enters before the break of dawn and exits after sunset, which differs from his view regarding the month."

Al-Layth, in one of his two opinions, and Zufar said: "He enters before the break of dawn, and for them the month and the day are the same." This was also reported similarly from Abu Yusuf. Al-Qadi Abd al-Wahhab held this view too, and said that the night enters into i'tikaf only by way of following (tabaʿ), as evidenced by the fact that i'tikaf cannot be except with fasting, and the night is not a time for fasting. Thus it is established that the intended object of i'tikaf is the day, not the night.

I say: The hadith of Aisha refutes these opinions, and it is the proof when there is dispute. It is a hadith whose authenticity is not disputed.

**Thirty-fourth issue:** Malik recommended that whoever observes i'tikaf during the last ten nights should spend the night of the Festival of Breaking the Fast (ʿId al-Fitr) in the mosque until he goes from it to the place of prayer (al-Musalla). Ahmad also held this view. Al-Shafi'i and al-Awza'i said: "He leaves when the sun sets." This was narrated by Sahnun from Ibn al-Qasim, because the ten days end when the month ends, and the month ends with the sunset of the last day of the month of Ramadan.

Sahnun said: "This is obligatory, so if he leaves on the night of the Festival, his i'tikaf is invalidated."

Ibn al-Majishun said: "This is refuted by what we have mentioned about the month ending. If remaining on the night of the Festival were a condition for the validity of i'tikaf, no i'tikaf that is not connected to the night of the Festival would be valid. The consensus on the permissibility of that is evidence that remaining on the night of the Festival is not a condition for the validity of i'tikaf."

These are sufficient principles of the rulings on fasting and i'tikaf appropriate to the verses. For one who confines himself to them, they are enough, and Allah is the One who grants success in guidance.

**Thirty-fifth issue:** The saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿These are the limits set by Allah﴾, meaning these rulings are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them. "These" (tilka) refers to these commands and prohibitions. The word ḥudūd (limits) means barriers, and ḥadd means prevention. From this the iron (ḥadīd) was named ḥadīd, because it prevents weapons from reaching the body. The doorkeeper and the jailer were called ḥaddād, because he prevents those inside the house from leaving it and prevents those outside from entering it. The limits of Allah are so called because they prevent anything that is not part of them from entering them, and anything that is part of them from leaving them. From this also the punishments for sins (ḥudūd) are so called, because they prevent their perpetrators from returning to the like of them. From this also the woman in the waiting period (ʿidda) who is in mourning (ḥādd) is so called, because she refrains from adornment.

**Thirty-sixth issue:** The saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Thus Allah makes His signs clear to the people﴾, meaning: just as He has made these limits clear, He makes all the rulings clear, so that you may guard against transgressing them. The word āyāt (signs) means the indicators guiding to the truth. The word "la'alla" (so that they may) expresses hope concerning them. Its apparent meaning is general, but its intended meaning is specific to those whom Allah has facilitated for guidance, by the evidence of the verses which state that Allah leads astray whomever He wills.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 2, verse 188:**

There are eight issues concerning it.

**The first issue:** His saying, ﴿Do not consume your wealth among yourselves wrongfully﴾. It is said that it was revealed concerning Abdan ibn Ashwa' al-Hadrami, who claimed a piece of land from Imru' al-Qays al-Kindi, and the two of them brought the matter before the Prophet (ﷺ). Imru' al-Qays denied the claim and wished to swear an oath, and then the verse was revealed. So he refrained from the oath, and he made Abdan the arbiter over his land and did not contest with him.

**The second issue:** The address in this verse includes the whole community of Muhammad (ﷺ). The meaning is: none of you should consume the property of another without right. This includes gambling, deception, usurpation, denying rights, and whatever the soul of its owner does not willingly give up, or whatever the Shari'ah has forbidden even if its owner willingly gives it up, such as the earnings of a prostitute, the gift (hulwan) of a soothsayer, the price of wine and pigs, and other such things. It does not include deception (ghabn) in sale when the seller knows the true nature of what he sells, because such deception is in effect like a gift, as will be explained in its place in Surah al-Nisa' [[See vol. 5, p. 152.]]. The word "wealth" is attributed to the pronoun of the addressees because each of them is both forbidden and the one forbidden from it, as in His saying: ﴿You kill yourselves﴾ [[See p. 19 of this part.]]. Some scholars said that the intended meaning of the verse, ﴿Do not consume your wealth among yourselves wrongfully﴾ [[See vol. 5, p. 150.]], is in amusements, singing-girls, drinking, and idleness. On this reading, the attribution of wealth to the pronoun of its owners is straightforward.

**The third issue:** Whoever takes the property of another not in the manner permitted by the Shari'ah has consumed it wrongfully. Among consuming wrongfully is that a judge rules in your favour while you know that you are in the wrong. The unlawful does not become lawful by the judge's ruling, because he only rules according to the outward appearance. This is a consensus (ijma') regarding property, although according to Abu Hanifa his ruling takes effect in matters of intimacy (furuj) inwardly as well. And if the judge's ruling does not change the inward reality of property, then it is even more so in matters of intimacy.

Al-A'immah narrated from Umm Salamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "You bring your disputes to me, and perhaps some of you are more eloquent in his argument than others, so I rule for him according to what I hear. Whoever I give him something from his brother's right, let him not take it, for I am only cutting off for him a piece of Fire." In another narration: "Let him carry it or leave it."

The majority of scholars and the leading jurists hold this hadith. It is explicit that the judge's ruling according to the outward appearance does not change the inward reality, whether in property, blood, or intimacy. The exception is what is reported from Abu Hanifa regarding intimacy. He claimed that if two false witnesses testified against a man concerning the divorce of his wife, and the judge ruled on their testimony because he considered them upright, then her intimacy becomes lawful to her new husband, provided he knows the case is false, after her waiting period (iddah). Likewise, if one of the two witnesses married her, it is permitted according to him, because once she has become lawful to husbands outwardly, the witness and others are equal, since the judge's ruling has severed her bond and brought about permissibility and prohibition both outwardly and inwardly. Were it not for that, she would not have become lawful to husbands. He argued from the ruling of li'an and said: It is known that the wife only reaches separation from her husband through false li'an, which, if the judge had known her to be lying in it, he would have punished her with the hadd and would not have separated them.
