So this case does not fall under the general meaning of his, peace be upon him, saying: "Whoever I give him something from his brother's right, let him not take it..." (the hadith).

**The fourth issue:** This verse is used against every opponent and proponent in every ruling that they claim is permissible for themselves. It is cited as evidence that it is not permitted, so the answer to them is: We do not accept that it is unlawful (batil) until you establish that with evidence. Then it enters into this general statement. Thus the verse is evidence that falsehood (batil) in dealings is not permitted, but it does not specify what the falsehood is.

**The fifth issue:** His saying, ﴿wrongfully﴾ (bil-batil). Linguistically, batil means that which goes away and vanishes. It is said: batala yabtulu butulan and butlanan. The plural of batil is bawatil. Al-abatil is the plural of butulah. Tabattala means he followed idle play. Abtala so-and-so means he came with falsehood. His saying: ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 367.]], Qatadah said: It is Iblis; it cannot add to the Qur'an nor diminish it. His saying: ﴿and Allah erases falsehood﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 25.]], meaning shirk. Al-batalah means sorcerers.

**The sixth issue:** His saying, ﴿and present them to the rulers﴾ (wa tudlu biha ila al-hukkam), the verse. It is said: it means the deposit and that which has no clear evidence supporting it, narrated from Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan. It is also said: it refers to the property of an orphan which is in the hands of guardians, who bring it to the rulers when they are asked for it, so that they may take part of it, and they have an outward argument in their favour.

Al-Zajjaj said: You act according to what the outward rulings require, while you abandon what you know to be the truth. It is said: adla al-rajul bi-hujjatihi (he put forward his argument) or bil-amr alladhi yarju al-najah bihi (the matter by which he hopes for success), by way of comparison with one who lowers a bucket into a well. It is said: adla dalwahu (he lowered his bucket), meaning he sent it down, and dallaha meaning he drew it up. The plural of dalw (bucket) is dilaa, adl, dilaa', and dulay.

The meaning of the verse is: Do not combine consuming wealth wrongfully with lowering your false arguments before the rulers. This is like His saying: ﴿and do not mix truth with falsehood, nor conceal the truth﴾ [[See vol. 1, p. 340.]]. It is of the same type as your saying: "Do not eat fish and drink milk."

It is also said: the meaning is: Do not curry favour with the rulers with your wealth and bribe them, so that they rule in your favour for more than it. On this reading, the (ba) in ﴿bil-batil﴾ is merely connective.

Ibn Atiyyah said: This view is preferred, because rulers are the likely place of bribery, except for one who is protected, and such a person is rare. Also, the two words are cognate: tudlu (you lower) comes from sending down a bucket, and rishwah (bribe) from rishaa' (rope), as if one draws with it to fulfil a need.

I say: What strengthens this is His saying, ﴿and present them﴾ (wa tudlu biha). Tudlu is in a jussive position, coordinated with ta'kulu (consume), as we have mentioned. In the codex of Ubayy, it reads ﴿wa la tudlu﴾ (and do not present), with the repetition of the particle of prohibition. This reading supports the jussive form of tudlu in the reading of the community.

It is said that tudlu is in the accusative position as an adverbial clause, and in such a construction, according to Sibawayh, an implied "an" (that) governs it.

The pronoun in His saying, ﴿biha﴾ (with them), refers to the wealth. On the first view, it refers to the argument, which has not been previously mentioned. Therefore the second view is strengthened by the mention of wealth. And Allah knows best.

In al-Sihah: "Bribery is well known. Rusubah with a dammah is the same. Its plural is rushan and rishan. Rashahu yarshuhu means he gave him a bribe. Irtasha means he took the bribe. Istarsha in his judgement means he sought a bribe for it."

I say: So the rulers today are the very essence of bribery, not merely its likely place. There is no power and no strength except with Allah!

**The seventh issue:** His saying, ﴿so that you may consume﴾ (li-ta'kulu). It is put in the accusative by the "li" of purpose (lam kay). ﴿A portion﴾ (fariqan) means a part and a share. He expressed the group by the portion and the part. Al-fariq is a piece of sheep that separates from the majority of the flock. It is said: there is inversion in the sentence, the implied meaning being: "so that you may consume the wealth of a group of people." ﴿With sin﴾ (bil-ith'm) means with wrongdoing and transgression. It is called ith'm because sin attaches to its doer. ﴿While you know﴾ (wa antum ta'lamun) means knowing its falsehood and its sinfulness. This is an intensification of audacity and disobedience.

**The eighth issue:** The People of the Sunnah agree that whoever takes anything that falls under the name of wealth, whether little or much, is thereby deemed a sinner (yufassaq), and that taking it is forbidden to him. This is in opposition to Bishr ibn al-Mu'tamir and those who followed him among the Mu'tazilah, who said: A person who has reached legal responsibility is not deemed a sinner unless he takes two hundred dirhams, and is not deemed a sinner for less than that. And in opposition to Ibn al-Jubba'i, who said: He is deemed a sinner for taking ten dirhams and is not deemed a sinner for less. And in opposition to Ibn al-Hudhayl, who said: He is deemed a sinner for taking five dirhams. And in opposition to some of the Qadariyyah of Basra, who said: He is deemed a sinner for taking one dirham or more, and is not deemed a sinner for less than that.

All of this is rejected by the Qur'an, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the scholars of the community. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed your blood, your wealth, and your honour are forbidden to you..." (the hadith), agreed upon as authentic.

There are twelve issues in it.

**First issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about the new moons﴾. The Jews asked about this and raised it as an objection against the Prophet (ﷺ). Mu'adh said: "O Messenger of Allah, the Jews visit us often and ask us a great deal about the new moons. What is the matter with the crescent that it appears thin, then grows until it becomes full and round, then wanes until it returns as it was?" So Allah revealed this verse. It is also said that the reason for its revelation was that some Muslims asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the crescent, and about the reason for its *mihaq* [[The *mihaq* (the vowel of the *mim* may be fatha, kasra or damma) is the period when the moon is hidden for two nights, so that it is not seen in the morning or the evening.]], its completion, and its difference from the state of the sun. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, al-Rabi' and others.

**Second issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿about the new moons﴾. *Al-ahilla* (the new moons) is the plural of *al-hilal* (the crescent). It is pluralised, although in reality it is singular in the sense that each month has one crescent, which is distinct from the crescent of another month. Its states are therefore expressed in the plural as *al-ahilla*. By *al-ahilla* is meant the months. The crescent is sometimes used to refer to the month because it occurs within it, as the poet said:

*Two brothers from Najd, in whom there is trust,*
*And the month is like the paring of a fingernail.*

It is also said that the month is called *shahr* because people point (*tushhiru*) with their hands to the place where it is seen and indicate it. The word *hilal* is applied to the two nights at the end of the month and the two nights at its beginning. It is also said that it applies to the first three nights of the month. Al-Asma'i said: "It is a crescent until it becomes thin and curved like a fine thread." It is also said: "Rather, it is a crescent until its light dazzles the sky, and that is on the seventh night." Abu al-Abbas said: "It is called *hilal* because people raise their voices in announcing it. From this comes *istahalla al-sabiyyu* (the child cried out loudly), when his life becomes evident through his crying. And *istahalla wajhuhu farahan* (his face lit up with joy) and *tahallala* when joy appears in it." Abu Kabir said:

*When you look at the bright lines of his face,*
*They shine like the lightning of the gleaming cloud.*

It is said: *ahlalna al-hilal* (we saw the new moon) when we have entered into it. Al-Jawhari said: "*Ahalla al-hilal* and *istahalla* are used in the passive voice (*ala ma lam yusamma fa'iluhu*). It is also said: *istahalla* in the sense of *tabayyana* (it became clear), but *ahalla* is not said. It is said: *ahlalna 'an laylati kadha* (we saw the new moon on such-and-such night), but one does not say *ahlalnahu fa-halla*, just as one says *adkhalnahu fa-dakhala*, although this is its analogical form." Abu Nasr Abd al-Rahim al-Qushayri said in his tafsir: "It is said: *ahalla al-hilalu* and *istahalla*, and *ahlalna al-hilal* and *istahlalna*."

**Third issue:** Our scholars said: whoever swears that he will repay his creditor, or that he will do such-and-such *fi al-hilal*, or *ra's al-hilal*, or *'inda al-hilal* (at the new moon), and does it one or two days after the crescent is sighted, has not broken his oath. All the months are suitable for all acts of worship and transactions, as will be explained.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: they are times marked out for people and for the Hajj﴾. This explains the wisdom in the waxing and waning of the moon. It removes ambiguity regarding fixed terms, transactions, oaths, the Hajj, the counting of periods, fasting, breaking the fast, the duration of pregnancy, hiring and rentals, and other benefits of the servants. A parallel is His saying, the Truth: ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs, then We effaced the sign of the night and made the sign of the day to give sight, that you may seek bounty from your Lord, and that you may know the number of the years and the reckoning﴾ [al-Isra' 17:12], as will be explained [[See vol. 10, p. 227.]]. And His saying: ﴿It is He who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light, and determined for it stations, that you may know the number of the years and the reckoning﴾ [Yunus 10:5] [[See vol. 8, p. 309.]]. Counting by the new moons is easier than counting by the days.

**Fourth issue:** On the basis of what we have established, a response is given to the Literalists (*Ahl al-Zahir*) and to those who hold their view, who say that *musaqah* (the contract of irrigating and tending palm trees for a share of the produce) is permitted for an unknown term, for uncertain years. They argue that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) dealt with the Jews over half of the crops and the palm trees for as long as it pleased the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), without a fixed term. This argument has no evidence in it, because he (peace be upon him) said to the Jews: "We will let you remain [in it] [[The addition from al-Muwatta'.]] for as long as Allah lets you remain." This is the clearest proof and the plainest indication that this was specific to him. He would wait for the decision of his Lord in such matters, which is not the case for anyone else. The Shari'ah has perfected the rules of hiring and of all other transactions, so nothing of them is permitted except in accordance with what the Book and the Sunnah have established, and what the scholars of the Ummah have affirmed.

**Fifth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿*mawaqit*﴾ (times marked out). *Mawaqit* is the plural of *miqat*, which means *waqt* (time). It is also said that *miqat* is the limit of a time. *Mawaqit* is not declined (it is diptote, not taking tanwin), because it is a plural with no singular counterpart, so it is a plural of a plural, as though the plural form were repeated within it. *Qawarir* in His saying: ﴿*qawarira*﴾ [al-Insan 76:16] is given tanwin because it occurs at the end of a verse, so it is given tanwin as rhyming words are, and this is not the tanwin of declension (*tanwin al-sarf*) which indicates the full nominal status of the noun.

**Sixth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿*wal-hajji*﴾ (and the Hajj). With fatha on the *ha'* is the reading of the majority. Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with kasra throughout the Qur'an, and in His saying: ﴿*hijju al-bayti*﴾ (the pilgrimage to the House) [Al 'Imran 3:97] in Al 'Imran [[See vol. 4, p. 142.]]. Sibawayh said: *al-hajj* is like *al-radd* and *al-shadd*, and *al-hijj* is like *al-dhikr*, so both are verbal nouns with the same meaning. It is also said: the fatha form is the verbal noun (*masdar*), and the kasra form is the name (*ism*).

**Seventh issue:** Allah, glorified is He, singled out the Hajj for mention because it requires knowledge of its time, and because it is not permissible to postpone it from its proper time. This is unlike what the Arabs used to do: they would perform the Hajj according to a count and interchange the months. Allah nullified their saying and their action. Its explanation will come, God willing, in *Bara'ah* [[See vol. 8, p. 136.]].

**Eighth issue:** Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, Abu Hanifa and their companions used this verse as evidence that entering the state of *ihram* for Hajj is valid outside the months of Hajj, because Allah, exalted is He, made all the new moons a time frame for it, so it is valid to enter into *ihram* for Hajj in all of them. Al-Shafi'i disagreed on this, citing His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:197], as will come. And the meaning of this verse, they said, is that some of them are times for people, and some of them are times for the Hajj. This is like saying: "The slave-girl belongs to Zayd and 'Amr," which requires that some of her belongs to Zayd and some belongs to 'Amr, and it is not permissible to say that the whole of her belongs to Zayd and the whole of her belongs to 'Amr. The answer is that the apparent meaning of His saying, "They are times marked out for people and for the Hajj," requires that all of them are times for people and all of them are times for the Hajj. Had He intended partition, He would have said: "Some of them are times for people and some of them are times for the Hajj." This is like saying: "The month of Ramadan is a fixed time for the fasting of Zayd and 'Amr." There is no disagreement that what is meant is that the whole of it is a fixed time for the fasting of each of them. As for what they cited about the slave-girl, it is correct, because for her to belong wholly to Zayd while also belonging wholly to 'Amr is impossible. This is not the case in our issue, since time can be a fixed time for Zayd and also a fixed time for 'Amr. Thus their argument is refuted.

**Ninth issue:** There is no disagreement among the scholars that whoever sells a known commodity for a known price up to a known term of the months of the Arabs, or up to days of known number, the sale is permissible. They said the same about *salam* (advance sale) up to a known term. They differed about one who sells up to the harvest, or up to threshing, or up to the stipend, and similar things. Malik said: that is permissible, because it is known. Abu Thawr agreed. Ahmad said: "I hope there is no harm in it." The same applies to the return of the raiders (*ghuzat*). It is reported from Ibn Umar that he used to buy up to the stipend. But another group said: that is not permissible, because Allah, exalted is He, set the appointed times and made them markers for their terms in their dealings and their interests. This is what Ibn Abbas said, and al-Shafi'i and al-Nu'man (Abu Hanifa) also held it. Ibn al-Mundhir said: "The saying of Ibn Abbas is sound."

**Tenth issue:** If the crescent is seen large, our scholars said: one does not rely on its largeness or its smallness; it is only the crescent of its night. Muslim narrated from Abu al-Bakhtari, who said: "We set out for the 'umrah, and when we descended at Batn Nakhlah, he (the narrator) said: 'We sighted the crescent.' Some of the people said: 'It is the crescent of three nights.' Others said: 'It is the crescent of two nights.' Then we met Ibn Abbas and said: 'We sighted the crescent.' Some of the people said: 'It is the crescent of three nights,' and others said: 'It is the crescent of two nights.' He said: 'On which night did you see it?' We said: 'On such-and-such a night.' He said: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah has extended it for sighting (*inna Allaha maddahu lil-ru'yah*), so it belongs to the night in which you saw it."'"

**Eleventh issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is not righteousness that you enter the houses from their backs﴾. This is connected to the mention of the times of the Hajj, because both matters occurred at the same time of the question about the new moons and about entering the houses from their backs, so the verse was revealed concerning both together. The Ansar, when they performed Hajj or 'umrah and returned, would not enter by the doors of their houses. When they had pronounced the *talbiyah* for Hajj or 'umrah, they bound themselves by a vow that nothing should stand between them and the sky. So if a man among them went out after his *ihram* from his house and returned for some need, he would not enter through the door of the chamber, because of the roof of the house standing between him and the sky. Instead he would climb onto the roof of his house over the walls, then stand in his chamber and give his command, and what he needed would be brought out to him from his house. They regarded this as a form of worship and righteousness, just as they held other things to be acts of worship, so He answered them concerning these, and the Lord, exalted is He, made clear that righteousness lies in obeying His command.

Ibn Abbas, in the narration of Abu Salih, said: "In the Jahiliyyah and in the early days of Islam, when a man among them entered *ihram* for Hajj, if he was one of the *ahl al-madar* (settled people, i.e. those who live in houses), he would breach the back of his house and enter and exit from it, or he would place a ladder and climb up by it and come down by it. If he was one of the *ahl al-wabar* (people of the tents, i.e. those who live in tents), he would enter the tent from behind it, except for those of the *Hums*." Al-Zuhri narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) entered *ihram* for 'umrah during the time of al-Hudaybiyah and entered his chamber, and a man from the Ansar of Banu Salamah entered behind him. He entered through the back, breaking the custom of his people. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Why did you enter while you are in *ihram*?" He said: "You entered, so I entered following your entry." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "I am *Ahmas*," meaning: from a people who do not follow this practice. The man said: "My religion is your religion," and then the verse was revealed. This was also said by Ibn Abbas, Ata' and Qatadah. It is also said that this man was Qutbah ibn Amir al-Ansari.

The *Hums* are: Quraysh, Kinanah, Khuza'ah, Thaqif, Jusham [[So in (j). In the rest of the manuscripts and in al-Razi's tafsir: "Khaythum". In Ibn Hayyan's al-Bahr: "Khath'am".]], Banu 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah, and Banu Nasr ibn Mu'awiyah. They were called *Hums* because of their strictness in their religion. *Al-hamasah* means severity. Al-Ajjaj said:

*And how many rugged, hard tracts (*qifaf*) of severity we have crossed.*

That is, severe ones. Then they differed about its interpretation. It is said that it is what we have mentioned, and this is the sound view. It is also said that it refers to *al-nasi'* (intercalation) and the postponement of the Hajj through it, so that they would make a permitted month forbidden by delaying the Hajj into it, and a forbidden month permitted by delaying the Hajj away from it. On this view, the mention of "houses" is an example of opposing what is obligatory in the Hajj and its months.

Its explanation will come in Surah Bara'ah (see vol. 8, p. 136), God willing.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: The verse is a parable (ḍarb mathal). The meaning is: "It is not righteousness that you ask the ignorant, but fear God and ask the scholars." This is like when you say: "I came to this matter from its door."

Al-Mahdawi and Makki related from Ibn al-Anbari, and al-Mawardi related from Ibn Zayd, that the verse is a parable concerning sexual intercourse with women, a command to approach them through the front (al-qubul) and not from the rear (al-dubur). Women are called "houses" (buyut) because one takes shelter with them, as one takes shelter in houses.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is far-fetched and it changes the style of the speech.

Al-Hasan said: They used to practice tiyarah (taking omens). Whoever travelled and did not achieve his need would come to his house from behind his back, out of pessimism about failure. So it was said to them: "There is no righteousness in taking omens; rather, righteousness is that you fear God and put your trust in Him."

I say: The first opinion is the most sound of these opinions, because of what al-Bara' narrated: He said: "The Ansar, when they performed Hajj and then returned, would not enter the houses through their doors. A man from the Ansar came and entered through his door, and he was reproached for this. Then this verse was revealed: ﴿And it is not righteousness that you enter houses from their backs﴾." This is explicit about actual houses. Al-Bukhari and Muslim recorded it.

As for those other opinions, they are taken from a different place, not from the verse, so consider it carefully.

It has also been said: The verse came as an admonition from God that people should approach righteousness from its proper direction, which is the direction God commanded. So He mentioned entering houses through their doors as an example, to indicate that we should approach matters from their proper source, which God has directed us to. I say: According to this, the opinions mentioned can all be valid.

Al-Buyut is the plural of bayt, and it is read qurā (with a ḍammah and a kasrah on the bā'). The meaning of taqwa (God-consciousness) and falah (success) and la'alla (perhaps) has already been discussed, so there is no point in repeating it.

Twelfth issue: This verse makes clear that what God has not prescribed as an act of worship or recommended does not become an act of worship merely because someone draws near to God through it.

Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: When it becomes unclear which act is righteousness and worship and which is not, one should examine that act. If it has a counterpart among the obligatory acts and the sunnah, it may be permissible; if it has none, then it is neither righteousness nor worship. He said: The reports from the Prophet ﷺ confirm this.

He mentioned the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "While the Messenger of God ﷺ was delivering a sermon, he saw a man standing in the sun. He asked about him, and they said: 'He is Abu Isra'il [Abu Isra'il: a man from the Ansar among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, whose name is disputed. See al-Isti'ab, al-Isabah and Usd al-Ghabah under 'the kunya chapter'], he vowed to stand and not sit, not seek shade, not speak, and to fast.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Tell him to speak, to seek shade, to sit, and to complete his fast.'" Thus the Prophet ﷺ nullified what was not an act of worship and had no basis in his Law, and affirmed what was an act of worship and had a counterpart among the obligatory acts and the sunnah.

There are three issues in it.

The first concerns His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fight﴾. This verse is the first verse revealed about the command to fight. There is no disagreement that fighting was forbidden before the Hijrah, based on His saying: ﴿Repel [evil] with that which is better﴾ [Fussilat: 34]; His saying: ﴿So pardon them and overlook﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 13]; His saying: ﴿And forsake them with graceful forsaking﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 10]; His saying: ﴿You are not over them a controller﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 22]; and what was similar to these of what was revealed in Makkah. When he migrated to Madinah, he was commanded to fight, and there was revealed: "And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you." This was said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas and others.

It is narrated from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq that the first verse revealed about fighting was: ﴿Permission is given to those who are being fought, because they were wronged﴾ [al-Hajj: 39]. The first view is more widely held. The verse of permission was revealed about fighting in general, for those who fight and for those among the polytheists who do not fight. That is because the Prophet ﷺ went out with his companions toward Makkah for the 'umrah. When he alighted at al-Hudaybiyah near Makkah (al-Hudaybiyah is the name of a well, and that place was named after that well), the polytheists prevented him from the House. He remained at al-Hudaybiyah for a month. They made a treaty with him that he would return that year as he had come, on the condition that Makkah be vacated for him in the coming year for three days. They also agreed with him that there would be no fighting between them for ten years, and he returned to Madinah.

When the following year came, he prepared for 'Umrat al-Qada'. The Muslims feared the treachery of the disbelievers and disliked fighting in the Sacred Precinct and in the sacred month. So this verse was revealed, meaning: fighting is permitted for you if the disbelievers fight you. Thus the verse is connected to what preceded it of the mention of the Hajj and of entering houses from their backs. He, peace be upon him, used to fight whoever fought him and refrain from whoever refrained from him, until ﴿Then kill the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5] was revealed, and this verse was abrogated (mansukhah). This was said by a group of scholars.

Ibn Zayd and al-Rabi' said that it was abrogated by ﴿And fight the polytheists all together﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36], so he was commanded to fight all the disbelievers.

Ibn 'Abbas, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz and Mujahid said that it is muhkamah (decisive, not abrogated). Its meaning is: fight those who are in the condition of those who fight you, and do not transgress in killing women, children, monks and the like, as will be explained.

Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: this is the more correct of the two views according to the Sunnah and sound reasoning. As for the Sunnah, it is the hadith of Ibn 'Umar that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw in one of his campaigns a woman who had been killed, and he disliked that, and forbade the killing of women and children. The imams narrated it. As for reasoning, "faʻala" (the form of mutual action) in general applies only between two parties, as in muqatalah (fighting each other), mushatamah (mutual cursing) and mukhasamah (mutual disputing). Fighting does not occur with women, children, or those resembling them, such as monks, the chronically disabled, the elderly and hired labourers, so they are not killed.

On this, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, enjoined Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan when he sent him to al-Sham, "except if these people have some hostility (adhah)." This was related by Malik and others.

The scholars have six cases concerning these groups.

The first: women. If they fight, they are killed. Sahnun said: this applies during the fighting and after it, based on the generality of His saying: "And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you," and ﴿And kill them wherever you overtake them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191]. Women have great effects in fighting. Among them is supplying money, and among them is urging on the fight. They may go out with their hair uncovered, wailing, stirring up [the men], reproaching them for fleeing, and this makes their killing permissible. However, if they fall into captivity, enslavement is more beneficial, because they quickly accept Islam and return from their religions, and their flight to their homelands becomes difficult, unlike men.

The second: children. They are not killed, because of the established prohibition against killing the offspring (dhurriyyah), and because they are not under obligation. If a child fights, however, he is killed.

The third: monks. They are not killed nor enslaved, but what they live on of their property is left to them. This applies when they are separate from the people of disbelief. This is based on Abu Bakr's words to Yazid: "You will find people who claim that they have confined themselves to Allah, so leave them and what they claim, that they have confined themselves to Him." If they are with the disbelievers in the churches, they are killed. If a woman takes up the monastic life, Ashhab related that she is not to be disturbed (la tuhaj),* while Sahnun said: monastic life does not change her ruling.

Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: "The sound view according to me is the narration of Ashhab, because she is included under His saying: 'leave them and what they have confined themselves to.'"

The fourth: the chronically disabled. Sahnun said they are killed. Ibn Habib said they are not killed. The sound view is that their conditions are taken into account: if they have hostility in them, they are killed; otherwise they are left alone with their state of disability, and they become a burden (mal) in their condition, and a surplus (hashwah).

The fifth: the elderly. Malik said in the Kitab Muhammad that they are not killed. What the majority of jurists hold is that if he is a very old man, decrepit, who cannot bear fighting and whose opinion or resistance is of no use, he is not killed. This was said by Malik and Abu Hanifah. Al-Shafi'i has two views: one of them is like the view of the majority, and the second is that he is killed, along with the monk. The sound one is the first, based on Abu Bakr's words to Yazid, and no one opposes it, so it is established as a consensus (ijma'). Also, he is one who does not fight and does not aid the enemy, so it is not permissible to kill him, like a woman. If, however, he is one whose harm is feared in war, in opinion, or in wealth, then if he is taken captive, the Imam has the choice among five things: killing, releasing without ransom, ransoming, enslavement, or a dhimmah contract on payment of the jizyah.

The sixth: the 'usafa', who are hired labourers and farmers. Malik said in the Kitab Muhammad that they are not killed. Al-Shafi'i said: farmers, hired labourers and the old men are killed unless they embrace Islam or pay the jizyah. The first view is more correct, based on his peace be upon him saying in the hadith of Rabah* ibn al-Rabi' (Go to Khalid ibn al-Walid, and do not kill any offspring or any hired labourer). 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "Fear Allah concerning the offspring and the farmers who do not raise war against you." 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz did not kill farmers; Ibn al-Mundhir mentioned this.

The second issue: Ashhab narrated from Malik that what is meant by His saying: "And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you" is the people of al-Hudaybiyah, who were commanded to fight those who fought them. The sound view is that it is an address to all Muslims: each one is commanded to fight whoever fights him, since nothing else is possible. Do you not see how He explained it in Surah al-Bara'ah with His saying: ﴿Fight those of the disbelievers who are near to you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 123]? That is because the first aim was the people of Makkah, so beginning with them was necessary. When Allah granted the conquest of Makkah, fighting became for those nearest to those who used to harm. This continues until the call spreads, the word reaches all the horizons, and no disbeliever remains. This continues and extends until the Day of Resurrection, to an end which is his peace be upon him saying: "Good is tied to the foreheads of horses until the Day of Resurrection: reward and spoils." It was also said that its end is the descent of 'Isa ibn Maryam, peace be upon him, and this agrees with the hadith before it, because his descent is one of the signs of the Hour.

The third issue concerns His saying, "And do not transgress." It was said about its interpretation what we have already mentioned, and so it is muhkamah. As for apostates, there is nothing but killing or repentance. Likewise the people of deviation and error: there is nothing but the sword or repentance. Whoever conceals belief in falsehood and then it becomes evident about him, he is like the zindiq (heretic who conceals disbelief): he is killed and is not asked to repent. As for the Kharijites against the just imams, it is obligatory to fight them until they return to the truth.

Others said: the meaning is "do not transgress in fighting for other than the sake of Allah," such as zeal and seeking reputation. Rather, fight in the way of Allah those who fight you, meaning for the religion and the elevation of the word. It was also said: "do not transgress" means do not fight those who do not fight. According to this, the verse is abrogated by the command to fight all the disbelievers. And Allah knows best.

There are five issues in this passage.

**The first issue** concerns God's words, ﴿thaqiftumuhum﴾ ("you overtake them" / "you come upon them"). It is said: *thaqifa yathqafu thaqfan wa thaqafan*. A man is called *thaqf laqf* when he is skilful and quick to grasp whatever matters come to him. This verse is evidence for killing a captive, and its explanation will come in *al-Anfal* (see vol. 8, p. 30), God willing. And ﴿wa-akhrijuhum min haythu akhrajukum﴾ ("and expel them from where they expelled you") refers to Makkah. Al-Tabari said: the address is to the Emigrants (*muhajirun*), and the pronoun refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh.

**The second issue** concerns God's words, ﴿wal-fitnatu ashaddu min al-qatl﴾ ("and persecution is worse than killing"). That means: the persecution by which they pressed you and sought to return you to disbelief is worse than killing. Mujahid said: that is, for a believer to be killed is lighter for him than the persecution. Others said: that is, their associating partners with God and their disbelief in Him is a greater crime and worse than the killing with which they reproached you. This is evidence that the verse was revealed concerning 'Amr ibn al-Hadrami, when Waqid ibn 'Abd Allah al-Tamimi killed him on the last day of Rajab, the sacred month, as is mentioned in the expedition of 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh, as will be explained (see vol. 3, p. 49). This was said by al-Tabari and others.

**The third issue** concerns God's words, ﴿wa-la tuqatilu-hum 'inda al-Masjid al-Haram hatta yuqatilukum fihi﴾ ("and do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque until they fight you there"), to the end of the verse. The scholars have two opinions on this verse: one, that it is abrogated (*mansukhah*); the other, that it is firm (*muhkamah*, not abrogated). Mujahid said: the verse is *muhkam*, and it is not permitted to fight anyone in the Sacred Mosque unless he has first fought. Tawus also said this, and it is what the wording of the verse requires. It is the sound of the two opinions, and Abu Hanifa and his companions adopted it. In the authentic reports from Ibn 'Abbas, he said: the Messenger of God ﷺ said on the day of the Conquest of Makkah: "Indeed this city, God made it sacred on the day He created the heavens and the earth, so it is sacred by the sanctity of God until the Day of Resurrection. Fighting in it was not permitted for anyone before me, and it was not permitted for me except for an hour of a day. So it is sacred by the sanctity of God until the Day of Resurrection." Qatadah said: the verse is abrogated by God's words, ﴿fa-idha insalakha al-ash-hur al-hurum faqtulu al-mushrikina haythu wajadtumuhum﴾ ("When the sacred months have passed, then kill the polytheists wherever you find them") [al-Tawbah: 5] (see vol. 8, p. 72). Muqatil said: God's words, ﴿waqtulu-hum haythu thaqiftumuhum﴾ ("and kill them wherever you overtake them") abrogated it, and then His words, "Kill the polytheists wherever you find them," abrogated that. So it is permissible to begin fighting within the sanctuary (*haram*).

Among the arguments they cited: *Bara'ah* (al-Tawbah) was revealed two years after *al-Baqarah*, and the Prophet ﷺ entered Makkah wearing a helmet (*mighfar*). The *mighfar*, like the *mighfarah* and *ghifarah* (all with a kasra), is a mail-like piece that is cut from armour to fit the head and is worn under a cap. It was said that Ibn Khatal was clinging to the curtains of the Ka'bah, and he said: "Kill him." Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: "And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque" is abrogated, because consensus was established that if someone seized Makkah and said, "I will fight you and prevent you from the Hajj, and I will not leave Makkah," it would be obligatory to fight him even if he did not begin the fighting. Makkah and other lands are equal. It was said of Makkah that it is sacred only to honour it. Do you not see that the Messenger of God ﷺ sent Khalid ibn al-Walid on the day of the Conquest and said: "Mow them down with the sword until you meet me at al-Safa"? Then al-Abbas came and said: "O Messenger of God, Quraysh is gone; there is no Quraysh after today." Do you not see that he said, in honouring it: "Its lost property may not be picked up except by one who announces it," and the picking up of lost property is the same there and elsewhere? It is possible that it is abrogated by His words, ﴿waqatilu-hum hatta la takuna fitnah﴾ ("and fight them until there is no persecution") [al-Baqarah: 193].

Ibn al-'Arabi said: "I was present in Bayt al-Maqdis, may God purify it, at the madrasa of Abu 'Uqbah al-Hanafi, and the judge al-Zinjani was giving us the lesson on a Friday. While we were like that, a handsome-looking man entered upon us, wearing rags, and he gave the greeting of the scholars and took the head of the assembly, wearing the garment of shepherds. The judge al-Zinjani said: 'Who is the master?' He said: 'A man whom the rogues (*shuttar*) plundered yesterday. My purpose was this sacred sanctuary, and I am a man from the people of Saghan, one of the students of knowledge.' The judge quickly said, as is the custom in honouring scholars, by hastening to ask them: 'Ask him.' The lot fell on the question of the disbeliever who takes refuge in the sanctuary: will he be killed or not? He ruled that he will not be killed. He was asked about the evidence, and he said God's words, ﴿wa-la tuqatilu-hum 'inda al-Masjid al-Haram hatta yuqatilukum fihi﴾, which were read as ﴿wa-la taqtulu-hum﴾ ("and do not kill them") and ﴿wa-la tuqatilu-hum﴾. If it is read as "and do not kill them," the matter is explicit; if it is read as "and do not fight them," it is an indication, because when He forbids fighting, which is the cause of killing, that is clear evidence for forbidding killing." The judge objected to him, defending al-Shafi'i and Malik, though he did not hold their school, as is customary: "This verse is abrogated by God's words, ﴿fa-uqtulu al-mushrikina haythu wajadtumuhum﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5]." Al-Saghani said to him: "This is not fitting for the rank of a judge and his knowledge. The verse you objected with is general in places, and the one I argued with is specific, and it is not permitted for anyone to say that the general abrogates the specific." Judge al-Zinjani was bewildered, and this is one of the remarkable statements.

Ibn al-'Arabi [the wording of his book differs somewhat from the originals] said: "If a disbeliever takes refuge in it, there is no way to him, by the text of the verse and the established Sunnah forbidding fighting in it. As for the adulterer and the murderer, the legal punishment (*hadd*) must be carried out on him, except that if the disbeliever begins the fighting, he is killed by the text of the Qur'an."

I say: As for what they cited concerning the killing of Ibn Khatal and his companions, there is no proof in it, for that was at the time when Makkah was made lawful to him, while it was a land of war and disbelief, and he had the right to shed the blood of whomever he wished of its people in the hour in which fighting was made lawful. So it is established and confirmed that the first opinion is more sound, and God knows best.

The disbeliever is killed if he fights in any case, whereas the rebel, if he fights, is fought with the intention of repelling him. A fleeing man is not pursued, and a wounded man is not finished off. This is as will be explained of the rules concerning rebels in *al-Hujurat* (see vol. 16, p. 315 and following), God willing.

Its parallel is His words, ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they cease, they will be forgiven what has already passed﴾ [al-Anfal: 38]. And it will come (see vol. 7, p. 401).

**Tenth Chapter:** Commentary on surah 2, verse 194 (part 1 of 2)

There are ten issues in this verse.

**The First Issue:** God's words, ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month﴾. The derivation of *al-shahr* (month) has already been discussed.[[See p. 290 of this volume.]] The occasion of revelation, as reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah, Mujahid, Miqsam, al-Suddi, al-Rabiʿ, al-Dahhak and others, is that they said: it was revealed concerning the ʿUmrat al-Qadiyyah (the making-up ʿUmrah) and the year of al-Hudaybiyyah. [That is because] the Messenger of God ﷺ set out as a pilgrim for ʿUmrah until he reached al-Hudaybiyyah [in Dhu al-Qaʿdah of the sixth year AH]. The disbelieving Quraysh polytheists barred him from the House, so he turned back. God, glory be to Him, promised him that he would enter it, and he entered it in the seventh year and performed his rites. Then this verse was revealed.[[The words between the square brackets are missing from manuscript B.]] It is also reported from al-Hasan that the polytheists said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Were you forbidden, O Muhammad, from fighting in the sacred month?" He said: "Yes." So they intended to fight him, and this verse was revealed. The meaning is: if they permit that in it, then fight them. Thus God, by this verse, permitted their repulsion. The first view is more well-known and is the view of most scholars.

**The Second Issue:** God's words, ﴿And the sacred prohibitions are subject to retribution﴾. *Al-ḥurumāt* is the plural of *ḥurmah* (sanctity), like *al-ẓulumāt* is the plural of *ẓulmah* (darkness), and *al-ḥujurāt* is the plural of *ḥujrah* (chamber). The plural *al-ḥurumāt* is used because He meant the sanctity of the sacred month, the sanctity of the sacred territory, and the sanctity of the state of ihram. The *ḥurmah* is that which is forbidden to be violated. *Al-qiṣāṣ* means equivalence, i.e., "I exacted retribution from them for you when they barred you in the sixth year, and you performed the ʿUmrah in the seventh year." On this view, "the sacred prohibitions are subject to retribution" is connected to what precedes it and linked to it. It was also said that it is separate from it, and that it is a ruling that existed at the beginning of Islam: whoever violates your sanctity, you may take from him the same as he transgressed against you; then this was abrogated (*nusikha*, i.e., naskh) by fighting. Another group said: what this verse covers of transgression among the community of Muhammad ﷺ, and of offences and the like, has not been abrogated. And it is permitted for one who has been wronged regarding property or a wound to transgress in the same manner in which he was wronged, if it has become apparent to him (*idhā khafiya*, the word is one of the words with opposite meanings; it is said *khafiya al-shay'* meaning he concealed it, and *akhfaytuhu* meaning I made it manifest; see vol. 11, p. 182).[[His words "idh khafiya" mean "when it became apparent." This term is one of the words with opposite meanings: it is said *khafiya al-shay'*, meaning he concealed it, and *akhfaytuhu*, meaning I made it manifest. See vol. 11, p. 182.]] There is no blame on him before God in that. This is the view of al-Shafiʿi and others, and it is a transmitted opinion in the school of Malik. A group among the companions of Malik said: that is not permitted for him, and matters of retribution are reserved for the judges. As for property, the saying of the Prophet ﷺ covers it: "Return the trust to the one who entrusted you, and do not betray the one who betrayed you." It was recorded by al-Daraqutni and others. So whoever has been betrayed by someone who was entrusted to him may not betray him and take his right from what he was entrusted with. This is the well-known position of the school, and Abu Hanifah said so, holding to this hadith, and also to God's words: ﴿Indeed, God commands you to render trusts to their owners﴾ [al-Nisa': 58]. This is also the view of ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurasani. Qudamah ibn al-Haytham said: I asked ʿAṭāʾ ibn Maysarah al-Khurasani, and I said to him: "I have a right against a man, and he has denied it to me, and I have failed to produce evidence. May I take retribution from his property?" He said: "Tell me, if he had done that with your slave-girl, what would you have done?" I say: The correct view is the permissibility of that, however one reaches the taking of one's right, so long as one does not become a thief. This is the position of al-Shafiʿi; al-Dawudi reported it from Malik; Ibn al-Mundhir also held it; and Ibn al-ʿArabi preferred it. That is not betrayal; it is only reaching a right. The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Help your brother, whether he is an oppressor or oppressed." Taking the right from the oppressor is helping him. He also said to Hind bint ʿUtbah, the wife of Abu Sufyan, when she said to him: "Abu Sufyan is a stingy man who does not give me enough maintenance to suffice me and my children, except what I take from his property without his knowledge. Is there any blame on me?" The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Take what suffices you and your child, in a reasonable manner." So he permitted her to take, but not to take more than what is due to her. All of this is established in the Sahih. And God's words: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾ are decisive in the place of disagreement.

**The Third Issue:** Scholars differed when one obtains property of a kind other than his own property. It was said: he may not take except by the ruling of a judge. Al-Shafiʿi has two opinions, the more sound of which is that he may take, by analogy with the case where he obtains property of the same kind as his own. The second opinion is that he may not take, because it is of a different kind. Some said: he should estimate the value of what he is owed and take an amount equal to that. This is the sound view, for the reason we have explained, and God knows best.

**The Fourth Issue:** If we accept the taking, is what the debtor owes to others (debts and so on) to be taken into account? Al-Shafiʿi said: No; rather he takes his due from him. Malik said: what he obtains is taken into account together with the creditors in the case of insolvency (*falas*), and this is the analogical view, and God knows best.

**The Fifth Issue:** God's words, ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾, are a general ruling agreed upon, whether by direct action if possible, or through the judges. People differed over whether requital is called transgression or not. Whoever said: there is no metaphor (*majāz*) in the Qur'an, said: requital is transgression, and it is a permissible transgression, just as metaphor in the speech of the Arabs is a permissible falsehood. Because the saying of the poet:

*"Then the two eyes said to him: 'Hearing and obedience.'"*

And likewise:

*"The basin filled and said: 'Enough for me!'"*

And likewise:

*"My camel complained to me of the length of the journey."*

It is known that these things do not speak. The definition of falsehood is: reporting about a thing contrary to what it is. Whoever said that there is metaphor in the Qur'an called this transgression by way of metaphor and as the matching of speech with its like, as ʿAmr ibn Kulthum said:

*"Let no one act ignorantly toward us, lest we outdo the ignorance of the ignorant."*

And another said:

*"For me is a horse for forbearance, bridled with forbearance; and for me is a horse for ignorance, saddled for ignorance."*

*"And whoever seeks to straighten me, I am straight; and whoever seeks to bend me, I am bent."*

He means: I repay the ignorant and the crooked, not that he praised himself with ignorance or crookedness.

**The Sixth Issue:** Scholars differed concerning one who destroys or damages some animal or some goods that are not measured by volume or weight. Al-Shafiʿi, Abu Hanifah and their followers, and a group of scholars said: he must pay its like, and one turns to its value only when there is no like, based on God's words: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾, and God's words: ﴿And if you retaliate, retaliate with the same as you were made to suffer﴾ [al-Nahl: 126]. They said: this is a general ruling covering all things. They supported this by the fact that the Prophet ﷺ detained the broken bowl in the house of the woman who broke it, and returned the intact one, saying: "A vessel for a vessel, and food for food." It was recorded by Abu Dawud, who said: Musaddad related to us, Yahya related to us (*ḥ*), and Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna related to us, Khalid related to us, from Humayd, from Anas: that the Messenger of God ﷺ was with one of his wives, and one of the Mothers of the Believers sent a servant with a bowl containing food. He said: she struck with her hand and broke the bowl. Ibn al-Muthanna said: the Prophet ﷺ took the two pieces and joined one to the other, and began gathering the food into them, saying: "Your mother has been jealous." Ibn al-Muthanna added: "Eat." So they ate until her bowl that was in her house came. Then we returned to the wording of the hadith of Musaddad, and he said: "Eat." The Messenger and the bowl were held until they finished, and he gave the intact bowl to the messenger and kept the broken one in his house. Abu Dawud related to us, saying: Musaddad related to us, Yahya related to us from Sufyan, who said: and Fulayt al-ʿAmiri related to us (Abu Dawud said: he is Aflat ibn Khalifah), from Jasrah bint Dajajah, who said: ʿAʾishah, may God be pleased with her, said: "I have not seen anyone prepare food like Safiyyah. She prepared food for the Messenger of God ﷺ and sent it to him, and jealousy seized me and I broke the vessel. I said: 'O Messenger of God, what is the expiation for what I did?' He said: 'A vessel like a vessel, and food like food.'"[[Al-afkal (on the pattern af'al): trembling. That is, I trembled from intense jealousy.]] Malik and his companions said: for animals and goods that are not measured or weighed, the obligation is the value, not the like, based on the fact that the Prophet ﷺ made the one who freed half of his slave compensate his partner with the value of the other half of the slave, and did not require him to pay the like of half of his slave. There is no disagreement among scholars that the like is required for foodstuffs, drinks and measured goods, based on his saying, peace be upon him: "Food for food."

**The Seventh Issue:** There is no disagreement among scholars that this verse is the basis for equivalence in retaliation (*qiṣāṣ*). Whoever kills with something is killed with the same thing he killed with. This is the view of the majority, unless he killed by an immoral means, such as sodomy or giving wine to drink, in which case he is killed by the sword. The Shafiʿis have an opinion that he is killed by that same means: a stick of that same kind is prepared and inserted into his anus until he dies, and water is poured down his throat in place of wine until he dies. Ibn al-Majishun said: one who kills by fire or by poison is not killed by the same means, because of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "None punishes with fire except God." And poison is an inward fire. The majority held that he is killed by the same means, based on the generality of the verse.

**The Eighth Issue:** As for retaliation by a stick, Malik said in one of two narrations: if killing with a stick involves prolonged torture, he is killed by the sword. Ibn Wahb transmitted this from him, and Ibn al-Qasim said it. In the other narration: he is killed by it even if it involves that. This is the view of al-Shafiʿi. Ashhab and Ibn Nafiʿ reported from Malik concerning the stone and the stick that he is killed by them if the blow is fatal; but if he strikes repeated blows, then no. Accordingly, one is not shot with arrows or stones, because that is torture. ʿAbd al-Malik said so. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: "The correct view among our scholars is that equivalence is obligatory, except when it enters the realm of torture, in which case it is abandoned in favour of the sword." Our scholars agreed that if he cut off his hands and feet and gouged out his eyes with the intent of torture, then the same is done to him, as the Prophet ﷺ did to the killers of the herdsmen.[[They were people from ʿUrayna who came to the Messenger of God ﷺ, embraced Islam, found Medina unhealthy, their bodies became weak, their complexions yellowed, and their bellies swelled. The Messenger of God ﷺ sent them to the camels of the charity and ordered them to drink from their milk and urine until they recovered. Then they killed the herdsmen and drove off the camels. The Prophet of God sent people to pursue them, and they were brought to him. He cut off their hands and feet and branded their eyes with hot iron. See the books of Sunnah for this hadith.]] If it was in a struggle or a fight, he is killed by the sword. A group held the opposite of all this, saying: there is no retaliation except by the sword. This is the position of Abu Hanifah, al-Tha'labi and al-Nakhaʿi.

The Jurists (al-Jumhur) and the Dispute over Equal Retribution

They based this on what is reported from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "There is no retaliation (qawad) except with an iron implement," and on the prohibition of mutilation (muthla), and on his saying: "None punishes with fire except the Lord of the Fire." The correct view is that of the majority (al-Jumhur), based on what the imams narrated from Anas ibn Malik: a slave girl was found with her head crushed between two stones. They asked her, "Who did this to you? Was it so-and-so, or so-and-so?" until they mentioned a Jew, and she nodded with her head. The Jew was arrested and confessed, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered that his head be crushed with stones. In another narration: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ killed him between two stones." This is an explicit, authentic text, and it is the implication of the words of the Exalted: ﴿And if you retaliate, then retaliate with the like of that with which you were afflicted﴾ [al-Nahl: 126], and of His words: "So retaliate against him with the like of what he did to you."

As for what they cited from the hadith of Jabir, it is a weak hadith according to the scholars of hadith, not transmitted by any sound chain. Even if it were sound, we would act upon its implication: that if one kills with an iron implement, he is killed with it. The hadith of Anas indicates this: a Jew crushed the head of a girl between two stones, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ crushed his head between two stones.

As for the prohibition of mutilation, we also act upon its implication when the killer did not mutilate; but if he mutilated, we mutilate him. This is indicated by the hadith of the people of 'Uraynah, which is authentic and was recorded by the imams. His saying, "None punishes with fire except the Lord of the Fire," is sound when one does not burn; but if he burns, he is burned, as indicated by the general meaning of the Qur'an.

Al-Shafi'i said: if he deliberately throws him into the fire, he is thrown into the fire until he dies. Al-Waqqar [[al-Waqqar (with a kasra): the epithet of Zakariyya ibn Yahya ibn Ibrahim, the Egyptian jurist, who studied with Ibn al-Qasim and Ibn Wahb.]] mentioned it in his Mukhtasar from Malik, and it is the view of Muhammad ibn Abd al-Hakam.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: the view of many scholars regarding a man who strangles another man is that retaliation (qawad) is due against him. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan disagreed, saying: if he strangled him until he died, or threw him into a well so that he died, or hurled him from a mountain or a roof so that he died, there is no retaliation against him, and the blood money (diyah) is due from his paternal kin ('aqilah). But if he was known for this, having strangled more than one person, then he is to be killed. Ibn al-Mundhir said: when the Prophet ﷺ imposed retaliation on the Jew who crushed the girl's head with a stone, this case is of the same meaning, so there is no sense in his statement.

I say: another scholar also related this view from Abu Hanifa, saying: Abu Hanifa stood alone regarding one who kills by strangling, by poison, by throwing from a mountain or into a well, or by a piece of wood. He said that such a killer is not killed nor is retaliation taken from him, except when he kills with a sharpened iron, a stone, or wood, or if he was known for strangling and throwing people down, and then the diyah is due from his paternal kin. This is a rejection of the Book and the Sunnah, and an innovation in matters the community of the Muslims did not follow, and a means to abolishing the retaliation (qisas) that Allah prescribed for the preservation of lives, so there is no escape from it.

The Ninth Issue: The scholars differed concerning one who detains a man and another kills him. Ata' said: the killer is killed, and the one who detained him is imprisoned until he dies. Malik said: if he detained him believing that the other intends to kill him, then both are killed. According to the view of al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr and al-Nu'man, the detainer is punished. Ibn al-Mundhir chose this view.

I say: the view of Ata' is sound, and it is the implication of the revelation. Al-Daraqutni related from Ibn Umar, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "If a man holds a man and the other kills him, the killer is killed and the one who held him is imprisoned." It was transmitted by Sufyan al-Thawri from Isma'il ibn Umayyah from Nafi' from Ibn Umar, while Ma'mar and Ibn Jurayj transmitted it from Isma'il as a mursal (a narration lacking a companion in its chain).

The Tenth Issue: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So whoever transgresses﴾. The transgression (i'tida') is exceeding the limit, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whoever transgresses the limits of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229], meaning, goes beyond them. So whoever wrongs you, take your right from him to the extent of his wrong against you. Whoever insults you, respond to him with the like of his words. Whoever takes your honor, take his honor, but do not extend it to his parents, his children, or his relatives. It is not permissible for you to lie about him even if he lied about you, for disobedience is not repaid with disobedience. So if he says to you, for example, "O unbeliever!", you may say to him, "You are the unbeliever." If he says to you, "O fornicator!", your retaliation is to say to him, "O liar! O false witness!" If you said to him, "O fornicator!", you would be lying and would have sinned by the lie. If he delays paying you while he is able, without excuse, then say: "O wrongdoer! O devourer of people's wealth!" The Prophet ﷺ said: "The delay of the one who is able (to pay) makes his honor and his punishment permissible" [[al-layy: delay. al-wajid: one who is able to pay his debt.]]. As for his honor, it is as we have explained; as for his punishment, it is imprisonment in which he is held.

Ibn 'Abbas said: this was revealed before Islam had become strong, so it commanded that whoever among the Muslims was harmed should repay with the like of what he was harmed with, or be patient, or pardon. Then this was abrogated (nusikh) by His saying: ﴿And fight the polytheists all together﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36]. It was also said: it was abrogated by referring the matter to the ruler (sultan). It is not lawful for anyone to exact retaliation from anyone except with the permission of the ruler.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 195:**

There are three issues here.

**The first issue:** Al-Bukhari narrated from Hudhayfah concerning ﴿And spend in the way of God, and do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾. He said: "It was revealed concerning spending (in charity)." Yazid ibn Abi Habib narrated from Aslam Abu Imran, who said: "We fought at Constantinople, and the commander of the army was Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Walid, while the Romans had their backs against the wall of the city. A man charged at the enemy, and the people said: 'Mah! (stop!) Mah! La ilaha illa Allah! He is throwing himself with his own hands into destruction!' Abu Ayyub said: 'Subhan Allah! This verse was revealed about us, the group of the Ansar, when God granted victory to His Prophet and made His religion prevail. We said to one another: "Come, let us remain with our wealth and set it right." So God, mighty and majestic, revealed: "And spend in the way of God..." (to the end of the verse). Throwing oneself with one's own hands into destruction means that we remain with our wealth, setting it right, and abandon jihad.'" Abu Ayyub continued to fight in the way of God until he was buried at Constantinople, where his grave is. Abu Ayyub thus informed us that throwing oneself with one's own hands into destruction is abandoning jihad in the way of God, and that the verse was revealed concerning this. Similar was narrated from Hudhayfah, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Dahhak.

I (al-Qurtubi) say: al-Tirmidhi narrated this report from Yazid ibn Abi Habib from Aslam Abu Imran, with the same meaning, saying: "We were in the city of the Romans, and they brought out to us a great battle-line of Romans. Muslims came out against them, equal to them or more. The people of Egypt were under Uqbah ibn Amir, and the commander of the whole force was Fudalah ibn Ubayd. A man from the Muslims charged at the line of the Romans until he penetrated into them. The people shouted and said: 'Subhan Allah! He is throwing himself with his own hands into destruction!' Abu Ayyub al-Ansari stood up and said: 'O people, you are interpreting this verse in this way, but this verse was only revealed concerning us, the group of the Ansar, when God honored Islam and its helpers became many. Some of us said to others secretly, without the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Our wealth has been lost, and God has honored Islam and its helpers have become many. So if we remain with our wealth and set right what was lost from it..." Then God revealed to His Prophet (ﷺ), responding to what we had said: "And spend in the way of God, and do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction." So destruction was remaining with our wealth and setting it right, and abandoning the raid.' Abu Ayyub kept marching in the way of God until he was buried in the land of the Romans." Abu Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: "This is a hadith that is hasan, gharib, sahih."

Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, Ata', Mujahid and the majority of the people said: the meaning is, "Do not throw yourselves with your own hands" by abandoning spending in the way of God and fearing poverty, so that a man says: "I do not have anything to spend." Al-Bukhari also took this meaning, since he mentioned no other. And God knows best.

Ibn Abbas said: "Spend in the way of God even if you have only an arrow or a mishqas (a broad blade, or an arrowhead fitted with a blade, used to shoot wild game), and let none of you say: 'I do not find anything.'" Similar was reported from al-Suddi: "Spend even a cord, and do not throw yourself with your hand into destruction by saying: 'I have nothing.'"

**A third view**, also from Ibn Abbas: when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) commanded the people to go out to jihad, some Bedouins who were present in Medina came to him and said: "With what shall we equip ourselves? By God, we have no provisions, and no one will feed us." Then God revealed: ﴿And spend in the way of God﴾, meaning: give charity, O people of means, in the way of God, that is, in obedience to God. "And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction" means: do not withhold your hands from charity and thus perish. Muqatil also said this. The meaning of Ibn Abbas is: do not withhold from charity and thus perish, that is, do not withhold spending on the weak, for if they fall behind you, the enemy will overpower you and you will perish.

**A fourth view:** It was said to al-Bara' ibn Azib concerning this verse: "Is it the man who charges at the battalion?" He said: "No, rather it is the man who commits a sin and then throws himself down and says: 'I have gone too far in sins, and there is no benefit in repentance.' He then despairs of God and thereafter plunges deeper into sins." So destruction is despair of God. Similar was said by Ubaydah al-Salmani.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: the meaning is, "Do not travel in jihad without provisions." Some people did this, and it led them to being cut off on the road, or to becoming a burden on people.

These are five views.

"The way of God" here means jihad, and the wording extends afterwards to all its paths. The ba' in "with your own hands" (bi-aydikum) is extra; the sense is "throw your hands into destruction."

**A parallel:** ﴿Did he not know that God sees?﴾ [al-Alaq: 14]. Al-Mubarrad said: "with your own hands" means "with yourselves," so a part is used to refer to the whole, as in His saying: ﴿for what your hands have earned﴾ [al-Shura: 30] and ﴿for what your two hands have sent forward﴾ [al-Hajj: 10]. It was also said that this is a figurative expression: one says, "So-and-so threw his hand into such-and-such a matter" when he surrenders, because the one who surrenders in battle throws down his weapon with his hands. Likewise is the act of every helpless person in whatever act he does. From this is the saying of Abd al-Muttalib: "By God, our throwing ourselves with our hands into death is helplessness..." (the statement of Abd al-Muttalib, as cited by Ibn Hisham in his Sirah in the discussion of digging Zamzam: "By God, our throwing ourselves with our hands into death in this way, not striking out in the earth and seeking for ourselves, is helplessness...").

Some said: the implied sense is "do not throw yourselves with your own hands," just as one says, "Do not corrupt your condition by your own opinion."

"Destruction" (al-tahlukah, with a damma on the lam) is a verbal noun from halaka, yahliku, halakan, uhlkan, and tahlukatan, meaning: do not engage in what destroys you. This was said by al-Zajjaj and others, meaning: if you do not spend, you disobey God and perish.

It was also said that the meaning of the verse is: do not hold back your wealth, lest others inherit it from you and you perish by losing the benefit of your wealth. Another meaning: do not withhold, lest recompense in this world and reward in the Hereafter be lost to you.

It is also said: "Do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction" means: do not spend from what is unlawful, for it will be returned to you and you will perish. Similar was reported from Ikrimah, who said concerning "and do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction": ﴿and do not aim at the bad, of which you spend﴾ [al-Baqarah: 267].

Al-Tabari said: His saying "and do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction" is general, covering all that has been mentioned, since it enters into all of them, for the wording allows it.

**The second issue:** The scholars differed about a man rushing into battle and charging alone at the enemy. Al-Qasim ibn Mukhaymirah, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad and Abd al-Malik from our scholars said: there is no harm in a man charging alone at a great army if he has strength and acts with pure intention for God. But if he has no strength, then that is destruction.

It was said: if he seeks martyrdom and his intention is pure, then let him charge, because his aim is one of them (i.e., the martyrs). This is clear from His saying: ﴿And among the people is one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 207].

Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: as for a man charging against a hundred or against the whole army, or against a group of thieves, bandits or Kharijites, there are two situations. If he knows, and it is his strong assumption, that he will kill the one he charges at and escape, then it is good. Likewise, if he knows and strongly assumes that he will be killed, but will inflict a blow (nikayah) or will be destroyed in a way that brings benefit to the Muslims, then it is also permissible.

It has reached me that when the army of the Muslims met the Persians, the Muslims' horses shied from the elephants. A man among them made an elephant of clay and got his horse accustomed to it until it became familiar with it. When morning came, his horse did not shy from the elephant, so he charged at the elephant that was leading them. He was told: "It will kill you." He said: "There is no harm if I am killed and victory is opened for the Muslims."

Likewise on the day of al-Yamamah, when the Banu Hanifah took refuge in the orchard, a man from the Muslims (he was al-Bara' ibn Malik, brother of Anas ibn Malik, as in the History of al-Tabari) said: "Put me in a hajfah (a shield made of hide; the ha' precedes the jim, with a vowel) and throw me to them." They did so, he fought them alone and opened the gate.

I (al-Qurtubi) say: among this is what is narrated: a man said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "What do you think if I am killed in the way of God, steadfast and seeking reward?" He said: "Then for you is Paradise." So he plunged into the enemy until he was killed.

In Sahih Muslim, from Anas ibn Malik: on the day of Uhud, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was left alone (ufrida, i.e., when the people had fled and the enemy reached him) with seven men from the Ansar and two men from Quraysh. When they overwhelmed him (rahiquhu, meaning they came upon him and reached him), he said: "Whoever turns them back from us, for him is Paradise," or "He will be my companion in Paradise." A man from the Ansar advanced and fought until he was killed. They overwhelmed him again, and he said: "Whoever turns them back from us, for him is Paradise," or "He will be my companion in Paradise." A man from the Ansar advanced and fought until he was killed. [Addition from Sahih Muslim.] So it continued until the seven were killed. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "We were not fair to our companions." This is the report as it stands: "anṣafnā" with a sukun on the fa', and "aṣḥābanā" with a fatha on the ba', meaning: we did not guide them to fight until they were killed. It is also narrated with a fatha on the fa' and a raf' on the ba', and its interpretation is that it refers to those of his companions who fled from him. And God knows best.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: if one man charged alone against a thousand polytheists, there would be no harm in it if he hoped for escape or for inflicting a blow on the enemy. But if he did not have such hope, it is disliked, because he would be exposing himself to destruction without benefit to the Muslims. If his purpose was to embolden the Muslims against the enemy, so that they would do as he did, its permissibility is not far-fetched, since there is benefit to the Muslims in some respects. If his aim was to terrify the enemy and to show the steadfastness of the Muslims in their religion, its permissibility is not far-fetched either. When there is benefit to the Muslims, and he is killed in order to exalt the religion of God and weaken disbelief, that is the noble station with which God praised the believers in His saying: ﴿Indeed, God has purchased from the believers their lives﴾ [al-Tawbah: 111], and other verses of praise by which God praised those who gave themselves. Accordingly, the ruling on enjoining good and forbidding evil should be that whenever one hopes for benefit in religion and gives himself to it until he is killed, he is in the highest ranks of the martyrs. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and bear patiently what afflicts you. Indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination﴾ [Luqman: 17].

Ikrimah narrated from Ibn Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "The best of martyrs is Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib, and a man who spoke a word of truth before an unjust ruler and was killed for it." The discussion of this will come later, God willing, in (surah) Al 'Imran.

**The third issue:** His saying ﴿And do good﴾ means: in spending in obedience (to God), and think well of God regarding His compensating you (for what you spend). It was also said: do good in your deeds by carrying out acts of obedience. This was narrated from some of the Companions.

**Ten issues arise from this verse.**

**The first issue:** God Most High says: ﴿So whoever does not find [an offering]﴾, meaning the sacrificial animal (al-hady), either because he lacks the wealth or because no animal is available. He fasts three days during the Hajj and seven when he returns to his home city. The three days of the Hajj end on the Day of 'Arafah. This is the view of Tawus. It is also reported from al-Sha'bi, 'Ata', Mujahid, al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Nakha'i, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Alqamah, 'Amr ibn Dinar, and the proponents of opinion (ashab al-ra'y). Ibn al-Mundhir related it. Abu Thawr reported from Abu Hanifah that he may fast them during his ihram for 'Umrah, because it is one of the two ihrams of tamattu' (the combined pilgrimage), so fasting the days during it is permissible, just as during his ihram for Hajj. Abu Hanifah and his companions also said: he fasts the day before the Day of Tarwiyah, the Day of Tarwiyah itself, and the Day of 'Arafah. Ibn 'Abbas and Malik ibn Anas said: he may fast them from the time he enters ihram for Hajj until the Day of Nahr (Sacrifice), because God Most High said: "Fasting three days in the Hajj." If he fasts them during 'Umrah, he has done so before their time, and it is not valid for him. al-Shafi'i and Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: he fasts them between his declaring the intention (ihlal) for Hajj and the Day of 'Arafah. This is the view of Ibn 'Umar and 'A'ishah. It is also related from Malik, and it is the implication of his statement in his Muwatta', "so that the Day of 'Arafah is a day of not fasting, for that is more in keeping with the Sunnah and stronger for worship," as will come. It is also reported from Ahmad that it is permissible to fast the three days before entering ihram. al-Thawri and al-Awza'i said: he fasts them from the first days of the ten (of Dhu al-Hijjah), and 'Ata' also said this. 'Urwah said: he fasts them as long as he is in Makkah during the days of Mina, and Malik and a group of the people of Madinah also said this.

The days of Mina are the three days of tashriq that follow the Day of Nahr. Malik related in the Muwatta' from 'A'ishah, Mother of the Believers, that she used to say: "Fasting is for one who performs tamattu' with 'Umrah until Hajj, for one who does not find an offering, between the time he declares the intention for Hajj and the Day of 'Arafah. If he has not fasted, he fasts the days of Mina." This wording implies the validity of fasting from the time one enters ihram for the Hajj of tamattu' until the Day of 'Arafah, and that this is the starting point. This is either because it is the time of performance (ada'), and what comes after it among the days of Mina is the time of making up (qada'), as the followers of al-Shafi'i hold, or because advancing the fast before the Day of Nahr clears the obligation (ibra' li-l-dhimmah), which is commanded. The more apparent position within the school is that these days are performed on time (ada'), although fasting before them is more virtuous, just as the time of prayer has a span for performance, and although its beginning is more virtuous than its end. This is the correct view: they are performance, not making up. For God's words "days in the Hajj" may mean the place of the Hajj, or may mean the days of the Hajj. If the intended meaning is the days of the Hajj, this view is correct, because the last of the days of the Hajj is the Day of Nahr, but the last of the days of the Hajj may also be the days of stoning (al-ramy), because stoning is an act of the Hajj, sincerely, even though it is not one of its pillars. If the intended meaning is the place of the Hajj, he fasts it as long as he is in Makkah during the days of Mina, as 'Urwah said, and this view is very strong. Some have said: he may postpone them initially until the days of tashriq, because fasting is obligatory on him only if he does not find the offering on the Day of Nahr.

**If it is said:** This is the second issue. A group of the people of Madinah and al-Shafi'i in his later view (al-jadid), with most of his companions, held that fasting the days of tashriq is not permissible, because the Messenger of God (ﷺ) forbade fasting the days of Mina. It is said in reply: if the prohibition is established, it is general, and the one performing tamattu' is excepted from it by what is established in al-Bukhari, that 'A'ishah used to fast them. Also from Ibn 'Umar and 'A'ishah, they said: "Fasting on the days of tashriq was not permitted except for one who does not find an offering." al-Daraqutni said: its isnad is sound, and it was narrated as a marfu' report from Ibn 'Umar and 'A'ishah through three chains, which he declared weak. Permission to fast them was granted only because no days remained of his [allotted] days except their measure, and by this the obligation of fasting for lack of an offering is fulfilled. Ibn al-Mundhir said: it has been related to us from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib that he said: "If he misses the fast, he fasts after the days of tashriq." al-Hasan and 'Ata' also said this. Ibn al-Mundhir said: and this is what we say.

A group said: if he misses the fast during the ten days, only the offering suffices for him. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Tawus, and Mujahid, and Abu 'Umar related it from Abu Hanifah and his companions from him, so consider it.

**The third issue:** The scholars agree that fasting has no place for one performing tamattu' when he is able to find the offering. They differed concerning one who is unable to find the offering, fasts, and then finds the offering before completing his fast. Ibn Wahb related from Malik, who said: "If he has begun the fast and then finds an offering, it is more beloved to me that he offer it. If he does not, the fasting suffices for him." al-Shafi'i said: he continues his fast, and that is his obligation. Abu Thawr also said so. This is the view of al-Hasan and Qatadah, and Ibn al-Mundhir chose it. Abu Hanifah said: if he becomes able (yasar) on the third day of his fast, the fast is void and the offering becomes obligatory for him. If he has fasted three days of the Hajj and then becomes able, he may fast the seven days and does not return to the offering. al-Thawri, Ibn Abi Najih, and Hammad also said this.

**The fourth issue:** God Most High says: ﴿and seven﴾. The reading of the majority is with the genitive (bi-l-khafd), by coordination (al-'atf): "wa-sab'atin." Zayd ibn 'Ali read "wa-sab'atan" with the accusative, meaning: "and fast seven."
