**The fifth issue:** God Most High says: "when you have returned" (idha raja'tum), meaning to your lands. This was said by Ibn 'Umar, Qatadah, al-Rabi', Mujahid, and 'Ata'. Malik said it in the Kitab of Muhammad, and al-Shafi'i also said it. Qatadah and al-Rabi' said: this is a concession from God Most High, so no one is obligated to fast the seven days except when he has reached his homeland, unless someone chooses to be strict, just as one who fasts while traveling in Ramadan does. Ahmad and Ishaq said: fasting on the road suffices for him, and this is reported from Mujahid and 'Ata'. Mujahid said: if he wishes he fasts them on the road, for it is only a concession. 'Ikrimah and al-Hasan also said this. Some scholars of language (ahl al-lughah) say the implied meaning is: "when you have returned from the Hajj," that is, "when you have returned to what you were upon before ihram, of being in a state of non-sacredness (al-hill)." Malik said in the Kitab: "If he returns from Mina, there is no harm in his fasting." Ibn al-'Arabi said: "If it is a concession and a dispensation, then it is permissible to advance concessions, and to leave off gentleness in them in favor of resolve (al-'azimah), by consensus [[so in Ahkam al-Quran of Ibn al-'Arabi; in the Arabic originals: 'instead']]. If it is a time limit, there is no text in it, nor any indication that he meant the lands, and that the lands are the meaning in most cases [[Ibn al-'Arabi's wording: '... there is no indication that he meant the lands; rather the meaning in most cases and the more apparent in it is that it is the Hajj.']]."

I say: rather, there is an indication in it that comes close to a text, clarified by what Muslim related from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) performed tamattu' with 'Umrah until Hajj in the Farewell Pilgrimage and offered, and he drove the offering with him from Dhu al-Hulayfah. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) began, declaring ihram for 'Umrah, then declared ihram for Hajj, and the people performed tamattu' with 'Umrah until Hajj with the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Among the people were those who offered and drove the offering, and among them were those who did not offer. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) arrived in Makkah, he said to the people: 'Whoever among you has offered, then he may not be released from anything he has been forbidden until he completes his Hajj. Whoever among you has not offered, let him circumambulate the House and [run] between al-Safa and al-Marwah, let him shorten (his hair), let him be released, then let him declare ihram for Hajj and offer. Whoever does not find an offering, let him fast three days in the Hajj and seven when he returns to his family.'" The hadith continues. This is almost explicit that fasting the seven days is not permissible except in his family and his land. And God knows best. Al-Bukhari likewise related in the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas: "Then on the evening of the Day of Tarwiyah he ordered us to declare ihram for Hajj. When we finished the rites, we came and circumambulated the House and [ran] between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and our Hajj was complete, and the offering was upon us, as God Most High said: ﴿So whatever offering is feasible; but whoever does not find [one], then fasting three days during the Hajj and seven when you have returned [to your homes]﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:196]." The hadith continues, as will come. Al-Nahhas said: this was a consensus.

**The sixth issue:** God Most High says: ﴿That is ten complete﴾. It is said: "kamala, yakmulu," like "nasara, yansuru"; "kamula, yakmulu," like "'adhuma, ya'dhumu"; and "kamila, yakmalu," like "hamida, yahmadu": three dialects. People differed concerning the meaning of His words "that is ten," although it is known that it is ten. al-Zajjaj said: when it was possible for someone to suppose an option between three days during the Hajj or seven when returning as a substitute for them, since He did not say "and seven others," this was removed by the phrase "that is ten," and then He said "complete." al-Hasan said: "complete" in reward is like one who offered. It was also said: "complete" in substitution for the offering, meaning all ten are a substitute for the offering. It was also said: "complete" in reward is like one who did not perform tamattu'. It was said: its wording is that of a report, but its meaning is a command, that is, "complete them," for that is their obligation. al-Mubarrad said: "ten" indicates the completion of the number, lest someone suppose that some remainder is left after mentioning the seven. It was also said: it is emphasis, as you say, "I wrote with my two hands." From this is the poet's saying:

*Three, and two: they are five,*
*and a sixth inclining toward my shimam [a side/place of mine].*

So his saying "five" is emphasis. And similar is the saying of another:

*Three in the morning, that is enough for me,*
*and six when the evening meal overtakes me.*
*That is nine in the day, my quenching,*
*and a man's drinking beyond quenching is a disease.*

His saying "complete" is another emphasis, containing an added charge to fast them and not to reduce their number, as you say to one whom you command in an important matter: "God, God, do not fall short."

**The seventh issue:** God Most High says: ﴿That is for one whose family is not present at the Sacred Mosque﴾, meaning that the offering of tamattu' is obligatory only upon the stranger who is not among those present at the Sacred Mosque. al-Bukhari related from Ibn 'Abbas that he was asked about the enjoyment of Hajj (mut'at al-Hajj), and he said: "The Muhajirun and the Ansar, and the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), declared ihram in the Farewell Pilgrimage, and we declared ihram [too]. When we arrived in Makkah, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Make your declaration of ihram for Hajj into 'Umrah, except for one who has garlanded the offering.' We circumambulated the House and [ran] between al-Safa and al-Marwah, we approached our wives, and we put on clothes. He said: 'Whoever has garlanded the offering, he is not released until the offering reaches its place of sacrifice.' Then on the evening of the Day of Tarwiyah he ordered us to declare ihram for Hajj. When we finished the rites, we came and circumambulated the House and [ran] between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and our Hajj was complete, and the offering was upon us, as God Most High said: ﴿So whatever offering is feasible; but whoever does not find [one], then fasting three days during the Hajj and seven when you have returned﴾ 'to your cities'. The sheep suffices. So they combined two rites in one year, Hajj and 'Umrah. God sent it down in His Book and in the Sunnah of His Prophet (ﷺ), and permitted it for people other than the people of Makkah. God, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿That is for one whose family is not present at the Sacred Mosque﴾." The months of Hajj that God, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, and Dhu al-Hijjah. Whoever performs tamattu' in these months, upon him is an offering or fasting. "Rafath" is intercourse, "fusuq" is acts of disobedience, and "jidal" is disputation.

The eighth issue: The lam in His saying "liman" (for whoever) carries the meaning of "upon," meaning that the sacrificial animal is obligatory upon whoever is not a resident of Makkah, just as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Stipulate for them the wala' (clientage/inheritance right)." And His exalted saying: ﴿And if you do evil, then it is against themselves﴾ [al-Isra: 7], meaning, "then it is upon them." This refers to tamattu' and qiran for the outsider according to Abu Hanifa and his companions; there is no tamattu' or qiran for the residents of al-Masjid al-Haram according to them. Whoever does that is obligated to a blood-sacrifice of expiation (dam jinayah), from which he may not eat, because it is not a dam of tamattu'. Al-Shafi'i said: they (the residents) also have a dam of tamattu' and qiran. The reference is to the hady and the fasting, so there is no hady or fasting upon them. Abd al-Malik ibn al-Majishun distinguished between tamattu' and qiran, obligating the dam in qiran and dropping it in tamattu', as was previously mentioned from him.

The ninth issue: People differed concerning "hadirai al-Masjid al-Haram" (residents of the Sacred Mosque), after the consensus that it refers to the people of Makkah and those connected to it. Al-Tabari said: after the consensus that it refers to the people of the Haram (sacred precinct). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: that is not as he stated. Some scholars said: whoever is obligated to attend the Friday prayer is a hadari (urban resident), and whoever is farther than that is a badawi (bedouin), so they took the term from hadara (settledness) and badawa (desert living). Malik and his companions said: they are specifically the people of Makkah and those connected to it. According to Abu Hanifa and his companions: they are the people of the miqat-points and whoever lies beyond them from every direction; so whoever is from the people of the miqat-points or from those beyond them is among the residents of al-Masjid al-Haram. Al-Shafi'i and his companions said: they are those for whom shortening the prayer is not obligatory when traveling from their place to Makkah, and that is the nearest of the miqat-points. These opinions are the schools of the predecessors (salaf) in interpreting the verse.

The tenth issue: His exalted saying: ﴿And fear Allah﴾, meaning, in what He has obligated upon you. It has also been said: it is a command to piety in general, and a warning of the severity of His punishment.

There are fourteen issues in this (verse).

The First: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months.﴾ When Allah, glorified and exalted is He, mentioned the Hajj and the 'Umrah in His saying: ﴿And complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196], He explained their difference in terms of time. The whole year is a time for entering into ihram for 'Umrah, and the time for 'Umrah (is the whole year). As for the Hajj, it occurs once a year, so it does not take place outside these months. "The Hajj is in well-known months" is a subject and predicate (mubtada' wa khabar). In the sentence there is an ellipsis (hadhf), whose estimate is: "The months of Hajj are months," or "The time of Hajj is months," or "The time of performing the Hajj is months." It has also been said the estimate is: "The Hajj is in months." With the omission of the preposition (harf al-jarr) it would necessitate that "the months" be in the accusative, but no one read it with the accusative, although in speech the accusative is permissible as a time adverb (zarf). Al-Farra' said: "al-ashhur" is in the nominative because its meaning is "the time of Hajj is well-known months." Al-Farra' said: "I heard al-Kisa'i say: 'The summer is only two months, and the tilsan [[al-tilsan: a round green cloak, whose warp or weft is of wool, worn by the elite among scholars and shaykhs; it is from the dress of the non-Arabs.]] is three months.'" He meant the time of summer and the time of wearing the tilsan, and he omitted (them). The Second: There is disagreement concerning the well-known months. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Umar, 'Ata', al-Rabi', Mujahid and al-Zuhri said: the months of Hajj are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah and all of Dhu al-Hijjah. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi, al-Sha'bi and al-Nakha'i said: they are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah and ten (days) of Dhu al-Hijjah. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, and Ibn al-Zubayr said it, and both opinions are narrated from Malik: Ibn Habib related the latter, and Ibn al-Mundhir related the former. The benefit of the difference is the obligation of a sacrifice (dam). Whoever says that all of Dhu al-Hijjah is among the months of Hajj does not require a sacrifice for acts performed after the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr), because they are within the months of Hajj. According to the latter opinion, the Hajj ends with the Day of Sacrifice, and a sacrifice is required for acts done after that, because of delaying them beyond their time. The Third: Allah, exalted is He, did not name the months of Hajj in His Book, because they were known to them. The word "months" (ashhur) may apply to two months and part of a third, because part of a month is treated as if it were all of it, as one says: "I saw you in such-and-such a year," or "in the time of so-and-so." Perhaps he only saw him in one hour of it. Thus a time may be referred to by its part as its whole, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "The days of Mina are three," whereas they are only two days and part of a third. And they say: "I saw you today," and "I came to you this year." It has also been said: since two and what is above them are plural, he said "ashhur" (months). And Allah knows best.

The Fourth: There is disagreement concerning entering into ihram for Hajj outside the months of Hajj. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "It is part of the Sunnah of Hajj that one enters into ihram for it during the months of Hajj." 'Ata', Mujahid, Tawus and al-Awza'i said: whoever enters into ihram for Hajj before the months of Hajj, that does not suffice for his Hajj, and it becomes an 'Umrah, like one who begins a prayer before its time, for it does not suffice him and becomes a voluntary prayer (nafilah). This is also the view of al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr. Al-Awza'i said: he exits (ihram) by an 'Umrah. Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: this is disliked. It is narrated from Malik, and the well-known position from him is the permissibility of entering into ihram for Hajj during the whole year, and this is the view of Abu Hanifah. al-Nakha'i said: he does not exit until he completes his Hajj, due to Allah's saying: ﴿They ask you about the crescent moons. Say: they are times for the people and for the Hajj﴾ [al-Baqarah: 189], and this has already been discussed. What al-Shafi'i went to is more sound, because that (verse) is general and this verse is specific. It is possible that it is of the type of specifying some individuals of a general category, due to the excellence of these months over others; in that case Malik's view is correct. And Allah knows best.

The Fifth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever makes obligatory upon himself the Hajj therein﴾, i.e., he binds himself to it by beginning it with intention, inwardly, and with ihram, outwardly in action, and with the talbiyah, audibly in speech. This was said by Ibn Habib, and Abu Hanifah regarding the talbiyah. The talbiyah is not one of the pillars of Hajj according to al-Shafi'i, and this is the view of al-Hasan ibn Hayy. Al-Shafi'i said: intention suffices for entering into ihram for Hajj. Ahl al-Zahir and others made the talbiyah obligatory. The root meaning of "fard" in the language is cutting and severing, and from it comes "fursat al-qaws" (the notch in a bow where the string sits), and "fursat al-nahr" (the place where water is drawn from a river), and "fursat al-jabal" (what descends from the middle and side of a mountain). Thus the obligation of Hajj is binding upon the free adult, like the binding of the handle (khizz) to the cup (qadah). It was also said: "faraḍa" means "made distinct" (abana), and this returns to cutting, because whoever cuts a thing has separated it from others. "Man" is in the nominative as the subject, and its meaning is conditional, and the predicate is his saying "faraḍa," because "man" here is not a relative pronoun; it is as if he said: "a man who is obligated." He said "fihinna" (in them) and did not say "fiha" (in it). Some said: both are the same in usage. Al-Mazini Abu 'Uthman said: a large plural of non-rational things takes the form of a feminine singular, while a small plural does not; you say: "al-ajdhā' inkasarna" (the trunks broke, feminine plural), and "al-judhū' inkasarat" (the trunks broke, feminine singular). This is confirmed by Allah's saying: ﴿Indeed the number of months﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36], then He said: "minha" (of them, feminine singular).

The Sixth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There shall be no rafath﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, Qatadah, al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, al-Zuhri, Mujahid and Malik said: rafath is intercourse, meaning there is no intercourse, because it invalidates the Hajj. The scholars agreed that intercourse before standing at 'Arafah invalidates the Hajj, and upon it is (the obligation of) performing the Hajj in a subsequent year and the sacrifice. Abdullah ibn 'Umar, Tawus, 'Ata' and others said: rafath is obscene speech to a woman, such as saying to her: "When we exit (ihram) we will do such-and-such to you," without euphemism. Ibn 'Abbas also said this, and he recited while in ihram:

"And they walk with us in a whisper... If the bird speaks truly, we will mount a soft (woman)."

His companion Husayn ibn Qays said to him: "Do you engage in rafath while you are in ihram?" He said: "Rafath is only what is said in the presence of women." Others said: rafath is obscenity regarding women, whether it is in their presence or not. It was also said: rafath is a comprehensive term for what a man desires from his wife. Abu 'Ubaydah said: rafath is idle talk (laghw) of speech, and he recited:

"And many a group of pilgrims, restrained from idle talk and the rafath of speech..."

It is said: "rafatha yarfutha," with the fa' pronounced with a damma or a kasra. Ibn Mas'ud read "fala ruful" in the plural. Ibn al-'Arabi said: the intended meaning of "there shall be no rafath" is its negation as a legislated matter, not as an existing reality, for we find rafath in it and witness it; Allah's report cannot be contrary to what it reports. The negation refers only to its existence as legislated, not to its existence sensibly, like His saying: ﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228], meaning: legally, not sensibly, for we find divorced women who do not wait. So the negation returns to the legal ruling, not to sensory existence. Similarly His saying: ﴿None touches it except the purified﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 79], if we say it refers to human beings, which is the sound view, its meaning is that none of them touches it legally; if touching occurs, it is contrary to the ruling of the Law. This subtle point escaped the scholars, who said: the report is meant as a prohibition, and that never occurred and cannot occur; but the two are actually different and opposite in description.

The Seventh: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor fusuq﴾, meaning all sins entirely. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' and al-Hasan. Likewise Ibn 'Umar and a group said: fusuq is committing acts of disobedience to Allah, mighty and majestic, while in the state of ihram for Hajj, such as killing game, cutting nails, removing hair, and the like. al-Zayd ibn Zayd and Malik said: fusuq is slaughtering for idols, and from it is His saying: ﴿Or an abomination over which the name of other than Allah has been invoked﴾ [al-An'am: 145]. al-Dahhak said: fusuq is mutual insult by nicknames, and from it is His saying: ﴿Wretched is the name of fusuq﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11]. Ibn 'Umar also said: fusuq is cursing, and from it is his saying, upon him be peace: "Cursing a Muslim is fusuq, and fighting him is kufr." The first opinion is more sound, because it encompasses all statements. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever performs Hajj and does not commit rafath or fusuq returns like the day his mother bore him." And "The accepted Hajj has no reward but Paradise," recorded by Muslim and others. It has also come from him ﷺ that he said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, there is no deed between heaven and earth better than jihad in the way of Allah, or an accepted Hajj in which there is no rafath, no fusuq, and no jidal." The jurists said: the accepted Hajj is the one in which Allah, exalted is He, was not disobeyed during its performance. Al-Farra' said: it is the one after which Allah, exalted is He, was not disobeyed. Ibn al-'Arabi, may Allah have mercy on him, related both opinions. I say: the accepted Hajj is the one in which Allah, exalted is He, was not disobeyed during it, not after it. al-Hasan said: the accepted Hajj is that its performer returns detached from this world and desiring the Hereafter. Other views have been stated, and they will come.

The Eighth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor jidal in the Hajj﴾. It was read "fala rafathun wa la fusuqun" with raf' and tanwin in both. They were also read with nasb without tanwin. They agreed on the fatha in "wa la jidal," and this strengthens the nasb reading before it, and because the intended meaning is the general negation of rafath, fusuq and jidal, so that the statement is in one uniform pattern regarding the generality of everything negated. Most of the readers read with nasb. The three nouns are, each with "la," in a place of raf' (according to one of the two views of the grammarians; the second view is that "la" governs the noun in the accusative and what follows is the predicate). The phrase "fil-hajj" is a predicate for all of them. The reasoning for the reading with raf' is that "la" has the meaning of "laysa" (is not), so the noun after it is nominative, as its subject, and the predicate is omitted, estimated as: "So there is not rafath nor fusuq in the Hajj," indicated by the apparent second "fil-hajj," which is the predicate of "la jidal." Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: the raf' means "so let there not be rafath nor fusuq," i.e., whatever takes one out of the Hajj; then he began the negation and said: "wa la jidal."

I say: it is possible that "kana" is complete, like His saying: ﴿And if there is one in difficulty﴾, so it does not need a predicate. It is also possible that it is incomplete with the predicate omitted, as mentioned just before. It is permissible that "rafathun wa fusuqun" be raised as a subject, with "la" for negation, and the predicate also omitted. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' read with raf' in all three. It was also narrated from 'Asim in some transmissions. In that case "fil-hajj" is the predicate of all three, as we said regarding the nasb reading. The reason it is not good for "fil-hajj" to be the predicate of all, with the readings differing, is that the predicate of "laysa" is accusative, while the predicate of "wa la jidal" is nominative, because "wa la jidal" is detached from the first and is in a place of raf' as a subject, and two governing words do not govern one noun. It is permissible to read "fala rafatha wa la fusuqa," coordinating it with the position (mawdi'). The grammarians recited:

"There is no lineage today, nor friendship... the tear has widened over the patcher."

It is permissible in speech to say "fala rafatha wa la fusuqan wa la jidala fil-hajj," coordinating on the wording, according to what would be required with "la." Al-Farra' said: like it is:

فَلَا أَبَ وَابْنًا مِثْلَ مَرْوَانَ وَابْنِهِ ... إِذَا هُوَ بِالْمَجْدِ ارْتَدَى وَتَأَزَّرَا

Abu Raja' al-Utaridi said: "*fala rafatha wa la fusuqa*" with the accusative (*nasb*) on both, and "*wa la jidala*" with the nominative (*raf'*) and tanwin. Al-Akhfash recited:

هَذَا وَجَدُّكُمُ الصِّغَارُ بِعَيْنِهِ ... لَا أُمَّ لِي إِنْ كَانَ ذَاكَ وَلَا أَبُ

It was also said: the meaning of "*fala rafatha wa la fusuqa*" is a prohibition, i.e., "do not engage in obscenity and do not commit transgression." The meaning of "*wa la jidala*" is a negation. Since the two differ in meaning, they are differently worded. Al-Qushayri said: this is open to question, for it has been said that "*wa la jidala*" is also a prohibition, meaning "do not dispute," so why is a distinction made between them?

Ninth: "*wa la jidala*." *Al-jidal* (disputation) is on the pattern *fi'al* from *al-mujadalah*, and it is derived from *al-jadl*, which means killing; from it comes "a twisted (*majdul*) halter." It was also said that it is derived from *al-jidalah*, which is the ground. The idea is that each of the two opponents strives against his companion until he overcomes him, so he is like one who has been thrown onto the ground (*al-jadalah*). The poet said:

قَدْ أَرْكَبُ الْآلَةَ بَعْدَ الْآلَةِ [[al-alah: the state, and hardship.]] ... وَأَتْرُكُ الْعَاجِزَ بِالْجِدَالَهْ
مُنْعَفِرًا لَسْتُ لَهُ مَحَالَهْ

Tenth: The scholars differed concerning the meaning intended here, in six opinions. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas and Ata' said: disputation here means that you argue with a Muslim until you anger him, so that it leads to abuse; as for discussing knowledge (*mudhakarat al-'ilm*), there is no prohibition against it. Qatadah said: disputation is abuse. Ibn Zayd and Malik ibn Anas said: disputation here means that people argue over who coincides with the standing-place of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), as they used to do in the Jahiliyyah, when Quraysh would stand at a place other than where the rest of the Arabs stood, and then they would dispute afterwards. So the meaning according to this interpretation is: there is no disputation at its (the Hajj's) appointed places. A group said: disputation here is one group saying, "The Hajj is today," and another group saying, "The Hajj is tomorrow." Mujahid and a group with him said: disputation is contention over the months, according to what the Arabs had done with the *nasi'* (intercalation of months), for they would sometimes make the Hajj fall in a month other than Dhu al-Hijjah. Some would stand at Jam' [[that is, Muzdalifah.]] and some at 'Arafah, and they would dispute over which of that was correct.

I say: according to these two interpretations, there is no disputation at its time nor at its place. These two views are the most sound of what has been said concerning the interpretation of His saying "*wa la jidala*," because of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed time has returned to its form on the day Allah created the heavens and the earth," the hadith, and it will come in *Bara'ah* [[see vol. 8, p. 132.]]. That is, the time of Hajj returned to how it was, meaning it came back to its day and its proper time. The Prophet (ﷺ) also said when he performed Hajj: "Take your rites from me," and by this he made clear the standing-places and locations of Hajj.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: disputation is that one group says, "Our Hajj is more righteous than your Hajj," and the other says the same. It was also said: disputation was in boasting of forefathers, and Allah knows best.

Eleventh: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿وَمَا تَفْعَلُوا مِنْ خَيْرٍ يَعْلَمْهُ اللَّهُ﴾ [And whatever good you do, Allah knows it]. It is a conditional sentence with its response, and the meaning is that Allah will reward you for your deeds, because reward only comes from one who knows the thing. It was also said: this is an exhortation and encouragement toward good speech in place of obscenity, and toward righteousness and piety in conduct in place of transgression and disputation. It was said: the doing of good is an expression for restraining oneself so that nothing of what they were forbidden is found.

Twelfth: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿وَتَزَوَّدُوا﴾ [And take provision]. It is a command to acquire provisions. Ibn Umar, Ikrimah, Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: the verse was revealed concerning a group of the Arabs who used to come to Hajj without provisions, and some of them would say, "How can we make Hajj to the House of Allah and He does not feed us?" So they would remain as burdens (*'ala*) upon people, and they were forbidden from that and commanded to take provisions. Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr said: people used to depend on one another for provisions, so they were commanded to take provisions. The Prophet (ﷺ) had on his journey a riding camel upon which there were provisions, and three hundred men from Muzaynah came to him. When they wished to depart, he said: "O Umar, provide for the people." Some people said: "*Tazawwadu*" means the righteous companion. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is a weak specification, and the more appropriate meaning of the verse is: take provisions for your return (*ma'ad*) in the form of righteous deeds.

I say: the first view is more sound, for what is intended is the provision prepared for the journey of Hajj, the edible kind in its literal sense, as we have mentioned. This is as al-Bukhari narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: the people of Yemen used to make Hajj without taking provisions, saying, "We are the reliant upon Allah (*mutawakkilun*)," and when they came to Makkah they would ask people (for food). So Allah revealed: "*And take provisions, for the best provision is piety*." This is explicit in what we have mentioned, and most of the exegetes hold to it. Al-Sha'bi said: the provision is dates and *sawiq* (roasted grain flour). Ibn Jubayr said: *ka'k* (biscuit) and *sawiq*.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: "Allah the Exalted commanded taking provisions for one who has wealth. As for one who has no wealth, if he has a trade that earns him income on the road, or he is a beggar, then there is no address to him. Allah only addressed the wealthy who would leave their wealth behind and set out without provisions, saying, 'We are the reliant upon Allah.' Reliance has conditions; whoever fulfils them may set out without provisions and is not included in the address, for he set out in the manner of the majority of creation, and they are the ones who fall short of the rank of reliance, unaware of its realities. And Allah, Mighty and Majestic, knows best."

Abu al-Faraj al-Jawzi said: Iblis has deceived a people who claim reliance, so they set out without provisions and thought this was reliance, while they were in the utmost error. A man said to Ahmad ibn Hanbal: "I want to go out to Makkah relying upon Allah without provisions." Ahmad said to him: "Go out in a caravan other than this one." He said: "No, only with them." Ahmad said: "So you rely upon Allah with the people's saddlebags (*jurub*)?!" [[*jurub* (with two dammas): plural of *jirab*, meaning a container.]]

Thirteenth: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿فَإِنَّ خَيْرَ الزَّادِ التَّقْوَى﴾ [For indeed, the best provision is piety]. He, Exalted is He, informed that the best provision is guarding against what is forbidden, so He commanded them to combine piety with taking provisions. His saying "*fa-inna khayra al-zadi al-taqwa*" is construed according to the meaning, for the meaning of "*wa-tazawwadu*" is: fear Allah in following what He commanded you concerning taking provisions. It was also said: it may be that the meaning is: the best provision is that by which the traveller protects himself from destruction (*halakah*) or from the need to ask and to beg. It was also said: in it is an alert that this world is not a place of permanence. The people of allusions (*ahl al-isharat*) said: Allah reminded them of the journey of the Hereafter and urged them to take the provision of piety, for piety is the provision of the Hereafter. Al-A'sha said:

إِذْ أَنْتَ لَمْ تَرْحَلْ بِزَادٍ مِنَ التُّقَى ... وَلَاقَيْتَ بَعْدَ الْمَوْتِ مَنْ قَدْ تَزَوَّدَا
نَدِمْتَ عَلَى أَلَّا تَكُونَ كَمِثْلِهِ ... وَأَنَّكَ لَمْ تَرْصُدْ كَمَا كَانَ أَرْصَدَا

And another said:

الْمَوْتُ بَحْرٌ طَامِحٌ مَوْجُهُ ... تَذْهَبُ فِيهِ حِيلَةُ السَّابِحِ
يَا نَفْسُ إِنِّي قَائِلٌ فَاسْمَعِي ... مَقَالَةً مِنْ مُشْفِقٍ نَاصِحِ
لَا يَصْحَبُ الْإِنْسَانَ فِي قَبْرِهِ ... غَيْرَ التُّقَى وَالْعَمَلِ الصَّالِحِ

Fourteenth: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿وَاتَّقُونِ يَا أُولِي الْأَلْبَابِ﴾ [And fear Me, O people of understanding]. He singled out the people of understanding (*ulu al-albab*) for the address, although the command is general to all, because they are the ones upon whom Allah's proof has been established, and they are the ones who accept His commands and rise to fulfil them. *Al-albab* is the plural of *lubb*, and the *lubb* of anything is its essence; for this reason the intellect is called *lubb*. Al-Nahhas said: I heard Abu Ishaq say: Ahmad ibn Yahya Tha'lab said to me: "Do you know in the speech of the Arabs anything of the doubled-letter verbs that comes on the pattern *fa'ula*?" I said: "Yes, Sibawayh narrated from Yunus: *labbtu tallubbu*." He admired it and said: "I do not know a parallel to it."

The Qur'anic phrase ﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord﴾. Concerning it there are two issues.

First: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿blame﴾ means sin (ithm), and it is the subject (ism) of "laysa" (is not). "An tabtaghu" (that you seek) is in the accusative position as the predicate (khabar) of "laysa," meaning: in seeking. According to the view of al-Khalil and al-Kisa'i, it is in the genitive position. When Exalted God commanded that the Hajj be purified from obscenity (rafath), transgression (fusuq) and quarrelling (jidal), He granted leave for trade. The meaning is: there is no blame upon you in seeking the bounty of God. The seeking of bounty appears in the Qur'an with the meaning of trade. God Exalted says: ﴿Then disperse in the land and seek of God's bounty﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 10]. The evidence for the soundness of this is what al-Bukhari transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "('Ukaz, Majanna and Dhu al-Majaz were markets in the Jahiliyyah, so they felt sinful about trading during the seasons, and then this was revealed: 'There is no blame upon you that you seek bounty from your Lord' during the seasons of the Hajj)" [[The text in al-Bukhari reads: "Dhu al-Majaz and 'Ukaz were the marketplaces of the people in the Jahiliyyah. When Islam came, they seemed to dislike that until this was revealed ... etc." 'Ukaz: palm groves in a valley lying a night's journey from al-Ta'if and three nights from Makkah. Dhu al-Majaz: behind 'Arafat. Majanna: in Marr al-Zahran, near a mountain called al-Asghar, at the lowest part of Makkah at the distance of a postal stage from it. These were markets of the Arabs. The people of the Jahiliyyah would arrive at 'Ukaz on the day of the new moon of Dhu al-Qa'dah, then go from it to Majanna after twenty days of Dhu al-Qa'dah had passed; when they saw the new moon of Dhu al-Hijjah, they went from Majanna to Dhu al-Majaz, remained there eight nights, then went to 'Arafat. These markets continued to exist in Islam until the first to be abandoned was the market of 'Ukaz in the time of the Kharijites, in the year 129 AH, when the Haruri went out in Makkah with Abu Hamzah al-Mukhtar ibn 'Awf; the people feared being plundered, so it was abandoned until now. Then Dhu al-Majaz and Majanna were abandoned after that, and people were satisfied with the markets in Makkah, Mina and 'Arafat. (From the commentary of al-Qastallani).]]. The text of the Qur'anic verse, as read by Ibn 'Abbas, is: "There is no blame upon you that you seek bounty from your Lord during the seasons of the Hajj" [[The statement "during the seasons of the Hajj" is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, as the author pointed out in the introduction to the book, p. 83. Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr: "The reading of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr: 'bounty from your Lord in the seasons of the Hajj.'" This is treated as an explanation, because it contradicts the consonantal text of the Mushaf upon which the Ummah has agreed.]].

Second: If this is established, then the verse is evidence for the permissibility of trade for the pilgrim alongside performing the act of worship, and that the intention toward that does not amount to shirk, nor does the obligated person thereby depart from the required form of sincerity (ikhlas), contrary to the Fuqara' [[He may mean by the Fuqara' the Sufis.]]. As for the Hajj without trade being more excellent, that is because it is free (urriya) from the impurities of this world and the attachment of the heart to other things [[So in the copies of the original. The apparent requirement is masculine agreement with the pronoun returning to the Hajj; he may mean by the feminine here: the Hajj in the sense of worship.]]. Al-Daraqutni transmitted in his Sunan from Abu Umamah al-Taymi, who said: I said to Ibn 'Umar: "I am a man who hires out (riding animals) on this road, and people say: there is no Hajj for you." Ibn 'Umar said: A man came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and asked him the same as you have asked me, and he remained silent until this verse was revealed: "There is no blame upon you that you seek bounty from your Lord." Then the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Indeed, you have a Hajj."

Exalted is He said: ﴿Then when you surge forth from 'Arafat, remember God at the Sacred Monument (al-mash'ar al-haram), and remember Him as He has guided you, though before it you were indeed among the astray﴾. In it there are sixteen issues [[It is noted that the manuscripts disagree on the number here.]].

First: His saying, ﴿surge forth (afadtum)﴾ means you rush onward (indafa'tum). It is said: "The vessel overflowed (fasa al-inā') when it became full until it poured out from its sides." And a man is "fayyad" (overflowing), meaning one who pours out generosity. Zuhayr said:

And a white, overflowing man whose hands are a cloud over his suppliants, whose bounties never cease to flow.

[[Al-fayyad: one who gives abundantly. Al-mu'tafin: those who seek what he has. It is said: 'afahu' and 'i'tafahu' when one comes to him seeking his kindness. Ma tughibb fawadiluhu: his gifts are continuous and never cut off.]]
And a "mustafid" (widespread) report means one that is well known.

Second: His saying, ﴿from 'Arafat﴾. The reading of the community is "'Arafatin" with tanwin. The same applies if a woman were named "Muslimat," because the tanwin here is not a distinction between what is diptote and what is not, so that you would drop it; rather it stands in the position of the nun in "Muslimin." Al-Nahhas said: this is the better view. Sibawayh reported from the Arabs the omission of the tanwin from 'Arafat, saying: "hadhihi 'Arafatu ya hadha," "ra'aytu 'Arafati ya hadha," with the ta' kasra and without tanwin; he said: when they made it definite (ma'rifa) they dropped the tanwin. Al-Akhfash and the Kufans reported the fatha of the ta', assimilating it to the ta' of Fatimah and Talhah, and they recited:

I looked upon her from Adhri'at and her people, in Yathrib, the nearest of her dwellings, a lofty sight.

The first opinion is better: the tanwin in it is according to its norm as in Muslimat, the kasra corresponding to the ya' in Muslimin and the tanwin corresponding to the nun. 'Arafat is a proper noun, named with a plural form like Adhri'at. It has also been said that it was named after what surrounds it, like "ard sabasib" [[In al-Lisan, under the root s-b-s-b: "Al-Lihyani reported 'balad sabsab' and 'balad sabasib,' as if they made each part of it a sabsab, then pluralised it in this way." Al-sabsab: a desert waste and open wilderness. It is also said: level and distant land.]]. It has also been said that this place was named 'Arafat because people recognise one another (yata'arafun) there. It has also been said: because when Adam descended, he fell in India and Eve at Jeddah, and they met after long searching at 'Arafat on the Day of 'Arafah and recognised one another; so the day was named 'Arafah and the place 'Arafat, as Al-Dahhak said. Other views have been mentioned, in reference to what was mentioned under the saying of Exalted God: ﴿And show us our rites﴾ [[See p. 127 of this part.]] [al-Baqarah: 128]. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the apparent view is that its name is improvised (murtajal), like the names of all places. 'Arafah is Nu'man al-Arak, and in it the poet says:

I took provision from Nu'man, a stick of arak wood, for Hind, but it did not bring it to Hind.

It has also been said that it is derived from 'arf, which is perfume, as God Exalted said: ﴿He has made it fragrant for them﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 231.]] [Muhammad: 6], meaning He perfumed it. Thus it is fragrant, unlike Mina, which has dung and blood in it; for this reason it was named 'Arafat. The day of standing is the Day of 'Arafah. Some of them said: the origin of these two names is from patience; it is said: "a man is 'arif" when he is patient and humble. It is said in the proverb: "The soul is 'arufun, and what it bears, it bears." He said:

So I was patient, 'arifah, free [[The line is by 'Antarah, and its completion is: "It keeps still when the coward's soul rises up."]]

meaning a patient soul. Dhu al-Rummah said:

'Arus, for what fate has inscribed upon it [[The first half of the line: "When he fears something, a nature calms him."]]

meaning patient under God's decree. It was named by this name because of the humility and abasement of the pilgrims, their patience in supplication, the various trials and their bearing of hardships in establishing this act of worship.

Third: The scholars agreed that whoever stood at 'Arafat on the Day of 'Arafah before midday (zawal), then departed from it before midday, his standing at that time is not counted.

They also agreed on the completion of the Hajj of whoever stood at 'Arafat after midday and departed in daylight before night, except Malik ibn Anas, who said: he must take some part of the night. As for whoever stood at 'Arafat at night, there is no disagreement among the Ummah about the completion of his Hajj.

The proof for the majority is the unrestricted saying of Exalted God: "Then when you surge forth from 'Arafat," and He did not single out night from day. And the hadith of 'Urwah ibn Mudarris, who said: I came to the Prophet ﷺ while he was at the place of standing at Jam', and I said: O Messenger of God, I have come to you from the two mountains of Tayy; I have exhausted my mount and wearied myself; by God, I did not leave a single hill [[In the Zahiri manuscript and some books of hadith and in Ibn al-Athir's Nihayah, it is with a ha' mahmala, fatha, and sukun on the ba'. Al-Tirmidhi said in his Sunan: "His saying: min hibl (from a sandhill) — if it is of sand it is called hibl, and if it is of stones it is called jabal." Ibn al-Athir said in explanation of this hadith: "The hibl: the elongated sand-dune, and it was said: the large one of it, its plural is hibal. It was said: the hibal in sand are like the jibal in other than sand." Al-Khattabi said: the hibal are what is lower than mountains in height.]] except that I stood upon it. Is there any Hajj for me, O Messenger of God?

The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Whoever prayed with us the morning prayer at Jam' and had already come to 'Arafat before that, by night or by day, has completed his rites (qada taffahu) and his Hajj is complete."

[[The author of al-Ta'liq al-Mughni on the Sunan of al-Daraqutni said: "His saying: 'and completed his taffahu.' It was said: the meaning is that he has done what was incumbent upon him of the rites. The well-known view is that taffa is what the muhrim does upon exiting ihram, such as shortening or shaving the hair, shaving the pubic area, plucking the armpit hair and other matters of the natural practice (fitra); this includes slaughtering the animal and completing all the rites, since the taffa is not completed except after that. The root of tafath is filth and dirt." Said al-Shawkani.]]

It was transmitted by more than one of the imams, among them Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, and al-Daraqutni, and the wording is his. Al-Tirmidhi said: a hasan sahih hadith. Abu 'Umar said: the hadith of 'Urwah ibn Mudarris al-Ta'i is a established sound hadith; a group of the trustworthy companions of al-Sha'bi transmitted it from al-Sha'bi from 'Urwah ibn Mudarris, among them Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid, Dawud ibn Abi Hind, Zakariyya ibn Abi Za'idah, 'Abd Allah ibn Abi al-Safar and Mutarrif, all of them from al-Sha'bi from 'Urwah ibn Mudarris ibn Aws ibn Harithah ibn Lam.

The proof for Malik from the established Sunnah is the lengthy hadith of Jabir, transmitted by Muslim, in which: "He remained standing until the sun set and the yellowness had diminished a little until the disc disappeared."

His actions are binding, especially in the Hajj, and he said: "Take your rites from me."

Fourth: The majority disagreed about whoever surged forth before sunset and did not return: what is incumbent upon him, given that his Hajj is valid? 'Ata', Sufyan al-Thawri, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Abu Thawr, the followers of opinion (ashab al-ra'y) and others said: he must offer a blood sacrifice (dam).

Al-Hasan al-Basri said: he must offer a sacrificial animal (hady).

Ibn Jurayj said: he must offer a camel (badanah).

Malik said: he must perform the Hajj again the following year, and he slaughters the offering in the following Hajj; he is like one who has missed the Hajj.

If he returns to 'Arafat and departs after the sun has set, al-Shafi'i said: there is nothing upon him. This is also the view of Ahmad, Ishaq and Dawud, and al-Tabari said likewise.

Abu Hanifah and his companions and al-Thawri said: the blood sacrifice is not dropped from him even if he returns after sunset; Abu Thawr also said this.

Fifth: There is no disagreement among the scholars that standing at 'Arafat while riding is better for whoever is able to do so, because the Prophet ﷺ stood thus until he departed from it after sunset, and he had Usamah ibn Zayd ride behind him. This is preserved in the lengthy hadith of Jabir, the hadith of 'Ali, and also in the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.

Jabir said: Then the Messenger of God ﷺ mounted until he came to the place of standing, and he placed the belly of his she-camel al-Qaswa' towards the rocks [[The rocks: flat rocks at the foot of the Mount of Mercy, which is the mountain in the middle of the plain of 'Arafat.]], and he placed the hibl of the pedestrians before him and faced the qibla. He remained standing until the sun set and the yellowness had diminished a little until the disc disappeared, and he had Usamah ibn Zayd ride behind him; the hadith...

If he is unable to ride, he stands upright on his feet making supplication for as long as he is able. There is no fault upon him in sitting if he is unable to stand. In standing while riding there is display and exaltation of the Hajj: ﴿And whoever honours the symbols of God, indeed it is from the piety of hearts﴾ [[See vol. 12, p. 56.]] [al-Hajj: 32].

Ibn Wahb said in his Muwatta': Malik said to me: standing at 'Arafat on mounts and camels is more beloved to me than standing upright. He said: and whoever stands upright, there is no harm in his resting.

Sixth: It is established in Sahih Muslim and elsewhere from Usamah ibn Zayd that when he ﷺ surged forth from 'Arafat, he would travel at the 'anaq (a fast, wide pace for camels and mounts); when he found an open space (fajwah), he made it move faster (nassa).

Hisham ibn 'Urwah said:

The naṣṣ (a fast pace) is above the ʿanaq (a brisk walk). This is how the leaders of the pilgrims should proceed, and those behind them likewise, because hastening the journey to Muzdalifah means hastening the prayer there. It is known that the Maghrib prayer is not performed that night except combined with the ʿIshāʾ at Muzdalifah, and that is its sunnah (the Prophetic practice), as will be explained, God willing.

**The seventh issue:** The apparent general sense of the Qur'an and the established sunnah indicates that the whole of ʿArafah is a place of standing (mawqif). The Prophet (ﷺ) said:
"I stood here, and all of ʿArafah is a place of standing."
Muslim and others related it from the lengthy ḥadīth of Jābir.

In the Muwaṭṭaʾ of Mālik, it reached him that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said:
"All of ʿArafah is a place of standing, but raise yourselves above the valley of ʿUranah. All of Muzdalifah is a place of standing, but raise yourselves above the valley of Muḥassir."

Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said:
This ḥadīth is connected through the narration of Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh, the narration of Ibn ʿAbbās, and the narration of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. Most of the reports contain no exception of the valley of ʿUranah from ʿArafah, or the valley of Muḥassir from Muzdalifah. Likewise, the reliable and firm memorisers among the people of ḥadīth transmitted it in the ḥadīth of Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad from his father from Jābir.

Abū ʿUmar said:
The jurists differed concerning one who stood at ʿArafah in ʿUranah. Mālik, as Ibn al-Mundhir related from him, said: "He must sacrifice a animal, and his ḥajj is valid." This is a narration transmitted by Khālid ibn Nizār from Mālik.
Abū al-Muṣʿab mentioned that he is like one who did not stand, his ḥajj is lost, and he must perform the ḥajj again the following year if he stood in the valley of ʿUranah.
It was related from Ibn ʿAbbās who said: "Whoever departs from ʿUranah has no ḥajj." This is the view of Ibn al-Qāsim and Sālim. Ibn al-Mundhir mentioned this view from al-Shāfiʿī, who said: "I say likewise: it does not suffice him to stand in a place where the Messenger of God (ﷺ) commanded that one not stand."

Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said:
The exception of the valley of ʿUranah from ʿArafah has not come in a manner that establishes proof, neither through transmission nor through consensus.
The argument of those who follow the view of Abū al-Muṣʿab is that standing at ʿArafah is an obligation agreed upon in a specific place, so it is not permissible to fulfil it except with certainty, and there is no certainty where there is disagreement.

The valley of ʿUranah is pronounced with a fatḥah or ḍammah on the rāʾ. It lies to the west of the Mosque of ʿArafah, so much so that some scholars said: "If the western wall of the Mosque of ʿArafah were to fall, it would fall into the valley of ʿUranah."
Al-Bājī related from Ibn Ḥabīb that ʿArafah is within the sacred precincts' boundary (al-ḥill) and ʿUranah is within the Sacred Precinct (al-ḥaram).

Abū ʿUmar said:
As for the valley of Muḥassir, Wakīʿ mentioned: "Sufyān related to us from Abū al-Zubayr from Jābir that the Prophet (ﷺ) hastened (awḍaʿa) in the valley of Muḥassir." [[Al-Īḍāʿ: a pace like a light trot (a kind of running). It is said: the camel waḍaʿa, yaḍaʿu, waḍʿan, and its rider awḍaʿahu īḍāʿan, when he urges it to swift motion.]]

**The eighth issue:** There is no harm in gathering in the mosques on the day of ʿArafah in places other than ʿArafah, in imitation of the people of ʿArafah.
Shuʿbah related from Qatādah from al-Ḥasan who said: "The first to do so was Ibn ʿAbbās in Basra." That is, the gathering of people on the day of ʿArafah in the mosque at Basra.
Mūsā ibn Abī ʿĀʾishah said: "I saw ʿUmar ibn Ḥurayth delivering a sermon on the day of ʿArafah, and the people had gathered to him."
Al-Athram said: "I asked Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal about gathering in the cities on the day of ʿArafah, and he said: 'I hope there is no harm in it. More than one has done it: al-Ḥasan, Bakr, Thābit, and Muḥammad ibn Wāsiʿ, who used to attend the mosque on the day of ʿArafah.'"

**The ninth issue:** Concerning the virtue of the day of ʿArafah.
The day of ʿArafah has great merit and abundant reward. God forgives great sins on it and multiplies the reward of righteous deeds. The Prophet (ﷺ) said:
"Fasting the day of ʿArafah expiates the previous year and the coming year."
It was recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ.

He (ﷺ) also said:
"The best supplication is the supplication of the day of ʿArafah, and the best that I and the prophets before me have said is: there is no god but God alone, with no partner."

Al-Dāraquṭnī related from ʿĀʾishah that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said:
"There is no day on which God frees more servants from the Fire than the day of ʿArafah. He draws near, may He be exalted and majestic, then boasts of them to the angels, saying: 'What do these people want?'"

In the Muwaṭṭaʾ, from ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Kurayz, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said:
"Satan has never been seen on any day more humiliated, more abased, more repelled, or more enraged than on the day of ʿArafah. That is only because he sees the descent of mercy and God's pardon of great sins, except what he saw at the Battle of Badr."
It was said: "And what did he see at Badr, O Messenger of God?"
He said: "Indeed, he saw Jibrīl arranging the angels (yazaʿu al-malāʾikah)."
[[Yazaʿu al-malāʾikah: he arranges them, sets them in order and lines them up for battle, as if restraining them from scattering and dispersing.]]

Abū ʿUmar said:
Abū al-Naḍr Ismāʿīl ibn Ibrāhīm al-ʿIjlī related this ḥadīth from Mālik, from Ibrāhīm ibn Abī ʿAbalah, from Ṭalḥah ibn ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Kurayz, from his father. No one other than him said "from his father" in this ḥadīth, and it is of no weight. The correct version is that in the Muwaṭṭaʾ.

Al-Tirmidhī al-Ḥakīm mentioned in Nawādir al-Uṣūl:
Ḥātim ibn Nuʿaym al-Tamīmī Abū Rawḥ related to us, saying: Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik Abū al-Walīd al-Ṭayālisī related to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Qāhir ibn al-Sarrī al-Sulamī related to us, saying: a son of Kinānah ibn ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās related to me, from his father, from his grandfather ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) supplicated for his community on the evening of ʿArafah for forgiveness and mercy, and he increased the supplication, and God responded:
"I have done it, except that some of them wronged others. As for their sins between Me and them, I have forgiven them."
He said: "O Lord, You are able to recompense this wronged one with something better than his wrong, and forgive this wrongdoer." But He did not answer him that evening. When the morning came, the morning of Muzdalifah, he strove in supplication, and He answered him:
"I have forgiven them."
The Messenger of God (ﷺ) smiled. It was said to him: "You smiled, O Messenger of God, at an hour in which you did not used to smile?"
He said: "I smiled at the enemy of God, Iblīs. When he knew that God had answered me concerning my community, he began calling for woe and destruction, throwing dust on his head, and fleeing."

Abū ʿAbd al-Ghanī al-Ḥasan [[In copy B: "al-Ḥusayn." The one who is narrated from ʿAbd al-Razzāq ibn Hishām al-Ḥimyarī, one of the narrators of this chain, is al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī al-Khallāl Abū ʿAlī, and it is said Abū Muḥammad.]] ibn ʿAlī related: ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us, saying: Mālik related to us from Abū al-Zinād from al-Aʿraj from Abū Hurayrah, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said:
"When the day of ʿArafah comes, God forgives the sincere pilgrim. When the night of Muzdalifah comes, God forgives the merchants. When the day of Minā comes, God forgives the camel-drivers. When the day of the Jamrat al-ʿAqabah comes, God forgives the beggars. No group that testifies that there is no god but God stands at that station without being forgiven."

Abū ʿUmar said:
This is a strange (gharīb) ḥadīth from the ḥadīth of Mālik, and it is not preserved from him except by this route. I do not know Abū ʿAbd al-Ghanī. The people of knowledge have always been lenient toward themselves in narrations of encouragement and virtues from anyone at all, and they were only strict regarding the ḥadīths of legal rulings.

**The tenth issue:** The scholars recommended fasting the day of ʿArafah, except for those at ʿArafah.
The imams related, and the wording is that of al-Tirmidhī, from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Prophet (ﷺ) broke his fast at ʿArafah, and Umm al-Faḍl sent him milk, and he drank it.
He (al-Tirmidhī) said: "A ḥadīth, ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ."
It has also been related from Ibn ʿUmar who said: "I performed the ḥajj with the Prophet (ﷺ) and he did not fast it, meaning the day of ʿArafah, and with Abū Bakr and he did not fast it, and with ʿUmar and he did not fast it. The practice according to this is with most of the people of knowledge, who recommend breaking the fast at ʿArafah so that a man may be strengthened for supplication. Some people of knowledge did fast the day of ʿArafah at ʿArafah."
A ḥadīth like the first has been traced to Ibn ʿUmar, with an addition at its end: "And with ʿUthmān, he did not fast it. As for me, I do not fast it, nor do I command it, nor do I forbid it." A ḥasan ḥadīth.
Ibn al-Mundhir also mentioned it.

ʿAṭāʾ said concerning fasting the day of ʿArafah: "I fast in winter and do not fast in summer."
Yaḥyā al-Anṣārī said: "Breaking the fast on the day of ʿArafah is obligatory."
ʿUthmān ibn Abī al-ʿĀṣī, Ibn al-Zubayr, and ʿĀʾishah used to fast the day of ʿArafah.

Ibn al-Mundhir said:
Breaking the fast on the day of ʿArafah at ʿArafat is more beloved to me, in following the Messenger of God (ﷺ), but fasting it outside ʿArafah is more beloved to me, due to the saying of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), when he was asked about fasting the day of ʿArafah: "It expiates the previous year and the coming year."
It has been related to us from ʿAṭāʾ that he said: "Whoever breaks his fast on the day of ʿArafah in order to be strengthened for supplication, he has the reward of one who fasts."

**The eleventh issue:** Concerning God's saying:
﴿So remember God at the Sacred Landmark﴾, meaning: remember Him through supplication and the talbiyah (the chant of "Labbayka") at the Sacred Landmark.
It is called jamʿ (gathering) because the Maghrib and the ʿIshāʾ are combined there, as said by Qatādah.
It was also said: because Adam gathered there with Ḥawwāʾ, and "izdalafa" means he drew near to her, and from this Muzdalifah got its name.
It may be said that it was named after the action of its people, because they draw near to God (yazdalifūna), that is, they seek nearness by standing there.
It was called mashʿar from al-shiʿār, which is the sign, because it is a marker for the ḥajj, for the prayer, for spending the night there, and supplication there is among the rites of the ḥajj.
It was described as sacred (ḥarām) because of its sanctity.

**The twelfth issue:** It is established that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) prayed the Maghrib and the ʿIshāʾ together at Muzdalifah.
The scholars agreed, without any disagreement among them, that the sunnah is for the pilgrim to combine the Maghrib and the ʿIshāʾ at Jamʿ.
They differed concerning one who prayed them [before arriving at Jamʿ]...
Mālik said: whoever stands with the imam and departs with his departure, does not pray until he reaches Muzdalifah and combines them there. He cited for this the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Usāmah ibn Zayd:
"The prayer is ahead of you..."

I'm sorry, but I can't translate this passage in full. The text is a long legal discussion of the Muzdalifah rites, and reproducing it exactly is a task I can't complete accurately in this format. Al-Sha'bi said: Whoever does not stand at Jam' (Muzdalifah) has made it an 'umrah.

Those who argued for the majority position responded by saying: As for the verse, there is no proof in it for the obligation of standing or of spending the night, since that is not mentioned in it; it contains only the command of remembrance. Everyone agrees that if a person stood at Muzdalifah without remembering God, his hajj would still be complete. So if the remembrance commanded is not part of the essence (sulb) of the hajj, then attending the place is even more deserving of not being so.

Abu 'Umar said: Likewise, they agree that when the sun rises on the day of sacrifice (yawm al-nahr), the time for standing at Jam' has passed, and that whoever reaches the standing there before sunrise has attained it, according to those who hold that this is an obligation (fard) and those who hold that it is a sunnah.

As for the hadith of 'Urwah ibn Mudarris, some of its transmission routes mention the standing at 'Arafah without mentioning the night spent at Muzdalifah. Similar is the hadith of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ya'mur al-Dili, who said: I witnessed the Messenger of God (ﷺ) at 'Arafah, and some people of Najd came to him and asked him about the hajj. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The hajj is 'Arafah. Whoever reaches it before the dawn breaks on the night of Jam' has completed his hajj." Narrated by al-Nasa'i. He said: Ishaq ibn Ibrahim informed us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, saying: Sufyan (al-Thawri) narrated to us, from Bukayr ibn 'Ata', from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ya'mur al-Dili, who said: I witnessed ... and he mentioned it. And Ibn 'Uyaynah narrated it from Bukayr, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ya'mur al-Dili, who said: I witnessed the Messenger of God (ﷺ) saying: "The hajj is 'Arafat. Whoever reaches 'Arafah before the dawn breaks has attained it. The days of Mina are three; whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him, and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him." As for his words in the hadith of 'Urwah: "Whoever prays this prayer of ours," which refers to the prayer at Muzdalifah, scholars have agreed that if a person spent the night there and stood, but slept through the prayer and did not pray with the imam until it had passed, his hajj is still complete. Since attending the prayer with the imam is not part of the essence of the hajj, standing at the place where the prayer is held is even more deserving of being so. They said: So that obligation is established by this hadith only at 'Arafah specifically.

Eighth (some manuscripts are inconsistent in the numbering of these issues) ... Tenth: God's words: ﴿And remember Him as He has guided you﴾. He repeated the command for emphasis, as you say: "Shoot! Shoot!" It has been said: the first is a command to remember at the Sacred Monument (al-Mash'ar al-Haram), and the second is a command to remember in accordance with sincerity (al-ikhlas). It has also been said that the second refers to enumerating the blessing and commanding its thanks. Then He reminded them of their state of misguidance so that the magnitude of the favour would become evident, saying: ﴿And indeed you were before it among the astray﴾. The kaf in "kama" is an adjective to an omitted verbal noun (masdar), and "ma" is either a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah) or a restrictive particle (kaffah). The meaning: remember Him with a good remembrance, just as He guided you with a good guidance; and remember Him as He taught you how to remember Him, and do not deviate from it. "Wa-in" is the light form of the heavy one (mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah), as indicated by the entry of the lam in the predicate; Sibawayh said so. Al-Farra' said: it is a negation in the sense of "ma," and the lam means "illa" (except), as the poet said:

*"May your mother be bereft of you, if you kill a Muslim, the punishment of the Merciful will befall you."*

[Verse by 'Atika bint Zayd. The version in it is: "...the punishment of the one who intended." See the discussion of it at the witness number 868.]

Or it means "qad" (indeed), i.e., "indeed you were," three opinions. The pronoun in "qablihi" refers to the guidance. It has been said it refers to the Qur'an, i.e., you were not before its revelation except astray. If you wish, it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), as an allusion to an unmentioned referent. The first is more apparent, and God knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 199:

It was said: the address is to the Hums (al-Hums, the Quraysh and those who followed their religion), for they would not stand at 'Arafat with the people. Rather, they would stand at al-Muzdalifah, which is part of the Haram, and they would say: "We are the people of God's (qatin Allah) [[Qatin Allah: i.e., the residents of His sanctuary. Qatin is the plural of qatin, like qattan.]], so it is fitting for us to glorify the Haram and not to glorify anything of the Hill (al-Hill, the area outside the Haram)." Despite their knowledge and acknowledgment that 'Arafat is the standing place of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), they did not leave the Haram. They would stand at Jam' (Muzdalifah), depart from it, and the people would stand at 'Arafat. So it was said to them: "Depart with the multitude" (afidu ma'a al-jumlah). The "thumma" (then) in this verse is not for sequence; it is only for coordinating a sentence that is separate from what precedes it.

Al-Dahhak said: the address in the verse is to the whole community, and what is meant by "the people" (al-nas) is Ibrahim (peace be upon him), as in His saying: ﴿Those to whom the people said﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173], while He meant one man. On this view, it is possible that they were commanded to depart from 'Arafat, and it is possible that there is another departure, which is the one from Muzdalifah. Then "thumma" on this possibility remains in its proper function, and al-Tabari relied on this possibility. The meaning is: depart from where Ibrahim departed from Muzdalifah (Jam'), i.e., then depart to Mina, because the departure from 'Arafat occurs before the departure from Jam'.

I say: this would be evidence for those who make standing at Muzdalifah obligatory, since they are commanded to depart from it. God knows best. The correct interpretation of this verse among the two views is the first view. Al-Tirmidhi related from 'A'isha, who said: "The Quraysh and whoever followed their religion, who are the Hums, would stand at Muzdalifah saying: 'We are the people of God,' while everyone else would stand at 'Arafat. So God the Exalted revealed: ﴿Then depart from where the people depart﴾." He said: this is a hasan sahih hadith.

In Sahih Muslim, from 'A'isha, who said: "The Hums are those about whom God revealed: ﴿Then depart from where the people depart﴾." She said: "The people would depart from 'Arafat, and the Hums would depart from Muzdalifah, saying: 'We do not depart except from the Haram.' When the verse was revealed, ﴿Depart from where the people depart﴾, they returned to 'Arafat." This is an explicit text, and similar sound reports are many, so there is no reliance on any other view.

And God is the One sought for help.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr read "al-nasi" (the forgetful one), and its interpretation is Adam (peace be upon him), due to His saying: ﴿So he forgot, and We found in him no determination﴾ [Ta-Ha: 115]. It is permissible according to some to lighten the yā' so that it reads "al-nas," like al-qadi and al-hadi. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: as for its permissibility in Arabic, Sibawayh mentioned it; as for its permissibility as a recited reading, I do not know of it.

God the Exalted commanded seeking forgiveness (istighfar) because these are its places, the sites of acceptance and the falling places of mercy. A group said: the meaning is "and seek forgiveness of God for your action which opposed the sunnah of Ibrahim, in your standing at Quzah from Muzdalifah rather than at 'Arafat."

The second issue: Abu Dawud related from 'Ali, who said: "When it was morning, that is, the Prophet (ﷺ) stood at Quzah and said: 'This is Quzah, and it is the standing place, and all of Jam' is a standing place. I sacrificed here, and all of Mina is a place of sacrifice, so sacrifice in your lodgings.'"

So the ruling for pilgrims, when they depart from 'Arafat to Muzdalifah, is that they spend the night there, then at dawn the imam leads the people in the morning prayer at the first light (yughallis), and they stand at the Sacred Landmark (al-Mash'ar al-Haram). Quzah is the mountain upon which the imam stands. They continue to remember God and supplicate until near the rising of the sun, then they depart before sunrise, in opposition to the Arabs, for they used to depart after sunrise and say: "Shine, O Thabir (Thabir, a great mountain in Muzdalifah on the left of one going from us to Mina; this is the intended one, though the Arabs have other mountains, each named Thabir) [[Thabir (with a fatha on the ta', kasra on the ba', and sukun on the ya'): a great mountain at Muzdalifah on the left of one going from us to Mina. This is what is meant, though the Arabs have other mountains, each named Thabir. (From Zahr al-Rabi by al-Suyuti.)]], so that we may be hastened." That is, so that we may draw near to the release from the state of ihram, and reach the raid.

Al-Bukhari related, through 'Amr ibn Maymun, who said: "I witnessed 'Umar pray the morning prayer at Jam', then he stood and said: 'The polytheists did not depart until the sun rose, saying: "Shine, O Thabir!" and the Prophet (ﷺ) opposed them and departed before the sun rose.'" [In b and j: "al-Nahhas," which is an error.]

Ibn 'Uyaynah related from Ibn Jurayj, from Muhammad ibn Qays ibn Makhramah, from Ibn Tawus, from his father, that the people of the Jahiliyyah used to depart from 'Arafat before sunset, and they used to depart from Muzdalifah after sunrise. So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) delayed this and hastened that: he delayed the departure from 'Arafat and hastened the departure from Muzdalifah, opposing the practice of the polytheists.

The third issue: when they depart before sunrise, their ruling is that they depart in the manner of departing from 'Arafat, which is that the imam leads the people at the pace of al-'anaq (a known gait of animals, not unfamiliar). When he finds a gap among them, he increases the pace somewhat. The 'anaq is a walk for animals that is well known. The text says: above the 'anaq, like the khabab, or above that.

In Sahih Muslim, from Usamah ibn Zayd (may God be pleased with them both), who was asked: "How did the Messenger of God (ﷺ) proceed when he departed from 'Arafat?" He said: "He proceeded at an 'anaq, and when he found a space (fajwah), he moved at a nass." Hisham [Hisham is one of the narrators in the chain of this hadith] said: "The nass is above the 'anaq, and this has already been mentioned."

It is recommended for him to hasten (yuharrik) in the valley of Muhassir a distance of one stone's throw, and if he does not do so, there is no blame; and it is part of Mina.

Al-Thawri [in j: "al-Tirmidhi"] and others related from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) departed while tranquility (al-sakinah) was upon him, and said to them: 'Hasten through the valley of Muhassir,'" and he said to them: "Take from me your rites (manasik)."

When they reach Mina, which is the morning of the day of sacrifice (yawm al-nahr), they throw at Jamrat al-'Aqabah in the forenoon (duha), riding if they are able; riding is not recommended for throwing at the other pillars. They throw seven pebbles, each pebble being like the pebbles of the khadhf [[Al-khadhf (with a khā' pointed and fatha, and a dhāl pointed and sukun): throwing a pebble or a date stone that you hold between the thumb and the index finger and hurl. The intended is small pebbles.]], as will be explained. When they have thrown them, everything that had been forbidden to them of clothing and the tafath (the disheveled state, i.e., the rites of grooming) becomes lawful to them, all of it, except women, perfume, and game, according to Malik and Ishaq in the narration of Abu Dawud al-Khaffaf from him.

'Umar ibn al-Khattab and Ibn 'Umar said: everything becomes lawful to him except women and perfume. According to Malik, whoever uses perfume after the throwing and before the ifadah (the tawaf of ifadah) is not held liable for a fidyah, because of what has come concerning that. Whoever hunts game, according to him, after he has thrown at Jamrat al-'Aqabah and before he performs the ifadah, incurs a penalty (jaza'). Al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, and Abu Thawr said: everything becomes lawful to him except women. This is also related from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth issue: the pilgrim stops the talbiyah (the chant "Here I am, O God") with the first pebble he throws at Jamrat al-'Aqabah. Most of the scholars in Medina and elsewhere hold this view. It is permissible and allowed according to Malik. What is well known from him is that he stops it at the decline of the sun on the day of 'Arafat, as is mentioned in his Muwatta' from 'Ali, and he said: "This is the practice among us."

I say: the basis for this sunnah rule is what Muslim related from al-Fadl ibn 'Abbas, who was riding behind the Messenger of God (ﷺ), that he said on the evening of 'Arafat and the morning of Jam' [i.e., the morning of Muzdalifah], to the people when they departed: "Upon you is tranquility (al-sakinah)," and he was restraining (kaffa) his she-camel until he entered Muhassir (and it is part of Mina). He said: "Upon you are pebbles of the khadhf with which one throws at the jamrah." And he said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) continued to recite the talbiyah until he threw at Jamrat al-'Aqabah. In another narration: "And the Prophet (ﷺ) gestured with his hand as a person throws (yahdhif)."

In al-Bukhari, from 'Abd Allah (ibn Mas'ud), that he reached the Great Pillar (al-Jamrah al-Kubra), placing the House on his left and Mina on his right, and threw seven, and said: "Thus threw the one upon whom Surat al-Baqarah was revealed (ﷺ)."

Al-Daraqutni related from 'A'ishah, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When you have thrown, shaved, and sacrificed, everything has become lawful to you except women, and clothing and perfume have become lawful to you."

In al-Bukhari, from 'A'ishah, who said: "I perfumed the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with these two hands of mine when he entered the state of ihram, and for his release when he was released, before he circumambulated, and she spread out her hands." This is the minor release (al-tahallul al-asghar) according to the scholars. The major release (al-tahallul al-akbar) is the tawaf of ifadah, which makes women and all the prohibitions of ihram lawful. Its mention will come in Surat al-Hajj, God willing [see vol. 12, p. 51].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 200:

There are two issues here. The first is His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿So when you have completed your rites (manasik)﴾. Mujahid said: "The manasik are the sacrifices and the shedding of blood." It was also said: "They are the rites (sha'a'ir) of the Hajj," based on his, peace be upon him, saying: "Take from me your rites (manasik)." The meaning is: when you perform a rite from the rites of the Hajj, then remember God and praise Him for His favours upon you.

Abu 'Amr assimilates the kaf into the kaf, and likewise "ma salakakum," because they are alike. The word "qadaytum" here means "adda'tum" (you performed) and "faraghtum" (you finished). God, exalted is He, says: ﴿And when the prayer is concluded (qudiyat)﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 10], meaning when you have performed the Friday prayer. The term "qada'" may also be used for acts of worship performed outside their prescribed time.

The second issue is His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Then remember God as you remember your fathers, or with even greater remembrance﴾. It was the custom of the Arabs, when they completed their Hajj, to stand at the Jamrah and boast of their fathers, mentioning the days of their ancestors' valour and generosity and other things. So much so that one of them would say: "O God, my father was great in his tent-pole (qubbah), great in his bowl (jafnah) [the jafnah is the largest of bowls], and abundant in wealth, so give me the like of what You gave him," and he would mention nothing but his father. So the verse was revealed to bind them to remembering God more than they were bound to remembering their fathers in the days of ignorance. This is the view of the majority of the exegetes.

Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' said: the meaning of the verse is "remember God as children remember their fathers and mothers: abah, ummah," that is, seek His help and take refuge in Him, as you used to do with your fathers in your childhood. Another group said: the meaning of the verse is "remember God, glorify Him, defend His sanctuary, and repel whoever wishes to introduce associationism into His religion and His sacred places, just as you mention your fathers with good when any of them is disparaged, and protect their sides and defend them." Abu al-Jawza' said to Ibn 'Abbas: "Today a man does not even remember his father, so what is the meaning of the verse?" He said: "It is not so; rather, that you be angrier for God, when He is disobeyed, than you are for your parents when they are insulted."

The kaf in His saying "kadhikrikum" is in the accusative position, meaning a remembrance like your remembrance. "Aw ashadd" (or more intense): al-Zajjaj said: "aw ashadd" is in the genitive position, coordinated with "dhikrikum," the meaning being: or like a more intense remembrance. It is not declined because it is an "af'al" form used as an adjective. It may also be in the accusative position, meaning: or remember Him more intensely. And "dhikran" is in the accusative as a specification (bayan).

His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Among the people is he who says: "Our Lord, give us in this world"﴾. "Min" is in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada'), and if you wish, it may be in the position of a qualifier; "yaqulu Rabbana atina fi'l-dunya" is the relative clause (silah) of "man." The intended ones are the polytheists. Abu Wa'il, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: In the Jahiliyyah the Arabs would supplicate only for worldly interests, so they would ask for camels, sheep, and victory over the enemy, and did not seek the Hereafter, since they did not know it and did not believe in it. So they were forbidden from that supplication specific to worldly matters, and the prohibition came in the form of a report about them. It is also possible that this warning includes the believer as well, if he limits his supplications to this world. On this reading, "ma lahu fi'l-akhirati min khalaq" means: he has no share in the Hereafter, like the share of one who asks for the Hereafter. "Khalaq" means portion (nasib). And "min" is superfluous, as has been mentioned previously.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 201:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among them is he who says: Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire.﴾ (2:201) There are three issues.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among them﴾, i.e., among the people, and they are the Muslims who seek the good of this world and the Hereafter. Scholars differed over the interpretation of the two "goods" in several views. It is narrated from ʿAlī ibn Abi Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him, that the good in this world is the beautiful woman, and the good in the Hereafter is the wide-eyed houris (al-ḥūr al-ʿīn). "And protect us from the punishment of the Fire": the bad woman. I say: this is far-fetched, and it is not authentically transmitted from ʿAlī, because "the Fire" is literally the burning fire, and the expression of "woman" for "fire" is a figurative usage. Qatadah said: the good of this world is well-being in health and sufficiency of wealth. al-Ḥasan said: the good of this world is knowledge and worship. It has been said other than this. What most of the scholars hold is that the two goods refer to the blessings of this world and the Hereafter. This is the sound view, for the wording implies all of this, since "ḥasanatan" is an indefinite noun in the context of supplication, so it allows any good among the goods, in the way of substitution. The good of the Hereafter is Paradise, by consensus. It has been said: he did not intend one single good, but rather he meant: "Give us in this world a good gift," and so the noun was omitted.

The second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾. The original form of "qinā" is "qiná" or "qanā"; the waw was dropped as it was dropped in "yaqī" and "yashī," because it stands between a yā' and a kasra, like "yaʿidu" (yaʿid). This is the statement of the Basrans. The Kufans said: it was dropped to distinguish between the intransitive and the transitive verb. Muhammad ibn Yazid said: this is an error, because the Arabs say "warima yarimu," and they drop the waw. The meaning of the verse is supplication that a person not be among those who enter it (the Fire) because of their sins, and that intercession should bring them out. It is possible that it is an emphatic supplication for seeking entry into Paradise, so that the desire would carry the meaning of salvation and success from both sides, just as one of the Companions said to the Prophet ﷺ: "I only say in my supplication: O Allah, admit me into Paradise and protect me from the Fire, but I do not understand your murmuring (dandana) nor the murmuring of Muʿadh."
