So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: "Around it (ḥawlahā) we murmur." Abu Dawud recorded it in his Sunan, and Ibn Majah also.

[Footnote: Al-dandana: that a man speaks words whose tune is heard but whose meaning is not understood, and it is a little louder than al-hainama.]
[Footnote: In al-Sindi's commentary on Sunan Ibn Majah: "In some copies it is ḥawlahumā in the dual. According to the first, its meaning is: around your statement, i.e., our speech is close to your speech. According to the second, its meaning is: around Paradise and the Fire, i.e., our speech also seeks Paradise and seeks refuge from the Fire."]

The third: this verse is among the comprehensive supplications that encompass this world and the Hereafter. It was said to Anas: "Pray to Allah for us." He said: "O Allah, give us in this world a good, and in the Hereafter a good, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire." They said: "Add more for us." He said: "What do you want? I have asked for this world and the Hereafter!" In the Two Sahihs, from Anas, who said: The most frequent supplication with which the Prophet ﷺ used to supplicate was: "O Allah, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good and protect us from the punishment of the Fire." He said: So whenever Anas wished to supplicate with a supplication, he supplicated with it, and whenever he wished to supplicate with a supplication, he supplicated with it in it. In the hadith of ʿUmar, that he used to circumambulate the House saying: "Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good and protect us from the punishment of the Fire." It was his constant habit (hijrā) other than it, recorded by Abu ʿUbayd. Ibn Jurayj said: It reached me that he would command that the most frequent supplication of the Muslim at the station (of ʿArafat) be this verse: "Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good and protect us from the punishment of the Fire." Ibn ʿAbbas said: Indeed, near the Corner (al-Rukn) there is an angel standing since Allah created the heavens and the earth, saying "Amin." So say: "Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good and protect us from the punishment of the Fire." ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abi Rabah was asked about the Yemeni Corner while he was circumambulating the House, and ʿAṭāʾ said: Abu Hurayrah related to me that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Seventy angels are entrusted with it. Whoever says: O Allah, I ask You for pardon and well-being in this world and the Hereafter, our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good and protect us from the punishment of the Fire, they say: Amin." The hadith in full. Ibn Majah recorded it in the Sunan, and it will come in full with its chain in (the chapter on) al-Hajj, if Allah wills.

The second part of Tafsir al-Qurtubi is complete. The third part, God willing, follows, beginning with His words: "And remember God during the appointed days..." [the verse].

Third Part

[Continuation of the commentary on Surat al-Baqarah]

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 203 (part 1 of 4):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And remember Allah during appointed days﴾. In this verse there are six issues.

The first: The Kufans said: the alif and ta' in "ma'dudat" (appointed, counted) indicate the least number. The Basrans said: they indicate both few and many, as evidenced by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and they will be secure in the lofty chambers﴾ [Surah Saba', 37], and the lofty chambers are many. There is no disagreement among the scholars that the "appointed days" in this verse are the days of Mina, which are the days of tashriq (the days of drying meat after the sacrifice), and that these three names apply to them; they are also the days of stoning the jamarat (pillars), and they apply to the three days from which the pilgrim may hasten after two days following the day of sacrifice (al-nahr). So understand this. Al-Tha'labi [in some copies: "al-Thawri"] and Ibrahim said: the appointed days are the days of the ten, and the known days (al-ayyam al-ma'lumat) are the days of sacrifice (al-nahr). Likewise Makki and al-Mahdawi reported that the appointed days are the days of the ten. This is not sound, due to the consensus we have mentioned, as transmitted by Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr and others. Ibn 'Atiyya said: either this is an error in the copy, or he means the ten that come after the sacrifice, but that is far-fetched.

The second: Allah, glorified and exalted, commanded His servants to remember Him during the appointed days, which are the three days after the day of sacrifice. The day of sacrifice is not among them, because people agree that no one departs on the day of departure (al-nafr), which is the second day after the day of sacrifice. Had the day of sacrifice been among the appointed days, it would have been permissible for whoever wished to depart hastily on the day of departure, since he would have taken two days of the appointed days. Al-Daraqutni, al-Tirmidhi and others narrated from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ya'mar al-Dili that some people from the people of Najd came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was at 'Arafat and asked him, so he commanded a caller who called out: "The Hajj is 'Arafat. Whoever comes on the night of Jam' [Jam': a name for Muzdalifa] before the dawn has attained it. The days of Mina are three. Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him, and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him." That is, whoever of the pilgrims hastens in two days of the days of Mina, his stay in Mina becomes three days including the day of sacrifice, and his total stoning becomes forty-nine pebbles, and the stoning of the third day is dropped from him. And whoever does not depart from it except at the end of the third day, he has a stay in Mina of four days because of the day of sacrifice, and he completes the number in the stoning, as will be explained later.

Among the evidence that the days of Mina are three, in addition to what we have mentioned, is the saying of al-'Arji:

We do not meet except for three Minas,
until the departure separates us.

So the days of stoning are the appointed days, and the days of sacrifice are the known days. Nafi' narrated from Ibn 'Umar that the appointed days and the known days together comprise four days: the day of sacrifice and three days after it. So the day of sacrifice is known but not appointed, the two days after it are known and appointed, and the fourth day is appointed but not known. This is the school of Malik and others. It is so because the first (the day of sacrifice) is not among the days that are specific to Mina in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And remember Allah during appointed days﴾, nor among those that the Prophet (ﷺ) specified by his saying: "The days of Mina are three", so it was known. Because Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿and mention the name of Allah on known days over what He has provided for them of the livestock of the grazing animals﴾ [Surah al-Hajj, 28], and there is no disagreement that what is meant is the sacrifice (al-nahr). The sacrifice took place on the first day, which is the day of al-Adha, and the second and third. There was no sacrifice on the fourth by consensus of our scholars, so the fourth was not intended by His saying "known", since no sacrifice takes place on it, and it was among the days of stoning, so it became appointed due to the stoning, not known due to the absence of sacrifice in it.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: the reality regarding it is that the day of sacrifice is counted by the stoning and known by the slaughter, but according to our scholars it is not intended in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And remember Allah during appointed days﴾.

Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i said: the known days are the ten, from the first day of Dhu al-Hijjah, and their last is the day of sacrifice. Their statements on this did not differ, and they narrated this from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Tahawi narrated from Abu Yusuf that the known days are the days of sacrifice. Abu Yusuf said: this was narrated from 'Umar and 'Ali, and to it I incline, because He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿and mention the name of Allah on known days over what He has provided for them of the livestock of the grazing animals﴾. Al-Karkhi narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan that the known days are the three days of sacrifice: the day of al-Adha and two days after it. Al-Kiya al-Tabari said: according to the view of Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, there is no difference between the known and the appointed days, because the appointed days mentioned in the Qur'an are the days of tashriq without disagreement, and no one doubts that the appointed days do not include the ten days, because Allah, may He be exalted, says: ﴿So whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾, and in the ten there is no ruling connected to two days but not the third. It has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the known days are the ten and the appointed days are the days of tashriq, and this is the view of the majority.

I say: Ibn Zayd said: the known days are the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah and the days of tashriq. This is far-fetched, for what we have mentioned, and the apparent meaning of the verse refutes it. Allah's making the remembrance during the appointed and known days indicates against his view, so there is no point in occupying oneself with it.

The third: There is no disagreement that the one addressed by this remembrance is the pilgrim. He is addressed with the takbir (saying Allahu akbar) at the stoning of the pillars, and over what has been provided of the livestock on the known days, and after the prayers, without talbiyah. Is anyone other than the pilgrim included in this or not? The position of the jurists of the regions and the notable Companions and Successors is that the intended takbir is for everyone, especially at the times of the prayers, so one says takbir at the end of each prayer, whether one prays alone or in congregation, clearly during these days, following the predecessors, may Allah be pleased with them. In al-Mukhtasar: women do not say takbir after the prayers. The first view is more famous, because the rule of ihram applies to them as it does to men; this is what he said in al-Mudawwana.

The fourth: Whoever forgets the takbir after a prayer says it if it is close; if the time has elapsed, there is nothing upon him. This was said by Ibn al-Jallab. Malik said in al-Mukhtasar: he says takbir as long as he is in his place; when he rises from his place, there is nothing upon him. In al-Mudawwana, from the saying of Malik: if the imam forgets the takbir, and it is close, he sits and says takbir; if it has elapsed, there is nothing upon him; and if he leaves without saying it while the people are seated, let them say takbir.

The fifth: The scholars differed about the two limits of the period of takbir. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn 'Abbas said: one says takbir from the dawn prayer on the day of 'Arafat until the 'asr prayer on the last day of the days of tashriq. Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Hanifa said: one says takbir from the morning of 'Arafat until the 'asr prayer on the day of sacrifice. His two companions disagreed with him and said with the first view, the view of 'Umar, 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them; thus they agreed on the beginning but not the end. Malik said: one says takbir from the noon prayer on the day of sacrifice until the dawn prayer on the last day of the days of tashriq; al-Shafi'i also said this, and it is the view of Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas too. Zayd ibn Thabit said: one says takbir from noon on the day of sacrifice until the last day of the days of tashriq. Ibn al-'Arabi said: as for one who said: one says takbir on the day of 'Arafat and cuts it off at the 'asr of the day of sacrifice, he has departed from the apparent meaning, because Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿in appointed days﴾, and their days are three, and these people said: one says takbir for two days, so they left the apparent meaning without evidence. As for one who said the day of 'Arafat and the days of tashriq, he said: Allah said: ﴿when you pour forth from 'Arafat﴾, so the mention of 'Arafat is included in the mention of the days. This would be valid if He had said: one says takbir from maghrib on the day of 'Arafat, because the time of pouring forth is then; but before that, the apparent wording does not require it, and it would entail that it begins from the day of tarwiyah upon arrival at Mina.

The sixth: They differed about the wording of the takbir. The well-known position of Malik is that one says takbir after each prayer three times; this was narrated by Ziyad ibn Ziyad from Malik. In the school there is a report: after the three takbirs one says: "There is no god but Allah, and Allah is greatest, and to Allah belongs praise." In al-Mukhtasar from Malik: "Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, la ilaha illa Allah, wa Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar wa lillahi al-hamd."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾. In this there are twenty-one issues. The first: His saying, may He be exalted: "whoever hastens" (fa-man ta'ajjala). Hastening (al-ta'jil) is never here except at the end of the day, and likewise the third day, because the stoning on those days is only after the decline of the sun (zawal).

Allah ﷺ granted a concession to someone to throw before dawn rises, but it is not permissible to throw them before dawn. If he threw them before dawn, he must repeat them. Abu Hanifa and his companions said likewise: it is not permissible to throw them. Ahmad and Ishaq also said this.

A group allowed throwing before the rising of dawn. It is narrated from Asma' bint Abi Bakr that she used to throw at night and say: "We used to do this during the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." Abu Dawud recorded it. This view is also narrated from 'Ata', Ibn Abi Mulayka and 'Ikrima ibn Khalid, and al-Shafi'i held it if the throwing was after midnight.

Another group said: one does not throw until the sun rises. This was said by Mujahid, al-Nakha'i and al-Thawri. Abu Thawr said: if one throws before sunrise, then if the scholars disagree about it, it does not suffice him; but if they agree, or if there is a Sunnah concerning it, it suffices him.

Abu 'Umar (Ibn 'Abd al-Barr) said: As for the view of al-Thawri and those who follow him, their proof is that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ threw at the pillar after sunrise and said: "Take from me your rites" (khudhu 'anni manasikakum). Ibn al-Mundhir said: The Sunnah is that one should not throw except after sunrise, and throwing before the rising of dawn does not suffice; if one throws, he must repeat it, since the one who does so opposes what the Messenger ﷺ prescribed for his community. As for one who throws after dawn but before sunrise, there is no repetition for him, since I know of no one who said it does not suffice him.

The second matter: Ma'mar narrated, saying: Hisham ibn 'Urwa informed me, from his father, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered Umm Salama to be in Makkah in the morning of the day of sacrifice (yawm al-nahr), and that was her day.

Abu 'Umar said: The narration from Hisham has been reported differently. One group narrated it from Hisham, from his father, as a mursal report (one where the Companion is omitted), as Ma'mar did. Others narrated it from Hisham, from his father, from 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her), that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered Umm Salama accordingly, as a connected report (musnad). Others narrated it from Hisham, from his father, from Zaynab bint Abi Salama, from Umm Salama, also as a musnad report. All of them are trustworthy (thiqat). It indicates that she threw at the pillar in Mina before dawn, because the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered her to be in Makkah in the morning of the day of sacrifice, and this could only happen if she had thrown at the pillar in Mina at night before dawn. And Allah knows best.

Abu Dawud also narrated it: He said, Harun ibn 'Abd Allah narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Fudayk narrated to us, from al-Dahhak ibn 'Uthman, from Hisham ibn 'Urwa, from his father, from 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her), that she said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent Umm Salama on the night of the sacrifice, and she threw at the pillar before dawn, then went on and performed the ifada (the tawaf al-ifada), and that was the day on which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would be with her.

If this is established, then throwing at night is permissible for one who does it, but the preferred time is from sunrise until its decline (zawal).

Abu 'Umar said: The scholars agreed that the preferred time for throwing at the Jamrat al-'Aqaba is from sunrise until the sun declines. They also agreed that if one throws it before sunset on the day of sacrifice, it suffices him and there is nothing upon him, except Malik, who said: I recommend that if he leaves the Jamrat al-'Aqaba until evening, he should shed blood (a sacrifice) which he brings from the area outside the sacred precinct (al-hill).

They differed concerning one who did not throw until the sun set, then threw at night or the next day. Malik said: he owes a sacrifice (dam), arguing that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ set a time for throwing the pillar, which is the day of sacrifice; so whoever throws after sunset has thrown after its time has passed, and whoever does something in the Hajj after its time owes a sacrifice. Al-Shafi'i said: he owes no sacrifice. This is also the view of Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, and Abu Thawr said likewise, because the Prophet ﷺ was asked by a questioner: "O Messenger of Allah, I threw after I had reached the evening," and he said: "There is no blame (la haraj)."

Malik said: Whoever forgets to throw the pebbles until evening should throw whenever he remembers, by night or by day, just as one prays at whatever hour he remembers. He throws only what he missed specifically. If it was only one pillar, he throws it, then throws what comes after it of the pillars, for the order (tartib) among the pillars is obligatory (wajib). It is not permissible for him to begin throwing at one pillar until he completes throwing at the first one, like the units (rak'at) of prayer. This is the well-known position in the school. It was also said: the order is not obligatory for the validity of the throwing; rather, if the entire throwing is within the time of performance (al-ada'), it suffices him.

The third matter: When the days of throwing have passed, there is no more throwing. If he remembers after he has departed (yasdur) while he is in Makkah, or after he has left it, he owes a hady (sacrificial offering). Whether he left all the pebbles, or one pillar of them, or one pebble from a pillar, until the days of Mina have passed, he owes a dam. Abu Hanifa said: if he left all the pebbles, he owes a dam; if he left one pillar, then for each pebble from that pillar he owes feeding one poor person half a sa' (a measure), until it reaches the value of a dam, and then he feeds as much as he wishes; except for the Jamrat al-'Aqaba, for which he owes a dam. Al-Awza'i said: he gives charity if he leaves one pebble. Al-Thawri said: he feeds for one pebble, two pebbles or three, but if he leaves four or more, he owes a dam. Al-Layth said: for one pebble there is a dam, and this is one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i. The other opinion, which is the well-known one, is that for one pebble there is one mudd of food, for two pebbles two mudds, and for three pebbles there is a dam.

The fourth matter: According to all, there is no way to throw what one missed of the pillars during the days of tashriq after the sun has set on its last day, which is the fourth day after the day of sacrifice, and is the third of the days of tashriq. Rather, a dam or feeding suffices him, according to what we have mentioned.

The fifth matter: It is not permissible to spend the nights of tashriq away from Mina, whether in Makkah or elsewhere, for this is not permitted according to all, except for the herdsmen (ri'a') and for those in charge of the water supply (siqaya) from the family of al-'Abbas. Malik said: whoever leaves the night's stay on one of the nights of Mina, other than the herdsmen and the people of the water supply, owes a dam. Al-Bukhari narrated from Ibn 'Umar that al-'Abbas asked the Prophet ﷺ for permission to spend the nights of Mina in Makkah because of his water supply, and he granted him permission. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: al-'Abbas used to oversee the water supply and attend to its affairs, and give the pilgrims its drink during the days of the season. Therefore he was granted a concession to stay away from Mina, just as the herdsmen of camels were granted a concession because of their need to graze the camels and their necessity to take them out toward the pastures which are far from Mina.

Mina was called "Mina" because of the blood that is shed (yumna) there, that is, poured out (yuraq). Ibn 'Abbas said: It was called Mina only because Jibril said to Adam, peace be upon him: "Wish (tamanna)." He said: "I wish for Paradise," so it was called Mina. He said: It was called Jam' because Hawwa' and Adam, peace be upon them both, gathered there. Jam' is also Muzdalifa, and it is al-Mash'ar al-Haram, as has been mentioned previously (see vol. 2, p. 421).

The sixth matter: The jurists agreed that spending the nights in Mina, for pilgrims other than those granted the concession for the nights of Mina, is one of the rites and acts of worship of Hajj, and analogy requires that every one who forfeits this rite owes a dam, by analogy with the rest of the Hajj and its rites.

In the Muwatta' (of Malik): Malik narrated from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, who said: 'Umar said: "None of the pilgrims shall spend the nights of Mina beyond the 'Aqaba." The 'Aqaba that 'Umar forbade anyone from spending the night beyond is the 'Aqaba near the pillar which people throw on the day of sacrifice, on the side nearest Makkah. Ibn Nafi' narrated it from Malik in al-Mabsut. He said: Malik also said: Whoever spends the nights of Mina beyond it owes a fidya (ransom), because he spent the night outside Mina during the nights of Mina, and that is a required stay in Hajj, so a dam becomes obligatory for abandoning it, like the stay at Muzdalifa. The meaning of fidya here, according to Malik, is the hady. Malik said: It is an offering brought from the area outside the sacred precinct (al-hill) to the Haram.

The seventh matter: Malik narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr ibn Muhammad ibn 'Amr ibn Hazm, from his father, that Abu al-Baddah ibn 'Asim ibn 'Adi informed him that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ granted a concession to the herdsmen of camels to stay away from Mina, throwing on the day of sacrifice, then throwing on the next day, and for two days after that, then throwing on the day of departure (yawm al-nafr). (Note: in the Muwatta' and Ibn 'Abd al-Barr's al-Istidhkar: "that Abu al-Baddah ibn 'Asim ibn 'Adi informed him, from his father.")

Abu 'Umar said: Malik did not act according to the implication of this hadith. He used to say: They throw on the day of sacrifice, that is, the Jamrat al-'Aqaba, then they do not throw on the next day. When it is the day after that, which is the second of the days of tashriq, and it is the day on which one who wishes to hasten the departure (ta'jil al-nafr), or one for whom hastening is permitted, departs, they throw for two days: that day and the day before it, because they are making up what was due upon them, and no one makes up anything in his view except after it has become obligatory upon him. This is the meaning of what Malik explained of this hadith in his Muwatta'. Others say: There is no harm in all of that according to the hadith of Malik, because all of these are days of throwing. Malik only disallowed for the herdsmen bringing forward the throwing, because it is not permissible for other than the herdsmen to throw any of the pebbles during the days of tashriq before noon (zawal). If one throws before noon, he must repeat it; they have no right to bring it forward. They were only granted a concession for the second day until the third.

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: What Malik said on this question is found in the narration of Ibn Jurayj, who said: Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr ibn Muhammad ibn 'Amr ibn Hazm informed me, from his father, that Abu al-Baddah ibn 'Asim ibn 'Adi informed him that the Prophet ﷺ granted a concession to the herdsmen to take turns, so they would throw on the day of sacrifice, then leave one day and one night, then throw the next day.

Our scholars said: The throwing of the third pillar (al-jamra al-thalitha) falls away for one who hastens (ta'ajjala) his departure.

Ibn Abi Zamanin [he is Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Isa ibn Abi Zamanin al-Murri, from the people of Elvira (al-Bira), which is a town in al-Andalus.

(From al-Takmilah li-Kitab al-Silah.) He throws them on the first day of departure, when he intends to hasten. Ibn al-Mawwaz said: The one who hastens (al-mutaʿajjil) throws in two days twenty-one pebbles, seven at each jamrah, so that the total of his throwing is forty-nine pebbles, because he has already thrown seven at Jamrat al-ʿAqabah on the Day of Sacrifice. Ibn al-Mundhir said: The throwing of the third day falls away.

The Eighth: Malik narrated from Yahya ibn Saʿid, from ʿAta' ibn Abi Rabah, that he heard him mention that he (the Prophet) granted leniency to the herdsmen (al-ruʿaa') to throw at night, saying: "In the earliest time." Al-Baji said: "His saying 'in the earliest time' requires that it be understood as the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), because it is the first era of this sharia. On this basis it is a mursal report. It is also possible that he meant by it the earliest time that ʿAta' witnessed, in which case it is mawquf (a report from a companion) and musnad (with a continuous chain)." [In the commentary of al-Baji: "mawquf muttasil."] And Allah knows best.

I say: It is musnad from the hadith of ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet (ﷺ), which al-Daraqutni and others transmitted, and we have mentioned it in al-Muqtabis fi Sharh Muwatta' Malik ibn Anas. The herdsmen were permitted to throw at night only because it is easier for them and more cautious regarding what they undertake of herding camels, since the night is a time when they do not graze or disperse, so they throw at that time.

The scholars differed concerning the one who misses the throwing until the sun sets. ʿAta' said: There is no throwing at night except for camel herdsmen; as for merchants, no. It is narrated from Ibn ʿUmar that he said: Whoever misses the throwing until the sun sets, let him not throw until the sun rises the next day. Ahmad and Ishaq said likewise. Malik said: If he leaves it by day, he throws it at night, and upon him is a sacrifice (dam) according to the narration of Ibn al-Qasim, though he did not mention in the Muwatta' that a sacrifice is due. Al-Shafiʿi, Abu Thawr, Yaʿqub and Muhammad said: If he forgets the throwing until evening, he throws and there is no sacrifice upon him. Al-Hasan al-Basri used to grant leniency in throwing the pebbles at night. Abu Hanifa said: He throws and there is nothing upon him if he mentions it during the night; but if he does not mention it until the next day, then he must throw it and a sacrifice is due upon him. Al-Thawri said: If he delays the throwing until night, whether forgetfully or deliberately, he must sacrifice an animal.

I say: As for whoever among the herdsmen of camels or the people of the water-supply (ahl al-siqayah) throws at night, no sacrifice is obligatory, because of the hadith. If he is other than them, then analysis (al-nazar) requires a sacrifice, but only with deliberate intent. And Allah knows best.

The Ninth: It is established that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) threw Jamrat al-ʿAqabah on the Day of Sacrifice while mounted on his riding beast (raahilah). Malik and others recommended that the one who throws it be mounted. Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn al-Zubayr and Salim used to throw it on foot. He throws on each of the three days twenty-one pebbles, saying "Allahu akbar" with each pebble, and his face is toward the Kaʿbah while he throws. He keeps the jamarat in order, gathers them together, does not separate them, and does not reverse them: he begins with the first jamrah and throws it with seven pebbles, throwing (rami) and not placing (wada') them. Thus said Malik, al-Shafiʿi, Abu Thawr and the Ahl al-Ra'y. If he casts them (tarh) rather than throws, it is valid according to the Ahl al-Ra'y. Ibn al-Qasim said: It is not valid in either case, and this is the sound view, because the Prophet (ﷺ) used to throw it, and according to them he did not throw two or more pebbles at once; if he does so, he counts it as one pebble. When he finishes with it, he moves forward before it and stands for a long time to supplicate with whatever is easy for him. Then he throws the second, which is the middle one, and turns away from it to the left, into the valley bed (batn al-masil), and lengthens his standing at it for supplication. Then he throws the third, at the place of Jamrat al-ʿAqabah, with seven pebbles as well; he throws it from its bottom and does not stand there. If he throws it from above it, it suffices him. In all of this he says "Allahu akbar" with each pebble he throws. The sunnah of remembrance in throwing the jamarat is takbir alone, without other remembrance. He throws them on foot, unlike the Jamrat of the Day of Sacrifice. All of this is a tawqif (a matter known only from revelation), raised by al-Nasa'i and al-Daraqutni from al-Zuhri that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used, when he threw the jamrah nearest the mosque (masjid Mina), to throw it with seven pebbles, saying "Allahu akbar" with each pebble he threw; then he moved forward before it and stood facing the qiblah with his hands raised, supplicating, and he would lengthen the standing. Then he came to the second jamrah and threw it with seven pebbles, saying "Allahu akbar" with each pebble; then he descended to the left, toward the side of the valley, and stood facing the qiblah with his hands raised, then supplicated. Then he came to the jamrah at the ʿAqabah and threw it with seven pebbles, saying "Allahu akbar" with each pebble, then he turned away and did not stand there. Al-Zuhri said: I heard Salim ibn ʿAbd Allah narrate this from his father, from the Prophet (ﷺ). He said: And Ibn ʿUmar used to do it. This is the wording of al-Daraqutni.

The Tenth: The rule regarding the pebbles is that they must be pure, not najis, and not previously thrown. If he throws with something that has already been thrown, it does not suffice him according to Malik; but Ibn al-Qasim related from him that if this is with a single pebble, it suffices him, and this was the case that befell Ibn al-Qasim, and he gave a fatwa accordingly.

**The Eleventh:** The scholars recommend taking the pebbles from Muzdalifah (the place between Mina and Arafat where pilgrims spend the night), not from the mosque's pebbles. If someone takes more than he needs and, after the stoning, still has some in his hand, he should bury them and not throw them away. This is the view of Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others.

**The Twelfth:** According to the majority (al-Jumhur), the pebbles are not washed, contrary to Tawus. It has been reported that if someone did not wash the pebbles that were najis (ritually impure), or threw pebbles that had already been thrown, he did wrong but his stoning was still valid. Ibn al-Mundhir said: "It is disliked to throw pebbles that have already been thrown, but it is valid if he does. I do not know of anyone who required a repeat of the stoning for one who did so. Nor do I know of any report from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he washed the pebbles or ordered them to be washed. It has been related to us from Tawus that he used to wash them."

**The Thirteenth:** Stoning is not valid with *al-madar* [[al-madar (with a vowel on the m): pieces of dried clay. It has also been said: moist clay with no sand in it.]] or with anything other than stone. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq. The people of opinion (Ashab al-Ra'y) said: it is valid with dried clay, and likewise with anything thrown from the ground. al-Thawri said: whoever throws with pottery shards or clods does not have to repeat the stoning. Ibn al-Mundhir said: stoning is valid only with pebbles, because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Take for yourselves pebbles of *al-khadhf*" [[al-khadhf (with a fatha on the kh and a sukun on the dh): throwing a pebble or a date stone that you hold between your forefinger and index finger and fling, or making a sling of wood and throwing with it between the thumb and index finger. The intended meaning of "pebbles of al-khadhf" is pebbles that are small.]], and with pebbles the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) threw.

**The Fourteenth:** The size of the pebbles has been disputed. al-Shafi'i said: they should be smaller than a finger joint in length and width. Abu Thawr and the people of opinion said: like the pebbles of *al-khadhf*. It has been related to us from Ibn Umar that he used to throw at the jamrah with pebbles the size of sheep droppings. There is no sense in Malik's statement, "Larger than that is more beloved to me," because the Prophet (ﷺ) prescribed throwing with pebbles like those of *al-khadhf*. It is permissible to throw with anything that is called a pebble. Following the Sunnah is better. So said Ibn al-Mundhir. I say: this is the correct view, and no one who seeks guidance and follows should oppose it. al-Nasa'i related from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me on the morning of al-Aqabah while he was on his mount: "Bring me pebbles." So I gathered some small pebbles of the kind used in *al-khadhf*. When I placed them in his hand, he said: "Like these. And beware of extremism in religion, for those before you were destroyed only by extremism in religion." His words "beware of extremism in religion" indicate that throwing large stones is disliked, and that it is a form of extremism. And Allah knows best.

**The Fifteenth:** Whoever is left with a pebble in his hand and does not know which jamrah it is meant for should count it as being for the first jamrah, and then throw at the middle and last jamrah after it. If a long time has passed, he should start over with all of them.

**The Sixteenth:** Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abd al-Malik, Abu Thawr and the people of opinion said, regarding one who throws at one jamrah before another: it is not valid for him unless he throws in succession. al-Hasan, Ata' and some others said: it is valid. Some people cited the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever performs one rite before another, there is no blame," and he added: "This is no more than a man who owes prayers or fasts and makes up some before others." The first view is more cautious, and Allah knows best.

**The Seventeenth:** The scholars differed regarding throwing on behalf of one who is sick. Malik said: one may throw on behalf of the sick person and the child who cannot throw. The sick person, when they are being thrown for, should intend it, and he should say seven takbirs for each jamrah. He must also offer a sacrificial animal (hady). If the sick person recovers during the days of stoning, he throws for himself, and according to Malik he must also offer a blood sacrifice (dam). al-Hasan, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq and the people of opinion said: one may throw on behalf of the sick, and they did not mention a sacrificial animal. There is no disagreement that a child who cannot throw may have someone throw on his behalf, and Ibn Umar used to do that.

**The Eighteenth:** al-Daraqutni related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: We said, "O Messenger of Allah, these are the pebbles that are thrown every year, and we think they are diminishing." He said: "What is accepted of them is lifted up. Had it not been so, you would have seen them like mountains."

**The Nineteenth:** Ibn al-Mundhir said: The scholars agreed that whoever among the pilgrims wishes to leave Mina, heading to his own country outside the Haram, without remaining in Makkah, may depart in the first departure (al-nafr al-awwal) after the sun has passed its zenith, once he has thrown on the day following the Day of Sacrifice, before evening falls. This is because Allah, exalted be His remembrance, said: ﴿Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾. So whoever wishes to depart may depart as long as some of the day remains. It has been related to us from al-Nakha'i and al-Hasan that they said: whoever is overtaken by the afternoon while in Mina on the second day of the Days of Tashriq should not depart until the next day. Ibn al-Mundhir said: It is possible that they meant this as a recommendation (istihbab). The first view is what we hold, based on the apparent meaning of the Book and the Sunnah.

**The Twentieth:** The scholars differed as to whether the people of Makkah depart in the first departure. It has been related to us from Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Whoever among all the people wishes to depart in the first departure may do so, except the family of Khuzaymah, who depart only in the last departure." Ahmad ibn Hanbal used to say: "I do not like it for someone who departs in the first departure to remain in Makkah." He also said: "The people of Makkah have it easier." Ahmad and Ishaq understood Umar's words "except the family of Khuzaymah" to mean that they are people of the Haram. Malik used to say regarding the people of Makkah: whoever has an excuse may hasten in two days. If he wishes to lighten his burden of the Hajj rites, then he may not. He permitted hastening for those who come from far away. Another group said: the verse is general, and the concession applies to all people, both the people of Makkah and others, whether one who leaves Mina intends to stay in Makkah or to return to his own land. Ata' said: it applies to people in general. Ibn al-Mundhir said: This resembles the school of al-Shafi'i, and we hold it. Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Ikrimah, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Nakha'i said: whoever departs on the second of the numbered days (al-ayyam al-ma'dudat) there is no blame, and whoever delays until the third, there is no blame either. So the meaning of the verse is that all of this is permissible. It was expressed in this division out of emphasis and affirmation, since some Arabs would blame the one who hastens, and vice versa. So the verse came lifting blame in every case.

Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i also said: the meaning of "whoever hastens, he has been forgiven, and whoever delays, he has been forgiven." They cited the Prophet's (peace be upon him) saying: "Whoever performs this House's pilgrimage without indecent speech or wickedness leaves his sins like the day his mother bore him." So His words "there is no sin upon him" are a general negation and an absolute exoneration.

Mujahid also said: the meaning of the verse is that whoever hastens or delays, there is no sin upon him until the coming year. A narration supports this view. Abu al-Aliyah said regarding the verse: there is no sin upon one who is mindful of Allah for the rest of his life, and the pilgrim is absolutely forgiven, meaning all his sin is gone if he fears Allah for the rest of his life. Abu Salih and others said: the meaning of the verse is that there is no sin upon one who is mindful of killing game and of what he must avoid during the Hajj. He also said: for one who is mindful in his Hajj, and performs it completely, until it is accepted (mabrur).

**The Twenty-First:** The "man" (*man*) in His words ﴿whoever hastens﴾ is in the nominative as the subject, and the predicate is ﴿there is no sin upon him﴾. Outside the Qur'an it would be permissible to say "there is no sin upon them," because the meaning of *man* is plural, as in His exalted words: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾ [[Qur'an 10:42.]] and likewise ﴿whoever delays, there is no sin upon him﴾. The lam in His words ﴿for one who is mindful﴾ is connected to the forgiveness, the estimated meaning being "forgiveness is for one who is mindful." This is according to the interpretation of Ibn Mas'ud and Ali. Qatadah said: We have been told that Ibn Mas'ud said: "Forgiveness was made for the one who is mindful after departing from the Hajj, from all disobedience." Al-Akhfash said: the estimated meaning is "that is for the one who is mindful." Some said: "for the one who is mindful," meaning the killing of game while in ihram and in the Haram. It was also said that the estimated meaning is permission for the one who is mindful; this is reported from Ibn Umar. And it was said: it is safety for the one who is mindful. It was also said: it is connected to the remembrance mentioned in His exalted words ﴿And remember Allah﴾, meaning the remembrance is for the one who is mindful.

Salim ibn Abdullah recited ﴿fa-la ithma alayhi﴾ with the alif connected, for lightness, and the Arabs do use this. A poet said:

*If I do not fight, then dress me in a veil.*

Then Allah, exalted, commanded taqwa (God-consciousness) and reminded of the gathering (on the Day of Resurrection) and the standing (before Allah).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 204:

There are three issues (masa'il) in this.

The first: God's statement, ﴿And among the people is one whose speech about the worldly life may impress you﴾. When He mentioned those whose aspirations were limited to this world, in His words, ﴿Among the people is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world"﴾, and the believers who asked for the good of both abodes, He mentioned the hypocrites, because they displayed faith and concealed disbelief. Al-Suddi and other exegetes said: it was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq, whose name was Ubayy; al-Akhnas is a nickname by which he was called, because he withdrew (khanasa) on the day of Badr, taking with him three hundred men of his allies from Banu Zuhra, from fighting the Messenger of God (ﷺ), as will be explained in Surat Al 'Imran. He was a man sweet of speech and appearance. He came afterwards to the Prophet (ﷺ), professed Islam, and said, "God knows that I am truthful." Then he fled, and he passed by a field of crops belonging to Muslim people and by donkeys, and he burned the crops and hamstrung the donkeys.

Al-Mahdawi said: concerning him was revealed, ﴿And do not obey every contemptible oath-swearer, a backbiter going about with slander﴾ [Qur'an 68:10-11], and ﴿Woe to every slanderer and defamer﴾ [Qur'an 104:1].

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is not established at all that al-Akhnas embraced Islam.

Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed concerning a group of hypocrites who spoke about those who were killed in the battle of al-Raji': 'Asim ibn Thabit, Khubayb, and others. They said, "Woe to these people! They neither stayed in their houses, nor did they deliver the message of their companion." So this verse was revealed concerning the attributes of the hypocrites. Then He mentioned the martyrs of the battle of al-Raji' in His words, ﴿And among the people is one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of God﴾ [Qur'an 2:207].

Qatada, Mujahid, and a group of scholars said: it was revealed concerning everyone who conceals disbelief, hypocrisy, lying, or harm, while outwardly displaying the opposite with his tongue. Thus it is general in application, and it resembles what is related in al-Tirmidhi: that in some of the books of God, the Exalted, it is said: "Among the servants of God are a people whose tongues are sweeter than honey while their hearts are more bitter than aloes; they wear sheepskins of softness before the people, buying the world with religion. God, the Exalted, says: 'Of Me do they feel secure, and at Me do they dare? By Me I swear I will surely send against them a trial that leaves the forbearing among them bewildered.'"

The meaning of ﴿and he calls God to witness﴾ is: he says, "God knows that I speak the truth." Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿وَيَشْهَدُ اللَّهُ عَلَى مَا فِي قَلْبِهِ﴾ with a fatha on the yā' and the hā' in "yashhadu," and ﴿Allah﴾ in the nominative, meaning: his speech impresses you, while God knows from him the opposite of what he says. Its proof is the words, ﴿And Allah testifies that the hypocrites are liars﴾ [Qur'an 63:1]. The reading of Ibn 'Abbas is: ﴿and Allah calls to witness what is in his heart﴾. The reading of the majority is more forceful in censure, because he had the strength to bind himself to fine speech, yet his inner state contradicted it. Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿وَيَسْتَشْهِدُ اللَّهَ عَلَى مَا فِي قَلْبِهِ﴾, and this is evidence for the reading of the majority.

The second: Our scholars said: in this verse there is a proof and an admonition regarding caution in matters pertaining to religion and worldly affairs, and in investigating the circumstances of witnesses and judges, and that a judge should not act merely on the outward circumstances of people and what appears of their faith and righteousness until he investigates their inner state, because God, the Exalted, has explained the states of people, and that among them is one who displays a beautiful statement while intending something ugly. If it is said: this is contradicted by his peace be upon him saying, "I have been commanded to fight the people until they say, 'There is no god but God'," the hadith, and his saying, "I judge for him according to what I hear." The answer: this was in the early period of Islam, when their Islam was their safety; but now that corruption has become widespread, it is not so. This was said by Ibn al-'Arabi.

I say: The correct view is that the outward is acted upon until the contrary becomes clear, based on the saying of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may God be pleased with him) in Sahih al-Bukhari: "O people, revelation has ceased, and we now judge you only by what has become apparent to us of your deeds. Whoever displays good to us, we grant him security and bring him near, and we have nothing to do with his inner state; God will call him to account for his inner state. And whoever displays evil to us, we do not grant him security nor do we believe him, even if he says his inner state is good."

The third: God's statement, ﴿and he is the most contentious of opponents﴾. Al-Aladd: the one strongly given to disputation. A man is "alladd," a woman is "laddaa," and they are "ahl ladad." One may say "laddta" (with kasra on the dal) "talodd" (with fatha) "laddan," meaning you became alladd. And "laddtuhu" (with fatha on the dal) "aluddu" (with damma) when you argue with him and overcome him. Al-alladd is derived from al-ladidayn, which are the two sides of the neck, meaning that whichever side he takes in the dispute, he prevails. The poet said:

"And one fierce against me, enraged, as if the enmity of his breast were boiling in a cauldron."

Another said:

"Indeed beneath the dust is resolve and firmness, and an opponent most contentious, one of firm locks."

Al-khisam in the verse is the verbal noun of khasama; this was said by al-Khalil. It was also said that it is the plural of khasm, as said by al-Zajjaj, like kalb/kilab, sa'b/si'ab, and dakhm/dikhám. The meaning: the most contentious of disputants in dispute; that is, he is one of argument, so that when he speaks to you and debates with you, you find his speech pleasing while its inner reality is falsehood. This indicates that argument is not permitted except with what is outwardly and inwardly the same.

In Sahih Muslim, from 'A'isha, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the most hated of men to God is the most contentious opponent."

"And when he turns away, he strives in the land to cause corruption therein and destroy crops and livestock." Some said: "tawalla" and "sa'a" are acts of the heart. So "tawalla" means he went astray, became angry and was indignant within himself. "Sa'a" means he strove, by his scheming and his will, to bring calamities upon Islam and its people, narrated from Ibn Jurayj and others. It was also said that both are acts of the person, so "tawalla" means he turned away and left you, O Muhammad. "Sa'a" means that he went on foot, cut the road and corrupted it, narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and others. Both kinds of striving are corruption. It is said: "sa'a al-rajul yas'a sa'yan," meaning he ran, and likewise when he worked and earned. And "fulan yas'a 'ala 'iyalihi" means he works for their benefit.

His saying, the Exalted: "wa-yuhlika" is conjoined to "li-yufsida." In the recitation of Ubayy it is "wa-li-yuhlika." Al-Hasan and Qatada recited "wa-yuhliku" with a nominative ending, and regarding its raising there are several views: it is conjoined to "yu'jibuka." Abu Hatim said: it is conjoined to "sa'a," because its meaning is "yas'a wa-yuhliku." Abu Ishaq said: "wa-huwa yuhliku." It is narrated from Ibn Kathir: "wa-yahlika" with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the kaf, with "al-harth wa-al-nasl" in the nominative as subject of "yahliku." This is the recitation of al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu Haywa, and Ibn Muhaysin, and 'Abd al-Warith narrated it from Abu 'Amr. Some people recited "wa-yahlaku" with a fatha on the ya' and the lam, and a raised "al-harth," in the dialect of "halaka yahlaku," like "rakana yarkanu," "aba ya'ba," "sala yasla," "qala yaqla," and similar. The verse is, in its intended sense, about al-Akhnas in his burning of the crops and his killing of the donkeys, as said by al-Tabari. Others said: but it has become general for all people, so whoever does a deed like his deserves that curse and punishment. Some scholars said: whoever kills a donkey or burns a heap [al-kudus: a heap of food, dates or dirhams] deserves reproach, and disgrace clings to him until the Day of Resurrection. Mujahid said: what is meant is that the wrongdoer corrupts the land, so Allah withholds the rain and so the crops and offspring perish. It was also said: "al-harth" means women and "al-nasl" means children, because hypocrisy leads to the division of the word and the outbreak of fighting, and in it is the destruction of creation; this was said by al-Zajjaj. And "sa'y fi al-ard" is walking swiftly; this is an expression for instigating strife and sowing discord among people, and Allah knows best. In a hadith: "If people see the wrongdoer and do not take hold of his hands, Allah is about to encompass them all with a punishment from Him." The explanation of this will come, God willing.

His saying, the Exalted: "al-harth wa-al-nasl." Al-harth in the language means tilling, and from it comes "al-mihrath," what the land is tilled with. Al-harth also means earning and gathering wealth; in a hadith: "Work for your worldly life as if you will live forever." Al-harth also means crops, and al-harrath means farmer. One says "harath and ihtarath," like "zara'a and izdara'a." It is also said: "uhrith al-Qur'an," meaning study it. "Harathtu al-naqa wa-ahrathtuha" means I rode her until she became lean. "Harathtu al-nar" means I stirred it. Al-mihrath is what is used to stir the oven fire, from al-Jawhari. Al-nasl is what comes out of every female as offspring; its origin is emergence and falling out, and from it comes "nasl al-sha'r" (hair growth) and "rish al-ta'ir" (bird's feathers). The present tense is "yansilu," and from it: "ila rabbihim yansiluna" and "min kulli hadabin yansiluna." Imru' al-Qays said:

"Fasulli thiyabi min thiyabiki tansulu"
[Verse half: "wa-in kunti qad sa'atka minni khalifatun" — "If you have been displeased by some disposition of mine, then strip my garments from yours," meaning: if there is in my character what you do not like, then depart and withdraw my affair from yours (from the commentary on the Diwan).]

I say: the verse indicates tilling and cultivating the land, and planting it with trees, as an analogy to crops, and seeking offspring, which is the growth of animals, and by this the existence of humanity is complete. This refutes those who say to abandon the means, and its explanation will come in this book, God willing.

His saying, the Exalted: "wa-Allahu la yuhibbu al-fasad." Al-Abbas ibn al-Fadl said: corruption is ruin. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: cutting coins is among corruption on earth. 'Ata' said: a man called 'Ata' ibn Munabbih entered ihram wearing a robe, and the Prophet ﷺ commanded him to take it off. Qatada said: I said to 'Ata': we used to hear that he should tear it. 'Ata' said: Indeed Allah does not love corruption. I say: the verse by its generality covers every corruption, whether in land, wealth, or religion, and this is the correct view, God willing. It was said: the meaning of "la yuhibbu al-fasad" is that He does not love it from people of righteousness, or that He does not love it as a religion. It is possible that the meaning is that He does not command it, and Allah knows best.

This is the description of the disbeliever and the hypocrite who goes off with pride in himself, and it is disliked for a believer to let himself be drawn into some of this. Abdullah said: "A person is sinful enough when his brother says to him, 'Fear God,' and he replies, 'Look to yourself! Someone like you advises me!' [[In another manuscript: "You are commanding me!"]]"

Al-ʿizzah means strength and dominance, from ʿazzahu, yaʿizzuhu, meaning he overpowered him. From this comes ﴿and he overpowered me in speech﴾ [[Sura Sad, verse 23.]]. It was also said that al-ʿizzah here means ḥamiyyah (zealous pride), and from this is the poet's saying:

Arrogance seized him out of his ignorance,
so he turned away angry, in the manner of one distressed.

It was also said that al-ʿizzah here means might and stubbornness of the soul, meaning that he became proud within himself and took a stance, and that pride took hold of him and compelled him to sin when it seized him and bound him to it. Qatadah said: the meaning is that when it is said to him, "Wait," he becomes more eager to commit disobedience. The meaning is that pride drove him to sin. It was also said: pride seized him because of what made him sinful, that is, he committed disbelief out of pride and the zealotry of the Age of Ignorance. A parallel is ﴿Rather, those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition﴾ [[Sura Sad, verse 2.]].

It was also said that the bāʾ in بِالْإِثْمِ has the sense of the lām, meaning that pride and zealotry seized him from accepting admonition for the sake of the sin that was in his heart, which is hypocrisy. From this is the saying of ʿAntarah describing the sweat of a she-camel:

As if the tar, or a thick, boiled bitumen,
whose fuel had been kindled beneath it, was blazing around the sides of a copper pot.

[Al-rubb (with a dammah on the rāʾ): boiled, thickened liquid. Al-kuḥayl (diminutive): naphtha or tar with which camels are coated. Al-muʿaqqad (with a fatḥah on the qāf): that which has had fire kindled beneath it until it congealed and thickened. Ḥashsha: was ignited. Al-qumqum (with a ḍammah): a type of vessel.]

That is, the fuel was kindled for it. It was also said that the bāʾ has the sense of maʿa (with), meaning that pride seized him along with the sin. Thus the meaning of the bāʾ differs according to the interpretations.

It is reported that a Jew had a need with Harun al-Rashid and came to his gate for a year, but his need was not fulfilled. One day he stood at the gate, and when Harun came out, he hurried until he stood before him and said: "Fear God, O Commander of the Faithful!" Harun dismounted from his mount and fell prostrate. When he raised his head, he ordered that the man's need be met, and it was. When he returned, it was said to him: "O Commander of the Faithful, you dismounted from your mount because of the words of a Jew!" He said: "No, but I remembered the saying of God Most High: ﴿And when it is said to him, 'Fear God,' pride takes hold of him for sin, so Hell suffices him, and how wretched a resting-place﴾."

Ḥasbuhu means that it suffices him as punishment and recompense, just as you say to a man: "What has befallen you is enough for you!" while you consider what has befallen him to be great and you magnify it for him. Al-mihād is the plural of al-mahd, which is the place prepared for sleep, and from it comes mahd al-ṣabī (the cradle of the infant).

God named Hell mihād because it is the resting-place of the disbelievers. It was also said: because it is a substitute for them in place of a resting-place, as in His saying ﴿so give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [[Sura Al ʿImran, verse 21.]]. A parallel to this in speech is their saying:

"Greeting among them is a painful blow."

[This is the second half of a line by Maʿdīkarib, whose first half is:
"And horsemen who had advanced upon them with horsemen."]

ابْتِغاءَ (ibtighā’) is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf‘ūl min ajlihi). When He mentioned the conduct of the hypocrites, He mentioned after it the conduct of the believers. It is said: it was revealed concerning Suhayb [Suhayb ibn Sinan ibn Malik al-Rumi. He was taken captive by the Romans while young, then brought to Mecca, where Abdullah ibn Jud‘an bought him. It is also said that he fled from the Romans, came to Mecca, and made an alliance with Ibn Jud‘an. Suhayb was among the foremost early Muslims; he witnessed Badr and all the battles. He died in Medina in the year 38 AH. (From al-Nujum al-Zahira.)] — for he set out as a emigrant (muhajir) toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and a group of the Quraysh pursued him. He dismounted from his riding-beast, emptied what was in his quiver [intatha ma fi kinanatihi: i.e., he drew out the arrows that were in it. The kinana is the quiver for arrows, made either of leather with no wood in it, or of wood with no leather in it], took his bow, and said: "You know well that I am among the best of you at archery, and by Allah, you will not reach me until I have shot with what is in my quiver, then I will strike with my sword as long as there remains anything in my hand of it; then do whatever you wish." They said: "We will not let you go away from us rich when you have come to us poor. But show us where your wealth is in Mecca and we will leave you alone." They made a covenant with him on that, and he did it. When he arrived before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the verse was revealed: "And among mankind is one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah," and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Profitable was the sale, Abu Yahya!" and he recited the verse to him. Razin related it, and Sa‘id ibn al-Musayyab said it, may Allah be pleased with them both.

The commentators said: The polytheists seized Suhayb and tortured him. Suhayb said to them: "I am an old man; it will not harm you whether I am from among you or from others. So will you take my wealth and leave me and my religion?" They did so. He had stipulated for them a mount and provisions. He set out for Medina, and Abu Bakr and ‘Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) and some men met him. Abu Bakr said to him: "Profitable was your sale, Abu Yahya!" Suhayb said to him: "And your sale will not lose. So what is that?" He said: "Allah revealed such-and-such concerning you," and he recited the verse to him.

Al-Hasan said: Do you know concerning whom this verse was revealed? It was revealed concerning a Muslim who met a disbeliever, and said to him: "Say, there is no god but Allah; when you say it, you will protect your wealth and your self." He refused to say it, so the Muslim said: "By Allah, I will sell myself to Allah," then advanced and fought until he was killed.

It is also said: It was revealed concerning one who enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong, and upon this interpretation ‘Umar, ‘Ali and Ibn ‘Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them) construed it. ‘Ali and Ibn ‘Abbas said: "The two men fought," meaning: the one who changes the wrong [in the copy "al-Muttaqi"] said to the corrupter: "Fear Allah," but the corrupter refused, and pride seized him; so the one who changes the wrong sold himself to Allah, fought him, and they fought each other.

Abu al-Khalil said: ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab heard a person reciting this verse, and ‘Umar said: "Indeed we belong to Allah and to Him we return; a man stood up enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, and was killed."

It is also said: ‘Umar heard Ibn ‘Abbas say: "The two men fought," when the reciter recited this verse. He asked him about what he had said, and he explained this interpretation to him. ‘Umar said to him: "By Allah, your inheritance is ancient, O Ibn ‘Abbas!"

It is also said: It was revealed concerning one who plunges into battle. Hisham ibn ‘Amir charged into the ranks at Constantinople and fought until he was killed. Abu Hurayrah recited "And among mankind is one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah," and the same was related from Abu Ayyub.

It is also said: It was revealed concerning the martyrs of the battle of al-Raji‘. Qatada said: They are the Emigrants and the Helpers.

It is also said: It was revealed concerning ‘Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) when the Prophet (ﷺ) left him on his bed the night he went out to the cave, as will be explained in "Bara’ah" if Allah the Exalted wills. It is also said: The verse is general, encompassing every fighter in the way of Allah, or one who is martyred for his own sake, or one who changes wrong. The ruling on one who charges into the ranks has already been mentioned [see the second issue, vol. 2, p. 363], and the mention of the one who changes wrong, his conditions and his rulings, will come in "Al ‘Imran" if Allah wills.

"Yashri" means "yabi‘" (sells), and from it [comes the verse]: "and they sold him for a paltry price" [verse 20, Surah Yusuf], i.e., they sold him. Its original sense is exchange (istibdal), and from it is the Exalted's saying: "Indeed Allah has purchased from the believers their selves and their wealth, for them is Paradise" [verse 111, Surah al-Tawbah]. And from it is the poet's saying:

"Even if the vicissitude of time has overtaken them in the first [generation], they sold this world for its eternal gardens."

And another said:

"I bought Burd, would that I had been, after Burd, a skull [i.e., would that I had died]..."

Here "Burd" is the name of a boy. And another said:

"He offers a price for her, yet withholds her, and her owner says: Ah, then sell!"

The selling of the self here is its expenditure for the commands of Allah. "Ibtighā’" is an object of purpose. Al-Kisa’i stopped on "marḍāt" with a tā’, while the others stopped with a hā’. Abu ‘Ali said: Al-Kisa’i stopped with the tā’ either following the dialect of those who say "ṭalḥat" and "‘alqamat," and from it is the poet's saying:

"Rather, a desert expanse like the back of a shield [ḥajfah]..."

[The ḥajfah (with vowelling and with ḥ before j): a shield when it is made of hides with no wood or core in it. (See Lisan al-‘Arab, root ḥ-j-f.)]

Or because this genitive complement is in the word by necessity, he kept the tā’ as it is kept in continuous speech, so that it is known that the genitive complement is intended. "Al-marḍāh" is "al-riḍā" (pleasure); it is said: radiya yarḍā riḍan wa marḍāh. Some have related that shara is used in the sense of ishtara (bought), and whoever interprets the verse as concerning Suhayb needs this, because he bought his self with his wealth and did not sell it. Unless it is said: Suhayb's offering himself to fight them is a sale of himself to Allah, and thus the wording is correct in the meaning of "sold."

The Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 208:

When Allah, glorified is He, distinguished people into believer, disbeliever and hypocrite, He said: "Be of one religion, unite upon Islam and remain steadfast in it." So al-salm here means Islam (submission). This is the view of Mujahid, and Abu Malik narrated it from Ibn Abbas. From it is the saying of the Kindi poet:

"I called my tribe to al-salm (peace/Islam) when I saw them turning their backs in retreat."

That is, to Islam, when Kindah apostatized after the death of the Prophet ﷺ along with al-Ash'ath ibn Qays al-Kindi. Also, the believers were never commanded to enter into al-musalamah (peace/truce), which is reconciliation. Rather, it was said to the Prophet ﷺ that he should incline to al-silm (peace) if they inclined to it, but as for initiating it himself, no. This was said by al-Tabari. It was also said: He commanded those who had believed with their tongues to enter into it with their hearts. Tawus and Mujahid said: Enter into the affairs of the religion. Sufyan al-Thawri said: into all kinds of righteousness.

It is also read as "al-silm" with a kasra on the sin.

Al-Kisai said: al-silm and al-salm have the same meaning, and so it is according to most of the Basran grammarians, and both may be used for Islam and for peace-making. Abu Amr ibn al-Ala' distinguished between them: he read it here as "ud-khulu fi al-silm" and said it means Islam, while he read the one in al-Anfal and the one in Surah Muhammad ﷺ as "al-salm" with a fatha on the sin, and said that with the fatha it means al-musalamah (peace-making). Al-Mubarrad rejected this distinction. Asim al-Jahdari said: al-silm is Islam, al-salm is reconciliation, and al-salam is submission (istislam). Muhammad ibn Yazid rejected these distinctions and said: language is not taken this way; it is taken by transmission, not by analogy, and whoever makes the distinction needs evidence. The Basrans have related: Bani Fulan are silm, salm and salam, with one meaning. Al-Jawhari said: al-silm is reconciliation, it may be pronounced with fatha or kasra, may be masculine or feminine, and its root is from istislam and inqiyad (submission and compliance), which is why reconciliation is called silm. Zuhayr said:

"You two have said: if we attain peace broadly, with wealth and good conduct in affairs, we shall be safe."

Al-Tabari preferred interpreting the word as meaning Islam, on the basis of what has preceded. Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman said regarding this verse: Islam has eight shares: prayer is a share, zakah is a share, fasting is a share, hajj is a share, umrah is a share, jihad is a share, enjoining good is a share, and forbidding evil is a share, and whoever has no share in Islam has indeed failed. Ibn Abbas said: the verse was revealed concerning the People of the Book, and the meaning is: O you who believe in Musa and Isa, enter into Islam with Muhammad ﷺ entirely.

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said: "By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, no one of this nation hears of me, be he Jew or Christian, and then dies without believing in what I have been sent with, except that he will be among the companions of the Fire."

Kaffatan means all together; it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) either of al-silm or of the pronoun of the believers. It is derived from their saying kaffaftu, meaning I prevented, that is, none of you should refrain from entering into Islam. Al-kaff means prevention, and from it is kuffat al-qamis (the collar/cuff of the shirt), with a damma, because it prevents the garment from spreading; and from it is kiffat al-mizan (the pan of the scale), with a kasra, which gathers what is weighed and prevents it from scattering; and from it is kaff al-insan (the human hand), which gathers his benefits and harms; every circular thing is called kiffah, and every elongated thing is called kuffah. A man who is kaff al-basar (blinded/restrained in sight) means he has been prevented from looking; so a group is called kaffah because they refrain from dispersing.

"And do not follow the footsteps of Satan": the prohibition, with "footsteps" as its object, and this has already been discussed [see the third issue, vol. 2, p. 208].

Muqatil said: Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions asked permission to read the Torah during prayer and to act by some of what is in the Torah, so the verse came down: "And do not follow the footsteps of Satan," for following the Sunnah is better, after Muhammad ﷺ was sent, than the footsteps of Satan. It was also said: do not take the path to which Satan calls you. "Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy," evidently hostile, and this has already been discussed [see the fourth issue, vol. 2, p. 209].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 209:

﴿Then if you slip﴾ means: if you turn aside from the path of uprightness (istiqamah). The original sense of zalal (slipping) is in the foot, and then it is used for beliefs, opinions and other things. It is said: zalla yazillu zallan, zalalan and zululan, meaning his foot slipped. Abu al-Simmal al-Adawi read ﴿zaliltum﴾ with a kasrah on the lam, and both are dialects (lughatan). The root of the letter is from zalaq (slipperiness), and the meaning is: you went astray and deviated from the truth. ﴿After clear proofs have come to you﴾ means the miracles and the verses of the Qur'an, if the address is to the believers. If the address is to the People of the Two Scriptures (ahl al-kitabayn), then the "clear proofs" are what appeared in their law (shar') of the announcement of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the description of him.

In the verse there is evidence that the punishment of one who knows of a sin is greater than the punishment of one who is ignorant of it, and that one whom the call of Islam has not reached does not become a disbeliever by abandoning the legal obligations (shara'i').

Al-Naqqash related that Ka'b al-Ahbar (Ka'b al-Ahbar), when he embraced Islam, was learning the Qur'an, and the one who was teaching him recited to him ﴿Know that Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾. Ka'b said: "I find it strange that it should be like this." A man passed by them, and Ka'b said: "How do you recite this verse?" The man said: "Know that Allah is Mighty, Wise." Ka'b said: "Thus it should be."

﴿Mighty ('Aziz)﴾ means that nothing He wills can be prevented from Him. ﴿Wise (Hakim)﴾ means He is wise in what He does.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 210:

Hal yanzuruna (هَلْ يَنْظُرُونَ), meaning those who refuse to enter into peace (al-silm) [[in man "al-Islam".]], and "hal" here is intended as a negation, meaning: they are not waiting for anything except that God should come to them in canopies of clouds (ظُلَلٍ مِنَ الْغَمامِ), and the angels. "Nazartuhu" and "intazartuhu" have the same meaning, and al-nazar is al-intizar (waiting). Qatadah, Abu Ja'far Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa' and al-Dahhak read "fi zilalin mina al-ghamam." Abu Ja'far read "wa al-malaikati" with a genitive (al-khafd) as a conjunction with al-ghamam, and its implied meaning is "with the angels," as the Arabs say: "aqbala al-amir fi al-'taskar," i.e., with the army. "Ẓulal" is the broken plural of "ẓullah," like "ẓulmah" and "ẓulam"; in the sound plural it is "ẓululat." Sibawayh recited:

When the wild beasts gather together in their shades... scattered from the heat, and it had become midday (The line is by al-Ja'di. Its meaning of "aẓhara": it became the time of midday. He describes his travel at the hottest time, when the wild beasts take refuge from the heat and the blazing of the sun, and he joins his herd.)

"Ẓulat" and "ẓilal" are plurals of "ẓill" in the common usage, and the rare form is "aẓlal." It is possible that "ẓilal" is the plural of "ẓullah," like "qullah" and "qilal," as the poet said:

Mixed with the water of the qilal [[The qilal (with kasra, plural of qullah with damma): the jar; it is said to be a vessel of the Arabs like a jar.]]

Al-Akhfash Sa'id said: "wa al-malaikati" with the genitive has the meaning of "wa fi al-malaikati." He said: the nominative is better, as in: "hal yanzuruna illa an ta'tiyahumu al-malaikatu" [[Verse 158, Surah al-An'am.]] and "wa ja'a rabbuka wa al-maliku saffan saffan" [[Verse 22, Surah al-Fajr.]]. Al-Farra' said: in the recitation of 'Abd Allah it is "hal yanzuruna illa an ya'tiyahumu Allahu wa al-malaikatu fi zulalin mina al-ghamam." Qatadah said: "al-malaikah" means they come to them to seize their souls, and it is said that it refers to the Day of Resurrection, and this is more evident. Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Rabi' said: the angels come to them in canopies of clouds, and God comes to them as He wills. Al-Zajjaj said: the estimated meaning is "fi zulalin mina al-ghamam wa mina al-malaikah." It was also said: the words are not to be taken in their apparent sense concerning Him, glory be to Him; rather the meaning is that the command and judgment of God come to them. It was also said: that is, with what He promised them of reckoning and punishment, in canopies, like: "fa ata-hum Allahu min haythu lam yahtasibu" [[Verse 2, Surah al-Hashr]], that is, with His abandonment of them. This is the view of al-Zajjaj, and the first is the view of al-Akhfash Sa'id. It is possible that the meaning of "ityan" (coming) returns to the requital, so requital is called "ityan," just as frightening and punishing in the story of Nimrod was called "ityan," so He said: "fa ata Allahu bunyanahum min al-qawa'id fa kharra 'alayhimu al-saqfu min fawqihim" [[Verse 26, Surah al-Nahl]]. And He said in the story of al-Nadir: "fa ata-hum Allahu min haythu lam yahtasibu wa qadhafa fi qulubihimu al-ru'b," and He said: "wa in kana mithqala habbatin min khardalin ataynا bi-ha" [[Verse 47, Surah al-Anbiya']]. The ityan could carry these meanings because the origin of ityan, according to the lexicographers, is intending a thing. So the meaning of the verse is: they await nothing except that God Most High manifests an act among His creatures, intending to requite them and deciding their affair as He decides; and just as He, glory be to Him, brought into being an act which He named descent and settling, so He brings into being an act which He names ityan, and His acts are without instrument or cause, glory be to Him! Ibn 'Abbas said, in the narration of Abu Salih: this is of the hidden matters which are not to be explained. Some of them remained silent about its interpretation, and some interpreted it as we have mentioned. It was also said: the fa' is in the sense of the ba', that is, He comes to them with canopies, and from it is the hadith: "Allah comes to them in a form" meaning "with a form," as a test for them. It is not permissible to take this and similar things that came in the Qur'an and the report in the sense of movement, transition and cessation, because that belongs to the attributes of bodies and physical forms; exalted is God, the Great, the Most High, Lord of Majesty and Honour, above resemblance to bodies, a great exaltation.

Al-ghamam: the thin white cloud, so called because it covers (yaghummu), that is, conceals, as has been mentioned earlier [[See the first issue, vol. 1, p. 405.]]. Mu'adh ibn Jabal read "wa qada'u al-amr." Yahya ibn Ya'mur read "wa qudiya al-umur" in the plural. The majority read "wa qudiya al-amr," so the meaning is: the requital took place and those who disobeyed were punished. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "turja'u al-umur" with the verb in the active voice, which is the original form; its evidence is "ala ila Allahi tasiru al-umur" [[Verse 53, Surah al-Shura]] and "ila Allahi marji'ukum" [[Verses 48 and 105, Surah al-Ma'idah]]. The rest read "turja'u" with the verb in the passive voice, and this too is a good reading; its evidence is "thumma turaddun" [[Verse 94, Surah al-Tawbah]], "thumma ruddu ila Allah" [[Verse 62, Surah al-An'am]], and "wa la'in rudidtu ila rabbi" [[Verse 36, Surah al-Kahf]]. Both readings are good and have the same meaning; the first is the original, and the passive form is an extension and a derivative. All affairs return to God, before and after. He mentioned this in relation to the Day of Resurrection to draw attention to the cessation of what belonged to the kings in this world.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 211:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We gave them﴾. "Sal" (ask) is from al-su'al (asking), with the hamza lightened. Since the sin (of the root) took a vowel, it did not need the alif of connection (alif al-wasl). It has also been said that the Arabs have two ways regarding the dropping of the alif of connection in "sal" and its retention in "wa-isal": the first is that it is dropped in one and retained in the other, and the Qur'an came with both, so one follows the script of the Mushaf in its writing or omission of the hamza. The second way is that its retention and dropping vary with the context in which the speech is used: the hamza is dropped in an initial (independent) utterance, as in His saying, "Sal Bani Isra'il," and His saying, "Salhum ayyuhum bi-dhalika za'im" [68:40]. It is retained in a conjoined construction, as in the saying, "Wasal al-qarya" [12:82], and "Wasalu Allaha min fadlihi" [4:32]. This was stated by Ali ibn Isa. Abu Amr, in the transmission of Ibn Abbas from him, read "isal" according to the original form. A group read "isal," transferring the vowel to the sin and retaining the alif of connection, according to the dialect of one who said: al-Ahmar.

"Kam" is in the accusative position, because it is the second object of "atainahum." It has also been said that it is governed by an implied verb, its estimate being: "kam atayna atainahum." The verb may not precede it, because it has the front position of the sentence.

"Min ayatin" is in the accusative position as a specification (tamyiz) according to the first estimate, and according to the second it is the second object of "atainahum." It may also be in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), with the predicate being "atainahum," and a pronoun referring back to "kam" arises in it, its estimate being: "kam atainahumuhu." "Kam" is not declined, since it is a noun that functions like particles, because it carries the meaning of interrogation. When you separate "kam" from the noun, the preferred form is to bring "min" as in this verse. If you omit it, you use the accusative in both the interrogative and the declarative, and the genitive is permitted in the declarative, as the poet said:

"Kam bi-judin muqrafin [the base, vile of lineage] nala al-ula... wa-karimin bukhluhu qad wada'ahu"

The intended meaning of "ayah" here is: how many signs came to them concerning the matter of Muhammad, peace be upon him, which make him known and indicate him. Mujahid, al-Hasan and others said: meaning the signs which Musa, peace be upon him, brought, such as the splitting of the sea, the clouds shading them, the staff, the hand, and other things. Allah, exalted is He, commanded His Prophet to ask them in the manner of rebuke and reproach.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever substitutes the blessing of Allah after it has come to him﴾. The wording is general for all people, even though the one referred to is the Children of Israel, because they altered what was in their books and denied the matter of Muhammad ﷺ; so the wording extends to every person who substitutes the blessing of Allah. Al-Tabari said: the blessing here is Islam, and this is close to the first. The wording also includes the Quraysh disbelievers, for the sending of Muhammad ﷺ among them is a blessing upon them, so they substituted its acceptance and gratitude for it with disbelief.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is severe in punishment﴾. This is a statement that includes a threat.
