"Al-iqab" (punishment) is derived from "al-aqib" (heel), as if the one who punishes walks, requiting him, in the traces of his heel. From it come "uqbat al-rakib" (the stopping place of the rider) and "uqbat al-qidr" (the portion of broth). So "al-iqab" and "al-uqubah" occur at the heel of a sin, and he punished him for his sin.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 212:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Adorned for those who disbelieve is the life of this world﴾, is in the passive form (ʿalā mā lam yusamma fāʿiluhu, the verb whose agent is not named). The intended referents are the chieftains of Quraysh. Mujahid and Humayd ibn Qays read it in the active form (ʿalā binā' al-fāʿil). Al-Nahhas said: "This is an irregular reading (qirāʾa shādhdha), because no agent (fāʿil) has been mentioned beforehand." Ibn Abi ʿAblah read ﴿zuyyinat﴾ with the feminine marker shown, and this is permissible because the feminine here is not real (ghayr ḥaqīqī). The one who adorns it is its Creator, its Originator, and the Creator of disbelief. Satan also adorns it through his whispering and seduction. The disbelievers were singled out for mention because they accepted the adornment entirely and turned toward this world, turning away from the Hereafter on account of it. God has made what is upon the earth an adornment for it, in order to test people as to which of them is best in deed (cf. ﴿That He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾). The believers, who are upon the ways of the Law, were not seduced by the adornment, whereas the disbelievers were overpowered by it, because they believe in nothing other than it. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, said when wealth was brought to him: "O Allah, we cannot help but rejoice in what You have adorned for us."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who believe they mock﴾ (wa-yaskhurūna min alladhīna āmanū), is a reference to the disbelievers of Quraysh, for they used to magnify their own worldly condition and exult in it, and they used to mock the followers of Muhammad (ﷺ). Ibn Jurayj said: "[They mocked them] for their pursuit of the Hereafter." It is also said: [they mocked them] for their poverty and their lack of means, such as Bilal, Suhayb, Ibn Mas'ud and others, may Allah be pleased with them. So God, glorified is He, drew attention to the lowliness of their station as a rebuke for their ugly conduct, by His saying: ﴿But those who are God-fearing will be above them on the Day of Resurrection﴾. ʿAli narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever humiliates a believing man or a believing woman, or belittles them because of their poverty and lack of means, Allah will expose him on the Day of Resurrection and then disgrace him. And whoever slanders a believing man or a believing woman, or says of them what is not in them, Allah the Exalted will set him upon a mound of fire on the Day of Resurrection until he comes out of what he said about them. Indeed, the esteem of a believer is greater with Allah and more honoured by Him than an angel brought near. Nothing is more beloved to Allah than a believing man who repents or a believing woman who repents. Indeed, the believing man is recognised in heaven just as a man is recognised by his family and his children."

Then it was said: the meaning of ﴿But those who are God-fearing will be above them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ is in rank, because they are in Paradise and the disbelievers are in the Fire. It is also possible that "above" refers to place, since Paradise is in the heaven and the Fire is at the lowest of the low. It is also possible that the preference is according to what the disbelievers' claim implies, for they say: "If there is a return, then we will have a greater share in it than you." From this is the report of Khabbab (1) with al-ʿAs ibn Wail. Khabbab said: "I had a debt owed to me by al-ʿAs ibn Wail, so I came to him to demand it, and he said to me: 'I will not pay you until you disbelieve in Muhammad (ﷺ).' I said to him: 'I will not disbelieve in him until you die and are resurrected.' He said: 'Am I really going to be resurrected after death?! Then I will pay you when I return to wealth and children,' and the report continues." It will come in full, God willing (2).

It is said: sakhirtu minhu and sakhirtu bihi (I mocked him), ḍaḥiktu minhu and ḍaḥiktu bihi (I laughed at him), and hazi'tu minhu and hazi'tu bihi (I ridiculed him); all of these are said, as related by al-Akhfash. The noun is al-suhriyya, al-sukhriyy and al-sikhriyy, and both are read in His saying: ﴿that they may take some of them as subjects of mockery (sukhriyyan)﴾ and His saying: ﴿so you took them as objects of mockery (sikhriyyan)﴾. A man who is a sukhra is one who is mocked, and sukhara (with a fatha on the kha') is one who mocks people. Fulan is a sukhra, meaning he is put to work; one says: "His servant is a sukhra," and sakhkharahu taskhiran means he assigned him a task without wages.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And God provides for whom He wills without reckoning﴾. Al-Dahhak said: "That is, without accountability in the Hereafter." It was also said: it refers to those who were oppressed, meaning He gives them a lofty station, so the verse is a reminder of the great blessing upon them. He made their provision "without reckoning" in that it is lasting and unending, and it does not run out. It was also said that His saying "without reckoning" describes God's provision in terms of how it is disbursed, since He, mighty is His power, does not spend by measure; so all of His bounty is without reckoning, whereas that which is "by reckoning" is what is given in return for a deed the servant has done. God, exalted is He, says: ﴿a reward from your Lord, a gift by count﴾. And God knows best. It is also possible that the meaning is "without the recipients' expectation," as He says: ﴿and provide for him from where he does not expect﴾.

---
(1) Khabbab (with a fatha on the kha' and a shaddah on the ba'): Ibn al-Aratt, a participant at Badr, who was among us in the Jahiliyya and among the earliest emigrants.
(2) See vol. 11, p. 145.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 213:

His saying, Exalted is He: "Mankind was one community" (kana al-nasu ummatan wahidatan), meaning: upon one religion. Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn Zayd said: the intended meaning of "mankind" is the children of Adam, when Allah brought them out as souls (nasam) from the loins of Adam, and they acknowledged His oneness. Mujahid said: "mankind" refers to Adam alone, and the singular was expressed with a plural form because he is the origin of the offspring. It was also said: Adam and Hawwa' (Eve). Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: the intended meaning of "mankind" is the generations that existed between Adam and Nuh (Noah), and they were ten, who were upon the truth until they differed, so Allah sent Nuh and those after him. Ibn Abi Khaythamah said: from the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, until the sending of Muhammad (ﷺ) was five thousand and eight hundred years. It was also said: more than that. Between him and Nuh there were one thousand and two hundred years. Adam lived nine hundred and sixty years, and the people in his time were one religious community, adhering to the religion, and the angels shook hands with them. They continued upon that until Idris, peace be upon him, was raised up, and then they differed. This view is open to question, because Idris is, according to the correct opinion, after Nuh. Some scholars, including al-Kalbi and al-Waqidi, said: the intended meaning is Nuh and those in the ark, and they were Muslims; then after Nuh's death they differed. Ibn 'Abbas also said: they were one community upon disbelief, meaning during the time of Nuh when Allah sent him. And it is also reported from him: the people in the time of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, were one community, all of them disbelievers, and Ibrahim was born in the age of ignorance, so Allah sent Ibrahim and other prophets. According to these opinions, "kana" (was) retains its proper sense of past completed time. Whoever takes the people in the verse to be believers must supply in the sentence: "so they differed, and He sent [prophets]." This omission is indicated by the phrase: "And none differed concerning it except those who were given it" (i.e., the Book), meaning: mankind was upon the religion of truth, then they differed, so Allah sent the prophets as bringers of good tidings to those who obeyed and warners to those who disobeyed. Whoever takes them to be disbelievers, the sending of the prophets was to them. It is possible that "kana" expresses a permanent state, and the meaning is an informing about mankind, the whole species, that they were one community in their lack of revealed laws and their ignorance of the realities, were it not for Allah's favour upon them and His grace in sending messengers to them. According to this interpretation, "kana" is not restricted to past time only, but its meaning is like His saying: "And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful" (an-Nisa' 4:96, 100, 152). The word "ummah" is derived from their saying: "I aimed at such a thing" (amamtu kadha), meaning I intended it. So the meaning of "ummatan" is that their aim is one. It is also said of an individual: "ummah," meaning his aim is different from the aim of other people. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) about Qass ibn Sa'idah: "He will be raised on the Day of Resurrection as an ummah alone." The same was said about Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl. "Al-ummah" also means the stature of a person, as if it were the aim of the whole body. "Al-imma" (with a kasra) means blessing, because people aim at its enjoyment. It was also said: "imma" means leader, because people aim to imitate what he does, according to al-Nahhas. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read: "Mankind (al-bashar) was one community," and Ibn Mas'ud read: "Mankind was one community, then they differed, so He sent [prophets]."

His saying, Exalted is He: "So Allah sent the prophets." Their total number was one hundred and twenty-four thousand, and among them the messengers were three hundred and thirteen. Those mentioned by name in the Qur'an were eighteen. The first of the messengers was Adam, according to what came in the hadith of Abu Dharr, which al-Ajurri and Abu Hatim al-Busti transmitted. It was also said: Nuh, because of the hadith of intercession, where people say to him: "You are the first of the messengers." It was also said: Idris. The explanation of this will come in al-A'raf, if Allah Exalted wills.

His saying, Exalted is He: "Bringers of good tidings and warners" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). "And He sent down with them the Book": "al-kitab" here is a collective noun with the meaning of "books." Al-Tabari said: the definite article in "al-kitab" is for a known referent, and the intended meaning is the Torah. "That they might judge" is linked to the Book according to the majority's view; it is in the accusative by the implied "an" (that), meaning "so that it might judge," and this is a metaphor, like His saying: "This Book of ours speaks against you with truth" (al-Jathiyah 45:29). It was also said: meaning that every prophet judged by his own book, and when he judged by the Book, it was as if the Book itself had judged. The reading of 'Asim al-Jahdari is "liyuhkama baynan-nas" (in the passive voice), which is an irregular reading, because the Book has already been mentioned. It was also said: the meaning is "that Allah might judge," and the pronoun in "fihi" refers to "ma" in His saying "fima" (concerning what). The second pronoun in "fihi" may refer to the Book, meaning: "and none differed concerning the Book except those who were given it." The position of "alladhina" (those who) is in the nominative as the agent of the verb "ikhtalafa" (differed). "Utuhu" means "given it." It was also said: it refers to the one to whom it was revealed, who is Muhammad (ﷺ), as al-Zajjaj said, meaning: "and none differed concerning the Prophet, peace be upon him, except those who were given his knowledge."

"By way of insolence among themselves" (baghyan baynahum) is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning: they did not differ except out of insolence (baghy), and its meaning has already been explained earlier. In this there is a warning about the folly of their action and the ugliness they committed. "So He guided" (fahada) means He directed. That is, Allah guided the community of Muhammad to the truth by making clear to them what those before them had differed about. A group said: the meaning of the verse is that some communities denied the books of others, so Allah the Exalted guided the community of Muhammad to affirm all of them. Another group said: Allah guided the believers to the truth regarding what the People of the Two Books (Jews and Christians) differed about, such as their claim that Ibrahim was a Jew or a Christian. Ibn Zayd and Zayd ibn Aslam said: (it refers to) their qibla, for the Jews faced Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) and the Christians faced the east; and (it refers to) the Friday, for the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "This is the day about which they differed, and Allah guided us to it: the Jews have Saturday, and the Christians have Sunday." (It also refers to) their fasting, and to everything else they differed about. Ibn Zayd also said: they differed about 'Isa (Jesus); the Jews made him a fabrication, and the Christians made him a lord, so Allah guided the believers by making them say that he was the servant of Allah. Al-Farra' said: this is an inversion (al-maqlub), and al-Tabari chose this view. He said: its implied meaning is "so Allah guided those who believed to the truth concerning what they differed about." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: what led him to this supposition is the fear that the wording might be understood as meaning that they differed about the truth, and then Allah guided the believers to some of what they differed about, while that thing itself might not be the truth. This is the view that al-Tabari pursued in his report from al-Farra'. But claiming an inversion in the wording of the Book of Allah without any necessity that compels it is weakness and poor reasoning, because the sentence can be understood in its own proper form and description: "fahada" implies that they reached the truth, and the meaning is complete with "fihi" (concerning it), and "min al-haqq" (of the truth) clarifies the kind of thing about which the disagreement occurred. Al-Mahdawi said: the word "ikhtilaf" (difference) was placed before "al-haqq" (the truth) out of concern, since the attention is directed to mentioning the difference. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is not strong in my view.

In the reading of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud: "lima ikhtalafu 'anhu min al-haqq," meaning: "from Islam." As for "bi-idhnihi" (by His permission), al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "by His knowledge." Al-Nahhas said: this is an error; the meaning is "by His command," for when you permit a thing you have commanded it. That is, Allah guided those who believed by commanding them to do what they must practise. His saying, Exalted is He: "And Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path" is a refutation of the Mu'tazila (a rationalist school), in their claim that the servant independently guides himself.

Qur'an 2:214: "Or did you think that you would enter Paradise without there having come to you the like of what came to those who passed away before you?"

Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Or do you think that you will enter Paradise?﴾ "Hasibtum" means "you supposed" (zanantum).

Qatadah, al-Suddi and most of the exegetes (mufassirun) said: this verse was revealed concerning the Battle of the Trench (al-Khandaq), when the Muslims suffered what they suffered of hardship and severity, heat and cold, bad living conditions, and all kinds of hardships, and it was as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the hearts reached the throats﴾ [Qur'an 33:10]. It was also said that it was revealed concerning the Battle of Uhud. Its counterpart in Al 'Imran is: ﴿Or do you think that you will enter Paradise while Allah has not yet made evident those of you who strove [in His cause]?﴾ [Qur'an 3:142].

A group said: the verse was revealed as consolation for the emigrants (muhajirun) when they left their homes and wealth in the hands of the polytheists, and preferred the pleasure of Allah and His Messenger. The Jews had shown enmity toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and a group of the wealthy had concealed hypocrisy, so Allah the Exalted revealed, to comfort their hearts: ﴿Or do you think...﴾.

Here "am" (أم) is disjunctive (munqati'ah), meaning "bal" (rather). Some linguists related that it may function as the interrogative alif, to begin with it. "Hasibtum" requires two objects, and the grammarians (al-nuhat) said: "an tadkhulu" (that you enter) takes the place of both objects. It was also said: the second object is omitted [this is so in the originals; in Ibn Atiyyah: its estimate is "a-hasibtum" (did you suppose)]: "a-hasibtum dukhulakum al-jannata waqi'an" (did you suppose your entering Paradise to be actual?).

"Lamma" means "lam" (not yet). "Mathal" means "shabah" (likeness), i.e., you were not tested with the like of what those before you were tested with, so that you would endure as they endured.

Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl [in some copies of the original: "the Basrans related"] related that "mathal" can mean "sifah" (attribute/description), and the meaning may be: "wa-lamma yusibkum mithlu al-ladhi asaba alladhina min qablikum" (and there has not yet come upon you the like of what came upon those before you), i.e., of affliction.

Wahb said: between Makkah and al-Ta'if there were found seventy dead prophets, whose death was caused by hunger and lice. A parallel to this verse is: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. Do people think that they will be left to say, "We believe," and they will not be tested? And We had already tested those before them﴾ [Qur'an 29:1-3], as will come, so He called them to patience and promised them victory for it, and said: ﴿Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near﴾.

"Al-zalzalah" is intense shaking; it occurs in persons and in conditions. It is said: Allah shook the earth with a shaking (zalzalatan), and with a shaking, zilzalan (with a kasrah), so it was shaken (tazalzalat) when it moved and convulsed. So the meaning of "zulziluu" is "they were frightened and shaken." "Al-zalzal" (with a fathah) is the noun. "Al-zalazil" means severe hardships. Al-Zajjaj said: the root of zalzalah is from "zalla al-shay'u 'an makanihi" (a thing slipped from its place); when you say "zalzaltuhu," its meaning is "I repeated its slipping from its place." Sibawayh's view is that "zalzala" is quadriliteral, like "dahraja."

Nafi' read ﴿until the Messenger says﴾ with the nominative (raf'), and the rest with the accusative (nasb). Sibawayh's position on "hatta" (until) is that the accusative after it is on two grounds and the nominative on two grounds. You say: "sirtu hatta adkhula al-madinah" (I traveled until I entered Madinah) with the accusative, meaning that both the traveling and the entering have passed, i.e., "I traveled up to the point of entering it," and this is a limit (ghayah); on this is the reading of whoever read with the accusative. The second way of the accusative, outside this verse, is "sirtu hatta adkhulaha," meaning "in order that I enter it" (kay). The two ways with the nominative are "sirtu hatta adkhulu-ha," meaning "I traveled, and then I entered it," and both have passed; i.e., "I had traveled and so entered."

"Hatta" does not govern by implied "an" here, because after it is a full clause (jumlah), as al-Farazdaq said:

"Fa-ya 'ajaban hatta Kulayb tasubbuni"
[Full line: "As if their father were Nahshal or Mujashi'."]

[Note from the source: Kulayb ibn Yarbu' was the clan of Jarir, and he satirized them, placing them in such lowliness that they are not reviled as such a man is, because of his nobility. Nahshal and Mujashi' were the clan of al-Farazdaq, and they are two sons of Darim (from the commentary on the verses of evidence).]

Al-Nahhas said: according to this, the reading with the nominative is clearer and sounder in meaning, i.e., "and they were shaken until the Messenger says," meaning such is his state, because the saying came from the shaking and was not cut off from it; whereas the accusative as a limit does not have this meaning. "Al-Rasul" here is Shi'ya according to Muqatil, and he is al-Yasa'. Al-Kalbi said: this applies to every messenger sent to his community who was exhausted in that, until he said: "When is Allah's help?" It is related from al-Dahhak that he said: it means Muhammad (ﷺ), and the revelation of the verse indicates this, and Allah knows best.

The other way outside this verse, "sirtu hatta adkhuluha," is that the traveling has passed and the entering is now. Sibawayh related: "marida hatta la yarjunahu" (he fell ill until they no longer hope for him), i.e., he is now one not hoped for; similarly, "sirtu hatta adkhuluha la umna'" (I traveled until I enter it, not being prevented).

Mujahid, al-A'raj, Ibn Muhaysin and Shaybah read with the nominative. The accusative was read by al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Shibl and others. Makki said: this is the preferred reading, because the majority of reciters follow it.

Al-A'mash read ﴿and they were shaken, and the Messenger says﴾ with "wa" in place of "hatta." In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: ﴿and they were shaken, then they were shaken, and [the Messenger] says﴾.

Most of the interpreters (mutawwilun) hold that the speech up to the end of the verse is the words of the Messenger and the believers: the hardship reached them until they grew impatient for victory, and then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near.﴾ This may be the saying of the Messenger, in seeking to hasten the victory, not out of doubt or suspicion. "Al-Rasul" is a generic noun (ism jins).

Another group said: there is inversion (taqdim wa-ta'khir) in the speech, and the intended sense is: "until those who believed say, 'When is the help of Allah?' and the Messenger says, 'Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near.'" The Messenger is placed first in rank because of his station, then the words of the believers are placed first because they come first in time. Ibn Atiyyah said: this is arbitrary, and bringing the speech to its proper sense is not impossible. It is also possible that "Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near" is an announcement from Allah the Exalted, beginning anew after the completion of the mention of the saying.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿When is the help of Allah?﴾ "Mata" is in the nominative (raf') as subject (ibtida') according to Sibawayh; according to Abu al-'Abbas it is in the nominative by a verb, i.e., "when does the help of Allah occur?" "Qarib" is the predicate of "inna." Al-Nahhas said: outside the Qur'an it is permissible to say "qariban," i.e., "a near place." The Arabs do not dual, pluralize or feminize "qarib" in this sense. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good﴾ [Qur'an 7:56]. The poet [it is Imru' al-Qays, as in his Diwan] said:

"Lahu al-waylu in amsa wa-la Umm Hashim ... qarib, wa-la Basbasah bintu Yashkura"

[Translation: Woe be to him if he should be the evening one — neither Umm Hashim is near, nor Basbasah, daughter of Yashkur.]

If you say, "So-and-so is near to me (qarib li)," you make it dual and plural, saying "qaribun," "aqriba'" and "qurba'."

**Fourth:** On its meaning

There are four issues in it.

**The first issue:** God's words, "They ask you," if you lighten the hamza (ء) by moving its vowel onto the sin (س) and making it fatha, and dropping the hamza, you say: "Yas'aluna" becomes "Yasaluna." The verse was revealed concerning 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh, who was an elderly man. He said: "O Messenger of God, my wealth is great, so what should I give in charity, and to whom should I spend?" Then the verse was revealed: "They ask you what they should spend."

**The second issue:** God's words, "what they should spend" (مَاذَا يُنْفِقُونَ). "Ma" (مَا) is in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), and "dha" (ذَا) is the predicate, meaning "alladhi" (the one which). The pronoun (the hā' at the end of the relative) is dropped because the phrase is long. The meaning is: "What is it that they spend?" If you wish, "ma" may be in the accusative position, governed by "yunfiquna" (they spend), and "dha" together with "ma" functions as a single word, and it does not need a pronoun. Whenever it is a compound noun, it is in the accusative position, except in what the poet said:

*"And what might the slanderers say,*
*Except that they say: 'I am truly in love with you'?"*

Here "'asa" (عَسَى, "might") does not govern it, so "lima dha" (لِمَاذَا) is in the nominative position, and it is compound, since "dha" has no relative clause.

**The third issue:** It has been said that the questioners were believers, and the meaning is: "They ask you which ways they should spend in, and where they should place what it is obligatory to spend." Al-Suddi said: "This verse was revealed before the obligatory zakat (obligatory alms) was prescribed, and then the prescribed zakat abrogated it (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later one)." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Al-Mahdawi made an error concerning al-Suddi in this, so it was attributed to him that he said the verse concerns the prescribed zakat, and then the parents were abrogated from it." Ibn Juraij and others said: "It is a recommendation (nadb), and zakat is other than this spending. On this view, there is no abrogation in it, and it clarifies the channels of voluntary charity (sadaqat al-tatawwu', optional charity). It is obligatory upon a wealthy man to spend on his needy parents what will suffice them, in proportion to his own means, in food, clothing and other things." Malik said: "He is not obliged to marry off his father, but he must spend on his father's wife, whether she is his mother or a stranger." Malik only said that he is not obliged to marry off his father because he saw that the father is generally able to do without marriage. If he were in dire need, it would be obligatory for him to marry him off. Were it not for this, he would not be obliged to spend on them both. As for what relates to acts of worship involving wealth, he is not obliged to give his father what he needs for the pilgrimage (hajj) or for military campaigns, but he must pay the charity of breaking the fast (sadaqat al-fitr) on his behalf, because it is due by reason of maintenance and Islam.

**The fourth issue:** God's words, "Say: whatever you spend" (مَا أَنْفَقْتُمْ). "Ma" is in the accusative position, governed by "anfaqtum" (you spent). Likewise, "wa ma tafʿaluu" (and whatever you do) and "wa ma tufʿaluu" are the conditional form, and the answer is "fa-lil-walidayn" (then it is for the parents). Likewise, "wa ma tafʿaluu min khayr" (and whatever good you do) is a conditional clause, and its answer is "fa-inna Allaha bihi 'alim" (then God knows it well). The discussion of the orphan, the needy, and the wayfarer has already passed. [[See the fifth issue and what follows, vol. 2, p. 14.]] The similar verse is God's words: "So give the kinsman his due, and the needy and the wayfarer" [[Qur'an 30:38]]. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib read "yafʿaluu" with the letter ya' (يَفْعَلُوا), referring to the third person absent. The apparent sense of the verse is a statement of fact, and it contains the promise of reward.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on Surah 2, verse 216:**

There are three issues here.

**The first issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you﴾. *Kutiba* means *furida*, "obligated," and its meaning has already been discussed before. [See the second issue, vol. 2, p. 244.] Some reciters read *"kutiba 'alaykumu al-qatl"* ("killing has been prescribed for you"). The poet [who is Umar ibn Abi Rabi'ah] said:

*"Killing and fighting have been prescribed for us,*
*and for the coquettes, trailing their skirts."*

This is the obligation of *jihad*. God, glorified is He, made clear that this is among the trials they were tested with, and that it was made a means of reaching Paradise. By "fighting" is meant fighting the enemies among the disbelievers, and this was known to them from the circumstances around them. The Prophet (ﷺ) was not permitted to fight during his residence in Makkah. When he emigrated, he was permitted to fight those among the polytheists who fought against him. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged﴾ [Qur'an 22:39]. Then he was permitted to fight the polytheists in general.

They differed over who is meant by this verse. It was said that it refers specifically to the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ). Fighting alongside the Prophet (ﷺ) was then an individual obligation (*fard 'ayn*, a duty incumbent on each person) for them. When the law became established, it became a collective obligation (*fard kifayah*, a duty that is fulfilled when enough people perform it). This is the view of 'Ata' and al-Awza'i. Ibn Jurayj said: "I said to 'Ata': Is the military campaign (*ghazw*) obligatory upon people by this verse?" He said: "No. It was only prescribed for those people."

The majority of the scholars of the community said: its initial obligation was a collective obligation, not a specific one for each person. However, when the Prophet (ﷺ) called them to mobilize (*istanfarahum*), mobilizing became obligatory upon them, because obedience to him is obligatory.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: jihad is an individual obligation upon every Muslim forever. This is related by al-Mawardi.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: What the consensus (*ijma'*) has settled upon is that jihad for every nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) is a collective obligation. When some of the Muslims undertake it, it is lifted from the rest. However, if the enemy descends upon the territory of Islam, then it becomes an individual obligation at that time. This will come up explained in detail in Surah *Bara'ah* [At-Tawbah], God willing. [See vol. 6, p. 136.]

Al-Mahdawi and others mentioned from al-Thawri that he said: jihad is voluntary (*tatawwu'*). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This statement, in my view, is only in response to a questioner who was already capable of jihad, and it was said to him: "That is voluntary."

**The second issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is hateful to you﴾. It is a subject and predicate (*mubtada' wa khabar*), and it means that it is hateful in human nature.

Ibn 'Arafah said: *al-kurh* (with a *damma*) means hardship, while *al-kurh* (with a *fatha*) means what you are compelled to do. This is the preferred usage. It is permissible to use the *damma* with the meaning of the *fatha*, so the two are dialects. One says: *karihtu al-shay'a karhan wa kurhan wa karahatan wa karahiyatan*, and *akrahtuhu 'alayhi ikraha*.

Jihad was hateful because it involves spending wealth, leaving one's homeland and family, and exposing the body to wounds, injuries, the loss of limbs, and the loss of life. So their aversion was to that, not to God's obligation.

'Ikrimah said regarding this verse: they hated it, then they came to love it and said: "We hear and we obey." This is because carrying out a command involves hardship, but when the reward is known, the suffering of hardships becomes easy in comparison.

I say: An example of this in the world is removing what causes a person pain and fear, such as amputating a limb, extracting a tooth, bloodletting, or cupping, all seeking health and lasting well-being. And there is no bliss better than the eternal life in the abode of eternity and honor, "in a seat of truth" [Qur'an 54:55].

**The third issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Perhaps you dislike a thing﴾. It was said: *'asa* here means *qad* (perhaps, indeed), as said by al-Asamm. It was also said: it is binding. *'Asa* from God is binding throughout the Qur'an, except for His saying: ﴿It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will substitute for him﴾ [Qur'an 66:5].

Abu 'Ubaydah said: *'Asa* from God is a binding affirmation. The meaning is: perhaps you dislike what is in jihad of hardship, and it is good for you, in that you will prevail, triumph, gain spoils, and be rewarded, and whoever dies, dies as a martyr. And perhaps you love ease and abandoning fighting, and it is evil for you, in that you will be overcome, humiliated, and your affairs will be lost.

I say: This is correct, without any doubt. As happened in the lands of al-Andalus, when they abandoned jihad, grew cowardly in fighting, and fled a great deal, so the enemy seized the lands. And what lands! They took captives, killed, enslaved, and reduced people to servitude. Surely we belong to God and to Him we return! ﴿This is because of what your hands have sent forth﴾ [Qur'an 8:51].

Al-Hasan said regarding the meaning of the verse: Do not dislike the calamities that befall you, for perhaps a matter you dislike contains your salvation, and perhaps a matter you love contains your destruction.

Abu Sa'id al-Darir recited:

*"Many a matter you guard against*
*drags you into a matter you are content with.*
*What is loved is hidden within it,*
*and what is hated is made apparent in it."*

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verses 217–218 (part 1 of 3):

There are twelve issues (masa'il) in it.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They ask you﴾ has already been discussed [[See p. 36 of this part.]]. Jarir ibn Abd al-Hamid and Muhammad ibn Fudayl narrated from Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "I have not seen a people better than the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ). They asked him only about thirteen issues, all of which are in the Qur'an: ﴿They ask you about menstruation﴾, ﴿They ask you about the sacred month﴾, ﴿They ask you about orphans﴾." They asked only about what would benefit them.

Ibn Abd al-Barr said: "In the hadith, of the thirteen issues, only three are found."

Abu al-Yasar narrated from Jundub ibn Abd Allah that the Prophet (ﷺ) sent a detachment (rahT) and appointed over them Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Harith, or Ubaydah ibn al-Harith. When he was about to set out, he wept out of longing for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). So he sent Abd Allah ibn Jahsh, wrote a letter for him, and ordered him not to read the letter until he reached such-and-such a place. He said: "Do not compel any of your companions to march." When he reached the place, he read the letter, uttered "Inna lillah" and said: "Hearing and obedience to Allah and His Messenger." He said: "Two men returned and the rest went on. They met Ibn al-Hadrami and killed him, and they did not realize that it was the day of Rajab. The polytheists said: 'You have killed in the sacred month.' So Allah sent down: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month﴾, the verse."

It is also reported that the cause of its revelation was that two men of Banu Kilab met Amr ibn Umayya al-Damri, not knowing that they had been with the Prophet (ﷺ), and that was on the first day of Rajab, so he killed them. Quraysh said: "He killed them in the sacred month," and the verse was revealed.

The view that its revelation concerns the story of Abd Allah ibn Jahsh is more prevalent and better known. The Prophet (ﷺ) sent him with nine men, and it was said eight, in Jumada al-Akhira, two months before Badr, and it was said in Rajab.

Abu Umar said in his book al-Durar: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned from pursuing Kurz ibn Jabir, an expedition known as the First Badr, he remained in Medina for the rest of Jumada al-Akhira and Rajab. In Rajab he sent Abd Allah ibn Jahsh ibn Ri'ab al-Asadi with eight men from the Emigrants: Abu Hudhayfah ibn Utba, Ukkasha ibn Mihsan, Utba ibn Ghazwan, Suhayl ibn Bayda' al-Fihri, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Amir ibn Rabi'ah, Waqid ibn Abd Allah al-Tamimi, and Khalid ibn Bukayr al-Laythi. He wrote a letter for Abd Allah ibn Jahsh and ordered him not to look into it until he had marched for two days, then to look into it, and to carry out what he had been ordered [[Addition from the Sirah of Ibn Hisham and the History of al-Tabari. See the expedition of Abd Allah ibn Jahsh.]], and not to compel any of his companions. He was their commander. Abd Allah ibn Jahsh did what he was ordered. When he opened the letter and read it, he found in it: 'When you have looked into this letter of mine, proceed until you alight at a palm grove between Mecca and al-Ta'if, and keep watch there on Quraysh, and learn for us some of their news.' When he read the letter, he said: 'Hearing and obedience.' Then he informed his companions of this, and that he would not compel any of them, and that he was setting out for his destination with whoever obeyed him, and that if no one obeyed him he would go alone. He said: 'Whoever loves martyrdom, let him set out, and whoever dislikes death, let him return.' They said: 'We all desire what you desire, and none of us is other than one who hears and obeys the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' They set out with him. He took the route toward the Hijaz. A camel that Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Utba ibn Ghazwan were riding in turns ran off, so the two of them fell behind in pursuit of it, while Abd Allah ibn Jahsh continued with the rest toward his destination until he alighted at Nakhla. A caravan of Quraysh passed by them, carrying raisins and merchandise, among it Amr ibn al-Hadrami (al-Hadrami's name was Abd Allah ibn Abbad of the Sadaf, and Sadaf is a clan of Hadramawt), and Uthman ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Mughira and his brother Nawfal ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Mughira, both of Makhzum, and al-Hakam ibn Kaysan, client of Banu al-Mughira. The Muslims consulted and said: 'We are on the last day of Rajab, the sacred month. If we fight them, we violate the sanctity of the sacred month; and if we leave them, tonight they will enter the Sacred Precinct.' Then they agreed to engage them. Waqid ibn Abd Allah al-Tamimi shot Amr ibn al-Hadrami and killed him. They captured Uthman ibn Abd Allah and al-Hakam ibn Kaysan, and Nawfal ibn Abd Allah escaped. Then they returned with the caravan and the two captives. Abd Allah ibn Jahsh said to them: 'Set aside the fifth (khums) of what we have taken as spoils for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' They did so, and it was the first fifth in Islam. Then the Qur'an was revealed: ﴿And know that whatever you obtain as spoils, a fifth of it belongs to Allah﴾ [[Verse 41 of surah al-Anfal.]]. Thus Allah and His Messenger approved the action of Abd Allah ibn Jahsh, were pleased with it, and established it as a sunnah for the community until the Day of Resurrection. It was the first spoil taken in Islam, the first commander, and Amr ibn al-Hadrami was the first person killed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) disapproved of the killing of Ibn al-Hadrami in the sacred month, so the people were at a loss. Then Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it﴾ up to His saying: ﴿they will abide therein forever﴾. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) accepted ransom for the two captives. As for Uthman ibn Abd Allah, he died in Mecca as a disbeliever. As for al-Hakam ibn Kaysan, he embraced Islam and remained with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) until he was martyred at the Well of Ma'una. Sa'd and Utba returned to Medina safe."

It was also said: "The departure of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Utba in pursuit of their camel was with permission from Abd Allah ibn Jahsh. When Amr ibn al-Hadrami and his companions saw the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), they were frightened of them, so Abd Allah ibn Jahsh said: 'The people are alarmed by you. Shave the head of one of you and let him show himself to them; when they see him shaved, they will feel secure and say: "They are pilgrims (umar); there is no harm upon you."' They consulted about fighting them..." (the hadith continues).

The Jews took it as an omen and said: "Waqid (the one who kindles) — the war has been kindled; Amr — the war has become populated (a'marat); al-Hadrami — the war has been present (hadarat)."

The people of Mecca sent for the ransom of their two captives. The Prophet (ﷺ) said [[That is, the Prophet (ﷺ), as in the Tafsir of al-Tabari.]]: "We will not ransom them until Sa'd and Utba come back. If they do not come back, we will kill them in exchange for them." When they came back, he ransomed them. As for al-Hakam, he embraced Islam and remained in Medina until he was martyred on the day of Ma'una. As for Uthman, he returned to Mecca and died there as a disbeliever. As for Nawfal, on the day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab) he struck the belly of his horse to make it leap into the trench against the Muslims, and he fell into the trench with his horse, and both were crushed; Allah caused him to die. The polytheists asked for his corpse in exchange for money, but the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Take it, for its corpse is vile and its blood-money is vile." This is the cause of the revelation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month﴾.

Ibn Ishaq mentioned that the killing of Amr ibn al-Hadrami took place on the last day of Rajab, as previously stated. Al-Tabari reported from al-Suddi and others that it was on the last day of Jumada al-Akhira, but the first is more well known, although it has come from Ibn Abbas that it was on the first night of Rajab, while the Muslims thought it was from Jumada.

Ibn Atiyyah said: "The Sahib ibn Abbad mentioned in his well-known epistle, al-Asadiyya, that Abd Allah ibn Jahsh was named Commander of the Believers at that time, because he was appointed over a group of believers."

The second: The scholars differed concerning the abrogation (naskh) of this verse. The majority hold that it is abrogated, and that fighting the polytheists in the sacred months is permissible. They differed about its abrogating verse. Al-Zuhri said: "It was abrogated by: ﴿and fight the polytheists all together﴾ [[Verse 36 of surah al-Tawba.]]." It was said: "It was abrogated by the Prophet's (ﷺ) raid on Thaqif in a sacred month, and his sending Abu Amir [[He is Abu Amir al-Ash'ari, cousin of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.]] to Awtas [[Awtas: a valley in the lands of Hawazin, where the Battle of Hunayn took place. See Tabaqat of Ibn Sa'd and the Sirah of Ibn Hisham on the Battle of Hunayn.]] in a sacred month." It was said: "It was abrogated by the Pledge of Ridwan on fighting in Dhu al-Qa'da." This is weak, for when the Prophet (ﷺ) received word of the killing of Uthman in Mecca and that they were determined to fight him, he then took the pledge from the Muslims to repel them, not to initiate fighting against them.

Al-Bayhaqi mentioned, from Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, outside the narration of Muhammad ibn Ishaq, after the story of al-Hadrami: "Then Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it﴾, the verse." He said: "Allah informed them in His Book that fighting in the sacred month is forbidden, as it was. What they consider lawful with regard to the believers is far greater than that: barring them from the way of Allah when they imprison them, torture them, and detain them from emigrating to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); their disbelief in Allah; their barring the Muslims from the Sacred Mosque for hajj, 'umrah, and prayer in it; their expelling its people, who are Muslims; and their tempting them away from their religion. We were informed that the Prophet (ﷺ) paid blood-money [[Aql the slain: he gave his heirs his blood-money after he was killed.]] for Ibn al-Hadrami and kept the sacred month sacred as he used to, until Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: ﴿A declaration of immunity from Allah and His Messenger﴾."

Ata' used to say: "The verse is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated), and fighting in the sacred months is not permitted, and he would swear to that, because the verses revealed after it are general regarding all times, while this one is specific, and the general does not abrogate the specific by consensus."

Abu al-Zubayr narrated from Jabir: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not fight in a sacred month unless he was attacked, or unless he attacked. [[So in the Tafsir of al-Fakhr al-Razi and many other tafsir books; in the originals: "unless he was attacked or attacked." In al-Tabari: "unless he was attacked or attacked; when that came, he remained until it ended."]]"

The third: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿fighting in it﴾. "Qital" (fighting) is, according to Sibawayh, a badal ishtimal (apposition of inclusion), because the question included both the month and the fighting. That is, the disbelievers asked you out of astonishment at the violation of the sanctity of the month, so their question about the month was only on account of fighting in it. Al-Zajjaj said: "The meaning is: They ask you about fighting in the sacred month." Al-Qutaybi said: "They ask you about fighting in the sacred month: is it permissible?" So he substituted qital for shahr. Sibawayh recited:

"Qays's death was not the death of a single man,
but it was the building of a people that collapsed."

[[The verse is by Abida ibn al-Tabib, who lamented Qays ibn Asim al-Minqari, chief of the people of the wabr (the tent-dwellers) of Tamim.
(From the Book of Sibawayh, vol. 1, p. 77, Bulaq edition.)]]

Ikrimah recited "يَسْأَلُونَكَ عَنِ الشَّهْرِ الْحَرَامِ قَتْلٍ فِيهِ قُلْ قَتْلٌ" without the alif in either word. It was also said that the meaning is "They ask you about the sacred month and about fighting in it," and Ibn Mas'ud recited it this way. On this reading it is in the genitive by "'an" (from), repeated, as al-Kisa'i said. Al-Farra' said: it is in the genitive by the intention of "'an." Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is in the genitive by *al-jiwar* (attraction, adjacency). Al-Nahhas said: it is not permissible for a thing to be given inflection by *al-jiwar* in the Book of God or in any speech. *Al-jiwar* is an error, and it occurs only in an anomalous case, namely their saying: "hadhā juḥru ḍabbin kharibin" (this is the hole of a dhabb lizard, a ruined one). The proof that it is an error is the Arabs' saying in the dual: "hadhāni juḥrā ḍabbin kharibāni." This is like *al-iqwa'* (the rhyme-vowel irregularity in poetry), and nothing from the Book of God may be interpreted this way. Only the most eloquent and soundest of dialects may be used. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Abu 'Ubaydah said it is in the genitive by *al-jiwar*, and this statement of his is an error. Al-Nahhas said: It is also not permissible to assume an elided "'an," and the correct view is that it is a substitute (*badal*).

Al-A'raj recited "يَسْأَلُونَكَ عَنِ الشَّهْرِ الْحَرَامِ قِتَالٌ فِيهِ" with *raf'* (nominative). Al-Nahhas said: This is obscure in Arabic grammar. The meaning is: "They ask you about the sacred month: is fighting in it permissible?" The phrase "yas'alūnaka" indicates interrogation, as Imru' al-Qays said:

"Do you see, O friend, a lightning flash whose glimmer I show you,
Like the flashing of two hands in a cloud-mass, crowned (with lightning)?"

[[*Al-wamīḍ*: the flash of lightning. "Kal-lam' al-yadayn": he meant like the movement and turning of the hands. *Al-ḥabā*: what rises of the cloud. It was also said: it is what extends across like a mountain before it covers the sky. *Al-mukallal* of the clouds: streaked with lightning. It is also said: it is that around which there are pieces of thick clouds.]]

The meaning is "Do you see lightning?" The alif of interrogation was elided, because the alif in "aṣāḥ" indicates it, even though it is the particle of address, as the poet said:

"Are you departing from the tribe, or are you hastening away?"

The meaning is "Are you departing?" The alif was elided because "am" indicates it.

Fourth: God's words, ﴿Say: Fighting therein is a great (matter)﴾, are an inchoative (*mubtada'*) and predicate (*khabar*), meaning: it is reprehensible, because the prohibition of fighting in the sacred month was established at that time, since the initiation of hostilities came from the Muslims. The word "al-shahr" (the month) in the verse is a generic noun. The Arabs had been given the sacred month by God as a foundation (*qiwām*) around which they balanced their affairs, so they did not shed blood or make changes in the sacred months. These are Rajab, Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah and al-Muharram: three consecutive months (*sard*) and one single month (*fard*) [[The three consecutive months: Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah and al-Muharram. *Sard* means consecutive. The single one is Rajab, and it is alone because Sha'ban, Ramadan and Shawwal come after it.]]. More explanation of this will come, God willing, in *al-Ma'idah*.

Fifth: God's words, ﴿and hindering from the way of God﴾, form an inchoative (*ibtida'*). "(And disbelief in Him)" is conjoined to "ṣadd." "(And the Sacred Mosque)" is conjoined to "sabīl Allāh" (the way of God). "(And expelling its people from it)" is conjoined to "ṣadd." The predicate of the inchoative is "(is greater in the sight of God)," meaning: it is greater in sin than fighting in the sacred month. This is what al-Mubarrad and others said, and it is the sound view, because of the long prevention of people from circumambulating the Ka'bah. "And disbelief in Him" means in God. It was also said: "And disbelief in Him" means in the pilgrimage and the Sacred Mosque. "And expelling its people from it is greater" means greater in punishment in the sight of God than fighting in the sacred month.

Al-Farra' said: "ṣadd" is conjoined to "kabīr" (great), and "al-masjid" is conjoined to the pronoun in "bihi" (in it/Him), so the sentence forms one continuous construction, not an interrupted one. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: That is an error, because the meaning leads to the conclusion that God's words "and disbelief in Him," meaning in God, are also conjoined to "kabīr," and from this it would follow that expelling the people of the Mosque from it is greater than disbelief in the sight of God. The corruption of this is obvious.

The meaning of the verse according to the majority view is: "You, disbelievers of Quraysh, consider fighting in the sacred month a great matter against us, but what you yourselves do, namely hindering from the way of God those who wish to embrace Islam, disbelieving in God, and expelling the people of the Mosque from it, as you did to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his companions, is greater in crime in the sight of God."

'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh (may God be pleased with him) said:

"You count the killing in the sacred month a great matter,
But greater than it, if he who sees the right path were to see it, is (your deed).
Your turning away from what Muhammad says,
And your disbelief in him, while God is Seeing and Witnessing.
And your expelling from the Mosque of God its people,
So that none may be seen prostrating to God in the House.
We, though you have wronged us by killing him (Ibn al-Hadrami),
And though the envious and the rebellious spread rumours against Islam,
We gave Ibn al-Hadrami a drink of our spears at Nakhlah,
When the one who kindles war (Waqid) kindled it,
A blood-price, while Ibn 'Abd Allah 'Uthman is among us,
Contended for by a shackle of rawhide, a stubborn one."

Al-Zuhri, Mujahid and others said: God's words, ﴿Say: Fighting therein is a great (matter)﴾, were abrogated by His words, "And fight the polytheists all together" [[Qur'an 9:36]], and by His words, "Then kill the polytheists" [[Verse 5, Surah al-Tawbah.]]. 'Ata' said: It was not abrogated, and fighting in the sacred months is not proper, as already mentioned.

Sixth: God's words, ﴿and persecution is greater than killing﴾. Mujahid and others said: "Fitnah" here means disbelief, meaning: your disbelief is greater than our killing of those people. The majority said: The meaning of "fitnah" here is their seducing the Muslims from their religion until they perish. That is, this is more gravely sinful than your killing in the sacred month.

Seventh: God's words, ﴿and they will not cease﴾, are an inchoative and a report from God, and a warning from Him to the believers against the evil of the disbelievers. Mujahid said: It refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh. "Yaruddūkum" (they will turn you back) is in the subjunctive after "ḥattā" (until), because it is a bare final limit.

Eighth: God's words, ﴿And whoever of you turns back﴾, meaning returns from Islam to disbelief, ﴿then those—their deeds are nullified﴾, meaning they become void and corrupt. From this comes "ḥabaṭ," which is a corruption afflicting livestock in their bellies from eating too much pasture, so that their bellies swell, and they sometimes die from it. Thus the verse is a threat to Muslims, so that they may remain steadfast in the religion of Islam.

Ninth: The scholars differed concerning the apostate: Is he to be asked to repent or not? Does his deed become void by the apostasy itself, or only if he dies in disbelief? Does he inherit or not? These are three questions.

The first: One group said he is to be asked to repent; if he repents, well, otherwise he is killed. Some said: for one hour. Others said: he is given a month. Others said: he is given three days, as narrated from 'Umar and 'Uthman, and this is the view of Malik, transmitted from him by Ibn al-Qasim. Al-Hasan said: he is asked to repent a hundred times. It is also narrated from him that he is killed without being asked to repent. This is also the view of al-Shafi'i in one of his two opinions, and it is one of the two views of Tawus and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr.

Sahnun mentioned that 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Abi Salamah al-Majishun used to say: The apostate is killed and is not asked to repent. He argued with the hadith of Mu'adh and Abu Musa, in which: When the Prophet (ﷺ) sent Abu Musa to Yemen, he sent Mu'adh ibn Jabal after him. When he arrived, he said, "Dismount," and threw him a cushion. And there was a man with him who was bound. He said, "What is this?" He said, "This was a Jew who became Muslim, then turned back from his religion to the evil religion, and became a Jew." He said, "I will not sit until he is killed, the judgment of God and His Messenger." He said, "Sit down." He said, "[Yes [[Addition from Sahih Muslim.]]] I will not sit until he is killed, the judgment of God and His Messenger," three times. So he ordered him, and he was killed. Muslim and others transmitted it.

Abu Yusuf reported from Abu Hanifah that the apostate is presented with Islam; if he embraces it, well, otherwise he is killed on the spot, unless he asks for a delay, in which case he is given three days. The well-known view from him and his companions is that the apostate is not killed until he is asked to repent. For them, the *zindiq* (heretic, one who conceals disbelief) and the apostate are alike. Malik said: The *zanadiqah* (heretics) are killed and are not asked to repent. This has already been discussed at the beginning of *al-Baqarah* [[See vol. 1, p. 198.]].

They differed concerning one who passes from one disbelief to another disbelief. Malik and the majority of jurists said: He is not interfered with, because he has moved to what, had he been upon it from the beginning, would have been left as it is. Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam reported from al-Shafi'i that he is killed, on the basis of the Prophet's (peace be upon him) words, "Whoever changes his religion, kill him," and he did not restrict it to a Muslim as opposed to a disbeliever. Malik said: The meaning of the hadith is one who leaves Islam for disbelief. As for one who passes from disbelief to disbelief, he is not meant by this hadith. This is also the view of a group of jurists.

The well-known view from al-Shafi'i, as reported by al-Muzani and al-Rabi', is that one among the *ahl al-dhimmah* (protected non-Muslims) who changes his religion is to be sent by the ruler to the land of war, expelled from his city, and his property is permitted along with the property of the non-Muslim combatants, if the Muslims prevail over the territory, because the protection was granted to him only upon the religion he held at the time the covenant was concluded.

They differed concerning the female apostate. Malik, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i and al-Layth ibn Sa'd said: She is killed just as the male apostate is killed. Their argument is the apparent meaning of the hadith, "Whoever changes his religion, kill him," and "man" (*man*) applies to both male and female. Al-Thawri, Abu Hanifah and his companions said: The female apostate is not killed. This is also the view of Ibn Shubrumah, and Ibn 'Ulayyah adopted it, and it is the view of 'Ata' and al-Hasan. They argued that Ibn 'Abbas narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said, "Whoever changes his religion, kill him." Then Ibn 'Abbas did not kill a female apostate, and whoever narrates a hadith knows best its interpretation. It is also narrated from 'Ali something similar. The Prophet (ﷺ) also forbade killing women and children. The first group argued with his (peace be upon him) words, "The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except in one of three cases: disbelief after belief..." It thus generalizes to everyone who disbelieves after his belief, and this is the sounder view.

Tenth: al-Shafi'i said: Whoever apostatizes and then returns to Islam, his deed is not nullified, nor his pilgrimage that he completed, but if he dies in apostasy, then at that point his deeds are nullified. Malik said: They are nullified by apostasy itself. The disagreement becomes evident in the case of a Muslim who performed the pilgrimage, then apostatized, then embraced Islam again. Malik said: He is obliged to perform the pilgrimage, because the first one was nullified by the apostasy. Al-Shafi'i said: There is no need to repeat it, because his deed remains.

Our scholars (the Malikis) cite in support God's words, ﴿If you associate partners with God, your deeds will surely be nullified﴾ [[Qur'an 39:65]]. They said: It is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and what is meant is his community, because apostasy is impossible for him in terms of the law. The companions of al-Shafi'i said: Rather, it is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ) in the manner of severe warning to the community, and a demonstration that if the Prophet (ﷺ), despite the nobility of his station, were to associate partners, his deeds would be nullified; so how about you! But he does not associate partners, because of the excellence of his rank, as He said: ﴿O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you commits a clear immorality, her punishment will be doubled twofold﴾ [[Qur'an 33:30]]. This is because of the nobility of their station; otherwise, no such act could be conceived from them, out of protection for their noble and honoured husband. (Ibn al-'Arabi.)

Our scholars said: God mentioned the condition of dying in that state (*muwafah*, dying upon a state) here only because He attached to it eternal dwelling in the Fire as its recompense. So whoever dies in disbelief, God makes him abide in the Fire by this verse, and whoever associates partners, his deeds are nullified by the other verse. Thus they are two verses.

Both verses yield two distinct meanings and two distinct rulings. What is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ applies to his community as well, unless his exclusive application is established. What is said concerning his wives is said about them to show that, if such a thing were conceivable, it would involve two violations: one of the sanctity of the religion, and the other of the sanctity of the Prophet ﷺ. Every violation of a sanctity incurs a punishment. This is comparable to one who disobeys during the sacred month, or in the sacred land, or in the Sacred Mosque, for whom the punishment is multiplied according to the number of sanctities he has violated. And Allah knows best.

The eleventh issue concerns the scholars' disagreement over the inheritance of the apostate (al-murtadd). Ali ibn Abi Talib, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, al-Hakam, al-Layth, Abu Hanifa and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh said: the apostate's estate passes to his Muslim heirs. Malik, Rabi'ah, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr said: his estate goes to the public treasury (bayt al-mal). Ibn Shubruma, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad and al-Awza'i, in one of two reports, said: whatever the apostate acquires after apostasy goes to his Muslim heirs. Abu Hanifa said: whatever the apostate acquired while in a state of apostasy goes to the public treasury, while whatever he had acquired while a Muslim and then apostatized passes to his Muslim heirs. As for Ibn Shubruma, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, they do not distinguish between the two situations. The unrestricted statement of the Prophet ﷺ, "There is no inheritance between the people of two religions," refutes their position. The scholars agreed that the apostate's heirs who are disbelievers do not inherit from him, except for Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, who said that they do inherit from him.

The twelfth issue concerns Allah's words: ﴿Indeed, those who have believed and those who have emigrated﴾, the verse. Jundab ibn Abd Allah, Urwa ibn al-Zubayr and others said: when Waqid ibn Abd Allah al-Tamimi killed Amr ibn al-Hadrami during the sacred month, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ held back from taking his fifth (khums) of the spoils, which Abd Allah ibn Jahsh had been granted as his share in the raid, and [he held back] regarding the two captives. The Muslims rebuked Abd Allah ibn Jahsh and his companions to the point that it grieved them. Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, consoled them with this verse concerning the sacred month and relieved them of their distress. He informed them that they would have the reward of those who emigrated and fought. So the reference to them is in His words, "Indeed, those who have believed," and then it remains applicable to everyone who does what Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has mentioned. It was also said: [[The meaning is that when Allah relieved the Muslims and the people of the expedition of what they were in, regarding the killing of Ibn al-Hadrami in the sacred month, by revealing His words, "They ask you about the sacred month" (2:217), they thought that it had only removed sin from them and that they would have no reward. So they became eager for it and said: "O Messenger of Allah, do we hope that there will be a raid in which we are given the reward of the fighters?" In another report: "If they had not committed a sin, then they have no reward?" So Allah revealed His words, "Indeed, those who have believed and those who have emigrated," the verse, and thereby Allah placed them at the highest hope in that.]]: if they had not committed a sin, then they have no reward. So Allah revealed, "Indeed, those who have believed and those who have emigrated," to the end of the verse.

Hijra (emigration) literally means moving from one place to another, with the intention of leaving the first for the sake of the second. Al-hajr is the opposite of joining, and one says hajarahu hajran and hijranan; the noun is hijra. Al-muhajara from one land to another is leaving the first for the second. Al-tahajur means severing ties. Whoever says that hijra is moving from the desert to the settled town has erred, on the ground that this was the most common case among the Arabs; but on his view the people of Makkah would not be emigrants. "Wa jahadu" (and struggled) is a form of the verb from jahada, meaning to exert effort, in the form mujahada and jihad. Ijtihad and tajahud mean exerting one's utmost ability and effort. Al-jahad (with a fatha) means hard ground. "Wa yarjun" (and they hope) means they aspire and regard it as near. He said "yarjun" (they hope) although He had praised them, because no one in this world knows that he will enter Paradise, however far he goes in obedience to Allah, for two reasons. The first: one does not know with what one's life will end. The second: so that one does not rely on one's deeds. Hope is pleasant, and hope is always accompanied by fear, just as fear is accompanied by hope. Al-raja' (hope) is from al-amal (expectation) and is a long-vowelled word. It is said: raja'tu fulanan rajwan wa raja'an wa rujaahu. It is said: "I did not come to you except in hope of good." Tarajjaytuhu, irtajaytuhu, rajaytuhu all mean the same as rajawtuhu. Bishr, addressing his daughter, said:

So hope for good and await my return
when the Qari' al-Anazi returns.

And I have no hope (rujayya) in so-and-so, meaning I do not hope for him. Rajw and raja' may also mean fear, as Allah says: "What is the matter with you that you do not expect (tarjuna) grandeur from Allah?" (71:13), meaning you do not fear the majesty of Allah. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

When the bee stings him, he does not fear its sting,
and it passes him by [to its honey] in a house of the bees' repeated returns.

That is, he did not fear and was not concerned. Al-raja (with the alif maqsura) means the side of a well and its two edges, and every side is a raja. The common people err in saying "O great raja," pronouncing it short rather than long.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verses 217–218 (part 1 of 3):

There are twelve issues (masa'il) in it.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They ask you﴾ has already been discussed [[See p. 36 of this part.]]. Jarir ibn Abd al-Hamid and Muhammad ibn Fudayl narrated from Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "I have not seen a people better than the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ). They asked him only about thirteen issues, all of which are in the Qur'an: ﴿They ask you about menstruation﴾, ﴿They ask you about the sacred month﴾, ﴿They ask you about orphans﴾." They asked only about what would benefit them.

Ibn Abd al-Barr said: "In the hadith, of the thirteen issues, only three are found."

Abu al-Yasar narrated from Jundub ibn Abd Allah that the Prophet (ﷺ) sent a detachment (rahT) and appointed over them Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Harith, or Ubaydah ibn al-Harith. When he was about to set out, he wept out of longing for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). So he sent Abd Allah ibn Jahsh, wrote a letter for him, and ordered him not to read the letter until he reached such-and-such a place. He said: "Do not compel any of your companions to march." When he reached the place, he read the letter, uttered "Inna lillah" and said: "Hearing and obedience to Allah and His Messenger." He said: "Two men returned and the rest went on. They met Ibn al-Hadrami and killed him, and they did not realize that it was the day of Rajab. The polytheists said: 'You have killed in the sacred month.' So Allah sent down: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month﴾, the verse."

It is also reported that the cause of its revelation was that two men of Banu Kilab met Amr ibn Umayya al-Damri, not knowing that they had been with the Prophet (ﷺ), and that was on the first day of Rajab, so he killed them. Quraysh said: "He killed them in the sacred month," and the verse was revealed.

The view that its revelation concerns the story of Abd Allah ibn Jahsh is more prevalent and better known. The Prophet (ﷺ) sent him with nine men, and it was said eight, in Jumada al-Akhira, two months before Badr, and it was said in Rajab.

Abu Umar said in his book al-Durar: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned from pursuing Kurz ibn Jabir, an expedition known as the First Badr, he remained in Medina for the rest of Jumada al-Akhira and Rajab. In Rajab he sent Abd Allah ibn Jahsh ibn Ri'ab al-Asadi with eight men from the Emigrants: Abu Hudhayfah ibn Utba, Ukkasha ibn Mihsan, Utba ibn Ghazwan, Suhayl ibn Bayda' al-Fihri, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Amir ibn Rabi'ah, Waqid ibn Abd Allah al-Tamimi, and Khalid ibn Bukayr al-Laythi. He wrote a letter for Abd Allah ibn Jahsh and ordered him not to look into it until he had marched for two days, then to look into it, and to carry out what he had been ordered [[Addition from the Sirah of Ibn Hisham and the History of al-Tabari. See the expedition of Abd Allah ibn Jahsh.]], and not to compel any of his companions. He was their commander. Abd Allah ibn Jahsh did what he was ordered. When he opened the letter and read it, he found in it: 'When you have looked into this letter of mine, proceed until you alight at a palm grove between Mecca and al-Ta'if, and keep watch there on Quraysh, and learn for us some of their news.' When he read the letter, he said: 'Hearing and obedience.' Then he informed his companions of this, and that he would not compel any of them, and that he was setting out for his destination with whoever obeyed him, and that if no one obeyed him he would go alone. He said: 'Whoever loves martyrdom, let him set out, and whoever dislikes death, let him return.' They said: 'We all desire what you desire, and none of us is other than one who hears and obeys the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' They set out with him. He took the route toward the Hijaz. A camel that Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Utba ibn Ghazwan were riding in turns ran off, so the two of them fell behind in pursuit of it, while Abd Allah ibn Jahsh continued with the rest toward his destination until he alighted at Nakhla. A caravan of Quraysh passed by them, carrying raisins and merchandise, among it Amr ibn al-Hadrami (al-Hadrami's name was Abd Allah ibn Abbad of the Sadaf, and Sadaf is a clan of Hadramawt), and Uthman ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Mughira and his brother Nawfal ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Mughira, both of Makhzum, and al-Hakam ibn Kaysan, client of Banu al-Mughira. The Muslims consulted and said: 'We are on the last day of Rajab, the sacred month. If we fight them, we violate the sanctity of the sacred month; and if we leave them, tonight they will enter the Sacred Precinct.' Then they agreed to engage them. Waqid ibn Abd Allah al-Tamimi shot Amr ibn al-Hadrami and killed him. They captured Uthman ibn Abd Allah and al-Hakam ibn Kaysan, and Nawfal ibn Abd Allah escaped. Then they returned with the caravan and the two captives. Abd Allah ibn Jahsh said to them: 'Set aside the fifth (khums) of what we have taken as spoils for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' They did so, and it was the first fifth in Islam. Then the Qur'an was revealed: ﴿And know that whatever you obtain as spoils, a fifth of it belongs to Allah﴾ [[Verse 41 of surah al-Anfal.]]. Thus Allah and His Messenger approved the action of Abd Allah ibn Jahsh, were pleased with it, and established it as a sunnah for the community until the Day of Resurrection. It was the first spoil taken in Islam, the first commander, and Amr ibn al-Hadrami was the first person killed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) disapproved of the killing of Ibn al-Hadrami in the sacred month, so the people were at a loss. Then Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it﴾ up to His saying: ﴿they will abide therein forever﴾. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) accepted ransom for the two captives. As for Uthman ibn Abd Allah, he died in Mecca as a disbeliever. As for al-Hakam ibn Kaysan, he embraced Islam and remained with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) until he was martyred at the Well of Ma'una. Sa'd and Utba returned to Medina safe."

It was also said: "The departure of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Utba in pursuit of their camel was with permission from Abd Allah ibn Jahsh. When Amr ibn al-Hadrami and his companions saw the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), they were frightened of them, so Abd Allah ibn Jahsh said: 'The people are alarmed by you. Shave the head of one of you and let him show himself to them; when they see him shaved, they will feel secure and say: "They are pilgrims (umar); there is no harm upon you."' They consulted about fighting them..." (the hadith continues).

The Jews took it as an omen and said: "Waqid (the one who kindles) — the war has been kindled; Amr — the war has become populated (a'marat); al-Hadrami — the war has been present (hadarat)."

The people of Mecca sent for the ransom of their two captives. The Prophet (ﷺ) said [[That is, the Prophet (ﷺ), as in the Tafsir of al-Tabari.]]: "We will not ransom them until Sa'd and Utba come back. If they do not come back, we will kill them in exchange for them." When they came back, he ransomed them. As for al-Hakam, he embraced Islam and remained in Medina until he was martyred on the day of Ma'una. As for Uthman, he returned to Mecca and died there as a disbeliever. As for Nawfal, on the day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab) he struck the belly of his horse to make it leap into the trench against the Muslims, and he fell into the trench with his horse, and both were crushed; Allah caused him to die. The polytheists asked for his corpse in exchange for money, but the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Take it, for its corpse is vile and its blood-money is vile." This is the cause of the revelation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month﴾.

Ibn Ishaq mentioned that the killing of Amr ibn al-Hadrami took place on the last day of Rajab, as previously stated. Al-Tabari reported from al-Suddi and others that it was on the last day of Jumada al-Akhira, but the first is more well known, although it has come from Ibn Abbas that it was on the first night of Rajab, while the Muslims thought it was from Jumada.

Ibn Atiyyah said: "The Sahib ibn Abbad mentioned in his well-known epistle, al-Asadiyya, that Abd Allah ibn Jahsh was named Commander of the Believers at that time, because he was appointed over a group of believers."

The second: The scholars differed concerning the abrogation (naskh) of this verse. The majority hold that it is abrogated, and that fighting the polytheists in the sacred months is permissible. They differed about its abrogating verse. Al-Zuhri said: "It was abrogated by: ﴿and fight the polytheists all together﴾ [[Verse 36 of surah al-Tawba.]]." It was said: "It was abrogated by the Prophet's (ﷺ) raid on Thaqif in a sacred month, and his sending Abu Amir [[He is Abu Amir al-Ash'ari, cousin of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.]] to Awtas [[Awtas: a valley in the lands of Hawazin, where the Battle of Hunayn took place. See Tabaqat of Ibn Sa'd and the Sirah of Ibn Hisham on the Battle of Hunayn.]] in a sacred month." It was said: "It was abrogated by the Pledge of Ridwan on fighting in Dhu al-Qa'da." This is weak, for when the Prophet (ﷺ) received word of the killing of Uthman in Mecca and that they were determined to fight him, he then took the pledge from the Muslims to repel them, not to initiate fighting against them.

Al-Bayhaqi mentioned, from Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, outside the narration of Muhammad ibn Ishaq, after the story of al-Hadrami: "Then Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it﴾, the verse." He said: "Allah informed them in His Book that fighting in the sacred month is forbidden, as it was. What they consider lawful with regard to the believers is far greater than that: barring them from the way of Allah when they imprison them, torture them, and detain them from emigrating to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); their disbelief in Allah; their barring the Muslims from the Sacred Mosque for hajj, 'umrah, and prayer in it; their expelling its people, who are Muslims; and their tempting them away from their religion. We were informed that the Prophet (ﷺ) paid blood-money [[Aql the slain: he gave his heirs his blood-money after he was killed.]] for Ibn al-Hadrami and kept the sacred month sacred as he used to, until Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: ﴿A declaration of immunity from Allah and His Messenger﴾."

Ata' used to say: "The verse is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated), and fighting in the sacred months is not permitted, and he would swear to that, because the verses revealed after it are general regarding all times, while this one is specific, and the general does not abrogate the specific by consensus."

Abu al-Zubayr narrated from Jabir: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not fight in a sacred month unless he was attacked, or unless he attacked. [[So in the Tafsir of al-Fakhr al-Razi and many other tafsir books; in the originals: "unless he was attacked or attacked." In al-Tabari: "unless he was attacked or attacked; when that came, he remained until it ended."]]"

The third: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿fighting in it﴾. "Qital" (fighting) is, according to Sibawayh, a badal ishtimal (apposition of inclusion), because the question included both the month and the fighting. That is, the disbelievers asked you out of astonishment at the violation of the sanctity of the month, so their question about the month was only on account of fighting in it. Al-Zajjaj said: "The meaning is: They ask you about fighting in the sacred month." Al-Qutaybi said: "They ask you about fighting in the sacred month: is it permissible?" So he substituted qital for shahr. Sibawayh recited:

"Qays's death was not the death of a single man,
but it was the building of a people that collapsed."

[[The verse is by Abida ibn al-Tabib, who lamented Qays ibn Asim al-Minqari, chief of the people of the wabr (the tent-dwellers) of Tamim.
(From the Book of Sibawayh, vol. 1, p. 77, Bulaq edition.)]]

Ikrimah recited "يَسْأَلُونَكَ عَنِ الشَّهْرِ الْحَرَامِ قَتْلٍ فِيهِ قُلْ قَتْلٌ" without the alif in either word. It was also said that the meaning is "They ask you about the sacred month and about fighting in it," and Ibn Mas'ud recited it this way. On this reading it is in the genitive by "'an" (from), repeated, as al-Kisa'i said. Al-Farra' said: it is in the genitive by the intention of "'an." Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is in the genitive by *al-jiwar* (attraction, adjacency). Al-Nahhas said: it is not permissible for a thing to be given inflection by *al-jiwar* in the Book of God or in any speech. *Al-jiwar* is an error, and it occurs only in an anomalous case, namely their saying: "hadhā juḥru ḍabbin kharibin" (this is the hole of a dhabb lizard, a ruined one). The proof that it is an error is the Arabs' saying in the dual: "hadhāni juḥrā ḍabbin kharibāni." This is like *al-iqwa'* (the rhyme-vowel irregularity in poetry), and nothing from the Book of God may be interpreted this way. Only the most eloquent and soundest of dialects may be used. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Abu 'Ubaydah said it is in the genitive by *al-jiwar*, and this statement of his is an error. Al-Nahhas said: It is also not permissible to assume an elided "'an," and the correct view is that it is a substitute (*badal*).

Al-A'raj recited "يَسْأَلُونَكَ عَنِ الشَّهْرِ الْحَرَامِ قِتَالٌ فِيهِ" with *raf'* (nominative). Al-Nahhas said: This is obscure in Arabic grammar. The meaning is: "They ask you about the sacred month: is fighting in it permissible?" The phrase "yas'alūnaka" indicates interrogation, as Imru' al-Qays said:

"Do you see, O friend, a lightning flash whose glimmer I show you,
Like the flashing of two hands in a cloud-mass, crowned (with lightning)?"

[[*Al-wamīḍ*: the flash of lightning. "Kal-lam' al-yadayn": he meant like the movement and turning of the hands. *Al-ḥabā*: what rises of the cloud. It was also said: it is what extends across like a mountain before it covers the sky. *Al-mukallal* of the clouds: streaked with lightning. It is also said: it is that around which there are pieces of thick clouds.]]

The meaning is "Do you see lightning?" The alif of interrogation was elided, because the alif in "aṣāḥ" indicates it, even though it is the particle of address, as the poet said:

"Are you departing from the tribe, or are you hastening away?"

The meaning is "Are you departing?" The alif was elided because "am" indicates it.
