Fourth: God's words, ﴿Say: Fighting therein is a great (matter)﴾, are an inchoative (*mubtada'*) and predicate (*khabar*), meaning: it is reprehensible, because the prohibition of fighting in the sacred month was established at that time, since the initiation of hostilities came from the Muslims. The word "al-shahr" (the month) in the verse is a generic noun. The Arabs had been given the sacred month by God as a foundation (*qiwām*) around which they balanced their affairs, so they did not shed blood or make changes in the sacred months. These are Rajab, Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah and al-Muharram: three consecutive months (*sard*) and one single month (*fard*) [[The three consecutive months: Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah and al-Muharram. *Sard* means consecutive. The single one is Rajab, and it is alone because Sha'ban, Ramadan and Shawwal come after it.]]. More explanation of this will come, God willing, in *al-Ma'idah*.

Fifth: God's words, ﴿and hindering from the way of God﴾, form an inchoative (*ibtida'*). "(And disbelief in Him)" is conjoined to "ṣadd." "(And the Sacred Mosque)" is conjoined to "sabīl Allāh" (the way of God). "(And expelling its people from it)" is conjoined to "ṣadd." The predicate of the inchoative is "(is greater in the sight of God)," meaning: it is greater in sin than fighting in the sacred month. This is what al-Mubarrad and others said, and it is the sound view, because of the long prevention of people from circumambulating the Ka'bah. "And disbelief in Him" means in God. It was also said: "And disbelief in Him" means in the pilgrimage and the Sacred Mosque. "And expelling its people from it is greater" means greater in punishment in the sight of God than fighting in the sacred month.

Al-Farra' said: "ṣadd" is conjoined to "kabīr" (great), and "al-masjid" is conjoined to the pronoun in "bihi" (in it/Him), so the sentence forms one continuous construction, not an interrupted one. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: That is an error, because the meaning leads to the conclusion that God's words "and disbelief in Him," meaning in God, are also conjoined to "kabīr," and from this it would follow that expelling the people of the Mosque from it is greater than disbelief in the sight of God. The corruption of this is obvious.

The meaning of the verse according to the majority view is: "You, disbelievers of Quraysh, consider fighting in the sacred month a great matter against us, but what you yourselves do, namely hindering from the way of God those who wish to embrace Islam, disbelieving in God, and expelling the people of the Mosque from it, as you did to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his companions, is greater in crime in the sight of God."

'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh (may God be pleased with him) said:

"You count the killing in the sacred month a great matter,
But greater than it, if he who sees the right path were to see it, is (your deed).
Your turning away from what Muhammad says,
And your disbelief in him, while God is Seeing and Witnessing.
And your expelling from the Mosque of God its people,
So that none may be seen prostrating to God in the House.
We, though you have wronged us by killing him (Ibn al-Hadrami),
And though the envious and the rebellious spread rumours against Islam,
We gave Ibn al-Hadrami a drink of our spears at Nakhlah,
When the one who kindles war (Waqid) kindled it,
A blood-price, while Ibn 'Abd Allah 'Uthman is among us,
Contended for by a shackle of rawhide, a stubborn one."

Al-Zuhri, Mujahid and others said: God's words, ﴿Say: Fighting therein is a great (matter)﴾, were abrogated by His words, "And fight the polytheists all together" [[Qur'an 9:36]], and by His words, "Then kill the polytheists" [[Verse 5, Surah al-Tawbah.]]. 'Ata' said: It was not abrogated, and fighting in the sacred months is not proper, as already mentioned.

Sixth: God's words, ﴿and persecution is greater than killing﴾. Mujahid and others said: "Fitnah" here means disbelief, meaning: your disbelief is greater than our killing of those people. The majority said: The meaning of "fitnah" here is their seducing the Muslims from their religion until they perish. That is, this is more gravely sinful than your killing in the sacred month.

Seventh: God's words, ﴿and they will not cease﴾, are an inchoative and a report from God, and a warning from Him to the believers against the evil of the disbelievers. Mujahid said: It refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh. "Yaruddūkum" (they will turn you back) is in the subjunctive after "ḥattā" (until), because it is a bare final limit.

Eighth: God's words, ﴿And whoever of you turns back﴾, meaning returns from Islam to disbelief, ﴿then those—their deeds are nullified﴾, meaning they become void and corrupt. From this comes "ḥabaṭ," which is a corruption afflicting livestock in their bellies from eating too much pasture, so that their bellies swell, and they sometimes die from it. Thus the verse is a threat to Muslims, so that they may remain steadfast in the religion of Islam.

Ninth: The scholars differed concerning the apostate: Is he to be asked to repent or not? Does his deed become void by the apostasy itself, or only if he dies in disbelief? Does he inherit or not? These are three questions.

The first: One group said he is to be asked to repent; if he repents, well, otherwise he is killed. Some said: for one hour. Others said: he is given a month. Others said: he is given three days, as narrated from 'Umar and 'Uthman, and this is the view of Malik, transmitted from him by Ibn al-Qasim. Al-Hasan said: he is asked to repent a hundred times. It is also narrated from him that he is killed without being asked to repent. This is also the view of al-Shafi'i in one of his two opinions, and it is one of the two views of Tawus and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr.

Sahnun mentioned that 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Abi Salamah al-Majishun used to say: The apostate is killed and is not asked to repent. He argued with the hadith of Mu'adh and Abu Musa, in which: When the Prophet (ﷺ) sent Abu Musa to Yemen, he sent Mu'adh ibn Jabal after him. When he arrived, he said, "Dismount," and threw him a cushion. And there was a man with him who was bound. He said, "What is this?" He said, "This was a Jew who became Muslim, then turned back from his religion to the evil religion, and became a Jew." He said, "I will not sit until he is killed, the judgment of God and His Messenger." He said, "Sit down." He said, "[Yes [[Addition from Sahih Muslim.]]] I will not sit until he is killed, the judgment of God and His Messenger," three times. So he ordered him, and he was killed. Muslim and others transmitted it.

Abu Yusuf reported from Abu Hanifah that the apostate is presented with Islam; if he embraces it, well, otherwise he is killed on the spot, unless he asks for a delay, in which case he is given three days. The well-known view from him and his companions is that the apostate is not killed until he is asked to repent. For them, the *zindiq* (heretic, one who conceals disbelief) and the apostate are alike. Malik said: The *zanadiqah* (heretics) are killed and are not asked to repent. This has already been discussed at the beginning of *al-Baqarah* [[See vol. 1, p. 198.]].

They differed concerning one who passes from one disbelief to another disbelief. Malik and the majority of jurists said: He is not interfered with, because he has moved to what, had he been upon it from the beginning, would have been left as it is. Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam reported from al-Shafi'i that he is killed, on the basis of the Prophet's (peace be upon him) words, "Whoever changes his religion, kill him," and he did not restrict it to a Muslim as opposed to a disbeliever. Malik said: The meaning of the hadith is one who leaves Islam for disbelief. As for one who passes from disbelief to disbelief, he is not meant by this hadith. This is also the view of a group of jurists.

The well-known view from al-Shafi'i, as reported by al-Muzani and al-Rabi', is that one among the *ahl al-dhimmah* (protected non-Muslims) who changes his religion is to be sent by the ruler to the land of war, expelled from his city, and his property is permitted along with the property of the non-Muslim combatants, if the Muslims prevail over the territory, because the protection was granted to him only upon the religion he held at the time the covenant was concluded.

They differed concerning the female apostate. Malik, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i and al-Layth ibn Sa'd said: She is killed just as the male apostate is killed. Their argument is the apparent meaning of the hadith, "Whoever changes his religion, kill him," and "man" (*man*) applies to both male and female. Al-Thawri, Abu Hanifah and his companions said: The female apostate is not killed. This is also the view of Ibn Shubrumah, and Ibn 'Ulayyah adopted it, and it is the view of 'Ata' and al-Hasan. They argued that Ibn 'Abbas narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said, "Whoever changes his religion, kill him." Then Ibn 'Abbas did not kill a female apostate, and whoever narrates a hadith knows best its interpretation. It is also narrated from 'Ali something similar. The Prophet (ﷺ) also forbade killing women and children. The first group argued with his (peace be upon him) words, "The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except in one of three cases: disbelief after belief..." It thus generalizes to everyone who disbelieves after his belief, and this is the sounder view.

Tenth: al-Shafi'i said: Whoever apostatizes and then returns to Islam, his deed is not nullified, nor his pilgrimage that he completed, but if he dies in apostasy, then at that point his deeds are nullified. Malik said: They are nullified by apostasy itself. The disagreement becomes evident in the case of a Muslim who performed the pilgrimage, then apostatized, then embraced Islam again. Malik said: He is obliged to perform the pilgrimage, because the first one was nullified by the apostasy. Al-Shafi'i said: There is no need to repeat it, because his deed remains.

Our scholars (the Malikis) cite in support God's words, ﴿If you associate partners with God, your deeds will surely be nullified﴾ [[Qur'an 39:65]]. They said: It is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and what is meant is his community, because apostasy is impossible for him in terms of the law. The companions of al-Shafi'i said: Rather, it is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ) in the manner of severe warning to the community, and a demonstration that if the Prophet (ﷺ), despite the nobility of his station, were to associate partners, his deeds would be nullified; so how about you! But he does not associate partners, because of the excellence of his rank, as He said: ﴿O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you commits a clear immorality, her punishment will be doubled twofold﴾ [[Qur'an 33:30]]. This is because of the nobility of their station; otherwise, no such act could be conceived from them, out of protection for their noble and honoured husband. (Ibn al-'Arabi.)

Our scholars said: God mentioned the condition of dying in that state (*muwafah*, dying upon a state) here only because He attached to it eternal dwelling in the Fire as its recompense. So whoever dies in disbelief, God makes him abide in the Fire by this verse, and whoever associates partners, his deeds are nullified by the other verse. Thus they are two verses.

Both verses yield two distinct meanings and two distinct rulings. What is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ applies to his community as well, unless his exclusive application is established. What is said concerning his wives is said about them to show that, if such a thing were conceivable, it would involve two violations: one of the sanctity of the religion, and the other of the sanctity of the Prophet ﷺ. Every violation of a sanctity incurs a punishment. This is comparable to one who disobeys during the sacred month, or in the sacred land, or in the Sacred Mosque, for whom the punishment is multiplied according to the number of sanctities he has violated. And Allah knows best.

The eleventh issue concerns the scholars' disagreement over the inheritance of the apostate (al-murtadd). Ali ibn Abi Talib, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, al-Hakam, al-Layth, Abu Hanifa and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh said: the apostate's estate passes to his Muslim heirs. Malik, Rabi'ah, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr said: his estate goes to the public treasury (bayt al-mal). Ibn Shubruma, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad and al-Awza'i, in one of two reports, said: whatever the apostate acquires after apostasy goes to his Muslim heirs. Abu Hanifa said: whatever the apostate acquired while in a state of apostasy goes to the public treasury, while whatever he had acquired while a Muslim and then apostatized passes to his Muslim heirs. As for Ibn Shubruma, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, they do not distinguish between the two situations. The unrestricted statement of the Prophet ﷺ, "There is no inheritance between the people of two religions," refutes their position. The scholars agreed that the apostate's heirs who are disbelievers do not inherit from him, except for Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, who said that they do inherit from him.

The twelfth issue concerns Allah's words: ﴿Indeed, those who have believed and those who have emigrated﴾, the verse. Jundab ibn Abd Allah, Urwa ibn al-Zubayr and others said: when Waqid ibn Abd Allah al-Tamimi killed Amr ibn al-Hadrami during the sacred month, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ held back from taking his fifth (khums) of the spoils, which Abd Allah ibn Jahsh had been granted as his share in the raid, and [he held back] regarding the two captives. The Muslims rebuked Abd Allah ibn Jahsh and his companions to the point that it grieved them. Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, consoled them with this verse concerning the sacred month and relieved them of their distress. He informed them that they would have the reward of those who emigrated and fought. So the reference to them is in His words, "Indeed, those who have believed," and then it remains applicable to everyone who does what Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has mentioned. It was also said: [[The meaning is that when Allah relieved the Muslims and the people of the expedition of what they were in, regarding the killing of Ibn al-Hadrami in the sacred month, by revealing His words, "They ask you about the sacred month" (2:217), they thought that it had only removed sin from them and that they would have no reward. So they became eager for it and said: "O Messenger of Allah, do we hope that there will be a raid in which we are given the reward of the fighters?" In another report: "If they had not committed a sin, then they have no reward?" So Allah revealed His words, "Indeed, those who have believed and those who have emigrated," the verse, and thereby Allah placed them at the highest hope in that.]]: if they had not committed a sin, then they have no reward. So Allah revealed, "Indeed, those who have believed and those who have emigrated," to the end of the verse.

Hijra (emigration) literally means moving from one place to another, with the intention of leaving the first for the sake of the second. Al-hajr is the opposite of joining, and one says hajarahu hajran and hijranan; the noun is hijra. Al-muhajara from one land to another is leaving the first for the second. Al-tahajur means severing ties. Whoever says that hijra is moving from the desert to the settled town has erred, on the ground that this was the most common case among the Arabs; but on his view the people of Makkah would not be emigrants. "Wa jahadu" (and struggled) is a form of the verb from jahada, meaning to exert effort, in the form mujahada and jihad. Ijtihad and tajahud mean exerting one's utmost ability and effort. Al-jahad (with a fatha) means hard ground. "Wa yarjun" (and they hope) means they aspire and regard it as near. He said "yarjun" (they hope) although He had praised them, because no one in this world knows that he will enter Paradise, however far he goes in obedience to Allah, for two reasons. The first: one does not know with what one's life will end. The second: so that one does not rely on one's deeds. Hope is pleasant, and hope is always accompanied by fear, just as fear is accompanied by hope. Al-raja' (hope) is from al-amal (expectation) and is a long-vowelled word. It is said: raja'tu fulanan rajwan wa raja'an wa rujaahu. It is said: "I did not come to you except in hope of good." Tarajjaytuhu, irtajaytuhu, rajaytuhu all mean the same as rajawtuhu. Bishr, addressing his daughter, said:

So hope for good and await my return
when the Qari' al-Anazi returns.

And I have no hope (rujayya) in so-and-so, meaning I do not hope for him. Rajw and raja' may also mean fear, as Allah says: "What is the matter with you that you do not expect (tarjuna) grandeur from Allah?" (71:13), meaning you do not fear the majesty of Allah. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

When the bee stings him, he does not fear its sting,
and it passes him by [to its honey] in a house of the bees' repeated returns.

That is, he did not fear and was not concerned. Al-raja (with the alif maqsura) means the side of a well and its two edges, and every side is a raja. The common people err in saying "O great raja," pronouncing it short rather than long.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In both there is great sin and benefits for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit.﴾

This contains nine issues.

**The first issue:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿They ask you﴾ [[See p. 37 of this volume.]]. The ones asking are the believers, as was mentioned earlier. *Al-khamr* (wine) is derived from *khamara*, meaning he covered or concealed, and from it comes *khimar*, a woman's head covering. Everything that covers something is said to have *khamarahu*. From this comes the saying "Cover (*khammiru*) your vessels." Wine covers the intellect (*takhmuru al-'aql*), meaning it veils and conceals it. From the same root comes the name *al-khamar* (with a fatha on the mim) for dense, interlacing vegetation, because it covers and conceals what is beneath it. From this it is said: *akhmarat al-ardu*, meaning the ground became abundant in such cover. The poet said:

*O Zayd and al-Dahhak, go on,*
*for you have passed the khamar of the road.*

That is, go on hiding yourselves, for you have passed the hollow in which the wolf and others conceal themselves. Al-'Ajjaj, describing an army that marches with banners and troops without concealing itself, said:

*In the gleaming eagles [[Al-'uqban (plural of 'iqab): banners. His saying "with the face of the earth" means that it passes nothing without making it a single direction, so its face goes with its face wherever it goes. His saying "drives the trees" means it passes over the *rimth* (a pasture of camels), the *'arfaj* and all other trees and drives them along with it, carrying them off because of their abundance. In manuscript B it is "al-'iqyan" with a ya', and he said: "al-'iqyan is pure gold; it is said to be what grows as a plant and is not obtained from stones." The same appears in manuscript J.]]*
*the khamar does not walk... it turns the earth and drives the trees.*

From the same usage comes their saying: "He entered the crowds of people and their *khimar*," meaning he is in a hidden place. Since wine conceals and veils the intellect, it was named for this. It was also said that wine was named *khamr* because it is left until it ripens, as they say: *qad ikhtamara al-'ajin*, meaning the dough reached its maturity; and *khumira al-ra'y*, meaning the opinion was left until its right course became clear. It was also said that wine was named *khamr* because it mixes with the intellect (*mukhamara*, from *al-mukhamara*, which is mixing), and from this comes their saying: "I entered among the *khimar* of the people," meaning I mingled with them. These three meanings are close to one another: wine is left and allowed to ferment until it ripens, then it mixes with the intellect, then it veils it. The root meaning is concealment.

*Al-khamr* is the juice of grapes that has begun to ferment or has been boiled. Whatever else overcomes the intellect has the same ruling, because the *ijma'* (scholarly consensus) of the scholars is that all gambling is forbidden. The gambling game (*maysir*) was singled out from among them, so the whole category was treated as an analogy (*qiyas*) to *maysir*. *Maysir* was only gambling in the form of the slaughtered camel in particular, so everything of the same kind as wine has the same status as wine.

**The second issue:** The majority of the Muslim community holds that whatever intoxicates in large quantity, other than grape wine, is forbidden in both small and large amounts, and the *hadd* (the prescribed punishment) for it is obligatory. Abu Hanifa, al-Thawri, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Shubrumah and a group of the jurists of Kufa said: whatever intoxicates in large quantity, other than grape wine, is *halal* [[That is, its small amount.]], and if someone becomes intoxicated from it without deliberately aiming to reach the state of intoxication, there is no *hadd* upon him. This view is weak, refuted by both reasoning and textual evidence, as will be explained in *al-Ma'idah* and *al-Nahl* [[See vol. 6, p. 285 onward, and vol. 10, p. 128 onward.]], if Allah the Exalted wills.

**The third issue:** Some of the exegetes said: Allah the Exalted did not leave any honour or virtue except that He gave it to this community. From His honour and kindness is that He did not impose the laws (*shara'i'*) upon them all at once, but imposed them one after another. Likewise was the prohibition of wine. This verse was the first revealed concerning wine. After it came: ﴿Do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾. Then His saying: ﴿Shaytan only wants to cause enmity and hatred among you through wine and gambling, and to turn you away from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. Will you then not desist?﴾ Then His saying: ﴿Wine, gambling, the stone altars and the divining arrows are only an abomination from the work of Shaytan, so avoid it﴾. This will be explained in *al-Ma'idah*.

**The fourth issue:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿and gambling﴾. *Al-maysir* is the gambling of the Arabs with the divining arrows. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: In the Jahiliyyah a man would stake his family and his wealth against another man, and whichever of them won over his companion took away his wealth and family. Then this verse was revealed. Mujahid, Muhammad ibn Sirin, al-Hasan, Ibn al-Musayyab, 'Ata', Qatadah, Mu'awiyah ibn Salih, Tawus, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) and Ibn 'Abbas also said: everything in which there is gambling, such as backgammon and chess, is *maysir*, even the children's games with walnuts and the dice-stones [[Al-ka'ab: the dice of backgammon.]], except what is permitted of racing horses and of drawing lots to determine rights, as will come later.

Malik said: *maysir* is of two kinds: the *maysir* of amusement and the *maysir* of gambling. The *maysir* of amusement includes backgammon, chess and all musical instruments. The *maysir* of gambling is whatever people stake against one another. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib said: chess is the *maysir* of the non-Arabs. According to Malik and other scholars, whatever is gambled upon is *maysir*. Further explanation of this subject will come in *Yunus* [[See vol. 8, p. 337 onward.]], if Allah the Exalted wills.

*Al-maysir* is derived from *al-yasar*, which means something becoming due to its owner. It is said: *yasara li kadha* when something became due to me, so he *yaysiru* *yasaran* and *maysiran*. *Al-yasir* is the one who plays with the arrows, and it is said *yasara yaysiru*. The poet said:

*So help them and gamble with what they gamble with,*
*and when they land in hardship, then land with them.*

Al-Azhari said: *al-maysir* is the slaughtered camel over which they gambled. It was called *maysir* because it is divided into parts, so it is as if it were the place of division, and everything you divide you have *yasartahu*. *Al-yasir* is the butcher, because he divides the meat of the camel. He said: this is the original meaning of *al-yasir*. Then those who strike with the arrows and gamble over the camel are called *yasirun*, because they are butchers, since they were the cause of this. In *al-Sihah* [it is said]: *wa yasara al-qawm al-jazura*, meaning they cut the camel into pieces and divided its limbs among themselves. Suhaym ibn Wathil al-Yarbu'i said:

*I say to them in the ravine when they gamble over me:*
*Did you not despair that I am the son of the knight Zahdam?* [[Tay'asu (from ya'isa) here means "to know." Zahdam (as Ja'far) is the name of a horse.]]

He had been taken captive and lots were cast for him with arrows. It is said: *yasara al-qawm* when they gambled. A man is *yasar* and *yasir*, with the same meaning. The plural is *ayasar*. Al-Nabigha said:

*That I complete my gamblers and give them*
*repeated favours, and clothe the leather pot.* [[His saying "repeated favours" means he repeats his kindness twice or three times.]]

Tarafah said:

*They are the gamblers of Luqman when*
*the winter [[Al-shatwah (singular of shita')... the Arabs regard winter as a time of famine, because people stay in their houses and do not go out to seek pasture. Ibda' (plural of bad'): great good in the camel. It is also said: it is the best share in it.]] makes them hungry, the first shares of the camel.*

Whoever volunteered to slaughter a camel was praised among them. The poet said:

*And I slaughtered a she-camel for a people of truth,*
*and I did not call out to the gamblers of the camel.*

**The fifth issue:** Malik narrated in the *Muwatta'* from Dawud ibn Husayn that he heard Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib say: "Among the gambling of the people of the Jahiliyyah was selling meat for a sheep or two sheep." According to Malik and the majority of his companions, this is applied to the same genus, where the animal is sold for its own meat, and for them it falls under *al-muzabana* [[al-Muzabana (muzabanah): selling fresh dates on the palm for dried dates. According to Malik: every *juzaf* (sale of an unmeasured lot) whose measure, count, or weight is not known is a sale for a named price of something measured, weighed, or counted, or a sale of a known thing for an unknown thing of the same kind, or a sale of an unknown thing for an unknown thing of the same kind.]] and *al-gharar* [[Al-gharar: selling fish in water and birds in the air. It is said: that which has an outward appearance that deceives the buyer and an unknown inner reality. Al-Azhari said: the sales of gharar include the unknown sales whose true nature is concealed from both contracting parties until it becomes known.]] and *al-qimar* [[Gambling (qimar).]], because it is not known whether the animal contains meat equal to what was given, less, or more. Selling meat for meat is not permitted when unequal, so selling a live animal for meat is like selling meat concealed in its hide, when both are of one genus. According to him, the one genus includes camels, cattle, sheep, gazelles, wild goats, and all other wild animals, and all quadrupeds that are eaten form one genus for him. It is not permitted to sell any animal of this category or genus for any single piece of its meat in any way, because for him it falls under *al-muzabana*, like selling raisins for grapes, olives for olive oil, sesame oil for sesame seeds, and the like. For him, all birds are one genus, and likewise fish, whether of the sea or otherwise. It is also narrated from him that locusts alone are a separate kind.

Al-Shafi'i, his companions, and al-Layth ibn Sa'd said: selling meat for a live animal is not permitted under any circumstances, whether the two are of one genus or of two different genera, based on the general wording of the hadith.

It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that a slaughtered camel was butchered in the time of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and divided into ten portions. A man said: "Give me a portion of it for a sheep." Abu Bakr said: "This is not permissible." Al-Shafi'i said: "I know of no companion who opposed Abu Bakr in this."

Abu Umar (Ibn Abd al-Barr) said: It has been narrated from Ibn Abbas that he permitted selling a sheep for meat, but this report is not strong. Abd al-Razzaq narrated from al-Thawri, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, that he disliked selling a living animal for a dead one, meaning a slaughtered sheep for a standing one. Sufyan said: "We see no harm in it."

Al-Muzani said: If the hadith on selling a live animal for meat is not authentic, then analogy (*qiyas*) [[Qiyas: analogical reasoning.]] permits it. If it is authentic, analogy is set aside and the report is followed.

Abu Umar said: The Kufans have many arguments, from analogy and reasoning, that selling meat for a live animal is permitted. However, once the report is authentic, analogy and reasoning are set aside.

Malik narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade selling a live animal for meat. Abu Umar said: I do not know of this being connected to the Prophet (ﷺ) through any firm chain, and the best of its chains is the *mursal* [[Mursal: a report in which the Successor (tabi'i) attributes a statement directly to the Prophet (ﷺ), omitting the Companion from the chain.]] of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, as mentioned by Malik in his *Muwatta'*. Al-Shafi'i followed this, although his principle is that he does not accept *mursal* reports. Yet he claimed that he examined the *mursal* reports of Sa'id and found them, or most of them, sound. So he disliked selling types of live animals for types of meat, according to the apparent meaning and general wording of the hadith, since no report or consensus specifies otherwise. For him, it is not permitted to specify the text by analogy. For him, the word "animal" (*hayawan*) refers to everything that lives on land and in water, even if its kinds differ, just as "food" (*ta'am*) refers to everything that is eaten or drunk. So understand this.

**The sixth issue:** The words of the Exalted: ﴿Say: In both of them is great sin﴾, meaning wine and gambling. The sin of wine includes what proceeds from the drinker of quarrelling, insulting, obscene speech, and false speech, the loss of reason by which one recognizes what is due to one's Creator, the neglect of prayers, and the diversion from the remembrance of Allah, and other such things. Al-Nasa'i narrated from Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "Avoid wine, for it is the mother of all evils. There was a man among those before you who was devoted in worship, and a corrupt woman fell in love with him. She sent her slave-girl to him, saying: 'We are calling you to give testimony.' So he went with the slave-girl, and she kept closing doors behind him each time he entered one, until she brought him to a beautiful woman who had a boy with her and a jar of wine. She said: 'By Allah, I did not call you to testify, but I called you so that you would have intercourse with me, or drink a cup of this wine, or kill this boy.' He said: 'Give me a cup of this wine.' So she gave him a cup. He said: 'Give me more,' and he did not stop until he had intercourse with her and killed the soul. So avoid wine, for by Allah, faith and persistence in wine never coexist, except that one of them soon drives out the other."

Abu Umar mentioned this in *al-Isti'ab*.

It is also narrated that al-A'sha, when he set out for Madinah to embrace Islam, met some polytheists on the road, who asked him: "Where are you going?" He told them that he wanted Muhammad (ﷺ). They said: "You will not reach him, for he will command you to pray." He said: "Serving the Lord is obligatory." They said: "He will command you to give wealth to the poor." He said: "Doing good is obligatory." It was said to him: "He forbids fornication." He said: "It is indecent and repugnant to reason, and I have become an old man, so I have no need of it." It was said to him: "He forbids drinking wine." He said: "As for this, I cannot endure without it!" So he turned back and said: "I will drink wine for a year, then return to him." He had not reached his home when he fell from his camel, broke his neck, and died.

Qays ibn Asim al-Minqari used to drink wine in the Jahiliyyah, then forbade it to himself. The reason for this was that he pinched his daughter's fold of flesh while he was drunk, insulted his parents, saw the moon and said something, and gave much of his wealth to the wine seller. When he came to his senses and was informed of this, he forbade wine to himself, and about it he said:

*I saw wine as good, but in it are qualities that corrupt the forbearing man.*
*By Allah, I will never drink it while healthy, nor be cured by it when ill.*
*I will never give my life's wealth for it, nor ever invite a companion to drink it.*
*For wine disgraces its drinkers, and brings upon them a great calamity.*

Abu Umar said: Ibn al-A'rabi narrated from al-Mufaddal al-Dabbi that these verses belong to Abu Mihjan al-Thaqafi, who said them when he gave up wine, and he is the one who said (may Allah be pleased with him):

*When I die, bury me beside a vine whose roots will water my bones after my death.*
*And do not bury me in the desert, for I fear that when I die I will not taste it.* [[In the nominative, either because "an" is neglected or because it is the light form of the heavy one.]]

Umar flogged him for drinking several times and exiled him to an island in the sea. He joined Sa'd, and Umar wrote to him to imprison him, so he imprisoned him. Abu Mihjan was one of the bravest of the *buhm* [[Al-buhm (plural of buhmah): a horseman whose attack cannot be anticipated because of his great valor.]]. When he took part in the battle of al-Qadisiyyah, which is well known, Sa'd released his shackles and said: "We will never flog you for wine again." Abu Mihjan said: "By Allah, I will never drink it again," and he never drank it after that.

In another report he said: "I used to drink it when the prescribed punishment was being applied to me [and I was purified by it] [[An addition from the book *al-Isti'ab*.]], but now, since you have nullified me by dropping the punishment from me, by Allah, I will never drink it again."

Al-Haytham ibn Adi mentioned that someone who saw the grave of Abu Mihjan at Badhir Bayjan, or he said: in the regions of Jurjan, told him that three vine roots had grown over his grave, had grown long and borne fruit, and were trellised over his grave, and written on the grave was: "This is the grave of Abu Mihjan." He said: "I began to marvel and recalled his words: 'When I die, bury me beside a vine.'"

Furthermore, the drinker becomes a laughing-stock for sensible people. He plays with his urine and excrement, and sometimes wipes his face with them, until some were seen wiping their faces with their urine and saying: "O Allah, make me one of those who repent and make me one of those who purify themselves." Some were seen while a dog was licking his face, and he was saying to it: "May Allah honour you."

As for gambling, it produces enmity and hatred, because it is consuming the property of others falsely.

**The seventh issue:** The words of the Exalted: ﴿and benefits for people﴾. As for wine, its benefit is the profit of trade, for they used to bring it from Syria cheaply and sell it in the Hijaz at a profit, and they did not regard bargaining over it as proper, so the one seeking wine would buy it at a high price. This is the most accurate of what has been said about its benefit. It has also been said about its benefits that it aids digestion, strengthens weakness, helps sexual potency, makes the miser generous, makes the coward brave, clears the complexion, and other pleasures derived from it. Hassan ibn Thabit (may Allah be pleased with him) said:

*We drink it, and it leaves us kings, and lions whom meeting does not restrain.*

And there are other verses about its joys. Another said [[He is al-Munakhkhal al-Yashkuri.]]:

*When I drink, I am the lord of al-Khawarnaq and al-Sadir.*
*And when I am sober, I am the lord of the little she-camel and the camel.*

The benefit of gambling is that a thing comes to a person through gambling without effort or toil. They used to buy a slaughtered camel and cast lots with their arrows. Whoever's arrow came out received his share of the meat without owing any of the price, and whoever's arrow remained last had to pay the price of the whole camel and received no meat. It has also been said that its benefit is providing for the needy, for whoever among them won would not eat from the camel, but would distribute it among the needy.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 219 (part 3 of 3):

The arrows of the maysir (gambling) were eleven arrows. Of them, seven had shares (ḥuẓūẓ), and on them were prescribed portions according to the number of shares. They are: "al-Fadh" (the single), which bears one mark: he who draws it gains a share, and he who draws it and loses owes a share. The second is "al-Tawam" (the twin), which bears two marks, and for it and against it are two shares. The third is "al-Raqib" (the watcher), which bears three marks, as we have mentioned. The fourth is "al-Hils", which has four. The fifth is "al-Nafiz", and also "al-Nafis", which has five. The sixth is "al-Musbil", which has six. The seventh is "al-Mu'alla", which has seven. That totals twenty-eight portions, and the shares of the slaughtered camel are likewise, according to the view of al-Asma'i. Four arrows remained, and these are the "aghfal" (blanks), which have neither portions nor shares. They are: "al-Musaddar", "al-Mudha'af", "al-Maniḥ" and "al-Safih". It was also said: the remaining blanks are three: "al-Safih", "al-Maniḥ" and "al-Waghd". These three are added so that the arrows are multiplied for the one who shuffles them (yujīluhā) [[yujīluhā: from ajāla, yujīlu, ijāla, meaning to move them; that is, he places his hand in the bag and moves them twice or thrice.]], so that he finds no way to favour anyone. The one who shuffles is called the mufīḍ [[al-ifāḍa bi-l-qidāḥ: striking with the arrows and shuffling them during gambling.]], the striker (ḍārib), the ḍarīb, and the plural is ḍurabā'. It was also said: a watcher (raqīb) is placed behind him so that he does not favour anyone. Then the ḍarīb kneels on his knees, wraps himself in a garment, puts his head out, and inserts his hand into the rabāba [[The author, may God have mercy on him, will mention the meaning of rabāba.]], and draws out.

It was the custom of the Arabs to strike the camel with these arrows in winter, in the hard season, when the cold was fierce upon the poor. The camel would be bought, and the well-off would bear its price, and its owner would be content to forgo his right. They used to take pride in this and would blame whoever among them did not do so, calling him "al-baram" (the stingy). Mutammim ibn Nuwayra said:

"Nor a stingy one for whose wedding the women offer gifts, when the skins rattle from the cold of winter."

Then it is slaughtered and divided into ten portions. Ibn 'Atiyya said: al-Asma'i erred in the division of the camel, for he mentioned that it is divided according to the shares of the arrows, twenty-eight portions, and that is not so. Then lots are cast over the ten, and whoever's arrow wins, by coming out of the rabāba first, takes his portions and gives them to the poor.

The rabāba (with a kasra on the rā'): it resembles a quiver (kinānah) in which the arrows of the maysir are gathered, and they sometimes call all the arrows a rabāba. Abu Dhu'ayb said, describing the donkey and his she-ass:

"And it is as if they were a rabāba, and he a yasar that dispenses the arrows and divides them."

The rabāba also means a covenant and a pact. The poet said [[He is 'Alqama ibn 'Abada, as in his Diwan.]]:

"I was a man who surrendered to you my rabāba, and before you it had owned me, so I was lost, a rubūb."

[[Rabbatnī means: kings' lords possessed me, so I was lost until I came to you. al-Rubūb (plural of rabb): the owners.]]

At times they gambled for themselves, and then the one whose arrow did not win would pay the price, as has been mentioned previously. The poor of the tribe lived by this way of life, and from this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"Those who feed the guest when they spend the winter, and who make sustenance dependent on the gambler."

And from it is the saying of another [[He is 'Umar ibn Qami'a, as in Taj al-'Arus and al-Lisan, entry "ghalaqa".]]:

"In their hands are the marked arrows (maqrūma), and the maghālīq (the winning arrows), which return by the gifts of the needy (al-'ufā) their maniḥ."

[[al-Maqrūma: marked with signs. The maghāliq are the arrows of the maysir. It was said: the maghāliq are among the attributes of the arrows of the maysir by which victory is achieved, and they are not among their names; they are what locks the stake and makes it due to the winning gambler, as a pledge is locked for its rightful claimant. (From al-Lisan.)]] [[Thus in the originals. al-'Ufā: the guests and seekers of kindness. What is in al-Lisan and Taj al-'Arus is "al-'iyāl" (dependants).]]

The "maniḥ" in this verse is the one who seeks a gift (al-mustamnih), because they used to borrow the arrow that had become smooth and whose winning was frequent; that is the praised maniḥ. As for the maniḥ which is one of the blanks, it is described only as "returning" (karr), and it is this that al-Akhtal meant in his saying [[In the originals: "Jarir", and the correction is from the Diwan of al-Akhtal. The verse is from a poem satirising Jarir, whose opening is:
"Your eye lied to you, or did you see at Wasit?"
See his Diwan p. 41, Beirut edition.]]:

"Indeed they turned upon Fazara a turn like the return of the maniḥ, and they circled there in a circle."

In al-Sihah: "The maniḥ is an arrow of the arrows of the maysir which has no share unless its owner is granted something." From the maysir is the saying of Labid [[Thus in the originals. What is in Ibn Qutayba's "al-Maysir wa-l-Qidah" and in al-Mufaddaliyyat is that it belongs to al-Muraqqish al-Akbar, from a poem of his, whose opening is:
"Absent are my neighbours, and I am not one who turns back."
See al-Mufaddaliyyat p. 474, Europe edition.]]:

"When they gambled, ease did not bring among them lewdness whose mention is lamented in the summer."

All of this is the benefit of the maysir, except that it is "the consuming of wealth falsely."

Eighth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And their sin is greater than their benefit﴾. God, mighty and majestic, informed that the sin is greater than the benefit, and more harmful in the Hereafter. The great sin is after the prohibition, while the benefits were before the prohibition.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "kathīr" with the three-dotted thā', and their argument is that the Prophet ﷺ cursed wine and cursed with it ten: its seller, its buyer, the one for whom it is bought, its presser, the one for whom it is pressed, its server, its drinker, its carrier, the one for whom it is carried, and the one who eats its price. Also, the plurality of benefits is fitting with the plurality of sins, and "kathīr" with the three-dotted thā' conveys that. The rest of the readers and the majority of people read "kabīr" with the single-dotted bā', and their argument is that the sin of gambling and drinking wine is among the major sins, so describing it as "great" is more fitting. Also, their agreement on "akbar" is an argument for "kabīr" with the single bā'. They agreed to reject "akthar" with the three-dotted thā', except in the codex of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, where there is "qul fihimā ithmun kathīr" and "wa-ithmuhumā akthar", with the thā' three-dotted in both letters.

Ninth: Some people of reasoning said: wine was prohibited by this verse, because God the Exalted said: "Say: My Lord has forbidden only indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is hidden, and sin" [[Verse 33 of surah al-A'raf.]]. So in this verse He informed that there is sin in it, and so it is forbidden. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this reasoning is not good, because the sin that is in it is the prohibited, not that it is itself, as this reasoning requires. I say: some of them said: in this verse there is what indicates the prohibition of wine, because He named it sin, and sin was prohibited in another verse, namely His saying, mighty and majestic: "Say: My Lord has forbidden only indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is hidden, and sin." Some of them said: by sin He meant wine, by the evidence of the poet's saying:

"I drank the sin until my mind went astray; so too sin takes away the intellects."

I say: this too is not good, because God the Exalted did not name wine sin in this verse; rather He said: "Say: in both there is great sin," and He did not say: "Say: they are great sin." As for the verse of al-A'raf and the poetry, the discussion of them will come there, explained, God willing, the Exalted. Qatada said: this verse only contains a censure of wine, while its prohibition is known from another verse, which is the verse of al-Ma'ida, and most of the commentators hold this view.

His saying, exalted is He: (They ask you what they should spend. Say: the surplus. Thus God makes clear to you the signs, that you may reflect. Upon this world and the Hereafter.) In it are three issues.

First: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: the surplus (al-'afw)﴾. The reading of the majority is with the accusative. Abu 'Amr alone read it with the nominative. It is reported differently from Ibn Kathir. With the nominative is the reading of al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Abi Ishaq. Al-Nahhas and others said: if you make "dhā" mean "alladhī", the nominative is the preferred, in the sense: "What they spend is the surplus", and the accusative is permissible. If you make "mā" and "dhā" one thing, the accusative is the preferred, in the sense: "Say: they spend the surplus", and the nominative is permissible. The grammarians related: "Mādhā ta'allamta: anaḥwan am shi'ran?", with the accusative and the nominative, both being good and fine, except that the interpretation in the verse is with the accusative.

Second: The scholars said: since the question in the previous verse, His saying, exalted is He, "They ask you what they should spend", was a question about the expenditure, to whom it is to be directed, as we have explained and as the answer indicated, and the answer came in accordance with the question, the second question in this verse was about the amount of expenditure, and it concerned the matter of 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh, as has passed. For when the verse "Say: whatever good you spend is for parents" was revealed, he said: How much shall I spend? So "Say: the surplus" was revealed. Al-'Afw is what is easy, facile and surplus, and whose removal from the heart is not burdensome, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Take the surplus from me, that my affection may endure, and do not speak in my anger when I am angry."

The meaning is: spend what exceeds your needs, and do not harm yourselves by it so that you become dependent. This is the best of what has been said in the interpretation of the verse, and it is the meaning of the saying of al-Hasan, Qatada, 'Ata', al-Suddi, al-Qurazi Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Ibn Abi Layla and others. They said: al-'afw is what exceeds the dependants, and similar to it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: it is charity from a surplus of wealth [[Ibn al-Athir said: "The word 'zahr' (back/surplus) may be added in such a context for emphasis and firmness, as if his charity were resting upon a strong back of wealth."]]. Likewise he, peace be upon him, said: "The best charity is that which is given out of richness", and in another hadith: "The best charity is that which is from a surplus of richness." Qays ibn Sa'd said: this is the obligatory zakat. The majority of scholars said: rather, these are voluntary expenditures. It was also said: it is abrogated. Al-Kalbi said: after the revelation of this verse, when a man had wealth of gold or silver, or crops or livestock, he looked at what would suffice himself and his dependants for a year, and retained it, and gave the rest in charity; and if he was one who worked with his hands, he retained what would suffice himself and his dependants for a day, and gave the rest in charity, until the verse of the obligatory zakat was revealed, which abrogated this verse and every charity they had been commanded. Others said: it is muhkam (not abrogated), and there is a right in wealth besides zakat. The apparent meaning supports the first view.

Third: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus God makes clear to you the signs﴾. Al-Mufaddal ibn Salama said: that is, in the matter of expenditure.
(That you may reflect. Upon this world and the Hereafter.) So that you withhold from your wealth what will suffice you in the livelihood of this world, and spend the rest on what benefits you in the next life. It was also said: there is inversion in the speech, meaning: thus God makes clear to you the signs concerning the matter of this world and the Hereafter, that you may reflect on this world and its passing and its ending, so that you become detached from it, and on the coming of the Hereafter and its permanence, so that you desire it.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 220:**

God Most High says: ﴿They ask you about orphans. Say: Setting things right for them is good﴾ up to His words ﴿...Mighty, Wise﴾. On this verse there are eight issues.

**The first issue:** Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: When God Most High revealed ﴿Do not approach the property of the orphan except in the way that is best﴾ [Qur'an 6:152] and ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly...﴾ [Qur'an 4:10], those who had an orphan in their care separated the orphan's food from their own food and drink from their own drink. They would set aside some of the food, keeping it for the orphan until he ate it or it spoiled. This became burdensome for them, so they mentioned it to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and God Most High revealed: ﴿They ask you about orphans. Say: Setting things right for them is good﴾ [Qur'an 2:220]. So they mixed their food with his food and their drink with his drink. This is the wording of Abu Dawud.

The verse is connected to what precedes it, because the command to protect the property of orphans is mentioned alongside the mention of property. It is also said that the questioner was Abdullah ibn Rawaha. And it is said that the Arabs would regard it as ill-omened to mix with orphans' property in eating together, so this verse was revealed.

**The second issue:** When God, Mighty and Majestic, permitted mixing with orphans with the intention of setting things right, by looking after them and their affairs, this became evidence for the permissibility of the guardian (wasi) disposing of an orphan's property, such as by selling, dividing and other such acts, in general terms, on the basis of this verse. If a man takes charge of an orphan and holds guardianship over him, and it is within his oversight, his action is valid even if no ruler has appointed him, because the verse is absolute and guardianship (kafalah) is a general authority. It is not reported from any of the caliphs that he appointed anyone over an orphan although they were present in their times; rather, they were content with the orphan being in their care.

**The third issue:** Reports have come through in abundance about entrusting an orphan's property to be traded with on the basis of mudarabah (profit-sharing partnership), and about trading with it. Also, mixing his property with one's own is evidence for the permissibility of disposing of his property by buying and selling when it is in the interest of his welfare, and for the permissibility of entrusting it on the basis of mudarabah, and other matters which we will explain in detail. It is disputed whether the guardian himself may act as the mudarib (the one who works with the capital). Ashhab forbade it, and he analogized it to the prohibition on selling to them from himself or buying from them for himself. Others said: if he takes it on a share of the profit at the going rate for such a mudarabah, it is permitted, just as buying something for the orphan with scrutiny (ta'aqqub) [scrutiny: that is, he examines the matter of the item being bought, raising it to the market to know its price], which is better for the orphan.

Muhammad ibn Abd al-Hakam said: He may also sell on credit for him if he sees that as beneficial. Ibn Kinana said: He may spend on the orphan's wedding what is fitting in terms of food and perfume, and his expenditure should be according to his own circumstances, the circumstances of the one he is marrying into, and the amount of his wealth. He said: Likewise for his circumcision. If he fears being accused, he should refer the matter to the ruler, who will order him to moderation. Whatever he does with a view to what is proper is permitted, and whatever he does out of favoritism and poor judgment is not permitted.

The apparent meaning indicates that the guardian of an orphan should teach him matters of this world and the next, should hire for him, and should hire him out to someone who will teach him crafts. If something is gifted to the orphan, the guardian may take possession of it, because of the benefit in that.

I will provide further explanation of this in the chapter of "Women" (al-Nisa'), God willing. [See vol. 5, p. 34 onward.]

**The fourth issue:** For what the guardian or the custodian spends from the orphan's property there are two situations. In one situation it is possible for him to have witnesses to it, so his word is not accepted except with evidence. In the other situation it is not possible for him to have witnesses, so his word is accepted without evidence. Whenever he buys real estate or other things for which it is customary to secure documentation, his word is not accepted without evidence.

Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: For this reason our companions distinguished between the orphan living in the guardian's house, whom he supports, in which case he is not required to produce witnesses for the cost of his maintenance and clothing, because it is impossible for him to have witnesses to what the orphan eats and wears at every moment; but if he says, "I spent such-and-such an amount for a year," his word is accepted. And between the orphan being with his mother or his foster-mother, when the guardian claims that he used to support him, or that he used to give the mother or the foster-mother the maintenance and clothing. In that case his word is not accepted against the mother or the foster-mother unless there is evidence that she used to receive that for him on a monthly or yearly basis.

**The fifth issue:** The scholars differed concerning a man who marries himself to his female orphan (ward), and whether he may buy for himself from the property of his orphan, male or female. Malik said: The authority to marry through guardianship and custody is stronger than authority through kinship, to the extent that he said regarding the Bedouins who hand over their children in times of famine: they marry them off as they marry them off [i.e., their marriage arrangements are binding]. As for the marriage of the guardian and custodian to himself, its explanation will come in "Women," God willing.

As for buying from the orphan, Malik said: he may buy, according to the well-known opinion. Likewise Abu Hanifa said: he may buy the property of the orphan child for himself at more than the market price, because it is a matter of setting things right, which the apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates. Al-Shafi'i said: That is not permitted in marriage or in sale, because the verse does not mention disposal; rather it says: ﴿Setting things right for them is good﴾, without mentioning who is permitted to act in their interest. Abu Hanifa says: if setting things right is good, then it is permitted to marry him off and permitted to marry someone to him. Al-Shafi'i does not regard marriage as setting things right except in terms of meeting a need, and there is no need before puberty. Ahmad ibn Hanbal permits the guardian to arrange marriage because it is setting things right. Al-Shafi'i permits the grandfather to arrange marriage alongside the guardian, and the father to arrange marriage on behalf of his child whose mother has died, but not by the ruling of this verse. Abu Hanifa permits the judge to arrange the marriage of an orphan by the apparent meaning of the Qur'an.

These schools of thought arose from this verse. If it is established that marriage is setting things right, then the apparent meaning of the verse requires its permissibility.

It is possible that the meaning of God's words ﴿They ask you about orphans﴾ is: the stewards over orphans, those who take charge of them, ask you. This is a general statement from which the identity of the custodian and the trustee, and the qualities required in them, are not known.

If it is said: Malik's principle regarding suspicion and means (dhara'i') would require him to abandon that principle, since he permitted buying from one's orphan, the answer is that this does not follow. Means (dhara'i') apply only where permissible acts lead to a forbidden thing that is explicitly stated as forbidden. Here, God, glorified be He, has permitted mixing in the situation of association, and He entrusted the custodians in this matter to their trustworthiness by His words: ﴿God knows the corrupter from the one who sets things right﴾. Every dangerous matter that God, glorified be He, has entrusted to the responsible person's trustworthiness is not said to be a means leading to a forbidden thing, such that he is prevented from it. Just as God made women trusted regarding their private parts, despite the great rulings that depend on what they say in this matter, and the permissibility and prohibition and lineages linked to it, even though they may lie.

Tawus, when asked about any matter concerning orphans, would recite: ﴿God knows the corrupter from the one who sets things right﴾. Ibn Sirin said that the most beloved thing to him regarding an orphan's property was that his advisers gather and consider what is best for him. This is mentioned by al-Bukhari. In this there is evidence for permissibility of buying from it for oneself, as we have mentioned.

The other opinion is that it is not appropriate for the guardian to buy anything from what is under his hand, because of the suspicion that attaches to him in that, unless the sale is a sale by the ruler before a crowd of people. Muhammad ibn Abd al-Hakam said: He should not buy from the estate, and there is no harm in his sending someone to buy from it on his behalf, provided it is not known that the buyer is acting on his behalf.

**The sixth issue:** God Most High says: ﴿And if you mix with them, then they are your brothers﴾. This mixing is like mixing like with like, such as dates with dates. Abu Ubayd said: Mixing with orphans means that one of them has property, and it is difficult for his custodian to separate his food from theirs, and he finds no alternative but to mix him with his dependents. He then takes from the orphan's property what he judges sufficient for him by good estimation, and combines it with his household's expenses. In this there may be excess or deficiency. This verse, which abrogates [naskh] earlier rulings, therefore came with a concession regarding it.

Abu Ubayd said: In my view this is a basis for what travelling companions do, for they share expenses among themselves equally, though they differ in how much they eat; not everyone who eats little is content to bear more than his companion. If this latitude is permitted concerning orphans' property, it is even more permissible regarding others. Were it not so, I would fear that the matter would become too constricting for people.

**The seventh issue:** God's words ﴿then they are your brothers﴾ are the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: then they are your brothers. The "fa" (then) is the response to the conditional. God's words ﴿God knows the corrupter from the one who sets things right﴾ are a warning, meaning: God knows who corrupts the property of orphans from the one who sets it right, and He will recompense each for his setting right and his corruption.

**The eighth issue:** God Most High says: ﴿Had God willed, He would have burdened you﴾. Al-Hakam reported from Miqsam, from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿Had God willed, He would have burdened you﴾, that he said: Had He willed, He would have made what you took from orphans' property a ruin (destruction). It is also said: "la'a'natakum" means "would have destroyed you," according to al-Zajjaj and Abu Ubayda. Al-Qutaybi said: He would have constricted and made it harsh for you, but He did not will anything except to make it easy for you. It is also said: that is, He would have imposed on you what is hard for you to carry out, and would have made you sinful in mixing with them, as He did with those before you, but He lightened it for you.

"Al-'anat" means hardship, and one who has been afflicted is "a'nata" by others. It is said of a bone that has been set when something strikes it and breaks it again: "a'natahu," so it is "'anat" and "mu'nit." And an animal "ta'nat 'anatan" when a break occurs in its legs after being set, such that it cannot run with it. A "'anut" hill is one whose ascent is difficult.

Ibn al-Anbari said: The root meaning of "al-'anat" is hardship. When the Arabs say, "So-and-so 'ata'annata so-and-so" or "'a'nataha," they mean that he makes things difficult for him and burdens him with what is hard for him to bear. Then the word was transferred to the meaning of ruin. The original meaning is what we have described.

God Most High says: ﴿Indeed, God is Mighty﴾, meaning nothing can prevail against Him. ﴿Wise﴾, He disposes of His dominion as He wills, with none to restrain Him, exalted be He,高 far above great exaltation.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 221 (part 1 of 5):**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And do not marry idolatresses until they believe. A believing slave woman is better than an idolatress, even though she may please you.﴾ In this verse there are seven issues.

**The first issue:** His saying, ﴿And do not marry﴾ (*tankihu*). The reading of the majority is with a *fatḥah* on the *tā'*. It was also read irregularly (*shādhdh*, a reading not transmitted through the standard channels) with a *ḍammah*, as if the meaning were that the one who marries her has given her in marriage from himself. *Nakaḥa* originally means sexual intercourse, and it is used for marriage figuratively and by extension. Its explanation will come, God willing.

**The second issue:** When Allah, glory be to Him, permitted mixing with orphans and mixing through marriage, He made clear that marrying idolaters is not valid. Muqatil said: this verse was revealed concerning Abu Marthad al-Ghanawi. It was also said: concerning Marthad ibn Abi Marthad, whose name was Kannaz ibn Husayn al-Ghanawi. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent him secretly to Makkah to bring out a man from among his companions. He had a woman in Makkah whom he had loved in the pre-Islamic period, called "Anaq." She came to him, and he said to her: "Islam has forbidden what was in the pre-Islamic period." She said: "Then marry me." He said: "Until I ask the permission of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." So he went to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked his permission, and he forbade him from marrying her, because he was a Muslim and she was an idolatress. Its explanation will come in *al-Nur*, God willing.[[See vol. 12, p. 168.]]

**The third issue:** The scholars differed in their interpretation of this verse. One group said: Allah forbade marriage to idolatresses in *Surat al-Baqarah*, then abrogated (*naskh*, the cancellation of a earlier ruling by a later one) from this general statement the women of the People of the Book, so He permitted them in *Surat al-Ma'idah*. This view was reported from Ibn Abbas, and Malik ibn Anas, Sufyan ibn Sa'id al-Thawri, and Abd al-Rahman ibn Amr al-Awza'i also held it. Qatadah and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the wording of the verse is general for every disbelieving woman, but the intended meaning is particular to the women of the People of the Book, and the verse of *al-Ma'idah* clarified that particularity. The general wording never included the women of the People of the Book at all. This is one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i. According to the first view, the general wording includes them, and then the verse of *al-Ma'idah* abrogated part of the generality. This is the position of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned by Ibn Habib, who said: marriage to a Jewish or Christian woman, although Allah has permitted it, is disliked and blameworthy. Ishaq ibn Ibrahim al-Harbi said: some people held that the verse in *al-Baqarah* is the abrogating one and the verse in *al-Ma'idah* is the abrogated one, so they forbade marriage to every idolatress, whether from the People of the Book or not.

Al-Nahhas said: among the evidence for the one who holds this view, from a soundly transmitted chain (*sanad*), is what Muhammad ibn Rayyan narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Rumh narrated to us, saying: al-Layth narrated to us from Nafi', that Abd Allah ibn Umar, whenever he was asked about a man marrying a Christian or Jewish woman, would say: "Allah has forbidden the idolatresses to the believers. I know of no association (*shirk*) greater than a woman saying that her lord is Jesus, or that he is one of the servants of Allah!"

Al-Nahhas said: this is a view outside the position of the consensus (*jama'ah*) on which proof rests, because a group of the Companions and the Successors (*tabi'un*) permitted marriage to the women of the People of the Book, among them Uthman, Talhah, Ibn Abbas, Jabir and Hudhayfah. From among the Successors: Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Tawus, Ikrimah, al-Sha'bi and al-Dahhak, and the jurists of the major cities agree with it.

Moreover, it is impossible that this verse of *al-Baqarah* abrogates the verse in *al-Ma'idah*, because *al-Baqarah* was among the first things revealed in Madinah, while *al-Ma'idah* was among the last. Only the later abrogates the earlier.

As for the hadith of Ibn Umar, there is no proof in it, because Ibn Umar, may Allah have mercy on him, was a man who withheld judgment. When he heard the two verses, one permitting and the other forbidding, and the abrogation had not reached him, he held back. The mention of abrogation was not taken from him; rather, his view was interpreted in that way. Abrogating and abrogated verses are not determined by interpretation.

Ibn Atiyyah mentioned: Ibn Abbas said, in some of what is reported from him: the verse is general, covering idolatresses, Magian women, and women of the People of the Book, and every woman who is not upon Islam is forbidden. On this view, it abrogates the verse in *al-Ma'idah*. Ibn Umar's saying in the *Muwatta'* refers to this: "I know of no association greater than a woman saying that her lord is Jesus."

It is reported from Umar that he separated Talhah ibn Ubayd Allah and Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman from two women of the People of the Book, and they said: "O Commander of the Faithful, we will divorce them, so do not be angry." He said: "If your divorcing them is valid, then your marrying them was valid! But I will separate you from them as a small, despised pebble." Ibn Atiyyah said: this is not well supported. A more firmly supported report is that Umar wanted to separate them, and Hudhayfah said to him: "Do you claim that they are forbidden, so that we should release them, O Commander of the Faithful?" He said: "I do not claim that they are forbidden, but I fear that you will take prostitutes from among them." Something similar is reported from Ibn Abbas.

Ibn al-Mundhir mentioned the permissibility of marrying women of the People of the Book from Umar ibn al-Khattab, and those mentioned from among the Companions and Successors in al-Nahhas's statement. He said at the end of his words: "Nothing is authentically reported from any of the earlier generations that they forbade this."

Some scholars said: as for the two verses, there is no contradiction between them, for the apparent meaning of the term "idolatry" (*shirk*) does not include the People of the Book, because of His saying: ﴿Neither those who disbelieve among the People of the Book nor the idolaters wish that any good should be sent down to you from your Lord﴾,[[Verse 105 of Surat al-Baqarah.]] and He said: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the idolaters were not going to depart﴾,[[Verse 1 of Surat al-Bayyinah.]] so He distinguished between them in wording. The apparent sense of the conjunction requires a difference between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined. Moreover, the term "idolatry" is general, not explicit, whereas His saying: ﴿And the chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture﴾,[[Verse 5 of Surat al-Ma'idah.]] following His saying: ﴿And the chaste women from among the believing women﴾, is explicit. So there is no contradiction between the probable and what is not probable.

If it is said: by His saying ﴿the chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture﴾ He meant "those who were given the Scripture before you and then embraced Islam," like His saying: ﴿And among the People of the Scripture there are those who believe in Allah﴾,[[Verse 199 of Surat Al 'Imran.]] and ﴿Among the People of the Scripture is an upright community﴾,[[Verse 113 of Surat Al 'Imran.]] it is answered: this contradicts the explicit wording of the verse, ﴿those who were given the Scripture before you﴾, and it contradicts what the majority said. Indeed, there is no ambiguity for anyone regarding the permissibility of marrying someone who has embraced Islam and become one of the notable Muslims.

If they say: Allah has said: ﴿Those invite to the Fire﴾,[[Verse 221 of Surat al-Baqarah.]] thereby making the reason for forbidding their marriage the invitation to the Fire. The answer is that this is the reason for His saying: ﴿a believing slave woman is better than an idolatress﴾, because the idolater invites to the Fire. This reason applies consistently to all disbelievers, so the Muslim is better than the disbeliever absolutely. This is clear.

**The fourth issue:** As for marrying women of the People of the Book when they are at war (*harb*), it is not permitted. Ibn Abbas was asked about this and said: "It is not permitted," and he recited the saying of Allah: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah nor in the Last Day﴾,[[Verse 29 of Surat al-Tawbah.]] up to His saying: ﴿humbled﴾. The narrator said: I related this to Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, and it pleased him. Malik disliked marrying women of the enemy territory (*harbiyyat*), because of the resulting neglect of children in the land of war, and because of their handling of wine and pork.

**The fifth issue:** His saying, ﴿and a believing slave woman is better than an idolatress﴾, is a statement that a believing slave woman is better than an idolatress, even if the latter is of noble descent and wealth.

﴿Even though she may please you﴾ in beauty and other things. This is the view of al-Tabari and others. It was revealed concerning Khansa', a black slave girl belonging to Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman. Hudhayfah said to her: "O Khansa', you have been mentioned in the Highest Assembly (*al-mala' al-a'la*) along with your blackness and ugliness," and Allah revealed:

Among the ways Allah, the Exalted, mentioned him in His Book: Hudhayfah freed her and married her. Al-Suddi said: It was revealed concerning Abdullah ibn Rawahah, who had a black slave-girl. In anger he slapped her, then regretted it, so he came to the Prophet ﷺ and informed him. He said, "What is she, O Abdullah?" He replied, "She fasts, prays, performs wudu' well, and bears witness to the two testimonies." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "She is a believer." Ibn Rawahah said, "I will free her and marry her." He did so. Some Muslims criticized him and said, "He married a slave-girl." They used to prefer marrying [their women] to polytheists, and they would marry them off for the sake of their lineage, so this verse was revealed. And Allah knows best.

Sixth issue: The scholars differed concerning marrying the slave-women of the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab). Malik said: It is not permissible to marry a Scripturist slave-woman. Ashhab said in the Kitab Muhammad, concerning one who embraces Islam while married to a Scripturist slave-woman: they are not to be separated. Abu Hanifah and his companions said: It is permissible to marry the slave-women of the People of the Book.

Ibn al-Arabi said: Shaykh Abu Bakr al-Shashi taught us in Madinat al-Salam (Baghdad), saying: The companions of Abu Hanifah argued for the permissibility of marrying a [Scripturist] slave-woman [al-kitabiyyah] by the words of Allah, the Exalted: "And a believing slave-woman is better than a polytheist." [[Ibn al-Arabi's wording in his Ahkam al-Quran: "Abu Hanifah argued."]] [[Addition from Ibn al-Arabi.]] The argument from the verse is that Allah, glorified is He, gave a choice between marrying a believing slave-woman and a polytheist, and if marrying a polytheist slave-woman were not permissible, Allah would not have given a choice between them, because choice is only between two permissible options, not between a permissible and a forbidden one, nor between two opposites. The reply is that giving a choice between opposites is permissible linguistically and in the Qur'an, for Allah, glorified is He, said: "The companions of the Garden on that Day will have a better abode and a finer resting place" [[Qur'an 25:24.]]. And Umar, in his letter to Abu Musa, said: "Returning to the truth is better than persisting in falsehood." Another reply: His words ﴿And a slave-woman﴾ do not refer to owned bondage, but refer to humanity, and all human beings, male and female, are the servants and handmaids of Allah. This was said by the judge in Basra, Abu al-Abbas al-Jurjani.

Seventh issue: They differed concerning marrying Magian women. Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah, al-Awza'i and Ishaq prohibited it. Ibn Hanbal said: It does not please me. It is narrated that Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman married a Magian woman, and Umar said to him, "Divorce her." Ibn al-Qassar said: Some of our companions said: According to one of the two opinions, since they have a Scripture, their intermarriage is permissible. Ibn Wahb narrated from Malik that a Magian slave-woman may not be taken as a concubine by right of ownership, and likewise idolatresses and other disbelieving women. This is the view of the majority of scholars, except what Yahya ibn Ayyub narrated from Ibn Jurayj, from Ata' and Amr ibn Dinar, that they were asked about marrying Magian slave-women, and they said: There is no harm in it. They interpreted the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: "And do not marry polytheistic women." According to them, this refers to the contract of marriage, not to a purchased slave-woman. They argued from the captives of Awtas, and that the Companions married slave-women from among them by right of ownership. Al-Nahhas said: This is an anomalous view. As for the captives of Awtas, it may be that the slave-women had embraced Islam, so their marriage was permissible. As for arguing from Allah's words, "And do not marry polytheistic women until they believe," it is an error, because they understood marriage as referring to the contract, whereas in the language marriage applies both to the contract and to sexual intercourse. When He said, "And do not marry polytheistic women," He forbade every marriage that applies to polytheistic women, whether by contract or by intercourse.

Abu Umar ibn Abd al-Barr said: al-Awza'i said: I asked al-Zuhri about a man who buys a Magian woman, may he have intercourse with her? He said: When she testifies that there is no god but Allah, he may have intercourse with her. And from Yunus, from Ibn Shihab, he said: It is not lawful for him to have intercourse with her until she embraces Islam. Abu Umar said: The statement of Ibn Shihab, "It is not lawful for him to have intercourse with her until she embraces Islam" (and he is the most knowledgeable of people about the campaigns and biographies) is evidence against the invalidity of the view of those who claim that the captives of Awtas were taken without embracing Islam. This was narrated from a group including Ata' and Amr ibn Dinar, who said: There is no harm in intercourse with a Magian woman. No jurist in the regions paid any attention to this. And there has come from al-Hasan al-Basri, who was among those whose campaigns, and the campaigns of his region, reached only the Persians and beyond them to Khurasan, and none of whom were People of the Book, what shows you how the practice was with their women when they were captured. He said: Abdullah ibn Muhammad ibn Asad informed us, saying: Ibrahim ibn Ahmad ibn Firas told us, saying: Ali ibn Abd al-Aziz told us, saying: Abu Ubayd told us, saying: Hisham told us, from Yunus, from al-Hasan, who said: A man said to him, "O Abu Sa'id, what did you do when you took them captive?" He said: "We would turn her toward the qiblah and order her to embrace Islam and to testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. Then we would order her to perform ghusl. When her master wished to have intercourse with her, he would not do so until he had ascertained her [womb is clear]."

On this basis is the interpretation of the majority of scholars concerning the words of Allah, the Exalted: "And do not marry polytheistic women until they believe," that they are the idolatresses and the Magian women, because Allah, the Exalted, has permitted Scripturist women by His words: "And chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you," meaning the chaste ones, not those whose unchastity is notorious among the Muslim women. Some of them disliked marrying them and having intercourse with them by right of ownership, unless they repented, because of what that entails for the corruption of lineage.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not marry polytheist men until they believe. Indeed, a believing slave is better than a polytheist, even though he may please you.﴾ In this there are eleven issues.

The first issue: His saying, ﴿And do not marry﴾, means: do not give a Muslim woman in marriage to a polytheist. The community (ummah) agrees that a polytheist may not have intercourse with a believing woman in any way, because of the disgrace this would bring upon Islam. The readers (qurra') read the letter ta' in "tankihu" with a damma (ضم), that is, ﴿tunkihu﴾ (as "do not marry" in the active form, with the ta' vowelled with a damma).

The second issue: This verse contains explicit textual evidence that there is no marriage except with a guardian (wali). Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn al-Husayn said: "Marriage with a guardian is in the Book of Allah," and then he recited, ﴿And do not marry polytheist men.﴾ Ibn al-Mundhir said: It is established that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no marriage except with a guardian."
