Scholars have differed concerning marriage without a guardian. Many scholars said: There is no marriage except with a guardian. This hadith is narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with them all. The same view was held by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, al-Hasan al-Basri, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, Jabir ibn Zayd, Sufyan al-Thawri, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Shubrumah, Ibn al-Mubarak, al-Shafi'i, 'Ubayd Allah ibn al-Hasan, Ahmad, Ishaq and Abu 'Ubayd. I say: This is also the view of Malik, Abu Thawr and al-Tabari, may Allah be pleased with them all.

Abu 'Umar (Ibn 'Abd al-Barr) said: The argument of those who say "There is no marriage except with a guardian" is that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is firmly established as having said: "There is no marriage except with a guardian." Shu'bah and al-Thawri narrated this hadith from Abu Ishaq, from Abu Burdah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), as a mursal report (one in which a Companion is omitted from the chain). Whoever accepts mursal reports must accept it. As for whoever does not accept mursal reports, he must also accept it, because those who linked it (to the Prophet through a Companion) were people of memorization and trustworthiness. Among those who linked it were Isra'il and Abu 'Awanah, both from Abu Ishaq, from Abu Burdah, from Abu Musa, from the Prophet (ﷺ). Isra'il and those who followed him are memorizers (huffaz), and the addition of a memorizer is accepted. This addition is supported by principles. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿So do not prevent them from marrying their husbands﴾ [2:232]. This verse was revealed concerning Ma'qil ibn Yasar, when he prevented (ʿadala) his sister from returning to her husband; this was reported by al-Bukhari. Had he had a right in the marriage, he would not have been forbidden from preventing (al-'adl). I say: Among what also indicates this from the Book is His saying: ﴿So marry them with the permission of their families﴾ [4:25], and His saying: ﴿And marry off the single ones among you﴾ [24:32]. He, exalted is He, addressed marriage only to men, and had it been up to women He would have mentioned them. The explanation of this will come in (the commentary on) Surah al-Nur. He, exalted is He, also said, relating the story of Shu'ayb concerning Musa, peace be upon them both: ﴿I wish to marry you﴾ [28:27], as will be explained in Surah al-Qasas. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Men are the protectors (qawwamun) of women﴾ [4:34]. Thus the Book and the Sunnah are unified in holding that there is no marriage except with a guardian.

Al-Tabari said: The hadith about Hafsah, when she became a widow (ta'ayyamat) and 'Umar contracted her marriage and she did not contract it herself, nullifies the view of those who say that a mature, self-possessed woman may contract her own marriage without her guardian. Had that been permitted to her, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would not have abandoned proposing to Hafsah for himself, if she had the right over herself more than her father, and proposed to her through one who has no authority over her affair nor the power to contract on her behalf. In this is the explanation of his peace be upon him saying: "The previously married woman (al-ayyim) has more right over herself than her guardian." Its meaning is that she has more right over herself in that no one may contract on her behalf except with her consent, not that she has more right over herself in that she may conclude the marriage contract herself without her guardian.

Al-Daraqutni narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A woman should not give another woman in marriage, nor should a woman give herself in marriage, for it is the adulteress who gives herself in marriage." He said: This is a sound hadith (hadith sahih).

Abu Dawud narrated, through the transmission of Sufyan from al-Zuhri, from 'Urwah, from 'A'ishah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Any woman who is married without the permission of her guardian, her marriage is invalid" (he said it three times), "and if he has consummated with her, then the dowry is hers in return for what he has enjoyed of her. And if they dispute, then the ruler is the guardian of whoever has no guardian." This hadith is sound.

There is no weight to the statement of Ibn 'Ulayyah, from Ibn Jurayj, that he said: "I asked al-Zuhri about it and he did not recognize it." No one other than Ibn 'Ulayyah has said this from Ibn Jurayj, and a group has narrated it from al-Zuhri without mentioning this. Even if this were established from al-Zuhri, it would be no proof, because trustworthy transmitters have related it from him, among them Sulayman ibn Musa, who is a trustworthy imam, and Ja'far ibn Rabi'ah. Even if al-Zuhri forgot it, that would not harm (the hadith), because forgetfulness is something no son of Adam is immune from. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Adam forgot, and his progeny forgot." He (ﷺ) used to forget, so others are more likely to forget, and whoever memorizes is a proof against the one who forgot. When a trustworthy transmitter narrates a report, the forgetfulness of one who forgot it does not harm it. This holds even if what Ibn 'Ulayyah related from Ibn Jurayj were correct. How much more so, when the people of knowledge have rejected that report from his account and did not give it any consideration.

I say: Abu Hatim Muhammad ibn Hibban al-Tamimi al-Busti also narrated this hadith in his Sahih Musnad (the sound collection arranged by chains), according to his classification of types (al-taqasim wal-anwa'), without any break in its chain and without any established defect in its transmitter. He narrated it from Hafs ibn Ghiyath, from Ibn Jurayj, from Sulayman ibn Musa, from al-Zuhri, from 'Urwah, from 'A'ishah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no marriage except with a guardian and two just witnesses. Any marriage other than that is invalid. If they dispute, then the ruler is the guardian of whoever has no guardian." Abu Hatim said: No one, in the report of Ibn Jurayj from Sulayman ibn Musa from al-Zuhri, has mentioned this, "and two just witnesses," except three persons: Suwayd ibn Yahya al-Umawi from Hafs ibn Ghiyath, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Wahhab al-Jumahi from Khalid ibn al-Harith, and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Yunus al-Raqqi from 'Isa ibn Yunus. Nothing concerning the two witnesses is sound except this report. Once this report is established, the Book and the Sunnah have explicitly stated that there is no marriage except with a guardian, so there is no sense in anything that opposes both of them.

Al-Zuhri and al-Sha'bi used to say: If a woman marries herself to a suitable match (kufu') with two witnesses, that is a permissible marriage. Likewise Abu Hanifah used to say: If a woman marries herself to a suitable match with two witnesses, that is a permissible marriage, and this is also the view of Zufar. If she marries herself to an unsuitable match, the marriage is valid, but the guardians have the right to separate them. Ibn al-Mundhir said: As for what al-Nu'man (Abu Hanifah) said, it contradicts the Sunnah and departs from the view of most of the people of knowledge. We say according to the report from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Abu Yusuf said: Marriage is not permissible except with a guardian. If the guardian consents, it is valid; if he refuses to consent while the husband is a suitable match, the judge may authorize it. The marriage is completed in his view only when the judge authorizes it. This is also the view of Muhammad ibn al-Hasan. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan used to say: The judge orders the guardian to authorize it, and if he does not do so, they must renew the contract. There is no disagreement between Abu Hanifah and his companions that if her guardian gives her permission and she then concludes the marriage herself, it is valid.

Al-Awza'i said: If a woman entrusts her affair to a man, and he marries her to a suitable match, the marriage is valid, and the guardian has no right to separate them, unless she is an Arab who married a non-Arab client (mawla). This is similar to the view of Malik, as will come. Those who held the view of al-Zuhri, Abu Hanifah and al-Sha'bi interpreted His, peace be upon him, saying: "There is no marriage except with a guardian" as meaning perfection (al-kamal), not obligation (al-wujub), just as he, peace be upon him, said: "There is no prayer for the neighbour of the mosque except in the mosque," and "There is no share in Islam for one who abandons prayer." They used as evidence His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿So do not prevent them from marrying their husbands﴾, and His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you for what they do with themselves in an acceptable manner﴾ [2:234], and what al-Daraqutni narrated from Simak ibn Harb, who said: A man came to 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and said: "A woman whose guardian I am married without my permission?" 'Ali said: "Look into what she has done. If she married a suitable match, we permit that for her. If she married someone who is not a suitable match for her, we leave that to you." In the Muwatta' it is reported that 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, married off the daughter of her brother, 'Abd al-Rahman, while he was absent, the hadith... It was also narrated by Ibn Jurayj from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr, from his father, from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that she married a man, who was al-Mundhir ibn al-Zubayr, to a woman from her brother's family. She placed a curtain between them, then she spoke until only the contract remained, and she ordered a man to conclude it. Then she said: "There is no marriage (inkah) for women." The correct understanding of the hadith in the Muwatta' is that 'A'ishah determined the dowry and the terms of the marriage, while one of her male relatives (' asabah) concluded the contract. The contract was attributed to 'A'ishah because its arrangement was entrusted to her.

Third issue: Ibn Khuwayz Mandad mentioned: The reports from Malik differ concerning who the guardians are. Once he said: Anyone who places the woman in a good position is her guardian, whether he is of the agnatic relatives ('asabah), of the relatives through the womb (dhawu al-arham), a stranger, the ruler or the executor (wasi). Another time he said: The guardians are from the agnatic relatives, so whoever among them places her in a good position is a guardian. Abu 'Umar said: Malik said, as Ibn al-Qasim reported from him: If a woman is married by someone other than her guardian with her permission, then if she is of noble standing among the people, her guardian is ...

Qurtubi, al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran, on 2:221 (part 4 of 5)

...she has the choice in annulling the marriage or upholding it. Even if she is of low standing, such as a freedwoman, a black woman [[Malik said: They are a people from the Copts who come from Egypt to Medina.]], a *si'aya* [[*Al-si'aya*: prostitution.]], or a *muslimaniyya* [[In the original texts: "al-Islamiyya." The correction is from the commentary of al-Kharashi and the gloss of al-Adawi.]], and she has no lineage, her marriage is permissible, and her guardian has no right to annul it, because each of them is *kufu'* (of equal standing) to her. It has been narrated from Malik that a woman of noble birth and a woman of low birth may be married only by her guardian or by the ruler. Ibn al-Mundhir chose this view. He said: As for Malik's distinction between the poor woman and the woman who has rank, it is not permissible, because the Prophet ﷺ made their rulings equal in matters of blood when he said: "The Muslims' blood is of equal value." If they are equal in matters of blood, they are one and the same in everything else.

Isma'il ibn Ishaq said: When Allah, glorified is He, commanded marriage, He made the believers guardians of one another. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The believing men and the believing women are protectors of one another﴾ [9:71]. The believers in general inherit from one another in this way. If a man died without an heir, his inheritance would go to the community of Muslims, and if he committed a crime, the Muslims would pay his blood money. Then one guardianship is closer than another, and one kinship is closer than another. When a woman is in a place where there is no ruler and no guardian for her, she entrusts her affair to a trustworthy man from among her neighbours, who marries her, and he becomes her guardian in this situation, because people must marry, and they act in the best way possible. On this basis Malik said about a woman of weak standing that she may be married by the one to whom she entrusts her affair, because she is one who is weak before the ruler, so she resembles one who has no ruler present. She thus ultimately returns to the principle that the Muslims are her guardians. But if she entrusts her affair to a man and leaves aside her guardians, she has taken the matter in an improper way, and has done what the judge and the Muslims would disapprove of. The marriage is annulled, not because it is known to be intrinsically unlawful, but because of what we have described, namely that the believers are guardians of one another, and because of the disagreement it involves. Rather, it is annulled because she took up the matter in an improper way, and because this is more cautious for the private parts and for protecting them. If consummation has taken place, the matter has been prolonged, children have been born, and the marriage was proper, then annulment is not permitted, because when matters have become varied, only what is unquestionably unlawful is to be rejected. This is comparable to what has passed through a judge's ruling: when a judge has ruled, it is not annulled unless it is a clear error beyond doubt.

As for al-Shafi'i and his companions, a marriage without a guardian is, in their view, void forever, both before and after consummation, and the spouses do not inherit from one another if either dies. For them the guardian is among the obligatory elements of marriage, since the evidence for this from the Book and the Sunnah is clear to them. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And marry the single among you﴾ [24:32], and He said: ﴿So marry them with the permission of their families﴾ [4:25]. He also addressed the guardians: ﴿So do not prevent them﴾ [2:232]. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "There is no marriage except with a guardian." They make no distinction between a woman of low standing and a woman of rank, because of the consensus of the scholars that there is no difference between them in matters of blood, based on the Prophet's words, peace be upon him: "The Muslims' blood is of equal value." The other rulings are likewise. Nothing in the Book or the Sunnah makes a distinction between the high and the low in this matter.

Fourth: Scholars differ concerning a marriage that is contracted without a guardian and then approved by the guardian before consummation. Malik and his companions, except Abd al-Malik, said: This is permissible, provided the approval comes promptly, whether or not consummation has taken place. This applies when the marriage was contracted by someone other than the guardian, and the woman did not contract it herself. But if the woman married herself and concluded the marriage contract without any guardian, near or distant, from among the Muslims, then this marriage is never upheld in any circumstance, even if it lasts long and children are born. Yet the child is attributed to the husband if consummation has occurred, the hadd punishment is waived, and the marriage must in every case be annulled. Ibn Nafi' narrated from Malik: Its annulment is without divorce.

Fifth: Scholars differ concerning the ranking of guardians and their order. Malik used to say: The first of them are the sons, however far down they may be, then the fathers, then the full brothers, then the paternal brothers, then the sons of full brothers, then the sons of paternal brothers, then the paternal grandfathers however far up they may be, then the paternal uncles in the order of the brothers, then their sons in the order of the sons of brothers, however far down they may be, then the freed master, then the ruler or his judge. The guardian of a ward has precedence over the other guardians in marrying off orphans, and he is the deputy and agent of the father, so his position is like that of the father were he alive.

Al-Shafi'i said: No one has any guardianship in the presence of the father. If the father dies, then the grandfather, then the father of the grandfather, because they are all fathers. After the grandfather, guardianship belongs to the brothers, then the nearest. Al-Muzani said: In the later doctrine he said: whoever is the sole full sibling of a woman has the better right to marry her, just as in inheritance. In the earlier doctrine he said: they are equal. I say: The Medinans narrated from Malik a view similar to al-Shafi'i's, and that the father has precedence over the son. This is one of the two opinions of Abu Hanifa, as al-Baji reported. It is narrated from al-Mughira that he said: The grandfather has precedence over the brothers. The well-known position of the school is what we have mentioned above. Ahmad said: The one with the most right over the woman is her father to marry her, then the son, then the brother, then his son, then the paternal uncle. Ishaq said: The son has precedence over the father, as Malik said, and Ibn al-Mundhir chose this view, because Umar, the son of Umm Salama, married her with her permission to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

I say: al-Nasa'i narrated it from Umm Salama and gave it the heading: "The marriage of a son to his mother." I say: Our scholars often cite this as evidence, but it is not conclusive. The evidence against it is what is established in the authentic collections, that Umar ibn Abi Salama said: I was a boy in the care of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and my hand would wander over the dish. He said: "Boy, mention the name of Allah, eat with your right hand, and eat from what is nearest to you." Abu Umar said in the Istiab: Umar ibn Abi Salama was called Abu Hafs. He was born in the second year of the Hijra in the land of Abyssinia. It is said that he was nine years old on the day the Messenger of Allah ﷺ died. I say: One of his age is not fit to be a guardian. But Abu Umar mentioned that Abu Salama had another son by Umm Salama named Salama, and it was he who concluded the marriage of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to his mother Umm Salama. Salama was older than his brother Umar ibn Abi Salama, and I do not know of any narration by him from the Prophet ﷺ, though his brother Umar narrated from him.

Sixth: Scholars differ concerning a man who marries off a woman when a more distant guardian is involved. (This is how it is worded, but the clearer expression would be: They differ concerning a woman whose marriage is arranged by a more distant guardian while a closer guardian, the *aq'ad* [[*Al-qa'ad* (with a damma on the qaf, sukun on the 'ayn, and damma or fatha on the dal): the one nearest to the great-grandfather. It is also said: the one most closely related in lineage.]] is present.) Al-Shafi'i said: The marriage is void. Malik said: The marriage is valid. Ibn Abd al-Barr said: If the nearer guardian does not object to any part of it and does not reject it, it takes effect. If he objects, and the woman is a previously married woman or a virgin who has reached maturity, an orphan with no guardian of her own, then the opinions of Malik and his companions and a group of the people of Medina differ on this. Some of them said: It is not rejected, and it takes effect, because it is a marriage concluded with the permission of a guardian from the same clan and tribe. Those who said it is not valid said: The ranking of guardians was ordained as the best and most preferred arrangement, and that is recommended, not obligatory. This is the summary of Malik's school according to most of his companions, and Isma'il ibn Ishaq and his followers chose this view. It is also said: The ruler examines the matter, asks the nearest guardian about what he objects to, and then, if he sees fit to uphold it, he upholds it, and if he sees fit to reject it, he rejects it. It is also said: Rather, the aq'ad has the right to reject it in every case, because it is his right. It is also said: He may reject it or approve it so long as she has not stayed long and borne children. All of these opinions are views of the people of Medina.

Seventh: If the nearest guardian is imprisoned or a fool, the woman is married by the guardian next to him, and he is counted as dead. Likewise, if the nearest of her guardians is absent for a long time, or an absence from which a quick return is not expected, the one next to him among the guardians marries her. It has been said: If the nearest of her guardians is absent, the one next to him has no right to marry her, and the judge marries her. The first view is the view of Malik.

Eighth: If the two guardians are equal in *al-qa'ad* [[*Al-qa'ad* (with a damma on the qaf, sukun on the 'ayn, and damma or fatha on the dal): the one nearest to the great-grandfather. It is also said: the one most closely related in lineage.]] and one of them is absent, and the woman entrusts her marriage contract to the one present, then the absent one, if he returns, has no right to object. If both are present and she entrusts her affair to one of them, he may not marry her without the permission of the other. If they disagree, the judge examines the matter and enforces the opinion of whichever of them is better for her. Ibn Wahb narrated this from Malik.

Ninth: As for witnessing the marriage, it is not a pillar of the marriage according to Malik and his companions. Sufficient is its being publicly known and announced, and then it is no longer a secret marriage. Ibn al-Qasim said, on the authority of Malik: If someone married a woman with witnesses but ordered them to conceal it, the marriage is not permissible, because it is a secret marriage. If he married without witnesses, not intending secrecy, it is permissible, and they should call witnesses for what follows. Ibn Wahb narrated from Malik concerning a man who marries a woman with the testimony of two men and asks them to keep it secret: He said: They are separated by a single pronouncement of divorce, the marriage is not valid, she receives her dowry if he has consummated it, and the two witnesses are not punished. Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i and their companions said: If he marries her with two witnesses and tells them to keep it secret, the marriage is valid. Abu Umar said: This is the view of Yahya ibn Yahya al-Laythi al-Andalusi, our companion. He said: Every marriage witnessed by two men has passed beyond the bounds of secrecy. I think he attributed this to al-Layth ibn Sa'd. A secret marriage, according to al-Shafi'i, the Kufans and those who follow them, is any marriage not witnessed by at least two men, and it is annulled in every case. I say: The view of al-Shafi'i is more sound because of the hadith we have mentioned. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: There is no marriage except with two just witnesses and an upright guardian. As far as I know, there is no dissent from him among the Companions on this point. Malik supported his position with the argument that the transactions Allah mentioned, in which witnessing at the contract is required, show that witnessing is not an obligatory condition of sales; and the marriage about which Allah mentions no witnessing is even more deserving of not having witnessing as one of its conditions or obligatory elements. The purpose is publicity and manifestation to preserve lineages. Witnessing is useful after the contract for resolving claims and disputes about what has been contracted between the spouses. It has been narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Announce the marriage." This is the view of Ibn Shihab and most of the people of Medina.

Tenth: His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And a believing slave is better than an idolater﴾ — that is, one who is owned (is better than an idolater), that is, one who is accountable.

(And even if a woman pleases you [or: and if she pleases you] by her lineage and her wealth, [the same applies], as mentioned before.) It is also said that the meaning is: "and a believing man [is better]," and likewise "and a believing slave-woman," i.e., "nor a believing woman," as we have explained. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "All your men are servants of Allah, and all your women are maidservants of Allah," and he said: "Do not prevent the maidservants of Allah from the mosques of Allah." And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿An excellent servant! Indeed, he was ever turning back (to Allah).﴾ [Qur'an 38:30, 38:44]. This is the best interpretation given to the statement regarding this verse, and by it the dispute is resolved and the disagreement dissolves; and Allah is the Granter of success.

The eleventh issue: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those﴾ is a reference to the polytheists, men and women.

(They invite to the Fire) i.e., to deeds that necessitate the Fire, for their companionship and association with them entail a decline into many of their desires, along with their raising of offspring.

(And Allah invites to Paradise) i.e., to the deeds of the people of Paradise.

(By His permission) i.e., by His command, as said by al-Zajjaj.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 222 (part 1 of 4):

There are fourteen issues in it.

The first issue: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And they ask you about menstruation﴾. Al-Tabari reported from al-Suddi that the questioner was Thabit ibn al-Dahdah. It was also said: Usayd ibn Hudayr and Abbad ibn Bishr, and this is the view of most scholars. The reason for the question, as Qatadah and others said, was that the Arabs in Madinah and its surroundings had adopted the practice of the Children of Israel in shunning eating with a menstruating woman and sharing a dwelling with her, so this verse was revealed. Mujahid said: they used to avoid women during menstruation and would have intercourse with them in their back passages for the duration of the menstrual period, so it was revealed. In Sahih Muslim, from Anas: the Jews, when a woman among them menstruated, would not eat with her or have intercourse with them in the houses [[The pronoun is plural because the intended meaning of "the woman" is the category.
(Muslim's margin) In A and H, "and would not have intercourse with her."]]. The Companions of the Prophet ﷺ asked the Prophet ﷺ, and Allah, exalted is He, revealed: "And they ask you about menstruation. Say: It is an injury, so keep away from women during menstruation" up to the end of the verse. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do everything except sexual intercourse." This reached the Jews, and they said: This man does not want to leave any of our matters without opposing us in it. Then Usayd ibn Hudayr and Abbad ibn Bishr came and said: O Messenger of Allah, the Jews say such and such; shall we not have intercourse with them? The face of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ changed, until we thought he had become angry with them [[Wajada 'alayhima: was angry. Its present tense (mudari'ah) may be read with a damma or a kasra on the jim.]]. They left, and a gift of milk was brought to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so he sent after them and gave them to drink, and they understood that he was not angry with them. Our scholars said: The Jews and the Magians used to shun the menstruating woman, the Christians used to have intercourse with menstruating women, so Allah commanded moderation between these two.

The second issue: His saying, ﴿concerning menstruation﴾. Al-mahid (menstruation) is al-hayd (the menstrual flow), which is a verbal noun. It is said: the woman menstruated (haddat al-mar'ah) a menstruation (hayd), mahad and mahid, so she is ha'id, and also ha'idah, according to al-Farra', who recited: "Like a menstruating woman who is fornicated with while impure." The plurals are nisa' hayd and hawa'id. A hayda (ḥayḍah) is a single occurrence. Al-hiyda (with a kasra) is the noun, and its plural is al-hiyad. Al-hayda also means the cloth with which a woman performs istithfar [[Istithfar: that a woman ties her private part with a broad cloth, or a wad of cotton which she stuffs and then ties its two ends to something, fastening it in place, to prevent the flow of blood.]]. A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "I wish I had been a cast-off cloth of menstruation." Likewise al-mahida, with plural al-mahayid. It was also said: al-mahid is an expression for the time and the place, and for the menstrual flow itself; its original usage is for time and place, and its use for the flow is metaphorical. Al-Tabari said: al-mahid is a name for the flow, and similar is Ru'bah's saying about hardship of living: "To you I complain of the severity of livelihood ... and years have passed, plucking my feathers." The root of the word is from flowing and gushing; it is said: the torrent flowed (hada al-sayl wa fada), and the tree menstruated (hadat al-shajarah), meaning its moisture flowed. From it comes al-hayd, meaning al-hawd (the pool), because water flows (yahid) into it, that is, flows. The Arabs interchange waw and ya', since they are from the same class. Ibn 'Arafah said: al-mahid and al-hayd are the gathering of blood at that place, and the pool (al-hawd) was named after it for the gathering of water in it. It is said: the woman menstruated and became menstruating (tahayyadat), and she was menstruating and bleeding (dara­sat, 'arakat, tamathat), tahid, hayd and mahad and mahid, when blood flows from her at known times. If it flows at times other than the known days, and not from the vein of menstruation, one says: she has become istihadah (bleeding irregularly), so she is musta'hadah. Ibn al-'Arabi.

She has eight names. The first: ha'id (menstruating). The second: 'arik. The third: farik. The fourth: tamis [[Thus in the originals and in Ibn al-'Arabi's Ahkam al-Quran.]]. The fifth: dasis. The sixth: kabir. The seventh: dahik. The eighth: tamith. Mujahid said regarding His saying, "So she laughed" [Q 11:71], that it means she menstruated. It was said regarding His saying, "When they saw him, they were struck with awe" [Q 12:31], that it means they menstruated. It will come in its place [[See vol. 9, p. 180]], Allah willing, exalted is He.

The third issue: The scholars have agreed that a woman has three rulings concerning seeing blood that visibly flows from her private part. Among these is the known menstruation, whose blood is black, thick, tinged with redness; prayer and fasting are left for it, and there is no disagreement about this. It may be continuous or interrupted. If it is continuous, the ruling applies to it. If it is interrupted, so she sees blood for a day and purity for a day, or blood for two days and purity for two days, or one day, then she leaves prayer during the days of blood, and washes at its cessation and prays; then she combines (yulaffiqu) the days of blood and disregards the days of purity that intervene, and does not count them as purity in the waiting period or as an istibra'. Menstruation is a natural occurrence in women, a known and habitual disposition among them. Al-Bukhari related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out on the day of Adha or Fitr to the musalla, and passed by the women and said: "O company of women, give charity, for I have seen that most of the people of Hell are you." They said: "Why, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "You curse much and you are ungrateful to your husbands. I have not seen anyone deficient in intellect and religion who takes away the intellect of a prudent man more than one of you." They said: "What is the deficiency in our intellect and religion, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Is not the testimony of a woman like half the testimony of a man?" They said: "Yes." He said: "That is from the deficiency of her intellect. Is it not that when she menstruates she does not pray and does not fast?" They said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "That is from the deficiency of her religion."

The scholars unanimously agreed that a menstruating woman makes up the fast but does not make up the prayer, based on the report of Mu'adhah, who said: I asked A'ishah, "What is the matter with the menstruating woman that she makes up the fast but not the prayer?" She said: "Are you a Harurite (Haruriyyah)?[[al-Haruriyyah: a sect of the Kharijites, named after "Harura'," a place near Kufa. They were the ones 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) fought, and they were known for their strictness in religion. When A'ishah saw this woman being strict about the matter of menstruation, she likened her to the Harurites. It was also said that she meant that the woman had opposed the Sunnah and departed from the community.]] I said, "I am not a Harurite, but I am asking." She said: "This used to happen to us, and we were commanded to make up the fast but were not commanded to make up the prayer." Muslim transmitted it.

When the bleeding stops, her purification from it is by ghusl (ritual bath), as will come. 

The fourth issue: The scholars differed over the duration of menstruation. The jurists of Madinah said: menstruation does not exceed fifteen days, and it is permissible for it to be fifteen days or less; anything beyond fifteen days is not menstruation but istihadah (irregular bleeding). This is the position of Malik and his companions. It has been reported from Malik that there is no fixed limit for the minimum or maximum of menstruation except what is found among women, as though he abandoned his first statement and returned to the custom of women. Muhammad ibn Maslamah said: the minimum period of purity is fifteen days. This is the choice of most of the Baghdadi Malikis, and it is the view of al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah and their companions, and al-Thawri, and it is the sound position on this topic, because Allah, exalted is He, made the waiting period (iddah) of women who have menstrual cycles three menstruations, and made the waiting period of one who does not menstruate, due to old age or youth, three months. So each qur' (menstrual cycle) is a substitute for a month, and the month comprises purity and menstruation. When menstruation is short, purity is long, and when menstruation is long, purity is short. Since the maximum of menstruation is fifteen days, its counterpart must be a minimum of fifteen days of purity, so that within a single month there is both menstruation and purity. This is what is customary in most cases of women's natural constitution and makeup, along with the indications of the Qur'an and Sunnah.

Al-Shafi'i said: the minimum of menstruation is one day and night, and the maximum is fifteen days. It has also been reported from him a view similar to Malik's: that this is referred back to women's customary practice.

Abu Hanifah and his companions said: the minimum of menstruation is three days, and the maximum is ten. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: whatever falls below three days according to them is istihadah, and it does not prevent prayer except at its first appearance, because its duration is not known. Then the woman must make up the prayers of those times. The same applies to what exceeds ten days according to the Kufans. According to the Hijazis, whatever exceeds fifteen days is istihadah. Whatever is less than a day and night according to al-Shafi'i is istihadah, and this is the view of al-Awza'i and al-Tabari. Among those who said the minimum is a day and night and the maximum fifteen days were 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, Abu Thawr and Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Al-Awza'i said: "Among us is a woman who menstruates in the morning and becomes pure in the evening."

We have covered what the scholars said on this topic, concerning the maximum and minimum of menstruation and the minimum of purity, and on precautionary waiting (istizhar). The evidence for this is in al-Muqtabas fi Sharh Muwatta' Malik ibn Anas.

If she is a virgin (bikr) experiencing bleeding for the first time (mubtada'ah), then according to al-Shafi'i she sits out fifteen days from when she first sees blood, then she performs ghusl and makes up the prayer of fourteen days. Malik said: she does not make up the prayer, and her husband refrains from her. 'Ali ibn Ziyad reported from him: she sits for the same number of days as her peers. This is also the view of 'Ata', al-Thawri and others. Ibn Hanbal: she sits for a day and night, then performs ghusl and prays, and her husband does not approach her. Abu Hanifah and Abu Yusuf: she leaves off prayer for ten days, then performs ghusl and prays for twenty days, then leaves off prayer for ten days after the twenty, and her condition remains like this until the bleeding stops for her. As for the woman who has known days, she adds three days of precaution to her known days. From Malik: as long as it does not exceed fifteen days. Al-Shafi'i: she performs ghusl when her days have ended, without precaution.

The second type of blood is postpartum bleeding (nifas) after childbirth. It also has a known limit according to the scholars, about which they differed. It was said: two months, which is the view of Malik. It was said: forty days, which is the view of al-Shafi'i. And it was said other than that. Her purity is when it stops, and ghusl from it is like ghusl from major impurity (janabah).

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad 'Abd al-Wahhab said: menstrual blood and postpartum blood prevent eleven things: the obligation of prayer and the validity of performing it, and the performance of fasting but not its obligation (the benefit of this distinction is that fasting must be made up and prayer need not be), sexual intercourse in the vagina and what is less than it, the waiting period (iddah), divorce, circumambulation (tawaf), touching the mushaf, entering the mosque and staying in it for i'tikaf, and reciting the Qur'an, on which there are two reports.

The third type of blood is blood that is neither a habit, nor a natural characteristic, nor a physical constitution of women, but is merely a severed vein. Its flow is red blood which never stops except when it is healed. The ruling for this is that the woman is pure from it, and it does not prevent her from prayer or fasting, by consensus of the scholars and agreement of the transmitted reports from the Prophet, provided it is known to be blood from a vein and not menstrual blood. Malik narrated from Hisham ibn 'Urwah, from his father, from A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) that she said: Fatimah bint Abi Hubaysh said: "O Messenger of Allah, I do not become pure! Should I leave off the prayer?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "That is only a vein, and it is not menstruation. When menstruation comes, leave off the prayer, and when its period has passed, wash the blood from yourself and pray."

In this hadith, along with its authenticity and brevity of wording, there is what clarifies for you the rulings of the menstruating woman and the woman with istihadah, and it is the most authentic report on this topic. It refutes what was reported from 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir and Makhul, that the menstruating woman performs ghusl and wudu' at every prayer time, and faces the qiblah sitting, remembering Allah, exalted is He. It also shows that the menstruating woman does not pray, and this is a consensus of all the scholars except some groups of the Kharijites, who hold that the menstruating woman must pray. It also contains an indication that the woman with istihadah is not obligated to anything beyond that ghusl which she performs for her menstruation; had anything else been obligatory for her, he would have commanded her to do it. It also refutes the view of those who held that she must perform ghusl for each prayer, the view of those who held that she must combine the two daytime prayers with one ghusl and the two nighttime prayers with one ghusl and perform ghusl for dawn, the view of one who said she performs ghusl from one purity to another, and the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab that it is from one purity to another, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not command her to do any of that. It also refutes the view of those who said precautionary waiting is required, because the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded her, when she knew that her menstruation had turned back and gone, to perform ghusl and pray, and he did not command her to leave off prayer for three days awaiting a menstruation that may or may not come. Precaution applies to performing the prayer, not to abandoning it.

The fifth issue: the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Say: it is harm (adha)﴾, meaning: it is something by which the woman and others are harmed, namely by the smell of menstrual blood. Adha is a metaphor for filth in general. It is also used for a disliked speech, as in Allah's saying: "Do not invalidate your charities with reminders and harm (al-adha)" [[Qur'an 2:264]], meaning by what you hear of what is disliked. And from it is His saying: "And leave off their harm (adhahum)" [[Qur'an 33:48]], meaning: leave off the harm of the hypocrites; do not requite them unless you are commanded regarding them. In a hadith: "Remove the adha from him," meaning by "adha" the hair on the head of a child at birth, which is shaved on the seventh day, and this is the 'aqiqah. In the hadith on faith: "The lowest of them is removing the adha from the road," meaning removing it, that is, thorns, a stone, and what resembles that of what harms the passerby. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there is no blame upon you if you have adha from rain﴾, which will come [[See vol. 5, p. 372]].

The sixth issue: those who prohibited intercourse with the woman with istihadah argued from the flow of istihadah blood, saying: every blood is adha, which must be washed from clothing and body, so there is no difference in physical contact between menstrual blood and istihadah blood, since all of it is impurity (rijs). As for prayer, it is a concession established by the Sunnah, just as one prays with dribbling urine. This is the view of Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Sulayman ibn Yasar, al-Hakam ibn 'Uyaynah, 'Amir al-Sha'bi, Ibn Sirin and al-Zuhri. It has been differed on regarding al-Hasan, and it is the view of A'ishah: her husband does not approach her. Ibn 'Uliyyah, al-Mughirah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, who was among the most eminent companions of Malik, and Abu Mus'ab also said this, and it was the basis of his fatwa.

The majority of scholars said: the woman with istihadah fasts, prays, performs tawaf, recites, and her husband may approach her. Malik said: the position of the people of jurisprudence and knowledge is on this, even if her bleeding is heavy; this was transmitted from him by Ibn Wahb. Ahmad used to say: "It is more beloved to me that he not approach her unless that lasts a long time for her." It was reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the woman with istihadah: "There is no harm in her husband approaching her, even if the blood flows down onto her heels." Malik said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "That is only a vein, and it is not menstruation." So if it is not menstruation, what prevents him from approaching her while she prays!

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: since Allah, mighty and majestic, ruled regarding the blood of istihadah that it does not prevent prayer, and she is charged with a worship different from the worship of the menstruating woman, it must not be ruled for it with anything of the rulings of menstruation, except regarding what they agreed upon, which is washing it, like all other bloods.

The seventh issue: the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So keep away from women during menstruation﴾, meaning during the time of menstruation, if you take al-mahid as a verbal noun, or in the place of menstruation, if you take it as a noun. The aim of this prohibition is abstention from sexual intercourse. The scholars differed concerning physical contact with a menstruating woman and what is permitted from her. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Abidah al-Salmani that the man must keep away from his wife's bed when she menstruates. This is an anomalous (shadh) view.

You are outside the view of the scholars. Even if the generality of the verse implies it, the established Sunnah is contrary to it. Maymunah, his (Ibn 'Abbas's) maternal aunt, once confronted him and said: "Are you averse to the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ?!"

Malik, al-Shafi'i, al-Awza'i, Abu Hanifah, Abu Yusuf and a great body of scholars said: he may enjoy with her everything above the waist wrapper (izar), based on his saying ﷺ to the questioner who asked him: "What is lawful for me of my wife when she is menstruating?" He said: "Let her tighten her izar around her, then do what you wish with her above it." ["Sha'nuka" (what you wish): it is in the accusative by an implied verb, and it may be read in the nominative as a beginning (mubtada'), with the predicate omitted, its estimate being "permissible" or "allowed" (Ibn al-Athir).] And his saying ﷺ to 'A'ishah when she menstruated: "Tighten your izar around yourself, then return to your bed."

Al-Thawri, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan and some companions of al-Shafi'i said: one avoids the place of the blood, based on his saying ﷺ: "Do everything except intercourse." This has already been mentioned. This is the view of Dawud, and it is the sound view of al-Shafi'i.

Abu Ma'shar narrated from Ibrahim, from Masruq, who said: I asked 'A'ishah, "What is lawful for me of my wife when she is menstruating?" She said: "Everything except the private part (farj)."

The scholars said: intimacy with a menstruating woman while she wears her wrapper is a matter of caution and of closing the means (dhari'ah) [to what is forbidden]. For if he permitted her thighs, that would be a means to the place of blood, which is forbidden by consensus. So he commanded this as a precaution, and the forbidden thing itself is the place of blood. Thus the meanings of the reports agree and do not conflict, and success is from Allah.

Eighth: They differed regarding one who has intercourse with his wife while she is menstruating, what is due from him. Malik, al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifah said: he should seek Allah's forgiveness, and there is nothing upon him. This is also the view of Rabi'ah and Yahya ibn Sa'id, and Dawud said likewise. It was narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan: he should give charity of half a dinar. Ahmad said: how excellent is the hadith of 'Abd al-Hamid, from Miqsam, from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet ﷺ: "He should give charity of a dinar or half a dinar." Abu Dawud transmitted it and said: "This is the sound narration: a dinar or half a dinar." al-Tabari recommended it. If he does not do so, there is nothing upon him; this is the view of al-Shafi'i in Baghdad. A group of the people of hadith said: if he has intercourse during the bleeding, he owes a dinar, and if he has intercourse when it has stopped, he owes half a dinar. al-Awza'i said: whoever has intercourse with his wife while she is menstruating gives charity of two-fifths of a dinar. The chains for all of this are in the Sunan of Abu Dawud and al-Daraqutni and others. In the Book of al-Tirmidhi, from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "If it is red blood, then a dinar; and if it is yellow blood, then half a dinar."

Abu 'Umar said: the argument of those who did not obligate an expiation upon him beyond seeking forgiveness and repentance is the instability (idtirab) of this hadith as transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, and that such a report cannot bear a proof, and that the obligation (dhimmah) rests on innocence, and nothing may be established in it for a poor person or anyone else except by a proof that cannot be repelled or challenged, and that is absent in this issue.

Ninth: The Most High said: ﴿And do not approach them until they have purified themselves﴾. Ibn al-'Arabi said: I heard al-Shashi in a session of disputation say: when it is said "la taqrab" (with a fatha on the ra'), its meaning is "do not engage in the act"; and if it is with a damma on the ra', its meaning is "do not draw near to it." Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim in the transmission of Hafs from him read "yathurna" with a sukun on the ta' and a damma on the ha'. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal read "yattahharna" with the ta' and ha' both doubled and vowelled with fatha. In the codex of Ubayy and 'Abd Allah it is "yatatahharna." In the codex of Anas ibn Malik: "And do not approach women during their menstruation, and keep away from them until they have purified themselves." al-Tabari preferred the reading with the doubled ta', and said: it means "they wash (yaghtasilna)," since there is consensus that it is forbidden for a man to approach his wife after the bleeding has stopped until she is pure. He said: the disagreement is only about what purity is. Some said it is washing with water. Some said it is wudu' like the wudu' for prayer. Some said it is washing the private part, and by that she becomes lawful to her husband even if she has not bathed from the menstruation. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi preferred the reading with the single ta', since it is a triliteral form opposite to "tamath," which is triliteral.

Tenth: The Most High said: ﴿So when they have purified themselves﴾, meaning with water. This is the view of Malik and the majority of scholars, that the purity by which intercourse with a menstruating woman becomes lawful, once the blood has gone from her, is her purifying herself with water like the purity of one in major ritual impurity (junub), and nothing else, such as tayammum, suffices for this. This is also the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, al-Tabari, Muhammad ibn Maslamah, the people of Madinah and others. Yahya ibn Bukayr and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: when the menstruating woman has become pure and performs tayammum where there is no water, she becomes lawful to her husband even if she has not bathed. Mujahid, 'Ikrimah and Tawus said: the cessation of the blood makes her lawful to her husband, but only once she performs wudu'. Abu Hanifah, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad said: if her bleeding stops after ten days have passed, it is permissible for him to have intercourse with her before she bathes; but if the bleeding stops before the ten days, it is not permissible until she bathes or the time of prayer enters upon her. This is an arbitrary ruling with no basis. They have ruled that for a menstruating woman after the cessation of her blood she is subject to the rule of confinement during the waiting period, and they said to her husband: he has the right of return so long as she has not bathed from the third menstruation. So by analogy with this view of theirs, she should not have to be approached until she bathes, in agreement with the people of Madinah. Our proof is that Allah, glorified is He, made the ruling in this matter conditional upon two conditions. The first is the cessation of the blood, which is His saying: ﴿until they have purified themselves﴾. The second is washing with water, which is His saying: ﴿So when they have purified themselves﴾, that is, they perform the washing with water. This is like His saying: ﴿And test the orphans until they reach marriageable age﴾, where the ruling, which is permission to hand over their property, is made conditional upon two conditions: first, that the one under obligation reach marriageable age; and second, that sound judgment be found in him. Likewise His saying concerning the divorced woman: ﴿then she is not lawful to him after that until she marries another husband﴾. Then the Sunnah came with the stipulation of the 'usaylah, so that the permission depends on both matters together: the validity of the marriage and the occurrence of intercourse. Abu Hanifah argued, saying: the meaning of the verse is that the limit in the condition is what is mentioned in the limit before it, so that His saying "until they have purified themselves," lightened, has the same meaning as "they purify themselves," doubled in the same form; but He combined the two dialects in the verse, as He said: ﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves, and Allah loves those who purify themselves﴾. al-Kumayt said:

"And the Ansar were not humbled therein,
nor were they absent therein when people were absent."

Moreover, the two readings are like two verses, so both must be acted upon. We interpret each of them with a distinct meaning. We take the lightened reading (*al-mukhaffafa*) to refer to the case where her bleeding has stopped for the lesser period, so we do not permit intercourse with her until she performs ghusl (the full ritual bath), because her bleeding may return. We take the other reading to refer to the case where her bleeding has stopped for the greater period, so intercourse with her is permitted even if she has not performed ghusl.

Ibn al-Arabi said: This is the strongest of their arguments. The answer to the first is that this is not the speech of eloquent speakers or of the masters of rhetoric, for it requires repetition in the enumeration. When a word can be understood as carrying a single, distinct meaning, it is not interpreted as repetition in human speech, so how much less in the speech of the All-Knowing, the All-Wise!

As for the second: each of the two readings is understood to have a meaning other than the meaning of the other. It follows for them that, when the bleeding has stopped, she should not be judged by the ruling of menstruation (*hayd*) before she performs ghusl with regard to the return (*raj'a*) of her husband. But they do not say this, as we have explained. So she is then in a state of menstruation, and it is agreed that intercourse with a menstruating woman is not permitted.

Also, what they say entails permission of intercourse when the bleeding has stopped for the greater period, while what we say entails prohibition. When what entails prohibition and what entails permission conflict, and the two motivations are weighed against each other, the motivation for prohibition takes precedence, as Ali and Uthman said regarding combining two sisters through ownership by right hand (*milk al-yamin*): "One verse permitted them and another verse forbade them, and prohibition is preferable." And Allah knows best.

**Eleventh issue.** Our scholars differed regarding the Jewish or Christian woman (*al-kitabiyya*): is she compelled to perform ghusl or not? Malik, in the transmission of Ibn al-Qasim, said: Yes, so that intercourse with her becomes lawful for her husband. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And do not approach them until they have become pure. Then, when they have purified themselves…﴾ [Qur'an 2:222], meaning with water, and He did not single out a Muslim woman from others.

Ashhab transmitted from Malik that she is not compelled to perform ghusl from menstruation, because she does not believe in it, based on the saying of Allah the Exalted: "And it is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs, if they believe in Allah and the Last Day" [Qur'an 2:228], meaning menstruation and pregnancy. Allah addressed the believing women alone with this, and He said: "There is no compulsion in religion" [Qur'an 2:256]. Mahmud ibn Abd al-Hakam used to say this.

**Twelfth issue.** The manner of the menstruating woman's ghusl is the same as the manner of her ghusl from major impurity (*janaba*), and she is not required to undo her hair for it. This is based on what Muslim transmitted from Umm Salama, who said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, I tightly braid my hair; shall I undo it for the ghusl of major impurity?" He said: "No. It is enough for you to pour three handfuls of water over your head, then pour water over your body, and you will be purified." In another narration: "Shall I undo it for menstruation and major impurity?" He said: "No." Abu Dawud added: "And rub your locks (*qurun*) with each handful."

**Thirteenth issue.** The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So come to them from where Allah has commanded you﴾. That means: have intercourse with them. This is a command of permission, and He used "coming" as a euphemism for sexual intercourse. This command reinforces what we have said, that the intended meaning of purification (*tathhur*) is washing with water, because a command from Allah the Exalted is only directed to the most complete manner.

And Allah knows best. The word "min" (from) here means "fi" (in): that is, in the place where Allah the Exalted has commanded you, which is the front passage. A parallel to this is the words of Allah the Exalted: "Show me what they have created from the earth" [Qur'an 35:40], meaning "in the earth." And His words: "When the call is made for prayer on the day of Friday" [Qur'an 62:9], meaning "on the day of Friday."

It was also said: the meaning is: from the way in which He has permitted you, that is, without fasting, ihram (the state of pilgrim consecration), or i'tikaf (retreat in the mosque). This was said by al-Asamm. Ibn Abbas and Abu Razin said: from the direction of purity, not from the direction of menstruation, and al-Dahhak said the same. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya said: the meaning is from the lawful direction, not from the direction of unlawful sex.

**Fourteenth issue.** The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who are constantly repentant and loves those who purify themselves﴾. This has been differed over. It was said: "those who are constantly repentant" are those who repent from sins and from association (with others with Allah), and "those who purify themselves" means those who purify themselves with water from major impurity and minor impurities (*ahdath*), as Ata' and others said. Mujahid said: from sins. He also said: from intercourse with women in their posterior. Ibn Atiyya said: It seems he took into account the words of Allah the Exalted, relating about the people of Lot: "Expel them from your town; indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure" [Qur'an 7:82].

It was also said: "those who purify themselves" are those who have not committed sins. If it is asked: why did He mention first those who sinned before those who did not sin? It is answered: He mentioned them first so that the repentant would not despair of mercy, and so that the one who is pure would not be self-admiring, as He mentioned in another verse: "Among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds" [Qur'an 35:32], as its explanation will come, God willing. [[See vol. 14, p. 347.]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 223 (part 1 of 2):

There are six issues.

The first concerns His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you﴾. The Imams narrated, and the wording is that of Muslim, from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who said: The Jews used to say: "If a man has intercourse with his wife from behind, in her vagina, the child will be cross-eyed." So this verse was revealed: "Your wives are a tilth for you, so go to your tilth however you wish." In another narration from al-Zuhri there is an addition: "Whether she is made to lie face down [[mujabbiyah: that is, his chest upon her face, likening it to the posture of prostration]] or not made to lie face down, provided it is in one orifice (ṣimām wāḥid)." It is also narrated as "in one ṣimām" with a sīn (sīmām wāḥid), related by al-Tirmidhi.

Al-Bukhari narrated from Nafi', who said: When Ibn Umar recited the Qur'an, he would not speak until he had finished it. One day I held the codex over him [[akhadhtu ʿalayhi: that is, I held the muṣḥaf while he was reciting from memory]], and he recited Surat al-Baqarah until he reached a point, and then said: "Do you know concerning what this was revealed?" I said: "No." He said: "It was revealed concerning such and such," and then he went on.

It is also narrated from Abd al-Samad, who said: My father related to me, who said: Ayyub related to me, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar: "So go to your tilth however you wish," and he said: "He comes to her in..." [[the genitive complement is omitted; see the commentary on al-Bukhari on the interpretation of this verse, where there is discussion of this omission]]. Al-Humaydi said: "That is, the vagina (al-farj)."

Abu Dawud narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Ibn Umar, may Allah forgive him, made an error. This was only the case of this clan of the Ansar, who were people of idolatry, together with this clan of Jews, who were people of the Book, and they regarded the Jews as having superiority over them in knowledge, so they followed much of their practice. It was among the affairs of the People of the Book that they would not approach women except in one manner [[ʿalā ḥarf]], and that is the most concealing position for a woman. So this clan of the Ansar took this up from their practice. And this clan of the Quraysh would treat their women with an objectionable mounting [[sharaḥa al-rajul jāriyatahu: when a man has intercourse with his slave-girl while she lies on her back]], and they would take pleasure from them facing forward, facing backward and lying on their backs. When the Emigrants came to Madinah, a man of them married a woman of the Ansar, and he went to do that with her, but she rejected it from him and said: 'We were only approached in one manner! So do this, or else keep away from me.' Their affair grew until it became serious [[sharā amruhumā: that is, it became great and escalated, and they persisted in it]], and this reached the Prophet ﷺ, and Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: 'So go to your tilth however you wish,' meaning: facing forward, facing backward and lying on the back, by which is meant the place of the child."

Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: Umar came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I am ruined!" He said: "What has ruined you?" He said: "I turned my mount around last night." He said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not answer him with anything. Then this verse was revealed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Your wives are a tilth for you, so go to your tilth however you wish," [and the addition:] "Approach from the front and from behind, but avoid the anus and menstruation." He said: "This is a hasan ṣaḥīḥ hadith." [[What is in the Ṣaḥīḥ of al-Tirmidhi is: "ḥasan gharīb."]]

Al-Nasai narrated from Abu al-Nadr that he said to Nafi', the freedman of Ibn Umar: "Many statements have been attributed to you. You say that Ibn Umar issued a ruling that women may be approached in their anuses." Nafi' said: "They have lied about me! But I will tell you how the matter actually was: One day Ibn Umar presented the codex to me while I was with him, until he reached: 'Your wives are a tilth for you.' Nafi' said: 'Do you know what the matter of this verse is? We, the company of the Quraysh, used to mount our women [[tajbiyah: its meaning has been mentioned before, p. 91 of this part]]. When we entered Madinah and married women of the Ansar, we wanted from them what we used to want from our wives, but they disliked that and considered it a great matter, for the women of the Ansar were only approached on their sides.' So Allah, glorified is He, revealed: 'Your wives are a tilth for you, so go to your tilth however you wish.'"

The second issue: these hadiths are explicit in permitting all the positions and postures, provided the intercourse is in the place of tilth, that is, however you wish, from behind or from the front, seated, lying on the back, or reclining. As for intercourse in other than the place of intercourse, it is not permitted; and the mention of "tilth" indicates that intercourse in other than the place of intercourse is forbidden. "Tilth" is a metaphor, for women are the fields of offspring. So the word "tilth" indicates that permission applies only to the vagina specifically, since it is the cultivated ground. Thaʿlab recited:

"Indeed the wombs are lands
for us, to be ploughed,
so upon us is the sowing in them,
and upon Allah is the growth."

So the woman's vagina is like the land, the semen is like the seed, and the child is like the growth. Thus "tilth" means "that which is ploughed." The word "tilth" is singular because it is a verbal noun, as one says "a man who fasts (ṣawm)" and "a people who fast (ṣawm)."

The third issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿however you wish﴾. Its meaning, according to the majority of the Companions, the Successors and the leading jurists, is: from whatever direction you wish, facing forward or facing backward, as we mentioned just above. "Anna" comes as a question and as an report about a matter that has several aspects, so in the language it is more general than "kayfa" (how), "ayna" (where) and "matā" (when). This is the Arabic usage of "anna." People have explained "anna" in this verse with these expressions. Sibawayh explained it as "kayfa" and "min ayna" together. A group among those who explained it as "ayna" held that intercourse in the anus is permitted. Among those to whom this view is attributed are Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, Nafi', Ibn Umar, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi and Abd al-Malik ibn al-Majishun, and this view has been related from Malik in a book of his called "Kitab al-Sirr" (the Book of the Secret). But the skilled scholars among the companions of Malik and his shaykhs deny that book, and Malik is too exalted to have a "secret book." This view has also appeared in al-Utbiyyah. Ibn al-Arabi mentioned that Ibn Shaʿban attributed the permissibility of this view to a large company of the Companions and the Successors, and to Malik through many narrations, in the book "Jimaʿ al-Niswan wa Ahkam al-Quran." Al-Kiya al-Tabari said: It is related from Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi that he saw no harm in it, and he interpreted in its favour the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic: "Do you approach the males of the worlds, and leave what your Lord has created for you of your spouses?"

[[Qur'an 26:165 note.]] He said: its meaning is "you leave what your spouses are for you," and if such [anal intercourse] were not permitted with wives, the phrase would not be valid. The permitted act in the other place is not a parallel to it, such that it could be said, "you do that and leave its permitted counterpart." Al-Kiya said: This is open to question, since its meaning is: "and you leave what your Lord has created for you of your spouses, through which your desire is calmed, and the pleasure of intercourse is obtained through both of them together." So rebuke is permissible on this meaning. In the verse ﴿So when they have purified themselves, come to them from where Allah has commanded you﴾ together with ﴿So come to your tilth﴾, there is something indicating that the place of intercourse is specific and restricted to the place of offspring. I say: This is the truth on the question. Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr mentioned that the scholars did not disagree that a woman with a closed passage (ratqa') who cannot be penetrated is a defect for which a marriage may be annulled, except for something reported from 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz through a route that is not strong, that a ratqa' is not returned, nor any other. All the jurists are against that, because touching (masis) is what is sought in marriage. Their consensus on this is evidence that the anus is not a place of penetration; had it been a place of penetration, a woman who cannot be reached in the vagina would not be returned. Also, there is their consensus that a barren woman who does not bear children is not returned. The correct view on this question is what we have explained. What is attributed to Malik and his companions on this is false, and they are free of it, because the permission of intercourse is specific to the place of tilth, by His saying ﴿come to your tilth﴾, and because the wisdom in creating spouses is the spreading of offspring, so a place other than the place of offspring is not reached by the one who holds the marriage contract. This is the truth. The companions of Abu Hanifa have said: "According to us, it is the same in ruling as the anus of a male." Also, the filth and harm in the place of excretion (al-najw) is greater than the blood of menstruation, so it is more abominable. As for the sphincter of urine, it is not the sphincter of the womb. Ibn al-'Arabi said in his Qabas: Our shaykh, the imam Fakhr al-Islam Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn al-Husayn, the jurist and imam of his time, told us: "The vagina most resembles thirty-five," and he extended his hand, folding its fingers. He said: "The passage of urine is below the thirty, and the passage of the penis and vagina is what the five encompasses." Allah the Exalted has forbidden the vagina during menstruation because of the accidental impurity. So it is more fitting that the anus be forbidden because of the constant impurity. Malik said to Ibn Wahb and 'Ali ibn Ziyad, when they informed him that some people in Egypt were narrating from him that he permitted this, that he recoiled from it and hastened to deny the one who transmitted it, saying: "They lied about me, they lied about me, they lied about me!" Then he said: "Are you not an Arab people? Did not Allah the Exalted say: ﴿Your women are a tilth for you﴾? Does a tilth exist except in the place of growth?" As for what the opponent used as evidence, that the saying of the Mighty and Majestic ﴿as you wish﴾ includes the [anal] passages by the ruling of its generality, there is no proof in it, since it is specified by what we have mentioned and by sound, good and well-known hadiths narrated from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ by twelve Companions, with differing wordings, all converging on the prohibition of coming to women in the anus. Ahmad ibn Hanbal mentioned them in his Musnad, as did Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, al-Tirmidhi and others. Abu al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzi collected them with their chains in a booklet he named "The Prohibition of the Hated Place." Our shaykh Abu al-'Abbas also has a booklet on this titled "Manifesting the Backside, Against One Who Permits Intercourse in the Anus." I say: This is the truth to be followed and the correct view on the question. It is not befitting for a believer in Allah and the Last Day to take the slip of a scholar as support in this matter once it has been authentically established from him. We have already warned against the slips of scholars. It has been reported from Ibn 'Umar the opposite of this, and that he declared disbelief in one who does it, and this is what is fitting for him, may Allah be pleased with him. Likewise Nafi' denied the one who reported this from him, as al-Nasa'i mentioned, and it has already been mentioned. Malik rejected this and considered it grave, and he denied the one who attributed it to him. Al-Darimi Abu Muhammad narrated in his Musnad from Sa'id ibn Yasar Abu al-Hubab, who said: I said to Ibn 'Umar: "What do you say about female slaves when I make them 'tahmid' (alternative intercourse)?" He said: "What is tahmid?" So I mentioned the anus to him, and he said: "Does any Muslim do that?" It is also transmitted from Khuzayma ibn Thabit: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "O people, indeed Allah is not shy of the truth. Do not come to women in their backsides." A similar report comes from 'Ali ibn Talq. It is also transmitted from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Whoever comes to a woman in her anus, Allah the Exalted will not look at him on the Day of Resurrection." Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi narrated in his Musnad from Qatada, from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "That is the lesser sodomy," meaning coming to a woman in her anus. It is narrated from Tawus that he said: "The beginning of the deed of the people of Lot was coming to women in their backsides." Ibn al-Mundhir said: When a matter is authentically established from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, one needs nothing else beside it.

The fourth issue: His saying the Exalted: ﴿And send forward for yourselves﴾, meaning: send forward what will benefit you tomorrow. The object has been omitted, and it has been stated explicitly in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And whatever good you send forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah﴾ [Qur'an 2:110]. So the meaning is: send forward for yourselves obedience and righteous deeds. It has been said: it means seeking offspring and progeny, because a child is the good of this world and the Hereafter; he may be an intercessor and a shield. It has been said: it means marrying chaste women, so that the child will be righteous and pure. It has been said: it means the advance of the afrat (children who died before reaching puberty), as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever sends forward three children who have not reached the age of responsibility, the Fire will not touch him except as a fulfillment of the oath," the hadith. It will come in Surah Maryam, if Allah the Exalted wills. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata' said: it means mention Allah's name at intercourse, as the Prophet ﷺ, peace be upon him, said: "If one of you, when he comes to his wife, says: 'In the name of Allah. O Allah, keep us away from Satan, and keep Satan away from what You have provided us,' then if a child is decreed between them, Satan will never harm him." Muslim transmitted it.

The fifth issue: His saying the Exalted: ﴿And fear Allah﴾ is a warning. ﴿And know that you will meet Him﴾ is a statement that calls for emphasis in warning, meaning: He will repay you for righteousness and sin. Ibn 'Uyayna narrated from 'Amr ibn Dinar, who said: I heard Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while he was delivering a sermon, saying: "Indeed you will meet Allah barefoot, naked, walking, uncircumcised" — then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited: ﴿And fear Allah, and know that you will meet Him﴾. Muslim transmitted it in meaning.

The sixth issue: His saying the Exalted: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾ is an encouragement to the doer of righteousness and the seeker of the paths of guidance.

The passage has four issues. The first: the scholars said, when God commanded spending and kind companionship with orphans and women, He said: do not refrain from any of the noble deeds on the pretext that "we have sworn not to do such-and-such." This was the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Nakha'i, Mujahid, al-Rabi' and others. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it is the man who swears that he will not be righteous, will not maintain ties of kinship, and will not reconcile between people. Then it is said to him, "Be righteous," and he says, "I have sworn." Some of the early exegetes said: the meaning is, "Do not swear by God falsely when you intend righteousness, piety and reconciliation," so there is no need to posit a "lā" (not) after "an" (that). It was also said: the meaning is, "Do not multiply oaths by God, for that diminishes awe in the hearts," and for this reason God said: ﴿And guard your oaths﴾ [[See vol. 6, p. 285.]]. He censured the one who multiplies oaths, saying: ﴿And do not obey every mean swearer﴾ [[See vol. 18, p. 231.]]. The Arabs praise few oaths, to the point that one of them said:

Few are his oaths, and he guards his oath,
And if an oath issues from him, it is fulfilled.

On this reading, ﴿that you be righteous﴾ means: make your oaths few, because of the righteousness and piety in that, for multiplying oaths is accompanied by breaking them and by little regard for the right of God. This is a good interpretation. Malik ibn Anas said: "It has reached me that it means swearing by God in every matter." It was also said: the meaning is, "Do not make oaths commonplace in every matter, true or false." al-Zajjaj and others said: the meaning of the verse is that when a man is asked to do a good deed, he makes an excuse by God, saying, "I swear by God," though he has not sworn. al-Qutabi said: the meaning is, if you swear that you will not maintain ties of kinship, not give charity, not reconcile, and similar acts of righteousness, then expiate the oath. I say: this is good, given what we have explained, and it is what indicates the occasion of revelation, as we will explain in the next issue.

The second issue: it was said that the verse was revealed concerning al-Siddiq (Abu Bakr), when he swore not to spend on Mistah when Mistah spoke against 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her, as in the hadith of the Slander (al-ifk), whose explanation will come in *al-Nur* [[See vol. 12, p. 207.]], on the authority of Ibn Jurayj. It was also said that it was revealed concerning al-Siddiq when he swore not to eat with the guests. It was said that it was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Rawaha when he swore not to speak to Bashir ibn al-Nu'man, who was his brother-in-law through his sister. And God knows best.

The third issue: God's words ﴿an obstacle to your oaths﴾ mean "a target," according to al-Jawhari. One says, "So-and-so is an 'ur<u>d</u>a for that," meaning he is a match for it and strong enough for it [[In the Sihah: "or 'urḍa li-dhalika."]]. The 'urḍa also means resolve. One poet said:

They are the Ansar; their 'urḍa is the encounter.
[Second half of a line by Hassan ibn Thabit, may God be pleased with him; the first half is: "And God said, 'I have prepared an army.'"]

"So-and-so is an 'urḍa for people" means they never cease to attack him. "I made so-and-so an 'urḍa for such-and-such" means I set him up as a target for it. It was also said that 'urḍa means strength and power, and from this comes their saying of a woman, "She is an 'urḍa for marriage," when she is fit for it and strong enough for it. "So-and-so has an 'urḍa" means he has strength for travel and war. Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said:

From every sweating, she-camel with a wide nape, whose 'urḍa (vigour) is an unknown, faded landmark.

'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr said:

These are for days of war, and these for pleasure, and these are an 'urḍa (provision) for our departure.

That is, a provision. Another said:

So do not make me an 'urḍa for the blamers.

Aws ibn Hajar said:

And a she-camel like a stallion, one day her 'urḍa (readiness) is for my saddle, and in her is a shaking and a jolting.

The meaning is: do not make the oath by God a strength for yourselves, and an excuse for refraining from righteousness.

The fourth issue: God's words ﴿that you be righteous and fear God﴾ are a subject whose predicate is omitted; that is, righteousness, piety and reconciliation are better and more fitting, like ﴿obedience and honorable speech﴾, according to al-Zajjaj and al-Nahhas. It was also said that its place is in the accusative: that is, the oath by God, Mighty and Majestic, should not prevent you from righteousness, piety and reconciliation. This is also from al-Zajjaj. It was also said that it is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi). It was also said that the meaning is "lest you be righteous," with "lā" omitted, like God's words ﴿God makes clear to you lest you go astray﴾ (4:176), meaning, "lest you go astray." This was said by al-Tabari and al-Nahhas. A fourth possibility in the accusative is: "from disliking that you be righteous," with it then omitted; this was mentioned by al-Nahhas and al-Mahdawi. It was also said that it is in the genitive position according to the view of al-Khalil and al-Kisa'i, the estimate being "in that you be righteous," so "in" was omitted and the noun was put in the genitive by it.

﴿All-Hearing﴾: of the sayings of the servants.

﴿All-Knowing﴾: of their intentions.
