Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 225:

There are four issues in this.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿by the idle oath﴾ (bi-l-laghw). Al-laghw is a verbal noun of laghā yalghū and yalghā, and laghiya yalghā laghan, meaning to say what is not needed in speech, or what contains no good, or what carries no sin (yulghī ithmuhu, i.e., its sinfulness is nullified). In a hadith: "If you say to your companion while the imam is delivering the Friday sermon, 'Be silent,' then you have committed laghw (laghawta)." The dialect of Abu Hurayra was "faqad laghayta." The poet said [[It is al-Ajjaj, as in his Diwan.]]:

"And many a flock of pilgrims, restrained from idle talk and obscene speech..."

Another said [[It is al-Farazdaq, as in al-Naqa'id, p. 344, Europe edition.]]:

"And I shall not be held to account for an idle word you utter, when you did not intend the firm resolutions that bind."

The second: The scholars differed concerning the oath that is laghw. Ibn Abbas said: it is a man's saying, in the flow of his speech and the haste of his discourse: "No, by Allah," and "Yes, by Allah," without intending an oath. Al-Marwazi said: the laghw of oaths, on which the scholars agree that it is laghw, is a man's saying, "No, by Allah," and "Yes, by Allah," in his talk and speech, without believing in the oath or intending it. Ibn Wahb narrated from Yunus, from Ibn Shihab, that Urwa told him that A'isha, the wife of the Prophet ﷺ, said: "The oaths of laghw are those uttered in disputation, jesting, joking, and in speech which the heart does not bind itself to." In al-Bukhari, from A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, she said: the words of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿Allah will not hold you to account for the idle oaths in your oaths﴾ were revealed concerning a man's saying: "No, by Allah," and "Yes, by Allah." It was also said: laghw is what one swears by on assumption, and it turns out to be otherwise; this was stated by Malik, related by Ibn al-Qasim from him, and a group of the early generation held it. Abu Hurayra said: when a man swears regarding a thing, thinking only that it is so, but it is not, that is laghw, and there is no expiation (kaffara) in it; and similar was reported from Ibn Abbas. It was also reported that some people were disputing a matter before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while shooting arrows in his presence, and one of them swore: "I was right and you were wrong, O so-and-so," but the matter was otherwise. The man said: "He has broken his oath, O Messenger of Allah." The Prophet ﷺ said: "The oaths of archers are laghw; there is no breaking (hinth) in them and no expiation." In the Muwatta', Malik said: the best I have heard on this is that laghw is a person's oath concerning a thing he is certain is so, and then it is found otherwise; there is no expiation in it. As for one who swears regarding a thing while knowing that he is sinful and lying in it, in order to please someone, or to excuse himself to a creature, or to seize property by it, this is far greater than being subject to expiation; expiation applies only to one who swears not to do a permissible act and then does it, or swears to do it and then does not do it, such as one who swears not to sell his garment for ten dirhams and then sells it for the same price, or swears he will beat his slave and then does not beat him. It was reported from Ibn Abbas, if it is authentically from him, that he said: the laghw of oaths is that you swear while you are angry; Tawus said the same. Ibn Abbas also related that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There is no oath in anger." Muslim recorded it. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it is the prohibition of what is lawful, so that one says: "My property is forbidden to me if I do such and such," and "the lawful is forbidden"; Makhul al-Dimashqi and Malik also said so, except that regarding a wife Malik held that the prohibition binds her, unless the one swearing intends to exclude her in his heart. It was also said: it is the oath of disobedience, as stated by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Abu Bakr ibn Abd al-Rahman, Urwa, and Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, such as one who swears that he will drink wine or sever the ties of kinship; his piety lies in abandoning that act, and there is no expiation for him. Their proof is the hadith of Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever swears an oath and then sees something else better than it, let him abandon it, for abandoning it is its expiation." Ibn Majah recorded it in his Sunan, and it will come again in (surah) al-Ma'ida [[See vol. 6, p. 265.]]. Zayd ibn Aslam said: the laghw of oaths is a man's supplication against himself: "May Allah blind his sight," "May Allah take away his wealth," "He is a Jew," "He is a polytheist," "He is a... if he does such and such." Mujahid said: they are two men trading, one of whom says: "By Allah, I will not sell to you for such and such," and the other says: "By Allah, I will not buy it for such and such." Al-Nakha'i said: it is the man who swears not to do a thing, then forgets and does it.

Ibn Abbas also said, as did al-Dahhak: the laghw of oaths is the one that is expiated; that is, when an oath is expiated it falls away and becomes laghw, and Allah does not hold one to account for expiating it and returning to what is better. Ibn Abd al-Barr related an opinion that laghw is the oath of one who is compelled. Ibn al-Arabi said: as for the oath made in forgetfulness, there is no doubt that it is nullified, because it came contrary to his intention, so it is pure laghw. I say: the oath of one compelled is of the same standing. The ruling on one who swears under compulsion will come in (surah) al-Nahl [[See vol. 10, p. 186.]], God willing. Ibn al-Arabi said: as for one who said it is the oath of disobedience, this is false, because the one who swears to abstain from disobedience has his oath valid as an act of worship, while the one who swears to commit disobedience has his oath valid as disobedience; it is said to him: do not do it and expiate. If he proceeds to the act, he sins in his proceeding but is faithful (barra) in his oath. As for one who said it is a person's supplication against himself, "if it is not so, may such and such befall him," this is vain speech as regards expiation, but it is binding in intention, disliked, and he may be held to account for it, because the Prophet ﷺ said: "Let none of you supplicate against himself, for it may coincide with an hour in which Allah is asked for nothing without granting it." As for one who said it is the oath of anger, the oath of the Prophet ﷺ in anger, that he would not carry the Ash'aris, and then he carried them and expiated his oath, refutes it. It will come in (surah) Bara'a [[See vol. 8, p. 228 and following.]]. Ibn al-Arabi said: as for one who said it is the expiable oath, there is no basis for it worth relating. Ibn Atiyya also weakened it and said: Allah, glorified and exalted is He, has lifted the holding to account absolutely in laghw, so its reality is that there is no sin in it and no expiation; and holding to account in oaths is by the punishment of the Hereafter for the perjurious oath (al-yamin al-ghamus al-masbura) [[The masbura oath is one by which the swearer is bound and detained, and which is binding on its owner by judgment; it is called "masbura" though its owner is in truth the one held, since he was held on account of it, that is, detained; so it is described as held and attributed to the oath figuratively. (Ibn al-Athir).]], and in what expiation was left undone where expiation is due, and by the punishment of this world in imposing expiation. Thus the view that it is the expiable oath is weakened, because holding to account has occurred in it, and restricting holding to account to the Hereafter alone is arbitrary.

The third: His saying, ﴿in your oaths﴾ (fi aymanikum). Al-aymān is the plural of yamin, and yamin means oath. Its origin is that when the Arabs made pacts or contracts, a man would take the right hand (yamin) of his companion with his own right hand; then this became common until the oath and the covenant themselves were called yamin. It was also said: yamin is on the pattern fa'il from al-yumn, which is blessing; Allah named it so because it preserves rights. Yamin is both masculine and feminine, and its plural is aymān and aymun. Zuhayr said:

"So the oaths of us and of you are gathered..." [[This is the first half of a line whose completion is: "by an oath whose blood spurts forth."]]

The fourth: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿but He will hold you to account for what your hearts have earned﴾. It is like His saying: "But He will hold you to account for the oaths you have bound." The discussion of it will come there in full, God willing [[See vol. 6, p. 266.]]. Zayd ibn Aslam said: His saying, ﴿but He will hold you to account for what your hearts have earned﴾ concerns a man who says: "He is a polytheist if he does it," that is, this laghw, unless he binds the association in his heart and earns it [[In manuscript B: "this is laghw."]].

﴿Forgiving, Forbearing﴾: two attributes fitting what has been mentioned of waiving accountability, since it is a matter of ease and latitude.

There are twenty-four issues (masa'il) in it.

The first issue: God's words, ﴿For those who take an oath of abstinence from their wives﴾. *Yu'lūna* means "they swear an oath." The verbal noun is *īlā'*, *aliyya*, *alwa* and *ilwa*. Ubayy and Ibn 'Abbas read *lilladhīna yuqsimūna* ("for those who swear"), and it is well known that *yuqsimūna* is an explanation of *yu'lūna*. It is also read *lilladhīna ā'law*. It is said: *ālā* (he swore) *yu'lī ī'lā'an*, *ta'allā* *ta'allīyan* and *i'talā* *i'tilā'an*, meaning "he swore." From this comes God's words, ﴿and let not those of virtue among you swear off﴾ [Q 24:22]. The poet said:

*So I swore that I would not cease urging on a poem*
*That will remain, and by it, after me, be a proverb.*

Another said:

*Few are his oaths; he keeps his oath,*
*And if an oath slips from him, he fulfils it.*

Ibn Durayd said:

*An oath by the swift camels that carry the riders*
*Between the wide open deserts.*

'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas said: The *īlā'* of the Jahiliyya (Age of Ignorance) lasted a year, two years or more, and they intended by it to harm the wife when they were displeased with her. So God set for them a period of four months. Whoever swears for less than that is not, by ruling, in *īlā'*.

I say: The Prophet (ﷺ) also took an oath of abstinence and divorced. The cause of his *īlā'* was that his wives asked him for maintenance that he did not have. This is so in Sahih Muslim. It is also said that Zaynab returned his gift to him, so he became angry (ﷺ) and swore off from them. This is mentioned by Ibn Majah.

The second issue: *Īlā'* binds everyone who is bound by divorce. The free man, the slave and the intoxicated person are bound by *īlā'*. Likewise the foolish person and the one under guardianship, if he is adult and not insane. Likewise the eunuch, if he is not castrated, and the old man if he still has some strength and vigour. Al-Shafi'i's opinion differed regarding the castrated man who takes an oath of abstinence. In one view, he has no *īlā'*. In another view, his *īlā'* is valid. The first is more correct and closer to the Book and the Sunnah, for *fay'* (return) is what cancels the oath, and return by words alone does not cancel it. So when the oath that prevents breaking it remains, the ruling of *īlā'* remains. The *īlā'* of the mute, by what is understood from him in writing or in clear gesture, binds him. Likewise the non-Arabic speaker, if he takes an oath of abstinence from his wives.

The third issue: The scholars differed about what kind of oath makes *īlā'* valid. Some said *īlā'* occurs only by an oath by God alone, based on the Prophet's (ﷺ) words, "Whoever swears, let him swear by God or keep silent." This is also the view of al-Shafi'i in his later opinion (*al-jadīd*). Ibn 'Abbas said: every oath that prevents intercourse is *īlā'*. This is also the view of al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, Malik, the people of the Hijaz, Sufyan al-Thawri, the people of Iraq, al-Shafi'i in his other opinion, Abu Thawr, Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: Every oath by which its taker cannot have intercourse with his wife except by breaking it is an oath of *īlā'* if the oath is for more than four months. So whoever swears by God, or by one of His attributes, or says, "I swear by God," or "I bear witness by God," or "Upon me is the covenant of God, His guarantee, His pledge and His trust," then *īlā'* binds him. If he says, "I swear" or "I resolve" without mentioning "God," it is said that *īlā'* does not apply to him, unless he intended "God" and meant it.

Whoever says that it is an oath to which it applies, its explanation will come in *al-Ma'ida* [Q 5], God willing. If he swears by fasting that he will not have intercourse with his wife, and says, "If I have intercourse with you, then upon me is the fast of a month or a year," then he is a *mūlī* (one who has taken the oath). Likewise everything that binds him, such as pilgrimage, divorce, manumission, prayer or charity. The basis for this whole matter is the generality of God's words, ﴿for those who take an oath of abstinence﴾, and He did not distinguish. So if he takes an oath by charity or by the manumission of a specific slave or of an unspecified slave, *īlā'* binds him.

The fourth issue: If he swears by God that he will not have intercourse, and makes an exception by saying, "If God wills," then he is a *mūlī*. If he has intercourse with her, there is no expiation (*kaffāra*) upon him, according to the transmission of Ibn al-Qasim from Malik. Ibn al-Majishun said in *al-Mabsut*: he is not a *mūlī*, and this is more correct, because the exception dissolves the oath and makes the one who swore as if he had not sworn. This is the view of the jurists of the great cities, because by the exception he has shown that he was not resolved to do the act. The basis of what Ibn al-Qasim transmitted is that the exception does not dissolve the oath, but it affects the removal of the expiation, as will be explained in *al-Ma'ida*. So, since his oath remains binding, the ruling of *īlā'* applies to him even if no expiation is due upon him.

The fifth issue: If he swears by the Prophet, or by the angels, or by the Ka'ba that he will not have intercourse with her, or says, "He is a Jew, or a Christian, or an adulterer if he has intercourse with her," then this is not *īlā'*, said Malik and others. Al-Baji said: In my view the meaning of that is that he made it not in the manner of an oath. As for if he presented it as *īlā'* by what he said of that or otherwise, then in *al-Mabsut* it is reported that Ibn al-Qasim was asked about a man who says to his wife, "No welcome," intending by that *īlā'*, and he said he is a *mūlī*. Malik said: every statement intended for divorce is divorce, and this and divorce are the same.

The sixth issue: The scholars differed about the *īlā'* mentioned in the Qur'an. Ibn 'Abbas said: he is not a *mūlī* until he swears that he will never touch her. A group said: if he swears that he will not approach his wife for a day, or less, or more, and then does not have intercourse for four months, she is separated from him by the *īlā'*. This was transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Hakam, Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman and Qatada, and Ishaq also said it. Ibn al-Mundhir said: Many people of knowledge rejected this view. The majority said: *īlā'* is that he swears not to have intercourse for more than four months. If he swears for four months or less, he is not a *mūlī*, and it is for them a pure oath. If he has intercourse during that period, nothing is due upon him, like other oaths. This is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Abu Thawr. Al-Thawri and the Kufans said: *īlā'* is swearing for four months or more, and this is the view of 'Ata'. The Kufans said: God made the waiting period in *īlā'* four months, as He made the waiting period for death four months and ten days, and for the waiting period there are three menstrual cycles. So there is no waiting after that. They said: After the period ends, the *īlā'* must lapse, and it lapses only by intercourse within the period, and by divorce after the four months have passed.

Malik and al-Shafi'i argued and said: God gave the one who takes the oath four months, and they are wholly his, and his wife has no objection to him during them, just as a deferred debt, its creditor may demand it only after the term is complete. The view of Ishaq, that for a short term the one who swears is a *mūlī* if he does not have intercourse, is based on analogy with one who swears for more than four months, for he is a *mūlī*, because he intended harm by the oath, and this meaning exists in the short period.

The seventh issue: They differed concerning one who swears not to have intercourse with his wife for more than four months, and the four months pass, and his wife does not demand it and does not bring him before the ruler to make him stop. According to Malik, his companions and most of the people of Medina, nothing is binding on him. Among our scholars, some say: by the end of the four months a revocable divorce (*ṭalāq rajʿī*) binds him. Among them and others, some say: a final divorce (*ṭalāq bā'in*) binds him at the end of the four months. The correct view is that of Malik and his companions, because the *mūlī* is not bound by divorce until the ruler makes him stop, upon his wife's demand, so that he returns (*fay'*) and resumes with his wife by intercourse and expiates his oath, or divorces. He is not left until he returns or divorces. *Fay'* is intercourse with one with whom intercourse is possible.

Sulayman ibn Yasar said: Nineteen men among the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) were made to stop in *īlā'*. Malik said: This is our practice, and it is the view of al-Layth, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq and Abu Thawr, and Ibn al-Mundhir chose it.

The eighth issue: The term of the *mūlī* is counted from the day he swore, not from the day his wife disputes with him and brings him before the judge. If she disputes with him and does not accept his refraining from intercourse, the ruler (*al-sultān*) [in another copy: the judge] sets for him a term of four months from the day he swore,

If he has intercourse with her, then he has returned (fa'a) to the wife's right and must make expiation (kaffara) for his oath. If he does not return, a single revocable divorce is pronounced against him. Malik said: If he takes her back, his taking back is not valid until he has intercourse with her during the waiting period ('idda). Al-Abhari said: The reason is that divorce was only imposed to remove harm. As long as he does not have intercourse, the harm remains, so there is no point in taking her back, unless he has an excuse that prevents him from intercourse, in which case his taking back is valid, because the harm has ended and his abstention is not for the sake of harm but for the sake of the excuse.

Ninth: Scholars differed about the ila' (oath of abstention from intercourse) when it is not made in a state of anger. Ibn 'Abbas said: There is no ila' except in anger. This is also reported from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, according to the well-known report from him, and it was said by al-Layth, al-Sha'bi, al-Hasan and 'Ata', all of whom said: The ila' only occurs when it is made out of anger, quarrelling, ill-humour and hostility, by which he refrains from having intercourse with her in her vagina, intending to harm her. It makes no difference whether there is in it a purpose of correcting a child or not. If it is not made out of anger, then it is not an ila'. Ibn Sirin said: Whether the oath is made in anger or not, it is an ila'. This was also said by Ibn Mas'ud, al-Thawri, Malik, the people of Iraq, al-Shafi'i and his companions, and Ahmad, except that Malik said: as long as he does not intend the correction of a child. Ibn al-Mundhir said: This is the more correct view, because they unanimously agreed that zihar (declaring one's wife unlawful like one's mother's back), divorce and all other oaths are the same whether made in anger or in contentment, so the ila' is likewise. I say: The general wording of the Qur'an supports it, and restricting it to the state of anger requires a proof, and none can be taken from a binding source. And Allah knows best.

Tenth: Our scholars said: Whoever refrains from intercourse with his wife without having sworn an oath, intending to harm her, is commanded to have intercourse with her. If he refuses and persists in his refraining, harming her, then he is separated from her without setting a term. It has been said that a term of ila' is set. It has also been said: the ila' does not apply to a man who abandons his wife and does not approach her, even if this lasts for years, but he is admonished and commanded to fear Allah, the Exalted, in not keeping her in harm.

Eleventh: They differed concerning one who swears not to have intercourse with his wife until she weans her child, so that the child is not harmed by pregnancy (al-maghl [[al-maghl (with the mim pronounced with fatha and the ghayn with sukun or fatha): that a nursing woman becomes pregnant while she is still nursing.]]), and he did not intend to harm her. Until the period of nursing ends, according to Malik, his wife has no claim, because the purpose is the welfare of the child. Malik said: It has reached me that 'Ali ibn Abi Talib was asked about this and did not consider it an ila'. Al-Shafi'i, in one of his two opinions, said the same. In the other opinion he is a muli (one who makes an ila'), and the nursing of the child is not taken into account. Abu Hanifa also said this.

Twelfth: Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and his companions, al-Awza'i, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal held that one who swears not to have intercourse with his wife in this house or this dwelling is not a muli, because he can find a way to have intercourse with her in another place. Ibn Abi Layla and Ishaq said: If he leaves her for four months, she is separated from him by the ila'. Do you not see that he is made to stop at the four months? If he swears not to have intercourse with her in his city or town, he is a muli according to Malik. This applies only to a journey that involves hardship and difficulty, not to his garden or nearby farm.

Thirteenth: The Almighty's words ﴿from their wives﴾ include free women, dhimmi women, and slave women when they are married. A slave is bound by ila' toward his wife. Al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Abu Thawr said: His ila' is like the ila' of a free man, and their argument is the apparent meaning of the Almighty's words: "for those who swear off from their wives," so this applies to all spouses. Ibn al-Mundhir said: I also hold this view. Malik, al-Zuhri, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah and Ishaq said: its term is two months. Al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i said: his ila' toward a slave wife is two months, and toward a free wife four months, and Abu Hanifa said the same. Al-Sha'bi said: the ila' of a slave woman is half the ila' of a free woman.

Fourteenth: Malik and his companions, Abu Hanifa and his companions, al-Awza'i, al-Nakha'i and others said: a woman who has been consummated with and one who has not are equal regarding the binding of the ila' in both cases. Al-Zuhri, 'Ata' and al-Thawri said: there is no ila' except after consummation. Malik said: There is no ila' from a young girl who has not reached puberty. If he makes an ila' against her and she then reaches puberty, the ila' binds him from the day she reaches puberty.

Fifteenth: As for the dhimmi, his ila' is not valid, just as his zihar and his divorce are not valid, because the marriage of polytheists is not a valid marriage in our view; they only have a claim of possession (shubhat yad). Also, they are not obligated to observe the sharia, so the expiations for oaths do not bind them. If they bring the matter of the ila' ruling before us, it is not proper for our judge to rule between them, and they go to their own judges. If it becomes an act of injustice among them, they are judged by the ruling of Islam, just as if a Muslim refrained from having intercourse with his wife out of harm, without an oath.

Sixteenth: The Almighty's words ﴿a waiting period of four months﴾. Al-tarabbus means delay and postponement, a metathesis of al-tasabbur (patience). The poet said:
Wait for her the calamity of fate, perhaps
She will be divorced one day, or her husband will die.
As for the purpose of fixing the four months, as Ibn 'Abbas mentioned about the people of the Jahiliyya, as has been stated earlier: Allah forbade that practice and gave the husband a period of four months in order to discipline the wife through abandonment, based on the Almighty's words: "And abandon them in the beds." The Prophet ﷺ swore off from his wives for a month as a means of disciplining them. It has also been said: The four months are the period beyond which a wife cannot endure being apart from her husband. It is reported that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, was walking one night in Medina and heard a woman reciting:
Oh, how long this night has grown, and its side has darkened,
And the lack of a beloved to play with keeps me awake.
By Allah, were it not for Allah, and nothing else,
The sides of this couch would be shaken from it,
Out of fear of my Lord, and modesty restrains me,
And honouring my husband, from having his mounts touched.
When morning came, 'Umar summoned that woman and said to her: Where is your husband? She said: You sent him to Iraq! He then summoned women and asked them how long a woman can endure being apart from her husband. They said: Two months; her patience decreases in three months, and her patience is exhausted in four months. So 'Umar made the period of a man's campaign four months. When four months passed, he recalled the fighters and sent other people. Allah knows best, and this strengthens the specification of the period of ila' as four months.

Seventeenth: The Almighty's words ﴿then if they return (fa'u)﴾ mean they came back, and from it comes the Almighty's words "until it returns to the command of Allah." From it also the shadow after noon is called fay', because it turns from the east side to the west side. It is said: fa'a yafi'u fay'atan wa fuyu'an, and: "He is quick to return (fay'a)," meaning returning. The poet said:
She returned without fulfilling what she came for,
And of a person's needs is that which is not fulfilled.

**Eighteenth issue:** Ibn al-Mundhir said: All the scholars from whom transmission is preserved agree that *fay'* (return, i.e., resuming marital relations) means intercourse, for one who has no excuse. If he has an excuse, such as illness, imprisonment, or the like, his *irtija'* (resumption of the marriage) is valid and she remains his wife. When the excuse ends, through his return from travel, his recovery from illness, or his release from prison, and he then refuses to have intercourse, they are separated if the waiting period has expired. Malik said this in *al-Mudawwana* and *al-Mabsut*. Abd al-Malik said: she becomes irrevocably separated (*ba'in*) from him on the day the period expired. If his claim of *fay'* during his excuse is confirmed when he is able to act on it, he is judged truthful regarding the past. If his claim of *fay'* is refuted by his refusal when he was able, his matter is taken as lying and obstinacy, and the rulings are applied as they would have been due at that time.

A group said: if witnesses testify to his *fay'* during the state of excuse, it suffices. This was said by al-Hasan, Ikrimah, and al-Nakha'i, and al-Awza'i also held it. Al-Nakha'i also said: *fay'* is valid by speech and calling witnesses alone, and the ruling of *ila'* (the vow of abstention from intercourse) falls away. [He asked]: "What do you think if he cannot have intercourse?" Ibn Atiyyah said: this view, if he does not have intercourse, returns to the principle of harm.

Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: if he has an excuse, he returns by his heart, and Abu Qilabah also said so. Abu Hanifah said: if he cannot have intercourse, he says, "I have returned to her." Al-Kiya al-Tabari said: Abu Hanifah holds, regarding one who made *ila'* while sick, with a distance of four months between him and her, or she is *ratqa'* (closed) or a child, or he is castrated, that if he returns to her by his tongue and the period passes while the excuse remains, that is valid. Al-Shafi'i disagrees with him in one of his two views.

A group said: *fay'* is only by intercourse, whether in a state of excuse or otherwise. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said so, and said: likewise if he is on a journey or in prison.

**Nineteenth issue:** Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah and their companions, and the majority of scholars, made expiation (*kaffarah*) obligatory on the one who makes *ila'* when he returns by intercourse with his wife. Al-Hasan said: there is no expiation for him, and al-Nakha'i said the same. Al-Nakha'i said: "They used to say, if he returns, there is no expiation for him." Ishaq said: some interpreters, regarding God's words ﴿if they return﴾, said it means [returning from] the oath they broke. This is a position on oaths held by some of the Successors (*tabi'un*), concerning one who swears not to do something righteous, pious, or good: he does it, and there is no expiation for him. The proof for this is God's words, ﴿then God is Forgiving, Merciful﴾, where He mentions no expiation. Also, this position rests on the premise that the vain oath (*laghw*) is an oath to commit sin, and abstaining from intercourse with one's wife is a sin.

I say: this view may be supported from the Sunnah by the hadith of Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever swears an oath and then sees something better than it, let him leave it, for leaving it is its expiation." Ibn Majah recorded it in his *Sunan*. More explanation of this will come in the verses on oaths, God willing.

The majority's proof is his (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever swears an oath and then sees something better than it, let him do what is better and expiate for his oath."

**Twentieth issue:** If he expiates for his oath, the *ila'* falls away. Our scholars said this. In it is evidence, according to the school, for the precedence of expiation over breaking the oath (*hinth*). This is a consensus in the matter of *ila'*, and it is evidence against Abu Hanifah in the matter of oaths, since he does not permit expiating before breaking the oath. Ibn al-Arabi said this.

**Twenty-first issue:** I say: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan used this verse to argue against permitting expiation before breaking the oath. He said: since God gave the one who makes *ila'* one of two rulings, either *fay'* or resolve to divorce, if expiation before breaking were permitted, the *ila'* would be nullified without *fay'* or resolve to divorce. This is because if he breaks the oath, nothing is required of him by the breaking, and when nothing is required of one who breaks the oath, he is not a *mu'li* (one who makes *ila'*). Also, permitting expiation before breaking nullifies the ruling of *ila'* by other than what God mentioned, which contradicts the Book.

**Twenty-second issue:** God said: ﴿And if they resolve on divorce, then God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾ The *'azimah* (resolve) is completing one's commitment to something. One says *'azama 'alayhi, ya'zimu, 'azman* (with a *damma*), *'azimatan*, *'azimán*, and *'azamán*, and *i'tazama, i'tizaman*. "I resolved upon you that you will do it" means "I swore to you." Shimr said: *al-'azimah* and *al-'azm* are what you have set your self upon, of a matter that you will do.

*Al-talaq* comes from *talaqat al-mar'ah* (the woman was divorced), *yatluqu* (on the pattern of *nasara yansuru*), *talaqan*. So she is *taliq* and also *taliqah*. Al-A'sha said:

*Ayya jaratā bayni fa-innaki taliqah*
*(O my neighbor, separate yourself, for you are divorced.)* [Note: "jarah" means his wife; "bayni" is from *al-baynunah*, separation. The second half of the verse: "Thus are the affairs of people: one departs and one arrives."]

It is also permissible to say *tulqat* (with a *damma* on the *lam*), like *'azuma, ya'zumu*, though al-Akhfash denied it. *Al-talaq* is the untying of the knot of marriage, and its origin is *al-inṭilaq* (departure). *Al-mutallaqat* are the women left free. *Al-talaq* means leaving free. One says: a ewe is *taliq*, a she-camel is *taliq*, meaning neglected, left in the pasture with no tether and no herder. A camel is *tulq* (with a *damma* on the *ta'* and *lam*), not tethered, and its plural is *atlaq*. Fulan was imprisoned in prison *talqan*, meaning without shackles. The *taliq* of camels is the one the herder leaves for himself, not milking it at the water. One says: the herder *istatlaqa* a she-camel for himself. The woman who is left free was named after what a ewe or she-camel whose affair is neglected is named. It was said that it is taken from *talaq al-faras* (the running of a horse), its going a course without restraint. So the woman who is released is called *taliq*, not prevented from herself after having been prevented.

**Twenty-third issue:** In His words ﴿and if they resolve on divorce﴾ is evidence that she is not divorced merely by the passing of four months, as Malik said, unless a pronouncement of divorce occurs after the period. Also, He said "All-Hearing," and "All-Hearing" implies something heard after the passing [of the period].

Abu Hanifah said: "All-Hearing" refers to his *ila'*, and "All-Knowing" refers to his resolve, which is indicated by the passing of four months.

Suhayl ibn Abi Salih narrated from his father, who said: "I asked twelve men of the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about a man who makes *ila'* with his wife. All of them said: there is nothing on him until four months pass, then he is made to stand [before the judge]. If he returns, [well and good]; otherwise, he divorces."

Qadi Ibn al-Arabi said: the truth of the matter is that the structure of the verse according to us is: ﴿For those who swear off their wives a waiting of four months. Then if they return﴾ after its expiry, ﴿then God is Forgiving, Merciful. And if they resolve on divorce, then God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾ Its structure according to them is: ﴿For those who swear off their wives a waiting of four months. If they return﴾ within it, ﴿God is Forgiving, Merciful. And if they resolve on divorce﴾ by abandoning the return within it, meaning the period of waiting within it, ﴿then God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾ Ibn al-Arabi said: this is an equally probable reading, and because of its equal probability, the Companions withheld judgment.

I say: when the probability is equal, the view of the Kufans is stronger, by analogy to the woman in the waiting period (*'iddah*) of months and menstrual cycles, since all of that is a term God set. Upon its completion, the bond of marriage ends and she is separated without disagreement, and her husband has no means over her except with her permission. Similarly with *ila'*: if he forgot the *fay'* and the period ended, the divorce would take effect. And God knows best.

**Twenty-fourth issue:** His words ﴿And if they resolve on divorce﴾ are evidence that a slave woman owned by right of possession (*milk al-yamin*) is not subject to *ila'*, since no divorce falls upon her. And God knows best.

There are twenty-four issues (masa'il) in it.

The first issue: God's words, ﴿For those who take an oath of abstinence from their wives﴾. *Yu'lūna* means "they swear an oath." The verbal noun is *īlā'*, *aliyya*, *alwa* and *ilwa*. Ubayy and Ibn 'Abbas read *lilladhīna yuqsimūna* ("for those who swear"), and it is well known that *yuqsimūna* is an explanation of *yu'lūna*. It is also read *lilladhīna ā'law*. It is said: *ālā* (he swore) *yu'lī ī'lā'an*, *ta'allā* *ta'allīyan* and *i'talā* *i'tilā'an*, meaning "he swore." From this comes God's words, ﴿and let not those of virtue among you swear off﴾ [Q 24:22]. The poet said:

*So I swore that I would not cease urging on a poem*
*That will remain, and by it, after me, be a proverb.*

Another said:

*Few are his oaths; he keeps his oath,*
*And if an oath slips from him, he fulfils it.*

Ibn Durayd said:

*An oath by the swift camels that carry the riders*
*Between the wide open deserts.*

'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas said: The *īlā'* of the Jahiliyya (Age of Ignorance) lasted a year, two years or more, and they intended by it to harm the wife when they were displeased with her. So God set for them a period of four months. Whoever swears for less than that is not, by ruling, in *īlā'*.

I say: The Prophet (ﷺ) also took an oath of abstinence and divorced. The cause of his *īlā'* was that his wives asked him for maintenance that he did not have. This is so in Sahih Muslim. It is also said that Zaynab returned his gift to him, so he became angry (ﷺ) and swore off from them. This is mentioned by Ibn Majah.

The second issue: *Īlā'* binds everyone who is bound by divorce. The free man, the slave and the intoxicated person are bound by *īlā'*. Likewise the foolish person and the one under guardianship, if he is adult and not insane. Likewise the eunuch, if he is not castrated, and the old man if he still has some strength and vigour. Al-Shafi'i's opinion differed regarding the castrated man who takes an oath of abstinence. In one view, he has no *īlā'*. In another view, his *īlā'* is valid. The first is more correct and closer to the Book and the Sunnah, for *fay'* (return) is what cancels the oath, and return by words alone does not cancel it. So when the oath that prevents breaking it remains, the ruling of *īlā'* remains. The *īlā'* of the mute, by what is understood from him in writing or in clear gesture, binds him. Likewise the non-Arabic speaker, if he takes an oath of abstinence from his wives.

The third issue: The scholars differed about what kind of oath makes *īlā'* valid. Some said *īlā'* occurs only by an oath by God alone, based on the Prophet's (ﷺ) words, "Whoever swears, let him swear by God or keep silent." This is also the view of al-Shafi'i in his later opinion (*al-jadīd*). Ibn 'Abbas said: every oath that prevents intercourse is *īlā'*. This is also the view of al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, Malik, the people of the Hijaz, Sufyan al-Thawri, the people of Iraq, al-Shafi'i in his other opinion, Abu Thawr, Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: Every oath by which its taker cannot have intercourse with his wife except by breaking it is an oath of *īlā'* if the oath is for more than four months. So whoever swears by God, or by one of His attributes, or says, "I swear by God," or "I bear witness by God," or "Upon me is the covenant of God, His guarantee, His pledge and His trust," then *īlā'* binds him. If he says, "I swear" or "I resolve" without mentioning "God," it is said that *īlā'* does not apply to him, unless he intended "God" and meant it.

Whoever says that it is an oath to which it applies, its explanation will come in *al-Ma'ida* [Q 5], God willing. If he swears by fasting that he will not have intercourse with his wife, and says, "If I have intercourse with you, then upon me is the fast of a month or a year," then he is a *mūlī* (one who has taken the oath). Likewise everything that binds him, such as pilgrimage, divorce, manumission, prayer or charity. The basis for this whole matter is the generality of God's words, ﴿for those who take an oath of abstinence﴾, and He did not distinguish. So if he takes an oath by charity or by the manumission of a specific slave or of an unspecified slave, *īlā'* binds him.

The fourth issue: If he swears by God that he will not have intercourse, and makes an exception by saying, "If God wills," then he is a *mūlī*. If he has intercourse with her, there is no expiation (*kaffāra*) upon him, according to the transmission of Ibn al-Qasim from Malik. Ibn al-Majishun said in *al-Mabsut*: he is not a *mūlī*, and this is more correct, because the exception dissolves the oath and makes the one who swore as if he had not sworn. This is the view of the jurists of the great cities, because by the exception he has shown that he was not resolved to do the act. The basis of what Ibn al-Qasim transmitted is that the exception does not dissolve the oath, but it affects the removal of the expiation, as will be explained in *al-Ma'ida*. So, since his oath remains binding, the ruling of *īlā'* applies to him even if no expiation is due upon him.

The fifth issue: If he swears by the Prophet, or by the angels, or by the Ka'ba that he will not have intercourse with her, or says, "He is a Jew, or a Christian, or an adulterer if he has intercourse with her," then this is not *īlā'*, said Malik and others. Al-Baji said: In my view the meaning of that is that he made it not in the manner of an oath. As for if he presented it as *īlā'* by what he said of that or otherwise, then in *al-Mabsut* it is reported that Ibn al-Qasim was asked about a man who says to his wife, "No welcome," intending by that *īlā'*, and he said he is a *mūlī*. Malik said: every statement intended for divorce is divorce, and this and divorce are the same.

The sixth issue: The scholars differed about the *īlā'* mentioned in the Qur'an. Ibn 'Abbas said: he is not a *mūlī* until he swears that he will never touch her. A group said: if he swears that he will not approach his wife for a day, or less, or more, and then does not have intercourse for four months, she is separated from him by the *īlā'*. This was transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Hakam, Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman and Qatada, and Ishaq also said it. Ibn al-Mundhir said: Many people of knowledge rejected this view. The majority said: *īlā'* is that he swears not to have intercourse for more than four months. If he swears for four months or less, he is not a *mūlī*, and it is for them a pure oath. If he has intercourse during that period, nothing is due upon him, like other oaths. This is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Abu Thawr. Al-Thawri and the Kufans said: *īlā'* is swearing for four months or more, and this is the view of 'Ata'. The Kufans said: God made the waiting period in *īlā'* four months, as He made the waiting period for death four months and ten days, and for the waiting period there are three menstrual cycles. So there is no waiting after that. They said: After the period ends, the *īlā'* must lapse, and it lapses only by intercourse within the period, and by divorce after the four months have passed.

Malik and al-Shafi'i argued and said: God gave the one who takes the oath four months, and they are wholly his, and his wife has no objection to him during them, just as a deferred debt, its creditor may demand it only after the term is complete. The view of Ishaq, that for a short term the one who swears is a *mūlī* if he does not have intercourse, is based on analogy with one who swears for more than four months, for he is a *mūlī*, because he intended harm by the oath, and this meaning exists in the short period.

The seventh issue: They differed concerning one who swears not to have intercourse with his wife for more than four months, and the four months pass, and his wife does not demand it and does not bring him before the ruler to make him stop. According to Malik, his companions and most of the people of Medina, nothing is binding on him. Among our scholars, some say: by the end of the four months a revocable divorce (*ṭalāq rajʿī*) binds him. Among them and others, some say: a final divorce (*ṭalāq bā'in*) binds him at the end of the four months. The correct view is that of Malik and his companions, because the *mūlī* is not bound by divorce until the ruler makes him stop, upon his wife's demand, so that he returns (*fay'*) and resumes with his wife by intercourse and expiates his oath, or divorces. He is not left until he returns or divorces. *Fay'* is intercourse with one with whom intercourse is possible.

Sulayman ibn Yasar said: Nineteen men among the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) were made to stop in *īlā'*. Malik said: This is our practice, and it is the view of al-Layth, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq and Abu Thawr, and Ibn al-Mundhir chose it.

The eighth issue: The term of the *mūlī* is counted from the day he swore, not from the day his wife disputes with him and brings him before the judge. If she disputes with him and does not accept his refraining from intercourse, the ruler (*al-sultān*) [in another copy: the judge] sets for him a term of four months from the day he swore,

If he has intercourse with her, then he has returned (fa'a) to the wife's right and must make expiation (kaffara) for his oath. If he does not return, a single revocable divorce is pronounced against him. Malik said: If he takes her back, his taking back is not valid until he has intercourse with her during the waiting period ('idda). Al-Abhari said: The reason is that divorce was only imposed to remove harm. As long as he does not have intercourse, the harm remains, so there is no point in taking her back, unless he has an excuse that prevents him from intercourse, in which case his taking back is valid, because the harm has ended and his abstention is not for the sake of harm but for the sake of the excuse.

Ninth: Scholars differed about the ila' (oath of abstention from intercourse) when it is not made in a state of anger. Ibn 'Abbas said: There is no ila' except in anger. This is also reported from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, according to the well-known report from him, and it was said by al-Layth, al-Sha'bi, al-Hasan and 'Ata', all of whom said: The ila' only occurs when it is made out of anger, quarrelling, ill-humour and hostility, by which he refrains from having intercourse with her in her vagina, intending to harm her. It makes no difference whether there is in it a purpose of correcting a child or not. If it is not made out of anger, then it is not an ila'. Ibn Sirin said: Whether the oath is made in anger or not, it is an ila'. This was also said by Ibn Mas'ud, al-Thawri, Malik, the people of Iraq, al-Shafi'i and his companions, and Ahmad, except that Malik said: as long as he does not intend the correction of a child. Ibn al-Mundhir said: This is the more correct view, because they unanimously agreed that zihar (declaring one's wife unlawful like one's mother's back), divorce and all other oaths are the same whether made in anger or in contentment, so the ila' is likewise. I say: The general wording of the Qur'an supports it, and restricting it to the state of anger requires a proof, and none can be taken from a binding source. And Allah knows best.

Tenth: Our scholars said: Whoever refrains from intercourse with his wife without having sworn an oath, intending to harm her, is commanded to have intercourse with her. If he refuses and persists in his refraining, harming her, then he is separated from her without setting a term. It has been said that a term of ila' is set. It has also been said: the ila' does not apply to a man who abandons his wife and does not approach her, even if this lasts for years, but he is admonished and commanded to fear Allah, the Exalted, in not keeping her in harm.

Eleventh: They differed concerning one who swears not to have intercourse with his wife until she weans her child, so that the child is not harmed by pregnancy (al-maghl [[al-maghl (with the mim pronounced with fatha and the ghayn with sukun or fatha): that a nursing woman becomes pregnant while she is still nursing.]]), and he did not intend to harm her. Until the period of nursing ends, according to Malik, his wife has no claim, because the purpose is the welfare of the child. Malik said: It has reached me that 'Ali ibn Abi Talib was asked about this and did not consider it an ila'. Al-Shafi'i, in one of his two opinions, said the same. In the other opinion he is a muli (one who makes an ila'), and the nursing of the child is not taken into account. Abu Hanifa also said this.

Twelfth: Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and his companions, al-Awza'i, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal held that one who swears not to have intercourse with his wife in this house or this dwelling is not a muli, because he can find a way to have intercourse with her in another place. Ibn Abi Layla and Ishaq said: If he leaves her for four months, she is separated from him by the ila'. Do you not see that he is made to stop at the four months? If he swears not to have intercourse with her in his city or town, he is a muli according to Malik. This applies only to a journey that involves hardship and difficulty, not to his garden or nearby farm.

Thirteenth: The Almighty's words ﴿from their wives﴾ include free women, dhimmi women, and slave women when they are married. A slave is bound by ila' toward his wife. Al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Abu Thawr said: His ila' is like the ila' of a free man, and their argument is the apparent meaning of the Almighty's words: "for those who swear off from their wives," so this applies to all spouses. Ibn al-Mundhir said: I also hold this view. Malik, al-Zuhri, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah and Ishaq said: its term is two months. Al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i said: his ila' toward a slave wife is two months, and toward a free wife four months, and Abu Hanifa said the same. Al-Sha'bi said: the ila' of a slave woman is half the ila' of a free woman.

Fourteenth: Malik and his companions, Abu Hanifa and his companions, al-Awza'i, al-Nakha'i and others said: a woman who has been consummated with and one who has not are equal regarding the binding of the ila' in both cases. Al-Zuhri, 'Ata' and al-Thawri said: there is no ila' except after consummation. Malik said: There is no ila' from a young girl who has not reached puberty. If he makes an ila' against her and she then reaches puberty, the ila' binds him from the day she reaches puberty.

Fifteenth: As for the dhimmi, his ila' is not valid, just as his zihar and his divorce are not valid, because the marriage of polytheists is not a valid marriage in our view; they only have a claim of possession (shubhat yad). Also, they are not obligated to observe the sharia, so the expiations for oaths do not bind them. If they bring the matter of the ila' ruling before us, it is not proper for our judge to rule between them, and they go to their own judges. If it becomes an act of injustice among them, they are judged by the ruling of Islam, just as if a Muslim refrained from having intercourse with his wife out of harm, without an oath.

Sixteenth: The Almighty's words ﴿a waiting period of four months﴾. Al-tarabbus means delay and postponement, a metathesis of al-tasabbur (patience). The poet said:
Wait for her the calamity of fate, perhaps
She will be divorced one day, or her husband will die.
As for the purpose of fixing the four months, as Ibn 'Abbas mentioned about the people of the Jahiliyya, as has been stated earlier: Allah forbade that practice and gave the husband a period of four months in order to discipline the wife through abandonment, based on the Almighty's words: "And abandon them in the beds." The Prophet ﷺ swore off from his wives for a month as a means of disciplining them. It has also been said: The four months are the period beyond which a wife cannot endure being apart from her husband. It is reported that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, was walking one night in Medina and heard a woman reciting:
Oh, how long this night has grown, and its side has darkened,
And the lack of a beloved to play with keeps me awake.
By Allah, were it not for Allah, and nothing else,
The sides of this couch would be shaken from it,
Out of fear of my Lord, and modesty restrains me,
And honouring my husband, from having his mounts touched.
When morning came, 'Umar summoned that woman and said to her: Where is your husband? She said: You sent him to Iraq! He then summoned women and asked them how long a woman can endure being apart from her husband. They said: Two months; her patience decreases in three months, and her patience is exhausted in four months. So 'Umar made the period of a man's campaign four months. When four months passed, he recalled the fighters and sent other people. Allah knows best, and this strengthens the specification of the period of ila' as four months.

Seventeenth: The Almighty's words ﴿then if they return (fa'u)﴾ mean they came back, and from it comes the Almighty's words "until it returns to the command of Allah." From it also the shadow after noon is called fay', because it turns from the east side to the west side. It is said: fa'a yafi'u fay'atan wa fuyu'an, and: "He is quick to return (fay'a)," meaning returning. The poet said:
She returned without fulfilling what she came for,
And of a person's needs is that which is not fulfilled.

**Eighteenth issue:** Ibn al-Mundhir said: All the scholars from whom transmission is preserved agree that *fay'* (return, i.e., resuming marital relations) means intercourse, for one who has no excuse. If he has an excuse, such as illness, imprisonment, or the like, his *irtija'* (resumption of the marriage) is valid and she remains his wife. When the excuse ends, through his return from travel, his recovery from illness, or his release from prison, and he then refuses to have intercourse, they are separated if the waiting period has expired. Malik said this in *al-Mudawwana* and *al-Mabsut*. Abd al-Malik said: she becomes irrevocably separated (*ba'in*) from him on the day the period expired. If his claim of *fay'* during his excuse is confirmed when he is able to act on it, he is judged truthful regarding the past. If his claim of *fay'* is refuted by his refusal when he was able, his matter is taken as lying and obstinacy, and the rulings are applied as they would have been due at that time.

A group said: if witnesses testify to his *fay'* during the state of excuse, it suffices. This was said by al-Hasan, Ikrimah, and al-Nakha'i, and al-Awza'i also held it. Al-Nakha'i also said: *fay'* is valid by speech and calling witnesses alone, and the ruling of *ila'* (the vow of abstention from intercourse) falls away. [He asked]: "What do you think if he cannot have intercourse?" Ibn Atiyyah said: this view, if he does not have intercourse, returns to the principle of harm.

Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: if he has an excuse, he returns by his heart, and Abu Qilabah also said so. Abu Hanifah said: if he cannot have intercourse, he says, "I have returned to her." Al-Kiya al-Tabari said: Abu Hanifah holds, regarding one who made *ila'* while sick, with a distance of four months between him and her, or she is *ratqa'* (closed) or a child, or he is castrated, that if he returns to her by his tongue and the period passes while the excuse remains, that is valid. Al-Shafi'i disagrees with him in one of his two views.

A group said: *fay'* is only by intercourse, whether in a state of excuse or otherwise. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said so, and said: likewise if he is on a journey or in prison.

**Nineteenth issue:** Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah and their companions, and the majority of scholars, made expiation (*kaffarah*) obligatory on the one who makes *ila'* when he returns by intercourse with his wife. Al-Hasan said: there is no expiation for him, and al-Nakha'i said the same. Al-Nakha'i said: "They used to say, if he returns, there is no expiation for him." Ishaq said: some interpreters, regarding God's words ﴿if they return﴾, said it means [returning from] the oath they broke. This is a position on oaths held by some of the Successors (*tabi'un*), concerning one who swears not to do something righteous, pious, or good: he does it, and there is no expiation for him. The proof for this is God's words, ﴿then God is Forgiving, Merciful﴾, where He mentions no expiation. Also, this position rests on the premise that the vain oath (*laghw*) is an oath to commit sin, and abstaining from intercourse with one's wife is a sin.

I say: this view may be supported from the Sunnah by the hadith of Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever swears an oath and then sees something better than it, let him leave it, for leaving it is its expiation." Ibn Majah recorded it in his *Sunan*. More explanation of this will come in the verses on oaths, God willing.

The majority's proof is his (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever swears an oath and then sees something better than it, let him do what is better and expiate for his oath."

**Twentieth issue:** If he expiates for his oath, the *ila'* falls away. Our scholars said this. In it is evidence, according to the school, for the precedence of expiation over breaking the oath (*hinth*). This is a consensus in the matter of *ila'*, and it is evidence against Abu Hanifah in the matter of oaths, since he does not permit expiating before breaking the oath. Ibn al-Arabi said this.

**Twenty-first issue:** I say: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan used this verse to argue against permitting expiation before breaking the oath. He said: since God gave the one who makes *ila'* one of two rulings, either *fay'* or resolve to divorce, if expiation before breaking were permitted, the *ila'* would be nullified without *fay'* or resolve to divorce. This is because if he breaks the oath, nothing is required of him by the breaking, and when nothing is required of one who breaks the oath, he is not a *mu'li* (one who makes *ila'*). Also, permitting expiation before breaking nullifies the ruling of *ila'* by other than what God mentioned, which contradicts the Book.

**Twenty-second issue:** God said: ﴿And if they resolve on divorce, then God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾ The *'azimah* (resolve) is completing one's commitment to something. One says *'azama 'alayhi, ya'zimu, 'azman* (with a *damma*), *'azimatan*, *'azimán*, and *'azamán*, and *i'tazama, i'tizaman*. "I resolved upon you that you will do it" means "I swore to you." Shimr said: *al-'azimah* and *al-'azm* are what you have set your self upon, of a matter that you will do.

*Al-talaq* comes from *talaqat al-mar'ah* (the woman was divorced), *yatluqu* (on the pattern of *nasara yansuru*), *talaqan*. So she is *taliq* and also *taliqah*. Al-A'sha said:

*Ayya jaratā bayni fa-innaki taliqah*
*(O my neighbor, separate yourself, for you are divorced.)* [Note: "jarah" means his wife; "bayni" is from *al-baynunah*, separation. The second half of the verse: "Thus are the affairs of people: one departs and one arrives."]

It is also permissible to say *tulqat* (with a *damma* on the *lam*), like *'azuma, ya'zumu*, though al-Akhfash denied it. *Al-talaq* is the untying of the knot of marriage, and its origin is *al-inṭilaq* (departure). *Al-mutallaqat* are the women left free. *Al-talaq* means leaving free. One says: a ewe is *taliq*, a she-camel is *taliq*, meaning neglected, left in the pasture with no tether and no herder. A camel is *tulq* (with a *damma* on the *ta'* and *lam*), not tethered, and its plural is *atlaq*. Fulan was imprisoned in prison *talqan*, meaning without shackles. The *taliq* of camels is the one the herder leaves for himself, not milking it at the water. One says: the herder *istatlaqa* a she-camel for himself. The woman who is left free was named after what a ewe or she-camel whose affair is neglected is named. It was said that it is taken from *talaq al-faras* (the running of a horse), its going a course without restraint. So the woman who is released is called *taliq*, not prevented from herself after having been prevented.

**Twenty-third issue:** In His words ﴿and if they resolve on divorce﴾ is evidence that she is not divorced merely by the passing of four months, as Malik said, unless a pronouncement of divorce occurs after the period. Also, He said "All-Hearing," and "All-Hearing" implies something heard after the passing [of the period].

Abu Hanifah said: "All-Hearing" refers to his *ila'*, and "All-Knowing" refers to his resolve, which is indicated by the passing of four months.

Suhayl ibn Abi Salih narrated from his father, who said: "I asked twelve men of the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about a man who makes *ila'* with his wife. All of them said: there is nothing on him until four months pass, then he is made to stand [before the judge]. If he returns, [well and good]; otherwise, he divorces."

Qadi Ibn al-Arabi said: the truth of the matter is that the structure of the verse according to us is: ﴿For those who swear off their wives a waiting of four months. Then if they return﴾ after its expiry, ﴿then God is Forgiving, Merciful. And if they resolve on divorce, then God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾ Its structure according to them is: ﴿For those who swear off their wives a waiting of four months. If they return﴾ within it, ﴿God is Forgiving, Merciful. And if they resolve on divorce﴾ by abandoning the return within it, meaning the period of waiting within it, ﴿then God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾ Ibn al-Arabi said: this is an equally probable reading, and because of its equal probability, the Companions withheld judgment.

I say: when the probability is equal, the view of the Kufans is stronger, by analogy to the woman in the waiting period (*'iddah*) of months and menstrual cycles, since all of that is a term God set. Upon its completion, the bond of marriage ends and she is separated without disagreement, and her husband has no means over her except with her permission. Similarly with *ila'*: if he forgot the *fay'* and the period ended, the divorce would take effect. And God knows best.

**Twenty-fourth issue:** His words ﴿And if they resolve on divorce﴾ are evidence that a slave woman owned by right of possession (*milk al-yamin*) is not subject to *ila'*, since no divorce falls upon her. And God knows best.

**The Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 2, Verse 228 (Part 1 of 4)**

God Most High says: ﴿The divorced women shall wait by themselves for three quru' (menstrual cycles or purity periods)﴾. On this verse there are five issues.

**The first issue:** God's words ﴿The divorced women﴾. When God mentioned the ila' (a husband's oath to abstain from intercourse with his wife) and that divorce may occur through it, He made clear the ruling concerning the woman after pronouncement of divorce. In the books of Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i, it is narrated from Ibn Abbas that, concerning God's words, ﴿The divorced women shall wait by themselves for three quru'﴾ up to the end of the verse, he said: "This was because a man, if he divorced his wife, had more right to her even if he had divorced her three times. So this was abrogated (naskh) and He said: ﴿Divorce is twice﴾ up to the end of the verse."

The word "divorced women" is a general term (lafz 'umum), but its intended meaning is particular: it refers to those who have been consummated with. A woman divorced before consummation is excluded by the verse of al-Ahzab: ﴿You have no waiting period (iddah) for them that you must count﴾, as will come. Likewise the pregnant woman is excluded by His words: ﴿And for those who are pregnant, their term is until they deliver their burden﴾. The purpose of the quru' is istibra' (establishing that the womb is clear), unlike the 'iddah of death, which is an act of worship. God made the 'iddah of the young girl who has not menstruated, and of the elderly woman who has despaired of menstruation, months, as will come.

Some people said that the generality of "divorced women" includes these categories, and then they were abrogated. This view is weak. The verse concerns only the woman who menstruates, and this is the common usage of women, and most of them follow it.

**The second issue:** God's words ﴿shall wait﴾ (yatarabbasna). Tarabbus means waiting, as we have already mentioned. This is a statement in the form of a report, but its intended meaning is a command, like His words: ﴿Mothers shall nurse their children﴾. [[See p. 160 of this volume.]]

The plural of "rajul" (man) is "rijal", and the phrase "'alayhi thiyabuh" (his garments are upon him) is similar, and "hasbuka dirham" (a dirham is enough for you) means "be content with a dirham." This is the view of the people of the language, without disagreement among them, as Ibn al-Shajari mentioned. Ibn al-Arabi said: "This is false. It is a report about the ruling of the Shari'ah. If a divorced woman is found who does not wait, then that is not from the Shari'ah, and it does not follow from this that God's report occurs contrary to what it reports." It was also said: its meaning is "li-yatarabbasna" (let them wait), so the lam was omitted.

**The third issue:** Most people recite ﴿quru'﴾ on the pattern fu'ul, with the lam being a hamzah. It is narrated from Nafi' that he recited "quruw" with a kasrah on the waw and shaddah, without hamz. Al-Hasan recited "qar'" with a fathah on the qaf, a sukun on the ra', and tanwin. Quru' is the plural of aqru' and aqra', and the singular is qar' with a dammah on the qaf, according to al-Asma'i. Abu Zayd said: "qar'" with a fathah on the qaf. Both said: "aqra'at al-mar'ah" when a woman menstruates, so she is muqri'. And "aqra'at" means she became pure. Al-Akhfash said: "aqra'at al-mar'ah" when she becomes a woman who has menstruation; when she menstruates you say "qara'at" without an alif. It is said: "aqra'at al-mar'ah haydatan aw haydatayn" (the woman completed one or two menstrual periods). Al-Qur' means the cessation of menstruation (in B and H: "the ending"). Some said: it is what lies between two menstrual periods. And "aqra'at hajatuk" means your need has drawn near, according to al-Jawhari. Abu Amr ibn al-'Ala said: Among the Arabs, some call menstruation qur', some call purity qur', and some combine both, calling purity together with menstruation a qur'. This was mentioned by al-Nahhas.

**The fourth issue:** Scholars differed about the quru'. The people of Kufa said: they are menstruation. This is the view of Umar, Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Musa, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Ikrimah and al-Suddi. The people of the Hijaz said: they are the periods of purity. This is the view of Aisha, Ibn Umar, Zayd ibn Thabit, al-Zuhri, Aban ibn Uthman and al-Shafi'i.

Whoever makes qur' a name for menstruation names it so because blood gathers in the womb. Whoever makes it a name for purity does so because the body gathers (blood) during it. What confirms for you this basic meaning of qur' is time. It is said: "hubbat al-rih li-qur'ihā wa-qari'ihā," meaning "the wind blew at its time." The poet said:

"I disliked the 'aqr, the 'aqr of Banu Shalil [[al-'Aqr: a place name. Shalil: the grandfather of Jarir ibn Abd Allah al-Bajali.]],
when the winds blew at its time (liqari'iha)."

So menstruation is called a time (waqt) and purity is a time, because both return at a known time. Al-A'sha said about the periods of purity:

"Each year are you a raider on a campaign
that fills its farthest reaches with your firm resolve?

Bringing glory and in the tribe a rise in standing,
for what was lost of the periods (quru') of your women in it."

Another said about menstruation:

"O Lord of one with enmity toward me who is hostile,
for him are periods like the periods of a menstruating woman."

He means that he stabbed him, and there was blood for him like the blood of a menstruating woman.

Some said: it is taken from the expression "qur' al-ma' fi al-hawd" (the gathering of water in the pool), and from it comes the Qur'an, because meanings are gathered in it. It is also said for the gathering of its letters. It is said: "ma qarat al-naqatu salan qatt," meaning she did not gather within her womb (a fetus). 'Amr ibn Kulthum said:

"The two forearms of a long-necked, white-skinned, virgin she-camel of pure color
have not gathered a fetus."

So the womb gathers the blood at the time of menstruation, and the body gathers it at the time of purity.

Abu Umar ibn Abd al-Barr said: The view of one who said that qur' is taken from the saying "qaraytu al-ma' fi al-hawd" is nothing, because qur' is hamzated and this (the verb) is not hamzated. I say: This is correct according to the transmission of the lexicographers, al-Jawhari and others. The name of that water is qira (with a kasrah on the qaf, and it is maqsur, i.e. a short-vowelled form).

It was also said: the qur' is the exit, either from purity to menstruation or from menstruation to purity. On this basis al-Shafi'i said in one of his opinions: the qur' is the transition from purity to menstruation, and he did not consider the exit from menstruation to purity to be a qur'. By the rule of derivation (ishtiqaq) it should be a qur' as well. The meaning of God's words ﴿The divorced women shall wait by themselves for three quru'﴾ would then be "three periods (adwar) or three transitions (intiqalat)." The divorced woman is characterized by only two states: at times she moves from purity to menstruation, and at other times from menstruation to purity. Thus the meaning of the statement is sound, and its indication of both purity and menstruation together. The term thus becomes mushtarak (having two meanings).

It is said: if it is established that the qur' is the transition, then her exit from purity to menstruation is not intended by the verse at all. For this reason, divorce during menstruation was not a sunni divorce (one prescribed and correct), commanded by the Shari'ah, which is divorce for the 'iddah. Divorce for the 'iddah is only that which takes place during purity. This indicates that the qur' is taken from the notion of transition. If divorce during purity is sunni, then the sentence means: "Their 'iddah is three transitions." The first of them is the transition from the purity in which the divorce took place, and that which is the transition from menstruation to purity was not made a qur', because the language does not indicate it. But we know by other evidence that God did not intend the transition from menstruation to purity. When one of the two is no longer intended, the other remains, namely the transition from purity to menstruation, which is intended. On this basis her 'iddah is three transitions, the first of which is purity. On this view it is possible to complete three full periods (qur') when the divorce takes place during purity, and this is not a case of figurative usage (majaz) in any way.

Al-Kiya al-Tabari said: This is a subtle analysis, most consistent with the school of al-Shafi'i. We can mention in this a secret which is not difficult to grasp from the fine points of the Shari'ah ruling: that the transition from purity to menstruation was made a qur' because it indicates the clearing of the womb. A pregnant woman generally does not menstruate, so by her menstruation it is known that her womb is clear. The transition from menstruation to purity is different, for a menstruating woman may conceive in the aftermath of her menstruation. When the period of pregnancy extends and the fetus grows strong, her blood stops. For this reason the Arabs praise their women for conceiving during purity. Aisha praised the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with the words of the poet [[Abu Kabir al-Hudhali (from al-Lisan).]]:

"And one free from every stain of a menstrual period,
and from the corruption of a nursing mother, and from the disease of the ghaylah (a child-harming condition of nursing)."

It means that his mother did not conceive him during the rest of her menstrual period. This is what the scholars and the linguists say regarding the interpretation of qur' (a term that can mean either a menstrual period or a state of purity between periods). They said: "The woman qara'at qur'an" when she menstruated or became pure. She also "qara'at" when she conceived. They agreed that qur' means a time period. So when you say, "And the divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods [quru']," the verse is explicit regarding the number but open regarding what is counted. Therefore it is necessary to seek clarification of what is counted from elsewhere. Our evidence is the word of God Most High: "So divorce them at their prescribed time [li-iddatihinna]" [[see vol. 18, p. 150]]. There is no disagreement that one is commanded to divorce during a time of purity, so that must be what is considered in the waiting period. He said, "So divorce them," meaning at a time during which she observes the waiting period. Then He said, "And count the waiting period" [al-'iddah], meaning what the divorced woman observes, which is the purity period in which she is divorced. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to 'Umar: "Let him take her back, then let him keep her until she becomes pure, then menstruates, then becomes pure again; that is the waiting period which God commanded for women to be divorced in." Muslim and others narrated it. This is explicit that the time of purity is what is called the waiting period, and it is the time in which women are divorced. There is no disagreement that whoever divorces during menstruation, she does not count that menstrual period as part of the waiting period, and whoever divorces during purity, she counts that purity as the waiting period according to the majority, and that is preferable. Abu Bakr Ibn 'Abd al-Rahman said: "We have not encountered any of our jurists except that they say according to the statement of 'A'ishah that the qur' are the periods of purity. So if a man divorces during a purity in which he has not had intercourse, she counts what remains of it, even an hour or a moment, then she begins a second period of purity after one menstruation, then a third after a second menstruation. When she sees blood from the third menstruation, she becomes lawful to marry and exits the waiting period. If a divorcer divorces during a purity in which he has had intercourse, the divorce is binding on him, though he has done wrong, and she counts what remains of that purity." Al-Zuhri said regarding a woman divorced during part of her purity: she counts three purities in addition to the remainder of that purity. Abu 'Umar said: "I know of no one who says that qur' are purities except Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri, who said: she discards the purity in which she was divorced, then counts three purities, because God, Mighty and Majestic, says: 'three qur'.'" I say: according to his view, the divorced woman does not become lawful until she enters the fourth menstrual period. The view of Ibn al-Qasim, Malik, the majority of his companions, al-Shafi'i and the scholars of Madinah is that when the divorced woman sees the first drop of the third menstrual period, she exits the marital bond. This is the position of Zayd ibn Thabit, 'A'ishah and Ibn 'Umar, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal said the same, as did Dawud ibn 'Ali and his companions. The argument against al-Zuhri is that the Prophet (ﷺ) permitted divorce during purity without intercourse, and he did not say at the beginning or end of the purity. Ashhab said: the marital bond and inheritance are not severed until it is certain that it is blood of menstruation, lest it be a single discharge of blood not from menstruation. The Kufans argued by the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him) to Fatimah bint Abi Hubaysh when she complained to him of bleeding: "That is only a vein. Look, and when your qur' comes, do not pray, and when the qur' passes, purify yourself and then pray from one qur' to the next qur'." God Most High said: "And those of your women who have despaired of menstruation, if you are in doubt, their waiting period is three months" [[see vol. 18, p. 162]]. He made the thing despaired of to be menstruation, which indicates that it is the waiting period, and made the replacement for it the months when it is absent. 'Umar said in the presence of the Companions: "The waiting period of a slave-woman is two menstrual periods, half the waiting period of a free woman; if I could make it one and a half menstrual periods, I would." No one objected to him, which indicates it is a consensus among them, and it is the view of ten of the Companions, including the four rightly-guided caliphs, and that is enough for you what they said! The words of God Most High: "And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three qur'" indicate this, because the meaning is "they shall wait three qur', meaning complete ones," and this is only possible according to our view that qur' are menstrual periods, because whoever says it is purity may count two purities and part of another, since if he divorces during purity she counts the remainder of that purity as one qur'. According to us, she begins from the start of menstruation until the name applies, so if a man divorces a woman during a purity in which he has not had intercourse, she begins one menstrual period, then another, then another, and when she bathes from the third, she exits the waiting period. I say: this is refuted by the words of God Most High: "He subjected it upon them for seven nights and eight days" [[see vol. 18, p. 259]], where He affirmed the ha' in "thamaniyata ayyam" (eight days), because yawm is masculine, and likewise qur', which indicates that this is what is meant. Abu Hanifah agreed with us that if she is divorced while menstruating, she does not count the menstrual period in which she was divorced, nor the purity that follows it; she counts only the menstruation that comes after the purity. According to us she counts the purity, as we have explained. The lexicographers permit referring to a part by the name of the whole, as God Most High says: "The Hajj is in well-known months" [al-Baqarah 2:197], and what is meant is two months and part of a third. Likewise His words: "three qur'." And God knows best. Some of those who hold the menstruation view said: when she becomes pure from the third, the waiting period ends after the bath, and the right of return is nullified. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Tawus, Ibn Shubrumah and al-Awza'i. Sharik said: if a woman neglects the bath for twenty years, her husband still has the right of return over her as long as she has not bathed. It is narrated from Ishaq ibn Rahawayh that he said: if the woman stabs (enters) the third menstruation, she is separated and the husband's right of return is cut off, except that it is not lawful for her to marry until she bathes from her menstruation. A similar report is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, but it is a weak view, on the evidence of God Most High's words: "Then when they have reached their term, there is no blame upon you for what they do with themselves" [al-Baqarah 2:234], as will come [[see p. 186 of this volume]]. As for what al-Shafi'i mentioned, that the mere transition from purity to menstruation is called qur', its benefit is to shorten the waiting period for the woman: if he divorces her in the last hour of her purity and she enters menstruation, that counts as one qur' for her, and by the mere transition from the third purity the bond is severed and she is lawful. And God knows best.

The fifth issue: The majority of scholars hold that the waiting period of a slave-woman who menstruates after her husband's divorce is two menstrual periods. It is narrated from Ibn Sirin that he said: "I do not see the waiting period of a slave-woman as other than that of a free woman, unless a sunnah has been established regarding it, for the sunnah has more right to be followed."
