Al-Asamm 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Kaysan, Dawud ibn 'Ali and the group of the people of the literal (zahir) said: the verses on the waiting period of divorce and death, by months and qur', are general regarding both slave-woman and free woman, so the waiting period of the free woman and the slave-woman is the same. The majority argued by his saying (peace be upon him): "The divorce of a slave-woman is two pronouncements, and her waiting period is two menstrual periods." It was narrated by Ibn Juraij from 'Ata' from Muzahir ibn Aslam from his father from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad from 'A'ishah, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The divorce of a slave-woman is two pronouncements, and her qur' are two menstrual periods," thus attributing both divorce and waiting period to her together. However, Muzahir ibn Aslam alone narrated this hadith, and he is weak. It is narrated from Ibn 'Umar: "Whichever of the two is lower in status, his divorce is reduced," and a group of scholars held this view.

The words of God Most High: "And it is not lawful for them to conceal what God has created in their wombs" contain two issues. The first: God Most High's words: "And it is not lawful for them to conceal what God has created in their wombs," meaning from menstruation, said by 'Ikrimah, al-Zuhri and al-Nakha'i. It was said: it means pregnancy, said by 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: both menstruation and pregnancy together, and this is based on the view that a pregnant woman menstruates. The intended meaning of the verse is that since the matter of the waiting period revolves around menstruation and purity, and there is no knowledge of it except from the women, the word is given to her when she claims the end of the waiting period or its absence, and they are entrusted with that. This is the requirement of God Most High's words: "And it is not lawful for them to conceal what God has created in their wombs." Sulayman ibn Yasar said: "We were not commanded to open the women and look at their private parts, but this is entrusted to them since they are trustworthy." The prohibition of concealment means the prohibition of harming the husband and nullifying his right. If the divorced woman says, "I have menstruated," when she has not, she nullifies his right of return; and if she says, "I have not menstruated," when she has, she obliges him to pay maintenance he is not bound to, harming him, or she intends by her lie about not menstruating that he not take her back until the waiting period ends and the law cuts off his right. Likewise the pregnant woman conceals the pregnancy to cut off his right of return. Qatadah said: "Their custom in the Jahiliyyah was to conceal pregnancy so that the child would be attributed to a new husband, and the verse was revealed concerning that." It is related that a man from Ash'ar came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of God, I divorced my wife while she was pregnant, and I am not safe from her marrying and my child becoming another's," so God revealed the verse, and the wife of the Ash'ari was returned to him. The second issue: Ibn al-Mundhir said: every scholar I have learned from said: if a woman says within ten days, "I have menstruated three menstrual periods and my waiting period has ended," she is not believed and that is not accepted from her, unless she says, "I have miscarried a fetus whose form has become clear." They differed regarding the period within which a woman is believed. Malik said: if she says her waiting period has ended within a period in which the waiting period normally ends, her word is accepted; if she reports the end of the waiting period within a period that rarely occurs, there are two views. He said in al-Mudawwanah: if she says, "I menstruated three menstrual periods in one month," she is believed if women confirm her, and Shurayh said the same. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib said to him: "Qalun!" meaning you are correct and you did well. He said in the Book of Muhammad: she is not believed except in a month and a half. Abu Thawr said something similar: he said, "The least that can be is in forty-seven days, since the least purity is fifteen days and the least menstruation is one day." Al-Nu'man said: she is not believed for less than sixty days, and al-Shafi'i said the same.

The words of God Most High: "If you truly believe in God and the Last Day": this is a severe and grave warning to stress the prohibition of concealment, and an obligation to fulfill the trust in reporting about the womb the reality of what is in it. That is, the way of believing women is not to conceal the truth. His words "if you believe in God" do not mean that concealment is permitted for one who does not believe, because that is not lawful for one who does not believe; rather it is like your saying: "If you are my brother, do not wrong me," meaning faith should restrain you from it, because this is not the conduct of the people of faith.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And their husbands have more right to take them back﴾. In this verse there are eleven issues.

**First:** His saying, ﴿And their husbands﴾. *Al-bu'ulah* is the plural of *al-ba'l*, which means the husband. He was called *ba'l* because of his superiority over the wife through the marital authority he has over her. From the same root is His saying: ﴿Do you call upon Ba'l and forsake the best of creators?﴾, meaning a lord, because of his superiority in lordship. It is said *ba'l* and *bu'ulah*, just as it is said for the plural of *dhakar* (male): *dhukurah*, and for the plural of *fahl* (stallion): *fuhulah*. This *ha'* is an extra, emphasizing letter marking the feminine of a collective noun. It is irregular, cannot be used as a basis for analogy, and depends on what is transmitted from the Arabs, so one does not say *lu'ubah* for *la'b*. It is also said that it is the *ha'* of the feminine that entered upon the pattern *fu'ul*. *Al-bu'ulah* is also the verbal noun of *ba'ala*: *ba'ala al-rajul yab'alu* (like *mana'a yamna'u*) *bu'ulah*, meaning he became a husband. *Al-mubaalah* and *al-bi'al* mean intercourse, and from this is his saying (ﷺ) concerning the days of tashriq: "They are days of eating, drinking and intercourse," which has already been mentioned. So the man is the *ba'l* of the woman, and the woman is his *ba'lah*. He had intercourse with her (*ba'ala mubaa'alah*) when he came into contact with her. *Fulan ba'l hadha* means its owner and its lord. The word has many other meanings, which will come, God willing. [See vol. 12, p. 231.]

**Second:** His saying, ﴿have more right to take them back﴾, meaning to restore them. Restoration (*al-murajaʿah*) is of two kinds: restoration during the waiting period (*ʿiddah*), according to the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, and restoration after the waiting period, according to the hadith of Maʿqil. If this is so, then the verse contains evidence that what the general wording includes is specified in terms of the cases it covers. His saying, ﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods﴾, is general regarding divorced women, both those divorced three times and those divorced fewer times, with no disagreement about that. Then His saying, ﴿And their husbands have more right﴾, is a specific ruling for the one whose divorce is less than three.

The scholars agreed that if a free man divorces his free wife, who had been consummated, with one or two divorces, he has more right to take her back as long as her waiting period has not ended, even if the woman dislikes it. If the divorcer does not take her back until her waiting period has ended, she has more right over herself, and she becomes a stranger to him. She is not lawful to him except through a proposal and a new marriage contract, with a guardian and witnesses, and not in the manner of restoration. This is a consensus among the scholars.

Al-Muhallab said: whoever takes a woman back during the waiting period is not bound by any of the rules of marriage except calling witnesses to the restoration alone. This is a consensus of the scholars, due to His saying: ﴿So when they have reached their term, retain them in kindness or part from them in kindness, and call to witness two just men among you﴾. He mentioned witnesses in the case of restoration and did not mention them in marriage or in divorce. Ibn al-Mundhir said: what we have mentioned from the Book of God, together with the consensus of the people of knowledge, is sufficient, so there is no need to mention what was narrated from the early generations on this subject. And God knows best.

**Third:** They differed about what makes a man a returner during the waiting period. Malik said: if he has intercourse with her during the waiting period while intending restoration, but he failed to call witnesses, it is a restoration. It is appropriate for the woman to prevent him from intercourse until he calls witnesses. Ishaq said the same, due to his (ﷺ) saying: "Actions are only by intentions, and every person will have only what he intended."

If he has intercourse with her during the waiting period without intending restoration, Malik said: he takes her back within the waiting period, but he does not have intercourse with her until he has cleansed her of his corrupt water (*istibraʾ*, the period of purification from a doubtful pregnancy). Ibn al-Qasim said: if her waiting period has ended, neither he nor anyone else may marry her during the rest of the period of *istibraʾ*. If he does, his marriage is annulled. Her prohibition upon him is not permanent, because the water is his water.

A group said: when he has intercourse with her, he has restored her. This was the view of Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan al-Basri, Ibn Sirin, al-Zuhri, ʿAtaʾ, Tawus and al-Thawri. He said: he should call witnesses. The same view was held by the people of opinion (the Hanafis), al-Awzaʿi and Ibn Abi Layla, as related by Ibn al-Mundhir.

Abu ʿUmar said: it has also been said that his intercourse is a restoration in every case, whether he intended it or not. This is related from a group of Malik's companions, and al-Layth went to this view. They did not disagree about one who sold his slave-girl with a right of option (*khiyar*), that he may have intercourse with her during the period of the option, and that by this he has taken her back into his ownership and chosen to annul the sale by his act. A revocable divorced woman has a ruling derived from this. And God knows best.

**Fourth:** Whoever kisses or touches (his wife) intending by that restoration, it is a restoration. If he does not intend restoration by kissing or touching, he is sinful, but he is not a returner. The sunnah is that he should call witnesses before he has intercourse, or before he kisses or touches. Abu Hanifa and his companions said: if he has intercourse with her, or touches her with desire, or looks at her private part with desire, it is a restoration. This is also the view of al-Thawri, and he should call witnesses. According to the view of Malik, al-Shafiʿi, Ishaq, Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Thawr, it is not a restoration, as Ibn al-Mundhir said.

In *al-Muntaqa*, he said: there is no disagreement about the validity of restoration by speech. As for restoration by action, such as intercourse or kissing, al-Qadi Abu Muhammad said: it is valid by these and by all forms of pleasurable enjoyment. Ibn al-Mawwaz said: like touching for pleasure, or looking at her private part, or what is close to that of her attractions, if he intends restoration by that. This is contrary to al-Shafiʿi's view that restoration is valid only by speech. Ibn al-Mundhir related this view from Abu Thawr, Jabir ibn Zayd and Abu Qilabah.

**Fifth:** Al-Shafiʿi said: if he has intercourse with her intending restoration, or not intending it, it is not a restoration, and she is owed the equivalent dower (*mahr al-mithl*). Malik said: she is owed nothing, because if he had taken her back there would be no dower upon him, so intercourse without restoration is no more deserving of a dower than restoration is.

Abu ʿUmar said: I know of no one who made the equivalent dower obligatory except al-Shafiʿi, and his view is not strong, because she has the status of a wife, and she inherits from him and he from her. How, then, can the equivalent dower be owed for intercourse with a woman whose status in most of its rulings is that of a wife! However, the doubt (*shubhah*) in al-Shafiʿi's view is strong, because she is forbidden to him except through a restoration to her. They agreed that a woman who has had intercourse under doubt is owed the dower, and that is enough for you!

**Sixth:** They differed about whether he may travel with her before he takes her back. Malik and al-Shafiʿi said: he does not travel with her until he takes her back. Abu Hanifa and his companions said the same, except Zufar, who, according to what al-Hasan ibn Ziyad related from him, held that he may travel with her before restoration. ʿAmr ibn Khalid related from him that he does not travel with her until he takes her back.

**Seventh:** They differed about whether he may enter upon her and see something of her attractions, and whether she may adorn herself and display herself for him. Malik said: he should not be alone with her, nor enter upon her except with permission, nor look at her except when she is wearing her clothes, and he should not look at her hair. There is no harm in eating with her if others are present with them, but he should not spend the night with her in a house, and he should move away from her.

Ibn al-Qasim said: Malik retracted this and said: he should not enter upon her, and he should not see her hair. (*Al-tashrruf*, in the sense of displaying oneself, means looking toward something and gazing at it.)

Abu Hanifa and his companions did not disagree that she may adorn herself for him, perfume herself, wear jewelry and display herself.

It is related from Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab that he said: when a man divorces his wife with one divorce, he asks permission to enter upon her, and she may wear whatever clothes and jewelry she wishes. If they have only one room, they should place a screen between them, and he should greet her when he enters. Similar was related from Qatadah. He should also alert her when he enters by clearing his throat and coughing.

Al-Shafiʿi said: the woman divorced with a divorce that allows him to take her back is forbidden to her divorcer with the prohibition of the irrevocably divorced woman until he takes her back, and he takes her back only by speech, as has already been explained.

**Eighth:** The scholars agreed that if the divorcer says, after the end of the waiting period, "I had taken you back during the waiting period," and she denies it, then her word is accepted with her oath, and he has no way to her. However, al-Nuʿman did not consider an oath to be required in marriage or in restoration, and his two companions disagreed with him and said as the rest of the scholars said.

Likewise, if the wife is a slave-girl and her master and the slave-girl disagree, and the husband claims restoration during the waiting period after its end while she denies it, the word is that of the slave-wife, even if her master contradicts her. This is the view of al-Shafiʿi, Abu Thawr and al-Nuʿman. Yaʿqub and Muhammad said: the word is that of the master, and he has more right to her.

**Ninth:** The word *radd* (return) implies the cessation of the marital bond. However, our scholars said that the revocably divorced woman is forbidden for intercourse, so the return restores permissibility. Al-Layth ibn Saʿd, Abu Hanifa and those who held their view, that restoration makes intercourse lawful again, said: the purpose of divorce is to reduce the number of divorces that was specifically allotted to it, and the rulings of marriage remain, none of them having been dissolved. They said: although the rulings of marriage remain, the woman, as long as she is in the waiting period, is moving toward ending by the expiry of the waiting period. So restoration is a turning back from this path that the woman had begun to follow. This is a figurative return. The return we have judged by is a real return, because there is a cessation that was sought, namely the prohibition of intercourse, so the return was in reality a return from it. And God knows best.

**Tenth:** The word *ahaqq* (more deserving, more right) is used when two rights conflict and one of them is given preference. The meaning here is that the husband's right during the period of waiting is more deserving than her right over herself, because she only owns herself after the waiting period has ended. Similar is his (ﷺ) saying: "The unmarried woman has more right over herself than her guardian." This has already been mentioned.

**Eleventh:** The man is recommended to take her back, provided he intends reform, by improving his condition with her and removing the estrangement between them. But if he intends harm, by prolonging the waiting period and cutting her off from being freed from the bond of marriage, it is forbidden, due to His saying: ﴿And do not retain them to harm them so that you transgress﴾. Then whoever does that, the restoration is valid, although he committed what is forbidden and wronged himself. If we knew that intention, we would divorce her upon him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 228 (part 4 of 4):

His the Exalted's saying: ﴿And they [the women] have rights similar to those [of men] over them, according to what is reasonable﴾. In this there are three issues.

The first: His the Exalted's saying: ﴿And they﴾, meaning: they have, from the rights of marriage over men, what is similar to what men have over them. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas said: "Indeed I adorn myself for my wife as she adorns herself for me, and I do not like to exhaust [istanzafa (to take all of something, i.e., to take everything)] all my right that I have over her, so that she would be owed her right that she has over me, because Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they have rights similar to those [of men] over them, according to what is reasonable﴾," meaning: adornment without sin. And from him also: meaning, they have, from good companionship and fine living with their husbands, what is similar to what is due upon them of obedience in what He has obligated them to their husbands. It was also said: they have over their husbands the abandonment of harming them, just as that is due from them to their husbands. Al-Tabari said: Ibn Zayd said: "You fear Allah regarding them just as they are obliged to fear Allah the Mighty and Majestic regarding you," and the meanings are close. The verse encompasses all of that from the rights of marriage.

The second: the saying of Ibn 'Abbas: "Indeed I adorn myself for my wife." The scholars said: As for men's adornment, it varies according to their conditions. They do this with propriety [al-labq (skill and dexterity)] and suitability, so sometimes an adornment suits one time and not another, and an adornment suits youth, and an adornment suits elders and does not suit youth. Do you not see that when an elder or a middle-aged man trims his moustache, that suits him and adorns him, whereas when a young man does that he appears unseemly and disliked, because his beard has not yet grown in? So when he trims his moustache at the very start of his face's emergence, he appears unseemly; but when his beard has grown full and he trims his moustache, that adorns him. It is narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "My Lord commanded me to let my beard grow and to trim my moustache." Likewise regarding clothing. In all of this is the seeking of rights, for he acts with propriety [in the text: al-la'iq (suitable)] and suitability so that he is with his wife in an adornment that pleases her and keeps her chaste from other men. Likewise kohl for men: some it suits and some it does not suit. As for perfume, the siwak, the khilal [meaning the use of the khilal, which is from the Sunnah, namely removing food remnants from between the teeth], shaking off grime and excess hair, purification, and cutting the nails, these are clear and suit everyone. Dyeing [the hair] is an adornment for elders, and the ring is an adornment for all, youth and elders alike, and it is the ornament of men, as its explanation will come in surah al-Nahl [see vol. 10, p. 87]. Then he should be attentive to the times when she needs the man, so that he keeps her chaste and spares her from looking toward others. If a man sees in himself an inability to fulfil her right in bed, he should take some of the medicines that increase his vigour [in z: his semen] and strengthen his desire, until he keeps her chaste.

The third: His the Exalted's saying: ﴿But men have a degree over them﴾, meaning: a rank. The madraja of the road is its beaten track, and its origin is folding [al-tayy], as it is said: "They folded [daraju], meaning they folded up their lives," and from it is the daraja (step) by which one ascends. It is said: "a man of clear vigour [al-rajla]," meaning strength, and he is "arjal of the two legs," meaning the stronger of them; and "a rujayl horse," meaning strong, and from it is the rijl (foot), for its strength in walking. So the increase in the man's degree is by his intellect and his strength [in b: and by spending] for spending, and by the blood-money, the inheritance, and jihad. Humayd said: "The daraja is the beard." If this is authentically from him, it is weak, and neither the wording of the verse nor its meaning requires it. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "Blessed is the servant who refrains from what he does not know, especially in the Book of Allah the Exalted!" The superiority of men over women is not hidden from anyone discerning, even if only because woman was created from man: he is her origin, and he may prevent her from acting except with his permission, so she does not fast except with his permission, nor perform Hajj except with him. It was said: the daraja is the dowry, said by al-Sha'bi. It was said: it is the permissibility of discipline. In general, daraja implies superiority, and suggests that the husband's right over her is more binding than her right over him; for this reason he (peace be upon him) said: "Had I commanded anyone to prostrate to other than Allah, I would have commanded the woman to prostrate to her husband." Ibn 'Abbas said: the daraja is an allusion to urging men toward good companionship and to being generous to women in wealth and character, meaning that the superior should constrain himself. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is a fine and excellent statement." Al-Mawardi said: it may be that it refers to the rights of marriage: he has the right to dissolve the contract without her, and she is obliged to answer him to the bed, while he is not obliged to answer her. I say: from this is his (peace be upon him) saying: "Any woman whose husband calls her to his bed and she refuses him, the angels will curse her until morning."

(And Allah is Mighty) meaning: unassailable in authority, with none to oppose Him.
(Wise) meaning: knowing, correct in what He does.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 229 (part 1 of 5):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Divorce is twice; then either retain in kindness or release with good treatment﴾. In this there are seven issues.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Divorce is twice﴾. It is established that in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance) there was no fixed number of divorces for them, and the waiting period ('iddah) was known and determined among them. This was the case for a while at the beginning of Islam: a man would divorce his wife as many times as he wished, and when her waiting period was about to end he would take her back as often as he wished. A man said to his wife during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I will neither shelter you nor let you become free (to remarry)." She said: "How?" He said: "I will divorce you, and when your waiting period is about to expire I will take you back." The woman complained of this to 'A'ishah, and she mentioned it to the Prophet (ﷺ). Then Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse, clarifying the number of divorces after which a man may take his wife back without renewing the dower and without a guardian, and it abrogated what they had been doing. This was said by 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, Qatadah, Ibn Zayd and others. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others said: the purpose of the verse is to define the Sunnah of divorce, that is, whoever has divorced twice, let him fear Allah regarding the third, so that either he leaves her without wronging her of any of her rights, or he retains her treating her well in companionship. The verse includes both of these meanings.

The second: Divorce (talaq) is the dissolution of the marital bond established between spouses by specific words. Divorce is permitted by this verse and by other evidence, and by his peace be upon him saying in the hadith of Ibn 'Umar: "If he wishes he may retain, and if he wishes he may divorce." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) divorced Hafsah and then took her back; this was narrated by Ibn Majah. The scholars agreed that whoever divorces his wife while she is pure, in a purity in which he has not had intercourse with her, has divorced in accordance with the Sunnah and the waiting period that Allah, exalted is He, commanded, and that he has the right of retraction if she has been consummated, before her waiting period ends. Once it has ended, he becomes one of the suitors. The Book, the Sunnah and the consensus of the Ummah thus establish that divorce is permissible and not forbidden. Ibn al-Mundhir said: there is no authentic report prohibiting it.

The third: al-Daraqutni narrated: "Abu al-'Abbas Muhammad ibn Musa ibn 'Ali al-Dulabi and Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim told me, both saying: al-Hasan ibn 'Arafah told us, Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash ibn Humayd ibn Malik al-Lakhmi told us, from Makhul, from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: 'O Mu'adh, Allah has created nothing on the face of the earth more beloved to Him than emancipation, and Allah has created nothing on the face of the earth more hateful to Him than divorce. So when a man says to his slave, "You are free, if Allah wills," he is free, and there is no exception for him. And when a man says to his wife, "You are divorced, if Allah wills," he has the right of exception, and there is no divorce upon him.'" Muhammad ibn Musa ibn 'Ali told us: Humayd ibn al-Rabi' told us: Yazid ibn Harun informed us: Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash, with his chain, similarly. Humayd said: Yazid ibn Harun said to me: "What a hadith it would be, if Humayd ibn Malik al-Lakhmi were known!" I said: "He is my grandfather!" Yazid said: "You have gladdened me; now it has become a hadith!" Ibn al-Mundhir said: Among those who held that an exception may be made in divorce were Tawus, Hammad, al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr and the people of opinion (Ashab al-Ra'y). It is not permissible to make an exception in divorce according to Malik and al-Awza'i; and it is the view of al-Hasan and Qatadah concerning divorce specifically. He said: I say with the first view.

The fourth: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿then either retain in kindness﴾. "Retain" (imsak) is the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate (khabar) is "in kindness" (bi-ma'ruf), or it is better or more excellent. It is also permissible that it be in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "upon you is retention in kindness," or "what is obligatory upon you is retention in what is recognised as right." Outside the Qur'an, "fa-imsakan" (in the accusative as a verbal noun) is permitted. The meaning of "in kindness" is that he does not wrong her of any of her rights and does not transgress, according to one view. "Imsak" is the opposite of releasing (iṭlaq). "Tasrih" is the release of a thing, and from it comes "tasrih al-sha'r" (combing the hair), so that some is separated from some; and "sarraha al-ma-shiyah" means he released the livestock. The word "tasrih" may carry two meanings. One: leaving her until the waiting period following the second divorce is complete, so that she is more in control of herself; this is the view of al-Suddi and al-Dahhak. The other meaning: that he divorces her a third time and thereby releases her; this is the view of Mujahid, 'Ata' and others, and it is more correct for three reasons. The first: what al-Daraqutni narrated from Anas, that a man said: "O Messenger of Allah, Allah, exalted is He, said: 'Divorce is twice,' so why did it become three?" He said: "'Then either retain in kindness or release with good treatment'—in another narration—'it is the third.'" Ibn al-Mundhir mentioned it. The second: tasrih is one of the words of divorce; do you not see that it has been recited as "in 'azamu al-sarah" (if they resolve upon release). The third: the form fa''ala (tafil) indicates that he has initiated a repeated action after the second divorce, and leaving her does not involve initiating an action that is expressed by the tafil form. Abu 'Umar said: The scholars agreed that His saying, exalted is He, "or release with good treatment," is the third divorce after the two divorces, and it is what He intended by His saying, exalted is He: "And if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him thereafter until she marries another husband." They also agreed that whoever divorces his wife once or twice has the right to take her back; if he divorces her a third time, she is not lawful to him until she marries another husband. This is among the clear (muhkam) verses of the Qur'an concerning whose interpretation there is no disagreement.

Similar reports have also been transmitted from reliable narrators:

Sa'id ibn Nasr told us, saying: Qasim ibn Asbagh told us, saying: Muhammad ibn Waddah told us, saying: Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah told us, saying: Abu Mu'awiyah told us, from Isma'il ibn Sumay', from Abu Razin, who said: A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, what do you say about the saying of Allah, exalted is He: 'Divorce is twice; then either retain in kindness or release with good treatment'? Then where is the third?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Then either retain in kindness or release with good treatment." Al-Thawri [[In some copies: "al-Tirmidhi"; the correction is from the book "al-Istidhkar" by Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr.]] and others narrated it likewise from Isma'il ibn Sumay' from Abu Razin.

I say: al-Kiya al-Tabari mentioned this report and said: it is not established in terms of transmission. He preferred the view of al-Dahhak and al-Suddi, and that the third divorce is only mentioned within the context of His saying, exalted is He: "And if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him thereafter until she marries another husband." So the third is mentioned within the very body of this address, conveying the irrevocable separation that requires prohibition except after another husband. Therefore it is necessary to understand His saying "or release with good treatment" as conveying a new meaning, namely the occurrence of irrevocable separation by two divorces at the end of the waiting period, and that the purpose of the verse is to clarify the number of divorces that require prohibition and to abrogate what had been permissible, namely divorce without a fixed limit. Had His saying "or release with good treatment" been the third, it would not have explained the intention regarding the imposition of prohibition by three divorces, for if it had been limited to it, it would not indicate the prohibitive irrevocable separation except after another husband; the prohibition is known only from His saying, exalted is He: "And if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him thereafter until she marries another husband." Therefore it must be that His saying "or release with good treatment" does not mean the third. And if His saying "or release with good treatment" meant the third, then His saying after it, "And if he divorces her," would be the fourth, since the fa' indicates sequence, and it would require a new divorce after what was mentioned earlier. Thus it is established that His saying, exalted is He, "or release with good treatment" is leaving her until her waiting period expires.

The fifth: al-Bukhari titled his chapter on this verse: "Chapter: on whoever permits three divorces by the saying of Allah, exalted is He: 'Divorce is twice, then either retain in kindness or release with good treatment.'" This is an indication from him that this repetition is in fact a limitation placed upon them; whoever constrains himself upon himself is bound by it.

Our scholars said: The jurists agreed that the pronouncement of three divorces in a single utterance is binding, and this is the view of the majority of the early scholars (salaf). Tawus and some of the Zahiri scholars deviated, holding that the three divorces pronounced in a single utterance count as one. This is reported from Muhammad ibn Ishaq and al-Hajjaj ibn Artah. It is also said of them that nothing follows from it, and this is the view of Muqatil. It is related from Dawud that he said it does not take effect. The well-known view of al-Hajjaj ibn Artah, the majority of the early scholars and the imams is that it is binding and takes effect as three. There is no difference between pronouncing three together in one utterance or separately in several utterances. As for those who held that nothing follows from it, they argued with the evidence of His saying, exalted is He: "And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods." This includes every divorced woman except what has been excepted from it, and this has already been discussed. And He said: "Divorce is twice," and the third is "then either retain in kindness or release with good treatment." Whoever divorces three times in one utterance is not bound, since it is not mentioned in the Qur'an. As for those who held that it takes effect as one, they relied on three hadiths. The first: the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas through the narration of Tawus, Abu al-Sahba' and 'Ikrimah. The second: the hadith of Ibn 'Umar according to the version which narrates that he divorced his wife three times, and that the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered him to take her back, and it was counted for him as one. The third: that Rukanah divorced his wife three times, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered him to take her back, and retraction implies the occurrence of one.

The response to the hadiths is what al-Tahawi mentioned: that Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, 'Ata', 'Amr ibn Dinar, Malik ibn al-Huwayrith, Muhammad ibn Iyas ibn al-Bukayr and al-Nu'man ibn Abi 'Ayyash narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning one who divorces his wife three times that he has disobeyed his Lord, and his wife is separated from him, and he may not marry her except after another husband. In what these imams narrated from Ibn 'Abbas there is that which agrees with the majority and indicates the weakness of the report of Tawus and others, and Ibn 'Abbas would not have opposed the Companions in favour of his own opinion.

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: The report of Tawus is an error and a mistake, and none of the jurists of the regions, in the Hijaz, al-Sham, Iraq, the East or the West, paid it any attention. It has been said that Abu al-Sahba' is not known among the clients of Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Qadi Abu al-Walid al-Baji said: "In my view the narration from Ibn Tawus regarding this is sound, for the imams narrated from him: Ma'mar, Ibn Jurayj and others, and Ibn Tawus is an imam. The hadith to which they refer is what Ibn Tawus narrated from his father from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: 'The divorce during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and of Abu Bakr, and two years of the caliphate of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, was one (counted) for three divorces. 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Indeed people have hastened in a matter in which they had been given deliberation; so if we were to enforce it upon them!" So he enforced it upon them.'" The meaning of the hadith is that they used to pronounce a single divorce in place of what people now pronounce as three pronouncements. What supports this interpretation is that 'Umar said:

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 229 (part 2 of 5):

Indeed, people have hastened in a matter in which they had been given respite. He therefore denounced them for introducing into divorce the hastening of a matter in which they had been given respite. Had that been their state at the beginning of Islam, in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), he would not have said it, nor would he have blamed them for hastening in a matter in which they had been given respite.

The soundness of this interpretation is supported by what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas through more than one chain, that he issued a ruling that three divorces pronounced together are binding on the one who pronounced them. If the meaning of the hadith of Ibn Tawus is this, then it is what we have said. And if the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas is taken in the sense that someone of no standing interprets it, then Ibn 'Abbas has returned to the view of the majority, and consensus (ijma') has been established upon it. Our evidence by way of analogy (qiyas) is that this is a divorce pronounced by one who has the right to pronounce it, so it must be binding on him; the basis for this is when it is pronounced singly.

I say:
What al-Baji interpreted is what al-Kiya al-Tabari mentioned as its meaning from the scholars of hadith, namely that they used to divorce with one pronouncement what these people now divorce with three; that is, they did not pronounce one divorce in each period of purity, but rather pronounced one throughout the whole waiting period until she became irrevocably separated and the waiting period ended.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad 'Abd al-Wahhab said:
Its meaning is that people used to limit themselves to a single pronouncement, then in the days of 'Umar they multiplied the pronouncement of three.

The Qadi said:
This is closer to the wording of the narrator: "People in the days of 'Umar hastened the three, so he enforced it upon them," meaning he obliged them to its ruling.

As for the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, al-Daraqutni narrated from Ahmad ibn Subayh, from Tarif ibn Nasih, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar al-Duhni, from Abu al-Zubayr, who said:
I asked Ibn 'Umar about a man who divorced his wife three times while she was menstruating. He said to me:
"Do you know Ibn 'Umar?"
I said:
"Yes."
He said:
"I divorced my wife three times in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) [while she was menstruating (addition from the Sunan of al-Daraqutni)], and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned her to the Sunnah."

Al-Daraqutni said:
"They are all from the Shi'a, and what is preserved is that Ibn 'Umar divorced his wife with one pronouncement during menstruation."

'Ubayd Allah said:
His divorcing her during menstruation was a single pronouncement, but he opposed the Sunnah.

Likewise Salih ibn Kaysan, Musa ibn 'Uqba, Isma'il ibn Umayya, Layth ibn Sa'd, Ibn Abi Dhi'b, Ibn Jurayj, Jabir, and Isma'il ibn Ibrahim ibn 'Uqba said, on the authority of Nafi':
that Ibn 'Umar pronounced one single divorce.

Likewise al-Zuhri said, on the authority of Salim, from his father; and Yunus ibn Jubayr, al-Sha'bi and al-Hasan.

As for the hadith of Rukana, it has been said:
It is a mudtarib (disturbed) and munqati' (broken) hadith, not supported by any chain that can be relied upon. Abu Dawud narrated it from the hadith of Ibn Jurayj, from some of the sons of Abu Rafi', none of whom is reliable, from 'Ikrima, from Ibn 'Abbas.
In it he said:
that Rukana ibn 'Abd Yazid divorced his wife three times, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him:
"Take her back."

It has also been narrated by Abu Dawud through other chains, from Nafi' ibn 'Ujayr, that Rukana ibn 'Abd Yazid divorced his wife with the absolute divorce (al-battah), so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made him swear what he had intended by it.
He swore he intended only one, so he returned her to him.
So there is disturbance in the name and in the action, and some are argued from such reports.

I say:
al-Daraqutni has transmitted this hadith in his Sunan through several chains. In one of them he said: "Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Mirdas narrated to us: Abu Dawud al-Sijistani narrated to us: Ahmad ibn 'Amr ibn al-Sarh, Abu Thawr Ibrahim ibn Khalid al-Kalbi and others narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafi'i narrated to us: my paternal uncle Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Shafi' narrated to me, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Ali ibn al-Sa'ib, from Nafi' ibn 'Ujayr ibn 'Abd Yazid [[In al-Daraqutni: Ibn 'Abd Yazid ibn Rukana. Etc.]]:
that Rukana ibn 'Abd Yazid divorced his wife Suhayma al-Muzaniyya with the absolute divorce (al-battah), and informed the Prophet (ﷺ) of that. He said: 'By Allah, I intended only one.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'By Allah, did you intend only one?' Rukana said: 'By Allah, I intended by it only one.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned her to him. Then he divorced her a second time in the days of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and a third time in the days of 'Uthman."
Abu Dawud said: "This hadith is sahih."

What is authentically established from the hadith of Rukana is that he divorced his wife with the absolute divorce (al-battah), not three. The absolute divorce has been disputed, as will be explained. Thus the argument falls, and praise be to Allah [[In MS ḥ: so the argument based on other than it falls.]]. And Allah knows best.

Abu 'Umar said:
The transmission of al-Shafi'i of the hadith of Rukana from his paternal uncle is more complete, and it adds an addition that the principles do not reject; therefore it must be accepted due to the reliability of its transmitters. Al-Shafi'i, his uncle and his grandfather are the family of Rukana, all of them from the Banu 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn 'Abd Manaf, and they know best the incident that befell them.

Section: Abu Muhammad Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Mughith al-Tulaytuli mentioned this issue in his documents, saying:
Divorce is divided into two kinds:
the divorce of the Sunnah and the divorce of innovation (bid'a).

The divorce of the Sunnah is that which occurs in the manner the Shari'a has encouraged.
The divorce of innovation is its opposite: that he divorces her during menstruation, or during postpartum bleeding, or three times in one utterance. If he does so, the divorce is binding on him.
Then the scholars differed, after their agreement that he is a divorcer, as to how much of divorce is binding on him. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn Mas'ud said: one single divorce is binding on him. Ibn 'Abbas also said this, and he said:
"His saying 'three' has no meaning, because he has not divorced three times. Saying 'three' is only valid when reporting what has passed, as when he says: 'I divorced three times,' reporting three acts he did at three times, like a man who says: 'I recited such-and-such a surah three times yesterday,' which is correct. But if he recited it once and said: 'I recited it three times,' he would be lying."
Likewise, if one swears by Allah three times, repeating the oath, it counts as three oaths. But if he says: "I swear by Allah three times," he has sworn only one oath. The divorce is similar.
Al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf also said so.
All of this has been transmitted to us from Ibn Wadah, and this was said by some of the scholars of Cordoba: Ibn Zinba' the sheikh of guidance, Muhammad ibn Taqi ibn Makhlad, Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Salam al-Hasani, the unique of his time and jurist of his age, Asbagh ibn al-Hubab, and a group besides them.

Among the proofs of Ibn 'Abbas is that Allah, exalted is His name, distinguished the word for divorce in His Book, saying: "Divorce is twice" [2:229], meaning the most that may be pronounced, after which there is retention in kindness, which is returning in the waiting period.
And the meaning of His saying: "or release with kindness" means leaving her without taking her back until her waiting period ends. In that there is kindness to her if regret arises between them. Allah says: "You do not know; perhaps Allah will bring about after that some matter" [65:1] [[See vol. 18 p. 147]].
This means regret over the separation and desire for return. The use of three is not good, because it abandons the latitude Allah granted and pointed out. Allah's mention of divorce in separate instances indicates that when it is combined it is a single expression. It may also be inferred by analogy, from outside the matter in the Mudawwana, what indicates this. Among it is a person saying: "My property is a charity for the poor," where a third suffices for him.

In al-Ishraf of Ibn al-Mundhir:
Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Tawus, Abu al-Sha'tha', 'Ata' and 'Amr ibn Dinar used to say: "Whoever divorces a virgin three times, it is one."

I say:
They sometimes argued on the ground that a woman not yet consummated has no waiting period. So when he says, "You are divorced three times," she is already irrevocably separated by the completion of his saying "You are divorced," and then "three" falls upon her while she is already separated, so it has no effect. Also, his saying "You are divorced" is independent in itself, so irrevocable separation in the case of a non-consummated woman must not depend on what comes after it. Its origin is when he says only "You are divorced."

The sixth point: al-Shafi'i used the saying of Allah, "or release with kindness" [2:229], and His saying: "or release them" [65:2], as evidence that this word is among the explicit (sarih) forms of divorce.
The scholars differed on this matter. Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad held that the explicit form is that which includes the word of divorce in any manner, such as saying "You are divorced," "You are a divorced woman," "I have divorced you," or "Divorce is binding on me." Whatever else among the words of divorce is used for it is an allusion (kinaya). This is also the view of Abu Hanifa.
Al-Qadi Abu al-Hasan said: The explicit words of divorce are many, and some are clearer than others: divorce (talaq), release (sarah), separation (firaq), "forbidden" (haram), "free of you" (khaliyya) and "apart" (bariyya).
Al-Shafi'i said: The explicit forms are three words, which the Qur'an has used: the word for divorce (talaq), release (sarah) and separation (firaq). Allah says: "or separate from them in kindness" [65:2], and "or release with kindness," and "divorce them for their waiting period" [65:1].

I say:
Given this established, divorce is of two kinds: explicit and allusive. The explicit is what we have mentioned, and the allusive is everything else. The difference between them is that the explicit does not require intention; divorce takes effect by the mere utterance. The allusive requires intention.
The argument of those who say that "forbidden" (haram), "free of you" (khaliyya) and "apart" (bariyya) are among the explicit forms of divorce is the frequency of their use for divorce, until they became known for it. They became clear and evident in the pronouncement of divorce, like the word "ghait" (lowland), which was originally for a depressed piece of ground, and then was used figuratively for relieving oneself. It became clearer and more evident and better known in that sense than in its original meaning. The same applies to our matter.

Then 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said:
"Were divorce a thousand, the absolute (al-batta) would leave nothing of it. Whoever says 'al-batta' has reached the furthest extreme." Related by Malik.

Al-Daraqutni also related from 'Ali, who said:
"Free of you (khaliyya), apart (bariyya), absolute (battah), irrevocable (ba'in) and forbidden (haram) are three, she is not lawful to him until she marries another husband."

And it has come from the Prophet (ﷺ) that al-batta is three, through a chain with some weakness, which al-Daraqutni recorded. It will come at His saying: "And do not take the signs of Allah in jest" [2:231], if Allah wills [[See p. 156 of this part.]].

Seventh point: The scholars did not differ regarding a man who says to his wife, "I have divorced you," that it is an explicit form of divorce, whether she has been consummated or not. Therefore if he says to his wife, "You are divorced," it is one, unless he intends more than that.
If he intended two or three, what he intended is binding on him. If he intended nothing, it is one, and he may take her back.
If he says, "You are divorced," and then says, "I meant from bondage (wathaq)," it is not accepted from him, and it binds him, unless there is something indicating his truthfulness.
If he says, "You are divorced, one, I have no right of return over you," then his saying "I have no right of return over you" is void, and he has the right of return due to his saying "one," since one cannot be three. If by his saying "I have no right of return over you" he intended three, then it is three according to Malik.

The scholars differed concerning a man who says to his wife:

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 229 (part 3 of 5):**

Al-Qurtubi's text: "I have separated from you" (قَدْ فَارَقْتُكِ), "I have released you" (أَوْ سَرَّحْتُكِ), "you are free" (أَوْ أَنْتِ خَلِيَّةٌ), "you are cut off" (أَوْ أَنْتِ بَرِّيَّةٌ), "you are irrevocably divorced" (أَوْ بَائِنٌ), "your rope is on your neck" (أَوْ حَبْلُكِ عَلَى غَارِبِكِ), "you are forbidden to me" (أَوْ أَنْتِ عَلَيَّ حَرَامٌ), "go back to your family" (أَوِ الْحَقِي بِأَهْلِكِ), "I have given you to your family" (أَوْ قَدْ وَهَبْتُكِ لِأَهْلِكِ), "I have left your way free" (أَوْ قَدْ خَلَّيْتُ سَبِيلَكِ), or "I have no way over you" (أَوْ لَا سَبِيلَ لِي عَلَيْكِ). Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf said: "It is an irrevocable divorce (talaq ba'in, a divorce that ends the marriage bond, reducing the number of permitted returns)."

It is also narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "If a man says to his wife, 'Take charge of your affair' (اسْتَقِلِّي بِأَمْرِكِ), or 'Your affair is in your hands' (أَمْرُكِ لَكِ), or 'Go back to your family' (الْحَقِي بِأَهْلِكِ), and they accept it, then it is one irrevocable divorce."

It is narrated from Malik concerning one who says to his wife, "I have separated from you" (قَدْ فَارَقْتُكِ) or "I have released you" (سَرَّحْتُكِ), that it is among the explicit (sarih) forms of divorce, like his saying, "You are divorced" (أَنْتِ طَالِقٌ).

It is also narrated from him that it is an implicit (kinaya) form, to be judged by the intention of the speaker, and he is asked how many (divorces) he intended, whether the wife was consummated or not.

Ibn al-Mawwaz said: "The more correct of his two opinions concerning the wife who has not been consummated is that it is one divorce, unless he intends more."

Ibn al-Qasim and Ibn Abd al-Hakam said the same.

Abu Yusuf said: "It is three (divorces). The same applies to 'I have divorced you through khul' (khalaʻtuka, divorce by compensation)' or 'You have no claim over me' (لَا مُلْكَ لِي عَلَيْكِ)."

As for all other implicit (kinaya) expressions, according to Malik they are three in the case of a wife who has been consummated, and the speaker's intention is not accepted for them. For a wife who has not been consummated, his intention is accepted. If he swears and says, "I intended one," he is like one of the suitors (khattab), because a consummated wife is not released, separated or cut off except by three pronouncements of divorce. An unconsummated wife is released, cut off, and her (divorce) is one.

It is also narrated from Malik and a group of his companions, and it is the view of a number of the people of Madina, that the speaker's intention is accepted in all these expressions, and he is bound by the number of divorces he intended. It has been narrated from Malik specifically concerning the word "al-batta" (absolute, final divorce) among all the implicit expressions that the speaker's intention is not accepted, whether the wife was consummated or not.

Al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa and his companions said: "He has his intention in all of that. If he intended three, then it is three. If he intended one, then it is one irrevocable divorce, and she has the right over herself. If he intended two, then it is one." Zufar said: "If he intended two, then it is two."

Al-Shafi'i said: "In all of that he is not a divorcer until he says, 'I meant by the wording of my speech a divorce,' and then it is what he intended. If he intended less than three, it is revocable (raj'i, allowing return during the waiting period). Even if he pronounced one irrevocable divorce, it would be revocable."

Ishaq said: "Every speech that resembles divorce is what he intended of divorce."

Abu Thawr said: "It is one revocable divorce, and he is not asked about his intention."

It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he did not regard a divorce as irrevocable except in khul' or ila' (a vow to abstain from intercourse), and this is what is preserved from him, as Abu Ubayd said.

Al-Bukhari entitled a chapter: "The chapter: if he says, 'I have separated from you,' or 'I have released you,' or 'free (al-bariyya),' or 'cut off (al-khaliyya),' or what is meant by it of divorce, then it is according to his intention." In this, he points to the view of the Kufans, al-Shafi'i and Ishaq, in his words, "or what is meant by it of divorce."

The proof for this is that every word that may be divorce or not divorce, it is not permissible to impose divorce by it unless the speaker says that he intended divorce by it, and then he is bound by that through his own confession. It is not permissible to annul the marriage, since they have unanimously agreed on its validity with certainty.

Abu Umar said: "Malik's opinion differed concerning the meaning of a man's saying to his wife, 'Observe your waiting period' (i'taddi), or 'I have released you' (قَدْ خَلَّيْتُكِ), or 'your rope is on your neck' (حَبْلُكِ عَلَى غَارِبِكِ). He said once: 'His intention is not accepted in them, and it is three.' He said at another time: 'His intention is accepted in all of them, for the consummated and the unconsummated wife, and this is what I hold.'"

I (al-Qurtubi) say: What the majority held, and what is narrated from Malik that the intention is accepted in these expressions and he is judged accordingly, is the correct view, because of the evidence we have mentioned, and because of the authentic hadith transmitted by Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah, al-Daraqutni and others, from Yazid ibn Rukana: that Rukana ibn Abd Yazid divorced his wife Suhayma with "al-batta," and he informed the Prophet (ﷺ) of that. He (ﷺ) said: "By Allah, did you intend only one?" Rukana said: "By Allah, I intended only one." So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned her to him.

Ibn Majah said: "I heard Abu al-Hasan al-Tanafisi say: 'How noble this hadith is!'"

Malik said concerning a man who says to his wife, "You are to me like carrion, blood and the flesh of swine": "I consider it al-batta (an absolute divorce) even if he had no intention, and she is not lawful to him except after another husband." According to al-Shafi'i's view: "If he intended divorce, it is divorce, and it is according to the number of divorces he intended. If he did not intend divorce, it is nothing, after he has sworn."

Abu Umar said: "The basis of this chapter, concerning every implicit expression of divorce, is what is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said, to the woman he married when she said, 'I seek refuge in Allah from you': 'You have sought refuge with the one who grants refuge. Go back to your family' (الْحَقِي بِأَهْلِكِ). So that was a divorce."

Ka'b ibn Malik said to his wife when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered him to separate from her: "Go back to your family." That was not a divorce. This indicates that this expression requires intention, and that it is not judged except by what the speaker intends by it. The same applies to all implicit expressions that may mean separation or other things.

And Allah knows best.

As for expressions that are not among the words of divorce and are not used as implicit references to separation, most scholars do not impose divorce by any of them, even if the speaker intended it. Malik said: "Whoever intends divorce with any wording, divorce is binding on him, even by saying, 'Eat, drink, stand, sit.'" No one followed Malik in this except his companions.

**The words of the Exalted:** ﴿And it is not lawful for you to take back anything of what you have given them, unless both fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah. But if you fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah, then there is no blame upon either of them concerning that by which she ransoms herself. These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them. And whoever transgresses the limits of Allah – it is those who are the wrongdoers.﴾

It contains fifteen issues.

**The first issue:** His saying, ﴿And it is not lawful for you to take back anything of what you have given them﴾. "That" (an, أَنْ) is in the position of nominative after "yahillu" (is lawful). The verse addresses the husbands. They were forbidden to take anything from their wives in a manner of harm. This is khul' (divorce by compensation), which is not valid unless the man does not solely inflict harm. The mention is specifically of what husbands gave their wives, because it is the custom among people that when there is discord and corruption, a man seeks back what he gave her as dower (sadaq) and provision (jihaz, ḥibā). For that reason it is mentioned specifically.

It has been said that His saying, "And it is not lawful," is a parenthetical clause between His saying, "Divorce is twice," and His saying, "And if he divorces her."

**The second issue:** The majority hold that taking a ransom (fidya) for divorce is permissible. They agreed on the prohibition of taking what is hers, except when the disobedience (nushuz) and corruption of the marriage come from her side.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from al-Nu'man that he said: "If the wrongdoing and disobedience come from his side, and she seeks khul' from him, then it is permissible and binding, but he is sinful. What he did is not lawful for him, and he is not compelled to return what he took."

Ibn al-Mundhir said: "This statement of his contradicts the apparent meaning of the Book of Allah, the established report from the Prophet (ﷺ), and what the general body of scholars have agreed upon in this matter. I do not think that if someone were told to exert himself in seeking an error, he would find anything greater than this: that the Book states the prohibition of something, and then an opponent contradicts it explicitly, saying, 'Rather, it is permissible, and he is not compelled to return what he took.'"

Abu al-Hasan ibn Battal said: "Ibn al-Qasim narrated the like of this from Malik." This view contradicts the apparent meaning of the Book of Allah, and it contradicts the hadith of the wife of Thabit, which will come.

**The third issue:** His saying, ﴿unless both fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah﴾. In this verse, Allah forbade taking anything except after fear that the two will not keep within the limits of Allah. He emphasised the prohibition with a threat for whoever transgresses the limit.

The meaning is that each of them thinks that they will not fulfil the right of marriage toward the other as is obligatory, because of a dislike they hold. Then there is no sin on the woman in seeking ransom, and no sin on the husband in accepting it.

The address is to the spouses. The pronoun in "yakhafa" (they fear) refers to both of them, and "allā yuqīmā" (that they will not keep) is the object. "Khifta" (you feared) transitively takes one object.

It has been said: this fear means knowledge, that is, that they know they will not keep the limits of Allah. It is true fear, which is apprehension of something disliked occurring, and it is close in meaning to supposition (zann).

It has also been said: "Illa an yakhafā" (unless they fear) is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), meaning: "But if there is disobedience from them, then there is no sin on you in taking the ransom."

Hamza read "illā an yukhāfā" with a dammah on the yā' (passive voice), where the subject is omitted, and it is the rulers and judges. Abu Ubayd preferred this reading. He said: "Because of His saying, 'But if you fear (khiftum),' He attributed the fear to others than the spouses. If He had meant the spouses, He would have said, 'If they both fear (khafa).'" In this there is evidence for those who make khul' a matter for the ruler (sultan).

I (al-Qurtubi) say: This is also the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin.

Shu'ba said: "I said to Qatada: 'From whom did al-Hasan take that khul' is to the ruler?'" He said: "From Ziyad, who was governor for Umar and Ali."

Al-Nahhas said: "This is known from Ziyad, and there is no sense in this view, because when a man arranges khul' with his wife, it is according to what they agree upon, and the ruler does not compel him to it. And there is no sense in the view of the one who says this is up to the ruler."

The preference of Abu Ubayd has been rejected and refuted. I know of no preference of his more remote than this letter, because neither the grammar, nor the wording, nor the meaning requires it.

As for the grammar: Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud read "illā an yakhāfā" as "takhāfū" (you fear). In Arabic, when this is turned into the passive, it is said "illā an yukhāfa" (unless it is feared).

As for the wording: if it were according to the wording of "yakhafā" (they both fear), it would have to be said "fa-in khīfa" (if it is feared). If it were according to the wording of "fa-in khiftum" (if you fear), it would have to be said "illā an takhāfū" (unless you fear).

As for the meaning: it is far-fetched to say, "It is not lawful for you to take anything of what you have given them, unless others fear," and He did not say, "Then there is no sin on you in taking from her a ransom," so that the khul' would be left to the ruler.

Al-Tahawi said: "It has been authentically reported from Umar, Uthman and Ibn Umar that it is permissible without the ruler, just as divorce and marriage are permissible without the ruler. So khul' is likewise, and this is the view of the majority of scholars."

**The fourth issue:** His saying, ﴿But if you fear that they will not keep﴾, that is, "that they will not keep (the limits)," meaning "that they should not keep."

(ḥudūd Allāh) That is, what is obligatory upon the two of them of good companionship and fair living together. The address is to the rulers and to those who mediate in such a matter, even if he is not a ruler. Failing to uphold the limits of Allah is the wife's disdain for her husband's right and her poor obedience to him; this is said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mālik ibn Anas and the majority of jurists. Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan and a group with him said: if the woman says, "I will not obey you in any matter, I will not bathe for you from impurity, and I will not fulfil any oath of yours," then khul' (divorce initiated by the wife through compensation) becomes permissible. Al-Shaʿbī said: "that they do not keep the limits of Allah" means that they do not obey Allah, because mutual resentment calls to abandoning obedience. ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ said: khul' and taking compensation are permissible if the woman says to her husband, "I hate you and do not love you," and the like. (fa-lā junāḥa ʿalayhimā fīmā iftadat bih) "There is no blame on them both for what she gives up to ransom herself."

Al-Bukhārī related, from the hadith of Ayyūb, from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbas, that the wife of Thābit ibn Qays came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I do not blame Thābit ibn Qays for his character or his religion, but I cannot bear him!" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Will you return to him his garden?" She said: "Yes." Ibn Mājah also related it from Qatādah, from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbas, that Jamīlah bint Salūl came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "By Allah, I do not fault Thābit in religion or character, but I dislike disbelief in Islam; I cannot bear him out of hatred!" The Prophet (ﷺ) said to her: "Will you return to him his garden?" She said: "Yes." So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded him to take back his garden from her and not to increase it. It is said that she hated him with the utmost hatred and he loved her with the utmost love, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) separated them by way of khul', and it was the first khul' in Islam.

ʿIkrimah related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The first to seek khul' in Islam was the sister of ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy. She came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, my head and his will never come together. I lifted the side of the tent and saw him approaching in a group, and he was the blackest of them, the shortest in stature, and the ugliest in face!" He said: "Will you return to him his garden?" She said: "Yes, and if he wishes I will add to it." So he separated them. This hadith is the basis for khul', and the majority of jurists act upon it.

Mālik said: I have always heard this from the people of knowledge, and it is the matter agreed upon among us: that if the man has not harmed the woman or mistreated her, and no fault has come from his side, and she wishes to leave him, then it is permissible for him to take from her everything she gave as ransom, as the Prophet (ﷺ) did in the case of the wife of Thābit ibn Qays. But if the ill-treatment (nushūz) comes from his side, by his restricting her and harming her, he must return to her what he took from her.

ʿUqbah ibn Abī al-Ṣahbāʾ said: I asked Bakr ibn ʿAbdullāh al-Muzanī about a man whose wife wants to seek khul' from him, and he said: it is not permissible for him to take anything from her. I said: then where is the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in His Book: "And if you fear that they will not keep the limits of Allah, there is no blame on them both for what she gives up to ransom herself"? He said: it was abrogated. I said: then where was it placed? He said: in Surah al-Nisāʾ: "And if you desire to exchange one wife for another, and you have given one of them a heap of gold, take nothing back from it. Would you take it by slander and manifest sin?" [See vol. 5, pp. 98 and 24.] Al-Naḥḥās said: this is an anomalous opinion, outside the consensus because of its aberrance, and neither of the two verses cancels the other so that abrogation occurs, because His saying "if you fear" is not removed by that verse, for if they fear this, the husband does not enter into "if you desire to exchange one wife for another," since that is for men specifically. Al-Ṭabarī said: the verse is muḥkam (not abrogated), and there is no sense in Bakr's saying. If she intends the gift, the Prophet (ﷺ) permitted Thābit to take back from his wife what he had given her, as already mentioned.

Fifth issue: Whoever holds that khul' is restricted to a state of discord and harm has adhered to this verse, and it is strengthened by what Abū Dāwūd related from ʿĀʾishah: that Ḥabībah bint Sahl was married to Thābit ibn Qays ibn Shammās, and he struck her and broke her nughḍ [In the originals: "baʿḍuhā" (some of it); the correction is from Sunan Abī Dāwūd. The nughḍ (with the nūn vowelled either way and the ghayn sukūn): the upper part of the shoulder; it is said to be the thin bone at its edge.], so she came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) after the dawn prayer and complained to him. The Prophet (ﷺ) summoned Thābit and said: "Take some of her property and part from her." He said: "Is that suitable, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then I have given her two gardens, and they are in her possession [In the originals: 'maʿa mā biyadihā'; the correction is from Sunan Abī Dāwūd.]," and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Take them both and part from her." So he took them and separated from her.

The majority of jurists hold that khul' is permissible without any complaint of harm, as the hadith of al-Bukhārī and others indicates. As for the verse, there is no proof in it, because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, did not mention it as a condition, but mentioned it because it is the usual circumstance of khul', so the statement came in accordance with what is usual. What removes the excuse and necessitates knowledge is His saying, Exalted is He: "But if they willingly give you a portion of it, then consume it with enjoyment and ease" [See vol. 5, pp. 98 and 24.].

Sixth issue: When Allah says, "There is no blame on them both for what she gives up to ransom herself," it indicates the permissibility of khul' for more than what he gave her. The scholars differ on this. Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Abū Ḥanīfah and their companions, and Abū Thawr said: she may ransom herself with whatever they mutually agree upon, whether it is less or more than what he gave her. This is related from ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, Ibn ʿUmar, Qabīṣah and al-Nakhaʿī. Qabīṣah argued from His saying: "There is no blame on them both for what she gives up to ransom herself." Mālik said: it is not among the noble morals, but I have not seen anyone among the people of knowledge disliking it. Al-Dāraquṭnī related from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī that he said: my sister was married to a man of the Anṣār, whom she wed for a garden, and there was some dispute between them, so they went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "Will you return to him his garden and he divorces you?" She said: "Yes, and I will add to it." He said: "Return to him his garden and add to it." In the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas: "And if he wishes, I will add to it," and it was not rejected. Another group said: he may not take from her more than he gave her; so said Ṭāwūs, ʿAṭāʾ and al-Awzāʿī. Al-Awzāʿī said: the judges would not permit him to take anything except what he had given her. Aḥmad and Isḥāq also said this. They argued by what Ibn Jurayj related: Abū al-Zubayr informed me that Thābit ibn Qays ibn Shammās had as his wife Zaynab, daughter of ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl, and he had given her a garden as her dower, but she disliked him, so the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "As for the increase, no, but his garden [returned]," and she said: "Yes." So he took it for him and released her. When this reached Thābit ibn Qays, he said: "I have accepted the judgement of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." Abū al-Zubayr heard it from more than one person; al-Dāraquṭnī related it. It is also related from ʿAṭāʾ as a mursal report that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "He shall not take from the woman who seeks khul' more than he gave her."

Seventh issue: According to Mālik, may Allah be pleased with him, khul' upon an unripened fruit, upon a stray camel, a runaway slave, a fetus in its mother's womb, or the like of these forms of gharar (uncertainty) is permissible, unlike sales and marriage. He has the right to pursue all of that: if it is delivered, it is his; if it is not delivered, he has nothing, and the divorce takes effect by its ruling. Al-Shāfiʿī said: khul' is permissible and he has the mahr al-mithl (the customary dower of such a woman); Ibn Khuwayz Mandād related it from Mālik, saying: because contracts of exchange, when they include an invalid counter-value and it is lost, are reverted to what is obligatory in similar cases as to the counter-value. Abū Thawr said: khul' is void. The companions of opinion (Abū Ḥanīfah's school) said: khul' is permissible, and he has what is in the belly of the female slave; if there is no offspring in it, he has nothing. Ibn al-Qāsim said in al-Mabsūṭ: it is permissible for the counter-value to be what his palm trees will yield this year and what his sheep will bear this year, contrary to Abū Ḥanīfah and al-Shāfiʿī. The proof for what Mālik and Ibn al-Qāsim held is the general wording of His saying, "There is no blame on them both for what she gives up to ransom herself." And by way of analogy: it is something that can be owned through gift and bequest, so it may serve as a counter-value in khul' like something known; furthermore, khul' is a divorce, and divorce is valid without any counter-value at all; so if it is valid without any counter-value, it is all the more valid with a defective counter-value, since the worst state of what is offered is that it is like what is left unmentioned. And since marriage, which is a contract of permission, is not invalidated by a defective counter-value, it is all the more fitting that it not invalidate divorce, which is the release and dissolution of a contract.

Eighth issue: If she ransoms herself from him by the nursing of her son for two years, it is permissible. Regarding khul' with her maintenance of the son after the two years for a known period, there are two opinions: the first is that it is permissible, the view of al-Makhzūmī, and Saḥnūn chose it. The second is that it is not permissible, related by Ibn al-Qāsim from Mālik; and if the husband stipulates it, it is void and is dropped from the wife. Abū ʿUmar said: whoever permits khul' upon a stray camel, a runaway slave and the like of such gharar must also permit this. Another of the Qayrawānīs said: Mālik did not prohibit khul' with maintenance beyond the two years because of gharar; he prohibited it because it is a right that belongs to the father in every state, so he may not transfer it to another. The difference between this and the maintenance of the two years is that this nursing maintenance may be owed by the mother during marriage and after divorce when the father is unable to pay, so it was permissible for this maintenance to be transferred to the mother, since she is its proper bearer. Mālik, in al-Mabsūṭ, argued for this by His saying, Exalted is He: "And mothers shall nurse their children for two complete years, for whoever wishes to complete the nursing."

Ninth issue: If khul' was concluded in the permitted manner with the son's maintenance, and the boy dies before the period ends, is the husband entitled to claim from her the remainder of the maintenance? Ibn al-Mawwāz related from Mālik: he cannot pursue her for anything. Abū al-Faraj related from him: he may pursue her, because it is a right that became established for him against the wife's liability through the khul', so it does not lapse by the boy's death, just as if he had ransomed her with property attached to her liability. The reasoning of the first view is that he did not stipulate for himself any property that he would own; he only stipulated the sufficiency of his child's support, so when the child dies he has no right to pursue her for anything, just as if a man voluntarily spent on a child for a year and the child then died, he could not be reimbursed for anything, since he intended by his voluntary act only to bear the child's maintenance. And Allah knows best. Mālik said: I have not seen anyone pursuing such a claim; and if he did pursue it, he would have some basis for that.

And they agreed that if she dies, the maintenance of the child is paid from her property, because it is a right that was established for him before her death, so it does not lapse with her death.

The tenth issue: If a man stipulates in the khul' (divorce by compensation, in which the wife pays to be released from the marriage) that his wife bear the maintenance of her pregnancy, while she has nothing, then the maintenance is on him if she has no property from which to spend. If she becomes wealthy after that, he may pursue her for what he spent and take it back from her. Malik said: "It is part of the right that a man be obligated to maintain his child, even if he stipulated on his wife that she maintain him, when she has nothing with which to maintain him."

The eleventh issue: The scholars differed over whether khul' is a talaq (a divorce pronouncement) or a faskh (an annulment). It is narrated from Uthman, Ali, Ibn Mas'ud and a group of the Successors that it is a talaq. Malik, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, Abu Hanifa and his companions, and al-Shafi'i in one of his two opinions held the same. So whoever intends by the khul' two or three pronouncements, it binds him according to Malik. The people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y) said: If the husband intends three, it is three; if he intends two, it is one irrevocable (ba'inah) divorce, "because it is a single utterance." Al-Shafi'i, in one of his two opinions, said: If he intends a talaq by the khul' and names it, it is a talaq; if he intends no talaq and does not name it, no separation takes place. He stated this in al-Qadim (his earlier school). His first opinion is more beloved to me. Al-Muzani said: "And it is the more correct according to them."

Abu Thawr said: If he does not name it a talaq, then the khul' is a separation and not a talaq; if he names it a single talaq, it is a single talaq, and the husband has more right to take her back during the 'iddah (waiting period) as long as she is in it.

Among those who said that khul' is a faskh and not a talaq, except if he intends it, were Ibn 'Abbas, Tawus, Ikrimah, Ishaq and Ahmad. They argued with the hadith narrated through Ibn 'Uyaynah, from 'Amr, from Tawus, from Ibn 'Abbas, that Ibrahim ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas asked him: "A man divorced his wife two times, then she sought khul' from him; may he marry her?" He said: "Yes, let him marry her. Khul' is not a talaq. Allah, mighty and majestic, mentioned talaq at the beginning of the verse and at its end, and khul' in between, so khul' is nothing." Then he said: "The divorce is twice; then either retention in kindness or release with good treatment." Then he recited: "But if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him after that until she marries another husband." They said: "And because, if it were a talaq, it would be a third after mentioning the two pronouncements, and his words 'if he divorces her' after that would indicate a fourth pronouncement, so prohibition would depend on four pronouncements."

They also argued with what al-Tirmidhi, Abu Dawud and al-Daraqutni narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: that the wife of Thabit ibn Qays sought khul' from her husband during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered her to observe a waiting period of one menstrual cycle. Al-Tirmidhi said: "A hasan gharib hadith." And from al-Rubayyi' bint Mu'awwidh ibn 'Afra', that she sought khul' during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered her, or she was ordered, to observe a waiting period of one menstrual cycle. Al-Tirmidhi said: "The hadith of al-Rubayyi' is the sound one: that she was ordered to observe a waiting period of one menstrual cycle." They said: "This indicates that khul' is a faskh and not a talaq, because Allah, exalted, said: 'And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods (qur').' If this woman were divorced, she would not be limited to one period."

I say: Whoever divorced his wife twice, then made khul' with her, then wished to remarry her, may do so, as Ibn 'Abbas said, even if she has not married another husband, because he has only two pronouncements left and the khul' is void. Whoever made khul' a talaq said: It is not permissible for him to take her back until she marries another husband, because by the khul' the three were completed. This is the correct view, God willing.

Qadi Isma'il ibn Ishaq said: "How is it acceptable to say about a man whose wife said to him, 'Divorce me for a sum of property,' and he divorced her, that it is not a talaq, when, if he had placed her affair in her hand without any compensation and she divorced herself, it would be a talaq?"
