As for the words of Allah, the Exalted: "But if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him after that until she marries another husband," it is connected to His words, "The divorce is twice," because His words, "or release with good treatment," mean only "or divorce." If khul' were connected to the two pronouncements, then khul' would not be permissible at all except after two pronouncements, and no one says this.

Others said: What they interpreted in the verse is an error, for His words, "The divorce is twice," convey the ruling for two pronouncements when they are issued not in the manner of khul', and with them He established the right of return by His words, "then retention in kindness." Then He mentioned their ruling when it is in the manner of khul', so the khul' returns to the two mentioned previously, since the purpose of that is to explain the unconditional talaq and the talaq for a compensation. The third talaq, whether for compensation or without compensation, cuts off lawfulness except after another husband.

I say: This is the answer concerning the verse. As for the hadith, Abu Dawud, when he cited the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas about the menstrual cycle, said: "This hadith was narrated by 'Abd al-Razzaq from Ma'mar, from 'Amr ibn Muslim, from Ikrimah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), as a mursal (a hadith missing a companion in the chain). And al-Qa'nabi narrated to us from Malik, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, who said: 'The waiting period of the woman who seeks khul' is the waiting period of the divorced woman.'" Abu Dawud said: "And the practice among us is according to this."

I say: This is the position of Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, al-Thawri and the people of Kufa. Al-Tirmidhi said: "And of the majority of the people of knowledge among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) and others." I say: The hadith of Ibn 'Abbas about the menstrual cycle, despite its rarity as al-Tirmidhi mentioned and its mursal character as Abu Dawud mentioned, has been said to contain: "The Prophet (ﷺ) made her waiting period one menstrual cycle and a half." Al-Daraqutni narrated it from the hadith of Ma'mar, from 'Amr ibn Muslim, from Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas: "The wife of Thabit ibn Qays sought khul' from her husband, so the Prophet (ﷺ) made her waiting period one menstrual cycle and a half." The narrator from Ma'mar here regarding the menstrual cycle and the half is the same narrator from him regarding the single menstrual cycle, namely Hisham ibn Yusuf Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-San'ani al-Yamani, from whom al-Bukhari alone narrated. So the hadith is disturbed (mudtarib) in both its chain and its text, and the argument from it falls, both regarding khul' being a faskh and regarding the waiting period of the divorced woman being one menstrual cycle. There remains the words of Allah: "And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods (qur')," which is explicit for every divorced woman who has been consummated with, except those specified, as preceded.

Al-Tirmidhi said: "Some of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'The waiting period of the woman who seeks khul' is one menstrual cycle.' Ishaq said: 'If someone goes to this, it is a strong position.'" Ibn al-Mundhir said: "'Uthman ibn 'Affan and Ibn 'Umar said: her waiting period is one menstrual cycle, and Aban ibn 'Uthman and Ishaq said the same." Ali ibn Abi Talib said: "Her waiting period is the waiting period of the divorced woman." Ibn al-Mundhir continued: "I say according to the words of 'Uthman and Ibn 'Umar, and the hadith of Ali is not established." I say: We have already mentioned from Ibn 'Umar that he said: "The waiting period of the woman who seeks khul' is the waiting period of the divorced woman," and this is sound.

The twelfth issue: Malik's opinion differed regarding one who intends to effect khul' without a compensation. Abd al-Wahhab said: "According to Malik it is a khul', and the divorce is irrevocable (ba'in)." It is also reported from him: "It is not irrevocable except with the existence of a compensation." This was said by Ashhab and al-Shafi'i, because it is a talaq stripped of compensation and of completing a number, so it is revocable, as if it were with the wording of talaq. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: "This is more correct in my view, and in the view of the scholars upon reflection." The reasoning of the first view is that the absence of the compensation in khul' does not take it out of its essential meaning, the basis of which is when one makes khul' with wine or with swine.

The thirteenth issue: The one who seeks khul' (al-mukhtali'ah) is the woman who releases herself from all that is hers. The one who ransoms (al-muftadiyah) is the woman who ransoms herself with part of it and keeps part of it. The one who is released (al-mubari'ah) is the woman who releases her husband before he has consummated with her, so she says: "I have released you, so release me." This is the statement of Malik. Isa ibn Dinar narrated from Malik: "The mubari'ah is the one who takes nothing and gives nothing; the mukhtali'ah is the one who gives back what he gave her and adds from her own property; the muftadiyah is the one who ransoms with part of what he gave her and keeps part of it. All of this happens before consummation and after it. What is before consummation has no waiting period. And al-musalahah (the settlement) is like al-mubara'ah."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad and others said: These four terms return to one meaning, though their descriptions differ with respect to the manner of pronouncement. It is an irrevocable single divorce, whether he named it or did not name it. He has no right of return during the waiting period, but he may remarry her during the waiting period and after it, with her consent, with a guardian (wali) and a dower, and before another husband and after him. This is contrary to Abu Thawr, because she only gave him the compensation so that she might own herself. If the talaq of khul' were revocable, she would not own herself, and the husband would then combine the compensation and what it was given for.

The fourteenth issue: This, with the unrestricted contract, is valid. If she offers him the compensation and stipulates the right of return, there are two narrations transmitted by Ibn Wahb from Malik. One of them: it is established, and this is the view of Sahnun. The other: it is negated. Sahnun said: "The reasoning of the first narration is that both have agreed that the compensation is in exchange for what is subtracted from the number of pronouncements, and this is permissible." The reasoning of the second narration is that he has stipulated in the contract what prevents its purpose, so it is not established, just as if he stipulated in a marriage contract: "I will not have intercourse with her."

The fifteenth issue: His words, the Exalted: "These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them." When Allah clarified the rulings of marriage and separation, He said: "These are the limits of Allah," which you are commanded to comply with, just as He clarified the prohibitions of fasting in another verse, saying: "These are the limits of Allah, so do not approach them." He divided the limits into two kinds: limits of command, to be complied with, and limits of prohibition, to be avoided. Then Allah, exalted, informed: "And whoever transgresses the limits of Allah, those are the wrongdoers."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 230 (part 1 of 3):

Allah's words: ﴿And if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him thereafter until she marries a husband other than him﴾. In this there are eleven issues.

The first: Some of the shaykhs of Khurasan from the Hanafis cited this verse as evidence that a woman divorced by khul' (khul' (a form of divorce initiated by the wife through compensation)) is subject to a further divorce. They said: Allah, glorified is He, legislated an explicit divorce after the ransoming by divorce, because the fa' (fa' (the particle of sequence, meaning "then")) denotes sequence. It is therefore unlikely that it refers back to His words, "The divorce is twice," because what intervened in the speech prevents building the phrase "And if he divorces her" upon "The divorce is twice." Rather, the closer reading is that it refers to what immediately follows it, as in the case of the exception, and it does not refer back to what precedes it except by an indication. Likewise, the words of Allah, the Exalted: "And your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship, born of your wives with whom you have consummated the marriage" [[See vol. 5, p. 112.]], which became restricted to what immediately follows it and not referring back to what precedes it, so that consummation is not a condition regarding the mothers of the women.

The scholars differed concerning divorce after khul' during the waiting period. One group said: If a man makes khul' with his wife and then divorces her while she is in the waiting period, the divorce falls upon her as long as she is in the waiting period. This was the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Shurayh, Tawus, al-Nakha'i, al-Zuhri, al-Hakam, Hammad, al-Thawri, and the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y (the adherents of personal reasoning, the Hanafi school in particular)). There is a second view, that the divorce does not bind her. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Zubayr, 'Ikrimah, al-Hasan, Jabir ibn Zayd, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, and Abu Thawr, and it is also the view of Malik, except that Malik said: If she ransoms herself from him on condition that he divorce her three times in immediate succession, at the moment he divorces her, then that is binding upon him. If there is a pause between them, then whatever he says after the pause is nothing. The reason for this is that the continuity of speech, one part following another without interruption, gives it a single ruling, and likewise when an exception is joined to an oath by God, it takes effect and the ruling of the exception is established; but when it is separated from it, it has no connection with what preceded in the speech.

The second: The intended meaning of Allah's words, "And if he divorces her," is the third divorce, "she is not lawful to him thereafter until she marries a husband other than him." This is agreed upon, with no disagreement.

They differed regarding what suffices of marriage, and what makes the lawful restoration (tahlil (the act of making a divorced woman lawful again to her former husband)) permissible. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and those who agreed with him said: Mere contract is sufficient. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: Mere intercourse does not suffice until there is emission of semen. The majority of scholars and the general body of jurists held that intercourse suffices for this, namely the meeting of the two circumcised parts, which requires the hadd punishment and ghusl, invalidates fasting and pilgrimage, makes the spouses muhsan (muhsan (married, so that adultery is punished by stoning)), and makes the full dower obligatory.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: No issue in jurisprudence has ever come before me that is more difficult than this one, because one of the principles of jurisprudence is whether a ruling attaches to the beginnings of names or to their ends. If we say the ruling attaches to the beginnings of names, we must follow the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib. If we say the ruling attaches to the ends of names, we must require emission together with the disappearance of the glans in order to make her lawful again, because that is the final taste of the 'usaylah (honey-sweetness, a metaphor for sexual pleasure), according to what al-Hasan said.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: The meaning of "tasting the 'usaylah" is intercourse, and the scholars are agreed upon this except Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib. He said: As for the people, they say, "She is not lawful to the first until the second has intercourse with her." But I say: If he marries her a valid marriage, not intending to make her lawful, then there is no harm in the first husband marrying her. We know of no one who agreed with him in this except a group of the Kharijites, and the Sunnah is sufficient without anything else.

I say: Sa'id ibn Jubayr also held the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib. Al-Nahhas mentioned this in his book Ma'ani al-Quran. He said: The people of knowledge hold that the marriage here means intercourse, because He said, "a husband other than him," and the husbandhood has already been mentioned, so the nikah becomes intercourse. Except Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: The nikah here is a valid marriage when one does not intend to make her lawful. I say: I think that they had not received the hadith of the 'usaylah, or it was not authentic in their view, so they took the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, which is His words: ﴿until she marries a husband other than him﴾. And Allah knows best.

The imams narrated, and the wording is that of al-Daraqutni, from 'A'ishah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If a man divorces his wife three times, she is not lawful to him until she marries another husband and each of them tastes the 'usaylah of the other."

Some Hanafi scholars said: Whoever contracts a marriage according to the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, the judge may annul it, and his disagreement is not taken into account, because it departs from the consensus of the scholars. Our scholars said: From the words of the Prophet (ﷺ), "until each of them tastes the 'usaylah of the other," it is understood that both are equal in attaining the pleasure of intercourse. This is evidence for one of the two views among us, that if he had intercourse with her while she was asleep or unconscious, she does not become lawful to her divorcer, because she has not tasted the 'usaylah, since she did not perceive it.

**The Third Issue:** Al-Nasa'i narrated from ʿAbd Allah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cursed the one who tattoos, the one who has herself tattooed, the one who joins hair (with false hair), the one who has her hair joined, the one who consumes usury (ribā), the one who pays it, the *muhallil* (the man who marries a divorced woman to make her lawful to her former husband), and the *muhallal lahu* (the former husband for whom she is made lawful)."

Al-Tirmidhi narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cursed the *muhallil* and the *muhallal lahu*." He said: "This is a ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ (good and sound) ḥadīth. This ḥadīth has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) through more than one chain." The practice according to the people of knowledge among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) is in accordance with this, among them ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar (in manuscript B: "ʿAmr," corrected in the margin), and others. It is also the view of the jurists among the Successors (*tābiʿūn*), and Sufyān al-Thawrī, Ibn al-Mubārak, al-Shāfiʿī, Mālik, Aḥmad and Isḥāq hold it. I heard al-Jārūd mention on the authority of Wakīʿ that he said the same, and said: "This topic should be thrown away from the statements of the people of opinion (*ahl al-raʾy*)." Sufyān said: "If a man marries a woman in order to make her lawful (to her former husband), and then it occurs to him to keep her, she is not lawful to him until he marries her again in a new marriage."

Abū ʿUmar Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: The scholars differed concerning the marriage of the *muhallil*. Mālik said: The *muhallil* does not remain in his marriage; rather he must begin a new marriage. If he has intercourse with her, she is owed the bridal gift of her equivalent (*mahr mithl*), and his intercourse does not make her lawful to her first husband, whether they both knew or did not know that he married her in order to make her lawful. His marriage is not allowed to continue and is annulled. This is also the view of al-Thawrī and al-Awzāʿī.

There is a second opinion, reported from al-Thawrī, concerning the marriage of option (*nikāḥ al-khiyār*) and the *muhallil*: that the marriage is permissible and the condition is void. This is the opinion of Ibn Abī Layla concerning this and concerning the temporary marriage (*nikāḥ al-mutʿa*). It is reported from al-Awzāʿī concerning the marriage of the *muhallil*: "What he did was wrong, but the marriage is permissible."

Abū Ḥanīfa, Abū Yūsuf and Muḥammad said: The marriage is permissible if he consummates it, and he may keep her if he wishes. Abū Ḥanīfa and his companions once said that she is not lawful to the first husband if he married her in order to make her lawful, and once they said that she becomes lawful to him through this marriage if he has intercourse with her and then divorces her. They did not differ that this husband's marriage is valid and that he may remain in it.

There is a third opinion: al-Shāfiʿī said: If he says, "I marry you in order to make you lawful (to your first husband), and there is no marriage between us after that," this is a form of temporary marriage, which is corrupt; it is not allowed to continue and must be annulled. And if he has intercourse on this basis, it does not make her lawful. But if he marries her with an unrestricted marriage, neither he nor she stipulated the *tahlīl*, then al-Shāfiʿī has two opinions on this in his Old Book (*al-Qadīm*): one is like the view of Mālik, and the other is like the view of Abū Ḥanīfa. His opinion did not change in his New Book (*al-Jadīd*), written in Egypt, that the marriage is valid if the condition is not stipulated. This is also the view of Dāwūd.

I (al-Qurṭubī) say: al-Māwardī related from al-Shāfiʿī that if the *tahlīl* was stipulated before the contract, the marriage is valid and she becomes lawful to the first husband; but if it was stipulated within the contract, the marriage is void and she does not become lawful to the first husband. He said: This is the view of al-Shāfiʿī.

Al-Ḥasan and Ibrāhīm said: If any of the three (the husband, the wife, or the guardian) intends the *tahlīl*, the marriage is corrupt. This is a strictness.

Sālim and al-Qāsim said: There is no harm in a man marrying her in order to make her lawful, if the two spouses do not know (the intention), and he is rewarded for it. Rabīʿa and Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd also said this, and Dāwūd ibn ʿAlī said it, provided that it is not made apparent by stipulating it at the time of the contract.

**The Fourth Issue:** According to our scholars, the permissibility of the *nikāḥ al-tahlīl* depends on the marrying husband. Whether he stipulated it or intended it, whenever either of these is the case, his marriage is corrupt, it is not allowed to continue, and his intercourse does not make her lawful to her husband. The knowledge and ignorance of the divorcing husband in this matter are the same. It has been said that when he knows that the one who marries her does so for this purpose, he should refrain from taking her back. According to Mālik, she is not made lawful except by a marriage of desire, for his need of her, not intended for *tahlīl*; and his intercourse with her must be lawful intercourse: she must not be fasting, nor in ihrām, nor in her menstruation; and the husband must be adult and Muslim.

Al-Shāfiʿī said: If he has intercourse with her in a valid marriage and the head of the penis (*ḥashafa*) enters her genitals, they have tasted the honey (*al-ʿusayla*, the sweetness of intercourse, a metaphor for consummation). This applies equally whether the husband is strong or weak in his sexual capacity, whether he inserted it with his own hand or hers, and whether he is a boy, an adolescent, or a castrated man who retains what enables penetration as a non-eunuch does. It also applies whether the husband had intercourse with her while she was in ihrām or fasting. All of this, as al-Shāfiʿī described it, is the view of Abū Ḥanīfa and his companions, al-Thawrī, al-Awzāʿī, al-Ḥasan ibn Ṣāliḥ, and some of Mālik's companions.

**The Fifth Issue:** Ibn Ḥabīb said: If he marries her, and if she pleases him he keeps her; otherwise, if he sought reward for making her lawful (to her former husband), it is not permitted, because the intention of *tahlīl* was mixed into his marriage. She does not become lawful to the first husband by this.

**The Sixth Issue:** A master's intercourse with his slave-girl whose husband has divorced her irrevocably does not make her lawful (to her former husband), because he is not a husband. This is narrated from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, and it is the view of ʿUbayda, Masrūq, al-Shaʿbī, Ibrāhīm, Jābir ibn Zayd, Sulaymān ibn Yasār, Ḥammād ibn Abī Sulaymān and Abū al-Zinād, and it is the view of the majority of jurists of the regions. It is narrated from ʿUthmān, Zayd ibn Thābit and al-Zubayr the opposite of this: that she becomes lawful to him if her master has intercourse with her without intending deception or *tahlīl*, and she returns to her husband with a proposal and a bridal gift. The first opinion is more sound, because of the words of the Exalted: ﴿until she marries another husband﴾, and the master only has authority through ownership of the right hand, and this is clear.

**The Seventh Issue:** In the *Muwaṭṭaʾ* of Mālik it is reported that it reached him that Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib and Sulaymān ibn Yasār were asked about a man who married his slave-girl to his slave; the slave then divorced her irrevocably (*al-battah*); then her master gave her to him as a gift. Is she lawful to him by right of ownership? They both said: "She is not lawful to him until she marries another husband."

**The Eighth Issue:** It is reported from Mālik that he asked Ibn Shihāb about a man whose wife was a slave-girl; he bought her, and he had divorced her once. He said: "She is lawful to him by right of ownership as long as he has not irrevocably divorced her. If he has irrevocably divorced her, she is not lawful to him by right of ownership until she marries another husband." Abū ʿUmar said: The community of scholars and the leading jurists hold this view: Mālik, al-Thawrī, al-Awzāʿī, al-Shāfiʿī, Abū Ḥanīfa, Aḥmad, Isḥāq and Abū Thawr. Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAṭāʾ, Ṭāwūs and al-Ḥasan used to say: If the one who irrevocably divorced her buys her, she becomes lawful to him by right of ownership, based on the general sense of the Mighty and Majestic's words: ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾ [see vol. 5, p. 20]. Abū ʿUmar said: This is an erroneous statement, because the words of the Mighty and Majestic, ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾, do not permit the mothers or the sisters; likewise all other forbidden women.

**The Ninth Issue:** If a Muslim irrevocably divorces his wife, a *dhimmī* (a non-Muslim under protection), three times, and then a *dhimmī* marries her and consummates the marriage, and then he divorces her, one group said: The *dhimmī* is a husband to her, and she may return to the first. This is what al-Ḥasan, [al-Zuhrī (the addition from manuscripts B and Z)], Sufyān al-Thawrī, al-Shāfiʿī, Abū ʿUbayd and the people of opinion said. Ibn al-Mundhir said: We also say this, because God the Exalted said: ﴿until she marries another husband﴾, and the Christian is a husband. Mālik and Rabīʿa said: He does not make her lawful.

**The Tenth Issue:** A corrupt marriage does not make a woman thrice-divorced lawful, according to the majority. Mālik, al-Thawrī, al-Shāfiʿī, al-Awzāʿī, the people of opinion, Aḥmad, Isḥāq and Abū ʿUbayd all say: She is not lawful to the first husband except by a valid marriage. Al-Ḥakam said: He is a husband. Ibn al-Mundhir said: He is not a husband, because the rulings of marriage concerning *ẓihār* (a pre-Islamic form of divorce by comparing the wife to a forbidden relative), *īlāʾ* (an oath of abstention from intercourse), and *liʿān* (mutual oath of condemnation) do not apply between them. All scholars whose views are preserved agree that if the woman tells the first husband, "I have married, and my husband has entered upon me," and he believes her, she becomes lawful to the first husband.

Al-Shāfiʿī said: The cautious course is that he should not do it if it occurs to him in his heart that she is lying to him.

**The Eleventh Issue:** Concerning this matter, a severe harshness has come from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, namely his saying: "I will not be brought a *muhallil* or a *muhallal lahu* except that I will stone them both." Ibn ʿUmar said: "*Tahlīl* is fornication (*siffāḥ*), and the two will not cease being adulterers even if they remain for twenty years." Abū ʿUmar said: ʿUmar's words admit only of strictness, because it is established from him that he waived the *ḥadd* (prescribed punishment) for one who had intercourse with a forbidden womb, having been ignorant of its prohibition and excusing him by his ignorance. Therefore the interpretation (that the statement is strict) is preferable. There is no disagreement that there is no stoning upon him.

**The Commentary on the Words of the Exalted:** ﴿Then if he divorces her, there is no blame upon them both if they return to each other, if they think they can keep within the limits of Allah. And these are the limits of Allah, which He makes clear to a people who know.﴾ On this there are four issues.

**The First:** The words of the Exalted, ﴿Then if he divorces her﴾, mean the second husband.

(So there is no blame upon them both)—that is, upon the woman and her first husband. Ibn ʿAbbas said: there is no disagreement on this. Ibn al-Mundhir said: the scholars (ahl al-ʿilm) have agreed that if a free man divorces his wife three times, then her waiting period (ʿiddah) ends, she marries another husband, he consummates the marriage with her, then divorces her, her waiting period ends, and she then marries her first husband, she returns to him with three divorces (i.e., the divorces are reset to none; rather, she is with him on three pronouncements of divorce).

They differed concerning a man who divorces his wife once or twice, then she marries someone else and then returns to her first husband. One group said: she remains under the remainder of her divorces. This is also what the senior Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, ʿImran ibn Husayn, and Abu Hurayrah. This is also reported from Zayd ibn Thabit, Muʿadh ibn Jabal, and ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs. Ubaydah al-Salmani, Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan al-Basri, Malik, Sufyan al-Thawri, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Shafiʿi, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu ʿUbayd, Abu Thawr, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, and Ibn Nasr also said this.

There is a second view: the marriage is new and the divorce is new. This is the view of Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbas, and it was held by ʿAta, al-Nakhaʿi, Shurayh, al-Nuʿman, and Yaʿqub. Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah mentioned, saying: Abu Muʿawiyah and Waki reported to us from al-Aʿmash from Ibrahim, who said: "The companions of ʿAbdullah used to say: does the husband demolish three but not one or two?" He said: and Hafs reported to us from Hajjaj from Talhah from Ibrahim that the companions of ʿAbdullah used to say: "The husband demolishes one or two just as he demolishes three, except ʿUbaydah, who said: she remains under the remainder of her divorces." Abu ʿUmar mentioned this. Ibn al-Mundhir said: "I say according to the first view."

There is a third view: if the last husband consummated the marriage with her, it is a new divorce and a new marriage; but if he did not consummate it with her, then she remains under the remainder. This is the view of Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi.

The second issue: the words of the Exalted, ﴿if they both think they can keep within the limits of Allah﴾, form a condition. Tawus said: "if they both think that each of them will treat the other well in companionship." It was also said: "the limits of Allah" are His obligations, meaning: if they both know that after the second marriage there will be goodness between them. Thus, whenever the husband knows that he will be unable to provide for his wife, or her dowry, or any of her obligatory rights upon him, it is not lawful for him to marry her until he makes it clear to her, or knows in himself the ability to fulfil her rights. Likewise, if he has a defect that prevents him from intimacy, he must make it clear, so that he does not deceive the woman about himself. It is also not permitted for him to deceive her about a lineage he claims, or about wealth [he has (the addition is from manuscript z)], or about a trade he mentions while lying about it. Likewise, it is obligatory upon the woman, if she knows in herself an inability to fulfil the husband's rights, or if she has a defect that prevents intimacy, such as madness, leprosy, vitiligo, or a disease of the private parts, that it is not permitted for her to deceive him, and she must make clear to him what she has of such things, just as the seller of goods must disclose the defects in his goods. Whenever either spouse finds a defect in the other, he or she has the right to annul. If the defect is in the man, the wife is owed the dowry if he consummated the marriage with her; if he did not consummate it, she is owed half of it. If the defect is in the woman, the husband may return her and take back what he gave her of the dowry. It has been narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) married a woman from the Banu Bayadah, found leprosy on her side, returned her, and said: "You have deceived me."

The narration from Malik differed concerning the wife of an impotent man (ʿinnin) who gave herself over to him and then they were separated because of impotence: once he said she is owed the full dowry, and once he said she is owed half the dowry. This depends on the difference in his statement: is the dowry owed by the handing over (of herself) or by consummation? There are two opinions.

The third issue: Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: "Our companions differed on whether the wife has a duty of service (khidmah) or not. Some of our companions said: the wife has no duty of service, because the contract covers enjoyment (istimtaʿ), not service. Do you not see that it is not a contract of hire nor of ownership of a person's body? It is a contract for enjoyment, and what is due by the contract is enjoyment alone, so she cannot be required to do more than that. Do you not see the words of the Exalted: ﴿then if they obey you, do not seek a way against them﴾." Other companions said: "She has a duty of service comparable to that of women like her. If she is of high standing, due to wealth or luxury, then it is her role to manage the household and direct the servant. If she is of middling condition, then she must spread the bedding and the like. If she is below that, then she must sweep the house, cook, and wash. If she is from the women of the Kurds, the Daylam, or the mountain regions, in their own lands, she is charged with what their women are charged with, because Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and they have rights similar to those upon them, according to what is reasonable﴾. The custom of the Muslims in their lands, in past and present times, has followed what we have mentioned. Do you not see that the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions used to undertake grinding, baking, cooking, spreading bedding, bringing food, and similar things, and we know of no woman who refused that, nor is refusal permissible for her; rather, they would strike their wives when they fell short in that, and hold them to service. Had she not been entitled to it, they would not have demanded it of them."

The fourth issue: the words of the Exalted, ﴿These are the limits of Allah; He makes them clear to a people who know﴾. The limits of Allah are what He prohibits. The word "hadd" (limit) is that which prevents, which bars one from committing indecencies. "Ahadda al-mar'ah" means the woman refrained from adornment. "Rajul mahdud" means a man prevented from good. "Al-bawwab haddad" means the doorkeeper who prevents (entry). This has already been discussed in full (see the thirty-fifth issue, vol. 2, p. 337). He said "for a people who know" because the ignorant person, when commands and prohibitions are abundant for him, does not memorize them or attend to them, whereas the knowledgeable person memorizes and attends to them. For this reason He addressed the scholars and did not address the ignorant.

**First issue: the meaning of "balaghna" (they reached).** Al-Qurtubi's commentary on surah 2, verse 231:

There are six issues in this verse. The first concerns God's words ﴿when they have reached their term﴾. The meaning of "balaghna" (reached) is "they drew near", by the consensus (ijma', scholarly agreement) of the scholars. The sense requires this, because after the term has been fully reached the husband has no choice of retaining her. In the next verse, the word carries the meaning of "coming to an end". The context requires this. So it is literal in the second instance and metaphorical in the first.

**Second issue: God's words ﴿then retain them honourably﴾.** Retaining honourably means fulfilling what is due to her from her husband in rights. For this reason a group of scholars said: among retaining honourably is that if the husband cannot find what to spend on the wife, he should divorce her. If he does not do so, he has gone beyond the bounds of what is honourable, and the judge (hakim) divorces her on his behalf because of the harm that befalls her from remaining with one who cannot provide for her, and hunger cannot be endured. This is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, Abu 'Ubayd, Yahya al-Qattan, and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi. It was also said by the Companions 'Umar, 'Ali and Abu Hurayra, and among the Successors by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, who said that this is a sunna (established practice). Abu Hurayra narrated it from the Prophet (ﷺ).

A group (in B: a faction) said: they are not to be separated. She must endure it, and the maintenance becomes a debt upon him by the ruling of the judge. This is the view of 'Ata' and al-Zuhri, and the Kufans and al-Thawri also held it. They argued with God's words: ﴿And if someone is in hardship, then let there be postponement until ease﴾ (2:280), and His words: ﴿Marry off the single among you﴾ (24:32). He commanded marrying off the poor, so poverty cannot be a cause of separation, since he is recommended to marry while poor. Also, the marriage between the spouses was concluded by consensus, so they cannot be separated except by a similar consensus or by a sunna from the Messenger (ﷺ) that has no contrary evidence.

The proof for the first view is the Prophet's (ﷺ) words in Sahih al-Bukhari: "The woman says: either you feed me, or you divorce me." This is an explicit text on the point of disagreement.

Separation due to inability to provide is, in our school, a revocable single divorce (talaq raj'i, one that permits return within the waiting period). This differs from al-Shafi'i's view that it is an irrevocable single divorce (talaq ba'in, one that does not permit return without a new marriage). His reasoning is that this is a separation after consummation, by which the number of divorces is not completed, and it was neither for a consideration nor for harm to the husband, so it is revocable. Its origin is the divorce of one who swears to abstain (talaq al-mūli, divorce through the oath of abstention, ila').

**Third issue: God's words ﴿or release them honourably﴾.** This means: divorce them. It has already been discussed.

(Concerning God's words ﴿and do not retain them to harm them, so that you transgress﴾): Malik narrated from Thawr ibn Zayd al-Dili that a man used to divorce his wife, then take her back, though he had no need of her and did not intend to keep her, in order to prolong her waiting period (idda) against her and to harm her. So God revealed: ﴿And do not retain them to harm them, so that you transgress. Whoever does that has wronged himself﴾ (2:231), admonishing them through it. Al-Zajjaj said: "he has wronged himself" means he has exposed himself to punishment, because doing what God has forbidden is an exposure to God's punishment.

This report agrees with the report that the verse ﴿Divorce is twice﴾ (2:229) came down to abolish what the people of the pre-Islamic age (jahiliyya) practised of divorce and taking back, as already explained at that verse. These two reports show that the revelation of the two verses mentioned had one closely related meaning, namely a man detaining a woman and taking her back with the intention of harming her. This is clear.

**Fourth issue: God's words ﴿And do not take the signs of God in jest﴾.** The meaning is: do not take God's rulings lightly, for they are all serious. Whoever jokes about them is bound by them. Abu al-Darda' said: a man in the jahiliyya would divorce and say, "I divorced only in play." He would free a slave and marry and say, "I was playing." So this verse was revealed. The Prophet (ﷺ) then said: "Whoever divorces, or frees, or marries, or gives in marriage, and claims he was joking, his claim is serious." Ma'mar narrated it, saying: 'Isa ibn Yunus told us from 'Amr from al-Hasan from Abu al-Darda', and he mentioned it in meaning.

In the Muwatta' of Malik it reached him that a man said to Ibn 'Abbas: "I divorced my wife a hundred times; what do you think is incumbent upon me?" Ibn 'Abbas said: "She was separated from you by three, and the other ninety-seven you took as God's signs in jest."

al-Daraqutni transmitted from the hadith of Isma'il ibn Umayya al-Qurashi from 'Ali, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) heard a man who had pronounced the final divorce (al-batta), and he became angry and said: "You take God's signs in jest—or the religion of God in jest and play. Whoever pronounces the final divorce, we bind him to three, so she is not lawful to him until she marries another husband." Isma'il ibn Umayya is a Kufan, weak in hadith.

It is also reported from 'A'isha that a man would divorce his wife and then say, "By God, I will not let you inherit from me, nor will I leave you." She said, "How is that?" He said, "When you are about to complete your waiting period, I take you back." So God revealed: ﴿And do not take the signs of God in jest﴾.

Our scholars said: all these views are included in the meaning of the verse, because it is said of one who mocks God's signs that he has taken them in jest. It is also said of one who disbelieves in them, and of one who discards them and does not act upon them but acts upon something else. So these views are included in the verse. The signs of God are His proofs, His commands and His prohibitions.

**Fifth issue:** There is no disagreement among the scholars that whoever divorces in jest, the divorce binds him. They differed about other matters, as will be explained in surah Bara'a (al-Tawba) if God wills (vol. 8, p. 197).

Abu Dawud transmitted from Abu Hurayra that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Three things, whether seriously or in jest, are binding: marriage, divorce and taking back." It is also reported from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn Mas'ud and Abu al-Darda', all of whom said: "There are three things in which there is no play, and the one who plays with them is serious: marriage, divorce and manumission."

It was also said: the meaning is, do not abandon God's commands and so become negligent players. Into this verse also enters seeking forgiveness for a sin with the tongue while persisting in it with the deed. Likewise everything of this kind; know it.

**Sixth issue: God's words ﴿and remember God's blessing upon you﴾.** That is, with Islam and the explanation of the rulings.

(And the wisdom): it is the sunna that clarifies, upon the tongue of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), God's intention regarding what is not explicitly stated in the Book.

(He admonishes you with it): that is, He warns you.

(And fear God, and know that God is Knowing of all things): already mentioned.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 232:**

There are four issues (masa'il) in this verse.

**The first issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So do not prevent them﴾ (fa-la ta'dulūhunna). It is narrated that the sister of Ma'qil ibn Yasar was married to Abi al-Badda (in the originals it reads "Abi al-Dahdah", which is an error). He divorced her and left her until her waiting period ('iddah, the period a divorced woman must observe before remarrying) had ended. Then he regretted it and proposed to her again. She agreed, but her brother refused to marry her to him and said: "My face is forbidden to your face if you marry him." So the verse was revealed. Muqatil said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) summoned Ma'qil and said: "If you are a believer, do not prevent your sister from Abi al-Badda." He said: "I believe in Allah," and he married her to him.

Al-Bukhari narrated from al-Hasan that the sister of Ma'qil ibn Yasar was divorced by her husband until her waiting period had ended. He then proposed to her, but Ma'qil refused, and so the verse was revealed: "So do not prevent them from marrying their husbands."

Al-Daraqutni also narrated it from al-Hasan, who said: Ma'qil ibn Yasar told me: "I had a sister who was asked for in marriage through me, and I used to keep her away from people. A cousin of mine came and proposed to her, and I married her to him. They lived together for as long as Allah willed. Then he divorced her with a revocable divorce (talaq raj'i), and left her until her waiting period ended. He then proposed to her among the other suitors. I said: 'I kept people away from her, and I married you to her. Then you divorced her with a divorce that allows you to take her back, and left her until her waiting period ended. Now that she has been asked for through me, you come to me proposing with the suitors! I will never marry her to you!'" So Allah revealed, or he said it was revealed: "When you divorce women and they reach their term, do not prevent them from marrying their husbands." So I made expiation for my oath and married her to him.

In another narration of al-Bukhari: Ma'qil took offense (hamiya... anfan) at this and said: "He let her go while he had power over her, and now he proposes to her!" So Allah revealed the verse. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) summoned him, recited the verse to him, and he gave up his offense and submitted to the command of Allah, Exalted is He.

It was also said that he was Ma'qil ibn Sinan (with an *n*). Al-Nahhas said: al-Shafi'i reported it in his books from Ma'qil ibn Yasar or Sinan. (The words "or Sinan" are not in the manuscripts Z and B.) Al-Tahawi said: He is Ma'qil ibn Sinan.

**The second issue:** If this is established, then the verse is evidence that marriage is not valid without a guardian (wali), because the sister of Ma'qil was a previously married woman (thayyib). If the matter had been entirely in her hands and not in her guardian's, she would have married herself and would not have needed her guardian Ma'qil. Therefore, the address in His saying, Exalted is He, "So do not prevent them," is directed to the guardians, and the matter of marriage rests with them provided the women consent.

It has also been said that the address in this is directed to the husbands, meaning that taking the woman back (irtija') would be harm, a prevention (adl) from marrying someone else, by prolonging her waiting period upon her. The followers of Abu Hanifa used this verse as evidence that a woman may marry herself. They said: Because Allah attributed this to her, as He said: "Then she is not lawful to him after that until she marries another husband" (2:230), and did not mention the guardian.

This question has been discussed fully earlier. The first view is more correct because of the reason for revelation that we have mentioned. And Allah knows best.

**The third issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They reach their term﴾ (fa-balaghna ajalahunna). The reaching of the term (bulugh al-ajal) in this context means its completion, because a new marriage can only be contemplated after the waiting period has ended.

"Ta'dulūhunna" (so you prevent them) means: you hold them back (tahbisūhunna). Al-Khalil reported: "A hen is mu'dil," meaning her eggs have been retained (ihtabasa bayduha). It was also said: al-'adl means constriction and prevention, and this goes back to the meaning of holding back. One says: "I wanted a matter and you prevented me from it (fa-'adaltani 'anhu)," meaning you kept me from it and constricted me. "A'dala al-amr" means when the stratagems are closed to you in a matter. From this comes the saying: "It is an 'udlah (a difficult problem) of the 'udal," when there is no way to find a stratagem for it. Al-Azhari said: The root of al-'adl comes from the saying: "'adalat al-naqah" when her offspring is stuck and its emergence is not easy, and "'adalat al-dajajah" when her eggs are stuck. In the hadith of Mu'awiyah: "A difficult question (mu'dilah) with no Abu Hasan," meaning a difficult question with narrow ways out. Tawus said: "Difficult judicial cases (udal aqdiyah) came, and none dealt with them except Ibn 'Abbas." Every problem that is unclear to the Arabs is mu'dil. From this is the saying of al-Shafi'i:

"When difficult matters confront me,
I uncover their realities through reflection."

It is also said: a'dala al-amr means when it became severe. Dā' 'udal (or 'udal) means a severe disease, difficult to cure, which has wearied the physicians. 'Adala fulan ayyimahu means he prevented her; the verb ya'duluha is pronounced with a *damma* or a *kasra*, both being acceptable dialects.

**The fourth issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿This is admonished by it, whoever among you﴾ (dhalika yu'azu bihi man kana). He did not say "dhalikum" (this, addressed to the plural), because it is taken according to the meaning of the group (al-jam'). Had He said "dhalikum," it would have been permissible, as in: ﴿That is purer for you and more pure, and Allah knows﴾ (2:232 in other readings / similar usage), meaning: what is good for you in it.

﴿And you do not know﴾ (wa antum la ta'lamun) that.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 233 (part 1 of 4):**

In it there are eighteen issues.

**The first:** His statement, exalted is He, ﴿The mothers﴾ is the subject (mubtada').

(﴿shall suckle their children﴾) is in the position of the predicate (khabar).

(﴿for two full years﴾) is an adverb of time (zarf zaman). When God, glorified is He, mentioned marriage and divorce, He mentioned the child, because the spouses may separate while there is a child. The verse is therefore about divorced women who have children from their husbands. al-Suddi, al-Dahhak and others said: that is, they have more right to suckling their children than strangers (non-mothers), because they are more compassionate and tender. Taking a young child away causes harm to him and to her. This indicates that even if the child has been weaned, the mother has more right to his custody (hadanah) because of the excellence of her affection and compassion. She has the right to custody only if she has not remarried, as will come.

On this basis, the statement ﴿And upon the father of the child is their provision and their clothing, according to what is reasonable﴾ raises a difficulty, because a divorced woman does not deserve clothing if she is not revocably divorced (raj'iyyah); rather she deserves a wage (ujrah). Unless it is understood as referring to noble conduct, in which case it is said: it is preferable that the wage not fall below what suffices her for her food and clothing.

It was also said: the verse is general, covering divorced women who have children and wives. The more apparent view is that it concerns wives while the marriage continues, because they are the ones entitled to maintenance (nafaqah) and clothing. A wife is entitled to maintenance and clothing whether or not she suckles. Maintenance and clothing are in exchange for submission and availability (al-tamkin). If she occupies herself with suckling, the availability is not complete, so it might be imagined that maintenance falls away. God removed that misconception by His statement ﴿upon the father of the child﴾, that is, the husband, ﴿is their provision and their clothing﴾ during the period of suckling, because it is an occupation in the husband's interests. So it is as if she had travelled for the husband's need with his permission, in which case maintenance does not fall away.

**The second:** (﴿shall suckle﴾) is a report whose meaning is a command, obligatory for some mothers and recommended (nadb) for others, as will come. It was also said: it is a report about what is legislated (mashru'iyyah), as has already been mentioned.

**The third:** People differed over whether suckling is a right of the mother or an obligation upon her, and the wording allows both. If He had intended to state explicitly that it is upon her, He would have said: "and upon the mothers is the suckling of their children," as He said: ﴿And upon the father of the child is their provision and their clothing﴾. But it is upon her during the marriage, and this is a custom that binds, since it has become like a condition, except that if she is a woman of high standing, possessing comfort (tarrafuh), then her custom is not to suckle, and that is like a condition. It is obligatory upon her if the child will not accept any other woman's milk. It is upon her if it is unavailable, because she is exclusively connected to him.

If the father dies and the child has no property, the school of Malik in al-Mudawwanah holds that suckling is binding upon the mother, unlike maintenance. In the Kitab of Ibn al-Jallab: his suckling is from the public treasury (bayt al-mal). Abd al-Wahhab said: he is one of the poor among the Muslims.

As for the woman divorced with an irrevocable divorce (talaq ba'innah), suckling is not obligatory upon her; it is upon the husband, unless she chooses it, in which case she has more right to the wage of the equivalent (ujrat al-mithl). This holds when the husband is wealthy. If he is destitute, suckling does not bind her, unless the child will not accept anyone other than her, in which case she is then compelled to suckle. Whoever is obligated to suckle, if an excuse prevents her from it, the obligation of suckling returns to the father.

It is narrated from Malik that if the father is destitute and the child has no property, the suckling falls upon the mother; if she has no milk and she has property, then suckling is upon her from her property.

al-Shafi'i said: suckling is binding only upon a father or a grandfather, however far up.

What the scholars say on this will come at His statement, ﴿And upon the heir is the like of that﴾.

It is said: ruda'a yarda'u radla'atan wa radaa'an, and ra'a yarda'u ridaa'an wa radla'atan (with a kasrah on the ra' in the first and a fathah in the second), and the active participle is ra'id in both. And al-radla'ah (with a fathah on the ra' only) means baseness (al-lu'm).

**The fourth:** His statement, ﴿two years﴾, that is, two years (sanatayn), from "hala al-shay'" when a thing changes (inqalaba). So the year (hawl) is a transformation from the first period to the second. It was also said: the year was called hawl because affairs change within it for the most part.

(﴿full﴾): It is qualified by "full" because a speaker may say: "I stayed with so-and-so for two years," meaning a year and part of another year. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿But whoever hastens in two days﴾, while one actually hastens in a day and part of the second.

His statement, exalted is He, ﴿for whoever wishes to complete the suckling﴾ is evidence that suckling for two years is not an absolute requirement, since weaning before two years is permitted. Rather, it sets a limit to end the dispute between the spouses over the period of suckling, so the husband is not obligated to give the wage for more than two years. If the father wishes to wean before this period and the mother does not agree, he does not have that right. Exceeding the two years or falling short of them is permissible only when there is no harm to the infant and when both parents consent.

Mujahid and Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿for whoever wishes that the suckling be completed﴾ with a fathah on the ta' and a raf' on "al-radla'ah," attributing the verb to it. Abu Haywah, Ibn Abi Ablah and al-Jarud ibn Abi Sabrah read "al-ridla'ah" with a kasrah on the ra', and it is a dialect like al-hadarah and al-hidarah. It is narrated from Mujahid that he read "al-radh'ah" on the pattern of al-fal'ah. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that he read "an yukmila al-radla'ah."

al-Nahhas said: the Basrans know "al-radla'ah" only with a fathah on the ra', and "al-ridaa'" only with a kasrah on the ra', like al-qitaal. The Kufans related a kasrah on the ra' with the ha', and a fathah without the ha'.

**The fifth:** Malik, may God have mercy on him, and those who followed him, along with a group of scholars, deduced from this verse that the suckling which creates prohibition (al-radla'ah al-muharrimah), functioning in the manner of kinship, is only that which occurs within the two years, because with the end of the two years the suckling is complete, and no suckling after the two years is considered valid. This is his statement in his Muwatta', and it is the narration of Muhammad ibn Abd al-Hakam from him. It is also the view of Umar and Ibn Abbas. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, and al-Zuhri, Qatada, al-Sha'bi, Sufyan al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad and Abu Thawr also said so.

Ibn Abd al-Hakam related from him: two years and a few additional days.

Abd al-Malik said: like a month or so.

Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik that he said: suckling is two years, and two months after the two years.

al-Walid ibn Muslim related from him that he said: whatever suckling occurs after the two years by a month, two months or three is part of the two years, and whatever is after that is futile (abath).

It is related from al-Nu'man that he said: whatever is after the two years up to six months is suckling. The sounder view is the first, because of His statement, ﴿And the mothers shall suckle their children for two full years﴾. This indicates that there is no ruling for what the infant suckles after the two years.

Sufyan related from Amr ibn Dinar from Ibn Abbas, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "There is no suckling except that which occurs within the two years." [Supporting this is what Ibn Majah related from him, peace and blessings be upon him: "There is no suckling except that which splits open the bowels."]

al-Daraqutni said: none related it from Ibn Uyaynah except al-Haytham ibn Jamil, and he is trustworthy and a memorizer (thiqah hafiz).

Al-Qurtubi, *al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*, commentary on Surah 2, verse 233 (part 2 of 4):

I say: this report, together with the verse and its meaning, negates the suckling of an adult, and that there is no prohibition (*hurmah*) arising from it. It has been reported from ʿĀʾishah that she held this view, and al-Layth ibn Saʿd among the scholars also holds it. It has been reported from Abu Musa al-Ashʿari that he used to hold the suckling of an adult to be valid, and it has also been reported from him that he retracted this. It will come in Surah "al-Nisa'" with full explanation, God willing [[See vol. 5, p. 109.]].

The sixth issue: The majority of exegetes (*mufassirun*) said: these two years apply to every child. It has been reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: it refers to the child who remains in the womb for six months. If he remains for seven months, his suckling is twenty-three months; if he remains for eight months, his suckling is twenty-two months; if he remains for nine months, his suckling is twenty-one months, based on God's words: "And his carrying and his weaning is thirty months." On this basis, the period of pregnancy and the period of suckling overlap, and each takes from the other.

The seventh issue: God's words, ﴿And upon the one to whom the child belongs﴾, meaning: upon the father. In Arabic it is permissible to say "upon those to whom the children belong" (*ʿalā al-mawludi lahum*), as in God's words, "And among them are those who listen to you" [[See vol. 8, p. 346.]], because the meaning is "upon the one to whom he was born," and *alladhi* (the one who) is used for the singular and the plural, as has already been explained.

The eighth issue: God's words, ﴿their provision and their clothing﴾. The "provision" (*rizq*) in this ruling is sufficient food. In this there is evidence that the maintenance of the child is obligatory upon the father, because of the child's weakness and inability. God attributed it to the mother because the nourishment reaches the child through her, in suckling, as He said: "And if they are pregnant, then spend upon them" [[See vol. 18, p. 168.]], because nourishment reaches the child only through her. The scholars agreed that a man is obligated to maintain his young children who have no property. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Hind bint ʿUtbah, when she said to him: "Abu Sufyan is a stingy man, and he does not give me enough maintenance to suffice me and my children, except what I take from his property without his knowledge. Is there any sin upon me in that?" He said: "Take what suffices you and your child, in a reasonable manner." The "clothing" (*kiswah*) is clothing. His words "in a reasonable manner" mean according to what is customary in the usage of the Sharia, without neglect or excess.

Then God explained that spending is according to the wealth and standing of the husband, without fixing a *mudd* or anything else, by His words, ﴿No soul is burdened except according to its capacity﴾, as will come with explanation in Surah "al-Talaq", God willing [[See vol. 18, p. 172.]]. It has also been said that the meaning is: the woman is not required to endure stinginess in the provision, and the husband is not required to do what is extravagance, but he should observe moderation.

The ninth issue: In this verse there is evidence for Malik that custody (*hadanah*, the right and duty of raising a child day to day) belongs to the mother. It applies to a boy until puberty, and to a girl until marriage, and this is her right. Abu Hanifa also held this view. Al-Shafiʿi said: when the child reaches eight years, which is the age of discernment (*tamyiz*), he is given the choice between his two parents, because at that stage his determination is stirred to learn the Qur'an, good manners, and the duties of worship, and this applies equally to a boy and a girl. Al-Nasa'i and others reported from Abu Hurayrah that a woman came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said to him: "My husband wants to take my son away." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "This is your father and this is your mother; take whichever of them you wish." So he took his mother's hand. In the book of Abu Dawud, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: A woman came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) while I was sitting with him, and she said: "O Messenger of God, my husband wants to take my son away, and he has given me water from the well of Abu ʿInabah [[The well of Abu ʿInabah is a well in Medina, where the Messenger of God (ﷺ) reviewed his companions when he set out for Badr. (Al-Nihayah).]], and it has benefited me." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Draw lots over him." Her husband said: "Who will dispute with me over my child?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "This is your father and this is your mother; take the hand of whichever of them you wish." So he took his mother's hand and she departed with him.

Our evidence is what Abu Dawud reported from al-Awzaʿi, who said: ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb told me, from his father, from his grandfather ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, that a woman came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of God, this son of mine, my belly was a vessel for him, my breast was a water-skin for him, and my lap was a shelter for him, and his father divorced me and wants to take him away from me." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to her: "You have more right to him as long as you do not marry."

Ibn al-Mundhir said: All the scholars whose transmission is preserved agreed that when a married couple separate and they have a child, the mother has more right to him as long as she does not marry. Likewise Abu ʿUmar said: I know of no disagreement among the early scholars that a divorced woman who has not remarried has more right to her child than his father, for as long as he is a small child who does not yet discern anything, when he is with her in safekeeping and adequate care, and when no corruption or immodesty is established against her. Then they differed after that concerning giving the child a choice when he has become discerning and understanding between his father and his mother, and concerning who is more entitled to him. Ibn al-Mundhir said: It is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) judged regarding the daughter of Hamzah in favour of the maternal aunt, without giving a choice.

Abu Dawud reported from ʿAli, who said: Zayd ibn Harithah went out to Mecca and returned with the daughter of Hamzah. Jaʿfar said: "I will take her; I have more right to her. She is my cousin, and her maternal aunt is with me, and the maternal aunt is a mother." ʿAli said: "I have more right to her. She is my uncle's daughter, and the daughter of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) is with me, and she has more right to her." Zayd said: "I have more right to her. I went out to her, travelled, and brought her back." So the Prophet (ﷺ) came out and mentioned a hadith, and he said: "As for the girl, I judge that she is to be with Jaʿfar, because her maternal aunt is with him, and the maternal aunt is only a mother."

The tenth issue: Ibn al-Mundhir said: All the scholars whose transmission is preserved agreed that the mother has no right of custody over the child if she remarries. I say: So he said in his book *al-Ashraf*. Al-Qadi ʿAbd al-Wahhab mentioned in his commentary on *al-Risalah* that al-Hasan held that her right of custody is not forfeited by remarriage. Malik, al-Shafiʿi, al-Nuʿman [Abu Hanifa] and Abu Thawr agreed that the paternal grandmother (the mother's mother) has more right to the custody of the child. They differed when the mother has no mother but has a grandmother who is the father's mother. Malik said: the father's mother has more right if the child has no maternal aunt. Ibn al-Qasim said: Malik said, and it reached me from him, that the maternal aunt has more right than the father's mother. According to the view of al-Shafiʿi and al-Nuʿman, the father's mother has more right than the maternal aunt. It has also been said that the father has more right to his son than the father's mother. Abu ʿUmar said: In my view this applies when he has no foreign wife. Then the sister after the father, then the paternal aunt. This applies when each of these is trustworthy regarding the child and is with him in safekeeping and adequate care. If they are not so, they have no right of custody, and what is considered is who protects the child, who treats him well, and who guards him and teaches him good. This is according to the view of those who say that custody is the child's right. This has been reported from Malik, and a group of his companions held it. Likewise, they do not allow custody to a dissolute woman, or to a weak woman who is unable to fulfil the child's rights because of illness or infirmity.

Ibn Habib reported from Mutarrif and Ibn al-Majishun, from Malik, that custody belongs first to the mother, then the maternal grandmother, then the maternal aunt, then the paternal grandmother, then the child's sister, then the child's paternal aunt, then the child's niece, then the father. The paternal grandmother has more right than the sister, the sister has more right than the paternal aunt, and the paternal aunt has more right than those after her, and more right than all the male guardians. The daughter of the maternal aunt, the daughter of the paternal aunt, and the daughters of the child's sisters have no right of custody. If the custodian is not feared to neglect the child or to introduce corruption, she remains his custodian until he reaches puberty. It has also been said: until he loses his milk teeth (*yuthghir*) [The *ithghar* is the falling out and replacement of a child's tooth. In manuscript H: "until he discerns" (*yumayyiz*).], and until a girl marries, except that if the father wants to move for travel and settlement, he then has more right to his child than the mother or others, if she does not wish to relocate. If he wants to leave for trade, he does not have that right. Likewise the child's guardians, whose charge is to be moved, when they relocate for settlement [In the manuscripts as they stand; perhaps it should read "whose charge reaches them"]. The mother may not move her child from the place where the father resides, except within a distance that does not allow the prayer to be shortened. If, at the time of her moving from her city, he stipulates that he will not leave his child with her unless she takes on his maintenance and expenses for specified years, and she agrees, then it binds her. If she dies, her heirs are not pursued for it from her estate. It has also been said that it is a debt taken from her estate, but the first view is more sound, God willing, just as if the child died, or as if he reached a settlement with her over the maintenance of pregnancy and suckling and she waived it, she is not pursued for anything of that.

The eleventh issue: If the mother remarries, her child is not taken from her until her husband has consummated the marriage with her, according to Malik. Al-Shafiʿi said: when she marries, her right has ended. If he divorces her, he does not have the right to take the child back, according to Malik, according to the more prevalent opinion in our school. Al-Qadi Ismaʿil mentioned, and Ibn Khuwaz Mindad also mentioned from Malik, that his opinion varied on this: once he said it is returned to her, and once he said it is not returned. Ibn al-Mundhir said: If the mother leaves the city where her child is and then returns to it, she has more right to her child according to al-Shafiʿi, Abu Thawr and the people of opinion (*ashab al-ra'y*). Likewise, if she remarries and is then divorced or widowed, she regains her right to the child. I say: Likewise al-Qadi Abu Muhammad ʿAbd al-Wahhab said: If the husband divorces her or dies leaving her, she may take him back, because the excuse that made it permissible for him to leave the child has ended.

The twelfth issue: If a woman leaves the custody of her child and does not intend to take him, and she is free and not occupied with a husband, and then afterward wishes to take him, consideration is given to her case. If her leaving him was due to an excuse, she may take him. But if she left him out of rejection of him and hatred, she may not take him after that.

The thirteenth issue: scholars differ concerning a married couple who separate through divorce while the wife is a dhimmi (a non-Muslim under Muslim protection). One group said there is no difference between a dhimmi wife and a Muslim wife, and she has the better right to her child. This is the view of Abu Thawr, of the Ashab al-Ra'y (the People of Opinion), and of Ibn al-Qasim, a student of Malik. Ibn al-Mundhir said: "We have related a hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) that agrees with this view, but there is a discussion about its chain of narration." A second view holds that the child stays with whichever of the two parents is Muslim. This is the view of Malik, Sawwar, and Abdullah ibn al-Hasan [[In B: Ubayd Allah.]], and it is attributed to al-Shafi'i.

Scholars also differ concerning a couple who separate when one is free and the other is a slave. One group said the free parent has the better right. This is the view of Ata, al-Thawri, al-Shafi'i, and the People of Opinion. Malik said: concerning a father who is free and has a free child, while the mother is a slave, the mother has the better right to the child, unless she is sold and transferred, in which case the father has the better right to him.

The fourteenth issue: the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿No mother shall be harmed on account of her child, nor shall a father be harmed on account of his child﴾. The meaning is: the mother should not refuse to nurse him in order to harm his father, nor demand more than the usual wage for her, and it is not permissible for the father to prevent the mother from this when she is willing to nurse. This is the view of the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun, scholars of tafsir, the explanation of the Qur'an).

Nafi', Asim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "tudarra" with a fatha on the second, doubled rā' [لَا تُضَارَّ], and its place is in the jussive mood as a prohibition. Its underlying form is "lā tuḍārarə" according to the original form, then the first rā' was assimilated into the second, and the second was given a fatha because two consonants came together (iltiqa' al-sakinayn). This is how doubled verbs are treated when a fatha or an alif precedes them. You say: "'add yā rajul" and "ḍārra fulānan yā rajul." The meaning is: the child should not be taken away from her when she is willing to nurse and the child has become accustomed to her.

Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir, Aban ibn Asim, and a group read "tuḍārru" with a ḍammah [بِالرَّفْعِ], in coordination with his saying "a soul is not burdened" (tukallafu nafs). It is a report in the form of a statement, but it is meant as a command. Yunus related from al-Hasan that he said: "It means: she should not harm her husband. She says, 'I will not nurse him,' and he should not harm her by taking him from her while she says, 'I will nurse him.'" It is also possible that the original form is "tuḍārir" with a kasrah on the first rā', and Aban related it from Asim, and this is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. Then "wālidatun" is the subject (fā'il). It is also possible that in "tuḍārar" the word "wālidatun" is the object of a verb in the passive voice (mā lam yusamma fā'iluhu).

It is related from Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he read "lā tuḍārar" with two rā's, the first with a fatha. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' read "tuḍār" with the rā' sukun and lightened. Likewise "lā yuḍār kātib" (Qur'an 2:282). This is unlikely, because when two identical letters come together and both are original, it is not permitted to delete one of them for lightness; there must be either assimilation (idghām) or full pronunciation (iẓhār). It is also related from him (Ibn al-Qa'qa') that he read with sukun and shaddah. It is related from Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan that they read "lā tuḍārir" with a kasrah on the first rā'.

The fifteenth issue: the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And upon the heir is the like of that﴾. It is coordinated with His saying: "and upon the one born to him" (al-mawlud lahu). Scholars differed in interpreting His saying: "and upon the heir is the like of that." Qatadah, al-Suddi, al-Hasan, and Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it refers to the heir of the child if he were to die. Some of them said: his male heirs only are obligated to nurse him, just as the child's father would have been obligated had he been alive. This was said by Mujahid and Ata. Qatadah and others said: it is the heir of the child, whether male or female, and they are obligated to nurse him according to the share of their inheritance from him. This is the view of Ahmad and Ishaq.

Al-Qadi Abu Ishaq Isma'il ibn Ishaq said in his book Ma'ani al-Qur'an: As for Abu Hanifah, he said: the maintenance (nafaqah) and nursing of a young child is obligatory on every relative within the prohibited degrees (dhu rahim mahram). For example, a man has a young nephew through his sister who is in need, and a young paternal cousin who is in need, and he is his heir. The maintenance is obligatory upon the maternal uncle for his sister's son, who does not inherit from him, and it falls away from the paternal cousin for his paternal cousin who is an heir. Abu Ishaq said: They said something that is not in the Book of Allah, and we know of no one who said it. Al-Tabari related from Abu Hanifah and his two companions that they said: the heir who is obligated to nurse is the heir if he is a relative within the prohibited degrees. If he is a paternal cousin or other, who is not a relative within the prohibited degrees, then nothing is obligatory on him.

It was said: the intended meaning is the father's agnatic relatives ('asabah), upon whom the maintenance and clothing are obligatory. Al-Dahhak said: If the child's father dies and the child has property, his nursing is paid from the property. If he has no property, it is taken from the agnatic relatives. If the agnatic relatives have no property, the mother is compelled to nurse him. Qabisah ibn Dhu'ayb, al-Dahhak, and Bashir ibn Nasr, the judge of Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, said: the heir is the child himself, and they interpreted His saying "and upon the heir" as referring to the one born, like what is upon the one to whom he is born, that is, upon him in his property when he inherits from his father, the nursing of himself. Sufyan said: the heir here is the surviving one of the child's two parents after the death of the other. If the father dies, the mother is obligated to provide for the infant if he has no property, and the agnatic relative shares with her in nursing the child according to his share of the inheritance.

Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: If the orphan is poor and has no property, it becomes obligatory upon the ruler (imam) to provide for him from the public treasury (bayt al-mal). If the ruler does not do so, it becomes obligatory upon the Muslims, beginning with those most closely related to him and then those next. The mother is most closely related to him, so it is obligatory upon her to nurse him and provide for him, and she has no claim for repayment from him or from anyone else.

Nursing is obligatory, while maintenance is recommended (istihbab). The basis for the recommendation is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And mothers shall nurse their children for two complete years﴾ (2:233). And it is obligatory upon husbands to provide for them. So when the right to receive it is impossible to collect because of the husband's death or his poverty, the right does not fall away from them. Do you not see that the waiting period ('iddah) is obligatory upon them, while maintenance and housing are upon their husbands? And when maintenance for them is impossible, the waiting period does not fall away from them.

Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim related in al-Asadiyyah from Malik ibn Anas, may Allah have mercy on him, that he said: A man is not obligated to maintain a brother, or a relative, or a kinsman within the prohibited degrees. He said: The saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: "and upon the heir is the like of that" is abrogated (mansukh). Al-Nahhas said: This is the wording of Malik, and neither Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim explained what abrogates it, nor do I know that any of their companions explained it. What seems likely to be the abrogating text for him, and Allah knows best, is that when Allah obligated for the widow, from the property of the deceased husband, maintenance for a year and housing, and then abrogated and lifted that, it was abrogated also for the heir. I say: According to this, the maintenance for the child is from his own property, and nothing from it is upon the heir, as will come.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: His saying "and upon the heir is the like of that," Ibn al-Qasim said from Malik that it is abrogated. This is a statement from which the hearts of the heedless recoil, and in which the minds of the deviant are perplexed, though the matter is simple! The reason is that the earlier scholars among the jurists and exegetes used to call specification (takhsis) abrogation (naskh), because it is the lifting of some of what the general wording includes, by way of leniency. This usage spread on their tongues until it became confusing to those who came after them. The verification of the matter is this: His saying, the Exalted, "and upon the heir is the like of that," refers to what came before. Some people related it to everything mentioned: the obligation of maintenance and the prohibition of harm. Among them is Abu Hanifah among the jurists, and among the early generation, Qatadah, al-Hasan, and a chain going back to Umar. Another group of scholars said: the meaning of His saying, the Exalted, "and upon the heir is the like of that" does not refer to everything mentioned before. It refers only to the prohibition of harm. The meaning is: upon the heir is, regarding the prohibition of harming the mother, the same as what is upon the father. This is the basic position. Whoever claims that the conjunction here returns to everything mentioned before, the burden of proof is upon him.

I say: His statement "and this is the basic principle" means that the pronoun refers to the nearest mentioned antecedent. This is sound, for if he had intended the whole group, namely breastfeeding, maintenance and not causing harm, he would have said, "And upon the heir is the like of these." This shows that it is coordinated with the prohibition of harm. On this reading, all the commentators agreed, as al-Qadi Abd al-Wahhab related, that the meaning is that the mother must not harm her child by refusing to nurse him when the father offers her the standard wage, and that the father must not harm the mother's child by refusing to pay her when the mother offers to nurse him for the standard wage. In that case she has the right to nurse him, because the mother is gentler and more compassionate toward him, and her milk is better for him than the milk of a stranger. Ibn Atiyya said: Malik, may God have mercy on him, all his companions, al-Sha'bi, al-Zuhri, al-Dahhak and a group of scholars said: the intended meaning of "the like of that" is that the heir must not cause harm. As for provision and clothing, nothing of them is obligatory. Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik that the verse included that provision and clothing are upon the heir, but this was abrogated (naskh) by the consensus (ijma') of the community concerning the heir not being harmed, and the disagreement is whether he owes provision and clothing or not. Yahya ibn Ya'mar read "and upon the heirs" in the plural, and this implies generality. If they argue from his words, peace be upon him: "God does not accept charity when a needy relative is present," it is said to them that "relative" is general for every relative, whether a mahram or not. There is no disagreement that directing charity to a relative is preferable, based on his words, peace be upon him: "Give it to the nearest of kin." So the hadith is understood in this way, and there is no proof in it for what they intended. And God knows best.

Al-Nahhas said: As for the one who says "and upon the heir is the like of that" means that he must not cause harm, his statement is good, because people's property is protected and nothing may be taken from it except by a decisive proof. As for the one who says it refers to the heirs of the father, the argument is that the maintenance was upon the father, so his heirs are more entitled to it than the heirs of the son. As for the argument of the one who says it refers to the heirs of the son, he says: just as they inherit from him, they must support them. Al-Nahhas said: Muhammad ibn Jarir used to prefer the view of the one who says that the heir here is the son. Although this is an unusual view, the inference from it is sound and its proof is clear, because his property is more entitled to it.
