The jurists have agreed, except for a few dissenters, that if a man has a young child who has property, and the father is well-off, the father is not obliged to pay for the maintenance or the nursing, and that this comes from the child's property. If it is said: God, mighty and majestic, has said, "And upon the one to whom the child belongs is their provision and clothing according to what is customary," it is answered: this pronoun refers to the feminine, and besides, consensus is a limit on the verse and clarifies it, and no Muslim may depart from it. As for the one who said: "that" refers to whichever of the two parents remains, his argument is that it is not permissible for the mother to neglect her child, since the one who used to support him and her has died. Al-Bukhari gave a chapter heading to refute this view: "Chapter: 'And upon the heir is the like of that'; and whether a woman bears any of it," and he cited the hadith of Umm Salama and Hind. Its meaning is that Umm Salama had sons from Abu Salama and they had no property, so she asked the Prophet, peace be upon him, and he told her that she would have a reward for that. This hadith shows that the maintenance of her sons is not obligatory upon her, for if it had been obligatory she would not have said to the Prophet, peace be upon him: "And I will not leave them." As for the hadith of Hind, the Prophet, peace be upon him, permitted her to take the maintenance for herself and her sons from the father's property, and he did not make it obligatory upon her as he made it obligatory upon the father. From this al-Bukhari inferred that since mothers are not obliged to maintain their children while the fathers are alive, likewise they are not obliged after the fathers die. As for the view of the one who said that maintenance and clothing are due to every mahram relative, his argument is that a man must maintain every mahram relative if he is poor. Al-Nahhas said: This view has been countered by the fact that it is not derived from the Book of God, nor from consensus, nor from a sound Sunnah, and indeed it is not known from any statement other than what we have mentioned. As for the Qur'an, God, mighty and majestic, said: "And upon the heir is the like of that." If maintenance and clothing were due from the heir, then they have contradicted this, for they said: if a man leaves a maternal uncle and a paternal cousin, then the maintenance is upon the maternal uncle and nothing is upon the paternal cousin. This contradicts the explicit text of the Qur'an, because the maternal uncle does not inherit alongside the paternal cousin by anyone's view, and does not inherit alone according to many scholars. What they argued from concerning maintenance for every mahram relative is opposed by most people of knowledge.

Sixteenth: God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And if they both desire weaning﴾. The pronoun in "desire" refers to the two parents.
"Fisal" means weaning from breastfeeding, that is, moving the child from feeding on his mother's milk to other foods. Al-fisal and al-fasl mean weaning, and its root is separation, for it is a separation between the child and the breast. From this the young camel is called al-fasil, because it is separated from its mother.
("by mutual consent from both of them") means before the two years are complete.
("there is no blame upon them both") means in the weaning of him. God, glorified be He, when He made the period of nursing two years, explained that their weaning is weaning, and their separation is separation, and no one has any objection to it. The only exception is when the two parents agree on a period less than that number without harming the child, and that is permitted by this explanation. Qatada said: Nursing was obligatory for two years and weaning before that was forbidden, then it was lightened and nursing for less than two years was permitted by His words: "And if they both desire weaning," and so on. In this is evidence for the permissibility of ijtihad (independent reasoning) in legal rulings, since God permitted the two parents to consult about what leads to the child's welfare, and that rests on their probable judgment rather than certainty and conviction. Tashawur (consultation) means extracting an opinion, and likewise mushawara and mashura, which is like ma' suna (help). "Shurtu al-'asal" means I extracted the honey; "shurtu al-dabba" and "shawwartuha" means I made the animal run to bring out its speed; al-shiwar means household goods because they show to the viewer; al-shara means a man's appearance; and al-ishara means extracting what is in yourself and displaying it.

Seventeenth: God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And if you wish to have your children nursed﴾, meaning for your children other than the mother. This was said by al-Zajjaj. Al-Nahhas said: The construction in Arabic is that you hire a stranger to nurse your children, like the expression "kalahum aw wazanuhum" (they measured for them or weighed for them), meaning they measured out for them or weighed out for them, and the preposition has been dropped because the verb takes two objects, one of which takes a preposition. Sibawayh cited:

"I commanded you to do good, so do what you were commanded,
for I have left you possessing wealth and property."

It is not permissible to say "da'awtu Zaydan" meaning "I called upon Zayd" in the sense of "I called for Zayd," because that leads to confusion, so in this type of usage hearing (the transmitted usage) is what counts.
I say: On this basis the verse contains evidence for permissibility of hiring a wet nurse when the fathers and mothers agree to that. Ikrimah said concerning God's words, "A mother shall not be harmed," that it means the wet nurse, related by Ibn Atiyya. The principle is that every mother is obliged to nurse her child, as God, mighty and majestic, has informed us. He commanded wives to nurse their children and obligated the husbands to provide them with maintenance and clothing while the marriage remains in effect. So if nursing were the father's obligation, He would have mentioned it along with the provision and clothing of the wives. However, Malik, may God have mercy on him, alone among the jurists of the regions, made an exception for the noble women (al-hasiba, women of high lineage), and said: nursing is not obligatory upon her. He thereby removed her from the verse and specified it by one of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), namely acting upon custom ('urf). This is a principle that no one noticed except Malik. The original insight behind it is that this practice existed in the Jahiliyya among people of high lineage; Islam came and did not change it, and the wealthy and high-born continued to free their mothers for enjoyment by handing their infants over to wet nurses, down to his time, and to our time, so we have come to regard it as established law.

Eighteenth: God, the Exalted, said: (when you pay) meaning the fathers, that is, when you pay the wage to the nursing woman, the wet nurse. Sufyan said. Mujahid said: "When you pay the mothers their wages according to the amount they have nursed up to the time of the desire for wet-nursing." The seven readers, six of them, read "ma ataytum" with the meaning "what you gave." Ibn Kathir read "ataytum" with the meaning "what you came with and did," as Zuhayr said:

"Whatever good they did, it is only
what the fathers of their fathers inherited before them."

Qatada and al-Zuhri said: the meaning is "when you pay what you had come to, of the desire for wet-nursing," that is, each of the two parents pays and consents, and this was by agreement between them, with a good intention and a desire for a fair matter. On this possibility, "when you pay" addresses both men and women, and on the two earlier interpretations the address is to men. Abu Ali said: the meaning is, "when you pay what you gave of its price or its provision," so the object was omitted and the pronoun was put in its place, so the construction was: "what you gave it," then the pronoun was dropped from the relative clause. On this interpretation the address is to men, because they are the ones who give the wage for nursing. Abu Ali said: It is possible that "ma" is a verbal noun, meaning "when you pay the coming," and the meaning is as in the first, but the one who drops the attributive phrase (the source of the idea) and then drops the pronoun can do without it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 234 (part 1 of 4):

There are twenty-five issues in this verse. The first is His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind﴾. When He, may He be exalted and majestic, mentioned the waiting period of divorce, and the mention of breastfeeding followed it, He also mentioned the waiting period of widowhood, lest it be thought that the waiting period of widowhood is like the waiting period of divorce. "Those who" means the men of you who die.

(﻿﻿﻿"Leave wives behind") means they leave wives, that is, they have wives, so the wives (﻿﻿﻿"must wait"). Al-Zajjaj said this, and al-Nahhas preferred it. Omitting the subject in speech is common, as in His saying: ﴿Shall I tell you of something worse than that? It is the Fire﴾ [[See vol. 12, p. 95.]], meaning: it is the Fire. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: the implied meaning is "those of you who die and leave wives behind, who must wait after them," and it is like your saying: "Samn (ghee) is two manas for a dirham," meaning two manas of it for a dirham. It was also said that the implied meaning is "and the wives of those of you who die must wait," so the expression came in the utmost brevity. Al-Mahdawi related from Sibawayh that the meaning is: "And among what is recited to you, those who die." Some grammarians of Kufa said: the predicate of "those who" is omitted, and the intent is to inform about their wives, that they must wait; and this wording is informing about the legislation in one of the two views, as has preceded.

The second issue: this verse concerns the waiting period of a woman whose husband has died. Its apparent meaning is general, but its meaning is specific. Al-Mahdawi related from some scholars that the verse included pregnant women, and then this was abrogated (naskh) by His saying: ﴿And for pregnant women, their term is until they deliver their burden﴾ [[See vol. 18, p. 162.]]. Most scholars hold that this verse abrogates His, may He be exalted and majestic, saying: ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind, [let there be] a bequest for their wives, provision for a year without eviction﴾, because people in the early period of Islam, when a man died and left his wife pregnant, his husband would bequeath to her a year's maintenance and lodging, so long as she did not leave and marry. Then this was abrogated by four months and ten days, and by inheritance. Some people said: there is no abrogation in this, rather it is a reduction from the year, like the prayer of the traveler, when it was reduced from four rak'ahs to two, and this was not abrogation. This is a clear error, because when her ruling was that she observe a year if she did not leave, and if she left she was not prevented, then this was removed and she was obligated to the waiting period of four months and ten days. This is abrogation, and the traveler's prayer is not of this kind at all. 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "Prayer was prescribed as two rak'ahs, two rak'ahs; then it was increased for the prayer of residence, and the prayer of travel was kept as it was." This will come later [[See vol. 5, p. 351.]].

The third issue: the waiting period of a pregnant woman whose husband has died is the delivery of her child, according to the majority of scholars. It is reported from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn 'Abbas that the complete end of her waiting period is the later of the two terms, and Sahnun of our scholars preferred this. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he retracted this.

The proof of those who (...) what was reported from 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas, an attempt to reconcile, is His saying: ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind, who must wait by themselves for four months and ten days﴾, and between His saying: ﴿And for pregnant women, their term is until they deliver their burden﴾. That is because if she observes the longer of the two terms, she has acted in accordance with both verses; but if she observes the waiting period by delivering the burden, she has abandoned acting by the verse of the waiting period of widowhood. Reconciliation is preferable to preference (tarjih), by the consensus of the people of usul al-fiqh (legal theory).

This is a good line of reasoning, were it not for what disturbs it: the hadith of Subay'a al-Aslamiyya, that she gave birth a few nights after her husband's death, and that she mentioned this to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he ordered her to marry. It was recorded in the Sahih.

So the hadith makes clear that His saying: ﴿And for pregnant women, their term is until they deliver their burden﴾ is to be understood in its generality regarding divorced women and women whose husbands have died; and that the waiting period of widowhood is specific to non-pregnant women of both categories. This is reinforced by the saying of Ibn Mas'ud: "Whoever wishes, I will invoke a curse upon him, that the verse of the shorter term for women (al-nisa' al-qusra) was revealed after the verse of the waiting period of widowhood."

Our scholars said: The apparent meaning of his words is that it abrogates it, but that is not what he meant. He only meant that it specifies it (takhsis), for it excluded some of its applications.

Likewise, the hadith of Subay'a is later than the waiting period of widowhood, because the story of Subay'a was after the Farewell Pilgrimage. Her husband was Sa'd ibn Khawla, from the Banu 'Amir ibn Lu'ayy, and he was among those who witnessed Badr. He died in Makkah at that time while she was pregnant, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) lamented for him, since he died in Makkah. She gave birth about half a month after him.

Al-Bukhari said: "forty nights."

Muslim related from the hadith of 'Umar ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Arqam that Subay'a asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about this, and she said: "He gave me a ruling that I had become lawfully free when I gave birth to my child, and he ordered me to marry if I wished."

Ibn Shihab said: "I see no harm in her marrying when she gives birth, even if she is still in her bleeding; but her husband does not approach her until she is purified. This is the view of the majority of scholars and the leading jurists."

Al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i and Hammad said: "A woman in postpartum bleeding (nifas) is not to be married while she is still in her postpartum bleeding."

So they stipulated two conditions: the delivery of the child, and purification from postpartum bleeding.

The hadith is a proof against them, and they have no proof in His saying (in the hadith): "When she had been freed (taʿallat) from her postpartum bleeding, she adorned herself for the suitors" [[Ibn al-Athir said: "It is also narrated as 'ta'allat,' that is, she rose up and became pure; and it may be that it comes from the saying: 'the man recovered from his illness' (ta'allā al-rajul min 'ilatihi), meaning he was healed, that is, she came out of her postpartum bleeding and was safe." Muslim, vol. 4, p. 201.]], as in the Sahih of Muslim and Abu Dawud. For "ta'allat," even if its root is "she became pure from her postpartum bleeding," according to what al-Khalil said, it may be that what is meant here is that she was freed from the pains of her postpartum period, that is, she was relieved of her pains.

Even if it is granted that its meaning is what al-Khalil said, there is no proof in it. The proof is only in his, peace be upon him, saying to Subay'a: "You have become lawfully free at the time you gave birth," where he attached lawful freedom to the time of delivery and made it dependent on it, and did not say "when your bleeding stops" or "when you become pure." So what the majority said is correct.

The fourth issue: there is no disagreement among scholars that the term of every pregnant divorced woman, whether her husband has the right to revoke her or not, and whether she is free, a slave-girl, a mudabbara (a slave promised freedom at her master's death), or a mukatiba (a slave under a contract of self-purchase), is that she must deliver her child.

They differed about the term of the pregnant widow, as has preceded. All agree without disagreement among them that if a man died and left a pregnant wife, and four months and ten days passed, she is not lawfully free until she gives birth. Thus it is known that the intended term is delivery.

The fifth issue: His saying: ﴿They must wait﴾. Tarabbus (waiting) means: to be patient and restrain oneself from marriage, and to refrain from leaving the marital residence; and that is by not separating from it at night.

Allah did not mention housing for the widow in His Book as He mentioned it for the divorced woman in His saying: ﴿Lodge them﴾. There is nothing in the wording of the waiting period in the Book of Allah that indicates mourning (ihdad). He only said: ﴿They must wait﴾, so the Sunnah explained all of that.

The hadiths from the Prophet (ﷺ) are consistent that waiting in widowhood is only with mourning, which is refraining from adornment, wearing dyed and beautiful clothing, perfume, and the like. This is the view of the majority of scholars.

Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: "Mourning is nothing; she only waits away from the husband, and she may adorn herself and use perfume." This is weak, because it contradicts the Sunnah, as we will explain, Allah willing.

It is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to al-Furay'a bint Malik ibn Sinan, who was a widow: "Remain in your house until the decreed term reaches its end." She said: "So I observed the waiting period in it for four months and ten days." This is an authentic hadith, which Malik related from Sa'd ibn Ishaq ibn Ka'b ibn 'Ujra. Malik, al-Thawri, Wuhayb ibn Khalid [in the originals: "Wahb," and the correction follows Sharh al-Muwatta and Tahdhib al-Tahdhib], Hammad ibn Zayd, 'Isa ibn Yunus, a large number of others, Ibn 'Uyayna, al-Qattan and Shu'ba related it from him. Malik related it from Ibn Shihab, and that is sufficient for you. Al-Baji said: "No one related it from him except him." 'Uthman ibn 'Affan acted upon it. Abu 'Umar said: "He judged by it regarding the waiting period of a widow in her house. It is a well-known and famous hadith among the scholars of the Hijaz and Iraq, that a widow must observe her waiting period in her house and not leave it. This is the view of the majority of jurists in the regions of the Hijaz, Syria, Iraq and Egypt."

Dawud used to hold that a widow is not required to observe her waiting period in her house, and she may observe it wherever she wishes, because housing was only mentioned in the Qur'an regarding divorced women. Among his arguments was that the matter is one of disagreement.

They said: "This hadith is only transmitted by a woman not known for carrying knowledge. Making housing obligatory is establishing a ruling, and rulings are not obligatory except by an explicit text of the Book of Allah, or the Sunnah, or consensus."

Abu 'Umar said: "As for the Sunnah, it is established, praise be to Allah. As for consensus, it is unnecessary given the Sunnah, because when disagreement arises over a matter, the authority is in the view that the Sunnah supports. And success is from Allah."

It is reported from 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, Jabir and 'A'isha the same as the view of Dawud, and Jabir ibn Zayd, 'Ata' and al-Hasan al-Basri also held it.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "Allah only said: ﴿They must wait by themselves for four months and ten days﴾, and He did not say: 'they must observe the waiting period in their houses'; and she may observe it wherever she wishes." This is also reported from Abu Hanifa.

'Abd al-Razzaq mentioned, saying: Ma'mar related to us from al-Zuhri from 'Urwa, who said: 'A'isha went out with her sister Umm Kulthum, when her husband Talha ibn 'Ubayd Allah was killed and left her, to Makkah for 'Umra, and she used to give legal opinions to the widows that they may go out during their waiting period.

He said: al-Thawri related to us from 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Umar that he heard al-Qasim ibn Muhammad say: "The people rejected that from her."

He said: Ma'mar related to us from al-Zuhri, who said: "Those who seek leniency among widows took the view of 'A'isha, and the people of caution and resolve took the view of Ibn 'Umar."

In the Muwatta': that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab used to send back widows from al-Bayda', preventing them from pilgrimage.

This from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, was an exercise of independent judgment (ijtihad), because he held that the woman's observing the waiting period in the house of her deceased husband was binding on her, and that this is what the Qur'an and the Sunnah require, so it is not permissible for her to go out for hajj or 'umra until her waiting period ends.

Malik said: "She is sent back, as long as she has not entered the state of ihram."

The sixth issue: If the husband owns the dwelling outright, the wife observes her waiting period in it. Most jurists hold this: Malik, Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and others, on the basis of the hadith of al-Furay'a.

As for whether it is permissible to sell the house if it was the property of the deceased and the heirs wish to sell it, the view of the majority of our companions is that this is permissible, and the wife's waiting period is a condition for it.

Ibn al-Qasim said: "Because she has more right to housing than the creditors."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 234 (part 2 of 4):

Muhammad ibn al-Hakam said:
The sale is invalid, because she may come to doubt (that she is pregnant), and then her waiting period would be prolonged.

The reasoning of Ibn al-Qasim:
The general rule is safety, and doubt is rare, and that does not affect the invalidity of contracts. If the sale took place with this condition and she then came to doubt, Malik said in the Kitab of Muhammad:
She has the greater right to remain (in the house) until the doubt is resolved. It is more beloved to us that the buyer have the option of cancelling the sale or upholding it, and he does not recover anything, because he entered knowing the customary waiting period. But if the sale took place on the condition that the doubt be removed, it would be invalid.

Sahnun said:
The buyer has no claim, even if the doubt extends to five years, because he entered upon the waiting period, and the waiting period may be five years. Abu Zayd related something similar from Ibn al-Qasim.

Seventh: If the husband had the right of residence without ownership of the property itself, she has the right of residence during the waiting period. This differs from Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i, based on his saying, upon him be peace, to al-Furay'a, and he knew that her husband did not own the dwelling itself:
"Remain in your house until the prescribed term reaches its end."
It cannot be said that the house was hers, which is why he said to her, "Remain in your house," for Ma'mar related from al-Zuhri that she mentioned to the Prophet ﷺ that her husband had been killed, and that he had left her in a dwelling that was not hers, and she asked his permission, and he mentioned the hadith.
Our argument from the standpoint of meaning is that he left a house whose residence he owned with a full right, with no obligation upon him concerning it, so it is necessary that the wife observe her waiting period in it, the basis of which is when he owns its ownership outright.

Eighth: This applies if he had paid the rent. As for if he had not paid the rent, what is in the Mudawwana is:
that she has no right of residence in the property of the deceased, even if he was wealthy, because her right is attached only to what he owns of residence with full ownership, and what he has not paid the consideration for, he has not owned with full ownership; he only owns the consideration that is in his hand. She has no right to that except through inheritance, not through residence, because that is property and not residence.
Muhammad related from Malik that the rent is binding upon the deceased in his property.

Ninth: His saying, upon him be peace, to al-Furay'a:
"Remain in your house until the prescribed term reaches its end" may be understood to mean that he ordered her to do so when her husband had already paid the rent of the dwelling, or he had resided in it until his death, or the people of the house permitted her to observe the waiting period in it, with or without rent, or whatever else God wills of such matters, by which he judged that remaining there is obligatory for her until her waiting period ends.

Tenth: They differ concerning a woman to whom the news of her husband's death comes while she is in a house other than her husband's house. Malik ibn Anas ordered her to return to his dwelling and residence, and this was related from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz [may Allah be pleased with him [[in h.]]].
Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and al-Nakha'i said:
She observes the waiting period wherever the news reaches her, and she does not leave that place until the waiting period ends.
Ibn al-Mundhir said:
The statement of Malik is correct, except that if the husband moved her to another place, then she must remain in that place.

Eleventh: She is permitted to go out for her needs from the time people disperse in the morning until the time they quiet down after the 'atama (night prayer), and she must not spend the night except in that house.

In al-Bukhari and Muslim, from Umm 'Atiyya, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:
"A woman must not mourn over a deceased person for more than three days, except over a husband, for four months and ten days. She must not wear dyed clothing except 'asb cloth [[al-'asb (with a fatha on the 'ayn and a sukun on the sad):
from the striped Yemeni cloths, whose yarn is tied, then dyed, then woven dyed, so it comes out patterned, because what was tied remains white and was not dyed. It is only the warp that is tied, not the weft.]], and she must not apply kohl, and she must not touch perfume except a little [[al-nabdha: a small amount.
al-qust and al-adhfar: two kinds of incense.
Nabdha is in the accusative as an exception, with the adverbial phrase placed before it (Sharh Muslim).]] of qust or adhfar."

And in the hadith of Umm Habiba:
"It is not lawful for a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day to mourn over a deceased person for more than three days, except over a husband, for four months and ten days," and the hadith continues.

Al-Ihdad (mourning):
It is the woman's abandonment of all adornment, of clothing, perfume, jewelry, kohl, and dyeing with henna, for as long as she is in her waiting period, because adornment invites husbands, so she is prohibited from it in order to cut off the means (to what is forbidden), and to protect the sanctities of Allah the Exalted from being violated. Oiling a woman's head with olive oil or sesame oil is not counted as perfume at all.
It is said:
A woman who is a mourner (haddad) and one who is mourning (muhiddah).
Al-Asma'i said:
We do not know "haddat."
The subject of "la yahillu" is the verbal noun that can be formed from "tuhiddu" with the implied "an", as if he had said: "al-ihdad" (mourning).

Twelfth: His, upon him be peace, describing the woman as believing indicates the soundness of one of the two opinions in our school concerning the Christian (or Jewish) widow, that she has no mourning obligation. This is the view of Ibn Kinana and Ibn Nafi', and Ashhab related it from Malik, and Abu Hanifa and Ibn al-Mundhir said so. It was also related from Ibn al-Qasim that she is obligated to mourn, like the Muslim woman, and this is the view of al-Layth, al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr, and most of our companions, because it is one of the rulings of the waiting period, so the Christian woman is bound by it just as a Muslim woman is bound by residence and the waiting period.

Thirteenth: In his, upon him be peace, saying:
"More than three days, except over a husband" is evidence of the prohibition for Muslim women to mourn over anyone other than their husbands for more than three days, and the permissibility of mourning over them for three days, beginning with the count from the night that follows (the death), until the end of the third (day). If a close relative dies in the remainder of a day [[in h.: its day or its night.]] or a night, she disregards it and counts from the following night.

Fourteenth: This hadith, by the force of its generality, includes all wives whose husbands have died, so it includes slave women and free women, adults and minors, and this is the position of the majority of scholars.
Abu Hanifa held that there is no mourning obligation for a slave woman or a minor girl, as related from him by the judge Abu al-Walid al-Baji.
Ibn al-Mundhir said:
As for the slave wife, she is included among the wives and in the generality of the reports, and this is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr, and the people of opinion. I know of no disagreement on this from anyone, and I do not know that they differ regarding mourning over an umm walad when her master dies, because she is not a wife, and the hadiths only concern wives.
Al-Baji said:
A minor girl, if she is of an age to understand commands and prohibitions and to comply with what is set for her, she is ordered to do so. If she is too young to understand any of that, Ibn Muzayn related from Isa that her family should keep her away from everything a grown woman avoids, and that is obligatory for her.
The evidence for the obligation of mourning upon a minor girl is what is related: that a woman asked the Prophet ﷺ about her daughter whose husband had died, and her eye was sore; may she apply kohl to it?
The Prophet ﷺ said, "No," twice or three times, each time saying "No," and he did not ask about her age. Had the ruling differed by youth and age, he would have asked about her age in order to clarify the ruling, and delaying clarification in such a matter is not permissible. Furthermore, anyone obligated to observe the waiting period due to death is obligated to mourn, like the adult woman.

Fifteenth: Ibn al-Mundhir said:
I know of no disagreement that dyeing (with henna) is included in the adornment that is forbidden.
They agreed that it is not permissible for her to wear dyed clothing or saffron-dyed clothing, except what is dyed black. Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, Malik, and al-Shafi'i permitted this, while al-Zuhri disliked it.
Al-Zuhri said:
She must not wear 'asb cloth, and this contradicts the hadith.
In the Mudawwana, Malik said:
She must not wear fine Yemeni 'asb cloth, but he allowed the thicker kind.
Ibn al-Qasim said:
Because fine 'asb is in the same position as dyed clothing, and she may wear fine and thick clothing of silk, linen, or cotton.
Ibn al-Mundhir said:
Every scholar I know of permitted wearing white garments.
The judge Iyad said:
al-Shafi'i held that every dye that is a form of adornment, which the mourner may not touch, whether fine or thick, is forbidden.
Similar to this is what the judge Abd al-Wahhab said:
Every color with which women adorn themselves for their husbands, the mourner must refrain from it.
Some of our later shaykhs prohibited fine white that is used for adornment, and likewise the choice black.
Ibn al-Mawwaz related from Malik:
She must not wear jewelry, even if it is of iron. In general, anything a woman wears in the manner in which jewelry is worn for beautification, the mourner must not wear it.
Our companions did not specify pearls, jacinths, and emeralds, though they fall within the meaning of jewelry.
And Allah knows best.

Sixteenth: The people have agreed on the obligation of mourning upon a widow, except al-Hasan, who said:
"It is not obligatory," and he argued with what 'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad ibn al-Had related from Asma' bint Umays, who said:
When Ja'far ibn Abi Talib was struck down, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me: "Mourn [[tasalli: wear black mourning garments, which are called al-salab (like kitab).]] for three days, then do what you wish."
Ibn al-Mundhir said:
Al-Hasan al-Basri, among all the scholars, did not hold that mourning was required, and he said:
A woman divorced three times and a widow may both apply kohl, dye, and do whatever they wish.
But the reports from the Prophet ﷺ concerning mourning are established, and there is no option for anyone who has received them except submission. Perhaps al-Hasan had not received them, or he had received them and interpreted them in light of the hadith of Asma' bint Umays, that she asked the Prophet ﷺ permission to mourn over Ja'far, who was her husband, and he permitted her three days, then after three days sent to her that she should purify herself and apply kohl.
Ibn al-Mundhir said: The scholars have rejected this hadith on several grounds, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal used to say:
"This anomalous hadith is not to be acted upon," and Ishaq said likewise.

**Seventeenth issue:** Malik and al-Shafi'i held that there is no *ihdad* (mourning, abstaining from adornment) for a divorced woman, whether her divorce was revocable (*raj'iyya*) or irrevocable (*ba'in*), whether it was one divorce or more. This is also the view of Rabi'a and 'Ata'. The Kufans, namely Abu Hanifa and his companions, al-Thawri, al-Hasan ibn Hayy, Abu Thawr and Abu 'Ubayd, held that a woman divorced three times must observe *ihdad*. This is also the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Sulayman ibn Yasar, Ibn Sirin and al-Hakam ibn 'Uyayna. Al-Hakam said: "It is more emphatic and more severe for her than for a woman whose husband has died." Another reason given on the basis of meaning is that both are in a *'idda* (waiting period) by which lineage is protected. Al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq said: "The precaution is that the divorced woman should avoid adornment." Ibn al-Mundhir said: The saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), "It is not lawful for a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day to mourn for a dead person for more than three days, except for a husband, for four months and ten [days]," is evidence that a woman divorced three times, while the divorcer is alive, does not observe *ihdad*.

**Eighteenth issue:** The scholars are unanimous that if a man divorces his wife with a divorce that allows him to take her back (*raj'a*), and then dies before the *'idda* ends, she must observe the *'idda* of widowhood, and she inherits from him. They differed regarding the *'idda* of a woman divorced three times during the husband's final illness. One group said she observes the *'idda* of divorce. This is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ya'qub, Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Thawr. Ibn al-Mundhir said: "This is what we say, because Allah, exalted is He, made the *'idda* of divorced women the menstrual periods (*quru'*), and they have unanimously agreed that if a woman divorced three times died, the one who divorced her would not inherit from her, because she is no longer his wife, and if she is not his wife, then he is not her husband." Al-Thawri said: She observes the longer of the two *'idda*s. Al-Nu'man (Abu Hanifa) and Muhammad said: She observes four months and ten [days], completing three menstrual cycles during it.

**Nineteenth issue:** They differed regarding a woman who learns of her husband's death or his divorce of her. One group said: The *'idda*, for both divorce and death, begins from the day he dies or divorces her. This is the view of Ibn 'Umar, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas. Masruq, 'Ata' and a group of the Successors (*tabi'un*) also said so, and it is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu 'Ubayd, al-Thawri, Abu Thawr, the people of opinion (*ashab al-ra'y*) and Ibn al-Mundhir. There is a second view, that her *'idda* begins from the day the news reaches her. This view is reported from 'Ali, and al-Hasan al-Basri, Qatada, 'Ata' al-Khurasani and Jalas ibn al-'Aziz also said so. [They said:] If a proof (*bayyina*) is established, then her *'idda* begins from the day of 'Amr. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and 'Umar ibn 'Abd [al-'Aziz] said: [The *'idda* begins from the day] he died or divorced her; but if no proof is established, then from the day the news comes to her. The correct view is the first, because Allah, exalted is He, linked the *'idda* to death or divorce. Also, if she knew of his death and abandoned *ihdad*, she would be shortening the *'idda* [in the text of Z: "expired"]; so if she abandons it without knowledge, that is lighter. Do you not see that a minor's *'idda* ends and there is no *ihdad* for her? Moreover, the scholars have unanimously agreed that if she were pregnant and did not know of the husband's divorce or death, and then gave birth, her *'idda* would be complete. There is no difference between this issue and the disputed issue. The argument of those who say the *'idda* begins from the day the news reaches her is that the *'idda* is an act of worship through abandoning adornment, and this is not valid except with intention and purpose, and purpose can only exist after knowledge. And Allah knows best.

**Twentieth issue:** The *'idda* of death applies to the free woman, the slave woman, the minor, the adult, the girl who has not reached menstruation, the woman who has menstruated, the woman past menstruation, and the Scripture-follower (*kitabiyya*), whether or not she has been consummated with, provided she is not pregnant. [The *'idda* of all of them, except the slave woman,] is four months and ten days, due to the generality of the verse in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They shall wait by themselves for four months and ten [days]﴾. The *'idda* of a slave woman whose husband has died is two months and five nights. Ibn al-'Arabi said: It is half the *'idda* of the free woman, by consensus, except what is reported from al-Asamm, who equated the free woman and the slave woman in this, but the consensus had already preceded him, and because of his deafness he did not hear it. Al-Baji said: We know of no disagreement on this except what is reported from Ibn Sirin, and it is not established from him that he said: Her *'idda* is the *'idda* of the free woman. I say: The view of al-Asamm is sound from the standpoint of reasoning, because the verses concerning the *'idda* of death and divorce, [specified by] months and menstrual periods, are general regarding the slave woman and the free woman. So the *'idda* of the free woman and the slave woman is the same according to this reasoning, since generalities do not distinguish between the free woman and the slave woman, and just as the slave woman and the free woman are equal in marriage, so they are equal in the *'idda*. And Allah knows best. Ibn al-'Arabi said: It is reported from Malik that the Scripture-follower observes three menstrual cycles, since by them the womb is cleared. This is extremely corrupt on his part, because he excluded her from the generality of the verse of death, while she is included in it, and he included her in the generality of the verse of divorce, while she is not included in it. [This is Ibn al-'Arabi's expression as it appears in *Ahkam al-Quran*. It appears disordered in the originals.] I say: The rule in the *Mudawwana* that there is no *'idda* for a woman who was not consummated with is based on this, because her womb's clearance is known. This implies that she may marry a Muslim or someone else immediately after his death, because if she has no *'idda* for death and no *istibra'* (ascertaining that the womb is clear) for consummation, then she is lawful for husbands.

**Twenty-first issue:** They differed regarding the *'idda* of an umm walad (a slave woman who bore her master's child) when her master dies. One group said: Her *'idda* is four months and ten [days]. This was said by a group of the Successors, among them Sa'id, al-Zuhri, al-Hasan al-Basri and others, and this is the view of al-Awza'i and Ishaq. Abu Dawud and al-Daraqutni reported from Qabisa ibn Dhu'ayb, from 'Amr ibn al-'As, who said: "Do not confuse for us the sunna of our Prophet (ﷺ): the *'idda* of a woman whose husband has died is four months and ten [days]," meaning concerning the umm walad. This is the wording of Abu Dawud. Al-Daraqutni said: It is *mawquf* (stopping at a Companion), and this is the correct view. It is *mursal* (with a missing link), because Qabisa did not hear from 'Amr. Ibn al-Mundhir said: Ahmad and Abu 'Ubayd weakened this hadith. It is reported from 'Ali and Ibn Mas'ud that her *'idda* is three menstrual cycles. This is the view of 'Ata', Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Sufyan al-Thawri and the people of opinion. They said: Because it is an *'idda* that is obligatory during a state of freedom, it must be a complete *'idda*, its origin being the *'idda* of the free woman. Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Abu Thawr said: Her *'idda* is one menstrual cycle, and this is the view of Ibn 'Umar. It is reported from Tawus that her *'idda* is half the *'idda* of a free woman whose husband has died, and Qatada said so. Ibn al-Mundhir said: I say what Ibn 'Umar said, because it is the least of what has been said on this, and there is no sunna to follow in it nor a consensus to rely upon. Their disagreement about her *'idda* upon manumission is the same as upon death, except that al-Awza'i made her *'idda* upon manumission three menstrual cycles. I say: The soundest of these views is the view of Malik, because Allah, glorified is He, said: ﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods﴾. So He made the waiting for menstrual periods conditional upon it being after divorce, and thereby it is excluded that it be after anything else. And He said: ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind shall wait by themselves for four months and ten [days]﴾. So He linked the obligation of this to the waiting woman being a wife, which indicates that the slave woman differs from her. Also, this is a slave woman who has been lawfully had by right of ownership (*milk al-yamin*), so her *istibra'* is one menstrual cycle, its origin being the slave woman.

**Twenty-second issue:** If this is established, is the *'idda* of an umm walad a pure *istibra'* or an *'idda*? What Abu Muhammad mentioned in his *Mu'ina* is that the menstrual cycle is an *istibra'* and not an *'idda*. In the *Mudawwana*, the umm walad is subject to the *'idda*, and her *'idda* is one menstrual cycle, like the *'idda* of the free woman, three menstrual cycles. The benefit of the disagreement is that if we say it is an *'idda*, Malik said: "I do not like that you make an arrangement with anyone who would marry her until she has had a menstrual cycle." Ibn al-Qasim said: "It has reached me from him that he said: She should not spend the night except in her house." Thus he gave the period of her *istibra'* the ruling of the *'idda*.

**Twenty-third issue:** The scholars unanimously agree that the maintenance (*nafaqa*) of a woman divorced three times, or of a woman divorced in a revocable divorce whom the husband may take back, if she is pregnant, is obligatory, due to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they are pregnant, then spend upon them until they give birth to their burden﴾. [See vol. 18, p. 166.] They differed regarding the obligation of maintenance for a pregnant woman whose husband has died. One group said: She has no maintenance. This was said by Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, 'Ata', al-Hasan, 'Ikrima, 'Abd al-Malik ibn Ya'la, Yahya al-Ansari, Rabi'a, Malik, Ahmad and Ishaq, and Abu 'Ubayd reported this from the people of opinion. There is a second view, that she has maintenance from the entire estate. This view is reported from 'Ali and 'Abd Allah, and Ibn 'Umar, Shurayh, Ibn Sirin, al-Sha'bi, Abu al-'Aliya, al-Nakha'i, Jalas ibn 'Amr, Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman, Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani, Sufyan al-Thawri and Abu 'Ubayd also said so. Ibn al-Mundhir said: I say what the first view says, because they have unanimously agreed that the maintenance of everyone whom one is compelled to maintain while he is alive, such as his young children, his wife and his parents, falls away from him. Likewise, the maintenance of a pregnant woman from among his wives falls away from him. Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad said: Because the maintenance of the fetus is not an established debt, so that it would attach to his property after his death. The proof is that it falls away from him in case of poverty, so its falling away by death is more fitting and more certain.

**Twenty-fourth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿four months and ten [days]﴾. The scholars differed concerning the four months and the ten [days], which Allah made the appointed term for the *'idda* of a woman whose husband has died: whether a menstrual cycle is required within them or not. Some said: She is not cleared if she is one who can be had, except by a menstrual cycle that she has within the four months and ten [days]; otherwise she is *mustariba* (one in whom doubt is possible). Others said: She is not obliged to more than four months and ten [days], unless she herself has a clear doubt, because in this period menstruation necessarily occurs in most women's cases, unless the woman is one who does not menstruate, or one who knows of herself, or is known, that her menses do not come to her except after more than this period.

**Twenty-fifth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and ten [days]﴾. Waki' reported from Abu Ja'far al-Razi, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, from Abu al-'Aliya, that he was asked: "Why were the ten [days] added to the four months?" He said: "Because the soul is breathed into the fetus during them." This will come in the chapter on Hajj, if Allah wills [see vol. 12, p. 6 onwards]. Al-Asma'i said: "It is said that the offspring of every pregnant woman kicks in the middle of her pregnancy, so she is *murkid* (one who has been kicked)." Someone else said: "She kicked, so she is *murkida*," and he recited:

*"A mare that kicks, pure-bred, whose sire is [a noble stallion],*
*For her, the foal and the colt are honored (or: pampered)."*

[The verse is by Aws ibn Ghalfa' al-Hujaymi, describing a mare. *Sarihi* is ascribed to *al-Sarih*, a famous stallion of the Arab horses.]
(From *Lisan al-Arab*.)

Al-Khattabi said: His saying "and ten" means, God knows best, ten days with their nights. Al-Mubarrad said: The word "ten" is feminine only because what is meant is the period ('ashr muddat), the meaning being ten periods, each period consisting of a day and a night. The night together with its day is a known period of time.

It was also said: [the number] was not stated as "ten" (masculine) in order to give precedence to the rule for the nights, since the night precedes the day, and the days are included within them. "And ten" is lighter in pronunciation, so the nights take precedence over the days when they are combined in reckoning, because months begin with the night at the sighting of the new moon. When the first night of the month comes, the night takes precedence. You say, "We fasted five of the month," and the nights are given precedence even though the fasting is done during the day.

Malik, al-Shafi'i and the Kufans held that what is meant by them is days and nights. Ibn al-Mundhir said: If someone contracted marriage with her on this view after four months and ten nights had passed, the contract would be void until the tenth day had passed.

Some jurists held that when four months and ten nights have passed for her, she becomes lawful for marriage to others. This is because they regarded the 'iddah (waiting period) as unspecified, so they gave precedence to the feminine form and interpreted it as nights. This view was held by al-Awza'i among the jurists and Abu Bakr al-Asamm among the theologians. It is also reported from Ibn Abbas that he recited "four months and ten nights."

God the Exalted said: ﴿Then when they have reached their term, there is no blame on you for what they do with themselves in an honourable manner, and God is Aware of what you do.﴾ On this verse there are three issues.

The first: God attributed the term (ajal) to them, since it is a fixed period set for their affairs, and it refers to the completion of the 'iddah.

The second: His saying ﴿there is no blame on you﴾ is addressed to all people, but the responsibility for enforcing this ruling falls upon the rulers and the guardians (awliya').

"What they do" refers to remarriage and what is less than it, such as adornment and abandoning mourning (ihdad).

"In an honourable manner" means in accordance with what the Law has permitted, such as choosing their husbands and fixing the dower, but not conducting the contract itself, since that is a right of the guardians, as has already been mentioned.

The third: This verse is evidence that guardians have the right to prevent women from displaying themselves (tabarruj) and from making themselves visible to a husband during the 'iddah. It also refutes Ishaq's view that when a divorced woman enters the third menstrual period (hayd) and the blood stops, she is separated, and the return (raj'ah) of her former husband ends, but she may not marry until she performs the ritual bath (ghusl). It is also reported from Shurayk that her husband has the right of return as long as she has not bathed, even after twenty years. God the Exalted said: ﴿Then when they have reached their term, there is no blame on you for what they do with themselves,﴾ and reaching the term here means the completion of the 'iddah by her entering the blood of the third menstrual period. He did not mention a ritual bath. Therefore, when her 'iddah is complete, she becomes lawful for marriage to others, and there is no blame on her for what she does in this respect.

As for the hadith from Ibn Abbas, if it is authentic, it may be understood as referring to a recommendation (istihbab), and God knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 235 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you imply in your proposal of marriage to women﴾ up to His saying (ma'ruf). In it are nine issues.

The first issue: His saying, ﴿there is no blame (junah)﴾, meaning there is no sin. The junah is sin, and this is the more correct usage in the Shari'ah. It was said: rather, it is a burdensome matter, and this is the more correct usage in the language. Al-Shammakh said:

When she climbs with her rider over a rugged ground, he remembers what he has of junah.

His saying, ﴿upon you for what you imply﴾: the address is to all people, and the intended ruling concerns a man who has in his mind to marry a woman in her waiting period (iddah) of widowhood. There is no blame upon you for implying a proposal during the waiting period of death. Ta'ridh (implication) is the opposite of tasrih (explicit statement). It is conveying a meaning through something that may bear that meaning and other meanings. It derives from 'ard al-shay', meaning its side, as if one circles around the matter without disclosing it. It was also said that it derives from your saying 'arradtu al-rajul, meaning I presented him with a gift. In a hadith: a group of Muslims presented (arradu) the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and Abu Bakr with white garments, meaning they gave them gifts. So the one who speaks by implication conveys to his counterpart words whose meaning is understood.

The second issue: Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the community (ummah) has agreed that speaking to a woman in her waiting period with what is explicit about her marriage, or an alert toward it, is not permitted. Likewise the community has agreed that speaking with her with what is sexual, or mention of intercourse, or an incitement to it, is not permitted, and similar things. Anything other than that is permitted. And how close to explicitness is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to Fatimah bint Qays: "Stay at the house of Umm Shurayk, and do not get ahead of me by yourself." Implicit proposal to a woman in revocable divorce (raj'iyyah) is not permitted by consensus, because she is like a wife. As for the woman in the waiting period of final separation (bayn), the sound view is that implicit proposal to her is permitted. And Allah knows best. Many expressions have been reported in explaining ta'ridh, and their sum returns to two categories. The first: that he mentions it to her guardian, saying to him, "Do not get ahead of me in her." The second: that he indicates it to her directly without an intermediary, saying to her: "I wish to marry," or "Indeed you are beautiful," "Indeed you are righteous," "Indeed Allah will bring good to you," "Indeed I am interested in you, and who would turn away from you!" "Indeed you are a nafiqah" (a woman whom many propose to and who is desired), "and indeed my need is for women, and if Allah decrees a matter, it will happen." This is the illustration of Malik and Ibn Shihab. Ibn 'Abbas said: there is no harm in saying, "Do not get ahead of me by yourself," and no harm in sending her a gift, and in attending to her affairs during the waiting period if that is his concern. Ibrahim said this. It is permissible for him to praise himself and mention his merits by way of implying marriage. Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Husayn did this. Sukaynah bint Handhalah said: Muhammad ibn 'Ali asked permission to see me, and my waiting period for the death of my husband had not ended. He said: "You know my kinship to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, my kinship to 'Ali, and my standing among the Arabs." I said: "May Allah forgive you, O Abu Ja'far! You are a man from whom knowledge is taken, and you propose to me during my waiting period!" He said: "I only informed you of my kinship to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and to 'Ali." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ also entered upon Umm Salamah while she was a widow of Abu Salamah, and he said: "You know that I am the Messenger of Allah, his chosen one, and my position among my people." That was a proposal. Al-Daraqutni reported it. Sending a gift to a woman in her waiting period is permissible, and it is a form of implication. Sahnun and many scholars said this, and Ibrahim said it. Mujahid disliked saying to her, "Do not get ahead of me by yourself," and considered it a secret promise. Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad ibn 'Atiyyah said: in my view, this is to be interpreted as the Prophet's ﷺ saying to Fatimah being a matter of advice to her regarding whom she marries, not that he wanted her for himself; otherwise it would contradict the saying of the Prophet ﷺ.

The third issue: His saying, ﴿of proposals to women﴾. Al-Khitbah (with a kasrah on the kha', proposal) is the act of the suitor, through speech, intention, and seeking to win favor by deed or word. One says: khataba-ha yakhtubu-ha khatban wa khitbatan. A man who is khattab is one who frequently engages in proposals. From this is the saying of the poet:

He has wearied the eyes, the khattab of the kuthab, who says, "Indeed I am a suitor," and he lies. He proposes only to ask for a bowl of milk from the one who milks.

Al-Khatib means the one who proposes. Al-Khitbi means proposal. 'Adi ibn Zayd, describing Jadhimah al-Abrash's intention to propose to al-Zabba', said:

The khitbi that betrayed and deceived, and they are women with treachery against us.

Al-Khitb is the man who proposes to a woman. It is also said: she is his khitb and his khitbah, the one he proposes to. Al-Khitbah is a form like jilsah and qi'dah. Al-Khutbah (with a dammah on the kha', the sermon) is the speech given at a marriage or other occasion. Al-Nahhas said: al-khutbah is what has a beginning and an end, and similarly what is in the form fa'lah, such as al-akalah and al-dagh'tah.

The fourth issue: His saying, ﴿or you conceal within yourselves﴾. Its meaning is that you hide and keep secret the intention to marry her after her waiting period has ended. Al-Iknan is concealment and hiding. It is said: kananthu and aknanthu with the same meaning. It was said: kanantu al-shay' means I protected it so that no harm reaches it, even if it is not hidden. From this come "eggs well-kept" (bayd maknun) and "a pearl well-kept" (durr maknun). Aknantu means I kept it secret and concealed it. It was said: kanantu al-shay' (of physical things) when I covered it with cloth, a house, land, or the like. And aknantu al-amr fi nafsi (I concealed the matter in my self). It has not been heard from the Arabs, "kanantuhu fi nafsi." It is said: al-bayt akanna al-insan (the house sheltered the person), and similar. So Allah lifted the blame from one who wishes to marry the woman in her waiting period, whether by implication or by concealment, and He forbade the mutual promise, which is an explicit statement of marriage, a basis for it, and an agreement upon a pledge. He permitted it, knowing the dominance and aspiration of souls and the weakness of humans in controlling them.

The fifth issue: The Shafi'is used this verse to argue that implication in slander does not entail the prescribed punishment (hadd). They said: since Allah lifted the blame for implication in marriage, this indicates that implication in slander does not require the hadd, because Allah, glorified is He, did not place implication in marriage in the position of explicit statement. We say: this argument is invalid, because Allah, glorified and exalted is He, did not permit explicit mention of marriage in the proposal, but He permitted implication, which is understood as marriage. This is evidence that implication may be understood as slander, and honor must be protected, and that requires the hadd on the one who implies, so that the immoral do not gain access to people's honor through implication that conveys what explicit speech conveys.

The sixth issue: His saying, ﴿Allah knows that you will mention them﴾, meaning either secretly or openly, in your souls and by your tongues. So He permitted implication but not explicit statement. Al-Hasan said: its meaning is "you will propose to them."

The seventh issue: His saying, ﴿but do not promise them in secret﴾, meaning "with secrecy," so the preposition is omitted, since it is among the verbs that take two objects, one of them by means of a preposition. The scholars differed concerning the meaning of His saying "sirran" (in secret). It was said: it means marriage, that is, a man should not say to this woman in her waiting period, "Marry me," but he should imply if he wishes, and not take from her a covenant and pledge that she will not marry anyone else in secret and hiddenness. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Malik and his companions, al-Sha'bi, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, al-Suddi, and the majority of the scholars. "Sirran" according to this interpretation is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, meaning "keeping it secret." It was also said: al-sirr is adultery, that is, there should not be a promise of adultery during the waiting period followed by marriage after it. Jabir ibn Zayd, Abu Mijlaz Lahiq ibn Humayd, al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Nakha'i, and al-Dahhak said this, and that the secret in this verse is adultery, meaning do not promise them adultery. al-Tabari chose this view. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

So do not approach a neighbor woman, for her secret is forbidden to you, so marry her or remain forever.

Al-Hutay'ah said:

The secret of their neighbor is forbidden to them, and their neighbor eats the nose of the bowls.

It was also said: al-sirr is intercourse, meaning do not describe yourselves to them with frequent intercourse in order to encourage them toward marriage, for mentioning intercourse with someone other than a spouse is indecent. This is the view of al-Shafi'i. Imru' al-Qays said:

Did not Basbasah claim today that I have grown old, and that those like me do not do well at the secret?

Ru'bah said:

So he withdrew from her secrets after the long clinging.

That is, he refrained from intercourse with her after being constantly attached to it. Al-sirr may also be the bond of marriage, whether secret or public. Al-A'sha said:

So they will not seek her secret for wealth, and they will not surrender her for her poverty.

He meant that they will not seek her marriage for the abundance of her wealth, and they will not give her up for the scarcity of her wealth. Ibn Zayd said: the meaning of His saying, "but do not promise them in secret," is that you should not marry them while concealing it; then, when the waiting period ends, you reveal it and consummate with them. This is the meaning of the first view, so Ibn Zayd, according to this, holds the first view, but he was odd in calling the contract a promise, and that is strained. Makki and al-Tha'labi reported from him that he said: the verse is abrogated by His saying, "and do not determine the bond of marriage (la ta'zimu 'uqdata al-nikah)."

The eighth issue: Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad ibn 'Atiyyah said: the community has agreed on the reprehensibility of a mutual promise during the waiting period on the part of the woman herself, and on the part of the father concerning his virgin daughter, and on the part of the master concerning his slave-woman. Ibn al-Mawwaz said: as for the guardian who does not have the power of compulsion, I dislike it, and if it occurs, I will not annul it. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said concerning one who makes a promise during the waiting period and then marries her after it: separation from her is more beloved to me, whether or not he has consummated with her, and it is one pronouncement of divorce; and when she is free, he may propose to her along with the other suitors. This is the narration of Ibn Wahb. Ashhab reported from Malik that they are separated by obligation, and Ibn al-Qasim said this. Ibn al-Harith related something similar from Ibn al-Majishun, and added what implies that the prohibition is permanent. Al-Shafi'i said: if he explicitly proposes and she explicitly accepts, and the contract is not concluded until the waiting period ends, then the marriage is valid, and the explicit proposal to her is disliked, because the marriage arises after the proposal. Ibn al-Mundhir said this.

The ninth issue: His saying, ﴿except that you say a fair word﴾. This is an exception that is disjunctive (munqati'), meaning "but," like His saying, "except by mistake," meaning "but by mistake." The fair word is what has been permitted of implication. Al-Dahhak mentioned that among the fair words is that one says to the woman in her waiting period, "Hold yourself back for me, for I have a desire for you," and she says, "And I am like that," and this is similar to a promise.

**Question 1: Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 235 (part 2 of 2)**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And do not determine upon the marriage contract until the decreed term reaches its prescribed end.﴾ There are nine issues concerning this.

**The first issue:** His saying, ﴿And do not determine﴾ (wa la ta'zimu). The meaning of *'azm* has already been discussed. It is said: *'azama al-shay'* and *'azama 'alayhi* (he resolved upon it). The meaning here is: "Do not resolve upon the marriage contract." It is clear that the Qur'an is the most eloquent speech, so nothing in it can be objected to, and there is no doubt about its soundness and eloquence. Allah the Exalted said, ﴿And if they resolve upon divorce﴾ [2:227], and here He said, ﴿Do not determine upon the marriage contract﴾. The meaning is: "Do not resolve upon the marriage contract during the waiting period," and then the preposition was omitted, as previously explained. Sibawayh reported: "*Daraba fulan al-zahra wa al-batna*," meaning "*'ala*" (upon). Sibawayh said: "Omission in these expressions is not to be generalised upon." Al-Nahhas said: It is also permissible that the phrase be ﴿Do not conclude the marriage contract﴾ (wa la ta'qidu), because *ta'zimu* and *ta'qidu* have the same meaning. It is also recited as *ta'zumu* with a *damma* on the *zay*.

**The second issue:** His saying, ﴿until the decreed term reaches its prescribed end﴾. It means the completion of the waiting period (*'iddah*). The "decree" (*kitab*) here is the limit that was set and the measure of the period that was fixed. He called it a "decree" because Allah's Book has determined and prescribed it, as He said, ﴿the decree of Allah upon you﴾ [[See vol. 5, p. 311, p. 123 and p. 373]], and as He said, ﴿Indeed, prayer has been upon the believers a decreed obligation at fixed times﴾ [[See vol. 5, p. 311, p. 123 and p. 373]]. So *al-kitab* means "the obligation," i.e., "until the obligation reaches its prescribed end." Similarly, ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ means "obligated." It is also said that there is an ellipsis in the sentence, i.e., "until the obligatory decree of the Book reaches its prescribed end," so *al-kitab* in this interpretation means the Qur'an. According to the first interpretation there is no ellipsis, so it is preferable, and Allah knows best.

**The third issue:** Allah prohibited concluding a marriage contract during the waiting period by His saying, ﴿And do not determine upon the marriage contract until the decreed term reaches its prescribed end﴾. This is among the clear (*muhkam*) rulings whose interpretation is agreed upon: that reaching its prescribed end means the completion of the waiting period. He permitted allusion (*ta'ridh*) during the waiting period by His saying, ﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you allude to of the proposal to women﴾ [2:235]. The scholars have not differed on the permissibility of this, but they differed on the wording of allusion, as previously mentioned. They also differed concerning a man who proposes to a woman during her waiting period while ignorant of the ruling, or who makes a promise to her and concludes the contract after the waiting period. This has been discussed in the previous verse.

They differed concerning a man who resolved upon the contract during the waiting period, and it was discovered and the judge annulled his marriage, and this was before consummation. This is the **fourth issue**: the statement of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and a group of scholars is that this does not make the prohibition permanent, and that he remains one of the suitors (*khattab*). Malik and Ibn al-Qasim said this in the *Mudawwana*, at the end of the chapter that follows it, "The Term for the Missing Husband." Ibn al-Jallab reported from Malik a narration that the prohibition becomes permanent with the contract even if it is annulled before consummation. Its reasoning is that it is a marriage during the waiting period, so the prohibition must become permanent through it, as with the original case where he consummated the marriage with her.

As for if he concluded the contract during the waiting period and consummated it after its completion, this is the **fifth issue**. A group of scholars said: this is like consummation during the waiting period, and the prohibition becomes permanent between them. Another group of scholars said: the prohibition does not become permanent through this. Malik said: the prohibition becomes permanent. On another occasion he said: "The prohibition is not clear through this." Both opinions are attributed to him in the *Mudawwana* in the section on the divorce of the Sunnah.

As for if he consummated the marriage during the waiting period, this is the **sixth issue**. Malik, al-Layth and al-Awza'i said: they are separated and she is never lawful to him again. Malik and al-Layth said: nor by ownership of the right hand (*milk al-yamin*), even though they permitted marriage with a woman who had been fornicated with. They argued that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "They shall never be together." Sa'id said: "She is entitled to her dower (*mahr*) for what he made lawful of her private part." Malik narrated this in his *Muwatta'*, and it will come later. Al-Thawri, the Kufans and al-Shafi'i said: they are separated, and the prohibition does not become permanent; rather they are separated and she observes a waiting period from him, after which he becomes one of the suitors. They argued by the scholars' consensus that if he fornicated with her, it would not prohibit him from marrying her, so likewise his intercourse with her during the waiting period. They said: this is the view of 'Ali, reported by 'Abd al-Razzaq. It is also reported from Ibn Mas'ud a similar view, and from al-Hasan as well. 'Abd al-Razzaq also reported from al-Thawri, from Ash'ath, from al-Sha'bi, from Masruq, that 'Umar retracted this and let them come together. Al-Qadi Abu al-Walid al-Baji mentioned in *al-Muntaqa* and said: The one who marries a woman during her waiting period and consummates it, either consummates during the waiting period or after it. If he consummated it during the waiting period, the well-known position of the school is that the prohibition becomes permanent, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal said the same. Abu al-Qasim reported in his elaboration that concerning a woman whom a man marries during a waiting period following divorce or death, while knowing the prohibition, there are two narrations: one is that his prohibition becomes permanent as we have mentioned; the second is that he is an adulterer, he receives the prescribed punishment (*hadd*), the child is not attributed to him, and he may marry her when her waiting period has ended. Al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa also said this. The reasoning for the first narration, which is the well-known one, is what was established from 'Umar's judgment on this, and his standing firm on it among the people; his judgments spread, circulated and were transmitted in the cities, and no opponent of it was known, so it is established as a consensus. Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad said: Similar was reported from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, and there is no opponent of these two with the fame and spread of this, and this is the ruling of consensus (*ijma'*). The reasoning for the second narration is that this is a prohibited intercourse, so its prohibition does not become permanent, just as if she had given herself in marriage or had entered a temporary marriage (*mut'a*) or had committed fornication. Al-Qadi Abu al-Hasan said: Malik's well-known position on this is weak from the standpoint of reasoning. And Allah knows best.

Abu 'Umar narrated with a chain: "'Abd al-Warith ibn Sufyan related to us, Qasim ibn Asbagh related to us, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from Nu'aym ibn Hammad, from Ibn al-Mubarak, from Ash'ath, from al-Sha'bi, from Masruq, who said: It reached 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that a woman from Quraysh had been married by a man from Thaqif during her waiting period. So he sent for them both, separated them, punished them, and said: 'Never marry her again.' He placed her dower in the treasury (*bayt al-mal*). This spread among the people and reached 'Ali, who said: 'May Allah have mercy on the Commander of the Believers! What is the matter with the dower and the treasury? They were only ignorant. It is fitting for the ruler to return them to the Sunnah.' It was said to him: 'What do you say about them?' He said: 'She is entitled to the dower for what he made lawful of her private part, they are separated, there is no lashing upon them, and she completes her first waiting period, then observes a complete waiting period from the second, which is three menstrual cycles (*qur'*), after which he may propose to her if he wishes.' When this reached 'Umar, he addressed the people and said: 'O people, return the ignorant to the Sunnah.'"

Al-Kiya al-Tabari said: There is no disagreement among the jurists that whoever contracts a marriage with a woman while she is in a waiting period from another man, the marriage is invalid. In the agreement of 'Umar and 'Ali on negating the prescribed punishment (*hadd*) from them both, there is an indication that an invalid marriage does not necessitate the prescribed punishment, except that with ignorance of the prohibition this is agreed upon, while with knowledge of it there is disagreement.

They differed on whether she observes a waiting period from both of them together. This is the **seventh issue**, the matter of the two waiting periods. The people of Madina narrated from Malik that she completes the remainder of her first waiting period and begins another waiting period from the second. This is also the view of al-Layth, al-Hasan ibn Hayy, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq. It is reported from 'Ali as we mentioned, and from 'Umar as will come. Muhammad ibn al-Qasim and Ibn Wahb narrated from Malik that her waiting period from the second suffices her from the day they were separated, whether it is by pregnancy, by menstrual cycles or by months. This is also the view of al-Thawri, al-Awza'i and Abu Hanifa. Their proof is the consensus that the first husband may not marry her during the remainder of his waiting period, which indicates that she is in a waiting period from the second; otherwise he could have married her during his own waiting period. The first group responded: This does not necessarily follow, because the first husband's prohibition from marrying her during the remainder of his waiting period is due only to what follows it, the waiting period of the second. These are two rights that have become due upon her for two husbands, like the rest of the rights of human beings, and neither one enters into the other.

Malik transmitted from Ibn Shihab, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and from Sulayman ibn Yasar, that Tulayha al-Asadiyya was married to Rashid al-Thaqafi, and he divorced her, and she married again during her waiting period. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab struck her and struck her husband with the *mikhfaqa* [[The *mikhfaqa* is a staff.]] several times and separated them. Then 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Whichever woman marries during her waiting period: if her husband who married her had not consummated with her, they are separated, then she completes the rest of her waiting period from her first husband, and then the other becomes one of the suitors. If he had consummated with her, they are separated, then she completes the rest of her waiting period from the first, then observes a waiting period from the other, and they shall never come together." Malik said: Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: "She is entitled to her dower for what he made lawful of her private part." Abu 'Umar said: As for this Tulayha, she is Tulayha bint 'Ubayd Allah, the sister of Talha ibn 'Ubayd Allah al-Taymi. In some copies of the *Muwatta'* from the narration of Yahya, it reads "Tulayha al-Asadiyya," but that is an error and ignorance, and I know of no one who said it.

**The eighth issue:** His saying, "'Umar struck her with the *mikhfaqa* and struck her husband several times," meaning as a punishment for what the two of them had committed of the forbidden act, which is marriage during the waiting period. Al-Zuhri said: "I do not know how many lashes that amounted to." He said: "'Abd al-Malik lashed each of them forty lashes in this matter." He said: "Qabisa ibn Dhu'ayb was asked about this, and he said: 'If only you had lightened it and lashed twenty!'" Ibn Habib said concerning a woman who marries during her waiting period, and the man touches her, kisses her, engages in intimacy with her, fondles her or looks at her with desire, that both spouses receive the punishment, and also the guardian (*wali*), the witnesses and whoever among them knew that she was in a waiting period; but whoever among them was ignorant of this receives no punishment. Ibn al-Mawwaz said: "The spouses are lashed the prescribed punishment (*hadd*) if they intentionally did this." So Ibn Habib's statement is understood as referring to one who knew of the waiting period, and perhaps he was ignorant of the prohibition and did not intentionally commit the forbidden act, and that is the one who is punished. On this basis was 'Umar's striking the woman and her husband with the *mikhfaqa* several times. The punishment and discipline are according to the condition of the one punished. Ibn al-Mawwaz's statement is understood as meaning that they knew the prohibition and boldly and presumptuously committed the forbidden act. Abu al-Qasim said: "There are two narrations concerning intentional offence: in one, they receive the prescribed punishment (*hadd*); in the second, they are punished but not with the *hadd*."

**The ninth issue:** His saying, ﴿And know that Allah knows what is within yourselves, so beware of Him.﴾ This is the utmost warning against falling into what He has forbidden.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 236 (part 1 of 2):

There are eleven issues in this verse. The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿There is no blame upon you if you divorce women﴾. This too is among the rulings concerning divorced women. It is an opening statement lifting blame from the one who divorces before consummation and intercourse, whether or not he has set a dower (mahr). When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade marriage for the sake of mere pleasure and the gratification of desire, and commanded marriage for the sake of seeking chastity, seeking the reward of Allah and intending lasting companionship, it came into the minds of the believers that whoever divorces before consummation has committed a part of this disliked act. So the verse was revealed, lifting blame in that case when the basis of the marriage was a good intention. Some people said: "There is no blame upon you" means there is no demand for the full dower; rather, you owe half of the stipulated dower to the one for whom a dower was stipulated, and provision (mut'ah) to the one for whom none was stipulated. It was also said: since the matter of the dower is emphasized in the Shari'ah, it might be supposed that a dower must be paid, either a named dower or the equivalent dower (mahr al-mithl). So He lifted blame from the divorcer at the time of divorce, even if no dower had been fixed in the marriage. Some people said: "There is no blame upon you" means regarding your releasing the divorce during menstruation, unlike the one who has been consummated with, since the one not consummated with has no waiting period ('iddah).

The second: Divorced women are of four kinds. A divorced woman who has been consummated with and for whom a dower was stipulated, whose ruling Allah mentioned before this verse, and that nothing of the dower is to be taken back from her, and that her waiting period is three menstrual cycles (quru'). A divorced woman for whom no dower was stipulated and who has not been consummated with: this verse concerns her, and she has no dower; rather, the Lord, exalted is He, commanded that she be provided for. In Surah al-Ahzab He explained that a woman not consummated with, if divorced, has no waiting period upon her, and it will come (see vol. 14, p. 202). A divorced woman for whom a dower was stipulated but who has not been consummated with, whom He mentioned after this verse when He said: ﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them, and you have already fixed for them a dower﴾. And a divorced woman who has been consummated with but for whom no dower was stipulated, whom Allah mentioned in His saying: ﴿So for what you have enjoyed of them, give them their wages﴾ (see vol. 5, p. 129).

So He mentioned this verse and the one after it concerning a woman divorced before touching and before a dower was fixed, and a woman divorced before touching but after a dower was fixed.
