If the prayer does not lapse because of fear, it is all the more fitting that it not lapse because of other things, such as illness or the like. So God, glorified and exalted, commanded the guarding of the prayers in every state, whether health or illness, residence or travel, ability or inability, fear or security. It does not lapse from the responsible person in any state, and no defect can reach its obligation. The explanation of the ruling on the sick person will come at the end of Al 'Imran (vol. 4, pp. 3–15, no. 310), God willing. The purpose of this is that the prayer should be performed however possible, and it does not lapse in any state; even if its performance is possible only by a sign with the eye, its performance is obligatory. By this it is distinguished from the other acts of worship, all of which lapse because of excuses and are relaxed by concessions.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: For this reason our scholars said: this is a great issue, that one who abandons the prayer is to be killed, because it resembles faith, which does not lapse in any state. They also said of it: it is one of the pillars of Islam, and no substitute for it is permitted by body or by wealth, so its abandoner is to be killed, its root being the two testimonies. What the scholars hold regarding one who abandons the prayer will come in Bara'a (vol. 8, p. 72), God willing.

**First issue:** The wording of this verse ("those who die among you and leave wives behind") is the basis of the discussion.

There are four questions (masa'il) in this passage. The first concerns God's words: ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind﴾. A group of exegetes (mufassirun) held that the interpretation (ta'wil) of this verse is that the widow used to remain in her late husband's house for a full year, and was provided for from his property so long as she did not leave the home. If she left, the heirs bore no blame for cutting off her maintenance. Then the year was abrogated (nusikha, naskh) by the four months and ten days, and the maintenance was abrogated by the quarter and the eighth in Surat an-Nisa' [[See vol. 5, p. 75.]]. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd and al-Rabi'.

Concerning residence (al-sukna), the scholars differed. al-Bukhari reported from Ibn al-Zubayr who said: "I said to 'Uthman: this verse in al-Baqarah, 'Those of you who die and leave wives behind… up to his words… without turning them out', has been abrogated by the other verse. So why do you leave it [in the Mushaf], or leave it [out]? He said: 'O son of my brother, I will not change anything of it from its place.'" [[This is as in the text of Sahih al-Bukhari. What appears in the原 manuscripts is: "...So why do you not write it? He said: Leave it, O son of my brother..." The phrase "or leave it" means leave it in the Mushaf; the doubt is from the narrator. Ibn al-Zubayr thought that a verse whose ruling is abrogated is not written down.]]

al-Tabari reported from Mujahid that this verse is muhkam (not abrogated), and that the waiting period had been fixed at four months and ten days; then God made for them a bequest from Himself of residence for seven months and twenty nights [[In ha': "days."]], so that if the woman wished, she would remain in accordance with the bequest, and if she wished, she could leave. This is the meaning of God's words: ﴿without turning them out; but if they leave, there is no blame upon you﴾.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: All of this has had its ruling removed by the abrogation that is agreed upon, except what al-Tabari attributed to Mujahid, may God have mercy on both of them. But there is a problem with al-Tabari's position.

al-Qadi 'Iyad said: There is consensus (ijma') that the year has been abrogated, and that her waiting period is four months and ten days.

Another scholar said: The meaning of His words "a bequest" is a bequest from God the Exalted, which was obligatory upon women after their husband's death, that they stay in their houses, as a sunnah; then it was abrogated.

I say: What al-Tabari attributed to Mujahid is sound and established. al-Bukhari reported: "Ishaq related to us, saying: Rawh related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind﴾, he said: This waiting period used to be observed at the household of her husband, as an obligation [[As in the original manuscripts. In al-Bukhari it reads "wajiban," meaning an obligatory matter.]]. Then God revealed: ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind… up to His words… reasonable﴾. He said: God made for her, for the completion of the year, seven months and twenty nights as a bequest; if she wished she could remain in her bequest, and if she wished she could leave. This is the saying of God: ﴿without turning them out; but if they leave, there is no blame upon you﴾."

However, the first view is more evident, because of his peace and blessings be upon him saying: "It is only four months and ten [days]. In the Jahiliyyah, one of you would throw a dung-pellet at the head of the year" — the hadith in full. This is a report from him ﷺ about the condition of the women whose husbands had died before the coming of the Shari'ah. When Islam came, God the Exalted commanded them to remain in their houses for a year, and then this was abrogated by the four months and ten days. This—together with its clarity in the established Sunnah transmitted through single reports (akhbar al-ahad)—is a consensus of the scholars of the Muslims, with no disagreement. Abu 'Umar [Ibn 'Abd al-Barr] said: "The same applies to the rest of the verse." So God the Exalted's words: ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind, [should make] a bequest for their wives of provision for a year without turning them out﴾ are, according to the majority of scholars, entirely abrogated. Then the bequest of residence for wives for the year was abrogated, except for an isolated, abandoned report that came from Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid, which no one followed. No one among the scholars of the Muslims—from the Companions, the Successors, or those after them, as far as I know—held it beyond the four months and ten days [[In the original manuscripts: "...and those after them from among the dissenters, as far as I know."]]. Ibn Jurayj reported from Mujahid the same as what the people hold; thus the consensus was established and the disagreement removed. And success is from God.

The second question concerns God's words: ﴿bequest﴾ (wasiyyah). Nafi', Ibn Kathir, al-Kisa'i, and 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr read "wasiyyatun" with a nominative (raf') ending, as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is (li-azwajihim, "for their wives"). It is possible that the meaning is "upon them is a bequest," and that "li-azwajihim" is then an attributive phrase (sifah). al-Tabari said: Some grammarians said: The meaning is "a bequest was prescribed for them," and "li-azwajihim" is an attributive phrase. He said: It is likewise in the reading of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.

Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and Ibn 'Amir read "wasiyyatan" with a accusative (nasb) ending, which is taken as governed by a verb, i.e. "let them make a bequest, a bequest." Then, the dead person does not make bequests, but He meant when they draw near to death. And "li-azwajihim" in this reading is also an attributive phrase. It was also said: The meaning is "God has bequeathed a bequest."

"Mata'an" (provision): i.e., provide them with provision, or God made this a provision for them, since the context indicates it. It may be in the accusative as a circumstantial (hal) or as a verbal noun governed by the word "wasiyyah," like His words: ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger, an orphan﴾ [[See vol. 20, p. 69.]]. "Mata'" here means the maintenance of her year.

The third question concerns God's words: ﴿without turning them out﴾. Its meaning is that the guardians of the dead man and the heirs of the house are not permitted to expel her. "Ghayra" (without) is in the accusative according to al-Akhfash as a verbal noun, as if he said: "No expulsion." It was also said: it is accusative because it is an attribute of "mata'" (provision). It was also said: it is accusative as a circumstantial state of those making the bequest, meaning: provide for them while they are not expelled. It was also said: by removing the preposition, meaning: "without expulsion."

The fourth question concerns God's words: ﴿but if they leave﴾, and the rest of the verse. Its meaning is by their own choice, before the year is over.

(﴿then there is no blame upon you﴾) means: there is no sin upon anyone, whether guardian, ruler, or other, because it is not obligatory for her to remain in her husband's house for a year. It was also said: meaning there is no blame in cutting off maintenance from them, or there is no blame upon them in seeking to attract husbands, since your watch over them, O heirs, has ended. Then it is incumbent on them not to marry before the waiting period of the year is over; or there is no blame in marrying them after the waiting period is over, because He said: ﴿reasonable﴾, which is what agrees with the Shari'ah.

(﴿And God is Mighty﴾) is an attribute that implies a threat concerning whoever transgresses the limit in this case, by expelling the woman when she does not want to leave.

(﴿Wise﴾) means: the One who perfects what He wills concerning the affairs of His servants.

The people differed concerning this verse. Abu Thawr said: it is *muhkamah* (definitive, not abrogated), and the *mut'ah* (a provision given at divorce) is due to every divorced woman. Al-Zuhri said likewise, [al-Zuhri said: "even for a slave-woman whose husband divorces her."] Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said likewise: every divorced woman has a *mut'ah*. This is one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i concerning this verse.

Malik said: every divorced woman, whether divorced twice or once, whether he has consummated the marriage or not, whether he has named a dowry for her or not, is due the *mut'ah*, except the woman divorced before consummation for whom a dowry was named; for her, half of that dowry suffices. If he had not named a dowry for her, she is due the *mut'ah*, whether less or more than the customary dowry (*mahr al-mithl*). There is no fixed limit to this *mut'ah*. This was related from him by Ibn al-Qasim.

Ibn al-Qasim said in *Irkha' al-sutur* from the *al-Mudawwanah*: "Allah the Exalted made the *mut'ah* due to every divorced woman by this verse, then in the other verse He made an exception for the one for whom a dowry has been fixed and who has not been consummated with, and excluded her from the *mut'ah*." Ibn Zayd claimed that the other verse abrogated it (*nasakhat-ha*).

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Ibn al-Qasim fled from the term *naskh* (abrogation) to the term *istithna'* (exception), and the exception is not tenable in this context; rather it is pure abrogation, as Zayd ibn Aslam said. And if Ibn al-Qasim holds that the phrase "﴿and for divorced women﴾" includes every divorced woman, he is necessarily bound to the view of abrogation.

Ata' ibn Abi Rabah and others said: this verse concerns the previously married women who have been consummated with, since the mention of the *mut'ah* for those with whom it was not consummated has already occurred in another verse. This is an opinion that the one for whom a dowry was fixed before touching (*al-masis*) never enters the generality at all. This would mean that Allah's words ﴿and if you divorce them before you have touched them﴾ specify this category of women. Whenever it is said that this general wording includes them, that is abrogation, not specification.

In the other opinion, al-Shafi'i said: there is no *mut'ah* except for the one divorced before consummation, where there has been neither touching nor a fixed dowry, because whoever is entitled to a portion of the dowry does not need the *mut'ah* in her case.

Allah's words concerning the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿So come, I will provide for you﴾ are understood to be a voluntary act (*tatawwu'*) of the Prophet (ﷺ), not an obligation upon him. His words ﴿So for them there is no waiting period you should count; so provide for them﴾ are also understood as referring to someone other than the one for whom a dowry was fixed. Al-Shafi'i said: the woman for whom a dowry was fixed, if divorced before touching, has no *mut'ah*, because she has taken half the dowry without any intercourse having taken place. But the woman who has been consummated with, if divorced, is due the *mut'ah*, because the dowry is given in exchange for intercourse, while the *mut'ah* is due by reason of the humiliation (*ibtidhal*) of the contract. Al-Shafi'i made the *mut'ah* obligatory for the woman who divorces by *khul'* (compensated divorce) and for the one divorced by *mubara'ah* (divorce by mutual release).

The companions of Malik said: how can a woman who ransoms herself (*al-muftadiyah*) be due a *mut'ah* when she is the one who pays? How can she take a provision! There is no *mut'ah* for a woman who chooses separation: whether she is a *mukhtali'ah* (divorcing by *khul'*), a *muftadiyah* (divorcing by ransom), a *mubari'ah* (divorcing by mutual release), a *musalihah* (divorcing by settlement), a *mula'anah* (cursed through *li'an*), or a *mu'taqah* who chooses separation, whether he has consummated with her or not, and whether he named a dowry for her or not. This has already been explained [See p. 200 of this volume.]

**Part 1 of the commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jāmiʿ li-Aḥkām al-Qurʾān) on Sūrah al-Baqarah, verse 243**

There are six issues (masāʾil) in this verse.

**The first issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you not considered?﴾ This is seeing of the heart, meaning "Have you not known?" According to Sībawayh (a leading grammarian), the meaning is "Pay attention to the matter of those who..." This seeing does not require two objects.

Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī read "Alam tara" with the rāʾ vowelless (jazm). The hamzah was dropped without transferring its vowel, since the original form is "Alam tara'" (with a hamzah at the end).

The story of these people is that they were a group from the Children of Israel among whom plague (wabāʾ) broke out. They were in a town called Dāwardān.[[Dāwardān (with a fatḥah on the wāw, a sukūn on the rāʾ, and a nūn at the end): one of the places east of Wāsiṭ, a farsakh away from it (Muʿjam Yāqūt). In Ibn ʿAṭiyyah it is written Dhāwardān with a dotted dhāl.]] They fled from it and camped in a valley, and God caused them to die. Ibn ʿAbbās said: they were four thousand who left to flee from the plague, saying, "We will go to a land where there is no death." So God caused them to die. Then a prophet passed by them, prayed to God, and He brought them back to life.

It is also said that they died for eight days, and it is said seven. God knows best.

Al-Ḥasan said: God caused them to die before their appointed times as a punishment for them, then He raised them up to complete the rest of their appointed terms.

It is also said that God did this to them as a sign (muʿjizah) for a prophet among their prophets. It is said his name was Shamʿūn.

Al-Naqqāsh reported that they fled from fever.

It is also said that they fled from jihad, when God commanded them to it through the tongue of the Prophet Ḥizqīl, peace be upon him. They feared death by killing in jihad, so they left their homes fleeing from that. God caused them to die in order to make them know that nothing can save them from death. Then He brought them back to life and commanded them to fight, by His saying: ﴿And fight in the way of God﴾. This is what al-Ḍaḥḥāk said.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: all this narrative has weak chains of transmission. What is necessarily derived from the verse is that God informed His Prophet Muḥammad (ﷺ) in a form of address that alerts and makes one attentive, about a people of humankind who left their homes fleeing from death. God caused them to die, then brought them back to life, so that they would see, and so that everyone who came after them would know that causing death is in the hand of God alone and not in the hand of anyone else. Therefore there is no sense in the fear of one who fears, nor in the deception of one who is deceived.

God placed this verse as an introduction before His command to the believers of the community of Muḥammad (ﷺ) to fight in jihad. This is the view of al-Ṭabarī, and it is the apparent sense of the verse's arrangement (rasf).[[In Ibn ʿAṭiyyah and manuscript Z: "rasf"; in the other manuscripts: "waṣf".]]

His saying, Exalted is He: (﴿and they were thousands﴾[[In manuscript Z, "and they were thousands" appears as the second issue, and then the issues are counted as seven. However, it is stated as six in the other manuscripts.]]). The majority said: "ulūf" is the plural of "alf" (thousand). Some of them said: they were six hundred thousand. It is also said: they were eighty thousand. Ibn ʿAbbās: forty thousand. Abū Mālik: thirty thousand. Al-Suddī: thirty-seven thousand. It is said: seventy thousand, reported by ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ. From Ibn ʿAbbās also: forty thousand and eight thousand, transmitted from him by Ibn Jurayj. From him also: eight thousand. From him also: four thousand. It is also said: three thousand.

The correct view is that they exceeded ten thousand, because of His saying, ﴿and they were thousands﴾, which is the plural of abundance (jamʿ al-kathrah), and "ulūf" is not said for ten or fewer.

Ibn Zayd said regarding the word "ulūf": its meaning is only "they were in agreement" (muʾtalifūn), that is, the separation of their people and no strife among them drove them out. They were in agreement, but this group opposed and left, fleeing from death and seeking life by their own claim. So God caused them to die in their place of safety, according to their claim. On this view, "ulūf" is the plural of "ālif," like "jālis" and "julūs" (sitting).

Ibn al-ʿArabī said: God caused them to die for a period as a punishment for them, then He brought them back to life. A death of punishment is followed by life, but a death at the appointed time has no life after it.

Mujāhid said: when they were brought back to life, they returned to their people knowing that they had been dead, but the look of death was on their faces. None of them wore a garment without it becoming a greasy shroud,[[al-dasm: filth, which is grease and dirt.]] until they died at their appointed times that had been decreed for them.

Ibn Jurayj reported from Ibn ʿAbbās: the odour remained on that tribe of the Children of Israel until today. It is narrated that they were in Wāsiṭ of Iraq. It is said that they were brought back to life after they had begun to stink, and that odour is still found among their descendants until today.

**The second issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: (﴿for fear of death﴾). That is, "for fear of death," so it is in the accusative because it is an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu, an object indicating the reason for an action). And ﴿Die﴾ is an imperative of creation (amr takwīn, a command that brings about what it orders). It is not far-fetched to say that they were called, and it was said to them, "Die." It has been reported that two angels called out to them, "Die," and they died. So the meaning is that God said to them through the two angels, "Die." And God knows best.

**Third point:** The most sound and clearest of these opinions, and the most widely known, is that they left their homes fleeing from the plague. Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "They went out fleeing from the plague and died. Then a prophet among the prophets asked Allah to revive them so that they would worship Him, and Allah revived them." 'Amr ibn Dinar said regarding this verse: "The plague struck their town. Some people left and some stayed, and more people left than stayed. Those who left survived, and those who stayed died. Then in the second year they all left, except for a few, so Allah caused them and their animals to die. Then He revived them, and they returned to their land, and their descendants had multiplied." Al-Hasan said: "They went out in fear of the plague, and Allah caused them and their animals to die at the same moment, and they numbered forty thousand."

I say: The rulings of this verse are based on this account. Al-Bukhari, and the other imams, narrated, with the wording belonging to al-Bukhari, from the hadith of 'Amir ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, that he heard Usama ibn Zayd telling Sa'd that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mentioned the plague[[The hadith appears in al-Bukhari in the Book of Medicine with the word "plague" (al-ta'un), and in the Book of Legal Stratagems (Kitab al-Hiyal) with the word "ache" (al-waja')]] and said: "It is a scourge or a punishment with which some nations were afflicted, and then a remnant of it remained. It goes away one time and returns another time. So whoever hears of it in a land, let him not enter upon it, and whoever is in a land where it has struck, let him not leave fleeing from it." Abu 'Isa al-Tirmidhi also narrated it, saying: "Qutayba narrated to us, Hammad ibn Zayd informed us, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from 'Amir ibn Sa'd, from Usama ibn Zayd, that the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned the plague and said: 'It is a remnant of a scourge or a punishment that was sent upon a group of the Children of Israel. So when it strikes a land while you are in it, do not leave it; and when it strikes a land while you are not in it, do not enter it.'" He said: "It is a hadith that is good and sound." In accordance with these hadiths, 'Umar and the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) acted when they returned from Sargh[[Sargh: a village in the valley of Tabuk on the road to Syria, thirteen stages away from Madinah.]], when 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf informed them of the hadith, as is well known in the Muwatta' and elsewhere.

Some people disliked fleeing from plague and from a diseased land. It is narrated from 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her) that she said: "Fleeing from plague is like fleeing from the advance of the enemy in battle[[Al-zahf: the advance of an army toward the enemy in battle.]]." The story of 'Umar's journey to Syria with Abu 'Ubayda is well known, and in it he returned. Al-Tabari said: The hadith of Sa'd indicates that a person must guard against harmful things before they befall him, and avoid dangerous things before they overtake him, and that he must be patient and avoid anxiety after they have befallen him. That is because the Prophet (peace be upon him) forbade someone who was not in the land of the plague from entering it once it had struck, and forbade someone who was in it from leaving it after it had struck, fleeing from it. Likewise, it is obligatory that the ruling for every matter one guards against, its harms, should be the same as the ruling for the plague. This meaning is similar to his (peace be upon him) saying: "Do not wish for an encounter with the enemy, but ask Allah for well-being. When you do meet them, then be patient."

I say: This is the correct position on this matter. It is what the words of the Messenger (peace be upon him) require, and it is the practice of his noble and righteous Companions (may Allah be pleased with them). 'Umar, when Abu 'Ubayda said to him, questioning him, "Are you fleeing from the decree of Allah?", said: "If someone other than you had said this, O Abu 'Ubayda!" Yes, we flee from the decree of Allah to the decree of Allah. The meaning is: there is no escape for a person from what Allah has decreed for him and against him. But Allah the Exalted has commanded us to take precautions against dangers and destructive things, and to exert full effort in guarding against what is disliked. Then 'Umar said to him: "Tell me, if you had camels and they descended into a valley that had two banks[[Al-'udwa (with a vowel on the 'ayn, or a kasra, and sukun on the dal): the bank or edge of a valley.]], one of them fertile and the other barren, would you not, if you pastured the fertile one, be pasturing it by the decree of Allah, and if you pastured the barren one, be pasturing it by the decree of Allah?" So 'Umar returned from that place to Madinah.

Al-Kiya al-Tabari said: We know of no disagreement that if disbelievers or highway robbers intend to attack a town whose people have no strength to face them, then the people may withdraw from before them[[In another manuscript: "they may escape"]], even though the appointed terms of life neither increase nor decrease. It has also been said that fleeing from it is forbidden only because a person who is in the place where the plague has struck may have already been touched by some of it, since the people of that place share in the cause of that general sickness. So fleeing gives him no benefit. Rather, he adds to the beginnings of the plague that have struck him the hardships of travel, so the sufferings multiply and the harm increases, and they perish along every road and are cast down into every hollow and narrow path. For this reason it is said: "No one has fled from the plague and survived," as related by Ibn al-Mada'ini. What is sufficient as an admonition in this matter is the statement of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Have you not considered those who left their homes, being thousands, fearing death? Then Allah said to them, "Die"﴾. Perhaps if a person flees and survives, he will say: "I survived only because I left it," and his belief will become corrupted. In summary, fleeing from it is prohibited for the reasons we have mentioned, and because it leaves the lands empty, while they are not free of the weak, who find it difficult to leave and cannot manage to do so, and who are harmed by the departure of the wealthy, who were the pillars of the land and the support of the weak. When the plague is in a land, no one should enter it, out of caution, vigilance, and guarding against places of harm, and to repel the confusing illusions that disturb a person's soul. Entering it leads to destruction, and that is not permitted under the ruling of Allah the Exalted, for protecting the self from what is disliked is obligatory. There is also a fear of corrupt belief, that a person will say: "If I had not entered this place, no harm would have befallen me." This is the benefit of the prohibition against entering a land where the plague is, or leaving it. And Allah knows best.

Ibn Mas'ud said: "The plague is a trial for the one who stays and for the one who flees. As for the one who flees, he says: 'By my fleeing I was saved.' As for the one who stays, he says: 'I stayed and so I died.'" Malik pointed to something similar when he was asked about disliking looking at a leper. He said: "I have not heard anything about disliking it, and I do not think the prohibition that came concerning it was anything but fear that it would frighten him or that something would occur in his mind that would distress him." The Prophet (peace be upon him) said regarding the plague: "If you hear of it in a land, do not go to it; and if it strikes while you are in it, do not leave fleeing from it." He was also asked about a town where death and diseases occur, and whether leaving it is disliked. He said: "I see no harm in leaving or in staying."

**Fourth point:** In his (peace be upon him) saying: "When the plague strikes a land while you are in it, do not leave fleeing from it," there is evidence that it is permissible to leave a town afflicted by plague, not in the manner of fleeing from it, provided one believes that what has befallen him would not have missed him anyway. Likewise, the ruling for someone entering is the same, if he is certain that entering it does not bring upon him a decree that Allah had not decreed for him. So it is permitted for him to enter it and to leave it within the limit we have mentioned. And Allah knows best.

**Fifth point:** Concerning the excellence of patience during the plague and its explanation. The word "ta'un" (plague) follows the pattern fa'ul, from "al-ta'n" (stabbing or piercing). However, when it was turned away from its original meaning, it was used to signify a general death by pestilence. This was stated by al-Jawhari. It is also narrated in a hadith from 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The death of my Ummah will be by stabbing and by plague." She said: "We know stabbing; what is plague?" He said: "A swelling like the swelling of a camel, which appears in the groin and the armpits[[Al-ghuddah: the plague of camels, from which few are spared.]]." The scholars said: This pestilence may be sent by Allah as a vengeance and a punishment upon whomever He wills among His disobedient servants and disbelievers, and He may send it as a martyrdom and a mercy for the righteous, as Mu'adh said regarding the plague of 'Amwas[[Amwas (it is narrated with a kasra on its first letter and sukun on the second, and also with a fatha on the first and second letters and a final sin): a district of Palestine near Bayt al-Maqdis. The plague began there in the days of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), then spread throughout the land of Syria, and a countless number died from it, including Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) and others, in the year 18 AH.]]: "It is a martyrdom and a mercy for you, and the supplication of your Prophet. O Allah, give Mu'adh and his family their share of Your mercy." Then he was stabbed in his palm (may Allah be pleased with him). Abu Qilaba said: "I have understood 'martyrdom' and 'mercy,' but I did not understand what 'the supplication of your Prophet' means. So I asked about it, and it was said: He (peace be upon him) prayed that the death of his Ummah would be by stabbing and plague, when he had prayed that their violence would not be among themselves, and that was refused, so he prayed for this instead."

It is also narrated from the hadith of Jabir and others, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "The one who flees from the plague is like the one who flees from the advance in battle, and the one who is patient in it is like the one who is patient in the advance in battle." In al-Bukhari, from Yahya ibn Ya'mar, from 'A'isha, that she informed him that she asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the plague, and the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) told her: "It was a punishment that Allah sends upon whomever He wills. Allah made it a mercy for the believers. There is no servant in whose land the plague strikes who remains there patiently, knowing that nothing will befall him except what Allah has written for him, except that he will have a reward like the reward of a martyr." This is an explanation of his (peace and blessings be upon him) saying: "The plague is a martyrdom, and the one who dies of it is a martyr." That is, the one who is patient in it, seeking reward from Allah, knowing that nothing will befall him except what Allah has written for him. For this reason Mu'adh wished to die of it, knowing that whoever dies of it is a martyr. As for the one who panics at the plague, dislikes it, and flees from it, he is not included in the meaning of the hadith. And Allah knows best.

**Sixth point:** Abu 'Umar said: I have not heard that any of the bearers of knowledge fled from the plague, except what Ibn al-Mada'ini mentioned, that 'Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an fled from the plague to al-Sayala[[Al-Sayala (with a fatha on its first letter and a lightened second letter): a place near Madinah, and it is the first stage for the people of Madinah when they intend to go to Makkah. It has also been said that it lies between Mall and al-Rawha on the road from Makkah to Madinah (from the commentary on al-Qamus).]], and he would lead the Friday prayer each week and then return. Whenever he led the prayer, they would shout at him: "He fled from the plague!" Then he died at al-Sayala. He said: 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd and Ribat ibn Muhammad fled to al-Ribatiyya. Then Ibrahim ibn 'Ali al-Fuqaymi said about that:

*When death provoked every deniер*
*I was patient, but Ribat did not persevere, nor did 'Amr.*

Abu Hatim reported from al-Asma'i, who said: One of the people of Basra fled from the plague, mounted his donkey, and set off with his family toward Safwan[[Safwan (with a fatha on the first letter): water about one stage from the gate of al-Mirbad in Basra (Mu'jam Yaqut).]]. He heard a driver singing behind him:

*Allah will not be outrun on a donkey,*
*nor on a swift, well-protected mount.*
*Or death will come at its appointed measure;*
*Allah may well come upon the traveler before he arrives.*

Al-Mada'ini mentioned: The plague (ṭā'ūn) broke out in Egypt during the governorship of Abd al-Aziz ibn Marwan, so he left, fleeing from it, and alighted in a village of the villages of Upper Egypt (al-Sa'id) called "Sukar" [[Sukar (on the pattern of Zufar): a place in the eastern part of Upper Egypt, two days' journey from Egypt, to which Abd al-Aziz ibn Marwan would often go out. (From Yaqut.) In the manuscripts it appears as "Sakan" with a nun, which is a distortion.]]. A messenger of Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan came to him when he had alighted there. Abd al-Aziz said to him: "What is your name?" He said: "Ṭālib ibn Mudrik." He said: "Awwah [[Awwah: a word a man says when complaining and expressing pain; its waw is silent and its ha' is kasra. Sometimes they change the waw into an alif, saying "awah min kadha" (alas for such-and-such). Sometimes they double the waw and vocalize it with kasra and make the ha' silent, saying "awwih". Some of them open the waw with doubling, saying "awwah".(From al-Nihayah.)]] — I do not think I will return to al-Fustat!" Then he died in that village.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 244:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah, and know that Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ (2:244). This is an address to the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ) to fight in the way of Allah, according to the majority (al-jumhur) opinion. It is that by which one intends that the Word of Allah be the highest. The ways of Allah are many, so it is general in every way, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: This is my way﴾ [see vol. 9, p. 274]. Malik said: The ways of Allah are many, and there is no way except that one fights for it or in it, and the greatest of them is the religion of Islam; there is no disagreement on this. It was also said: the address is to those who were brought back to life from the Children of Israel, related from Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak. In this view, the waw in His saying "and fight" is conjunctive, joining it to the preceding command, and in the speech there is an omitted element whose implied meaning is: and He said to them, "Fight." In the first view, the waw conjoins a new sentence to the preceding sentence, and there is no need to posit an implied element in the speech. Al-Nahhas said: "And fight" is a command from Allah the Exalted to the believers not to flee as those fled.

(And know that Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing): that is, He hears your speech if you say the like of what those said, and He knows what you intend by it. Al-Tabari said: There is no basis for the view of those who say that the command to fight was addressed to those who were brought back to life. And Allah knows best.

There are eleven issues in this passage. The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah a goodly loan?﴾ When Allah, exalted is He, commanded jihad (striving in the way of God) and fighting for the truth, since there is nothing in the sharia (sacred law) for which fighting is not permitted, for it or against it, and the greatest of these is the religion of Islam, as Malik said, He urged spending for that purpose. This report therefore includes the one who fights in the way of Allah, for he lends with it, hoping for reward, as 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, did at the Army of Hardship [[Jaysh al-'Usra: at the Battle of Tabuk, there was hardship and severity from the heat and the barrenness of the land. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded the people to prepare, and urged the wealthy to spend in the way of Allah. 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, spent a great sum in this. Ibn Hisham said: "Someone I trust told me that 'Uthman spent a thousand dinars, apart from the camels, provisions and what relates to them. The Prophet ﷺ then said: 'O Allah, be pleased with 'Uthman, for I am pleased with him.'"]]. "Man" is in the nominative as the subject, "dha" is its predicate, "alladhi" is an adjective modifying "dha", and if you wish it may be an apposition. When this verse was revealed, Abu al-Dahdah hastened to give his property in charity, seeking the reward of his Lord.

Our shaykh, the jurist, imam, traditionist, judge Abu 'Amir [[In (copies) J, H and Z: "Abu 'Amir Yahya ibn Ahmad ibn Rabi' al-Ash'ari."]] Yahya ibn 'Amir ibn Ahmad ibn Mani' al-Ash'ari, by lineage and school, in Qurtuba (may Allah restore it), in Rabi' al-Akhir of the year 628 AH, informed us by reading from me to him, saying: My father informed us by ijazah (licence) saying: I read to Abu Bakr 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Khalaf ibn Madyan al-Azdi, from Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'dun, by listening to him, who said: Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn Mihran narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Hasan Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Zakariyya ibn Hayawa al-Nisaburi narrated to us in the year 366 AH, saying: My paternal uncle Abu Zakariyya Yahya ibn Zakariyya informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Mu'awiya ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Khalaf ibn Khalifa narrated to us from Humayd [[In all the originals: "from al-A'raj." This is incorrect, because Humayd al-A'raj al-Kufi is the narrator from Ibn al-Harith and from Khalaf ibn Khalifa.]] al-A'raj, from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith, from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: When the verse "Who is it that will lend Allah a goodly loan" was revealed, Abu al-Dahdah said: "O Messenger of Allah, or does Allah, exalted is He, want a loan from us?" He said: "Yes, O Abu al-Dahdah." He said: "Show me your hand." [He said] so he gave him his hand. He said: "I have lent Allah a garden in which there are six hundred palm trees."

Then he went walking until he came to the garden, where Umm al-Dahdah and his dependants were. He called out: "O Umm al-Dahdah!" She said: "At your service!" He said: "Come out, for I have lent my Lord, mighty and majestic, a garden in which there are six hundred palm trees."

Zayd ibn Aslam said: When it was revealed, "Who is it that will lend Allah a goodly loan," Abu al-Dahdah said: "May my father and mother be your ransom, O Messenger of Allah! Allah asks us for a loan while He is free of need of loans?" He said: "Yes, He wants to admit you to Paradise by it." He said: "If I lend my Lord a loan, will He guarantee me and my children, the Dahdah family with me, Paradise?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then give me your hand," and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave him his hand. He said: "I have two gardens, one in the lower part and the other in the upper part, and by Allah I own nothing but these two. I have made them a loan to Allah, exalted is He." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Make one of them for Allah, and leave the other as a livelihood for you and your dependants." He said: "I call you to witness, O Messenger of Allah, that I have dedicated the better of the two to Allah, exalted is He, and it is a garden in which there are six hundred palm trees." He said: "Then Allah will reward you with Paradise for it."

Abu al-Dahdah set off until he came to Umm al-Dahdah, who was with her children in the garden, moving among the palm trees. He then began to recite:

My Lord has guided you to the paths of right guidance,
to the way of goodness and rectitude.
Clear out for me from the garden with affection,
for it has gone forward as a loan until the Day of Reckoning.
I have lent it to Allah, relying on Him,
willingly, without reproach or retraction,
seeking only the doubling of reward in the Hereafter.
So depart with your souls and your children,
for piety, without doubt, is the best provision
that a person sends ahead to the Hereafter.

Umm al-Dahdah said: "May your sale profit! May Allah bless you in what you have bought." Then Umm al-Dahdah replied to him, and began to say:

May Allah give you good news and joy;
one like you fulfils what he has and gives sincere advice.
Allah has granted my dependants enjoyment and bounty,
with the black 'ajwa dates and the ripe bald dates.
The servant strives, and has what he has laboured for
through the long nights, and bears what he has committed.

Then Umm al-Dahdah turned to her children, taking out what was in their mouths and shaking out what was in their sleeves, until she reached the other garden. The Prophet ﷺ said: "How many a heavy-laden palm cluster and a wide, spacious dwelling belong to Abu al-Dahdah!" [[Al-'idhq (with fatha and then sukun): the palm tree. With kasra and sukun: the stalk with its fruit-strands. Radah: heavy.]] [[Al-fayyah (with shadda and without): wide.]]

The second issue: Ibn al-'Arabi said: "Creation was divided, by the judgement of the Creator, His wisdom, power, will, decree and destiny, when they heard this verse, into three categories, and they split into three groups. The first group, the base ones, said: 'The Lord of Muhammad is needy and poor, and we are rich.' This is ignorance that is not hidden from anyone of understanding. Allah answered them with His saying: ﴿Allah has indeed heard the saying of those who said, 'Surely Allah is poor and we are rich.'﴾ [[See vol. 4, p. 294.]] The second group, when they heard this saying, preferred stinginess and miserliness and gave precedence to desire for wealth. So they did not spend in the way of Allah, nor did they free a captive, nor did they help anyone, out of laziness towards obedience and inclination towards this world. [The group [[In Ibn al-'Arabi.]]] The third group, when they heard it, hastened to comply with it, and among them the one who answered quickly gave precedence to his wealth, like Abu al-Dahdah, may Allah be pleased with him, and others." And Allah knows best.

The third issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a goodly loan﴾. "Qard" (loan) is a name for anything for which a reward is sought. And "aqrada fulan fulanan" means he gave him what would repay him. The poet, who is Labid, said:

If you are repaid with a loan, then repay it,
for a young man is only repaid in kind, not with a camel.

The word "qirḍ" with a kasra is also a dialectal form of it, as transmitted by al-Kisa'i. "Istaqradtu min fulan" means I asked him for a loan and he lent it to me. "Iqtaradtu minhu" means I took the loan. Al-Zajjaj said: "Qard in the language means a good trial and an evil trial." Umayya said:

Every man will be repaid for his loan,
whether good or evil, and debts are repaid as he has repaid.

And another said:

Loans are repaid with their likes,
so good is repaid with good, and evil with evil.

Al-Kisa'i said: "Al-qard (loan) is what you send ahead of yourself of good deeds or bad deeds." The root meaning of the word is cutting, and from it comes al-miqrad (scissors). "Aqraztuhu" means "I cut for him a portion of my wealth, for which he will repay me." "Inqarada al-qawm" means their traces were cut off and they perished. Here al-qard is a noun; were it not so, the verb would have been "iqraadan" [The addition is from manuscript Z; in manuscript H it reads: "laqalu iqradan."]. The calling of this verse to a loan is only a means of familiarizing people and bringing it close to them in terms they understand. God is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy, but He, exalted is He, likened the giving of the believer in this world, by which he hopes for its reward in the Hereafter, to a loan, just as He likened the giving of souls and wealth in order to attain Paradise to buying and selling, as its explanation will come in Surat Bara'a (al-Tawba) [See vol. 8, p. 266], God willing, Exalted is He.

It has also been said that the intent of the verse is to urge charity, spending wealth on the poor and the needy, and widening their means, and (spending) in the way of God by supporting the religion. God, glorified is He, referred to the poor by His own exalted Self, which is beyond needs, as an encouragement to charity, just as He referred to the sick, the hungry and the thirsty by His own Self, which is sanctified above deficiencies and pains. In the sound hadith, reported from God, Exalted is He: "O son of Adam, I was sick and you did not visit Me; I asked you for food and you did not feed Me; I asked you for drink and you did not give Me drink." He said: "My Lord, how could I feed You, and You are the Lord of the worlds?" He said: "My servant so-and-so asked you for drink and you did not give him drink. Had you given him drink, you would have found that with Me." And similarly what came before. It was narrated by Muslim and al-Bukhari. All of this came in the form of honouring the one referred to, and as encouragement for the one addressed.

Fourth: It is obligatory on the borrower to repay the loan, because God, Exalted is He, made clear that whoever spends in the way of God is not lost with God, Exalted is He, but rather the reward is certainly returned to him, and He left the reward unspecified. In a report: "Spending in the way of God is multiplied up to seven hundred times and more," as will come in explanation in this surah at His saying, Exalted is He: "The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of God is as the likeness of a grain that grows seven ears" [See p. 302 of this part], and He said here: "So that He may multiply it for him many times over." This has no limit or boundary.

Fifth: The reward of lending is great, because in it there is a widening for the Muslim and a relief of his distress. Ibn Majah reported in his Sunan from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "On the night I was taken on the Night Journey, I saw written at the gate of Paradise: 'Charity is (rewarded) tenfold, and a loan eighteenfold.' I said to Jibril: 'Why is a loan better than charity?' He said: 'Because the one who asks, asks while he has (means), whereas the one who borrows borrows only out of need.'"

He said: Muhammad ibn Khalaf al-Asqalani narrated to us, Ya'la narrated to us, Sulayman ibn Yasir narrated to us, from Qays ibn Rumi, who said: Sulayman ibn Udhanan [In al-Taj: Sulayman ibn Adhnan (dual of adhn), and Alqama: he is Ibn Qays al-Nakha'i al-Kufi, and the hadith is as in the Sunan] used to lend Alqama a thousand dirhams until his stipend came. When his stipend came out he demanded it from him, and pressed him, so he repaid him. Alqama seemingly became angry and stayed away for months [The hadith is authenticated by Ibn Majah, though there is disagreement about it in the originals]. Then he came to him and said: "Lend me a thousand dirhams until my stipend." He said: "Yes, and with honour! O Umm Utba, bring that sealed bag that you have." She brought it, and he said: "By God, these are your dirhams which you repaid me; I have not moved a single dirham from them." He said: "May your father be blessed! What led you to do what you did to me?" He said: "I did not hear from you." He said: "What did you hear from me?" He said: "I heard you narrate from Ibn Mas'ud that the Prophet ﷺ said: 'No Muslim lends a Muslim a loan twice except that it is like its charity once.'" He said: "Thus Ibn Mas'ud informed me."

Sixth: A loan from one human to another is of the same kind, that is, what he lent is returned to him in its like. The scholars agreed that borrowing dinars, dirhams, wheat, barley, dates, raisins and all things that have a like among the rest of foodstuffs is permissible. The Muslims also agreed, transmitted from their Prophet ﷺ, that stipulating an increase in a loan is riba, even if it is a handful of fodder, as Ibn Mas'ud said, or a single grain. It is permissible for the borrower to return something better than what he borrowed, if he did not stipulate that, because that is of the category of kindness. This is based on the hadith of Abu Hurayra concerning the young camel: "The best of you are those who are best in repayment." It was narrated by the imams al-Bukhari, Muslim and others. So the Prophet ﷺ praised the one who repays well, and he stated it without restriction and did not limit it by a description. Likewise he himself repaid for the young camel a choice, four-year-old male camel. Al-khiyar means the chosen, and al-rab'i is the one that has entered its fourth year, because in it he sheds his rubai'a (the tooth that follows the incisors), and these are four rubai'at, lightly pronounced in the letter ba'. This hadith is evidence for the permissibility of lending animals, which is the view of the majority, while Abu Hanifa prohibited that, as has been previously mentioned.

Seventh: It is not permissible for the one who has borrowed to give a gift to the lender, and it is not lawful for the lender to accept it, unless it was their custom to do so. The Sunnah came with this. Ibn Majah reported: Hisham ibn Ammar narrated to us, saying: Isma'il ibn Ayyash narrated to us, Utba ibn Humayd al-Dabbi narrated to us, from Yahya ibn Abi Ishaq al-Hana'i, who said: I asked Anas ibn Malik about a man among us who lends his brother money and then gives him a gift? He said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "If one of you lends his brother a loan and then he gives him a gift or carries him on his animal, he should not accept it nor ride it, unless there was dealing between them before that."

Eighth: A loan may be of wealth, and we have already explained its ruling, and it may be of one's honour (ird). In a hadith from the Prophet ﷺ: "Is one of you unable to be like Abu Damdam, who, when he left his house, would say: 'O God, I have given my honour in charity to Your servants'?" It is also reported from Ibn Umar: "Lend from your honour for the day of your poverty," meaning: whoever reviles you, do not take from him any right and do not impose any punishment on him, until you come on the Day of Resurrection with your reward complete. Abu Hanifa said: It is not permissible to give honour in charity, because it is a right of God, Exalted is He, and it was also narrated from Malik. Ibn al-Arabi said: This is corrupt. He, peace be upon him, said in the sound hadith: "Indeed your blood, your wealth and your honour are forbidden to you," the hadith. This indicates that these three prohibitions run in one course in that by their being respected they are a right of the human being.

Ninth: "Hasanan" (a goodly loan). Al-Waqidi said: seeking reward, with his soul content with it. Amr ibn Uthman al-Sadafi said: he does not boast about it nor cause harm. Sahl ibn Abd Allah said: he does not expect any compensation for his loan.

Tenth: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿fa-yudā'ifahu lahu﴾ (so that He may multiply it for him). Asim and others read "fa-yudā'ifahu" with an alif and a fatha on the fa'. Ibn Amir and Ya'qub read with shaddah on the 'ain, with the alif dropped and a fatha on the fa'. Ibn Kathir, Abu Ja'far and Shayba read with shaddah and a damma on the fa'. The others read with an alif and a damma on the fa'. Whoever reads it with a damma makes it a coordinated clause following His saying "yuqridu" (lends), and it was said: it is on the presumption of "huwa yudā'ifuhu" (He multiplies it). Whoever reads it with a fatha makes it an answer to the interrogative with the fa'. It was also said: by the implied "an" (that). The shaddah and the lightened forms are two dialects. Evidence for the shaddah is "adā'ifan kathīratan" (many multiples), because the shaddah indicates multiplicity. Al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: We do not know this multiplying except for God alone, based on His saying: "and gives from Himself a great reward" [See vol. 5, p. 195]. Abu Hurayra said: This refers to the expenditure for jihad, and we used to reckon, while the Prophet ﷺ was among us, the expense of a man on himself, his companions, and his mount, at two thousand thousand.

Eleventh: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿wallahu yaqbidu wa-yabsutu﴾ (And God withholds and extends). This is general over everything; He is the Withholder, the Extender. We have discussed both of them in "Sharh al-Asma' al-Husna" (Explanation of the Beautiful Names) in the book "al-Asna."

﴿wa-ilayhi turja'un﴾ (And to Him you will be returned) is a warning, so He will recompense each one for his deed.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 246:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Have you not considered the chiefs (al-mala') of the Children of Israel after Moses, when they said to a prophet of theirs, "Send us a king, and we will fight in the way of God"? He said, "Would you perhaps, if fighting is prescribed for you, not fight?" They said, "And why should we not fight in the way of God, when we have been driven out of our homes and our children?" But when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away, except for a few of them. And God is Knowing of the wrongdoers.﴾ (2:246)

He mentioned, in urging people to fight, another story that happened among the Children of Israel. "Al-mala'" means the nobles of the people, as if they were "filled" (mumtali'un) with nobility. Al-Zajjaj said: They were named so because they are filled with what the people need from them. In this verse, "al-mala'" means "the people" (al-qawm), because the meaning requires it. "Al-mala'" is a collective noun, like "al-qawm" and "al-rahat." "Al-mala'" also means good character. From this is the hadith: "Be good to the mala' (in manners), for all of you will be satisfied (sayarwa)," related by Muslim.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿from after Moses﴾, that is, after his death. (When they said to a prophet of theirs, "Send us a king.") It is said that he was Shamwil ibn Bal (ibn Bali) ibn 'Alqamah, and he is known as Ibn al-'Ajuz. He is also called Shim'un (Shamʿun). Al-Suddi said: He was called "Ibn al-'Ajuz" because his mother was an old woman; she asked God for a child when she had grown old and barren, and God granted her him. He is also called Sam'un, because she called on God to grant her a child, so He heard (sami'a) her supplication, and she bore a boy, whom she named "Sam'un," saying: "God has heard my prayer." In the Hebrew language the sin becomes a shin. He was from the descendants of Ya'qub (Jacob). Muqatil said: He was from the offspring of Harun (Aaron), peace be upon him. Qatadah said: He was Yusha' ibn Nun (Joshua). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is weak, because the period of Dawud (David) is many generations after Moses, and Yusha' was the young servant (fata) of Moses. Al-Muhasibi mentioned that his name was Isma'il, and God knows best.

This verse is a report about a group of the Children of Israel who suffered humiliation and the domination of an enemy. They asked for permission to fight and to be commanded to do so. When they were commanded, most of them shrank back (ka'a), and a few remained steadfast, so God gave them victory. [[Editor's note: It is said that "rajul ka'" and "ka''" are said of a man who is cowardly in fighting. It is also said that he is one who does not persist in resolve or firmness, and who turns back on his heels.]] In a report, these people mentioned are those who were made to die and then were brought back to life, and God knows best.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿nuqatil﴾ is read with the nun and with the jazm (short vowel), and the reading of the majority of the reciters is as the answer to the imperative (jawab al-amr). Al-Dahhak and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read it with the ya' and with a raf' (damma) on the verb, so it is in the position of a description (sifah) of the king. The words of the Exalted: (He said, "Would you perhaps") — "'asaytum" with fath and with kasr are two dialects, and Nafi' read with the second, while the rest read with the first, which is the more well-known. Abu Hatim said: There is no justification for the kasr, though al-Hasan and Talhah read with it. Makki said regarding the active participle: "'Asin," which indicates the kasr of the sin in the past tense. The fath of the sin is the common dialect. Abu 'Ali said: The basis for the kasr is the saying of the Arabs: "Huwa 'asin bi-dhalika" (he is likely to do that), like "harin" and "shajin." The forms fa'ala and fa'ila have come in words such as "na'ama" and "ni'ima," and likewise "'asaytu" and "'asiytu." If the verb is attributed to a noun, the analogy of "'asaytum" would be to say "'asiya Zayd," like "radiya Zayd." If that is said, it is the analogy; and if it is not said, it is permissible to take both dialects, so that one is used in place of the other. The meaning of this statement is: Are you close to turning away and fleeing?

(If fighting is prescribed for you, [would you] not fight?) Al-Zajjaj said: "Alla tuqatiluu" is in the position of an accusative, meaning: "Would you perhaps [have] fighting?"

(They said, "And why should we not fight in the way of God?") Al-Akhfash said: "An" is extra (za'idah). Al-Farra' said: It is taken according to the meaning, that is, "what prevented us," as you say: "Ma laka alla tusalliya?" meaning "What prevented you?" It is also said: The meaning is "And what is it for us regarding not fighting in the way of God?" Al-Nahhas said: This is the best of these views. "An" is in the position of an accusative.

(When we have been driven out of our homes) is a cause (ta'lil), and likewise (and our children), meaning, because of our offspring.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿When fighting was prescribed for them﴾, that is, obligated upon them, (they turned away). God informed that when fighting was obligated upon them and they saw the reality, and their thoughts turned to engaging in war, and that their souls might perhaps recoil, "they turned away," that is, their intentions were disturbed and their resolves weakened. This is the condition of pampered nations that incline to ease: they wish for war in times of pride, but when war arrives, they shrink back and yield to their nature. On this meaning the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do not wish to meet the enemy, but ask God for well-being. When you do meet them, then stand firm." Related by the imams. Then God, the Exalted, reported about a few of them that they remained steadfast upon the first intention, and their resolve continued in fighting in the way of God, the Exalted.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 247:**

Allah's words: ﴿And their prophet said to them, "Indeed, Allah has sent Talut (Saul) to you as king."﴾ That is, He responded to what you asked for. Talut was a water-carrier. It is also said he was a tanner, and it is said he was a hired camel-driver. He was a scholar, and for this reason Allah raised him up, as will come. He was from the tribe of Benjamin and was not from the tribe of prophethood or the tribe of kingship. Prophethood was among the Banu Lawi, and kingship was in the tribe of Judah. For this reason they denied him.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: When the chiefs of the Children of Israel said to Samuel ibn Bal what they said, he asked Allah, exalted is He, to send them a king and to show him who it was. Allah, exalted is He, said to him: "Look at the horn (al-qarn) [[al-qarn (with vowelling): a leather container made of hides, split and then sewn.]] in your house that contains the oil. When a man enters upon you and the oil in the horn makes a sound (nashsha) [[nashsha: made a sound.]], he is the king of the Children of Israel. Anoint his head with it and make him king over them."

He said: Talut was a tanner. He went out searching for an animal he had lost, and he headed to Samuel, hoping he would pray for him regarding the matter of the animal or find relief with him. The oil made a sound, as they claim. [[In manuscripts h, w, j: "as they allege."]] Samuel stood up to him, took the oil, anointed Talut's head with it, and said to him: "You are the king of the Children of Israel whom Allah, exalted is He, commanded me to appoint." Then he said to the Children of Israel: "Indeed, Allah has sent Talut to you as king."

Talut and Jalut are two non-Arabic names that have been Arabized, and for this reason they are not declined. The same applies to Dawud, and their plurals are Tawalit, Jawalit and Dawawid. If you named a man Tawus or Raqud [[al-raqud: a large jar, or a jar with a long base; its plural al-rawaqid is an Arabized form.]], you would decline them even though they are non-Arabic. The difference between these and the former is that you say "al-Tawus," adding the definite article, which is possible in Arabic, and this is not possible with those.

Allah's words: ﴿"How can he have kingship over us?"﴾ That is, how can he rule us when we have a better claim to kingship than he does? They followed their customary way of harassing the prophets and deviating from the command of Allah, exalted is He. They said, "How (anna)," meaning, "from what direction." So "anna" is in the accusative position as an adverb of place. "We are of the tribe of kings, and he is not like that; he is poor." They abandoned the stronger cause, which is the decree of Allah, exalted is He, and His prior judgment, until their prophet argued against them with his words: (Indeed, Allah has chosen him), that is, He selected him. This is the decisive proof. Together with this, he explained to them the reason for Talut's selection, which is his superiority in knowledge, the thing on which a person's worth depends, and his physical stature, which helps him in war and is his equipment at the encounter. Thus the verse includes a description of the qualities of the imam and the conditions of the imamate, and that it is deserved through knowledge, religion and strength, not through lineage. Lineage has no share in it alongside knowledge and excellence of the soul, and these take precedence over it, because Allah, exalted is He, informed that He chose him over them for his knowledge and strength, even though they were of more noble lineage. The matter of the imamate and its conditions has already been discussed at the beginning of the surah sufficiently and fully. [[See the fourth issue and what follows, vol. 1, p. 264.]] This verse is a foundation for it.

Ibn Abbas said: Talut was at that time the most knowledgeable man among the Children of Israel, the most handsome and the most complete. Largeness of body is something that inspires awe in the enemy. It is also said: Talut was named so because of his height. It is also said: The increase in his body was through the abundance of goodness and courage, and it does not mean largeness of body alone. Do you not see the words of the poet [[He is al-Abbas ibn Mirdas, as in al-Hamasa and elsewhere.]]:

You see a slender man and you despise him,
while in his garments there is a lion, fierce and rending.

And you are impressed by a man of splendid appearance, and you test him,
but the splendid man disappoints your expectation.

[[Al-tarir: one of fine appearance and aspect. In manuscript h: "so his body does not avail him."]]

A camel may be large without intellect,
and the large camel is not made sufficient by its size.

I say: From this meaning is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to his wives: "The one of you who will join me soonest is the one with the longest hand." So they used to measure their hands. Zaynab was the first of them to die, because she used to work with her hand and give charity. Muslim recorded it. Some of the interpreters said: The intended meaning of knowledge is knowledge of war. This is restricting a general statement without evidence. It has also been said: The increase in knowledge was that Allah revealed to him. According to this, Talut was a prophet, as will come.

Allah's words: ﴿And Allah gives His kingship to whom He wills.﴾ Some of the interpreters held that this is from the words of Allah, exalted is He, to Muhammad ﷺ. It has also been said: It is from the words of Samuel, and this is the more apparent view. He said this to them because he knew of their obstinacy and their disputing over proofs, so he wished to complete his speech with a decisive matter against which there is no objection, and so Allah, exalted is He, said: "And Allah gives His kingship to whom He wills." Attributing worldly dominion to Allah, exalted is He, is the attribution of a possession to its owner. Then he said to them, by way of encouragement and reminder, without any question from them: "Indeed, the sign of his kingship." It is possible that they had asked him for evidence of the truth of his statement: "Indeed, Allah has sent Talut to you as king." Ibn Atiyya said: The first view is more apparent from the context of the verse, and the second is more fitting with the blameworthy character of the Children of Israel. Al-Tabari also held this view.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 248:

Allah's words: ﴿And their Prophet said to them, "Indeed, the sign of his kingship is that the chest (al-tabut) will come to you, containing tranquility from your Lord and a remnant of what the family of Musa and the family of Harun left behind, carried by the angels. Indeed, in that is a sign for you, if you are believers."﴾

Allah's words: ﴿And their Prophet said to them, "Indeed, the sign of his kingship is that the chest will come to you"﴾: The coming of the chest. It was said that the chest had been sent down by Allah upon Adam, peace be upon him, and it remained with him until it reached Ya'qub, peace be upon him. It was among the Children of Israel, and by it they would overcome whoever fought against them, until they disobeyed, and were overcome, and the Amalekites, Jalut (Goliath) and his companions according to al-Suddi, overpowered them regarding the chest and seized the chest from them. I say: this is the clearest evidence that disobedience is the cause of defeat, and this is evident. Al-Nahhas said: The sign in the chest, according to what is related, is that a sound (anin) was heard from it, and when they heard that they would march to their battle, and when the sound subsided they would not march, and the chest did not move. It was also said: they would place it at the crisis of the battle, and they would keep overcoming until they disobeyed and were overcome, the chest was taken from them, and their affair became humiliated. When they saw the sign of total destruction (al-istisal, meaning annihilation and extermination) and the loss of remembrance, some of them became indignant, and they spoke about their affair until their leaders gathered and said to the prophet of the time: "Send us a king." When he said to them, "Your king is Talut," they disputed with him about him, as Allah related about them. When he overcame them with the proof, they asked him for a clear sign confirming that, according to al-Tabari's account. When they asked their prophet for a sign of what he had said, he prayed to his Lord, and a disease descended upon the people who had taken the chest, because of it, according to differing accounts. It was said: they placed it in a church of theirs in which there were idols, and the idols would be found upside down in the morning. It was also said: they placed it in the house of their idols beneath the great idol, and in the morning they found it above the idol; they took it and tied it to its feet, and in the morning the idol's two hands and two feet had been cut off and thrown beneath the chest. They took it and placed it in the village of a people, and those people were afflicted with pains in their necks. It was also said: they placed it in the latrine of a people, and they would be afflicted with hemorrhoids (al-basur) [in MS z and Ibn 'Atiyya: "al-nasur" with a nun]. When their affliction became great wherever it was, they said: "This is nothing but because of this chest! Let us return it to the Children of Israel." They placed it on a cart between two bulls and sent them off into the land toward the lands of the Children of Israel, and Allah sent angels who drove the two cows [as in the originals; in al-Tabari: "the two bulls"] until they arrived among the Children of Israel, who were in the matter of Talut, and they became certain of victory. This is the carrying of the chest by the angels according to this narration. It is also related that the angels came bringing it, carrying it, and Yusha' ibn Nun had placed it in the wilderness. It is related that they saw the chest in the air until it descended among them; this was said by al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: the chest was about three cubits by two cubits. Al-Kalbi said: it was made of shimsar wood (in MSS ḥ, w, j with the shin, mim and sin; what is in h and al-Bahr is with two dotted letters with a mim between them; and in Mu'jam asma' al-nabat it is "shamsad," p. 34), from which combs are made. Zayd ibn Thabit read "al-tabut" (with a ha), which is his dialect, and the people read it with a ta; this has been mentioned before. It is related from him "al-taybut," mentioned by al-Nahhas. Humayd ibn Qays read "yahmiluhu" with a ya.

Allah's words: ﴿containing tranquility from your Lord and a remnant﴾: The scholars differed regarding the tranquility (al-sakinah) and the remnant (al-baqiyyah). Al-sakinah is a form (fa'ila) derived from al-sukun, dignity and calm. So His words "containing tranquility" mean: it is the cause of the calm of your hearts regarding what you disputed about concerning Talut's affair. Its parallel is: "Then Allah sent down His tranquility upon him" [see vol. 8, p. 148], meaning He sent down upon him what calmed his heart. It was also said: he meant that the chest was the cause of the calm of their hearts, so wherever they went they would be at ease with it, and would not flee from the chest when it was with them in battle. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: al-sakinah is a spirit from Allah that speaks; whenever they disagreed on a matter, it would speak clarifying what they wanted, and when it cried out in battle, victory was theirs. Ali ibn Abi Talib said: it is a swift wind that has a face like a human face. It is also related from him that he said: it is a violent wind (rih khajuj, one that passes strongly and unevenly) having two heads. Mujahid said: it is an animal like a cat, having two wings and a tail, and its eyes have rays; when it looks at the army, they are routed. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is a basin of gold from Paradise, in which the hearts of the prophets were washed; and al-Suddi said the same. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the correct view is that the chest contained excellent things from the remnants and relics of the prophets, and souls would find calm in it, feel at ease with it, and grow strong. I say: In Sahih Muslim, from al-Bara', who said: A man was reciting Surat al-Kahf, and beside him was a horse tied with two ropes (shatanayn, al-shatan: a rope, plural ashtan). A cloud covered him and began to circle and draw near, and his horse began to shy away from it. When morning came, he went to the Prophet ﷺ and mentioned that to him, and he said: "That was tranquility descending for the Qur'an."

In the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: that Usayd ibn al-Hudayr, one night while he was reciting in his threshing ground (mirbad, with a kasra, sukun, and fatha: the place where dates are dried)... the hadith. And in it: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Those were the angels who were listening to you; had you continued reading, they would have become visible to the people, they would not have hidden from them." Related by al-Bukhari and Muslim. So he ﷺ informed of the descent of tranquility once, and of the descent of the angels another time, which indicates that tranquility was in that cloud, and that it descends always together with the angels. In this is evidence for those who say that tranquility is a spirit or something that has a spirit, because hearing the Qur'an is valid only for one who understands; and Allah knows best.

Allah's words: ﴿and a remnant﴾: Scholars differed about the remnant in several opinions. It was said: the staff of Musa, the staff of Harun, and the fragments (rudad, its crumbs) of the tablets, because they broke when Musa threw them; this is said by Ibn 'Abbas. 'Ikrimah added: the Torah. Abu Salih said: the remnant is the staff of Musa, the garments of Musa, the garments of Harun, and two tablets from the Torah [in MS z and Ibn 'Atiyya: "and the manna"]. 'Ativa ibn Sa'd said: it is the staff of Musa [and the staff (from h, j, z)] of Harun, their garments, and the fragments of the tablets. al-Thawri said: some people say the remnant is two qafizes (measures) of manna in a basin of gold, the staff of Musa, the turban of Harun, and the fragments of the tablets. Others say: the staff and the two sandals. The meaning of this is what is related: when Musa came to his people with the tablets and found them worshipping the calf, he threw the tablets in anger and they broke; he took out what was intact and gathered the fragments of what was broken and placed them in the chest. Al-Dahhak said: the remnant is jihad and fighting the enemies. Ibn 'Atiyya said: that is, the command regarding that in the chest, either because it was written in it, or because the very bringing of it is like the command to that; and the leaving behind is attributed to "the family of Musa and the family of Harun," since the matter included people from one group to another, and all of them are the family of Musa and the family of Harun. The "family" (al) of a man is his relatives. This has been mentioned before [see vol. 1, p. 381, second and third issues].

In this there are eleven issues.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿When Talut set out with the troops﴾. *Fasala* means he went out with them. One says *fasaltu al-shay'a fa-infasala*, meaning "I cut it and it was cut off." Wahb ibn Munabbih said: When Talut set out, they said to him, "The waters will not carry us, so pray to God that He make a river flow for us." Talut said to them, "God will test you with a river." According to al-Suddi, the number of troops was eighty thousand. [Wahb said: None stayed behind except one with an excuse, through youth, old age, or illness.] *Al-ibtila'* means testing (*al-ikhtibar*). *Al-nahar* and *al-nahr* are two dialectal forms. Its derivation is from breadth (*al-si'a*), and from it comes *al-nahar* (daytime), which has been discussed earlier. Qatada said: The river by which God tested them was a river between Jordan and Palestine. The majority of readers recited *bi-nahar* with a fatha on the ha'. Mujahid and Humayd al-A'raj recited *bi-nahar* with a sukun on the ha'. The meaning of this trial is that it was a test for them: whoever's obedience was evident in abstaining from the water is known to be obedient in other matters, and whoever was overcome by his desire for the water and disobeyed the command would be even more likely to disobey in hardships. It is narrated that they came to the river while thirst had overtaken them, and it was at the height of sweetness and beauty. Therefore the obedient were granted leniency to take a handful, so that the harm of thirst would be lifted from them to some degree, and so that they would break the soul's resistance in that state. It is clarified that a handful suffices to avert the harm of thirst for the resolute, the patient who endure the hardship of life, whose concern lies beyond comfort, as Urwa said:

*"They sip the pure water, though the water is cold."*

I say: From this meaning is His saying, peace be upon him: "A person's sufficiency is a few morsels that keep his back upright." Some who engage in the subtle meanings said: This verse is a parable God has coined for the world. God likened it to the river, the one who drinks from it, the one who leans toward it, the one who takes much of it, the one who abandons drinking from it, the one who turns away from it and renounces it, the one who takes with his hand a single handful, and the one who takes only the amount of need. The conditions of these three are different in the sight of God. I say: How good this would be, were it not for the distortion in interpretation and departure from the apparent sense. Yet its meaning is sound apart from this.

The second: Those who held that Talut was a prophet cited His saying, "God will test you," and that God revealed this to him and inspired him, and that the inspiration was a trial from God for them. Those who said he was not a prophet said: Their prophet Shmuwil informed him by revelation when Talut told his people this. The trial occurred so that the truthful would be distinguished from the liar. Some have held that Abdullah ibn Hudhafa al-Sahmi, a companion of the Messenger of God, ﷺ, only ordered his companions to light a fire and enter it as a test of their obedience, but that he carried his jest to the point of making the command they were given harsher. Its explanation will come, God willing, in *al-Nisa'*.

The third: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Whoever drinks from it is not of me﴾. It has been said that *shariba* means *kara'a* (to drink by lapping directly with the mouth). The meaning of "is not of me" is that he is not of my companions in this war, and this does not remove them from faith. Al-Suddi said: They were eighty thousand, and there was undoubtedly among them the believer and the hypocrite, the diligent and the lazy. In the hadith, "Whoever deceives us is not of us" means he is not of our companions and not upon our way and our guidance. [The poet said, this being the poet al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani, saying it to Uyayna ibn Hisn al-Fazari, who had invited him and his people to break with Bani Asad and annul their alliance; he refused them and threatened them with it, and by *fujur* he meant breaking the alliance; (from *Sharh al-Shawahid*)]:

*"If you attempt treachery against Asad, then I am not of you and you are not of me."*

This is a clear and broad path (*mahay'*) in the speech of the Arabs: a man says to his son when he follows a course other than his manner, "You are not of me."

The fourth: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And whoever does not taste it, he is of me﴾. One says *ta'imtu al-shay'* meaning I tasted it, and *at'amtuhu al-ma'* meaning I gave him water to taste. He did not say "whoever does not drink from it," because it is a habit of the Arabs, when they repeat something, to repeat it with a different word. The language of the Qur'an is the most eloquent of languages, so no weight should be given to the criticism of one who says, "One does not say *ta'imtu al-ma'*."

The fifth: Our scholars have used this as evidence for the doctrine of blocking the means (*sadd al-dhara'i'*, the principle of preventing what leads to a prohibited act). This is because even the slightest tasting falls within the scope of the word "eating," so when the prohibition on eating is stated, there is no way for drinking to occur from one who avoids eating. Because of this emphasis, the text did not say "and whoever does not drink from it."

The sixth: When He said, exalted is He, "And whoever does not taste it," this shows that water is food. And if it is food, it is sustenance, since life is maintained by it and bodies are sustained by it, so it is obligatory that the rules of usury (*riba*) apply to it. Ibn al-Arabi said: This is the correct position of the school. Abu Umar said: Malik said, "There is no harm in selling water on the bank of a river for water, with unequal amounts and on deferred terms." This is also the position of Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf.
