Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: It is among what is measured by volume and weight, so according to this view, unequal exchange is not permissible for him, and that is usury for him, because its effective cause for usury is measure and weight. Al-Shafi'i said: It is not permissible to sell water for unequal amounts, nor is deferral permissible in it, and its effective cause for usury is that it is an edible of the same kind.

The seventh: Ibn al-Arabi said: Abu Hanifa said: If someone says, "If the slave of so-and-so drinks from the Euphrates, he is free," then he is not freed unless he drinks by lapping (*kara'*) from it. *Al-kara'* is that a man drinks from the river with his mouth. If he drinks with his hand or scoops from it with a vessel, he is not freed, because God, glorified is He, distinguished between lapping in the river and drinking with the hand. He said: This is unsound, because the drinking of water applies to every form and manner in the language of the Arabs, whether by scooping with the hand or lapping with the mouth, in one and the same sense; so when the drinking sworn to occurs linguistically and literally, the oath is broken. Know this.

I say: Abu Hanifa's position is more correct, since the people of language distinguished between the two, just as the Book and the Sunnah distinguished them. Al-Jawhari and others said: *Kara'a fi al-ma' kurw'an* means when one takes it with the mouth from its place without drinking with the palms or with a vessel. There is another dialect, *karia* with a kasra on the ra', *yakra'u kara'an*. *Al-kara'* is rainwater that is lapped from. As for the Sunnah, Ibn Majah mentioned in his *Sunan*: Wasil ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us: Ibn Fudayl narrated to us from Layth, from Sa'id ibn Amir, from Ibn Umar, who said: We passed by a pool and began to lap from it, and the Messenger of God, ﷺ, said: "Do not lap, but wash your hands and then drink from it, for there is no vessel better than the hand." This is an explicit text. Layth ibn Abi Sulaym is one whose narrations Muslim included, though he has been declared weak.

The eighth: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Except one who takes a handful with his hand﴾. *Al-ightiraf* is taking from a thing with the hand or with an instrument, and from it comes *al-mighrafa* (ladle). *Al-gharf* is like *al-ightiraf*. It was recited *ghurfatan* with a fatha on the ghayn, and it is a verbal noun, and He did not say *ightirafatan* because the meaning of *al-gharf* and *al-ightiraf* is one and the same. *Al-ghurfa* is one single instance. It was also recited *ghurfatan* with a damma on the ghayn, meaning the thing that is scooped. Some exegetes said: *Al-ghurfa* is with one palm, and *al-ghurfa* with two palms. Others said: Both are dialects with one meaning. Ali, may God be pleased with him, said: The palms are the cleanest of vessels, and from this is the saying of al-Hasan:

*"They do not approach water with vessels, except by scooping from the pools with the palms."*

*Al-dalif* means a slow walk.

I say: Whoever wants pure lawful sustenance in these times, free of doubt, uncertainty, or suspicion, let him drink the water with his palms from the springs and rivers made subservient to flowing through the hours of the night and the day, seeking thereby from God the acquisition of good deeds, the removal of burdens, and joining the righteous leaders. The Messenger of God, ﷺ, said: "Whoever drinks with his hand while he is able to use a vessel, intending humility, God writes for him good deeds equal to the number of his fingers, and it is the vessel of Jesus son of Mary, peace be upon them both, when he threw away the cup and said, 'Uff, this is with the world!'" Ibn Majah narrated it from the hadith of Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of God, ﷺ, forbade us to drink by lapping on our bellies, which is *al-kara'*, and forbade us to scoop with one hand, and said: "Let none of you lap as a dog laps, nor drink with one hand as the people drink whom God has been angry with, and let none drink at night from a vessel without stirring it, unless it is a covered vessel. Whoever drinks with his hand while he is able to use a vessel..." the hadith as previously mentioned. In its chain is Baqiyya ibn al-Walid. Abu Hatim said: His hadith is written down but not used as evidence. Abu Zur'a said: When Baqiyya narrates from trustworthy transmitters, he is trustworthy.

The ninth: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So they drank from it, except a few of them﴾. Ibn Abbas said: They drank according to the measure of their certainty. The unbelievers drank like the thirst-stricken camels (*al-hiym*, camels afflicted with a disease so that they cannot be quenched by water, singular *ahyam*, feminine *haya'*), the disobedient drank less than that, and seventy-six thousand of the people turned back. Some believers did not drink anything, and some of them took a single handful. As for the one who drank and was not quenched, thirst overcame him. As for the one who abandoned the water, his condition was good, and he was more steadfast than the one who took a handful.

The tenth: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So when he had crossed it, he and those who believed with him﴾. The pronoun *hu* refers to the river, and *huwa* is for emphasis. *Al-ladhina* is in the nominative position, conjoined to the pronoun in *jawazahu*. One says *jawaztu al-makan mujawazatan wa jawazan*. *Al-majaz* in speech is that which is permitted in usage, passes through, and continues in its proper form. Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi said: There crossed the river with him four thousand men, among them those who had drunk. When they saw Jalut and his troops, who were one hundred thousand, all of them armed, three thousand six hundred and some eighty turned back. According to this view, the believers who were certain of the resurrection and the return to God, the Almighty, at that moment, and they were the number of the people of Badr, said: ﴿How many a small company has overcome a great company by the permission of God﴾. Most exegetes hold that only those who did not drink at all crossed the river with him. Some of them said: How can we withstand the enemy with their multitude? Then the resolute among them said: ﴿How many a small company has overcome a great company by the permission of God﴾. Al-Bara' ibn Azib said: We used to say that the number of the people of Badr equaled the number of Talut's companions who crossed the river with him, three hundred and some ten men (in another narration, and thirteen men), and none crossed with him except a believer.

The eleventh: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Those who thought﴾. Here *al-zann* means certainty, and it may also mean doubt rather than knowledge; that is, those who supposed that they would be killed with Talut and would meet God as martyrs said this, so the doubt concerned the killing.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 249 (part 2 of 2):

The Exalted One said: ﴿How often has a small company overcome a large company by Allah's permission﴾. Al-fi'ah (the company) is a group of people, and a portion of them, from the root fa'a'tu ra'sahu bi-al-sayf, "I split his head with the sword," and fa'aytuhu, meaning "I cut it." In their saying, may Allah be pleased with them, "How often has a small company..." up to the end of the verse, there is an exhortation to fight, an instilling of patience, and an example to follow for those who were truthful to their Lord. I say: Is this how we ought to act? But ugly deeds and corrupt intentions have prevented us from this, so that our large number is broken before the small number of the enemy, as we have witnessed more than once. That is because of what our own hands have earned!

In al-Bukhari, Abu al-Darda' said: "You only fight by your deeds." In the same work there is a connected report (musnad) that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Are you provided for and given victory except through your weak ones?" So the deeds are corrupt, the weak are neglected, patience is scarce, reliance is weak, and piety is fading! The Exalted One said: ﴿O you who believe, be patient, outdo others in patience, stand firm, and fear Allah, that you may succeed﴾. He said: ﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely﴾. He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him and those who are doers of good﴾. He said: ﴿Allah will surely help those who help Him﴾. He said: ﴿When you encounter a company, stand firm and remember Allah often, that you may succeed﴾.

These are the causes of victory and its conditions, and they are absent among us, not present in us. To Allah we belong and to Him we return, for what has befallen us and descended upon us! Indeed, nothing remains of Islam but its name, and nothing of the religion but its outward traces, because corruption has become apparent, tyranny has multiplied, and right guidance has become rare, until the enemy has taken control east and west, by land and by sea. Trials have spread, calamities have grown severe, and there is no protector except the one whom Allah has mercy upon!

"بَرَزُوا" means they came out into the open (al-barāz), which is the wide, spacious part of the land (al-afyaḥ min al-arḍ al-mutta'si'). Jalut was the commander and king of the Amalekites (al-'Amāliqa), and his shadow was a mile (mīl) long. It is said that the Berbers (al-Barbar) are from his descendants. It is narrated that he had three hundred thousand horsemen. ʿIkrima said: ninety thousand.

When the believers saw the great number of their enemy, they humbled themselves before their Lord. This is like His saying: ﴿And how many a prophet fought, and with him were many devoted followers; and they did not weaken for what befell them in the way of Allah, nor did they become weak, nor did they submit. And Allah loves the steadfast﴾, up to His saying: ﴿And their words were only that they said: "Our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excesses in our affairs, and make firm our feet and help us against the disbelieving people"﴾, the verse.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he met the enemy, would say in the battle: "O Allah, by You I attack and by You I defend." And the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would say when he met the enemy: "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from their evils, and I place You against their throats." He also supplicated on the Day of Badr until his cloak fell from his shoulders, pleading with Allah to fulfil His promise, as will be explained in Āl ʿImrān, if Allah the Exalted wills.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 251 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they routed them by the permission of Allah﴾, meaning: Allah sent victory down upon them. "Fa-hazamuhum" (فَهَزَمُوهُمْ): they broke them. Al-hazm (الْهَزْمُ) means breaking. From it comes the expression siqa'un mutahazzim (سِقَاءٌ مُتَهَزِّمٌ), meaning a waterskin in which parts have folded over one another as it dried out. From the same root is what is said about Zamzam: that it is the "hazmah of Jibril" (هَزْمَةُ جِبْرِيلَ), meaning that Jibril struck it with his foot and the water came forth. Al-hazm also means the dry firewood that has been broken up.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Dawud killed Jalut﴾. The reason is that King Talut (طَالُوتَ) chose him from among his people to fight Jalut (جَالُوتَ). He was a short, sickly, sallow, small, blue-eyed man. Jalut was among the strongest and most powerful of people, and he would rout armies single-handedly. Jalut, who was the head of the Amalekites (الْعَمَالِقَةِ), was killed at his hand. He was Dawud ibn Iysha (داوُدُ ابْنُ إِيشَى) [[Thus in the manuscripts; what is in al-Bahr and elsewhere is Iysha.]], with a kasra on the hamza, and it is also said: Dawud ibn Zakariyya ibn Rashwa (دَاوُدُ بْنُ زَكَرِيَّا بْنِ رَشْوَى). He was of the tribe (sibt) of Yahudha ibn Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, peace be upon them all. He was of the people of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). Prophethood and kingship were combined for him after he had been a shepherd, the youngest of his brothers, and he used to tend sheep. He had seven brothers who were among Talut's companions. When the battle came, he said to himself: "I will certainly go to see this battle." When he set out on his way, he passed by a stone which called out to him: "O Dawud, take me, for by me you will kill Jalut." Then another stone called out to him, and then another, so he took them and placed them in his satchel (mikhlah) and went on.

Jalut came out seeking a single combatant, but the people shrank from him (kaʿʿa al-nas, كَعَّ النَّاسُ) [[Ka'a: became cowardly and weak.]] until Talut said: "Whoever will come out to him and kill him, I will marry him to my daughter and make him the manager of my wealth." Dawud, peace be upon him, came and said: "I will come out to him and kill him." Talut despised him when he saw him because of his young age and small stature, and turned him away. Dawud was blue-eyed and short. Then Talut called out a second and a third time, and Dawud came out. Talut said to him: "Have you tested yourself against anything?" He said: "Yes." Talut said: "Against what?" He said: "A wolf entered my flock, so I struck it, then I took its head and cut it off from its body." Talut said: "The wolf is weak. Have you tested yourself against anything else?" He said: "Yes. A lion entered my flock, so I struck it, then I seized it by its jaws and tore them apart. Do you think this is stronger than the lion?" He said: "No."

Talut had a coat of mail which would fit only the one who would kill Jalut. So Dawud informed him of this, and he put it on, and it fitted him. Talut said: "Mount my horse and take my weapons." He did so, but when he had walked a little way he returned. The people said: "The lad has become cowardly!" Dawud said: "If Allah does not kill him for me and help me against him, this horse will not benefit me, nor will this weaponry. But I want to fight him in my own way." He said: "Dawud was among the best of people at the sling (al-miqla'). So he dismounted, took his satchel, slung it over his shoulder, took his sling, and went out to Jalut. Jalut was armoured on his head with a helmet weighing three hundred ratl, according to what al-Mawardi and others mention. Jalut said to him: "You, lad, are coming out to me?" He said: "Yes." He said: "In this way, as you would come out to a dog!" He said: "Yes, and you are more contemptible." He said: "I will certainly feed your flesh today to the birds and the beasts." Then they drew close, and Jalut intended to take Dawud by the hand in contempt of him. Dawud put his hand into the stones, and it is reported that they joined together and became one stone. He took it and placed it in the sling, invoked the name of Allah, whirled it and threw it, and it struck Jalut's head and killed him. He cut off his head and placed it in his satchel. The people were thrown into confusion, and the companions of Talut attacked, and so the rout came.

It has been said that the stone struck the helmet at the place of his nose. It has also been said that it struck his eye and came out through the back of his neck, and it struck a group of his army and killed them. It has also been said that the stone broke into fragments until every man in the army was struck by some of it. It was like the handful of pebbles with which the Prophet (ﷺ) struck Hawazin on the day of Hunayn. And Allah knows best.

People have said a great deal about the stories of these verses. I have mentioned to you from them what is intended, and Allah is the One to be praised.

I say: The meaning of Talut's words, "Whoever will come out to him and kill him, I will marry him to my daughter and make him the manager of my wealth," is established in our sharia: that the Imam says, "Whoever brings a head, he will have such-and-such; or a captive, he will have such-and-such," as will come with its explanation in surah al-Anfal [[See vol. 7, p. 363.]], if Allah the Exalted wills. In it is evidence that single combat (al-mubarazah, الْمُبَارَزَةُ) is not permitted except with the permission of the Imam, as Ahmad, Ishaq and others say. This has been reported differently from al-Awza'i. It is related from him that he said: "No one should charge except with the permission of his Imam." It is also related from him that he said: "There is no harm in it, but if the Imam forbids single combat, no one should engage in it except with his permission." A group permitted single combat and did not mention permission from the Imam or the lack of it; this is the view of Malik. Malik was asked about a man who says between the two lines: "Who will come out for single combat?" He said: "That is up to his intention. If he intends thereby Allah, then I hope there is no harm in it. This was done in the past." Al-Shafi'i said: "There is no harm in single combat." Ibn al-Mundhir said: "Single combat with the permission of the Imam is good, and there is no sin upon one who engages in single combat without the Imam's permission, and it is not disliked, for I know of no report that prohibits it."

﴿And Allah gave him the kingdom and the wisdom﴾. Al-Suddi said: "Allah gave him the kingship of Talut and the prophethood of Shamun." What He taught him was the craft of making coats of mail, the speech of birds, and other kinds of things which He taught him (ﷺ). Ibn Abbas said: "It is that Allah gave him a chain linked to the Milky Way and the sphere, its top being at the sanctuary (sawma'a) of Dawud. Whenever an event occurred in the air, the chain would resound, and Dawud would know what had happened. No one afflicted with a disease would touch it without being healed. The sign of his people's entry into the religion was that they would touch it with their hands and then wipe their palms over their chests. They would judge by it after Dawud, peace be upon him, until it was lifted up."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿of what He wills﴾, meaning "of what He willed." The future tense is sometimes placed in the position of the past, and this has been mentioned before.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And had Allah not repelled some people by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted, but Allah is full of bounty to the worlds﴾. In this are two issues.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿had Allah not repelled some people by means of others﴾. This is the reading of the majority, except that Nafi' read "difa'" (دِفَاعُ). It is possible that it is a verbal noun (masdar) of a verb, as one says: "hasibtu al-shay' hisaban" (I reckoned the thing), "aba iyaban" (he returned), "laqitu-hu liqa'an" (I met him). Similar is "kataba-hu kitaban" (he wrote it), and from this comes: "kitaba Allahi 'alaykum" (the decree of Allah upon you) [[Vol. 5, p. 123.]]. Al-Nahhas said: "This is good, so difa' and daf' are both verbal nouns of dafa'a, and this is the view of Sibawayh." Abu Hatim said: "Dafa'a and daf'a have the same meaning, like taraqtu al-na'l and tarraqtu" [meaning I patched the sandal and I patched it repeatedly], i.e., I stitched one piece on top of the other, and al-khasf is stitching. Abu Ubayda chose the reading of the majority, "wa-law-la daf'u Allah," and he rejected reading it as "difa'," saying: "Because no one overpowers Allah, the Mighty and Majestic." Makki said: "This is a mistake; he imagined that it has the pattern of mufa'ala (the reciprocal form), and it does not. The name 'Allah' is in the nominative position as the agent of the verb, meaning: 'Had Allah not repelled.' And 'difa'' is nominative as the subject of the sentence according to Sibawayh. 'Al-nas' (the people) is the object; 'ba'dahum' (some of them) is a substitute for 'al-nas'; 'bi-ba'd' (by means of others) is in the position of the second object according to Sibawayh. It is, in his view, like your saying: 'dhahabtu bi-Zayd' (I took Zayd away), where Zayd is in the position of the object. So understand it."

The second issue: The scholars differed about who the people are through whom corruption is repelled. It was said: They are the Abdal (الْأَبْدَالُ, the substitutes), and they are forty men. Whenever one dies, Allah replaces him with another. When the Resurrection comes, they will all have died: twenty-two of them in al-Sham and eighteen in Iraq. It is related from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'The Abdal will be in al-Sham, and they are forty men. Whenever one of them dies, Allah replaces him with another man, through whom the rain is sent down, through whom victory is given over the enemies, and through whom affliction is turned away from the people of the earth.'" This was mentioned by al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim in Nawadir al-Usul. He also related from Abu al-Darda' who said: "The prophets were the pegs of the earth. When prophethood ceased, Allah replaced them with a people from the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) called the Abdal. They did not surpass people in much fasting or prayer, but through good character, sincere scrupulousness, good intention, purity of hearts toward all Muslims, giving them sincere counsel seeking the pleasure of Allah, with patience, forbearance, intellect, and humility without degradation. They are the successors of the prophets, a people whom Allah chose for Himself and singled out by His knowledge for Himself. They are forty truthful ones, thirty of whom are upon the certainty of Ibrahim, the Friend of the All-Merciful. Through them Allah repels hardships from the people of the earth and calamities from people, and through them rain is sent down and sustenance is given. None of them dies until Allah has brought forth one who will succeed him."

Ibn Abbas said: "Had Allah not repelled the enemy by means of the armies of the Muslims, the polytheists would have prevailed, killed the believers, and destroyed the lands and the mosques." Sufyan al-Thawri said: "They are the witnesses through whom rights are extracted." Makki related that most of the exegetes hold that the meaning is: "Had it not been that Allah repels, through those who pray, [harm] from those who do not pray, and through those who are God-fearing [harm] from those who are not God-fearing, people would have been destroyed for their sins." Al-Nahhas and al-Tha'labi also mentioned this. [Al-Tha'labi said [[In ha' and waw-jim.]]] And the rest of the exegetes said: "Had it not been for Allah's repelling of the righteous believers from the wicked and the disbelievers, the earth would have been corrupted," meaning it would have perished.

He mentioned a hadith that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah repels punishment through those of my community who pray, from those who do not pray; and through those who give zakat, from those who do not give zakat; and through those who fast, from those who do not fast; and through those who perform the Hajj, from those who do not perform it; and through those who strive (in jihad), from those who do not strive. And if they were to unite in abandoning these things, Allah would not give them respite for the blink of an eye." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿And had Allah not repelled some people by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted﴾.

And from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "Indeed, Allah has angels who call out every day: 'Were it not for worshippers bowing in prayer, infants nursing, and beasts grazing, the punishment would have been poured upon you, pouring.'" Abu Bakr al-Khatib related it in meaning from the hadith of al-Fudayl ibn Iyad. Mansur related to us from Ibrahim, from Alqama, from Abd Allah [ibn Mas'ud], who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Were it not for men among you who are humble, beasts grazing, and children nursing, the punishment would have been poured upon the believers, pouring."

Some of them took this meaning and said:

*Were it not for worshippers of God who bow in prayer,*
*and infants of the orphans who nurse,*
*and beasts left to graze in the wilderness,*
*the most painful punishment would have been poured upon you.*

Jabir narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah rectifies the offspring of a man because of his righteousness, and his children's children, and the household of his dwelling, and the dwellings around him, and they will not cease to be under the protection of Allah for as long as he is among them."

Qatadah said: Allah tests the believer through the disbeliever, and He protects the disbeliever through the believer.

Ibn Umar said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah repels calamity through a righteous believer from a hundred members of his household and his neighbours." Then Ibn Umar recited: ﴿And were it not for Allah's repelling some people by means of others, the earth would be corrupted﴾.

It was said: This repelling is by means of the laws that He prescribed through the tongues of the Messengers. Were it not for that, people would plunder one another and seize one another's goods and perish. This is a good opinion, for it is general in restraint, repelling, and other things, so reflect upon it.

﴿But Allah is full of bounty to the worlds﴾. He, glory be to Him, explains that His repelling the evil of the disbelievers through the believers is a bounty and a favour from Him.

﴿That﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿the signs of Allah﴾ is its predicate (khabar). If you wish, it may be an appositive (badal), with the predicate being ﴿We recite them to you in truth﴾.

﴿And indeed you are among the messengers﴾: here the predicate of inna is ﴿among the messengers﴾, meaning "and indeed you are a messenger." Allah Most High alerted His Prophet (ﷺ) that these verses mentioned earlier are not known except by a messenger.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 253:

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Those are the messengers⦄. He said: "Tilka" (those) and not "dhalika" (that), observing the feminine form of the word "jama'ah" (group). It is in the nominative case as the subject (mubtada'), "al-rusul" (the messengers) is its adjective (na't), and the predicate of the subject is the sentence (that follows). It was also said: "al-rusul" is an explanatory apposition ('atf bayan), and "fadalna" (We have preferred) is the predicate. This is a problematic verse, and the hadiths are established that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not make distinctions among the prophets" and "Do not prefer one of the prophets of Allah over others," narrated by the trustworthy imams. That is, do not say: "So-and-so is better than so-and-so," nor "So-and-so is more excellent than so-and-so." It is said: "Khayyara fulan bayna fulan wa fulan" and "faddala" (with the doubled letter) when one says that. The scholars have differed in interpreting this meaning. A group said: This was before he was revealed the (verse about) preference, and before he knew that he was the master of the children of Adam, and that the Qur'an abrogates (naskh) the prohibition of preference. Ibn Qutaybah said: He only meant by his saying: "I am the master of the children of Adam" on the Day of Resurrection, for he will be the intercessor on that day, and he will have the banner of praise and the Pool. And he meant by his saying: "Do not prefer me over Musa" as a matter of humility, just as Abu Bakr said: "I have been put in charge of you, and I am not the best of you." Likewise the meaning of his saying: "No one should say, I am better than Yunus ibn Matta" is in the sense of humility. And in His words, Exalted is He: "And be not like the companion of the fish" [see vol. 18 p. 253], there is an indication that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is more excellent than him, because Allah Exalted says: "Be not like him," which shows that his saying "Do not prefer me over him" is out of humility. It is also possible that he meant: "Do not prefer me over him in deeds," for perhaps he (Yunus) is more excellent in deeds than I am, nor in trial and testing, for he (Yunus) had a greater ordeal than I did. What Allah gave our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ of lordship and excellence on the Day of Resurrection over all the prophets and messengers is not by his deeds, but by Allah's preference for him and His singling him out, and this interpretation was chosen by al-Muhallab. Some said: He only forbade delving into this matter, because delving into it is a means to disputation, and that leads to mentioning about them what should not be mentioned, and diminishes their honour in arguing. My teacher said: So one should not say, "The Prophet is more excellent than all the prophets," nor "than so-and-so," nor "is better," as is the apparent meaning of the prohibition, because of the imagined deficiency in the one who is preferred, since the prohibition requires refraining from uttering the expression, not forbidding belief in that meaning. Allah Exalted has informed that the messengers are differing in excellence, so you do not say: "Our Prophet is better than the prophets," nor "than so-and-so the prophet," in avoidance of what is forbidden, in good manners toward him, and in acting on the belief in what the Qur'an contains of preference. And Allah knows the realities of matters. I say: Better than this is the view of one who said: The prohibition of preference is only from the aspect of prophethood, which is one quality in which there is no difference; rather, preference lies in the additional states, special distinctions, honours, graces and distinct miracles. As for prophethood itself, it does not vary, but they differ by other matters added to it. For this reason among them are messengers and possessors of resolve, and among them is one taken as a friend (khalil), and among them one to whom Allah spoke, and He raised some of them in rank. Allah Exalted said: ﴿And We preferred some of the prophets over others, and We gave David the Psalms⦄ [see vol. 10 p. 278], and He said: ﴿Those are the messengers; We preferred some of them over others⦄. I say: This is a fine view, for it reconciles the verses and the hadiths without abrogation, and the statement of preference of some over others is only by what they were granted of virtues and given of means. Ibn 'Abbas alluded to this when he said: Allah preferred Muhammad over the prophets and over the people of heaven. They said: "In what, O Ibn 'Abbas, did He prefer him over the people of heaven?" He said: Allah Exalted said: ﴿And whoever among them says, "I am a god besides Him," that One We will recompense with Hell; thus do We recompense the wrongdoers⦄ [see vol. 11 p. 272]. And He said to Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿Indeed, We have opened for you a clear victory, that Allah may forgive you what preceded of your sin and what follows⦄ [see vol. 16 p. 260]. They said: "Then what is his preference over the prophets?" He said: Allah Exalted said: ﴿And We did not send any messenger except in the language of his people to make things clear for them⦄ [see vol. 9 p. 340], and Allah Mighty and Majestic said to Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿And We have not sent you except comprehensively to mankind⦄ [see vol. 14 p. 300]. So He sent him to the jinn and mankind. Abu Muhammad al-Darimi mentioned it in his Musnad. Abu Hurayrah said: The best of the children of Adam are Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa and Muhammad ﷺ, and they are the possessors of resolve among the messengers. This is an explicit statement from Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Hurayrah in specifying them, and it is known that whoever is sent is more excellent than whoever is not sent, for whoever is sent is preferred over others by the messengership, and they are equal in prophethood, with regard to what the messengers encounter from the denial of their peoples and their killing of them, and this is something with no obscurity in it. However, Ibn 'Atiyyah Abu Muhammad 'Abd al-Haqq said: The Qur'an requires preference, and that in general, without specifying any particular one as the lesser, and so too are the hadiths. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: "I am the most honoured of the children of Adam before my Lord," and he said: "I am the master of the children of Adam," without specifying. And he, peace be upon him, said: "It is not befitting for anyone to say, I am better than Yunus ibn Matta," and he said: "Do not prefer me over Musa." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: In this there is a strong prohibition against specifying the lesser one, because Yunus, peace be upon him, was a young man and buckled (tafassakh) under the burdens of prophethood. [It is said: "Tafassakh al-ba'ir" when the camel cannot bear the heavy load.] If this is the caution regarding Muhammad ﷺ, then regarding others it is more fitting.

I say: What we have chosen is preferable, if Allah wills, for when Allah Exalted informed that He preferred some of them over others, He began to explain some of those who were preferred and mention the states by which they were preferred, saying: "Among them is one to whom Allah spoke, and He raised some of them in rank, and We gave Isa son of Maryam the clear proofs." And He said: "And We gave David the Psalms" [see vol. 6 p. 17]. He Exalted said: "And We gave him the Gospel" [see vol. 17 pp. 262 and 239], "And We gave Musa and Harun the Criterion and a light and a reminder for the God-fearing" [see vol. 11 p. 295]. He Exalted said: "And We gave David and Sulayman knowledge" [see vol. 13 p. 163]. He said: "And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you and from Nuh" [see vol. 14 p. 126], so He generalized, then specified, and began with Muhammad ﷺ, and this is evident. I say: The same applies to the Companions, if Allah wills: they shared in companionship, then differed in virtues by what Allah bestowed upon them of gifts and means, so they are differing in those, although all of them are encompassed by companionship, uprightness and praise. Sufficient for you is the saying of the Truth: ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and those with him are severe against the disbelievers⦄ [see vol. 16 pp. 292, 288 and 274] to the end of the surah. And He said: ﴿And He made them adhere to the word of piety, and they were most deserving of it and worthy of it⦄ [see vol. 16 pp. 292, 288 and 274]. Then He said: ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent before the conquest and fought⦄ [see vol. 17 pp. 262 and 239]. And He said: ﴿Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree⦄ [see vol. 16 pp. 292, 288 and 274]. So He generalized and specified, and removed from them blemish and deficiency. May Allah be pleased with them all, and benefit us with their love. Amen.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Among them is one to whom Allah spoke⦄. The one spoken to is Musa, peace be upon him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about Adam: "Was he a sent prophet?" He said: "Yes, a prophet spoken to." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Some people have interpreted that Adam's speaking was in Paradise, and on this view the distinction of Musa remains. The "ha'" (pronoun) is omitted due to the length of the name, and the meaning is "the one whom Allah spoke to."

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And raised some of them in rank⦄. Al-Nahhas said: "Some of them" here, according to Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sha'bi and Mujahid, is Muhammad ﷺ. He ﷺ said: "I was sent to the red and the black, the earth was made for me a mosque and a purifier, I was supported with awe [al-ru'b: fear and dread. Allah had placed fear in the hearts of the enemies of the Prophet ﷺ, so that if between him and them was a month's journey, they would be in awe of him and flee from him (from al-Nihayah)] over a month's distance, spoils were made lawful for me, and I was given intercession." Among this is the Qur'an, the splitting of the moon, his speaking with the tree, and his feeding a great multitude from a few dates, and the milk of Umm Ma'bad's sheep after drought. Ibn 'Atiyyah said its meaning and added: He is the greatest of people in community, and the prophets were sealed with him, and other such noble character that Allah gave him. The wording may admit that it means Muhammad ﷺ and others whose signs were great, and the statement would then be emphatic. It may also mean the raising of Idris to a lofty place, and the ranks of the prophets in heaven, as in the hadith of the Night Journey, which will come. The clear proofs of Isa are the raising of the dead, the healing of the blind and the leper, and the creating of a bird from clay, as explicitly stated in the revelation.

(﴿And We supported him⦄) We strengthened him.

(﴿with the Holy Spirit⦄) Jibril, peace be upon him, and this has been mentioned earlier [vol. 2 p. 24].

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And if Allah had willed, those who came after them would not have fought one another⦄. That is, after the messengers. It was said: The pronoun refers to Musa and Isa, and the two are plural. It was said: after all the messengers, and this is the apparent meaning of the wording. It was said: fighting occurred only among those who came after them, but that is not the meaning; rather the intended meaning is that people did not fight after each prophet. This is like your saying: "I bought horses, then I sold them," which is permissible for you to say though you only bought one horse and sold it, then another and sold it, then another and sold it. Likewise these incidents: people differed after each prophet, some believed and some disbelieved out of rebellion, envy and for the goods of this world, and all of that is by the decree, destiny and will of Allah Exalted. Had He willed otherwise, it would have been, but He alone holds the secret of wisdom in that act for what He wills. The nun was vowelled with kasra in "wa-lakini ikhtalafu" due to the meeting of two unvocalised letters, and it is permissible to omit it outside the Qur'an. Sibawayh recited:

"So I will not come to him nor am I able to,
But, [oh] by Allah, give me water if your water has surplus."

[The verse is by al-Najashi, describing that he accompanied a wolf in a desolate wilderness with no water in it, and claimed that the wolf replied to him: "I am not coming to what you call me to in companionship, nor am I able to, because I am wild and you are human, but give me water if your water is surplus over your need" (from Sharh al-Shawahid by al-Shantamari).]

(﴿So among them are those who believed and among them are those who disbelieved⦄) "Man" (who) is in the nominative position as the subject, and the relative clause.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 254:

Al-Hasan said: "It is the obligatory zakat." Ibn Jurayj and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "This verse includes both the obligatory zakat and voluntary charity." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This is correct, but what precedes this verse, concerning fighting and that Allah repels [harm] through the believers from the breasts of the disbelievers, indicates that this exhortation is specifically in the way of Allah. This is reinforced at the end of the verse by His saying: ﴿And the disbelievers are the wrongdoers﴾, meaning: so confront them with fighting, with your lives and by spending your wealth."

I say: According to this interpretation, spending wealth is sometimes obligatory and sometimes recommended, depending on whether jihad is individually obligatory or not. Allah, exalted is He, commanded His servants to spend from what Allah has provided them and bestowed upon them, and warned them against withholding until there comes a Day on which there is no buying, no selling, and no making up for any expenditure, as He said: ﴿...so that he says, "My Lord, if only You would delay me to a near term, so I would give charity..."﴾ [see vol. 18, p. 130].

Al-khullah (خُلَّة): pure affection, derived from the penetration of secrets between two friends (takhallul al-asrar). Al-khilalah, al-khalalah and al-khulalah: friendship and affection. The poet said [it is al-Nabigha al-Ja'di, as in Lisan al-Arab]:

"How can you keep up relations with one whose friendship has become like that of Abu Marhab?"

Abu Marhab is a kunya for shade, and it is said that it is the kunya of 'Urqub, about whom it was said: "the promises of 'Urqub" (mawa'id 'Urqub). Al-khullah (also with a damma): what remains of the vegetation after grazing; it is said: "the khullah is the bread of camels and the hamd is their fruit." Al-khallah (with a fatha): need and poverty. Al-khallah: a young she-camel in her second year (ibn makhad), from al-Asma'i. It is said: "He brought them a loaf as if it were the hoof-bone (firsin) of a khallah." The feminine is also khallah. It is said of the dead: "O Allah, make right his khallah," meaning the gap he left behind. Al-khallah: sour wine. Al-khillah (with a kasra): one of the linings of swords, which were covered with linings inlaid with gold and other materials; it is also the thongs worn on the back of the two ends of a bow (siyat al-qaws: what is bent over of its two ends). Al-khillah also: what remains between the teeth. The derivation and meaning of "al-khalil" will come in "al-Nisa'" [vol. 5, p. 399]. Thus Allah, exalted is He, informed that there is no khullah in the Hereafter, and no intercession except by His permission. Its reality is a mercy from Him, exalted is He, by which He honours the one whom He permits to intercede.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ﴿la bay'a fihi wa la khullatun wa la shafa'ah﴾ with a fatha and without tanwin, and likewise in surah Ibrahim: ﴿la bay'a fihi wa la khilal﴾ [vol. 9, p. 366], and in al-Tur: ﴿la laghwa fiha wa la ta'thim﴾ [vol. 17, p. 66]. Hassan ibn Thabit recited:

"Surely there is no spear-thrust nor any raiding horsemen, except your belching at the cooking-pots."

[He says this to the Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b, among whom was al-Najashi, and he was satirising them, making them people of gluttony and greed for food, not people of raids and fighting. Al-'adiyah: the long one. It is narrated as ghadiyah (with a ghayn), which is the one that goes out in the morning for a raid; 'adiyah is more general, since it can be in the morning or otherwise.

(From Sharh al-Shawahid of al-Shantamari.)]

The alif of interrogation does not change the function of "la": as in your saying, "Is there not a man with you?" and it is permissible to say "Is there not a man and not a woman?" just as it is permissible in other than interrogative contexts, so know this. The rest of the readers recited all of these with a raised (marfu') form and tanwin, as al-Ra'i said:

"I did not cut you off until I said, announcing it, 'There is no she-camel of mine in this, nor any male camel.'"

It is also narrated as "wa ma hajartuki" (I did not forsake you). The fatha is on the general negation encompassing all aspects of that category, as if it were an answer to one who asks, "Is there any sale in it?" so he asks a general question and is answered with a general negation. "La" together with the negated noun is like a single noun in a raised position as subject, and the predicate is "fihi". If you wish, you may make it an attribute of "yawm". Whoever raises it makes "la" function like laysa, and makes the answer non-general, as if it were an answer to one who says, "Is there in it a sale?" with the "min" omitted; so the answer comes without changing the raised form, and the raised noun is the subject or the ism of laysa, with "fihi" as the predicate. Makki said: "The preferred reading is the raised form, because most of the readers recite it so; and in other than the Qur'an one may say: la bay'a fihi wa la khullatun." Sibawayh recited, from a man of Madhhij:

"This, by your lives, is the very smallness; may I have no mother if that is so, nor any father."

It is also permissible to build the first and make the second accusative with tanwin, so you say: la rajula fihi wa la imra'atan. Sibawayh recited:

"No kinship today, nor any friendship; the tear has widened over the mender."

So "la" is extra in both positions: the first is coordinated with the position, and the second with the wording. A fifth way is to raise the first and build the second, as in your saying: la rajulun fiha wa la imra'ata. Umayyah said:

"There is no idle talk nor sinful speech therein, and what they utter is never lasting."

These five ways are permissible in your saying: la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah. This has already been mentioned, praise be to Allah.

(wa al-kafirun) is the beginning (mubtada').

(hum) is a second beginning, and (al-zalimun) is the predicate of the second. If you wish, "hum" may be an intervening pronoun (damir al-fasl) and "al-zalimun" the predicate of "al-kafirun." 'Ata' ibn Dinar said: "Praise be to Allah who said: ﴿And the disbelievers are the wrongdoers﴾, and did not say: ﴿and the wrongdoers are the disbelievers﴾."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 255 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah, there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all existence﴾. This is Ayat al-Kursi (the Verse of the Throne), the master of the verses of the Qur'an and its greatest verse, as its explanation has already passed in al-Fatiha. It was revealed at night, and the Prophet (ﷺ) summoned Zayd and had him write it down. It is narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah that he said: When the Verse of the Throne was revealed, every idol in the world fell down, and likewise every king in the world fell down, and crowns fell from their heads, and the devils fled, striking one another, until they came to Iblis and informed him of this. He ordered them to investigate the matter, so they came to Medina and it reached them that the Verse of the Throne had been revealed.

The imams narrate from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Abu al-Mundhir, do you know which verse of the Book of Allah that is with you is the greatest?" He said: I said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "O Abu al-Mundhir, do you know which verse of the Book of Allah that is with you is the greatest?" He said: I said: "Allah, there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all existence." So he struck me on the chest and said: "May knowledge be pleasant for you, O Abu al-Mundhir."

al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim Abu Abd Allah added: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, this verse has a tongue and two lips that sanctify the King at the foot of the Throne."

Abu Abd Allah said: This is a verse which Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, sent down, and He made its reward for its reciter both in this world and in the next. As for the reward in this world, it is a guard for whoever recites it against calamities. It has been related to us from Nawf al-Bikali that he said: The Verse of the Throne is called in the Torah "the Friend of Allah." He means: its reciter is called, in the kingdom of the heavens and the earth, "mighty." He said: When Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf entered his house, he would recite the Verse of the Throne in the four corners of his house. Its meaning is that he sought by this to have it as a guard for him from its four sides, and to repel the devil from the corners of his house.

It is narrated from Umar that he wrestled with a jinn, and Umar threw him down. The jinn said to him: "Let me go, and I will teach you what you protect yourselves with from us." So he released him, and asked him, and he said: "You protect yourselves from us with the Verse of the Throne."

I say: This is authentic. And in a report: Whoever recites the Verse of the Throne after every prayer, the One who takes charge of seizing his soul is the Lord of Majesty and Honor, and he is like one who fought alongside the prophets of Allah until he is martyred.

And from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: I heard your Prophet (ﷺ) say while he was on the steps of the pulpit: "Whoever recites the Verse of the Throne after every prayer, nothing prevents him from entering Paradise except death. And none persists in it except a truthful one (siddiq) or a worshipper. And whoever recites it when he takes his bed, Allah will grant him security for himself, his neighbor, his neighbor's neighbor, and the houses around him."

In al-Bukhari, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entrusted me with guarding the zakat of Ramadan, and he mentioned a story in which it says: I said: "O Messenger of Allah, he claimed that he would teach me words by which Allah would benefit me, so I released him." He said: "What are they?" I said: "He said to me: When you go to your bed, recite the Verse of the Throne from its beginning until you finish, 'Allah, there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all existence.' And he said to me: 'There will never cease to be a guardian over you from Allah, and no devil will come near you until morning.'" And they were the most eager of people for good. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "As for him, he has told you the truth, though he is a liar. Do you know whom you have been addressing these three nights, O Abu Hurayrah?" He said: "No." He said: "That was a devil."

In Musnad al-Darimi, Abu Muhammad, al-Sha'bi said: Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: A man from the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) met a man from the jinn and wrestled with him, and the human threw him down. The human said to him: "I see you are slight and lean, as if your two forearms were the forearms of a dog. Is that how you jinn are, or are you particularly like that among them?" He said: "No, by Allah! I am stout among them. But wrestle with me a second time, and if you throw me down, I will teach you something that will benefit you." He said: "Yes." So he threw him down. He said: "Do you recite the Verse of the Throne: 'Allah, there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all existence'?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Indeed, the devil will leave any house in which you recite it, passing wind like the braying of a donkey, and he will not enter it until morning."

Abu Nu'aym narrated it from Abu Asim al-Thaqafi, from al-Sha'bi. Abu Ubayd mentioned it in Gharib Hadith Umar: Abu Mu'awiyah narrated it to us from Abu Asim al-Thaqafi, from al-Sha'bi, from Abd Allah, who said: It was said to Abd Allah: "Was it Umar?" He said: "Who else could it be but Umar!"

Abu Muhammad al-Darimi said: al-Dhai'il means slender; al-Shakhit means emaciated; al-Dhali' means well-boned; and al-Khabaj means wind. Abu Ubayd said: al-Khabaj means flatulence, and it is also al-Habaj with a ha'.

In al-Tirmidhi, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Ha Mim (the Believer) up to 'to Him is the final return' and the Verse of the Throne in the morning will be protected by them until evening, and whoever recites them in the evening will be protected by them until morning." He said: This is a strange (gharib) hadith.

Abu Abd Allah al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim said: It has been related that the believers were urged to be constant in reciting it after every prayer. From Anas, who raised the hadith to the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "Allah revealed to Musa (peace be upon him): Whoever is constant in reciting the Verse of the Throne after every prayer, I will give him more than I give the grateful [in the original: 'I gave him the hearts of the grateful'; the correction is from the book al-Sirr al-Qudsi fi Tafsir Ayat al-Kursi], and the reward of the prophets and the deeds of the truthful, and I will spread My right hand over him with mercy, and nothing will prevent Me from admitting him into Paradise except that the Angel of Death comes to him." Musa (peace be upon him) said: "O Lord, who will hear of this and not be constant in it?" He said: "I give it only to a prophet, a truthful one, a man whom I love [in another manuscript: 'whom I have chosen'], or a man whom I intend to kill in My cause."

From Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: Allah the Exalted said: "O Musa, whoever recites the Verse of the Throne after every prayer, I will give him the reward of the prophets." Abu Abd Allah said: Its meaning, in my view, is that I will give him the reward of the deeds of the prophets. As for the reward of prophethood, it belongs to no one except the prophets.

This verse contains tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness) and the sublime attributes. It consists of fifty words, and in each word there are fifty blessings. It equals one third of the Qur'an, and the hadith concerning this has been reported; it was mentioned by Ibn Atiyyah.

"Allah" is a mubtada' (subject of a nominal sentence). "La ilaha" is a second subject, and its predicate is omitted, the estimate being "ma'bud" (worshipped) or "mawjud" (existent). "Illa Huwa" is a substitute (badal) for the position of "la ilaha." It was also said: "Allah, la ilaha illa Huwa" is a beginning and a predicate, and it is in the nominative case, governed by meaning, i.e., "there is no deity except Him." Outside the Qur'an it is permissible to say "la ilaha illa iyyahu" in the accusative, as an exception.

Abu Dharr, in his long hadith, said: I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Which verse of the Qur'an that Allah sent down to you is the greatest?" He said: "Allah, there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all existence."

Ibn Abbas said: The most noble verse in the Qur'an is the Verse of the Throne. Some scholars said: That is because the name of Allah, Exalted is He, is repeated in it, between pronoun and noun, eighteen times.

"Al-Hayy al-Qayyum" (the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all existence) is an epithet (na't) of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. If you wish, it may be a substitute (badal) for "Huwa"; if you wish, it may be a predicate after a predicate; and if you wish, it may be by supposing an omitted subject. Outside the Qur'an the accusative is permissible, as praise.

"Al-Hayy" is one of His Most Beautiful Names, by which He is named, and it is said that it is the Greatest Name of Allah. It is said that Jesus son of Mary (peace be upon him), whenever he wished to raise the dead, would supplicate with this invocation: "Ya Hayy, ya Qayyum." It is said that Asaf ibn Barkhiya, when he wished to bring the throne of Bilqis to Sulayman, supplicated with the words "Ya Hayy, ya Qayyum." It is said that the Children of Israel asked Musa about the Greatest Name of Allah, and he said to them: "Ayya hayya sharaya hayya," meaning "Ya Hayy, ya Qayyum." It is said that it is the supplication of the people of the sea when they fear drowning, and they call upon it with it.

al-Tabari said, regarding some people: It is said that He is "Hayy Qayyum" as He described Himself, and this is accepted without investigation. It was also said: He named Himself "Hayy" because He directs affairs to their courses and determines things according to their measures.

Qatadah said: al-Hayy is the One who does not die. al-Sudda said: What is meant by al-Hayy is the Everlasting. Labid said:

Though you see me today, having become safe,
I am not more alive than Kilab and Ja'far.

It has been said that this name is the Greatest Name of Allah.

"Al-Qayyum" derives from qama, meaning the one who stands in managing what He created, according to Qatadah. al-Hasan said: Its meaning is the one who stands over every soul with what it has earned, until He recompenses it for its deed, since He is knowing of it and nothing of it is hidden from Him. Ibn Abbas said: Its meaning is the One who does not change and does not cease. Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said:

The heaven was not created, nor the stars,
nor the sun with the moon moving alongside it,
Measured by the Protector, the Sustainer,
nor the Gathering, nor Paradise, nor bliss,
Except for a matter whose affair is great.

al-Bayhaqi said: I saw in "Uyun al-Tafsir" by Isma'il al-Darir the explanation of al-Qayyum, where he said: It is said that He is the One who does not sleep, and it seems he took this from His saying, Mighty and Majestic, right after it in the Verse of the Throne: "Slumber does not seize Him, nor sleep." al-Kalbi said: al-Qayyum is the One for whom there is no substitute (la badil lahu), mentioned by Abu Bakr al-Anbari. The original form of qayyum is qayyum, where waw and ya' came together and one of them was preceded by a sukun, so the first was assimilated into the second after the waw was changed to ya'. Qayyum cannot be fa'ul, because it derives from waw, so it would have been "qayyuwum."

Ibn Mas'ud, Alqamah, al-A'mash, and al-Nakha'i read "al-Hayy al-Qayyam" with an alif, and this is related from Umar. There is no disagreement among the lexicographers that al-Qayyum is better known among the Arabs, sounder in form, and more firmly founded in its root. al-Qayyam is transferred from al-Qawwam to al-Qayyam, shifted from fa''al to fayy'al, as it was said of the goldsmiths al-Sayyagh (from al-Sawagh). The poet said:

Indeed, the Lord of the Throne is the One who provides for the people,
and the Living, over them, is the Sustainer.

Then Mighty and Majestic negated that slumber or sleep should seize Him. Sinah (slumber) is drowsiness, according to the consensus. Drowsiness is what is from the eye; when it reaches the heart it becomes sleep. 'Adi ibn al-Riqa' said, describing a woman by the languor of her gaze:

Drowsy, sleep has overcome him, and its haze
has clouded his eye with slumber, though he is not asleep.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 255 (part 2 of 3):

Al-Mufaddal distinguished between the two, saying: "Drowsiness (sinah) is in the head, slumber (nu'as) is in the eye, and sleep (nawm) is in the heart." Ibn Zayd said: "The wasnan (one who is drowsy) is the one who rises from sleep without understanding, to the extent that he may draw his sword against his own family." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "What Ibn Zayd said is open to question, and that is not what is understood from the speech of the Arabs." As-Suddi said: "Al-sinah is the breeze of sleep that comes over the face, so that a person becomes drowsy."

I say: In general, it is a lethargy that overtakes a person without his losing his reason along with it. The meaning of this verse is that Allah, exalted is He, is not overtaken by any defect and is not affected by any weariness in any state. The original form of sinah and wasnah is that the waw was dropped, just as it was dropped from yasin (the verb, which in the books of lexicography is from the pattern of "fariha").

Nawm is the deep sleep in which the mind departs, in the case of human beings. The waw is for coordination (conjunction), and "la" is for emphasis.

I say: People mention on this subject, from Abu Hurairah, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) relate from Musa on the pulpit, he said: "It occurred to the soul of Musa: Does Allah, exalted is His praise, sleep? So Allah sent to him an angel who kept him awake for three nights, then gave him two flasks, one in each hand, and commanded him to guard them. He said: So he began to sleep, and his hands were almost meeting; then he would wake and move one away from the other, until he slept a sleep, and his hands jerked and the two flasks broke." He said: "Allah struck a parable for him: If He were to sleep, the heavens and the earth would not be held firm." "This hadith is not sound; many have declared it weak, among them al-Bayhaqi."

The words of His, exalted is He: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth﴾, meaning by ownership, so He is the Owner of all of it and its Lord. The expression used is "ma" (what), although among those in it are those who have reason, because the intent is the whole and what exists. Al-Tabari said: This verse was revealed when the disbelievers said: "We worship idols only so that they may bring us near to Allah in closeness."

His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ "Man" is in the nominative case as the subject, and "dha" is its predicate, and "alladhi" is an attribute of "dha"; if you wish, it may be an apposition. It is not permissible for "dha" to be redundant, as it is redundant with "ma," because "ma" is indefinite, so "dha" was added with it due to its resemblance to it. It is established in this verse that Allah permits whomever He wills to intercede, and they are the prophets, the scholars, the martyrs, the angels, and others whom Allah has honored and distinguished. Then they do not intercede except for those whom He approves, as He said: ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ [see vol. 11, p. 381]. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: What appears is that the scholars and the righteous intercede for those who have not reached the Fire and are between the two ranks, or who have reached it but have good deeds. In al-Bukhari, in the chapter "a remainder from the chapters on the vision": "The believers will say: Our Lord, our brothers used to pray with us and fast with us." This is intercession for those whose affair is near, and as the child who is stubborn (al-muhbanti'), [al-muhbanti': one who clings to the ground; and in the hadith, "the miscarried child will sit stubbornly (yuzallil muhbanti'an) at the gate of Paradise." Ibn al-Athir said: al-muhbanti' (with or without hamza): one who is angry and impatient for something. It is said: he is one who refuses by way of seeking, not by way of refusal of denial.] intercedes at the gate of Paradise. This is only regarding their relatives and acquaintances. And the prophets intercede for those among the sinful of their nations who have entered the Fire through sins, without kinship or acquaintance, but solely through faith itself. Then the intercession of the Most Merciful of the merciful remains for those who are immersed in sins and transgressions, upon whom the intercession of the prophets has had no effect. As for the intercession of Muhammad (ﷺ) in hastening the reckoning, it is specific to him.

I say: Muslim has clearly explained the manner of intercession in his Sahih, and it seems that he (al-Qurtubi's critic) did not read it, and that the interceders enter the Fire and bring out people who deserved punishment. Accordingly, it is not far-fetched that the believers have two intercessions: an intercession for those who have not reached the Fire, and an intercession for those who have reached it and entered it, may Allah save us from it. He mentions from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: "Then the bridge will be laid over Hell, and intercession will be permitted, and they will say: O Allah, grant safety, grant safety." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is the bridge?" He said: "A slippery place (dahd) with hooks, claws and a thorny plant (hasakah) in Najd, with a shrub called al-sa'dan. The believers will pass over it like the blink of an eye, like lightning, like the wind, like birds, and like the swiftest horses and riding camels. Some will be saved and unharmed, some will be scratched and released (mursal, i.e. wounded without restraint), and some will be thrown (makdus) into the Fire of Hell. When the believers have been delivered from the Fire, by Him in whose hand is my soul, none of you is more insistent in appealing to Allah for the recovery of rights from the believers on the Day of Resurrection than they are for their brothers who are in the Fire. They will say: Our Lord, they used to fast with us, pray with us and perform pilgrimage. It will be said to them: Bring out those whom you recognise. Their forms will be forbidden to the Fire, and they will bring out a great number, whom the Fire has seized up to the middle of their shins and their knees. Then they will say: Our Lord, none remains in it of those You commanded us about. He, Mighty and Majestic, will say: Return, and whoever you find in his heart the weight of a dinar of good, bring him out. They will bring out a great number. Then they will say: Our Lord, we have not left in it anyone of those You commanded us about. Then He will say: Return, and whoever you find in his heart the weight of half a dinar of good, bring him out. They will bring out a great number. Then they will say: Our Lord, we have not left in it anyone of those You commanded us about. Then He will say: Return, and whoever you find in his heart the weight of an atom (dharrah) of good, bring him out. They will bring out a great number. Then they will say: Our Lord, we have not left in it any good." Abu Sa'id used to say: "If you do not believe me in this hadith, then recite, if you wish: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong (anyone) an atom's weight; and if there is a good deed, He multiplies it and gives from Himself a great reward﴾ [see vol. 5, p. 194]." Then Allah, exalted is He, says: "The angels have interceded, the prophets have interceded, and the believers have interceded, and none remains except the Most Merciful of the merciful. He will grasp a handful from the Fire and bring out from it a people who never did any good; they have become charcoal (hummam)." [Al-hummam (with a damma on the ha and a fatha on the first, lightened mim): charcoal, singular hummamah, like hutamah.] He mentioned the hadith in full. And from the hadith of Anas from the Prophet (ﷺ): "I will say: O Lord, permit me regarding those who said: There is no god but Allah. He will say: That is not for you, or he said: That is not up to you. By My might, My majesty and My greatness [and My grandeur (jibriya'i)] I will surely bring out whoever said: There is no god but Allah." And it is mentioned from the hadith of Abu Hurairah, from him (peace and blessings be upon him): "When Allah has finished judging among the servants and wishes to bring out, by His mercy, whomever He wills from the people of the Fire, He will command the angels to bring out from the Fire whoever did not associate anything with Allah, of those whom Allah wished to have mercy upon, who say: There is no god but Allah. They will recognise them in the Fire by the mark of prostration. The Fire consumes the son of Adam except the mark of prostration; Allah has forbidden the Fire to consume the mark of prostration." The hadith in full.

I say: These hadiths indicate that the intercession of the believers and others is only for the one who has entered the Fire and been in it, may Allah save us from it! As for Ibn 'Atiyyah's words, "for those who have not reached it or have reached it," it may be that he took it from other hadiths, and Allah knows best. Ibn Majah has reported in his Sunan, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "People will be arranged in rows on the Day of Resurrection, (and Ibn Numayr said: the people of Paradise), and a man from the people of the Fire will pass by a man and say: O so-and-so, do you not remember the day you asked me for a drink and I gave you a drink? He will intercede for him. And a man will pass by a man and say: Do you not remember the day I handed you water for purification? He will intercede for him." (Ibn Numayr added): "And he will say: O so-and-so, do you not remember the day you sent me on such-and-such an errand and I went for you? So he will intercede for him."

As for the intercessions of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), they are differed over: it is said there are three, two; and it is said five, whose explanation will come in (the commentary on) Surah Subhan, if Allah wills. We have dealt with them in the book "al-Tadhkirah," and praise be to Allah.

His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾. The two pronouns refer to everyone who has reason among those included in His saying: "To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth." Mujahid said: "What is before them" is this world, "and what is behind them" is the Hereafter. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: All of this is correct in itself and there is no harm in it, because what is before a person is everything that precedes him, and what is behind him is everything that comes after him; and in the same vein as Mujahid's statement is what as-Suddi and others said.

His, exalted is He, saying: (And they do not encompass anything of His knowledge except what He wills). "Knowledge" here means "what is known," i.e., they do not encompass anything of what is known to Him. This is like the saying of al-Khidr to Musa, peace be upon him, when the sparrow pecked in the sea: "My knowledge and your knowledge, compared with the knowledge of Allah, are no more than what this sparrow has taken from this sea." This and what resembles it refers to the things known, because the knowledge of Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, which is an attribute of His essence, is not divisible.

The meaning of the verse is: No one knows anything except what Allah wills for him to know.

His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth﴾. Ibn 'Asakir mentioned in his History, from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Kursi is a pearl, and the Pen is a pearl; the length of the Pen is seven hundred years, and the length of the Kursi is such that none knows it except Allah." [In some copies: "none knows it except the knowledgeable."] And Hammad ibn Salamah related from 'Asim ibn Bahdalah, who is 'Asim ibn Abi al-Najud, from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Between every two heavens is a journey of five hundred years, and between the seventh heaven and the Kursi is five hundred years, and between the Kursi and the Throne is a journey of five hundred years, and the Throne is above the water, and Allah is above the Throne, knowing what you are in and what you are upon." It is said: kursiyy and kirsiyy, and the plural is al-karasiyy. Ibn 'Abbas said: "His Kursi is His knowledge." Al-Tabari preferred this and said: From it comes the al-kurrasah (notebook) that contains knowledge, and from it the scholars are called karasiyy, because they are the ones relied upon, as one says: "the pegs of the earth."

The poet said:
Around them are fair-faced men and a band
of kursi (pillars) in calamities when they befall.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 255 (part 3 of 3):

That is, scholars of the events of affairs. It has also been said: His Kursi is His power, by which He holds up the heavens and the earth, just as you would say: "Make a kursi for this wall," meaning that which props it up. This is close to the statement of Ibn 'Abbas concerning the words "His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth," as reported by al-Bayhaqi. We have also related from Ibn Mas'ud and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning the words "His Kursi extends over," that he said: "His knowledge." All the other reports from Ibn 'Abbas and others indicate that what is meant is the well-known Kursi together with the Throne. Israil narrated from al-Suddi, from Abu Malik, concerning His words "His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth," that he said: "The rock upon which the seventh earth rests, and the limit of creation is at its edges, upon it are four angels, each of whom has four faces: the face of a man, the face of a lion, the face of an ox, and the face of an eagle. They stand upon it, having encompassed the earths and the heavens, and their heads are beneath the Kursi, and the Kursi is beneath the Throne, and Allah places His Kursi above the Throne." Al-Bayhaqi said: In this there is an indication of two Kursis: one beneath the Throne, and the other placed upon the Throne. In the narration of Asbat from al-Suddi, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Murrah al-Hamdani from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Murrah al-Hamdani from Ibn Mas'ud, from some of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, concerning His words "His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth," that the heavens and the earth are within the hollow of the Kursi, and the Kursi is before the Throne. The heretics interpret these as referring to the greatness of the kingdom and the majesty of the sovereignty, and deny the existence of the Throne and the Kursi, but this is not correct. The people of truth affirm both, since in the power of Allah there is ample room, so it is obligatory to believe in that. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari said: "The Kursi is the place of the two feet, and it has a creaking (atit) like the creaking of a saddle." Al-Bayhaqi said: We have also related this from Ibn 'Abbas, and we have mentioned that its meaning, as it appears, is that it is placed from the Throne at the place of the two feet of a bed. There is in it no affirmation of place for Allah, exalted is He. And from Ibn Buraydah, from his father, who said: When Ja'far came from Abyssinia, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: "What is the most astonishing thing you have seen?" He said: "I saw a woman with a basket of food on her head, and a horseman passed by and scattered it, so she sat down gathering her food. Then she turned to him and said: 'Woe to you on the day when the King places His Kursi and takes for the oppressed from the oppressor!'" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, confirming her words: "A nation is not sanctified—or how can a nation be sanctified—in which the weak does not take his right from the strong." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: As for Abu Musa's statement "The Kursi is the place of the two feet," he means that it is, from the Throne of the Most Merciful, like the place of the two feet of the beds of kings. It is a great created thing before the Throne, its relation to it being like the relation of the stool to the king's seat. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: The Kursi is the Throne itself, but this is not acceptable, and what the hadiths indicate is that the Kursi is a creature before the Throne, and the Throne is greater than it. Abu Idris al-Khawlani narrated from Abu Dharr, who said: I said: "O Messenger of Allah, which of what was revealed to you is greatest?" He said: "The Ayat al-Kursi," then he said: "O Abu Dharr, the seven heavens with the Kursi are nothing but like a ring thrown in a desert land, and the excellence of the Throne over the Kursi is like the excellence of the desert over the ring." Al-Ajurri and Abu Hatim al-Busti in his Sahih Musnad, and al-Bayhaqi, related it, and he said it is sahih. Mujahid said: The heavens and the earth in the Kursi are nothing but like a ring thrown in a desert land. This verse indicates the greatness of Allah's creations, and from this is derived the greatness of Allah's power, the Mighty and Majestic, since the preservation of this great matter does not burden Him. "Yauduhu" means it burdens Him; it is said: "Adani al-shay'" meaning "the thing burdened me," and "I bore hardship from it." By this meaning Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah and others explained the word. Al-Zajjaj said: It is permissible that the pronoun refers to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and it is permissible that it refers to the Kursi; and if it refers to the Kursi, then it is from the affair of Allah, exalted is He. As for "al-'Ali," it is meant as elevation of rank and station, not elevation of place, because Allah is exalted above being confined to a direction. Al-Tabari related from some people that they said: He is "al-'Ali" above His creation by the elevation of His place above the places of His creation. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is the saying of ignorant anthropomorphists, and it would have been better not to relate it. It is narrated from Abd al-Rahman ibn Qurt that on the night of the Isra' the Messenger of Allah ﷺ heard glorification in the highest heavens: "Glory be to Allah, the Most High, the Supreme, glory be to Him and exalted is He." "Al-'Ali" and "al-'Ali" mean the Dominant, the Victorious over things; the Arabs say: "Fulan 'alā Fulānan," meaning he overcame him and subdued him. The poet said:
"When we rose over them and prevailed upon them, we left them prostrate for the eagle and the hawk."
From this is His saying, exalted is He: "Indeed Pharaoh exalted himself in the land" [see vol. 13, p. 248]. "Al-'Azim" is an attribute meaning great in rank, worth and nobility, not in the sense of the largeness of bodies. Al-Tabari related from some people that "al-'Azim" means "al-Mu'azzam" (the one who is magnified), as one says "al-'Atiq" meaning "al-Mu'attaq" (the freed), and he recited the verse of al-A'sha:
"As if the old wine of al-Isfinṭ [a kind of drink, Persian, arabicized], mixed with clear water..."
And it is related from some people that they denied this and said: If it meant "magnified," it would necessarily follow that He would not be "great" before He created creation and after their annihilation, since then there would be no one to magnify Him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 256:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾. In this there are two issues.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion.﴾ The word "religion" (din) in this verse means belief (al-mu'taqad) and creed (al-millah), as indicated by His saying: (The right course has become clear from the error). The compulsion that appears in the rulings concerning faith (iman), sales, gifts and other matters does not belong in this place; it belongs rather in the explanation of His saying: "except one who is compelled" [[see vol. 10, p. 180]].

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read "Qad tabayyana al-rushdu min al-ghayy" (the right course has become clear from the error), and the same is related from al-Hasan and al-Sha'bi. It is said: rashada yarshudu rushdan and rashida yarshadu rashadan, meaning he attained what he loves. Its opposite is ghawa, related from al-Nahhas. Ibn 'Atiyyah related from Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami that he read "al-rashad" with an alif. It is also related from al-Hasan (al-rushud) with a dammah on the ra' and the shin.

(Al-ghayy) is a verbal noun from ghawa yaghwi, when one goes astray in a belief or an opinion. Al-ghayy is not used for misguidance in an absolute sense.

The second issue: The scholars differed regarding the meaning of [[in h, j and b: "the meaning of"]] this verse, in six opinions.

(The first) It is said that it is abrogated (mansukhah), because the Prophet ﷺ compelled the Arabs to the religion of Islam and fought them, and he did not accept from them anything but Islam. This was said by Sulayman ibn Musa, who said: it was abrogated by "O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites" [[see vol. 8, p. 240]]. This is also related from Ibn Mas'ud and many of the exegetes.

(The second) It is not abrogated; rather it was revealed specifically concerning the People of the Book, who are not compelled to accept Islam once they pay the jizyah, whereas those who are compelled are the people of idols, from whom nothing is accepted except Islam; they are the ones concerning whom "O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites" was revealed. This is the view of al-Sha'bi, Qatadah, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak. The evidence for this view is what Zayd ibn Aslam related from his father, who said: I heard 'Umar ibn al-Khattab say to an old Christian woman: "Embrace Islam, O old woman, and you will be safe; indeed God sent Muhammad with the truth." She said: "I am an old woman, and death is near to me!" So 'Umar said: "O God, bear witness," and recited "There is no compulsion in religion."

(The third) What Abu Dawud related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: this was revealed concerning the Ansar. A woman among them would be barren, and would vow that if a child lived for her, she would make it a Jew. When the Banu al-Nadir were expelled, many of the sons of the Ansar were among them, and they said: "We will not leave our sons!" So God, exalted is He, revealed: "There is no compulsion in religion. The right course has become clear from the error." Abu Dawud said: "The muqlat is the woman for whom no child survives." In another narration: "We only did what we did because we considered their religion better than what we were upon; but when God brought Islam, we would compel them to it."
