So "There is no compulsion in religion" was revealed: whoever wishes may join them, and whoever wishes may enter Islam. This is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Sha'bi and Mujahid, except that he said: the cause of their being among the Banu al-Nadir was fostering (al-istirda'). Al-Nahhas said: Ibn 'Abbas's statement concerning this verse is the most preferable of the opinions, because its chain is sound, and such a matter is not taken by personal opinion.

(The fourth) Al-Suddi said: the verse was revealed concerning a man from the Ansar called Abu Husayn, who had two sons. Merchants came from Syria to Medina carrying olive oil, and when they wished to leave, the two sons of al-Husayn came to them and they invited them to Christianity, so both became Christians and went with them to Syria. Their father came to the Messenger of God ﷺ complaining of their affair, and he desired that the Messenger of God ﷺ send someone to bring them back. So "There is no compulsion in religion" was revealed. At that time the fighting against the People of the Book had not yet been commanded, and [the Prophet] said: "May God distance them; they are the first to disbelieve!" Abu Husayn was resentful toward the Prophet ﷺ because he did not send anyone in pursuit of them. So God, whose praise is exalted, revealed: "But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge in what is disputed among them" [[see vol. 5, p. 266]], to the end of the verse. Then it abrogated "There is no compulsion in religion," and commanded fighting the People of the Book in the surah of "Bara'ah" [[see vol. 8, p. 109]].

The sound view regarding the occasion of His saying, "But no, by your Lord, they will not believe," is the hadith of al-Zubayr with his Ansari neighbour concerning the irrigation, as will come in explanation in "al-Nisa'" [[see vol. 5, p. 266]], God willing.

It is said: its meaning is: do not say to one who embraced Islam under the sword, compelled and forced, [this is the fifth view]. And a sixth view: it was revealed concerning captives, whenever they were of the People of the Book, they are not compelled if they are adults; but if they are Magians, young or old, or idolaters, they are compelled to Islam, because whoever takes them captive gains no benefit from them while they are idolaters. Do you not see that their slaughtered animals are not eaten and their women may not be taken as concubines, and they hold to eating carrion and impurities and the like, and their owner finds them repugnant, and benefit from them through ownership is impossible for him, so it is permissible for him to compel them? Ibn al-Qasim related something similar from Malik. As for Ashhab, he said: they follow the religion of whoever captured them, so if they refuse, they are compelled to Islam; and children have no religion, so they are compelled to enter the religion of Islam, lest they go to a false religion. As for all other kinds of disbelief, when they offer the jizyah we do not compel them to Islam, whether they are Arabs or non-Arabs, Quraysh or others. The explanation of this and of what the scholars hold concerning the jizyah and from whom it is accepted will come in "Bara'ah" [[see vol. 8, p. 109]], God willing.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in the Taghut and believes in God﴾: this is a conditional with the jussive (jazm). Al-taghut is feminine in form, from taghā yatghā [the root "taghiya" in the source]. Al-Tabari related "yatghu" when one exceeds the limit by an addition to it. Its pattern is fa'lut. Sibawayh's view is that it is a masculine singular noun, as though it were a collective noun used for the few and the many. Abu 'Ali's view is that it is a verbal noun like rahabut and jabarut, which is applied to both the singular and the plural; its final radical was moved to the position of the middle radical and its middle radical to the position of the final, as in jabadha and jadhaba, so the waw became an alif because it is vowelled and what precedes it is vowelled, and it became "taghut." Al-Nahhas chose this view. It is said that the root of taghut in the language is derived from al-tughyan and conveys its meaning without derivation, as it is said: la'al min al-lu'lu'. Al-Mubarrad said: it is a plural. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: that is rejected. Al-Jawhari said: al-taghut is the soothsayer, the devil, and all of these are heads of misguidance; it may be singular, as God, exalted is He, said: "They wish to take their disputes to the taghut, though they were commanded to reject it" [[see vol. 5, pp. 263 and 280]]. It may also be plural, as God, exalted is He, said: "Their protectors are the taghut" [Qur'an 2:257], and the plural is tawaghit. "And believes in God" is a conjunction (ataf).

(Then has he grasped the most trustworthy handhold.) This is the answer to the condition. The plural of al-wuthqa is al-wuthuq, like al-fudha and al-fudl. So al-wuthqa is fu'la from al-wathaqah (trustworthiness). This verse is an analogy (tashbih). The exegetes differed in the expression of what is the thing compared: Mujahid said: the handhold is faith (iman). Al-Suddi said: Islam. Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak said: "There is no god but God." These expressions return to one meaning. Then He said: (There is no breaking for it.) Mujahid said: that is, He does not change what is with a people until they change what is in themselves, i.e., He does not remove from them the name of faith [[in j: Islam]] until they disbelieve. Infisam (breaking) is breaking without separation into parts, while qasm is breaking with separation. In the sound hadith: "Then the revelation leaves him (fayafsimu 'anhu al-wahy), and his forehead drips with sweat," meaning it ceases (yuqli'u). Al-Jawhari said: fasm of a thing is breaking it without it separating into pieces; you say: fasamtuhu fa-infasama. God, exalted is He, said: "There is no breaking for it," and tafassama is similar. Dhu al-Rummah, describing a gazelle, compares it to a silver bracelet:

As though it were a silver bracelet, forgotten (nabah) ... in a playground of the tribe's maidens, broken (mafsum).

[[al-nabah (with fatha on the nun and the ba') is anything fallen from a person that is forgotten and not found. He likened the gazelle, while sleeping, to a silver bracelet that has been dropped and forgotten. In the Diwan: "'adhara" (maidens).]]

He made it "mafsum" only because it bends and curves when it sleeps. He did not say "maqsum" with a qaf, which would mean separated into two. Afsama al-matar: it ceased (aqla'a); and afsamat 'anhu al-humma: the fever left him. Since disbelief in the taghut and belief in God are things the tongue utters and the heart believes, it is fitting that the attributes be (Samee'un) "All-Hearing" because of the utterance, and (Aleem) "All-Knowing" because of the belief.

(ALLAH is the Protector (al-Wali) of those who believe) Al-Wali is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of fa'il (active participle): the one who takes charge of and helps. Al-Khattabi said: al-Wali is the helper, who gives victory to His believing servants. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Allah is the Protector of those who believe; He brings them out of darkness into light﴾, and He said: ﴿That is because Allah is the Master (Mawla) of those who believe, and because the disbelievers have no master﴾ [see vol. 16, p. 234].

Qatadah said: "The darknesses" are misguidance, and "the light" is guidance. Al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' said the same in meaning.

Mujahid and Abdah ibn Abi Lubabah said: His saying "Allah is the Protector of those who believe" was revealed concerning a people who believed in Jesus, and when Muhammad (ﷺ) came they disbelieved in him. That is their being brought out from the light into the darknesses.

Ibn Atiyyah said: It is as if this believer had secured a light in belief, from which he came out into darknesses. But the wording of the verse is independent of this specification; rather, it applies to every disbelieving nation in which some have believed, such as the Arabs. Whoever among them believed, Allah is his Protector, bringing him out of the darkness of disbelief into the light of faith. And whoever disbelieved after the existence of the Prophet (ﷺ), the summoning messenger, his devil misleads him, as if he had been brought out of faith, since he was already prepared and fit to enter it. And He judged them to enter the Fire for their disbelief, as an act of justice on His part; He is not questioned about what He does.

Al-Hasan recited "their protectors are the tawaghit (false deities/transgressors)," meaning the devils. And Allah knows best.

This passage has two issues. The first is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Have you not considered﴾, where this is the interrogative alif of drawing attention, and the sentence carries a sense of wonder, meaning: wonder at this matter. Al-Farra' said: "Alam tara" means "hal ra'ayta" (have you not seen), i.e., have you seen the one who argued with Ibrahim, and have you seen the one who passed by a village, and he is Namrud [[Namrud, with a dammah on the nun and the letter dhal marked. Shihab.]] ibn Kush ibn Kan'an ibn Sam ibn Nuh, the king of his time and the owner of the fire and the gnat! This is the statement of Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Rabi', al-Suddi, Ibn Ishaq, Zayd ibn Aslam and others. His destruction came when he intended to wage war against Allah, the Exalted: Allah opened upon him a door of gnats, and they covered [[As it stands in all the manuscripts; the correct reading in al-Tabari is: Allah sent them against them, and they ate their flesh and drank their blood.]] the sun and devoured his army, leaving nothing but the bones. One of them entered his brain and kept eating it until it became like a mouse. After that, the most honoured of people with him was the one who struck his brain with a prepared hammer for that purpose. He remained in this affliction for forty days. Ibn Jurayj said: he was the first king on earth. Ibn Atiyyah said: this is rejected. Qatadah said: he was the first tyrant, and he is the owner of the tower in Babylon. It is also said that he ruled the whole world, and he was one of the two disbelievers, the other being Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar). It is said that the one who argued with Ibrahim was Namrud ibn Falikh ibn Abir ibn Shalikh ibn Arfakhshad ibn Sam; Ibn Atiyyah related all of this. Al-Suhayli related that he was Namrud ibn Kush ibn Kan'an ibn Ham ibn Nuh, and he was king over al-Sawad [[That is, the Sawad of Iraq. In manuscript H: al-Sudan.]]. His king was al-Dahhak, who is known as al-Izdihaq, whose name was Biwarasb ibn Andarast, and he was king of all the regions. He is the one whom Afridun ibn Athfayan killed. Habib [[Ibn Aws, Abu Tammam.]] says concerning him:

"As if he were al-Dahhak in his slaughters among the worlds, while you are Afridun."

Al-Dahhak was a tyrant and a despot, and his rule lasted a thousand years, as they report. He was the first to crucify and the first to cut off hands and feet. Namrud had a son of his own loins called "Kusha" or a name close to this, and he had a son called Namrud the Younger. The rule of Namrud the Younger was one year, while the rule of Namrud the Elder was four hundred years, as they report.

Concerning the story of this argument there are two narrations. The first is that they went out to a festival of theirs, and Ibrahim entered upon their idols and smashed them. When they returned, he said to them: "Do you worship what you carve?" They said: "Then whom do you worship?" He said: "I worship my Lord who gives life and causes death." Some said: Namrud used to hoard food, and when the people were in need of food they would buy it from him, and when they entered upon him they would prostrate to him. Ibrahim entered and did not prostrate to him. He said: "What is wrong with you that you do not prostrate to me?" He said: "I do not prostrate except to my Lord." Namrud said to him: "Who is your Lord?" Ibrahim said: "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death." Zayd ibn Aslam mentioned that this Namrud used to sit and command the people regarding provisions (al-mirah, meaning the bringing in of food, as Ibn Sayyidah said). Whenever a people came, he would say: "Who is your Lord and your god?" They would say: "You." He would say: "Give them provisions." Ibrahim, peace be upon him, came seeking provisions, and he said to him: "Who is your Lord and your god?" Ibrahim said: "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death." When Namrud heard this, he said: "I give life and cause death." Ibrahim countered him with the matter of the sun, so the one who disbelieved was confounded, and he said: "Do not give him provisions." Ibrahim returned to his family without anything. He passed by a heap of sand like flour and said to himself: "If I fill my two sacks with this and enter with it, the children will be delighted, until I look after them." He took it, and when he reached his home the children rejoiced and began playing on top of the two sacks, while he himself slept from exhaustion. His wife said: "If I prepare food for him that he will find ready when he wakes up." She opened one of the two sacks and found the finest white flour (al-hawwara, meaning fine white flour, the best and purest part of the flour), so she baked it. When he got up, she placed it before him. He said: "Where is this from?" She said: "From the flour you brought." Ibrahim knew that Allah, the Exalted, had made this easy for them.

I say: Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah related from Abu Salih, who said: The Prophet Ibrahim, peace be upon him, set out seeking provisions but was unable to obtain food. He passed by a red sandy place (sahlah, meaning coarse sand that is not fine and smooth; and sahlah with a fatha on the sin is the opposite of hazanah, which is the rougher part of the land), and he took some of it, then returned to his family. They said: "What is this?" He said: "Red wheat." They opened it and found it was red wheat. He said: "Whenever he sowed some of it, its ear would come from its base to its tip, full of grain, one piling upon another."

Al-Rabi' and others said concerning this story: When Namrud said, "I give life and cause death," he summoned two men, killed one of them and released the other, and said: "I have given life to this one and caused this one to die." When Ibrahim answered him with the matter of the sun, he was confounded. It is also reported in a tradition that Allah, the Exalted, said: "By My might and My majesty, the Hour will not come until I bring the sun from the west, so that it may be known that I am the One who is able to do that." Then Namrud gave orders regarding Ibrahim and he was thrown into the fire, for this is the custom of tyrants: when they are opposed with something and are unable to produce an argument, they resort to punishment. So Allah rescued him from the fire, as will come later [[See vol. 11, p. 303.]]. Al-Suddi said: When Ibrahim came out of the fire, they brought him in to the king, who had not previously entered upon him. He spoke with him and said to him: "Who is your Lord?" He said: "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death." Namrud said: "I give life and cause death. I take four men and put them into a house where they are not fed or given drink until they are hungry. Then I bring them out, feed two of them, and they live, and I leave two of them, and they die." Ibrahim countered him with the sun, and he was confounded.

The scholars of legal theory (al-usuliyyun) mentioned concerning this verse that when Ibrahim, peace be upon him, described his Lord, the Exalted, with what is an attribute of Him, namely giving life and causing death, which is a matter having both a literal and a figurative sense, Ibrahim, peace be upon him, pursued the literal sense, while Namrud fled to the figurative sense and deceived his people. So Ibrahim accepted this from him in the manner of debate and moved on from the example and brought him a matter with no figurative sense in it: "So the one who disbelieved was confounded," meaning his argument was cut off, and he could not say, "I am the one who brings it from the east," because people of understanding would have called him a liar.

The second issue concerns the ruling: this verse indicates the permissibility of calling a disbeliever a king when Allah gives him kingship, honour and elevation in this world. It also indicates the establishment of debate, disputation and the presentation of proof. The Qur'an and the Sunnah contain much of this for whoever reflects upon it. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say: "Bring your proof, if you are truthful."﴾ and ﴿You have no authority for this﴾, meaning, no proof. He described the dispute of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, with his people and his refutation of them regarding the worship of idols, as in Surat al-Anbiya' and elsewhere. He said in the story of Nuh, peace be upon him: ﴿They said: "O Nuh, you have argued with us and multiplied our argument"﴾ up to His words ﴿And I am free of what you commit as crime﴾. Likewise the debate of Musa with Pharaoh, and other verses. All of this is instruction from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in question, answer and debate concerning the religion, for the difference between truth and falsehood does not become manifest except by the manifestation of the proof of truth and the refutation of the proof of falsehood. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) debated the People of the Book and invoked a curse upon them [[Mubahalah means mutual cursing. It means that the people gather when they differ over a matter and say: "May the curse of Allah fall upon the wrongdoer among us." See vol. 4, pp. 103 and 108.]] after the proof was established, as will be explained in Surat Al 'Imran. Adam and Musa disputed, and Adam overcame him with proof. The Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) disputed on the day of Saqifah, pushed against one another, deliberated and debated until the truth emerged among its people. They also debated after the allegiance to Abu Bakr concerning the apostates, and there are other things too numerous to mention. In the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Why do you argue about what you have no knowledge of?﴾ is evidence that argument based on knowledge is permissible and widespread for whoever reflects. Al-Muzani, the companion of al-Shafi'i, said: It is part of the right of debate that it be intended for the sake of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and that what becomes clear from it be accepted. They also said: Debate is not valid, and the truth does not become manifest between the debaters, unless they are close to one another or equal in rank in religion, intellect, understanding and fairness; otherwise it is mere wrangling and obstinacy.

Readings: Ali ibn Abi Talib read "Alam tar" with the ra' vowelled with a sukun, while the majority read it with a fatha, and the ya' was dropped for the jazm. ﴿that Allah gave him the kingdom﴾ is in the accusative position, meaning because Allah gave him, or on account of Allah giving him.

The majority of reciters read "Ana uhyi" by omitting the alif after the nun in "ana" when connected, but Nafi' and Ibn Abi Uways retained it whenever a hamzah followed it throughout the Qur'an, except in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿I am only a warner﴾, where he omits it in this position like the other reciters, because it occurs rarely. In the Qur'an it occurs in only three places, and he treated these as places where no hamzah follows, due to their rarity, so he dropped the alif in connected speech.

The grammarians said: The pronoun of the first person has the hamzah and the nun. When you say "ana" or "innahu," the alif and the ha' are there to show the vowel in pausal position. When the word is connected to something, both drop, because what the word is connected to takes the place of the alif. So one does not say "ana fa'altu" with the alif retained, except as an irregular usage in poetry, as the poet said:

"I am the sword of the tribe, so recognise me,
Humayd, indeed I have ploughed the hump." [[So in J, W and H. In B and J: Humayd, a second time; and collectively, another time. In al-Taj: collectively.]]

Al-Nahhas said: Nafi' retained the alif, reading "Ana uhyi wa umitu," and there is no justification for it. Makki said: The alif is superfluous according to the Basrans, and the implied pronoun for them is the hamzah and the nun, and the alif was added for emphasis. It is also said that it was added for pausing so that the vowel of the nun would show. According to the Kufans the noun is "ana" in its entirety, so Nafi's retention of the alif is, by their view, in accordance with the original form, and whoever dropped it did so for lightness, and because the fatha indicates it. Al-Jawhari said: As for their saying "ana," it is a pronoun for the first person singular, and it is built on the fatha to distinguish it from "in," which is a particle that governs the verb. The final alif is only there to show the vowel in pausal position. If it appears in the middle of the speech, it drops, except in a poor dialect [[In al-Samin: retaining the alif in both connected and pausal speech is the dialect of Tamim.]], as he said:

"I am the sword [[In Ibn Atiyyah: I am a shaykh. Humayd is Ibn Mujdal.]] of the tribe, so recognise me,
Humayd, indeed I have ploughed the hump."

And Arabic "baha tha al-rajul," "bahata," and "buhita" mean that the man was silenced and fell silent, bewildered, when he had no answer; from al-Nahhas and others.

Al-Tabari said: It has been related from some Arabs, with this meaning, "bahata," with a fatha on the ba' and the ha'.

Ibn Jinni said: Abu Haywa recited "fa-bahuta alladhi kafara" (﴿so the one who disbelieved was confounded﴾), with a fatha on the ba' and a damma on the ha', and this is a dialectal form of "buhita" with a kasra on the ha'. He said: Ibn al-Sumayqa recited "fa-bahata" with a fatha on the ba' and the ha', meaning "fa-bahata Ibrahim alladhi kafara" (﴿so Ibrahim, the one who disbelieved, was confounded﴾), so that "alladhi" is in the accusative position. He said: It is also possible that "bahata" with a fatha on its letters is a dialectal form of "bahuta." He said: Al-Akhfash Abu al-Hasan related the reading "fa-bahita" with a kasra on the ha', like "ghariqa" (to drown), and "dahisha" (to be dismayed). He said: Most readers use a damma on the ha'.

Ibn Atiyya said: Some people have interpreted the reading of those who recited "fa-bahata" with a fatha on the ha' to mean "insulted and slandered," and that Nimrod was the one who insulted when he was cut off and had no way out.

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 259 (part 1 of 3):

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Or like the one who passed by a town that had fallen into ruin over its roofs﴾. The "or" (aw) is a conjunction, understood according to the sense. According to al-Kisa'i and al-Farra', the implied construction is: "Have you not seen [something] like the one who argued with Ibrahim about his Lord, or like the one who passed by a town?" Al-Mubarrad said: the meaning is, "Have you not seen the one who argued with Ibrahim about his Lord? Have you not seen who he is? [He is] like the one who passed by a town." So "who he is" is understood in the speech.

Abu Sufyan ibn Husayn read "aw ka-alladhi marra" with a fatha on the waw, so that the waw is the conjunction, and the interrogative alif, whose meaning is affirmation (taqrir), has entered upon it.

The town was called qaryah (town) because people gather in it (ijtima'), from their saying qaraytu al-ma' (I gathered the water), meaning I collected it. This has been mentioned before (see vol. 1, p. 409).

Sulayman ibn Buraydah, Najiyah ibn Ka'b, Qatadah, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Rabi' and 'Ikrimah and al-Dahhak said: the one who passed by the town was 'Uzayr.

Wahb ibn Munabbih, Abd Allah ibn 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr and Abd Allah ibn Bakr ibn Mudar said: he was Irmiya', and he was a prophet.

Ibn Ishaq said: Irmiya' is al-Khadir (al-Khidr), and al-Naqqash reported this from Wahb ibn Munabbih.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This is as you see it, unless it is a name that coincides with another name, because al-Khadir was a contemporary of Musa, whereas the one who passed by the town was, according to what Wahb ibn Munabbih related, a later figure, after a period of time, from the tribe of Harun."

I say: If al-Khadir is Irmiya', then there is no unlikelihood in it, because al-Khadir has remained alive from the time of Musa until now, according to the sound view on this matter, as will be explained in surah al-Kahf (see vol. 11, p. 16). But if he died before this story, then the statement of Ibn 'Atiyyah is correct, and Allah knows best.

Al-Nahhas and Makki reported from Mujahid that he was a man from the Children of Israel who was not named. Al-Naqqash said: It is also said that he was the boy (ghulam) of Lut, peace be upon him. Al-Suhayli reported from al-Qutabi that he was Shi'ya in one of his two opinions.

The one who revived it after its ruin was Kushak al-Farisi.

The town mentioned is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) according to the view of Wahb ibn Munabbih, Qatadah, al-Rabi' ibn Anas and others. He said: He was coming from Egypt, and his food and drink mentioned were figs (tin), green [...], grapes, and a rakwah (a small vessel made of leather from which water is drunk, and a small bucket) of wine. It was also said: of grape juice. It was also said: a jug of water was his drink.

The one who laid waste Bayt al-Maqdis at that time was Bakht Nassar (Nebuchadnezzar), who was governor of Iraq for Lahrasib, then for Istasib the son of Lahrasib, the father of Isbindiyad.

Al-Naqqash reported that some people said: the town is al-Mu'tafikah (the overturned towns).

Ibn 'Abbas, in a report from Abu Salih, said: Bakht Nassar raided the Children of Israel and took captive many people from them, and he brought them, and among them was 'Uzayr ibn Shar-khiya, who was one of the scholars of the Children of Israel. He brought them to Babil (Babylon). One day he went out on some business of his to the monastery of Hirqal on the bank of the Dijlah (Tigris). He alighted under the shade of a tree while he was on his donkey. He tied the donkey under the shade of the tree, then went around the town, but he saw no inhabitant in it, and it was fallen into ruin over its roofs. He said: "How will Allah bring this to life after its death?"

It was also said: it is the town from which thousands went out for fear of death, according to Ibn Zayd. And it is also reported from Ibn Zayd that the people who went out of their homes, and they were thousands, fearing death, were told by Allah: "Die." A man passed by them while they were bones, scattered and bleached, and he stopped to look and said: "How will Allah bring this to life after its death?" So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This statement of Ibn Zayd contradicts the wording of the verse, since the verse only includes a town in ruin with no one in it, and the demonstrative "this" (hadhihi) refers only to the town. And its revival is only by rebuilding and the existence of buildings and inhabitants.

Wahb ibn Munabbih, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, al-Rabi' and 'Ikrimah said: The town is Bayt al-Maqdis, when Bakht Nassar the Babylonian destroyed it.

In the long hadith: when the Children of Israel committed their misdeeds, Irmiya' or 'Uzayr stopped at the town, and it was like a great mound in the middle of Bayt al-Maqdis, because Bakht Nassar ordered his troops to carry the dirt to it until he made it like a mountain. Irmiya' saw the houses whose walls had fallen onto their roofs and said: "How will Allah bring this to life after its death?"

Al-'Arish means the roof of a house, and everything prepared to give shade or shelter is an 'arish, and from it comes 'arish al-daliyah (the trellis of the vine). From it is the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿and what they build (ya'rishun)﴾.

Al-Suddi said: it means "it is fallen onto its roofs," that is, the roofs collapsed and then the walls fell upon them. Al-Tabari chose this view.

Other than al-Suddi said: The meaning is "empty of people and houses while the houses are still standing." Khawiyah means khaliyah (empty). The root of khawa' is emptiness (khuluww). It is said: the house became empty (khawat al-dar) and khawiyat yakhwa khawa'an (mamdud) and khuwiyyan: it became desolate, and likewise when it collapsed. From it is the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Those are their houses, empty (khawiyah) because of what they did wrong﴾, meaning empty. It is also said: fallen down, as it is said: ﴿so it is empty over its roofs﴾, meaning fallen onto its roofs. [The editor's note: this is how it stands in all the manuscripts, but the correct reading is "qala" (he said), since this is a verse; see vol. 12, p. 73.]

Al-khawa' also means hunger, because the belly is empty of food. A woman (khawat al-mar'ah, khawiyat) also means her womb emptied at childbirth. And I prepared (khawwaytu) for her a takhwiyah when I made for her a khawiyyah which she eats, and it is food. Al-khawiyy is the low-lying, soft part of the land, on the pattern of fa'il. And a camel (khawwa al-ba'ir) when it keeps its belly away from the ground when kneeling, and likewise a man in his prostration.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿How will Allah bring this to life after its death?﴾ mean: by what way and by what cause. The apparent sense of the wording is a question about reviving the town with construction and inhabitants, just as it is said now about ruined cities that are unlikely to be rebuilt and inhabited: "How will this be rebuilt after its ruin?" So this is a grieving lament from the reflecting man over his city in which he knew his people and loved ones. And an example was struck for him in his own self with something greater than what he asked about. The example struck for him in his own self may be understood to mean that his question was about the revival of the dead among the children of Adam, that is, "How will Allah bring its dead to life?"

Al-Tabari reported from some of them that he said: This statement was a doubt about Allah's power to give life, and for that reason the example was struck for him in his own self.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: No doubt enters into Allah's power to bring a town to life by bringing construction to it. Doubt can only be imagined (from an ignorant person) in the other sense. The correct view is that no doubt should be ascribed to the verse.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years﴾. "Mi'ata" is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf). And al-'Am means the year (sanah). It is said: sinun 'awwam (years of abundance). It is an emphasis of the first word, just as it is said: "Between them is a busy occupation (shughl shaghil)." Al-'Ajjaj said:

"From the passing of the years, the swimming years (al-sinin al-'awwam)."

In meaning it is the plural of 'a'im, but it is not used alone, because it is not a noun but an emphasis, as al-Jawhari stated. Al-Naqqash said: al-'am is a verbal noun like al-'awm (swimming), and this amount of time was named after it, because it is a "swim" of the sun in the sphere. Al-'awm is like al-sabh (swimming), and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿each in an orbit they swim﴾. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This has the same meaning as the statement of al-Naqqash, and on this view al-'am is like al-qawl and al-qal (the word and its verbal form). The apparent meaning of this causing to die is that it was by the departure of the soul from the body. It is reported in the narratives about this verse that Allah the Exalted sent to it a king of the kings who rebuilt it and worked diligently at it, until its full reconstruction was complete at the time of the one who spoke. It has also been said: when seventy years had passed from his death, Allah sent a great king of the kings of Persia called Kushak, and he rebuilt it in thirty years.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Then He raised him up﴾. It means He brought him to life, and the discussion of it has already passed.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿He said: How long have you remained?﴾ There is disagreement about who said to him, "How long have you remained?" It has been said: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, but He did not say to him "if you are truthful," as He said to the angels, according to what has been mentioned before. It has also been said: he heard a voice (hatif) from the sky saying that to him. It has been said: Jibril addressed him. It has been said: a prophet. It has been said: a believing man from among those who witnessed him at his death from his people, who lived until the time of his revival, and he said to him: "How long have you remained?" I say: The more apparent view is that the one who said it is Allah the Exalted, because of His words: ﴿And look at the bones, how We raise them, then clothe them with flesh﴾. And Allah knows best.

The people of Kufa read "kam labitta" with idgham (assimilation) of the tha' into the ta', because they are close to each other in articulation point, for their point of articulation is from the tip of the tongue and the roots of the front teeth, and both are whispered letters (al-huruf al-mahmusah, the ten letters gathered in the phrase "hathahu shakhsun fasakata"). Ibn Jinni said: As for the letters of whispering, the sound that comes out with them is breath, not from the chest, but emerges softly, and it is not like the blowing of the za' and the zay. Al-Nahhas said: Clear pronunciation (al-izhar) is better, because the articulation point of the tha' differs from that of the ta'. It is also said: this question was asked through the king in the form of affirmation (taqrir). And "kam" is in the position of the accusative as an adverb of time.

(He said: I remained a day or part of a day.) He said this according to what he had and what he thought, and on this basis he was not lying in what he reported. A similar statement is the words of the People of the Cave: ﴿They said: We have remained a day or part of a day﴾, though they remained three hundred and nine years, as will be explained later, and they were not liars, because they reported what they had, as if they said: What we have and what we think is that we remained a day or part of a day. A parallel to this is the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the story of Dhu al-Yadayn: "I did not shorten and I did not forget." Some people say: it is a lie in the sense that the reality of lying exists in it, but there is no blame for it. Otherwise, lying is reporting something contrary to what it is, and that does not vary with knowledge or ignorance, and this is clear in the view of the principles of jurisprudence (usul). On this basis it is permissible to say that the prophets are not protected from reporting something contrary to what it is when it is not intentional, just as they are not protected from forgetfulness and heedlessness. This is what relates to this verse, but the first view is more correct.

Ibn Juraij, Qatadah and al-Rabi' said: Allah caused him to die at the morning of a day, then he was raised before sunset, so he thought that this day was one day, and he said: "I remained a day." Then he saw a remnant of the sun, and feared that he might be lying, so he said: "Or part of a day." It was said to him: "No, you remained a hundred years." He saw from the construction of the town, its trees and its buildings, what showed him that.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So look at your food﴾, which is the figs (al-tin) that he had gathered from the trees of the town through which he passed.

(وَشَرابِكَ لَمْ يَتَسَنَّهْ) [And your drink, it has not changed with years]. Ibn Mas'ud recited, "وَهَذَا طَعَامُكَ وَشَرَابُكَ لَمْ يَتَسَنَّهْ" [And this is your food and your drink, it has not changed with years]. Talha ibn Musarrif and others recited, "وَانْظُرْ لِطَعَامِكَ وَشَرَابِكَ لِمِائَةِ سَنَةٍ" [And look at your food and your drink over a hundred years].

The majority (al-Jumhur) recited with the ha' (هاء) retained in continuous recitation (wasl), except al-Akhawan [[Text of al-Bahr: Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited with the ha' deleted in continuous recitation, treating it as the pausal ha' (ha' al-sakt); the remaining seven recited with the ha' retained both in continuous recitation and in pause. In manuscripts B, H and J: "al-Akhawan", the correct form being "al-Akhawayn" (the two brothers).]], who delete it. There is no disagreement that pausing (waqf) on it is with the ha'.

Talha ibn Musarrif also recited, "لَمْ يَسَّنَّ وَانْظُرْ" [with the ta' assimilated into the sin (idgham)]. According to the recitation of the majority, the ha' is original (asliyyah) and the vowel was dropped for the jussive (jazm). "يَتَسَنَّهْ" would then be from al-sanah (the year), meaning: the years have not changed it. Al-Jawhari said: it is said sununa (the plural), and al-sanah is the singular of al-sinin (the years). Regarding the elision of its radical, there are two opinions: one is that it is a waw, the other that it is a ha'. Its original form is sanhah, like al-jabhah (forehead), because it derives from sanihat al-nakhlah and tasannahat, when years have passed over the palm tree. A date palm that is sanna' bears fruit one year and not the next, and also sanha'. One of the Ansar said [[This is Suwayd ibn al-Samit (from Lisan al-'Arab).]]:

"Fa-laysat bi-sanha'a wa-la rujabiyyah..." [She is not a sanha' (alternate-bearing palm) nor a rujabiyyah]

[[Rujabiyyah: a palm tree that is rujjibat (its clusters are gathered with its fronds and tied with palm-fiber so the wind does not shake them off), or it is that thorns are placed around its clusters so that no eater reaches them and they are not stolen; this is done when the palm is rare and prized.]] ... "Wa-lakin 'araya" [but rather a palm given as a gift] "fi al-sinin al-jawa'ih" [in the years of disaster] [[In the originals: "al-mawahil"; the correction is from lexicographical books. Before this verse is: "Adinu wa-ma dini 'alaykum bi-maghram / Wa-lakin 'ala al-shumm al-jilad al-qaraw'ih" (I pay what I owe, and my debt is not a loss to you, but to the lofty ones of hard, firm hides). Al-Jawa'ih: the harsh years that destroy wealth.]]

"Wa-asnahtu 'inda Bani Fulan" means: I stayed with them; "tasannaytu" likewise. "Istajartuhu musanatan wa-musanahatan" (I hired him for a year's service). In the diminutive: sunayyah and sunayhah. Al-Nahhas said: whoever recites "lam yatasanna wa-unzur" says in the diminutive sunayyah, the alif is deleted for the jussive, and one pauses on the ha', saying "lam yatasannah"; the ha' is to show the vowel.

Al-Mahdawi said: it may be that its origin is from sanaytuhu musana'tan, meaning I dealt with him year after year, or from sanahtu [with the ha' [[From H.]]]. If it is from sanaytu, its origin is yatasanna, the alif fell away for the jussive, and it is from the waw, as evidenced by their saying sanawat (years). The ha' in it is then the pausal ha'. If it is from sanahtu, the ha' is the final radical of the verb, and the origin of sanah on this basis is sanhah. On the first view it is sanawah.

It was also said that it comes from asina al-ma' (the water became stagnant/changed) when it changed; on this view it would have to be yata'assan. Abu 'Amr al-Shaybani said: it is from His saying "ḥama'in masnun" [black, malleable mud] [[See vol. 1, p. 21.]], so the meaning is "has not changed." Al-Zajjaj said: this is not so, because His saying "masnun" does not mean changed; it means poured in the manner of the earth's way (sunnat al-ard).

Al-Mahdawi said: its origin according to al-Shaybani's view is "yatasannan," and one of the two nuns was changed to a ya' to avoid doubling (idgham), becoming yatasanna; then the alif fell away for the jussive and the ha' was added for the pausal ha'.

Mujahid said: "lam yatasannah" means it did not become foul-smelling (lam yuntin). Al-Nahhas said: the most correct of what has been said about it is that it is from al-sanah, meaning the years have not changed it. It is possible that it is from al-sanah in the sense of drought (al-jadb), and from this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وَلَقَدْ أَخَذْنا آلَ فِرْعَوْنَ بِالسِّنِينَ﴾ [And We certainly seized the people of Pharaoh with years (of drought)] [[See vol. 7, p. 263.]], and His saying, peace be upon him: "O God, make them years like the years of Joseph." From this it is said: asnata al-qawm, meaning they suffered drought. So the meaning would be: drought and famine have not changed your food, or the years and seasons have not changed it, meaning it remains in its freshness and freshness of youth.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وَانْظُرْ إِلى حِمارِكَ﴾ [And look at your donkey]. Wahb ibn Munabbih and others said: "And look at the joining of its bones and its revival piece by piece." It is related that God revived it in this manner until it became bones joined together; then He clothed it with flesh until it was complete as a donkey; then an angel came and breathed the spirit into it, and the donkey stood up braying. This is the view of most exegetes (mufassirun).

It is also related from al-Dahhak and Wahb ibn Munabbih that they both said: rather, it was said to him: "And look at your donkey" standing in its tether, untouched by anything for a hundred years. The bones he looked at were the bones of himself, after God had revived his eyes and head, while the rest of his body was dead. They said: God blinded the eyes from Irmiya and his donkey throughout this period.

His saying, exalted is He: (وَلِنَجْعَلَكَ آيَةً لِلنَّاسِ) [And so that We may make you a sign for the people]. Al-Farra' said: He placed the waw in His saying "wa-li-naj'alaka" to indicate that it is conditional upon an act after it; the meaning is: "and so that We may make you a sign for the people" and as an indication of resurrection after death, We did that. If you wish, you may consider the waw superfluous and extra.

Al-A'mash said: the point of him being a sign is that he came as a young man in the state he was in on the day he died, and he found the sons and grandchildren old men. Ikrimah said: he died at forty years of age. It is related from 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, that 'Uzayr left his family and left his wife pregnant, while he was fifty years old; God caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him, and he returned to his family while he was fifty years old, and he had a son who was a hundred years old, so his son was fifty years older than him.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: when God revived 'Uzayr, he rode his donkey and came to his neighborhood, but the people did not recognize him and he did not recognize them. He found in his house a blind old woman who had been their slave-girl; 'Uzayr had left them when she was twenty years old. He said to her: "Is this the house of 'Uzayr?" She said: "Yes!" Then she wept and said: "'Uzayr left us so many years ago." He said: "I am 'Uzayr." She said: "We lost 'Uzayr a hundred years ago." He said: "God caused me to die for a hundred years, then raised me." She said: "'Uzayr was one whose supplication was answered for the sick and the afflicted, so that they recovered. Pray to God that He return my sight to me." He prayed to God and wiped her eyes with his hand, and they were healed at once, as if she had been released from a fetter. She said: "I bear witness that you are 'Uzayr!" Then she went to the assembly of the children of Israel, among whom was a son of 'Uzayr, a shaykh of a hundred and twenty-eight years, and his sons' sons were old men. She said: "O people, by God, this is 'Uzayr!" His son came to him along with the people and said: "My father had a dark birthmark like the crescent moon between his shoulders." He looked at it and it was indeed 'Uzayr.

It was also said: he came after everyone who knew him had died, so he was a sign for those among his people who were still alive, since they were certain of his condition by report. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: in his being made to die for this period and then revived after it is the greatest sign, and his whole affair is a sign for all time, and there is no need to restrict this to one part over another.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وَانْظُرْ إِلَى الْعِظامِ كَيْفَ نُنْشِزُها﴾ [And look at the bones, how We raise them]. The Kufans and Ibn 'Amir recited with the zay (ز), and the rest with the ra' (ر). Aban related from 'Asim: "nanshuruha" with a fatha on the nun, a damma on the shin and the ra' [i.e., "nanshuruha," with ra']. Likewise Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Abu Haywah recited. It was said: they are two dialects with the same meaning for reviving, as one says raja'a and raja'tuhu (he returned and I returned him), ghada al-ma' and ghidtuhu (the water receded and I made it recede), khasirat al-dabbah and khasirtuha (the animal was lost and I lost it). However, the known usage in the language is: Allah anshara al-mawta, so they came to life (nasharu), meaning God revived them and they came to life. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿ثُمَّ إِذا شاءَ أَنْشَرَهُ﴾ [Then when He wills, He will raise him] [[See vol. 19, p. 215.]]. And "nashrahā" may be like nashara al-thawb (he spread the garment). Nasha al-mayyit yanshuru nushuran, meaning he lived after death. Al-A'sha said:

"Hatta yaqula al-nasu mimma ra'aw / ya 'ajaban li-l-mayyit al-nashir" [until people say, seeing what they saw: "How strange, for the dead man who came back to life!"]

It is as if death folds the bones and the limbs, and as if reviving and joining the limbs one to another is an unfolding (nashr). As for the recitation "nunshiziha" with the zay, its meaning is "We raise it." Al-nashz is the elevated part of the ground. He said:

"Tara al-tha'laba al-hawliyya fiha / ka-annahu idha ma 'ala nashzan hasanun mujallal" [You see the fox of the year in it, as if, when it climbs a high ground, it is a well-caparisoned mare].

Makki said: the meaning is: look at the bones, how We raise some of them upon others in the assembling for revival, because al-nashz is elevation; from it comes the word nushuz for a woman who is raised above agreement with her husband. From it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وَإِذا قِيلَ انْشُزُوا فَانْشُزُوا﴾ [And when it is said, "Rise up," then rise up] [[See vol. 17, p. 296.]], meaning: rise up and come together. Also, the recitation with the ra' has the meaning of revival, and bones do not come to life individually until some of them are joined to others; the zay is more suitable for that meaning, since it has the meaning of joining, not reviving. So the one described as revived is the man, not the bones on their own; one does not say "this is a living bone." The meaning is: look at the bones, how We raise them from their places in the earth to the body of their owner for revival.

Al-Nakha'i recited "nunshuzuha" with a fatha on the nun, a damma on the shin and the zay; this is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah. Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited "nunshiyuha" with the ya' (ي).

Al-kiswah (clothing) is what covers from garments, and flesh was likened to it. Labid [[In the originals and Ibn 'Atiyyah: "al-Nabigha, the well-known famous one"; what we have written is correct. Its first hemistich: "al-hamdu li-llahi idh lam ya'tini ajali" (Praise be to God that my appointed time has not come to me)]] used it as a metaphor for Islam, saying:

"Hatta iktasaytu min al-Islam sirbalan" [until I was clothed in a garment of Islam]

It was mentioned earlier at the beginning of the surah [[See vol. 1, p. 153.]].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿فَلَمَّا تَبَيَّنَ لَهُ قالَ أَعْلَمُ أَنَّ اللَّهَ عَلى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ﴾ [So when it became clear to him, he said: "I know that God is capable of all things."] It is recited with the alif cut (qat' al-alif), meaning the initial alif is pronounced as a full alif. It has been related that God, mighty is His remembrance, revived part of him and then showed him how He revived the rest of his body. Qatadah said: he began to look at how some of his bones were joined to others, because the first thing God created from him was his head, and he was told: "Look." Then he said at that point: "a'lamu" with the cut alif, meaning: "I know this."

Al-Tabari said: the meaning of His saying "fa-lamma tabayyana lahu" is: when it became clear to him by direct sight what he had considered implausible about God's power before seeing it, he said: "I know." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is an error, because it imposes what the wording does not require, and interprets according to an odd reading and a weak possibility. In my view this is not an admission of what he had previously denied, as al-Tabari claims; rather it is a statement prompted by contemplation, as a believing person says when he sees something strange from God's power: "There is no god but God," and the like. Abu 'Ali said: the meaning is: "I know this kind of knowledge which I had not known."

I say: this meaning has been mentioned from Qatadah, and likewise Makki, may God have mercy on him, said: he informed about himself when he witnessed God's power in reviving the dead, so he was certain of that through observation, and he acknowledged that he knows that God is capable of all things; that is, "I know this kind of knowledge which I had not known by direct witnessing." This is according to the recitation of those who recite "a'lamu" with the cut alif, and they are the majority of the reciters.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited with the alif joined (wasl al-alif), and this allows two possibilities. One: the angel said to him: "Know (i'lam)!" The other is that he placed himself in the position of a distant, separate addressee, so the meaning is: when it became clear to him, he said to himself: "Know, O self, this certain knowledge which you did not know by direct witnessing." Abu 'Ali cited in this sense:

"Wada'a Hurayrata inna al-rakba murtahil / ... alam taghtamid 'aynaka laylatan armadah" [Bid farewell to Hurayrah, for the caravan is departing... did your eyes not close, one night, with ophthalmia?] [[The two verses are by al-A'sha; the second half of the first is: "Wa-hal tutiq wada'an ayyuha al-rajul" (and can you bear farewell, O man). The second's second half is: "Wa-adaka ma 'ada al-saleem al-musahhadah" (and it has returned to you as the sleepless snake-stung one returns).]]

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Abu 'Ali found support for this meaning in the words of the poet:

"Tadhakkar min anna wa-min ayna shurbuhu / yu'ami nafsayhi ka-dhi al-hajmati al-ibil" [Remember whence and whither his drinking is: he consults his two selves like the owner of a large herd of camels] [[The hajmah (with fatha and sukun): a large portion of camels; it is said it is between thirty and a hundred. A rajul abal (with kaf-like pattern): one skilled at managing camels.]]

Makki said: It is far-fetched that this was a command from God, exalted is His remembrance, to him to have knowledge, because He had already shown him His power and let him see a matter of which he became certain of its truth and acknowledged the power. So there is no sense in God commanding him to know that; rather, he himself is commanding himself to that, and this is permissible and good. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud (Abdullah) there is something that indicates it was a command from God Most High to him to have knowledge, in the sense of "Hold to this knowledge, since you have witnessed and become certain," for in his reading it is: "qīla i'lam" (it was said: know). Also, it agrees with what precedes it of commands in His saying "﴿Look at your food﴾" and "﴿Look at your donkey﴾" and "﴿Look at the bones﴾," so likewise "﴿Know that God﴾". Ibn Abbas used to recite it "qīla i'lam" and would say: "Is it better, or Abraham?" when it was said to him: "﴿And know that God is Mighty and Wise﴾." This shows that it is part of God's speech to him, because of what he witnessed of the living creatures.

The Muslim scholars differed over whether this question came from Abraham out of doubt or not. The majority (al-jumhur) said: Abraham, peace be upon him, never doubted God's giving life to the dead. He only asked to witness it, because souls long to see what they have been told about. For this reason he, peace be upon him, said: "The report is not like seeing with one's own eyes." This was related by Ibn Abbas, and no one else related it, as Abu Umar stated. Al-Akhfash said: he did not mean the sight of the heart, but the sight of the eye.

Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Rabi' said: he asked so that his certainty would increase above his certainty.[[In manuscripts C and H: "to his own self."]]

Ibn Atiyyah said: al-Tabari, in his tafsir, gave the heading: "Others said: he asked his Lord this because he doubted God's power, the Exalted." Under this heading he included a report from Ibn Abbas, who said: "There is no verse in the Qur'an that I find more hopeful than this one." It is also reported from Ata' ibn Abi Rabah that he said: "Some of what enters the hearts of people entered the heart of Abraham, so he said: 'My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.'" He also mentioned the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "We have more right to doubt than Abraham," and so on. Then al-Tabari preferred this opinion.

I say: The hadith of Abu Hurayrah was recorded by al-Bukhari and Muslim from him, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "We have more right to doubt than Abraham, when he said: 'My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.' He said: 'Do you not believe?' He said: 'Yes, but so that my heart may be at rest. And may God have mercy on Lut, for he took refuge in a strong pillar. Had I remained in prison as long as Joseph did, I would have answered the summoner.'"

Ibn Atiyyah said: What al-Tabari headed with is, in my view, rejected, and what he included under the heading is a matter of interpretation. As for Ibn Abbas's words, "It is the most hopeful verse," this is because it contains the proof of God and the request for life to be given in this world, and it is not the place for that. It is possible to say: it is the most hopeful verse because of God's words, "Do you not believe?" That is, faith is sufficient, and with it there is no need for searching and inquiry. As for Ata's words, "Some of what enters the hearts of people entered the heart of Abraham," their meaning, in terms of seeing with the eyes, is as we explained earlier. As for the Prophet's words (ﷺ), "We have more right to doubt than Abraham," their meaning is that if he had been a doubter, we would have had more right to it, and we do not doubt. So Abraham, peace be upon him, is even more deserving of not doubting. The hadith, then, is built on the negation of doubt from Abraham. What was reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) about it, that he said, "That is the pure essence of faith," refers only to passing thoughts that do not settle. As for doubt, it is hesitation between two matters with neither of them having a preference over the other, and that is what is negated from the Friend (al-Khalil), peace be upon him. The giving of life to the dead is established only through revelation (al-sam'), and Abraham, peace be upon him, knew it better. This is shown by his saying: "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death." Doubt is far-fetched even for one whose foot is firm in faith alone, so how much more for one at the rank of prophethood and friendship (al-khullah)? The prophets are protected from major sins and from minor sins that involve baseness, by ijma' (scholarly consensus). When you consider his question, peace be upon him, and the rest of the wording of the verse, they give no indication of doubt. This is because the interrogative "how" (kayfa) asks about the state of a thing which is established in existence for both the questioner and the one asked, like your saying: "How is Zayd's knowledge?" or "How is the weaving of the cloth?" and similar. When you say: "How is your garment?" or "How is Zayd?" the question is only about one of his states. "How" may also be used as an indication of something about which the question is normally asked with "how," like your saying: "However you wish, so let it be," and like al-Bukhari's words: "How the beginning of revelation was." The "how" in this verse is a question about the form of giving life, and giving life is established. But since we find that some who deny the existence of a thing express their denial by asking about a state of that thing which is known to be impossible, it follows that the thing itself is impossible. An example of this: a claimant says, "I will lift this mountain," and the one who denies him says, "Show me how you will lift it!" This is a figurative way of speaking, and its meaning is a dialectical concession, as if he were saying: "Suppose that you lift it, then show me how you lift it!" Since Abraham's expression, peace be upon him, had this figurative ambiguity, God made it clear for him, and led him to explain the truth, saying to him: "Do you not believe?" He said: "Yes." So the matter was complete and he was free of all doubt. Then he, peace be upon him, gave the reason for his question as being to attain tranquility.

I say: This is what Ibn Atiyyah mentioned, and it is excellent. It is not permissible for the prophets, may the blessings of God be upon them, to have such doubt, for it is disbelief, and the prophets agree on belief in resurrection. God, the Exalted, has informed us that His prophets and His friends have no authority for Satan over them. He said: "Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them." The accursed one said: "Except Your sincere servants among them." If Satan has no authority over them, how could he cause them doubt? Abraham only asked to witness how the scattered parts of the dead are gathered again, and how the sinews and skins are reconnected after being torn apart. So he wanted to rise from ʿilm al-yaqīn (knowledge by certainty) to ʿayn al-yaqīn (knowledge by seeing). His words "Show me how" were a request to witness the manner.

Some scholars of meanings said: Abraham only asked his Lord to show him how He gives life to hearts. This is corrupt and rejected by the explanation that follows it. al-Mawardi mentioned it. The alif in "Do you not believe?" is not an interrogative alif. It is an alif of affirmation and confirmation, as Jarir said:

"Are you not the best of those who rode the mounts?"

The waw is the waw of the circumstantial clause (waw al-hal). "Tu'min" (you believe) means belief in an unrestricted sense, which includes the excellence of giving life to the dead.

("He said: Yes, but so that my heart may be at rest") meaning: I asked You so that my heart might be at rest through the gaining of the difference between what is known by proof and what is known by sight. Tranquility (al-tuma'nina) is calm and stillness. The tranquility of the limbs is well known, as the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Then bow until you are at rest in bowing," and so on. The tranquility of the heart is that its thought becomes still regarding the thing believed. Reflection on the form of giving life is not forbidden, just as it is permitted for us today to reflect on it, since it is a thought containing lessons. So the Friend wanted to see it, so that his thought about the form of giving life would be settled.

Al-Tabari said: The meaning of "so that my heart may be at rest" is "so that he may be certain." Something similar was reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and it was also reported from him: "so that he may increase in certainty." Ibrahim and Qatadah also said it. Some said: "so that I may increase in faith along with my faith." Ibn Atiyyah said: No increase in this meaning is possible except through stillness from thought, for otherwise certainty does not divide into parts.

al-Suddi and Ibn Jubayr also said: "Do you not believe that you are My friend?" He said: "Yes, but so that my heart may be at rest through the friendship."

It was said: He asked that God show him how He gives life to the dead, so that he would know whether his supplication would be answered. So God said to him: "Do you not believe that I answer your supplication?" He said: "Yes, but so that my heart may be at rest that You answer my supplication."

There is disagreement about what moved him to this. It was said: God had promised him that He would take him as a friend, so he wanted a sign of this. This was said by al-Sa'ib ibn Yazid.[[Thus in H, B and J, which is correct as in al-Tahdhib and al-Isti'ab; in C and A: Zayd.]] It was also said: it was the words of Nimrod: "I give life and cause death."

al-Hasan said: He saw a carcass, half of it on land being torn apart by beasts, and half of it in the sea being torn apart by sea creatures. When he saw its scattering, he preferred to see its gathering, so he asked, so that his heart might be at rest by seeing the manner of gathering, just as he had seen the manner of scattering. Then it was said to him: "Take four birds." It was said: they were the rooster, the peacock, the dove and the crow. Ibn Ishaq related this from some scholars, and it was said by Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj, Ata' ibn Yasar and Ibn Zayd. Ibn Abbas said that instead of the crow it was the kurki (a crane), and also from him, instead of the dove it was the vulture (nasr).

So he took these birds as he was commanded, slaughtered them, cut them into small pieces, and mixed the flesh of some with the flesh of others, along with the blood and feathers, so that it would be more wondrous. Then he placed a portion of this mixed mass on every mountain. He stood where he could see those portions, and held the heads of the birds in his hand. Then he said: "Come, by God's permission!" The portions flew, the blood flew to the blood and the feathers to the feathers, until they were joined together as they had been before, and they remained without heads. Then he called again, and they came to him running, that is, hastening on their feet. One does not say of a bird that it "strove" (saʿā) when it flies, except in a figurative sense, as al-Nahhas said. Whenever he pointed to one of them without its head, the bird moved away; and whenever he pointed to it with its head, it came close, until each bird reached its head, and they flew by God's permission.

al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: "Then place upon every mountain a portion from each one of them." Abu Bakr, from Asim, and Abu Ja'far read "juzan" as "juz'an" with the pattern fu'ul. Abu Ja'far also read "juzzan" with a shadda on the zay. The rest read it hamzated and unstressed. These are dialectal variants, and its meaning is "portion."

"Yatinanaka sa'yan" (they will come to you hastening) is in the accusative as a circumstantial (ḥāl). "Fa-ṣurhunna" means: cut them up. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Abu Ubaydah and Ibn al-Anbari. It is said: "sara al-shay yasuruhu," meaning he cut it. Ibn Ishaq also said this. Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali said: in Syriac it means "cutting." Tawbah ibn al-Humayyir said, describing it:

"When I pulled the rope, its strands creaked,
with the ends of firm sticks whose cords were strong,
the ropes brought me close until I reached them,
by my rising, when my climbing had nearly cut them."

That is, it cuts them. Ṣawr means cutting. al-Dahhak, Ikrimah, and Ibn Abbas, in some of what is related from him, said: it is a word in Nabatean meaning "cut them up." It was also said: the meaning is "incline them toward you," that is, gather them and bring them together to you. It is said: "a man is aṣwar" when his neck is leaning. One also says: "I am aṣwar toward you," meaning longing and inclining. A woman is ṣawrā', and the plural is ṣuwar, like aswad and sud. The poet said:

"God knows that we, in our glancing
on the day of parting toward our neighbors, are ṣuwar."

So "ilayka" (toward you), on the interpretation of cutting, is connected to "fa-khudh" (take), and no omitted element is needed. On the interpretation of inclining and gathering, it is connected to "fa-ṣurhunna," and in the speech there is an omitted element: "So incline them toward you, then cut them up."

There are five readings of it: two among the seven (canonical readings), which are with ḍamma on the ṣād and with kasra on it, and with the rā' lightened. Some read "fa-ṣurrahunna" with ḍamma on the ṣād and a shadda on the rā' with fatḥa, as if he were saying "fa-shuddahunna" (bind them), and from this comes "ṣurrat al-danānīr" (a purse of dinars). Some read "fa-ṣirrahunna" with kasra on the ṣād and a shadda on the rā' with fatḥa, meaning "ṣayyiḥhunna" (call them out), from your saying: "ṣarra al-bāb wa al-qalam" when they make a sound. This was related by al-Naqqash. Ibn Jinni said: this is a strange reading, because yafʿil with kasra on the ʿayn in a doubled transitive verb is rare. Its pattern is yafʿul with ḍamma on the ʿayn, like shadda yashuddu and similar. But there have come from it "namma al-ḥadīth yanummuhu" and "yanimmuhu," and "harra al-ḥarb yahurruhā" and "yahirruhā." From this is the line of al-A'sha:

"Speech will certainly lead you on until you are excited by it,
and you will know that I am not guilty toward you."[[In the Diwan it reads: "Speech will certainly lead you on until you are excited by it, and you will know that I am not guilty toward you."]]

Among other readings in a few letters. Ibn Jinni said: As for the reading of ʿIkrimah with a ḍammah on the ṣād, the rāʾ may take ḍammah, fatḥah or kasrah [like maddа and shaddа (addition from MS h, b, j and Ibn ʿAṭiyyah)]. The preferable form is a ḍammah on the rāʾ, because of the ḍammah on the hāʾ after it. The fifth reading is "ṣarrihinna" with a fatḥah on the ṣād and a shaddah on the rāʾ with a kasrah, transmitted by al-Mahdawi and others from ʿIkrimah, meaning "hold them back" (fa-ḥbishunna), from their saying ṣarra yuṣerrī, meaning he held back; and from this comes the "muṣarrāh" sheep (a sheep whose udder is tied to withhold its milk). Here there is an objection raised by al-Mawardi [and he is (from MS h, b, j)]: It is said: How then was Abraham granted the signs of the Hereafter but not Moses, in his saying "My Lord, show me Yourself that I may look upon You" [see vol. 7, p. 278]? To this there are two answers: The first is that what Moses asked for cannot be granted while the obligation of religious duty remains, whereas what Abraham asked for is a specific matter with which the continuation of religious duty is compatible. The second is that circumstances differ, so granting a request may be the better course at one time, while at another time refusal is better in matters for which no permission has been given beforehand. Ibn ʿAbbas said: God Most High commanded Abraham to do this before a child was born to him and before the scriptures were sent down to him. And God knows best.

There are five issues in this passage.

The first: When Allah, glorified is He, related the proofs contained in it, He urged jihad, and informed that whoever strives in jihad after this proof, which none brings except a prophet, will have a great reward for his jihad. Al-Busti (Ibn Hibban) narrated in his *Sahih Musnad*, from Ibn Umar, who said: When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "My Lord, increase my ummah." Then ﴿Who is it that would lend Allah a goodly loan, so He may multiply it for him manifold?﴾ was revealed. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "My Lord, increase my ummah." Then ﴿Only the patient will be given their reward without measure﴾ was revealed. [See p. 237 of this part and vol. 15 p. 240.]

The wording of this verse is an illustrative example of the nobility of spending in the way of Allah and its excellence, and it includes an exhortation to that. In the speech there is an elision of a modifier, its estimated form being: "The likeness of the spending of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a grain." Another reading: "The likeness of those who spend their wealth is like a sower who sowed a grain in the earth, and the grain produced seven ears of grain," meaning it brought forth seven ears, with one hundred grains in each ear. Thus the one who gives charity is likened to the sower, and the charity is likened to the seed. Allah gives him seven hundred good deeds for every act of charity. Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾, meaning beyond seven hundred. So the likeness of the one who gives charity is the likeness of the sower, if he is skilled in his work, the seed is good, and the land is fertile: the crop will be greater. Likewise, the one who gives charity, when he is righteous and his wealth is good, and he places it in its proper place, his reward becomes greater. This is contrary to those who say that the verse contains no multiplication beyond seven hundred, as we will explain, Allah willing.

The second: It is narrated that this verse was revealed concerning Uthman ibn Affan and Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, may Allah be pleased with them both. This was because when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ urged the people to give charity when he intended to set out for the Battle of Tabuk, Abd al-Rahman came to him with four thousand and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I had eight thousand. I kept four thousand for myself and my dependents, and I lent four thousand to my Lord." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "May Allah bless you in what you kept and in what you gave." Uthman said: "O Messenger of Allah, I will provide the equipment for whoever has none." So this verse was revealed concerning them both.

It was also said: It was revealed concerning voluntary spending. It was also said: It was revealed before the verse of zakat and then abrogated (naskh) by the verse of zakat. There is no need to claim abrogation, because spending in the way of Allah is recommended at all times. The ways of Allah are many, and the greatest of them is jihad, so that the Word of Allah may be the highest.

The third: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿like a grain﴾. The word *habbah* (grain) is a generic noun for everything that the son of Adam sows and eats, and the most well-known of these is wheat. The word *habb* is often used to mean grain, and from it is the verse of al-Mutalammis:

*I have sworn never to eat the grain of Iraq as long as I live,*
*while the weevil eats the grain in the village.*

*Habbat al-qalb* is its core (*suwaydaa'*), and it is said its fruit, and both are the same. *Al-hibbah* with a kasra on the ha is the seeds of herbs that are not staple food. In the hadith of intercession: "They will sprout as the seed sprouts in the debris (*hamil*) of a flood." [Hamil al-sayl: what the flood carries of foam and mud.] The plural is *hibab*. *Al-hubbah* with a damma on the ha is love (*al-hubb*); it is said: "a blessing, a love, and an honor." *Al-hubb* is affection (*al-mahabbah*), and likewise *al-hibb* with a kasra. *Al-hibb* also means the beloved, like *khidn* and *khadin* (both meaning close friend). *Sunbulah* is on the pattern *fun'ulah*, from *asbala al-zar'*, when the crop develops ears, that is, the ear extends with its spike, as a curtain extends when let down (*al-israb*). It is said its meaning is: there came to be concealed grain in it, as a thing is concealed by letting down a curtain over it. The plural is *sanabil*.

Then it was said: The intended meaning is the ear of millet (*al-dukhn*), for it is in the ear of it that this number occurs. I say: This is nothing, for the ear of millet contains more than this number by two times or more, as we have observed. Ibn Atiyah said: It may be found in an ear of wheat with one hundred grains, but in the rest of the grains there are more, yet the example was given with this amount. Al-Tabari said concerning this verse: His saying "in every ear a hundred grains" means if that is found, and if not, then it is supposed. Then it was transmitted from al-Dahhak that he said: "In every ear a hundred grains" means every ear that produced a hundred grains. Ibn Atiyah said: Al-Tabari made al-Dahhak's statement similar to what he said, but that does not necessarily follow from al-Dahhak's statement.

Abu Amr al-Dani said: Some read "*mi'ata*" (a hundred) in the accusative, on the assumption of "it produced a hundred grains." I say: Yaqub al-Hadrami said: Some read "*fi kulli sunbulatin mi'ata habbatin*" as "it produced a hundred grains." Similarly, some read "*wa li-lladhina kafaru bi-rabbihim adhabu jahannam*" as "*wa a'tadna lahum adhaba al-sa'ir*" [see vol. 18 p. 211], and "*wa a'tadna lil-ladhina kafaru adhaba jahannam*."

Abu Amr and Hamzah and al-Kisai read "*anbatat sab'a sanabil*" with the assimilation of the *ta'* into the *sin*, because both are voiceless consonants; do you not see that they interchange? Abu Amr recited:

*O curse of Allah upon the sons of al-Sa'lah* [al-Sa'lah: the most wicked of the ghouls; when a woman is ugly of face and bad of character, she is likened to the sa'lah], *Amr ibn Maymun* [In the books of language (root n-w-t): "Amr ibn Yarbu'"], *base of birth!*

He intended "*al-nas*" (the people), and changed the *sin* to *ta'*. The rest read with clear pronunciation according to the original form, because they are two separate words.

The fourth: The Qur'an has established that a good deed in all acts of righteousness is multiplied tenfold, and this verse indicates that the good deed of spending in jihad is multiplied by seven hundred. The scholars differed concerning the meaning of His saying: ﴿And Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾. One group said: It explains and emphasizes what was mentioned earlier of the seven hundred, and there is no multiplication beyond seven hundred. Another group of scholars said: Rather, it is an announcement that Allah, exalted is He, multiplies for whom He wills more than seven hundred times. I say: This view is more sound because of the hadith of Ibn Umar mentioned at the beginning of the verse.

Ibn Majah narrated: Harun ibn Abd Allah al-Hammal narrated to us, Ibn Abi Fudayk narrated to us, from al-Khalil ibn Abd Allah, from al-Hasan, [from [Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abu al-Darda, Abd Allah ibn Amr, Abu Umamah al-Bahili, Abd Allah ibn Amr, Jabir ibn Abd Allah, and Imran ibn Husayn, all of whom narrate from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he said: "Whoever sends forth expenditure in the way of Allah and remains in his house, for him is seven hundred dirhams for every dirham; and whoever fights himself in the way of Allah and spends in its cause, for him is seven hundred thousand dirhams for every dirham." Then he recited [this verse]: "And Allah multiplies for whom He wills." [Footnote: from the editions ج وب، وابن ماجة، وفية في الهند: وأبى هريرة (in Ibn Majah: "in wajh"). These are variant readings noted in the printed edition.]

It has been narrated from Ibn Abbas that the multiplication reaches, for whom Allah wills, up to two thousand thousand. Ibn Atiyah said: This is not authentically transmitted from him.

The fifth: In this verse there is evidence that cultivating crops is among the highest trades that people practice and the livelihoods in which laborers engage, and for this reason Allah struck it as an example, saying: ﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth﴾, to the end of the verse.

In *Sahih Muslim* from the Prophet ﷺ: "No Muslim plants a plant or sows a crop, and a bird or a person or an animal eats from it, except that it is for him a charity."

Hisham ibn Urwah narrated from his father, from Aisha, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Seek provision in the hidden places of the earth," meaning agriculture. It was recorded by al-Tirmidhi.

And he ﷺ said concerning the palm tree: "It is the firmly rooted in the mud, providing food in the time of dearth." This came in the form of praise.

Agriculture is among the communal obligations (*furud al-kifayah*), so the ruler must compel the people to it, and what is similar to it, such as planting trees.

Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Malik met Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri and said: "Direct me to a property I may work at." Ibn Shihab began to say:

*I say to Abd Allah on the day I met him, when he had tightened the saddle-girths of the riding camels, setting out toward the east:*
*Seek out the hidden places of the earth and call upon its Owner, perhaps one day you will be answered and provided for.*
*Then He will give you abundant wealth, lasting and of great return, when the waters of the earth have sunk, gushing forth.*

It is related from al-Mu'tadid that he said: I saw Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, in a dream, handing me a hoe, and he said: "Take it, for it is the keys to the treasuries of the earth."

There are three issues in this verse.

The first concerns God's words: ﴿Those who spend their wealth in the way of God﴾. It is said that this was revealed concerning Uthman ibn Affan (may God be pleased with him). Abd al-Rahman ibn Samura said: "Uthman came with a thousand dinars for the Army of Hardship (jaysh al-'usrah), and poured them into the lap of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). I saw him (ﷺ) put his hand into them and turn them over, and he said: 'Whatever Uthman does after today will not harm him. O God, do not forget this day for Uthman.'" Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: "I saw the Prophet (ﷺ) raising his hands and supplicating for Uthman, saying: 'O Lord of Uthman, I am pleased with Uthman, so be pleased with him.' He kept supplicating until dawn broke, and then this was revealed: ﴿Those who spend their wealth in the way of God, and then do not follow what they have spent with reminders of their generosity or injury﴾, and the rest of the verse."

The second issue: Since the previous verse mentioned spending in the way of God in general terms, this verse clarifies that this ruling and reward belong only to those who do not follow their spending with reminders of generosity or with injury, because reminder (mann) and injury (adha) nullify the reward of charity (sadaqah), as God states in the verse after this one. A person should intend by his spending on the recipient the face of God and His reward, expecting nothing from him and looking at his circumstances only in order to fulfil his entitlement. God says: ﴿We do not want from you any reward or thanks﴾. Whoever spends in order to seek from the recipient some kind of reward is not seeking the face of God; if such a person's expectation is disappointed, he reminds the recipient of his giving and injures him. Likewise, whoever spends under compulsion, to ward off a debt, either out of obligation to the recipient or because of some other connection, such as the attention of someone who takes care of him, has not intended the face of God. What is accepted is the gift given for God's sake, where the greater part of the intention is to seek what is with God, like what is related of Umar ibn al-Khattab (may God be pleased with him): a bedouin came to him and said:

"O Umar of goodness, may you be rewarded with Paradise,
clothe my daughters and their mother.
Be for us a shield against time,
I swear by God that you will surely do it."

Umar said: "What will happen if I do not?" He said:

"Then, O Abu Hafs, I will surely leave."

He said: "And if you leave, what will happen?" He said:

"You will be questioned about my condition,
on a day when gifts are weighed,
and the standing of the one questioned is between them,
either to a fire or to Paradise."

Umar wept until his beard was soaked, then said: "O boy, give him this shirt of mine, for that day, not for his poetry! By God, I have no other." Al-Mawardi said: When giving is of this kind, free from seeking reward or thanks and free from reminder and publicity, it is more honourable for the giver and more pleasant for the receiver.
