As for the giver who seeks by his gift a reward and asks for gratitude and praise, he is one who seeks reputation and show (riya'), and these two carry blame that is incompatible with generosity. If he seeks such things, he is a merchant seeking profit, who does not deserve praise or commendation. Ibn Abbas, concerning God's words ﴿And do not give in order to receive more﴾, said: "that is, do not give a gift seeking something better in return." Ibn Zayd held that this verse concerns those who do not go out to fight but spend while sitting at home, while the previous verse concerns those who go out themselves; he said: "For this reason a condition is set for these, but not for the former." Ibn Atiyya said: "There is scrutiny in this view, because the arbitrariness in it is apparent."

The third issue concerns God's words: ﴿reminder or injury﴾. Mann (reminder) is recalling the favour in order to enumerate it and reproach with it, such as saying: "I have done good to you, I have supported you," or similar. Some have said: mann is speaking about what one has given until it reaches the recipient and injures him. Mann is among the major sins; this is established in Sahih Muslim and other collections, and it is one of the three whom God will not look at, nor purify, and for whom there is a painful punishment. Al-Nasa'i related from Ibn Umar who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Three whom God will not look at on the Day of Resurrection: the one who disobeys his parents, the woman who dresses like a man imitating men, and the cuckold (dayyuth). And three who will not enter Paradise: the one who disobeys his parents, the habitual drinker of wine, and the one who reminds of what he has given." In one of the chains in Sahih Muslim: "The mannan is the one who gives nothing except with reminder."

Adha (injury) is reviling and complaining. It is more general than mann, because mann is a part of injury, but it was specifically mentioned because it occurs frequently. Ibn Zayd said: "If you think that your greeting burdens the one you have spent upon, while you seek the face of God, then do not greet him." A woman said to him: "O Abu Usamah, point me to a man who truly goes out in the way of God, for they go out only to eat fruits. I have arrows and a quiver." He said: "May God not bless your arrows and your quiver, for you have injured them before you gave them."

Our scholars (may God have mercy upon them) said: whoever spends in the way of God and does not follow it with reminder or injury, such as saying: "How you press me! May God free us from you!" and similar words, God has guaranteed him the reward, and the reward is Paradise. God has negated fear for him after his death concerning what lies ahead, and grief over what has passed of his worldly life, because he rejoices in his hereafter. He said: ﴿Their reward is with their Lord, and there is no fear for them, nor will they grieve﴾. This is sufficient as excellence and honour for spending in the way of God, the Exalted. It also provides evidence for those who prefer the rich over the poor, as will be explained if God wills.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 263:

There are three issues concerning this.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a kind word﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate (khabar) is omitted, meaning: a kind word is better and more fitting. This was mentioned by al-Nahhas and al-Mahdawi. Al-Nahhas said: It is also permissible for "a kind word" to be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: that which you have been commanded is a kind word. The kind word is supplication, comforting, and hope in what is with Allah, which is better than a charity that outwardly is charity but inwardly is nothing, because mentioning a kind word carries a reward, whereas there is no reward in that. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A good word is charity, and indeed among what is good is that you meet your brother with a cheerful face." Related by Muslim. So he should receive the one asking with cheerfulness and welcome, and meet him with warmth and closeness, so that he is thanked if he gives and excused if he refuses. Some of the wise have said: Meet the person in need with cheerfulness; if you do not earn his thanks, you will not lose his excuse. Ibn Lankak [he is Abu al-Hasan Muhammad ibn Muhammad, the unique one of Basra and the foremost of its men of letters] (from Yatimat al-Dahr, vol. 2, p. 116) reported that Abu Bakr ibn Duraid went to some of the ministers regarding a need that was not fulfilled, and he showed displeasure, so he said:

Let not the displeasure at a petitioner enter you, for the best of your age is that you be seen as one who is asked.
Do not confront with refusal the face of one who hopes, for the endurance of your honour is that you be seen as one who is hoped in.
You meet the noble and are guided by his cheerfulness, and you see frowning upon the base as a sign.
Know that before long you will become a report, so be a report that pleases with beauty.

It is narrated from the hadith of Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When the petitioner asks, do not cut off his request until he finishes; then respond to him with dignity and gentleness, or with a small gift, or with a gracious refusal, for there may come to you one who is neither human nor jinn, watching your conduct regarding what Allah Exalted has entrusted to you." I say: Its evidence is the hadith of the leper, the bald man and the blind man, related by Muslim and others, that an angel appeared in the form of a leper once, a bald man another time, and a blind man another time, as a test for the one being asked. Bishr ibn al-Harith said: I saw Ali in a dream and said: O Commander of the Faithful, tell me something that Allah may benefit me by. He said: How excellent is the inclination of the prophets toward the poor, seeking the reward of Allah Exalted; and more excellent than that is the pride of the poor over the rich, out of trust in the promise of Allah. I said: O Commander of the Faithful, increase it for me. He turned away while saying:

You were dead and became alive, and before long you will become dead.
So lay waste the house of perishing, and build a house in the abode of enduring.

The second: His saying, exalted is He: (forgiveness) — "forgiveness" here means concealing the need and the bad condition of the one in want. From this is the saying of the Bedouin, when he asked a group of people with eloquent speech, and someone said to him: "Who is this man?" He said: "O Allah, a pardon!" Bad earnings prevent one from claiming lineage. It was also said: The meaning is that overlooking the petitioner when he presses, becomes harsh and rude, is better than giving him charity accompanied by reproach and harm. This is the meaning reported by al-Naqqash. Al-Nahhas said: This is difficult, and the grammatical analysis (i'rab) clarifies it. "Forgiveness" is in the nominative as the subject, and the predicate is (better than charity). The meaning, Allah knows best, is: an act that leads to forgiveness is better than a charity followed by harm. Its grammatical estimate is: "and an act of forgiveness." It is also permissible that it be like your saying: Allah's favour upon you is greater than the charity with which you reproach, meaning: Allah's forgiveness is better than this charity of yours with which you reproach.

The third: His saying, exalted is He: (and Allah is Rich, Forbearing). He, exalted, informs of His absolute richness, that He is free of the charity of His servants, and He only commanded it so that He might reward them; and of His forbearance, that He does not hasten to punish whoever reproaches and harms with his charity.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 264:

There are three issues in this.

The first concerns His saying, ﴿with reminders of generosity and injury﴾. Its meaning has already been explained. God expressed the non-acceptance of the charity and the deprivation of reward by the word "nullification" (ibtal). The intended meaning is the charity over which one reminds of one's favour and causes injury, and nothing else. The creed (al-'aqidah) is that bad deeds do not cancel good deeds or nullify them. So reminding of favour and injury in one act of charity does not nullify another act of charity. Most scholars said regarding this verse: the charity which God knows its giver reminds of or injures with is not accepted. It has also been said: rather, God has set a sign for the angel regarding it, so he does not record it, and this is a good view. The Arabs say of what is reminded of: "a black hand" (yad sawda'). Of what is given without a request: "a white hand" (yad bayda'). Of what is given in response to a request: "a green hand" (yad khadra'). Some eloquent writers said: "Whoever reminds of his kindness, his thanks are lost, and whoever is pleased with his deed, his reward is lost." Some poets said:

"A companion from whom a favour came to me,
who was slow to repay it, and so he became my enemy.
When he became certain that fate had made war on me,
he showed regret for what he had done for me."

Another said:

"You spoiled with reminding the good you had done;
the noble man, when he does a favour, does not remind."

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said, and excelled:

"The best of every good,
at every time and in every era,
is a favour that is nurtured
and free of reminders."

Ibn Sirin heard a man say to another: "Did I not do this for you and do that for you!" He said to him: "Be silent, for there is no good in kindness when it is counted."

It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Beware of reminding of kindness, for it nullifies gratitude and destroys the reward." Then he recited: ﴿Do not nullify your charities with reminders and injury﴾.

The second issue: Our scholars, may God have mercy on them, said: Malik disliked, in light of this verse, that a man give his obligatory charity (zakah) to his relatives, lest he thereby receive from them praise and commendation, and reveal his favour over them, and they reward him for it, so it would not be purely for the sake of God, the Exalted. He preferred that it be given to strangers. He also preferred that he entrust its distribution to someone else if the ruler was not just, so that it would not be nullified by reminders, injury, gratitude, praise, and repayment by service from the recipient. This differs from voluntary secret charity, because if its reward is nullified, it is free from the threat and is in the position of one who did not do it. But the obligatory act, if its reward is nullified, the threat falls upon him, since he is in the position of one who did not do it.

The third issue: His saying, ﴿like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people﴾. The kaf (like) is in the accusative position, meaning "nullification like..." so it is a description of an omitted verbal noun (masdar). It is also permissible for it to be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). God made the one who reminds of and injures with his charity a parable for the one who spends his wealth to be seen by people and not for the sake of God, and for the disbeliever who spends so that he will be called generous and be praised with various kinds of praise. Then He made this spender also a parable with a smooth rock (safwan) covered with dust, which an observer thinks is fertile, good earth. When a heavy rain strikes it, it removes the dust and leaves it bare. Likewise is this show-off. Reminders, injury, and showing off reveal the intention in the Hereafter, so the charity is nullified, as the heavy rain reveals the smooth rock. The safwan is the large, smooth stone. It has also been said: the verse intends the nullification of the merit (fadl) but not the reward. So the one who spends with the intention of showing off is not rewarded, like the disbeliever, because he did not intend by it the face of God, so he does not deserve reward. The one who reminds and injures, however, intended the face of God and deserves his reward, even though he repeated his giving, and his excellence is nullified. It has also been said: only the reward of his charity from the time of his reminding and injury is nullified, while what came before that is recorded for him and multiplied. When he reminds and injures, the multiplication ceases, because charity is made to grow for its owner until it becomes greater than a mountain. When it leaves its owner's hand purely, in the lawful manner, it is multiplied. When reminding and injury come upon it, it stops there, and the extra multiplication is cut off from it. The first view is more apparent (in manuscript H: "more preferable"). And God knows best.

As for al-Saf'wan: its plural is safa'in, its singular is safwanah, said al-Akhfash. He said: some of them said: safwan is singular, like hajar (stone). Al-Kisa'i said: safwan is singular, and its plural is sifwan, suffi, and sifi. Al-Mubarrad rejected this and said: rather, suffi is the plural of safa, like qafa and qufiy. From this meaning come al-saf'a' and al-safa (see the second issue, vol. 2, p. 179). Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and al-Zuhri read "safawan" with a vowelled fa', and this is a dialect. Qutrub transmitted "sifwan." Al-Nahhas said: safwan and safawan may be plural or singular, but it is more proper that it be singular, because of His saying, ﴿upon it is dust, and a heavy rain strikes it﴾. Even though it is permissible to masculinize a plural, a thing does not depart from its pattern except with conclusive evidence. As for what al-Kisa'i reported regarding the plural, it is not correct according to careful analysis. Rather, sifwan is the plural of safa, and safa has the meaning of safwan. Its parallel is warl (a lizard-like creature larger than the dabb, found in sands and deserts, which the Arabs find repulsive and do not eat), with plural warlan, and akh (brother) with plural ikhwan, and karaw (a kind of bird) with kirwan, as the poet said:

"For us is a day, and for the karawan a day:
the wretched ones fly, and we do not fly."

The weak view in Arabic is that kirwan is the plural of karawan, and sifiy and sifiy are the plural of safa, like asa. Al-Wabil: heavy rain. The sky "wabalat" (poured heavily), and the earth is "mawbulah." Al-Akhfash said: from this is His saying, ﴿So We seized him with a severe seizure (akhdh wabil)﴾ (see vol. 19, p. 47), meaning severe. A "wabil" blow and a "wabil" punishment mean severe. Al-Sald: the smooth of stones. Al-Kisa'i said: salida yaslidu saladan with the lam vowelled, so it is salid with the lam sukun, and it is everything that does not produce anything. From this is jabin asladu (a bare forehead). Al-Asma'i recited for Ru'bah:

"Bright, bare-foreheaded, with the hairline receded."

Al-Naqqash said: al-asladu is the bare one in the dialect of Hudhayl. The meaning of "they are not able" (la yaqdiruna) refers to the show-off, the disbeliever, and the one who reminds, "over anything," meaning to benefit from the reward of any of their spending, which is their earning when they need it, since it was for other than God. So the spending is called earning, because they intended by it earning. It has also been said: this was given as a parable for the show-off regarding the nullification of his reward, and for the one who reminds and injures regarding the nullification of his merit. This is mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 265:

His saying, exalted is He: "And the likeness of those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of Allah and for the firming of their own souls" ("ibtighā'" is an object of purpose [maf'ūl min ajlihi]. "wa-tathbītan min anfusihim" is coordinated with it. Makki said in al-Mushkil: both of them are objects of purpose. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is rejected. It is not valid for "tathbītan" to be an object of purpose, because spending is not for the sake of firming. "Ibtighā'" is in the accusative as a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and the accusative as an object of purpose was also possible, but the accusative as a verbal noun is the correct view, because of the coordination of the verbal noun "tathbītan" with it." When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the description of the charities of the people for whom their charities have no value, and forbade the believers from engaging in anything resembling that in any way, He followed in this verse by mentioning the expenditures of the people whose charities grow, since they were in accordance with the Law and its purpose. "Ibtighā'" means seeking. "Marḍāt" is a verbal noun from radiya, yarḍā. "Tathbītan" means that they make sure (yatathabbatūn) where they place their charities, said Mujahid and al-Hasan. Al-Hasan said: "When a man intended to give charity, he made sure. If it was for Allah, he carried it out, and if doubt mixed with it, he refrained." It was also said: its meaning is confirmation and certainty, said by Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn 'Abbas also said, and Qatada: its meaning is seeking reward (ihtisāban) from their own souls. Al-Sha'bi, al-Suddi, Qatada also, Ibn Zayd, Abu Salih and others said: "Tathbītan" means and certainty, that is, their souls have insights, so they firm them up in spending in obedience to Allah, exalted is He, a firming. These three opinions are more correct than the saying of al-Hasan and Mujahid, because the meaning they adopted is expressed as "tathbītan" being a verbal noun of a different form. Ibn 'Atiyya said: This is not permissible except when the verbal noun is mentioned and the verb that precedes it is explicit, as in His saying, exalted is He: "And Allah has caused you to grow from the earth [[see vol. 18 p. 305]] a growth," and "And devote yourself [[see vol. 19 p. 42]] to Him with devotion." As for when no verb is made explicit, it is not permissible for you to bring a verbal noun not in its meaning and then say: I take it to mean such and such, for a verb that has not been mentioned before. Ibn 'Atiyya said: This is the most common style of Arabic speech as far as I know. Al-Nahhas said: If it were as Mujahid said, it would be "wa-tathabbutan" from "tathabbata," like "karramat, takarrumam." Qatada's saying "ihtisaban" is not known except if it means that their souls firm them up while seeking reward, and this is far-fetched. Al-Sha'bi's saying is good, that is, a firming from their own souls for them in spending that in obedience to Allah, mighty and majestic is He. It is said: "thabbattu fulanan fi hadha al-amr," meaning I corrected his resolve and strengthened his opinion in it, "uthabbituhu tathbitan," that is, their souls are certain of Allah's promise regarding their firmness in that. It was also said: "And a firming from their own souls" means they acknowledge that Allah, exalted is He, makes them firm upon it, that is, a firming from their own souls for its reward, unlike the hypocrite who does not seek the reward.

His saying, exalted is He: "As the likeness of a garden on a height" ("al-jannah" is the orchard, and it is a piece of land in which trees grow until they cover it, and it is derived from the word "jinn" and "janin" because of their concealment. This has already been mentioned. "Al-rabwah" is a place raised a slight height, usually with it a density of soil, and what is like that its vegetation is finer, and for that reason He singled out the height for mention. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The meadows of Hazn are not of this, as al-Tabari claimed, rather those are the meadows attributed to Najd, because they are better than the meadows of Tihama, and Najd's plants are more fragrant, and its breeze is cooler and gentler, and Najd is called Hazn. The air of Tihama is rarely suitable except at night, and for that reason the Bedouin woman said: "My husband is like the night of Tihama." Al-Suddi said: "bi-rabwah" means "bi-rabawah," which is what has sunk from the land. Ibn 'Atiyya said: This is an unsteady expression, and the word "rabwah" is derived from "raba, yarbu," when it increases. I say: al-Suddi's expression is worthless, because the root "r-b-w" in the speech of the Arabs means increase, and from it is "al-rabw" for a high breath. "Raba, yarbu" when he was seized by asthma. "Rabā al-faras" when the horse was seized by asthma from running or fright. Al-Farra' said regarding His saying, exalted is He: "So He seized them with a seizure increasing [[see vol. 18 p. 262]]," meaning increasing, as when you say: "arbaytu" when you take more than you give. "Rabawtu fi bani fulan" and "rabaytu," meaning I grew up among them. Al-Khalil said: "al-Rabwah" is a high, good land. Allah, exalted is He, singled out for mention the one in which no water flows, in terms of the custom in the lands of the Arabs, so He gave them a likeness of what they sense and perceive. Ibn 'Abbas said: "al-Rabwah" is the high place in which rivers do not flow, because His saying, exalted is He: "a heavy rain struck it" to the end of the verse indicates that there is no running water in it, and He did not intend the type in which rivers flow, because Allah, exalted is He, has mentioned a height with a dwelling place and a spring. What is well known in the speech of the Arabs is that "rabwah" is what is raised above what is adjacent to it, whether or not water flows in it. There are five dialects: "rubwah" with a damma on the ra', and with it Ibn Kathir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read. "Birabwah" with a fatha on the ra', and with it 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir and al-Hasan read. "Ribwah" with a kasra on the ra', and with it Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Ishaq al-Sabi'i read. "Rabawah" with a fatha, and with it Abu Ja'far and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read, and the poet said:

"Who is my dwelling in a meadow of Rabawah, between the palm trees and the Baqi' al-Gharqad?"

"Ribawah" with a kasra, and with it al-Ashhab al-Uqayli read. Al-Farra' said: It is said "birabawah" and "biribawah," and all of it is from "al-rabiyah," and its verb is "raba, yarbu."

His saying, exalted is He: "It was struck by" ("it" refers to the rabwah) "a heavy rain," meaning a strong rain. The poet said [[It is the verse of A'sha Maymun; in his diwan, al-Tabari, al-Lisan and al-Taj under (ḥ-z-n) it reads: "musbil, hatil"]]:

"No meadow of the meadows of Hazn is abundant in vegetation, green, upon which a heavy rain has poured, abundant."

"Fa-ātat" means gave.

"Ukulahā" with a damma on the hamza: the fruit that is eaten, and from it His saying, exalted is He: "It yields its produce [[see vol. 9 p. 358]] every season." And what is eaten of anything is called "ukul." And "al-ukulah" is a morsel. From it is the hadith: "If the food is meager [mashfūh, meaning little; its root is water that many lips have drunk until it became scant. It is also said: he meant the food is heaped upon, i.e., its eating is abundant. Al-Nihayah], then let him put in his hand from it one or two morsels." Meaning one morsel or two morsels, recorded by Muslim. Its attribution to the garden is an attribution of particularity, like the saddle of the horse and the door of the house. Otherwise, fruit is not something the garden eats. Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "ukuluhā" with a damma on the hamza and a sukun on the kaf, and likewise every feminine noun in annexation. Abu 'Amr differed from them in what is annexed to a masculine noun, such as "ukulihi," or what is not annexed to anything, such as "ukulin khamt" [[see vol. 14 p. 285]], so Abu 'Amr made those heavy and light. 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read all of what we have mentioned with the heavy form. It is said: "akl" and "ukul" have the same meaning.

"Ḍi'fayn" means it gave double the fruit of other lands. Some scholars said: it bore twice in the year, and the first is more, meaning it produced from the crop what other land produces in two years.

His saying, exalted is He: "But if a heavy rain does not strike it, then a light rain" is an emphasis from Him, exalted is He, in praise of this height: that if a heavy rain does not strike it, the light rain suffices for it, and it takes the place of the heavy rain in producing the fruit double, and that is due to the nobility and goodness of the land. Al-Mubarrad and others said: its estimate is "fa-tallun yakfīhā" (a light rain suffices for it). Al-Zajjaj said: "fa-alladhi yuṣībuhā ṭallun" (so what strikes it is a light rain). "Al-Tall" is the weak rain, the fine drizzle of light rainfall, said Ibn 'Abbas and others, and it is the well-known meaning in the language. Some people, including Mujahid, said: al-Tall is dew. Ibn 'Atiyya said: This is a figurative and metaphorical usage. Al-Nahhas said: The lexicographers transmitted "wabalat" and "awbalat," and "tallat" and "atalla." In al-Sihah: al-Tall is the weakest of rain, and its plural is al-tilal. One says from it: "tullat al-ardu" and "atallahā al-nadā," so it is "matlūlah" (dew-soaked). Al-Mawardi said: Crop from light rain is weaker than crop from rain and yields less, yet in it, though small, there is firmness and benefit. Some of them said: In the verse there is inversion and reordering, and its meaning is: "like a garden on a height struck by a heavy rain; if a heavy rain does not strike it, a light rain, then it yields its produce double," meaning its leaves became green and its fruit came out double. I say: the first interpretation is more correct, and there is no need for inversion. So Allah, exalted is He, likened the growth of the charities of these sincere people, whose charities Allah makes grow, to the raising of a foal (fulu) and a weanling (fasil) to the growth of the plants of the garden on the described height, unlike the smooth rock whose soil was uncovered so that it remained bare. Muslim and others transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "No one gives charity of a date from lawful earnings except that Allah takes it with His right hand and makes it grow for him, as one of you raises his foal or weanling, until it becomes like a mountain or greater." Al-Muwatta' also recorded it.

His saying, exalted is He: "And Allah is seeing of what you do" is a promise and a warning. Al-Zuhri read "ya'malūn" with the ya', as if he meant all people, or meant only the spenders, so it is a pure promise.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 266:**

His saying, may He be exalted: "Would any of you like to have a garden of date palms and grapevines, with rivers flowing beneath it, in which he has every kind of fruit, and then old age overtakes him while he has weak offspring, and a fiery whirlwind strikes it so that it is burned? Thus God makes the signs clear to you, so that you may reflect." (266)

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Would any of you like to have a garden of date palms and grapevines﴾, the verse. Al-Tabari reported from al-Suddi that this verse is another parable for the spending (nafaqah) of riya' (showing off), and al-Tabari preferred this view. I say: It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "This is a parable God struck for those who show off in their deeds, whose deeds He nullifies on the Day of Resurrection, when they are most in need of them, like a man who had a garden and had children who were no help to him. Then he grew old, and a whirlwind (i'sar, meaning a violent wind) with fire struck the garden and burned it, so he lost it when he was most in need of it." It is also reported from Ibn Zayd that he recited God's saying: "O you who believe, do not nullify your charities with reproach and injury" (2:264), the verse, and then said: "Then He struck a parable concerning that, saying: 'Would any of you like...'" the verse. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This is clearer than what al-Tabari preferred, and this verse is not another parable for the spending of riya'; this is what the context of the speech requires. As for its meaning outside this context, it resembles the condition of every hypocrite or disbeliever who does a deed while supposing he is doing good, and when the time of need comes he finds nothing."

I say: It has been reported from Ibn 'Abbas that it is a parable for one who acts for other than God, whether a hypocrite or a disbeliever, as will come, except that what is established in al-Bukhari from him is contrary to this. Al-Bukhari transmitted from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, who said: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said one day to the companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "About what do you think this verse was revealed: 'Would any of you like to have a garden of date palms and grapevines'?" They said: "God and His Messenger know best." 'Umar became angry and said: "Say: we know, or we do not know!" Ibn 'Abbas said: "There is something in my heart about it, O Commander of the Faithful." He said: "O son of my brother, speak and do not belittle yourself." Ibn 'Abbas said: "It was struck as a parable for a deed." 'Umar said: "What deed?" Ibn 'Abbas said: "For the deed of a wealthy man who works in obedience to God, then God sends Satan to him, and he works in disobedience until he burns up his deed." In another narration: "When his life is spent and his term draws near, He concludes it with a deed of wretchedness," and 'Umar was pleased with this.

Ibn Abi Mulaykah reported that 'Umar recited this verse and said: "This is a parable struck for a person who does a righteous deed, until, when he is at the end of his life and most in need of it, he does an evil deed." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This is a view that carries the verse to everything that falls under its wording, and Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Rabi' and others said something similar." The date palms and grapevines were singled out for mention because of their nobility and their excellence over the rest of the trees. al-Hasan read "jannat" (gardens) in the plural.

(with rivers flowing beneath it) This has been mentioned before.

(in which he has every kind of fruit) He means that there is no fruit except that it grows in it.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and old age overtakes him﴾: here the past tense (asabahu) is joined (by the conjunction wa) to a future-tense verb, which is "takun" (would be). It was said that the sense is "and old age had overtaken him," and it was said that it is governed by the meaning, since the meaning is "Would any of you like, if he had a garden...?" It was also said that the wa is the wa of circumstance (hal), and likewise in His saying "and he has" (wa lahu).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and a fiery whirlwind strikes it so that it is burned﴾. Al-Hasan said: "i'sar fihi nar" (a whirlwind with fire in it) is a wind with intense cold. Al-Zajjaj said: al-i'sar in the language is the violent wind that blows from the earth to the sky like a column, and this is what is called zawba'ah. Al-Jawhari said: al-zawba'ah is a chief of the jinn, and from it the i'sar was named zawba'ah. It is also said: "Umm Zawba'ah," which is a wind that raises dust and rises to the sky like a column. It was also said: al-i'sar is a wind that stirs up a cloud with thunder and lightning. Al-Mahdawi said: it was called i'sar because it coils like a garment when it is wrung out (u'sira). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This is weak." I say: Rather, it is sound, because it is what is observed and perceived, for it rises as a coiled column. It was also said: the wind was only called i'sar because it wrings (ya'sir) the cloud, and the clouds are called mu'sirat (wringing clouds), either because they are pregnant, so they are like the mu'sir (a woman who is near to conceiving) among women, or because they are wrung by the winds. Ibn Sidah reported that some people explained the mu'sirat as winds and not clouds. Ibn Zayd said: al-i'sar is a violent wind and intense scorching heat, and al-Suddi likewise said: al-i'sar is the wind, and the fire is the scorching heat. Ibn 'Abbas said: a wind with intense scorching heat in it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This may occur in intense heat, and it may occur in intense cold, and all of it comes from the blaze (fayh) and breath of Hell, just as the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) includes: "When the heat intensifies, delay the prayer until it cools, for the intensity of heat is from the blaze of Hell," and "The Fire complained to its Lord," the hadith.

It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas and others: this is a parable God struck for the disbelievers and the hypocrites, in the likeness of a man who planted an orchard and abundantly produced fruit in it, then old age overtook him while he had weak offspring, meaning young daughters and sons, and his livelihood and the livelihood of his offspring came from that orchard. Then God sent upon his orchard a wind with fire in it, and it burned it, and he had no strength to plant it again, and his children had no good in them so that they could return to their father. Likewise, the disbeliever and the hypocrite, when they come to God on the Day of Resurrection, have no return, so that they are raised and sent back a second time, just as this man had no strength to plant his orchard again, and he had no one with him, in his old age and the weakness of his offspring, whom he could rely on for support.

(Thus God makes the signs clear to you, so that you may reflect) He means: so that you may return to My greatness and My lordship, and not take allies besides Me. Ibn 'Abbas also said: "So that you may reflect on the passing away and perishing of this world, and the coming and enduring of the Hereafter."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 267 (part 1 of 2):

[The text of the commentary begins here.]

His saying, exalted is He: O you who have believed, spend of the good things you have earned and of what We have produced for you from the earth, and do not aim at the defective therefrom to spend [from] while you would not accept it except with disdain toward it. And know that Allah is Free of need and Praiseworthy. (2:267)

It contains eleven issues.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: "O you who have believed, spend." This is an address to the whole of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). The scholars differed about the meaning intended by "spending" here. Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ubaydah al-Salmani and Ibn Sirin said: it is the obligatory zakat (obligatory almsgiving), and He forbade people from spending the inferior in it instead of the good. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The apparent meaning of the statements of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, al-Hasan and Qatadah is that the verse concerns voluntary charity, and they recommended that one not give voluntary charity except with a chosen good item. The verse includes both meanings. But the proponents of zakat rely on two points: that it is a command, and commands imply obligation; and that He forbade the inferior, and that prohibition is specific to the obligatory. As for voluntary charity, just as a person may give voluntarily a small amount, so too he may give voluntarily something lower in quantity, and a dirham is better than a date. The proponents of recommendation relied on the fact that the form "fa'al" (imperative) is suitable for recommendation just as it is suitable for obligation, and the inferior is forbidden in voluntary giving just as it is forbidden in obligatory giving, and God is most worthy of the best that is chosen for Him.

Al-Bara' narrated that a man hung a cluster (qinw) of dates (ḥashaf), so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw it and said: "How evil is what he has hung." Then the verse was revealed. Al-Tirmidhi related it, and it will come in full.[[The qinw: the cluster of the palm, which is the spikes bearing fruit. The ḥashaf: dates that dry before ripening, so they are inferior and have no flesh.]]

According to this view, the command is one of recommendation: they were recommended not to give voluntary charity except with a good, chosen item. The majority of interpreters said: the meaning of "of the good things" (min ṭayyibāt) is of the good and chosen "what you have earned" (mā kasabtum). Ibn Zayd said: of the lawful (ḥalāl) of what you have earned.

The second: Earning (al-kasb) is either by bodily labour, which is hiring (al-ijārah), whose ruling will come, or by a contract in trade, which is sale (al-bay'), whose explanation will come. Inheritance is included in this, because the non-heir has earned it.

Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah said: Ibn al-Mubarak was asked about a man who wants to earn, and intends by his earning to maintain family ties, to strive in the way of God, and to do good deeds, and to enter the hazards of earning for this purpose. He said: If he has with him a sufficiency of livelihood sufficient to keep himself from people, then leaving this is better, because if he seeks what is lawful and spends in what is lawful, he will be questioned about it, about his earning, and about his spending. Leaving that is asceticism (zuhd), for asceticism is in abandoning what is lawful.

The third: Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: By this verse it is permissible for a father to eat from his son's earnings, because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Your children are of the good of your earnings, so eat from your children's wealth, wholesome and pleasant."

The fourth: His saying, exalted is He: "and of what We have produced for you from the earth." It means vegetation, minerals and buried treasure (al-rikāz). These are three categories that this verse encompasses. As for vegetation, al-Daraqutni related from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: The practice was established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "There is no zakat on what is less than five wasqs." A wasq is sixty ṣāʿs, so that is three hundred ṣāʿs of wheat, barley, dates and raisins. And there is no zakat on what the earth produces of vegetables.

Some people have argued, in support of Abu Hanifah, from God's saying: "and of what We have produced for you from the earth," that this is general in both the small and the large of what the earth produces and in all kinds, and they regarded the apparent meaning of the command as obligation. The explanation of this will come fully in [the commentary on] "al-An'am."[[See vol. 7, p. 47.]]

As for the mine (al-ma'dan), the imams related from Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he said: "The wound caused by a beast is unrecompensed (jubār), and the well is unrecompensed, and the mine is unrecompensed, and in buried treasure there is one-fifth." Our scholars said: When he (ﷺ) said "and in buried treasure there is one-fifth," it indicates that the ruling regarding mines is different from the ruling regarding buried treasure, because he (ﷺ) separated between the mines and buried treasure with the separating "and" (wa), and if the ruling concerning both were the same, he would have said "and the mine is unrecompensed, and in it there is one-fifth." When he said "and in buried treasure there is one-fifth," it is known that the ruling for buried treasure differs from the ruling for the mine regarding what is taken from it, and God knows best.[[Al-'ajmā': the beast. Jubār: wasted, unrecompensed. The ma'dan: a place in the earth from which come forth substances and metals such as gold, silver, iron, copper, lead, sulphur and others, from 'adana bi'l-makān, meaning to reside in a place. The meaning of the hadith is that if a beast gets loose and strikes a person or thing with its escape, its wound is unrecompensed; likewise an old well into which a person falls and dies, his blood is unrecompensed; and a mine that collapses on the one digging it and kills him, his blood is unrecompensed. See the lexicons and books of hadith.]]

The original meaning of rikāz in the language is what is embedded in the earth of gold, silver and jewels, and it is so according to the other jurists as well, for they say concerning the nadrah (a piece of gold or silver found in a mine) that is found embedded in the earth in a mine, which is not obtained by work, effort or toil, that there is one-fifth in it, because it is rikāz. It has been related from Malik that the nadrah in a mine has the ruling of what requires labour to extract from the mine, as with rikāz; but the first is the established position of his school, and on it is the fatwa of the majority of jurists.

Ruh (?) ibn Sa'id ibn Abi Sa'id al-Maqburi narrated from his father, from his grandfather, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about rikāz, and he said: "It is the gold that Allah created in the earth on the day He created the heavens and the earth." Abd Allah ibn Sa'id is this one, a matrūk al-ḥadīth (a narrator abandoned in hadith), as Ibn Abi Hatim mentioned. It has also been related by another route from Abu Hurayrah, but it is not authentic, as al-Daraqutni mentioned.

The hoards of the people of ignorance (jāhiliyyah) are also rikāz according to the majority of scholars, and they do not differ about this if their burial was before Islam and consisted of old (ʿādiyyah) wealth. As for what was minted in Islam, its ruling according to them is the ruling of the lost property (luqṭah).

The fifth: They differed about the ruling on rikāz when it is found. Malik said: What is found of the burial of the jāhiliyyah in the land of the Arabs, or in the open deserts of land that Muslims possess without war, belongs to the one who finds it, and in it is one-fifth. As for what is in the land of Islam, it is like lost property. He said: What is found of that in land conquered by force (ʿanwah) belongs to the group who conquered it, not to its finder; and what is found of that in land taken by treaty (ṣulḥ) belongs to the people of those lands, not the general people, and there is nothing for the finder in it, unless he is from the people of that dwelling, in which case it belongs to him rather than them. It was said: rather, it belongs to the totality of the people of the treaty.

Ismail said: Rikāz has been ruled by the ruling of booty (ghanīmah) only because it is the property of an unbeliever that a Muslim found, so he is placed in the position of one who fought him and took his property, and so he has four-fifths of it.

Ibn al-Qasim said: Malik used to say about goods, jewels, iron, lead and the like that are found as rikāz: there is one-fifth in it. Then he retracted and said: I do not see anything in it. Then the last thing he departed from us with was that he said: there is one-fifth in it. This is the sound position, due to the generality of the hadith, and it is the position of the majority of jurists.

Abu Hanifah and Muhammad said concerning rikāz found in a house: it belongs to the owner of the house, not the finder, and there is one-fifth in it. Abu Yusuf disagreed, saying: it belongs to the finder, not the owner of the house, and this is the position of al-Thawri. If it is found in the open wilderness (al-falāt), it belongs to the finder according to all of them, and there is one-fifth in it. There is no difference in their view between land taken by treaty and land conquered by force, and whether it is the land of the Arabs or others is the same for them. It is permissible for the finder, according to them, to keep the fifth for himself if he is needy, and he may give it to the poor.

Among the people of Medina and the companions of Malik were those who did not differentiate between any of that, and they said: whether the rikāz is found in land conquered by force, or in land taken by treaty, or in the land of the Arabs, or in the land of war, provided it does not belong to anyone and no one claims it, it belongs to its finder, and there is one-fifth in it, according to the general apparent meaning of the hadith. This is the position of al-Layth, 'Abd Allah ibn Nafi', al-Shafi'i and most of the people of knowledge.

The sixth: As for what is extracted from mines and comes out of them, it has been differed about. Malik and his companions said: there is nothing in what comes out of mines of gold or silver until it reaches twenty mithqāls of gold or five awqiyah of silver. When these two reach this amount, zakat becomes obligatory in them, and whatever exceeds it is by proportion so long as there is extraction (nayl) from the mine. If it stops and then another extraction comes afterward, zakat begins anew in it at that point. The rikāz according to them is like crops: zakat is taken from it at its time, and one does not wait a year for it.

Sahnun said concerning a man who has mines: he does not add what is in one of them to another, and he does not pay zakat except on two hundred dirhams or twenty dinars in each one. Muhammad ibn Maslamah said: he adds some of them to others and pays zakat on the whole, like crops.

Abu Hanifah and his companions said: the mine is like rikāz; whatever is found in a mine of gold or silver, after the fifth is removed, each of them is considered on its own. Whoever has in his hand what zakat is obligatory upon pays zakat on it when a full year has passed over it, if it is a nisab in his possession. This is when he has no gold or silver on which zakat is obligatory. If he has of that which zakat is obligatory upon, he adds it to that and pays zakat on it. Likewise, according to them, every profit that is added during the year to the nisab of its kind is paid as zakat at the year of the principal. This is the position of al-Thawri.

Al-Muzani related from al-Shafi'i, who said: As for what I am undecided about, it is what comes out of mines. Al-Muzani said: The more appropriate ruling according to his principle is that what comes out of the mine is a profit (fā'idah), and zakat is paid on it by its own year after its extraction.

Al-Layth ibn Sa'd said: what comes out of mines of gold and silver is in the position of a profit, and one begins a year anew with it. This is the position of al-Shafi'i in what al-Muzani derived from his school. Dawud and his companions also held this, when a year has passed over it, according to Malik, if ownership is sound, because of his (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever acquires wealth, there is no zakat upon him until a year passes over it." Al-Tirmidhi and al-Daraqutni related it.

They also argued by what 'Abd al-Rahman ibn An'um narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that the Prophet (ﷺ) gave to some of those whose hearts were to be reconciled (al-mu'allafah qulūbuhum) a little gold (dhuhaybah) in its earth, which 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, had sent from Yemen.[[It is the diminutive of dhahab, and the feminine ending was added to it because gold is feminine, and a triliteral feminine noun when made diminutive takes the ha' in its diminutive, like shamsiyyah. It was said: it is by intention a piece of it, so he made the diminutive of its wording.]] Al-Shafi'i said: The "mu'allafah qulūbuhum" have their share in zakat, so it became clear by this that the ruling on mines is the ruling of zakat.

The argument of Malik is a hadith from Rabi'ah ibn Abi 'Abd al-Rahman that the Prophet (ﷺ) granted Bilal ibn al-Harith the mines of al-Qabaliyyah,[[Al-Qabaliyyah (with a vowelled qaf and ba): attributed to Qabal, a place on the seashore five days from Medina. Al-Fur' (with damma and sukun): a village in the districts of al-Rabadhah, on the left of al-Suqya, between it and Medina eight post-stages on the Mecca road; it is also said four nights. It has a pulpit, palm trees and abundant water.]] which are from the region of al-Fur', and those mines are not taken from them until...

[The text ends here, mid-argument.]

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 267 (part 2 of 2):

...the zakat (obligatory almsgiving). This is a hadith whose isnad (chain of narration) is broken (munqati'), and the people of hadith do not use such a report as evidence. However, it is a practice (amal) that was followed among them in Madinah. al-Darawardi related it from Rabi'ah, from al-Harith ibn Bilal al-Muzani, from his father. al-Bazzar mentioned it. Kathir ibn Abdullah ibn Amr ibn Awf also related it from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he granted Bilal ibn al-Harith the mines of the Qabaliyyah, their high ground (jalsiyyuha) and their low ground (ghawriyyuha) [[al-Jals (with a fatha and then a sukun): every elevated part of the land. al-Ghawr: what lies low in it.]], and wherever it is suitable for cultivation from Quds [[al-Quds (with a damma on the qaf and a sukun on the dal): a well-known mountain. It is also said: it is the elevated place suitable for cultivation.]], and he did not give him the right of a Muslim. al-Bazzar also mentioned this, and Kathir is agreed upon as weak.

This is the ruling concerning what the earth produces. The ruling concerning what the sea produces will come in surah "al-Nahl", since it is the counterpart of the land [[See vol. 10, p. 85.]]. And the meaning of his (peace be upon him) saying "The wound of the animal is unrequited (jubar)" will come in "al-Anbiya'" [[See vol. 11, p. 315.]]. Each in its place, if Allah the Exalted wills.

The seventh matter: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not aim at the bad of it, to spend from it﴾. Tayammamu means taqsidu (intend, aim at). The evidence from the poetry of the Arabs that tayammum means qasd (intention) will come in "al-Nisa'" [[See vol. 5, p. 231.]], if Allah the Exalted wills. The verse indicates that earnings contain good and bad.

al-Nasa'i related from Abu Umamah ibn Sahl ibn Hunayf, concerning the verse in which Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And do not aim at the bad of it, to spend from it﴾, that he said: "It is al-Ju'rur and the dates of Lawn Hubayq" [[al-Ju'rur (with a damma on the jim, a sukun on the ayn, and a doubled ra'): a poor kind of date that bears small unripe dates with no good in them. Hubayq (with a damma on the ha' and a fatha on the ba'): a poor type of date, attributed to Ibn Hubayq, which is the name of a man.]], so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade that these two be taken in charity.

al-Daraqutni related from Abu Umamah ibn Sahl ibn Hunayf, from his father, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered a charity, and a man from this al-Suhhal [[al-Suhhal (with a damma on the sin, and a fatha on the ha' with a shaddah): dates that have not fully ripened and whose strength is not complete.]] came with bundles (kaba'is) of dates. Sufyan said: meaning the shis (inferior dates). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Who brought this?!" And whenever anyone brought something, it was attributed to the one who brought it. So the verse was revealed: ﴿And do not aim at the bad of it, to spend from it﴾. He said: The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade that al-Ju'rur and Lawn al-Hubayq be taken in charity. al-Zuhri said: they are two kinds of the dates of Madinah. al-Tirmidhi also related it from the hadith of al-Bara', and graded it sahih (sound), and it will come.

al-Tabari and al-Nahhas reported that in the recitation of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) it was "wa la ta'ammamu", and both are two dialects. Muslim ibn Jundub recited "wa la tuyammimu" with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the mim. Ibn Kathir recited "tayammamu" with a shaddah on the ta'. In the word there are several dialects, among them "ammamtu al-shay'" with a lightened first mim, and "ammamtuhu" with it doubled, and "yammamtuhu" and "tayammamtuhu". Abu Amr related that Ibn Mas'ud recited "wa la tu'ammimu" with a hamzah after the damma-marked ta'.

The eighth matter: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿to spend from it﴾. al-Jurjani said in his book "Nazm al-Quran": A group of people said: the speech is complete at His saying "the bad", then a new statement begins describing the bad, saying: "to spend from it", while you do not take it except when you overlook (ughmadtum), that is, you are lenient. It is as if this meaning is a reproach and a rebuke to the people. The pronoun in "minhu" refers to "al-khabith", which is the inferior and the poor. al-Jurjani said: Another group said: the speech is connected up to His saying "minhu", so the pronoun in "minhu" refers to "ma kasabtum", and "tunfiqun" comes as if it were in an accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), like your saying: "I go out fighting in the way of Allah."

The ninth matter: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And you would not take it except that you overlook in it﴾. That is: you would not take it in your debts and your rights from people, except that you are lenient in that and forgo some of your rights while disliking it and not being pleased with it. That is, do not do with Allah what you would not be pleased with for yourselves. This was said by al-Bara' ibn Azib, Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak. al-Hasan said: The meaning of the verse is: you would not take it even if you found it being sold in the market, unless its price were reduced for you. Something similar was related from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him). Ibn Atiyyah said: These two statements resemble the verse being about obligatory zakat. Ibn al-Arabi said: If it were about the obligation, He would not have said "and you would not take it", because the inferior and the defective may by no means be taken in an obligation, neither with leniency nor without it; it is taken only without leniency in the transfer. al-Bara' ibn Azib also said its meaning is: "and you would not take it" if it were given to you as a gift, "except that you overlook in it", that is, you are shy before the giver and accept from him what you have no need of and no value for in yourself. Ibn Atiyyah said: This resembles the verse being about voluntary charity. Ibn Zayd said: "And you would not take the forbidden except that you overlook its objectionable quality."

The tenth matter: His saying, the Exalted: (﴿except that you overlook in it﴾). This is the reading of the majority (al-Jumhur), from aghmada al-rajulu fi amrin kadha, when he is lenient in it, accepts part of his right and lets it pass. From this is the saying of al-Tirimmah:

*He did not get the better of us in vengeance, and to the humiliated are people who accept leniency (al-ighmad).*

It may be that it is derived either from closing the eye (taghmid al-ayn), because the one who wants to endure something disliked closes his eyes. He said:

*How many, and how many things from you trouble me? I overlook them, I am not blind to them.*

This is like turning a blind eye at what is disliked. al-Naqqash mentioned this meaning in this verse, and Makki pointed to it. Or it is derived from the saying of the Arabs: aghmada al-rajulu, when he came to a hidden matter, as you say: a'mana, that is, he came to Oman; and a'raqa, that is, he came to Iraq; and anjada and aghwara, that is, he came to Najd and al-Ghawr, which is Tihamah. That is, he seeks an interpretation for his taking it. Al-Zuhri read with a fatha on the ta' and a kasra on the mim, lightened, and also from him: "tughammidu" with a damma on the ta', a fatha on the ghayn, a kasra on the mim, and doubled. The first is in the sense of: you diminish its price from the seller, so he reduces it for you. The second, which is the reading of Qatadah as reported by al-Nahhas, means: you take it with a deficiency. Abu Amr al-Dani said: the meaning of the two readings of al-Zuhri is: until you take it with a deficiency. Makki related from al-Hasan "illa an tughammadu" with the mim doubled and fatha-marked. Qatadah also read "tughmadu" with a damma on the ta', a sukun on the ghayn, and a fatha on the mim, lightened. Abu Amr al-Dani said: its meaning is: except that it be overlooked for you, and al-Nahhas related this from Qatadah himself. Ibn Jinni said: its meaning is: you are found to have overlooked the matter by your interpretation or by your leniency, and you went along with what is not what first comes to the souls. This is like your saying: ahmadtu al-rajul (I found the man praiseworthy), that is, I found him praised, along with other examples. Ibn Atiyyah said: The reading of the majority is understood as forgiveness and as closing the eye, because aghmada is equivalent to ghammada, and also in the sense of: until you come upon a hidden matter of interpretation and consideration in taking it, either because it is forbidden according to the view of Ibn Zayd, or because it is a gift or something taken in religion according to the view of others.

al-Mahdawi said: As for the one who reads "tughmidu", the meaning is: you close the eyes of your insight from taking it. al-Jawhari said: I closed my eyes to so-and-so (ghammadtu 'an fulan) when I was lenient with him in a sale or purchase, and I overlooked (aghmadtu). Allah the Exalted said: "And you would not take it except that you overlook in it." It is said: "Overlook for me in what you sold me," as if you want an increase from him because of its inferiority, and a reduction of its price. And "an" is in an accusative position, and the estimate is: "except by overlooking."

The eleventh matter: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And know that Allah is Rich, Praiseworthy﴾. He, glorified and exalted, drew attention to the attribute of richness, that is: He has no need of your charities. So whoever draws near and seeks reward, let him do that with his wealth, which has value; otherwise it is a burden, for he is only advancing for his own self. And "Hamid" means praised in every state. We have covered the meanings of these two names in "al-Kitab al-Asna", and praise belongs to Allah. al-Zajjaj said concerning His saying: "And know that Allah is Rich, Praiseworthy": that is, He did not command you to give charity out of need, but He tested your affairs, and He is Praiseworthy for that, for all His blessings.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 268:

There are three issues here.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿The Shaytan (Satan)﴾. The meaning of shaytan and its derivation has already been discussed, so there is no point in repeating it [see the tenth issue, vol. 1, p. 90]. "Yaʿiduakum" (promises you) means yukhawwifukum (frightens you) "al-faqr" (poverty), i.e., with poverty, so that you do not spend. This verse is connected to what precedes it, and that Satan has a role in discouraging a person from spending in the way of God, while he also commands him to indecency (al-fahshaʾ), which is sins and spending on them. It has also been said: [that is], by telling you not to give charity, so that you disobey and sever ties. It is also read "al-futr" with a damma on the fa', and this is a dialect. Al-Jawhari said: "al-futr" is a dialect of "al-faqr," like "al-duʿf" and "al-daʿf" (weakness).

The second: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And God promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty﴾. In Arabic usage, when "waʿd" (promise) is used without qualification, it refers to good, but when the thing promised is specified, it may be understood as good or evil, as with "bishara" (glad tidings). This verse is one in which the promise is qualified by both meanings together. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "In this verse there are two [promises] from God, exalted is He, and two from Satan."

Al-Tirmidhi narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, Satan has a whisper (lamma) to the son of Adam, and the angel has a whisper. As for the whisper of Satan, it is a promise of evil and a denial of the truth; as for the whisper of the angel, it is a promise of good and an affirmation of the truth. Whoever finds that, let him know that it is from God, and whoever finds the other, let him seek refuge in God from Satan." Then he recited: ﴿Satan promises you poverty and commands you to indecency﴾. He said: "This is a hadith that is ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ" [as it stands in the originals; but what is in the Sunan of al-Tirmidhi is: "...ḥasan gharīb"].

[Footnote: "Lamma" (with a fatḥa on the lam): the thought or impulse that falls upon the heart. It means the angel or Satan's visitation to it and nearness to it; so whatever comes as an impulse toward good is from the angel, and whatever comes as an impulse of evil is from Satan. (From Ibn al-Athir's al-Nihaya.)]

In speech other than the Qur'an, it is permissible to say "wa-yaʾmurukum al-fahshaʾa" with the bāʾ omitted. Sibawayh cited the verse:

"I commanded you the good, so do what you were commanded,
For I have left you possessing wealth and property."

Forgiveness (maghfira) is God's concealing of His servants' faults in this world and the next, and bounty (fadl) is provision in this world, and expansion and delight in the next; God has promised both.

The third: Al-Naqqash mentioned that some people took comfort in this verse for the claim that poverty is better than wealth, because Satan only keeps the servant away from good, and by frightening him with poverty he keeps him away from it. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: There is no decisive proof in the verse; rather, the counter-argument from it is strong. It is also narrated that in the Torah: "My servant, spend from My provision, and I will extend My bounty over you, for My hand is outstretched over every outstretched hand." The Qur'an confirms this, in His saying: ﴿And whatever you spend, He will replace it, and He is the best of providers﴾ [see vol. 14, p. 307]. Ibn ʿAbbas mentioned this.

(﴿And God is All-Embracing, All-Knowing﴾) Its meaning has already been discussed [see the fifth issue, vol. 2, p. 84]. What is intended here is that He, glory be to Him, gives from abundance, and knows where to place that, and knows the unseen and the witnessed. These are two of His names, which we have mentioned among the names in the book "al-Kitab al-Asna," and praise be to God.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 269:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He gives wisdom to whomever He wills﴾, meaning: He gives it to whomever He wills of His servants. The scholars differed concerning the meaning of wisdom (al-hikmah) here. Al-Suddi said: it is prophethood. Ibn Abbas said: it is knowledge of the Qur'an, its jurisprudence (fiqh), its abrogating (nasikh) and abrogated (mansukh) verses, its clear (muhkam) and allegorical (mutashabih) verses, its rare expressions (gharib), and its earlier (muqaddam) and later (mu'akhkhar) parts. Qatadah and Mujahid said: wisdom is understanding (fiqh) of the Qur'an. Mujahid also said: correctness in speech and action. Ibn Zayd said: wisdom is intellect in religion. Malik ibn Anas said: wisdom is knowledge of the religion of Allah, understanding of it, and following it. Ibn al-Qasim related from him that he said: wisdom is reflection upon the command of Allah and following it. He also said: wisdom is obedience to Allah, understanding of the religion, and acting upon it. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: wisdom is fear (of Allah). Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: wisdom is comprehension of the Qur'an, and Zayd ibn Aslam said the same. Al-Hasan said: wisdom is scrupulousness (wara'). I say: all these sayings, apart from the sayings of al-Suddi, al-Rabi' and al-Hasan, are close to one another, because hikmah is a verbal noun from ihkam, which is perfection in speech or action. So everything that has been mentioned is a type of the wisdom which is the genus. The Book of Allah is wisdom, the Sunnah of His Prophet is wisdom, and everything mentioned of excellence is wisdom. The root meaning of hikmah is that by which one is restrained from foolishness (safah). Knowledge is therefore called hikmah, because one is restrained by it, and by it one knows restraint from foolishness, which is every ugly action. So too the Qur'an, intellect and understanding. In al-Bukhari: "Whomever Allah wills good for, He gives him understanding of the religion." Here He said: "Whoever is given wisdom has indeed been given much good." He repeated the mention of wisdom and did not use a pronoun for it, out of care for it and to draw attention to its nobility and excellence, as has been explained earlier at His saying: "But those who did wrong substituted a saying" [see the third issue, vol. 1, p. 416]. Abu Muhammad al-Darimi mentioned in his Musnad: Marwan ibn Muhammad related to us, Rifda al-Ghassani related to us, who said: Thabit ibn Ajlan al-Ansari informed us, who said: It used to be said: Indeed Allah intends punishment for the people of the earth, but when He hears a teacher teaching wisdom to children, He turns that away from them. Marwan said: by wisdom he means the Qur'an.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whoever is given wisdom has indeed been given much good. And none will be reminded except the people of understanding﴾. It is said: whoever is given wisdom and the Qur'an has been given the best of what was given to one who gathered the knowledge of the books of the former peoples, including the scrolls and others, because He said to them: "And you have been given of knowledge only a little" [see vol. 10, p. 323]. He called this "much good", because this is the comprehensive words (jawami' al-kalim). Some of the wise said: whoever is given knowledge and the Qur'an should make himself known (by it) and should not humble himself before the people of this world for the sake of their worldly life, for he has only been given the best of what the people of this world were given, since Allah, exalted is He, called this world "a little enjoyment" when He said: "Say: the enjoyment of this world is little" [see vol. 5, p. 281], and He called knowledge and the Qur'an "much good". The majority (al-Jumhur) read "wa-man yu'ta" with the verb in the passive. Al-Zuhri and Ya'qub read "wa-man yu'ti" with a kasrah on the ta', meaning: and whoever Allah gives wisdom, so the subject (al-fa'il) is the Name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. "Man" is the first object (maf'ul awwal), placed first, and "al-hikmah" is the second object (maf'ul thani). "Al-albab" means intellects; its singular is "lubb", and it has been discussed earlier [see the fourteenth issue, vol. 2, p. 412].

A conditional clause and its response. The vows (nudhur) were something the Arabs frequently made, so Allah mentioned both kinds: what a person does voluntarily (mutabarri'an), and what he does after binding it upon himself. The verse carries the sense of both promise and threat: whoever is sincere in intention will be rewarded, and whoever spends out of showing off (riya') or for some other purpose, such as that which brings him reminders of favour and harm (al-mann wa'l-adha) and the like, is a wrongdoer (zalim); his action goes to waste and he will find no helper in it. The meaning of "ya'lamuhu" is "yuhsihi" (He counts it), as said by Mujahid.

He used the singular pronoun although two things were mentioned. Al-Nahhas said: the estimated sense is (wa ma anfaqtum min nafaqatin) fa-inna Allaha ya'lamuha, (aw nadhartum min nadhrin fa-inna Allaha ya'lamuhu), and then he omitted [one of them]. It is also permissible that the estimate be: wa ma anfaqtum fa-inna Allaha ya'lamuhu, with the pronoun returning to "ma", as Sibawayh recited [from Imru' al-Qays [[The addition is in B.]]]:

Tawdih and al-Miqra'a have not had their traces effaced / by what the south and north winds have woven over them. [[Tawdih and al-Miqra'a are two places, and they are in apposition to "Hawmal" in the line before it.]]

And "aw nadhartum min nadhrin" would be coordinated with what precedes it. Ibn 'Atiyya said: He used the singular pronoun in "ya'lamuhu" although two things were mentioned, because He intended what was mentioned or the sense of it.

I say: this is good, for the pronoun may be intended to refer to all that has been mentioned, even if it is many.

The precise definition of the vow (nadhr) is: it is what a legally responsible person (mukallaf) makes obligatory upon himself of acts of worship, which would not have become binding upon him had he not made it obligatory. One says: "nadhara al-rajulu kadha" when he commits himself to doing it; the verb is yanduru (with the dhal vowelled with damma) and yandhiru (with it vowelled with kasra). It has rulings whose explanation will come in another place, God willing. [[See vol. 19, p. 125.]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 271 (part 1 of 2):

The majority of the exegetes (mufassirun) held that this verse concerns voluntary charity (sadaqat al-tatawwu'), because concealing it is better than displaying it. Likewise, in all acts of worship, concealment is better in their voluntary forms, since showing off (riya') is absent from them, whereas this is not the case with obligatory acts. Al-Hasan said: "Displaying the zakat is good, but concealing voluntary charity is better, for it is more indicative that it is intended for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, alone." Ibn 'Abbas said: "Allah made secret charity in the voluntary category surpass its public form by seventy times, and He made the public obligatory charity better than its secret form by twenty-five times." He said: "And likewise all obligatory and voluntary acts in all things." I say: Such a matter is not stated on the basis of opinion (ra'y); it is a matter of divine determination (tawqif). In the Sahih of Muslim, it is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The best prayer of a person in his house is other than the prescribed prayer (al-maktubah)." [[The wording in Muslim's Sahih is: "... for the best prayer of a person in his house is other than the prescribed prayer."]] The reason is that obligatory acts are not open to showing off, whereas voluntary acts are liable to it. Al-Nasa'i related from 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The one who recites the Qur'an aloud is like the one who gives charity openly, and the one who recites the Qur'an quietly is like the one who gives charity quietly." And in a hadith: "Secret charity extinguishes the anger of the Lord."

Ibn al-'Arabi said: "There is no authentic hadith for preferring public charity over secret charity, nor secret charity over public charity, but it is an established consensus (ijma'). As for voluntary charity, the Qur'an explicitly states that it is better in secret than in public. Nevertheless, our scholars said that this is the general (ghalib) meaning. The precise assessment is that the situation regarding charity differs according to the state of the giver, the recipient, and the people who witness it. As for the giver, there is for him in publicity the benefit of displaying the Sunnah and the reward of being an example. I say: This applies to one whose state is strong, whose intention is good, and who is safe from showing off regarding himself. As for one who is too weak for this level, secrecy is better for him. As for the recipient, secrecy is safer for him from people's contempt for him, or from their attributing to him that he took it while being wealthy and abandoned restraint (ta'affuf). As for the people, secrecy regarding them is better than publicity to them, because they may slander the giver with showing off and the taker with seeking charity while wealthy; and for them there is in publicity a stirring of hearts toward charity, but this is rare today."

Yazid ibn Abi Habib said: "This verse was revealed only concerning charity given to Jews and Christians, so he would order the zakat to be distributed in secret." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This is rejected, especially among the righteous predecessors (al-salaf al-salih). Al-Tabari said: 'The people have agreed that displaying the obligatory is better.'" I say: Al-Kiya al-Tabari mentioned that this verse indicates that concealing charities is preferable in every case, that they are the right of the poor, and that it is permissible for the owner of the wealth to distribute them himself, according to one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i. According to the other opinion, they said that what is meant by charities here is voluntary charity, not the obligatory, whose display is preferable so that the giver is not subject to suspicion. For this reason it has been said: voluntary prayer alone (furada) is better, while congregational prayer is for the obligatory, further from suspicion.

Al-Mahdawi said: "The verse refers to the obligatory zakat and what is given voluntarily. Concealment was better during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), but afterwards people's suspicions worsened, so the scholars regarded displaying the obligatory charities as good, lest anyone be suspected of withholding." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This view contradicts the reports, and in our time it may be good to conceal the obligatory charity, since withholding it has become widespread and giving it out openly has become liable to showing off."

Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: "It is possible that the verse refers to both obligatory charities, such as zakat, and voluntary ones, since it mentioned concealment and praised it, and mentioned displaying and praised it, so it may be directed to both together." Al-Naqqash said: "This verse was abrogated by the saying of the Exalted: 'Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly...' (2:274)."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿فَنِعِمَّا هِيَ﴾ ("how excellent it is") is praise for displaying the charity, then He judged that concealment is better than that. For this reason some of the wise said: "When you do a good deed, conceal it; and when a good deed is done to you, publicize it." Di'bil al-Khuza'i said:

"When they take revenge they announce their affair,
and when they bestow favour they bestow it with concealment."

Sahl ibn Harun said:

"A friend who, when you come to him one day seeking his help,
gives you what his hands possess and apologizes,
conceals his good deeds, and Allah makes them manifest;
indeed, the good deed, when you conceal it, becomes apparent."

Al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "A good deed is not complete except with three qualities: hastening it, minimizing it, and concealing it. When you hasten it, you make it pleasant; when you minimize it, you magnify it; and when you conceal it, you perfect it." And one of the poets said, excellently:

"Your good deed increases greatly in my estimation,
that it is hidden with you and considered small.
You forget it as though you had never done it,
while among people it is famous and great."

The readers differed concerning His saying "fa-ni'imma hiya." Abu 'Amr, Nafi' in the narration of Warsh, 'Asim in the narration of Hafs, and Ibn Kathir read "fa-ni'immā hiya" with a kasra on the nun and the 'ayn. Abu 'Amr also, and Nafi' in other than the narration of Warsh, and 'Asim in the narration of Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal read "fa-ni'mā" with a kasra on the nun and sukun on the 'ayn. Al-A'mash, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "fa-na'immā" with a fatha on the nun and a kasra on the 'ayn, and all of them made the mim sakin. Outside the Qur'an it is permissible to say "fa-ni'ma mā hiya." Al-Nahhas said: "But in the written text it is joined, so idgham (assimilation) is required." The grammarians related four dialects for "ni'ma": "na'ima al-rajulu Zayd" — this is the original. "Ni'ima al-rajulu" with a kasra on the nun because of the kasra on the 'ayn. "Na'ma al-rajulu" with a fatha on the nun and sukun on the 'ayn, the original being "na'ima," with the kasra removed because it is heavy. "Ni'ma al-rajulu," and this is the most eloquent of the dialects, its original being "na'ima." It is used for every praise, so it was lightened, the kasra of the 'ayn was transferred to the nun, and the 'ayn was made sakin. Whoever reads "fa-ni'immā hiya" has two interpretations: one, that he came with it according to the dialect of one who says "ni'ima"; the other, that it is according to the better dialect, the original being "ni'ma," then the 'ayn was given a kasra because of the meeting of two sakins. Al-Nahhas said: "As for what is related from Abu 'Amr and Nafi' concerning sukun of the 'ayn, it is impossible. It is related from Muhammad ibn Yazid that he said: 'As for sukun of the 'ayn with the mim doubled, no one can pronounce it; rather, one intends to join two sakins, and moves it without lingering.'" Abu 'Ali said: "Whoever reads with sukun on the 'ayn, his statement is not sound, because he joined two sakins, the first of which is not a letter of madd and lin. It is permitted among the grammarians only when the first is a letter of madd, since the madd becomes a substitute for the vowel, as in dabbah and dawall and the like. Perhaps Abu 'Amr concealed the vowel and reduced it, as in his taking the idgham in 'bari'ikum – wa-ya'murukum,' so the listener thought the concealment was sukun, owing to its subtlety in hearing and its obscurity." Abu 'Ali said: "As for whoever reads 'ni'immā' with a fatha on the nun and a kasra on the 'ayn, he has brought the word according to its original form, and from it is the poet's saying:

"My two feet have not carried, indeed they are
excellent the runners in the matter that is grave."

Abu 'Ali said: "The 'mā' in His saying 'fa-ni'immā' is in the position of an accusative, and His saying 'hiya' is an explanation of the implied subject mentioned before. The meaning is: 'How excellent a thing is its displaying'; the displaying is what is praised, except that the mudaf (the governed noun) was omitted and the mudaf ilayhi (the governing noun) was put in its place. What indicates this is His saying 'it is better for you' (fa-huwa khayrun lakum), i.e., concealment is better. Just as the pronoun here refers to concealment, not to the charities, so too, the subject is the displaying, which is what the pronoun is attached to; the displaying was omitted and the pronoun of the charities was put in its place likewise."

(wa-in tukhfuwha) is a conditional clause, therefore the nun was dropped.
(wa-tu'tuwha) is conjoined to it. And the response is (fa-huwa khayrun lakum).

(وَيُكَفِّرُ) The readers differed over its recitation. Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir and 'Asim (in the transmission of Abu Bakr), along with Qatadah and Ibn Abi Ishaq, read "wa-nukaffiru" with the nun and a raised ra' (nu­kaffiru, with damma). Nafi' [in the originals: al-A'mash, but the correct reading is what we have recorded, from al-Bahr, Ibn 'Atiyyah and others] and Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with the nun and a jazm (sukun) on the ra'; the same is also reported from 'Asim. Al-Husayn ibn 'Ali al-Ju'fi related from al-A'mash "yukaffira" with a fathah on the ra'. Ibn 'Amir read it with the ya' and a raised ra' (yukaffiru), and Hafs related it from 'Asim; likewise it is reported from al-Hasan, and it is also reported from him with the ya' and the jazm. Ibn 'Abbas read "wa-tukaffir" with the ta', a kasrah on the fa' and a jazm on the ra'. 'Ikrimah read "wa-tukaffar" with the ta', a fathah on the fa' and a jazm on the ra'. Al-Mahdawi reported from Ibn Hurmuz that he read "wa-tukaffiru" with the ta' and a raised ra'. It is related from 'Ikrimah and Shahr ibn Hawshab that both read with the ta' and a fathah on the ra'. So these are nine readings. The clearest of them is "wa-nukaffiru" with the nun and the raised ra'. This is the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh. Al-Nahhas said: Sibawayh said: "The raising here is the preferred form and it is the good one, because the clause after the fa' runs in the same manner as it does when it is not a conditional." He permitted the jazm by taking it as conveying the meaning: "If you conceal them and give them to the poor, it will be better for you, and We will remove (nukaffir) from you [some of your sins]." Abu Hatim said: al-A'mash read "yukaffiru" with the ya' without a waw before it. Al-Nahhas said: What Abu Hatim related from al-A'mash without a waw, with the jazm, is in the manner of a substitution (badal), as if it were in the position of the fa'. What is related from 'Asim, "wa-yukaffiru" with the ya' and the raising, means "and Allah will remove (yukaffiru Allah)"; this is the view of Abu 'Ubayd.
