Al-Naqqash related from Muqatil ibn Sulayman that he said: "in" in this verse means "idh" (when). Ibn ʿAtiyya said: this is rejected and not known in the language. Ibn Fawrak said: it is possible that by "O you who believe" is meant those before Muhammad ﷺ among the prophets, [and] "give up what remains of usury, if you are believers" in Muhammad ﷺ, since the former benefits only through this. This is rejected by what has been related concerning the occasion of the verse.

The thirty-first point: His saying, Exalted is He: (But if you do not do so, then be informed of war from God and His Messenger). This is a threat if they do not abandon usury, and war calls for killing. Ibn ʿAbbas related that it is said on the Day of Resurrection to the one who consumes usury: "Take your weapon for war." Ibn ʿAbbas also said: whoever persists in usury and does not desist from it, it is incumbent upon the imam of the Muslims to ask him to repent; if he desists, well and good, otherwise he strikes his neck. Qatada said: God threatened the people of usury with killing, making them "bahraj" (lawful prey) wherever they are "thuqifu" (found, seized). It was also said: the meaning is that if you do not desist, then you are war on God and His Messenger, that is, enemies. Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: if the people of a city agreed upon usury as lawful, they would be apostates, and the ruling concerning them is the ruling concerning the people of apostasy; and if it is not from them as lawful, it is permissible for the imam to fight them, do you not see that God, Exalted is He, has permitted this, saying: "then be informed of war from God and His Messenger." Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, read "fa-adhanu" (then announce), meaning: then inform others that you are at war with them.

The thirty-second point: Ibn Bukayr said: a man came to Malik ibn Anas and said: "O Abu ʿAbd Allah, I saw a drunk man staggering, wanting to seize the moon, and I said: my wife is divorced if anything enters the belly of the son of Adam that is worse than wine." He said: "Return until I consider your question." He came the next day, and he said: "Return until I consider your question." He came the next day and he said: "Your wife is divorced. I have examined the Book of God and the Sunna of His Prophet, and I have found nothing worse [in j, h and b: more severe] than usury, because God has permitted war against it."

The thirty-third point: This verse indicates that consuming usury and practising it is among the major sins, and there is no disagreement about this, as we shall explain. It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "There will come upon people a time when no one will remain who has not consumed usury, and whoever does not consume usury will be struck by its dust." Al-Daraqutni related from ʿAbd Allah ibn Hanzala [In al-Istiʿab it is stated that Hanzala al-Ghasil was killed as a martyr at the battle of Uhud, killed by Abu Sufyan. He had been with his wife at the time he went out to Uhud, then the urgency of going out to the fighting overtook him, so that it made him forget the ritual bath and hastened him from it. When he was killed as a martyr, the Messenger of God ﷺ informed that the angels had washed him.] "al-Ghasil al-Malaika" (the one washed by the angels), that the Prophet ﷺ said: "A single dirham of usury is more grievous in the sight of God, Exalted is He, than thirty-six acts of fornication." It is also related from him, peace be upon him, that he said: "Usury has ninety-nine gates, the lowest of which is like a man lying with his mother," meaning fornication with one's mother. Ibn Masʿud said: "The consumer of usury, its payer, its scribe and its witness are cursed upon the tongue of Muhammad ﷺ." Al-Bukhari related from Abu Juhayfa who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ forbade the price of blood [that is, the wage for its cupping, and it was called a price by way of figurative speech], the price of a dog, the earnings of a prostitute, and he cursed the consumer of usury, its payer, the tattooer and the one tattooed, and the image-maker. [We have relied on the hadith as in Sahih al-Bukhari; see al-ʿAsqalani, vol. 10, p. 220.] In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayra, that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Avoid the seven destructive sins..." — and among them — "and consuming usury." In the Musannaf of Abu Dawud, from Ibn Masʿud, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ cursed the consumer of usury, its payer, its scribe and its witness.

The thirty-fourth point: His saying, Exalted is He: "And if you repent, then you have your capital (principal)..." — the verse. Abu Dawud related from Sulayman ibn ʿAmr from his father, who said: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say during the Farewell Pilgrimage: "Verily every usury of the Jahiliyya is void. You have your capital: you do not wrong and you are not wronged," and he mentioned the hadith. So God, Exalted is He, returned them with repentance to their capital and said to them: "you do not wrong" by taking usury, "nor are you wronged" by having something of your capital held back so that your wealth is lost. It is possible that "you do not wrong" refers to delay, because the delay of the wealthy is injustice; so the meaning is that repayment occurs with the removal of usury, and this is the sunna of reconciliation, and this is the most similar thing to reconciliation. Do you not see that the Prophet ﷺ, when he indicated to Kaʿb ibn Malik regarding the debt of Ibn Abi Hadrad to waive half, Kaʿb said: "Yes," and the Messenger of God ﷺ said to the other: "Stand up and pay him." The scholars received his command to pay as a sunna in settlements. It will come in al-Nisa' [see vol. 5, pp. 405, 385] an explanation of reconciliation and what is permissible of it and what is not, God willing.

The thirty-fifth point: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you repent, then you have your capital﴾ is an emphasis on annulling what has not been received from it, and taking the principal in which there is no usury. Some scholars used this as evidence that whatever befalls a sale before possession, of what necessitates the prohibition of the contract, nullifies the contract, as when a Muslim buys game and then the buyer or the seller enters the state of ihram before possession, the sale is void, because there befell it before possession what necessitated the prohibition of the contract, just as God nullified what was not received, because there befell it what necessitated its prohibition before possession; and if it had been received it would have had no effect. This is the position of Abu Hanifa, and it is an opinion of the companions of al-Shafiʿi. It is also used as evidence that the destruction of the sold item before possession, in the hand of the seller, and the lapse of possession in it, necessitates the nullity of the contract, contrary to some of the early scholars; and this disagreement is related from Ahmad. This only holds according to the view of those who say that the contract in usury was originally concluded, and that it was only voided by the arising of Islam before [possession].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 275–279 (part 7 of 8):

...the taking (al-qabd). As for the one who denies that usury (riba) was valid in the first place, this statement is not correct. Usury was forbidden in the (earlier) religions, and what they did in the Jahiliyyah was the custom of the polytheists, and what they took from it was like wealth that came to them by usurpation [[In A: "by gift, so it is not addressed, and there is no sense in it; it is not addressed only because Islam wipes out what came before it." In J: "by plunder."]] and seizure, so it is not addressed. Accordingly, it is not valid to cite as evidence what they have mentioned of the issues. The inclusion of the prohibition of usury in the laws of the prophets before us is well known and mentioned in the Book of God, as is related about the Jews in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and their taking of usury, although they had been forbidden from it﴾ [[See J. 6, p. 12.]]. And it is mentioned in the story of Shu'ayb that his people objected to him and said: ﴿Does your prayer command you that we abandon what our fathers worshipped, or that we not do what we wish with our wealth?﴾ [[See J. 9, pp. 86 and 87.]] Accordingly, it is not sound to derive evidence from it. Yes, it is understood from this that contracts made in the territory of war, if the ruler (al-imam) gains control over them, are not to be challenged by annulment if they were concluded on a corrupt basis.

The thirty-sixth issue: Some of the extremists among the people of scrupulousness (wara') held that lawful wealth which has become mixed with unlawful wealth to the point that it cannot be distinguished, and then the quantity of the unlawful mixed into it is removed, does not become lawful and is not pure, because it is possible that what was removed was the lawful and what remained is the unlawful. Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is an extremism in religion. For everything that is not distinguished, what is intended from it is its monetary value, not its specific substance, and if it perishes, its equivalent takes its place. Mixing is a destruction of its distinguishability, just as ruin is a destruction of its substance, and the equivalent stands in place of what has gone. This is clear in sense and clear in meaning. And God knows best.

I say: Our scholars said that the path of repentance from the unlawful wealth in one's hand, if it is from usury, is that he returns it to the one from whom he took the excess, or to his heirs if he is not present. If he despairs of finding him, then he gives it in charity on his behalf. If he took it by wrongdoing, then he does the same regarding the one who wronged him. If the matter becomes confused for him and he does not know how much of what is in his hand is unlawful and how much is lawful, then he should estimate the amount in his hand that he must return, until he is certain that what remains has become purely his, and he returns from that which he removed from his hand to whoever is known among those who wronged him or took usury from him. If he despairs of finding him, he gives it in charity on his behalf. If the injustices encompass his liability and he knows that he owes from that what he can never fully pay because of its quantity, then his repentance is that he removes all that is in his hand, either to the poor or to what benefits the Muslims, until nothing remains in his hand except the least clothing that suffices him in prayer, which is what covers the 'awrah, from his navel to his knees, and the food of his day, because that is what he is entitled to take from the property of another if he is compelled to it, even if the one from whom he takes it dislikes that. Here the bankrupt (muflis) differs, according to the view of most scholars, because the wealth of people did not come to the bankrupt through aggression; rather, they are the ones who transferred it to him. So what covers him and what is the appearance of his clothing is left to him. Abu 'Ubayd and others hold that the bankrupt should not be left with clothing except the least that suffices him in prayer, which is what covers him from his navel to his knee, and then whenever anything comes into this man's hand he removes it from his hand and retains from it only what we have mentioned, until he and whoever knows his condition know that he has paid what is owed.

The thirty-seventh issue: This threat that God made concerning usury, of war, has been transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ in a similar form concerning mukhabara. Abu Dawud related, saying: Yahya ibn Ma'in informed us, saying: Ibn Raja' [[So in J and H, and it is correct as in the Sunan of Abu Dawud; in A, B, and J: Abu Raja'.]] informed us, saying: Ibn Khaythama told me, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: "Whoever does not abandon mukhabara, let him be warned of war from God and His Messenger." This is evidence for the prohibition of mukhabara, which is taking land for a half, a third, or a quarter (of its produce), and it is called muzara'a (sharecropping). All the companions of Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and their followers, and Dawud agreed that it is not permissible to give land for a third or a quarter, nor for a part of what it produces, because it is unknown. Except that al-Shafi'i and his companions and Abu Hanifa said that renting land for food is permissible if it is known, based on his peace be upon him saying: "As for something known and guaranteed, there is no harm in it," related by Muslim. This was also the view of Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Hakam. Malik and his companions prohibited it, based on what Muslim also related from Rafi' ibn Khadij, who said: We used to rent out land (yuhaqil) during the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ, renting it for a third, a quarter, and a stated amount of food. One day a man from my paternal uncles came to us and said: The Messenger of God ﷺ forbade us from a matter that was beneficial to us, and obedience to God and His Messenger is more beneficial to us. He forbade us to rent out land (nuhaqil) and to rent it for a third, a quarter, and a stated amount of food, and he commanded the owner of the land to cultivate it or have it cultivated [[So in A: this is what he forbade. What is in B, J, H, and Ḥ: "yuzri'uha aw yuzari'uha" (he cultivates it or has it cultivated). That is, he enabled another to cultivate it, and this is in the sense of the hadith: "Whoever has land, let him cultivate it or grant it to his brother."]]. And he disliked renting it and anything other than that. They said: It is not permissible to rent land for any food, whether edible or drinkable, in any case, because that is in the sense of selling food for food on credit. Likewise, in their view it is not permissible to rent land for anything that comes out of it, even if it is not edible or drinkable food, except wood, reeds, and firewood, because for them that is in the sense of muzabana [[Muzabana: every item of guesswork whose measure, weight, or count is not known, exchanged for something specified by measure, weight, or count. That is when a man says to another who has a heap of food whose measure is unknown, of wheat, dates, or the like, or who has a commodity of khabat, nawa, qadb, 'usfur, kirsuf, kattan, or the like whose measure, weight, or count is unknown, and the man says to the owner of that commodity: I will take all your commodity, or I will send someone to measure it, or weigh it, or count it, for so much; whatever falls short of such-and-such measure of sa' by a stipulation he stipulates, or such-and-such ratls by weight, or such-and-such count, what falls short will be on my liability, and I guarantee what falls short of that, on condition that what exceeds is mine. That is not a sale, but gambling, uncertainty, and chance, and this is included. It was also said: muzabana is the name for selling dates for dates by measure, and fresh of each kind for its dry, and unknown for known (from the Muwatta').]]. This is what is preserved from Malik and his companions. Ibn Sahnun related from al-Mughira ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Makhzumi al-Madani that he said: There is no harm in renting land for food that does not come out of it. Yahya ibn 'Umar related from al-Mughira that this is not permissible, like the view of all the other companions of Malik. Ibn Habib mentioned that Ibn Kinana used to say: Land is not rented for anything if vegetation is restored in it, and there is no harm in renting it for anything else of all things, whether edible or not, whether it comes out of it or not. Yahya ibn Yahya said the same and said it is from the view of Malik. He said: Ibn Nafi' used to say: There is no harm in renting land for any food or other things, whether it comes out of it or not, except wheat and its kind, for that is muhaqala [[Muhaqala: selling crops before their ripeness appears. It was also said: selling the crop in its ear for wheat. It was also said: muzara'a for a known share of a third, a quarter, or less or more than that. It was also said: renting land for wheat.]], which is what is forbidden. Malik said in the Muwatta': As for the one who gives his white (unplanted or barren) land for a third or a quarter of what it produces, that involves uncertainty, because the crop sometimes decreases and sometimes increases, and sometimes it perishes entirely, so the landowner has left a known rent. The likeness of that is the likeness of a man who hires a laborer for a journey for a known amount, then the one who hired him says to the laborer: Would you like me to give you a tenth of what I profit on my journey? This is not lawful and is not appropriate. Malik said: It is not appropriate for a man to hire himself, his land, his ship, or his animal except for a known thing that does not change. Al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa and their companions say the same. Ahmad ibn Hanbal, al-Layth, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, al-Hasan ibn Hayy, Abu Yusuf, and Muhammad said: There is no harm in a man giving his land for a portion of what it produces, such as a third or a quarter. This is also the view of Ibn 'Umar and Tawus. They argued from the story of Khaybar, that the Messenger of God ﷺ dealt with its people for a share of what their land and fruit trees produced. Ahmad said: The hadith of Rafi' ibn Khadij concerning the prohibition of renting farmland has unsettled wording and is not sound, and the view based on the story of Khaybar is better, and it is a sound hadith. A group of the Successors and those after them permitted a man to give his ship and his animal, just as he gives his land, for a portion of what God provides from working with them. They took as their basis for this the qiradh [[Qiradh (with a kasra on the qaf) according to the Malikis is what is called mudaraba among the Hanafis: giving the muqarid (the owner of the capital) to the muqarad (the worker) money to trade with, on condition that he has a known portion of the profit.]] upon which there is consensus, as will be explained in "al-Muzzammil," God willing, at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and others who travel through the land seeking of God's bounty﴾ [[See J. 19, p. 54.]]. Al-Shafi'i, regarding the saying of Ibn 'Umar, "We used to do mukhabara and saw no harm in it until Rafi' ibn Khadij informed us that the Messenger of God ﷺ forbade it," meant that they used to rent out land for part of what it produces. He said: In that there is an abrogation of the sunna of Khaybar. I say: What confirms al-Shafi'i's view on abrogation is what the Imams related, and the wording is that of al-Daraqutni, from Jabir, that the Prophet ﷺ forbade muhaqala, muzabana, muKhabara, and thunya, unless it is known. Sahih. Abu Dawud related from Zayd ibn Thabit, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ forbade muKhabara. I said: And what is muKhabara? He said: That you take the land for a half, or a third, or a quarter.

The thirty-eighth issue: Concerning the readings. The majority read "مَا بَقِيَ" with the yaʼ vowelled, and al-Hasan read it with sukun, and similar to it is the saying of Jarir:

He is the caliph, so be content with what he is content with for you,
one of firm resolve, in whose ruling there is no deviation.

And 'Umar ibn Abi Rabi'a said:

How often I have remembered you, were I rewarded for remembering you,
O you who most resemble all people in the moon!
Indeed I rejoice that I should be in the evening opposite him,
out of love to see the one whom you resemble in form.

The original is "مَا رَضِيَ" and "أَنْ أُمْسِيَ", and he made them sukun, and this is frequent in poetry. Its basis is that he likened the yaʼ to the alif: just as a vowel does not attach to the alif, so here it does not attach to the yaʼ. From this dialect come "uḥibbu an adʿūka" and "ashtahī an aqḍīka" [[In J: awsīka.]], with sukun on the waw and the yaʼ. And al-Hasan read "مَا بَقَى" with an alif, and this is the dialect of Tayy, who say for the girl: jārāh, and for the forelock: nāṣāh, and the poet said:

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 275–279 (part 8 of 8):

By your life, I do not fear poverty (tasa'luk) so long as there remains on earth a man of the Qays who drives camels.

Abu al-Sammal alone, among all the reciters, read "min al-Ribu" with a kasra on the doubled ra', a damma on the ba', and a sukun on the waw. Abu al-Fath Uthman ibn Jinni said: this reading is anomalous for two reasons: first, the movement goes from kasra to damma, and second, a waw falls after a damma at the end of the noun. Al-Mahdawi said: its explanation is that he emphasized the alif and inclined it toward the waw from which the alif derives, and it should not be understood otherwise, since there is no noun in the language ending in a sakin waw preceded by a damma. Al-Kisa'i and Hamza read "al-Riba" with imala because of the kasra on the ra'. The rest read it with tafkhim because of the fatha on the ba'.

Abu Bakr, from Asim and Hamza, read "fa-ädhinu" (fa-adhinu) in the sense of "fa-adhinu ghayrakum" (then notify others), omitting the object. The rest read "fa'dhanu" (fa'dhanu), meaning "be on knowledge (idhn)," from your saying: "I am upon knowledge (ilm)," which Abu Ubayd related from al-Asma'i. The lexicographers reported that one says: "adhintu bihi idhnan," meaning "I knew of it." Ibn Abbas and others among the exegetes said: the meaning of "fa'dhanu" is "then be certain of war from Allah, the Exalted," and it has the sense of idhn.

Abu Ali and others preferred the reading with the madd (fa'dhanu with lengthening), saying: when they are commanded to inform others who have not desisted from this, they will certainly know it themselves. He said: in informing them is their knowledge, but in their knowledge is not their informing others. Al-Tabari preferred the qasr reading (fa-adhinu without madd), because it is specific to them. On the reading with madd, they were commanded to inform others.

All the reciters read "la tazlimuna" with a fatha on the ta', and "wa-la tuzlamuna" with a damma on it. Al-Mufaddal related from Asim: "la tuzlamuna wa-la tazlimuna," with a damma on the ta' in the first and a fatha on it in the second, the reverse. Abu Ali said: the reading of the majority is preferred, because it accords with his saying "wa-in tubtum" in the attribution of both verbs to the subject; so "tazlimuna" with a fatha on the ta' fits better with what precedes it.

The verses (three verses) included the rulings on riba (usury) and the permissibility of contracts of exchange, and the threat against those who consider riba lawful and persist in practising it. On this there are thirty-eight issues.

The First: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who consume riba﴾. "Consume" means "take." He expressed taking by consuming, because taking is only intended for consumption. Riba in language means increase in general; one says "riba al-shay'" (the thing increased) when it grows, and from this is the hadith: "By Allah, we did not take a morsel but that it grew (rabā) beneath it," meaning the food over which the Prophet ﷺ had invoked blessing; Muslim, may Allah have mercy on him, transmitted the hadith. The analogy for writing it with a yā' (ربا) is the kasra at its beginning [meaning imalah], but they wrote it in the Qur'an with a wāw. Then the Shari'ah has restricted this general usage to some of its applications: at one time it applied it to unlawful earnings, as Allah the Exalted said about the Jews: ﴿and their taking of riba, though they had been forbidden from it﴾ [see vol. 6, pp. 182 and 236]. He did not mean by it the riba of the Shari'ah whose prohibition has been legislated for us; rather He meant unlawful wealth, as He the Exalted said: ﴿listeners to falsehood, devourers of unlawful gain (suht)﴾ [see vol. 6, pp. 182 and 236], meaning by it unlawful wealth from bribery, and what they considered lawful from the wealth of the unlettered, when they said: ﴿there is no blame on us regarding the unlettered﴾ [see vol. 4, p. 115]. On this basis, the prohibition includes every unlawful wealth, by whatever means it was acquired. The riba which is recognized in the terminology of the Shari'ah is of two kinds: the prohibition of delayed exchange (nasa'), and excess in contracts [in the manuscripts: "al-nuqud" (money)] and in foodstuffs, as we will explain. Most of it was what the Arabs used to do, such as saying to the debtor: "Will you pay, or will you increase (turbi)?" So the debtor would increase the amount and the creditor would be patient with him. All of this is prohibited by the consensus of the Muslim community.

The Second: Most of the prohibited sales are prohibited because of an element of increase, either in the subject of the sale itself or in a benefit for one of the two parties, such as delay and the like. Among sales there are some in which there is no element of increase, such as selling fruit before it has ripened, and selling at the time of the call to prayer on Friday. If someone calls its doer "a consumer of riba," that is figurative usage and a comparison.

The Third: The imams transmitted, and the wording is Muslim's, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Gold for gold, silver for silver, wheat for wheat, barley for barley, dates for dates, and salt for salt, like for like, hand to hand; whoever gives more or asks for more has committed riba; the taker and the giver in it are equal."

"And in the hadith of ʿUbadah ibn al-Samit: "When these kinds differ, sell as you wish, provided it is hand to hand." Abu Dawud related from ʿUbadah ibn al-Samit that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Gold for gold, raw and minted, silver for silver, raw and minted, wheat for wheat, mudy for mudy [[That is, a measure for a measure. The mudy (with a damma on the mim, sukun on the dal, and a yaʾ) — Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: it is a large measure used by the people of Syria and Egypt, its plural being amdaʾ. Ibn Barri said: al-mudy is a measure used by the people of Syria, called al-jarib, which holds forty-five ratl. It is other than the mudd (with a damma on the mim and a shaddah on the yaʾ). Al-Jawhari said: the mudd is a measure, and it is a ratl and a third according to the people of the Hijaz and al-Shafiʿi, and two ratl according to the people of Iraq and Abu Hanifa.]], barley for barley, mudy for mudy, dates for dates, mudy for mudy, salt for salt, mudy for mudy. Whoever gives more or takes more has engaged in riba. There is no harm in selling gold for silver, with silver being the greater of the two, hand to hand, but as for deferred, no. And there is no harm in selling wheat for barley, with barley being the greater of the two, hand to hand, but as for deferred, no."

The scholars have unanimously agreed to act according to the requirement of this Sunnah, and the body of jurists of the Muslims holds to it, except regarding wheat and barley: Malik made them one kind, so two of them may not be exchanged for one, and this is the view of al-Layth, al-Awzaʿi, and the majority of the scholars of Madinah and Syria. Malik added to them al-sult [[Al-sult: a type of barley that has no husk.]]. Al-Layth said: al-sult, al-dukhn and al-dhurah are one kind, and Ibn Wahb said the same. I say: once the Sunnah is established, no opinion stands against it. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "When these kinds differ, sell as you wish, provided it is hand to hand." His saying: "Wheat for wheat and barley for barley" is evidence that they are two different kinds, like the difference between wheat and dates, and because their characteristics differ and their names differ; there is no consideration of the place of growth or harvest when the Law has not considered it, rather it has specified and clarified. This is the view of al-Shafiʿi, Abu Hanifa, al-Thawri, and the people of hadith.

The fourth issue: Muʿawiyah ibn Abi Sufyan used to hold that the prohibition and the ban came from the Prophet (ﷺ) only regarding the minted dinar and the minted dirham, not regarding raw gold and silver exchanged for minted, nor regarding worked (manufactured) items exchanged for minted. It has been said that this was from him only regarding worked items, until there occurred with ʿUbadah what Muslim and others narrated. He said: We went on a campaign, and Muʿawiyah was over the people, and we gained many spoils, among what we gained were silver vessels. Muʿawiyah ordered a man to sell them in the people's stipends, and the people disputed about that. The matter reached ʿUbadah ibn al-Samit, so he stood and said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbid the sale of gold for gold, silver for silver, wheat for wheat, barley for barley, dates for dates, and salt for salt, except equal for equal, like for like, hand to hand; whoever gives more or takes more has engaged in riba." So the people returned what they had taken. The matter reached Muʿawiyah, so he stood to deliver a sermon and said: "Behold, what is wrong with men who narrate from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) hadiths that we were present for and accompanied him, yet we did not hear them from him!" Then ʿUbadah ibn al-Samit stood and repeated the story, then said: "We will certainly narrate what we heard from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), even if Muʿawiyah dislikes it" — or he said "even if it displeases" — "and I do not care that I do not accompany him in his army on a black night." Hammad [[He is Hammad ibn Zayd, one of the narrators of this hadith.]] said: "This, or something similar."

Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: It has been related that this incident was actually between Abu al-Darda and Muʿawiyah. It is possible that it occurred to both of them with him, but the hadith is well known as preserved from ʿUbadah, and it is the foundational principle upon which the scholars relied in the chapter on riba. There is no disagreement that Muʿawiyah's action in this was not permissible. It is not a reprehensible matter that Muʿawiyah was unaware of what Abu al-Darda and ʿUbadah knew, for they were both eminent among the jurists and senior companions, and what was hidden from Abu Bakr and ʿUmar was found with others who were below them, so Muʿawiyah is more excusable. It is possible that his view was like the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, for he was an ocean of knowledge and did not see a dirham for two dirhams as harmful until Abu Saʿid turned him away from that. The incident of Muʿawiyah with ʿUbadah was during the governorship of ʿUmar. Qabisah ibn Dhuwayb said: ʿUbadah objected to something of Muʿawiyah's and said: "I will not live with you in a land where you are." And he entered Madinah. ʿUmar said to him: "What brought you?" So he informed him. He said: "Return to your place. May Allah disfigure a land in which you are not, nor those like you!" And he wrote to Muʿawiyah: "You have no authority over him."

The fifth issue: The imams related — and the wording is that of al-Daraqutni — from ʿAli (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Dinar for dinar and dirham for dirham, with no excess between them. Whoever needs silver should exchange it for gold, and whoever needs gold should exchange it for silver, hand to hand" [[Ibn al-Athir said: "It means that each of the two parties says 'ha' and gives what is in his hand, meaning exchange in the session. It was said its meaning is 'take and give' (hak and hat), i.e., take and give." Al-Khattabi said: "The people of hadith pronounce it 'ha wa ha' with the alif quiescent, but the correct form is to elongate it and vowel it, since its origin is hak, meaning take; the kaf was dropped and compensated by the elongation and the hamzah. For one it is said haʾ, for two haʾuma, and for many haʾum. Other than al-Khattabi permits quiescence in it, dropping the compensation and treating it like the 'ha' used for alerting. There are other dialectal forms."]]. The scholars said: his saying (peace be upon him): "Dinar for dinar and dirham for dirham, with no excess between them" points to the kind of the minted original, as evidenced by his saying: "Silver for silver and gold for gold," the hadith. White silver and black silver, and red gold and yellow gold, all of this, it is not permissible to sell some of it for some except like for like, equal for equal, in every case; on this is the body of the scholars, as we have explained. The transmission from Malik differed regarding fulus (copper coins): he attached them to dirhams insofar as they served as a price for things, and at another time he refused to attach them, insofar as they are not a price in every land, but rather a particular land specializes in them over another.

The sixth issue: No consideration is given to what has been related from many of Malik's companions, and some of them transmit it from Malik, concerning the merchant who is urged by the need to depart and has a need for minted dirhams or minted dinars, so he comes to the mint with his silver or gold and says to the minter: "Take this silver of mine or this gold of mine, and take the amount of your labor, and give me minted dinars in exchange for my gold or minted dirhams in exchange for this silver of mine, because I am urged to depart and I fear that I will miss those I am to go with." That this is permissible out of necessity, and that some people have acted on it. Ibn al-ʿArabi related it in his Qabas from Malik, regarding someone other than a merchant, and that Malik was lenient in that. So in form he has sold his silver, whose weight is one hundred and five dirhams, for one hundred [plus] his wage, and this is pure riba. What made its permissibility obligatory is that if he had said to him: "Mint this for me," and contracted with him for a wage on that, then when he minted it, he received it from him and gave him his wage, then what Malik did first is what would be the outcome. Malik only looked at the money and applied to it the ruling of the transaction, while the rest of the jurists rejected it. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: The proof for Malik in it is clear. Abu ʿUmar, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is the very riba which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade by his saying: "Whoever gives more or takes more has engaged in riba." Ibn Wahb rejected this issue against Malik and denied it. Al-Abhari claimed that this is from the category of leniency for the pursuit of trade and so that the market does not pass by, and that riba applies only to one who intends to make profit from someone who aims at that and seeks it. Al-Abhari forgot his principle regarding blocking the means, and his statement regarding one who sold a garment on credit, having no intention of buying it, then finds it being sold in the market: that it is not permissible for him to buy it from him for less than what he sold it for, even if he did not intend that and did not seek it, and there are many like this. If riba applied only to one who intended it, it would not have been forbidden except to jurists. ʿUmar said: "None trades in our market except one who has understanding, or else he eats riba." This is clear to one who has been granted fairness and inspired with right guidance.

I say: Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, went to great lengths in prohibiting excess, to the point that he treated the presumed as the actual, so he forbade a dinar and a dirham for a dinar and a dirham, as a blocking of the means and a cutting off of suspicions, since were it not for the suspicion of excess they would not have exchanged. The prohibition of that has been explained by the difficulty of equality at the time of distribution, for it would lead to gold and silver for gold. More evident than this is his prohibition of nominal excess: he forbade a dinar of superior gold and a dinar of inferior gold in exchange for the superior, and disregarded the inferior, and this is from his subtle insight, may Allah have mercy on him. This shows that that narration from him is rejected and is not authentic. And Allah knows best.

The seventh issue: Al-Khattabi said: al-tibr is pieces of gold and silver before they are struck and stamped as dirhams or dinars, its singular being tibrah. And al-ʿayn is the minted dirham or dinar. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade selling a mithqal of minted gold for a mithqal and a portion of unminted raw gold. Likewise he forbade the disparity between minted silver and unminted silver, and this is the meaning of his saying: "Its raw and its minted are equal."

The eighth issue: The scholars have unanimously agreed that dates for dates is permissible only like for like. They differed regarding exchanging one date for two dates, and one grain of wheat for two grains: al-Shafiʿi, Ahmad, Ishaq, and al-Thawri prohibited it, and it is the analogy of Malik's view, and it is the correct view, because what riba applies to by excess in its quantity, its small amount also falls under it by analogy and reasoning. Those who permitted that argued that one who consumes one date or two dates is not obligated to pay its value, he said: because it is neither measured nor weighed, so excess in it is permissible.

The ninth issue: Know, may Allah have mercy on you, that the issues of this chapter are many and its branches are widespread, and what ties all of that together for you is that you look at what each of the scholars considered as the effective cause (ʿillah) of riba. Abu Hanifa said: its cause is being a measured or weighed commodity of the same kind; so whatever is subject to measure or weight in his view, of one kind, then selling some of it for some in excess or—

NASIY'AN lā yajūz, so he forbade selling dust for dust of the same kind in unequal amounts, because it is subject to measure (kayl). He permitted selling one loaf of bread for two loaves, because in his view it is not subject to measure, which is its essential characteristic; thus it has left the category of goods subject to riba for what lies beyond it. Al-Shafi'i said: the effective cause ('illa) is that it is a foodstuff (matcum) of a single genus. This is his view in al-Jadid (his later doctrine), so according to him it is not permissible to sell flour for bread, nor bread for bread in unequal amounts, nor on credit, whether the bread is leavened or unleavened. It is also not permissible, according to him, to sell one egg for two eggs, one pomegranate for two pomegranates, or one watermelon for two watermelons, whether hand to hand or on credit, because all of that is edible food. In al-Qadim (his earlier doctrine) he said: the cause is that it is measured (makil) or weighed (mawzun). The expressions of our Maliki colleagues differed on this, and the best formulation is that it is a staple food, stored for sustenance, generally of a single genus, such as wheat, barley, dates and salt, which were specified in the hadith, and what is in their meaning, such as rice, maize, millet and sesame, and legumes such as broad beans, lentils, lupin and chickpeas. Likewise meats, milk products, vinegars and oils; fruits such as grapes, raisins and olives; and figs, about which there is disagreement. Honey and sugar are attached to these. All of this is subject to riba because of deferment (nasa'). Unequal exchange is permissible in it, based on the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "When these kinds differ, sell as you wish provided it is hand to hand." There is no riba in fresh fruits that do not keep, such as apples, watermelons, pomegranates, pears, cucumbers, melons, aubergines and other vegetables. Malik said: it is not permissible to sell eggs for eggs in unequal amounts, because they are stored, though it is permissible in his view equal for equal. Muhammad ibn 'Abdullah ibn 'Abd al-Hakam said: it is permissible to sell one egg for two eggs or more, because they are not stored; this is the view of al-Awza'i.

The tenth issue: the grammarians differed about the word "riba". The Basrans said it is from the "waw" roots, because you say its dual is ribawan, as Sibawayh stated. The Kufans said it is written with a "ya", and its dual is with a "ya", because of the kasra at its beginning. Al-Zajjaj said: I have never seen a mistake more ugly or more shameful than this! They are not content with the error in writing until they err in the dual, while they recite: "And what you give as riba that it may increase within the wealth of people" (30:39) [see vol. 14, p. 36]. Muhammad ibn Yazid said: "riba" was written in the Mushaf with a "waw" to distinguish it from "zina", and riba was more fitting with a "waw", because it derives from rabá yarbú.

The eleventh issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who consume riba will not stand except as one stands who is being beaten by Satan into insanity﴾. The clause is the predicate of the subject, which is "alladhina". The meaning is: from their graves. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, Qatada, al-Rabi', al-Dahhak, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. Some of them said: a devil is made to accompany him and choke him. All of them said: he is raised like a madman, as punishment for him and as a mark of shame before all the people of the gathering. What strengthens this interpretation, on which there is consensus, is that in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "They will not stand on the Day of Resurrection except as one stands." Ibn 'Atiyya said: The wording of the verse could allow a comparison of the state of one who stands with greed and avarice for worldly trade with the standing of a madman, because desire and longing agitate him until his limbs tremble, as you say of someone hurrying in his walk who stumbles in the form of his movements, whether from fright or otherwise: "This one has gone mad!" Al-A'sha compared his camel in its vigour to madness, in his saying:

"In the morning after the weariness of travel, as though a madness from the jinn's haunt had struck her."

Another said:

"By your life, I am mad with love for Asma'."

However, what the reading of Ibn Mas'ud brings, and what the statements of the exegetes agree upon, weakens this interpretation. "Yatakhabbatuhu" is yatafa'aluhu from khabata yakhbitu, as you say: tamallakahu and ta'abbadahu. God made this sign for the consumers of riba, because He made it swell in their bellies and so weighed them down; when they rise from their graves they stand and fall. It is said that on the Day of Resurrection they will be raised with their bellies swollen like pregnant women, and whenever they stand they fall, while people walk over them. Some scholars said: this is only a mark for them by which they are recognised on the Day of Resurrection, and the punishment comes after that, just as the one who embezzled (ghall) will come with what he embezzled on the Day of Resurrection, with a notoriety by which he is made known, and then the punishment follows. He said, exalted is He: "They consume" and what is meant is that they earn riba and practise it. The consumption is specifically mentioned because it is the strongest aim of a person regarding wealth, and because it indicates greed, which is the most intense covetousness. It is said: a man is jash, clearly greedy, and people are jashun, as stated in al-Mujmal. Thus this part of the means of earning is put in the place of all earning: clothing, housing, saving and spending on dependants are included in His saying: "those who consume."

The twelfth issue: In this verse there is evidence for the corruption of the view of those who deny that possession (sar') is caused by jinn, and who claim that it is from the nature of the bodily humours, and that Satan does not enter a person and there is no touch (mass) from him. The refutation of them has already passed earlier in this book. Al-Nasa'i related from Abu al-Yasar, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to supplicate, saying: "O God, I seek refuge in You from falling from a height, from collapse, from drowning and from burning, and I seek refuge in You from Satan striking me at the time of death, and I seek refuge in You from dying in Your way while turning back, and I seek refuge in You from dying by a snake bite." And it was narrated from the hadith of Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna: Abu Dawud told us, Hammam told us, from Qatada, from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he used to say: "O God, I seek refuge in You from madness, leprosy, vitiligo and evil diseases." Al-mass means madness; it is said: the man was musst and ul'is, so he is mamsus and ma'lus if he is mad. That is the sign of riba in the Hereafter. It was related in the hadith of the Night Journey: "Gabriel took me, and I passed by many men, each of whom had a belly like a huge house, standing on the path of the people of Pharaoh, and the people of Pharaoh are displayed before the Fire morning and evening, so they come like thirsty camels afflicted with haymah [al-muhayyam: a disease afflicting camels from water they drink standing stagnant, so they wander the earth and do not graze; it is said: a disease that makes them thirsty so they cannot be quenched; it is said: a disease from intense thirst], they trample stones and trees, not hearing nor understanding. When the people of those bellies perceive them, they rise, and their bellies make them lean over, so they fall. Then one of them rises, his belly makes him lean, and he falls, and they cannot move at all until the people of Pharaoh overtake them, trampling them coming and going. That is their punishment in the barzakh between this world and the Hereafter. The people of Pharaoh say: O God, do not establish the Hour ever, for God, exalted is He, says: 'And on the day the Hour is established: Admit the people of Pharaoh to the severest punishment' [see vol. 15, p. 318]." I said: "O Gabriel, who are these?" He said: "These are those who consume riba, who will not stand except as one stands who is being beaten by Satan into insanity." Al-mass is madness, and likewise al-ulq, al-als and al-rawd [as in the originals and in Ibn 'Atiyya, who did not change it, and there is no way to explain it except what was reported: "Satan seeks the son of Adam with every ridah", i.e., with every aim and desire; al-ridah is a noun from al-iradah. (Al-Nihaya)].

The thirteenth issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is because they said: "Trade is only like riba."﴾ Its meaning, according to all the commentators, concerns the disbelievers, and about them it was said: "Then what has passed is for him." That is not said of a believing sinner; rather his sale is annulled and his act rejected even if he was ignorant, and for this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever does an action which is not according to our command, it is rejected." But sinners in riba may take a portion of the threat in this verse.

The fourteenth issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Trade is only like riba﴾, meaning that the increase at the due date, at the end, is like the principal price at the beginning of the contract. The Arabs did not know riba except this. So when their debt fell due, they would say to the debtor: "Either you pay or you increase it," that is, add to the debt. God, glory be to Him, forbade this and answered their statement with His true word: "God has permitted trade and forbidden riba." He made clear that if the term came due and he did not have what he could pay, he should be given time until a time of ease. This riba is what the Prophet (ﷺ) abrogated by his saying on the Day of 'Arafah, when he said: "Indeed every riba is abolished, and the first riba I abolish is our riba, the riba of 'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, for it is entirely abolished." He began with his paternal uncle and the person closest to him. This is one of the ways of justice for the leader: to bestow justice first upon himself and his close circle, so that it then spreads among the people.

The fifteenth issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿God has permitted trade and forbidden riba﴾. This is from the general wording of the Qur'an, and the "al" is for the genus, not for specific reference, since no previously mentioned trade is being referred to, as He said: "By time, indeed mankind is in loss, except those who believe and do righteous deeds" [see vol. 20, p. 178]. Once it is established that trade is general, it is specified by what we have mentioned of riba and other things forbidden and whose contract is prohibited, such as wine, carrion, and the sale of the unborn young of the unborn young (habal al-habala) [al-habl (with vowelling) is a verbal noun used for what is carried, as "hamal" is; the feminine ta' was added to indicate the female sense in it. The first habl refers to what is in the wombs of she-camels of pregnancy, and the second habl to what is in the wombs of she-camels. He forbade it for two reasons: first, that it is gharar, the sale of something not yet created, namely selling what the foetus in the she-camel's belly will bear on the assumption that it will be female, which is a sale of the offspring of the offspring. It was also said that by habl al-habala he meant selling it on a term at which the pregnancy in the she-camel's belly would deliver, which is an unknown term and not valid (from Ibn al-Athir's Nihaya)], and other things that are established in the Sunnah and the consensus of the community as prohibited. Its parallel is: "Then kill the polytheists" [see vol. 8, p. 71], and all the other apparent texts that imply generality and into which specification may enter. This is the position of most jurists. Some of them said: it is the mujmal (general, unspecified) of the Qur'an, which was explained as permitting certain trade and forbidding other trade. So it cannot be used to permit or forbid trade unless it is accompanied by a clarification from the Sunnah of the Messenger (ﷺ), although it indicates the permissibility of sales in general without detail. This is the difference between the general ('amm) and the unspecified (mujmal).

The general wording indicates the permissibility of sales in principle, and the details stand unless they are specified by evidence. An unspecified (mujmal) text does not establish the permissibility of a particular sale in its details until it is accompanied by a clarification (bayan). The first view is more sound, and God knows best.

**The Sixteenth Issue:** *Bay'* (sale) linguistically is the verbal noun of *bā'a kadhā bi-kadhā*, meaning he gave a compensation and took a counter-value. It requires a seller (*bā'i'*), who is the owner or one who stands in his place; a buyer (*mubtā'*), who offers the price (*thaman*); and a sold item (*mabī'*), which is the priced good (*muthmūn*), the thing for which the price is offered. Accordingly, the pillars (*arkān*) of sale are four: the seller, the buyer, the price, and the priced item. Further, among the Arabs, exchange (*mu'āwaḍah*) varies according to what it is attached to. If one of the two counter-values is in exchange for a physical thing (*raqabah*), it is called a sale (*bay'*). If it is in exchange for the usufruct of a thing, then if the usufruct is of a *bud'* (a woman's body), it is called marriage (*nikāh*); if the usufruct is of something other than that, it is called hire (*ijārah*). If it is currency for currency, it is the sale of money, which is *ṣarf* (currency exchange). If it is for a deferred debt, it is *salam* (forward sale), and its explanation will come in the verse on debt [[See p. 376 of this part.]]. The ruling on *ṣarf* has already passed, the ruling on hire will come in *al-Qaṣaṣ* [[See vol. 13, p. 72 onward.]], and the ruling on the bridal gift (*mahr*) in marriage will come in *al-Nisā'* [[See vol. 5, p. 23 and p. 99.]]. Each will be in its place, God willing.

**The Seventeenth Issue:** Sale is an offer and acceptance (*qabūl wa-ījāb*) that occurs by the present or past tense. The past tense in it is literal (*ḥaqīqah*), and the present tense is allusive (*kināyah*). It takes place by explicit wording (*ṣarīḥ*) and by allusive wording from which the transfer of ownership is understood. So whether he says, "I sold you this item for ten," and he replies, "I bought it," or the buyer says, "I bought it," and the seller says, "I sold it to you," or the seller says, "I will sell it to you for ten," and the buyer says, "I will buy," or "I have bought," it is the same. Likewise, if he says, "Take it for ten," or "I gave it to you," or "Take it," or "May it be blessed for you for ten," or "I handed it over to you," while both intend sale, all of that is a binding sale. If the seller says, "I sold you for ten," and then retracts before the buyer accepts, then he said [[His words "then he said" mean Malik, as will come in his words: "the transmission from him has differed," etc.]]: he has no right to retract until he hears the buyer's acceptance or rejection, because he has offered that from himself and made it obligatory upon him, and it was said to him for that reason, since the contract has not been completed through it. If the seller says, "I was joking," the transmission from him has differed. Once he said that the sale is binding and his statement is not to be considered, and once he said that the value of the goods is to be examined. If the price resembles its value, the sale is binding. If it is disproportionate, like a slave for a dirham or a house for a dinar, it is known that he did not intend sale by it, and he was only jesting, so it is not binding upon him.

**The Eighteenth Issue:** His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah has forbidden riba﴾. The definite article here is for a known reference (*'ahd*), which is what the Arabs used to practice, as we have explained. Then it extends to what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade and prohibited from sale that involves *ribā* and what is similar in meaning to it among the prohibited sales.

**The Nineteenth Issue:** A contract of *ribā* is void and is never permissible under any circumstance, due to what the imams narrated, with the wording being Muslim's, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: Bilal came with *barnī* dates [[*Barnī* (with a fatha on the *bā'*, sukun on the *rā'*, and a shaddah on the final *yā'*): a kind of date that is reddish with yellowness, having thick skin (the covering of the pit), and sweet in taste.]]. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him, "From where is this?" Bilal said, "From dates we had that were inferior, so I sold two *ṣā'* of them for one *ṣā'* for the food of the Prophet ﷺ." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ then said: "Oh! That is the very *ribā*! Do not do that. But when you want to buy dates, sell them in another sale and then buy with it." In another narration: "This is *ribā*, so return it, then sell our dates and buy for us from this." Our scholars said: his statement "Oh! That is the very *ribā*" means it is the forbidden *ribā* itself, not something resembling it. His statement "return it" indicates the obligation to annul the transaction of *ribā* and that it is not valid in any way. This is the view of the majority, in contrast to Abu Hanifa, who says that the sale of *ribā* is permissible in its essence insofar as it is a sale, and prohibited in its attribute insofar as it is *ribā*, so the *ribā* is dropped and the sale is valid. If it were as he claims, the Prophet ﷺ would not have annulled this transaction, and he would have ordered him to return the excess over the *ṣā'*, and he would have validated the transaction in exchange for the *ṣā'*.

**The Twentieth Issue:** Whatever is clearly forbidden and is annulled, the buyer must return the item itself. If it is destroyed in his possession, he returns its value for what has a value, such as real estate, goods, and animals, and its equivalent for what has an equivalent, such as measured or weighed foodstuffs or goods. Malik said: the clearly forbidden is to be returned whether it has been consumed or not. As for what people have disliked, it is returned unless it has been consumed, in which case it is left.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verses 275–279 (part 5 of 8)**

The twenty-first issue: God's words, ﴿Whoever receives an admonition from his Lord﴾. Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq (may God have mercy on them both) said: God forbade riba (usury, interest) so that people would lend to one another. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "A loan made twice is equal in reward to giving charity once." Al-Bazzar recorded it. This meaning has already been discussed in full.

Some people said: God forbade it because it destroys wealth and ruins people. The feminine marker is dropped in God's words ﴿jā'ahu﴾ ("came to him") because the feminine form of "admonition" (mawi'za) is not a true feminine, and it carries the sense of "exhortation" (wa'z). Al-Hasan recited ﴿jā'athu﴾ with the feminine marker retained.

This verse was recited by 'A'isha when she was told of the action of Zayd ibn Arqam. Al-Daraqutni related from al-'Aliya bint Anf, who said: "I and Umm Muhabba went out to Makkah, and we entered upon 'A'isha (may God be pleased with her), greeted her, and she said to us: 'Where are you from?' We said: 'From the people of Kufa.' She seemed to turn away from us, so Umm Muhabba said to her: 'O Mother of the Believers! I had a slave-girl, and I sold her to Zayd ibn Arqam al-Ansari for eight hundred dirhams on credit until his stipend came. Then he wanted to sell her, so I bought her back from him for six hundred dirhams in cash.' She said: 'Then 'A'isha turned to us and said: "What a wretched bargain you made, and what a wretched thing you bought! Tell Zayd that he has nullified his jihad with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) unless he repents." She said: "Suppose I take from him only my principal?" 'A'isha said: ﴿Whoever receives an admonition from his Lord and desists, he shall have what is past﴾."

Al-'Aliya is the wife of Abu Ishaq al-Hamdani al-Kufi al-Sab'i, the mother of Yunus ibn Abi Ishaq.

This hadith was recorded by Malik, through the transmission of Ibn Wahb from him, in the chapter on deferred sales (buyu' al-ajal). If a transaction leads to falling into what is forbidden, it is prohibited, even if its outward form is a permissible sale. Most jurists disagreed with Malik on this principle and said: "Rulings are based on what is apparent, not on suspicions." Our evidence is the doctrine of blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i', the principle of closing the avenues that lead to what is forbidden). If this is accepted, well and good; otherwise we argue for its validity, as has already been discussed.

This hadith is an explicit text. 'A'isha could not have said, "Tell Zayd that he has nullified his jihad unless he repents," except on the basis of revelation (tawqif), since such a statement is not made by personal opinion. The nullification of deeds cannot be known except through revelation, as discussed earlier.

In Sahih Muslim, from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "What is lawful is clear and what is unlawful is clear, and between them are doubtful matters that many people do not know. Whoever avoids doubtful matters has safeguarded his religion and his honour. Whoever falls into doubtful matters falls into what is unlawful, like a shepherd who grazes around a protected pasture, who is about to enter it. Verily, every king has a protected pasture, and the protected pasture of God is His prohibitions." [The hadith is as recorded in Sahih Muslim, Istanbul edition, p. 50, vol. 5. In manuscripts B, H and J: "is about to fall into it" (yuwshik an yuwaqi'ahu).]

The point of its evidence is that it forbade approaching doubtful matters out of fear of falling into what is forbidden, and this is blocking the means.

The Prophet (ﷺ) also said: "Among the major sins is a man cursing his parents." They said: "How can a man curse his parents?" He said: "He insults the father of a man, and he insults his father; he insults his mother, and he insults his mother." Thus he made indirect insult of a person's parents equivalent to insulting one's parents directly.

He (ﷺ) also cursed the Jews when they consumed the price of what they had been forbidden to consume.

Abu Bakr said in his letter: "Nothing that is separate may be joined together, and nothing that is joined may be separated, out of fear of charity (being evaded)."

Ibn 'Abbas forbade dirhams for dirhams with a surplus between them. [In manuscripts H and A: "a surplus" (jarira). In manuscripts Ḥ, B and J: "harira". The apparent meaning is: dirhams for dirhams with something added that may involve excess; perhaps the original reading is "bayna-huma jadida", meaning there is a difference because of the distinction between new and old coins.]

The scholars agreed on prohibiting the combining of a sale with a loan (bay' wa-salaf), on the prohibition of even a small quantity of wine, even if it does not intoxicate, on the prohibition of a man being alone with a non-mahram woman even if he is impotent, and on the prohibition of looking at the face of a young woman, along with other matters that are numerous and known with certainty and firm consensus, that the Law has ruled prohibited, because they are means (dhara'i') to what is forbidden.

Riba is the most deserving of having its pastures fenced off and its paths blocked. Whoever permits these causes should also permit digging a well and setting up snares for the destruction of Muslim men and women, and no one would say that. Furthermore, we agree on prohibiting one who sells by 'ina (a deceptive sale) when he is known for it and it is his habit, and this is of the same category.

God is the one who grants success to what is right.

The twenty-second issue: Abu Dawud related from Ibn 'Umar, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "When you engage in 'ina sales, take the tails of cows, are content with agriculture, and abandon jihad, God will send upon you a humiliation that He will not remove from you until you return to your religion."

In its chain of transmission is Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Khurasani, who is not well known. [In the margin: In its chain is Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Khurasani, whose name is Ishaq ibn Usayd, a resident of Egypt, whose narrations are not used as proof. Also in its chain is 'Ata' al-Khurasani. The shaykh, may God be pleased with him, did not mention it; it is not well known.]

Abu 'Ubayd al-Harawi explained 'ina as follows: it is that a man sells a commodity to another man for a known price up to a stated term, and then buys it back from him for less than the price at which he sold it. He said: If, in the presence of the 'ina seeker, the seller buys a commodity from a third party for a known price and takes possession of it, then sells it to the 'ina seeker for a higher price than he paid, up to a stated term, and then the buyer sells it back to the original seller for cash at less than the price, this is also 'ina. It is less serious than the first, and some scholars consider it permissible.

It was called 'ina because of the immediate availability of cash (hudur al-naqd) for the one seeking 'ina, since 'ayn means present wealth, and the buyer buys it only in order to sell it for present cash that reaches him immediately.

The twenty-third issue: Our scholars said: If a man sells a commodity for a price on credit, and then buys it back for a price of the same kind as the price at which he sold it, then he must either buy it from him for cash, or on a term shorter than the term of his sale, or on a longer term, and at the same price, or less, or more. These are three cases.

As for the first and second cases, if the price is equal to or greater than the original price, it is permissible. It is not permissible for less, according to the content of 'A'isha's hadith, because he gave six hundred to receive eight hundred, while the commodity is nothing; this is riba itself.

As for the third case, a longer term: if he buys the whole commodity, or more, then it is permissible at the same price or less, but not more. If he buys only part of it, then it is impermissible in every case, whether at the same price, less, or more.

Our scholars counted the issues of this chapter at twenty-seven, and their basis is what we have mentioned, so understand.

The twenty-fourth issue: God's words ﴿so he shall have what is past﴾ mean: concerning riba, there is no liability upon him for it, in this world or the next. This was said by al-Suddi and others. This is a ruling from God for those among the Quraysh and Thaqif unbelievers who embraced Islam and for those who used to trade in that region. Salaf (past) means what has gone before in time and has ended.

The twenty-fifth issue: God's words ﴿and his affair is with God﴾ have four interpretations. The first is that the pronoun refers to riba, meaning the matter of riba rests with God regarding the continuation of its prohibition or otherwise. The second is that the pronoun refers to "what is past," meaning his affair rests with God in pardoning it and removing liability for it. The third is that the pronoun refers to the person who engaged in riba, meaning his affair rests with God as to whether He will keep him on abstention or return him to disobedience in riba. al-Nahhas chose this view and said: "This is a good and clear view," i.e., his affair in the future is with God: if He wills He will keep him upon the prohibition, and if He wills He will permit it. The fourth is that the pronoun refers to the one who has desisted, but with the meaning of reassurance to him and expanding his hope for good, as you say: "His affair is toward obedience and goodness," and as you say: "His affair is in growth and prosperity, toward God and toward His obedience."

The twenty-sixth issue: God's words ﴿and whoever returns﴾ mean: returns to the practice of riba until he dies. This was said by Sufyan. Others said: whoever returns and says, "Trade is only like riba," has disbelieved. Ibn 'Atiyya said: If we take the verse as referring to an unbeliever, then "abiding" (khulud) is true eternal abiding. If we take it as referring to a disobedient Muslim, then this is figurative abiding, in the sense of emphasis, as the Arabs say "a lasting kingdom," meaning the continuance of what does not last forever, not true eternity.

The twenty-seventh issue: God's words ﴿God destroys riba﴾ mean in this world: He removes its blessing, even if it is abundant. Ibn Mas'ud related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Verily, riba, even if it increases, its end is to diminish." It has also been said that ﴿God destroys riba﴾ means in the Hereafter. Ibn 'Abbas, regarding God's words ﴿God destroys riba﴾, said: He does not accept from it charity, pilgrimage, jihad, or kinship ties.

Al-mahq means decrease and loss, and from it comes muhaq al-qamar (the waning of the moon), which is its diminishing.

(Wayuribi al-sadaqat) — that is, He makes them grow in this world through blessing, and multiplies their reward in the Hereafter through doubling. In Sahih Muslim [[So in (j); in all other manuscripts: "in the Sahih of al-Hadith."]]: "Indeed, the charity of one of you falls into the hand of God, and He nurtures it for him just as one of you nurtures his foal or his young camel, until it comes on the Day of Resurrection, and indeed a morsel is (as large) as Mount Uhud." Ibn al-Zubayr read "yumahhiq" with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the ḥā' with shaddah, and "yurabbi" with a fatḥa on the rā' and shaddah on the bā'; and this was also transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ.

The twenty-eighth point: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And God does not love every ungrateful sinner﴾. Describing "kaffar" (ungrateful) with "athim" (sinner) is an intensification, since the two words differ. It was also said: it is to remove the ambiguity in "kaffar," since it may apply to the farmer who covers the seed in the earth; this was said by Ibn Fawrak. The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He: (Indeed those who believe and do righteous deeds and establish prayer and give zakat) has already passed. He singled out prayer and zakat for mention, although they are included in righteous deeds, to honour them and to draw attention to their rank, since they are the foundation of deeds: prayer among bodily deeds, and zakat among deeds of wealth.

The twenty-ninth point: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, fear God and give up what remains of usury, if you are believers﴾. Its apparent meaning is that He nullified of usury what had not been received, even if it had been contracted before the revelation of the verse of prohibition, and what had been received is not to be reversed. It has been said: the verse was revealed concerning the tribe of Thaqif, who had made a covenant with the Prophet ﷺ that what was owed to them from usury by people was theirs, and what they owed to people was waived. When the due dates of their usury came, they sent to Mecca to demand payment. The debts were owed to the Banu ʿAbd Amr, and they were the sons of ʿAmr ibn ʿUmayr of Thaqif, and they were owed by the Banu al-Mughira of the Makhzum. The Banu al-Mughira said: "We will not give anything, for usury has been abolished." They referred their matter to ʿAttab ibn Asid, who wrote about it to the Messenger of God ﷺ, and the verse was revealed, and the Messenger of God ﷺ wrote with it to ʿAttab, and Thaqif learned of it and desisted. This is the cause of the verse in summary of what Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jurayj, al-Suddi and others narrated. The meaning: make between you and the punishment of God a shield by your leaving what remains of usury for you and your forgoing it.

The thirtieth point: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿if you are believers﴾ is a pure condition regarding Thaqif, on its proper footing, because it was at the beginning of their entry into Islam. If we assume the verse concerns those whose faith has already been established, then it is a figurative condition in the form of intensification, as you say to one whom you want to rouse: "If you are a man, then do such-and-such." Al-Naqqash related from Muqatil ibn Sulayman that he said: "in" in this verse means "idh" (when). Ibn ʿAtiyya said: this is rejected and not known in the language. Ibn Fawrak said: it is possible that by "O you who believe" is meant those before Muhammad ﷺ among the prophets, [and] "give up what remains of usury, if you are believers" in Muhammad ﷺ, since the former benefits only through this. This is rejected by what has been related concerning the occasion of the verse.

The thirty-first point: His saying, Exalted is He: (But if you do not do so, then be informed of war from God and His Messenger). This is a threat if they do not abandon usury, and war calls for killing. Ibn ʿAbbas related that it is said on the Day of Resurrection to the one who consumes usury: "Take your weapon for war." Ibn ʿAbbas also said: whoever persists in usury and does not desist from it, it is incumbent upon the imam of the Muslims to ask him to repent; if he desists, well and good, otherwise he strikes his neck. Qatada said: God threatened the people of usury with killing, making them "bahraj" (lawful prey) wherever they are "thuqifu" (found, seized). It was also said: the meaning is that if you do not desist, then you are war on God and His Messenger, that is, enemies. Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: if the people of a city agreed upon usury as lawful, they would be apostates, and the ruling concerning them is the ruling concerning the people of apostasy; and if it is not from them as lawful, it is permissible for the imam to fight them, do you not see that God, Exalted is He, has permitted this, saying: "then be informed of war from God and His Messenger." Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, read "fa-adhanu" (then announce), meaning: then inform others that you are at war with them.

The thirty-second point: Ibn Bukayr said: a man came to Malik ibn Anas and said: "O Abu ʿAbd Allah, I saw a drunk man staggering, wanting to seize the moon, and I said: my wife is divorced if anything enters the belly of the son of Adam that is worse than wine." He said: "Return until I consider your question." He came the next day, and he said: "Return until I consider your question." He came the next day and he said: "Your wife is divorced. I have examined the Book of God and the Sunna of His Prophet, and I have found nothing worse [in j, h and b: more severe] than usury, because God has permitted war against it."

The thirty-third point: This verse indicates that consuming usury and practising it is among the major sins, and there is no disagreement about this, as we shall explain. It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "There will come upon people a time when no one will remain who has not consumed usury, and whoever does not consume usury will be struck by its dust." Al-Daraqutni related from ʿAbd Allah ibn Hanzala [In al-Istiʿab it is stated that Hanzala al-Ghasil was killed as a martyr at the battle of Uhud, killed by Abu Sufyan. He had been with his wife at the time he went out to Uhud, then the urgency of going out to the fighting overtook him, so that it made him forget the ritual bath and hastened him from it. When he was killed as a martyr, the Messenger of God ﷺ informed that the angels had washed him.] "al-Ghasil al-Malaika" (the one washed by the angels), that the Prophet ﷺ said: "A single dirham of usury is more grievous in the sight of God, Exalted is He, than thirty-six acts of fornication." It is also related from him, peace be upon him, that he said: "Usury has ninety-nine gates, the lowest of which is like a man lying with his mother," meaning fornication with one's mother. Ibn Masʿud said: "The consumer of usury, its payer, its scribe and its witness are cursed upon the tongue of Muhammad ﷺ." Al-Bukhari related from Abu Juhayfa who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ forbade the price of blood [that is, the wage for its cupping, and it was called a price by way of figurative speech], the price of a dog, the earnings of a prostitute, and he cursed the consumer of usury, its payer, the tattooer and the one tattooed, and the image-maker. [We have relied on the hadith as in Sahih al-Bukhari; see al-ʿAsqalani, vol. 10, p. 220.] In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayra, that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Avoid the seven destructive sins..." — and among them — "and consuming usury." In the Musannaf of Abu Dawud, from Ibn Masʿud, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ cursed the consumer of usury, its payer, its scribe and its witness.

The thirty-fourth point: His saying, Exalted is He: "And if you repent, then you have your capital (principal)..." — the verse. Abu Dawud related from Sulayman ibn ʿAmr from his father, who said: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say during the Farewell Pilgrimage: "Verily every usury of the Jahiliyya is void. You have your capital: you do not wrong and you are not wronged," and he mentioned the hadith. So God, Exalted is He, returned them with repentance to their capital and said to them: "you do not wrong" by taking usury, "nor are you wronged" by having something of your capital held back so that your wealth is lost. It is possible that "you do not wrong" refers to delay, because the delay of the wealthy is injustice; so the meaning is that repayment occurs with the removal of usury, and this is the sunna of reconciliation, and this is the most similar thing to reconciliation. Do you not see that the Prophet ﷺ, when he indicated to Kaʿb ibn Malik regarding the debt of Ibn Abi Hadrad to waive half, Kaʿb said: "Yes," and the Messenger of God ﷺ said to the other: "Stand up and pay him." The scholars received his command to pay as a sunna in settlements. It will come in al-Nisa' [see vol. 5, pp. 405, 385] an explanation of reconciliation and what is permissible of it and what is not, God willing.

The thirty-fifth point: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you repent, then you have your capital﴾ is an emphasis on annulling what has not been received from it, and taking the principal in which there is no usury. Some scholars used this as evidence that whatever befalls a sale before possession, of what necessitates the prohibition of the contract, nullifies the contract, as when a Muslim buys game and then the buyer or the seller enters the state of ihram before possession, the sale is void, because there befell it before possession what necessitated the prohibition of the contract, just as God nullified what was not received, because there befell it what necessitated its prohibition before possession; and if it had been received it would have had no effect. This is the position of Abu Hanifa, and it is an opinion of the companions of al-Shafiʿi. It is also used as evidence that the destruction of the sold item before possession, in the hand of the seller, and the lapse of possession in it, necessitates the nullity of the contract, contrary to some of the early scholars; and this disagreement is related from Ahmad. This only holds according to the view of those who say that the contract in usury was originally concluded, and that it was only voided by the arising of Islam before [possession].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 275–279 (part 7 of 8):

...the taking (al-qabd). As for the one who denies that usury (riba) was valid in the first place, this statement is not correct. Usury was forbidden in the (earlier) religions, and what they did in the Jahiliyyah was the custom of the polytheists, and what they took from it was like wealth that came to them by usurpation [[In A: "by gift, so it is not addressed, and there is no sense in it; it is not addressed only because Islam wipes out what came before it." In J: "by plunder."]] and seizure, so it is not addressed. Accordingly, it is not valid to cite as evidence what they have mentioned of the issues. The inclusion of the prohibition of usury in the laws of the prophets before us is well known and mentioned in the Book of God, as is related about the Jews in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and their taking of usury, although they had been forbidden from it﴾ [[See J. 6, p. 12.]]. And it is mentioned in the story of Shu'ayb that his people objected to him and said: ﴿Does your prayer command you that we abandon what our fathers worshipped, or that we not do what we wish with our wealth?﴾ [[See J. 9, pp. 86 and 87.]] Accordingly, it is not sound to derive evidence from it. Yes, it is understood from this that contracts made in the territory of war, if the ruler (al-imam) gains control over them, are not to be challenged by annulment if they were concluded on a corrupt basis.

The thirty-sixth issue: Some of the extremists among the people of scrupulousness (wara') held that lawful wealth which has become mixed with unlawful wealth to the point that it cannot be distinguished, and then the quantity of the unlawful mixed into it is removed, does not become lawful and is not pure, because it is possible that what was removed was the lawful and what remained is the unlawful. Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is an extremism in religion. For everything that is not distinguished, what is intended from it is its monetary value, not its specific substance, and if it perishes, its equivalent takes its place. Mixing is a destruction of its distinguishability, just as ruin is a destruction of its substance, and the equivalent stands in place of what has gone. This is clear in sense and clear in meaning. And God knows best.

I say: Our scholars said that the path of repentance from the unlawful wealth in one's hand, if it is from usury, is that he returns it to the one from whom he took the excess, or to his heirs if he is not present.
