In this verse there is a clear text that reward and punishment are tied to the acquisition (kasb) of deeds, and this is a refutation of the Jabriyya (determinists), which has already been discussed.

In this verse there are fifty-two issues (masā'il). The first: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, when you contract a debt for a specified term, then write it down﴾, to the end of the verse. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: "It has reached me that the last part of the Qur'an to be revealed concerning the Throne is the verse of debt." Ibn 'Abbas said: "This verse was revealed specifically concerning salam (forward sale)." The meaning is that the forward sale practice of the people of Madina was the occasion of the revelation, but the verse then encompasses all debt transactions by consensus. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: "It contains thirty rulings." Some of our scholars have used it as evidence for permitting deferred payment in loans, according to what Malik said, since it does not distinguish between a loan and other contracts in debts. The Shafi'is disagreed and said: "The verse does not indicate the permissibility of deferral in all debts. It only contains the command to call witnesses when the debt is deferred. Then the permissibility or impermissibility of deferral in debt is known from another proof."

The second: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿بِدَيْنٍ﴾ ("for a debt") is emphatic, like His saying: "nor any bird that flies with its two wings" [6:38], and "so all the angels prostrated themselves together" [15:30]. The true meaning of debt is an expression for every transaction in which one of the two counter-values is cash and the other is deferred in liability (dhimma). Among the Arabs, 'ayn (cash) is what is present, and dayn (debt) is what is absent. A poet said:

"She promised us two dirhams' worth of wine,
and immediate roast meat, not on credit (dayn)."

Another said:

"Let death hurl me wherever it wills,
if it does not hurl me into the two pits.
When they kindle wood and fire,
that is death in cash, not on credit."

God, Exalted is He, has clarified this meaning with His true saying: ﴿for a specified term﴾.

The third: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿for a specified term﴾. Ibn al-Mundhir said: "God's saying 'for a specified term' indicates that salam for an unknown term is not permitted, and the Sunna of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) indicates the same meaning as the Book of God, Exalted is He. It is established that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) came to Madina while they were paying in advance for dates for two or three years. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever pays in advance for dates, let him pay in advance for a known measure and a known weight, for a known term.'" It was narrated by Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Bukhari, Muslim and others recorded it. Ibn 'Umar said: "The people of the Jahiliyya used to sell the meat of a she-camel for the 'pregnancy of the pregnancy' (habal al-habala)." Habal al-habala means that a she-camel gives birth and then the offspring she gives birth to is sold. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) forbade them from this. All the scholars from whom knowledge is transmitted agreed that permissible salam is that a man pays in advance to his companion for a known, described food, from the food of a common region whose like does not fail, by a known measure, for a known term, with known dinars or dirhams, and the goods paid for are handed over before the two part from the place where they made the sale, and they name the place where the food is to be received. If they do this, and the one who pays is legally competent, it is a valid salam, and I know of no scholar who invalidates it.

I say: Our scholars said that salam for harvest time, cutting time, Nawruz and Mihrajan (Persian festivals) is permitted, since these are tied to a known time and period.

The fourth: Our scholars, may God have mercy on them, defined salam. They said: it is a known sale in liability (dhimma), restricted by description, with a present cash item, or what is in its ruling, for a known term. Its restriction to "known in liability" guards against the unknown, and against salam in specific identified items, like what they used to pay in advance for in Madina when the Prophet (peace be upon him) came to them. They would pay in advance for the fruits of specific palm trees, and he forbade them from this because of the gharar (uncertainty) in it, since those trees might fail and bear nothing. Their saying "restricted by description" guards against the merely general knowledge without detail, as if one paid in advance for dates, clothes or fish without specifying their type or the particular description. Their saying "with a present cash item" guards against debt for debt. Their saying "or what is in its ruling" guards against the two or three days during which it is permitted to delay the capital (ra's al-mal) of salam. It is permitted in our school to delay it that amount, with or without a condition, because of its proximity, but it is not permitted to make it a condition. Al-Shafi'i and al-Kufi did not permit delaying the capital of salam beyond the contract and separation, and they held that it is like sarf (currency exchange). Our evidence is that the two categories differ in their most distinctive characteristics: sarf is a narrow category with many conditions, unlike salam, where the impurities of transactions are more numerous. And God knows best. Their saying "for a known term" guards against immediate salam, which is not permitted according to the well-known view, as will come. Describing the term as "known" guards against the unknown term which they used to pay in advance for in the Jahiliyya.

The fifth: Salam and salaf are two expressions for one meaning, and both occur in the hadith. However, the term specific to this category is "salam", because salaf is said of a loan (qard). Salam is one of the permissible sales by consensus, excepted from his (ﷺ) prohibition on selling what you do not have. He permitted salam because salam, being a sale of a known item in liability, is a sale of an absent item, which the need of each of the two parties calls for. The owner of the capital needs to buy the fruit, and the owner of the fruit needs its price before its season so that he can spend it on it. It is thus evident that the sale of salam is among the needs-based benefits (maslaha hajiyya), and the jurists have called it "the sale of the needy" (bay' al-mahawij). If it were permitted as an immediate sale, this wisdom would be nullified and this benefit would be removed, and its exception from the prohibition on selling what you do not have would serve no purpose. And God knows best.

The sixth: Concerning the conditions of salam, agreed and disputed, there are nine: six concerning the item paid for (al-muslam fihi), and three concerning the capital of salam (ra's mal al-salam). As for the six concerning the item paid for: that it be in liability, that it be described, that it be quantified, that it be deferred, that the term be known, and that it exist at the time the term falls due. As for the three concerning the capital: that its kind be known, that it be quantified, and that it be cash. These three conditions concerning the capital are agreed upon, except for cash, as already stated.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: "As for the first condition, that it be in liability, there is no difficulty in the fact that what is intended is that it be in liability, because it is a debt transaction (mudayana). Were it not so, it would not have been legislated as debt, and people would not have sought profit and ease through it. On this view, people have agreed." However, Malik said: "Salam for a specific item (al-mu'ayyan) is not permitted except with two conditions: first, that it be from a secure village, and second, that one begin to take it, like milk from a sheep or fresh dates from a palm." No one other than him has said this. These two issues are sound according to the evidence, because specification was prohibited in salam out of fear of muzabana (a sale of dried fruit for fresh on the tree, a form of gharar) and gharar, lest the item become unavailable when it falls due. When the place is secure and what is in it generally cannot fail to be available, it is permitted, since the outcome cannot be certainly guaranteed in matters of jurisprudence, and some minor gharar must be tolerated, and this is common in subsidiary issues, whose enumeration is in the books of issues.

As for salam for milk and fresh dates with the beginning of taking them, this is a Medinan issue on which the people of Madina agreed, and it is based on the principle of benefit (maslaha). A person needs to take milk and fresh dates day by day, and it is hard for him to take them anew each day, because cash may not be available to him, and because prices may vary on him. The owner of the palm and the milk needs cash, because what he has is goods that he cannot dispose of. Since both share the need, this transaction was permitted for them by analogy with 'araya (a permitted sale of dates on the tree for dried dates) and other roots of needs and benefits.

As for the second condition, that it be described, it is agreed upon, and likewise the third condition. Quantification comes in three ways: by measure (kayl), by weight (wazn), and by count ('adad). This depends on custom, which is either the custom of the people or the custom of the Shari'a.

As for the fourth condition, that it be deferred, there is disagreement concerning it. Al-Shafi'i said: "Immediate salam is permitted," but the majority of scholars prohibited it. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "The Malikis were inconsistent in determining the term, until they reduced it to a day. Some of our scholars even said: immediate salam is permitted." The correct view is that the term is necessary in it, because the item sold is of two kinds: immediate, which is cash, and deferred. If it is immediate and the one who pays does not have it, it falls under the category of "selling what you do not have." Therefore a term is necessary so that each contract may stand according to its description and its conditions, and so that the Shari'i rulings may take their proper places. Its limit according to our scholars is a period in which markets differ on such a thing. The saying of God, Exalted is He, "for a specified term", and His (peace be upon him) saying "for a known term", suffices against the saying of any speaker.

I say: What our scholars permitted of immediate salam is what places differ on in their prices, so salam is permitted for an item whose distance from its place is a day, two days or three days. But within a single city it is not permitted, because its price is one. And God knows best.

As for the fifth condition, that the term be known, there is no disagreement about it among the community, because God and His Prophet described the term in that way. Malik alone among the jurists of the cities permitted sale until the time of cutting (jadhdh) and harvest (hasad), because he considered it known. The discussion of this has already passed under His saying: "They ask you about the new moons" [2:189].

As for the sixth condition, that it exist at the time the term falls due, there is also no disagreement about it among the community. If the item sold is cut off at the time the term falls due by a decree of God, Exalted is He, the contract is annulled according to all the scholars.

The seventh: It is not a condition of salam that the one who receives payment (al-muslam ilayhi) own the item paid for, contrary to some of the early scholars, because of what al-Bukhari narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Mujalid, who said: "'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad and Abu Burda sent me to 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Awfa, and they said: 'Ask him whether the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) used to pay in advance for wheat during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ).' 'Abd Allah said: 'We used to pay in advance to the Nabit [[The Nabit (with a fatha on the nun, a kasra on the ba' with a single dot, and a ta' at the end) are people of agriculture. It is said: a people who settle in the marshes, and they were so named because they were guided to extracting water from springs due to their extensive working of farming. It is also said: the Christians of Syria who cultivated it.]]

(from al-Qastallani)] the people of Syria regarding wheat, barley and olive oil, by a known measure and until a known term. I said: "To whom does the one who has the capital belong?" He said: "We did not used to ask them about that." Then they sent me to Abd al-Rahman ibn Abza, and I asked him, and he said: "The companions of the Prophet ﷺ used to make advance payments (salaf) during the time of the Prophet ﷺ, and we did not ask them whether they had produce or not."

Abu Hanifa stipulated that the goods contracted for (al-muslam fihi) must exist from the time of the contract until the time of the term, out of fear that the goods would be sought and not found, which would be gharar (uncertainty). The rest of the jurists disagreed with him and said: what is taken into account is their existence at the time of the term. The Kufans and al-Thawri stipulated that the place of delivery be mentioned for goods that have carriage and transport costs, and they said: the salam contract is invalid if the place of delivery is not mentioned. Al-Awza'i said: it is disliked. For us, if they remain silent about it, the contract is not invalidated, and the place of delivery is determined by default. This is also the view of Ahmad, Ishaq and a group of the people of hadith, based on the hadith of Ibn Abbas, for there is no mention in it of the place where the salam is to be delivered; had it been one of its conditions, the Prophet ﷺ would have specified it just as he specified the measure, the weight and the term. Ibn Abi Awfa is similar.

Eighth: Abu Dawud related from Sa'd (i.e., al-Ta'i), from Atiyya ibn Sa'd, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever makes an advance payment for something, let him not divert it to something else." Abu Muhammad Abd al-Haqq ibn Atiyya said: He is al-Awfi [al-Awfi: the epithet of Atiyya ibn Sa'd], and no one takes proof from his hadith, although the eminent scholars have related from him. Malik said: The practice among us regarding one who makes an advance payment for food at a known price until a stated term, and when the term falls due the buyer does not find with the seller the fulfilment of what he bought from him, and he cancels the contract: it is not proper for him to take from him anything except his silver or his gold, or the price he paid him in its very same form; and he should not buy anything with that price from him until he receives it from him. That is because if he takes other than the price he paid him, or spends it on a commodity other than the food he bought from him, then it is the selling of food before it is taken in full. Malik said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ has indeed forbidden the selling of food before it is taken in full.

Ninth: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿so write it﴾, meaning the debt and the term. It is said: He commanded writing, but what is meant is writing and calling witnesses, because writing without witnesses is not proof. It is also said: We were commanded to write so that we would not forget. Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi related in his Musnad, from Hammad ibn Salama, from Ali ibn Zayd, from Yusuf ibn Mihran, from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said concerning the words of Allah, mighty and majestic, "When you contract a debt for a stated term, then write it" to the end of the verse: "The first to deny was Adam, peace be upon him. Allah showed him his offspring, and he saw a man radiant, his light shining, and said: 'O Lord, who is this?' He said: 'This is your son Dawud.' He said: 'O Lord, what is his lifespan?' He said: 'Sixty years.' He said: 'O Lord, add to his lifespan.' He said: 'No, unless you give him from your lifespan.' He said: 'And what is my lifespan?' He said: 'A thousand years.' Adam said: 'Then I have given him forty years.' So Allah wrote a document concerning that and called His angels to witness it. When death came to Adam, the angels came to him. He said: 'There remain forty years of my life.' They said: 'You have given them to your son Dawud.' He said: 'I have given nothing to anyone.' So Allah, may He be exalted, brought out the document, and His angels bore witness to it." In another narration: "And He completed for Dawud a hundred years, and for Adam his lifespan of a thousand years." Al-Tirmidhi also related it.

In His saying "so write it" there is a clear indication that he should write it with all its descriptions that clarify it and express it, because of the apparent disagreement between the two contracting parties, and so that the judge knows what to rule when they come before him. And Allah knows best.

Tenth: Some people held that writing down debts is obligatory on their creditors, made obligatory by this verse, whether it is a sale or a loan, so that no forgetting or denial occurs regarding it; this is the view preferred by al-Tabari. Ibn Jurayj said: Whoever incurs a debt should write it, and whoever sells should call witnesses. Al-Sha'bi said: They used to hold that His saying "But if one of you trusts the other" abrogates His command to write. Ibn Jurayj related something similar, Ibn Zayd said the same, and it is related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri. Al-Rabi' held that this is obligatory by these words, then Allah lightened it by His saying: "But if one of you trusts the other." The majority said: The command to write is a recommendation for preserving wealth and removing doubt, and if the debtor is pious, the writing does not harm him; and if he is otherwise, then writing is a safeguard for his religion and a protection for the rights-holder. Some said: If you call witnesses, that is prudence; and if you rely on trust, there is latitude and ease. Ibn Atiyya said: This is the correct view. There is no abrogation in this, because Allah recommended writing for what a person may give away or leave by consensus; so its recommendation is only by way of precaution for people.

Eleventh: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And let a scribe write between you with justice﴾. Ata and others said: It is obligatory upon the scribe to write. Al-Sha'bi said: That is when no other scribe is found; then it is obligatory upon him to write. Al-Suddi said: It is obligatory when he is free. The lam was dropped in the first and retained in the second, because the second is a third-person imperative and the first is addressed to the second person. The lam is retained with the second person, as in His saying: ﴿فَلْتَفْرَحُوا﴾ [see vol. 8, p. 354] with the taa'; and it is dropped with the third person, as in the line: "Muhammad, ransom yourself; every soul, when you fear any evil, [let it be ransomed]..."

Twelfth: His saying: ﴿with justice﴾, that is, with truth and equity, meaning he should not write for the rights-holder more than he stated nor less. He said "between you" and not "between one of you" because the creditor is suspected in what the debtor writes, and likewise the reverse; so Allah, glorified is He, prescribed a different scribe who writes with justice, in whose heart and pen there is no partiality toward either of them over the other. It was also said: since people used to deal with one another, and some of them could write while others could not, Allah commanded that a scribe write between them with justice so that none of them would be left out of the transaction.

Thirteenth: The ba' in His saying "with justice" is connected to "let him write," not to "scribe," for otherwise it would follow that only a just person in himself may write a document; yet a child, a slave, or one who is restrained may write it when they have mastered its jurisprudence. As for those who set themselves up for writing it, it is not permissible for the authorities to leave them unless they are just and acceptable. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: No one writes documents between people except one who knows them, is just in himself and trustworthy, according to His saying: "And let a scribe write between you with justice." I say: On this view the ba' is connected to "scribe," meaning let a just scribe write between you, so "with justice" is in the position of a descriptive qualifier.

Fourteenth: His saying: ﴿And let not the scribe refuse to write﴾. Allah forbade the scribe from refusing. People differed over whether writing is obligatory on the scribe and testimony on the witness. Al-Tabari and al-Rabi' said: It is obligatory on the scribe when he is commanded to write. Al-Hasan said: It is obligatory on him in a place where no other scribe can be found, so that the creditor would be harmed if he refused; in that case it is an obligation, but if another scribe can be found, he is under no obligation when another can carry it out. Al-Suddi: It is obligatory upon him when he is free, as has already been mentioned. Al-Mahdawi related from al-Rabi' and al-Dahhak that His saying "And let not [the scribe refuse]" is abrogated by His saying "Let not a scribe or a witness be harmed." I say: This accords with the view of one who saw or thought that it had been obligatory at first upon everyone whom the two contracting parties chose that he should write, and that it was not permissible for him to refuse until the saying of Allah, "Let not a scribe or a witness be harmed," abrogated it. But this is far-fetched, for it has not been established that writing is obligatory upon everyone whom the two contracting parties desire, whoever he may be.

If writing were obligatory, it would not be valid to hire someone for it, because hiring for performing obligations is invalid; and the scholars have not disagreed about the permissibility of taking a fee for writing a document. Ibn al-'Arabi: The correct view is that it is a command of guidance, so one should not write until he takes his right. "Abā" (yaʾbā) is an anomalous verb, and there came only "qalā yaqlā," "abā yaʾbā," "ghasā yaghsā" (it became dark), and "jabā al-kharāj yajbā" (he collected the tax); this has been discussed earlier.

Fifteenth: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿as Allah has taught him, so let him write﴾. The kaf in "kamā" is connected to "an yaktub" (that he write), meaning: writing as Allah taught him. It is possible that it is connected to the meaning implied in "wa lā ya'ba" (let him not refuse), that is: as Allah has bestowed upon him the favour of knowledge of writing, let him not refuse, and let him show generosity as Allah has shown generosity to him. It is also possible that on this meaning the sentence is complete at "an yaktub," and then "as Allah has taught him" begins a new sentence, with the kaf connected to "so let him write."

Sixteenth: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And let the one upon whom the right lies dictate﴾. This is the debtor, the one being claimed against, who acknowledges with his tongue what is upon himself, so that he may be informed of what he owes. "Imlā'" and "imlāl" are two dialects: amalla and amlā. Amalla is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz and Banu Asad, while Tamim says amlaytu. The Qur'an came in both dialects; the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿فَهِيَ تُمْلَى عَلَيْهِ بُكْرَةً وَأَصِيلًا﴾ [see vol. 13, p. 3]. The original is amlalta, the lam being changed to a ya' because it is lighter. So Allah commanded the one upon whom the right lies to dictate, because testimony is only given on the basis of his acknowledgment. He also commanded him, may He be exalted, to fear Allah concerning what he dictates, and forbade him to diminish anything of the right. Al-bakhs means shortfall. From this meaning is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿وَلا يَحِلُّ لَهُنَّ أَنْ يَكْتُمْنَ مَا خَلَقَ اللَّهُ فِي أَرْحامِهِنَّ﴾ [see p. 118 of this part].

Seventeenth: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But if he upon whom the right lies is foolish or weak﴾. Some people said: that is, a minor. This is an error, for the foolish person may be an adult, as will be explained. "Or weak" means an adult who has no understanding.

﴿Or if he is unable to dictate﴾. God made the person who owes the debt fall into four categories. One is capable of dictating for himself. The other three categories cannot dictate, and their cases arise in every age. The right (al-haqq) may also be due to them in areas other than transactions, such as inheritances when they are divided, and in other matters. These three are the *safih* (one who is weak in judgment or wastes property), the *da'if* (the weak), and the one who is unable to dictate. The *safih* is one whose opinion about property is flimsy, who does not know how to take for himself or give from it well. He is likened to a *thawb safih*, a garment that is *safih*, meaning one that is thinly woven. A person of foul speech is also called *safih*, because foul speech is hardly ever found except among ignorant people and those with light minds. The Arabs use *safah* to mean weakness of intellect at times and weakness of body at other times. The poet said:

*We fear that our forbearance will be made foolish,*
*and that time will show ignorance to the forbearing one.*

Dhu al-Rummah said:

*They walked as spears sway, whose tips were made weak*
*by the passing of the scattering winds.*

That is, he made them weak and soft, and shook them. They have said: *al-du'f* with a *dammah* on the *dad* refers to bodily weakness, and with a *fathah* refers to weakness of opinion. It is also said that they are two dialects. The first is more sound, because Abu Dawud related from Anas ibn Malik that a man in the time of the Prophet ﷺ used to buy and sell, and he had weakness in his mind. His family came to the Prophet of God ﷺ and said: "O Prophet of God, place a *hajr* (legal interdiction on his dealings) over so-and-so, for he buys and sells and has weakness in his mind." The Prophet ﷺ summoned him and forbade him from trading. He said: "O Messenger of God, I cannot be patient to refrain from trade for a single hour." The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "If you are not going to give up trading, then say *ha wa ha* and no *khilabah* (deception)." [[Al-khilabah: deception. The words of the Prophet, peace be upon him, "haw ha," have been discussed earlier on p. 350 of this part.]] At-Tirmidhi, Abu 'Isa Muhammad ibn 'Isa as-Sulami, also narrated it from the hadith of Anas and said: "It is sound." He said: "A man had weakness in his mind," and he mentioned the hadith. Al-Bukhari also mentioned it in *at-Tarikh* and said in it: "When you trade, say, 'No deception,' and you have the option (*khiyar*) for three nights in every item you buy." This man was Hibban [[Hibban is with a *fathah*.]] ibn Munqidh ibn 'Amr al-Ansari, father of Yahya and Wasi' the two sons of Hibban. It is also said that he was Munqidh, the grandfather of Yahya and Wasi', the two shaykhs of Malik, and his father was Hibban. He lived to be one hundred and thirty years old. He had received a severe head wound (*ma'mumah* [[A *shajjah ammah* and *ma'mumah* are head wounds that reach the brain.]]) in one of his military campaigns with the Prophet ﷺ, and his mind and tongue were impaired by it. Ad-Daraqutni related that he said: Hibban ibn Munqidh was a weak man, blind in sight. He had been struck on the head with a *ma'mumah*, so the Messenger of God ﷺ gave him the option regarding what he buys for three days. His tongue had become heavy, so the Messenger of God ﷺ said to him: "Sell, and say, 'No deception.'" So I used to hear him say: "*La khidhabah, la khidhabah*" [[Lā khidhābah: a mispronunciation of *khilābah*.]]. He narrated it from the hadith of Ibn 'Amr. *Al-khilabah* means deception, and from it the saying: "If you cannot overcome, then deceive" [[In Lisan al-'Arab: "Whoever says it with a *dammah* means: deceive. Whoever says it with a *kasrah* means: take a little, a small amount after another, as if he took it from the claw of a beast of prey. Ibn al-Athir said: its meaning is, if the matter is difficult to overcome by contention, then seek it by deception."]]. 

The eighteenth issue: The scholars differed concerning the one who is deceived in transactions because of his lack of experience and weakness of mind. Is he to be placed under *hajr* or not? Ahmad and Ishaq held that he should be placed under *hajr*. Others said that he should not be placed under *hajr*. Both opinions exist within the school (*madhhab*). The sounder of the two is the first, because of this verse and because of the words in the hadith: "O Prophet of God, place a *hajr* over so-and-so." The reason the Prophet ﷺ left off placing him under *hajr* was his statement: "O Prophet of God, I cannot be patient to refrain from trade." So he permitted him to trade and made this a special concession for him, because one who is deceived in transactions should be placed under *hajr*, especially when that is due to impairment of his mind. Among what indicates that this was a special concession is what Muhammad ibn Ishaq related, saying: Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Hibban told me, saying: He is my grandfather Munqidh ibn 'Amr, who had been struck on the head with a *ama*, which broke his tongue and disturbed his mind. He did not give up trade and was constantly being cheated. He came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and this was mentioned to him. He said: "When you sell, say, 'No deception,' then for every item you buy you have the option for three nights. If you are pleased, keep it, and if you are displeased, return it to its owner." He lived a very long life, reaching one hundred and thirty years. In the time of 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may God be pleased with him, when people had multiplied and become numerous, he would buy items in the market and return home with them, having been cheated in a shameful way. People would blame him and say: "Are you buying?" He would say: "I have the option. If I am pleased I take it, and if I am displeased I return it. The Messenger of God ﷺ gave me the option for three days." Then he would return the item to its owner the next day and the day after, and he would say: "By God, I will not accept it. I have taken my item and you have given me dirhams." He said: He would say: "The Messenger of God ﷺ gave me the option for three days." A man from among the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ would pass by and say to the merchant: "Woe to you! He has spoken the truth. The Messenger of God ﷺ had given him the option for three days." Ad-Daraqutni narrated it. Abu 'Umar mentioned it in *al-Isti'ab* and said: al-Bukhari mentioned it in *at-Tarikh* from 'Ayyash ibn al-Walid, from 'Abd al-A'la, from Ibn Ishaq.

The nineteenth issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿or weak﴾. The weak (al-da'if) is the one who is mentally impaired (al-madkhul al-'aql), deficient in natural disposition [[As written in the manuscripts H and J. Al-fitra means nature and innate constitution. In J and A it reads: al-fiṭna (shrewdness).]], unable to dictate, either because of a speech impediment ('ayy) [[As written in H and J; in Ḥ and A: la'ah (mental derangement).]], or muteness, or ignorance of how to express speech. Such a person may also have a guardian who is a father or an appointed executor (wasi). Also, one who is unable to dictate is a minor, whose guardian is his executor or his father. Also, one absent from the place of witnessing, whether due to illness or another excuse. His guardian is his agent. As for the mute, he may be counted among the weak, but it is more appropriate that he be among those unable to dictate. These are categories that are distinguished, and their explanation and discussion will come, God willing, in "al-Nisa'" [[See vol. 5, p. 28]].

The twentieth issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then let his guardian dictate with justice﴾. Al-Tabari held that the pronoun in "his guardian" refers to "the truth" (al-haqq), and this was attributed to al-Rabi' and to Ibn 'Abbas. It was also said that it refers to "the one upon whom the right lies," and this is the correct view. What is related from Ibn 'Abbas is not authentic. How can the witnesses testify to something and bring property into the liability of the foolish person through the dictation of the one to whom the debt is owed? This is something not in the Sharia. Unless its proponent means: the one who cannot dictate due to illness, or old age, with a heavy tongue that prevents dictation, or due to muteness. In that case, the sick person and the one whose tongue is heavy for dictation due to muteness have no guardian according to one scholar, just as is established for the child and the foolish person according to those who place them under interdiction. If that is so, then the creditor dictates with justice and makes the one who is incapable hear it, and when the dictation is complete, he acknowledges it. This is a meaning the verse does not intend. This interpretation is valid only for one who cannot dictate due to illness, and those mentioned with him.

The twenty-first issue: When God, exalted is He, said: ("and let the one upon whom the truth lies dictate"), this indicates that he is trusted regarding what he reports and issues. This entails accepting the statement of the pledgor (al-rahin) under oath when he and the pledgee (al-murtahin) disagree about the amount of the debt while the pledge still exists. The pledgor says: "I pledged it for fifty," and the pledgee claims a hundred. The pledgor's word is accepted while the pledge still exists. This is the position of most jurists: Sufyan al-Thawri, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, and the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y). Ibn al-Mundhir also chose it, saying: "Because the pledgee is claiming an excess," and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The burden of proof is upon the claimant, and the oath is upon the one who denies." Malik said: The word of the pledgee is accepted regarding what is between him and the value of the pledge, and he is not believed regarding more than that. It seems he regards the pledge and the pledgee's oath as evidence for the pledgee. God's saying, "and let the one upon whom the truth lies dictate," is a refutation of this, for the one upon whom the truth lies is the pledgor. This issue will come later. If someone says that God made the pledge a substitute for the witness and the document, and the witness indicates the truthfulness of the claimant regarding what is between him and the value of the pledge, then once it reaches its value there is no security for the excess. It is said to him: the pledge does not indicate that its value must equal the amount of the debt, for one may pledge an object for a small or large amount. Yes, the pledge usually does not fall below the amount of the debt, but it need not match it exactly. This speaker says: the pledgee is believed with his oath regarding the amount of the debt until it equals the value of the pledge. But custom does not follow that, for often the debt is less than the pledge, and this is the usual case, so their statement has no real basis.

The twenty-second issue: Since it is established that the intended one is the guardian, there is evidence that his acknowledgment is valid against his ward, because when he dictates, his word is binding upon him regarding what he dictated.

The twenty-third issue: The disposal (tasarruf) of the interdicted foolish person without the permission of his guardian is invalid by consensus (ijma') and is always annulled. It does not establish a ruling nor produce any effect. If a foolish person disposes of property while no interdiction has been imposed on him, there is a disagreement about it, whose explanation will come, God willing, in "al-Nisa'" [[The manuscript text here reads "the child" (al-sabi) in Ḥ and A; the correct reading is what we have established from H and J.]].

The twenty-fourth issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and call upon two witnesses from among your men﴾. Istishhad means requesting testimony. People differed as to whether it is obligatory (fard) or recommended (nadb), and the correct view is that it is recommended, as its explanation will come, God willing.

The twenty-fifth issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿two witnesses﴾. God, glory be to Him, in His wisdom, prescribed testimony in financial rights, bodily rights, and the hudud (fixed punishments), and made two witnesses required in every category except adultery, as its explanation will come in Surat "al-Nisa'" [[See vol. 5, p. 39 and p. 83]]. "Shahid" is an intensive form (bina' mubalagha), and this indicates one who has testified and this has been repeated from him. It is therefore a hint toward justice ('adala). And God knows best.

The twenty-sixth issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from among your men﴾ is explicit in excluding unbelievers, children, and women. As for slaves, the wording includes them. Mujahid said: The intended meaning is free men, and al-Qadi Abu Ishaq chose this and elaborated on it. The scholars differed concerning the testimony of slaves. Shurayh, 'Uthman al-Batti, Ahmad, Ishaq, and Abu Thawr said: the testimony of a slave is permissible if he is upright, and they gave preference to the wording of the verse. Malik, Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i, and the majority of scholars said: the testimony of a slave is not permissible, and they gave preference to the deficiency of slavery. Al-Sha'bi and al-Nakha'i permitted it in minor matters. The correct view is the position of the majority, because God, exalted is He, said: "O you who have believed, when you contract a debt..." and the address continues to His saying "from among your men," so the apparent address includes those who incur debts, and slaves do not have that right without the permission of their masters. If they say: the particularity of the beginning of the verse does not prevent relating its generality at the end, it is said to them: this is restricted by God's saying: ﴿and let not the witnesses refuse when they are called﴾, as its explanation will come. His saying "from among your men" is evidence that the blind are among those eligible to testify, but only if he knows with certainty, as related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about testimony and he said: "Do you see this sun? Testify to the like of it, or refrain." This indicates the requirement that the witness directly observe what he testifies to, not one who testifies by inference which may be mistaken. Yes, a man may have intercourse with his wife if he recognizes her voice, because proceeding with intercourse is permissible on the basis of preponderant assumption (ghalabat al-zann). If a woman were escorted to him and it was said: "This is your wife," while he did not know her, it would be permissible for him to have intercourse with her, and it is lawful for him to accept a gift brought to him on the word of the Messenger. But if someone informed him about Zayd regarding an acknowledgment, a sale, a slander, or usurpation, it would not be permissible for him to testify against the one he was informed about, because the proper basis of testimony is certainty, whereas in other matters the use of preponderant assumption is permissible. For this reason al-Shafi'i, Ibn Abi Layla, and Abu Yusuf said: if he knew the matter before he became blind, his testimony is valid after he became blind, and the blindness that comes between him and the one testified against is like absence or death of the one testified against. This is the position of these scholars. What prevents the blind man from giving testimony about what he witnessed while he was sighted has no basis, and his testimony is valid regarding lineage, which is established by widely transmitted reports, just as he reports what has been widely transmitted as a ruling from the Messenger (ﷺ). Some scholars accepted the testimony of a blind man in matters whose means is voice, because they saw that reasoning from this reaches the level of certainty, and they saw that the confusion of voices is like the confusion of forms and colors. This view is weak, for it entails permitting reliance on voice for the sighted as well. I say: Malik's position on the testimony of a blind man based on voice is that it is valid in divorce and other matters when he recognizes the voice. Ibn al-Qasim said: I said to Malik: "A man hears his neighbor from behind a wall and does not see him, hears him divorcing his wife, and testifies against him, having recognized the voice?" He said: Malik said: "His testimony is valid." This was also said by 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, Shurayh al-Kindi, al-Sha'bi, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, Yahya ibn Sa'id, Rabi'a, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Malik, and al-Layth.

The twenty-seventh issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if they are not two men, then a man and two women﴾. The meaning is: if the claimant does not bring two men, then let him bring one man and two women. This is the view of the majority. "Fa-rajul" is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), "wa-imra'atan" is coordinated with it, and the predicate is omitted, meaning: "then a man and two women stand in their place." It is permissible to use the accusative outside the Qur'an, meaning: "then call upon a man and two women." Sibawayh related: "in khinjaran fa-khinjaran" [[an idiomatic construction]]. Others said: Rather the meaning is: "if there are not two men," meaning they are not found, so the testimony of two women is not permissible except when men are absent. Ibn 'Atiyya said: This is weak; the wording of the verse does not support it. Rather, the apparent meaning is the view of the majority, that is: if the one to be called upon is not two men, meaning if the claimant overlooks this or intends it for some excuse, then let him call upon one man and two women. Thus God made the testimony of two women together with one man permissible when two men are present in this verse, and He did not mention it elsewhere. It was therefore permitted in financial matters specifically according to the majority, on condition that a man be with them. The reason it was so in financial matters and not others is that God multiplied the means of securing property because of the many ways of acquiring it, the general trial with it, and its frequency. So He provided security for it sometimes through writing, sometimes through witnesses, sometimes through a pledge, and sometimes through a guarantee, and He included the testimony of women alongside men in all of these. No rational person should imagine that God's saying "when you contract a debt" includes the dower debt in marriage, or settlement regarding deliberate bloodshed, for that testimony is not testimony regarding a debt but testimony regarding marriage. The scholars permitted the testimony of women alone in matters that no one other than women can witness, due to necessity. On the same basis, the testimony of children was permitted in injuries among themselves, due to necessity. The scholars differed concerning the testimony of children in injuries, and this is: The twenty-eighth issue. Malik permitted it so long as they have not disagreed and have not separated. It is not permissible for fewer than two of them to testify against a younger child, or for a older one against a younger one. Among those who used to judge by the testimony of children in...

[Part 5 of 8 — Commentary of al-Qurtubi on Surah 2:282]

...between them of the wounds: ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr. Mālik said: "This is the matter upon which we agree (al-ʿamr ʿindanā al-mujtamaʿ ʿalayhi)." Al-Shāfiʿī, Abū Ḥanīfa and his companions (in one manuscript: "their companions") did not permit their testimony (i.e., the testimony of children), on account of His Exalted saying: ﴿from among your men﴾, and His saying ﴿from among those you approve﴾, and His saying ﴿two men of justice from among you﴾ (ḏawā ʿadlin minkum) [see vol. 18, p. 157]. These qualities do not apply to a child.

The twenty-ninth issue: When God, glorified is He, made the testimony of two women a substitute for the testimony of one man, it became necessary that their ruling be like his ruling. Thus, just as the one (male) witness must swear an oath along with his testimony according to us, and according to al-Shāfiʿī too, so it is necessary that an oath be sworn along with the testimony of two women, by the general application of this substitution (ʿiwaḍiyya). Abū Ḥanīfa and his companions disagreed on this; they did not regard the oath with a witness, and said: God, glorified is He, divided the testimony and enumerated it, and did not mention a witness plus an oath. Therefore it is not permissible to judge by it, because it would be an additional division (qisman zāʾidan; in manuscripts ḥ, h and j: "a third division") beyond what God has divided, and this is an addition to the text, and that is abrogation (naskh). Among those who held this view were al-Thawrī, al-Awzāʿī, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ḥakam ibn ʿUtayba and a group.

Some of them said: The ruling by an oath with a witness is abrogated... [the text here reads: "the ruling by an oath with a witness is abrogated — 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwān, and he said: the ruling is by the Qur'an."] ʿAṭāʾ claimed that the first to judge by it was ʿAbd al-Malik... "The judgment by the oath and the witness is an innovation (bidʿa)," and the first to rule by it was Muʿāwiya. All of this is error and conjecture that avails nothing against the truth, and one who negates and is ignorant is not like one who affirms and knows! Nothing in God's saying ﴿And call upon two witnesses from among your men﴾ (the verse) offers grounds for rejecting the judgment of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) regarding the oath with a witness, nor that rights cannot be reached or claimed except by what is mentioned in it, for that is refuted by the defendant's refusal (nukūl) and the claimant's oath; by this, property is established by consensus, though this is not in the Book of God. This is a decisive refutation of them.

Mālik said: Among the proofs against one who says that view is to be asked: "Tell me, if a man claimed property against another man, would the defendant not swear that the claim is not due from him? If he swears, that right is void from him; if he refuses to swear, the claimant swears that his right is true, and his right is established against the other party." This is something on which no one among people or in any land disagrees. From what, then, did they take this, and in which Book of God did they find it? Whoever accepts this must accept the oath with a witness.

Our scholars said: Then the wonder is that despite the fame and soundness of the hadiths, they labelled as innovators those who act upon them, until they annulled his ruling and belittled his opinion, although the four caliphs acted upon this, as did Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Muʿāwiya, Shurayḥ, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz (who wrote to his governors with it), Iyās ibn Muʿāwiya, Abū Salama ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, Abū al-Zinād and Rabīʿa. For this reason Mālik said: "It suffices in this what has passed of the practice of the Sunna. Do you think these men's rulings are to be annulled and judged as innovation? This is severe heedlessness and an unsound view."

The imams related from Ibn ʿAbbās, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he judged by the oath with a witness. ʿAmr ibn Dīnār said: "In property matters specifically." It was narrated by Sayf ibn Sulaymān from Qays ibn Saʿd ibn Dīnār, from Ibn ʿAbbās. Abū ʿUmar said: This is the most sound chain for this hadith, and it is a hadith against which no one has any criticism in its chain, and there is no disagreement among the people of knowledge of hadith that its narrators are trustworthy (thiqāt). Yaḥyā al-Qaṭṭān said: "Sayf ibn Sulaymān is reliable (thabt); I have not seen anyone more retentive than him." Al-Nasāʾī said: "This is a good chain; Sayf is trustworthy and Qays is trustworthy." Muslim also transmitted this hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās. Abū Bakr al-Bazzār said: "Sayf ibn Sulaymān and Qays ibn Saʿd are both trustworthy, and those after them need not be named, due to their fame for trustworthiness and integrity."

No one among the Companions is reported to have denied the oath with a witness; rather, the saying in its favour came from them, and it is the view of the majority of the people of knowledge in Medina. It was differed about regarding ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr and Ibn Shihāb: Maʿmar said: "I asked al-Zuhrī about the oath with a witness, and he said: 'This is something people introduced; there must be two witnesses.'" But it is also reported from him that when he first assumed the judiciary, he ruled by a witness and an oath. This is what Mālik and his companions, al-Shāfiʿī and his followers, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, Abū ʿUbayd, Abū Thawr, Dāwūd ibn ʿAlī and the body of the people of narration (ahl al-athar) held, and it is the view whose opposition I hold to be impermissible, because of the mass-transmitted (mutawātir) reports from the Prophet (ﷺ) and the practice of the people of Medina generation after generation.

Mālik said: Judgment by the oath with a witness is given in all lands. He did not argue in his Muwaṭṭaʾ for any question other than this one. No disagreement is reported from him on judging by the oath with a witness, nor from any of his companions in Medina, Egypt or elsewhere, and the Mālikīs in every land know no other position of their school except in our land of al-Andalus, where Yaḥyā [ibn Yaḥyā (in manuscripts j, h and t)] claimed that he did not see al-Layth issuing fatwa by it or holding to it. Yaḥyā opposed Mālik in this, despite opposing the Sunna and the practice of the Abode of Migration (Medina).

Furthermore, the oath with a witness is an additional ruling upon the tongue of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), like his prohibition of marrying a woman together with her paternal aunt or her maternal aunt, alongside God's saying ﴿and lawful to you is what lies beyond that﴾ (according to the reading of Nāfiʿ; see vol. 5, p. 124). Like his prohibition of eating the flesh of domestic donkeys, and of every carnivorous animal with fangs, alongside His saying ﴿Say: I find not...﴾ (see vol. 7, p. 115). And like wiping over the leather socks (khuffayn), whereas the Qur'an came only with washing the feet or wiping them; and similar examples are many. If it were permissible to say that the Qur'an abrogated the Messenger of God's ruling on the oath with a witness, it would be permissible to say that God's saying ﴿and God has permitted trade and forbidden usury﴾ and His saying ﴿unless it be trade by mutual consent among you﴾ (see vol. 5, p. 151) abrogates his prohibition of muzabana, gharar sale, the sale of what has not yet been created, and all else he forbade in sales. This is not permissible for anyone, because the Sunna explains the Book.

If it is said: What came in the hadith is a case concerning a particular matter, so there is no generality. We say: Rather, that is an expression establishing this as a general rule, as if he had said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) made obligatory the judgment by the oath with a witness. What bears witness to this interpretation is what Abū Dāwūd related in the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) judged by a witness and an oath in rights (ḥuqūq). And from the standpoint of analogy and reasoning, we find the oath stronger than two women, because they have no role in li'an, whereas the oath does have a role in li'an. And when the Sunna is sound, acting upon it is obligatory, and the Sunna does not need anything to support it, because whoever opposes it is refuted by it. And success is from God.

The thirtieth: When this is established and the ruling by the oath with a witness is confirmed, the judge Abū Muḥammad ʿAbd al-Wahhāb said: That applies to property and what relates to it, excluding bodily rights, due to consensus on this from every proponent of the oath with a witness. He said: Because rights of property are lower than rights of the body, as evidenced by the acceptance of women's testimony in them. The view of Mālik differed concerning intentional wounds: whether retaliation (qawad) is due therein by a witness and oath. There are two narrations: one holds that by it there is an option between retaliation and blood-money (diya); the other that nothing is due by it, because it is among rights of the bodies. He said: This is the sound view. Mālik said in the Muwaṭṭaʾ: "That is only in property specifically." ʿAmr ibn Dīnār said likewise.

Al-Māzarī [Abū ʿAbd Allāh Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn ʿUmar ibn Muḥammad al-Tamīmī, the Mālikī jurist, died in 536 AH. Al-Māzarī, with a fatḥa on the mīm, an alif, then a zāy, and the zāy may also be kasra, then a rāʾ; the nisba is to "Mazar", a small town in the island of Sicily (from Ibn Khallikān)]:
It is accepted in pure property matters without disagreement, and it is not accepted in pure marriage and divorce matters without disagreement.
If the content of the testimony is not property but leads to property, such as testimony concerning a bequest and marriage after death, such that from establishing it only property is sought, and so on, then there is disagreement about its acceptance: whoever considers the property accepts it, as one accepts it in property; whoever considers the circumstance does not accept it.

Al-Mahdawī said:
The testimony of women in hudud is not permissible according to the consensus of the majority of jurists; likewise in marriage and divorce according to the view of most scholars, and this is the school of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and others; women testify only in property matters.
Whatever they do not testify in, they do not testify upon the testimony of others in it, whether or not a man is with them; and they do not transmit testimony except together with a man, whom they transmit from, about a man and a woman.
And judgment is given on the basis of two of them in every matter that no one else attends, such as childbirth, the crying out of a newborn (istihlāl), and the like.
All of this is the school of Mālik, and there is disagreement on some of it.

The thirty-first issue: God's saying ﴿of those you approve of among the witnesses﴾ is in the place of nominative case as an adjective (ṣifa) to "a man and two women."
Ibn Bukayr and others said: This is addressed to the judges.
Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: This is not a sound view; the address is to all people, but those concerned with this matter are the judges, and this is common in the Book of God, where address encompasses what some of them are involved in.

The thirty-second issue: When God, exalted is He, said ﴿of those you approve of among the witnesses﴾, it indicates that among witnesses there are those who are not approved, from which it follows that people are not presumed to be just until their justice is established; and that is a meaning beyond being Muslim. This is the view of the majority.
Abū Ḥanīfa said: Every Muslim who outwardly manifests Islam, free of manifest wickedness, is just, even if his condition is unknown.
Shurayḥ, ʿUthmān al-Battī and Abū Thawr said: They are the just among the Muslims, even if they are slaves.
I say: They generalized the ruling, and it entails the acceptance of the testimony of a Bedouin against a townsman if he is just and approved; this is the view of al-Shāfiʿī and those who agree with him, and he is among our men and the people of our religion.
His being a Bedouin is like his being from another town, and the general statements in the Qur'an indicating the acceptance of the testimony of the just make no distinction between the Bedouin and the townsman. God says ﴿of those you approve of among the witnesses﴾ and He says ﴿and call to witness two men of justice from among you﴾ — ﴿from among you﴾ being an address to Muslims.
This necessarily entails that justice is, by necessity, something beyond Islam, since the attribute is additional to the thing described; likewise ﴿of those you approve of﴾ is similar, contrary to what Abū Ḥanīfa said. Further, one cannot know that he is approved until his condition is tested, and so it follows that one should not rely on the outward appearance of Islam.
Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal and Mālik, in the narration of Ibn Wahb from him, went to rejecting the testimony of a Bedouin against a townsman, on account of the hadith of Abū Hurayra from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "The testimony of a Bedouin against the people of a village is not permitted."
The sound view is the permissibility of his testimony if he is just and approved, as will come in "al-Nisāʾ" and "Barāʾa," God willing.

وَلَيْسَ فِي حَدِيثِ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ فَرْقٌ بَيْنَ الْقَرَوِيِّ فِي الْحَضَرِ أَوِ السَّفَرِ، وَمَتَى كَانَ فِي السَّفَرِ فَلَا خِلَافَ فِي [قَبُولِهِ [[كذا في ط.
وفى باقى الأصول:
فلا خلاف في قوله.]]].

قَالَ عُلَمَاؤُنَا:
الْعَدَالَةُ ('adala، uprightness) هِيَ الِاعْتِدَالُ فِي الْأَحْوَالِ الدِّينِيَّةِ، وَذَلِكَ يَتِمُّ بِأَنْ يَكُونَ مُجْتَنِبًا لِلْكَبَائِرِ (the major sins) مُحَافِظًا عَلَى مُرُوءَتِهِ (murū'a، personal integrity) وَعَلَى تَرْكِ الصَّغَائِرِ (minor sins)، ظَاهِرَ الْأَمَانَةِ غَيْرَ مُغَفَّلٍ.
وَقِيلَ:
صَفَاءُ السَّرِيرَةِ وَاسْتِقَامَةُ السِّيرَةِ فِي ظَنِّ الْمُعَدِّلِ، وَالْمَعْنَى مُتَقَارِبٌ.

الثَّالِثَةُ وَالثَّلَاثُونَ- لَمَّا كَانَتِ الشَّهَادَةُ (testimony) وِلَايَةً عَظِيمَةً وَمَرْتَبَةً مُنِيفَةً، وَهِيَ قَبُولُ قَوْلِ الْغَيْرِ عَلَى الْغَيْرِ، شَرَطَ تَعَالَى فِيهَا الرِّضَا وَالْعَدَالَةَ.
فَمِنْ حُكْمِ الشَّاهِدِ أَنْ تَكُونَ لَهُ شَمَائِلُ يَنْفَرِدُ بِهَا وَفَضَائِلُ يَتَحَلَّى بِهَا حَتَّى تَكُونَ لَهُ مَزِيَّةٌ عَلَى غَيْرِهِ، تُوجِبُ لَهُ تِلْكَ الْمَزِيَّةُ رُتْبَةَ الِاخْتِصَاصِ بِقَبُولِ قَوْلِهِ، وَيُحْكَمُ بِشُغْلِ ذَمِّهِ الْمَطْلُوبِ بِشَهَادَتِهِ.
وَهَذَا أَدَلُّ دَلِيلٍ عَلَى جَوَازِ الِاجْتِهَادِ (ijtihad، independent reasoning) وَالِاسْتِدْلَالِ بِالْأَمَارَاتِ وَالْعَلَامَاتِ عِنْدَ عُلَمَائِنَا عَلَى مَا خَفِيَ مِنَ الْمَعَانِي وَالْأَحْكَامِ.
وَسَيَأْتِي لِهَذَا فِي سُورَةِ" يُوسُفَ [[راجع ح ٩ ص ١٧٣ فما بعد وص ٢٤٥.]] "زِيَادَةُ بَيَانٍ إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى.
وَفِيهِ مَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى تَفْوِيضِ الْأَمْرِ إِلَى اجْتِهَادِ الْحُكَّامِ، فَرُبَّمَا تَفَرَّسَ فِي الشَّاهِدِ غَفْلَةً أَوْ رِيبَةً فَيَرُدُّ شَهَادَتَهُ لِذَلِكَ.

الرَّابِعَةُ وَالثَّلَاثُونَ- قَالَ أَبُو حَنِيفَةَ:
يُكْتَفَى بِظَاهِرِ الْإِسْلَامِ فِي الْأَمْوَالِ دون الحدود.
وهذه مناقضة تُسْقِطُ كَلَامَهُ وَتُفْسِدُ عَلَيْهِ مَرَامَهُ، لِأَنَّنَا نَقُولُ:
حَقٌّ مِنَ الْحُقُوقِ.
فَلَا يُكْتَفَى فِي الشَّهَادَةِ عَلَيْهِ بِظَاهِرِ الدَّيْنِ كَالْحُدُودِ، قَالَهُ ابْنُ الْعَرَبِيِّ (Ibn al-'Arabi).

الخامسة والثلاثين- وَإِذْ قَدْ شَرَطَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى الرِّضَا وَالْعَدَالَةَ فِي الْمُدَايَنَةِ كَمَا بَيَّنَّا فَاشْتِرَاطُهَا فِي النِّكَاحِ أَوْلَى، خِلَافًا لِأَبِي حَنِيفَةَ حَيْثُ قَالَ:
إِنَّ النكاح ينعقد بشهادة فاسقين.
فنفى الِاحْتِيَاطَ الْمَأْمُورَ بِهِ فِي الْأَمْوَالِ عَنِ النِّكَاحِ، وَهُوَ أَوْلَى لِمَا يَتَعَلَّقُ بِهِ مِنَ الْحِلِّ وَالْحُرْمَةِ وَالْحَدِّ وَالنَّسَبِ.
قُلْتُ:
قَوْلُ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ فِي هَذَا الْبَابِ ضَعِيفٌ جِدًّا، لِشَرْطِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى الرِّضَا وَالْعَدَالَةَ، وَلَيْسَ يُعْلَمُ كَوْنُهُ مَرْضِيًّا بمجرد الإسلام، وإنما يعلم بالنظر في أحوال حَسَبَ مَا تَقَدَّمَ.
وَلَا يُغْتَرُّ بِظَاهِرِ قَوْلِهِ:
أَنَا مُسْلِمٌ.
فَرُبَّمَا انْطَوَى عَلَى مَا يُوجِبُ رَدَّ شَهَادَتِهِ، مِثْلَ قَوْلُهُ تَعَالَى:
﴿وَمِنَ النَّاسِ مَنْ يُعْجِبُكَ قَوْلُهُ فِي الْحَيَاةِ الدُّنْيَا وَيُشْهِدُ اللَّهَ عَلَى مَا فِي قَلْبِهِ﴾ إِلَى قَوْلِهِ ﴿وَاللَّهُ لَا يُحِبُّ الْفَسَادَ﴾ [[راجع ص ١٤ من هذا الجزء.]].
وَقَالَ:
﴿وَإِذَا رَأَيْتَهُمْ تُعْجِبُكَ أَجْسَامُهُمْ﴾ الآية [[راجع ج ١٨ ص ١٢٤.]].

السادسة والثلاثون- قوله تعالى:
(﴿أَنْ تَضِلَّ إِحْدَاهُمَا﴾) قَالَ أَبُو عُبَيْدٍ:
مَعْنَى تَضِلَّ تَنْسَى.
وَالضَّلَالُ عَنِ الشَّهَادَةِ إِنَّمَا هُوَ نِسْيَانُ جُزْءٍ مِنْهَا وَذِكْرُ جُزْءٍ، وَيَبْقَى الْمَرْءُ حَيْرَانَ بَيْنَ ذَلِكَ ضَالًّا.
وَمَنْ نَسِيَ الشَّهَادَةَ جُمْلَةً فَلَيْسَ يُقَالُ:
ضَلَّ فِيهَا.
وَقَرَأَ حَمْزَةُ "إِنْ" بِكَسْرِ الْهَمْزَةِ عَلَى مَعْنَى الْجَزَاءِ، وَالْفَاءُ فِي قَوْلِهِ ﴿فَتُذَكِّرَ﴾ جَوَابُهُ، وَمَوْضِعُ الشَّرْطِ وَجَوَابُهُ رَفْعٌ عَلَى الصِّفَةِ لِلْمَرْأَتَيْنِ وَالرَّجُلِ، وَارْتَفَعَ ﴿فَتُذَكِّرَ﴾ عَلَى الِاسْتِئْنَافِ، كَمَا ارْتَفَعَ قَوْلُهُ ﴿وَمَنْ عَادَ فَيَنْتَقِمُ اللَّهُ مِنْهُ﴾ [[راجع ج ٦ ص ٣٠٢.]] هَذَا قَوْلُ سِيبَوَيْهِ (Sibawayh).
وَمَنْ فَتَحَ "أَنْ" فَهِيَ مَفْعُولٌ لَهُ وَالْعَامِلُ [فِيهَا [[كذا في ط وج.]]] مَحْذُوفٌ.
وَانْتَصَبَ ﴿فَتُذَكِّرَ﴾ عَلَى قِرَاءَةِ الْجَمَاعَةِ عَطْفًا عَلَى الفعل المنصوب بأن.
قَالَ النَّحَّاسُ (al-Nahhas):
وَيَجُوزُ "تَضَلَّ" بِفَتْحِ التَّاءِ وَالضَّادِ، وَيَجُوزُ "تِضَلَّ" بِكَسْرِ التَّاءِ وَفَتْحِ الضَّادِ.
فَمَنْ قَالَ:
"تِضَلَّ" جَاءَ بِهِ عَلَى لُغَةِ مَنْ قَالَ:
ضَلِلْتَ تِضَلُّ.
وَعَلَى هَذَا تَقُولُ تِضَلُّ فَتَكْسِرُ التَّاءَ لِتَدُلَّ عَلَى أَنَّ الْمَاضِيَ فَعِلْتُ.
وَقَرَأَ الْجَحْدَرِيُّ وَعِيسَى ابْنُ عُمَرَ "أَنْ تُضَلَّ" بِضَمِّ التَّاءِ وَفَتْحِ الضَّادِ بِمَعْنَى تُنْسَى، وَهَكَذَا حَكَى عَنْهُمَا أَبُو عَمْرٍو الدَّانِيُّ (Abu 'Amr al-Dani).
وَحَكَى النَّقَّاشُ (al-Naqqash) عَنِ الْجَحْدَرِيِّ ضَمَّ التَّاءِ وَكَسْرَ الضَّادِ بِمَعْنَى أَنْ تُضِلَّ الشَّهَادَةَ.
تَقُولُ:
أَضْلَلْتُ الْفَرَسَ وَالْبَعِيرَ إِذَا تَلِفَا لَكَ وَذَهَبَا فَلَمْ تَجِدْهُمَا.

السَّابِعَةُ وَالثَّلَاثُونَ- قَوْلُهُ تَعَالَى:
﴿فَتُذَكِّرَ﴾ خَفَّفَ الذَّالَ وَالْكَافَ ابْنُ كَثِيرٍ وَأَبُو عَمْرٍو، وَعَلَيْهِ فَيَكُونُ الْمَعْنَى أَنْ تَرُدَّهَا ذَكَرًا فِي الشَّهَادَةِ، لِأَنَّ شَهَادَةَ الْمَرْأَةِ نِصْفُ شَهَادَةٍ، فَإِذَا شَهِدَتَا صَارَ مَجْمُوعُهُمَا كَشَهَادَةِ ذَكَرٍ [[في ج:
رجل.]]، قَالَ سُفْيَانُ بْنُ عُيَيْنَةَ وَأَبُو عَمْرِو بْنُ الْعَلَاءِ.
وَفِيهِ بُعْدٌ، إِذْ لَا يَحْصُلُ فِي مُقَابَلَةِ الضَّلَالِ الَّذِي مَعْنَاهُ النِّسْيَانُ إِلَّا الذِّكْرُ، وَهُوَ مَعْنَى قِرَاءَةِ الْجَمَاعَةِ ﴿فَتُذَكِّرَ﴾ بِالتَّشْدِيدِ، أَيْ تُنَبِّهُهَا إِذَا غَفَلَتْ وَنَسِيَتْ.
قُلْتُ:
وَإِلَيْهَا تَرْجِعُ قِرَاءَةُ أَبِي عَمْرٍو، أَيْ إِنْ تَنْسَ إِحْدَاهُمَا فَتُذْكِرُهَا الْأُخْرَى، يُقَالُ:
تَذَكَّرْتُ الشَّيْءَ وَأَذْكَرْتُهُ غَيْرِي وَذَكَّرْتُهُ بِمَعْنًى، قَالَهُ فِي الصِّحَاحِ (al-Sihah، al-Jawhari).

الثَّامِنَةُ وَالثَّلَاثُونَ- قَوْلُهُ تَعَالَى:
﴿وَلَا يَأْبَ الشُّهَدَاءُ إِذَا مَا دُعُوا﴾ قَالَ الْحَسَنُ:
جَمَعَتْ هَذِهِ الْآيَةُ أَمْرَيْنِ، وَهُمَا أَلَّا تَأْبَى إِذَا دُعِيَتْ إِلَى تَحْصِيلِ الشَّهَادَةِ، وَلَا إِذَا دُعِيَتْ إِلَى أَدَائِهَا، وَقَالَهُ ابْنُ عَبَّاسٍ.
وَقَالَ قَتَادَةُ وَالرَّبِيعُ وَابْنُ عَبَّاسٍ:
أَيْ لِتَحَمُّلِهَا وَإِثْبَاتِهَا فِي الْكِتَابِ.
وَقَالَ مُجَاهِدٌ:
مَعْنَى الْآيَةِ إِذَا دُعِيَتْ إِلَى أَدَاءِ شَهَادَةٍ وَقَدْ حَصَلَتْ عِنْدَكَ.
وَأَسْنَدَ النِّقَاشُ إِلَى النَّبِيِّ ﷺ أَنَّهُ فَسَّرَ الْآيَةَ بِهَذَا، قَالَ مُجَاهِدٌ:
فَأَمَّا إِذَا دُعِيَتْ لِتَشْهَدَ أَوَّلًا فَإِنْ شِئْتَ فَاذْهَبْ وَإِنْ شِئْتَ فَلَا، وَقَالَ أَبُو مِجْلَزٍ وَعَطَاءٌ وَإِبْرَاهِيمُ وَابْنُ جُبَيْرٍ وَالسُّدِّيُّ وَابْنُ زَيْدٍ وَغَيْرُهُمْ [[في ب:
وعطية فلا يجب إلخ.]].
وَعَلَيْهِ فَلَا يَجِبُ عَلَى الشُّهُودِ الْحُضُورُ عِنْدَ الْمُتَعَاقِدَيْنِ، وَإِنَّمَا عَلَى الْمُتَدَايِنَيْنِ أَنْ يَحْضُرَا عِنْدَ الشُّهُودِ، فَإِذَا حَضَرَاهُمْ وَسَأَلَاهُمْ إِثْبَاتَ شَهَادَتِهِمْ فِي الْكِتَابِ فَهَذِهِ الْحَالَةُ الَّتِي يَجُوزُ أَنْ تُرَادَ بِقَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى:
﴿وَلَا يَأْبَ الشُّهَدَاءُ إِذَا مَا دُعُوا﴾ لِإِثْبَاتِ الشَّهَادَةِ، فَإِذَا ثَبَتَتْ شَهَادَتُهُمْ ثُمَّ دُعُوا لِإِقَامَتِهَا عِنْدَ الْحَاكِمِ فَهَذَا الدُّعَاءُ هُوَ بِحُضُورِهِمَا عِنْدَ الْحَاكِمِ [[في ب:
الحكم.]]، عَلَى مَا يَأْتِي.
وَقَالَ [[في ط وب:
قاله أبن عطية.]] ابْنُ عَطِيَّةَ:
وَالْآيَةُ كَمَا قَالَ الْحَسَنُ جَمَعَتْ أَمْرَيْنِ عَلَى جِهَةِ النَّدْبِ، فَالْمُسْلِمُونَ مَنْدُوبُونَ إِلَى مَعُونَةِ إِخْوَانِهِمْ، فَإِذَا كَانَتِ الْفُسْحَةُ لِكَثْرَةِ الشُّهُودِ وَالْأَمْنِ مِنْ تَعْطِيلِ الْحَقِّ [[في هـ:
الحقوق.]] فَالْمَدْعُوُّ مَنْدُوبٌ، وَلَهُ أَنْ يَتَخَلَّفَ لِأَدْنَى عُذْرٍ، وَإِنْ تَخَلَّفَ لِغَيْرِ [[في ط:
العذر.]] عُذْرٍ فَلَا إِثْمَ عَلَيْهِ وَلَا ثَوَابَ لَهُ.
وَإِذَا كَانَتِ الضَّرُورَةُ وَخِيفَ تَعَطُّلُ الْحَقِّ أَدْنَى خَوْفٍ قَوِيَ النَّدْبُ وَقَرُبَ مِنَ الْوُجُوبِ، وَإِذَا عُلِمَ أَنَّ الْحَقَّ يَذْهَبُ وَيَتْلَفُ بِتَأَخُّرِ الشَّاهِدِ عَنِ الشَّهَادَةِ فَوَاجِبٌ عَلَيْهِ الْقِيَامُ بِهَا، لَا سِيَّمَا إِنْ كَانَتْ مُحَصَّلَةً وَكَانَ الدُّعَاءُ إِلَى أَدَائِهَا، فَإِنَّ هَذَا الظَّرْفَ آكَدُ، لِأَنَّهَا قِلَادَةٌ فِي الْعُنُقِ وَأَمَانَةٌ تَقْتَضِي الْأَدَاءَ.
قُلْتُ:
وَقَدْ يُسْتَلْوَحُ مِنْ هَذِهِ الْآيَةِ دَلِيلٌ عَلَى أَنَّهُ جَائِزٌ لِلْإِمَامِ أَنْ يُقِيمَ لِلنَّاسِ شُهُودًا وَيَجْعَلَ لَهُمْ مِنْ بَيْتِ الْمَالِ كِفَايَتَهُمْ، فَلَا يَكُونُ لَهُمْ شُغْلٌ إِلَّا تَحَمُّلَ حُقُوقِ النَّاسِ حِفْظًا لَهَا، وَإِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ ذَلِكَ ضَاعَتِ الْحُقُوقُ وَبَطَلَتْ.
فَيَكُونُ الْمَعْنَى وَلَا يَأْبَ الشُّهَدَاءُ إِذَا أَخَذُوا حُقُوقَهُمْ أَنْ يُجِيبُوا.
وَاللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
فَإِنْ قِيلَ:
هَذِهِ شَهَادَةٌ بِالْأُجْرَةِ، قُلْنَا:
إِنَّمَا هِيَ شَهَادَةٌ خَالِصَةٌ مِنْ قَوْمٍ اسْتَوْفَوْا حُقُوقَهُمْ مِنْ بَيْتِ الْمَالِ، وَذَلِكَ كَأَرْزَاقِ الْقُضَاةِ وَالْوُلَاةِ وَجَمِيعِ الْمَصَالِحِ الَّتِي تَعِنُّ [[في ج:
تعين المسلمين.]] لِلْمُسْلِمِينَ وَهَذَا مِنْ جُمْلَتِهَا.
وَاللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَقَدْ قَالَ تَعَالَى: ﴿وَالْعَامِلِينَ عَلَيْهَا﴾ [[راجع ج ٨ ص ١٧٨.]] فَفَرَضَ لَهُمْ.

التَّاسِعَةُ وَالثَّلَاثُونَ- لَمَّا قَالَ تَعَالَى: ﴿وَلَا يَأْبَ الشُّهَدَاءُ إِذَا مَا دُعُوا﴾ دَلَّ عَلَى أَنَّ الشَّاهِدَ هُوَ الَّذِي يَمْشِي إِلَى الْحَاكِمِ، وَهَذَا أَمْرٌ بُنِيَ عَلَيْهِ الشَّرْعُ وَعُمِلَ بِهِ فِي كُلِّ زَمَانٍ وَفَهِمَتْهُ كُلُّ أُمَّةٍ، وَمِنْ أَمْثَالِهِمْ: "فِي بَيْتِهِ يُؤْتَى الْحَكَمُ".

الْمُوفِيَةُ أَرْبَعِينَ- وَإِذَا ثَبَتَ هَذَا فَالْعَبْدُ خَارِجٌ عَنْ جُمْلَةِ الشُّهَدَاءِ، وَهُوَ يَخُصُّ عُمُومَ قَوْلِهِ: ﴿مِنْ رِجَالِكُمْ﴾ لِأَنَّهُ لَا يُمْكِنُهُ أَنْ يُجِيبَ، وَلَا يَصِحُّ لَهُ أَنْ يَأْتِيَ، لِأَنَّهُ لَا اسْتِقْلَالَ لَهُ بِنَفْسِهِ، وَإِنَّمَا يَتَصَرَّفُ بِإِذْنِ غَيْرِهِ، فَانْحَطَّ عَنْ مَنْصِبِ الشَّهَادَةِ كَمَا انْحَطَّ عَنْ مَنْزِلِ الْوِلَايَةِ.
نَعَمْ!
وَكَمَا انْحَطَّ عَنْ فَرْضِ الْجُمُعَةِ وَالْجِهَادِ وَالْحَجِّ، عَلَى مَا يَأْتِي بَيَانُهُ إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى.

الْحَادِيَةُ وَالْأَرْبَعُونَ- قَالَ عُلَمَاؤُنَا:
هَذَا فِي حَالِ الدُّعَاءِ إِلَى الشَّهَادَةِ.
فَأَمَّا مَنْ كَانَتْ عِنْدَهُ شَهَادَةٌ لِرَجُلٍ لَمْ يَعْلَمْهَا مُسْتَحِقُّهَا الَّذِي يَنْتَفِعُ بِهَا، فَقَالَ قَوْمٌ:
أَدَاؤُهَا نَدْبٌ لِقَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: ﴿وَلَا يَأْبَ الشُّهَدَاءُ إِذَا مَا دُعُوا﴾ فَفَرَضَ اللَّهُ الْأَدَاءَ عِنْدَ الدُّعَاءِ، فَإِذَا لَمْ يُدْعَ كَانَ نَدْبًا، لِقَوْلِهِ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ (ﷺ):
"خَيْرُ الشُّهَدَاءِ الَّذِي يَأْتِي بِشَهَادَتِهِ قَبْلَ أَنْ يُسْأَلَهَا" رَوَاهُ الْأَئِمَّةُ.
وَالصَّحِيحُ أَنَّ أَدَاءَهَا فَرْضٌ وَإِنْ لَمْ يُسْأَلْهَا إِذَا خَافَ عَلَى الْحَقِّ ضَيَاعَهُ أَوْ فَوْتَهُ، أَوْ بِطَلَاقٍ أَوْ عِتْقٍ عَلَى مَنْ أَقَامَ عَلَى تَصَرُّفِهِ عَلَى الِاسْتِمْتَاعِ بِالزَّوْجَةِ وَاسْتِخْدَامِ الْعَبْدِ إِلَى غَيْرِ ذَلِكَ، فَيَجِبُ عَلَى مَنْ تَحَمَّلَ شَيْئًا مِنْ ذَلِكَ أَدَاءُ تِلْكَ الشَّهَادَةِ، وَلَا يَقِفُ أَدَاؤُهَا عَلَى أَنْ تُسْأَلَ مِنْهُ فَيُضَيِّعَ الْحَقَّ، وَقَدْ قَالَ تَعَالَى: ﴿وَأَقِيمُوا الشَّهَادَةَ لِلَّهِ﴾ [[راجع ج ١٨ ص ١٥٩.]] وَقَالَ: ﴿إِلَّا مَنْ شَهِدَ بِالْحَقِّ وَهُمْ يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ [[راجع ج ١٦ ص ١٢٢.]].
وَفِي الصَّحِيحِ عَنِ النَّبِيِّ ﷺ:
"انْصُرْ أَخَاكَ ظَالِمًا أَوْ مَظْلُومًا".
فَقَدْ تَعَيَّنَ عَلَيْهِ نَصْرُهُ بِأَدَاءِ الشَّهَادَةِ الَّتِي لَهُ عِنْدَهُ إِحْيَاءً لِحَقِّهِ الَّذِي أَمَاتَهُ الْإِنْكَارُ.

The Forty-Second Issue: There is no doubt that whoever is obligated to give testimony in one of the ways we have mentioned, and does not give it, has thereby disqualified himself as a witness and his testimony. There is no difference in this between the rights of God, exalted is He, and the rights of human beings. This is the view of Ibn al-Qasim and others. Some scholars held that if that testimony concerns a right of human beings, the disqualification applies only to that particular testimony itself, so it is not permissible for him to give it afterward. The correct view is the first one, because what makes him disqualified is his wickedness (fisq) in refraining from carrying out what was obligatory upon him without an excuse, and wickedness removes the eligibility to testify absolutely. This is clear.

The Forty-Third Issue: There is no contradiction between the Prophet's saying, peace be upon him, "The best of witnesses is the one who brings his testimony before he is asked for it," and his saying, peace be upon him, in the hadith of Imran ibn Husayn: "The best of you is my generation, then those who follow them, then those who follow them, then those who follow them." Imran said: "I do not know whether the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said 'after his generation' twice or three times. Then there will come after them a people who will give testimony without being asked to testify, who will betray and not be trusted, who will make vows and not fulfil them, and among whom corpulence will appear." [Note: this is the wording of Muslim.] Both are reported in the two Sahihs. This hadith is to be understood in three ways. The first is that it refers to the false witness, who testifies to what he was not asked to testify about, that is, to what he neither bore nor was entrusted with. Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shayba mentioned that Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, delivered a sermon at the Bab al-Jabiya and said: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, stood among us as I stand among you, and then said: 'O people, fear God regarding my companions, then those who follow them, then those who follow them, then lies will spread and false testimony.'" The second way is that it refers to one whose greed drives him to carry out what he testifies to, so he hastens to give testimony before being asked for it. This testimony is rejected, for it indicates a desire that dominates the witness. The third is what Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, a narrator of some of the chains of this hadith, said: "They used to forbid us, while we were boys, from [hastening to bear] covenants and testimonies."

The Forty-Fourth Issue: The words of the Exalted: "And do not be weary of writing it down, whether it is small or large, along with its term." "Tas'amu" means "tamalluna" (you become bored). Al-Akhfash said: one says "sa'imtu as'amu sa'man, sa'amatan, sa'aman," as the poet said:
"I have grown weary of the burdens of life, and whoever lives eighty years, without a father to you, grows weary."
"An taktubuhu" is in the accusative position governed by the verb. "Saghiran aw kabiran" are two circumstantial clauses (hal) from the pronoun in "taktubuhu," and the "small" is placed first out of concern for it. This prohibition of weariness came because debts were frequent among them, so it was feared they would become bored with writing, and one of them would say: "This is little; I have no need to write it down." So God, exalted is He, emphasized the urging regarding both small and large amounts. Our scholars said: except for what is a qirat or the like, because of its insignificance and because the soul does not strive for it, whether to acknowledge or deny it.

The Forty-Fifth Issue: The words of the Exalted: "That is more just in the sight of God." Its meaning is "more equitable" (a'dal), that is, that both small and large amounts be written down and witnessed.
"And more upright for testimony," that is, more correct and more protective.
"And nearer" means "closer."
"And that you may not doubt" means "that you may not be in doubt."

The Forty-Sixth Issue: The words of the Exalted:
And the words "and more upright for testimony" are evidence that a witness, if he sees the document but does not remember the testimony, should not give testimony, because of the doubt that has entered into it. He should not testify except to what he knows; rather, he may say: "This is my handwriting, but I do not now remember what I wrote in it."
Ibn al-Mundhir said: Most of the scholars from whom it is transmitted prohibit a witness from testifying on the basis of his own handwriting when he does not remember the testimony.
Malik argued for the permissibility of this with the words of the Exalted: "And we testify only to what we know." [See vol. 9, p. 244.]
Some scholars said: Since God attributed the writing to the just, it is permissible for him to testify on the basis of his handwriting even if he does not remember.
Ibn al-Mubarak related from Ma'mar, from Ibn Tawus, from his father, concerning a man who testifies to a testimony and forgets it: "There is no harm in his testifying if he finds its mark in the document or in his own handwriting."
Ibn al-Mubarak said: "I find this excellent."
In what has come in reports from the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, is that he judged in many matters by evidences and proofs, and from the prophets before him there is what indicates the soundness of this position.
And God knows best.
More explanation of this will come, God willing, in "al-Ahqaf" [see vol. 16, p. 181 ff.].

The Forty-Seventh Issue: The words of the Exalted: "Except that it be a present trade that you conduct among yourselves." "An" is in the accusative position as an exception, not from the first part. Al-Akhfash [Abu Sa'id] said: meaning "except that a trade occurs," so it has the sense of "waqa'a" and "hadatha" (occurred and happened).
Others said: "tudirunaha" is the predicate.
'Asim alone read "tijaratan" as the predicate of "kana," with its subject concealed within it.
"Hadirah" is an attribute of "tijara." The implied meaning is "except that the trade be trade," or "except that the transaction be trade." This is how Makki and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi estimated it, and its parallels and evidence have already been mentioned.
When God, exalted is He, knew the hardship of writing for them, He stated the abandonment of this and lifted the blame in it for every sale made in cash, and this, in the majority of cases, is only for small items such as foodstuffs and the like, not for large amounts such as properties and the like.
Al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: This applies to what is hand to hand (yadan bi-yad).

The Forty-Eighth Issue: The words of the Exalted: "That you conduct among yourselves" require mutual receipt and separation with the item received.
Since real estate, land, and many animals do not admit of separation and cannot be hidden, writing was recommended in them, and debt transactions were attached to this, so writing became a guarantee against whatever changes of circumstances and shifts of hearts may arise.
As for when the two parties settle the transaction, take possession, and each separates from the other with what he bought from his companion, then in custom the fear of dispute becomes small, except through obscure causes.
The Law drew attention to these benefits in the cases of deferred payment and cash, and of what is hidden and what is not hidden, through writing, witnessing, and pledge.
Al-Shafi'i said: Sales are of three kinds: a sale with writing and witnesses, a sale with a pledge, and a sale with trust. And he recited this verse.
Ibn Umar, when he sold for cash, would call witnesses, and when he sold on credit, he would write.

The Forty-Ninth Issue: The words of the Exalted: "And call witnesses when you trade." Al-Tabari said: its meaning is "and call witnesses over its small and its large."
People differed on whether this is obligatory or recommended. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Ibn Umar, al-Dahhak, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Jabir ibn Zayd, Mujahid, Dawud ibn Ali and his son, and Abu Bakr said that it is obligatory. Among the most strict in this was 'Ata', who said: "Call witnesses when you sell and when you buy, even for a dirham, or half a dirham, or a third of a dirham, or less than that, for God, mighty and majestic, says: 'And call witnesses when you trade.'"
From Ibrahim: "Call witnesses when you sell and when you buy, even if it is a bundle of herbs."
Among those who held this view and preferred it was al-Tabari, who said: "It is not lawful for a Muslim, when he sells or buys, unless he calls witnesses; otherwise he would be opposing the Book of God, mighty and majestic. Likewise, if it is for a term, he must write and call witnesses if he finds a scribe."
Al-Sha'bi and al-Hasan held that this is recommendation and guidance, not a binding requirement.
It is reported that this is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, and the people of opinion.
Ibn al-'Arabi claimed that this is the view of the majority, and said: "It is the sound one."
He related from no one who held the obligation except al-Dahhak.
He said: The Prophet, peace be upon him, sold and wrote. And he said: He copied his book: "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. This is what al-'Adda' ibn Khalid ibn Hawdhah bought from Muhammad, the Messenger of God, peace be upon him: he bought a slave or a female slave, without any defect (da') [the da' is a hidden fault or an inward illness that is not seen; the doubt is from the narrator, as in al-Isti'ab], without any secret flaw (ghaila) or corruption (khubtha), the sale of a Muslim to a Muslim."
And he sold without calling witnesses, and bought, and pledged his coat of mail to a Jew without calling witnesses.
Had calling witnesses been obligatory, it would have been obligatory alongside the pledge, for fear of dispute.
I say: We have already mentioned the obligation from other than al-Dahhak.
The hadith of al-'Adda' was recorded by al-Daraqutni and Abu Dawud.
His conversion was after the Conquest and Hunayn, and he is the one who said: "We fought with the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, on the day of Hunayn, and God did not grant us victory and did not help us. Then he embraced Islam and his Islam was good." Umar mentioned him and related this hadith, and at its end he said:
"Al-Asma'i said: I asked Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah about the ghaila, and he said: 'Running away (ibaq), theft, and adultery.' I asked him about the khubtha, and he said: 'The sale of the people of the covenant to the Muslims.'"
Abu Muhammad ibn 'Atiyya said: "Obligation in this is unsettled. As for small transactions, it is difficult and burdensome; as for large ones, a merchant may intend to win favor by not calling witnesses, and it may be a custom in some lands, and one may feel shy before a scholar or an honored elder so that witnesses are not called upon him. All of that falls under trust. The command to call witnesses remains recommended, because of the benefit it generally carries, so long as no excuse arises that prevents it, as we have mentioned."
Al-Mahdawi, al-Nahhas, and Makki related from some people that they said: "'And call witnesses when you trade' is abrogated by His words: 'But if one of you trusts another...'"
Al-Nahhas traced it back to Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, that he recited "O you who believe, when you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down," up to "But if one of you trusts another, let the one trusted fulfil his trust," and said: "This verse abrogated what came before it."
Al-Nahhas said: This is the view of al-Hasan, al-Hakam, and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd.
Al-Tabari said: "This has no meaning, because this is a different ruling; rather, this is the ruling for one who does not find a scribe. God, mighty and majestic, said: 'And if you are on a journey and do not find a scribe, then a pledge taken into possession. But if one of you trusts another—that is, if he does not demand a pledge from him—let the one trusted fulfil his trust.'"
He said: "If it were permissible for this to abrogate the first, it would be permissible for His words, 'And if you are sick or on a journey, or one of you comes from the place of relieving himself...' to abrogate His words, 'O you who believe, when you rise to prayer...', and it would be permissible for His words, 'Then whoever does not find [the means], then fasting two consecutive months,' to abrogate His words, 'Then the freeing of a believing slave.'"
