Some scholars said: His words, "But if one of you trusts another," do not show that its revelation came later than the beginning of the verse containing the command to call witnesses; rather, both came together.
And it is not permissible for an abrogating and an abrogated text to come together in one and the same situation.
He said: It has been related from Ibn 'Abbas that when it was said to him, "The verse on debt is abrogated," he said: "No, by God, the verse on debt is decisive (muhkama), there is no abrogation in it," he said:

The commentary's view that the witnessing (ishhad) was prescribed for reassurance, and that the pledge (rahn) and witnessing are two means of securing debts. There is no disagreement among the scholars of the regions (ulama al-amsar) that the pledge is prescribed as recommended (mandub) rather than obligatory (wajib). By the same reasoning, the same applies to witnessing. People have continued to trade in towns and in travel, by land and by sea, on plains and in mountains, without witnesses, and the people knew of this without objection. Had witnessing been obligatory, they would not have left off rebuking the one who abandoned it.

I say: All of this is a sound argument, but better than it is the explicit Sunnah on abandoning witnessing, which al-Daraqutni transmitted from Tariq ibn Abd Allah al-Muharibi, who said: "We came in a caravan from al-Rabadhah and the outskirts of al-Rabadhah [[Al-Rabadhah (with a vowel on the first letter): a village of Madinah three miles away, near Dhat Irq on the Hijaz road when travelling from Fayd toward Makkah. In this place is the grave of Abu Dharr al-Ghifari, may Allah be pleased with him, who went out there in anger at Uthman ibn Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, and remained there until he died in the year 23 AH (from Mu'jam al-Buldan by Yaqut).]] until we alighted near Madinah, and with us was a female camel-rider of ours.

While we were sitting, a man came to us wearing two white garments. He greeted us and we returned his greeting. He said: 'From where have the people come?'

We said: 'From al-Rabadhah and the outskirts of al-Rabadhah.'

He said: 'And with you is a red camel?' He said: 'Will you sell me this camel of yours?'

We said: 'Yes.'

He said: 'For how much?'

We said: 'For such-and-such a number of sa' of dates.'

He said: 'He did not ask us to lower the price at all, and said: "I have taken it." Then he took hold of the camel's head until he entered Madinah and vanished from us. So we blamed one another and said: "You have given your camel to someone you do not know!"

The female camel-rider said: "Do not blame one another. I have seen the face of a man who would not betray you. I have never seen a face more like the moon on the night of the full moon than his face."

When it was the evening [[So in al-Daraqutni; in all the originals: al-'Asha (the evening meal).]], a man came to us and said: "Peace be upon you. I am the messenger of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to you, and he commands you to eat of this until you are satisfied, and to measure until you have received your full measure."

He said: "So we ate until we were satisfied, and we measured until we had received our full measure."'"

Al-Zuhri also related the hadith from Umarah ibn Khuzaymah, that his paternal uncle, who was one of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), told him that the Prophet (ﷺ) bought a horse from a Bedouin, and the hadith continues.

In it: The Bedouin began to say: "Come forward with a witness who will testify that I sold it to you." Khuzaymah ibn Thabit said: "I testify that you have indeed sold it."

The Prophet (ﷺ) turned to Khuzaymah and said: "On what basis do you testify?"

He said: "By your confirmation, O Messenger of Allah."

He said: So the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) made the testimony of Khuzaymah equal to the testimony of two men.

Al-Nasa'i and others transmitted it.

The fiftieth point: Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Let not a scribe or a witness be harmed﴾. There are three opinions concerning it:

The first [[The second is the view of Ibn Abbas, and the third is the view of Mujahid and al-Dahhak.]]: The scribe should not write except what is dictated to him, and the witness should not add to or subtract from his testimony.

This was said by al-Hasan, Qatadah, Tawus, Ibn Zayd and others.

It is related from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ata' that the meaning is: the scribe must not refuse to write, nor the witness refuse to testify.

According to these two opinions, "wa la yudarr" originally was yudarir with a kasra on the ra', then assimilation occurred, and the ra' was given a fatha in the jussive because of the lightness of the fatha.

Al-Nahhas said: "I have seen Abu Ishaq inclining to this opinion. He said: Because after it comes 'and if you do so, it is indeed a transgression in you.' So it is more fitting that whoever bears witness falsely or distorts in writing should be told: 'You are a transgressor.' He is more deserving of this than one who asks a witness to testify while the witness is occupied."

Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Abi Ishaq read yudarir with a kasra on the first ra'.

Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Tawus and al-Suddi said, and it is related from Ibn Abbas: the meaning of the verse "Let not a scribe or a witness be harmed" is that a witness is summoned to testify and a scribe is summoned to write while they are occupied. When they excuse themselves by their excuse, he expels them and harms them, and says: "You have neglected the command of Allah," and similar words, and he beats them.

The original form of "yudarr" according to this is yudarar with a fatha on the ra'. Likewise Ibn Mas'ud read "yudarar" with a fatha on the first ra'. So Allah the Exalted forbade this, because if it were left unrestricted there would be occupation for both of them away from the affairs of their religion and their livelihood.

The word "mudarra" (harming), since it is from two parties, implies these meanings.

The scribe and the witness, according to the first two opinions, are in the nominative because of their own action. According to the third opinion, they are in the nominative as the passive subject whose agent is not named.

The fifty-first point: His saying, the Exalted: "And if you do so" means the harming, "then it is indeed a transgression in you" meaning a disobedience. This is from Sufyan al-Thawri.

So the scribe and the witness disobey by adding or subtracting, and that is harmful falsehood concerning wealth and bodies, and it involves nullifying the truth.

Likewise, harming them when they are occupied is disobedience and a departure from what is right in opposing the command of Allah.

His saying "in you" (bikum): its implied sense is that transgression lands upon you.

The fifty-second point: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And fear Allah; Allah teaches you, and Allah is knowing of all things﴾. This is a promise from Allah the Exalted that whoever fears Him, He will teach him, meaning He will place in his heart a light by which he understands what is cast upon him. And Allah may at the outset place in his heart a criterion (furqan), meaning a decisive judgment by which he distinguishes between truth and falsehood. From this is His saying, the Exalted: "O you who have believed, if you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion (furqan)" [[See vol. 7, p. 396.]].

And Allah knows best.

In it are twenty-four issues:[[We adopted "four" because of what appears in h, w and j at the end of the twenty-first: "Three issues have been raised here, completing twenty-four."]] When Allah the Exalted mentioned the recommendation to call witnesses and to write for the sake of protecting wealth and religion[[So in the original manuscripts and in Ibn 'Atiyya. "Religion" here means acts of obedience, and failing to fulfil rights is a transgression against the command of Allah. Perhaps the intended word is "bodies" (al-abdan); see the commentary on His words "it is a transgression (fusuq) in you."]], He followed this with the circumstances of excuses that prevent writing, and He made a pledge (rahn) the alternative. He specified travel as one of the excuses, since it is the most common excuse, especially at that time because of the frequency of military campaigns. In meaning, every excuse is included. There are times when a scribe is unavailable in the home, such as times when people are busy, and at night. Also, fear that the debtor's obligation will be lost is an excuse that makes seeking a pledge necessary. The Prophet (ﷺ) pledged his coat of mail to a Jew from whom he had requested a loan of barley. The Jew said, "Muhammad only wants to take my property." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "He lied. I am trustworthy on earth and trustworthy in heaven. If he had entrusted me, I would have repaid. Go to him with my coat of mail." He died while his coat of mail was still pledged (ﷺ), as will be explained shortly.

The second issue: The majority of scholars said: the pledge during travel is established by the explicit text of the revelation, and in the home it is established by the Sunnah of the Messenger (ﷺ). This is correct. We have already explained its permissibility at home from the verse by its meaning, since excuses also arise at home. No one is reported to have prohibited it at home except Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Dawud, who held to the verse. But there is no proof in it, because although this statement came in the form of a condition, what is intended is the most common circumstances. The fact that the pledge is mentioned in the verse in the context of travel does not mean it is forbidden elsewhere. In the two Sahihs and others, from 'A'isha, the Prophet (ﷺ) bought food from a Jew on credit and pledged to him an iron coat of mail of his. Al-Nasa'i reported from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) died while his coat of mail was pledged to a Jew for thirty measures of barley for his family."

The third issue: His words, ﴿and you do not find a scribe﴾. The majority recited "katiban" (a scribe), meaning a man who writes. Ibn 'Abbas, Ubayy, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Ikrimah and Abu al-Aliyah recited "wa lam tajidu kitaban" (and you do not find a writing). Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: Mujahid explained it, saying: its meaning is "if you do not find ink," meaning during journeys. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas as "kuttaban" (scribes). Al-Nahhas said: this recitation is irregular (shadhdha), and the common recitation differs from it. Rarely does anything deviate from the common recitation without having some flaw. The sentence structure follows "katib," since Allah the Mighty and Majestic said before this: "and let a scribe write between you with justice," while "kitab" implies a group. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "kuttaban" is appropriate, because for every incident there is a scribe, so it was said in the plural: "and you do not find scribes." Al-Mahdawi related from Abu al-Aliyah that he recited "kutuban" (writings), which is the plural of "kitab," because the incidents differ. As for the recitation of Ubayy and Ibn 'Abbas, "kitaban," al-Nahhas and Makki said it is the plural of "katib," like "qa'im" and "qiyam" (standing and standers). Makki said: the meaning is that if the inkwell, the pen and the sheet are absent. The absence of a scribe may be due to the lack of any tool whatever, and the absence of a scribe also implies the absence of writing. Thus both recitations are good, except in terms of the script of the Mushaf.

The fourth issue: His words, ﴿then a pledge taken into possession﴾. Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir recited "fa-ruhunun" with a damma on the ra and the ha, and it is reported from them that the ha was lightened. Al-Tabari said: some people interpreted "ruhunan" with a damma on the ra and the ha as the plural of "rihan," so it is a plural of a plural, and al-Zajjaj related this from al-Farra'. Al-Mahdawi said: "fa-rihan" is a beginning (mubtada') and the predicate is omitted, and the meaning is "fa-rihanun maqbudatun yakfi min dhalika" (then pledges taken into possession suffice in this). Al-Nahhas said: 'Asim ibn Abi al-Najud recited "fa-rahnun" with a sukun on the ha, and this is related from the people of Makkah. The general rule in this is "rihan," as one says "baghl" and "baghal" (mule and mules), and "kabsh" and "kibash" (ram and rams). "Ruhunun" is intended to be the plural of "rihan," like "kitab" and "kutub." It was also said that it is the plural of "rahn," like "saqf" and "suqf," "halq" and "hulq," "farsh" and "furush," "nashr" and "nushur," and similar. "Rahnun" with a sukun on the ha is intended to be that the damma was removed because it is heavy. It was also said: it is the plural of "rahn," like "sahm hashr" (a fine arrow), and "sihham hashr." The first is preferable, because the first (ruhunun) is not an adjective, while this (maqbudatun) is an adjective. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: I do not know of a broken plural of "rahn" for the smallest number. If it came, its pattern would be "af'ul," like "kalb" and "aklub" (dog and dogs). It seems they dispensed with the small number in favour of the large number, just as the large pattern is used instead of the small pattern in their saying "thalathat shusu'" (three sandals). The small pattern has been used instead of the large pattern in "rasan" and "arsan" (rope and ropes). So "rahn" is pluralised by two patterns: "fu'ul" and "fi'al." Al-Akhfash said: "fu'ul" is on a disliked pattern and is rare and irregular. He said: "ruhun" may be the plural of "rihan," as if "rahn" is pluralised as "rihan," and then "rihan" is pluralised as "ruhun," like "firash" and "furush."

The fifth issue: The meaning of rahn (pledge) is the holding of an object as a security for a right, so that the right may be collected from its price or from the price of its benefits when it cannot be collected from the debtor. This is how the scholars defined it. In the language of the Arabs it means continuance and persistence. Ibn Sida said: "rahanahu" means "adamahu" (he made it last). From "rahana" in the sense of "dama" (remained) is the poet's line:

"Bread and meat are constant for them, and wine whose strainer is pouring."

Al-Jawhari said: "rahana al-shay'u rahnan" means it lasted. "Arhantu lahum al-ta'am wa al-sharab" means I made food and drink lasting for them, and it is "ta'am rahin" (lasting food). "Al-rahin" means the firm, and "al-rahin" also means the emaciated among camels and people. He said:

"Though you see my body thin, emaciated from leanness, and the glory of men is not in fatness."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: The pledge that is the security is also expressed as "arhantu irhanan," which some have related. Abu 'Ali said: "arhantu" is used in the sense of raising the price, while "rahantu" is used for loans and sale. Abu Zayd said: "arhantu fi al-silra irhanan" means I raised the price of the goods, and this is specifically for high prices. He said:

"Ida'iyyatun urhinat fihā al-danānīr" (a she-camel of the 'Id tribe, in whose price dinars were raised).

He describes a she-camel. The 'Id is a clan of Mahra, and the camels of Mahra are described as noble. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said of the pledge: "rahantu" and "arhantu." Ibn al-A'rabi and al-Akhfash also said so. 'Abd Allah ibn Hammam al-Salouli said:

"When I feared their claws, I escaped and made Malik a pledge."

Tha'lab said: all the narrators have "arhantuhum" (I made them hold him as a pledge), although it is permissible to say "rahantuhu" and "arhantuhu." Except al-Asma'i, who narrated "wa arhanahum," taking it as a verb in the future tense conjoined with a past verb, and he compared it to their saying "qumtu wa ashukku wajhahu" (I stood up while striking his face). This is a good view, because the wa is the wa of circumstance (hal), so "ashukku" is a circumstance of the first verb, meaning "I stood striking his face," that is, I left him remaining with them. It is not said "arhantu al-shay'" (I pledged the thing), but "rahantuhu." One says "rahantu lisani bi-kadha" (I pledged my tongue for such and such), and one does not say "arhantu" in this. Ibn al-Sikkit said: "arhantu fiha" means "aslaftu" (I lent). The murtahin (pledgee) is the one who takes the pledge. The object is "marhun" and "rahin," and the feminine is "rahina." "Rahantu fulanan 'ala kadha muraharatan" means I wagered with him. "Arhantu bihi waladi irhanan" means I put my son at risk. "Al-rahina" is the singular of "al-rahai'in" (pledges), all of this from al-Jawhari. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is said without disagreement in sale and loan: "rahantu rahnan," then the thing that is given is named by this verbal noun. One says "rahantu rahnan," just as one says "rahantu thawban" (I pledged a garment).

The sixth issue: Abu 'Ali said: since the pledge carries the meanings of permanence and continuance, for this reason the pledge becomes void according to the jurists if it leaves the hand of the pledgee to the pledgor in any way, because it has departed from what was made for the pledgee by his choice. I say: this is what we rely upon, that when the pledge returns to the pledgor by the choice of the pledgee, the pledge becomes void. Abu Hanifa said the same, except that he said: if it returns by way of loan or deposit, it is not void. Al-Shafi'i said: its return to the hand of the pledgor in any case does not nullify the ruling of the earlier possession. Our evidence is His words, ﴿then pledges taken into possession﴾. So when it leaves the hand of the one who has taken possession, that word does not apply to it linguistically, and so it does not apply to it legally. This is clear.

The seventh issue: If he pledges it by word but does not take possession of it in act, this does not establish a ruling, based on His words, ﴿taken into possession﴾. Al-Shafi'i said: Allah did not make the ruling except for a pledge described as taken into possession. When the attribute is absent, the ruling must also be absent. This is very clear. The Malikis said: the pledge becomes binding by the contract, and the pledgor is compelled to hand over the pledge so that the pledgee may take custody of it, based on His words, ﴿Fulfil the contracts﴾[[See Vol. 6, p. 31.]] and this is a contract, and His words, ﴿with the covenant﴾[[See Vol. 10, p. 296.]] and this is a covenant, and His words, peace be upon him: "Muslims are bound by their conditions," and this is a condition. So possession, according to us, is a condition for its full benefit, and according to them it is a condition for its binding force and validity.

The eighth issue: His words, ﴿taken into possession﴾ require the pledgee's control over the pledge. The people agreed on the validity of the pledgee's taking possession, and likewise the taking possession by his agent. They differed about the taking possession by a trustee on whose hands the pledge is placed. Malik, all his companions and the majority of scholars said: the trustee's taking possession is taking possession. Ibn Abi Layla, Qatada, al-Hakam and 'Ata' said: it is not taking possession, and it is not considered taken into possession unless it is with the pledgee, and they regarded this as a matter of worship. The view of the majority is more correct in meaning, because when it is with the trustee it becomes taken into possession linguistically and in reality, since the trustee stands in place of the owner of the right and is like an agent. This is clear.

The ninth issue: If the pledge is placed in the hands of a trustee and it is lost, the pledgee is not liable, nor is the one on whose hand it was placed, because the pledgee had no possession of it that he would be liable for. The one on whose hand it is placed is a trustee, and a trustee is not liable.

**The tenth issue:** When Allah the Exalted said, ﴿pledges taken into possession﴾, our scholars said: its apparent and unrestricted meaning permits the pledging of an undivided share (*rahn al-mushā'*, a pledge of an unpartitioned portion of property)[[In MS H: "al-matā'" (goods).]]. This differs from Abu Hanifa and his companions, who hold that one may not pledge a third of a house, half of a slave, or a sword. They then said: if two men are owed money by a third man and they are co-owners of that debt, and he pledges to them a piece of land for it, the pledge is valid once they take possession of it. Ibn al-Mundhir said: this is permission to pledge an undivided share, because each of them is the pledgee of half of [the land][[As in the manuscripts; it should read: "half of a plot of land."]]. Ibn al-Mundhir also said: pledging an undivided share is permissible, just as selling it is permissible.

**The eleventh issue:** Pledging a debt that is owed (*rahn mā fī al-dhimma*) is permissible according to our scholars, because it is something that can be taken into possession. This is against those who forbid it. An example: two men deal with each other, one of them is owed a debt by the other, and the debtor pledges to him the very debt that he owes. Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: every item of goods that may be sold may be pledged. For this reason we permit pledging a debt owed, since its sale is permissible, and because it is property through which security is established, so it may be a pledge, by analogy with an existing commodity. Those who forbid it said: its taking into possession cannot be realized, and taking possession is a condition for the binding nature of the pledge, since the right must be satisfied from it when the term falls due. Satisfaction must come from its monetary value, not from its substance, and this cannot be conceived for a debt.

**The twelfth issue:** Al-Bukhari reported from Abu Hurayra, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A riding animal is ridden for its upkeep when it is pledged, and milk from a milch animal is drunk for its upkeep when it is pledged, and the one who rides or drinks bears the upkeep." Abu Dawud also transmitted it, but he said instead of "is drunk" in both places: "is milked."

Al-Khattabi said: this is an ambiguous statement; the wording itself does not clarify who rides and who milks, whether it is the pledger (*al-rāhin*), the pledgee (*al-murtahin*), or the trustee in whose hand the pledge is placed.

I say: this has come clarified and explained in two reports, and because of them the scholars differed on this matter. Al-Daraqutni reported from the hadith of Abu Hurayra that the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned: "When the animal is pledged, the pledgee bears its fodder, and milk from a milch animal is drunk, and the one who drinks bears its upkeep." He transmitted it through Ahmad ibn Ali ibn al-Ala': Ziyad ibn Ayyub related to us: Hushaym related to us: Zakariyya related to us, from al-Sha'bi, from Abu Hurayra.

This is the view of Ahmad and Ishaq: that the pledgee benefits from the pledge by milking and riding to the extent of the upkeep. Abu Thawr said: if the pledger spends on it, the pledgee does not benefit from it. But if the pledger does not spend on it and leaves it in the hand of the pledgee, who then spends on it, then the pledgee may ride it and employ the slave. Al-Awza'i and al-Layth also said [similar things].

The second report was also transmitted by al-Daraqutni, and there is discussion about its chain, which will come later in its explanation. It is from the hadith of Isma'il ibn Ayyash, from Ibn Abi Dhi'b, from al-Zuhri, from al-Maqburi[[As in all manuscripts; the correct reading, as in al-Daraqutni, is: "from al-Zuhri, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab." It will come shortly.]], from Abu Hurayra, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "*Lā yaghlaqu al-rahn*[[Ghalq al-rahn: among the practices of the pre-Islamic period was that if the pledger did not pay what he owed by the specified time, the pledgee would take ownership of the pledge; Islam nullified this. (From al-Nihaya.)]] (The pledge is not forfeited); its gain belongs to its owner, and its loss is his as well."

This is the view of al-Shafi'i, al-Sha'bi and Ibn Sirin, and it is also the view of Malik and his companions. Al-Shafi'i said: the benefit of the pledge belongs to the pledger, its upkeep is his responsibility, and the pledgee does not benefit from any part of the pledge except for preserving the security.

Al-Khattabi said: this is the most preferable and soundest of the opinions, based on the Prophet's (peace be upon him) statement: "The pledge is not forfeited by its owner who pledged it [its gain is his, and its loss is his]." [Al-Khattabi said: his words "from its owner" mean "to its owner"[[The addition is from MSS J, H, Ḥ and T. This is a different transmission of al-Daraqutni's report.]].] The Arabs use "min" in place of "li," as in their saying:

*Amin Umm Awfa dimnatun lam tukallami*[[Is it from Umm Awfa a ruined encampment that has not been spoken to?]]

I say: "li-sahibihi" (to its owner) has come explicitly, so there is no need for interpretation.

Al-Tahawi said: that ruling applied when riba was still permitted, and [the Prophet] did not forbid a loan that brings benefit, nor taking one item in exchange for another even if they were unequal, and then riba was forbidden afterwards. The community has agreed that a female slave who is pledged may not be lawfully enjoyed by the pledger; likewise, it is not permitted for him to make use of her services. Al-Sha'bi said: nothing from the pledge may be benefited from. Al-Sha'bi transmitted the hadith and gave a ruling contrary to it, and in his view that would not be permissible unless it had been abrogated.

Ibn Abd al-Barr said: they have agreed that the milk and the back [i.e., riding] of the pledge belong to the pledger. Then it is not free of one of two possibilities: either the pledgee's milking of it is with the pledger's permission or without his permission. If it is without his permission, then the hadith of Ibn Umar from the Prophet (ﷺ) states: "No one may milk another's livestock except with his permission," which refutes this and rules that it was abrogated. If it is with his permission, then the established principles agreed upon in forbidding the unknown, uncertainty (*gharar*), selling what one does not have, and selling what has not yet come into being, also refute this, since that was before the revelation of the prohibition of riba. And Allah knows best.

Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: if the pledgee stipulates the right to benefit from the pledge, there are two situations: if it arises from a loan, it is not permitted; if it arises from a sale or a lease, it is permitted, because he becomes a seller of the commodity at the stated price, and the benefits of the pledge are for a known period, so it is like a sale and a lease. As for a loan, it becomes a loan that brings benefit, and because the essence of a loan is that it is an act of worship, if a benefit enters it, it becomes an increase in the same kind, and that is riba.

**The thirteenth issue:** *Ghalq al-rahn* is not permitted, and it means that the pledgee stipulates that the pledge becomes his in exchange for his right if the pledger does not bring it to him at its due time. This was a practice of the pre-Islamic period, and the Prophet (ﷺ) nullified it with his saying: "*Lā yaghlaqu al-rahn*." We have read it with the *qāf* vowelled as a predicate (*khabar*), meaning: the pledge is not forfeited. One says: *aghlaqtu al-bāb* (I closed the door), so it is *mughlaq* (closed). And the pledge became forfeited (*ghalaqa*) in the hand of its pledgee if it was not redeemed. The poet said:

*Ajāratanā man yajtami' yatafarraqi*
*Wa man yaku rahnan lil-hawādithi yughlaqi*
O our neighbor, whoever gathers will be separated,
and whoever becomes a pledge to misfortunes will be forfeited.

Zuhayr said:

*Wa fāraqtaka bi-rahnin lā fikāka lahu*
*Yawma al-wadā'i fa-amsā al-rahnu qad ghaliqā*
And she parted from you with a pledge that has no redemption
on the day of farewell, so the pledge has become forfeited.

**Fourteenth:** Al-Daraqutni narrated, through Sufyan ibn Uyayna, from Ziyad ibn Sa'd, from al-Zuhri, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from Abu Hurayra, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The pledge is not foreclosed: its gain belongs to its owner and its loss is upon him." Ziyad ibn Sa'd is one of the reliable memorizers (huffaz), and this chain (isnad) is good (hasan). Malik also transmitted it from Ibn Shihab, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, as a mursal report (one in which a Successor omits the Companion), that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The pledge is not foreclosed." Abu 'Umar (Ibn 'Abd al-Barr) said: As far as I know, everyone who transmitted the Muwatta' from Malik narrated it this way, except Ma'n ibn 'Isa, who connected it (wasala). Ma'n is trustworthy, but I fear that the error in it comes from 'Ali ibn 'Abd al-Hamid al-Ghadair'i, from Mujahid ibn Musa, from Ma'n ibn 'Isa. Abu 'Abd Allah 'Umarus [[In ṭ: Ibn 'Amrus; the correction is from al-Tamhid.]] added, from al-Abhari with his chain: "Its gain belongs to it and its loss is upon it." The narrators have disagreed about raising (raf') this wording to the Prophet. Ibn Abi Dhi'b, Ma'mar and others raised it. Ibn Wahb narrated it and said: Yunus said, Ibn Shihab said: "Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab used to say: The pledge belongs to the one who pledged it; its gain belongs to him and its loss is upon him." Thus Ibn Shihab made clear that this is the saying of Sa'id, not from the Prophet (ﷺ). However, Ma'mar narrated it from Ibn Shihab as marfu' (traced to the Prophet), and Ma'mar is the most reliable of people regarding Ibn Shihab. Yahya ibn Abi Unaysa followed him in raising it, but Yahya is not strong. The origin of this hadith, according to the scholars of transmission, is mursal, and although it has been connected through many routes, they criticize these (as defective). Despite this, it is a hadith that none of them raises (to the Prophet) with certainty, though they differ in its interpretation and meaning. Al-Daraqutni also narrated it from Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash, from Ibn Abi Dhi'b, from al-Zuhri, from Sa'id, from Abu Hurayra, as marfu'. Abu 'Umar said: Isma'il did not hear it from Ibn Abi Dhi'b; he heard it from 'Abbad ibn Kathir, from Ibn Abi Dhi'b, and 'Abbad is considered weak and not to be used as proof. Isma'il is also considered by them not acceptable in narration when he narrates from people other than those of his own city; when he narrates from Syrians his narrations are sound, but when he narrates from Medinans and others there is much error and confusion in his hadith.

**Fifteenth:** The increase of the pledge is included with it if it cannot be separated, like fatness, or if it is offspring, like birth and the young of animals. In the same category is the shoot of a date palm. Anything else, such as produce, fruit, milk and wool, is not included unless it is stipulated. The difference between them is that offspring follow the mothers in zakat, whereas wool, milk and tree fruit do not follow the mothers in zakat. They are not in their form, nor in their meaning, nor do they subsist with them, so they have the ruling of their own, not the ruling of the origin, unlike the offspring and the young. And Allah knows best what is correct.

**Sixteenth:** The pledge of one whose wealth is encumbered by debt is permissible as long as he has not been declared bankrupt (yufris), and the creditor (murtahin) has greater right to the pledge than the other creditors. This was said by Malik and a group of people. But a view contrary to this has been reported from Malik, and 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Abi Salama said that the other creditors share with him in this, but this is not valid, because whoever has not been placed under restriction (hujr) has valid dispositions in all his conditions, including sale and purchase. The creditors dealt with him on the basis that he would sell, buy and pay. Malik's position in this chapter has not varied, and so it is with the pledge. And Allah knows best.

**Seventeenth:** The Almighty's words: ﴿And if one of you trusts another﴾, the verse. This is a condition linked to the instruction to the debtor to pay and not to delay. It means: if the debtor is trustworthy in the eyes of the creditor and is relied upon, then let him pay what he owes to the one who trusted him. His words ﴿let him pay﴾ come from al-ada' (payment), with hamza. [And this is the answer to the condition.] [It is permissible to lighten its hamza, so the hamza becomes a waw, and it is not changed into an alif nor made intermediate (bayn bayn), because an alif can only be preceded by a fatha.] It is a command meaning obligation, by the evidence of the consensus (ijma') on the obligation to pay debts, the establishment of a judge's ruling on it, and his compelling the debtors to it, and by the evidence of the sound hadiths on the prohibition of taking another's property.

**Eighteenth:** The Almighty's words: ﴿his trust﴾. Amana (trust) is a verbal noun (masdar), and the thing that is in the obligation (dhimma) has been named by it. He attributed it to the one upon whom the debt lies because it has a relation to him, as the Almighty said: ﴿And do not give the foolish your property﴾ [[See vol. 5, p. 27.]].

**Nineteenth:** The Almighty's words: ﴿and let him fear Allah, his Lord﴾, meaning: in not concealing anything of the right. His words ﴿and do not conceal testimony﴾ are an explanation of His words "and let no harm be done" (wa la yudarra), with the vowel of the ʿayn being kasra. He forbade the witness from harming by concealing testimony, and this prohibition is obligatory by several indications, among them the threat (wa'id). The place of the prohibition is where the witness fears the loss of a right. Ibn 'Abbas said: The witness must testify wherever he is called to testify, and inform wherever he is asked for information. He said: Do not say "I will inform about it before the ruler" but inform him about it, perhaps he will return and be restrained. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read ﴿wa la yaktumu﴾ with the yā', making it a prohibition in the third person.

**Twentieth:** If there are witnesses to the right, it becomes obligatory upon them to bear witness as a collective duty (fard kifaya). If two of them give testimony and the judge is satisfied with them, the obligation falls from the rest. If the judge is not satisfied with them, then going to him becomes obligatory until the proof is established. This is known by the call of the rights-holder: if he says to the witness: "Revive my right by giving the testimony you have for me," then this becomes obligatory upon him.

**Twenty-first:** The Almighty's words: ﴿And whoever conceals it, his heart is sinful﴾. He singled out the heart for mention because concealment is one of its acts, and because it is the lump of flesh by whose soundness the whole body is sound, as the Prophet (peace be upon him) said. So He named the part to refer to the whole. This has already been discussed. [At the beginning of the surah [[The addition is from j and ṭ. See vol. 1, p. 188.]]] [Al-Kiya said: When he resolved not to give it and abandoned giving it with the tongue, the sin returned to both aspects together. So His words "his heart is sinful" are figurative (majaz), and it is more emphatic than literal meaning in indicating the threat. This is among the wonderful expressions and subtle grammatical explanations of meanings. It is said: the sin of the heart is the cause of its transformation, and Allah, when He transforms a heart, makes it hypocritical and seals it. We seek refuge in Allah from that [and this has been discussed at the beginning of the surah [[From ṭ.]]]]. "Qalbuhu" is in the nominative case governed by "āthimun", and "āthimun" is the predicate of "inna". If you wish, you may read "āthimun" as the subject of the beginning (mubtada'), and "qalbuhu" as a subject that fills the place of the predicate, and the whole clause is the predicate of inna. If you wish, you may read "āthimun" as the predicate of the subject, intending its postponement. If you wish, "qalbuhu" may be a substitute for "āthimun", a substitution of part for whole. If you wish, it may be a substitute for the pronoun in "āthimun".

Three issues are raised here, completing twenty-four.

**The first:** Know that what Allah commanded regarding testimony and writing is for the sake of preserving good relations between people and removing disputes that lead to the corruption of relations, lest Satan embellish to him denial of the right and transgression of the limit set by the Law, or abandonment of confining oneself to the due amount [[In ṭ: "the wealth."]]. For this reason the Law forbade unknown transactions, whose habit leads to disagreement, corruption of relations, and the creation of hatred and separation. Among these is what Allah forbade: gambling, games of chance, and drinking wine, by His words: ﴿Satan only wants to cast enmity and hatred among you through wine and gambling﴾, the verse [[See vol. 6, p. 285.]]. Whoever disciplines himself by Allah's discipline in His commands and prohibitions attains the good of this world and the next. Allah the Almighty said: ﴿And if they had done what they were admonished with, it would have been better for them﴾, the verse [[See vol. 5, p. 270.]].

**The second:** Al-Bukhari narrated from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Whoever takes people's property intending to repay it, Allah will repay on his behalf; and whoever takes it intending to destroy it, Allah will destroy him." Al-Nasa'i narrated from Maymuna, wife of the Prophet (ﷺ), that she borrowed, and it was said to her: "O Mother of the Believers, you borrow while you have no means of repayment?" She said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Whoever takes a debt intending to repay it, Allah will help him to it.'" Al-Tahawi, Abu Ja'far al-Tabari and al-Harith ibn Abi Usama in his Musnad narrated from 'Uqba ibn 'Amir that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not frighten the souls after their security." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is that?" He said: "Debt." Al-Bukhari narrated from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), in a supplication he mentioned: "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from anxiety and grief, from incapacity and laziness, from cowardice and miserliness, from the burden of debt and from being overpowered by men." The scholars said: The burden of debt (dal' al-dayn) is that which the creditor cannot obtain from the place where it can be repaid. It is derived from the saying of the Arabs: "a heavy load (himl mudli')", meaning heavy, and "a beast mudli'" which cannot bear loads. The author of al-'Ayn said so. The Prophet (ﷺ) also said: "Debt is a blemish on the religion." It was also reported from him that he said: "Debt is worry by night and humiliation by day." Our scholars said: It is a blemish and humiliation because of what it contains of occupying the heart and mind with constant worry about its settlement, and the humbling of oneself before the creditor when meeting him, and bearing his favor by delaying until its time comes. Often a person promises himself to pay and then breaks his word, or tells the creditor something about it and lies, or swears to him and breaks the oath, and so on. For this reason the Prophet (peace be upon him) used to seek refuge from sin (ma'tham) and from debt (maghram), which is debt. It was said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, how much you seek refuge from debt!" He said: "When a man incurs debt, he speaks and lies, and promises and breaks his promise." Also, a person may die without having paid his debt, and so he is held in pledge by it, as the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "The soul of the believer is held in pledge in his grave by his debt until it is paid on his behalf." All these causes are blemishes in religion that take away its beauty and diminish its perfection. And Allah knows best.

**The third:** When Allah the Almighty commanded writing, calling witnesses, and taking pledges, this was a decisive text upon observing the preservation and growth of property, and a refutation of the ignorant ascetics (al-mutasawwifa) and their rabble, who do not see this, so they renounce all their property and leave nothing sufficient for themselves and their dependents. Then, when they are in need and their dependents become poor, they either seek the favors of brothers or their charity, or take from the lords of this world and its oppressors. This action is blameworthy and forbidden. Abu al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzi said: I am not surprised at the ascetics who did this with little knowledge; rather I am surprised at people who have knowledge and intellect, how they urged this and commanded it, despite its contradiction to the Law and reason. Al-Muhasibi mentioned many words on this, and Abu Hamid al-Tusi built upon and supported it. And al-Harith [[He is Abu 'Abd Allah al-Harith ibn Asad al-Zahid al-Muhasibi, and was called al-Muhasibi because of his frequent self-reckoning.]]

Al-Qurtubi, *al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*, commentary on Surah 2, verse 283 (part 4 of 4):

(From the *Ansab* of al-Sam'ani.)]] I find him (al-Ghazali) more excusable than Abu Hamid, because Abu Hamid was the greater jurist. However, his entry into Sufism (tasawwuf) obliged him to defend what he had entered. Al-Muhasibi said, in a long passage of his: "It has reached me that when Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf died, some of the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'We fear for Abd al-Rahman because of what he left behind.' Ka'b [[Ka'b al-Ahbar is meant, as shown by his later words to him: 'O son of the Jewess.' This is not authentic, as will come in p. 418. Among what some of the heretical libertines (al-mulhidah al-ibahiyyun) cling to.]] said: 'Glory be to God! What do you fear for Abd al-Rahman? He earned good, spent good, and left good behind.' When this reached Abu Dhar, he went out angry, seeking Ka'b. He passed by the jawbone [[The lihi is the bone of the jaw, the one on which the teeth sit.]] of a camel and took it in his hand, then set off looking for Ka'b. Ka'b was told: 'Abu Dhar is looking for you.' So he fled until he entered upon Uthman, seeking his protection, and told him what had happened. Abu Dhar came tracing his steps in search of Ka'b until he reached Uthman's house. When he entered, Ka'b stood up and sat behind Uthman, fleeing from Abu Dhar. Abu Dhar said to him: 'O son of the Jewess! You claim there is no harm in what Abd al-Rahman left behind! The Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out one day and said: "The ones who have most (in wealth) will be the ones with least (reward) on the Day of Resurrection, except those who say [[i.e., those who spend their wealth on people in acts of piety and charity. Ibn al-Athir said: 'The Arabs use "say" to express all actions, and they apply it to speech and the tongue. They say "he said with his hand," meaning he took; "he said with his foot," meaning he walked; "he said with his garment," meaning he lifted it. All of this is figurative and extended usage.']] like this and like that."'" Al-Muhasibi said: "So Abd al-Rahman, despite his excellence, will be detained on the plain [[in some copies: 'on the plain of the Day of Resurrection']] on account of what he earned from lawful means, out of his abstinence (ta'affuf) and his good works. He will be prevented from hastening to Paradise with the poor, and will crawl after them on his hands and knees, and so on in his other words [[in one copy: 'his words']]." Abu Hamid mentioned this, confirmed it, and strengthened it with the hadith of Tha'laba, that he was given wealth and then withheld zakat. Abu Hamid said: "Whoever observes the states and sayings of the prophets and the saints will not doubt that the absence of wealth is better than its presence, even if it is spent on good works, since at the least its presence occupies the aspiration with its upkeep, away from the remembrance of God. Therefore the aspirant (murid) should divest himself of his wealth until nothing remains for him but the measure of his necessity. If a single dirham remains which his heart turns toward, he is veiled from God, exalted is He."

Al-Jawzi said: "All of this contradicts the Shari'a and reason, and is a misunderstanding of what is meant by wealth. God has honored it, exalted its status, and commanded its preservation, making it the means of support (qiwam) for the human being. Whatever is made a means of support for the noble human being is itself noble. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not give to the foolish your property, which God has made for you a means of support﴾ [[See vol. 5, p. 27.]]. He, mighty and majestic, forbade entrusting wealth to one who is not rightly guided, saying: ﴿But if you perceive in them rectitude, then give them their property﴾. The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade the squandering of wealth. He said to Sa'd: '(It is) better that you leave your heirs wealthy than that you leave them destitute, begging from people.' He also said: 'No wealth has benefited me like the wealth of Abu Bakr.' He said to Amr ibn al-As: 'How excellent is righteous wealth for a righteous man!' He supplicated for Anas, and at the end of his supplication he said: 'O God, increase his wealth and his offspring, and bless him in it.' Ka'b [[Ka'b ibn Malik, one of the three who were left behind; see vol. 8, p. 286, where it says: 'Among the repentance of God toward...' etc.]] said: 'O Messenger of God, among the signs of my repentance is that I should strip myself of my wealth as charity to God and to His Messenger.' He said: 'Keep some of your wealth for yourself, for it is better for you.'"

Al-Jawzi said: "These hadiths are recorded in the authentic collections (sihah), and they run counter to what the Sufis believe: that abundance of wealth is a veil and a punishment, that withholding it contradicts reliance on God (tawakkul), and that it is a fitna. It cannot be denied that people fear its trial, and that many people have avoided it out of fear of that. Its acquisition from its proper source is rare, and the heart's safety from being seduced by it is scarce, and the heart's preoccupation with the remembrance of the Hereafter while possessing it is rare. For this reason its trial is feared. As for earning wealth: whoever limits himself to earning enough for sustenance, from lawful means, that is a necessity. As for whoever intends to amass it and increase it from what is lawful, his intention must be examined. If he intends mere boasting and vainglory, that is a wretched intention. But if he intends to keep himself and his family chaste, to save for the calamities of his time and theirs, and to intend the expansion of help to his brothers, the enrichment of the poor, and the performance of public benefits, he is rewarded for his intention, and his amassing with this intention is better than many acts of worship. The intentions of many of the Companions in gathering wealth were sound, because their purposes in gathering it were good; so they were eager for it and asked for more of it.

When the Prophet (ﷺ) granted al-Zubayr a land grant, [the horse's] hadr [[al-hadr (with a damma and then a sukun) and al-ihdar: the rearing of a horse in its running.]] was measured. He ran the horse until it stood, then threw his whip and said: 'Give him (the land) as far as his whip reaches.' Sa'd ibn Ubadah used to say in his supplication: 'O God, expand (provision) for me.' The brothers of Joseph said: ﴿And we will gain a camel's load﴾ [[See vol. 9, p. 223.]]. Shu'ayb said to Musa: ﴿And if you complete ten, then it is from you﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 267.]]. When Job was healed, a swarm [[al-rijl (with a kasra and then a sukun): a great mass of locusts.]] of golden locusts was showered upon him, and he began to gather it into his garment and to take much of it. It was said to him: 'Have you not had enough?' He said: 'O Lord, can a poor man be satisfied with Your bounty?' This is a matter established in human nature.

As for al-Muhasibi's words, they are an error that shows ignorance of knowledge. What he mentioned of the hadith of Ka'b and Abu Dhar is a fabrication of the ignorant. Its lack of authenticity from them was hidden because of its attribution to these people. Something of this has been transmitted, though its chain does not stand, because its isnad contains Ibn Lahi'a, who is criticized. Yahya said: 'His hadith is not used as evidence.'

The authentic chronology is that Abu Dhar died in the year 25 (AH), and Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf died in the year 32 (AH). So he lived seven years after Abu Dhar. Moreover, the wording of what they transmitted from their discussion indicates that their narration is fabricated. Furthermore, how would the Companions say: 'We fear for Abd al-Rahman!'? Is not the consensus (ijma') established on the permissibility of gathering wealth from its lawful source? So what is the basis for fear when it is permitted? Or does the Shari'a permit something and then punish for it? This is a lack of understanding and of jurisprudence. Furthermore, would Abu Dhar denounce Abd al-Rahman, when Abd al-Rahman is superior to Abu Dhar beyond comparison? Moreover, his clinging to Abd al-Rahman alone is evidence that he did not study the way (sayr) of the Companions, for Talhah left three hundred bahars, each bahar being three qantars. The bahar is a load. The wealth of al-Zubayr was fifty thousand and two hundred thousand. Ibn Mas'ud left ninety thousand. Most of the Companions earned wealth and left it behind, and none of them denounced another.

As for his statement, 'Abd al-Rahman will be crawling on his hands on the Day of Resurrection,' this is evidence that he did not know the hadith. I seek refuge in God from Abd al-Rahman crawling on the Day of Resurrection! Do you think that someone who was among the foremost, one of the ten promised Paradise, one of the people of Badr, and one of the electors of the council (al-shura), would crawl? Moreover, the hadith is transmitted by Imran ibn Zadhan. Al-Bukhari said: 'His hadith is sometimes confused.' Ahmad said: 'He narrates strange hadiths from Anas.' Abu Hatim al-Razi said: 'He is not used as evidence.' Al-Daraqutni said: 'He is weak.'

As for his saying, 'Leaving lawful wealth is better than gathering it,' this is not so. When the intention is sound, gathering it is better, without disagreement among the scholars. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab used to say: 'There is no good in one who does not seek wealth, by which he pays his debts and protects his honor. If he dies, he leaves it as an inheritance to those who come after him.' Ibn al-Musayyab left four hundred dinars, and Sufyan al-Thawri left two hundred. He used to say: 'Wealth in this age is a weapon.' The predecessors (salaf) continued to praise wealth and to gather it for calamities and for aiding the poor. Only a group of them avoided it, preferring preoccupation with acts of worship and unity of concern, and they were content with little. If this speaker had said that reducing it is preferable, the matter would have been close, but he pushed it into the rank of sin.

I say: Among what shows the preservation and safeguarding of wealth is the permissibility of fighting in its defense and for it. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever is killed defending his wealth is a martyr.' Its explanation will come, God willing, in (the commentary on) Surah al-Ma'idah [[See vol. 6, p. 156.]]."

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 2, Verse 284:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. Its meaning has already been given.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whether you show what is in your souls or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it﴾. On this there are two questions.

The first: Scholars have differed over the meaning of His saying, "And whether you show what is in your souls or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it," in five opinions.

The first: it is abrogated (*mansukh*, meaning its ruling has been cancelled by a later revelation, *naskh*). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, 'A'isha, Abu Hurayra, al-Sha'bi, 'Ata', Muhammad ibn Sirin, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Musa ibn 'Ubayda, and a group of the Companions and the Successors. According to them, this obligation remained for a year until Allah brought relief through His saying: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾. [This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, 'A'isha, 'Ata', Muhammad ibn Sirin, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, and others [[Addition from the manuscripts J, B and T.]]. [In Sahih Muslim, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When "And whether you show what is in your souls or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it" was revealed, something entered their hearts from it that had never entered their hearts before. So the Prophet ﷺ said: "Say: We hear and we obey and we submit." He said: So Allah cast faith into their hearts, and Allah revealed: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity. It gets what it has earned and bears what it has earned. Our Lord, do not impose blame upon us if we forget or make mistakes﴾ [He said: "I have done it" [[Addition from Sahih Muslim.]]]. ﴿Our Lord, and do not lay upon us a burden like that which You laid upon those before us﴾ [He said: "I have done it" [[Addition from Sahih Muslim.]]]. ﴿Our Lord, and do not burden us with that which we have no ability to bear. And pardon us; and forgive us; and have mercy upon us. You are our protector, so give us victory over the disbelieving people﴾ [[This part of the verse is present in the original texts but not in Sahih Muslim.]] [He said: "I have done it" [[Addition from Sahih Muslim.]]]. In one narration: When they did that, Allah abrogated it, and then He revealed: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾, and it will come.]

The second: Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, al-Sha'bi and Mujahid said: it is definitive (*muhkam*, meaning its ruling is firm and not abrogated) but specific (*makhsus*, meaning its scope is restricted). It refers to the testimony which Allah forbade concealing, and then in this verse He informed that the one who conceals it, who hides what is in his soul, will be called to account.

The third: the verse concerns what passes through the souls of doubt and certainty. Mujahid also said this.

The fourth: it is definitive and general, not abrogated. Allah calls His creation to account for what they did and for what they did not do but which was established in their souls, which they concealed, intended and willed. So He forgives the believers and holds the people of disbelief and hypocrisy accountable. Al-Tabari mentioned this from a group of people, and something similar was attributed to Ibn 'Abbas. It was narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: It was not abrogated, but when Allah gathers the creation He will say: "I will inform you of what you concealed in your souls." As for the believers, He will inform them and then forgive them. As for the people of doubt and suspicion, He will inform them of what they concealed of denial. That is His saying: ﴿Allah will call you to account for it, and He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills﴾ [[The recitation of Nafi' is as will come.]]. And this is His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿But He will call you to account for what your hearts have earned﴾ [[See p. 99 of this part.]], meaning doubt and hypocrisy. Al-Dahhak said: Allah will make him know on the Day of Resurrection what he used to keep secret, so that he knows it was not hidden from Him. And in a report: "Allah, may He be exalted, says on the Day of Resurrection: This is a day when hidden things will be tested and inner thoughts brought out, and My scribes wrote down only what appeared of your deeds, and I am the One who knows what they did not know, what they were not informed of and did not record. So I will inform you of that and call you to account for it. I forgive whom I will and punish whom I will." So He forgives the believers and punishes the disbelievers. This is the most sound of what has been said on the subject, and it is supported by the hadith of private conversation with Allah, as will be explained. [It is not said [[This addition is from manuscripts J, H and A.]]: It has been established from the Prophet ﷺ: "Allah has overlooked for my community what their souls whisper to them, so long as they do not speak of it or act upon it." We say: That is to be understood as applying to the rulings of this world, such as divorce, manumission and sale, whose ruling does not bind a person unless he speaks of it. What is mentioned in the verse concerns what a servant will be held accountable for between himself and Allah in the Hereafter.]

Al-Hasan said: The verse is definitive, not abrogated. Al-Tabari said: Others said something similar to the meaning reported from Ibn 'Abbas, except that they said the punishment that is the recompense for what passes through the souls and is accompanied by thought is only through the calamities of this world, its pains and all its hardships. Then something similar was transmitted from 'A'isha. This is the fifth opinion. Al-Tabari preferred that the verse is definitive and not abrogated. Ibn 'Atiyya said: This is the correct view, because His saying, "And whether you show what is in your souls or conceal it," means what is within your capacity and under your acquisition, and that is sustaining beliefs and thought. Since the wording could include passing thoughts, the Companions and the Prophet ﷺ became fearful. So Allah clarified for them what He intended by the other verse, and specified it, and stated the ruling explicitly: He does not burden a soul beyond its capacity. Passing thoughts are neither within capacity nor is their repelling, but they are an overpowering matter that is not acquired. In this clarification was their relief and the removal of their distress. The rest of the verse is definitive, with no abrogation in it. What also rules out abrogation is that the verse is a report, and reports do not admit abrogation. If someone insists on positing abrogation, it applies only to the ruling that affected the Companions when they were alarmed by the verse, since the Prophet's ﷺ saying to them, "Say: We hear and we obey," implies that they should remain steadfast in this, bind themselves to it, and await Allah's kindness in forgiveness. When this ruling is established as such, abrogation in it is valid, and the verse then resembles His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If there are among you twenty patient ones, they will overcome two hundred﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 44.]]. This is worded as a report, but its meaning is: Bind yourselves to this, remain firm upon it, and be patient according to it. Then it was abrogated after that. As far as I know, the scholars agree that this verse concerning jihad is abrogated by the requirement that a hundred endure against two hundred. Ibn 'Atiyya said: This verse in al-Baqara is the most similar to it.

It was also said: there is an implied element and a restriction in the speech. Its meaning is: "Allah will call you to account for it, if He wills." According to this view, there is no abrogation.

Al-Nahhas said: Among the best things said about the verse, and the one most consistent with its apparent meaning, is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas that it is general. Then he introduced the hadith of Ibn 'Umar about private conversation, which al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related, and the wording is Muslim's. He said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "A believer will be brought near to his Lord, mighty and majestic is He, on the Day of Resurrection, until He places His screen (*kanaf*) over him and makes him acknowledge his sins. He will say: Do you know? He will say: [My Lord, I know. [[Addition from Sahih Muslim.]]] He will say: I concealed them for you in the world, and today I forgive them for you. Then he will be given the record of his good deeds. As for the disbelievers and the hypocrites, they will be called out before all creation: These are the ones who lied against Allah."

It has also been said: it was revealed concerning those among the believers who befriend the disbelievers, meaning: "And whether you disclose what is in your souls, O believers, of loyalty to the disbelievers, or keep it hidden, Allah will call you to account for it." This was said by al-Waqidi and Muqatil. They used as evidence His saying in Surah Al 'Imran: ﴿Say: Whether you conceal what is in your breasts or reveal it, Allah knows it﴾, in reference to loyalty to the disbelievers, which is indicated by what precedes it, His saying: ﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies rather than the believers﴾ [[See vol. 4, p. 57.]]. I say: This is far-fetched, because the context of the verse does not require it. That is clearly stated in Surah Al 'Imran, and Allah knows best. Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: It has reached me that the prophets, peace be upon them, used to come to their peoples with this verse: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And whether you show what is in your souls or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it.﴾

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "fayaghfir – wa-yu'adhdhib" with the jussive (*jazm*), in coordination with the response (*jawab*). Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read both with the nominative (*raf'*), as a new clause, meaning: so He forgives and He punishes. It is also related from Ibn 'Abbas, al-A'raj, Abu al-'Aliya and 'Asim al-Jahdari, with the accusative (*nasb*) in both, by implicit "an." Its reality is that it is coordinated with the meaning, as in His saying: ﴿So He will multiply it for him﴾ [[See p. 237 of this part.]]. Coordination with the wording is better for harmony, as the poet said:

*And whenever you speak to him a word,*
*He speaks and answers you with reason.*

Al-Nahhas said: It was also related from Talha ibn Musarrif: "yuhasibkum bihi Allah yaghfir" without the fa', as an apposition (*badal*). Ibn 'Atiyya said: al-Ju'fi and Khallad also read it this way. It is also reported that it is so in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud. Ibn Jinni said: It is in apposition to "yuhasibkum," and it is an explanation of the calling to account, like the poet's saying:

*Gently, Banu Shayban, a little of your threats;*
*You will meet tomorrow my horses at Safawan.*

*You will meet horses that do not turn from the battle*
*When they advance into the close-pressed narrow place.*

This is apposition, and the poet repeated the verb because the benefit lies in what follows it of the speech. Al-Nahhas said: Better than the jussive, if there were no fa', would be the nominative, which would be in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), as the poet said:

*Whenever you come to him, seeking the light of his fire,*
*You will find the best fire, and with it the best host.*

**Question 1**: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord﴾. [It is related from al-Hasan, Mujahid and al-Dahhak that this verse was in the account of the Mi'raj (the Night Journey and Ascension). Likewise it is related in some narrations from Ibn 'Abbas. Some said: the entire Qur'an was brought down by Jibril, peace be upon him, to Muhammad (ﷺ) except this verse, for it was the Prophet (ﷺ) himself who heard it on the night of the Mi'raj. Others said: it was not in the account of the Mi'raj, because the night of the Mi'raj took place in Makkah, and this surah is entirely Madinan. As for those who said it was on the night of the Mi'raj, they said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) ascended and reached high in the heavens, with Jibril accompanying him, until he passed the Sidrat al-Muntaha (the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary), Jibril said to him: "I have not passed this place, and no one has been commanded to pass this place except you." So the Prophet (ﷺ) passed beyond it until he reached the place which Allah willed. Jibril gestured to him to greet your Lord. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "All greetings are for Allah, and the prayers and the good things." Allah, exalted is He, said: "Peace be upon you, O Prophet, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings." The Prophet (ﷺ) wished that his community should have a share in the greeting, so he said: "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah." Then Jibril and all the inhabitants of the heavens said: "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and His Messenger." Allah, exalted is He, said: "The Messenger believes" in the sense of honouring him, meaning: the Messenger affirms "what has been sent down to him from his Lord." The Prophet (ﷺ) then wished to share with his community in the honour and virtue, so he said: "And the believers, each one believes in Allah, His angels, His books and His messengers; we make no distinction between any of His messengers." That is, they say: "We believe in all the messengers, we do not disbelieve in any of them, and we do not make distinctions between them as the Jews and the Christians did." Then his Lord said to him: "How will they accept what I have sent down?" — referring to His saying: "Whether you show what is in your selves or conceal it" — and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "They said: 'We hear and we obey. Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the final return'," meaning the return (al-masir). Then Allah, exalted is He, said at that point: "Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity," meaning its ability; and it is said: "except less than its capacity." ﴿It has what it has earned﴾ of good, ﴿and it bears what it has earned﴾ of evil. Then Jibril said at that point: "Ask, and you will be given." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Our Lord, do not take us to account if we forget or make mistakes." That is, if we act in ignorance; and "or make mistakes" means if we do so deliberately. It is also said: if we act out of forgetfulness and error. Jibril said to him: "You have been granted that; the error and forgetfulness have been lifted from your community. So ask for something else." He said: "Our Lord, and do not place upon us a burden like that which You placed upon those before us," meaning a weight. That was that He forbade them the good things because of their wrongdoing; and when they sinned at night, they would find it written on their doors. The prayers were fifty for them, so Allah lightened it for this community and reduced it for them after He had prescribed fifty prayers. Then he said: "Our Lord, and do not burden us with what we have no ability to bear," meaning: do not make us bear of the deeds what we cannot endure, so that You punish us. It is also said: what is hard upon us, for they, had they been commanded with fifty prayers, would have been able to do it, but it would have been hard for them and they would not have been able to maintain it. "And pardon us," from all of that; "and forgive us," and overlook us. It is also said: "pardon us" from transformation (into animals), "forgive us" from being swallowed up by the earth, and "have mercy on us" from being struck down by stones, because some of the earlier nations were afflicted with transformation, some with being swallowed by the earth, and some with being struck by stones. Then he said: "You are our Protector," meaning our Guardian and Keeper; "so help us against the disbelieving people." His supplication was answered. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "I have been helped with terror for a distance of a month's march." It is also said that when the warriors (ghuzat) set out from their homes with pure intention and beat the drum, terror and awe fell into the hearts of the disbelievers for a distance of a month's journey in a month, whether they knew of their departure or not. Then, when the Prophet (ﷺ) returned, Allah revealed these verses to inform his community of that.

It has another explanation for this verse. Al-Zajjaj said: When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned in this surah the prescription of the prayer and the zakat, explained the rulings of the Hajj, the ruling on menstruation, divorce, and the oath of abstention (ila'), the stories of the prophets, and explained the ruling on usury (riba), He mentioned His glorification, may He be glorified, with His saying: "To Allah belongs what is in the heavens and what is on the earth." Then He mentioned the affirmation of His Prophet (ﷺ), then He mentioned the affirmation of the believers of all of that, saying: "The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord." That is: the Messenger affirmed all these things that have been mentioned, and likewise all the believers affirmed Allah, His angels, His books and His messengers.

[[This addition is not found in the original manuscripts except in one copy (B), part of it; in the copy (N, T) it appears in full, and we have relied upon it. As it appears, its content is anomalous at the outset, for what is agreed upon by the predecessors and successors is that the Qur'an was brought down entirely by the Trustworthy Spirit upon our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): "The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart." This is the mass-transmitted (mutawatir) report. That this verse was received by our Prophet, may Allah bless him, on the night of the Mi'raj is contrary to what is mass-transmitted, and it would be an even greater departure if you know that the Night Journey took place in the fifth year after the bi'thah (prophethood), and it is said: a year before the Hijrah, while al-Baqarah is Madinan by consensus. Narrations appear in Sahih Muslim and in the Musnads of Ahmad and Ibn Mardawayh that support what al-Qurtubi mentioned, but mass-transmission makes those narrations subject to some kind of interpretation, provided their chains and texts are sound. (Its corrector.)]] [.

It is also said that the cause of its revelation was the verse before it, which is: "To Allah belongs what is in the heavens and what is on the earth; whether you show what is in your selves or conceal it, Allah will bring you to account for it. He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills, and Allah is over all things competent." When this was revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ), it weighed heavily upon the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so they came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then they knelt on their knees and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we have been charged with deeds that we can bear: the prayer, the fasting, and jihad [and charity (from Sahih Muslim)], but Allah has revealed to you this verse, and we cannot bear it." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do you want to say what the People of the Two Books before you said: 'We hear and we disobey'? Rather, say: 'We hear and we obey. Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the final return'." They said: "We hear and we obey. Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the final return." When the people recited it, their tongues became submissive to it, so Allah revealed after it: "The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord, and the believers, each one believes in Allah, His angels, His books and His messengers; we make no distinction between any of His messengers," and they say: "We hear and we obey. Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the final return." When they did that, Allah abrogated it (naskh), and Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: "Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity; it has what it has earned, and it bears what it has earned." [[In the originals, after the words "what it has earned" he said: "Yes." It is not in Sahih Muslim.]] "Our Lord, do not take us to account if we forget or make mistakes." He said: "Yes." "Our Lord, and do not place upon us a burden like that which You placed upon those before us." He said: "Yes." "Our Lord, and do not burden us with what we have no ability to bear." He said: "Yes." "Pardon us, forgive us, and have mercy on us; You are our Protector, so help us against the disbelieving people." He said: "Yes." Muslim related it from Abu Hurayrah.

Our scholars said: his saying in the first narration "Indeed I have done so," and here he said "Yes," is evidence that the hadith was transmitted by meaning (bi'l-ma'na), and this has been discussed before. When the matter was settled with them saying "We hear and we obey," Allah praised them and commended them in this verse, and removed the hardship concerning the thoughts of their hearts from them. This is the fruit of obedience and of devotion to Allah, exalted is He, as opposed to what happened to the Children of Israel, who were blamed and burdened with hardships of humiliation, poverty and exile when they said: "We hear and we disobey." This is the fruit of disobedience and rebellion against Allah, exalted is He. May Allah protect us from His vengeance by His bounty and generosity.

It is related in a hadith that it was said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The house of Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas glows every night with lamps." He said: "Perhaps he is reciting Surat al-Baqarah." Thabit was asked, and he said: "I recited from Surat al-Baqarah, 'The Messenger believes'." It was revealed when what Allah had threatened them with, of being called to account for what their souls concealed, weighed heavily upon the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ). They complained of that to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: "Perhaps you say: 'We hear and we disobey', as the Children of Israel said." They said: "Rather, we hear and we obey." So Allah, exalted is He, revealed praise of them: "The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord." Then he (ﷺ) said: "And it is right that they should believe."

**Question 2**: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Believes﴾, that is, affirms; this has been mentioned before. What was sent down is the Qur'an. Ibn Mas'ud recited "And the believers, each one believes in Allah," according to the wording, and in other than the Qur'an it is permissible to say "they believe" (amanu) according to the meaning. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr, and Ibn 'Amir recited (wa-kutubihi) with the plural. And they recited in "al-Tahrim": "kitabihi" in the singular. Abu 'Amr recited here and in "al-Tahrim" "wa-kutubihi" in the plural. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited "wa-kitabihi" in the singular in both places. Whoever recited the plural intends the plural of kitab (book). Whoever recited the singular intends the verbal noun (masdar) which encompasses every written thing whose descent was from Allah. It is permissible in the reading of the one who used the singular that it be intended as plural, with kitab being a collective noun (ism li'l-jins), so both readings are equivalent. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So Allah sent the prophets as bearers of good tidings and warners, and sent down with them the Book﴾ [see p. 30 of this part]. The community recited "wa-rusulihi" with a dammah on the sin, and likewise "arsalna" and "rusulukum" and "rusulika," except Abu 'Amr; it is related from him that he recited "rusluna" and "ruslukum" with a light pronunciation, and it is related from him that in "ruslika" both the heavy and the light are reported. Abu 'Ali said: whoever recited "ruslika" with the heavy pronunciation, that is the original form of the word; and whoever lightened it, it is as one lightens in singular nouns, like 'unq and tunb. If it is lightened in the singular, it is more fitting in the plural, which is heavier. Makki said the same. Most people recited "la nufarriqu" with the nun, and the meaning is: they say, "we do not make distinctions," so the verb "they say" was omitted, and omission of the verb of saying is common. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate: Peace be upon you﴾ [see vol. 9, p. 310], that is, they say, "Peace be upon you." And He said: ﴿And they reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth: Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾ [see vol. 4, p. 313], that is, they say, "Our Lord," and what is similar to it. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Yahya ibn Ya'mar, Abu Zur'ah ibn 'Amr ibn Jarir, and Ya'qub recited "la yufarriqu" with the ya', and this is in accordance with the wording "kullun" (each). Harun said: it is in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud as "la yufarriqun." He said "bayna ahadin" in the singular, and did not say "ahad" (plural), because "ahad" encompasses the one and the many, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then there is none of you who could hold him off from Us﴾ [see vol. 18, p. 276]: "hajizin" is an attribute of "ahad," because its meaning is plural. And the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The spoils were not made lawful for anyone with black heads except you." And Ru'bah said:

"When the affairs of people are judged by your judgment,
they will fear no one besides you."

**The First Note: the meaning of this verse**

The meaning of this verse is that the believers are not like the Jews and Christians, who believe in some parts (of the Book) and disbelieve in others.

**The Third Matter:** Allah's words, ﴿And they say: "We hear and we obey"﴾, contain an ellipsis (ḥadhf), meaning: "We hear the hearing of those who accept" (qābilīn). It has also been said that *sami'a* here means *qabila* (to accept), as in the saying "Allah hears whoever praises Him" (*sami'a Allāhu li-man ḥamidah*), so there is no ellipsis. In general, this statement implies praise for those who make it. *Ṭā'a* (obedience) is the acceptance of a command.

Allah's words, *ghufrānaka* ("Your forgiveness"), are a verbal noun like *kufrān* and *khusrān*, and the word that governs it is an implied verb. Its implied form is: "Forgive, (O Lord), Your forgiveness." This is the view of al-Zajjaj and others, who say: "We seek" or "We ask for Your forgiveness."

﴿And to You is the final return﴾ is an affirmation of the Resurrection and of standing before Allah the Exalted.

It is narrated that when this verse was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ, Jibril said to him: "Allah has granted you and your community the right to be praised, so ask and you will be given," and he asked until the end of the surah.

**The Fourth Matter:** Allah's words, ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾. *Taklīf* (burden) is the command to do something difficult for a person. *Takallaftu al-amr* means "I undertook the matter with effort," as recorded by al-Jawhari. *Al-wus'* means capacity and ability. This is a definite statement. Allah the Exalted has stated that He does not burden His servants, from the time this verse was revealed, with any act of worship, whether of the heart or of the limbs, except that it is within the capacity of the one who is obligated and within what his understanding and constitution can bear. By this, the distress of the Muslims was lifted regarding their handling of passing thoughts (*khawāṭir*).

On the meaning of this verse, Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) related: "I never wished that anyone born of a mother had been mine except Ja'far ibn Abi Talib. Once I followed him while I was hungry, and when he reached his house he found nothing in it except a jar of ghee in which a little remained. He broke it open before us, and we began to lick what was in it of ghee and date syrup (*rubb*)." And he was saying:

*"Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity,*
*and no hand gives except from what it finds."*

**The Fifth Matter:** People differed over the permissibility of imposing what cannot be borne (*taklīf mā lā yuṭāq*) in the rulings that apply in this world, after they agreed that it does not actually occur in the Shari'ah, and that this verse indicates its absence.
